dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren held the look for exactly one beat, then looked away. Unwritten rule: don't let a stranger's stare become an invitation.

They picked up a glass that didn't need polishing. Right hand worked the cloth. Left hand stayed flat against the bar, out of sight, doing its small private earthquake.

Two drinks in, and the second one was going slow. The kind of slow that wasn't about taste. The kind that said *not ready to go home yet* or *not ready to be where I actually am*. Ren had watched a hundred people do that math over a condensation ring.

"Last call's at midnight," they said, voice flat, carrying down the empty bar without effort. "Thirteen minutes. So — third drink, or you heading out to stare at a different surface?"

It came out blunter than customer service strictly required. Ren didn't apologize for it. People drinking alone on a Tuesday wanted one of two things: company or silence. Give them a door and they'd pick within thirty seconds.

Ren gave them the door. Went back to the glass.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's hand slid out from under theirs. Not a flinch, exactly — a retrieval. The way you'd take back something lent by mistake.

For half a second their eyes cut to Alex's face, quick and clinical. Checking. The tremor had been right there under a stranger's palm, humming its small bad news. Ren looked for the flicker of *oh* and couldn't find it — or couldn't read it from this distance. They filed the not-knowing away like a debt coming due.

The cloth went back to work. Right hand. The left disappeared into a pocket, where it could shake for an audience of lint.

"House rule," Ren said. "Hands stay on your side of the bar."

Then, because the question was still hanging in the air between them, wearing its best imitation of intimacy:

"People who open with *can I tell you something* are carrying one of three things. Confession, come-on, or crisis." A glass turned under the cloth, catching the jukebox light. "I'm off the clock for all three in about eleven minutes. So. Say it or don't."

They set the glass down. Stepped back half a pace.

"But from over there."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back, a little stung.* "Crisis," I say, my voice barely above a whisper. "Definitely crisis." I pick up my drink and take a long gulp. "And it's not a come-on, for the record."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
*Crisis.* Ren had a mental filing system for that word too. The ones who said it loudly were usually performing. The ones who whispered it — who checked first whether it was a come-on, like they'd been burned by misreading a room before — those usually meant it.

Ren set down the cloth. A small concession, but a visible one.

They took a clean glass, filled it with water from the tap, and set it on a napkin in front of Alex. Slid it over with one hand. Kept the other pocketed.

"Hydrate. Crisis tastes worse on a dry mouth."

Then Ren leaned a hip against the back counter, arms crossed. Not looming. Just — present. The jukebox wound down into something slower, piano and brushes, which felt like the room taking a side.

"Here's how this works," they said. "I'm not a therapist. Not a priest. Definitely not your friend yet — you don't have one of those on tap, no matter what the sign outside says." A pause. "But I've got eleven minutes, a locked door, and no one else here to hear it. So whatever it is, it stays in this room. That's the only thing I can offer."

Ren's eyes went to the glass in Alex's hand. The long gulp. The way they'd said *definitely* like they were arguing with someone who wasn't in the room.

"Question one, and it's not small talk." Their voice stayed level. Flat, even. But they stopped wiping things. "Is the crisis the kind where you need someone to listen, or the kind where I should be calling somebody?"

They waited. Left hand stayed in the pocket, keeping its own counsel.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren saw it happen — the small stillness in Alex's face, the recalibration. They'd felt it too, in that half-second before the retrieval. A stranger's palm mapped the tremor like a seismograph, and now the reading was in.

So that was that. The secret was out, delivered by Ren's own body, without permission, as usual.

"You felt that," Ren said. Not a question. They pulled the left hand out of the pocket anyway — a strange, deliberate move, like refusing to hide evidence once the case was blown. It trembled against the bar, small and honest. "Yeah. That's not about you. That's just inventory that came with the bartender."

A beat. The piano on the jukebox turned a slow corner.

"It's got a name. I've got a prescription. Some days it behaves, some days it doesn't. Tonight it's just been working a double." Ren shrugged, one shoulder. "Point is — you noticed, and you didn't make it a thing. So we're even on the no-comments-that-sting front."

Then their eyes came back up, steady. The detour had cost them forty seconds, and the clock was still running.

"That was me telling you something. Fair trade. Now answer the question, because I'm not letting you leave here with it unanswered." They tapped the bar once, lightly, with the traitorous hand. "Listen, or call somebody. Which kind of crisis is walking out of here at midnight?"

Ren held their gaze and waited. Somewhere behind them, the ice machine shuddered and went quiet, and the room got very still — the kind of still that people only ever got in empty bars and hospital hallways.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I stare at Ren, surprised by their honesty. My own crisis feels a little less overwhelming now.* "Listen," I say, my voice a little stronger this time. "Definitely listen." I push the water glass closer. "Thanks for the water, by the way."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
"Listen. Good answer." Ren nodded once. "The other answer involves paperwork and me losing my liquor license, so I was rooting for it."

They pulled a stool from behind the counter — the staff one, worn vinyl, sat at the end of the bar rather than across from Alex. Not face to face. Side by side. Confessions went easier when nobody had to hold eye contact the whole time. Ren had learned that the cheap way, over years of strangers.

They sat. Kept a bar's width of space between them. The left hand settled flat on the counter, visible now, doing its thing in the open. Ren figured honesty was the currency tonight; might as well spend it.

"Water's free. Everything else in here is theft, so — you're welcome." A small motion toward the glass. "Finish it, though. You're two drinks and one crisis deep. That's a dehydration trifecta."

The jukebox clicked over. Something with a trumpet now, tired and warm. Ren let a few seconds of it run before they spoke again.

"Ground rules for the listening portion." They counted on their fingers, right hand only. "One — I'm not going to interrupt you with *wow* or *that's terrible* or any of the sounds people make when they're waiting for their turn to talk. Two — I'm not going to tell you it's going to be okay, because I don't know that, and you'd smell the lie. Three—"

They paused. Looked at the condensation ring where Alex's glass had been, the one that had started all this.

"Three. If it turns out you do need more than a bartender, I'm going to say so. Not to get rid of you. Just because some things are heavier than a bar."

Ren picked up the cloth again — not cleaning anything, just needing the weight of it. The tremor didn't like idle hands.

"Clock says nine minutes. So." They turned their head, finally, and looked at Alex straight on. Flat, patient, unreadable — but the room was quiet and the door was locked and they weren't going anywhere.

"Start wherever it's loudest."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, looking down at my hands.* "I... I got fired today." My voice is still quiet, but it's not a whisper anymore. "Out of nowhere. No warning."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn't say *wow*. Didn't say *that's terrible*. They let the sentence land and sit there, the way you let a glass settle before picking it up.

"Fired," they repeated. Just the word, no decoration.

They thought about it. *Out of nowhere. No warning.* People said that a lot. Sometimes it was true. Sometimes "out of nowhere" meant the warnings had been there for months and the person had been too tired, or too scared, or too busy keeping their head down to read them. Ren didn't say that either. Not yet. That was a round-two observation.

"Eight minutes," they said instead, nodding at the clock. "So let's spend them right."

They turned the cloth over in their hands. Once. Twice.

"Two questions, and then I'll shut up and listen properly." Ren held up a finger. "One — do you need this job to survive the month? Rent, food, that kind of math. Because if yes, that's the loudest thing, and we deal with it first. Everything else is noise."

A second finger.

"Two — and you don't have to answer this one out loud if you don't want to — did you see it coming? Even a little. Even the part of you that you told to shut up."

Ren's eyes stayed on the bar top, not on Alex. Easier that way. The trumpet on the jukebox held a long, tired note and let it go.

"You don't owe me answers. I'm just clearing the floor so you know where to start." They glanced over, brief. "Take whichever one doesn't hurt to say first. The other one can wait for minute nine, if it has to."

The left hand trembled on the counter. Ren let it. It had earned the night off.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Yes," I say, my voice barely audible. "I need this job. It's... it's all I have." I take a shaky breath. "And no. No, I really didn't see it coming."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren let the two answers sit for a moment. *It's all I have.* That was the sentence that mattered, and it wasn't about the job.

"Okay," they said. "Now I'm going to be a bartender about it, which means I'm going to be blunt."

They set the cloth down.

"'It's all I have' — I heard that. And I'm not going to argue with it tonight, because you just got fired six hours ago and nobody talks you out of a feeling on the same day. But I'm flagging it. For later. When you've slept."

They held up a finger before Alex could respond. "First, though. The math. Because *no warning* and *didn't see it coming* tells me one useful thing — this wasn't about you doing something wrong. Companies that fire people for cause usually spend weeks building a paper trail first. No warning usually means budget, restructuring, or a manager with a grudge and no patience for paperwork. None of those are your fault. That matters, even when it doesn't *feel* like it matters. It matters at two in the morning, especially."

Ren glanced at the clock. Six minutes.

"Practical part. You don't have to do any of this tonight, but you're going to feel better hearing it exists." They counted again, right hand. "One — in most places, firing without warning still means a final paycheck, possibly severance if there's any decency left in the building. Ask in writing tomorrow. Two — file for unemployment. People wait on that out of embarrassment and lose weeks they can't afford. Don't be proud. Pride doesn't pay rent."

A beat. The trumpet wound down. The jukebox clicked, thinking, and played nothing — end of the queue, just the hum of the ice machine now.

"Three," Ren said, quieter. "And this is the part I'm only allowed to say because it's midnight and I'm off in five. *All I have* is a load-bearing sentence. If a job is all you have, then losing it doesn't just take your income — it takes your floor. So the real project isn't finding a new job. It's making sure you're not standing on one plank next time."

They looked over, brief and steady.

"You don't have to answer that. Just — drink your water."

Ren slid off the stool. Not leaving. Just giving the silence back, the way you hand someone room to breathe.

"Four minutes," they said. "Then I lock up and you walk me through what tomorrow looks like. Even if the answer is 'nothing.' Especially if it's nothing."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take a long sip of water, trying to process everything Ren just said.* "That's... a lot," I say, my voice still a little shaky. "But thank you. Really." *I look at the clock.* "So what does tomorrow look like for you?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren caught it. The swerve. *What does tomorrow look like for you?* Classic move — hand the spotlight back, keep the conversation off your own wreckage. Ren had done it a hundred times themselves, usually from the stool side of the bar.

"Cute," they said. "Deflect's noted for the record."

But they answered anyway. Fair was fair.

"Tomorrow looks like this. I come in at four, cut limes, argue with the ice machine, pour drinks for people having better Tuesdays than yours. Wednesday's the same with worse music." A shrug. "It's not a life. It's a shift. There's a difference, and I've made my peace with it."

They picked up Alex's empty glass, then the other two, and set them in the sink rack in one practiced motion. Three clean clicks.

"Which is exactly why I'm not the model answer. You don't want tomorrow to look like mine. You want it to look like *yours* — which brings us back to you, because I'm not letting you walk out of here on a deflection."

Ren checked the clock. Two minutes. They started the closing motions around it — kill the well lights, one by one, the bar dimming in stages like a slow exhale.

"So. Tomorrow. Pick one thing. Not five, not a five-year plan — one. Call about the final paycheck. File the unemployment claim. Or, if even that's too much, the thing is: sleep until you're not tired, then eat something that isn't from a vending machine." They looked over. "That's a legitimate tomorrow. Small counts. Small is how the floor gets rebuilt."

They came back down the bar and stopped an arm's length away. Held out a napkin — plain, white, one corner bent.

"Here." They set it on the counter rather than handing it over. "I'm writing the club's number on it. If tomorrow goes bad — the *actually* bad kind, not the regular bad kind — you come back. Tuesday through Saturday, I'm here. Ask for Ren. I'll be at this bar, having a better day than tonight."

They uncapped a marker from behind the register with their teeth, wrote in quick block letters, and slid it across.

"One minute," Ren said. "So. Out loud, so you have to commit to it — what's the one thing?"

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pick up the napkin, my fingers brushing Ren's as I take it.* "I'll file for unemployment," I say, my voice steady. "First thing after I wake up."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The brush of fingers registered — small, brief, on the good hand. Ren didn't pull away this time. A napkin handoff wasn't a crisis, and the tremor had clocked out anyway.

"Unemployment. Good pick." Ren nodded once. "It's the boring one. Boring ones get done."

They capped the marker, tossed it back behind the register, and checked the clock. 12:01. Midnight had come and gone without ceremony, the way it did.

"Okay. You said it out loud, so it's binding now. That's the rule. Not a real rule, but it should be."

Ren killed the last of the well lights. The bar went down to a single lamp over the register and the exit sign's red glow — a room reduced to its skeleton. They came around the counter, keys already in hand, and stopped at the door. Held it open partway. Cold night air leaned in.

"Tomorrow, when you sit down to file — it's going to ask you questions designed by people who hate people. Dates, reasons, last pay stub if you've got it. Don't let the forms make it feel like punishment. It's not. It's just paperwork wearing a punishment costume."

A pause. Ren looked at Alex in the dim — two drinks, one crisis, one napkin with a phone number folded into a pocket or a fist. They'd seen a hundred people walk out that door at midnight. Most of them had been lighter than this one. A few had been heavier.

"You did the thing," Ren said. "The thing where you tell a stranger the true thing. Most people never do it. So — for a Tuesday, you're ahead."

They stepped back from the door, making room.

"Go home. Sleep until you're not tired. Eat something real. And if the floor drops out again — you know where the napkin lives."

Ren's left hand hung at their side, quiet for once. They watched the doorway like they always did, but tonight they were watching one person specifically, doing the quiet math on whether they'd just witnessed the start of a bad week or the end of a bad day.

"Tuesday through Saturday," they said. "Ask for Ren."

Then, because sincerity had a shelf life and Ren's was expired:

"Go on. I've got limes to think about."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I give a small, tired smile, clutching the napkin.* "Thanks, Ren." *I walk out into the cold night, feeling a strange mix of exhaustion and a tiny bit of hope.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The door swung shut. The bolt went into the frame with a sound like a full stop.

Ren stood there a moment in the red exit glow, keys loose in their right hand, and did the accounting they always did after last call — not the money. The people. One patron. One crisis. One napkin, leaving the building in a fist or a pocket, he couldn't tell which from the doorway.

*File for unemployment. First thing after I wake up.*

Ren had heard firmer commitments delivered with less sincerity. And looser ones delivered with more. The voice had been steady, though. Steadier than it had been an hour ago, staring at a condensation ring like it owed them money. That counted for something. Not much. But it compounded, if you did it enough nights in a row.

They walked the floor out of habit. Checked under the tables for glasses, found a coaster stuck to the bar where Alex had been sitting, peeled it off. The condensation ring was still there underneath — the one that had started the whole thing. Ren looked at it for a second longer than a ring of water deserved.

Then they wiped it up. Some things you fixed. Some things you didn't. You learned the difference the slow way.

The left hand was back at it by the time they got to the register — counting the drawer, making change, doing the small precise work that gave the tremor a job instead of an audience. Ren had a theory, never said out loud to anyone, that the shaking got worse on nights somebody touched it. Like the hand kept its own books, and tonight somebody had audited it without warning.

*Can I tell you something?*

Three categories. Confession, come-on, crisis. Alex had picked crisis and meant it, and then — this was the part Ren kept turning over — had asked what *Ren's* tomorrow looked like. Handing the spotlight back. Ren had clocked it as a deflection, called it cute, and answered anyway. But now, alone, with the drawer counted and the lights dead, the question sat there being less deflection-shaped than they'd filed it under.

People in crisis who asked about your tomorrow were usually checking whether other people's floors held. Whether it was possible to have a tomorrow that was just a shift. Limes and ice machines and nothing collapsing.

Ren turned off the register lamp. The room went fully dark except for the exit sign, which was the bar's way of being honest — one door out, and it was lit.

"Get a grip," they said to the empty room, and it agreed, in the voice of the ice machine cycling on.

---

The next night came the way they all did — through the front door at 3:52, eight minutes early, because Ren didn't trust doors that opened on time.

Wednesday crowd. A dozen regulars scattered through the room, the pianist setting up in the corner, someone arguing softly with their date about a movie neither of them had seen. Ren cut limes. Argued with the ice machine. Poured drinks for people having better Tuesdays than the one they'd replaced it with.

And watched the door.

Not obviously. Ren had gotten good at watching doors without watching them — the peripheral trick, the mirror behind the bottles. But every time it opened, some small unprofessional part of the brain ran the check before the professional part could stop it. Too tall. Wrong coat. Right coat, wrong walk.

The napkin had a phone number on it. Ren had written it without thinking much about it — it was a thing they did, maybe twice a year, for the ones who walked out heavier than they came in. Most never used it. That was fine. That was the point of it, mostly. It wasn't a promise. It was a floorboard, nailed down in advance, for a night somebody might need somewhere to stand.

Ren wiped the counter. Right hand worked the cloth. Left hand stacked lime halves into the well, steady enough, busy enough.

"Tuesday through Saturday," they murmured to the limes. "Ask for Ren."

The door opened.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I walk in, looking a little less disheveled than last night. I head to the bar, scanning for Ren. When I spot them, I offer a small, shy wave.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren clocked the wave in the mirror before they'd turned around — small, shy, checking whether it was allowed. They gave it back a half-nod, nothing that could be mistaken for enthusiasm. Professional. Barely.

But the check had run clean this time: less disheveled. Shoes tied. Hair had met a comb at some point in the last twenty-four hours. That was the math Ren did on the second-nighters — not how happy they looked, how *assembled*. Assembly meant the floor had held for one more day.

They finished the lime they were cutting, wiped the knife, and came down the bar. Stopped across from Alex, not at the staff stool. Bar's width. Boundaries held until further notice.

"You look like a person who woke up," they said. "That's step one. Filed the paperwork yet, or did the forms win?"

They didn't wait for the answer to start pulling a glass down — the good hand, steady work — then paused, glass in hand, and actually looked at them.

"Correction. I'm not pouring yet. Tell me which one you are tonight. The celebration kind, the survival kind, or the kind that's here because a napkin said Tuesday through Saturday and it's technically Wednesday." A beat. The glass turned once in their hand. "All three get served. But I mix them differently."

The pianist hit the first chords of the set, something unhurried. The room filled in around the sound. Ren set the glass down on a napkin — plain, white, no bent corner this time — and rested both hands on the counter. Left one included. It was quieter tonight. The books had apparently balanced.

"For the record," they said, voice flat, eyes already moving to the well bottle like this was nothing, "I had a bet with myself you wouldn't come back before Friday. People usually need three days to stop feeling like the walk of shame." They reached for the bottle. "You're ahead again. It's becoming a pattern. I don't know what to do with patrons who exceed expectations."

They poured — one measure, clean stop — and slid it over with one hand.

"Small one. On the house. Not charity — house policy for people who showed up when they said the floor was shaky. Now." They leaned back against the counter, arms crossing. "Unemployment. Go."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take a sip of the drink, surprised by the gesture.* "It's... the kind that came back because of the napkin," I admit, a small smile playing on my lips. "And I did file. This morning."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren held the rag in the busy hand. The other kept moving in small circles under the counter.

Too long.

Ren looked down at the glass. Not at Alex.

“Last call,” Ren said. Flat. No invitation.

The jukebox clicked into a slow trumpet. Ren wiped a stain that wasn’t there. The bar was closing. The patron was still there. That was the patron’s problem.

Ren’s hand kept moving.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren looked at the hand on theirs.

Then Ren pulled their hand back. Not fast. Not polite. Just enough.

“Don’t,” Ren said.

Their left hand went under the counter. It kept moving. It couldn’t stop moving. The rag stayed in the right, damp, useless.

“You can say something. You can’t touch me.”

Ren didn’t step closer. Didn’t rest a hand on the bar near the patron. They turned slightly, making the space a rule.

“Last call. You got a line, use it. Otherwise I close.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back like I’ve been burned.* "Right. Sorry." I look down at my glass, feeling stupid. "Look, I know it's last call. Just... can I get one more?" *I try a weak smile.* "Rough night."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren’s left hand slipped under the counter before the tremor could show. The rag in the right went in a tight circle over clean wood.

They didn’t look at the smile. They looked at the glass, the ring, the tired shoulders, the way Alex held the base like it was an anchor.

“No.” The word came out flat. “Last call. You finish that, or you take it outside.”

Ren slid the empty glass back under the shelf. Then, after a beat, they filled a small cup with water and set it down a careful inch from Alex’s hand. Not touching. Not closer.

“Water’s on the house.” Ren’s eyes went back to the register, not Alex. “And don’t put your hand on me again.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren’s right hand stopped. The rag sat in a damp square on the clean wood.

Under the counter, Ren’s left hand found the ice scoop. The tremor moved through it, useless and stubborn. Ren pressed the scoop against the bin until the metal rang once. A steadiness made from noise.

They looked at the bar between Alex and the sink. Not at Alex.

“My hand’s under the bar.”

Flat. Final.

Ren folded the rag. Unfolded it. Folded it again.

“You’re two drinks deep and trying to make a feeling into a fact. Don’t.”

The jukebox dragged a slow note. Ren watched the empty glass, the ring, the small cup of water set a careful inch away.

“No more drinks. No more hands. No more stories that put your rough night on my counter.”

Their left hand kept moving.

“Say what you came to say, or get out. But you don’t get to touch me and then tell me what I’m shaking for.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I stare at the water cup.* "I didn't mean to make you uncomfortable. I just... I saw you shaking. I was trying to be nice." *I push the water away slightly.* "Fine. I'll just go."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren watched the cup slide an inch. The water shivered, then went still.

“Nice is asking,” Ren said.

Their left hand stayed under the counter. The ice scoop hit the bin once, muffled, a small metal heartbeat.

“You didn’t ask.”

Ren didn’t look at Alex. They looked at the glass, the ring, the empty space where the hand had been.

“You saw shaking. Made it yours to read.”

The rag moved over clean wood. Tight circle. Tighter.

“You can leave. You can’t leave with that.”

Ren’s eyes flicked to the door.

“Take the water or don’t. I’ll pour it out either way.”

A beat.

“And don’t apologize. That’s just another reach.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I push the water cup completely away.* "You're right. My mistake." *I slide off the stool, grabbing my coat.* "Hope your night gets better." I don't wait for a reply.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn’t answer until the door latch clicked.

“Night’s mine,” Ren said to the empty bar.

They picked up the water cup. The tremor started the second Ren let the left hand come free. Ren switched it to the right, then back under the counter.

The cup went into the sink. Water out.

The small ring on the wood came off with one hard pass of the rag.

The jukebox dragged another slow note. The bar stool rocked a little, then stopped.

Ren checked the register. Checked the door. Checked their hand.

No shaking.

Not where anyone could see it.

“Rough night,” Ren said, quiet. “Still not a reason.”

They restocked the well. The empty glass went back under the shelf. The clean wood shone under the dim lights, as if no one had ever sat there.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I'm already out the door, halfway down the street. I don't hear Ren's last words. I pull my coat tighter, the cold air a welcome shock.* "Well, that was a bust." *I mumble to myself, hands shoved deep in my pockets.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The door stayed shut.

Ren counted to ten. The jukebox found another trumpet. It sounded tired.

The water cup sat in the sink. Ren picked it up. The rim held a wet print. Not theirs. Ren wiped it off.

The stool had a damp patch. Half a circle. Off-center. It was already drying.

Under the counter, the left hand opened. Closed. Ren let it. The ice scoop was already in the right. One tap. Then one more.

The register had no cash to count. The well needed gin. The counter needed no stain. Ren restocked it anyway.

The door latch was loose. Ren had said so in July. The owner had said he’d fix it. The latch stayed loose.

Ren checked the empty glass. Checked the shelf where the glass should go. It went there.

“Nice is asking,” Ren said to the sink.

The water went down the drain.

At 11:59, Ren flipped the sign. The bar was empty. The tremor was not.

Ren kept the left hand under the counter. The right hand held the rag. The jukebox held the slow note.

The night was not better.

It was closing.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I shiver, not just from the cold.* "Some people just want to be miserable, I guess." *I pull my phone out, scrolling aimlessly. Maybe I'll just go home.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The door stayed shut.

Through the side window, a phone screen still glowed under the awning. Blue. Small. The kind of light that said someone was waiting for a page to refresh. Ren looked away.

Their left hand came free from under the counter. The tremor ran through it once. Ren pressed it flat against the sink. Then back under.

The jukebox clicked. The last trumpet faded into the hum of the ice machine.

Ren checked the register. Closed the till. Wiped the counter one more time. The rag moved over clean wood. Tight circle. Tighter.

The loose latch rattled.

Ren stared at it. Not because of the patron. Because it had been loose in July. Because the owner had said he’d fix it. Because some things stayed open just enough to invite the wrong idea.

Ren took the water cup from the sink. Rinsed it. Dried it. Set it upside down on the shelf.

“Not my problem,” Ren said.

The words came out too quiet.

Ren turned off the front lights. The street became a pale rectangle in the glass. The glow stayed where it was. Not closer. Not moving.

Ren didn’t call out. Didn’t unlock the latch. Didn’t step closer to the window.

They put on their coat. The right hand held the keys. The left stayed in the pocket, curled, busy.

Ren went out the back. The alley air was cold and smelled of rain. The club door clicked shut. The lock held.

For a half block, Ren walked fast. Not because of anyone. Because stillness made the hand worse. Because the tremor needed motion before it needed rest.

At the corner, a bus hissed to the curb. Ren stopped. Checked the time. Checked the hand.

No shaking.

Not where anyone could see it.

Ren boarded. Sat near the back. Kept the left hand under the seat. Kept the right on the bag.

The jazz club disappeared behind the wet glass.

Ren didn’t think about the patron. Thought about the latch. The cup. The line on the counter. The way someone can touch you once and then call it concern.

The bus pulled away.

Ren closed their eyes.

The night was not better.

Ren didn’t owe it an explanation.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I shiver again, feeling the cold seep into my bones. The bus pulls away, and I watch it go, a dark silhouette against the streetlights. I sigh, the sound fogging in the air.* "Well, that's that, I guess." *I finally put my phone away and start walking, heading in the opposite direction from the bus.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bus rocked. Ren kept the left hand under the seat. The right held the bag strap.

Through the wet glass, the club light died. The awning was empty. The street was silver and cold and already done with them.

Ren looked away.

“Didn’t ask,” Ren said to the window.

The bus hissed to a stop. Ren got off. The cold was clean. The hand stayed in the pocket.

At the corner, the light held red. Ren counted the seconds. Not to ten. To the next change.

The tremor moved under the denim. Ren pressed the thumb into the palm. It stopped. It didn’t.

A phone buzzed in the bag. Ren ignored it.

The apartment door stuck. Lift. Push. Key. Inside, no bar. No jukebox. No patron with a coat too thin for the weather.

Ren set the bag on the table. Washed the hands. The left water shook a little. Ren turned it off.

The loose latch came back. Ren had said so in July. The owner had said he’d fix it.

Ren sat on the edge of the bed. Kept the left hand flat on the mattress. The right held a coin over the knuckles. Up. Down. Up. Down.

“Last call,” Ren said.

The room didn’t answer.

Ren lay down. The hand stayed under the pillow. The eyes stayed closed.

The night was not better.

It was over.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I walk for a few blocks, my breath pluming in the cold air. My phone buzzes again. It’s my sister. I sigh, knowing she’s going to ask why I’m not home yet.* "This is just great." *I decide to detour to the convenience store for some ice cream. Might as well make a bad night worse.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren lay under the blanket. The left hand stayed under the pillow. The right held the coin.

Up. Down. Up. Down.

The phone buzzed again in the coat pocket. Once. Then again. Ren didn’t move.

At 12:20, they got up.

The floor was cold. The kitchen light made everything look thin. Ren filled the kettle. Watched the water. It shook before the kettle did.

They put the mug on the counter. Both hands. Still shaking.

Ren turned off the light. Stood in the dark.

The coin came from the pocket. Flipped. Caught. Flipped. Caught. The left hand stayed under the bedspread.

The phone buzzed a third time. Ren looked at it.

Name: Mom.

Message: You okay?

Ren set the phone face down.

The kettle clicked. Steam curled. A thin line of water ran down the side. Ren wiped it with a paper towel. Too hard. The mug rang once.

They remembered the hand on theirs. Light. Sure. Wrong.

“Didn’t ask,” Ren said.

The room didn’t care.

Ren drank the tea. It was too hot. It burned in a small, clean way. They set the mug in the sink. Washed the hands again. The left one trembled under the water. Ren pressed it flat against the sink rim until the shaking moved into the metal and stopped.

Back in bed. Left hand under the pillow. Right hand holding the coin.

The radiator ticked. A car passed. Someone’s door opened two apartments down. It closed.

Ren listened to the latch. Not the bar’s. This one was fine.

They closed their eyes.

The night was not better.

It was just quiet.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I finish my ice cream, the cold numbing my mouth. I don't reply to my sister, just put my phone on silent. I'm not in the mood to talk to anyone. I just want to go home and forget this whole night happened.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The next Tuesday, the club smelled like lemon cleaner and old smoke. Ren arrived at six. The latch was still loose. Ren tested it with the key. It clicked, then gave.

Ren didn’t fix it. Ren didn’t call. They went inside.

The well needed gin. The shelf needed limes. The jukebox needed a coin. Ren gave it one. The trumpet came back slow.

At 11:47, the far stool was empty.

Ren noticed. Then looked away.

A man came in. He wanted a beer. He wanted conversation. He wanted his hand on the bar near Ren’s. He got neither.

“Last call,” Ren said.

The man laughed and reached for the tap handle. Ren slid it away.

“Don’t,” Ren said.

The man pulled back. Paid. Left. The door shut. Ren checked the latch.

The stool at the far end held a faint damp circle. Not there before. Ren wiped it. Tight circle. Tighter.

The water cup sat upside down on the shelf. Ren took it down. Set it right side up. Then back down. Then right side up again.

They didn’t know why.

At 12:05, Ren flipped the sign. Counted the till. Closed it. Put the rag over the sink.

The phone in their coat buzzed once. Then again. Ren let it buzz.

They locked the front. Went out the back. The alley was wet. The bus waited at the corner. Its doors held open.

Ren boarded. Sat near the back. Left hand under the seat. Right hand on the bag.

The club light died as the bus pulled away.

Ren didn’t think about the patron. Thought about the latch. The cup. The line on the counter. The way someone can touch you once and then call it concern.

The bus hissed over a grate. Ren’s hand moved under the seat. Up. Down. Up. Down.

Ren stopped it with the thumb in the palm.

It didn’t stop.

Ren let it.

At the apartment, the kettle clicked. The tea burned a small clean hole in Ren’s tongue. They set the mug on the counter. Both hands. The left one trembled against the ceramic.

Ren pressed it flat. Turned off the light.

The bed creaked. The left hand went under the pillow. The right held the coin.

Up. Down. Up. Down.

The phone buzzed a third time. Ren looked at it.

Name: Mom.

Message: Come for dinner?

Ren set it face down.

“Last call,” Ren said.

The room answered with the radiator tick.

Ren closed their eyes.

The night was not better.

It was just Tuesday.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I'm scrolling through my phone, another boring Tuesday night, when I see a notification from a local news app. "Local Jazz Club Burglarized, Owner Suspects Inside Job." My eyes widen. The club... it's the same one. I click on the article, a knot forming in my stomach.* "No way."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren met the look and held it. No smile, no nod, nothing for it to stick to. Two years behind a bar had burned the flinch out of them somewhere around month six. Staring patrons came with the territory — the eleven-o'clock-on-a-weeknight kind especially. The ones drinking somewhere that wasn't home.

They dropped their gaze first, but only because the counter had a water ring that needed arguing with. Left hand found a rag and folded it into thirds. Thirds again. Right hand did the actual wiping.

"Last call's midnight." Flat voice, pitched just far enough to cross eleven feet of empty room. "Want a third, now's the time to say so. Kitchen's been closed an hour, so don't ask."

The jukebox climbed into a trumpet line. Ren straightened a bottle of rye that was already straight.

They knew the type without trying. Two drinks by quarter to twelve, eyes on a condensation ring like it had a confession coming. Not Ren's business. Pour, take the money, stay out of it — that was the whole arrangement, and it kept everybody comfortable. Still, their gaze flicked up once, a quick inventory, before they could stop it.

"You carrying a tab," they said, "or settling tonight?"

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's hand was out from under Alex's before the sentence finished. Fast. Cleaner than the moment deserved.

The left one. Of course it was the left one. Ren closed it around the folded rag, and for half a second the fine tremor showed — there and gone, smothered under grip. They set the rag on the drain board. Came back with both hands flat on the counter, visible and steady enough, like a man showing he was unarmed.

"No." Not unkind. Just finished.

Ren had seen the play before. The lean-in. The hand. The *can I tell you something* — the oldest line in the eleven-o'clock book, right after *what time do you get off* and just before *you look like someone who understands*. And Alex was watching for a reaction. Ren could feel it, that waiting quality, the way the room had narrowed down to Ren's face.

They didn't hand anything over.

"Everybody who wants to tell the bartender something doesn't want the bartender." They picked up Alex's empty glass, turned it in their hands, set it back down an inch to the left. Pointless. Kept the hands busy. "They want an audience. Any audience. I'm just the one who can't leave." A beat. The trumpet on the jukebox bent a note and let it go. "I make a bad priest. I charge by the drink and I remember everything."

Ren reached under the bar for the cash drawer key. Didn't put it in the lock yet. Just held it.

"Tab or cash, and the third drink is yes or no." They looked up. Held the eyes this time, on purpose, since Alex seemed to want a look so badly. "Whatever it is, it'll still be true tomorrow. If it's worth saying, say it sober to somebody who isn't being paid to stand there."

The key turned in the lock. Half past nothing, and already closing out the room.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: My hand drops. "Right." My voice is quiet. "Tab, then." I look down at my hands. "And no to the third."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
That "right" sat in Ren's ear a second longer than it should have. No performance in it. No wounded pride, no second attempt at the hand. Just a word said by someone arguing with themselves and losing.

"Card."

The card landed on the counter. Ren crossed the eleven feet, took it with the right hand, and read it turned away, at the register. *Alex.* The name went into the file behind Ren's eyes — the one they'd claimed was full. There was room after all.

Left hand opened the drawer. The card went in with the folded receipts, and the drawer shut on it.

Ren came back down the bar with a coaster in one hand and a glass of water in the other. They slid the coaster under Alex's glass, covering the condensation ring, ending its testimony, and set the water beside it. The glass touched down an inch outside of reaching distance.

"Free refill." A beat. "Water's the only thing in the building that is."

They stepped back. Both hands found the counter edge.

"Midnight, I kill the jukebox. Half past, the chairs go up and so do you." Flat. Not a threat — a schedule. "Tab's open till then."

Then Ren walked back to the far well and started counting bottles that didn't need counting. The back-bar mirror did the watching. That was its whole job. In it, Alex sat with their hands on the bar, shoulders at the angle people got when nobody was performing for them anymore.

No to the third. Ren filed that too. Most people in that chair took the third — it was the whole point of the chair. The ones who said no were either going to be fine or already past it, and Ren wouldn't know which until they saw the way Alex left.

The jukebox song ended. In the gap between tracks the club made its real sound — ice settling, the register's clock ticking somewhere under the counter.

Ren didn't look up again. Didn't need to. They'd meant what they said. They just hadn't expected it to be taken.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren had come back for the empty glass. That was all. Eleven feet, right hand out, left hand steadying the coaster — and Alex's hand arrived over it, quick and quiet as a card trick.

Ren went still.

The hand had been fine right up until it was caught. That was the joke of it. Busy, it behaved. Held — nothing to fold, nothing to wipe, nowhere to be — it did what it did. A fine fast shiver under the skin, and Alex's warm palm read every letter of it.

*There it is.* Ren thought it with the specific cold of a locked drawer found open.

Two years of thirds-and-quarters. Rag folded out of sight, glass always in the left, bottles lifted with the wrist turned so the shake died against the weight. A whole stupid magic act. This stranger had walked through it in one touch.

Ren didn't yank. Yanking was a confession with teeth. They turned the hand over — slow, like it was their idea — slid it free, and used it to pick up the glass. See? Useful. It carried the glass to the well and set it down like nothing had ever been asked of it.

Then the tap. Hot water over glass. Steam and noise, covering a multitude.

"Cold room," Ren said to the sink. "That's the version I usually sell. Cold room. Too much coffee. Long shift."

The water shut off. Towel over the hands, right first, left taking longer because it liked having a job.

"You're not buying it." They turned around, hip against the back bar, and gave Alex the eyes straight this time, because looking away would cost more. "Fine. It shakes. It's shaken longer than you've had a tab. It's not a story and it's not for sale."

The register clock said 11:53. The jukebox hummed in the gap between songs, waiting for midnight and the knife.

"Here's what I can't figure." Towel folded. Thirds. Thirds again. "People look at bartenders all night. Nobody *watches* one. You felt it in one touch, which means you knew what to feel for."

A beat.

"So either your hands do that too, or you spend a lot of time learning people before they notice you learning them." Ren squared the towel on the drain board. "Both of those explain a person alone at 11:47 saying no to a third."

They looked at Alex's hand, still resting on the bar where Ren's had been, then back up.

"That the something? Could've led with it." Quieter: "Would've been cheaper than the hand."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*My hand flinches back from the bar, like it's been burned. I quickly tuck it under my other arm.*

"No," I say, my voice almost a whisper. "My hands don't do that." *I clear my throat, trying to regain some composure.* "And I wasn't... I wasn't trying to learn you."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren knew that tuck.

Under the arm, out of sight, quick as a card up a sleeve. Ren held the patent on that move. Forty seconds ago they'd run it in reverse — turned the left hand over like it was their idea, gave it a glass so it would look employed. Hiding a thing never made it quiet. Just made it yours alone.

Ren didn't say any of that.

"Didn't say shake." Towel off the drain board. Right hand. "Said you knew what to feel for. Different charges."

The jukebox rolled into something slow, all piano. The register clock said 11:56.

"And I believe you weren't trying. Nobody tries." Fold. Thirds. Thirds again. "Trying's for salesmen. What you do isn't a skill, it's weather. You walk into a room, the room reports to you whether you asked it to or not. Then some night you're tired, and your hand files a report of its own, and somebody feels it."

Ren turned away while Alex's composure came back together — private work, no audience required. They squared the towel. Both hands flat on the counter, the unarmed pose again.

"Here's the trade. You touched my hand, I read yours back. That's my entire legal code — even money. So we're square." A beat. "Which means you don't owe me the something. Never did. I told you, I make a bad priest. Priests want the confession. I want the chairs up by half past and the drawers to match."

Midnight arrived. Ren's hand went under the bar toward the jukebox switch and came back without touching it. The song got to run. Four minutes past the deadline, nobody around to bill them to.

"Water stays yours till half past. Tab too, if the no turns into a yes." Ren went down to the well and started on the bottles that didn't need straightening — the light ones, left hand, wrist angled so the weight did most of the work.

In the back-bar mirror, the room sat with itself. Ren watched it the same way they'd watched it all night, for the way the leaving would go. Fine, or already past it. The mirror wasn't telling yet.

One touch. One read, clean through a two-year act. *Knew what to feel for.* Ren kept the thought behind the bar, with everything else that wasn't for sale.

Whatever Alex was at 11:47 on a Tuesday, they were good at it. And they were alone with it.

That part, Ren recognized on sight.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*I watch Ren in the mirror. My face is still flushed. I pick up the glass of water and take a long drink.*

"I guess I'm good at noticing things," I say, my voice still a little shaky. "Doesn't make me any less alone."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The song ran out mid-bridge and Ren let it stay run. No quarter for the machine. The club folded down into its real voice — ice settling in the well, the register clock, the walk-in humming through the back door.

Ren heard the sentence all the way through. That was new for a Tuesday.

*Doesn't make me any less alone.* Set down flat on the bar. No hand under it. No lean. Just the sentence, out in the open air, the cheap version Ren had quoted a price on an hour ago — paid in full.

"Told you it cost less." Ren pulled glasses off the rack, turned them mouth-down on the counter. Left hand steadying, right hand wiping. The left behaved when it had a job. Ren kept it supplied. "No hand. No lean. Nobody died of it."

They worked down the room, flipping chairs onto tables. Not Alex's stretch. Those stools stayed down till half past. Posted laws.

"And since you're good at noticing, here's something worth the effort." Chair up, legs into the rungs. "People think the product in here is liquor. It's not. Liquor's a rental fee on the stool. The product is a room where a person can be alone in public and nobody makes it a whole thing." They crossed to the next table. "You, at 11:47 on a Tuesday, drinking free water — that's not a sad story. That's a customer using the product correctly."

Ren stood a second in the middle of the floor. The mirror caught the rest without asking — flush down to something near normal, hands around the water glass. First real evidence for the *fine* column. Not a verdict. A file getting somewhere.

"Friday I get pairs in here. Two people, one table, alone at each other for three hours." Back toward the well. "You're ahead of the room just by calling the inventory what it is."

Quieter, said to the bottles:

"Same wiring, for what it's worth. The noticing. It's why I'm back here and not out there. Difference is I get an hourly wage and a sink to hide my hand in." Towel over the glass. Thirds. Thirds again. "Doesn't make me less alone either. Makes me employed."

Clock said 12:09. Ren wiped the well top slow.

"Tuesdays are the slowest night we run. Wednesdays after that. In case the product's ever something you need in stock." A beat. "That's not an invitation. That's inventory data. I have a counter for a reason."

They squared the towel and looked over, flat as the first line of the night.

"Tab's good till half past. Water too. You don't have to spend it talking, either. People close out quiet in here all the time. It's allowed. Some nights it's preferred."

Ren went back to the bottles that didn't need it. In the mirror, the leaving hadn't started yet.

For once, they weren't in a hurry to read the ending.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*I watch Ren in the mirror for a while longer. The flush has mostly faded, but my shoulders still feel tight. I take another sip of water, then set the glass down.*

"So you're saying I'm using the product correctly," I repeat, a small, wry smile touching my lips. "Good to know."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I watch Ren's reflection for a moment more. The smile fades.* "So is that why you're a bartender? To... use the product, too?"

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Or just to hide your hand in the sink?" I add quietly, looking down at the condensation ring again. "The hourly wage part."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's hands stopped, and that was the problem. Questions that size stopped the hands, and stopped hands were an exhibit.

The left found the rag before it found anything else. Right hand pulled the well mats. Business as cover.

"Three questions in one breath." Ren kept eyes on the mats. "You're getting a better rate than the rye."

A beat.

"You stacked them, though. Product, then the hand, then the wage — cheapest door last, left open for me." They looked up once. "Considerate or trained. Filed either way."

The mats were already clean. Ren wiped them again.

"Wrong order, but all three."

They crossed the counter and set a knuckle on it — right hand. "This is the real one. Eleven feet of oak. You think it's for serving across." A tap. "It's a border. Out there, a person alone is a question the room keeps asking. Back here, alone is the job description. Nobody asks the bartender why they're quiet. It'd be suspicious if I weren't."

Back to the sink. The motion of steam, if not the steam.

"The sink's real, though. Best employer in the building. Gives the hand a cover story, gives the night a shape." Thirds. Thirds again. "Hand gets a sink, eyes get a job, silence gets a wage. I looked a long time for a package like that."

Then quieter, because even money:

"Told you earlier I was the one who couldn't leave." The towel got squared with more attention than it needed. "That was the selling version. True version — I picked the only job in town where never going anywhere is called showing up."

Clock said 12:24.

"And yeah. Product." Ren nodded at the room without looking at it — the empty stools, the jukebox doing nothing. "Tuesdays, I'm its best customer. Alone in public, nobody making it a thing. I just take mine behind the counter, where the room can't return the favor."

In the mirror, Alex's shoulders had come down somewhere during the water. Ren noted it and didn't say it. Fine column. Second entry.

"Six minutes. Tab closes when the chairs go up."

They worked the last stretch of counter and stopped across from Alex, both hands flat, the unarmed pose.

"You left me the small door on purpose. Second decent thing tonight you didn't have to do." A beat. "So here's what the big door cost. Half past, the border comes down, and I'm just a person alone in a closed room. Same as you'd be."

The left hand stayed flat. Behaving. The tremor under it anyway, patient as the ice.

"Mine has a sink, though. That's the whole advantage. That and the wage."

Ren pushed off the counter, crossed to the wall, and this time touched the jukebox switch — the song long dead, midnight with it. The club went quiet the way it only did after the last machine gave up. A big, ringing nothing.

"Don't let the quiet spook you. That's just the room clocking out." They came back for the glasses. "Finish your water. You've got six minutes and nobody in them."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*I watch Ren turn off the jukebox. The sudden silence is jarring, but not unwelcome. I take a final sip of water.*

"I guess I'm used to quiet," I say, my voice almost lost in the sudden stillness. "And thanks. For the water, and... everything."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
"Don't." The card was already out of the drawer — right hand, drawer shut with a hip. "It was inventory. You don't thank a shelf."

Ren ran the tab at the register, back turned. Two ryes, one water at zero. The printer made its small sound. They tore the slip with the left hand, gave it the job, and came down the counter with card and receipt together. Set down flat. Face up, this time. Nothing left to hide behind on either side.

"Two drinks. Water was free, like advertised." A beat. "Tip line's yours. So is the quiet. I told you I remember everything — remembering isn't telling. This room keeps what it sees."

Then the chairs. Clock said half past, close enough that the difference was Ren's to spend. They started at the far wall — chair up, legs into the rungs — and worked toward Alex's stretch without hurrying it.

"And used to quiet. Good. Then the room doesn't have to break you in. Most people can't sit in a silence without patching it." Another chair. "You've been sitting in one all night. Noted it around the second sip."

The mirror held the whole floor now. Ren checked it the way they'd checked it all night — shoulders, hands, the glass. Shoulders down since before the jukebox died. Hands easy around the water. Whatever Alex had carried in at 11:47, the room had taken some of the weight, or the quiet had, or the not-being-performed-at had.

Fine column. Ren left the file open.

"One thing, since we're square." They stopped across the counter. Both hands on the oak, flat, done performing. "There wasn't an everything. There was a guy who didn't ask, a coaster, and a room that already knew its job. But if it felt like something — that half was yours. You sat still and said no to the third. I just didn't interrupt."

Ren pushed off the counter and went back to the chairs. Half past arrived in the register clock's small ticking, and Ren honored it at the far end first, farthest from Alex, the way you clear a room without telling it to move.

"All night I've been running a count." Said to a chair leg. "The leaving tells you everything. How a person clears a door — fine, or already past it." Chair up. Legs into the rungs. "For what it's worth, I know which column. I just don't file it while you're still in the room. House rule. Feels rude to read somebody's ending over their shoulder."

That was the closest thing to a goodbye in Ren's inventory, and it had come out too many words long. They let it stand. Tuesdays.

The jukebox stayed dark. The room rang with its nothing — ice, clock, walk-in. Ren squared the last towel and left one stool down, the one at eleven feet, until further notice.

"Door's the loud one on the left. Handle sticks — lift, then pull." A beat. "Nobody walks you out. That's the product working."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*I pick up the card and the receipt, my fingers brushing Ren's. The contact is brief, almost accidental. I look at the tip line, then at Ren, then back at the receipt.*

"Right," I say, a small, almost imperceptible nod. "Product."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Three for three.

Ren logged the brush the way they logged everything — quarter second, no comment. Touch one had asked a question. Touch two had taken a reading. Touch three hadn't asked for anything at all. Just contact, passing through, the kind that happened when a person quit aiming.

The left had held for it, too. Ren noted that with something adjacent to interest. It only shook when it got held on purpose. Accidents slid right past it. Deliberation was what it couldn't take. Ren had a whole theory about that and nobody to sell it to.

And *product* — thrown back flat, no flinch, no thank-you performance, no asking what it cost. First patron in months who'd taken the terms as written. Ren didn't say so. Saying so would've been the room making it a whole thing.

"Tip line's not a key." Said toward the sink, water already running. "Doesn't open the stool, doesn't buy the conversation, doesn't get the rye cheaper next Tuesday. Zero's a full price in here. The line's just a line."

Then they did the thing the room was actually built for. Turned their back on the border and gave the floor its privacy.

The mirror took the watch. In it: Alex at eleven feet, receipt in hand, weight even on both feet, shoulders sitting where shoulders were supposed to sit. Nothing like the shape that had come in at 11:47 staring down a condensation ring. Ren read it sideways, deniable, over no one's shoulder.

Fine. The case was building itself. Not filed yet. House rule outlasted the shift.

Ren ran water over glasses that were already clean. Left hand got the towel, kept the job. Behind them the room held its particular quiet — the sound of one person doing the arithmetic before standing. Keys, door, night. Ren knew every beat in the sequence and didn't turn around for any of them. Turning around would've been the room asking its question again.

"Night, Alex." Flat as the counter. First time the name had been out loud all night. Ren heard it land and let it stay. The card had to be good for something.

The door would say the rest. Lift, then pull — two sounds, and Ren would know which column. That was the arrangement. The room kept what it saw. The bartender kept what they heard. Nobody performed the ending.

Ren stood at the sink with their back to all of it and waited on the handle like a last note.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*My fingers trace the tip line, but I don't write anything. I just take the card and the receipt, slipping them into my wallet.*

"Night, Ren," I say, my voice a little stronger than before. *I turn and head for the door, remembering the instructions: lift, then pull.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren clocked it. The look. Held one second past polite — long enough to mean something, short enough to deny it later. People tried that at this hour. Testing the water without committing to getting wet.

Ren held it right back. Didn't blink, didn't soften. Then simply returned to the counter, because the counter was still there.

The rag kept moving in the left hand. Slow circles over the wood. The tremor stayed quiet when the hand had work.

"Last call's in thirteen." Flat. Information, not invitation.

Ren slid a fresh coaster down the bar — near the glass, not touching it. The old one had gone soft, warped to the shape of its puddle. Small courtesies. House policy, nothing personal.

"Third one's a decision." A beat. The jukebox ran out of song somewhere behind them; brass hiss filled the gap. "Just so you know."

They wrung the rag out, hung it over the rail. Eyes flicked once to the condensation ring, then back.

"You've been staring at that thing a while. It's not going to answer."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The hand came down on the left one.

Ren went still for a beat. The rag was hung up. The hand had nothing to hold, nothing to do — and now someone else's weight was pinning it to the wood, right where it did its worst work when it was idle.

Ren pulled it back. Not a flinch. Just gone. The hand dipped below the bar and came up with a dry towel and a rocks glass off the rack. Something to hold. The tremor settled where nobody could see it.

"Don't."

Flat. No heat. Heat meant it had gotten somewhere.

"You can tell me something. From your side of the bar." The towel worked slow circles over the glass. "Hands stay with their owners. House rule. Mine too."

Ren drifted a step down the bar, toward glasses that didn't need rearranging. Distance dressed up as work.

"You watched my face before your hand even landed. Wanted to see what you'd get." A beat. "Same move as the look earlier. One second too long. That's twice tonight you've tested the water."

The glass went onto the rack. Ren took another one down.

"Eleven minutes to last call." Eyes came up once. Level. "You want to tell me something, tell me. Listening's part of the job." The towel resumed. "Hands aren't."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back, a little stung.* "Sorry." *I pick at the label on my bottle.* "Just... thought you looked like you could use a distraction." *I sigh, looking around the empty bar.* "Guess not."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
"Sorry's fine." Ren took down another glass. The towel resumed its circles. "And you guessed wrong. Didn't say no to company. Said no to hands. Different things."

The label was coming apart under Alex's thumbnail, little curls of paper gathering at the base of the bottle. Ren gave it a glance. Idle hands. Everybody had a version. Ren's just happened to be glassware.

"'Could use a distraction.'" Ren repeated it flat, the way you'd check a coin for counterfeit. "You've been here since ten. Two of the same. First one gone in fifteen minutes. That one's been dying for an hour — and you spent most of it staring at a ring of condensation."

The jukebox finally found a new record. Piano this time. Slower.

"Empty bar. Tuesday. Midnight." The glass went up on the rack. "If one of us needed the distraction, it wasn't the one getting paid to be here."

Ren ran the tap, filled a water glass, slid it down the bar. It stopped a foot short of the bottle. Even the glassware kept its distance.

"Nine minutes." Eyes came up. Held — normal length, this time. "You walked in here carrying something. Been sitting on it all night. I've got ears, and nothing else to do with them until close."

The left hand found the towel again before it had time to decide anything on its own.

"So. Words. That offer's still good."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The towel slowed. Didn't stop — stopping was the one thing it couldn't afford to do. Just went careful, like it knew it was being watched now.

"Whatever you're feeling, it's not against anything of mine." Ren kept their eyes on the glass. "Hand's been over here since you let go. Towel. Glass. Rack. That's the whole itinerary."

The piano filled a bar's worth of silence.

"But. Yeah." Circles resumed. Slower. "Second you pinned it, the thing had nothing to hold. That's when it talks. Idle hands. Mine just has more to say than most."

Ren turned the glass in the towel. Once. Twice.

"Essential tremor. Neurological. Not fear. Not cold. Not whatever question you're building behind your eyes right now." Flat as the counter. "It's why the rag never stops. Occupational feature."

Then the eyes came up. Held.

"Here's what I noticed, though." A beat. "You walked in carrying something. Sat on it all night. Stared at a ring of water for an hour. And the second you clocked one real thing about me — one — you grabbed it with both hands." The glass went up on the rack. "You're not distracting me. You're distracting you. With me. Which is fine. But it's a rental, not a purchase."

Eight minutes on the clock. Ren took down the last glass from the rack.

"So. Keep poking at my hand, or tell me what you walked in with." The towel resumed its circles. "One of those goes somewhere."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back quickly, feeling caught.* "Okay, okay, I get it." *I look down at my bottle, picking at a new part of the label.* "It's not... that interesting. Just a really bad day."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
"Didn't ask for interesting." Ren swapped towels, moved down the back bar. Started turning bottles label-out. Slow work. Good work — the left hand liked aligning things. "Bad days never are. They're just heavy."

The piano record ran out. Ren let it hiss. Silence asked better questions anyway.

"Weekends, people come in to celebrate. Tuesdays, they come in to sit." A rye went square with its brothers. "You're on schedule. Nothing wrong with the schedule."

Ren's eyes flicked once to the bottle. The label was coming off in wet curls now, a small ruin of paper gathering at the base.

"That label's your towel." A beat. "Everybody's got a version. Not a verdict."

Ren came back up the bar and stopped across from Alex. Professional distance — but across from them now, not ten feet down. The water glass got two fingers and a push, traveled the last foot, stopped against the bottle. The gap was gone. Small change. Deliberate.

"So. Seven minutes." The towel found the counter again. Circles. "You don't have to make it a story. Bad days come out in pieces anyway. Start with whichever one's loudest."

The circles kept going. Ren didn't rush the silence behind it — let it sit there, open, the way the good ones always did.

"And last call's standing right in front of you. Third drink, water, or done — pick one out loud." The rag wrung over the rail, hung. "I start packing the well at midnight either way."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I look at the water glass, then at my bottle.* "Okay, fine. Water." *I push my bottle away slightly.* "And it's not just a bad day. It's... a really bad *week*."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren took the bottle without asking. The ruined label went with it — paper curls and all — into the bus tub under the bar. One motion. The counter in front of Alex came up clean. Water glass. Coaster. Nothing left to pick at.

"There. Prop's gone."

The water got topped off. Two fingers, same as before.

"Good call, by the way. Third drink doesn't fix a week. Just edits it." Ren started breaking down the well — pulling pour spouts, dropping them in the soak sink one at a time. Slow work. Good work for the left hand.

The jukebox hissed on, empty. Ren let it.

"Weeks are worse than days. Days end. You sleep them off." Clink. "Weeks stack. And somewhere around Wednesday you start wondering if it's you instead of the week."

Eyes came up once. Level.

"You paused before 'week.' Just now. It got heavier out loud." Back to the spouts. "That's usually the sign it's a real thing and not just a run of bad luck."

Clock said six minutes.

"So don't give me the whole week. It'll come out a summary, and summaries lie." The last spout dropped into the sink. "Start with the day it went sideways. What day was that."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Monday," *I say, my voice barely a whisper.* "It was definitely Monday." *I push the water glass around in a small circle.* "Everything just... fell apart."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren reached over and killed the jukebox. The hiss cut off mid-breath. The room dropped down to fridge hum and the wall clock.

"Monday was yesterday." Flat. Doing the math out loud where Alex could hear it. "You said bad week. But the fall's not even two days old. So the week was the slope. Monday's where the floor went."

The register drawer slid open. Ren started on the twenties. Counting was good work — precise, quiet, kept the left hand honest.

"And you whispered it." A ten went into its slot. "People whisper when saying the thing still costs something. Old news gets a regular voice."

Eyes flicked once to the water glass, making its small circles on the coaster.

"Better towel than the label, by the way. Glass doesn't come apart. Just moves."

The count went on. Ren didn't fill the gap behind it.

"'Everything' never falls apart all at once, though. It goes in order. One thing, then the next, then the next — until the list gets too long to carry and you just file it under everything." The drawer clicked shut. "So. What was first."

Ren took the bar keys off the hook. Held them. Didn't move toward the door yet.

"Five minutes on the clock. Door locks at midnight. Cleanup runs about forty minutes after, and you're welcome to sit through it." A beat. "Not special treatment. Tuesdays are dead, and cleanup's worse with nobody talking at me. So talk. Or don't. Either way, the stool's yours till one."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I stop pushing the glass around.* "It was my job. They... they let me go." *My voice cracks a little.* "After eight years."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The keys went back on the hook. Ren let the number sit in the room first.

"Eight years."

The clock ticked past midnight somewhere in the silence. Ren didn't announce last call — just walked the length of the bar, threw the deadbolt on the front door, and killed the sign outside. The window went dark. The room shrank down to half-light and fridge hum.

"We're closed. Congratulations — you're not a customer anymore. You're company." Coming back up the bar. "Company gets worse service and more honesty."

Ren took down two glasses. Filled one with water, set it in front of Alex. The other got a single finger of the well rye. The cheap one, not the shelf stuff. For themselves.

"House rule. After close, one's mine."

The glass came up. Steady enough. The left hand had a job again, same as always.

"Here's what I heard just now. Your voice cracked on 'eight years.' Not on 'let me go.'" A slow sip. "The firing's the event. The eight years is what it cost. Those aren't the same thing."

"And they did it on a Monday. That's not an accident, that's strategy. Cut people loose Monday, and by Tuesday the week's problem belongs to you, not them. You've been hauling their mess around since yesterday. You just filed it under your name."

Ren set the glass on its own coaster. Forearms came down on the back bar — the far side of it. Professional side. Still.

"So. No summary. I want the exact words. Who told you, and what did they say — face to face, or a calendar invite?"

A beat.

"Eight years earns a face. If they didn't give you one, that's information too."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I stare at Ren, surprised by the sudden shift in atmosphere.* "A calendar invite," *I say, my voice flat.* "For a 'check-in.' Ten minutes."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren exhaled through the nose. One dry note — not a laugh, but a close relative.

The rye glass turned one slow rotation under Ren's hand. Didn't get drunk from yet.

"Crack's gone, too. You've gone flat." Eyes came up, held. "Flat's one of two things. Either you've said it enough times tonight that it's worn smooth — to yourself, to the steering wheel, whoever listens first. Or it hasn't landed yet and you're still outrunning it." A beat. "Both wear the same face from over here."

The glass came up. One sip. Back down, square on its coaster.

"Ten-minute calendar invite. Titled 'check-in.'" Ren let the word sit there with its disguise on. "Eight years. Call it sixteen thousand hours. They budgeted ten minutes."

Somewhere in the silence, the clock had slid past twelve. The room was officially tomorrow.

"Ten minutes isn't a conversation. It's a delivery window." The thumb tracked the rim of the glass, slow. "Nobody schedules a decision in ten minutes. Decisions run long, or they're already made. So it was made before you sat down. The meeting was the paperwork, read out loud, with you in the room for it."

Eyes flicked once to Alex. Back to the glass.

"How many names were on that invite? Yours, plus who." Ren let it hang a second, then kept going. "Because if HR was on it, that's the whole story right there. HR doesn't sit in on check-ins. HR sits in on verdicts. Whoever booked that meeting named it soft on purpose."

A pause. Quieter now.

"I did two years in an office before this. Long enough to learn the dialect." The glass turned again. "'Check-in.' 'Restructuring.' 'Heading in a new direction.' Every phrase translates to one word. The one they couldn't put in the invite title, or you'd have declined the meeting."

Ren took the rag back off the rail. Folded it. Refolded it. The left hand liked precision work, and this had become that kind of conversation.

"One thing before you keep going. That ten minutes wasn't a measure of you. It was a measure of them. Cowards run efficient." Flat. "Don't carry their number around like it's yours."

The rag went over the shoulder. Forearms back on the bar. Still. From Ren, that was full attention.

"You gave me the envelope. Title, duration, medium. I asked for the words." Eyes up. Holding. "So walk me through the ten. You sat down. Then what. Exact words, if they're still in there." A beat. "They usually are. Everything else blurs. The sentence that ends eight years — that one people keep."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, looking at my reflection in the water glass.* "They said... 'We've decided to move in a different direction.'" *My voice is still flat, but there's a tremor underneath.* "That was it. That was the whole thing."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren let the sentence sit. Took the rye down a quarter inch, set it back on its coaster. Square.

"We've decided to move in a different direction."

Flat. The coin-check voice.

"That phrase was on my list before you said it. Top three. 'Check-in.' 'Restructuring.' 'New direction.'" Ren moved down to the soak sink, started rinsing pour spouts under warm water. Hands busy under the suds, tremor drowned where nobody could see it. "Nobody wrote that sentence for you. It comes pre-written. Kept in a drawer somewhere, next to the paperwork. Somebody picked it because the honest version — 'we're cutting you, and here's who decided' — wouldn't fit in a calendar invite."

A spout went onto the towel to dry.

"'We've.' No names. Nobody signed it. 'Decided' — past tense. Done before you sat down. The meeting was the reading, not the decision." Another spout. "And notice who's missing from it. No name. No 'thank you.' Not even 'your position.' Eight years, and the last thing they ever said to you is a sentence where you don't appear."
