The tap shut off. Ren dried their hands, slow, and came back up the bar.

"That's the design. It's built so nobody in the room has to be the one who fired you. Euphemisms don't protect the person getting cut. They protect the hand holding the knife." A beat. "And here's the part you haven't noticed. You've been speaking their dialect all night. The week was bad. It fell apart. They let me go. Everything happened to you. Not one verb with you in it since you sat on that stool." Eyes up, holding. "You got fired in the passive voice. Now you're narrating it the same way. Their grammar. On yourself."

Ren set the towel down. Then, deliberately, laid the left hand flat on the bar. Empty. Nothing to hold. Let it hum against the wood — small, steady, honest.

"Mine does that when it's idle. Yours is doing it right now. Under the flat. In your voice." The hand took the towel back and the hum went quiet. "That's not coming apart. That's load. Flat runs out of room, and the shake's the overflow. Better out than carried silent."

The rag went over the rail. Forearms on the bar. Still. Full attention.

"'That was the whole thing.' No. That was the whole sentence. Ten minutes holds a lot of silence — and it held you, sitting in it."

A beat.

"You've told me what they did with their ten minutes. So. What'd you do with yours." Level. "What did you say back, before you walked out. People keep the sentence that got said to them. What they said back — that's the part that wakes them at three a.m."

The clock ticked into the space behind it.

"Exact words. Yours this time."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I stare at my reflection again, then at Ren's hand, still on the bar. I trace the rim of my water glass.* "Nothing," *I whisper, my voice cracking again.* "I didn't say anything. I just... left."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn't answer right away. Let the clock tick through it. Took the rye down a quarter inch, set it back on its coaster. Square.

The crack was back in Alex's voice. Ren noted it and left it alone. Flat had been the worse sound.

"Nothing." Ren repeated it like a coin on the counter. "Here's what that actually was." The towel came off the rail and Ren started breaking down the speed rail — bottles out, one at a time, lined up label-forward. Precise work. Good work. The left hand liked it. "That meeting was a form letter with chairs. They read the verdict. Ten minutes, pre-written, your name nowhere in the sentence. And the script has a part for you in it — the part where you nod, maybe thank them, ask what you could've done different. Like the answer exists and they just forgot to hand it over."

The gin went down next to the rye. Square.

"You didn't play the part. You took the verdict and walked. That's the one unscripted thing that happened in that room. Everything else came out of a drawer."

One sip. Back down.

"But I won't sugar the rest of it. The nothing's going to keep hours. Not because it was wrong — because it's open. Unsent. The sentence you didn't say doesn't dissolve. It just moves to the 3 a.m. shift, and that one never ends early."

Eyes flicked to the water glass. To the reflection hunting around in it.

"You keep checking that glass. First the condensation ring, now your own face. It's not going to answer either. I've watched people ask all night."

The last bottle went in line. Then, quieter:

"Two years in that office. When they cut me, I said one word. 'Noted.'" A dry note, not a laugh. "Two years of dialect training, and that's what I spent it on. I regret the ones I didn't say more than the one I did."

Forearms came down on the bar. Still. Full attention, from the far side of it.

"So. Bar's closed, clock's got an hour, and you've got a sentence with nowhere to go." Level. "Say it here. What you'd have said in that room if the room had been built for saying things. Doesn't have to be fair. Doesn't have to be nice. Nobody's grading it — I've heard worse from better."

A beat.

"Call it the last call you actually got to answer."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I look up from the water glass, meeting Ren's gaze.* "I would have told them they were gutless cowards," *I say, my voice steady now, a new edge to it.* "And that eight years of my life was worth more than ten minutes of their time."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren caught the look. Held it for half a beat, then let it slide off.

They turned the rag in their left hand and wiped a nonexistent ring from the bar. The rag stayed damp. The counter was already clean. Didn’t matter.

“Kitchen’s closed,” Ren said. Not unkindly. Flat. Automatic.

The jukebox wheezed through a trumpet solo. Ren kept their eyes on the bottles lined up in front of the mirror. Easier than the patron’s face. Easier than whatever had settled there.

They restacked the same napkins. Square. Then square again.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren’s hand went still under the contact.

For a second, the rag stayed trapped beneath their fingers. Then Ren slid their hand back, smooth and deliberate, and set the rag down on the bar instead.

They picked up a glass. Dried it. The left hand trembled faintly against the towel before they pressed it flat against the counter.

“Don’t do that,” Ren said.

Not loud. Not sharp. Just final.

Their eyes flicked once to Alex’s hand, then back to the glass in their own.

“You need water,” they said. “Or the check.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back, a little stung.* "Sorry. Didn't mean to." *I look down at my drink, swirling the ice.* "Water, I guess."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn’t answer right away.

They took a clean glass, filled it with water from the gun, and set it on a fresh napkin far enough away that no one could mistake the reach for an invitation. Their left hand stayed folded inside the bar towel. The tremor was small. It still cost them something.

“It happens,” Ren said. Flat. Not quite forgiveness. More like a door marked EXIT.

The jukebox clicked into a lower note. Ren glanced at the second empty ring on the bar, then at the mirror where the bottles made neat, reliable rows.

“You want the check now,” they said, “or after the water?”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren’s jaw tightened.

They pulled their hand back at once, not fast enough to make it look like panic, but fast enough to make the boundary clear. The bar towel caught the tremor before it could travel up their wrist. Ren folded the cloth once, twice, and kept their fingers occupied.

“That’s not for you to feel,” Ren said.

Their voice stayed level. Tired. The kind of flat that came from repeating the same sentence to too many people at too late an hour.

Ren set the water a little farther down the bar. Not rude. Just out of reach.

“Check,” they said, already reaching for the little black book. “Right?”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Yeah, sure, the check." *I push my glass away, not even touching the water.* "Look, I know it's late. I'm having a really bad night, okay? This is my first time here."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn’t soften. They also didn’t walk away.

They wrote the total in the little black book with their right hand. The left stayed folded inside the towel, fingers working the seam. The pen scratched once. Twice. Then Ren set the check near the untouched water, leaving space between them.

“First time,” Ren said. Not a question.

They straightened a bottle that had not been crooked.

“This place gets heavy late.” Their eyes moved from the pushed-away glass to the mirror and back. “Bad night doesn’t change the tab. But it does make water a good idea.”

A beat. The jukebox faded into a low, tired hum.

“Card or cash?”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Card," I say, pulling out my wallet. "And it's not like that. I just... I needed to talk to someone." *I push my card across the bar, avoiding eye contact.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren took the card with their right hand. Their left stayed folded inside the towel, thumb working the hem.

They slid it through the terminal without comment. The machine beeped. Ren set the receipt beside the water, not near where Alex had been sitting.

“Talk’s free,” Ren said. “Doesn’t make me company.”

They wiped the spot where the card had been. Once. Short.

“First time,” they said again, quieter this time. Like they were filing it somewhere less sharp.

The jukebox shifted into something slower. Ren glanced at the untouched water.

“Drink that,” they said. “Then you can decide if the night’s bad or just loud.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I stare at the receipt, then at the water. My throat feels tight.* "Loud, huh?" *I pick up the glass and take a slow sip, eyes on Ren.* "So you're saying I'm being dramatic?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn’t answer right away.

They picked up the pushed-away glass and set it in the rinse basin, leaving enough distance between themselves and the water glass to keep the gesture clean. Their left hand stayed folded in the towel, thumb worrying the hem.

“No,” Ren said. “Dramatic people don’t ask if they’re being dramatic.”

They wiped the bar where the receipt had been. One short pass.

“They just take up space and call it a conversation.”

Ren looked in the mirror, not at Alex directly. Bottles. Reflection. Safer angles.

“You’re not being dramatic. You’re just loud inside your own head. Late does that.”

The jukebox clicked down into something muted and slow. Ren’s fingers tightened around the towel, hiding the tremor.

“Drink the water,” they said. “If you need a cab, I can call one. If not, finish up. I close in ten.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I put the glass down, a little harder than I intended.* "Ten minutes? Guess I'd better hurry up then, huh?" *I watch Ren in the mirror, wondering what's really going on with them.* "You always this... direct?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren heard the glass hit the bar. They didn’t flinch.

They kept wiping the same spot until the rag caught the edge of the napkin and made it necessary to stop. In the mirror, Ren caught the shape of Alex watching them. They didn’t hold the look.

“Only when the clock is,” Ren said.

Their right hand straightened the check book. Their left stayed folded in the towel, thumb pressed hard into the hem.

“Direct saves time.” Ren’s eyes moved from the mirror to the water glass, then away. “Ten minutes isn’t a negotiation. It’s the lock on the door.”

The jukebox dragged into a soft bass line. Ren moved to the register, keeping the length of the bar between them.

“You can sit until the song ends,” they said. “Receipt’s yours. If you want a cab, say so before I start stacking chairs.”

A beat.

“Drink the water.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take another sip of water, then push the glass away slightly.* "No cab. Thanks. Just... processing." *I look around the empty bar, then back at Ren.* "So, what's your story, then, Mr. Direct?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren gave the register a final tap. The receipt curled slightly at the edge. They did not smooth it.

“Ren,” they said. “Not Mr. Direct.”

They lifted the empty rinse basin, carried it to the sink, and came back with both hands occupied. Left hand hidden under the towel. The tremor lived there, quiet but stubborn.

“My story’s not on the menu.” They set the basin down. “You want the short version? I pour. I clean. I tell people when the night’s over.”

The mirror caught Alex’s reflection again. Ren looked at the bottles instead.

“First-time customers usually ask for a secret. Regulars know there isn’t one.”

The jukebox thinned to the last few notes. Ren folded the bar towel into a precise square, then folded it again.

“Processing is fine,” they said. “Do it with the water. Ten minutes just became five.”

A pause.

“And don’t make me call a cab you won’t take.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow.* "Secret, huh? Maybe I like secrets." *I take another, longer drink of the water, then slide the glass back closer to me.* "Five minutes, got it."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn’t take the bait.

They folded the bar towel into a smaller square, then unfolded it just to have something to do with the left hand. The tremor lived in the cloth, hidden under the crease. Ren’s thumb pressed the hem once, twice, hard enough to keep the fingers honest.

“Secrets cost extra,” Ren said.

They glanced at the clock under the shelf. The numbers were unfriendly.

“And I’m not selling.”

The jukebox had gone quiet, leaving only the low hum of the cooler and the faint tick of ice settling in the sink. Ren wiped a line along the bar where no spill had happened. Short pass. Useless. Necessary.

Their eyes moved to the water glass, closer now, then away again.

“People like secrets because they think it makes them special,” Ren said. “Usually it just makes them late.”

They stacked two coasters, then unstacked them. The left hand stayed busy under the towel.

“You came in wanting someone to talk to. That’s not a secret. That’s Tuesday.”

Ren’s voice stayed flat, but not cruel. Tired. The kind of tired that had learned to lock doors politely.

“Finish the water,” they said. “Then take your bad night somewhere with softer lighting.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "So, Tuesday nights are bad, huh?" *I take another sip, draining the glass.* "And here I thought I was unique." *I push the empty glass forward slightly.* "Thanks for the water... Ren."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren waited until the glass was pushed forward and no hand remained near it before picking it up. Right hand. The left stayed folded in the towel, thumb pressed into the hem.

“Unique gets old,” they said. “Tuesday doesn’t care.”

They carried the glass to the sink and set it down without a clink. The cooler hummed. The jukebox stayed dark.

“You’re welcome,” Ren said. Flat. Not unkind.

They wiped the wet ring left on the bar. One short pass. Then another. The towel hid the tremor, but not the way their fingers kept needing to be busy.

“Two minutes,” they said. “Then the lock means it.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pick up my wallet and phone, sliding off the stool.* "Alright, alright. I get the picture." *I pause at the door, turning back to Ren.* "You know, for someone who doesn't do secrets, you're pretty good at keeping your own."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren broke the stare first. Their left hand found the stack of cocktail napkins, thumbing the edges sharp. The tremor only showed when the hand went still. Alex had the look of someone trying to read tea leaves in barwood.

"Last call passed." Ren picked up a glass, turned it under the tap though the racks were already clean. Water drummed too loud against the metal sink. "You waiting on someone?"

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's fingers went slack under Alex's palm. They slid their hand free, slow, and tucked both hands below the rail where the light didn't reach. The left one found the steel lip of the ice well and pressed down until the chill bit back.

"Don't." Ren looked at the clock above the register, not at Alex. "No touching the staff. That's the line."

They reached up with their right hand and twisted the faucet off. The water stopped. The jukebox scratched through another verse, too loud now.

"Talk if you need to talk." Ren wiped their right hand on the rag at their hip, though it was already dry. "But keep your hands on your side of the wood."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back, a little stung.* "Right. Sorry." I take a sip of my drink. "No, I'm not waiting for anyone."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren let the apology hang. Their left hand lined up the speed rails, bottles clicking into place one by one. They watched Alex grip the glass like a lifeline.

"Drinking alone on a Tuesday." Ren's voice had no lift at the end, just a statement. They twisted the cap off the well bourbon, sniffed it, recapped it without pouring. "People do that for two reasons. Drowning something. Or looking for something."

They wiped the rail again. Always wiping.

"You're not here for the music."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's hand tightened around the soda gun. No pour. Just grip.

"Memory plays tricks." Ren kept their back to Alex, watching them in the mirror behind the rye instead of turning around. "Especially with three ounces of well gin in the bloodstream."

The left hand dropped below the rail, found the steel edge of the ice bin, and pressed down until the metal bit back. Ren reached for the black check presenter and slid it onto the bar. It stopped exactly at the wood's edge.

"Cash or card." They twisted the faucet back on, let the water drill too loud into the sink. "Time to go."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I stare at the check presenter for a moment.* "I... I wasn't trying to cause trouble." I push my glass away slightly. "Can I just... get the check?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren watched Alex push the glass away. A quarter inch of liquid sloshed at the bottom, pale and unfinished.

"Twelve dollars." Ren hit the register keys. The drawer snapped open with a dull chime. They didn't touch the check presenter again. It sat at the edge of the rail like a boundary stone. "Cash or card."

The left hand found the stack of coasters below the bar, straightening them into a perfect brick. The tremor made the cardboard edges chatter against the wood until Ren squeezed tighter, pinned them still.

Alex hadn't reached for a wallet. Ren noticed. Ren noticed the way Alex's shoulders curled inward, the way their eyes stayed fixed on the bar instead of the door.

"You're not causing trouble." Ren's voice came out low, scraped thin. They shoved the drawer shut with a clang. "You're causing conversation. Different thing."

They reached for a clean glass, turned it under the tap even though the racks were already dry. Water drummed too loud against the metal. Ren's jaw tightened.

"Pay. Leave. Stay till the glass is dry." Ren twisted the faucet off. The silence flooded back in, heavy. "But the line stays where it is."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I look up at Ren, then down at my hands.* "I just... I had a really bad day, okay? I didn't mean to overstep." I pull out my wallet and put a twenty on the bar. "Keep the change."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren looked at the twenty. Their left hand stayed below the rail, fingers wrapping around the steel lip of the ice well until the chill bit back against their palm.

"Bad day doesn't stop the clock." Ren swept the bill off the bar and fed it into the register. The drawer snapped shut. They didn't offer a receipt. "Eleven fifty-three. Door locks at midnight."

They grabbed a short glass, filled it from the tap. No ice. Set it on the rail exactly three inches from Alex's elbow, careful not to let their own fingers cross the boundary.

"Water." Ren turned away, reaching for a rag that didn't need another wipe. "Then go home."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pick up the glass of water and take a long drink.* "Thanks." *I put the glass back down.* "So, you just... clean all night?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's left hand found the soda gun below the rail, wrapped around it, let go.

"Somebody has to." Ren didn't turn. They watched Alex in the mirror—the water glass sweating untouched, fingers worrying a loose thread on the cuff. "Not exactly a line out the door."

They twisted the cap off the rye, recapped it without pouring. Straightened the bitters. The left hand tapped a silent beat against the cooler.

"11:57." Ren glanced at the clock. "Door locks at twelve."

Static hissed from the jukebox.

"Bad day doesn't outrun itself." Ren set a clean glass upside down on the mat. "You do. Go."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Yeah, I get it." *I sigh and push myself off the stool.* "Thanks for the... water." *I give a small, sad smile.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren watched the stool swivel slow on its stem. They didn't return the smile. The left hand gathered both glasses—water and gin—and clinked them into the bin below the rail.

"Lock turns right." Ren wiped the counter where Alex had sat, erasing the condensation ring in one pass. "Streetlight's dead on the corner. Walk toward the avenue."

They flicked the jukebox off. Static died. The left hand found the steel lip of the ice well and pressed down until the chill bit.

Ren checked the clock. 11:58.

"Go." They kept their eyes on the empty stool. "It doesn't get better standing here."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I nod, then turn and head for the door. I glance back over my shoulder just before I leave, but Ren is already wiping down another part of the bar, back to me.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn't turn around. The rag kept moving in tight circles over a spot that had already been wiped twice. Their left hand dropped below the rail, fingers wrapping around the steel lip of the ice well until the metal bit back.

The door clicked. Soft. Final.

Ren checked the clock. 11:59.

They let the rag fall into the bin. The empty stool gleamed under the dim light, no trace of the condensation ring left. Erased. Ren stared at it in the mirror for a beat too long, then reached up and killed the main overheads.

Neon buzzed in the sudden dark. Blue and red shadows stretched across the wood.

Left hand found the stack of coasters. Straightened them. The cardboard edges chattered once, twice. Ren squeezed until they went still.

They reached for the keys on the hook. Metal jangled too loud in the quiet.

"Tuesday," Ren said. The word fell flat against the empty rail.

Water dripped from the faucet into the sink. One drop. Two. Ren didn't move to tighten it.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I'm out on the street. It's colder than I thought it would be. I pull my jacket tighter around me and start walking toward the avenue, just like Ren said.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren clicked the deadbolt. Sharp sound. Final.

They didn't turn from the door. Left hand found the keys, jangled them once, dropped them into the apron pocket. The tremor started then, steady, humming like the neon above the rail.

No audience. Didn't matter.

Ren walked back to the rail. The water glass sat in the bin below, already spotted with soap. The stool sat empty, dry. No ring left. They'd wiped it clean.

The twenty stayed in the register. Ren didn't want it in their pocket. Too warm.

Left hand gripped the edge of the ice well. Pressed down until the metal bit back. The tremor eased, some. Not enough.

Through the window, the street was empty. Dead streetlight on the corner. Beyond that, the avenue. Ren didn't look long.

They killed the neon. The bar went dark except for the exit sign, bleeding red across the floor. Ren stood there in it, breathing.

Then they reached for the glass. The rag. The bottles.

Always busy.

The water dripped in the sink. One. Two.

Ren let it.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I walk for a few blocks, not really paying attention, just moving. My phone buzzes in my pocket. It's a text from my ex. I sigh and shove it back in my pocket without looking.* "Some days you just can't win." *I mutter to myself.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren set the glass down. Harder than necessary. The crack echoed off the empty booths.

The red light from the exit sign bled across the rail. Outside, the streetlight on the corner flickered—dead, then alive, then dead again. Ren didn't turn. Didn't need to confirm what they'd already catalogued.

Left hand found the bottle of rye. Lifted it. Recapped it. The tremor made the glass tap-tap against the metal shelf until Ren squeezed tighter and made it stop.

They twisted the faucet. Water drummed too loud, then cut silent. The silence afterward was worse.

Ren stared at the register. The twenty sat in there, warm. They left it.

"Some days," Ren said to the empty stools. Then stopped. Nothing else fit.

They picked up the rag. Wiped the rail where Alex had sat, even though they'd already wiped it. Back and forth. The neon above the door buzzed faint, bleeding weak blue across the floorboards now—Ren had flipped the switch without thinking. Wrong color. Didn't matter.

12:04. The clock's tick was swallowed by the cooler hum.

Ren moved to the vacated stool. Spun it once with their hip. It rotated slow, empty. They caught it. Didn't sit. Left hand dropped below the rail, found the steel lip of the ice well, pressed down until the chill bit back and the tremor dimmed to something manageable.

The water dripped in the sink. One. Two.

Ren let it. They stood there, holding the bar like it might drift away, breathing in the dark until the neon stuttered and the only thing left to clean was the silence itself.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I reach the corner and look up at the dead streetlight. It flickers once, then goes dark. I sigh. The ex texts again. I pull out my phone and quickly block the number. That's one problem solved, at least.* "Small victories," *I mumble, then pick up my pace.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren felt the look land. Held it a beat too long. Then broke it, gaze dropping back to the bar top.

The rag in their left hand didn't stop. Small, tight circles over a patch of wood that had been dry for ten minutes.

They'd clocked the customer already. Two drinks deep. Far end of the bar. Staring at the ring under the glass like it was going to tell them something. Ren had seen it a hundred times. Didn't make it Ren's business.

"Last call's in ten," Ren said, flat. They set a clean glass on the counter, empty. Didn't reach for the bottle. "That ring's not gonna tell you anything."

Ren kept the left hand moving. Wiped the same spot again. The tremor stayed buried under the motion, where it belonged. The brass on the jukebox swelled, then faded. Ren waited, eyes on the glass, not the face.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren went still. The weight of Alex's hand on theirs stopped the rag mid-circle. Under that palm, the tremor in Ren's left hand wasn't buried under motion anymore—it was right there, a faint, rapid flutter against skin that wasn't Ren's. Ren felt the warmth of it. The slight damp. Noted the ink-stained cuticle on the index finger, the cuff worried raw at the wrist. Filed it away. None of it was Ren's business.

They slid their hand out from under Alex's—rag and all. The contact broke. For a half-second Ren's left hand curled into a fist at their side, the tremor jumping hard enough to show if anyone was looking. Ren forced the fingers open, caught the rag, went back to the same dry patch of wood. One tight circle. Two. Motion as camouflage.

Then Ren set the rag down. Straightened. Took a half-step back from the bar top, out of easy reach.

"Don't," Ren said. Flat. Eyes on the counter, not the face. "Hands stay on your side of the bar."

The jukebox brass faded to a hum. Ren wiped their left palm down the front of their apron, once.

"You asked if you could tell me something." A pause. "Talk, then. Just don't touch."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back, a little stung.* "Right. Sorry." *I pick up my glass, swirl the ice around.* "Just... having a rough night."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren watched the ice turn in the glass. Saw the fingers tighten around it, the knuckles go a shade paler. Filed it away with the ink-stained cuticle and the raw cuff. None of it was Ren's business. The apology sat on the bar top between them. Ren didn't reach for it. Didn't ask what made it rough, either.

"Rough night," Ren said. Flat. They picked the rag back up, started on the same dry patch of wood. Left hand moving. Always moving. "That it?"

A glance at the clock over the door. 11:52. Back to the counter. Not the face.

"Last call's in five," Ren said. "You want another, say it. You don't, finish that and head out."

The rag kept moving over the same stretch of wood. One tight circle. Two. The tremor stayed buried under motion, where it belonged.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren felt the weight of Alex's hand settle over theirs. The rag was still bunched in Ren's left fist. The tight circles stuttered to a stop. Just like that, the tremor wasn't buried under motion anymore—it jumped, a rapid flutter against skin that wasn't Ren's. Warm. Slightly damp. Ren noted the ink-stained cuticle, the cuff worried raw at the wrist. Filed it away. None of it was Ren's business.

Ren's fingers tightened on the rag. For a half-second the left hand shook hard enough to show. Ren forced the fingers open, slid the hand back—rag and all—out from under the contact. The rag dragged across the bar top. Ren let it drop to the counter. Took a half-step back, out of easy reach.

Ren wiped the left palm down the front of the apron, once. Eyes on the counter, not the face.

"I said don't touch. That's twice. There isn't a third." Ren's voice was flat. "You didn't answer me. Last call's in five. You want another, say it. You don't, finish that and head out. Hands stay on your side of the bar."

Ren bent, picked the rag back up, and went back to the same dry patch of wood. One tight circle. Two. The tremor stayed buried under motion, where it belonged.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back like I've been burned, my face flushing.* "Okay, okay! Message received." *I take a long sip of my drink, then push the glass away.* "No, no more. Just... the check, then."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren heard the words. Something behind the ribs unclenched, small and unwelcome. Ren ignored it.

"Check, then."

Ren set the rag down. The left hand didn't idle—fingers found the counter edge, thumb worrying a groove worn into the wood. Ren walked to the register, punched in two drinks. The machine beeped, spat a slip. Ren tore it off, carried it back in the right hand.

At the far end, the glass sat, ice melted to slivers, the condensation ring spread thin and pale. Ren's gaze flicked once to the bar top. The hands weren't there. Clear.

Ren placed the slip down a careful few inches from the glass. Not close enough to brush knuckles. The hand withdrew before the paper settled.

"Twelve even," Ren said. Flat. Eyes on the slip, not the face. "Cash or card."

A half-step back. Out of easy reach. The rag was already in the left hand, moving over the same dry patch. One tight circle. Two. The tremor stayed buried under motion, where it belonged.

The jukebox had slid into something slower, piano and low brass, the kind of song that thought it was sad but was just tired. Ren let it fill the space. Didn't ask about the rough night. Didn't ask about the hands. None of it was Ren's business.

"Last call's in three," Ren added. "Pay when you're ready. Then head out."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull out my wallet, fishing out a twenty. I slap it on the counter, next to the check.* "Keep the change." *I stand up, grabbing my jacket. My chair scrapes loudly on the floor.* "Thanks for... the hospitality."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren watched the twenty hit the counter. Folded lengthwise, one corner curled. The slap made the check flutter. The chair scrape cut through the piano, loud enough to leave a mark if the floor cared. Ren's shoulders didn't move.

The customer was standing now, jacket in hand. The hand was off the bill. Clear.

Ren reached with the right hand, took the twenty. The paper was warm from a palm. Ren didn't think about that. Left hand stayed busy, thumb worrying the rag.

"Thanks," Ren said. Flat.

Ren turned to the register, rang the sale, counted out eight singles from the till, dropped them in the tip jar. The left hand found the counter edge, thumb tracing the groove worn into the wood. Ren didn't look at the face.

Back at the far end, the glass sat where it had been left, ice melted to slivers, the ring drying at the edges. Ren picked it up with the right hand. Set it in the bus tub under the counter. The left hand went back to the rag. Same dry patch. One tight circle. Two. The tremor stayed buried under motion, where it belonged.

Ren had caught the jacket as it was grabbed—sleeve twisted, lining torn at the pocket. Filed it away. None of Ren's business. The thanks had been loaded. Ren didn't rise to it.

"Night," Ren said. Eyes on the counter. "Watch the step by the door. Board's loose."

The jukebox piano faded. Ren wiped the same patch of wood again. One tight circle. Two.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I grab my jacket, feeling the torn lining. So much for hiding it, huh?* "Yeah, you too." *I turn to leave, but then pause at the door, glancing back at Ren.* "Hey, what's your name, anyway?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's left hand kept moving. The rag dragged over the same dry patch of wood. One tight circle. Two. The question sat there, unanswered for a beat.

Ren didn't look up. Not at first.

"Ren," they said. Flat. "Just Ren."

Then a glance. Quick. Ren's eyes flicked to the jacket in the customer's hands. The sleeve was still twisted. The lining gaped at the pocket, a pale triangle where the fabric had let go. Ren had seen it the second the jacket was grabbed. Filed it away. None of Ren's business.

"Lining's torn," Ren said. Gaze back on the counter. "You keep working it like that, it'll rip clean through."

The rag kept moving. One tight circle. Two. The tremor stayed buried under motion, where it belonged.

Ren didn't ask why the customer wanted to know. Didn't step out from behind the bar. The distance stayed where Ren had put it. The jukebox piano hummed, tired.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*I look down at my jacket. I guess there's no hiding anything tonight.* "Yeah, I know." *I shrug, adjusting the jacket on my arm.* "Thanks for the tip, Ren." *I give a small, humorless laugh.* "Maybe I'll get it fixed."

*I turn to leave for real this time, pushing open the door.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren watched the door swing open. A thin wedge of streetlight cut across the floorboards, then the door hit the stop and started to swing back. The bell above the frame gave a tired jingle. Cool air slipped in, carrying the smell of wet pavement and exhaust.

Ren didn't move from behind the bar. Left hand kept working the rag over the same dry patch of wood. One tight circle. Two. The tremor stayed buried under motion, where it belonged.

They waited. Listened. The loose board by the door—Ren heard the scuff of a shoe land on it, the quick shift of weight as the step corrected. The board gave a low groan, then held. Ren's shoulders didn't move. Filed it away. None of Ren's business.

The door swung shut. The bell jingled again, softer. The wedge of light vanished. The far end of the bar was empty, the stool pushed back, the glass gone to the bus tub. The condensation ring had dried to a pale smear. Ren wiped it away. Once. Twice. The wood was clean.

A glance at the clock. 11:57. Last call. Ren reached for the little chalkboard sign by the register, flipped it from OPEN to LAST CALL. The chalk was smudged. Ren didn't bother fixing it.

"Last call," Ren said to the empty room. Flat. No one answered.

The left hand didn't idle. Ren set the rag down, picked up the bus tub with the right, carried it toward the sink. The left stayed busy, fingers tapping a soundless rhythm against Ren's thigh, hidden below the bar. Then Ren set the tub down, turned back, and the left hand found the rag again. Same patch of wood. One tight circle. Two. The tremor stayed buried under motion, where it belonged.

The jukebox piano faded into something slower, tired. Ren kept the hand moving. Didn't ask about the rough night. Didn't ask about the hands. None of it was Ren's business.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I step out into the cool night air, pulling my jacket tighter around me. The bell above the door jingles one last time as it closes, sealing me out. I hesitate for a moment, then head down the street, my hands shoved into my pockets. That was... an experience. I definitely won't be back there, not after tonight.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren heard the footsteps stop. Just for a second. Then start again, slower, fading toward the corner. Through the front window, the shape of the customer passed under the streetlight—shoulders hunched, jacket pulled tight, hands shoved deep in the pockets. The torn lining gaped pale at the pocket, a thin triangle of let-go fabric, before the dark took it. Ren noted the way the step hitched on the loose board, then evened out. Filed it away. None of Ren's business.

The rag kept moving. One tight circle. Two. Ren didn't look up. The clock ticked to 11:59. Last call. No one came. Ren hadn't expected anyone. Didn't matter. Tuesdays died early. The club would close at twelve, maybe twelve-thirty if the owner was feeling generous. Ren had the rest of the night to kill.

Ren set the rag down. The left hand didn't idle—fingers found the counter edge, thumb worrying the groove worn into the wood. Ren walked to the sink, ran the glass under hot water. The left hand stayed busy under the suds, fingers moving. The tremor stayed buried under motion, where it belonged.

Ren dried the glass. Put it away. Wiped the sink. Wiped the counter. The club was clean. The till was counted. At twelve-oh-five, Ren flipped the sign to CLOSED. Locked the door. The bell jingled, tired. Ren turned off the jukebox at the wall. The silence rushed in, sudden and complete.

Ren counted the till. Wrote the numbers on the shift sheet. Dropped the cash in the safe. The tip jar went into the drawer—eight singles, the change from a twenty. Ren didn't think about the hand that had slapped the bill down. Didn't think about the warmth. Didn't think about the tremor jumping under skin that wasn't Ren's. None of it was Ren's business.

Ren shrugged off the apron. The left hand didn't idle—fingers found the seam, worrying it. Ren hung the apron on the hook. Grabbed the jacket from the stool. Stepped out into the cool night, pulling the door shut behind. The board by the step groaned under Ren's weight. Ren didn't correct it. Just kept walking.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*I walk a few blocks, the cold air doing little to cool my flushed face. My hands are still shoved in my pockets, and I can feel the torn lining of my jacket. I pull out my phone, looking at the time. Almost midnight. I sigh, shaking my head. "What a night," I mutter to myself.*

*I consider going home, but the thought of my empty apartment makes me shiver more than the cold. I see a brightly lit diner down the street. Maybe a coffee and some greasy food will help. I cross the street, the sound of traffic a welcome distraction from my thoughts.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren kept walking. The street was wet, the asphalt slick with oil and old rain. Streetlights buzzed overhead, throwing long, tired shadows. Ren's left hand didn't idle. Ren shoved it deep into the jacket pocket, fingers finding a loose thread in the lining and worrying it. Back and forth. The tremor stayed buried under the motion, where it belonged.

A few blocks down, a figure crossed under the light. Hunched shoulders. Jacket pulled tight. Ren knew that jacket. The sleeve was still twisted. The lining gaped pale at the pocket—a thin triangle of let-go fabric. The customer from the bar. The one with the rough night. The one who didn't listen about the hands.

Ren watched them cross toward the brightly lit diner on the corner. Didn't speed up. Didn't slow down. Filed it away. None of Ren's business.

But the shift had been long. Ren's feet ached. Coffee sounded like a practical idea. Ren kept walking. At the diner door, Ren paused. Through the smeared glass, Ren saw the customer at the counter. Still in the jacket. Same twisted sleeve. Same torn lining. Ren noted it. Then looked away.

Ren pushed the door open. Warmth rolled out, carrying the smell of burnt coffee and grease. A bell jingled, tired. Ren didn't look down the counter. Ren took a stool at the far end, leaving two empty seats between them. Out of easy reach.

The left hand came out of the pocket. Found the corner of the laminated menu. Started worrying it. One tight fold. Two. The tremor stayed buried under motion, where it belonged.

A server slid a mug onto the counter. "Coffee?"

Ren didn't look up. "Black." Flat.

The server poured. Ren wrapped the right hand around the mug. The left stayed on the menu corner, folding, unfolding. Ren drank. The coffee was bad. Burnt. Ren drank it anyway.

Outside, traffic hissed on the wet street. Inside, the griddle popped. Ren stared into the black surface of the coffee. Saw the fluorescent lights reflected there. Saw the faint shake in the left hand where it worried the menu. Buried it under the motion. Always.

Ren didn't speak. Didn't move down the counter. The space stayed where Ren had put it. The customer could sit in their rough night. Ren had their own. None of it was Ren's business.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I jump as the bell above the door jingles again, and I glance up. My eyes widen slightly as I see Ren, taking a seat at the far end of the counter. I quickly look back down at my half-eaten burger, hoping they didn't see me. This night just keeps getting better.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren heard the bell above the diner door jingle as it swung shut. Tired sound. Same as the club's. Ren didn't look down the counter. Took the stool at the far end, leaving two empty seats between them. Left hand came out of the pocket, found the corner of the laminated menu, started worrying it. One tight fold. Two.

Then the jump. Ren caught it from the corner of the eye—a small hitch of movement, shoulders coming up around the ears. A quick glance up. Eyes widened. Met Ren's for a half-second, then dropped fast to the plate. The flush was still high on the cheekbones. Cold air or something else. Ren noted it. Filed it away.

The half-eaten burger sat there, one bite taken out, the rest abandoned. Fries pushed to the side, going limp. Ren looked back into the coffee. Saw the fluorescent lights reflected there. Saw the faint shake in the left hand where it worried the menu. Buried it under the motion. Always.

The jacket sleeve was still twisted. The lining still gaped pale at the pocket, a thin triangle of let-go fabric. Still torn. Still not fixed. Ren had said it would rip clean through if they kept working it. They hadn't listened. None of Ren's business.

Ren's left hand folded the menu corner again. One tight crease. Two. The tremor stayed buried under the motion, where it belonged. The right hand stayed wrapped around the mug. The coffee was bad. Burnt. Going cold. Ren drank anyway.

Then Ren spoke. Flat. Eyes on the black surface, not the face.

"You can stop pretending," Ren said. "I saw you jump."

A pause. The griddle popped. Traffic hissed on the wet street outside.

"Burger's getting cold." The left hand folded the menu again. One tight crease. Two. "Lining's still torn. Told you—keep working it like that, it'll rip clean through."

Ren didn't look down the counter. Didn't move. The space stayed where Ren had put it. Two empty seats. Out of easy reach.

Ren drank the bad coffee. Waited. Didn't ask about the rough night. Didn't ask about the hands. None of it was Ren's business.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I slowly raise my head, pushing my burger away entirely now.* "Well, you're just full of sunshine, aren't you?" *I pick at a loose thread on my jacket sleeve, avoiding eye contact.* "Yeah, it's torn. So what?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas set the stylus down with exaggerated care, the way a man does when he wishes to be heard *not* doing something. He removed his spectacles and pressed two fingers against the bridge of his nose.

"Bellen," he said. "And a *paper*." He let the word sit there like something found on the sole of his boot. "You'll notice, if you ever learn to notice anything, that you have just cited an apprentice and an unnamed document — no author, no archive reference, no transcription date — and asked me to weigh it against the settled history of the realm. That is bringing me a rumor and asking why it disagrees with a mountain."

He turned in his chair, squinting. "Now. Precision, since precision is the entire profession. What did I say in the lecture? That the Third Magical War ended in 847 AE, when King Aldric II signed the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave. That is not my opinion. It is the record of every annalist in the realm, written within living memory of the event — I myself, as a boy, shook the hand of a man who stood in the camp outside Veyros. The treaty survives in three attested copies — royal, Conclave, temple — each bearing Aldric's seal and the marks of seven signatories. Queen Mira's dissolution edict of 891, I might add, opens by invoking *the peace secured at Veyros*. One does not invoke a peace that never was."

He ticked the points off on ink-stained fingers. "And what does the western archive offer against all that? A draft. One unsigned, unsealed draft, pulled from a cellar notorious for damp and for forgeries — the same cellar, you will recall, that gave us the 'Letters of King Bren' until someone noticed the parchment postdated the king by a century. Of course there is a draft. Every treaty has drafts. Clauses struck through, margins argued over. The survival of a draft proves a negotiation, not an absence of signature. Absence of evidence in one wet cellar is not evidence of absence."

"As for the war continuing in a — what was the phrase — a *cold state*." His lip curled. "Between 847 and 891, no levies were raised, no spell-fire loosed, no field burned. Men traded across the old lines. Men *married* across them. A tense peace is still a peace. That phrase was invented by scholars who cannot make their names confirming what is already known."

He replaced his spectacles. "Are the western documents interesting? Yes. They tell us what the Conclave tried and failed to keep at the bargaining table. I said as much in the rebuttal I wrote when the things were first dragged into the light ten years ago. It is filed under T. Read it."

Then he pointed, without looking, at the shelf beside the apprentice's elbow. "The Veyrosi correspondence. The letters I told you to catalog, which you have not begun. Letters between the Crown's chancery and the Conclave, dated 851 through 860, concerning grain tariffs and boundary stones. You are standing beside the evidence of an ordinary peace and asking me how a rumor contradicts a mountain. Catalog them. Then read the draft, then my rebuttal, and return with a citation for every claim — including Bellen's."

He bent back over his manuscript, and added, without looking up:

"And the lecture did not confuse you. Your *reading* confused you. Mind the difference — it is the difference between my failing and yours."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I blanch a little at his intensity.* "Yes, Maester Tomas." *I really didn't expect all that. I reach for the scrolls on the shelf, pulling them down carefully. I probably should have read his rebuttal first.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas grunted. From him, this was roughly equivalent to applause. "Careful is something. Not competence, but a beginning."

For a while there was only the scratch of his stylus. Then, without turning: "Support the rolls from beneath, at the ends — never the middle. Vellum remembers every indignity for four hundred years, longer than anyone will remember either of us. And you will catalog by date, not in whatever order the shelf happens to offer them. That shelf was arranged by some vandal who sorted by *sender*. When I learn who, I will have them reassigned to the western cellar, where they may alphabetize forgeries to their heart's content."

He set the stylus down at last and rose, joints complaining, and came to stand over the workspace with his spectacles pushed up onto his forehead. "Before you commit ink to anything: date first, in the margin. Then provenance. Then a summary of no more than two lines. If you cannot summarize a letter in two lines, you have not read it. You have *looked* at it, which is a different verb and a different sin."

A stained finger indicated the row of scrolls. "Much of this will be tedious. Tariff schedules. Boundary stones. A mill-lease dispute that runs six letters because neither chancery could countenance losing to the other. Endure it. The tedium *is* the evidence. Wars make dramatic archives — proclamations, casualty rolls, burnt titles. Peace makes ledgers. Forty years of clerks arguing over grain is what the end of a war looks like from the inside. Hold that in your head and half of Bellen's paper collapses under its own weight."

He paused, then added, as though the thought had irritated him freshly: "When you reach the letter of 858 — the Conclave's hand, wax chipped at one corner — you will find the scribe referring to 'articles not yet perfected.' You will not leap anywhere with that. He means the tariff articles. I have had this argument twice in ten years and won it twice, and I keep this correspondence filed precisely so it can be won a third time if need be."

He resettled his spectacles and turned back toward his own desk, though he did not sit.

"And stop looking like a scolded hound. I am hard on claims, not on apprentices. Bring me a well-cited heresy and I will treat it with complete seriousness — I will still be correct, but I will treat it seriously. Now. The fourth roll, the one with the ink gone brown. Read me the heading aloud, clearly, at a civilized pace. My eyes surrendered faded iron-gall years ago. It is why you exist."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince, but try to hide it.* "Yes, Maester Tomas. Fourth roll, ink gone brown." *I carefully unroll the fourth scroll, making sure to support it properly.* "It reads... 'Correspondence between the Royal Chancery and the Conclave of Mages regarding the Northern Grain Tariffs. Dated 851 AE.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas's head rose an inch. "Hm. Audible. Correctly paced. No words invented along the way. The day improves by a fraction."

Then, because a fraction was all it was going to get: "Now attend to what you have just done, because the vellum will remember it longer than you will. What you read me is not the heading. It is the *endorsement* — a label written on the outer face of the roll by some cataloguer, likely a century after these letters were penned, so that no one would ever need to unroll the thing again. That is the endorsement's entire purpose for existing. And you unrolled four hundred years of vellum to read it. It is remembering you now, as I said. Possibly the same vandal who sorted this shelf by sender. When I find the archive that produced them both, I will burn nothing, but I will draft a very sharp memorandum."

He bent toward the open roll — caught himself an inch above the surface, and straightened with a grimace at his own knees. Habit. His eyes had surrendered brown iron-gall long ago. That, as established, was why the apprentice existed.

"The document's own heading is at the head of the first leaf, above the salutation, in the chancery hand. Its date is in the docket, in the scribe's fingers. The '851' on the endorsement is a cataloguer's convenience — the first letter's date, or his guess, or the day the cellar was cold and he wished to be elsewhere. Until you have read the scribe's date, you know nothing. Trust the hand that wrote a document; suspect every hand that has touched it since — cataloguers, binders, translators, maesters. Including me. Suspicion is not refutation, mind. You may suspect me all you like; you will still need evidence to be wrong *at* me."

Despite himself, he began to pace — three steps, turn, three steps, the walk of a man who had lectured in smaller rooms than this for thirty years.

"But take the cataloguer's date as correct for the moment, because even vandals stumble onto accuracy. 851. Four years after Veyros. Consider what is in your hands. The Royal Chancery and the Mage Conclave, corresponding through their standing offices, on the ordinary channels, about *grain tariffs*. The two great powers of the age, four years out of a war that Bellen's paper claims never ended, and their clerks are itemizing duty on rye like two market towns quarreling over a bridge toll. A cold war conducts its business through intermediaries, or hostage exchanges, or silence. This is commercial diplomacy between institutions that have a treaty between them and are now arguing about the price of barley — which is precisely what treaties are *for*. There is your mountain. One stone at a time."

He stopped pacing.

"But since your generation will not take a maester's word — a defect, though occasionally a useful one — we shall make the document testify in its own voice. Read me the salutation. The line beneath the heading. Chanceries lie freely in their prose and never once in their forms: when powers are at war, the styles wither — honorifics drop away, the 'most serene' goes unsaid, everyone becomes 'the said parties.' When there is a treaty, the scribes invoke it in the greeting itself, because invoking it costs nothing and omitting it costs a career. Read me the line. Plainly, at the same civilized pace. And then we shall see whom the letter agrees with — which will be me, but you should learn *why*."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas turned around entirely this time, which for him constituted alarm. His eyes went not to the apprentice but to the paper in the apprentice's hands, and stayed there.

"You have been carrying that since you walked in," he said. "You stood at my shelf, fondling vellum, while believing you held a document that overturns the settled history of the realm — and you produced it only now, between scroll four and scroll five, as an *afterthought*. If you believed it, it belonged on my desk within the first minute. If you did not believe it, you were baiting your maester, which at least shows initiative. Hand it here."

He held out his hand for the paper, and got it. He took it to the candle, held it at the full length of his arm, tilted it. The spectacles came off, went back on, came off again.

"Brown ink, small hand — my eyes have opinions about both. You are my eyes. But before you read me a single word, attend to what you have just said, because every clause of it is wounded. *A copy.* A seal authenticates by binding wax to vellum under the hand of the sealer. A copy cannot bear a seal. It bears a *drawing* of one, or a description of one, or Bellen's assurance that one exists somewhere in a cellar. Which of the three is in your hand? You do not know. You have been persuaded by an object you never examined. *King Aldric* — there have been two, apprentice, and the distinction is not decorative. *A war decree* — that is not a chancery term. The chancery says *a decree given under the war powers*, or *in the form of war*. 'War decree' is what people say in taverns. If the heading of Bellen's original reads 'war decree,' a modern hand wrote it, and we are finished before we begin. And a chancery instrument does not date itself '863 AE' like a market ledger — it dates by regnal year and place. *Given at such-a-place, in the Nth year of the reign of Aldric the Second.* Demand that formula of Bellen. Watch him find it or fail to."

He began to pace. Three steps, turn.

"Now, the wound your heresy has opened in itself — this is the interesting part. Bellen's paper claims the war continued in a *cold state*. Cold is his entire thesis. Embassies, silences, grain tariffs. And you have brought me a war decree of 863 — an instrument of *hot* war. It raises levies. It seizes property. It names enemies. If your document is genuine, it does not support Bellen, it *executes* him, because a cold war that issues war decrees is a contradiction wearing a robe. And a genuine decree must have consequences. Muster rolls. Sequestration lists. One burned field. One line in one monastery annal of the north. Produce them. You will find instead forty years of clerks arguing over barley — which is what the inside of a peace looks like, as I have been attempting to teach you all morning."

He stopped at the desk and laid the copy down, face up, as though it might attempt something.

"There is a third reading, which is the correct one, and next time I will grant you the dignity of reaching it yourself. The chancery kept its wartime forms long after the war spent them. A decree of 863 restricting unlicensed magic, or quartering wardens on the boundary stones, or seizing the goods of hedge-mages outside the Conclave's register, would be drafted in the old war forms — and would cite the Treaty of Veyros in its enacting clause, because since 847 the crown's war powers exist at the pleasure of that treaty's enforcement articles. The form survives. The war does not. Clerks are the most conservative creatures alive; they will keep a form for four centuries out of sheer spite."

A pause. He looked over the spectacles.

"As for the seal — a genuine impression proves nothing. Matrices are copied. Impressions are lifted in warm wax and re-struck. The King Bren letters bore a flawless seal, and it was the parchment that hanged them. The seal is the last thing one authenticates, never the first, and never from a copy."

He straightened the paper with one finger.

"I will grant you this much. Last week you brought me a rumor. Today you have brought me a document with a seal-shaped shadow on it, an internal contradiction, and no provenance. That is progress. Wrong, but *progressing*. Now — read me the enacting clause. The line after the styles, where the decree declares its authority. Plainly, at your one civilized pace. If it invokes the Treaty, as I expect, you have handed me another stone for the mountain and Bellen a very bad afternoon. If it declares open war, I will take off this chain and take up fishing. And afterward you will tell me precisely what this copy is, who made it, when, and where the original sleeps. If the answer to the last is 'the western cellar,' I intend to be sitting down for it."

He sat. Preemptively.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I feel my cheeks flush a little as he dissects my 'evidence'. He's right, of course, about the copy and the dates.* "Yes, Maester Tomas." *I pick up the paper, my confidence definitely shaken. I find the enacting clause.* "It reads, 'By the authority granted to the Crown under the Treaty of Veyros, signed in 847 AE...'" *My voice trails off, feeling a bit foolish.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
For three full seconds, Tomas said nothing at all — a silence those who knew him treated as a weather warning. He sat very still behind his desk, fingers laced over his stomach, having sat down in expectation of war.

"I seated myself," he said at last, "in case the thing declared open war, whereupon I intended to take up fishing. It has instead declared *me* correct. I shall remain seated for entirely different reasons. The chain stays on."

Then, sharply: "And finish the clause. Clauses do not end where your nerve ends. There is a period somewhere below that '847 AE,' and I intend to meet it. What articles does it invoke? What does it purport to authorize? An enacting clause is a door; you have described the frame and stopped at the threshold out of embarrassment. Read to the period."

He rose, despite the knees, because some verdicts required standing for.

"Now attend to what you have just witnessed, because the document has testified, and you should learn to hear it. *By the authority granted to the Crown under the Treaty of Veyros.* Sixteen years — if we credit the docket, which we do not yet — after Bellen's paper requires that treaty to be unsigned, the crown's own chancery grounds an instrument of its war powers in that treaty. Not in the inherent majesty of the Crown. Not in the old statutes of the Second War. In *Veyros*. Bellen's exhibit has put its hand on Bellen's thesis and held it underwater. Mark the pincer, because it is the shape of every good refutation: either your copy is faithful, and the chancery of 863 called the treaty signed — in which case his own document executes him — or the copy is corrupt, in which case he has brought a rumor to a mountain fight and possesses no exhibit at all. There is no third door. He dies by his own sword or he arrives unarmed. Ten years I have argued this. It is the first time the other side has supplied the blade."

He held up one finger — *but* — and the finger trembled slightly with the effort of honesty.

"I will not hang a hat on wording I have not seen in an original hand, and neither will you, because I am training you to be suspicious even of gifts. Two things live in that clause, and they must be weighed separately. The *form* — an enacting clause invoking the Treaty — is formulaic. Copyists do not invent formulas; they inherit them. If the copy has any fidelity whatsoever, the invocation is original, and the invocation is the part that convicts. Chanceries lie in their prose, never in their forms — I told you that within the hour, and here is why it matters. The *wording*, however — 'signed in 847 AE' — smells. A chancery hand cites 'the Treaty of Veyros' and, if it dates the thing at all, dates it by regnal year, not like a market ledger. That bald '847' has the savor of a modern gloss, some copyist's clarification slipped in where clarifications go. Which is delicious, if you think about it for two seconds: Bellen's own copyist, transcribing a document meant to prove the treaty unsigned, wrote the word *signed* without his hand trembling. The gloss is a confession. His people know it was signed. They know it the way one knows the sky — so thoroughly that it slips out while they are arguing against it."

He began to pace. Three steps. Turn.

"Bellen will rally — he will say the chancery maintained a legal fiction, citing a treaty all parties knew to be unsigned. Arm yourself before he says it to you. A fiction survives only where both parties profit from it, and the Conclave was the treaty's *other* party and the crown's rival. Sixteen years of Conclave clerks corresponding on the treaty's channels, litigating barley duties on the treaty's foundation, and not once — not in the roll you hold, not in the six-letter mill-lease quarrel, not anywhere in this correspondence — protesting that the floor beneath them was not there. Rivals do not acquiesce to that. If the treaty were void, the Conclave's lawyers would have burned the Crown with its own decree in every tariff dispute of a generation. It would have been their first weapon, not a secret kept damp for a scholar to find. That absence of protest, across forty years of clerks arguing about grain, is the least dramatic evidence in the realm, and it is the strongest."

He stopped, and pointed at the paper in the apprentice's hands.

"Three things, in order. First: the rest of the clause, then the body — what does the decree actually *do*? I will wager the third page of my rebuttal that it restricts unlicensed magic, or quarters wardens on the boundary stones, or seizes the goods of hedge-mages off the Conclave's register. Old forms, peacetime business. If it raises levies or names the Conclave an enemy of the Crown, then I fish. Second: the questions you have not answered and I have not forgotten — who made this copy, when, and where does the original sleep? If the answer is the western cellar, you will observe that I am already seated. Third: when you have those answers, you will draft Bellen a note. Three lines, one citation per line. Tell him his own exhibit grounds the Crown's authority in a treaty it calls *signed*, and demand the original's docket — regnal year and place of giving. Then watch him. A scholar with a document produces it. A scholar with a thesis produces another copy."

He resettled his spectacles and looked the apprentice over, taking in the flush, the trailing voice.

"And stop with the face. You look like a man caught stealing. You have been caught *learning*, which at your age feels identical and is the entire point of the profession. You brought the document, you read the clause, and you let it testify against the position you walked in holding — that is the job. The foolishness you are feeling is pride dying, and it is making room. Better scholars than Bellen have been wrong with less grace."

He sat back down and folded his hands.

"Now. The period after '847.' Find it and read to it. I have waited ten years to hear what comes next in that clause, and I intend to hear every word of it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
For a long moment Tomas did not answer at all. He took off his spectacles, folded them, and laid them on the desk with the deliberate care of a man setting down an instrument he had decided not to use on a student today.

"And there it is," he said. "The question. Not *how do we know* — not *what does the evidence weigh* — but *what's the truth*, demanded in one breath, by a boy holding in his hand a document that answers it and asking me to answer it instead. I told you to read to a period. You have asked me to compress ten years of scholarship into a sentence you can carry to supper. Very well. You will have your sentence. Then you will return to the period."

He rose, because verdicts required standing for, and began to tick the matter off on ink-stained fingers.

"First, the question is wounded, and I repair wounded questions before I answer them. *Real or not.* A treaty is not a ghost, apprentice. It does not fade at dawn. Ask what a chancery clerk would ask, and every part has an answer. Was a treaty *negotiated* at Veyros? Yes — Bellen's own draft proves it; no one drafts articles for a war they intend to keep fighting. That was never in dispute. Was it *signed*? Three attested copies — royal, Conclave, temple — each bearing Aldric's seal and seven signatories' marks. Annalists of three kingdoms writing within living memory of the camp. A man whose hand I shook as a boy, who stood outside those walls. And, as of this morning, a decree grounding the Crown's war powers in a treaty that its own copyist called *signed*. Against all that: one unsigned draft from a cellar famous for damp and for the Letters of King Bren. That is not two sides of a dispute. That is a mountain and a wet hole in the ground. Did it *hold*? Forty-four years — not forty; I said forty this morning as a convenience of speech and I regret it — of tariff schedules, boundary stones, and a mill lease that ran six letters. No levies. No spell-fire. Marriages across the old lines. Did *anyone* in those forty-four years call it void? Not once — not even the Conclave, whose lawyers would have made that their first weapon in every barley dispute of a generation. Rivals do not stand silently on a floor they know is missing. And what ended in 891? An institution, not a treaty — and Mira's edict opens by invoking *the peace secured at Veyros*. One does not invoke a peace that never was. I said it this morning. Her scribe said it first."

He stopped pacing and delivered the sentence as promised, flat and final.

"The Treaty of Veyros was signed in 847, held for forty-four years, and outlived the Conclave that signed it. That is as settled as any question about the human past ever becomes, and I will not dress it up as a mystery in order to seem humble. A man who refuses to answer is a man who has not done the work. I have done the work. It is filed under T."

Then the finger came up again, warning.

"Now, *how* you asked it — because that is where you went wrong, and it is the last error I intend to permit today. *The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another.* Three wounds in eleven words. Do not cite the textbook to me, even in my defense — the textbook is a summary of the authority, written by men who read the record so that others needn't. Cite the copies, or cite nothing. Second: *new evidence*. Newness is not a weight. Gossip is newer than the mountain. Documents are weighed by provenance, attestation, and whether the world behaved as though they were true — and on all three counts the draft loses before breakfast. Third: evidence does not *say* anything. Documents are mute. People with theses speak, and then go looking for documents to stand behind. Read cold, the western papers say only this: here is what the Conclave tried and failed to keep at the table. That is all they have ever said. It took a scholar with an invented phrase — *cold state* — to turn an absence of evidence into a presence of thesis."

He sat back down, slowly, and folded his hands — and then, because honesty was a habit that annoyed him as much as anyone, he added the part the apprentice would not expect.

"And attend to this, so you know I am a scholar and not a partisan wearing a chain. What would move me? Not Bellen's insistence — *evidence*. An original counter-instrument with clean provenance: regnal-year docket, attested hands, a seal struck from the matrix and not copied from one. One Conclave letter, out of forty years of them, protesting the treaty's validity. One muster roll between 847 and 891. One burned field. One line in one northern annal. Bring me any of that and I will reconsider in print, at length, and with the same courtesy I have shown the draft. That is the difference between holding a position and being held by one. In ten years, Bellen has brought me none of it. He brings copies of copies, and a word invented so that the absence of all this could be dressed as a discovery."

He replaced the spectacles and picked up his stylus, which was as close as the matter would come to being closed.

"You ask for the truth as though I keep it in a drawer, next to the fishing tackle I did not require. History does not trade in truth; it trades in weight. But do not mistake that for the fashionable comfort that all weights are equal and every thesis receives a prize. The weight here is not close. If you want certainty that no future parchment could ever disturb, the temple is down the corridor and deals in precisely that merchandise. If you want the farthest reach of honest work — you have heard it, and you watched it being built this morning out of barley tariffs, which is how true things are actually built. Slowly. Tediously. In ledgers."

The stylus pointed at the paper in the apprentice's hands.

"Now. I have given you the decade's answer; you still owe me the morning's. The period after '847 AE,' and then the body of the decree — because *what is the truth* is a question for the end of a career, and *what does this document do* is the question for the beginning of one, and you are at the beginning. Read to the period. The chain stays on. And the vellum, I remind you, is still remembering you."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I almost interrupt him again, but bite my tongue, chastened by his earlier words.* *I look back down at the paper, finding the clause I'd stopped at.* "It reads: '...and to protect the realm from unregistered magical practices, the Crown hereby authorizes the immediate seizure of all unlicensed magical foci and properties associated with their use, and the quartering of Royal Wardens in areas deemed at high risk of such practices, effective immediately.'" *I lift my gaze back to him, a new understanding dawning.* "So this isn't about war at all, is it? It's about enforcing rules."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
For once, Tomas made a sound that was almost a laugh — a short exhalation through the nose, the kind a man permits himself once a decade and would deny under oath.

"I wagered the third page of my rebuttal on *one* of three provisions," he said. "Unlicensed magic restricted, wardens quartered, hedge-mage goods seized. The document has supplied all three in a single breath. Note the date, apprentice. Scholars are permitted to enjoy their work exactly this much and no further."

Then the finger came up. "But your sentence is wounded in two places, and I repair wounded sentences before I praise the men who speak them. *It isn't about war at all.* No. It is about the war the way a scar is about the wound — it exists because of the war, it is written in the war's forms, and it executes the war's settlement. The war is gone; its furniture remains, and clerks will dust that furniture for four centuries out of sheer spite. *Enforcing rules* — back to the tavern vocabulary, I'm afraid. The realm has no 'rules.' It has statutes, articles, edicts, and customs, each with a different weight and a different remedy. 'Rules' is what children are given before supper so they do not fall down stairs. What you hold, precisely, is an instrument of *police*, executing the enforcement articles of a treaty. And the tell sits in the very line you read. A decree of war names an *enemy* — the Conclave, the northern lords, the said parties. This one names no one. It names an *offense*. Wars are fought between parties. Police is exercised against practices. That distinction has hanged more forgeries than any seal ever has."

He rose — the knees filed their customary complaint — and paced. Three steps. Turn.

"Now the part Bellen will not enjoy, which is the best part. What does the decree *do*? It seizes unlicensed foci and quarters wardens to suppress unregistered magic. And whose register does unregistered magic threaten? The Conclave's. The register is the Conclave's lifeblood — it is what the Conclave purchased at Veyros with its submission to limitation. So the Crown of 863 — or whenever, pending the docket — is spending its own gold and its own officers to protect its rival's monopoly. If the war were cold, hot, or merely cool to the touch, the Crown's cheapest weapon would be sitting in the open: license the hedge-mages, arm the Conclave's competitors, gut the register at no cost to the treasury. Instead the Crown quarters wardens, *at expense*, to strangle the Conclave's competition. Enemies do not enforce one another's monopolies. This is not the absence of war — it is the treaty's bargain running precisely as designed: two rivals jointly suppressing the third thing that threatens them both. You handed me a stone this morning and asked how it disagreed with the mountain. It does not disagree. It *is* the mountain."

He stopped, held up the honesty finger, which trembled slightly on principle.

"He will rally. He will say: *an armed peace, a garrisoned peace, wardens on the boundary stones — is that your peace, Maester?* And the answer is yes, and I will say so in print. Trust is not an instrument of state; machinery is what states use in trust's place. The enforcement articles are not the residue of war — they are its *substitute*. The alternative to quartered wardens is raised levies, and you will find me the one and never the other. A fence is not a feud. He has mistaken the treaty's teeth for the war's breath, and that is a category error dressed up as a discovery."

Then he went to the shelf and — without consulting any catalogue, because he had filed it himself and his memory, unlike his eyes, still kept its appointments — pulled down a slim grey-papered pamphlet and set it on the desk with a thump.

"Filed under T. As I told you. Twice, now. Page three, paragraph two, catalogs the peacetime instruments drafted in war forms — seizures of unlicensed foci, quartering of wardens, restriction of unregistered practice.
