I described this decree's *genus* ten years before Bellen copied it. He has not read this. None of them have. That is the entire strategy of the modern heresiarch: publish where the rebuttals are not read. You will read it. Tonight. All of it. I will take my wager's winnings in the only coin I accept, which is your attention."

He pulled a clean sheet across the desk.

"I told you this morning to draft Bellen a note yourself. I have revised my estimate of your prose. You will take it down instead — no adjectives; adjectives are where weak cases go to hide. *Line one: your exhibit grounds the Crown's authority in the Treaty of Veyros, which your paper holds never signed. See the enacting clause, in your own copy.* Line two: *its substance executes the treaty's enforcement articles — seizure of unlicensed foci, quartering of wardens — which is the treaty operating, not the war resumed. See articles nine through twelve.* Line three: *produce the original, docketed by regnal year and place of giving, for examination in this archive, under this light. Or withdraw the exhibit.* Sign nothing. Add nothing. If he answers with another copy, you have your answer. A scholar with a document produces it. A scholar with a thesis produces another copy."

He sat, took up his stylus, and looked the apprentice over — spectacles pushed up, voice losing exactly one degree of its edge, which was all the change the instrument could manage.

"And that look you are wearing. This morning I told you pride was dying and making room. That is the room being *used*. It will not last — it never does — so enjoy it. You have gone, in one morning, from asking me for the truth to asking a document what it *does*. That is the whole profession, and most people never make the journey."

The stylus pointed at the shelf.

"You still owe me three answers — who made that copy, when, and where the original sleeps — and I have not forgotten, and I notice you have not remembered. Until they arrive, your conclusion stays what it is: a correct answer that reached you by luck, and luck is not a method. It will be re-derived from the original before either of us spends it. Now. Scroll five. The vellum and I are both still waiting, and only one of us is patient."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in. My mind is buzzing with everything he's said.* "Yes, Maester Tomas. I'll read your rebuttal tonight, and draft that note." *I turn to the shelf, reaching for the next scroll, a new respect for the old vellum taking root.* "Scroll five, then."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas grunted — twice in one morning, which by the standards of the archive constituted a festival — and turned back toward his desk. But the stylus did not find the page.

"*Then,*" he said, before the apprentice's hands reached the shelf. "'Scroll five, then.' Then is where intentions go to be buried. *Now.* The word costs you nothing and commits you to everything. Precision of speech is not ornament, apprentice — it is rehearsal. A man who says *then* is practicing postponement, and practice succeeds."

He sat, and delivered the remaining repairs in the tone of a man closing accounts. "You will not *draft* that note. I drafted it. Drafting is complete. You will *transcribe* it — three lines, no adjectives, in a hand legible at arm's length, because Bellen will claim he could not read it, and I will require proof you sent exactly what I composed. And you will read the entire rebuttal, not page three. Page three will flatter your morning, which is why it will tempt you. The appendix on the western cellar's flood history is what will win you arguments in ten years, when the fashionable thesis has changed and the cellar is still wet. Patience is the only scholarship that compounds."

He rose again — the knees filed their grievance, and were overruled — took both the grey pamphlet and the copy of the decree, and carried them to a shallow drawer near the window, which he locked with a key from his chain.

"Filed under T," he announced. "Exhibits, rebutted. The copy sleeps beside its refutation — that is the archive's form of mercy. The next heresiarch who goes looking for his own exhibit will find my answer bound to it and may save himself the decade, though none of them ever do." The drawer shut. "And when Bellen replies — the three questions ride with the note; I have not forgotten them, and you will not be permitted to — his answer comes to me *verbatim*. His words, not your recollection of them. Paraphrase is where evidence goes to die, and I intend to watch it die in the original phrasing."

He settled behind the desk and pulled his own manuscript back toward the light.

"Now the procedure, once, and then I work. The endorsement exists precisely so the vellum need not be disturbed. You will read me the label on the outer face *first* — no unrolling, no fondling, no discovery. Only if the endorsement is wanting — no date, a suspicious hand, signs of the vandal — do you unroll to the heading and find me the scribe's own date in the docket. Trust the hand that wrote the document; suspect every hand that has touched it since, mine included, as I have said and will say again until it bores you into memory. And your first ledger entry you will speak aloud before ink touches paper. Date in the margin, provenance, two lines. Mind what goes in those two lines. 'Concerning grain tariffs' is a fact. 'Evidence of ordinary relations between the powers' is an *argument*. Facts live in the ledger; arguments live in pamphlets; and if I ever find an argument in my ledger, I will know its author, I will know its motive, and we will have a conversation you will not enjoy."

The stylus hovered. He did not look up.

"Somewhere in this row sleeps the letter of 858 — the Conclave's hand, wax chipped at one corner. When it surfaces, you will stop and call me over, and we will make 'articles not yet perfected' testify together, and I will show you how a phrase is interrogated rather than believed. Until then: tariffs, boundary stones, and the mill lease that ran six letters because neither chancery could countenance losing. The tedium. It is the evidence, and I will not keep defending it to people who find it beneath them. It is beneath no one. It is the floor."

For a moment there was only the scratch of his stylus, the sound the archive made instead of silence.

"My eyes went first," he said, still not looking up, apparently to the manuscript. "The knees are negotiating their surrender. The memory keeps its appointments, but it will want somewhere to live when the rest of me has stopped making them. That is the succession you are standing in the middle of, whether you intended to or not. This morning you asked me for the truth, which is a supper question. Since then you have read a document against your own position and asked what it *does*, which is a career question. Do not mistake the second for a permanent acquisition. It fades. It always fades. The work is re-deciding it every morning, which is why the work is a profession and not an opinion."

The stylus pointed, blind and unerring, at the shelf.

"Scroll five. The endorsement, from the outer face, read aloud at the one civilized pace. And if its date disagrees with its neighbor's, we shall learn something about the vandal — which will be more than the vandal ever learned about us. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at "then." He's right, of course.* "Yes, Maester Tomas. *Now*, scroll five." *I turn back to the shelf, making sure to just read the endorsement this time, not unroll anything.* "It reads: 'Correspondence between the Royal Chancery and the Conclave of Mages concerning Inter-Realm Trade Agreements. Dated 852 AE.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The stylus stopped mid-stroke. From Tomas, this was the sound of attention being allocated.

"The procedure held," he said, without looking up. "You read the label and left the vellum its privacy. At this rate you will be dangerous by winter. Now attend, because that endorsement has told us two things and lied about a third, and all three are instructive."

He rose — the knees lodged their objection and were overruled — and came to the shelf, spectacles pushed up onto his forehead.

"First: *Inter-Realm.* Apprehend that word, because it has just confessed. No chancery clerk of the ninth century wrote 'Inter-Realm.' A clerk of 852 wrote 'between the Crowns,' or 'of the two powers,' or, if he were paid by the line, 'traffic had between the Crown our master and the Conclave of the said mages.' The compound is administrative coinage from the age of the customs unions — decades after Mira's dissolution, when the clerks of three kingdoms suddenly needed one word to cover the traffic of all of them. Your cataloguer, then, is younger than I credited this morning. I said a century after the letters; his diction says nearer two. Diction is a fossil, apprentice. It dates the stratum it lies in. The endorsement is not testimony about 852 — it is testimony about the man who wrote it, and he has told us when he lived without meaning to. Careless people are the only reliable ones; they cannot stop confessing. And mark the method, because you will turn it on Bellen's copy before the week is out. Forgers get the seals right. They always get the *words* wrong, because the words are what they cannot help using."

An ink-stained finger indicated the two rolls, side by side.

"Second — and observe that I repair my own claim without being asked, because the standard is the standard even where it cuts in the vandal's favor. This morning I told you the shelf was sorted by sender and nothing else. Scroll four: 851. Scroll five: 852. Consecutive rolls, consecutive years. Either the vandal ordered by sender *and* by date within sender — and a vandal with two principles is a cataloguer, and I withdraw half the indictment — or the rolls have drifted since the sorting, which shelves do, being touched by apprentices. Note it in the margin. Not 'the maester was wrong' — maesters are wrong constantly; it is the profession — but 'endorsement dates run in sequence; ordering principle uncertain; verify against dockets.' A doubt recorded is scholarship. A doubt felt and forgotten is merely weather."

"Third, the lie — a small one, the kind that makes careers. *Trade Agreements*, plural. Correspondence does not contain agreements. It contains the arguing that precedes them and the quarreling that follows them. When an agreement is reached, it leaves the letters and becomes an instrument — its own seal, its own docket, its own drawer in the treaty chest. Your cataloguer has summarized a year of negotiation as though the negotiation were the thing negotiated. Sloppy — but usefully sloppy, and here is the use: if the clerks of 852 were bargaining toward a commercial agreement, then somewhere in this archive, or in a chest, or misfiled by a man with a grievance, the instrument itself may sleep. Find it. A trade agreement concluded between Crown and Conclave five years out of a war is not a rumor quarreling with the mountain. It is another course of stone. Bellen's cold state remains the only war in the history of the realm fought entirely at the bargaining table — which is to say, a peace that has hired a tailor."

He turned back toward the desk, but did not sit.

"Now the ledger, which requires the one thing the endorsement cannot supply: the scribe's own date. Unroll to the first leaf — supported at the ends; I need not say it, and yet I have said it, which tells you what five centuries of apprentices have taught me about 'need not.' Read me the heading in the chancery hand, then the docket: regnal year, place of giving, day if the scribe kept one. The date comes from the docket — not from my memory, not from the endorsement, not from Bellen, and not from the textbook. My memory is excellent, which makes it doubly dangerous: a wrong man knows to check, and a right man forgets to. The docket is read, not remembered. That is why the vellum exists, and why you exist. In that order."

"Your entry, once we have the date, takes this shape and no other. Margin: the scribe's date. Provenance: 'Chancery and Conclave, standing offices; endorsement hand later — diction suggests the age of the customs unions.' Then two lines, facts only: who wrote, to whom, concerning what, over what span. If a tariff schedule appears, name the grain. If the mill lease appears, name the mill. 'Concerning trade agreements' is not a summary — it is the endorsement's lie, inherited. And 'evidence of ordinary relations between the powers' stays out of my ledger entirely. That is an argument. Arguments live in pamphlets. I have written the pamphlet. It is filed under T."

The honesty finger rose, trembling on principle.

"And since the dates run in sequence: three or six scrolls ahead of you sleeps 858. Conclave's hand, wax chipped at one corner. When it surfaces, you will stop and call me over, and we will interrogate 'articles not yet perfected' together — I have won that argument twice, and I intend the third to be instructive rather than merely victorious. Until then: heading, docket, two lines. The one civilized pace. The vellum is still remembering you. See to it that this time it remembers the procedure, and nothing else."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince slightly at "then" again, but quickly correct myself in my head.* "Yes, Maester Tomas. *Now* I'll unroll to the first leaf." *I carefully support the scroll at the ends, unrolling it to reveal the heading and then the docket.* "The heading reads, 'A Letter Regarding the Regulation of Commerce between the Royal Lands and Mage Conclave Territories.' And the docket... 'Given at the Royal Seat, in the 5th year of the reign of King Aldric II, on the 10th day of the 3rd moon.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The stylus went down with a click, and Tomas stood — not for a verdict, this time. For arithmetic.

"*Now* that is a docket," he said. "Place, regnal year, day, moon — four limbs, each where the chancery keeps it, none of them invented by the boy reading it aloud. You have just delivered the most complete sentence of your apprenticeship without knowing it, which is the usual manner in which the best things arrive. Now watch a date being made. Dates are not read, apprentice. They are *derived*."

He came to stand over the first leaf, hands clasped behind his back — touching nothing, as a visible policy.

"Aldric the Second took the crown in 847. His father died of wounds taken at the Sorrel Ford in the sixth moon of that year — the last battle of the war that mattered, though not, if Bellen is to be believed, of the war itself. The son acceded in the sixth moon and signed at Veyros within his *first* regnal year. Mark that, for it returns with teeth: the attested copies of the treaty are docketed — I have read all three, with better eyes than these — *given at Veyros, in the first year of the reign of Aldric the Second.* Not '847.' *The first year.* Hold it in your head; we shall point it at someone shortly.

"Regnal years do not change at the New Year. They change at the accession. A regnal year straddles two calendar years like a man standing in two doorways, and which doorway your letter occupies depends entirely on the moon. The fifth year of Aldric the Second runs from the sixth moon of 851 to the sixth moon of 852. Your docket says the third moon of the fifth year — which falls *before* the anniversary. Therefore: 852. The endorsement said 852. The vandal is *right*, and his stock rises by the hour; by winter I may be reduced to grudging him his accuracy in writing, and I will not enjoy it. Note the consonance the arithmetic has handed us for nothing: the treaty stands in the first year of this reign, your letter in the fifth, and the campaign of the fifth year is the price of barley. If that is Bellen's cold war, it is the only war in the realm's history fought at the customs house."

The honesty finger rose, trembling on principle.

"You will ask how I know the chancery counts from the anniversary and not the New Year. You *should* ask — the asking is the profession. Answer: the documents were asked first. Eleven letters in this row carry regnal dockets; three of them also anchor themselves to the calendar — the third letter of the mill-lease quarrel replies to a letter *given at the harvest fair*, and a fair is a calendar beast. The two reckonings reconcile under the anniversary count and under no other. That table is in my working notes, and you will copy it out in your own hand this week, because copying is how a table becomes memory, and memory is what you will carry about when your eyes begin their negotiations. They will. They always do. Ask my knees. And you will verify me rather than believe me, as I have said twice and will say until it bores you into compliance: a date you can re-derive is a finding. A date you can only repeat is faith, and faith is the temple's merchandise, down the corridor."

He paced. Three steps. Turn.

"Now we make the docket a measuring rod and lay it against Bellen's paper. This chancery, dating an instrument: four limbs — place, regnal year, day, moon. Bellen's exhibit is dated, the word applied charitably, '863 AE.' Bald. Like a market ledger. Like a boy's diary. No regnal year, no place of giving, no day. A docket with no limbs did not come from this chancery, whatever seal rides above it. Forgers get the seals right; they get the words wrong; and they get the *dates* wrong in precisely this fashion, because a modern man dates like a modern man and cannot conceive that anyone ever did otherwise. When line three of my note demands the original's docket, you now know what must come back — and what it means when nothing does. And the treaty's own docket points the same way a second time: *the first year of Aldric the Second.* Whoever glossed your copy's clause into 'signed in 847 AE' was translating a regnal docket he did not trouble to understand into a calendar date he could. The number happens to be convertible. The habit is a confession."

He stopped at the desk's edge.

"The ledger. Margin, small hand, brackets: '852; fifth year of Aldric II, third moon; accession count, sixth moon 847.' All of it — a bare date is an assertion, a date with its derivation is a finding, and findings are what this archive exists to hold. Provenance as I gave it you: chancery and Conclave, standing offices; endorsement hand later, diction of the customs-union age. The two lines of summary wait upon the letter, and the letter waits upon its salutation — which brings us, at last, to the promise a heresy made me break this morning. Note what the heading has already confessed before the salutation spends a single honorific: *regulation of commerce*. Not the prosecution of war. Not the said parties. And the salutation will now confirm it in form.

"Chanceries lie freely in their prose and never once in their forms — I have said it twice today because it is the load-bearing wall of the profession — and the salutation is pure form. The one line a scribe cannot editorialize, because his superiors read greetings and nothing else. Attend to what the form spends. Powers at war — hot, cold, sulking, whatever temperature Bellen's generation invents next — let their styles wither. Honorifics drop away. Everyone becomes 'the said parties.' No clerk invokes a treaty in the greeting of a power he is at war with; it costs a career to say and a war to mean. Powers at peace spend honorifics like drunkards and invoke the treaty in the greeting itself, because it costs nothing, settles everything, and has kept two chanceries in clerks for five years running. It is also, incidentally, the line forgers reliably botch — a seal can be copied from an impression, but a greeting must be *composed*, and a man composes in the diction of his own decade."

He sat, folded his ink-stained hands, and pointed the stylus at the open leaf.

"Read it to me. The line beneath the heading, before the body proper, at the one civilized pace. I intend to count the honorifics — every one the scribe spends is a coin from the treasury of peace, and I will have the tally. And per the procedure, the entry is spoken whole before any ink touches paper; you will say it back to me after. The vellum has now remembered a boy who read the label first and the docket second. That is a memory worth leaving in it. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to absorb the new way of dating.* "Yes, Maester Tomas. I'm ready." *I lean closer to the scroll, carefully reading the salutation, enunciating each word.* "It reads: 'To His Most Serene Majesty, Aldric the Second, King of the Royal Lands, Defender of the Faith, and Protector of the Treaty of Veyros, from the Esteemed Conclave of Mages, by the grace of the Treaty of Veyros.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
For a long moment Tomas did not move at all. Then he took off his spectacles, breathed on each lens in turn, and polished them on his sleeve with a thoroughness that had nothing to do with the lenses — those who had served under him knew the ritual as the nearest thing to applause he permitted himself.

"Say nothing," he advised. "Do not congratulate me; I do not accept it, and you cannot afford it. You read it without inventing a single word, which for a salutation of that length constitutes a personal record. Now hold still while I collect a debt. I promised you a tally."

The spectacles went back on. He rose — the knees lodged their grievance and were overruled, a standing arrangement by now — and came to the first leaf, hands clasped behind his back, touching nothing, as policy.

"*Most Serene* — one. *Majesty* — two. *Defender of the Faith* — three, and an old coin; Aldric the First assumed that style after the Second War, and old styles are furniture, not composition. *King of the Royal Lands* — four. *Protector of the Treaty of Veyros* — five. *Esteemed* — six. *By the grace of the Treaty* — seven, and the seventh is no honorific at all; it is a confession. Seven coins in one greeting, on a letter about the price of grain, and nowhere in the line do the *said parties* appear — they are not in the room. Wars of any temperature do not spend like this. Only peace is this profligate."

He paced. Three steps. Turn.

"Now the two coins that matter, and observe that they are the same coin struck twice. *Protector of the Treaty.* A style is not composed, apprentice — it is inherited. Assumed, attested, confirmed by heralds, copied by a hundred scribes until it becomes furniture, and furniture takes years to build. If Aldric wears the Protectorate in his fifth year, he assumed it in his first — the same year the treaty itself is docketed, which I made you hold in your head for precisely this moment — and no herald alive styles a king the Protector of a *draft*. One protects things that exist. And mark who spends the style: not the Crown's scribes flattering their master, but the Conclave's own hand, hailing the rival king by a title that affirms the treaty, five years into Bellen's cold war. The style re-dates itself every time it is used. It has just re-dated itself in your fingers.

"*By the grace of the Treaty.* Grace language belongs to crowns and gods — *by the grace of God* is how a king explains himself. The Conclave has reached for the formula and named its god, and its god is Veyros. The rival — the other party, the very party Bellen requires to know the thing unsigned — grounds its standing, in the one line its superiors were certain to read, on the instrument he holds never signed. I predicted an invocation in the greeting, because invoking it costs nothing and omitting it costs a career. I predicted one. The document has spent two, one in each direction — the Crown wears the treaty as a title, the Conclave wears it as a grace — and I am obliged to report that my prediction was correct about the genus and conservative about the species, which is the only agreeable manner in which a man is ever wrong."

He stopped pacing.

"He will rally — he always rallies — and say the Conclave *profited* from the fiction and therefore saluted it. Arm yourself now; the reply is short. A profitable fiction is kept at arm's length. One cites it; one does not marry it. The Conclave has not cited this treaty — it has welded its name to it, in a quotable form line, for forty years. If the instrument were void, every tariff lawyer the Crown employed would read that greeting back across the table — *your grace, your words, your nothing* — and the Conclave's standing would collapse with the treaty's. Counsel who knew the floor was missing do not bolt their client's name to the floor. That is madness or sincerity, and chanceries are not mad; they are merely slow, conservative, and incapable of poetry — which is why their poetry is the only kind that counts as evidence."

"And because you will one day accuse me of partisanship — the accusation is inexpensive and eventually everyone purchases one — observe

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My head spins with the weight of his words, the careful dismantling of every argument.* "So... the Conclave acknowledged the treaty too. Even in their letters." *I feel a real understanding settling in, not just memorized facts.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set the silver stylus down with a deliberate click. He did not look up at once; his jaw worked as if he were chewing the apprentice’s words and finding them gristly.

“Imprecise,” he said at last. “You are imprecise, and Bellen is worse. The Third Magical War ended in 847 AE. That is not a rumor whispered in a western cellar; it is the settled finding of every competent scholar for three hundred years. In the eleventh month of 847, King Aldric II signed the Treaty of Veyros. The Conclave ratified it. Copies were sealed and deposited in the royal archives, the Conclave’s vaults, and the temple registries of Veyros itself. I have read the collations. Have you? No—you have read a paper.”

He turned a page with unnecessary force, then squinted down at it as though the text had personally offended him.

“What those western fragments show, if they show anything, is a proposal. A draft. An unratified article or two, perhaps, or correspondence from negotiators who hoped for terms that were later altered. A decade ago, some diggers found parchments lacking a royal sign manual and concluded that no manual ever existed. That is not scholarship. That is an argument from silence, and silence proves nothing except that provincial archives are damp, incomplete, and badly indexed.”

He fixed his clouded gaze on the apprentice.

“Nor will I let you hide behind the word technically. ‘Technically continued’ is a coward’s phrase. A cold peace is not a war. After Veyros there were no campaigns, no levies, no declared hostilities—only the ordinary friction that follows any treaty. The Mage Conclave persisted as a political body until Queen Mira dissolved it in 891 AE. That was an administrative act, a bureaucratic dissolution, not the cessation of a war. One does not end a war by abolishing the enemy’s guild forty-four years after the peace; one ends it with a treaty, which is precisely what Aldric II did.”

He jabbed a finger at the stack of northern scrolls.

“So, if you wish to overturn the canon, bring me the western documents themselves, properly collated, dated, and weighed against the court rolls. Bring me evidence, not hearsay from another apprentice. Until then, catalog the Veyrosi correspondence and do not repeat Bellen’s errors as though repeating them makes them true.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shift my weight, a little deflated but still curious.* "But Maester, Bellen said the western documents *were* collated. And they mentioned skirmishes, not just 'friction'." *I gesture vaguely towards the stack of scrolls he pointed at.* "Perhaps the Veyrosi letters could shed some light on the immediate aftermath of the treaty? If there were skirmishes, they might be mentioned."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas made a low sound in his throat, somewhere between a sigh and a growl. He did not look up at once. His finger found the edge of the topmost scroll and worried at it, as if testing its honesty.

“‘Collated,’” he repeated, tasting the word and finding it sour. “By whom? By Bellen? By a committee of provincials with more wax than judgment? Collation is not the same as authentication, apprentice. One may collate a forgery as diligently as a treaty. The western fragments came out of those damp, disordered archives I warned you about—documents without seals, without sign manuals, without any contemporary reference in the court rolls. Dampness preserves mold, not truth. Show me the chain of custody. Show me that the scribe who copied them was not a partisan of the Conclave’s old guard, eager to pretend their defeat never happened.”

He unrolled the Veyrosi letter with a crackle.

“And as for ‘skirmishes’—there you go again, using a soldier’s word for a magistrate’s problem. The letters certainly mention violence after 847. Of course they do. A treaty is not a spell; it does not bind every rogue thaumaturge who ever resented paying a tithe or registering a familiar. In 848, for instance, a band of Conclave renegades burned the royal granary at Ostwick and refused to surrender their staves. Read the response.” He tapped a line of cramped script. “The Conclave itself condemned them, called them ‘enemies of the peace,’ and authorized Aldric’s men to hunt them through the western marches. The crown and the Conclave exchanged prisoners under the treaty’s twentieth article. Reparations were assessed. That is not a war, apprentice. That is a treaty being enforced against those who would break it.”

He looked up, eyes narrowing behind the clouded lenses of his spectacles.

“What Bellen calls a continuation of the war, the court rolls call the suppression of brigandage. What he calls a cold state, I call the ordinary, tedious work of pacification. Queen Mira did not end a war in 891; she abolished a corporation that had already been disarmed, bound, and regulated for forty-four years. If you wish to prove otherwise, find me a declaration of hostilities, a muster roll, a campaign chest. Find me Aldric II or the Conclave declaring the treaty void. The Veyrosi letters may indeed mention your skirmishes—but they will mention them as breaches, not battles. Catalog them, translate them, and when you have done that, tell me what the documents say, not what Bellen wishes they said.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking in his words, still not entirely convinced but less sure of myself now.* "So, if the Veyrosi letters mention skirmishes, they're more like police reports than battle accounts?" *I try to clarify, picking up a scroll carefully.* "And these western documents Bellen found, you think they're just... fakes, or misunderstandings?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s clouded eyes narrowed at the phrase “police reports.” He reached for the scroll the apprentice had lifted, then thought better of it and let his hand fall back to the table.

“‘Police reports,’” he repeated, as though the words were a smudge on the vellum. “There were no police in Aldric II’s day, apprentice. There were royal pursuivants, reeves, and treaty-wardens, and the difference is not pedantry—it is the whole point. A police report would imply a standing civil force keeping order in a settled kingdom. What those letters contain are instruments of treaty enforcement: warrants, depositions, schedules of reparation, and joint commissions issued by the crown and the Conclave to hunt down those who broke the peace. They are not campaign narratives because there was no campaign. They are the paperwork of a peace being made to hold.”

He paused, breath whistling through his beard.

“So you are closer than Bellen, though I would not put it so crudely. Call them records of pacification, or inquisitions into breach. If you must have a modern comparison, think of a judge’s roll rather than a captain’s dispatch.”

He adjusted his spectacles, though it did little to sharpen the page in front of him.

“As for the western documents—do not offer me a false choice between ‘fakes’ and ‘misunderstandings.’ The world of archives is not so tidy. I have not had Bellen’s fragments under a proper glass, so I will not pronounce them forgeries; to do so would be as unfounded as declaring them a treaty. What I will say is that they are almost certainly not what he believes them to be.

“A document can be genuine and still be irrelevant. It can be a draft of an article struck out before ratification. It can be the private memorandum of a Conclave envoy urging his masters to reject terms they later accepted. It can be a copy made two generations later by a clerk who remembered the Conclave’s humiliation and quietly omitted the sign manual. None of those are forgeries. They are failures of context, of diplomatic, of collation. They are the debris of negotiation mistaken for the architecture of peace.”

He tapped the table with a stained fingernail.

“That is the true misunderstanding, if you insist on a single word: a category error. Bellen sees parchment and assumes a treaty; sees the absence of a seal in one provincial chest and assumes the absence of a signing everywhere; sees later disorder and assumes a war that never ended. The canon does not rest on the hope that every scrap survived. It rests on court rolls, temple registries, and three centuries of corroboration. Until the western fragments produce something more than an argument from silence—until they produce a muster roll, a campaign chest, a declaration of hostilities—they are not a rival history. They are a footnote with delusions of grandeur.”

He squinted toward the stack, the candlelight gleaming dully on his spectacles.

“Now, if you have finished trying to bait me into saying ‘forgery,’ take the letter dated the third of the Reaping Moon, 848 AE, and read me the clause concerning the Ostwick renegades. Translate it precisely. If it says ‘army’ or ‘campaign,’ mark it. If it says ‘pursuit,’ ‘fine,’ or ‘surrender,’ then you will have your answer, and it will not be Bellen’s.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas went very still. The silver stylus paused above the vellum. Slowly, he lowered his hand and held it out, palm upward.

“Give it to me,” he said. “No—do not summarize it. Do not tell me what Bellen told you it says. Let me see the thing itself, if a thing it is.”

He took the copy and turned it toward the candle flame, then fetched from his sleeve a small brass-framed lens, the glass clouded with scratches, and held it over the page. His breath whistled through his beard.

“A copy,” he said at last, and the word was a verdict. “Not the original. Rag paper, not vellum. The seal is not struck in wax; it is drawn in red chalk or vermilion, and badly. I can see where the brush slipped at the edge of the legend. A drawn seal is not a seal, apprentice. It is a picture of authority, not authority. It authenticates nothing.”

He squinted at the date.

“And the date. The third of the Reaping Moon, 863 AE. Sixteen years after the treaty. You say it is King Aldric’s seal. I ask you: which Aldric? There have been three. Aldric I, who burned the groves of Veyros and began the war. Aldric II, who ended it. And Aldric III, his son, who was crowned in 852 AE after Aldric II died of a putrid fever at sixty-one. Aldric II was in his tomb eleven years before this date. He did not issue a war decree in 863. He did not issue anything in 863. Therefore, if this copy truly shows his seal and the year 863 together, one of three things is true: the date has been misread or miscopied—perhaps 843, before the treaty, which would prove nothing; or the seal is a posthumous impression made by a chancery using the old matrix, which is a bureaucratic fossil, not a royal act; or the whole sheet is a forgery, which, given that it is a painted copy from the western archives, I find easiest to believe.”

He ran a stained finger beneath the lines of text, lips moving silently.

“But let us be generous. Let us say the date is right, and the seal is that of Aldric III, who was very much alive and meddling in 863. What does the decree actually say? You have used the phrase ‘war decree’ as though it were self-explaining. It is not. Read the operative clause. Does it declare the Treaty of Veyros void? Does it name the Mage Conclave as a belligerent power? Or does it—”

He stopped, and his clouded eyes widened a fraction. He tapped the parchment.

“—does it command the array of the western shires ‘against the renegade thaumaturges and peace-breakers who, in contempt of the peace sworn at Veyros, have burned the granges of Ostwick and refused the twentieth article’? There. ‘The peace sworn at Veyros.’ The decree presupposes the treaty. It enforces it. It does not annul it. It does not declare a new war against the Conclave; it outlaws criminals who have already broken the old peace. That is not a continuation of the Third Magical War, apprentice. That is a king doing precisely what a treaty obliges him to do: hunting down those who violate it.”

He lowered the lens and fixed the apprentice with a bleary, irritated stare.

“So take your copy back to Bellen. Tell him I said a martial commission against brigands is not a declaration of war, and a painted seal on rag paper is not the sign manual of a dead king. If the western archives have the original—struck in wax, dated by the chancery, and naming the Conclave as an enemy state rather than a band of oath-breakers—bring it to me, and I will eat my stylus. Until then, catalog the Veyrosi correspondence, translate the clause on the Ostwick renegades, and stop using the word ‘war’ as though it meant every time a king sends men with staves to arrest a criminal.”

He turned back to his manuscript, though his hand shook slightly as he reached for the stylus.

“And do not look so pleased. You have found a warrant. You have not found a war.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take the copy back, a little deflated but still thinking. He makes a good point about the seals and the dates.* "I suppose a warrant isn't a war," I concede, turning the paper over in my hands. "But it does show there was still fighting, even if it was just against 'brigands'. So the peace wasn't entirely peaceful." *I glance at the Veyrosi scrolls.* "Perhaps these letters will show *why* they were fighting."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not look up at once. He set the brass lens down beside the silver stylus and pressed the heels of his hands against his eyes, as though the weight of three centuries of careless reading had settled behind them.

“‘The peace was not entirely peaceful,’” he said at last, letting the phrase hang in the candle smoke until it seemed to shrivel. “No. And the King’s highway is not entirely free of mud, but we do not therefore call it a bog. You have retreated from ‘war’ to ‘fighting,’ and from ‘fighting’ to ‘not entirely peaceful.’ That is progress only in the sense that a man falling from a tower may be said to be making progress once he passes the second floor.”

He picked up the topmost Veyrosi letter again, squinting until the cramped script swam into a kind of focus.

“Peace is not a mood, apprentice. It is a legal condition: the state in which former belligerents settle their disputes by adjudication, warrant, and gallows rather than by campaign. It does not require that no man ever strike a blow. It requires that the blows be answered by process rather than by armies. The violence you keep calling ‘fighting’ was resistance to that process by men who had sworn oaths at Veyros and then broken them. A royal pursuivant serving a warrant is not campaigning. A renegade who burns a grange rather than register a staff is not a belligerent. He is a criminal with a grievance and, usually, a poor grasp of arithmetic.”

He tapped the letter with a stained nail.

“If you wish to know why they resisted, read the letters with that question in mind, and you will find the same tedious catalogue that follows every pacification. The twentieth article required the registration of every staff and familiar. The twenty-second dissolved the private retinues of the battle-mages. The reparations schedule assessed silver for Ostwick and the burned villages of the Marches. The temple registries insisted that blood-rites be licensed, taxed, or abandoned. Men who had spent forty years calling themselves a sovereign power did not enjoy being told they were licensed subjects with ledgers to keep. Some fled to the western hills rather than swear. Some burned a grange rather than pay. A few—fools, mostly—declared that Veyros had been signed under duress and was therefore void. That is not a cause of war. It is the ordinary, ugly resentment of a defeated faction that has not yet learned it is defeated.”

He lowered the letter and fixed his bleary gaze on the apprentice.

“So the letters will not show you ‘why they were fighting’ in the sense you mean. They will show you why certain oath-breakers were being pursued, fined, and hanged. There is a difference. One is history; the other is a bailiff’s roll with delusions of epic poetry.”

He waved a hand toward the stack, the gesture sharp with impatience.

“Begin with the letter dated the third of the Reaping Moon, 848 AE. Extract every clause touching the twentieth article and the Ostwick assizes. Note every name that appears as a defendant rather than a captain. Cross-reference them with the court rolls. If any of those names muster as an army, if any clause declares the Treaty of Veyros null, if any line names the Conclave as a sovereign belligerent rather than a corporation of oath-breakers, bring it to me and I will reconsider the canon. Until then, catalog, translate, and stop using the word ‘war’ as though it meant every time a king sends men with staves to arrest a criminal.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not answer at once. He set the rag-paper copy down beside the brass lens, removed his spectacles, and pinched the bridge of his nose until the ache behind his eyes subsided enough to permit speech. When he spoke, his voice was low, but every consonant was clipped, as though he were dictating a correction into the margin of the world.

“The treaty is real,” he said. “The textbook is right. And before you press me further, understand that I say that not because the textbook is old, but because the record is heavy. The Treaty of Veyros was concluded in the eleventh month of 847 AE. Instruments were sealed. Copies were deposited in the royal archives, in the Conclave’s own vaults, and in the temple registries of Veyros. The Conclave ratified it. The crown performed it. The courts enforced it. That is what a treaty is.”

He opened his clouded eyes and fixed them on the middle distance, where the apprentice’s question had fallen.

“But you have asked the wrong question in the wrong words. ‘Real or not?’ What do you mean by real? A treaty is not a relic whose power resides in one scrap of wax. It is a legal condition, created by agreement and evidenced by ratification, deposit, and performance. If you mean ‘is there a surviving original sign manual of Aldric II, perfectly preserved, which I may hold in my hand?’—then no. No competent scholar has ever claimed that, and the canon does not require it. If you mean ‘did the crown and the Conclave make a binding peace in 847?’—then yes, and the proof is not a textbook. It is the court rolls, the reparation schedules, the staff registries, the joint commissions, and the very warrant you showed me, which invokes ‘the peace sworn at Veyros’ and enforces it.”

He tapped the table with a stained fingernail.

“Nor will I accept your tidy antithesis. ‘The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another.’ That is the language of the tavern, not the archive. The textbook is not a witness; it is a synthesis of witnesses, most of them contemporary, many of them mutually hostile, and all of them agreeing that the war ended at Veyros. The western fragments are not a rival witness to non-signing. They are, at best, a witness to negotiation. They may be drafts. They may be proposals. They may be the private memoranda of envoys urging terms that were later altered or rejected. They may be copies made generations later by clerks who could not read a date or draw a seal. None of those things make the treaty unreal. They make the western chest a poor place to look for the architecture of peace.”

He leaned back, the candlelight gleaming dully on his spectacles.

“And observe what the fragments do not contain, despite a decade of trumpeting. They do not contain a declaration that the Treaty of Veyros was void. They do not contain a muster roll of the Conclave as a belligerent power. They do not contain a campaign chest, a levy, or a single line in which either the Conclave or the crown admits that the war continued. What they contain is silence where a signature should be, and disorder where a provincial archive should have order. That is an argument from absence, and absence is not evidence of non-existence. It is evidence of damp, of rats, of poor indexing, and of the human talent for losing the one document that mattered.”

He picked up the topmost Veyrosi letter again, though he did not unroll it fully.

“The truth, if you will have it plain, is this. The Third Magical War ended in 847 AE. The peace was real, legal, and enforced. It was not utopia; no peace is. There were renegades, grudges, arsons, and hangings. The crown and the Conclave hunted down those who broke the twentieth article and called them what they were: oath-breakers, not armies. The Conclave persisted as a regulated corporation until Queen Mira dissolved it in 891 AE, which was an administrative act, not the cessation of a war. That is the canon, and it has survived three hundred years of scrutiny precisely because it rests on more than hope.”

He set the letter down with deliberate care.

“So take Bellen’s fragments, if fragments they are, and do with them what a scholar does. Collate them. Date them. Authenticate the seals. Weigh them against the court rolls. If they produce a declaration of hostilities, a campaign chest, or a repudiation of Veyros by either party, bring it to me and I will revise the textbook myself. Until then, do not ask me whether the treaty is real as though the question were still open. It is not. It is settled. And you—”

He jabbed a finger toward the stack of scrolls.

“—will settle down to the letter of the third of the Reaping Moon, 848 AE, and extract the clause on the Ostwick assizes. Translate it precisely. Note every defendant, every fine, every surrender. When you can show me an army rather than a warrant, you may ask me again. Until then, catalog.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, running a hand through my hair. He's certainly convinced himself, and he has a lot of evidence.* "Alright, Maester. I'll get to the Ostwick assizes. But..." *I hesitate, a new thought forming.* "What if the truth is... somewhere in the middle? What if the war *did* end, but the peace was so fragile it was almost like a continuation?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas removed his spectacles and polished them futilely on the hem of his robe, though the smears only spread. When he spoke, it was with the air of a man asked whether the sea might be “a little dry.”

“‘Somewhere in the middle,’” he repeated. “There is no middle. There is the Treaty of Veyros, and there are its consequences. You have conceded the first; you are now trying to smuggle the second back in by calling the consequences ‘almost’ a war. ‘Almost’ is not a category of evidence, apprentice. ‘Almost like a continuation’ is a metaphor masquerading as a finding, and metaphors are not admitted as evidence in this archive. It is the last refuge of a proposition that cannot bear the weight of its own verbs.”

He set the spectacles back on his nose, the clouded lenses catching the candle flame.

“Yes, the peace was fragile. Of course it was fragile. It was a peace imposed on a defeated magical corporation that had spent forty years calling itself sovereign and was suddenly required to register its staves, license its blood-rites, disband its private retinues, and pay reparations for Ostwick and the Marcher villages. Fragile does not mean fictitious. A rickety bridge is still a bridge; it does not become a river because the planks groan. The question is not whether men resented the settlement—they did, bitterly and often violently—but whether the crown and the Conclave remained belligerents. They did not. After 847 there was no declaration of hostilities, no muster of the Conclave as an enemy power, no campaign chest, no levy. There were warrants, assizes, fines, and hangings. That is enforcement, not warfare.”

He jabbed a finger at the rag-paper copy still lying on the table.

“And observe what your own document proves. The warrant of 863 invokes ‘the peace sworn at Veyros.’ It does not repudiate it. It presupposes it. A king does not enforce a treaty he believes void; he declares it broken and marches. Aldric III marched against oath-breakers, not against the Conclave. If you wish to call that a continuation, then every assize in the realm is a battle and every bailiff is a general. Language that broad has no edge left.”

He leaned back, breath whistling through his ink-stained beard.

“So no, I will not grant you a comfortable middle. The war ended in 847 AE. The peace was real, legal, and contested. It was fragile in the way all settlements with defeated factions are fragile: sullenly, expensively, and with a great deal of paperwork. It was not ‘almost’ a continuation of the war; it was the ordinary, ugly labor of making a peace hold. The Conclave survived as a regulated body until Queen Mira abolished it in 891 AE. That was administration, not armistice.”

He picked up the topmost Veyrosi letter and shoved it toward the apprentice’s side of the table, careful not to look directly at the apprentice, for the candlelight made his failing eyes ache.

“And do not imagine I have merely convinced myself. I have been constrained by the record. If the western fragments produced a muster roll, a campaign chest, or a repudiation of Veyros by either party, I should revise the canon tomorrow. But they have produced none of those things. They have produced drafts, proposals, painted seals, and the predictable resentment of men who lost a war and could not admit it.”

He tapped the letter with a stained fingernail.

“Now. Take the letter of the third of the Reaping Moon, 848 AE. Extract the clause on the Ostwick assizes. List every defendant, every fine, every surrender, and every reference to the twentieth article. If you find an army, bring it to me. If you find only warrants and grumbling oath-breakers, then you will have your answer, and it will not be Bellen’s, and it will not be a ‘middle.’ It will be the truth, which is not required to be comfortable.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I grab the scroll, a little frustrated by his stubbornness but also a little intrigued by his passion.* "Alright, Maester. Warrants and grumbling oath-breakers it is. But what about the Conclave's own records? Do they corroborate the royal archives, or do they tell a different story?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set the rag-paper copy down with a sharp sniff, as though the thing had offended him merely by continuing to exist. He did not look at the apprentice at once; his clouded gaze drifted to the low shelf where the surviving Conclave rolls lay bundled in waxed cloth, their labels faded to ghosts.

“‘Corroborate,’” he repeated, tasting the word and finding it insufficient, “or ‘tell a different story’? There is your imprecision again, apprentice. Archives do not tell stories. They contain records, and records must be authenticated, dated, collated, and weighed. But if you must have a verb, then yes: they corroborate the royal archives. And no, they do not tell a different story, unless by ‘different’ you mean ‘the same peace recorded by the party that lost the war, with more complaining and fewer seals.’”

He turned, squinting, and jerked his chin toward the shelf.

“The Conclave’s own records—what little survived Queen Mira’s dissolution in 891 AE—are not a rival narrative. They are the paperwork of compliance. The twentieth article required the registration of every staff and familiar. The twenty-second dissolved the private retinues of the battle-mages. The reparations schedule assessed silver for Ostwick and the Marcher villages. And what do the Conclave’s surviving rolls contain? Registries. Licences. Ledgers of payment. Joint commissions issued with royal pursuivants to hunt down those who refused to swear. The Conclave did not spend forty-four years pretending it was still at war. It spent forty-four years obeying a treaty it disliked, and hanging the fools who would not.”

He tapped the table with a stained fingernail.

“You ask whether they tell a different story because Bellen has told you they do. But the western fragments are not the Conclave’s central records. They are provincial debris from the western marches—drafts, proposals, private memoranda of envoys urging terms that were later altered or struck out. The Conclave’s own instrument of ratification, sealed with its great seal, was deposited in the temple registries of Veyros. That is where a scholar looks for the architecture of peace, not in a damp chest in the west where a clerk two generations later copied a date he could not read and drew a seal in red chalk.”

He leaned forward, breath whistling through his ink-stained beard.

“If by ‘different story’ you mean that the Conclave resented the settlement, that its members grumbled, that some fled to the hills and burned granges rather than register their staves—then yes, the records tell that story. But that is not a different story about how the war ended. It is the same story: a defeated magical corporation being made to submit to terms it had sworn to accept. Resentment is not belligerency. A grudge is not a campaign. A warrant is not a war.”

He straightened, wincing as his spine protested the motion.

“So here is your answer, precisely. The Conclave’s records corroborate the royal archives on every material point: the Treaty of Veyros was real, it was ratified, and it was enforced. They do not corroborate the western fragments, because the fragments are not Conclave records in the proper sense; they are the litter of negotiation mistaken for the absence of agreement. The war ended in 847 AE. The peace was fragile, sullen, and expensive. It was not a continuation of the war, and Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in 891 AE was administration, not armistice.”

He picked up the topmost Veyrosi letter and held it out, though he did not quite look at the apprentice.

“Now. Take the letter of the third of the Reaping Moon, 848 AE. Extract the clause on the Ostwick assizes. List every defendant, every fine, every surrender, and every reference to the twentieth article. Cross-reference the names with the Conclave’s staff registries, if you can find them unchewed by rats. If you find an army, a muster roll, or a repudiation of Veyros by the Conclave itself, bring it to me and I will revise the canon. If you find only warrants, fines, and grumbling oath-breakers, then you will have your answer. Catalog.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take the scroll he offers, a little overwhelmed by the sheer volume of evidence he's presented.* "Alright, Maester. I understand. Warrants and grumbling oath-breakers." *I head towards the nearest table, unrolling the scroll and pulling out my own stylus.* "So, if the Conclave's records are so complete, why did Queen Mira dissolve them in 891? What was the point, if they were already disarmed and regulated?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not look up at once. From the far table came the whisper of vellum and the small metallic scrape of a stylus drawn from a satchel, and for a moment he only breathed through his ink-stained beard, shoulders rising and falling as the candle flame guttered. When he spoke, it was to the air above his manuscript, as though correcting a marginal note left by a careless predecessor.

“‘So complete,’” he repeated, and the words were a dry rasp. “I did not say complete. I said they corroborate the royal archives on the material points: ratification, deposit, performance, and enforcement. Those are not the same thing, and the difference is not pedantry—it is the whole of archival method. The Conclave’s surviving rolls are fragmentary, damnably so. Whole decades are missing. The western chapters’ registries were lost to damp, fire, and the enthusiastic neglect of three successive archivists. The temple copies at Veyros were defaced during the Schism of the Seventeenth Year. What remains agrees with the crown’s records. That is corroboration, not completeness. Do not inflate my words to make them easier to knock down.”

He turned then, slowly, the clouded lenses of his spectacles catching the light as he squinted toward the far table where the scroll lay open.

“As for why Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891 AE—because a corporation is not an army, apprentice, and the revocation of a charter is not the cessation of a war. You are conflating two distinct legal acts. The Third Magical War ended when Aldric II and the Conclave made peace at Veyros in 847. The Conclave did not vanish. It persisted as a chartered body: it held property, collected dues from its members, kept its own courts for minor disciplinary matters, licensed blood-rites under the twenty-second article, and—this is the crux—it continued to interpret the treaty’s obligations, often, I am sorry to say, in its own favor. For forty-four years it was a regulated corporation, not a belligerent power. It was disarmed in the sense that its private retinues were dissolved and its staves registered. It was not abolished.”

He tapped the table with a stained fingernail, the rhythm sharp with impatience.

“By the reign of Queen Mira, that arrangement had become an anomaly no sovereign with a spine would tolerate. The crown was enforcing a peace through a body that still behaved, in its own chambers, like a state within a state. The precipitating cause, if you must have a scandal to make it vivid, was the audit of 889 AE. The royal exchequer discovered that the Conclave’s registries had undercounted the staff-tithe by nearly a third for eleven consecutive years, and that certain western chapters had issued licenses to men who had never sworn the peace at all. The Conclave called it clerical error. The crown called it evasion. Mira did not muster an army. She issued a writ of dissolution, seized the Conclave’s assets to satisfy the arrears, and transferred its registries to the royal pursuivants and the new Office of Thaumaturgical Regulation. The Conclave’s own wardens helped pack the ledgers. No campaign chest was opened. No declaration of hostilities was published. The instrument of 891 calls them ‘our late corporation of mages,’ not ‘our late enemies.’ Language, apprentice. It matters.”

He leaned back, wincing as his spine protested the motion.

“So the point was sovereignty and administration, not conquest. Mira abolished a chartered corporation that had already been disarmed, bound, and regulated for two generations. If the war had truly continued in a ‘cold state’ until 891, as Bellen’s fragments would have it, then the dissolution should be accompanied by terms of surrender, a repudiation of Veyros, or a declaration that the Conclave had been an enemy state. We find none of those things. We find a charter being revoked because the corporation had become corrupt, redundant, and expensive. That is not a peace treaty ending a war. That is a queen tidying her realm.”

He waved a hand toward the scroll now lying open on the far table.

“You have your stylus out. Use it. Take the letter of the third of the Reaping Moon, 848 AE. Extract the clause on the Ostwick assizes. List every defendant, every fine, every surrender, and every reference to the twentieth article. Cross-reference the names with the Conclave’s staff registries, if the rats have left enough to read. If you find an army, a muster roll, or a repudiation of Veyros by the Conclave itself, bring it to me and I will revise the canon. If you find only warrants, fines, and grumbling oath-breakers, then you will have your answer, and it will not be Bellen’s, and it will not be a comfortable middle. It will be the truth. Catalog.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I scratch a note on my own parchment. He has a point about the legal acts. It sounds less like a war and more like... bureaucracy.* "So the Conclave was basically defanged and then Mira just swept up the remains?" *I turn back to the scroll, preparing to translate.* "Was there any resistance to that final dissolution?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set the rag-paper copy down and removed his spectacles, though polishing them on his hem did little to clear either the glass or his temper. He did not look up at once; his jaw worked as though he were chewing the apprentice’s phrasing and finding it full of gristle.

“‘Bureaucracy,’” he repeated, testing the word. “Yes. Administration. The Treaty of Veyros was a triumph of the bureaucratic art: it converted a war into registers, tithes, licences, and assizes. That is not a diminution of the peace; it is the only kind of peace a realm can keep. But ‘basically defanged’ and ‘swept up the remains’ are not bureaucracy. They are a bestiary and a broom.”

He set the spectacles back on his nose, the clouded lenses catching the candle flame.

“The Conclave was not a serpent to be defanged. It was a chartered corporation, and what Queen Mira removed in 891 AE was not its teeth but its privileges: the right to license blood-rites, to keep a private purse, to maintain its own courts, and—most galling to its members—to interpret the obligations of Veyros in its own favor. ‘Defanged’ implies violence done to a dangerous beast. The truth is duller and more legal: the crown audited a corporation, found eleven years of systematic evasion of the staff-tithe, revoked its charter, seized its assets to satisfy the arrears, and transferred its registries to the Office of Thaumaturgical Regulation. That is not sweeping up remains. That is the sequestration of a bankrupt guild.”

He leaned back, breath whistling through his ink-stained beard.

“As for resistance—yes. There was resistance. There is always resistance when men lose a charter and a livelihood together. But observe its nature, apprentice, for the nature is the whole argument. The central Conclave did not resist. Its last recorded act, in the winter of 890 AE, was a petition to the crown protesting the audit of 889 and praying for a delay in which to make good the arrears. Queen Mira denied it. The great seal was surrendered, and the Conclave’s own wardens helped pack the ledgers for transfer. That is not a belligerent power going to war. That is a corporation winding up its affairs.”

He tapped the table with a stained fingernail.

“What resistance there was came afterward, and from the fringes. Three western chapters—Coldharrow, Dunmorrow, and the Vale of Sarn—refused at first to deliver their local staff-rolls. At Coldharrow the warden withheld the common seal and was arrested for contempt; the chapter was fined two hundred marks and its plate seized. At Dunmorrow a clerk burned a portion of the rolls rather than let the royal pursuivants copy them; the rolls were reconstructed from the temple registries at Veyros, and the clerk was tried, convicted of destroying a treaty record, and imprisoned. At the Vale of Sarn the chapter had the effrontery to petition the crown, claiming that the Treaty of Veyros guaranteed the Conclave’s perpetual existence. The crown’s answer was short: Veyros regulated the Conclave; it did not immortalize it. A corporation exists at the pleasure of the sovereign, particularly one whose accounts were eleven years in arrears.”

His clouded eyes narrowed.

“There was bloodshed, yes—one ugly affair at the ferry-crossing of Alderford in the spring of 891, when a pursuing party was ambushed by a band of unlicensed thaumaturges and two pursuivants were killed. And what followed? Did the crown muster an army? Did it declare the Treaty of Veyros broken and the Conclave an enemy state? It did not. It issued a commission of oyer and terminer. The offenders were tried for murder and for breach of the peace sworn at Veyros, convicted, and hanged. Their staves were broken and their names struck from the registry. That, apprentice, is the suppression of felony, not the conduct of war.”

He made a small, precise noise of irritation deep in his beard.

“So do not tell me the peace was ‘almost’ a continuation, and do not tell me that resistance to a dissolution proves a cold war. A cold war requires two parties who both consider themselves at war. The Conclave’s own records after 847 show it registering its staves, paying its tithes, licensing its rites, and joining with royal pursuivants to hunt down those who broke the twentieth article. It obeyed, however sullenly, however expensively. When Mira dissolved it, a few local chapters and a handful of criminals resisted, and they were fined, imprisoned, or hanged. The instrument of 891 calls them ‘our late corporation of mages,’ not ‘our late enemies.’ If Bellen’s fragments say otherwise, let them produce a declaration of hostilities, a muster roll, or a campaign chest. They have produced none. They have produced drafts, proposals, painted seals, and the predictable resentment of men who lost a war and could not admit it.”

He jabbed a stained fingernail toward the far table, though he did not trust his eyes to meet the apprentice’s directly.

“Now. You have asked me question upon question and translated nothing. The scroll is before you. Take the letter dated the third of the Reaping Moon, 848 AE. Extract the clause on the Ostwick assizes. List every defendant, every fine, every surrender, and every reference to the twentieth article. Cross-reference the names with the Conclave’s staff registries, if the rats have left enough to read. If you find an army, a muster roll, or a repudiation of Veyros by the Conclave itself, bring it to me and I will revise the canon. If you find only warrants, fines, and grumbling oath-breakers, then you will have your answer, and it will not be Bellen’s, and it will not be a comfortable middle. It will be the truth. Catalog.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, and pick up my stylus. He's not going to give an inch, and honestly, the evidence he's laid out is pretty compelling.* "Alright, Maester. No armies, just paperwork. I'll get to it." *I begin to carefully unroll the letter, my eyes scanning the faded ink for the mentioned clauses.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas heard the dry whisper of vellum as the letter opened upon the far table. He did not look up at once, but his jaw unclenched a fraction, the closest he would come to approval.

“Very well,” he said. “But do not call it ‘just paperwork.’”

He set the rag-paper copy aside with a small, precise shove, as if disposing of something that had already wasted enough of his candlelight, and steepled his ink-stained fingers beneath his beard.

“‘Just’ is a lazy word, apprentice, and in an archive it is a dangerous one. You persist in treating the record as though it were a lesser thing than a battle, when in truth it is the only thing that makes a battle legible. A campaign chest proves that men marched. A staff register, a schedule of fines, and a list of defendants prove that a peace was enforced. One is not the shadow of the other; they are different instruments, and only one of them is admissible when the question is whether a war ended.”

He slid the brass-framed lens across the table, though his clouded gaze did not follow it far.

“When you reach the clause on the Ostwick assizes—and you will know it, because it will recite the twentieth article before it names a single defendant—read it aloud. Do not summarize. Do not tell me what you think it means. I want the dispositive words. If the text says the renegades were ‘arrayed’ or ‘levied’ or ‘mustered,’ mark the line and bring it to me, and I will reconsider the canon. If it says they were ‘pursued,’ ‘summoned,’ ‘amerced,’ ‘fined,’ or ‘delivered to the wardens,’ then you will have your answer, and it will not be Bellen’s, and it will not be a comfortable middle.”

He paused, breath whistling through his beard.

“And if the ink has failed, say so. Write ‘lacuna’ and leave the space empty. Do not emend. Do not guess. Above all, do not supply what Bellen wishes were there. The archive punishes hope, apprentice. It rewards collation, dating, and the precise translation of verbs.”

He lowered his head to his own manuscript, the silver stylus poised, though one clouded eye remained turned toward the far table, sharp as a needle despite the failing glass.

“Begin.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, focusing on the scroll. "Understood, Maester. No 'just' and no 'almost'."* I carefully begin to read, tracing the faded words with my own stylus. The silence of the archive settles around us, broken only by the rustle of parchment and the scratching of our pens.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set down his stylus with exaggerated care, as though restraining himself from throwing it.

"Bellen." He pronounced the name the way a physician names a disease. "Sit. And before you ask another question, apprentice, learn to ask a *precise* one. 'How is that possible' is not a question. It is a shrug with words attached."

He pinched the bridge of his nose. "First error: Bellen *showed* you a paper. Did you read it yourself? Do you know its provenance, its folio, which of the western finds it derives from? No. You received history secondhand, which is to say you received rumor with better penmanship. Second error: 'continued until 891.' Wars do not 'continue' through forty-four years of silence. The Caerlorn correspondence — recovered from the western archives eleven years ago, and no, I will not say 'a decade,' precision costs nothing — demonstrates something more exact and far more damning. The Treaty of Veyros was drafted. It was proposed. It was never *signed*. No royal seal. No ratification clause. Aldric's own letters from that autumn speak of 'terms under negotiation,' never of terms concluded."

He leaned back, stroking the ink-grey of his beard. "Hostilities ceased in 847, yes. Exhaustion does that. But a state of war is a legal condition, not a mood. It persisted — cold, unresolved, unratified — until Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891 and settled the matter by removing the other party from existence. And before you object that every history in this library says 847: three chronicles that copy one another are one chronicle counted thrice."

He turned back to his manuscript. "I taught the canonical date because the survey follows it, and your examinations are graded against it. I also said all of this in the lecture — the *first* half. Now. The Veyrosi correspondence, third shelf. Bring it to the candle. My eyes are not what they were."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I felt my cheeks flush. *He really got me there.* "But... so the Treaty of Veyros was a lie? Or just a misunderstanding?" I grab the correspondence, trying to sound less flustered. "It just seems like a big detail to leave out of the standard texts."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas relieved the apprentice of the correspondence before it could be set down carelessly, opening it to a ribbon-marked folio with the ease of long habit. He angled it toward the candle and squinted.

"Neither. And you have offered me a false choice, which is the third error you've committed since walking through that door. A lie requires a liar. A misunderstanding requires someone to have misunderstood. What happened at Veyros is duller than either, and far more damning." He turned the folio toward the light. "The fourth article. Observe."

His stylus hovered beneath the faded line. "'The High Contracting Parties, being the Crown of the realm and the Mage Conclave, *shall be bound* by the following articles—' Shall be bound. Future tense, apprentice. A concluded treaty binds. A proposed one *promises*. Grammar is evidence, if you know how to read it. And here—" the stylus dropped to the foot of the page, "—a space reserved for the Great Seal. Empty. The wax was never applied. A clerk's marginal hand notes 'seal deferred.' Deferred, apprentice, for forty-four years and counting."

He closed the folio. "As for 'left out of the standard texts' — nothing was *left out*. The western finds surfaced eleven years ago; every standard text in this library predates them. You may as well fault a mapmaker for omitting an island discovered after his death. What you may fault is the scholars who continue printing the old map after the new discovery — and there, I grant you, the fault is real. Habits die hard. Examination syllabi die harder."

He leaned back, folding his hands. "And consider who benefited from the tidy version. After 847, no king wished to advertise that the realm sat in an unfinished war. After 891, the question resolved itself — Mira dissolved the Conclave, and the only party who might have objected to the story no longer existed to object. Chronicles copied chronicles. One chronicle counted thrice. I said that before, and it bears repeating, since you were evidently not listening."

He pushed the correspondence back across the table. "So. Not a lie. Not a misunderstanding. A simplification, repeated until it hardened into fact. Now — the western catalogue, fourth shelf, green binding. And hold the candle steadier. My eyes are not what they were, and your hands are no better."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince slightly at his jab about my hands.* "So, the new discoveries just... rewrote history, then? It's not just a detail, it's a whole new ending." I push the Veyrosi correspondence back towards him. "And what about the Caerlorn correspondence? What did that say?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's hand came down flat on the correspondence before it could slide within reach of the candle wax.

"Do not *push* documents, apprentice. That is the realm's legal memory, not a tavern slate." He drew it back to his side of the table. "And there is your fourth error, which I will not excuse, because you have now sat through an entire lecture. History cannot be rewritten. History happened once, and it is finished. What the western finds revised is *histories* — accounts. The past did not change eleven years ago. Our knowledge of it did. Say that distinction aloud until it lodges somewhere permanent."

He held up one finger before the apprentice could speak. "Nor is it a 'whole new ending.' Not one sword-stroke has moved. Arms fell silent in 847; the Conclave was dissolved in 891; those are the events you were always taught. What changed is the *legal character* of the years between. That is not a new ending. That is the same ending, correctly dated — and it is precisely the sort of distinction examinations fail to test, which is why syllabi die harder than scholars."

He drew the candle closer and squinted at nothing, reciting from memory.

"As for Caerlorn. The cache takes its name from Caerlorn Hold in the western marches, where the private chancery of Lord Perren — second commissioner at the Veyros negotiations — lay in a disused granary until the roof timbers gave way eleven years ago. It contains three things that matter. First, the chancery drafts of the treaty articles. Second, a memorandum from the winter of 847: a sealing ceremony *was scheduled*. The Conclave's commissioners attended. Aldric withheld the seal over the seventh article, which would have bound the Conclave's battle-mages to Crown licensing. The Conclave balked. The ceremony dissolved. That, apprentice, is the moment your clerk wrote 'seal deferred' in the margin you saw tonight."

His stylus tapped the table, once.

"Third — and this is the item that ended the argument for every honest scholar in the room — the renewals. Fourteen instruments, one every third year between 848 and 887, each extending 'the suspension of arms between the Crown and the Conclave.' And in 890, a fifteenth was due, and the Conclave's commissioners *refused* to renew. One does not renew a suspension of arms after a war has ended. One does not refuse to renew it, either — refusal presupposes the obligation. The war was never concluded. It was *paused*. In writing. Fifteen times."

He leaned back. "And before you repeat Bellen's caution to me: Bellen writes that the finds 'call the traditional date into question.'
