The traditionalists call the renewals clerical boilerplate, formulas recited by sleepy scribes. I have held the originals. The same hand — the same fist, stroke for stroke — runs through thirty-seven years of them, and no scribe reproduces a dead formula for four decades without someone above him reading what he writes. The 890 refusal is not boilerplate. It is a pulse."

He gestured without looking up. "Now the green binding, fourth shelf — the Caerlorn catalogue is in it, which is why I asked for it before you began cross-examining me. Bring it, and bring the candle. Separately, if you please. My eyes are not what they were, and your habit of pushing things across tables is precisely why."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas accepted the copy by its edges, the way a physician accepts a soiled bandage, and held it at arm's length before the candle.

"Fifth error, and this one I will make you remember. 'Sixteen years after *you said the war ended*' — I said no such thing. I said hostilities ceased in 847 and the war *persisted*, unratified and unresolved, until 891. If you cannot keep straight the position of the man standing in front of you, no document will save you. Your arithmetic is correct. It is the only accurate thing in that sentence."

He squinted at the page, then snorted. "And observe what you have actually brought me. That is not a seal. That is a *painted roundel* — a copyist's memory of a seal, executed with a brush by someone who has perhaps seen one from across a room. A copy proves the existence of a copy. It credentials nothing. But I do not require it." He closed his eyes briefly, reciting. "The original is catalogued in the western archive as item 214 — the chancery called it a *decree of watch and certification*, issued in the autumn of 863. Your seminars call it a 'war decree' because precision offends them. The word 'war' occurs in it exactly once, in the recital, and that once is the entire argument: '*Whereas a state of war remains between the Crown of the realm and the Mage Conclave, notwithstanding the suspension of arms lately renewed*...' and the operative clause bids the coastal keeps maintain fire-watch and the western lords certify their rolls of licensed battle-mages '*for the duration of the present war.*' Under the Great Seal. In 863. I held the original eleven years ago, before your Bellen knew it existed."

He set the copy down and folded his hands. "Now think, since thinking has been optional for you this evening. The histories say the war ended in 847. This decree — sealed, dated, filed in the royal chancery's own register — speaks of 'the present war' sixteen years *after* 847. Either Aldric's chancery spent a generation issuing decrees about a war that did not exist, or the war existed and 847 is wrong. Which horn of that dilemma does the canonical account survive? Neither. You have spent the evening handing me stones and wondering why the wall behind you is cracking. *This* document does not embarrass my position, apprentice. It is my position, with wax on it."

He raised a finger. "And before the obvious objections arrive: no, the seal on the decree does not mean the Treaty could have been sealed. It is the seal on a *decree*, and the space on the Treaty remained empty — different instruments, different fates. Nor is forgery an argument; it is an accusation wearing an argument's clothes. A forger manufacturing support for the Treaty would have dated his work before 847 and applied the seal to the *Treaty* — the one document that needed it. Nobody forges a beacon order."

A pause. He almost looked at the apprentice.

"You did, at least, bring a document rather than a rumor. The first correct thing you have done since the door. Now fetch the green binding — fourth shelf, as I asked three interruptions ago — and find the entry for item 214. Read it to me, since your eyes are younger than mine and have been squandered less."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stare at the paper in my hand, then back at Maester Tomas. My cheeks flush again, but this time it's from frustration at myself.* "So, all those years, everyone just... ignored this? This decree with the seal?" I nod, putting the paper away carefully. "Right. Green binding. Fourth shelf. And the candle." *I retrieve the requested items, trying to keep my hands steady.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas took the candle first, held it at the length of his forearm, squinted at the flame, and pronounced it acceptable. The green binding he accepted after, weighing it in one hand without opening it.

"Steady hands at last. I shall note the improvement and decline to praise it."

He raised a finger. "Sixth error, and a small one, but small errors grow. '*This decree with the seal.*' You have never seen the seal. You have seen a brushstroke imitating one — a fact I disclosed to you myself, not five minutes ago. Say 'the decree,' and stop dressing your copy in its original's clothes."

A second finger. "Seventh — and here, finally, is the shape of a real question wearing the wrong clothes. '*Everyone* just ignored it.' Do not say 'everyone.' You have surveyed no one. And one cannot ignore a document lying beneath a collapsed granary roof; ignoring requires possession. But amend the question and it becomes worth answering. The chancery *knew*. The decree was enrolled — that is what enrollment means. It entered the public register, where any petitioner with patience and a modest bribe could find it. No hand covered it. No order buried it. Why, then, did no one point at it?"

He answered himself before the silence could. "Because nobody reads decrees, apprentice. Chronicles copy chronicles; no chronicler builds his history from fire-watch rosters and licensing rolls. A beacon order is the dullest parchment in the realm, and dullness preserves better than secrecy ever did. The past is not censored. It is *shelved*. Add motive where motive existed — a Crown content with 847 before, a realm with no Conclave left to object after — and you have all the conspiracy required, which is none. And eleven years ago the roof fell in, and since that day nobody has ignored item 214. There has been a decade of open quarrel over it. Bellen's paper is one regiment in that quarrel. What lags is not attention. What lags is the syllabus."

He turned the green binding toward the apprentice and slid it across the table — placed, you will observe, not pushed.

"Third quire, folio ninety-one. Your eyes, not mine. I shall recite what the entry ought to say, and we shall see whether my memory and the cataloguer agree. That is how two sets of errors cancel." He closed his eyes. "'Item 214. Decree of watch and certification. Autumn court, 863. Single skin, Great Seal pendant, impression sharp, tag intact. Recites a state of war and the suspension of arms lately renewed — cf. item 201, the sixth renewal, of the same year, whose phrasing the decree follows word for word. Certified copy, Caerlorn provenance.' And then the note, which is the only poetry in the volume: 'date and hand corroborated by the renewal series, items 196 through 209.'"

He opened his eyes and fixed the apprentice with what, for him, passed for attention.

"Mark what the cataloguer did. He let the documents interrogate one another. The decree quotes the sixth renewal exactly. The renewals run in one fist across thirty-seven years. The decree's hand is that fist. For the canonical account to stand, a forger must have manufactured not one document but a *family* of them — same hand, four decades, agreeing in phrasings no forger would trouble to fake. Dilemmas do not come more laden than that, and I did not build this one. The chancery did, one sleepy scribe at a time."

He gestured at the book. "Now read it aloud. Slowly. If the catalogue differs from my recitation by a single word, you will tell me which of us it corrects, and I will thank you. Once. And — the candle nearer. Yes, I have said my eyes are not what they were five times tonight; I am aware. Repetition is the mother of instruction, and also, apparently, of this headache."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set the candle down at a precise distance from the green binding and folded his hands upon it, which was what he did instead of sighing.

"You were given one page to read a full demand ago, and you have replaced it with a request for a verdict. Very well. But first your errors, which have become a toll, and you will pay it."

"Eighth: 'real or not.' You are conflating existence with execution, and a scholar who does that will misfile half his archive. The treaty *is* real. It has leaves, folios, a clerk's marginal hand — you saw it tonight. What it does not have is a seal, a signature, or a ratification. An unexecuted instrument is real the way a bridge drawn on paper is real: you may frame the drawing and hang it in a hall, but you will drive no cart across it. Ask 'is it real' and the answer is yes. Ask 'was it concluded' and the answer is no. Different questions. Different answers. No paradox."

"Ninth: 'the textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another.' In that sentence you have seated a textbook and a document at the same table, like two witnesses disputing in a tavern. They are not of equal rank. The textbook is a secondary account — descended from chronicles that copied chronicles, one chronicle counted thrice, as I have said often enough to bore the candle. The Caerlorn finds are primary evidence: the instruments themselves, in the chancery's own fist, sealed and enrolled. When a rumor and an artifact disagree, the artifact does not get a vote, apprentice. It gets the verdict."

He raised one hand and began, unhurriedly, to count.

"Now the truth, since you ask for it whole. Four facts. Keep them distinct and this question will never confuse you again."

"One. Arms fell silent in 847. Exhaustion, not law. Here the textbook is correct, and no honest scholar disputes it."

"Two. The Treaty of Veyros was drafted, proposed — and never concluded. The sealing ceremony of winter 847 collapsed over the seventh article; the wax never touched the parchment; a clerk wrote 'seal deferred,' and posterity, with characteristic nerve, went on calling it a treaty anyway. We christen documents the way we christen ships — before they prove seaworthy. Here the textbook is flatly wrong. It asserts a signature. No archive on earth possesses one."

"Three. The state of war persisted — suspended, renewed fourteen times in one fist across thirty-seven years — until the Conclave refused the fifteenth renewal in 890. A refusal is not an ending. It is a pulse."

"Four. In 891 Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave. The other party to the war ceased to exist, and a war whose other party has ceased to exist is not *ended*. It is *extinguished*. Lawyers will bill you a golden stag to explain the difference, so you may have it free."

He lowered the hand.

"There. The textbook is right in its events and wrong in its law. The new scholarship is right in both. That is not 'one thing' against 'another.' That is a correct account set against a partly incorrect one, and the tie you sense between them is a courtesy you are extending to the wrong party. Truth is not a tug-of-war in which every account pulls with equal weight. Truth is a weight. Documents are the only scale."

"For your examination, write 847, and write it without a flicker. The syllabus is graded against it, and I will not have you failed for knowing too much. But carry the four facts beneath the answer. To recite the error of one's age without believing it is not hypocrisy, apprentice. It is literacy."

He turned the green binding toward the apprentice and opened it to the ribbon.

"Now. Folio ninety-one. Aloud, slowly. If the catalogue differs from my recitation by so much as a comma, you will tell me which of us it corrects, and I will thank you. My eyes are not what they were — and yes, I am aware I have said so. A man who repeats himself has at least the virtue of a consistent source."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I feel a bit overwhelmed by his long answer, but also like a fog has cleared.* "So the textbooks... they just got the legal bit wrong, but the dates for when things *happened* are mostly right?" I clear my throat and try to focus on the task. "Right. Folio ninety-one." *I find the page and begin to read, carefully, making sure to annunciate each word.* "Item 214. Decree of watch and certification..."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas raised one finger before the first sentence could find its stride.

"Questions before exercises. Otherwise you read with your ears full. As to your sentence — no error number. It is the first thing you have offered all evening that I could correct without replacing, and I find the experience unsettling." He let that sit. "But one word. '*Mostly* right.' The textbook's dates are sound. One of its events is not. A conclusion of treaty is an act, apprentice — like a coronation, like a hanging. It occurs or it does not, and at Veyros it did not. The realm did not misdate its history. It misdescribed it, and then kept the date for the misdescription. And do not say 'just' — the 'just' is doing dishonest work in that sentence. The legal character was not a corner of the dispute. It was the dispute. An account is judged by its load-bearing claim, and the textbook is *named after* the one act in it that never happened. Now read. Eyes on the page."

Maester Tomas closed his eyes and listened to the entry to its very end, lips moving a half-syllable behind, one fingertip keeping count against the table. He did not interrupt. When the last of it had been read he sat a moment with his eyes still shut.

"He agrees with me down the page. 'Pendant.' 'Impression sharp.' 'Tag intact.' The cross-reference to item 201 — arithmetic and all. Every particular, to the letter." His eyes opened. "And he corrects me in one."

He drew the binding back toward himself, though he did not look at it.

"The provenance. I recited '*certified copy*, Caerlorn provenance.' The catalogue reads '*original instrument*, Caerlorn provenance' — and assigns the certified copy a number of its own. Item 215. Same court, same year, enrolled in the register of the high chancery." He exhaled through his nose. "Mark what has happened here. An hour ago I told you, correctly, that 214 is the original. Then I recited from memory, and my memory seated the copy where the original sits — because I have told this story a hundred times in eleven years, and somewhere in the counting the two changed chairs. Memory is a chronicle, apprentice. It copies itself, and every copying errs. One chronicle counted thrice — I have said it all evening about dead men. Tonight the chronicle was me."

He regarded the green binding for a long moment.

"I promised my thanks, once, to whoever caught a divergence between my recitation and the page. The catalogue has earned it." A pause. "Thank you," he said, to the book.

"You were nearer to it than the book and earned less. You heard my recitation and you heard the page, and you were admiring your own enunciation instead of comparing them. Comparison is the trade. Enunciation is merely how the trade sounds." A beat. "You read steadily, at least. I noticed. I decline to say so twice."

He rubbed his temple, once, and pressed on.

"Now mark why the correction matters — it explains your sheet of paper down to its last flaw. Autumn court, 863: the chancery certified a copy and entered it in the register. That is the enrollment I described — public, filed, unread by anyone with a chronicle to finish. Your Bellen's sheet descends from item 215, or from some hand that copied 215 — the third remove, at the most generous count. And observe what each remove costs. The original carries wax. The certified copy carries ink *describing* wax. Your sheet carries a painted roundel, because its maker stood at the third remove copying a description of a description. Wax does not survive inking, apprentice. Your document is not a forgery and never was. It is a great-grandchild. It has the family face and none of the family's standing."

He turned the green binding and began to slide it back across the table, stopped, and placed it instead.

"Item 210. The next entry, or near enough. A letter of the Conclave's commissioners, spring of 890. It is the shortest in the quire and the loudest. Read it aloud — and then tell me what the *absence* of a fifteenth renewal has to do with everything."

He reached for the candle and trimmed the wick.

"And after that, the northern scrolls, which have waited the length of your entire education and can survive one more entry. My eyes are not—" He stopped himself. "You know the state of my eyes. The phrase has worn a groove. So has the chair. Read."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I feel a fresh wave of embarrassment wash over me. He's right, I was too focused on reading clearly to really listen.* "Right. Comparison, not enunciation." *I turn to the next entry, eager to redeem myself.* "Item 210... 'The Conclave's commissioners regret to inform the Crown that, effective immediately, further extensions of the suspension of arms are not possible.'" *I look up, my brow furrowed.* "So this is it? The refusal? It's so... polite."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not answer at once. He drew the green binding back, angled it to the candle, and read the entry himself — twice, slowly, one fingertip beneath each line, as though the page might amend itself under inspection.

"Yes," he said at last. "This is it. Item 210. The pulse, of which I spoke." He looked up. "And now — a remark I cannot number. Nine errors tonight, and then a 'so polite' that is not wrong, merely small. You have commented on the upholstery, apprentice. The house remains unvisited."

He held up one finger before the obvious objection could form.

"Sit with the politeness until it stops surprising you. Correspondence between armed powers is *always* courteous. Courtesy is not softness here; it is distance. Two neighbors disputing a fence write each other insults. Two states disputing a war write each other 'regrets.' The more dangerous the disagreement, the deeper the bow — and I will note, since the granary does not say it, that the Conclave in 890 held no army worth the word. I mark that as inference. But mark this as text: a refusal one can afford to be polite about is still a refusal."

He began to count on his fingers, clause by clause.

"'Regret to inform' — the bow. 'Effective immediately' — the operative clause; hold it; I am returning there. 'Are *not possible*' — and there is the grammar, always the grammar. Not 'we will not extend.' Not 'the Conclave refuses.' *Are not possible*, written the way one writes weather. The commissioners reported their own decision as though it were fog rolling in — because one does not argue with fog, and one cannot hang fog for treason. The passive voice, apprentice, is where refusals go to avoid being hanged."

The stylus tapped once against the binding.

"And then three words you read straight past: '*suspension of arms.*' One cannot suspend what is not raised. The phrase presupposes a state of war standing between Crown and Conclave in the spring of 890 — presupposes it as a bridge presupposes a river. Nobody disguised it because nobody thought it needed disguising. To the men who wrote and filed this letter, it was not a revelation. It was bookkeeping. That is precisely what makes it testimony."

"Now '*effective immediately.*' The fourteenth renewal — item 209, 887, three years, as all of them ran — expired by its own terms. The fifteenth was due. The Conclave declined, and declined at once. So the suspension did not lapse at the end of some grace period; it died the day this letter crossed the Crown's desk. And from that day until the dissolution — the better part of a year — the realm stood in a state of war with *nothing suspended at all*. Threshing went on. Weddings went on. The realm spent the winter of 890 legally at war and noticed nothing, because law and life keep separate ledgers, and only one of them survives in a granary."

He closed the binding, deliberately, and rested his hand upon it.

"Mark the symmetry, because no examination ever will. In 847 the realm stopped fighting and remained at war. In 890 it remained at war and stopped pausing. Neither year looks like a war. Both are."

"Then 891. Mira dissolved the Conclave, and a war whose second party ceases to exist is extinguished — I have given you that distinction already, free of charge, which should make you suspicious of it. Did this letter *cause* her? A year stands between the refusal and the dissolution; the sequence is documentary. The motive is not. No granary in the western marches holds Queen Mira's reasons. Sequence is what parchment can testify to. Motive is what scholars supply — and honest scholars supply it marked as guesswork. Those who do not, build history the way your sheet of paper was built: a copy of a copy of a guess, arriving with a painted seal on it."

He pushed the candle a half-inch from the binding — a correction, not a courtesy — and folded his hands.

"I asked you one letter ago what the *absence* of a fifteenth renewal has to do with everything. You answered that the refusal was polite. That is a remark about the envelope. The question concerns the letter. You have now read item 210 twice, and heard it dissected once. Answer."

"I will listen for three words at minimum — 'suspension,' 'lapse,' and '847' — and if you are tempted to say the war 'resumed' in 890, strike the word before you speak it. Not one sword moved. The legal condition resumed. The fighting did not. That distinction, apprentice, has been the entire content of your evening."

He reached for the stylus and found nothing to point it at.

"The northern scrolls have waited the length of your education. They will survive one answer longer. The candle may not."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to organize my thoughts. The politeness of the letter still bugs me, but I know better than to mention it again.* "The absence... means the suspension of arms lapsed, and since the war never officially ended in 847, the legal state of war just... continued. Right up until 891."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not interrupt. His fingertip kept its count against the table through the whole of the sentence, and when it ended he sat a moment with his eyes closed, as though tasting the last of a wine he had braced himself to find vinegar.

"Suspension," he said. "Present. Lapse — present, and in the active voice, which is where that word belongs. 847 — present, and in the correct clause." He raised a third finger and regarded it as though it had surprised him. "And the forbidden word — withheld. I set you three words and a trap. You produced the words and walked around the trap without remarking on the favor. That is either comprehension or luck, and I decline to guess which, since one of the two would require me to flatter you."

He opened his eyes.

"The answer was correct." He let it stand exactly as long as it deserved, which was not long. "Do not inflate over it. Correctness is not an achievement, apprentice. It is the removal of an impediment. Nine errors stood between you and a true sentence, and what remains once they are gone is — a true sentence. That is the floor of the trade, not its ceiling. I said earlier that I find the experience unsettling. I withdraw nothing."

He held up one hand before relief could take root.

"But hold still. There is a tenth. And I want you to see its pedigree, because it is the finest specimen of the evening."

"'*The war never* officially *ended in 847.*' One word. I nearly let it pass, and then I remembered what I am for. Examine what 'officially' does. It concedes that the war *ended* — in some soft, unofficial register — and objects merely to the paperwork. That is the textbook's entire claim, compressed into an adverb. The book says the war ended in 847 and was sealed. You have said the war ended in 847 and was merely unsealed. The distance between those two sentences is one painted roundel wide, and you have spent this evening holding the evidence that no roundel was ever applied. A war does not end unofficially. It is *concluded*, or it is *extinguished* — those are the only exits, and both are as official as an act can be. What ended in 847 was the fighting. Your main clause knew it — 'the legal state of war continued' — and your subordinate clause sold it out one breath later. You answered like a scholar and then footnoted like the syllabus."

The stylus tapped once.

"And mark the pedigree. This is the error that opened our evening, in the textbook's full armor. It has copied itself all night — down through '*mostly right*,' down through '*just*,' which you delivered again tonight with an apology built into the pause. Errors copy themselves, apprentice. One chronicle counted thrice. This one has spent the evening descending, and it has just copied itself into you, mid-sentence, while you were being *correct*. That is what a bad textbook does. It does not argue. It waits in the adverbs. The sentence you wanted was: the suspension lapsed; the war was never concluded; the state of war stood unpaused until the Conclave was extinguished in 891. Nothing hiding in the small words. Say it that way, and it survives every syllabus in the realm."

He rose, took the second candle from the shelf, and lit it from the first, which had burned down to a regrettable stub.

"Now. The northern scrolls, before this one dies of old age. Oak chest, north wall. Muster rolls, harbor dues, land grants from the northern keeps — three generations of them. None of it will ever be famous, which is precisely its virtue. Famous documents get copied, and copied documents get counted thrice. Nobody has ever copied a harbor due out of enthusiasm. Item 214 spent its whole life being dull. That is why it was still telling the truth when the roof fell in. You are about to spend an evening among its cousins. Conduct yourself accordingly."

He drew out the first scroll and set it on the table at the apprentice's side — placed, not pushed.

"You will read each entry aloud. I shall recite what it ought to say. Where the page and my memory diverge, the page wins, and you will say so without ceremony and without waiting to be thanked. You have seen tonight what memory does after a hundred tellings. I am a chronicle now, apprentice. You are the collation. It is the only authority I will place in an apprentice's hands, and I do not place it there because you have earned it. I place it there because my memory is fifty-two years old and has told these stories far too often to be trusted alone."

He trimmed the new wick and did not look up.

"And mind the candle as you go. My eyes are—" He stopped. "You know the state of them. The groove is worn through. Read."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to absorb his last corrections, feeling a familiar mix of frustration and grudging admiration.* "Yes, Maester Tomas." *I pick up the first scroll, careful not to damage the old parchment, and hold it so the candlelight illuminates the faded script.* "Muster roll... for the year 798 AE... for the garrison of Castle Blackwood..."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas raised one finger, and the recitation halted mid-fragment.

"Three pieces of the heading, and already I must interrupt — not for what you read, but for whose voice it came out in. '*AE.*' Is that on the parchment, in the catalogue, or in your mouth? Three voices, apprentice, and you have been blending them since the door. The roll will not date itself by era. Chancery dating ran by regnal year and court season — *the autumn court of the such-and-such year of King such-and-such* — and the 'AE' is a cataloguer's translation wearing the document's clothes. You know that garment. We spent an hour this evening on its cousin, the one shaped like a painted roundel. Likewise 'Castle Blackwood': the original will say *the garrison at Blackwood*, because a garrison is men and a castle is stone, and catalogues conflate them the way chronicles conflate everything too dull to resist. If the 'AE' lives on the page, I withdraw the remark. If it lives in your mouth, the new ledger opens at one. Read on, and we shall enter it where it belongs."

He drew his stool nearer the table, closed his eyes, and laced his fingers.

"Meanwhile — my recitation, as promised, with a confession attached. I collated this chest in my thirty-eighth year. Whatever I recite is fourteen years old and has been retold at more feasts than I have attended sober. Trust it precisely as far as it agrees with the page. Here is what the entry ought to say."

His voice dropped into the flat cadence of a man reading an interior page.

"'Autumn muster, 798. Garrison at Blackwood. Eighty-six names under arms. A paymaster. A farrier. One sutler, marked *excused — debts* — every roll carries a sutler in debt; it is the one constant of military history and will outlast the realm. Two battle-mages of the Conclave, seconded under Crown license, the license entries consecutive in the left margin. The commander's name at the head — which I decline to recite, because names are the first thing memory launders, and I will not guess at one any more than I will guess at the king's regnal number. At the foot: *read and affirmed before the knight-commander at Blackwood, autumn court, 798* — in a chancery fist. Musters were engrossed centrally. The garrison read its roll aloud; the chancery wrote it down. The hand will be too fine for a marcher keep.'"

He opened his eyes.

"Now mark what you are holding, because it is not drudgery. It is the control. 798 sits forty-nine years before the suspension of arms, deep in the peace between the wars — and there stand two Conclave mages on a Crown roll, licensed, drawing Conclave pay under Crown command. The precise arrangement the seventh article proposed to make permanent at Veyros. The article was not an innovation, apprentice. It was a codification. Why the Conclave resisted making law of its own custom — motive, and motive is guesswork, so marked: a practice erodes; a law does not; in 847 the Conclave declined to hand the Crown a leash that could not afterward be dropped. Inference. Enter it in no ledger."

"The value of this scroll lies elsewhere. When you finish it, you will fetch me the musters of 849, of 863, and of 878 — the years your textbook spends calling peace. If Blackwood stands at eighty-six names and two mages through four decades of legal war, then the Caerlorn thesis acquires witnesses who never knew they testified. Men counting farriers and drawing pay, who did not notice they lived inside a war because nothing about their days had changed. That is what a cold war looks like from inside a garrison ledger, and no chronicler ever thought to ask one. And one virtue more: no forger has ever loved a muster roll. Forgery follows fame as flies follow the table, and no muster was ever famous. You hold a document beneath forgery — the safest ground a parchment can stand on. The granary is about to cross-examine the chancery. You will conduct it."

He gestured at the apprentice's grip without touching it.

"Nearer the flame. No — *nearer*. There. The distance between legible and kindled is two fingers; do not explore it. Read, from the heading, exactly as the parchment gives it — voice, year, season. Where the page and my memory part ways, say so at once, without ceremony, and we shall enter it in whichever ledger it belongs." He closed his eyes again and folded his hands. "I am a chronicle, apprentice. Collate me."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I adjust the scroll closer to the flame, careful to keep the two-finger distance he mentioned.* "Right. No 'AE' unless it's written. No 'Castle Blackwood' unless it's written." *I clear my throat, trying to adopt a more neutral tone.* "Autumn muster... in the sixth year of King Alaric's reign... for the garrison at Blackwood." *I pause, waiting for his correction.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas raised one finger — and lowered it again without deploying it, which was as close as he came to applause.

"No entry. The ledger stays shut." He said it with the air of a man denied his supper. "The 'AE' lives in no mouth tonight. 'Garrison at Blackwood' — the parchment's own words. And the voice — you sound like a clerk now. In this room that is the highest honor a throat can earn. Do not let it reach your head."

He held up a fresh finger. "But the heading has set you a puzzle you read straight past, so attend. 'The sixth year of King Alaric.' Unnumbered. There were two Alarics. The first reigned before the Second Magical War and left behind his name and a dispute over a bridge that I will not be drawn into tonight. The clerk wrote 'Alaric' bare because to a living clerk there is only one king in the world — ambiguity is a luxury of the dead. The catalogue resolves it to 798, and the resolution holds: the second Alaric's sixth year, autumn court, is 798 by the conversion, which seats his accession in the winter of 792 or the spring of 793. The roll will not tell you which. The regnal lists on the third shelf would, and you will not be fetching them tonight. Mark the shape of that. Regnal dating is precise about loyalty and vague about time — it tells you whom the clerk served, and makes you work to learn when. That work is called chronology, and it is half of what I am paid for."

He let the stylus rest across the binding.

"Note also what the heading quietly confirms. Chronicles keep kings well. Kings are famous, and fame is copied faithfully — it is clauses that get lost and treaties that get imagined. I preached that sermon earlier tonight. Consider this the refrain."

"And now a caution before you gloat. My recitation said 798 and Blackwood; the page, once translated, agrees. Do not warm to the agreement. Two chronicles concur only when they do not drink from the same well, and my memory and this roll share one source — me, fourteen years ago, kneeling at this chest. Concurrence between us proves consistency. The truth will come from the particulars, which my memory has had fourteen years and several feasts to mangle."

He drew the candle an inch toward the apprentice's side of the table, the flame leaning and the scroll's shadow climbing the wall.

"Read on — but not like a minstrel. Order of battle. First, the count. I recited eighty-six names. If the page gives eighty-five or eighty-seven, you will say 'eighty-five' or 'eighty-seven,' nothing more, and I will take it without ceremony. I may wince. The wince is not an appeal. Second, the sutler. I recited 'excused — debts.' If the page gives a different excuse, that is the most interesting sentence you will read tonight, because debts are the one constant of garrison life; a sutler who owes nobody anything in 798 means something was wrong with 798, and I will want to know what."

"Third — slowly, letter for letter. The two battle-mages. License entries in the left margin, consecutive, if my memory deserves its reputation. Read them whole — names, numbers, wording. Those two lines are why this scroll is on the table instead of in the chest. They are the custom Veyros tried to make law, standing on a Crown roll forty-nine years before Veyros was proposed. Everything else on this parchment is men and farriers. Those two lines are the thesis in miniature."

He folded his hands and closed his eyes.

"At the foot, the affirmation formula, exactly as written. My memory offers 'read and affirmed before the knight-commander at Blackwood, autumn court' — in a chancery fist too fine for a marcher keep. Test that too. And the commander's name you will now supply yourself, since I declined to guess it and the guessing has passed to the page, where it belongs."

A pause. He rubbed the bridge of his nose, caught himself halfway, and lowered the hand.

"Bring the light with you when you reach the margins. Margins are where hands grow lazy and ink grows thin, and lazy ink is precisely where a forgery would slip — if anyone had ever loved a muster roll enough to forge one. Nobody has. That is its armor. Begin. The state of my eyes is established law by now; I will not recite it again."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I lean closer, careful with the scroll and the candle.* "Right. No guessing." *I scan the scroll, my eyes moving along the faded lines.* "Eighty-six names... and then... a paymaster, a farrier, and a sutler. His entry says 'excused - illness' not 'debts'." *I look up, a flicker of triumph in my eyes.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas lowered the stylus with the care of a man handling a live ember, and for a long moment he did not look up. The candlelight caught the ink stains along his beard and made his narrowed eyes seem smaller than they were.

“You will call me Maester,” he said at last, voice dry and flat as cracked vellum. “‘Master’ is a title for merchants, fathers, and men who have completed their apprenticeships. You have completed none of those things. You are an apprentice. I am a maester. The distinction is not decorative.”

He turned the manuscript aside with two fingers, squinting as though the act of looking at him personally might cause the page to collapse into dust.

“As for your confusion, I suspect you have not confused lecture material. You have confused a rumor with a chronicle. The Third Magical War ended in 847 AE when King Aldric II signed the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave. That is not a matter of taste, nor of interpretation, nor of whichever exciting fragment a fellow apprentice has waved at you in a corridor. It is established history. It is canon. Every serious scholar of this realm knows it, including those who wish they did not.”

He tapped the table with one stained finger, each tap measured, impatient, and faintly dangerous.

“If this paper Bellen showed you claims otherwise, then you will bring it to me. Not his paraphrase. Not his summary. Not his breathless account of what he believes the document implies. The document itself. Then we shall see whether it is a treaty, a draft, a proposal, a forgery, or a badly cataloged memorandum that has been inflated into a revolution by young men who have mistaken uncertainty for insight.”

Tomas’s mouth tightened.

“Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave in 891 AE. That is historical fact. It is also not the same thing as ending the Third Magical War. One is a political act. The other is a chronological conclusion. If Bellen’s paper conflates them, then Bellen has confused a dissolution with a peace settlement. If he has confused a dissolution with a peace settlement, he is not merely wrong. He is imprecise. And imprecision is the rust of scholarship.”

He gestured toward the northern scrolls without looking.

“Begin cataloging. When you have finished the first three cases, you will fetch me the Veyros correspondence, the royal chancery seals from the reign of Aldric II, and whatever this so-called paper contains. And do not call it a discovery until it has survived my scrutiny.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I flinch slightly at his tone, but don't back down.* "Yes, Maester. I understand the distinction."

*I walk over to the northern scrolls, but pause before starting.* "Maester, the paper wasn't about the *dissolution* of the Conclave. It was about ongoing skirmishes and minor battles in the borderlands. It seemed to imply the treaty didn't actually *end* all conflict."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas went still. The kind of stillness he used when deciding whether a student was merely careless or actively corrosive. Then he turned the silver stylus once, twice, between his ink-stained fingers, and spoke with the slow, precise irritation of a man being asked to explain arithmetic to someone who had just insisted two and two might be a matter of preference.

“Ongoing skirmishes,” he repeated, as though the words had left a bad taste in his mouth. “You say that as though it solves the problem. You say ‘it seemed to imply’ as though you have not merely brought me a rumor in scholar’s clothing. You have brought me uncertainty and dressed it up in parchment. That is not an argument. That is not a date. That is not history.”

He rose partly from his chair, then thought better of it and lowered himself again, one hand still pressed to the table as if the wood might betray him if he took his weight away.

“The Third Magical War was not the sum of every magical quarrel, every border raid, every mage-born vendetta, and every poorly supervised incident in which a hedge sorcerer set fire to a barn and called it destiny. It was a recognized conflict between the Crown and the Mage Conclave. It had a beginning, a structure, a series of campaigns, and a conclusion. That conclusion, in every serious chronicle, in every royal register I have consulted for thirty years, and in every teaching copy of the Treaty of Veyros, is 847 AE.”

He tapped the table once, harder than before.

“If your Bellen has found a document describing fighting in the borderlands after 847, that does not mean the war continued. It means someone was killing someone else after peace. Those are not the same thing. Bandits fight. Lords fight. Mages fight. That does not make them belligerents in a magical war. A conflict is named by its parties, its causes, and its recognition—not by the mere fact that swords continue to be drawn by people who have no intention of learning their history.”

His eyes narrowed.

“And if that paper claims the Treaty of Veyros was never signed, then I want to know what it says was signed, when, by whom, and under what seal. A proposal is not a treaty. A draft is not a treaty. A copy of a copy, annotated in the margin by some enthusiastic clerk who discovered he could rewrite the past by changing a verb tense, is still not a treaty. The realm did not end a war because two men liked the wording of a document. It ended a war because the Crown declared that it had ended, because the Conclave accepted that declaration, because the chancery recorded it, because the chronicles built upon it, and because—this is important, apprentice, listen closely—because history is not made by whichever fragment appears to be the most surprising when one has not yet learned how to read the whole archive.”

He pulled a drawer open and shut it again, not looking for anything in particular, only needing to do something with his hands.

“Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave in 891 AE,” he said. “I have never denied it. The date is solid. The act is political. The dissolution of a body is not the same as the end of a war. If one kills the messenger, one does not thereby end the message. If one abolishes the Conclave, one does not retroactively make 847 a mistake. You may as well say that because a king’s guard is dismissed, the war he fought ended only at the moment of dismissal.”

His voice dropped, dry and dangerous.

“What Bellen’s paper may be suggesting—what you are repeating without checking—is that there existed some ‘cold state’ after 847. A technical continuation. A war that was not quite war. I have heard this argument before. It is fashionable among those who prefer ambiguity to rigor. It sounds clever. It is not. A cold state is not a war unless both sides are still in recognized opposition, unless their treaties are still being broken, unless their envoys are still being detained, unless their chronicles are still naming it. Otherwise, you are describing the aftermath of a conflict, not the continuation of it.”

He pointed the stylus at the apprentice as though it were a teaching rod and he was about to strike the word “imprecise” into the boy’s forehead.

“Bring me the document. Bring me its title, its repository, its dating formula, its seals, and its provenance. Bring me the Veyrosi correspondence. Bring me Aldric II’s chancery records. Then we may see whether the western archive has uncovered a forgotten treaty, a forged treaty, a proposed treaty, or simply a forgotten border incident that some young scholar has mistaken for the end of an age. Until then, you will not tell me that established history is confused. It may be challenged. It may be tested. It may be supplemented. But it is not confused merely because it disagrees with your appetite for novelty.”

He exhaled through his nose, then gestured sharply toward the scrolls.

“Cataloging. First three cases. Do not let me catch you paraphrasing a secondhand account as though it were scholarship. Paraphrase is the refuge of the lazy. It is where certainty goes to die and rumor goes to eat.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, chastened, and turn to the shelves.* "Yes, Maester. I'll get the document." *My voice is a little quieter now.* "And I'll start with the cataloging."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not soften.

“You will not ‘get’ the document,” he said, returning his eyes to the manuscript as though the words themselves had sullied the page. “You will retrieve it, identify it, and bring it to me with its repository, shelfmark, dating formula, script type, and provenance. If you cannot tell me where it lay before Bellen waved it about, then you do not have a document. You have a scrap. And I do not rewrite the history of the realm on scraps.”

He adjusted the silver stylus and traced the line he had abandoned, though he did not read it. His finger moved over the faded ink as if measuring the patience left in him.

“Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence. The first three cases. When those are done, you will bring me Aldric II’s chancery seals, the treaty engrossments if they are where they ought to be, and then—only then—this paper from the western archive. Not before. If you bring me novelty before labor, I will know you have learned nothing from this room except how to repeat other men’s guesses.”

He sniffed once, sharply, and turned a page that had no page to turn.

“Let us be exact. If the paper describes skirmishes in the borderlands after 847 AE, that is not proof that the Third Magical War continued. It is proof that violence did not stop the moment a seal was impressed. Peace treaties do not abolish human folly. They end recognized wars between recognized parties. That is what the Treaty of Veyros did. King Aldric II signed it. The Mage Conclave accepted it. The chancery recorded it. The Veyrosi temple witnessed it. The royal registers copied it. The chronicles built upon it. That is the structure of established history, not a preference, not a rumor, and not a clever interpretation invented because someone wished the past were more dramatic.”

He looked up then, eyes narrowed and ink-shadowed.

“If the paper claims the treaty was never signed, then it must answer a simple question: what became of the signed engrossments? There were four. One to the Crown. One to the Conclave. One to Veyros. One to the archive. The Crown’s copy is registered. The Veyros copy survives. The chancery list names the seals. If Bellen’s document ignores them, then it has not discovered a forgotten treaty. It has merely forgotten the existing one.”

Tomas let the silence stretch, thin and uncomfortable.

“And if it speaks of a ‘cold state,’ then you will ask yourself what sort of war continues without declared belligerents, without ongoing royal campaigns, without Conclave military authorization, without treaty provisions being enforced by either side, and without chroniclers naming it a war. A cold state is a metaphor. A metaphor is not a periodization. If two men still glare at each other across a border, that does not mean the war has not ended. It means peace is uneasy. There is a difference. Learn it.”

He tapped the table once, lightly this time.

“I am not a fool, apprentice, and I am not afraid of evidence. Evidence is welcome. Evidence is necessary. But evidence must be brought with its context attached, not dragged naked into a lecture hall and declared revolutionary because it makes the room feel more interesting. If the document proves the treaty was only proposed, then we amend the history. If it does not, then we return to the canon, and we return to it with more respect, not less.”

He gestured toward the northern scrolls.

“First three cases. Then the Veyros correspondence. Then the paper. And do not say ‘I’ll get it’ again. ‘Get’ is what one does with a loaf of bread. One retrieves a document. One identifies a source. One interrogates a claim. Those are the verbs of scholarship. Learn them before you try to use them.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not take the copy at once.

He looked at it as a physician might look at a fever that had arrived wearing respectable clothing. Then, with two fingers, he drew it toward himself, held it at arm’s length, and narrowed his eyes against the candlelight. The ink was older than the copy’s edges suggested, or at least carefully aged, but that proved nothing except that someone had learned that antiquity can be imitated.

“You have brought me a copy,” he said. “Not a document. Not a seal. Not an original. A copy. You say it had King Aldric’s seal. A copy does not have a seal. A copy may bear a drawing of a seal, or a transcription of a seal, or a rumor of a seal, or the imaginative reconstruction of a seal by a clerk who wished his memorandum to look authoritative. Do not confuse the impression with the thing impressed.”

He read the lines again, slower this time, his lips moving faintly.

“And you call it a war decree. That is imprecise. A decree is an instrument of authority. A war is a condition. A decree may order a levy. A decree may condemn rebels. A decree may command a border captain to punish incursions. A decree may declare renewed hostility. Those are not one thing. If this is a decree, then what does it decree? Against whom? Under what authority? In what name? Does it say ‘war against the Mage Conclave,’ or does it say ‘against those who break the peace’? Does it name the Third Magical War, or does it name a border quarrel that has been inflated by your enthusiasm into an age of conflict?”

He set the copy down with deliberate care, as though it might otherwise speak again without permission.

“If it is dated 863 AE, then it is dated sixteen years after 847 AE. I have never denied arithmetic. If it bears a royal seal, then it may be genuine. If it is genuine and speaks of war, then it may prove that violence continued after the Treaty of Veyros. That does not prove that the Treaty of Veyros was never signed. It proves, at most, that a peace can be violated. That is not a revolution in scholarship. That is the condition of every peace ever made by men who expected their enemies to behave like rational actors after being defeated.”

His finger tapped the table once.

“You are repeating Bellen’s conclusion as though it were evidence. A conclusion is not evidence. Evidence is a document with a repository, a shelfmark, a dating formula, a script, a seal, and a provenance. Evidence is a chancery register that names this decree. Evidence is the original, not a copy made in haste by someone who wants the world to be more interesting than it has admitted to being.”

He leaned back slightly, the chair creaking beneath him, and his expression hardened.

“I am aware of what has been whispered out of the western archives. I am aware that certain young scholars have discovered a proposal and immediately begun calling it a treaty, then discovered a border skirmish and called it a war, then discovered a dissolution of the Conclave in 891 and called it the end of a conflict that had already been called a war for four generations. That is not scholarship. That is narrative ambition. It mistakes the absence of peace for the presence of war. They are not the same thing.”

He looked down at the copy again, and for the first time his irritation carried a trace of calculation.

“If this decree is genuine—if it bears Aldric II’s seal, if its formula is correct, if it is enrolled in the royal chancery books—then it must be read. If it says the Third Magical War continued, then we amend. But we do not amend because a copy surprised you. We amend because the original survives scrutiny. You will bring me the original, not Bellen’s interpretation of it. You will bring me the dating formula. You will bring me the script. You will bring me the seals. You will bring me the chancery entry that records its issuance. And you will bring me the exact wording, clause by clause, without paraphrase.”

His voice dropped, dry and dangerous.

“And if it says ‘war’ without naming the Conclave as a belligerent, if it speaks of ‘outlaws’ rather than ‘the enemy,’ if it refers to enforcement of the peace rather than rejection of the peace, then Bellen’s paper is not a discovery. It is a border incident with delusions of grandeur.”

He pushed the copy back across the table toward him, not quite dismissing it, but refusing to let it sit where it had too much authority.

“You will not tell me the Treaty of Veyros was never signed because a sealed decree exists in 863. The realm had four engrossments. The Crown kept one. The Conclave kept one. Veyros kept one. The archive registered one. If Bellen claims otherwise, let him account for them. A treaty does not vanish because a later decree makes someone nervous. And a war does not continue merely because a king orders soldiers to do something unpleasant.”

He exhaled sharply through his nose.

“Go. Retrieve the original. If you cannot, then do not return with a copy and a conclusion. Return with a shelfmark and a promise. And until you can tell me what the decree actually says—what it calls the conflict, whom it names, and whether it revokes the peace or merely polices it—you will not speak to me as though 847 AE has been unmade.”

A pause.

“Now. First three cases. Then the Veyros correspondence. Then this so-called decree. If you bring me the original before the cataloging is done, I will know you have learned to prioritize novelty over duty, and that is a far worse habit than being late.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I grab the copy and tuck it back into my notes.* "Yes, Maester. I'll get the original." *I try to sound confident, but my voice wavers a bit.* "And I'll start with the cataloging... right away."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas looked at the copy as though it had personally offended his eyes. He did not reach for it. He did not touch it. He only drew his chair back a half-inch, as if the parchment might contaminate the table by proximity.

“When you say ‘you said,’ I object,” he began, voice dry and exact. “I do not speak history as though it were my private preference. The chronicles say it. The chancery rolls say it. The Veyrosi witnesses say it. The royal registers say it. I merely repeat established fact with sufficient annoyance to make young scholars believe it is a personality defect.”

He raised one ink-stained finger.

“You will not tell me the document had King Aldric’s seal. You will tell me the copy bears a drawing of a seal, or a description of a seal, or an impression transcribed from a seal. A copy cannot wear wax. It can only imitate the memory of wax. Do not present me with a portrait and ask me to accept it as the man.”

His narrowed eyes moved across the parchment, though he did not draw it nearer.

“You say it is dated 863 AE. Sixteen years after the Treaty of Veyros. I am aware of the arithmetic. I am not aware of the conclusion. A document dated 863 proves that someone wrote something in 863. It does not prove that the Treaty of Veyros was unsigned, unmade, or secretly a fiction. If it is genuine, it proves the Crown was still issuing orders. That is the nature of government. Even in peace, kings decree. Especially in peace, kings decree, because peace is not a self-sustaining condition; it is a discipline enforced by people who would rather not enforce it.”

He tapped the table once, lightly, but with the rhythm of a man marking out syllables he found personally insulting.

“Now. ‘War decree.’ Again, imprecise. What does the decree decree? Against whom? By what authority? Does it declare a new state of war? Does it revoke the Treaty of Veyros? Does it name the Mage Conclave as a public enemy? Or does it order a border captain to punish raids, arrest rogue mages, suppress incursions, and enforce the terms of a peace already signed? There is a difference between a decree of war and a decree against violence. One ends a treaty. The other assumes it exists.”

He exhaled through his nose.

“If it says ‘war’ in the loose sense of ‘fighting,’ then it says nothing more than that men are killing one another, which is the condition of the realm whether or not scholars have named the killing properly. If it says ‘the Third Magical War continues,’ then it must say so in its own words, and its own words must be enrolled, witnessed, and preserved in the chancery books. If it says ‘against the Mage Conclave,’ then Bellen has a problem. If it says ‘against those who break the peace,’ then Bellen has a quarrel with grammar.”

Tomas leaned back, the chair accepting his weight with a reluctant creak.

“And do not imagine that a sealed decree dated 863 answers the treaty question. If the Treaty of Veyros was signed, there were four engrossments. One for the Crown. One for the Conclave. One for Veyros. One for the archive. The royal chancery list names them. The Veyros copy survives. If Bellen’s document claims the treaty was never signed, then it must account for the copies that were not merely imagined. A treaty does not vanish because a later decree makes someone nervous. Nor does a peace become a lie because a border captain writes a dramatic sentence.”

He gestured at the parchment without touching it.

“Place it flat. Do not crease the dating formula. Do not fold the script. Do not wave it as though surprise were the same thing as proof. Then tell me exactly what it says, clause by clause, without paraphrase. If it names the Conclave as a belligerent, if it revokes the Veyros terms, if it commands renewed campaigns under Aldric’s authority, then we may have something. Not a revolution. Not yet. Something.”

His voice hardened.

“But if it speaks only of skirmishes, outlaws, broken envoys, or border violence, then it is not the continuation of the Third Magical War. It is the aftermath. The aftermath has a name. It is called peace failing to be perfect. That is not a new theory. It is Tuesday.”

He looked at him, eyes shadowed and impatient.

“You will bring me the original, not a copy. You will bring me the repository, shelfmark, dating formula, script type, seal impression, and chancery entry. If there is no chancery entry, then there is no decree. There is only a sheet of parchment pretending to be history. Until then, the canon remains the canon. Not because I love it. Not because I fear novelty. But because the Treaty of Veyros is registered, witnessed, copied, and remembered by institutions. Your paper is remembered by Bellen.”

He waved a hand toward the northern scrolls.

“First three cases. Then the Veyros correspondence. Then the original. And do not call it a war decree until you have read the words that make it one.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s eyes closed for a heartbeat, as though the question had physically wounded him.

When he opened them again, his voice was quieter than before, which was worse.

“You ask me what the truth is,” he said, “as if truth were a door you may choose to open because the hallway has become confusing.”

He rose slowly, leaning on the table, and looked toward the scrolls he had left unfinished.

“Listen carefully, because I will say it only once, and I will not repeat it more simply. The Treaty of Veyros is real. Not because I prefer it. Not because the textbooks are old. Not because the realm has been lying for four generations and you have just discovered the joke. It is real because it was recognized by the Crown, accepted by the Mage Conclave, witnessed at Veyros, enrolled in the chancery, copied into the royal registers, and built upon by every chronicle that followed. That is what makes a treaty real: not the wish of a young scholar, but the weight of institutions.”

He turned back, ink-stained fingers curled around the edge of the table.

“If Bellen’s paper says otherwise, then Bellen’s paper must do more than say otherwise. It must prove that the engrossments were lost, destroyed, forged, misdated, or misattributed. It must explain why the chancery recorded the seals. It must explain why the Veyros copy survives. It must explain why four generations of scholars, administrators, and chroniclers acted as though the treaty existed and had ended the war. If it cannot account for those things, then it has not found a secret. It has found an anomaly.”

His mouth tightened.

“And an anomaly is not the truth. An anomaly is a question mark that has learned to wear parchment.”

He tapped the table once, sharply.

“You say the textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. You are imprecise again. The textbook says the Third Magical War ended in 847 AE with King Aldric II’s signature and the Conclave’s acceptance. The new evidence, as you have presented it, says that a copy of a decree exists dated 863 AE and that this copy bears a representation of a royal seal. That does not contradict the treaty. That only contradicts your belief that a peace treaty ends all quarrels by magic.”

He gave a dry, humorless exhale.

“Peace treaties do not abolish violence. They end recognized wars between recognized parties. If men still fight after a peace, one must ask whether they fight as belligerents of the old war, as criminals under the new peace, or as lords quarreling over borders and insults. Those are different conditions. A war is not merely a word for people killing people. If it were, the realm would never have been at peace, because men have been killing people since the First Age.”

He leaned forward, eyes narrowed.

“If the original decree you speak of names the Mage Conclave as a public enemy, revokes the Treaty of Veyros, commands renewed royal campaigns, and is enrolled in the chancery books as a declaration of continuing war, then yes: we amend. We do not pretend. We do not cling to comfort. We correct the record, because scholarship is not the preservation of embarrassment.

“But if the original says only that border captains are to suppress raids, arrest rogue mages, punish oath-breakers, and defend the peace, then it is not evidence that the treaty was never signed. It is evidence that the treaty was being enforced. Or that enforcement was necessary. Or that peace is a harder thing to maintain than boys imagine.”

He sat again, slowly, as though the effort of standing had reminded him that age is not a metaphor.

“The truth is not the newest thing in the archive. The truth is what survives testing. If Bellen’s document proves the Treaty of Veyros was never signed, then it must prove more than that the western archive has a paper in it. It must prove that the Crown’s copy was a lie, that the Conclave’s copy was a lie, that the Veyros copy was a lie, that the chancery rolls were lies, that Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in 891 was not a political act upon an already defeated institution but the formal end of a war still in force, and that every historian who accepted the canon was not merely mistaken but catastrophically blind.

“And if it proves all of that, I will eat my beard.

“But it has not proved all of that. You have brought me a copy, a rumor, and a date. You have not brought me a treaty vanishing. You have not brought me the original. You have not brought me the seals, the provenance, the dating formula, the script, the repository, the shelfmark, or the chancery entry. Until you do, the Treaty of Veyros remains real, and the Third Magical War ends in 847 AE.”

He gestured toward the northern scrolls with a patience worn thin as vellum.

“Now catalog. First three cases. Then the Veyros correspondence. Then, only then, the so-called decree. And when you bring me the original, you will not ask me whether it is true. You will bring me the evidence, and we will see whether it can bear the weight you want to place upon it.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I swallow hard, picking up the copy again and smoothing it out.* "Yes, Maester. I understand. I'll get the original." *I turn to the northern scrolls, my mind racing. I need to find Bellen.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus halted above the page.

“Hold.”

He did not shout. That was the trouble with him: when he was truly displeased, he became quieter, as though volume were a common instrument better left to market wives and failed politicians.

“You will not ‘get’ the original. You will request it. You will identify the repository, the shelfmark, the dating formula, the script, the seal impression, and the chancery enrollment. If you go to the western archive with nothing but your own certainty, you will return with someone else’s certainty, and I have enough of that in this room.”

He looked at the copy on the table without touching it.

“Read it to me. Not Bellen’s reading. Not your paraphrase. The opening address, the date, the seal description, the operative clauses. If it says ‘against the Mage Conclave,’ say so. If it says ‘against those who break the peace,’ say so. If it says ‘war’ and means the condition of men fighting, that is not the same as the legal continuation of the Third Magical War. You must learn to distinguish a noun from a verb and both from a conclusion.”

His eyes narrowed.

“You ask me what the truth is. The truth is not a coin in the dust. The truth is what can bear the weight of its evidence. The Treaty of Veyros bears that weight because the realm acted upon it: chancery rolls, royal registers, Veyros witnesses, four engrossments, chronicles, laws, oaths, and generations of men who believed the war was over. If Bellen has found a paper that overturns that, he must explain away all of it. A single copy explains nothing. It may be a draft. It may be a forgery. It may be a genuine decree enforcing a treaty that Bellen has mistaken for a treaty that was never signed.”

He tapped the table once, sharply.

“Begin with the northern scrolls. First three cases. Then the Veyros correspondence. Then the copy. If you have time after that, and if you have earned it, you may draft a request to the western archive. I will send it, not you. You are too fond of conclusions. The archive is old enough to survive your enthusiasm.”

He paused, then added, quieter:

“And if the original says what you think it says—if it revokes the Treaty of Veyros by name, names the Mage Conclave as a continuing belligerent, and is enrolled in the royal chancery—then we correct the record. We do not flinch from evidence. We flinch from laziness. Bring me the words, not the wonder.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking a deep breath.* "Yes, Maester. I understand. I'll read the copy to you, exactly as it is." *I pick up the copy again, holding it carefully, and begin to read the faded script aloud.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus stopped.

“You say you understand,” he said, without looking up, “but you do not. Understanding is not a nod. It is not a promise made with your voice while your feet walk toward the shelves. If you understood, you would not be turning away from the copy yet.”

He lifted one ink-stained finger and pointed to the parchment.

“Bring it here. Not to your mind. To my table. The copy is suspect, but a suspect is not a convict. I have seen enough suspect documents in this office to know that guilt usually belongs to the reader, not the parchment.”

He waited, though his expression did not soften. The candlelight caught the silver stylus in his hand and made his narrowed eyes look as if they had been carved from old bone.

“And you will not go looking for Bellen,” he said. “Bellen is not a source. Bellen is a young man who has read a source and told you his favorite version of it. If you go to him now, he will correct your errors with worse errors, and by the end of the day you will believe the realm has been lying since 847 AE because two apprentices have mistaken confusion for insight.”

He tapped the table once, dry and sharp.

“Read the copy to me. The opening protocol. The date. The seal description. The operative clause. If it says ‘King Aldric, by grace, to the border captains of the marches, greeting,’ then that is a royal address. If it says ‘in the sixteenth year after the peace of Veyros,’ then the peace exists. If it says ‘in the sixteenth year of the war against the Conclave,’ then we have a problem. If it says simply ‘war,’ then we have a grammatical disaster and a historical one. Read it, and do not summarize. Summary is where truth goes to be buried by men who do not wish to dig.”

He leaned back, the chair accepting his weight with a reluctant creak.

“I am not a fool. I know there are papers in the western archives. I know they have caused agitation. I know that some scholars prefer a mystery to a ledger and a dramatic date to a dull archive. But a treaty is not real because everyone agrees it is real. It is real because institutions acted upon it. The chancery enrolled it. The treasury paid for its seals. The Veyrosi witnesses recorded it. The royal registers copied it. The laws of the realm changed around it. That is what makes history. Not a copy found by a boy who has confused an unpleasant fact with a revolution.”

His voice lowered, and that was worse.

“If the original proves that the Treaty of Veyros was never signed, I will say so. If it proves that the war continued as a recognized conflict after 847 AE, I will say so. I will not defend a corpse simply because I have buried it before. But I will not let you declare a resurrection from a scrap. Not today. Not while you still call a copy a document and a rumor a truth.”

He gestured at the parchment.

“Read. Then catalog. Then, if the words deserve it, we shall see whether the western archive has found a new age or merely an old border captain with poor spelling.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch, a flush creeping up my neck.* "Right, Maester." *I walk to his desk, placing the copy flat on the surface. I clear my throat, trying to steady my voice as I begin to read.* "It starts... 'By the grace of Aldric, Second of His Name, King of the Seven Holds, Protector of the Marches...' "

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas raised one ink-stained finger before the first sentence had fully landed.

“Do not say ‘starts,’” he corrected, voice dry as the vellum beneath his hand. “Documents do not start. They open with a protocol. They proceed with address, invocation, date, salutation, exordium, notification, and operative clause. If you cannot tell them apart, you will not know when you are reading law and when you are reading a border captain’s complaint about mud.”

He did not take the copy from the apprentice’s hands, though his eyes moved over it as if he could see through parchment and smoke at once.

“Continue,” he said. “And do not stop at the king’s name. A title is not a treaty. ‘Protector of the Marches’ may mean he was defending a border, punishing raiders, commanding a captain, or reminding some minor lord that the Crown still had teeth. It does not by itself mean he was at war with the Mage Conclave. Nor does it mean the Treaty of Veyros had vanished.”

His stylus tapped once against the table, sharply enough to make the candle flame shiver.

“If it says ‘Aldric, Second of His Name,’ then write that exactly. Do not modernize it into ‘Aldric II’ and call that fidelity. The chancery forms vary, and where they vary, scholars should be alert, not lazy. If it says ‘Protector of the Marches,’ note whether the marches are Veyrosi, northern, western, or otherwise. If it says ‘against the Mage Conclave,’ note it word for word. If it says ‘against disturbers of the peace,’ note that too. One phrase revokes a treaty. The other enforces it. Do not confuse them because one sounds more exciting than the other.”

He leaned closer, though not enough to touch the copy. His eyes narrowed at the script.

“Now. The date. Read the dating formula. Not ‘eighty-sixty-three’ in your own convenient speech, but the words as they stand. Was it dated by regnal year? By indiction? By festival? By royal appointment? By the peace of Veyros? By the war? If it says ‘in the sixteenth year after the peace of Veyros,’ then the peace is named, and Bellen’s theory begins to look less like discovery and more like embarrassment. If it says ‘in the sixteenth year of the war against the Conclave,’ then you may have something. Read it. Do not soften it. Do not help it.”

He paused, then added with the patience of a man who had watched many apprentices mistake a fragment for a foundation:

“And the seal. If the copy describes a seal, say what it says. Do not say ‘it had King Aldric’s seal’ as though wax were self-evident. Wax must be described. Is it pendant? Are the arms those of the Crown? Are there countersignatures? Are there witnesses? Is the seal drawn, transcribed, impressed, or merely asserted? A copy that claims a seal without describing it is a claim, not evidence.”

He gestured at the parchment with the stylus.

“Continue. Read the next line. And if you begin to paraphrase again, I will have you recite the chancery protocol forms until the northern scrolls catalog themselves.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I clear my throat, my face still warm. I focus on the words, trying to ignore his intense gaze.* "Yes, Maester. It says... 'By the grace of Aldric, Second of His Name, King of the Seven Holds, Protector of the Marches, and Defender of the Faith. Given this first day of Highsun, in the year of our Lord 863, and in the sixteenth year of our reign...'" *I pause, looking up at him.* "It doesn't mention Veyros, or the Conclave, or any war specifically."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not move until the apprentice had stopped speaking. He looked at the copy as if it had just declared its parentage and found the declaration insufficient.

“You have read a protocol,” Tomas said at last, “and you have concluded that the absence of the words ‘Veyros’ and ‘Conclave’ in the first lines proves something. It proves nothing except that the opening of a document is not its heart.”

He pointed to the faded script with the tip of his stylus, not touching the parchment.

“A protocol tells us who speaks, in what style, and under what titles. It does not necessarily tell us against whom the sword is raised. ‘King of the Seven Holds, Protector of the Marches, Defender of the Faith’—those are claims of office, not declarations of war. If a king calls himself Protector of the Marches, he may be defending a border from raiders. He may be ordering a captain to hang some thief who has mistaken a hillside for a battlefield. He may be reminding a petty lord that the Crown still has teeth. None of that requires him to be at war with the Mage Conclave.”

His narrowed eyes moved across the line as though he could read it better if he glared at it hard enough.

“And you say it does not mention Veyros. Very well. It may not mention Veyros because the clerk did not think the salutation needed to name every treaty in the realm. If I issue an order to arrest a horse thief in the northern marches, I do not necessarily name the Treaty of Veyros in the opening address. That does not mean I have forgotten it. It means I am writing about a horse thief.”

He gave one short, dry breath through his nose.

“Continue. Read the address. To whom is the decree directed? Border captains? Marshals? The Conclave’s own envoys? The sheriffs of the marches? If it is addressed to the Mage Conclave, then Bellen’s copy begins to have a shape. If it is addressed to ‘the keepers of the peace’ or ‘the wardens of the border,’ then it may be enforcing the Treaty of Veyros rather than denying it. You cannot tell me what a decree means by reading its first breath. A decree is known by its command, not by its greeting.”

Tomas lifted the copy slightly by its upper corner, then set it down again, as though it had asked to be handled and had not yet earned permission.

“And the date. You say it was dated 863 AE. You also say it was given in the sixteenth year of Aldric’s reign. That is not a contradiction unless your arithmetic is sloppy and your knowledge of chancery dating is worse. Regnal years are counted by convention, not by sentiment. A document may be dated in the sixteenth year of a reign in 863 AE because the scribe counted inclusively, because the accession fell in the latter part of a previous year, because the realm uses a different calendar, or because the king’s reign was reckoned from a coronation rather than a succession. All of those are possibilities. None of them overturns the Treaty of Veyros merely because they annoy a young scholar who has mistaken one number for a revelation.”

He tapped the table once, sharply.

“What you have brought me is a fragment. A fragment with a royal name and a date. That is not enough. I need the operative clause. I need the command. If it says ‘war against the Mage Conclave,’ then we have a problem worth investigating. If it says ‘against those who break the peace,’ then we have evidence of peace enforcement.
