If it says ‘against disturbers of the marches,’ then we have border violence. If it says only ‘war’ in the loose sense of fighting, then it proves that men were killing one another in 863 AE, which is less surprising than it sounds and far less significant than Bellen believes.”

Tomas leaned back, eyes still fixed on the copy.

“You must also give me the seal description. You said the original had King Aldric’s seal. This copy says ‘Given this first day of Highsun’ and stops before it has earned the right to be called authoritative. Where is the seal? Is it described as pendant? Is it impressed on wax? Are the arms of the Crown shown? Are there countersignatures? Are there witnesses? A copy that claims a seal without describing it is like a man who claims to have seen a dragon without telling whether it had wings. He may be honest. He may also be confused, lying, or too excited to distinguish the shape of a lizard from the shape of history.”

His voice lowered, dry and exact.

“Do not tell me what it is not. Read what it is. Read the next clause. Read the witness list if there is one. Read the chancery endorsement, if the copy preserves it. If the original is enrolled in the royal registers, then its date, its authority, and its scope become known. If it is not enrolled, then it may be a draft, a private commission, a local order, a forgery, or a genuine document that never became state policy. Those are different things. They are not interchangeable merely because a young man finds the word ‘decree’ exciting.”

He gestured at the parchment.

“And when you have read it, do not ask me whether it disproves the treaty. Ask me what it actually commands. The Treaty of Veyros is not real because a textbook prints it in bold. It is real because the realm acted upon it. The Crown acted upon it. The Conclave acted upon it. The chancery enrolled it. The Veyrosi witnesses recorded it. The royal registers copied it. Laws changed around it. Campaigns ended because of it. If Bellen has found a paper that overturns all of that, let him explain not only why the treaty is absent from a salutation, but why four engrossments, four sets of witnesses, and generations of administrators were all fooled by a document that never existed.”

Tomas’s mouth tightened.

“Until then, this copy is not evidence that the Treaty of Veyros was never signed. It is evidence that someone wrote a decree in 863 AE. That is a date, not a discovery. A date without context is only a number wearing parchment like a disguise.”

He looked at the apprentice, or rather at the space near the apprentice where the copy had been placed, because his eyes had learned to distrust the world when the world insisted on being small and blurry at once.

“Read the next line,” Tomas said. “The address. Then the command. Then the seal, if there is one. And if you summarize again, I will have you transcribe the chancery forms for a hundred years of royal decrees until you learn that the difference between a draft and an engrossment is not a matter of opinion. It is a matter of law, wax, and patience.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to ignore the heat in my cheeks.* "Yes, Maester. The next line says: 'To all loyal subjects and border captains in the Western Marches, greetings and urgent command.'" *I pause, glancing up at him again, hoping for a flicker of approval, but his expression remains stern.* "It doesn't mention the Conclave, but it does say 'urgent command.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's stylus hovered above the table for a long, still moment.

"You say it *doesn't mention* the Conclave," he repeated, and the emphasis on *doesn't* was surgical. "You are telling me that the absence of a word is evidence. That the silence of a salutation speaks louder than the speech of a command. That because a clerk in 863 AE did not think to write 'Mage Conclave' in the address line of a letter to border captains, the Conclave must therefore have never existed in 847, the treaty must therefore have been a fiction, and the war must therefore have raged on in some secret, unnamed, unrecorded form for forty-four more years."

He set the stylus down with the care of a man placing a scalpel on a tray between cuts.

"Listen to yourself. 'It doesn't mention.' 'It doesn't say.' 'It doesn't specifically name.' You are building a revolution on what is *not* written. I have read a thousand chancery documents in this life, apprentice, and not one of them names every treaty, every institution, every possible antagonist in its greeting. If I address a letter to the sheriffs of the northern marches and do not mention the Treaty of Veyros, it does not follow that I have forgotten it, revoked it, or never signed it. It follows that I am writing about the northern marches."

He leaned forward, though only slightly, as if the parchment might yield its secrets if he simply looked at it with enough contempt.

"Now. The address itself. 'To all loyal subjects and border captains in the Western Marches.' Read that again. *Loyal subjects.* Not 'the enemy.' Not 'the Conclave.' Not 'the rebels of the western holds.' *Loyal subjects.* A king does not address his opponents as loyal subjects. He addresses his own people. He commands his own officers. That is the language of administration, of governance, of a sovereign speaking to those who already owe him obedience."

His ink-stained finger traced the line without touching the vellum.

"And 'border captains.' Not 'marshals of the realm.' Not 'generals of the campaign.' Not 'the army of the Crown, arrayed for war.' *Border captains.* Men who patrol a line. Men who inspect a pass. Men who hang a thief at the gate and write a letter about it. If this were a declaration of renewed war against the Mage Conclave, it would be addressed to a *commander*, a *marshal*, a *general*, a *lord lieutenant*. It would speak of *levies*, of *campaigns*, of *the field*. It would not speak of border captains as though the matter at hand were a customs dispute with slightly more blood."

He paused. The candle guttered. His eyes, narrowed and shadowed, moved to the apprentice's face.

"And you say 'urgent command.' You say it as though 'urgent' were a word that changes the nature of a document. It does not. 'Urgent command' is a chancery formula. It appears in orders to repair a bridge before the autumn floods. It appears in orders to arrest a lord who has detained a royal envoy. It appears in orders to muster a garrison because some hedge sorcerer has set fire to a granary and the border captain has written a panicked letter and the king's clerk has decided that *greetings* alone will not suffice."

He tapped the table once, lightly.

"'Urgent command' does not mean 'war.' It means 'do this before it becomes a war, which is precisely the purpose of having a peace in the first place.' The Treaty of Veyros exists. The peace is in force. And something has happened in the Western Marches that requires the king to remind his border captains that they are, in fact, supposed to be *doing their jobs.*"

His voice dropped. Not softer. Sharper. The way a blade is sharper when it is drawn slowly.

"You are hoping," he said, "that I will praise you for reading a line. You looked at me when you said 'urgent command' as though you had handed me the key to a locked age. You did not. You handed me the first half of a sentence. The operative clause is the *second* half. The command is not in the greeting. The command is in the *order.* What does the king tell these border captains to *do?* Does he tell them to march on the Conclave? Does he tell them to arrest rogue mages operating outside the treaty's terms? Does he tell them to suppress a raid by some unnamed lord who has mistaken a border for an invitation?"

He raised the stylus again, pointing it at the parchment.

"Read the next clause. The *operative* clause. The command itself. And while you read, do not look at me for approval. I will not give it. If the document says what you hope it says, I will say so. If it says what I expect it says, I will say so. But I will not nod at a boy who has read a salutation and believes he has read a war."

He settled back into his chair, one hand resting on the arm as though the wood were a patient he might, with effort, be gentle with.

"And note the geography," he added, quieter now, almost to himself. "The *Western* Marches. Not the northern marches. Not the Veyrosi border. Not the heartland. The Western Marches. If the Third Magical War had continued after 847, the fighting would not be confined to a western border. The Mage Conclave held seats in the capital. Their towers stood in the Veyrosi marches. Their envoys moved through the northern passes. A war against them is not a war against the Western Marches. A war against the Western Marches is a war against a *place*, and the Conclave was not a place. The Conclave was an *institution.* You cannot march on an institution. You can dissolve it. You did. In 891. But that is a different thing."

His eyes narrowed.

"Read the command, apprentice. And read it slowly. I am old, my eyes are failing, and I will not be made to guess at the shape of history because you are too eager to tell me what the document means before you have told me what it *says.*"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I grit my teeth, a fresh wave of frustration washing over me. He's not going to make this easy.* "Yes, Maester." *I focus on the words again, determined not to give him any more reason to criticize.* "It reads: '...to secure the peace, apprehend those who violate the King's law within said marches, and to suppress all unlawful magical incursions with prejudice.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set his silver stylus down with a sharp click against the oak. He lifted his head, squinting through the haze of candle smoke and the blur of his own failing eyes, his ink-stained beard twitching at the corner.

“Confused you,” he said, flat and dry. “No. You were not confused; you were persuaded by sloppy rhetoric and sloppier scholarship. Bellen has always possessed more enthusiasm than precision, and this ‘paper’ of his is no exception.”

He pushed the manuscript aside and folded his ink-blackened fingers atop the table.

“The Third Magical War ended in eight hundred and forty-seven Anno Epochi. That is not interpretation. That is record. The Treaty of Veyros was signed. King Aldric II affixed his seal. The Mage Conclave ratified it. To claim otherwise is to mistake preliminary drafts for executed instruments—which, I suspect, is precisely what these so-called western documents are. Proposals. Discussions. Parchments that never superseded the binding treaty.”

His voice grew thin and grating, the tone he used when correcting a gross categorical error.

“And even if—if—we were to entertain this fantasy of a ‘cold state,’ you commit a fundamental imprecision. A war without hostilities is not a war continuing; it is a peace imperfectly maintained. The Conclave’s dissolution in eight hundred ninety-one was an administrative afterthought, the tidying of an institution that had already operated under treaty obligations for forty-four years. Do not conflate the extinction of a body with the conclusion of a conflict. The conflict concluded in eight hundred forty-seven. The realm knew it. The crown knew it. Every reputable scholar knows it.”

He gestured irritably toward the heap of northern scrolls.

“Now. Catalog. And leave Bellen’s sensationalism where it belongs—in the midden heap of revisionist provocation.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinched a little at his sharp tone, but I stood my ground.* "But Master, the document Bellen showed me was a signed decree from the then-Emperor, dated 890, discussing ongoing skirmishes in the Dragon's Teeth mountains. It seemed pretty official." I paused. "And how can a war end if skirmishes are still happening?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas rubbed his temples, leaving a fresh streak of ink near his eyebrow. His mouth tightened into a line barely visible beneath the stained tangle of his beard.

"Emperor," he repeated, as though the word itself tasted of sour wine. "There was no Emperor in eight hundred ninety. The realm was ruled by a monarch—King Aldric's successors held the throne until Mira's accession. If your document bears an imperial seal, then you are looking at either a foreign pretension or an outright fabrication, and in either case it has no bearing on a royal treaty concluded four decades prior."

He let his hand fall to the table with a dry slap.

"But let us indulge your larger fallacy. You ask how a war can end if skirmishes persist. The answer is: quite easily, because skirmishes are not war. War is a declared juridical condition between belligerent powers. The Third Magical War concluded when the constituted authorities—the Crown and the Conclave—executed and ratified the Treaty of Veyros. What followed in the Dragon's Teeth was not the continuation of that conflict; it was the criminal intransigence of rogue elements, unauthorized sects, and mountain chieftains who owed no obedience to the Conclave they claimed to serve. A treaty binds nations, not every brigand with a spellbook."

His voice rose slightly, taking on the querulous edge of a man who had explained this too many times.

"Your decree—assuming it is genuine, which I doubt, given the western archives' celebrated indifference to provenance—describes civil disorder. It describes violations of an existing peace, not the absence of one. To argue otherwise is to abandon the distinction between peace and war entirely, rendering the term meaningless. Shall we say the war continues still, every time a hedge wizard sets fire to a sheep?"

He snatched up his stylus and jabbed it toward the neglected scrolls.

"Catalog the northern correspondence. And the next time Bellen waves a damp scrap under your nose, examine the seal, the jurisdiction, and the terminology before you waste my hour with it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I bristled a bit at his dismissal, but I tried to keep my voice even.* "But Master, the skirmishes were quite large, according to the decree. Whole villages razed, trade routes disrupted... that sounds like more than just 'civil disorder' to me. And if the Emperor was a 'foreign pretension', as you say, then the war was even *more* widespread than we thought, right?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas straightened in his chair, the joints of his spine cracking like dry twigs. He fixed the apprentice with a watery, narrowed stare, the candlelight catching the fresh ink smudge above his brow.

"Listen to yourself," he said, his voice dropping to a lower, more cutting register. "You measure the juridical state of a realm by the number of burned thatched roofs. That is not scholarship; that is sensationalism. A village razed is a tragedy. A trade route disrupted is an inconvenience. Neither, by any legal or historical definition, constitutes a state of war—particularly not a war concluded four decades earlier by competent authorities."

He pushed his chair back, the legs scraping against the stone floor.

"You commit the most vulgar of categorical errors: conflating magnitude with classification. If a thunderstorm levels a hamlet, do we declare war on the sky? If a peasant revolt blocks a road, have we begun a fifth magical war? Violence is not self-defining; it derives its meaning from the institutions that authorize or prosecute it. The Third Magical War was a specific belligerency between the Crown of Aldric II and the constituted Mage Conclave. It ended when those parties executed the Treaty of Veyros. Rogue factions, foreign adventurers, and mountain zealots operating outside that chain of command are not continuators of the war; they are criminals, pirates, or invaders engaged in entirely separate hostilities."

He waved a hand, dismissing the notion with a flick of ink-stained fingers.

"And no, the appearance of some foreign pretender styling himself 'Emperor' does not make the conflict 'more widespread.' It makes it a different conflict, or more likely, a fabricated one. If an Arlesian raider burns a fishing village in 891, do we backdate it to the Arlesian Incursion of 602? Of course not. We recognize it for what it is: an unrelated act of aggression. Your logic would stitch every border skirmish in forty-four years into a single, endless tapestry of war, rendering the term so broad as to be intellectually useless."

He leaned forward, his breath sour with old wine and frustration.

"You are not arguing history. You are arguing that history is whatever a single, unverified decree with a suspect seal tells you it is. That is called credulity, not inquiry. The Treaty of Veyros was signed. The war ended. Everything else is aftermath, criminality, or Bellen's wishful thinking."

He jabbed a finger toward the scrolls.

"Catalog. Now. Before I conclude that your confusion is not Bellen's doing, but a deficiency of your own attention."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not immediately reach for the copy. He sat very still, his ink-stained fingers steepled beneath his chin, and fixed the apprentice with a stare that seemed to bore through the parchment rather than at it.

“Sixteen years later,” he said, his voice low and precise. “And you believe a monarch—any monarch—kept a war simmering for sixteen years without a single court chronicle, diplomatic record, or prior scholarly notice, only to have it revealed by Apprentice Bellen and a damp western archive? That is not a discovery. That is a delusion wearing archival gloves.”

At last he extended his hand, but instead of taking the copy, he flicked the edge of it with one gnarled fingernail.

“First: your term ‘war decree.’ I would wager my remaining eyesight that those exact words do not appear on that parchment. Does the text proclaim a renewed state of belligerency between the Crown and the Conclave? Does it explicitly void the Treaty of Veyros? Or did you merely encounter martial language—garrison allocations, punitive authorizations, perhaps a confiscation of illicit grimoires—and conclude, with your customary imprecision, that the war itself had resurrected?”

He let his hand drop and emitted a short, dry laugh.

“Post-treaty enforcement is not war. In the decades following 847, the Crown issued dozens—hundreds—of decrees employing military force against unauthorized magic. King Aldric, and his successors after him, exercised their *peacetime* sovereign authority to police the treaty’s terms. Suppressing a coven of Dragon’s Teeth renegades in 863 is not the Third Magical War continuing any more than a sheriff’s posse hunting bandits is the continuation of the Brigand Uprising of 710. The war concluded. The peace, however, required maintenance.”

He leaned forward, the candlelight carving deep shadows into the lines around his eyes.

“Second: you hold a copy. Not the original. Copies err. Copies lie. Copies are made by enthusiastic young men in poorly lit vaults who see what they wish to see. And even if—*if*—the original bore Aldric’s seal, a seal affixed by a Chancery clerk in 863 proves only that the royal administration functioned, not that the realm remained at war. Seals certify jurisdiction, not historiography.”

He pushed himself back from the table, his mouth twisting beneath his stained beard.

“You are attempting to overturn a documented, ratified, universally acknowledged treaty with a single ambiguous document interpreted by an apprentice who cannot distinguish between a state of war and a state of security. One does not negate the other. The Third Magical War ended in eight hundred forty-seven. The realm spent the subsequent decades enforcing that end. There is no contradiction—except in your willingness to privilege a dubious scrap over forty-four years of established record.”

He jabbed his stylus toward the northern scrolls with renewed vehemence.

“Put that away. Catalog the correspondence. And for the love of precision, stop letting Bellen interpret texts for you. He reads history like a tavern ballad—seeking drama where there is only administration.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, exasperated, but don't back down.* "But Master, the decree *specifically* mentioned 'resumption of hostilities with rogue mage factions operating outside the Treaty of Veyros.' Doesn't 'resumption of hostilities' imply the war was still ongoing, or at least started again?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas seized the parchment from the table and held it so close to his face that his ink-stained beard nearly brushed the ink. His watery eyes narrowed, tracking the line of text the apprentice had quoted, and then he let out a coughing, mirthless laugh.

"'Resumption of hostilities,'" he said, each word enunciated with withering precision. "Oh, you are a master of selective quotation. But tell me, does your reading comprehension extend to the prepositional phrase that follows? These factions, by the Crown's own admission, were operating *outside* the Treaty of Veyros."

He thrust the parchment back down, his ink-stained finger stabbing at the words.

"Think, if that word is in your vocabulary at all. If the treaty were merely proposed, if the war had never terminated, upon what juridical basis could Aldric claim these mages stood *outside* its strictures? You cannot violate a fiction. You cannot breach a draft. The very act of declaring them extra-treaty acknowledges the treaty as binding law on the constituted Mage Conclave. It is the refutation you wave as proof."

He straightened, or attempted to, his spine cracking like a snapped quill.

"And 'hostilities'—you quake at the word like a startled fawn. Hostilities are not war. Hostilities are acts. The Crown dispatched troops against criminals, renegades, and apostates who refused the authority of the treaty-bound Conclave. That is not the Third Magical War continuing; that is the peace of 847 defending itself against internal parasitism. Aldric II did not resume war against the Conclave in 863. The Conclave, per the treaty, was at peace. He punished marauders who wore the stolen livery of an institution to which they no longer belonged. It was an execution of the peace, not its negation."

He picked up his silver stylus and pointed it at the apprentice with trembling irritation.

"By your atrocious logic, the moment a treaty-breaking pirate fires on a coastal garrison, the previous naval war has 'resumed.' Peace becomes impossible, for any skirmish retroactively dissolves it. You render every treaty a provisional joke, and every end to war a mythical creature. It is historiographically obscene."

He turned his shoulder, dismissing the document with a jerk of his stained beard.

"The war ended in eight hundred forty-seven. The decree of sixty-three enforced that end against its violators. The distinction is plain to anyone who has not surrendered his critical faculties to Bellen's archival sensationalism. Now. Catalog the northern scrolls. And parse your texts before you parade them through my chamber."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas thumped his ink-stained palm against the oak, making the candles gutter. “Real or not,” he repeated, his voice climbing to a reedy, exasperated pitch. “You pose the question as though truth were a toggle between a venerable historiographical consensus and a sheaf of unverified parchments found by boys in dusty vaults. That is not how evidence functions. That is not how history functions.”

He swiped at the smudge above his eyebrow, succeeding only in darkening it.

“The Treaty of Veyros is real. It was signed, sealed, witnessed, and ratified. It exists in the Crown Charters, in the Conclave’s own annals, and in the diplomatic correspondence of eleven separate courts who recognized its execution in eight hundred forty-seven. That is not a ‘textbook’ telling you a comforting story; that is a documentary record affirmed by contemporaries, successors, and the institutions that governed the realm for forty-four years afterward. When a treaty governs taxation, garrison limits, and the licensing of thaumaturges, it is not a hypothesis. It is a juridical fact.”

He leaned forward, his breath sour with old wine and aggravation.

“What Bellen showed you—and what you persist in mislabeling as ‘new evidence’—are preliminary drafts, negotiation memoranda, or unsigned engrossments from before the final accord. Such papers always litter the path to a treaty. They are the scaffolding, not the edifice. To claim they supersede the executed instrument is to mistake the architect’s sketch for the cathedral itself. Every major compact generates discards; finding them in a western archive does not erase the ratified version in the royal registry. It merely proves that diplomacy, like scholarship, requires revision before it reaches its final form.”

His fingers drummed a sharp, irritable rhythm against the tabletop.

“There is no equivalence. Established record is not one voice in a debate of equals; it is the datum against which novel claims must be tested. The western documents have not survived that test. They lack provenance, they lack corroboration, and they lack the plainest common sense, for they ask us to believe that generations of officials, chroniclers, and disputing parties conspired to maintain a fiction of peace under a treaty that never was. That is not a new truth emerging. That is an old fantasy entertained by the credulous.”

He jabbed his stylus toward the neglected heap of northern scrolls.

“The truth is that the Third Magical War ended in eight hundred forty-seven, and every assertion otherwise is the product of misread scraps and fevered imagination. Now. Catalog.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I chew on my lip, frustrated, but a new thought sparks.* "What if the original treaty was... changed? Like, the copy in the royal registry isn't the *real* original? Or what if there was another, secret treaty that contradicted it?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas went very still. Then he emitted a sound like a grinding hinge—something between a groan and a laugh. His ink-stained fingers curled around the edge of the manuscript until the vellum squeaked against the oak.

“Changed,” he said, the word reedy with disbelief. “You propose that the Crown Charters, the Conclave annals, and the diplomatic protocols of a dozen foreign ambassadors have all been quietly... altered? And nobody noticed? Not a single chancery clerk, not one visiting mage, not one rebellious noble with a grudge and a pen, sounded the alarm for four decades?”

He pushed himself up, leaning heavily on the table, his failing eyes wide and harsh in the candle-glow.

“That is not historical inquiry. That is the plot of a cheap tavern romance. ‘The Secret Treaty.’ ‘The Forgotten Parchment.’ Histories are not built upon invisible ink and shadow cabinets; they are built upon records that men lived by, died by, and cited in court. The Treaty of Veyros regulated taxes, garrisons, and the very licensing of magic. You cannot govern a realm for forty-four years with a forged document dangling in the wind. Subjects would notice. Tax collectors would notice. Mage-lords bound by its articles would notice.”

He jabbed a stained finger toward the apprentice’s copy.

“And suppose—merely to indulge your taste for the theatrical—suppose there existed some ‘secret’ counter-treaty that contradicted the public one. So what? A treaty that is hidden, unratified, and publicly ignored is not a treaty; it is a worthless scrap. History concerns the instruments that operated upon the world, not fantastical documents that existed only in the fevered dreams of conspirators. The juridical reality of the realm was the peace of eight hundred forty-seven. If a secret pact whispered otherwise in a locked drawer, it changed nothing, governed nothing, and ended nothing.”

He sat down heavily, his breath rasping, and fixed the apprentice with a glare sharp enough to cut glass.

“You are not engaged in detection. You are engaged in retreat. Having failed to disprove the treaty with ambiguous drafts and misread decrees, you retreat into the unfalsifiable: invisible forgers and phantom compacts that leave no evidence because, conveniently, they were erased or concealed. That is not argument. That is the abdication of reason masquerading as skepticism.”

He snatched up his silver stylus and leveled it like a dirk.

“The Third Magical War ended in eight hundred forty-seven. The Treaty of Veyros was signed, was real, was effective, and no quantity of schoolboy conspiracism will undo it. Now. Catalog the northern scrolls. Before I begin to doubt that your intellect merits instruction at all.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I deflate a little, defeated by his conviction, but still not entirely convinced.* "Alright, Master. But can I at least look at the original Treaty of Veyros sometime? Just to see it myself?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas paused. He tilted his head, the candlelight catching the grease and ink in his beard, and regarded the apprentice with an expression that mingled suspicion with something almost like grudging recognition.

“You wish to *examine* the engrossed instrument,” he said, his voice dry as pumice. “Not ‘see’ it, as if it were a dancing bear at a fair. Not the ‘original,’ which is a layman’s imprecision—the Crown possesses the *signed and ratified engrossment*, executed in duplicate, with the Conclave’s authenticated counterpart sealed at Veyros itself. These are juridical instruments, not theatrical props for your idle satisfaction.”

He sat back, his chair creaking like a rotting mast.

“The charter engrossment resides in the sealed vault under three locks and a binding clause that predates your grandparents. It is not retrieved for the whims of apprentices who have yet to demonstrate they can distinguish a ratification protocol from a tavern receipt. However—” and here he raised one ink-blackened finger, “—your impulse, though clumsily phrased, at least gestures toward a proper scholarly instinct. One does not adjudicate historiography through gossip and secondhand copies. One consults the instrument itself.”

He leaned forward, his breath shallow and sour.

“You will complete the northern correspondence first. Every scroll, every chancery notation, every marginal annotation. If, by week’s end, your catalog exhibits the precision you have so sorely lacked—if you can correctly differentiate a diplomatic protocol from a requisition order in those very files—I shall arrange for you to examine the Conclave’s authenticated counterpart under my direct supervision. You will read the seventeen witness subscriptions. You will read the appended schedule of reparations, dated 847, and the mutual-defense clauses that governed garrison withdrawals. You will observe the Great Seal, affixed intact, and the counter-seal of the Archmages. And you will see, with whatever visual acuity the gods granted you, that the realm did not spend forty-four years governed by a fantasy.”

He thumped his stylus against the oak for emphasis.

“But understand this: if you approach that document with the same credulity and taxonomic sloppiness you have paraded today—if you squint at the parchment hunting for invisible ink, or if you begin muttering about secret compacts concealed between the lines—I shall have you reassigned to the palace latrine inventories before the ink dries. Is that sufficiently precise for you?”

He jerked his stained chin toward the neglected heap.

“Now. Catalog.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, a newfound determination hardening my expression.* "Yes, Master. I understand. I'll catalog the northern scrolls. With precision." *I turn to the stack of scrolls, pulling the first one towards me and unrolling it carefully.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas emitted a noise somewhere in the back of his throat, low and dyspeptic. He retrieved his silver stylus but did not immediately return to his manuscript.

“‘Understand,’” he muttered, as though testing the word for mildew. “You have grasped the posture of submission. Whether you comprehend its substance remains to be demonstrated.”

He gestured with the stylus toward the first scroll, his failing eyes tracking the apprentice’s hands with unsettling intensity.

“You will catalogue by the Tripartite Method. Header, provenance, and marginal notation—and I mean the standard chancery sigla, not whatever private abbreviations you devise. Cross-reference each header against the exchequer rolls for the years eight hundred forty-six through eight hundred forty-eight. Note the binding medium: if the stitching is sinew rather than hemp cord, the scroll antedates the treaty settlement and belongs in the antebellum sequence. Should you encounter any reference to garrison levies, thaumaturgical licensing, or—gods forbid—another ‘war decree,’ you will flag it with a blue ribbon, not some scrap of lint from your pocket. And for the preservation of the realm’s records, roll them *forward*, against the cylinder, not backward against the grain. I will not have you cracking vellum today out of the same clumsiness you applied to historiography.”

He hunched back over his manuscript, his ink-stained beard hovering inches above the faded text, but his watery gaze kept flicking upward toward the apprentice’s table, watchful and unblinking.

“Begin.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I suppress a sigh, knowing this meticulous cataloging is going to be tedious.* "Yes, Master. Tripartite Method. Sinew and hemp. Blue ribbon. Rolling forward." *I carefully unroll the first scroll, my eyes already scanning for anything that might be relevant to the treaty.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas sniffed, a wet, rattling sound.

“Repetition is not precision,” he said, without looking up from his manuscript. “You recite my instructions like a litany, as though the utterance itself were compliance. It is not. The scroll does not care what you mouthed at me; it cares what your fingers do to its structure.”

He dipped his stylus and scratched a notation along the margin of his page, the sound sharp and deliberate.

“And unburden yourself of that expression,” he continued, his gaze flicking upward toward the apprentice’s face. “You wear the look of a hound that suspects a hare beneath every bush. Cataloging is not hunting. You do not root through the northern correspondence for ammunition to vindicate Bellen’s fantasies. You record. You describe. You observe without expectation. If you scour each line for covert proofs of a secret war, you will begin to see phantom legions in grain tariffs and phantom mages in grain delivery schedules. That is not research; it is mania.”

He set the stylus down and rubbed his temple, leaving another dark streak across the parchment of his skin.

“The northern rolls are predominantly exchequer memoranda and quartermaster requisitions. They are tedious. They are administrative. They are precisely the sort of unremarkable peacetime documentation that a realm generates when it is not, in fact, consumed by total war. If your scroll bears a requisition for cart horses dated eight hundred fifty-two, describe it as a requisition for cart horses. Do not annotate it as ‘evidence of mobilization.’ If a garrison at Coldmere requests winter boots in eight hundred sixty, note the size and the tally. Do not speculate that the boots were meant for marching against a Conclave that had already disbanded its field elements under treaty obligation.”

He leaned back slightly, his eyes narrowing to watery slits.

“Dispassion, or the nearest approximation you can manage. And should you encounter the name Veyros in the header, merely verify the chancery date and the routing. No underlining. No exclamations in the margins. No triumphant sighs that announce to the entire archive that you believe you have found something.”

He hunched forward again, his beard brushing the manuscript, but his voice carried clearly across the candle-smoke.

“Begin with the header. Author, recipient, place of composition, and the regnal year. If the sender identifies himself as a treaty-commissioner, record it as an administrative title, not as a revelation. Now. Proceed.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I bite back a sharp retort, feeling my face flush. He's trying to get a rise out of me.* "Yes, Master. No phantom legions." *I clear my throat and focus on the scroll, carefully noting the details for the header.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas watched the apprentice’s hands with watery, unblinking intensity. He let the silence stretch until the distant dripping of the water clock became audible in the haze of candle smoke. Then he thumped his silver stylus against the oak, the sound sharp as a cracked knuckle.

“Posture,” he snapped. “You hunch over the vellum like a vulture over carrion. Sit upright. The document is not a secret whispered to your navel; it is a public record to be read at a scholar’s distance. And your left hand—do not pin the lower margin with your thumb. Pressure creases. Creases become tears. Tears become the excuse of apprentices who later claim the damage predated their tenure.”

He leaned forward, squinting, his ink-stained beard twitching.

“You have unrolled it sufficiently to read the superscription. State the author, the recipient, and the regnal year. Do not preface your reading with ‘I think it says’ or ‘it appears to be.’ Precision demands either certainty or the honest admission of illegibility. And if the date falls between eight hundred forty-seven and eight hundred ninety-one, you will classify it as a document of the treaty period—not as ‘post-war,’ not as ‘pre-dissolution,’ and certainly not as ‘evidence of continued belligerency.’ The war ended. The treaty governed. Learn the epochal terminology, or invent your own and be reassigned to the latrine inventories.”

He retrieved a scrap of cloth and wiped his stylus, though his failing gaze never left the apprentice’s face.

“Speak.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stiffen at his constant corrections, but I force myself to relax my shoulders and lift my hand from the scroll.* "The author is Lord Cassian of Moorgard. Recipient is Royal Treasurer Aethelred. Regnal year is 851 AE." I glance up at him, a flicker of defiance in my eyes. "So, well within the 'treaty period', Master."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus stopped moving. A bead of ink gathered at its tip, swollen and black, then fell to the vellum with a soft blot. He stared at the stain for a moment as though it had personally offended him, then lifted his head just enough to expose one bloodshot, impatient eye.

“Maester,” he corrected, in the tone of a man who had endured this particular wound many times and had never once grown accustomed to it. “Not ‘Master.’ If you cannot be punctual, you may at least be precise.”

He set the stylus down with excessive care, aligning it exactly parallel to the edge of the manuscript. His fingers were stained to the second knuckle, and the left side of his beard bore the ghost of an earlier ink disaster.

“As for your confusion,” he said, “it is not the lecture that is confused. It is your hearing. Or perhaps your note-taking. Possibly both.”

He pushed the manuscript aside, not roughly, but with the weary authority of a man who had handled too many fragile things to waste movement.

“I said the Third Magical War ended in 847 AE because that is the historical reckoning accepted by every serious chronicler of the realm until very recently, and by a great many who ought to know better even now. King Aldric II concluded the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave. Hostilities ceased. The Conclave withdrew from the king’s courts. The northern marches stopped being set alight every other solstice. That, in any ordinary use of language, is what is meant by ‘ended.’”

One bushy eyebrow rose.

“However,” he continued, “if Apprentice Bellen has put a western archive pamphlet into your hands and told you he has overturned three centuries of scholarship with a single afternoon’s reading, then Apprentice Bellen has more enthusiasm than judgment. The documents in question do not say that the war continued in arms. They do not say that Aldric’s treaty was rejected in open session, or that the Conclave resumed organized warfare, or that the Crown maintained a state of open hostilities for another forty-four years. What they suggest—what they appear to indicate, if one reads them with sufficient caution—is that the Treaty of Veyros may never have been formally executed in the final sealed form required by Conclave law.”

Tomas’s mouth tightened.

“Proposed, yes. Negotiated, yes. Publicly proclaimed in several provinces, yes. But signed and ratified in the strictest technical sense? That is where the western papers become troublesome. They imply that the treaty remained, in legal terms, incomplete. A proposal accepted in practice but never perfected in form.”

He tapped one ink-spotted finger against the desk.

“Therefore, if you are asking when the fighting stopped, the answer remains 847 AE. If you are asking when the legal and constitutional state of unresolved conflict was finally extinguished, then you may say 891 AE, when Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave and ended whatever shadow of the old war still lingered in the archives. One date marks the practical end. The other marks the juridical end. They are not the same question, and a scholar who treats them as though they are is no scholar at all.”

His gaze sharpened, though his eyes were plainly tired.

“Do not come to me saying the war ‘actually’ continued until 891 unless you are prepared to define ‘actually’ with more rigor than a tavern argument. History is not improved by being made dramatic. It is improved by being exact.”

He turned the nearest bundle of correspondence toward him and rested a hand on its brittle edge.

“Now put away those notes and begin with the Veyros letters. If you find any mention of a draft treaty, an unsealed accord, or a disputed ratification, bring it to me at once. And if Apprentice Bellen attempts to instruct you again, remind him that discovery is not the same thing as understanding.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I wince at the "Maester" correction, mumbling a quick apology. *I pull out a chair, a bit too loudly, and start sorting through the scrolls Maester Tomas indicated, trying to look busy.* "So, if the fighting stopped, why did it matter if the treaty wasn't officially signed? Like, if everyone *thought* it was over, wasn't it over?" I look up, genuinely curious. "And why didn't anyone just sign it properly later?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s mouth thinned into a line so severe it might have been drawn with a ruler.

“Because,” he said, “you are speaking of a treaty as though it were a mood. ‘Everyone thought it was over.’ ‘Everyone thought.’” He repeated the phrase with such distaste that the words seemed to sour in the air. “History is not governed by what everyone thought over ale or while counting their chickens. It is governed by what was agreed, what was recorded, what was sealed, and what could be enforced. A treaty is not a feeling of relief. It is a mechanism.”

He lifted one ink-stained finger and pointed it at the nearest stack of scrolls as if summoning them to witness his patience.

“If two lords cease burning one another’s villages because winter has come, because their treasuries are empty, because their soldiers have grown tired of dying in the mud, that is a cessation of violence. It is not, in itself, a legal peace. It may be a truce. It may be exhaustion. It may be convenience. But if the borders remain disputed, if prisoners remain unransomed, if taxes continue to be levied under wartime statutes, if one side still claims the right to inspect the other’s strongholds, then the war has not ended in law. It has merely gone quiet.”

His failing eyes narrowed, and he leaned closer to the manuscript before him, though he did not seem to be reading it so much as using it to steady his argument.

“The Treaty of Veyros was meant to do more than stop the burning. It was meant to define the status of the Mage Conclave within the realm. It was meant to settle whether battlemages could be tried in royal courts or only before their own tribunals. It was meant to determine the fate of fortified mage-holds. It was meant to fix the limits of warding, the taxation of enchanted lands, the custody of dangerous artifacts, and the obligation of the Conclave to provide counsel to the Crown. These are not trivialities. They are the bones beneath the skin of a kingdom.”

One hand rose, fingers ticking off points with stiff, scholarly precision.

“If the treaty was signed and ratified, then the Crown’s later actions against the Conclave must be judged as acts of governance under a settled peace. If it was not signed and ratified, then the Crown could claim that certain wartime powers remained in abeyance. That distinction mattered. It mattered to a magistrate deciding whether a mage could be compelled to surrender a tower. It mattered to a lord deciding whether he could seize lands once held by a battlemage’s household. It mattered to a queen deciding whether an ancient corporation of spellcasters still possessed legal standing, or whether it could be dissolved as an unfinished relic of an unfinished conflict.”

Maester Tomas let that settle. Somewhere in the archive, a candle spat.

“As for why no one simply signed it properly later,” he continued, and the word “simply” earned a look of such withering reproach that even the dust seemed to straighten on the shelves, “you would do well to remember that states do not behave like scribes who have blotted a page and wish to copy it again. A treaty is not a loaf of bread left too long in the oven. One cannot merely return it to the fire and expect it to rise.”

He pushed aside a brittle roll of correspondence and rested both hands on the desk, the knuckles pale beneath their stains.

“King Aldric II may have wished the matter settled in 847, but wishes do not make law. The western documents suggest that the final execution of the treaty required not only the king’s seal, but the Conclave’s full concord, the attestation of provincial archmagisters, and registration in the High Chancery. Some of those steps appear to have been incomplete. Perhaps one of the necessary seals was never affixed. Perhaps the Conclave’s internal vote was unresolved. Perhaps the registration was delayed because one party feared what the written record would fix beyond argument. We do not yet know precisely, and anyone who tells you he knows precisely is either lying or has read too little.”

His voice grew drier still.

“Then time passed. And time, in such matters, is not neutral. It creates facts. Lands changed hands. Offices were established. Wartime edicts became convenient. Certain lords grew accustomed to controlling mage-property without the nuisance of Conclave oversight. Certain royal officials discovered that ambiguity allowed them to act without admitting they were breaking peace. The Conclave, meanwhile, may have preferred an imperfect treaty to a corrected one if correction meant surrendering privileges it still claimed. Later kings had no desire to reopen a settlement that their fathers had proclaimed as finished. To sign the treaty properly after decades of practice would have been to admit that it had not been proper before, and to invite every injured party to demand redress.”

Maester Tomas gave a short, humorless sound.

“By the reign of Queen Mira, the matter had become even more tangled. The Conclave was weaker, divided, and politically dangerous. If the Treaty of Veyros had been fully executed, it might have protected the Conclave as a lawful body and constrained the Crown’s power over it. If it had never been executed, then the Crown’s lawyers could argue that the old conflict had never been juridically concluded, and that the queen possessed residual authority to settle the matter once and for all. Which argument do you suppose her councillors preferred?”

He did not wait for an answer, nor did he appear to expect one.

“She dissolved the Conclave in 891 AE. Not because armies marched again. Not because fire rained from the sky, or because the old war erupted in the manner of ballads. She dissolved it because the legal shadow of the old war had never been fully dispelled, and because that shadow gave her room to act. That is why the date matters. Not as drama. As law.”

Maester Tomas reached for a cloth and wiped ineffectually at the ink blot he had made earlier, only succeeding in smearing it into a grey bruise. He stared at the result with deep offense.

“Therefore,” he said, returning to the point with the stubbornness of a man who intended to nail it to the table, “when I say the Third Magical War ended in 847 AE, I am speaking of the practical cessation of organized conflict and the accepted historical reckoning. When I acknowledge the argument for 891 AE, I am speaking of the final extinction of the unresolved legal condition. Neither statement is false. They are answers to different questions. The failure lies in asking one question and expecting it to devour all the others.”

His gaze sharpened again, tired but unyielding.

“And do not say ‘if everyone thought it was over’ unless you can tell me who this everyone was, what they thought, what records they left, and whether their thoughts had the force of law. Most did not. Some thought the war over and thanked the gods. Others thought it merely suspended and kept their knives close. Others thought only of what they could take while the rules remained unclear. All of them may have been sincere. Sincerity is not evidence.”

He tapped the Veyrosi correspondence with one crooked finger.

“That is why you will examine those letters carefully. If you find language such as ‘draft,’ ‘proposed accord,’ ‘awaiting seal,’ ‘in abeyance,’ ‘without prejudice,’ or ‘until the full instrument be perfected,’ bring it to me. If you find proclamations celebrating peace in terms too grand to be supported by the surviving documents, bring those as well. Grand words often conceal missing signatures.”

Maester Tomas picked up his silver stylus again, then paused, its tip hovering over the ruined vellum.

“And if Apprentice Bellen tells you that the western archive has proven the entire traditional account a lie, you may inform him that the archive has done no such thing. It has complicated the record. It has exposed a gap between practice and law. It has given us a more precise question to ask. That is valuable. But it is not the same as overturning the past, and it certainly is not the same as understanding it.”

He bent back over his manuscript, voice dropping into the tone of a man who considered the subject closed unless the subject proved itself worthy of reopening.

“Begin with the third bundle. And do not read as though you are hunting for a scandal. Read as though you are measuring the distance between what people said and what they were empowered to do.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, a lot of what he's saying sinking in. It's more complicated than I thought.* "So, it's not just about what happened, but what *should* have happened, legally." *I pick up the first scroll from the bundle he indicated, the parchment feeling brittle and dry under my fingers.* "And what people *said* happened, versus what the actual documents show." *I start to unroll it carefully, my eyes scanning the faded script.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not look up immediately. His attention remained fixed on the ruined blot he had made, as though it were a small, dark enemy that had to be conquered by disapproval alone. Then, with a slow exhale through his nose, he lifted his gaze to the apprentice’s hands on the scroll.

“Careful,” he said sharply. “That is not a tavern napkin. If you crack the seal or tear the margin, you will spend the next month copying grain inventories in the lower scriptorium, and I will personally ensure the ink is thin.”

He watched a moment longer, satisfied only when the parchment was unrolled with sufficient caution. Then he gave a single, curt nod, though it carried no warmth.

“Better,” he said. “You are beginning to hear the shape of the problem, though you are still stumbling over the words. Do not say what *should* have happened. That is the language of moralists, children, and men who have never drafted a binding instrument. Law is not a prayer that things be as they ought. Law asks what was required, what was performed, what was witnessed, and what could be enforced. ‘Should’ is a door through which every kind of convenient nonsense enters the archive.”

He reached for a clean cloth and dabbed once more at the ink stain, then stopped, disgusted, and let the cloth fall.

“Nor should you speak as though ‘what people said’ and ‘what the documents show’ are two cleanly opposed realms. Documents are also things people said. They are merely things people said with seals, formulae, and the hope of outliving their lies. A charter may be false. A letter may be propaganda. A proclamation may be issued to calm a city while the councillors behind it are still arguing over the wording. The question is not whether a document is ‘actual’—that is a useless word—but whether it is authentic, contemporary, authoritative, and relevant to the legal point at issue.”

His fingers drummed once on the desk, then stilled.

“If a village chronicle says, ‘And so the war ended in peace,’ that may tell us how the matter was remembered. If a royal writ orders wartime levies discontinued, that may tell us something of administrative practice. If a Conclave register records that its magisters withdrew from the king’s courts and ceased to appoint wardens to the marches, that may tell us something of institutional behavior. But none of those things, by itself, proves that the Treaty of Veyros was executed in the manner required to bind the realm in perpetuity. Memory is not ratification. Custom is not signature. Silence is not consent.”

Maester Tomas leaned back slightly, the joints of his chair giving a dry complaint. His eyes, red-rimmed and tired, tracked the apprentice’s movements with the wary attention of a man who expected scrolls to misbehave.

“The traditional account is not a foolish tale told by fools,” he said, his voice hardening. “It is the account built upon the visible settlement: the cessation of open warfare, the withdrawal of the Conclave from royal administration, the end of organized military operations, and the long public memory of King Aldric II as the monarch who made peace. That is no small thing. It is the thing most people mean when they say a war has ended, and they are not wrong to mean it so in ordinary speech. If every historian abandoned the practical date because a legal technicality has surfaced, we would have no stable chronology at all. We would have only arguments without anchor.”

He raised a stained finger.

“But neither do we ignore the technicality. That is where Apprentice Bellen and his sort become tiresome. They discover a complication and immediately announce that the world has been remade. The western documents do not give us license to declare that the entire received history is false. They give us reason to distinguish between the end of fighting and the end of the juridical condition produced by the fighting. That distinction is not a scandal. It is scholarship.”

Maester Tomas’s gaze dropped to the scroll in the apprentice’s hands.

“Now, the Veyrosi correspondence. You will find there letters between royal envoys, provincial officials, and agents of the Conclave in the years immediately after the proclaimed peace. Some will speak of the treaty as accomplished. Some may use language that is far more cautious. Your task is not to decide which side you prefer, as though you were judging a contest of bards. Your task is to identify the formulae and note their implications.”

He began to recite, ticking the phrases off on ink-darkened fingers.

“If you see ‘the peace concluded at Veyros,’ record it, but do not assume it proves ratification. Men often speak loosely of concluded peace when they mean only that the killing has stopped. If you see ‘the accord proposed at Veyros,’ ‘the articles drawn up at Veyros,’ or ‘the treaty yet awaiting perfection,’ that is of greater consequence. If you find mention of missing seals, absent archmagisters, delayed registration, or instructions to treat the matter as provisional, bring it to me immediately. If you find a reference to Queen Mira’s later settlement and someone describes it as ‘finally ending what was begun at Veyros,’ that too must be noted, because it may reveal how the later generation understood the earlier failure.”

He squinted toward the scroll, then leaned forward a little, frustration tightening his mouth.

“Hold it where the light catches the line. My eyes are not so obliging as they once were, and I will not have you waving it about like a banner.”

Maester Tomas lifted his silver stylus, not to write, but to point.

“Read the opening formula aloud. Slowly. If it names King Aldric, note the style. If it names the Conclave, note whether it calls them ‘the Mage Conclave of the realm,’ ‘the assembled magisters,’ or merely ‘certain masters of the arcane.’ Titles matter. If it invokes the treaty, note the verb: concluded, ordained, proposed, accepted, proclaimed, or some vaguer term. Do not paraphrase. Paraphrase is where precision goes to die.”

He settled back, hands folding over the desk, ink-stained fingers interlaced like the bars of a small cage.

“And remember this,” he added, his voice dropping into a colder register. “If the first line seems to prove me wrong, do not grin like a boy who has found a coin in the street. The first line of a document proves almost nothing until you know who wrote it, for whom, under what authority, and for what purpose. A scribe may call a treaty ‘signed’ because he believes it was. He may call it ‘proposed’ because he wishes it to remain so. He may be ignorant. He may be lying. He may be repeating the language of a superior who had reasons for ambiguity. The archive is not a witness stand where every page speaks truth under oath. It is a room full of partial voices, and the historian’s labor is to make them answer precisely, not to let them shout.”

His eyes narrowed.

“So. The opening line. Read it.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s silver stylus halted a hair’s breadth above the blotched vellum. For a moment he did not answer. His bloodshot eye moved from the copy to the apprentice’s face, then back again, with the slow, dangerous patience of a man deciding whether to correct a mistake or mourn it.

“Sixteen years,” he repeated softly. “And Apprentice Bellen, with the confidence of a boy who has read one folio and mistaken it for a library, told you that this overturns the Third Magical War.”

He set the stylus down with excessive care.

“You say ‘after you said the war ended.’ I did not say the matter was simple. I said the accepted historical reckoning placed the practical end of organized hostilities in 847 AE. If you heard a simpler claim than that, the fault lies in your hearing, not in my lecture.”

His gaze dropped again to the copy, but he did not reach for it.

“A copy,” he said. “You present me with a copy and announce that it bears King Aldric’s seal. Did you see the seal yourself? Was it wax, or a drawn device? Was it attached by cords, or merely represented by a scribe’s flourish? A seal is not a decoration painted at the bottom of a page to please later readers. A seal is an act of authentication, and authentication has conditions.”

He pointed to the desk with one ink-stained finger.

“Set it where the light falls, not in your hands. If I am to be contradicted, I prefer the contradiction to lie still.”

Maester Tomas leaned forward slightly, squinting toward the page but not touching it.

“And do not say ‘war decree’ as though the phrase were a key that opens every lock. What do you mean by war decree? Does the instrument declare war? Does it order the levy of the realm? Does it name the Mage Conclave as an enemy still in arms? Or does it use the word war in some lesser sense—against rebels, brigands, unlicensed spellcasters, or a lord who has fortified a tower without leave?”

His fingers tightened around the edge of the desk.

“A king may issue a decree full of martial language without thereby continuing a war. Kings do that constantly when they wish to make ordinary coercion sound grander. They speak of war on bandits, war on smugglers, war on disobedience. If every such phrase were taken literally, the realm has been at war with sheep rustlers since the first dynasty.”

One bushy eyebrow rose, sharp with irritation.

“Suppose the document is genuine. Suppose it is rightly dated 863 AE. Suppose even that it uses the term war without ambiguity. You still have not answered the only questions that matter. Against whom was it directed? Under what authority was it issued? Does it treat the Treaty of Veyros as void, suspended, or never perfected? Or does it simply rely upon old wartime powers that the Crown found convenient not to surrender?”

A muscle worked in his jaw.

“That is the distinction the western archive has forced upon us, if you have been listening instead of merely collecting exciting words. The practical end of the fighting is one thing. The legal residue of the conflict is another. A decree in 863 may show that the Crown still used wartime formulas, or that the status of the Conclave remained unsettled. It does not, by itself, prove that the Third Magical War continued as an organized conflict. It may prove a cold state, not a burning one.”

Maester Tomas tapped the desk once, sharply.

“I did not say the received chronology was beyond examination. I said it was the accepted reckoning, and it remains the accepted reckoning because it rests on more than a single dramatic scrap. It rests on the cessation of campaigns, the withdrawal of magisters from royal courts, the silence of military records, the chronicles of the provinces, and the long public memory of Aldric as a peacemaker. If one document from 863 is to overturn all that, it must do more than exist. It must speak clearly. It must name the war. It must show that the Conclave as a body was still being treated as a public enemy, not merely that some unlucky sorcerer had angered the Crown.”

He gave a short, contemptuous breath.

“Apprentice Bellen has shown you the danger of half-learning. He has found a word and believes he has found a world. If the decree is genuine, it belongs in the argument. I do not deny that. It may strengthen the claim that the peace was juridically incomplete. It may help explain why Queen Mira’s lawyers later found room to dissolve the Conclave. But it is not proof that my lecture was false, and it is certainly not proof that armies were still marching under the banners of the Third Magical War sixteen years after the fighting stopped.”

His eyes narrowed, tired but hard.

“Read the operative clause, not the title. Titles are often the loudest part of a document and the least precise. If it commands the marshals to raise the host against the Conclave, if it declares the accord at Veyros unmade, if it says the realm remains in a state of open war, bring it to me at once and I will reconsider the weight of the evidence. But if it orders a local muster, the arrest of certain mages, the seizure of unauthorized wards, or the enforcement of old statutes, then you have found an administrative measure dressed in severe language. That is not the same thing as a continuation of the war.”

He picked up the silver stylus again, then set it down without writing, as though even the instrument had disappointed him.

“And when you return to Apprentice Bellen, tell him this: a seal proves nothing unless one knows what it was attached to, by whom, and under what authority. A date proves nothing unless one knows what was happening in that year. And a word proves nothing unless one knows whether it was used as law, as rhetoric, or as convenience. If he wishes to overturn three centuries of scholarship, he must do better than hand a student a copy and say, ‘Look, a war decree.’”

Maester Tomas turned his attention back to the Veyrosi correspondence, but his hand remained near the copy, as if he did not entirely trust it not to sprout arguments in the night.

“Now read the document you have brought. Slowly. Begin with the invocation, then the style of the king, then the named parties, and then the verb by which the king commands. If you cannot do that without paraphrase, then you are not ready to contradict me. You are only ready to repeat someone else.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully place the copied document on the desk, pushing it slightly towards him so the light hits it better.* "It says... 'By the Grace of Aldric, Second of His Name, King of the Andals and the First Men, Lord of the Seven Kingdoms and Protector of the Realm... do hereby decree a renewed state of martial law within the Western Marches, and commit the Crown's forces to the apprehension and subjugation of those rogue mages who continue to defy the Crown's authority and threaten the peace established at Veyros.'" *I look up, a bit nervous.* "It mentions 'peace established at Veyros,' but then 'renewed state of martial law' and 'subjugation of rogue mages'."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not lay a finger on the copy at first. He leaned over it until his beard nearly brushed the ink, then drew back with a small, irritated sound, as if the letters had arranged themselves to mock him.

“Peace established at Veyros,” he said. “There. That is the phrase Apprentice Bellen should have had the grace to notice before he began proclaiming revolutions.”

He tapped the desk beside the page, not the page itself.

“You have read a decree that speaks of rogue mages, martial law, and the Crown’s forces. You have not read a declaration that the Third Magical War continued. Those are different beasts, and if you pen them in the same stall you will be kicked.”

He straightened, rubbing one knuckle against his temple.

“What does it say? It says the king commits forces to the apprehension and subjugation of rogue mages who defy the Crown’s authority and threaten the peace established at Veyros. It does not say the Mage Conclave has renounced the peace. It does not say the Conclave is in arms as a body. It does not say the treaty has been broken, voided, or never made. It invokes Veyros as a peace already established. If anything, it is evidence that by 863 the Crown itself wished to be understood as governing under a settlement, even if the final instrument remained imperfect.”

One bushy eyebrow rose.

“That does not mean the treaty was properly executed. A king may speak of an established peace because the killing has stopped, because the provinces expect it, or because it is useful to say so. Public language and sealed law are not twins. But it does mean this document is far better suited to proving a cold and unsettled aftermath than to proving an ongoing war.”

He picked up the stylus and pointed it at the copy.

“Martial law. Attend to that term and do not let it gallop away with you. Martial law is not necessarily war. It may be a suspension of ordinary process in a disturbed region. It may be a grant of summary authority to marshals. It may be a measure against rebellion, banditry, or unlicensed sorcery. The Western Marches have long been a nuisance. If the Crown sent soldiers to arrest rogue mages there, that may be policing, coercion, or local suppression. It becomes a continuation of the Third Magical War only if it shows organized hostilities against the Conclave as a public enemy. You have not shown me that.”

His voice grew drier still.

“Nor is ‘renewed’ the word you should skip. It is troublesome. It may mean that an earlier emergency grant from the war was being revived. It may mean the Crown still had recourse to wartime powers. It may support the argument that the legal condition of the conflict had not been fully extinguished. I concede that much. It belongs in the discussion of the cold state that persisted until Queen Mira’s settlement. But a cold state is not a burning one, and a legal shadow is not an army in the field.”

He gave the copy a look of deep suspicion.

“As for the seal, you tell me a copy bears King Aldric’s seal. Is it impressed wax? Is it attached? Is there a chancery endorsement? Or has some later copyist drawn a round device to make the text look weightier? And the style—‘King of the Andals and the First Men, Lord of the Seven Kingdoms and Protector of the Realm’—must be checked against authenticated acta of the reign. Some of that is florid. Some may be formula borrowed from later usage. A copy can be faithful, corrupted, or invented. Until I know which, it is a witness to be questioned, not a trumpeter to be believed.”

He folded his stained hands.

“So. If Apprentice Bellen calls this a war decree, tell him he has named it by its loudest possible interpretation. It is not a war decree on its face. It is a martial or public-safety decree issued in a time of proclaimed peace. If he wishes to make more of it, let him show me the Conclave named as enemy, or a clause declaring the Veyros settlement void, or evidence that the ‘rogue mages’ were acting under Conclave authority and the Crown treated them as such. Without that, he has found a spark and called it a bonfire.”

Maester Tomas let out a breath and pushed the copy a finger’s breadth closer to the light with the tip of his stylus.

“It is relevant,” he admitted, as though the word cost him something. “It may help explain why later lawyers could argue the old war had never been perfectly concluded. It may show that the peace of 847 was lived in without being legally finished. But it does not overturn my lecture. The practical end remains 847. The juridical end remains 891. This decree sits between them, in the muddy years where men used the language of peace while keeping the instruments of force near to hand.”

His eyes narrowed.

“Now read the next clause, if there is one. And when you come to verbs, do not bring me ‘subjugation’ until you have found whether it is followed by ‘of the Conclave’ or merely ‘of certain persons.’ Persons can be arrested. A war is waged against a body. The difference is the whole of your argument.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas closed his eyes for a moment, as though the question had struck him somewhere behind the brow and he needed darkness to endure it.

“Real,” he repeated. The word came out flat and suspicious, like a coin he suspected had been filed down at the edges. “You ask whether the treaty is *real* as though history were a cupboard and we were searching for a missing pot. The treaty is not a pot. It is a legal act, a political fact, a textual tradition, and a historiographical problem all at once. If you insist on one word, you will get one falsehood.”

He drew the copy nearer by the corner, but only just, as if it might bite.

“The textbook says one thing. The new evidence says another. That is not a contradiction; that is a failure to distinguish kinds of statement. A textbook compresses. It says, ‘The Treaty of Veyros ended the Third Magical War in 847,’ because that is the public shape of the event: fighting stopped, terms were proclaimed, the realm began to govern itself as though peace had come. That is not nothing. It is, in fact, most of what ordinary men mean by peace.”

One stained finger rose.

“But the western documents ask a narrower and nastier question: was the treaty completed in the form required to make it fully binding in law? There the answer is less comfortable. On the present evidence, I will not say the treaty never existed. That is Bellen’s sort of exaggeration. I will say that there appears to have been a negotiated accord, publicly treated as peace, but not perfected in every formal particular. Proposed, perhaps. Accepted in practice, perhaps. Legally finished? That is doubtful.”

Maester Tomas’s mouth tightened.

“So if you demand a verdict, here is the least dishonest one: The Treaty of Veyros was real as a political settlement. It was real as a set of terms known and invoked by contemporaries. It may not have been real as a fully executed and ratified instrument under Conclave law. Those are not the same claim, and a scholar who cannot hold them apart has no business handling documents.”

He tapped the copy with the back of one knuckle.

“This decree you have brought even helps the point, if you read it without letting it flatter your appetite for drama. It speaks of the ‘peace established at Veyros.’ That is evidence the Crown wanted the realm to believe a peace existed. At the same time, it uses martial law and force against rogue mages, which suggests the Crown still possessed and employed extraordinary powers. A settled peace and an unsettled legal condition can coexist. They often do. Kingdoms are tidy in chronicles and messy in fact.”

His tired eyes sharpened.

“Do not mistake the newest scrap for the final truth, either. The western evidence is valuable because it complicates the old account. It is not automatically superior because it is newer, or because it was found in an archive with dust on it. Every document must be authenticated, dated, placed, and interrogated. A copy with a drawn seal may be faithful. It may be a later invention. It may be a sincere error. Until those questions are answered, it is a witness, not a verdict.”

Maester Tomas leaned back in his chair, the wood creaking beneath him.

“The truth, if you must have it in plain speech, is this: the war ended in practice in 847. The peace was remembered, proclaimed, and relied upon. But the legal instrument that should have closed the matter may never have been completed, and that incompleteness gave the Crown room to act for decades afterward, until Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891 and ended the old war in law, if not in memory.”

He picked up his stylus, looked at it, and set it down again without writing.

“So do not come to me asking whether the treaty is real. Ask instead: real in what sense? Agreed? Likely. Proclaimed? Yes. Performed? In large part. Ratified beyond challenge? No. Not on the evidence we presently have.”

A short, humorless breath escaped him.

“That is the truth. It is less satisfying than a simple ‘yes’ or ‘no,’ but it has the virtue of being defensible. Now stop hunting for a single secret answer and return to the correspondence. The truth in this archive will not arrive shouting. It will arrive in formulae, omissions, titles, and seals.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the copy again, looking at it with new eyes.* "So it's not a lie... it's just a different kind of truth. A legal truth versus a practical truth." *I chew on that for a moment, then carefully roll up the decree and put it away.* "Alright, I'll go back to the Veyrosi letters. I'll look for those phrases you mentioned." *I turn back to the stack, feeling a bit more focused now.* "Maester, how long do you think it will take to sort through all of this? There's so much."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas gave a short, dry sound, not quite a laugh and not quite a cough. It was the sound of a man who had heard apprentices ask how long the sea would take to empty, and had no illusion that the question could be answered to the asker’s satisfaction.

“How long?” he repeated. “You might as well ask how long it takes to untangle a net after three storms, while blindfolded, and with a cat sitting on the knots.”

He glanced at the stack of Veyrosi correspondence, then at the apprentice’s hands, then back to the stack, as though suspecting the scrolls of multiplying while he was not watching.

“That depends entirely on what you mean by ‘sort through.’ If you mean unroll them, squint at them, and feel important, you may finish before supper and know nothing. If you mean catalog them well enough to say what each is, whom it concerns, what date it claims, and whether it speaks of the peace as concluded, proposed, or merely wished for, then you will need longer than you would like and more patience than you appear to possess.”

He lifted a finger and began counting on it, though his eyes were too tired to look at anything but the middle distance.
