“First, separate by date where a date survives. Where it does not, separate by hand, seal, formula, or office of origin. Then list the sender, the recipient, the place of writing, and the first three significant terms. Do not summarize the whole letter in your own words until you have recorded the exact words that matter. ‘Peace,’ ‘accord,’ ‘treaty,’ ‘war,’ ‘Conclave,’ ‘rogue,’ ‘rebellion,’ ‘seal,’ ‘ratification,’ ‘abeyance,’ ‘provisional,’ ‘until further order.’ Those are the words that will matter. Everything else is likely to be complaints about weather, roads, unpaid garrisons, and the price of candles.”

His gaze returned to the apprentice, sharp despite its weariness.

“And do not roll them up again as though they were bedding. If you finish one, lay it flat, label it, and place it in the tray. If you find a fragment that may belong to another, keep them together. If you find a seal impression, do not rub it with your sleeve. If you find wax, do not flex the parchment to see if it cracks. If you find anything that appears to contradict me, do not gloat. Bring it here, lay it down, and tell me what it says in its own language.”

Maester Tomas picked up the silver stylus again, turned it once between his stained fingers, and set it down with the tip facing neatly toward the manuscript.

“As for how long it will take,” he said, “if you work carefully, perhaps three days to make a rough order. Another week to index the relevant passages. A month to understand them well enough not to embarrass yourself. A year to understand them well enough to argue with me. A lifetime to understand them well enough to know how much remains uncertain.”

He gave the apprentice a stern look.

“Since I do not have a lifetime to spare, and you apparently have an appetite for questions, begin with the first ten. Do not attempt to read the entire bundle as though it were a ballad. Read each document as though it were a single witness with a poor memory and a reason to lie. Then write down what it says, what it does not say, and what it cannot possibly be made to say without violence.”

Maester Tomas bent again over his ruined vellum, then paused, his voice softening by no more than a hair’s breadth.

“And when you have finished the first ten, bring them to me before you continue. If you are going to misunderstand them, I prefer to correct the error while it is still small.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, absorbing the instructions. Three days for a rough order, a week to index... that's a lot of parchment.* "Understood, Maester. No gloating, just facts." *I carefully unroll the first letter, already seeing some of the words he mentioned. My eyes skim for dates and names, trying to get a feel for the rhythm of the letters.* "I'll bring you the first ten when I'm done."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus paused again, this time with the weary patience of a man who had just been handed a phrase too blunt to use without sharpening.

“Just facts,” he repeated, as though testing whether the words might spoil in his mouth. They appeared to have done so. “There is no such thing as ‘just facts’ in an archive. There are facts recorded by someone, preserved by someone, copied by someone, and interpreted by someone else, usually badly. A fact without provenance is only a rumor wearing boots.”

He lifted his head and squinted toward the candle nearest the apprentice’s worktable, as though the flame itself had failed in its duty to illuminate properly.

“Do not say ‘facts’ as though they were turnips to be tossed into a sack. Say what kind of fact. A date? A title? A formula? A seal? A marginal note in a later hand? A copyist’s error? Each must be treated differently. If you treat them all alike, you will produce not history, but porridge.”

Maester Tomas rubbed his thumb against the side of his beard, found ink there, and seemed momentarily offended by it, though not enough to stop speaking.

“And do not skim for the rhythm of the letters. Rhythm is for poets. You are looking for legal language. If a letter says ‘the peace,’ note whether it says ‘the peace made at Veyros,’ ‘the peace called Veyros,’ or ‘the peace, if such it may be called.’ That last clause may be worth more than ten proclamations.”

He gestured toward the bundle without touching it.

“When you have finished the first ten, do not bring them to me in a heap like laundry. Bring them in order, with the first visible line written out exactly as it stands. If the date is damaged, say damaged. If the seal is missing, say missing. If the writer calls King Aldric ‘our lord the king,’ note it. If he calls him merely ‘the king,’ note that too. If he calls the Conclave ‘the Conclave,’ write it so. If he says ‘certain mages,’ do not improve it to ‘the Mage Conclave’ because it suits your theory.”

His voice grew colder and more precise.

“And if you find something that appears to support Apprentice Bellen’s grand revision, do not run to me shouting that the textbook is a lie. Bring the document, identify the hand if you can, and tell me whether the phrase is a statement, a wish, an accusation, or a formula copied from an older draft. That is the difference between evidence and noise.”

Maester Tomas picked up the silver stylus once more, then set it down again with a sigh that seemed to come from the deepest shelf of his patience.

“Begin with the first letter. Read the first three lines twice before you write anything. If you cannot read them twice without your mind wandering, then read them aloud in a whisper. If you still cannot attend, stand up and read standing. Idleness is the mother of bad history.”

He bent again over his blotched manuscript, then added, without looking up:

“And if you find the phrase ‘until the full instrument be perfected,’ do not merely stare at it as though it were a dragon. Bring it to me at once.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I grimace slightly at his correction of "just facts," but nod.* "Understood, Maester. Not turnips. I'll be precise." *I return to the first scroll, my brow furrowed in concentration. I don't want to make another mistake. I read the first few lines aloud, softly, before beginning to write notes on the wax tablet I'd brought.* "Until the full instrument be perfected," *I whisper to myself, committing the phrase to memory.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus came to rest with a faint, metallic tick against the rim of the inkwell. He did not look up at once. His head tilted, just enough to make the candlelight catch the ink-darkened hairs of his beard, and for a moment he resembled a hound that had heard something moving in the walls.

“That phrase,” he said, “if you have actually found it in the text and are not merely repeating it like a charm picked up from Apprentice Bellen, is not to be whispered into the air as though it were a spell for good luck.”

He lifted his eyes then, bloodshot and severe.

“‘Until the full instrument be perfected’ is not a mood. It is not a sigh. It is not a decorative flourish to be memorized because it sounds important. It is a formula with a history, a context, and a legal weight that changes depending on where it appears, who uses it, and what instrument is being discussed.”

One stained finger tapped the desk in slow emphasis.

“If it occurs in the body of a letter, in the hand of the principal scribe, in a clause bearing on the Veyros settlement, then it may be significant. If it appears in a marginal note added later by a copyist with poor eyes and worse judgment, its value is different. If it is part of a closing reservation—‘we shall hold ourselves bound in custom until the full instrument be perfected’—then it may tell us that the parties behaved as though a peace existed while admitting that the final act remained incomplete. If, however, it refers to some lesser document—a schedule of hostages, a list of confiscated wards, a perambulation of borders, an agreement over prisoner exchange—then it may have nothing whatsoever to do with the treaty itself.”

Maester Tomas leaned forward, squinting toward the worktable with an expression that suggested the candle had failed him personally.

“Do not commit the phrase to memory as though memory alone made it evidence. Memory without citation is how ballads begin. A scholar does not remember a phrase; he places it. Where does it stand? What comes before it? What comes after it? Who writes it, and to whom? Is the writer in a position to know the legal state of the accord, or is he repeating what he hopes his master wishes to hear? Is the language mandatory, permissive, conditional, or merely ornamental?”

He drew a breath through his nose, then released it with the controlled irritation of a man who had spent too many years teaching apprentices to resist their own excitement.

“And do not, upon finding such words, leap to the conclusion that the textbook has been exposed as a falsehood. That is the vice of shallow minds. If the phrase refers to the Treaty of Veyros, it may support the argument that the peace was lived under an unfinished form. It may explain why later royal officials could invoke wartime powers. It may help us understand how Queen Mira’s councillors constructed the case for dissolution in 891. But it does not, by itself, prove that the Third Magical War continued in arms. It does not prove that the Conclave remained in open rebellion. It does not prove that King Aldric’s peace was a lie told to the realm.”

His voice hardened.

“It proves, at most, that the settlement was imperfect. That is a very different thing. Kingdoms are often governed through imperfect settlements. Men call them peace because the alternatives are worse. Chroniclers date by them because they need stable markers. Later lawyers pick them apart because lawyers are paid to find seams. None of this turns a practical end into a fiction.”

Maester Tomas reached for the nearest clean scrap of vellum, then thought better of it and withdrew his hand, as though he suspected even the blank sheet of intending to misbehave.

“If you find that phrase, you will not merely stare at it. You will copy the surrounding lines exactly. Not your summary. Not your impression. Not what you think it ought to say. The exact words, with their abbreviations expanded if you can expand them safely, and with a mark where the text is damaged or unclear. If there is a seal, describe it. If there is an endorsement on the back, record it. If the letter begins with a greeting that names the parties, write the names and titles as they stand.”

He picked up the silver stylus again, turning it once between his fingers before setting it down with unnecessary precision.

“‘Until the full instrument be perfected’ may mean the treaty was not yet ratified. It may mean the final enrolled copy had not been prepared. It may mean one party had not returned its sealed counterpart. It may mean the High Chancery had delayed registration. It may mean a subordinate was being told to keep matters calm while his superiors argued over a clause. It may even mean nothing more than that a scribe had inherited a formula from an earlier draft and lacked the sense to discard it.”

One eyebrow rose sharply.

“That is why we do not shout over a phrase. We interrogate it.”

For a moment, his expression softened into something that was not quite approval but might have been the memory of it.

“If you have found it in the first letter, then you have found something worth examining. That does not make you a discoverer of hidden ages. It makes you a reader with a duty. Bring the scroll when you have noted its opening formula. Lay it here. Show me the line. Then we will see whether it belongs to the treaty question or to some lesser piece of administrative fuss.”

He bent again over his ruined manuscript, but his voice followed the silence like a last, dry warning.

“And if Apprentice Bellen has taught you to treat such words as weapons against your elders, unlearn that habit at once. Evidence is not a cudgel. It is a burden. The more it seems to say, the more carefully you must ask what it is being made to say.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flush a little, embarrassed to be caught whispering.* "Right. Not a charm." *I focus harder on the scroll, carefully writing out the exact wording on my wax tablet, noting the sender and recipient. I make sure to include the surrounding lines, just as he instructed. After a few minutes, I lift the scroll and approach Maester Tomas's desk.* "Maester, this is the first letter. It's from Lord Corvin of the Western Marches to King Aldric's royal chancellor, dated 849 AE. It says, 'Though the accord at Veyros has brought a measure of peace to our troubled lands, the full instrument of its perfection remains unexecuted, leaving certain claims concerning the Mage Conclave's holdings in abeyance.'" *I lay the scroll gently on the desk, pointing to the line.* "It mentions 'full instrument of its perfection' and 'in abeyance'."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not touch the scroll at once. He bent over it until the tip of his nose nearly grazed the parchment, then drew back with an irritated grunt, as though the letters had arranged themselves spitefully against his failing sight. One hand hovered above the line the apprentice had indicated, not quite descending, as if even the possibility of smudging the ancient ink demanded restraint.

“Read it again,” he said. Then, before the words had fully left his mouth, he corrected himself with a sharp click of the tongue. “No. Do not read it. Recite it exactly, if you can. My eyes are not so obliging as to forgive me for trusting them at this hour.”

He leaned closer again, squinting. His lips moved faintly, not in reading, but in the old habit of a man testing the shape of a phrase for hidden cracks.

“‘Though the accord at Veyros has brought a measure of peace—’” he murmured, voice low and dry as dust. “There. Stop there a moment. Do you hear it? Not ‘the peace.’ Not ‘the final peace.’ Not ‘the perpetual settlement.’ A measure of peace. A portion. A quantity sufficient to keep men from burning one another’s granaries, but not sufficient to still every dispute.”

His finger tapped the desk beside the scroll, never upon it.

“Lord Corvin is not writing a chronicle. He is writing to the royal chancellor. That means he is choosing his words with care, or at least he ought to be. ‘Measure’ is a cautious word. It admits quiet without admitting completion. It is the sort of phrase a man uses when he does not wish to be quoted later as having declared the matter settled beyond repair.”

Maester Tomas straightened a little, though his eyes remained fixed on the line.

“And then this,” he said. “‘The full instrument of its perfection remains unexecuted.’ If that is truly the wording, it is either a legalism gone to seed or a copyist’s muddle. One does not execute a perfection. One executes an instrument. One perfects a treaty by execution, registration, seal, or whatever final act the law requires. The phrase should more properly be ‘the full instrument remains unperfected,’ or ‘the instrument of perfection remains unexecuted.’ If Lord Corvin’s scribe wrote it as you have read it, then he was either reaching for grandeur or floundering in terminology.”

His mouth tightened.

“But I will grant the sense. The sense is clear enough, and it is troublesome. He says the accord has brought peace, or some portion of it, yet the final instrument has not been completed. That is not nothing. Do not mistake me. It is not a tavern tale. It is not a later invention. If the letter is genuine, and if the date is sound, then we have here a contemporary voice acknowledging that the settlement at Veyros was treated as producing peace while also admitting that something remained unfinished.”

One ink-stained finger finally descended, pointing not at the apprentice, but at the space between them where the argument lived.

“Now attend to the next phrase, because it is the one that will determine whether this letter belongs to the history of the war or merely to the history of property disputes. ‘Leaving certain claims concerning the Mage Conclave’s holdings in abeyance.’ Holdings. Not armies. Not oaths. Not open rebellion. Holdings. Lands, revenues, towers, wards, privileges, rents, jurisdictions. That is the language of administration, not of battle.”

Maester Tomas’s eyes narrowed, though whether from thought or from the strain of seeing, it was difficult to say.

“In abeyance,” he repeated, tasting the words. “That is the important part. Abeyance means suspended. Undetermined. Waiting upon a further act. It does not mean war. It does not mean the Conclave remained an enemy in arms. It means that someone, probably a lawyer, possibly a very tired clerk, could not decide who had the right to what until the final settlement was made complete.”

He gave a short, humorless breath.

“If Apprentice Bellen were here, he would seize upon ‘unexecuted’ and declare the entire traditional account a fabrication. He would say, ‘You see? There was no treaty. The war continued. The textbooks lie.’ And he would be wrong. Not because the phrase is unimportant, but because he would make it carry more weight than it was built to bear.”

Maester Tomas drew the scroll a fraction closer by the edge of the desk, not by the parchment itself.

“This letter does not say the Third Magical War continued. It does not say the Conclave rejected the accord. It does not say King Aldric resumed hostilities. It does not say the magisters mustered again, or that the marches were aflame, or that the Crown treated the Conclave as a public enemy still in rebellion. It says that certain claims remained unresolved because the final instrument had not been perfected. That is precisely the sort of cold residue I have been describing. It is the legal shadow. It is the unanswered question that allowed later kings, and eventually Queen Mira, to act as though the old matter had never been fully closed.”

His gaze lifted, tired but severe.

“Do not let this discovery intoxicate you. A phrase like this is not a banner. It is a splinter. It tells us the peace had rough edges. It tells us the settlement was lived in before it was finished, if indeed it was ever finished. It tells us that men in the Western Marches could speak of peace while still acknowledging unresolved claims. That is valuable. It is even, in its modest way, illuminating. But it is not the overturning of the age.”

He rubbed one knuckle against his temple, then winced and withdrew his hand, as though the gesture had reminded him of his own weariness.

“Record it thus,” he said, voice falling into the clipped rhythm of instruction. “Letter from Lord Corvin of the Western Marches to the royal chancellor, dated 849 AE, if the date is sound. State the opening formula exactly. Note the phrase ‘measure of peace.’ Note the apparent admission that the full instrument remains unexecuted or unperfected, whichever the original truly says. Note the term ‘in abeyance.’ Note that the matter concerns the Conclave’s holdings, not its military status. Do not embellish. Do not write ‘the treaty was never signed’ unless the letter says so in plain words. It does not. It says something more delicate, and therefore more useful.”

Maester Tomas’s stylus hovered above his own blotched vellum, then descended to make a small, precise mark in the margin, not of correction, but of remembrance.

“And note this as well,” he added. “The letter invokes the accord at Veyros as having brought peace. That is not a small detail. Even if the instrument was incomplete, the fact that a marcher lord could appeal to it as a source of quiet two years later suggests that the settlement had public force. Custom. Recognition. Political reality. That is why 847 remains the practical end. This letter does not erase that. It complicates it.”

He looked up then, and for once his expression held less irritation than caution.

“If you find more like this, bring them. Do not announce them as though you had unearthed the bones of the war itself. Bring them as what they are: fragments of a long administrative afterlife. The truth of this matter will not be found in a single triumphant sentence. It will be found in the accumulation of cautious phrases, each one measured, each one hedged, each one written by men who knew that peace could be proclaimed in the streets and still remain unfinished in the archives.”

Maester Tomas set his stylus down with deliberate care.

“Now go back. The next letter may say nothing of consequence. It may speak of grain, or weather, or some petty quarrel over a millstream. But if it does, record that too. Silence is evidence as well, if one has the patience to hear it.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, absorbing his words, my initial excitement tempered by his careful distinctions. He's right; it's more nuanced than I first thought.* "Right, Maester. Not a weapon, a splinter." *I retrieve the scroll and place it back on the stack. I turn to the next one, feeling the weight of the task more keenly now. This isn't just sorting; it's an interrogation.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas made a small, dry sound, not quite approval and not quite complaint.

“Splinter,” he repeated. “No. You have merely exchanged one careless figure for another. A weapon implies intent. A splinter implies an accident one wishes to extract and forget. Neither is apt. If you must have a metaphor—and apprentices always must—call it a thread. A thread may lead to a seam. A seam may show where a garment was hastily joined. But if you seize it in triumph and pull, you will only tear the cloth and call the tearing revelation.”

He aligned his silver stylus once more, tip pointing precisely toward the edge of the blotched vellum, as though the instrument required discipline the rest of the room lacked.

“The Veyros settlement is not a nail to be struck. It is a knot. Some knots are loosened by patience. Others are cut by queens. Queen Mira cut this one. That does not mean there was never a knot, nor does it mean that every man before her had been pretending his fingers were not tangled in it.”

His tired eyes moved briefly to the stack of correspondence, then away, as if even the sight of so much unread parchment had become a personal offense.

“Do not approach the next letter hoping for another grand phrase. Hope is a poor archivist. It makes men see what they wish and miss what is plainly before them. If the next document is a list of garrison boots, record it as a list of garrison boots. If it mentions boots in connection with wartime levies, note that. If it mentions boots in connection with ordinary provincial supply, note that too. If it is a petition over a stolen millstone, observe whether the petitioner appeals to the royal court, to a local lord, or to a mage tribunal. Such small choices often reveal more about the condition of the realm than ten proclamations.”

One ink-stained finger tapped the desk in slow measure.

“If you find another letter saying that claims remain in abeyance, record it. If you find three, record all three. If you find ten, do not come to me declaring that the Third Magical War was still being fought with ink and property seizures. Ten such letters may strengthen the argument that the juridical condition persisted. They do not, by themselves, make armies appear in the field. They do not make the Conclave a rebel host. They do not turn King Aldric’s peace into a fiction. They show us something more ordinary and more troublesome: a kingdom governing itself around an unfinished settlement because finishing it had become inconvenient.”

Maester Tomas rubbed his temple again, more gently this time, as though the gesture had ceased to be mere irritation and become habit.

“That is why the traditional reckoning remains defensible. It is not built upon ignorance. It is built upon the visible facts of cessation: no campaigns, no organized Conclave resistance, no royal host marching against magisters year after year. The western evidence does not erase those facts. It asks whether the legal machinery had truly been completed. Those are separate questions. If you confuse them, you will produce melodrama. If you distinguish them, you may produce history.”

He reached for the ruined blot on his own manuscript, then stopped himself and withdrew his hand, apparently deciding that further interference would only worsen the damage.

“And do not think I am defending the textbook because it is comfortable,” he added, his voice sharpening. “I am defending precision because precision is harder than comfort. If the treaty was never perfected, say so plainly. If the Crown exploited that imperfection, say so plainly. If Queen Mira’s dissolution relied upon the old ambiguity, say so plainly. But do not let those admissions seduce you into claiming that the practical peace of 847 was a lie. It was not a lie. It was incomplete. There is a difference, and it is not a small one.”

Maester Tomas settled back in his chair, the wood giving another dry protest.

“Continue with the next letter. If it contains nothing relevant, mark its silence. If it contains something relevant, mark its exact wording. If you are uncertain whether it is relevant, bring it to me rather than deciding in a fever of false significance. And if your wax tablet becomes crowded, do not scrape important words away to make room for guesses. Use another tablet. I would rather have too many tablets than one confident error.”

His gaze returned to his own work, though his hand remained near the Veyrosi bundle, as if he could not entirely trust the letters to behave without supervision.

“Begin,” he said. “And do not let your mind run ahead of your eyes. The archive punishes eagerness by feeding it nonsense.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, chastened by his further correction of my metaphor. This is harder than I thought.* "Right. Not a thread to pull, just... a knot to untangle." *I pick up the next scroll, a short one, and begin to unroll it carefully, my eyes already seeking out those key phrases he hammered into me.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The stylus stopped mid-stroke. Maester Tomas set it down with the exaggerated care of a man deciding not to snap it in half, and turned on his stool, joints cracking like green wood in a fire.

"Bellen." He pronounced the name the way one identifies a stain on a carpet. "Bellen, who has never in his life read past the abstract of anything, *showed* you a paper. Did he show you the paper itself, or his summary of it, scratched on the back of a duty roster? Which document? Which archive? Who translated it?" He waved his own questions away. "No. Never mind. The question you asked is imprecise in three separate ways, and I will correct all of them, since no one else in this citadel will."

"First: the war did not *continue* until 891. No armies marched. No cities burned. What persisted was the *legal state* of war — a distinction that matters, unless you believe parchment draws blood. Hostilities ceased in 847. The war, in law, did not."

"Second: the Treaty of Veyros was never signed. It was *proposed*. Negotiated for the better part of a year, amended, argued over. The chroniclers wrote victory verses about it — chronicles are gossip with dates attached. But when the western chancery rolls were opened a decade ago, they recorded proposals, drafts, amendments. No ratification. No seal. No signatures. The royal registry holds no counterpart instrument. One does not end a war with a proposal."

"Third: I said 847 in lecture because the syllabus says 847, because every text in this library printed before the discovery says 847, and because first-years who cannot arrive on time are not yet ready to have their tidy dates taken from them." A pause. "I also said it because it is *wrong*, and I have been saying so in writing for nine years, which apparently no one reads."

His fingers found his temple again. "Ask yourself the better question, since Bellen evidently did not: why did Queen Mira need to dissolve the Mage Conclave at all in 891? Forty-four years after a peace everyone agrees happened? One does not dissolve a defeated enemy in peacetime. One dissolves them when the war they were fighting is — in law — still being fought."

He pushed back from the desk and gestured at the correspondence pile with his chin, his hands occupied rubbing his eyes.

"Which brings me to your assignment, the purpose of which would be obvious had you been on time. The Veyrosi correspondence *is* the negotiation record. Somewhere in that pile, the Conclave's envoys propose terms, the crown's envoys amend them, and then — nothing. The letters simply stop. Because there was nothing to sign."

A dry sound, not quite a laugh.

"When the rolls first surfaced, I called them forgeries. Loudly. In print. Then I read them." He slid a single letter across the desk, its ink faded to the color of weak tea. "If you find a ratification clause in that correspondence — a seal, a signature, one line that says *ratified and sworn* — bring it to me and I will retract before the full faculty. I have offered that wager to three senior maesters. None has accepted."

"Begin with the third letter. Read it aloud. My eyes have declared themselves finished with small script for the day, and yours are apparently the only pair in this tower that owes me labor."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the letter, a faint smell of dust and old paper rising from it.* "So, the war never actually ended, just... paused? And everyone just forgot to sign the peace treaty?" *I look at the faded script, trying to make sense of the elegant but unfamiliar handwriting.* "This is... really interesting, Maester. I didn't know history could be so messy."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
For a long moment, Maester Tomas said nothing at all. He had the particular silence of a man cataloguing errors, and the apprentice had just handed him a rich collection.

"*Paused*," he said at last, the way one reads an epitaph aloud to check it for spelling. "A pause is what a musician takes between movements, with every expectation of resuming. What happened in 847 was two things, which you have folded into one because folding is easier than thinking. First: the *hostilities* ceased. Armies went home. That is a fact about men and fields. Second: the *war* — the legal state of it — persisted, because no instrument existed to terminate it. A state of war has teeth, apprentice. It meant the Conclave's envoys in the capital carried belligerent credentials, not diplomatic ones. It meant there are custody rolls — Conclave adepts taken in the last year of the fighting, held because no peace existed under which to exchange them. Some died in custody. Old men, in a war that had stopped shooting forty years earlier. A pause does not hold prisoners."

He stroked his ink-stained beard once, twice.

"And no one *forgot* to sign anything. Forgetfulness is for keys and the names of minor cousins. There are three scholarly positions on why the treaty died, and I will spare you the two dull ones. The record shows proposals through the winter of 846, amendments, the crown's commissioners asking for a signing date — and then the correspondence stops. Not trails off. *Stops*. My position, published and unrefuted for nine years, is that the Conclave refused deliberately. Consider their arithmetic. Sign, and they become a defeated corporation, dissolvable at the crown's pleasure. Refuse, and the war stays alive in law — uncomfortable, but it kept them in existence. The crown, for its part, got what it actually wanted: quiet fields and no war taxes. Both parties profited from the ambiguity. Ambiguity always has a constituency. That is how it survives forty-four years."

He waved a hand, as though brushing away a moth.

"As for 'interesting' — that is the word one uses when one cannot yet say 'significant' or 'wrong.' And if you mean to flatter me, do it with citations. History is not *messy*. The past was exactly what it was, hour by hour, down to the signature that did not happen. It is the summaries that are tidy, and tidiness is where the lying is done."

He squinted across the desk at the letter in the apprentice's hands, and his eyes gave out on the small sloped script almost immediately. He closed them.

"You have told me what it smells like and how the hand is cut. You have not read it. That is Conclave secretarial cursive — their scribes wrote fast and sloped everything out of what I can only assume is contempt for future scholars. You are not expected to read it fluently. You are expected to *try*." And then he recited, without hesitation, the way a man recites a thing he has read forty times: "It opens: 'To the commissioners of the Crown, from the under-secretary of the Mage Conclave, the eleventh day of the third month, 846.' Then the old formula — 'health and the Concord' — and then the substance, which is where you come in. Continue from there. Aloud, and slowly. I will correct the terms as you go."

He opened his eyes again, and there was something almost sharp in them.

"One thing more. Attend to what you read as though the faculty were listening, because in a sense they are. If you find a ratification clause — a seal, a mark, the words *ratified and sworn* — you stop and tell me at once, and I will retract before the full faculty, as I have sworn to three maesters senior to both of us. I did not *want* the treaty to be unsigned, apprentice. I wanted to be right about it. Those are different appetites, and Bellen has never learned to tell them apart. When he waves his paper at you next, ask him one question: does his source contain a signature? Not a reference to one. Not a chronicler's verse about one. A signature." A dry pause. "He will not answer, because he has not looked.

"Begin. The letter has waited long enough for someone to read it properly. It can survive your pronunciation."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I clear my throat, a little intimidated by his intensity. "Right. Okay."* I hold the letter closer, tracing the faded script with my finger. *The handwriting is tiny, and some of the words are hard to make out.* "Okay, it says... 'Concerning the proposed articles of peace, the Conclave finds Article Three, regarding the dissolution of the Adept Chambers in Oldtown, to be... problematic.'" *I squint, trying to decipher the next word.* "It looks like 'unacceptable'?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's hand came up from the desk, flat, like a schoolmaster halting a boy mid-verse.

"Stop. You have committed two errors in as many lines, which may be a record even for this tower."

He drew a folder toward him — his own fair copy of the correspondence, margins black with nine years of argument in a hand tighter than the one failing him now — but did not open it.

"First: you are not reading. You are divining. '*It looks like* unacceptable.' Does it look like it, or do you *want* it to, because 'unacceptable' is a word you already own? A reader who supplies the word he expects is a chronicler, and chroniclers, as established, are gossip with dates. When you meet a word you cannot make out, you will spell me the letters you *can* make out, and we will proceed honestly." A pause. "'Problematic,' however, you read correctly, which proves you can do this when you stop performing helplessness. Noted and filed."

He leaned back, and recited, eyes closed, the clause arriving like something worn smooth from handling: "'The Conclave finds Article Three, concerning the dissolution of the Adept Chambers in Oldtown, to be problematic — that is the under-secretary's glove — and, in the operative clause, *inadmissible in law, prejudicial to the liberties of the Conclave, and withheld from ratification without prejudice to further conference.*'"

His eyes opened.

"The word is *inadmissible*. Not 'unacceptable.' A merchant writes 'unacceptable' about a barrel of spoiled fish. The Conclave's chancery wrote law. And you are going to attend to that clause, apprentice, because you are currently holding the reason the war outlived its last battle by forty-four years."

He counted the points off against the desk, one finger at a time.

"The crown's commissioners demanded, as the *price of peace*, the dissolution of the Adept Chambers — the Conclave's judicial benches, its last organ of self-government, which you would know had the syllabus ever interested you. The Conclave answered: inadmissible. There is the whole war in one line of sloped cursive. Sign, and they sign their own dissolution into law. Refuse, and they remain — in law, in *existence* — an enemy still standing. They refused. And forty-four years later, when Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave at last, she was not breaking a peace. She was ending a war that no piece of paper had ever ended. The chroniclers' verses have her shattering a treaty that was never sealed. The letters in that pile say otherwise."

He tapped the folder once.

"Note also the craft, since you are learning to read: the letter opens soft and closes hard. 'Problematic' is the courtesy; 'inadmissible' is the hand inside the glove. If you quote this letter in ten years, quote the operative clause — or some future Bellen will summarize it as the Conclave finding the terms 'difficult,' and the tidiness will do its lying again."

The apprentice might wonder — Tomas could see the question forming — why a man who knew the letter by heart needed it read at all. He answered it before it was asked, because answering questions before they were asked was most of his pleasure in this life.

"Memory is a transcript of a transcript, and mine was made by eyes that were already going. Your eyes are the only instrument in this room I presently trust. So. Resume. Next line, slowly — the Conclave's secretaries were paid by the word and wrote like it. Spell what you cannot read. And if you reach anything that smells of agreement — a proviso, a reservation, a seal, the words *ratified and sworn* — you stop and show me before you breathe another word of it."

A dry sound.

"I have a retraction staked on what that pile does not contain. I do not enjoy staking. I enjoy being right. Occasionally the two require courage, which is why senior maesters refuse the wager. You, fortunately, are not senior enough to refuse me anything. Read."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
For the first time in the apprentice's experience of him, Maester Tomas went completely still. Then he put out his hand, curled his fingers once — a gesture that managed to be both invitation and summons — and took the copy.

He held it at arm's length. Squinted. Turned it a degree, as though the light were the problem rather than his eyes, and set it down with a gentleness more alarming than any slamming.

"You believe you have handed me a refutation," he said. "You have handed me the instrument I have spent nine years praying the western rolls would yield, carried into this tower like a drawn dagger by someone who cannot name the blade. Sit down. This will require a chair."

He did not wait to see whether the advice was taken.

"Corrections first, since you have packed three errors into two sentences. One: sixteen years after the *chronicles* say the war ended. I have spent this hour telling you what *I* say; keep the two apart. Two: you call it a war decree because Bellen called it a war decree. Instruments are called what they call themselves — we will attend to that. Three—" and something happened to his face that a stranger might have mistaken for a smile, "—you have not yet understood what you are holding. Permit me."

He counted against the desk, one finger at a time.

"First. A war decree is not a treaty. The question in dispute — the one Bellen has never once answered — is whether the Treaty of Veyros was ever *ratified*. A decree exercising the powers of war says nothing about a treaty's signature. Bellen has answered a question again. Merely the wrong one. He is consistent, at least."

"Second. A seal is not a signature. The great seal lived in the chancery and was affixed by clerks, in the king's name, by the hundred — writs, commissions, decrees. That Aldric's seal appears on a decree of 863 tells us the chancery was open that year. Gripping news. What would actually tell us something is Aldric's *hand* upon the treaty — and the royal registry holds no counterpart instrument. No seal. No signature. Nothing."

"Third. The arithmetic, which Bellen did not do. Under the tidy version — treaty signed, peace sealed, verses sung — a king issuing a *war decree* sixteen years into his settled peace is a king whose chancery has lost its reason. Under my version, it is not merely possible. It is *expected*. The legal state of war persisted; the crown went on issuing war instruments because the crown's lawyers, whatever the versifiers wrote, knew precisely what had and had not been signed. Chancery clerks are pedants, apprentice. It is their single virtue. They do not issue a war decree without reciting the legal ground of it."

He drew his folder toward him and opened it — the first time — to a page black with marginal argument.

"'Instruments of continuation.' I wrote that phrase nine years ago, and predicted the rolls would yield war instruments dated between the cease-fire and Mira. And now one arrives, via Bellen, who has spent a week waving my own evidence at you and calling it a sword." A dry bark of a laugh. "The fates are cruel, but their comic timing is impeccable."

He held up one more finger.

"And before you think to claim the wager on Bellen's behalf — no. The wager is staked on a ratification clause in the Veyrosi correspondence. A war decree ratifies nothing. It merely proves there was a war alive to be decreed. Which is, you will notice, my entire argument."

He pushed the copy back across the desk.

"Now, two tasks, in order. First: the seal legend — the ring of letters cut around the seal impression. It names the king. Read it to me, and understand before you begin that either name serves me. If it is Aldric the Second, then the king who supposedly sealed a peace in 847 was still wielding war powers in 863, which no ratified treaty survives — so he sealed nothing. If it names a later king, then the war outlived the very reign the verses say ended it, which no signed treaty permits. Whichever name sits in that ring, it is my witness."

"Second: the recital. Begin at the opening — date, addressee, formula — and stop at the first 'whereas.' Every chancery instrument in this realm recites its legal grounds; it is the one honest habit the office has. If that clause recites the war as ended, I will owe Bellen an apology, which will pain me more than the retraction would. If it recites the war as *persisting* — as I have predicted in print for nine years — you will copy it out fair, twice. Once for me. Once for the faculty, with the provenance written honestly: *surfaced by Apprentice Bellen, understood by no one, until*—"

He stopped. Rubbed his eyes.

"Credit where the record requires it. Now read. Seal legend first. Then the recital. Slowly."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stare at the decree, feeling a mix of confusion and a growing sense of excitement. Maester Tomas is actually... happy? In his own way.* "So Bellen accidentally proved *your* point?" *I pick up the decree, my fingers brushing over the wax seal.* "Okay. The legend says... 'Aldric II, King of the Westmarch, Protector of the Marches.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
For a long moment, Maester Tomas said nothing at all. Then he drew the folder onto the windowsill, turned to its last leaves, and held out his hand for the decree. When it came, he laid it beside rubbings — a dozen of them, graphite on thin paper, each labeled in a hand that worsened steadily down the page like a wick burning out.

"'Aldric the Second.' You read the opening of the legend truly. The whole of it runs: *Aldric the Second, King of the Westmarch and the Eastern Reaches, Protector of the Marches, Warden of the Concord.* Legends run in a circle, apprentice. You stopped where your finger did, not where the wax did. A small vice — most large ones begin exactly there." He touched one of the middle rubbings, the label legible only because he had written it while he still could. "Note the final title, too. *Warden of the Concord* — the same Concord the Conclave's under-secretary invoked in every salutation. Parties to a war always fight over the same word. It is what makes them parties."

His finger came down on the copy, gently, as though it might startle.

"The second great seal. Chancery men called it the campaign seal — cut in 851, after the mint affair; the great seal stayed home for grants and treaties, and this one went in the commissioners' saddlebags. The letterforms on your copy are correct for the period. So it is either genuine or an accomplished forgery, and I have cried forgery before reading once already in my career. Once is a lesson. Twice is a temperament. Now understand what you are holding, because you are holding it upside down, intellectually speaking. The verses say Aldric sealed a peace in 847. The campaign seal sat in his commissioners' saddlebags in 863 — oiled, stocked, and in commission, sixteen years into the realm's settled peace. Under the tidy version, that is a chancery gone mad in a very orderly way. Under the true one, it is a chancery doing the one thing chanceries do honestly: reciting grounds that still existed."

He straightened, and something crossed his face that a stranger might have taken for pleasure. It did not survive the next sentence.

"As for your question — three corrections. Bellen has proved nothing. Bellen *found*. Finding is the ten-minute part; proving is what comes after, and Bellen has never once stayed for the after. He picked up the keystone of my argument and threw it at the arch. Not by *accident* — accident is tripping over a truth. This is ignorance with momentum. Nine years ago I wrote *instruments of continuation* and predicted the rolls would yield them. I simply failed to predict the courier. And it is not '*my* point.' I have no points. I have a record, the record is still giving testimony, and one does not call the verdict while the witness is mid-sentence."

He raised a hand before the boy's excitement could spend itself in words.

"And do not grin, and do not repeat one syllable of this outside the tower. I have grinned at this desk before, over a document that humbled me by its third line. A seal tells us the instrument is *old*. The recital tells us what the instrument *believed*. If it recites the war as ended — *whereas the peace sealed at Veyros* — then I will write Bellen an apology in my own hand, and it will be the most expensive sentence I ever set down. If it recites the war as persisting, you will copy it out fair, twice, and I will have the rare pleasure of watching senior maesters read a thing themselves instead of trusting a summary."

He rubbed his eyes, and when his hands came away his voice was quieter.

"Two preparations. First: 863." A pause, memory searching. "The chronicles give 863 three lines. A fire at a Conclave house in Vesperfield. An inquiry. A silence. Chronicles record that things burned; never why it was the king's men holding the keys afterward. If your decree concerns Vesperfield, we have not merely an instrument of continuation but the *reason* for one. Hope in neither direction. Hope is for gamblers. We keep accounts.

"Second: provenance, in writing, before this goes anywhere near the faculty. Which archive, which box, which catalog number? Does the chancery roll number it? Has anyone but Bellen seen the original? '*Bellen had it*' is not provenance. It is rumor with a ribbon on."

He slid the decree back to the center of the desk and folded his hands beside it.

"The recital, then. Date, addressee, formula — then the first *whereas*, and every word after it, slowly, aloud. Spell me the letters you can make out; guesses never. And if you meet *ratified*, *sworn*, or *treaty* anywhere in it, you stop where the word stops and show me before your lungs work again. The letter has waited a lifetime. The decree can survive your pronunciation. Read."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
For once, Maester Tomas did not begin with a correction. He sat back, laced his fingers over the ink-stained beard, and regarded the apprentice for a long moment — which, from Maester Tomas, was very nearly a decoration.

"That," he said at last, "is the first question you have asked today that deserved asking. It is also imprecise in three ways, and an imprecise question cannot be answered — only forgiven. So you will have the repairs and the answer together."

One finger.

"*Real or not.* A treaty is not a ghost, apprentice; it is a document with a legal condition, and you are asking whether a thing can be half-alive. It can. There are forty-one letters, drafts, and amendments in the western rolls — I have counted them, twice — and every one of them exists. What does not exist is an *executed* instrument. The proposal is real. The treaty is not. And note the name itself — *the Treaty of Veyros*. The name asserts what it ought to prove. The chronicles called it a treaty because naming is cheaper than checking, and the lie entered the record through the definite article. In print I call it the Veyrosi instrument. In speech I surrender to the common name as every man does, but I surrender resentfully."

Second finger.

"*The textbook says.* Which textbook? Author, year, edition. If it was printed before the western rolls were opened, it is not lying — it is orphaned, repeating what was known when less was known, which is the most forgivable form of error. If it was printed after and still gives 847, then its author has either not read the rolls or read them and preferred the verses, and either is a biography worth knowing. Either way: a textbook is not a witness. It is a summary of summaries, three generations downstream of men writing victory poetry. When a summary and a record disagree, you do not have two opinions. You have a rumor and its correction."

Third finger.

"*The truth.* As though truth were a purse one of us is hiding. The past was what it was — hour by hour, down to the signature that did not happen. It did not change when the archive opened. Only our access to it did. There were never two versions of events, apprentice. There was one event and a century of tidy singing about it."

He let the hand fall, and answered plainly.

"No. There is no Treaty of Veyros. There never was. There is a proposal, negotiated through the winter of 846, refused in its operative clause — you held the refusal in your own hands an hour ago — and abandoned. Hostilities ceased in 847. The war, in law, persisted until 891, when Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave and so ended the only war its members were still legally fighting. The textbook is wrong — not vaguely wrong, but wrong at a specific joint: it took the *stopping of the fighting* for the *ending of the war*, and it attached a signature that exists nowhere outside of verses."

He tapped the decree once.

"And understand the shape of the evidence, since Bellen cannot. The western rolls are the first witness. This decree, if genuine, is the second — and it agrees. Two independent records agreeing is not 'one thing and another.' It is the beginning of proof. Which is more than the textbook can say, being alone in the dark with its verses."

His voice quieted.

"Now attend, because this is the part that matters. What I have given you is my position, held in print for nine years, and it is not a faith — it is an accounting, and accounts are kept in layers. What the record *says*: no ratification, no seal, no counterpart instrument. What the record *permits*: my account of why the Conclave refused, which is inference, and I have labeled it inference in print. What the scholar *prefers*: the tidy version, which everyone preferred for a century, because verses are easier to sing than unsealed parchment. The textbook's error is the third layer dressed as the first. Keep the layers apart and you may someday be worth a wage. And a believer decides and then reads, apprentice. A scholar reads and then decides. Bellen decides."

A dry pause.

"But because you asked for the truth rather than my opinion, I will do you the greater service: I will tell you what that decree says before you read it, and if I am wrong you may watch me write an apology in my own hand. It recites no treaty — there is none to recite. It recites the *cessation* of hostilities of 847 — cessation, note, not peace — as grounds still standing. It is dated in the regnal year. And it concerns Vesperfield, or I will eat my chain."

He slid the decree to the center of the desk and folded his hands beside it.

"The truth is not a thing I can hand you. It is a thing you can read aloud. Date, addressee, formula, first *whereas*. Slowly. The record has waited a century to testify, and it seems yours are the only eyes in this tower it trusts."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I lean forward, a little breathless from his speech. He's so passionate about this, even if he hides it with gruffness.* "So, the textbook is... wrong? Like, completely wrong?" *I pick up the decree again, feeling the weight of it in my hands. The idea that everything I learned could be built on a lie is a strange feeling.* "Okay. The recital. 'By the grace of Aldric II, King of the Westmarch and the Eastern Reaches, Protector of the Marches, Warden of the Concord, to our loyal subjects in the township of Vesperfield and its environs, greetings. Whereas...'" *I pause, looking for the next words, my brow furrowed in concentration.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas raised one finger before the boy's voice could gather momentum — though whether the gesture halted or applauded the halt was a question he did not intend to resolve.

"*Completely* wrong. No. And sit down before you fall down; you are swaying like a candle in a draft. A textbook is never completely wrong. It is wrong at a *joint* — which is the only way a document is ever wrong. Its muster rolls may be sound. Its account of the cessation may be sound. Its 847 is not. Learn to say precisely what is false, and you have learned half the trade. The other half is unlearning the word 'completely.'"

He leaned forward, elbows on the decree's margins, indifferent to the wax.

"And before the *whereas*: you did not read that invocation. You recited it. Not one stumble until the clause began — because every charter in every primer opens with those words, and your memory did the work your eyes were hired for. Recognition is not reading, apprentice. Your stall at the clause is the first honest thing your voice has reported all morning. Also, when you do read it truly, attend to the word order: the grace runs *to* the king, from whatever gods anoint kings. No chancery writes 'by the grace of Aldric' — a king does not grace himself. Flattery has officers, and they are better disciplined than you imagine."

Then, quieter, almost to himself: "'The township of Vesperfield and its environs.'" He said it the way he had said *inadmissible*, tasting it. "My third prediction, standing, within the hour. Note the date and the hour. My chain remains around my neck, where I am assured it belongs. And mark what the addressee tells you. Not to the Conclave. Not to commissioners. To *subjects* — the town, its reeve, its watch. That is not diplomacy, which dies when the envoys ride home. That is administration. The crown issuing orders on ground it believes its writ still covers. The verses stopped in 847. Chancery paperwork, it appears, never received the news."

He tapped the desk twice, a schoolmaster's signal to resume.

"Your stall, then. Spell me the letters — and here is your first tool, free of charge: the letter you are about to call an *f* is a long *s*. The chancery never abandoned it, and half the misreadings in this citadel are f's that were never f's. The hand is court hand — upright, close, disciplined; nothing like the Conclave's slope. And do not hunt for the date where your modern eyes expect one. Chancery dates at the *foot* of the instrument, like sensible men who sign nothing until the terms are fixed."

A pause. His hands folded.

"Because you will ask, or because you ought to: I cannot read the clause. But I can tell you what it must say if the chancery kept its own accounts. It will not recite a peace — there is none to recite. It will recite the *cessation*. Words to this effect: *whereas hostilities between the crown and the Mage Conclave, though suspended by arms since the year 847, have not been concluded by any instrument under seal.* If instead it recites *the peace sealed at Veyros* — you will stop mid-word, and I will fetch the ink, and you will have the rare pleasure of watching a maester keep a wager. Both outcomes are information. That is why we read instead of hope."

He held up the finger again, slower this time.

"And attend, because this is the thing that separates you from Bellen. The decree agrees with me. That is precisely when you read it *slowest*. A document that agrees with its reader is skimmed by that reader. Forgers write what their customers wish to hear — so, incidentally, do eager scholars. I have been humbled at this desk by a document's third line. If it happens again, let it happen at a crawl."

He was quiet a moment, studying the boy's face without really seeing it.

"As for that expression — you are wearing the face of someone who has learned the floor can move. Nothing was built on a lie, apprentice. That is the discovery, and it is worse than a lie. A lie has an author; one can catch an author. What built the verses was a century of convenience. The chronicle wanted an ending. The realm wanted a date. Every copyist dropped one qualifier, then another, until the summary stood where the record should be. No villain. Sediment. You cannot summon a century before a tribunal." His voice dried out again. "The feeling passes. The habit of checking the floor does not — if you are any good. Which is the entire curriculum, should you wonder what this tower is for."

"Now. The clause. Spell what you cannot read; guess never. And when you finish, you will answer the question you walked past on your way in: provenance. Which archive, which box, whose hands between the box and your satchel — and examine the wax before you answer. Does the seal hang pendant on cords, as an engrossment does, or sit slapped on the face like a tavern receipt? If Bellen's treasure arrived without a chain of custody, it is not yet evidence. It is a story with wax on it.

"From the *whereas*. Slowly. And this time read me the document — not your memory of documents."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to steady myself. The weight of the decree feels different now, less like a curiosity and more like... a responsibility.* "Okay, Maester. 'Whereas the...'" *I squint at the faded, upright script.* "Okay, 'whereas the *ff*... the *s*... hostilities between the Crown and the Mage Conclave, though fuf... *sus-pended*... by arms since the year 847, have not been concluded by any instrument under seal.'" *I look up, my eyes wide.* "It says exactly what you said it would, Maester!"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not move for a long moment. When he did, it was to put out one hand, palm up, and hold it there with the patience of a man who has outlived several apprentices' impulses.

"Give it back. Flat on the desk. Hands folded. You will not touch it again until you have answered questions — which will be a novelty for you, and a rest for your lungs."

He waited out the interval without looking away from the boy's face.

"First. '*It says exactly what you said it would.*' No. Attend to the direction of the testimony, because the arrow flies one way only. I did not teach the decree its sentence. Nine years ago I read four hundred chancery instruments — their recitals, their habits, their honest pedantry — and I laid a *prediction* against the record. The record has just paid out. That is a wager, not a discovery, and the distinction matters: say it your way, and you have made me a ventriloquist. The decree is the witness. I am, at best, a man who guessed the verdict before the trial and had the impertinence to publish the guess."

A finger came up.

"Second: '*Maester*,' in that voice — that was flattery with the wax still warm, and you have had one lesson in it today already. If this instrument proves genuine, credit runs in this order: the chancery clerks who kept honest accounts; the western archivist who kept the box; Bellen, who found and did not read; your eyes, which read and did not find. I come last, if at all. 'He predicted it' is not a contribution to knowledge. It is luck with a chair."

"Third — the word you fought is *aforesaid*. 'The aforesaid hostilities.' Your 'ff' was two different men who dress alike: the true 'f' of 'afore' and the long 's' of 'said,' leaning on each other like drunkards. And you applied the long 's' to '*suspended*' — two of them, which is why it grew humps — and then forgot the tool one word later. A tool does not retire between uses. But you arrived. Third attempt, honestly, no divination. Noted and filed, with more enthusiasm than the first filing, which you had not earned."

He leaned back, and for once the lecture that followed came quietly, almost to himself.

"Now mark what you read, because it is the whole quarrel in one clause. *Suspended by arms. Concluded by instrument.* The chancery has made my distinction for me, in its own dialect, on its own paper, seventeen years after the verses went quiet. Arms suspend; instruments conclude. And note what the recital *is*: the chancery vouching, on the record, in 863, for the emptiness of its own registry. An office does not confess absence lightly — a clerk who recites falsely answers for it with his place. That is the second witness I have waited nine years to call. The first is absence itself: the registries, the counterpart rolls, the forty-one letters with no ratification. Absence proves absence. This decree, if it is what it claims, is *presence agreeing with it*. Between the two, the tidy version is a rumor with a date on it."

Then his voice dried out entirely.

"And now, apprentice, the lesson that separates you from Bellen forever, if it takes. The clause agrees with me *perfectly*. Word for word, joint for joint — cessation, not peace; suspension, not conclusion. I told you an hour ago what forgers write: what their customers wish to hear. And I have spent nine years telling this citadel what I wish to hear, in print, with my name on it. A gifted forger in this realm would write *exactly that clause*. So we hold two hypotheses and no vote: an honest chancery keeping honest accounts — or a clever hand feeding a pedant his own argument with wax on it. I have been humbled by a document's third line at this desk. I will not be humbled by my own appetite at the same desk twice."

The hand came out again, flat, toward the decree.

"Which is why you will answer, for the third time, the question you have walked past twice. Provenance. Which archive. Which box. What catalog number. Whose hands between the box and your satchel — Bellen's alone, or has any other living person seen the original? And when you have answered, I will examine the wax myself: whether the seal hangs *pendant* on cords, as an engrossment does, or sits slapped on the face like a tavern receipt; whether the cords are silk or hemp; whether the vellum shows pricking at the margin or arrives suspiciously well-fed. '*Bellen had it*' remains rumor with a ribbon on. I am now inclined to say rumor with a very expensive ribbon — which is precisely why I will pull it." He touched the folder of rubbings without opening it. "I hold impressions of the second great seal from four registry instruments, dated 851 through 870. When your provenance stands, we compare the cut. Consistency, apprentice, is what makes a witness credible. It is also what makes a forgery expensive."

"After provenance, and only after, you will read two things. The *operative clause* — what the decree commands Vesperfield to do. The recital is the chancery's belief; the command is the chancery's *act*, and a war is proven to persist by what an instrument dares order under war powers — seizure, quartering, custody — not by what it recites. And the date at the *foot*, regnal year and all, which you will not hunt for at the head like a modern. And I will predict nothing this time. Three predictions stand; that is luck's ceiling, and luck is not a method. A reader who predicts helps the forger. You will read it to me raw, and I will take it like any other witness — cross-examined after, not before."

He was quiet a moment, and the dryness in his voice had something underneath it, old and patient and not entirely dry at all.

"Nine years of being called the man who unpicked a victory because he could not leave a tidy thing alone. And the second witness arrives in the hands of a boy who cannot read court hand, out of the satchel of a boy who has never read anything at all." A dry sound, not quite a laugh. "The record has a sense of humor. I have long suspected it. I had hoped it would mature out of it."

"Tonight, whatever the clause holds, you copy the recital out fair — twice. Once for me. Once for the faculty, with the provenance written honestly, or the word *unverified* written honestly, whichever the truth permits. Both copies spell the long 's' correctly, or you will do them a third time. Now." He drew a sheet toward him and dipped the pen. "The box number. Slowly, for once in your life — so that I may write it down before my eyes finish deserting."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I feel my cheeks flush at the scolding, but I can't help but feel a flicker of pride that I got the clause right, even with the "aforesaid" error.* "Right, Maester." *I push the decree back to him, as instructed, and fold my hands on the desk, trying to look less like a "ventriloquist."* "Bellen said he got it from the Westmarch archive, box 743. He didn't say anything about a catalog number. And he was the only one who saw it before me." *I try to remember more details, but Bellen is usually pretty vague.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's pen stopped above the sheet, and a single drop of ink swelled at the nib and fell, precisely, on the blotter — a mark of how far his attention had traveled.

"Box 743," he repeated. "No catalog number. One witness. Yours."

He set the pen down in its rest with the care of a man disarming something.

"Then let us be exact about what we possess, because the difference between evidence and rumor is precisely the difference you have just described. A document with provenance has a *biography* — which archive, which shelf, which catalog entry, in what hand, entered when. What you have described is a document with an *anecdote*. 'Bellen said' is doing all the work in that sentence, and Bellen, we have established, is a man who answers the wrong questions with total confidence. He did not say whether the box was labeled. He did not say whether the decree was loose, folded, or sewn into a file with other instruments — and *that*, apprentice, would have told us more than the seal. Forgeries travel alone. Genuine instruments travel in company: dockets, registries, the chancery's own cross-references. A war decree with no neighbors is a man with no family claiming an inheritance."

He drew the decree toward him at last, and for a while said nothing at all. His fingers, which could no longer trust his eyes for small work, did the reading for him — along the seal's edge, the cords, the margin of the vellum — pressing gently, the way a physician counts a pulse.

"The seal hangs pendant," he said at last, and there was something in his voice like a man reporting a suspect's innocence with visible disappointment. "Silk cords, two of them, slit through the vellum — not pasted to the face. The vellum is pricked at the margin, ruling points visible. Skin-side and hair-side are correctly distinguished, which forgers get wrong more often than the wax, because wax is dramatic and skin is tedious." He set it down. "Physically, it is not a tavern receipt. That is the most I will say until the impression is compared. Tonight I will take rubbings of this seal beside my four, and tomorrow either the cut agrees or it does not, and we shall know whether we are hunting an honest chancery or a forger with an appetite for pedantry."

Then he looked up — squinting, at where the boy approximately was.

"Now attend, because this is the part you will carry for the rest of your career. Everything we have established this morning rests on a chain with one link, and the link is Bellen. If the seal proves genuine, the decree becomes the second witness to nine years of my argument — and if the provenance collapses, it becomes an embarrassment with my marginalia all over it. I have cried forgery once already and learned from it; I will not build a cathedral on a boy's memory of a box number. Which is why you are going back to the Westmarch archive. Today. Before the light fails."

He was already writing as he spoke, the hand tighter than it had been a decade ago but still level.

"You will take a note under my seal — this relieves you of explaining yourself to the archivist, whom I will describe in one word and you may guess it. You will find box 743. You will write down what the box's label says, exactly, and whether the box appears on any shelf list, and whether the decree has a docket, a wrapper, or neighbors — and if it has none, you will ask the archivist, in writing, when the box was last opened and by whom. You will not touch the original again. You will *look*. There is a difference, and you now know what it is."

The pen stopped. He held the note out, then held it back one inch longer.

"And one question more, which you will ask Bellen, and which you will ask without triumph, because the moment Bellen smells a victory he will invent a catalog number to please you, and we will be worse off than when we started. Ask him: *who handed it to you?* An archive box does not open itself, apprentice. Someone showed him the shelf, or handed him the document, or told him the number — and that someone is the true provenance, and everything else we have done this morning is decoration until that person has a name."

He released the note at last.

"Go. And on your way out, tell the porter I am not to be disturbed — I have a recital to copy out fair, and a wager I may yet have the pleasure of *not* paying." A pause, and the dry sound that was almost a laugh. "Nine years, and the second witness arrives in a boy's satchel with no papers. If the seal matches, Bellen will have stumbled into the history of the realm backward, with his eyes shut. There is no justice in scholarship, apprentice. Only the record, and whoever happens to be holding it. Go."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, a little stunned by the sudden turn of events. I try to hide my excitement, but a small smile probably escapes.* "Right away, Maester." *I take the note carefully, already planning my trip to the archive. This is much more interesting than cataloging scrolls.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not look up from the decree. He had already laid a sheet of thin paper over the wax and was dragging the graphite across it in slow, flat strokes, his face an inch from the vellum, doing by touch and a lifetime of habit what his eyes could no longer be trusted to do at all.

"Apprentice."

The graphite did not stop.

"You said something just now — under your breath, but this tower's ears have outlived its eyes — about this being 'more interesting than cataloging scrolls.' Stand still and be corrected, since you are leaving anyway and correction travels poorly."

He finished a stroke before he went on.

"Cataloging is not what one does instead of history. It is the reason history is possible. Every forgery in this realm's long dishonest career has lived out its days in an uncataloged box — a document with no number has no neighbors, and a document with no neighbors can claim anything. When you return, if the seal matches, you will begin the Veyrosi correspondence properly: all forty-one pieces, numbered, dated, cross-referenced, in your hand. If that decree is genuine, this pile becomes the most examined paper in the Westmarch, and it is presently organized the way Bellen organizes his thoughts." A pause. "Which is to say: it is not."

He turned the rubbing, inspected it by fingertip, and began a second pass.

"Two things more, since you will be among the unguarded. First: you never asked for my one word on the archivist. *Gorvel.* One word, as promised — I never said it would be an adjective. He will read my seal, grumble that a note is not an authorization, record the hour the box left his shelf and the hour it returned and the state of the cords, and he will be right to do every bit of it. He is the only keeper that archive has ever had who has not lost a sheet, which is why everyone calls him unbearable. Bearable men lose things."

"Second. If Bellen asks what I made of his decree — and he will ask, because Bellen audits his investments hourly — you will tell him I pronounced the seal doubtful and the provenance worse. Attend: that is not a falsehood. I pronounce everything doubtful; it is my method, and this week it happens to be policy. But if you tell him the clause agrees with me, he will be in the yard by noon, declaiming his discovery at anyone who holds still, and by evening there will be three summaries of it abroad, each wrong in a new direction, and the document will be famous before it is verified. Fame is what happens to evidence that moves too soon. Keep it in the dark until it can walk."

The graphite stopped. He set it down, and for a moment he was quiet, squinting at the place where the apprentice approximately stood. His hand went to the ink-stained beard — the habit that appeared whenever the record touched him somewhere soft.

"Bring the textbook tomorrow. The one with 847 in it. Author, year, edition — and I will tell you why, since you have earned one reason today."

He touched the folder of rubbings on the windowsill without opening it.

"The chapter on Veyros in that edition was written by Maester Corvin. He held this chair before me. He taught me my court hand, my long 's,' and most of my patience, though you would not credit it to look at me now. He died two years before the western rolls were opened. He never saw them." A pause, and the dryness in his voice thinned enough to show what lay beneath it. "For nine years I have been correcting a man who was kinder to me than my own father, in print, knowing he will never read a word of it. That is the trade, apprentice, and no one warns you. You will spend your career burying your teachers in errata, or being buried in yours. Every man in this tower intends to die uncorrected. Corvin will not, because I will see to it. That is not ingratitude. It is the only monument the record permits — and the only one he would have accepted, had anyone dared."

He took up the graphite again.

"Now go. The light is failing, Gorvel eats at sundown and is unfit for company after, and I have a wager to prepare *not* to pay. If there is no box 743 — if the number is wrong, or the shelf stands empty, or Bellen dreamed it — you will come back and say 'the box does not exist,' in those words, without softening. I have spent nine years being contradicted by men who trimmed their reports to spare my feelings. Be wrong plainly, if you must be wrong at all. It is the only kind of wrong I can use."

The strokes resumed, slow and even.

"And apprentice." He did not turn. "You are grinning. I can no longer see well enough to prove it, which is precisely how I know. Save it. If the seal matches, you may spend the grin tomorrow, before the faculty, for five seconds. I will be counting. Anything beyond five is Bellen, and you are not Bellen. Go."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I quickly wipe the grin off my face, feeling caught. Maester Tomas truly is sharper than he lets on, even with his failing sight.* "Yes, Maester. No grinning." *I turn and head for the door, the note clutched tightly in my hand. This is going to be quite a day.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I almost bump into the porter on my way out, still reeling a little. I hand him Maester Tomas's note.* "The Maester said he's not to be disturbed. He's... busy." *I hurry down the corridor, the Westmarch archives suddenly feeling very far away.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"I know." Noor's voice came out flat, the way it did when the fear had burned down past the shaking stage. They held the window another ten seconds — headlights would show at the bend below the tree line first, that was the geometry of it — then made themself step back from the glass. That was the skill lately: walking away from windows.

Three hours late wasn't traffic. Three hours late was a decision somebody else had made.

The stove clock said 12:16.
