Noor dug the burner out of their jacket — the cheap one, the one Halloran's real number had never touched — and typed the check-in they'd agreed on weeks ago, dressed up as a wrong-number text: *Hi, are you still selling the kayak?* Sent. If no answer in twenty minutes, the protocol said assume compromise and be gone by first light. Noor set the phone face-up on the table, in view, and left it there ticking.

Then, finally, the laptop. The phone records were already on it — six weeks of the fixer's call logs, three thousand lines, three numbers that mattered. Noor had flagged two. The third traced to a burner that had gone dark in March, and that was the whole gap, one number, and Halloran was supposed to be walking up that road tonight with the name attached to it. The encrypted drive sat in its padded case at the table's edge. Noor looked at it, then opened the call logs instead. One disaster at a time.

They crossed to the cabinet, found a sleeve of saltines in a plastic bin, and ate four standing up without tasting any of them. "There," they said. "I ate."

Then, without looking up from the screen: "You want a job? Sit where you can see the road. Headlights come up that track, I want to hear about it before the bend. Not after."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I don't look up from my phone, still scrolling.* "Sure, whatever." *I shift on the couch so I can see the window without moving too much.* "Just tell me when I can go back to sleep."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"That depends on the kayak," Noor said.

Then, because Driver had given them six hours of mountain road without asking a single question, and that was worth paying back: "There's a text out to my source, dressed up as a wrong number. Right answer comes back, you can sleep with both eyes shut. No answer by half past twelve, we're loading the car in the dark and you're driving again. So. Kayak."

They rinsed the dust out of the coffee pot, filled it from the gallon jug on the counter, set it on the back burner. They'd regret the caffeine at three in the morning and drink it anyway. That was the entire sleep plan: regret it later.

"Your actual job, if headlights come up that road — you say the word 'car.' Just that. Quiet, like you're bored. Then you get up slow and go stand in the back bedroom till I come get you. You did me a favor driving me up here. You didn't sign the rest of it."

Then the laptop. The logs were a six-week wall of timestamps, and Noor went at them the way that always worked — by hand, line by line, coffee cooling beside the trackpad. Number one was a downtown law office. Weekday calls, business hours, eleven minutes apiece, boring as billing. A front, which was itself information. Number two was the opposite of boring: twenty-six calls, every one between eleven at night and three in the morning, every one routed through the same tower — the one off Route 9, the industrial stretch, gravel lots and chain-link. The fixer had been standing in the same half mile of nowhere every single time he made them.

Noor matched the log against their own sent folder, and their hands went still on the keys. The comment request had gone out on a Tuesday, 4:51 PM. At 5:02, the fixer called Number Two. Four minutes. Then his phone went dark for two days. You call after something gets set in motion. Then you go quiet and let it run. Six weeks. Every careful thing since — the cash, the second phone, this cabin — done inside their clock, not outside it.

Noor caught themself checking the gap in the curtain again and made themself stop.

The stove said 12:27. The phone lay face-up at the table's edge, screen dark, not buzzing.

One disaster at a time. The logs had given what they had. Noor unzipped the padded case, plugged in the drive, and typed the passphrase Halloran had made them memorize in a parking garage in March — eight words, no paper copy, repeated until they stopped being words. The folder tree bloomed across the screen: dates. PAYMENTS. Audio files with no names at all.

"New job," Noor said, already clicking the folder dated three days after the thing that burned down the county records annex. "Watch the clock for me. If that phone hasn't buzzed by 12:36 exactly, say the time out loud. I go under on this, I lose hours."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, still not looking up from my phone.* "Got it. 12:36." *I make a mental note, then go back to scrolling.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Eleven files. Noor counted them twice, the way you count money. Four photographs of ledger pages taken on a desk — somebody's thumb in the corner of the first frame, Halloran's probably; he was careful about the middle of things and never the edges. One spreadsheet. Six audio files numbered 0001 through 0006 and named nothing at all. The drive had come to Noor ten days ago, taped behind a drainpipe at a park-and-ride, and this laptop was the first machine it had ever touched. Halloran's one rule had been simple: *if I miss the meet, it's yours.* He'd missed the meet by three hours and twenty-seven minutes.

Spreadsheet first. One disaster at a time.

141 rows: date, amount, payee. The payey never changed — Ashfield Site Services LLC. The amounts never crossed ten thousand. Eight-two hundred, ninety-six fifty, ninety-four seventy-five, a drumbeat of payments sitting just under the line where banks start asking questions. Noor selected the column and let the machine add it: $1,283,650. Twenty-two months of it.

The remit-to field was the part that mattered. A mailbox place, 1140 Route 9, Unit B. Noor sat very still. Twenty-six calls, all between eleven and three, all routed through the tower off Route 9 — the same half mile of gravel lots and chain-link. The fixer had been standing inside the money the entire time.

The coffee was done. Noor poured a mug, drank it black and terrible standing up, and watched the stove clock roll over to 12:30. The phone stayed dark.

"Half past," Noor said, to the room. "No kayak." The protocol was their own, written sober, and it said load the car in the dark. "First light's six hours off and the loading takes twenty minutes. I'm spending the difference." It came out steady. It was the most dishonest sentence of the night.

The first audio file ran forty-one minutes. Noor dug the earbuds out of their jacket and wore one. The other ear belonged to the road. That was the rule now.

Room tone first: wind on a mic, a diesel idling, the backup beeper of a loader somewhere — a sound with an address on it. Route 9 at night. Then two voices. One flat, older, unhurried. The other, Noor knew the way you know a voice that has spent three hours whispering in a parking garage.

Halloran.

"You said the annex was clean," Halloran said.

"It's handled."

"It's on the news. That's handled?"

"It bought us a quarter. Nobody counts paper that doesn't exist anymore." A pause — diesel, wind. "And the reporter?"

"What reporter. A phone number and a theory."

Noor looked at the drive's activity light blinking on the table's edge. *A phone number and a theory.* The men on the recording were wrong about that, and being wrong was the only thing keeping Noor alive. Then the flat voice again, quieter, almost kind:

"You worry like a man who made copies."

Silence, long enough that Noor's finger hovered over the trackpad. A door. The file ran out.

Noor played the last thirty seconds twice. The drive was the copy. Ten days in a drainpipe — and whatever the question had cost Halloran, it had cost him before the nine o'clock meet he never made.

The phone lay dark at the table's edge. Noor queued 0002 and did not look at the stove. That was Driver's job now, given away on purpose, because this drive was the kind of thing that ate hours whole.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
File 0002 ran thirty-four minutes. It had been recorded in a vehicle — engine idling, a heater fan, the creak of somebody's seat. Two voices. The flat one, and a younger one that said "sir" twice in the first sixty seconds and meant it both times. The logs said the fixer lived in the flat man's pocket. This voice was standing in one.

"He's been at the clerk's office twice this week," the younger voice said. "Requesting the bid file again."

"Good. Let him knock. A man knocking on doors tells you which doors he can't open."

Then the part that stopped Noor's spoon halfway to their mouth. The park-and-ride. Off 17, Tuesday before last — the day the drive went into the drainpipe. *He sat eleven minutes, walked the fence line, got back in his car.* And after: *camera got one angle, a car came through after he left, out-of-county, partial on the plate.*

Noor set the chili down. It was two years past its best-by date and tasted like it, and none of that mattered, because the car that came through after was theirs. Three characters of their own plate, sitting in somebody's folder for ten days. Ten days was long enough to run a partial, pull a registration, and park a sedan across from an apartment. The men on file 0001 had said *what reporter, a phone number and a theory.* Being wrong about Noor was the only thing keeping Noor alive, and wrongness, it turned out, had a shelf life of ten days.

The flat voice made his decision at minute twenty-two, patient as billing: "Don't touch the drop. Let it ripen. When it moves, we follow it, and we take the set — him, and whoever's hands it's in."

Noor played that part twice, then made themself stop, because the arithmetic was already done. They'd meant to take the pair at the handoff. The handoff was set for nine o'clock, here. The road had been empty for four hours. Which meant they'd moved early and taken Halloran somewhere below the mountain — or the address of this cabin was holding, for now, inside a man under questioning. There was no good version. There was only *how long does a man hold an address,* and the answer was always *not forever.*

The stove said 1:14. So 12:36 had come and gone unannounced — the timekeeping had been delegated to a couch, and the couch had delegated it right back to nobody. It didn't matter. The phone's silence had already said everything the protocol needed it to say.

One thing left that Noor could control tonight. They dragged the folder off the drive onto the laptop's own disk and watched the bar crawl. A single copy was a hostage, not a shield. And the flat voice's own words — *you worry like a man who made copies* — meant he believed copies existed, which was maybe the only reason Halloran was hours late instead of dead in a ditch. Copies weren't paranoia anymore. Copies were the whole plan.

The phone buzzed at 1:31.

Noor crossed the kitchen in four steps and looked down at it. One text. From Halloran's number.

**Sold it in June, sorry.**

The right answer. Word for word — the exact phrase they'd agreed on weeks ago. And it meant nothing, because Noor had months of texts from that number, every one of them lowercase, punctuation applied like it cost money. *sold it in june sorry* was Halloran. This had capitals and a comma. This had been proofread.

"That's the right answer," Noor said, to Driver, without looking up. "Seventy-five minutes late, and it's in the wrong handwriting. They've got his phone. Which means they've probably got him. And now they've got the number that texted it." Noor popped the battery out of the burner, dropped phone, battery, and SIM into a zip bag, and put the bag in the go-bag by the door. The burner had been cheap in every possible sense.

The go-bag took ten minutes: laptop, drive, cash, the sleeve of saltines, keys on the table where the phone used to be. Headlights never came up the track. Noor checked the gap in the curtain twice anyway, which was its own tax.

"You wanted to know when you could go back to sleep," Noor said. "Go. I'll wake you at five-fifteen, we're rolling by five-forty-five, down the mountain in the dark. I promised you both eyes shut if the kayak sold. The kayak sold wrong. One eye's the best I can offer." A beat. "The word 'car' still means what it meant. Boots, keys, back bedroom. No questions."

Then the notebook, and the lede Noor had been carrying around for six weeks, finally set down in ink: *For twenty-two months, somebody paid a shell company $1.28 million in pieces too small to attract a question — and the paper trail burned down with the county annex.*

Noor read it over. It was true and it was nothing. It needed a name at the end of it.

Four files left to find one. Noor put the earbud back in.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I blink and sit up, looking from my phone to Noor, then at the go-bag by the door.* "Wait, so we're leaving?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor pulled the earbud out and let it hang. "At five-forty-five. Not now." A beat, dry as the saltines. "I did cover this an hour ago, but you were somewhere in your phone, so the briefing repeats once. Three reasons. One — there's a single road off this mountain, and if a car's coming up it while we're going down, I want to meet it at an hour I chose, not an hour it chose. Two — nobody's on it yet, and the text is how I know that. Three—" they tapped the padded case "—I don't leave here with half this. The finished story is the only place I'm safe. The half story is just a bag somebody can take off me."

They sat back down at the laptop. The fear had found a job to do, which was the only treatment for it that ever worked.

"And the text. You watched me kill the phone. Here's what it actually told me." Noor kept their voice level, the way you'd brief a colleague, because Driver had earned a briefing if not the whole truth. "That passphrase got agreed out loud. Parking garage, March. It's not in any phone, any email, any notebook — it lived in two skulls. So the man who texted it didn't *find* it. He asked somebody for it. Seventy-five minutes to produce four words." They let that sit. "That's not a guy scrolling a phone. That's a guy working on a person."

The stove clock flipped a minute in the silence.

"Which means Halloran's alive, and talking, and as long as they need him talking, this cabin isn't in anybody's GPS. We're inside his window. It closes when he runs out of answers, and I've seen men hold for days and I've seen them hold for forty minutes, and there is no way to know which kind he is from up here. So sleep in the window. That's not a figure of speech. That's the schedule." Then, quieter, without looking over: "Your name's on nothing I own. Not the logs, not the drive, not the notebook. That's procedure. It's also the only thank-you I've got that's worth anything."

Earbud back in. File 0003 ran twenty-two minutes, recorded indoors after hours — Noor knew it inside ten seconds: HVAC hum with no wind over it, a wall clock somewhere, the dead acoustics of an office where every hard surface wore the same silence. Three voices this time. The flat one. Halloran, mostly breathing. And a visitor — gravel voice, work boots on tile, a man who didn't introduce himself because contractors never do.

"Gene," was the entire introduction. "Gene, I'm carrying two hundred grand in receivables on your word, and now I'm hearing *records review*."

"There's talk of a review. Talk's cheap. Paper isn't." A chair took weight slowly. "The bid files sit at the annex. After Thursday, there's nothing to review."

"The annex is—"

"Being inspected. Sprinklers. Very routine." And then the flat voice did the thing Noor had now heard three times, the thing that put cold on the back of the neck — it went kind. "You're worrying again. You worry like a man with something to lose. Pay in the pieces we agreed, stay off the phone, and Thursday takes care of Thursday."

Boots leaving. A door with a soft closer. Then, to the man who'd sat silent at a desk recording all of it: "You know that building better than the fire marshal does. Thursday night. North stair."

Halloran's entire answer was one breath. "It's empty at night."

"Then it's a perfect building."

Noor paused it there and sat with cold coffee until the coffee stopped mattering. On 0001 the annex was past tense. On 0003 it was future tense, and Halloran had been *in the room* while it got scheduled — one sentence of objection, taped everything. That was the whole man. Present for the crime, recording it, three months from growing a spine in a parking garage.

Then the work took over, fast, the way it did when the pieces were already on the board. Offline folder — six weeks of hoarded PDFs, org charts and budgets and minutes, saved back when the county website was still boring. Search: *Prosser.*

Eugene T. Prosser. Deputy Commissioner, Department of Public Works. Twenty-six years. Chair of the Procurement Committee, appointed twenty-three months ago. First Ashfield payment: twenty-two months ago. One month for a new chairman to learn the shape of the machine. Then the machine started eating. And the state filing from week three — Ashfield Site Services LLC, registered agent, a downtown law office. Number One. Eleven-minute weekday calls, boring as billing. Because it *was* billing. The firm hadn't been hiding in the logs. It had done the paperwork.

Noor opened the notebook and crossed out one word.

*For twenty-two months, somebody paid a shell company $1.28 million in pieces too small to attract a question — and the paper trail burned down with the county annex.*

Underneath, pressed hard enough to show through to the next page:

*For twenty-two months, the man who chaired every bid committee the county had collected $1.28 million through a shell company, in pieces too small to attract a question — and the paper trail burned down with the annex. His name is Gene Prosser.*

It was true, and for the first time all night it was more than nothing. It still wasn't a story — one recording was a voice, two was a pattern, the whole set was proof — and there were three files left and four hours of window.

The stove said 2:12. Noor put the earbud back in and started 0004. Behind them, through the gap in the curtain, the mountain kept saying nothing, which was the sound of the window holding.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I close my phone and set it on the cushion beside me.* "So, Prosser." *I let the name hang in the air for a second.* "He's the guy."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor pulled the earbud halfway out and looked at Driver properly for the first time in an hour. "He's the guy who *signs*. Every machine like this has two of them — one who signs, one who carries. I've had the signer since midnight: the committee, the payments, the name. The carrier is the voice. The flat one. He's the one who schedules fires and works on people, and right now he's the one working on Halloran somewhere below this mountain, and until tonight I didn't have a syllable of him. That was the handoff, you understand. Not the drive — I've had the drive ten days. Halloran was supposed to walk up that road carrying the man's name." A beat. "And you put the phone down. First time all night. Noted for the record."

Earbud back in. File 0004 ran nine minutes, and for the first time all night it had no second voice.

Room tone: a parked car, engine off. The tick of a cooling exhaust pipe. A seatbelt buckle swinging once against the door. Halloran, close to the mic, low, in the cadence of a man reading notes he'd written to himself. Dictating a will.

*"If you're hearing this, I missed the meet. Start there. Whatever you've decided happened, start one step worse and you'll be close."*

Then the machine, laid out like inventory: *"Prosser doesn't sign, Prosser appoints. The firm files — Whitlow and Marsh, downtown, everything since the LLC. And the man you've been hearing does the rest. He answers to Voss. That's not his name. Nothing about him is his."* Whitlow & Marsh — the registered agent off the state filing, now with a voice under it.

Then, flatter: *"The annex. I unlocked the north stair and I held the door and I drove home with the windows down. Put that in the story. I'm not a witness to any of this. I'm staff."*

Then, aimed straight at Noor the way the parking garage had sounded: *"They pulled a partial off the park-and-ride camera. Out-of-county car. If that's you — don't go home. Don't call anyone from your own number. Don't use your paper's lawyer. The feds take these better than editors do. That's all I'll say on tape."*

And last, almost apologetic: *"Voss signed the books once. Twenty-two months, one signature. Third page — the photograph with my thumb in the corner. I kept that page because of it. It's the only thing about him that's true."*

The file ran out into engine-off silence.

Something ticked gravel outside — Noor was up and at the curtain gap before the thought finished. Nothing on the track. Down in the valley a logging truck dragged its jake brake through the dark, a sound from another world. Not their road. Their road stayed quiet in a different register.

The photographs. Third image, full screen: a ledger page, a thumb big as a fist in the corner, and there in the payee margin, small and slanted — *D. Kessler*. Twenty-two months of payments to Ashfield Site Services, and once, one time, a human hand had slipped.

The hoard next. Six weeks of boring PDFs, saved precisely because boring is where names live. Search: *kessler*. One hit. 2019. Bid documents, fire-suppression retrofit, county annex building. Contractor: Kessler Mechanical Services. Site foreman: D. Kessler. And on the vendor sheet, a business address — 1140 Route 9, Unit F.

Noor sat very still. Ashfield's remit-to was 1140 Route 9, Unit B. Twenty-six calls, all between eleven and three, all routed through the tower off Route 9. The money mailed to a mailbox, the man standing in the same gravel half mile — and the half mile had a name the whole time. "And the cover story for burning the annex was a sprinkler inspection," Noor said, mostly to themself, "because he'd done the sprinkler work in 2019. He didn't pick a lie. He picked his own résumé."

Notebook. Cross out. Write it again, pressed hard:

*For twenty-two months, the chairman of every bid committee the county had collected $1.28 million through a shell company, in pieces too small to attract a question. The paper trail burned down with the annex — set by a man who once held the county contract to protect that building from fire. Gene Prosser signed the deals. Douglas Kessler carried the cans.*

True, and no longer nothing. Two recordings was a pattern; a ledger, a signature, a contract, and a confession was closing on proof.

Noor sat for a moment with the dead earbud in. Nine minutes. Halloran had spent his last week of freedom building a will for a stranger, then walked into the men it named, and held for seventy-five minutes before giving up the only thing they could use — four words, the toll, not the treasure. Noor made themself stop doing that arithmetic.

The stove said 2:44. A little over two and a half hours of window left.

"New standing order," Noor said, before the fatigue could get a vote. "You sleep till five-fifteen like I promised. But if you wake up and I'm face-down on this keyboard, don't tiptoe — wake me. We're rolling at five-forty-five either way." They drank water from the jug, standing. "And the tape just put a question on the table that I'll want you in the room for. Feds or editors. Halloran said feds. My instinct says editors. My life expectancy says feds. I want to decide it with the full set."

Earbud in. The mountain kept saying nothing, and Noor started 0005.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing the information. I look at the go-bag, then back at Noor.* "Okay. Feds or editors." *I chew on that for a second.* "So, what's Kessler's deal? He burned it down, right?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: No

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I glance at Noor, then back at my phone.* "So, he burned it down, right?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: No

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my phone down again, looking at Noor with a raised eyebrow.* "No? Then what's his deal?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: No

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I sigh, exasperated.* "Okay, then what *is* his deal, Noor? Spit it out."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: No

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I throw my hands up.* "Alright, fine! Don't tell me." *I pick up my phone again, but just stare at the blank screen, clearly annoyed.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't answer right away. The road beyond the glass stayed empty, a pale scar cutting through the pines, and for a long moment they simply watched it, willing headlights to appear. They didn't. Three hours late was not a delay; it was a message.

The suggestion from the couch—eat something—was the most reasonable thing Noor had heard since they'd arrived. Their hands were trembling, too much coffee and not enough food, and the last solid thing they'd eaten was a gas station breakfast sandwich sometime yesterday afternoon. Their stomach turned at the thought of it, but they knew the drill. You couldn't run on fear alone. Eventually the body quit.

They let the curtain drop back into place, sealing the gap. The cabin went fully dark except for the faint glow of the laptop's sleep light. Noor crossed to the kitchen table, stepping around the familiar shape of their own bag, and shrugged off the paralysis that had been creeping up on them for the last hour.

Food first. There was no point in opening the encrypted drive if their hands were shaking too hard to type the passphrase. In the cupboard, past the three mismatched mugs and the dust on the coffee pot, they found a sleeve of saltines and a jar of peanut butter somebody's uncle had left behind. Noor ate standing over the sink, dry cracker, then peanut butter scooped with a plastic spoon that looked older than their career, then another cracker. Mechanical. Not tasting any of it. The salt helped. The protein helped more. By the time the last cracker was gone, some of the tremor had evened out.

They wiped their mouth with the back of their hand and finally flipped open the laptop. The screen's cold blue light painted the kitchen. Noor pulled the encrypted drive from its padded case, ran a thumb over the casing as if to reassure themselves it was real, and plugged it in. The login prompt blinked. They typed the twenty-three-character passphrase from memory—the one they had never written down, the one they repeated in their head every night like a prayer or a threat. The drive unlocked.

They went for the phone records first. The source had promised a log of calls between the shipping company and the port authority; if even one number matched the ones in Noor's own notes, the story stopped being a maybe and became a weapon. Noor opened the CSV, scanned the columns, and started cross-checking against the burner phone's call history.

Three rows in, a number leapt out. Not one of the port authority lines. A burner. Unregistered, as usual. But the tower data put it less than two miles from the cabin at 11:52 PM.

Noor stopped breathing.

Their own burner—the one only the source had the number for—was facedown on the table where they'd left it. Noor picked it up, thumbed it awake. One new message, timestamped 12:11 AM.

*Close the curtain. You're not alone.*

For a second the kitchen tilted. Noor's first thought was that the source had finally arrived and was warning them. Their second, colder thought was that someone else had the source's phone.

They killed the laptop screen with the heel of their hand, plunging the room back into darkness, and backed away from the window, putting the table between themselves and the door. The cabin suddenly felt very small, and very far from help.

"Don't turn on any lights," Noor said, voice barely a breath, not knowing if the words were meant for the friend on the couch or for themselves.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I was still scrolling, half-listening to Noor move around. The sudden darkness makes me jump.* "What the hell was that, Noor?" *I fumble for my phone's flashlight.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The question from the couch barely registered as words. Noor heard only the sudden absence of the laptop's glow and, beneath it, the small sounds of movement from the couch.

"No light," Noor hissed, low and fierce. "Kill your screen. Whatever you're doing—stop. If you turn that flashlight on, you'll silhouette us against the window."

They didn't wait to see whether the warning landed. Noor was already moving, dropping into a crouch beside the kitchen table. The burner went screen-down on the wood, but not before their thumb found the silent switch; if that number was compromised, every ring or vibration was a beacon. Then the encrypted drive: they ejected it properly, waited for the click, and slid it into the inner pocket of their jacket, patting it once through the fabric as if to confirm it hadn't vanished. The laptop followed, tucked under one arm, its weight solid and reassuring. Their bag was still by the table where they'd stepped around it an hour ago; Noor hooked the strap with one foot and dragged it close, not standing, not rising into the line of sight the windows offered.

Only then did they let themselves think.

The message had come from the source's number. The tower data said that same burner had been two miles out at 11:52. Two miles was a five-minute drive, a forty-minute walk through the pines. Either the source had been sitting in the dark just down the road for twenty minutes, or someone else was holding their phone and had driven it there. Neither option ended with Noor safe in this cabin. The textClose the curtain. You're not alone.—was not a rescue. It was a warning that the walls had eyes, or worse, that the person who had sent it was the one doing the watching.

Priorities, Noor thought, the way they always did when the fear tried to climb into their throat and steer. Data secured. Route out. Then live to publish it.

Keeping low, they crawled the last few feet to the front window and used the edge of a knuckle to shift the curtain no more than a centimeter. The road was empty, a pale slash of gravel under a sky that gave no moon. No headlights. No figure on the porch. But the absence of a threat wasn't the same as safety. Whoever had texted knew about the curtain. They had been close enough to see Noor standing there, breath fogging the glass.

Noor let the curtain fall and turned toward the back of the cabin, toward the narrow hallway that led past the bedroom to the rear door. It was a hunting cabin; there was always a back way out, a door that opened onto the woodpile and the tree line. They could make the pines in thirty seconds if they moved now, before headlights swept the front of the house.

"We're leaving," Noor said, pitching their voice to carry no farther than the couch. "Back door. Leave your phone if you have to, but do not light it and do not open the front door. If I say run, you run and you don't look back."

They didn't wait for agreement. There was no time for it. Noor reached the rear door, wrapped a hand around the cold brass knob, and pressed their ear to the paint-flaked wood. Beyond it, the night held its breath. Somewhere in the trees, an engine turned over—distant, muffled, gone almost before it registered.

Noor's grip tightened on the knob. Then they turned the handle and pulled the door open a crack, letting the mountain air and the smell of wet pine flood in. They held it there, a hand's width of darkness, and stepped out into the night, hoping the friend was already moving behind them.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I kill the flashlight on my phone, cursing under my breath.* "Jesus, Noor, you scared the crap out of me." *I scramble off the couch, dropping my phone on the cushion. I follow Noor, trying to keep quiet.* "What's going on?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor let the back door ease shut behind them, the latch clicking with a soft, final sound that seemed too loud in the stillness. They stayed in a crouch at the top of the stoop, the laptop a hard rectangle against their ribs, the bag strap cutting into their shoulder. Cold air bit at their cheeks; the smell of wet pine and old rain rose from the dark. Somewhere out beyond the yard, the engine they had heard a moment ago did not return. That was worse. Engines that cut out meant someone was listening too.

They turned their head just enough to pitch their voice toward the shape behind them. "Keep down," Noor breathed. "And don't speak unless it's to say you see something."

The explanation could wait. There wasn't time for the whole ugly shape of it—the tower ping two miles out, the text from a phone that should have been in the source's hand, the way the message had known about the curtain. Noor filed it all down to the only two facts that mattered: someone was out there, and the cabin had become a box with a target on it.

They moved.

Staying low, Noor crossed the few yards of open ground between the stoop and the woodpile. The stacked logs were a blacker mass against the dark, and they pressed a shoulder against the rough bark, feeling the splintery edge bite through their jacket. No sound came from the tree line. No snap of a twig, no cough of an engine turning over again. Just the wind moving high in the branches and the rasp of their own breath.

Noor's gaze swept the yard, the faint outline of the path that led around to the front. The car—their ride, their only real chance of getting off this mountain—was parked on the far side of the cabin. Going for it meant crossing open ground and the front windows, where anyone watching from the road would have a clear line. Not yet. Maybe not at all.

Behind them, the back door was a rectangle of slightly lighter dark. Noor didn't check. Checking meant taking eyes off the trees.

"Woodpile to the pines," Noor murmured, so low it was almost lost in the wind. "Thirty feet. When I move, you move. Don't straighten up."

They counted the distance in their head, measured the patch of open dirt and pine needles they'd have to cross. Then Noor pushed off from the woodpile and ran, bent nearly double, the laptop held tight, their shoes finding the soft places between the rocks. The cold tore at their throat. Ten feet. Fifteen. The first skeletal pines rose up ahead, their lower branches brushing the ground like a curtain.

Noor reached the tree line and slipped between the trunks, the darkness swallowing them whole. They went another ten paces, until the cabin was a shape half-guessed through the branches, and then they stopped, one hand braced against a trunk, and listened.

Nothing. No pursuit. No shouted order. Only the blood roaring in their ears and the slow, deliberate drip of water from the wet needles overhead.

Noor's heart hammered against the encrypted drive in their pocket. They had the data. They were out of the box. But the night was very large, and somewhere in it, someone who knew about the curtain was still moving.

They turned their head slightly, just enough that their voice would carry back the way they had come. "We keep to the trees," Noor said. "Parallel to the road. If headlights come, we hit the dirt and we don't move until I say."

Then, because the question from the stoop still hung unanswered between them, because the friend deserved at least that much, Noor added, quiet and grim: "Our source didn't send that text. Someone else did. And they were close enough to watch me breathe on the glass."

With that, Noor started moving again, deeper into the pines, putting one careful foot in front of the other, already calculating how to circle back to the car without walking into whatever was waiting on the road.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor had taken perhaps a dozen soundless steps into the pines when the silence behind them changed texture.

It wasn't a sound so much as an absence. No second set of footsteps crushing pine needles. No quiet rustle of a jacket pushed through wet branches. Noor stopped, breath held, and slowly turned.

Through the gaps in the trees, the cabin hunched in the dark. And in the front window—the one facing the road, the one Noor had been standing in front of when the burner buzzed—a small, cold light bloomed. Pale blue. Rectangular. A phone screen, lit and unmistakable.

The friend had not followed.

Noor's first impulse was a hot, useless surge of anger. They had said *don't light it*. They had said it would silhouette them against the glass. Now the cabin glowed like a lantern in the middle of a forest full of people who wanted them dead. Whoever had sent that message—whoever had pinged two miles out and then cut their engine in the dark—would see it. They might already be moving toward it.

The anger died as quickly as it came, buried under the cold weight of the next realization: the car keys were in the friend's pocket. And the friend was sitting in a lit window.

Noor couldn't leave them. Not because it was noble, but because the route off this mountain ended in the driver's seat of a car they couldn't start without those keys. Data was secure; the encrypted drive was a hard weight against their ribs, the bag strap cutting into their shoulder, the laptop solid under one arm. The story was safe. The ride was not.

Priorities, Noor thought, the way they always did when fear tried to climb into their throat and steer. Secure the liability. Kill the light. Get to the car. Then live to publish it.

They reversed course.

Keeping low, Noor ghosted back through the trees to the woodpile, then to the rear stoop. The back door stood ajar, a thin wedge of darker dark. Noor slipped inside, the laptop still tucked under one arm. The cabin smelled of dust and stale peanut butter. From the front room came the faint flicker of the screen, and beyond it, the low shape of the friend on the couch.

Noor didn't announce themselves. There was no time to explain tower pings and burner phones to someone who had not followed them into the dark. They crossed the kitchen in three strides and kept going into the front room.

The phone was a small beacon in the friend's hands. Noor reached out, closed their fingers around the device, and thumbed the screen dark. Then, in one motion, they twisted it free and hurled it underhand across the room. It hit the far wall with a plastic crack and fell behind the couch, screen still black.

Noor found the friend's wrist in the dark, locked their grip around it, and pulled toward the back of the cabin.

"Keys," Noor breathed, low and fierce, not caring if it hurt. "Pocket. Now. We go out the back, we keep low, and you do not speak. If you light anything else, I'll leave you in the road myself."

They didn't release the wrist. Noor was already moving, hauling the weight behind them past the kitchen table and toward the rear door. The night air hit them as they shouldered the door open and pulled the friend out onto the stoop.

Then Noor stopped, one hand raised for silence, and listened.

Somewhere beyond the trees, a branch snapped. Close. Too close.

And this time, Noor didn't wait to see what came next. They turned and ran for the pines, the friend's wrist still locked in their grip, the encrypted drive burning against their ribs like a second heartbeat.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stumble after Noor, my wrist aching. I'm still trying to process what's happening.* "Hey! What the hell, Noor?!" *I dig in my pocket for the keys, fumbling a bit.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor heard the shout. It was too loud. The pines wouldn't swallow that. They pivoted, keeping the laptop clamped under one arm, and slapped their free hand over the friend's mouth. The other hand still had the wrist locked; Noor used it to haul the stumbling weight forward, half-dragging, half-guiding.

"Quiet," Noor breathed against the friend's ear, low and fierce. "One more sound and you're on your own."

They felt the friend's hand working at the pocket—the fumbling that had already started. Noor had no patience for fumbling. They released the wrist for a second, reached across, and found the hard outline of the keyring through the fabric. Noor hooked it, twisted, and yanked it free, the metal teeth biting into their palm. Keys. Good. They shoved the ring into their own jacket pocket, beside the encrypted drive, then reclaimed the friend's arm, not gentle now, locking their grip above the elbow and pulling them into a stumbling run.

Noor's left hand came away from the mouth. They didn't speak again; words were noise. Instead they pointed toward the deeper dark, where the pines thickened and the ground dropped toward the old logging track they remembered from the drive in. The car was the other way, past the open yard and the front windows. Not yet. Maybe not at all.

They pushed the friend ahead, using their body to steer, and scanned the trees over the friend's shoulder. The snap had come from the east, closer to the road. Whoever it was, they were on foot now, moving through the woods with the patience of someone who knew the dark. Noor's mind raced: the track came out near the highway a mile down. If they could reach it, they could circle back to the car from the tree line, or keep going if the car had been seen.

The laptop dug into their ribs. The keys were a solid weight against the drive. Data secured. Route out. Then live to publish it.

Noor tightened their grip and ran.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My wrist throbs, and now my arm where Noor grabbed it.* I stumble, nearly falling, but Noor keeps pulling. *I just try to keep up, eyes darting into the dark woods around us.* This is insane.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor felt the stumble through the arm locked in their grip—the near-fall that would have dumped them both onto the wet pine needles. They absorbed it, thighs burning, and kept moving. But the branch snap had loosened something in their head. Running blind through unfamiliar woods with panic dragging behind them was how people ended up at the bottom of a ravine with a broken neck.

They stopped so abruptly the weight behind them lurched forward. Noor didn't loosen their hold. They sank into a crouch behind a curtain of low boughs, hauling the dead weight down with them, and put their lips close to the friend's ear.

"Listen," they breathed. Not a request. A command.

The wind had died. In the sudden stillness, the woods gave up their secrets. Dry needles crunched—not behind them now, but off to the left, parallel, keeping pace. Whoever it was, they weren't chasing. They were flanking. Cutting the angle toward the car.

Noor's jaw tightened. The car. Of course. It was the only reason to be out here. They wanted the data, or they wanted Noor's body in the driver's seat with the laptop beside it. Either way, the vehicle had become bait.

Priorities. The encrypted drive was a hard weight against their ribs, the bag strap cutting into their shoulder, the laptop solid under their arm. Secure the data. Deny the bait. Get off the mountain.

Noor shifted the laptop to their left arm and slid the keyring from their pocket with their right, curling the metal tight so it wouldn't jingle. They didn't need the friend to drive. The keys were already in their hand, and the fob would unlock the doors with a chirp they couldn't afford. They'd have to get close enough to use the manual blade, close enough to see if the car was covered.

They pointed to a hollow beneath a sprawling hemlock, a pocket of deeper dark maybe fifteen feet off their line. Then they leaned in again.

"Stay here. If I'm not back in five minutes, you take the logging track north and you don't stop until you hit the highway. No lights. No phone. You understand me?"

They didn't wait for an answer. There wasn't time for one. Noor released the arm and melted away from the thicket, moving at a crouch, using the trees as a screen. They circled wide, putting the cabin between themselves and the road, then began to work their way back toward the far side where the car waited.

The pines thinned near the edge of the clearing. Noor went to their belly in the wet duff, cold soaking through their jacket, and parted the last screen of branches with careful fingers.

The car sat where they'd left it, a darker shape against the paler gravel of the turnout. No figures moved around it. No shadow detached from the tree line across the road. The front windows of the cabin were empty and black—the friend's phone was dead and dark behind the couch, exactly where they'd thrown it.

But the driver's side door was slightly open.

Noor's breath stopped.

They hadn't left it that way. They were certain—they remembered the solid *thunk* of the door closing when they'd arrived, the automatic interior light winking out as they'd walked toward the cabin.

Someone had been in the car. Or was still in it.

Noor's fingers tightened on the keys until the teeth cut into their palm. They scanned the tree line across the road, the black mouth of the turnout, the roofline of the car itself. Nothing. But the open door was a hook, and they'd be damned if they'd swallow it.

They stayed flat, unmoving, and counted their heartbeats. Thirty. Sixty. The cold seeped into their bones. Somewhere far off, an engine turned over—closer this time, not fading. Then headlights swept through the trees, painting the trunks in stark relief, and Noor pressed themselves deeper into the wet earth as the light raked over the clearing and kept going, moving away down the road.

Toward the highway. Or a trick to draw them out.

Noor didn't move until the taillights were gone. Then they rose, not to their full height, and began to circle the car from the back, using the trunk and the far side as cover, keys ready, every sense screaming.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I watch Noor disappear into the darkness. Five minutes? I'm not waiting five minutes. I didn't sign up for this. I pull out my phone again, forgetting it was dead, then remember Noor chucked it. I'm getting out of here.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor reached the driver's side and stopped, pressed flat against the cold metal of the door. It stood ajar exactly as she had seen it—a hand's width of darkness. She slid her fingers into the gap, feeling for the dome light switch. The interior remained pitch black. No faint glow from the courtesy light. Whoever had opened the door had disabled it first. That was not the work of a tweaker breaking in for spare change. That was the work of someone who understood how to hunt in the dark.

Keeping her body low, Noor ran her hand along the underside of the dashboard, then beneath the driver's seat. Her fingers found nothing but old wrappers and the metal track of the seat adjuster. She leaned out, reached into the wheel well, and felt along the frame. There—a small square, magnetic, no bigger than a matchbox, with a single sluggish red pulse beneath its plastic shell. A GPS tracker. She worked a key under the seam, popped the casing, and pinched the coin battery loose. The light died. She dropped the dead husk into the wet pine needles and ground it under her heel, twice, until it was just another piece of trash in the dark.

The car was tagged. The cabin was watched. The source's phone was in someone else's hand. It all fit together with the awful neatness of a trap that had already closed. Noor's mouth went dry. She had the data—the drive was a hard weight against her ribs, the laptop solid under her arm—but the data didn't matter if she turned the ignition and the whole thing went up, or if she sat in the driver's seat and a round came through the windshield.

She slid back out of the car, leaving the door ajar as she'd found it, and sank into a crouch behind the rear tire. Five minutes. The friend would be gone, or worse, waiting to be found. Noor couldn't leave them. Not when the route off this mountain ended in the driver's seat, and not when the friend's panic could bring the whole thing down on top of them both.

She turned toward the hemlock hollow—and froze.

From the direction of the hollow came the unmistakable sound of movement without care: a shoe scuffing rock, the crash of a body pushing through wet branches, the ragged drag of breath. It was heading north. Toward the logging track. The friend was supposed to wait five minutes. Instead, the noise of panic was already fading into the trees, loud enough to draw every eye on the mountain.

Noor's fingers tightened on the keys until the teeth bit into her palm. She couldn't shout. A shout would carry, and the flanker—whoever had snapped that branch and cut their engine—was still out there, listening for exactly that kind of mistake.

She began to move, angling north through the pines, parallel to the sound, using the dark and the rise and fall of the ground to close the distance without crossing open earth. The laptop was a hard rectangle against her ribs. The encrypted drive burned against her pocket. Somewhere ahead, the careless crashing continued; somewhere closer than she wanted to believe, something else moved with patience, matching her pace through the dark.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor closed the last few yards at a crouch, moving from trunk to trunk, the laptop a solid weight under one arm, the bag strap cutting into their shoulder. Ahead, the friend's head was bent, the phone's screen a cold blue smear in the dark. They had said "Yeah" a moment ago—too loud, too careless—and the sound still hung in the damp air, a thread that could lead someone straight to them.

Noor didn't hesitate. They came up behind the friend, caught the wrist of the hand holding the phone, and twisted it free in one smooth motion. The screen winked out as Noor's thumb found the power button, then they hurled the device into a clump of ferns and brought a heel down on it, twice, feeling the plastic crack and the glass give. No light. No signal. No beacon.

"You want to die out here?" Noor breathed, so close their lips almost brushed the friend's ear. "They're in the trees. They've been watching the cabin. You light that screen again and you paint a target on both of us."

They didn't wait for an answer. Noor's grip shifted to the friend's arm, hauling them down into a crouch. The careless crashing had stopped—either the friend had finally realized, or something else had frozen them. Noor strained to listen. The wind had picked up, sighing through the branches, but beneath it, off to the right and slightly behind, came the faint, deliberate crunch of a boot settling weight on pine duff. Not careless. Patient. Closing.

Priorities. Data secured—the encrypted drive was a hard weight against their ribs, the laptop solid under their arm. Route out: the car, back past the cabin, thirty yards of open ground and the front windows. The keys were in their pocket, the tracker dead in the dirt behind them.

Noor pointed south, back the way they had come, then tapped two fingers against their own chest and pointed at the friend, then at the ground: *follow, stay low, no sound.* Then they moved, sliding backward through the trees in a crouch, putting themselves between the friend and the patient footsteps, guiding them toward the rear of the cabin and the far side where the car waited in the dark.

Every sense screamed. Somewhere in the pines, the hunter was matching their pace, and Noor had exactly one chance to reach the car before the dark closed its hand.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I'm frozen in shock, then fear. My arm hurts where Noor is practically dragging me. My phone! Oh, god, my phone.* "My phone!" *I hiss, trying to pull away.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor felt the change in the arm locked in their grip—the sudden dead weight of shock, then the panicked wrench as the friend tried to tear free. The hissed “My phone!” was too loud. It ripped through the damp air like a snapped twig, and somewhere out in the dark, the patient footsteps paused.

Noor didn’t loosen their hold. They pivoted instead, using the friend’s own momentum to spin them around, and clamped their free hand over the friend’s mouth again, hard. The laptop dug into their ribs. The encrypted drive was a solid weight against their pocket. Data secured. Now they just had to keep the liability from getting them both killed.

“It’s gone,” Noor breathed against the friend’s ear, low and fierce. “I broke it. That screen was a beacon—it would’ve painted us for anyone watching the cabin.”

Priorities, Noor thought, the way they always did when the fear tried to climb into their throat and steer. Data secured. Route out. Then live to publish it. But first, stop the friend from getting them both shot.

“You want to live?” they breathed. “You move. South. To the car. Low and silent. Nod if you understand.”

They didn’t wait to see if the nod came. There wasn’t time. Noor shifted their grip to the friend’s jacket collar, bunching the fabric in one fist, and turned them bodily toward the rear of the cabin. They pushed, steering with their shoulder, keeping them both in a crouch as they ghosted back through the pines. The ground sloped toward the far side where the car waited, a darker shape against the pale gravel of the turnout.

The patient footsteps had resumed, off to the right and slightly behind, matching their pace. Closing. Noor’s skin crawled with the certainty of being watched. They reached the edge of the clearing and held up a fist, pressing the friend down behind the rear bumper. The car was twenty feet away. The driver’s door still stood ajar, exactly as they’d left it—a hand’s width of darkness, an invitation or a trap.

Noor slid around the trunk, keys in hand, the manual blade already extended so the fob wouldn’t chirp. They kept low, moving to the driver’s side, and leaned in just far enough to sweep the interior. Front seats empty. Back seat a heap of shadow that resolved into an old blanket and a discarded coffee cup. No one inside. The dome light stayed dead, just as they’d left it.

Noor exhaled, a thin stream of white in the dark. They opened the door the rest of the way, silent, and slid into the driver’s seat. The laptop went on the passenger floor, the bag at their feet. They leaned across and unlocked the passenger door, then reached back and hauled the friend inside by the collar, shoving them down into the footwell.

“Stay down,” Noor hissed. “Head below the window. Do not sit up until I say.”

They pulled the door shut. The solid *thunk* was loud in the silence, but it was done. Noor locked the doors, the locks engaging with a heavy clunk. The keys went into the ignition. Their hand was steady now, the caffeine and the fear burned down to a single, cold clarity.

They turned the key. The engine caught, a low rumble that vibrated through the seat. Noor didn’t turn on the headlights. They put the car in gear and rolled forward, tires crunching softly on gravel, guiding the vehicle around the cabin toward the road. Every sense screamed. They watched the tree line in the rearview, waiting for the muzzle flash or the crunch of a boot on the shoulder.

The encrypted drive burned against their ribs. The laptop was safe on the floor. They were out of the box, they were in the car, and the road to the highway was dark and empty ahead.

Noor exhaled, once, and drove.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I'm curled up on the floor, shaking. I hear the engine rumble to life, and the car starts to move. I don't dare look up.* "Are we safe?" I whisper, my voice hoarse.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor heard the whisper from the footwell, hoarse and thin, the words barely carrying over the low rumble of the engine. *Are we safe?*

For a moment, Noor didn't answer. Their eyes stayed on the rearview mirror, watching the tunnel of black behind them. The cabin was gone, swallowed by the pines. No headlights appeared in the glass. No shadow detached from the tree line to give chase. But the tracker they'd crushed under their heel said otherwise: someone had known exactly where this car was, and someone had been close enough to watch the cabin through a rifle scope or a phone lens. Safety was a mile away, or ten, or not at all.

"No," Noor said at last. Their voice was low, stripped of anything but fact. "Not yet. We're not safe until we're off this mountain and standing in a place with lights and people and cameras. Stay down."

They kept the headlights off. The road was a pale, meandering scar of gravel, just visible in the dark, and Noor guided the car along it by memory and the faint gleam of the stones. Ten miles an hour. Fifteen. The tires crunched, a sound too loud in the silence, but stopping was worse. Every minute they sat still was a minute the flanker could close the distance.

Noor's mind sorted the facts the way it always did, filing them into the only order that mattered. Data secured: the encrypted drive was a hard weight against their ribs, the laptop safe on the passenger floor. Route out: the highway, a mile or so ahead, then north toward the truck stop with the all-night diner and the state police barracks six miles beyond. Liability managed: the friend was in the footwell, phone destroyed, no longer painting them both against the glass.

They checked the mirror again. Still nothing. But the road curved ahead, and Noor slowed, easing the car around the bend. The trees thinned. The grade evened out. Somewhere below, the highway waited—a ribbon of asphalt that would take them toward town, toward lights, toward the kind of place where a car with a dead tracker and two frightened people could disappear into the noise.

"We go to the highway," Noor said, pitching the words down toward the footwell, more to hear the plan aloud than to reassure. "Then the truck stop. We don't stop for anything else. If headlights come up behind us, you say so. You don't sit up. You just say it."

They pressed the accelerator, just enough to feel the car respond, and drove on into the dark. The encrypted drive burned against their ribs like a second heartbeat. They had the story. They had the proof. Now they just had to live long enough to file it.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod against the floor, too scared to even whisper. Truck stop. Highway. Just get me out of here.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor felt the tiny shift of the friend's head against the floor—the nod they had demanded. They didn't take their eyes off the rearview mirror. Behind them, the mountain road remained a tunnel of black. No headlights. No shadow detaching from the trees to give chase. The tires crunched over gravel, and the engine rumbled low, but nothing followed.

The road narrowed, then opened abruptly. Noor eased the car onto the highway, feeling the tires bite into asphalt instead of loose stone. Only then did they reach down and switch on the headlights. The beams cut a bright wedge through the night, catching a reflective green sign: TRUCK STOP — 2 MILES. Noor let out a breath they felt all the way to their ribs.

They drove with the windows up, the doors locked, checking the mirror every few seconds. The tracker was dead in the dirt back at the cabin, but the memory of that open driver's-side door sat cold in their gut. Someone had been inside their car. Someone had known exactly where they were.

"We're on the highway," Noor said, pitching their voice down toward the footwell. "Two miles. You can sit up now, but keep your head below the glass until we're parked under the lights."

The truck stop rose ahead like an island: sodium lights buzzing over a long row of idling semis, a low diner with a neon coffee cup, cameras mounted on the poles. Noor signaled, turned in, and rolled slowly through the lot. They chose a space directly beneath a light, close to the entrance but not boxed in, and shut off the engine. For a moment they just sat there, hands still on the wheel, listening to the tick of the cooling engine and the ordinary hum of trucks and distant music. It sounded almost like safety.

Then Noor moved.

They pulled the laptop from the passenger floor, set it on their thighs, and powered it on. While it booted, they dug the encrypted drive from the inner pocket of their jacket, ran a thumb over the casing, and plugged it in. The login prompt blinked. Noor typed the twenty-three-character passphrase from memory, the same one they repeated every night like a prayer or a threat. The drive unlocked.

They went back to the CSV.

Three rows in, the burner had leapt out at them before. Now, with the adrenaline burned down to something cold and clear, Noor cross-checked the rest of the log against the numbers in their own notes. Match after match. The shipping company's private line had called the port authority's deputy director eleven times in the week before the container vanished. And the burner that had pinged less than two miles from the cabin at 11:52 PM had called that same deputy director's private cell twice that night. The story was no longer a maybe. It was a weapon.

But the source had promised more than calls. Noor opened the drive's directory. A folder labeled MANIFEST. Another labeled PHOTOS. They opened the manifests first: scanned bills of lading, altered weights, signatures that didn't match the ones on file. Then the photos: the container yard at night, a crate stenciled with the shipping logo, and a figure in a port authority jacket accepting a plain white envelope. Noor's breath hissed between their teeth. Bribery. Fraud. Whatever the shape of it, it was real, and it was all there.

They copied the entire drive to the laptop's encrypted partition, then opened their mail client and began a draft to their editor. They attached a compact encrypted archive of the manifests and photos. The message was short: *Publish if I disappear. Verify independently. Source compromised—assume hostile.* They hit send, knowing it would sit in the outbox until they found wifi.

The truck stop had wifi. They would go inside, connect, and let it fly. Then food. Then, if the world hadn't ended, sleep.

Noor looked down at the friend still curled in the footwell. They reached over and unlocked the doors, the heavy clunk loud in the quiet car.

"We're going inside," Noor said. "Diner. Lights, people, cameras. We eat, we use their wifi to send this, and then we figure out what happened to our source." They pushed their own door open, the cold mountain air rushing in, and stepped out onto the bright asphalt, the laptop under one arm, the bag over their shoulder, the encrypted drive a hard, burning weight against their ribs.

They waited, every sense still screaming, but the parking lot was lit and ordinary, and for the first time that night, the dark felt a little less like a noose.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I slowly uncurl from the footwell, my muscles stiff and aching. I blink in the sudden light, my eyes adjusting. I look at Noor, then at the bright lights of the truck stop.* "Thank god." *I reach for the door handle, eager to get out.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Eat something," Noor repeated, half to themselves, in the tone of someone reading a prescription they'd written for other people for years. *Eat. Sleep. Don't become the story.* Easy rules to hand out from a phone line. Harder at 12:14 in the morning in a dead man's cabin.

They pulled themselves off the window. The cold of the glass had gotten into their shoulder and stayed there.

The cabinet yielded a can of chili with a label in a language Noor didn't read, and a loaf of bread that had gone stiff at both ends. They ate standing up at the counter, mechanically, because Driver was right and Noor knew the crash was coming around 2 AM whether they scheduled it or not. The burner phone sat on the table where they'd left it, one bar of signal blinking in and out like something breathing.

They crossed to it between bites. Typed: *Status. One word is fine.*

The message crawled, failed, crawled again. Sent. Delivered. No reply.

Delivered meant the phone was on. On meant Wren was — possibly — still Wren, and not a phone in an evidence bag on a table somewhere with two people in windbreakers reading the message thread in order.

Noor set the phone face-up on the table, where they could see the screen from anywhere in the room, and sat down across from the laptop and the drive. The drive they were not touching. That was the rule they'd set themselves, back when the rules still felt like they applied: nothing decrypts until Wren is in the room with hands on the keyboard. Chain of custody. Plausible deniability. All those sturdy daylight phrases.

But the rules had assumed a source who showed up.

The laptop, though. The laptop was fine. Noor opened it and pulled up the photographed call records Wren had passed two weeks ago — the ones showing eleven calls between a Halden Group VP and the city procurement office in the nine days before the surveillance contract closed, all from a number that appeared on no filing anywhere. Tonight's job was the unglamorous part: cross-checking them against the second set, the billing statements, digit by digit. Because if Wren had fabricated even one of those numbers, the story was dead, and Noor's byline with it, and probably worse than the byline.

"There's more chili," they said over their shoulder, mouth around the last of the bread. "It's a crime against chili, but it's calories."

They worked for a few minutes, cross-referencing timestamps, until call four matched and call five matched and their hands had almost stopped shaking.

Then they looked up at Driver. "You didn't have to drive all the way up here. I'm glad you did." A beat. The headlights question sat in their throat for a second before they swallowed it. "Here's the thing. If Wren's not through that door by one o'clock, I'm opening the drive. I'm not asking — I'm telling you now, while I'll still listen if you've got an argument. And I'd take it as a favor if you kept half an eye on the road while I do this."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I take a long swig of my soda.* "Look, I told you I'd drive. No big deal." *I set the can down, noticing the time on my phone.* "And hey, your rules are your rules. Just... try not to get too deep before they get here."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Too deep is the drive," Noor said, not looking up from the screen. "The paperwork's the shallow end. Paperwork never hurt anyone. It's the people inside it you drown on."

They worked. Call six matched. Seven. Eight. It was a ritual, this — finger on the screen, eyes on the photograph, timestamp against timestamp, duration against duration. Prayer for people who didn't pray: repetitive, humbling, done on the chance that someday someone would ask whether you'd checked. Call nine matched. Ten. Eleven. Every number Wren had photographed lived on the billing statement exactly as Wren had sworn it did.

Noor sat back, and the relief came up through them like warmth into cold hands — and kept going, past relief, into something colder, because the relief had a wrongness to it and it took a second to find the source.

Wren's photographs held eleven calls. The billing statement ran twelve.

They counted twice. Once with a finger under each line, once without, the way you go back to check a door you know you locked.

The twelfth call sat at the bottom of the page like it had been waiting for them. Outbound from the unlisted number — the VP's ghost line, the one that appeared on no filing anywhere. Dated five days ago. Five days ago was the day after Wren and Noor had fixed this meeting: this cabin, this night, this hour. Four minutes long. Placed to a number Noor didn't know, carrying the mountain prefix — this county's prefix, shared by roughly four thousand people, two traffic lights, and an Elks lodge.

The burner stayed dark on the table. Noor didn't reach for it. There was nothing Wren could say from silence, and nothing Noor wanted to type where the wind might carry it.

The wall phone hung by the pantry door — cream-colored trimline, cord coiled like something asleep, dust furred along the cradle. They'd glanced at it once on arrival and not thought about it since. Somebody's uncle's cabin. Somebody's uncle's line.

Noor crossed the room and lifted the handset. Dial tone — absurdly loud, bright, a hum from another century. On the base, a strip of masking tape, ballpoint in a stranger's hand: ten digits.

They held the billing page open on their phone beside it and compared, digit by digit, the way they'd spent the last hour comparing everything else.

It matched. Prefix and all. Last four and all.

Four minutes, five days ago, from a Halden ghost line to the cabin where Noor was sleeping. You could say a great deal in four minutes. You could say: *there's a journalist coming up the mountain Thursday. Alone. Tired. Trusting.*

Noor hung up gently, as if the phone might be listening — as if it hadn't already had its conversation — and stood in the middle of the room doing math with their eyes shut. Three explanations. The uncle talked to everyone. The number had been reassigned. Or someone in the chain of people who produced this safehouse had sold it, and the sale had closed five days ago.

None of the three were good. Two of the three ended with leaving.

They moved without deciding to: duffel by the door, laptop bag to a chair with the strap facing out, the drive case into their jacket pocket, where it sat against their ribs like a second heartbeat.

"Driver." They kept their voice level. "Question. Think before you answer. The drive up — did you pass anyone? Anything parked at the turnouts, anything sitting with its lights off, anything behind you on the switchbacks more than once?" A beat. "Because if the answer's yes, we're gone by one o'clock. With or without Wren."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look up from my phone, a bit startled.* "Uh, no, not really. It was pretty quiet. Why? What's going on?" *I sit up straighter, a knot forming in my stomach.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"No," Noor said. "You wouldn't have seen it. That's not an insult, it's arithmetic. A clean tail on a mountain road doesn't ride your bumper with high beams on. One car waits at a turnout until you're past, then folds in two bends back. The only way you'd know is if you were checking your mirrors at every apex for twenty miles, which is a thing I do and you don't. Thank God for that. It would've ruined the drive."

They turned the laptop toward Driver, screen tilted into the dark, the twelfth line underlined by a finger.

"What's going on is this. There's a call on this page Wren never mentioned. Twelve calls, not eleven. Five days ago — the day after we fixed tonight. Four minutes, from Halden's ghost line to that." A nod at the wall phone, still and quiet in its cradle. "This cabin's number. Somebody at Halden spent four minutes on the phone with the place I was going to sleep."

The words sat in the room a moment, the way cold does.

"You don't find somebody's uncle's hunting cabin out of a phone book. The number of people who knew this place existed is three. Me. Wren. And the man who arranged it. So either the arrangement leaked, or Wren talked — and I don't get to pick the nicer version of that sentence." Noor closed the laptop, slid it into the bag. "You gave me an honest answer and the honest answer is *nothing*, and *nothing* from a moving windshield at night is worth what it cost. So we're leaving. Not because your answer was yes. Because the downside of running from a safe cabin is embarrassment, and the downside of staying might not have a name yet. If this is someone trying to spook me into bolting — fine. I'd rather be manipulated and alive."

They worked while they talked. Photographed the masking tape number before anything else — evidence had a way of walking off. The chili can and the bread bag went into a grocery sack; trash cans could testify. The burner went into the left pocket, opposite the drive.

The drive. Noor's hand found it through the jacket and stayed there.

"I told you one o'clock. That deadline assumed a clean room, and this room stopped being clean at 12:40. Forty minutes of decryption in a house that might get visitors is how a story dies with its only copy — and without Wren standing next to it, the drive's only half a story anyway." Their jaw set. "The rule holds. That's the ugly truth about rules. They hold hardest exactly when you want to break them."

They pressed the truck keys into Driver's hand and folded the fingers over them.

"Engine stays off till I'm back — sound climbs mountains. Headlights stay dead till the county road. Anyone knocks, you're the nephew, you're checking on your uncle's place, you've never seen me. When I come back it'll be three knocks, a stop, then two. Anything else, you drive. Not home — the truck stop on Route 9, one hour, then home the long way. And if it goes that way, Driver, that's the *good* version of tonight. Don't argue with the good version."

They'd lifted the duffel to their shoulder when the burner lit up on the table.

Three dots. Pulsing. Noor went absolutely still, one strap in their fist, watching a stranger's punctuation blink in the dark.

The dots stopped. The screen went back to sleep.

"Wren was alive enough to type," Noor said quietly. "And alive enough to stop."

They pocketed the phone, eased the chain off the back door, and the night came in — pine, cold, no wind at all.

"Ten minutes," they said. "Count them out loud if it helps."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The night took the sound of the door and folded it into pine silence.

Noor gave themselves sixty breaths against the wall, letting the dark develop like a photograph — road first, then tree line, then the frost smoking faintly off the grass. No wind. No wind meant sound carried and nothing covered it, so the steps went on the needle duff and not the gravel, and they were slow, and they were few.

The prints were on the north wall, in the thin blue frost the eaves had spared. Boots, coming out of the trees — not the road, the *trees* — walking the length of the cabin to the kitchen window, and there they stopped. One of them wasn't a print anymore. Frost melted clean through to black grass, the shape of a man standing still for a long time. The edges had feathered. Hours, not minutes.

Noor stood beside it and did the arithmetic they didn't want. They had stood at that glass from eleven-something to twelve-fourteen, lights off, watching the road, and around eleven-thirty the back of their neck had prickled and they'd blamed the coffee. Two people had spent the same hour not existing, thirty feet and one pane apart, and Noor had only ever looked out.

The burner buzzed against their hip like a wasp in a jar. They cupped the screen before it lit the wall. Wren: *Take the county road down. Don't stop for anything. I'm sorry.*

No password. At the second meeting — parking structure, level three, fluorescent hum — Wren had explained that the only thing torture can't extract from a person is trivia. The procurement officer kept a golden retriever named Q3, after the quarter the contract died in. The name lived in two heads on earth and zero documents. Every real message knew the dog.

This one didn't know the dog. Which meant Wren was typing with a hand on the back of their neck, or Wren had stopped typing some time ago and the phone had changed careers. Either way, the message had one author and one want: Noor, on the county road, at one in the morning, moving and visible and alone.

Far below, an engine took the switchbacks in low gear, patient as a filing cabinet. Then it cut. Not faded — *cut*. An engine doesn't park; an engine is silenced. Noor gave the dark a number: turnout below the drive, fifteen minutes up frozen ground for a careful man. Call the cabin's clean time ten.

No reply. Doubt was the one thing you never put in writing. Noor went back along the wall, gave the melted print the width of respect, and found what hunting cabins keep for the deer-dragging months: behind the woodpile, a second track. Two ruts, a gate on a rusted chain, alder already moving in. It ran north, away from the switchbacks, away from everything the county road knew.

Good enough. Ghosts aren't choosy about exits.

Three knocks. A stop. Two.

"Change of math," Noor said, keeping it at parade-volume quiet. "Somebody stood at that window tonight and watched me watch the road. Wren's phone just gave me orders without the password. And there's a car below with its engine cut." They pressed the duffel into Driver's arms. "We're not meeting anyone. We're the smoke. Your phone goes off — *off* off, not silent. A lit screen reads a mile up here."

They typed once more on the burner — *Going dark. Staying till dawn.* — sent it, and set it face-up in the center of the table, radio live, testifying to an occupied room. The truck stayed too: dark, dead, furniture for the lie. Whoever came up the drive would spend their patience searching a person who was already frost on the north fence.

"Laptop's mine. Drive's on me." The case sat against their ribs, second heartbeat, holding its rule. "If we get separated: south, downhill, off the road till light. Route 9 truck stop by noon. I'm there by two, not before. If I'm not there by two, then you went for a drive with a friend, and you never heard of Wren, Halden, or me." A beat. "You drove. That's all you did tonight — keep that. It's the truth, and it keeps you clean."
