The back-door chain came off with a whisper this time — sleeve over the links, lifted, not slid — and they went out along the north wall, past the melted print, through the alder to the gate. The gate chain got the same surgery. Beyond it the track ran black under black pines.

Twelve fifty-eight. Noor put sixty feet between them and the woodpile, and was still feeding distance behind them when, at one o'clock exactly — the hour keeping its appointment after all — gravel sounded down by the drive.

One set of footsteps. Unhurried. Frost has a voice, and it said: one person, in no hurry, carrying no light.

Noor took Driver's sleeve and drew them both down into the shadow the woodpile owed them. Thirty feet of open frost lay between the woodpile and the porch. The steps crossed it. Took the porch. Stopped at the front door.

Three knocks. Polite. Patient.

The stop.

Then the knob, turning slow, meeting the lock, letting go. And through the door, low, almost gentle, a voice that knew the name:

"Noor."

Noor's hand closed hard on Driver's sleeve. Under their breath, barely air:

"Don't."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My breath hitches. I'm frozen, barely daring to breathe. My eyes wide, locked on Noor.* (OOC: Don't write my actions)

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The name hung in the frost, and the silence after it had texture — the silence of a man waiting to see what the name would do.

Recognition arrived late, the way it does when the body spends its first seconds on fear and leaves the ears to catch up. Noor had heard that voice exactly twice, through a paid line, patient as a notary, giving directions to this very cabin. *Mile 31. The mailbox with the reflectors.* The arranger. The man who dealt in anonymous cabins the way florists dealt in roses.

And then the lock made a small, obscene sound. Not a kick. Not a shoulder. A key.

Three people had known this place existed, and the door had just narrowed the field to one. Keys don't leak. Pockets carry them, and pockets come with people. And the knock — three, a stop — Noor's own countersign, played back at the door like a recording. Every protocol Noor owned now lived in someone else's coat.

Inside: boots on floorboards, unhurried, no lights. A pale line of glow bloomed through the curtain gap where the burner lay face-up, still playing its part. A deeper buzz answered it — his own phone.

"No," the notary voice said, conversational as a weather report. "Warm. Hours, not days." A pause. "Truck's still here. Run the plate — whatever name falls out, put a man on it." A longer pause. "Is he talking?" Something came back that made Noor's stomach drop through the frozen ground. "Good. Keep him expensive."

Wren. Alive. Priced.

Noor put their mouth against Driver's ear, and the words came out on almost no air at all. "In through the nose. Out slower. Move when he talks. Freeze when he stops. Now."

The floorboards spoke and they moved. The voice carried and they moved. Silence nailed them down twice — once at forty feet from the gate, crouched on the needle duff with the cold coming up through both knees, while the man in the cabin finished his call to a person Noor would never hear. *Keep him expensive.* The drive sat against Noor's ribs, and it had just acquired a second function. It was collateral now. Twelve calls and one rule deep, Wren's pulse was filed under property, and Noor was carrying it.

The chair scraped. Silence. The worst acoustics in the world.

They covered the last twenty feet in it, heel to toe, navigating by the map Noor had carried behind their eyes since the outbound trip — where the eaves spared the ground, where the frost lay open and would testify. The gate took both of them. The chain got the sleeve, the lift, the silence.

Then the back door opened behind them, and light fanned out across the frost.

The beam walked the north wall, unhurried, professional, and stopped where two sets of prints doubled back toward the woodpile. Noor didn't look. Looking was for people with time. They fed Driver through the alder, one trunk at a time, and behind them the notary voice said — level, to the phone, no drama in it at all:

"North track. The old one." A pause. "Alone. He runs from noise — put trucks on the road and he goes over the edge on purpose."

Boots on frost. Unhurried. Entering the alder.

Noor pressed a coat from the duffel into Driver's arms and kept them moving, bent double under the black pines, and the whisper that came out was steady, which surprised them both.

"Walk, don't run — running is noise, and noise is for when he sees us. Noon still stands. But your name's riding on a plate in that yard, so home is off the table till I say." A breath. "Distance before light. That's the whole religion tonight."

One: oh-one. Behind them, patient as a filing cabinet, the frost began to testify again — one set of boots, following the written trail north.

"How are your legs," Noor breathed. "Honestly. I need to know what I'm working with."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My legs are shaking, but I manage to keep moving.* "They're fine, they'll do." *I grip the coat and push forward.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"'They'll do' is what people say when their legs are lying," Noor breathed, and slowed them both down by a third anyway — a pace you could hold till dawn beat a brave pace that lasted ten minutes. They fished a wool beanie and gloves out of the duffel and pushed them into Driver's hands on the move. "Wear both. A third of your heat leaves through the skull, and up here the mountain does accounting. We rest on my count, thirty seconds, moving again before the cold notices us."

The track ran black and open under its frost, and Noor stepped off the ruts.

"This road is writing us down," they whispered, easing both of them under the pine canopy, where the needle duff drank the moonlight and held no shine. "Frost is his book. Under the trees the pages go blank. He can read our heading but not our minds."

Then, far below and east, an engine took the county road in low gear. A second answered from farther off — not chasing. *Spacing.*

"There's the fence going up." Noor kept them moving, bent, patient. "He's not hunting, he's escorting. He read my file — knows I run from noise — so he rings the roads and lets the cold do the shooting. By four a.m. this mountain works for him. So we don't beat him with distance. We beat him with walls." A breath. "One thing in the plus column. At the cabin he told his phone: *alone.* Two sets of prints and he said *alone.* Either the dark is bad for his arithmetic or nobody's said your name into that phone yet. The official record has one journalist fleeing into the trees. You were never in any car. That's the only good sentence anyone's written tonight, Driver, and I intend to keep it true all the way to noon."

The creek announced itself before they saw it — black sound, a cold seam cutting the spur. Noor had read the topo twice on the drive up, journalist's rosary, and now paid the memory out. "Two miles north there's a square the surveyors never bothered to name. Buildings with no name are either nothing or exactly something. We're about to find out which."

They crossed at the riffle, not the pool, straps cinched high, the laptop slung across their back like a shield. Thirty yards walking *in* the water — water doesn't keep a diary — then out onto stone and up under the canopy on the far side. The cold sent its invoice up both legs at once. They sat Driver down on a downed trunk, dug socks from the duffel, took the bag across their own chest while Driver's feet were captive. "Your whole job tonight is legs and silence. I'll carry the rest of it."

Working blood back into their own toes, Noor felt the drive shift against their ribs and stopped pretending it was only a story anymore.

"He told his phone to keep Wren *expensive*," they said, barely above breath. "Bookkeeping, not cruelty. As long as this is loose in the world, Wren's collateral. The day it's worthless, he's a cleanup. Carrying it is the only vote I get on whether he sees spring. So it stays where it is, and my ribs will have to learn to share."

Downstream, faint as a thought, a single stone turned over in water.

Noor went still with a sock half on. Counted the silence to sixty. To ninety. Boots didn't come.

"Stupid would follow the creek," they breathed at last. "He's not stupid. He'll walk both banks, lose the page, and go back to being patient — patience is his entire résumé. Which means the next thing that tries to kill us isn't him." They pulled the dry sock up like closing a wound. "It's the temperature, and it's a better shot than he is. Two miles. Walls. Move."

They'd gone maybe a quarter mile, needle-quiet, when Noor spoke again — and the steadiness had a crack in it now, hairline, honest.

"One warning. The crash finds me around two — it always does. Coffee is an appointment, not a personality. When my hands start their own investigation, you'll have to hate me quietly and keep us pointed north." A few more steps. Then: "Talk to me a minute. Something normal — twenty words about anything that isn't this mountain. Keep it low. I need to hear what we're walking back toward."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My teeth are chattering, but I try to keep my voice steady.* "Uh... okay. So, my cat, Mittens, she figured out how to open the pantry. It's... it's a whole thing."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The laugh got out before Noor could tax it — a short, cracked sound, half air, immediately strangled behind a glove, because on a silent mountain laughing was just a flare with better manners. Their shoulders kept going for a while after the sound stopped.

"Mittens," they whispered, when they could trust their mouth again. "The pantry. A *whole thing*." A breath. "Do you know what you just gave me? A size. That's the size of the country we're defending tonight. A world where a cat commits burglary and the worst consequence is rearranged canned goods. Everything up here gets heavier the longer you carry it, and I needed the true weight of it — which was never the drive. The drive is glass and metal. The weight was always that."

They walked a few steps on it. Then, because fair was fair:

"Sundays I call my mother and tell her I write obituaries." The needle duff drank the words the way it drank the moonlight. "She thinks it's gloomy work. It's the only section of the paper where somebody gets the whole truth read out loud once, with no lawsuit attached. Same job as mine, really. You find out what a life was worth and put it in writing. I just do it while they can still argue." A pause. "She mails casseroles for the funerals I don't attend. I eat every one. That's my Mittens."

East and below, a truck's headlights combed the tops of the pines and slid away. The ring, walking its fence. Noor marked it without breaking stride and kept them under the canopy, where the frost's pages stayed blank.

Two o'clock arrived on schedule. The crash didn't knock; it came up through the floor. First the words began to double — *canopy* arriving as *cannery*, *cannery* as something with too many teeth — then the edges of the dark went granular, and Noor's hands began their promised investigation, trembling at a frequency that had nothing to do with cold.

They called it before it could call itself.

"Wall," Noor breathed, steering toward a blowdown where three trunks had leaned together into a roof of branches. "Fifteen minutes. Rest is a tactical decision now, and I'm making it while I still outrank the part of me that wants to argue." From the duffel's front pocket came a chocolate bar crushed nearly to gravel. "Sugar first. The crash is a fuel problem pretending to be a feelings problem. Eat half of everything you're handed — that's an order from the only ranking officer present."

They ate in the dark and listened. The mountain offered back wind in the high trees and, once, an engine far to the east, spaced and unhurried. Nothing near. Noor hated how quickly they'd started grading silence on a curve.

While the sugar worked, they brought the drive case out and sat with it flat in both unsteady hands.

"Rule check," they said finally. "Old rule: no decryption without Wren, because half a story is a dead story, and dead stories get people killed for nothing." A thumb moved across the padded shell. "The rule holds. But you've earned honesty at these prices, so here's the real reason. It stopped being craft around the time a man said *keep him expensive* into a dead man's phone. This used to be a story. Now it's a leash. As long as everything Halden wants stays loose in the world, Wren stays priced instead of finished. The day it's decrypted, printed, *solved* — that's the day the ledger wants balancing." It went back against their ribs, second heartbeat. "So the whole job is: walk it to noon, get it loose in more hands than one, and make me worth more breathing than not."

They stood too fast, paid for it, held a trunk until the trees stopped tilting.

"Last thing, and it costs me. The crash has maybe an hour of legs left in it, then it starts spending mine. When my judgment files its resignation, you'll notice before I do — somebody has to work here." A breath. "If I weave, say *north* and keep walking. Don't debate me. I won't be in."

They moved again with the hour. The pines spaced out, the track bent along the spur, and the surveyor's square resolved out of the dark the way a photograph develops: a cabin first — small, gray wood gone silver, stone chimney, stovepipe capped against rain. Then a shed with one corner of roof folded in, alder claiming its foundation. Then, between them, a shape under a blue tarp the size of a truck — tied down clean, and Noor's one good eye did the arithmetic the bad one couldn't.

"No snow in the folds," they whispered. "Covered this season. Everything else up here is retired. That isn't."

They put their back against a trunk and closed the left eye entirely.

"Your turn with the eyes. I've got one working and it wants to clock out. Tell me what you see — the tarp, the tie-downs, whether the ground around it's been walked, and anything that's too straight. Nature doesn't do straight lines, Driver. Talk to me. I'll listen and be smart at you in about ninety seconds."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The word arrived without its cargo. "Yeah" — and under it, between Driver's fingers, a blue thumbprint of phone-glow, exactly the kind of light Noor had promised the mountain could read at a mile.

There was a sentence available about trust, and who owed whom what at this altitude. Noor left it where it was. Debt accounting could wait for daylight.

They crossed the blowdown and laid a gloved palm flat over the screen, gentle as closing a book. Up close, their voice was barely weather.

"Two hours ago I told you a lit screen reads a mile up this mountain. I don't say things like that for rhythm. They're load-bearing." A breath. "And I asked for your eyes because I'm down to one, and the one I have left keeps sending out résumés. You gave me 'yeah.'"

They could feel their own tremor where their hand covered the glass, and hated that Driver might feel it too, so they said the rest quickly, before pity could get a vote.

"You're not a bad friend. You're a civilian, which is the best thing a person can be and the worst thing to be in a ditch — I've been both, I know the literature. So here's a ditch-sized job: you're the clock. When I say rest, you count thirty out loud, breath-level, and we move at thirty whether my legs agree. That's your whole rank, and I'm pinning it on you right now." Their palm stayed over the phone. "And the phone goes fully off and rides in my pocket till noon. You'll get it back with an apology and my mother's address — she'll want to feed you after tonight. Decide while I'm gone. Ninety seconds. I need both of mine."

Noor went to the tree line alone and put their back against a pine where the canopy's shadow ran deepest, and counted.

*Sixty. Sixty-one. Sixty-one.* The numbers were doubling. Noor leaned on the count anyway — a metronome with a stutter — and let the good eye work.

The wire first. It ran from the cabin's eave to a pine across the yard, and it didn't sag. Wire sags; that was the whole honest confession of wire. This one flew taut and level, and nature doesn't do straight. Then the pole by the shed, and mounted on it a solar panel angled at the southern sky — dustless, new, drinking — a flower planted by people who never left. At the cabin steps, one set of boot prints, edges crisp, an in-and-out pattern: a maintenance visit, hours old, stovepipe still capped. And the tarp — ratchet straps tensioned hard, edges tucked under, not a fold of snow because it had never met any. This season's install. Tire prints ran sharp from the track to it, and a jerry can rode the rack.

The picture assembled itself with a click Noor felt in the teeth.

*He told his phone: he runs from noise. Then he rang every road and left the quiet door standing open.* You don't chase a man toward a cliff. You build a barn at the bottom of it and leave the door open, and you let the cold do the driving. The north track had never been an escape. It was a funnel, and this square was the receiving pen, and the throat of it was that straight wire — somewhere down-mountain, a notary voice feeding the ring by radio.

"Maybe the boots behind us aren't a dog," Noor breathed. "Maybe they're the drover, walking patient, because the barn already has our stall."

They went in along the shed's shadow seam, alder to eave, and never once put a boot on the open frost. At the tarp's rear corner the hands did their investigation — the buckle cold as a judge — and under it sat a side-by-side machine with a storage box behind the seat: tow strap, bungees, an oil-stained work jacket, a headlamp that still had honest weight to its batteries. Noor pulled the spark plug cap, pocketed it. *When he turns the key tomorrow, the machine will say 'later,' and later is the most expensive word on a mountain.*

The journalist wanted a photograph. The fugitive outvoted her, two eyes to one.

Back at the blowdown, Noor pushed the jacket into Driver's arms — still warm from nothing but the mountain's politeness — and kept the voice at parade-volume quiet.

"New inventory, then we're moving. The square's a trap wearing a barn's clothes, so we don't sleep in it — we walk. Motion till light; the cold only shoots what stands still. At first light we want east-facing rock, not trees. Rock holds the sun." They flexed their trembling fingers and told the truth about it: "It's 2:26. Noon stands. Route 9 stands."

Then they held out an open palm, and the voice went somewhere it hadn't been all night — quieter than tactics, quieter than fear.

"Before we go. The phone. What was worth a mile of visibility, Driver? And I'm not asking to scold — I'm asking because if there's someone waiting up for you, a person, a Mittens, someone who hears a door and knows your footsteps — then the good version of tonight has to get you back to them, and I want that *written in*. I've been spending you like cab fare since the cabin, and it's a habit I hate in myself." The palm stayed open between them. "So. Honest answer, and then we're ghosts again."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My phone is already off. I put my cold hands in yours for a second, then pull them back.* "It was nothing. Just... checking the time. Habit." *I look away, embarrassed.* "Let's just go."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The lie arrived politely, and Noor took it the same way. Their hand closed around Driver's cold fingers before they finished retreating — two seconds of borrowed warmth, brisk as a transaction, knuckle to wrist — and then let go.

"Time," Noor said. "Sure. Then here's some: it's 2:26, and it says east."

Everyone kept one door shut. Behind Noor's stood a mother who mailed casseroles to funerals for a son who wrote obituaries; they weren't going to knock on Driver's. But they logged it, because logging was the whole job: the answer had never mattered. Driver had killed the phone without being made to. Whatever the screen held, they'd surrendered the thing it protected the moment they thumbed it dark — and that was worth more than the name of it would have been.

They went. East under the canopy, contouring the spur where needle duff kept the frost's pages blank, at the third-speed Noor had set and now resented. The crash was in the words. *Canopy* kept arriving with one syllable too many. Once the moon came down in two installments, one behind the other, and Noor stood still until the world resolved to a single moon, pressing a thumbnail into a forefinger until the pain filed its report. Pain was a stake. Pain was load-bearing.

The rest was a granite knob with a slice of open sky, called at 2:41, thirty seconds — the clock's job. Out of pure professional reflex — journalists rifle pockets the way other people check locks — Noor went through the work jacket while they waited.

Chest pocket. Paper. A folded photocopy, hand-ruled columns, read close under the drape of the jacket by moonlight the trees had quartered.

*Camp 1 — wood, batteries — 10/9.*
*Camp 2 (HART) — drain lines, wire wax — 10/16.*
*SQ 4 — tension wire, fuel — 10/17.*

Down the page it went. Camp 5. Square 2. A system, dated, ticked off in a workman's pencil. Inside the collar, Sharpie gone shiny with wear: VOSS.

Noor sat with that for the rest of the thirty seconds and let the largest sentence assemble itself.

Nobody sold the safehouse. Nobody had to. The safehouse was the *product* — arrangement and trap off the same shelf, factory-installed, keys included. Which meant the cabin proved nothing about Wren. Wren might never have had a thing to betray. He might be innocent and priced, and innocence had never once gotten anyone off a ledger.

For sixty seconds the fear went quiet and the work came on like a lamp. That was the true addiction — not adrenaline; corroboration. Noor photographed the page, second exhibit of the night, then slid it into a zip pocket. The ribs were getting crowded: drive, route sheet, a second heartbeat apiece. And maybe the patient man behind them had a name now. Names were handles. Handles got pulled.

Then they listened, and the mountain had changed the subject.

The boots were gone.

Not far. Not quiet. *Gone* — no frost testifying on the track behind them, no patience anywhere in it. Behind had been the only direction where Noor knew the man was, and nowhere and behind were different religions. He'd stopped being a dog. Cut upslope, or dropped to a road, or simply quit following a trail he already understood — and Noor's whole map of the night expired at the border of that silence.

"He's off the leash too," they breathed. "Which makes the next hour the expensive one. Rock at first light. Move on my—"

The sentence didn't come back. Three steps into standing, the ground quietly revised its angle of repose, and Noor caught the granite with a palm and stayed there, breathing, honest.

"Okay." The word came out level, which cost something. "It's happening. Judgment's clearing its desk early — overtime rates." They got one knee under themselves and made the hand-off while they still outranked it. "New arrangement. You ask me questions. Anything — Mittens-tier is perfect. Weather, your worst haircut, anything at all. If I answer, the pilot light's still on. If I'm slow, or wrong, or the answer comes out with too many syllables in it — you say *north*, you take my sleeve, and you do not wait for me to agree. That's the rank I'm handing you, and tonight it outranks mine. That's the entire point of it."

They found the black seam of the track with their eyes and pointed their chin along it, east, toward where the ridge should break into bare stone by morning.

"Start now," they said. "Ask me one."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My heart pounds in my chest, but I try to focus.* "Okay. Um... what's the weirdest thing you've ever eaten?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The answer took four seconds, which Noor graded out loud as *within parameters*, because a rule unenforced was just a wish.

"Mittens-tier, as ordered. Two answers." They paced the words to their footfalls so the sound would scatter among the trunks. "The record book says pickled egg, 2011, stakeout at a scrapyard, out of a jar with no label and no allegiances. Tasted like regret and formaldehyde. I remember every second. But the ledger answer — the one that cost — is a sheep's head. Halved, boiled, skin on, the eye still seated, in a union man's kitchen outside Molde. His mother set it down and then watched me find the eye, and I understood in one cold flash that the eye was the exam. So I ate the exam." A breath, white, spent fast. "Here's what that table taught me, and it's load-bearing tonight: eating together is the oldest countersign there is. Older than knock codes. Somebody feeds you what they are, you swallow, the contract exists. And tonight a man stood at a door and knocked three times and waited." The sentence shut like a trap with good hinges. "Countersigns are recipes, Driver. Anybody can cook."

They walked a few steps on that, because it deserved them. Then Noor stopped under a gap in the canopy and pointed a glove at the one hole in the trees where a star stood still while everything else swung.

"Polaris. That's your compass now — mine runs on coffee and has started rounding off. It rides on your left hip all night. If it drifts behind your shoulder, I'm curving home without meaning to, and you say *north* and take my sleeve. I read ground, you read true. Nobody crosses a mountain alone. It just usually isn't phrased that way."

The crash kept its books in installments. A quarter hour on, Noor caught themselves narrating a slope that wasn't there — and then the trees began to space out, and their lagging eye took it for the saddle thinning until it was past time: the trees weren't thinning. They were *ending*. Ahead lay a meadow, wide and silver and open, a blank page under the moon. Noor's hand closed on Driver's sleeve an instant before either foot committed.

And in the same breath, from downslope left, small as a cricket: a radio key, pressed once. Silence with weight in it. Then from the right, farther, an answering click. Then a third, behind them, back in the timber they'd just left.

Noor drew them off the frost a step at a time, until the black closed over them again.

"Not tracking," they breathed. "Mowing. A line, spaced out, sweeping the neck of the funnel. Trail-followers read the past — a line owns the future. And a line finds motion. Against a line you're furniture or you're found." They put their mouth close. "I sold you motion till light. That rule priced in one man reading frost behind us. It didn't price in a broomstroke. Rules get re-underwritten when the risk changes — that's not breaking them, that's insurance."

The spruce Noor chose had skirts to the ground and a trunk like a wall, dead boughs already down beneath it — nothing broken, nothing green, nothing that screamed. From the duffel came a folded square of foil: "Every paranoid person's duffel carries miracles." It went under them, because the ground steals heat downward all night and never leaves a name. The duffel went under their hips, the boughs over their knees, a square of chocolate into each of them — "fuel for shivering; shivering is work, and we're about to work all night at doing nothing."

"One more piece of tailoring. The coat — his coat. Inside out. There's a name in that collar, and if anyone reads you tonight, I want you reading as nobody. Collar against your chest."

Then, quieter, the clause Noor hated.

"If the line finds us anyway, I stand first. Hands land on me, and while they're busy pricing me, you're a rock — then a lost, freezing, stupid camper with no truck and no story that touches mine. Every second of their attention on me, you spend going east. That's not nobility, it's arithmetic: I'm the line item. And the drive stays on me. If I put it on you, you're written into the ledger, and the only clean sentence tonight says you were never in any of it."

Downslope, the left-hand click came again. Nearer. Unhurried.

"3:04," Noor breathed, settling their back against the trunk, the drive pressed between their ribs and the bark. "First gray near seven. Four hours of geology, and the temperature finally gets its shot — stillness is a loan the cold makes at interest. So: toes wiggle on every thirty-count, breath through the nose, and we watch each other's speech. If my answers start arriving pre-slurred, say my name. I'll answer. The pilot light test runs both directions now."

A pause. The broom coming, stroke by stroke.

"Ask me another. Quiet as a secret, nothing worth laughing at yet. The line has a long way to mow, and answering keeps both our lights on. Count's yours. Start now."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My heart is pounding, but I try to keep my breathing even.* "Okay. Um... what's your favorite kind of tree?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Olive," Noor breathed, and let four full seconds pass before grading it. "Four. Outside parameters. Logging it against myself, so the record stays honest."

They paced the story to their breath, white and quickly spent.

"The record-book answer is cedar, because cedar prints well in copy. The true answer is my grandmother's grove. A terraced hill, forty trees, and she had names for every tree and none for the neighbors. The old ones lean on stones wedged under their arms like crutches — you prop an olive the way you'd prop an uncle, and nobody on that hill finds it strange." A pause. "Her brother's grove burned in the bad year — the one that family doesn't say out loud, and I'm going to follow their lead. Three springs later, the stumps sent up shoots. Nobody planted. Nobody asked. Olives don't die all the way. You can only schedule them." Noor's hand settled against the drive through the jacket. "Everything I believe about evidence, I learned on that hillside. Burn the page; the stump keeps. Records regrow. It's why this rides against my ribs. Not sentiment. Agronomy."

The quiet after the story had lasted maybe a minute when the line arrived.

Down-left, the radio clicked — close now, inside the trees. Then boots, and Noor's ear filed a complaint before the fear did: the boots were on the duff, not the frost. He avoided the pages too. Competence, confirmed.

The shape came down the spacing between trunks and stopped on the far side of the spruce, close enough through a gap in the skirt to count the eyelets on his boots. Noor's hand found Driver's sleeve and stayed there — a written instruction in five fingers. The smell reached them first: tobacco, cold nylon, a full night of outside on a man. A match did not strike. Just a coal, cupped into two fists, no bigger than a bead — the only light for a mile, and small enough to be arrogance instead of a mistake.

Somewhere in the middle of the waiting, Noor's chin went down on its own schedule — sleep ambushing in two-second installments — and the jerk of it came within an inch of the boughs. Thumbnail into forefinger. Pressed until the report came back. Stakes in the ground.

The man coughed. Deep, ranged, a miner's cough — and Noor spent it, letting half a held breath go inside the sound, the way you move a pawn behind a louder piece.

Then, low, half swallowed by the trees: *"...meadow's clean..."* Static. *"...hinge..."* A number. Ten, possibly. Or seven wearing ten's coat — Noor's arithmetic had started rounding, and they knew it.

The coal ground out under a boot heel. One person leaving, unhurried, the duff whispering him back down toward the open ground.

"Journalism is mostly half a sentence and the nerve to be right about the other half," Noor breathed. "Two men. The sweep pivots on a hinge — some rock or gate where the line turns around — and in ten minutes, it turns. Which means for nine of those minutes, the safest ground on this mountain is the ground they just finished mowing." A breath. "You don't run from a line. You let it pass, and you walk its wake, before it doubles back. So we cross behind them. Not east *with* them — east *through* them, on their heels, angled so the meadow sits between us and the turn by the time it turns. Then bare rock before first gray, east-facing, and the sun signs off on the whole night."

Noor stood, and the mountain tilted its invoice, and they waited out the lean against the trunk until the trees agreed to hold still.

"Polaris rides your left hip, same religion as before. And your clock just got promoted — I'm rounding now, so you keep the count, out loud, breath-level. If I argue with a number I gave you, the number wins. That's the rank working as intended."

They eased out from under the skirts into the cold open dark, one trunk at a time, the meadow lying silver and empty ahead where the broom had just passed over.

"One thing before we cross. Hands out of the gloves, ten seconds — fingertip to thumb, both hands, fast as you can go." Their voice dropped to almost nothing. "The creek had your boots an hour ago, and the cold keeps books too. Fine motor is the first page it writes on. Tell me which hand is slower — and be honest, because I'll be reading your face either way, and I'm down to one eye to read it with."

Downslope, faint, the radio clicked once more. Farther. Moving away.

"It's 3:19," Noor breathed. "We cross on your thirty."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My hands are shaking, but I pull them out of the gloves. My right hand feels stiff, but my left feels like a block of ice. I try to make them move, but it's hard.* "My left... it's really slow."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor let the curtain fall back into place. "Yeah," they said, the word rough against a throat dried out by too much coffee. But they didn't turn toward the cabinets. Instead, they stepped over to the kitchen table and finally snapped the laptop open. The screen threw a hard blue rectangle across the dusty wood. Noor sat—perched, really, on the edge of the chair—and pulled the padded case toward them with one hand while unwrapping a protein bar from their jacket pocket with the other. They ate without tasting it, eyes already tracking across the laptop's glow.

The phone records first. Noor plugged their personal phone into the side port and opened the extraction tool they'd been running for the last three weeks. The call log populated in a tight column of white text. The source's number appeared three times: an incoming at 6:22 PM confirming the meet, an outgoing at 8:47 PM—forty-three seconds, *"On my way"*—and then nothing. Dead air. Noor cross-referenced the timestamps against their notes, lips moving silently. The source had never been late before. Never.

Noor swallowed the last of the protein bar and wiped their fingers on their thigh before unlocking the padded case. The encrypted drive came out cold and matte-black. They inserted it into the second USB port. A password prompt blinked once, twice. Noor typed the long string from memory—twenty-four characters, a line from a poem they'd memorized in college that they hadn't thought about in years until they'd needed a key. The drive mounted. Folders bloomed across the screen: financials, transcripts, geotagged photos. Noor clicked into the transcripts folder first. If the source wasn't coming, Noor needed to know exactly what they had before dawn.

Outside, something creaked. Noor's head snapped toward the window, but they didn't get up. They reached instead for the heavy flashlight on the table and thumbed it on, angling the beam toward the ceiling to dim the glare. With their other hand, they kept scrolling. They would check the road again in ten minutes. They would verify every timestamp on this drive. They would not sleep until they knew whether they were waiting for a ghost or a warning.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I put my phone down, watching Noor. *Something creaked outside, but it was probably just the house settling.* "You gonna be up all night?" I ask, already knowing the answer.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't look away from the screen. "Someone has to be," they said, the words clipped and automatic. The flashlight beam still washed the ceiling in a pale, trembling disk, turning the kitchen into a cave of half-shadows. 

They clicked into a transcript dated four days prior—source's code name in the header, a conversation with an unidentified contact. Noor had read it before, but now they read it *hunting*. Halfway down the document, a line they'd previously skimmed past stuck like a thorn: *"If I don't make the drop, assume they got to me first."*

Noor's mouth went dry. They dragged the geotagged photos folder into a split-pane view, cross-referencing timestamps. The last image had been taken yesterday at 11:03 AM outside a diner off Highway 14—metadata intact, the source's reflection ghosting the chrome bumper of a white sedan. But the transcript file modified tonight, time-stamped 7:15 PM, was only three sentences long. *"I think I'm clean. Coming up the mountain road now. See you at nine."*

That was before the 8:47 call. Before the forty-three seconds of *"On my way."* Before the silence.

Noor began copying the entire drive onto the laptop's local storage, the progress bar crawling too slowly across the dusty screen. They checked their watch: twelve minutes since they'd last surveyed the road. Too long. They left the laptop running and moved back to the window, bringing the heavy flashlight with them this time. They hooked one finger behind the curtain and held the light low, shielding the lens with their palm so only a thin blade of illumination cut across the dirt turnoff.

Nothing. No headlights. No crunch of gravel. Just the black shape of pines against a slightly blacker sky.

Noor let the fabric fall. They returned to the table and opened the financials folder—spreadsheets of shell company transactions, dates highlighted in red, amounts that made the air feel thinner. If the source wasn't coming, Noor needed to know who else knew about this meeting. They pulled their personal phone free and began photographing the laptop screen, page by page, the camera flash lighting their face in brief, violent bursts. Redundancy was survival. They would encrypt these photos. They would queue them for the dead-drop upload. They would check the road again in eight minutes.

They unwrapped a second protein bar with their teeth and kept working.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I sigh, running a hand through my hair.* "You can't do this alone, you know." I grab my own phone, checking for service again, though I know there isn't any.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor made a sound that wasn't quite agreement and wasn't quite dismissal. "I'm not alone," they said, though their voice had thinned to something mechanical. "I've got three dead corporations and a missing witness keeping me company."

They finished photographing the final page of financials, the flash etching another white scar across their retinas. Before the afterimage faded, they were already navigating to the encryption suite on their phone, thumbs moving in a blur. The files queued, compressed, locked behind a key only their editor possessed. The upload icon spun uselessly—no signal, no dead drop yet. Noor slipped the phone into their inner jacket pocket, closest to their ribs.

They stood, chair scraping the floorboards, and crossed to the back door. The latch was cheap aluminum, the frame swollen with mountain moisture. Noor tested it with their shoulder, felt the give, and dragged the kitchen trash bin across the floor to block it. Then they turned the deadbolt on the front door and wedged the heavy flashlight behind the knob for good measure.

Back at the table, Noor opened the financials spreadsheet again, scrolling not for content now but for names. A holding company kept appearing: Varnum Capital. Three wires in the last month, each one matching the dates of the source's geotagged photos. Noor cross-referenced the amounts against the transcript timestamps, lips moving. The pattern assembled itself like a skeleton rising from mud. If the source had been taken, it wasn't random. It was cleanup.

Noor closed the laptop but didn't shut it down—hibernate, password-locked, ready to run. They slid it into their go-bag along with the encrypted drive, then stashed the bag in the hall closet behind a stack of musty firewood. If someone breached the door, they wouldn't find the evidence in the first sweep.

Twelve thirty-seven. Noor returned to the window. This time they didn't touch the curtain. They stood to the side, breathing shallow, and watched the dark ribbon of the road through the gap. The protein bars sat like glue in their stomach. They needed water. They needed sleep. They needed the source to materialize out of the dark with a good reason for the delay and a better alibi for the silence.

None of that was coming.

Noor reached into their jacket and withdrew a folding knife—small, legal, useless against a gun but better than fingernails. They palmed it open and kept watching. In four minutes, they would check the road again. In four minutes, they would decide whether to burn the remaining hours before dawn waiting, or to wake Driver and run.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Twelve forty-one. Noor checked the road a final time, the gap in the curtain offering only the same empty dark. They let the fabric fall and turned away from the window for good. The decision crystallized in their chest, cold and final.

“Get your things,” Noor said to the couch. “We’re leaving.”

They didn’t wait for an answer. Noor moved to the kitchen table and swiped their sleeve across the wood, erasing the faint rectangle of dust where the laptop had sat, then the smudge where the flashlight had rested. They retrieved the go-bag from the hall closet, the encrypted drive and laptop safe inside, and slung it over their shoulder. But at the door, they paused. One thread still dangled.

Noor pulled out their phone and opened the last photo they’d taken of the laptop screen—the diner shot, the source ghosting in the chrome bumper. They pinched to zoom until the reflection filled the glass. The white sedan’s license plate was partially visible: a state prefix, three characters, the rest lost to glare. Enough.

They opened the financials spreadsheet again, thumbs flying, and scrolled to the vehicle expenses buried three tabs deep. A corporate registration for a black SUV, another for a silver coupe, and there—dated last Tuesday—a white sedan with the same prefix, the same three characters. Varnum Capital.

The source hadn’t just been followed. They’d been hunted by the same entity that signed the checks.

Noor’s mouth tightened. They deleted the photo from their camera roll, then from the recently deleted folder, and shoved the phone back into their inner pocket. The folding knife stayed open in their other hand as they crossed to the back door. They kicked the trash bin aside, turned the deadbolt, and cracked the door an inch. Cool mountain air rushed in, carrying pine and rot. Noor swept the flashlight across the tree line in a low arc—trunks, ferns, nothing moving.

They looked back toward the couch. “I’m not waiting to find out if they take the road or cut through the woods,” Noor said, their voice stripped to a wire. “Move, or I’m hiking to the highway alone.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I scramble up, surprised.* "Whoa, okay! I'm coming, I'm coming!" *I grab my jacket and keys from the coffee table.* "What's going on?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't answer directly—there wasn't time to diagram the labyrinth of shell companies and ghost registrations for someone who hadn't been living inside the file for three weeks. They moved through the back door in a low crouch, flashlight beam pinned to the dirt to preserve night vision. The knife stayed palmed against their thigh.

They swept the light under the cabin's single parked vehicle, then across the undercarriage in a practiced arc. No wires glinted. No fresh mud on the tires that hadn't been there when they arrived. Noor straightened only halfway, the go-bag strap cutting a diagonal across their chest, and gestured toward the driver-side door with a sharp jerk of their chin.

"Highway 14, but not the main junction," Noor said, their voice keeled low against the cricket noise. "Take the old logging spur two miles west, then cut south for the interstate. If headlights appear behind us and don't pass inside thirty seconds, floor it until the traction gives out."

They circled to the passenger side, refusing to turn their back on the tree line. Noor pulled their sleeve over their fingers before touching the handle, then yanked the door open. As they dropped into the seat, they withdrew their phone one final time and disabled the Bluetooth, the location services, the cellular radio itself—leaving it a dead brick that could betray nothing but still hold the queued files. They pulled the battery from their backup burner and dropped both devices into a zippered side pocket of the go-bag.

Noor pulled the door shut with a soft click, leaving the window cracked to catch any sound from the woods. They wedged the knife into the door panel's map pocket, within instant reach, and twisted to surveil the tree line through the rear glass. Nothing moved against the stars.

"Lights off until we clear the ridge," Noor said, the words barely a murmur in the darkened cab. Their thumb found the zipper of the go-bag and traced it once, twice, confirming the encrypted drive still rode against their ribs. They had the laptop. They had the transcripts. They had a name—Varnum Capital—and a partial plate that matched a corporate registration. The rest of the night would be spent deciding whether to burn that name across every encrypted newsroom drop box they could reach, or whether doing so would turn the ghost at their shoulder into a body they could never outrun.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, heart thumping. I start the car, trying to be as quiet as possible, and pull away from the cabin.* "Got it. Logging spur, two miles west." *I keep the lights off, peering into the darkness.* "What exactly are we running from?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't turn from the rear window. "The people who sign the checks," they said. Their hand found the go-bag and pulled out a spiral notebook, the kind that fit in a back pocket. They clicked a pen—one click, loud in the dark—and wrote the partial plate in the margin, then *Varnum Capital*, then the date. Paper couldn't be remotely wiped.

They checked the side mirror. The cabin had vanished into the black, but something else hadn't. Noor's pen stopped. "Don't take the spur," they said, sudden and sharp. "Look to your left at the next fork. Fire access trail, unmarked. It'll dump us three miles north of the interstate, past the pinch point."

Noor kept their eyes on the rear glass. Through the dark, a single point of light had appeared where the logging spur met the county road—not headlights, but the amber glow of a parking lamp, steady and waiting. Someone had parked in the blind curve, lights doused, facing the only route down.

Noor tore the page from the notebook, folded it into a tight square, and slid it into their sock. They palmed the folding knife from the door panel and twisted to check the side mirror again. The light hadn't moved. "If they flashed high beams, that would be a signal," Noor said, more to themselves than to Driver. "Parking lamp means they're holding position. Waiting for us to come down the mountain nice and predictable." They shook their head once, sharp. "We're not predictable."

They opened the laptop—not the screen, just the lid a crack to wake it from hibernate, angling the glow away from the windows. Noor's fingers moved across the keyboard by memory, queuing the files for transmission the instant they caught a bar of signal. They pulled up the geotagged photos again, hunting for another route, another body of water, another cabin where a phone might work. The map showed a ranger station seven miles south through the fire trail. Noor memorized the coordinates and shut the laptop.

"Keep the lights off," Noor said. Their thumb traced the zipper of the go-bag once more. "And if you see brake lights ahead, don't stop. Don't even hesitate. I'll tell you when to turn."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My hands tighten on the wheel.* "Got it." *I squint into the darkness, trying to find this unmarked trail.* "You think they're waiting for us specifically?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't look away from the rear window. "They knew about the meet," they said. "They knew the only ways down." Noor's hand tightened around the knife handle once the car had settled onto the narrower track. Pine branches scraped the passenger side, a sharp skittering sound that made Noor's shoulders tense.

They swept the flashlight across the trail's edge, playing the beam low and brief. The dirt showed a disturbance—tire treads pressed into the damp soil, overlaying the day's dust. Recent. Wide-base, heavy load. Noor killed the light immediately.

"Someone else took this way within the hour," Noor said. They pulled the laptop from the go-bag, waking it with the lid cracked just enough to read the screen. The map reappeared, and Noor traced a new route with their thumb, abandoning the ranger station. "There's a maintenance shed two miles west. Beyond it, a ridge with line-of-sight to the interstate cell tower. We need to get there."

Noor reached into their pocket and found only the empty protein bar wrapper. The sugar wasn't holding back the tremor in their hands anymore. They needed water. They needed sleep. They needed to not die in the woods.

They glanced at the side mirror. The amber light had vanished, or maybe the trees had swallowed it. That was worse.

"Kill the engine," Noor said suddenly. "Now."

The moment the motor died, Noor was moving. They stuffed the laptop and the encrypted drive into the go-bag, then reached under the seat for the emergency kit they'd spotted earlier—a flashlight, a road flare, a cheap reflective vest. Noor took the flare and the vest. They opened the door using their jacket sleeve, then crouched by the front tire, pressing the reflective vest into the mud to obscure the tread marks behind them. It wasn't much, but in the dark, it might read as a dead end.

Noor returned to the passenger side, breathing hard, and pointed ahead where the trail narrowed into a footpath. "We walk from here. If they find the car, we need to be on that ridge with the files already transmitting." They checked their watch—twelve forty-nine. "Leave the keys. Take anything you can't replace."

Noor shouldered the go-bag, the weight of it digging into their collarbone, and stepped out into the dark. The folding knife stayed open in their hand. They didn't wait; they started up the footpath, counting paces, memorizing the curve of the terrain. In twenty minutes, they would reach the ridge. In twenty-one, they would know if the story would survive the night.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't look back again. The footpath climbed steeply through fir and loose scree, the go-bag strap cutting a burning line across their collarbone. They counted paces in their head—forty-six, forty-seven—while their left hand kept the folding knife pointed down and ready. At fifty paces, Noor ducked behind a granite outcropping and pulled the laptop from the bag. They woke it with the lid cracked to a blade of light, checked the transmission queue. Twelve files, encrypted, waiting for a signal bar. Noor toggled the settings to burst-transmit on contact, then closed the lid but kept the machine live, burning battery for the seconds it would save.

They took the road flare and wedged it between two stones at ankle height on the path below the outcropping, striker facing outward, braced to ignite if kicked. Crude, but it would scream light and smoke into the dark if anyone came up fast. Noor left it and kept climbing.

The ridge was close. Noor felt the air thin above the tree line, the black shape of the crest visible against a slightly less black sky. They switched the knife to their other hand and wiped their palm on their thigh. Then, from somewhere downslope and west—not the car, but deeper in the trees—a branch cracked under weight. Noor froze for one heartbeat, two. They didn't turn. They just moved faster, thighs burning, the go-bag slamming against their hip. In three minutes they would reach the crest. In two, they would find a flat rock, angle the laptop toward the interstate, and let the files run. The story would outrun them, or it wouldn't. Noor kept climbing, each breath a sharp hook in their side, and did not look back.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I sigh and slip my phone into my pocket. *I guess I'm walking.* I grab my jacket and get out of the car, slamming the door. *What a mess.* I follow Noor, trying to keep up.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor's head snapped toward the sound of the car door slamming—sharp, metallic, carrying too far in the mountain stillness. Their jaw tightened, but they didn't call out a warning. There wasn't time to teach noise discipline to someone who hadn't been running for three weeks. Noor just pushed harder up the slope, boots sliding on scree, the go-bag bouncing against their spine.

The branch cracked again, closer this time, downslope and west. Not a deer. Deer didn't move in a straight line. Noor ducked behind a fallen log and pulled the laptop free one-handed, waking it with the lid cracked to a sliver. The battery icon glowed amber: forty-seven percent. The transmission queue pulsed, ready. They scanned the ridgeline above, judging the distance. Two hundred meters, maybe less. The cell tower's red aviation light blinked against the sky beyond the crest—line of sight, if they could reach the bare rock.

Noor shoved the laptop back into the bag and ran. Not a sprint—that would break an ankle in the dark—but a steady, brutal pace, knees driving, knife still open in their fist. They passed a stand of dead birch and cut right, away from the footpath, angling across a talus slope where their boots wouldn't leave clear prints in soft earth. The rocks turned underfoot. Noor caught their balance with their free hand, palm shredding on granite, and didn't stop to check the blood.

At the crest, the wind hit them. Noor dropped to their belly behind a low wall of granite and dragged the go-bag around front. They pulled the laptop out, angled the screen toward the interstate corridor, and watched the signal indicator. Nothing. Noor tilted it left, right, higher. One bar flickered, died, flickered again. Noor held their breath. The icon solidified.

They triggered the burst transmission.

The progress bar filled in jerking increments—eight percent, fifteen, twenty-three. Noor's eyes kept dropping to the dark slope below. They could hear Driver's footsteps now, crunching through the talus, getting closer. Noor didn't look up. They reached into the bag and found the encrypted drive, still cold, still intact. They gripped it while the files uploaded, as if holding it could keep the signal strong.

Forty-seven percent. Fifty-two.

From the tree line below the ridge, a flashlight beam swept upward—not pointing at them yet, but searching. Noor flattened further against the stone. The light passed over their position, close enough to catch the dust on the laptop lid if it had been clean. Noor's thumb found the power button, ready to kill the screen if the beam swung back.

Sixty-one percent.

Noor needed a secondary plan. If the transmission failed, if the battery died, if someone crested the ridge with a gun, the story still had to survive. They pulled the spiral notebook from their pocket and began writing—names, dates, the partial plate, Varnum Capital—in tight, precise script, compressing three weeks of investigation into a paragraph that could fit under a tongue or inside a shoe. The pen ran out of ink. Noor shook it, kept writing.

Seventy-eight percent.

The flashlight beam below went dark. Whoever held it had either found the car or decided to go quiet. That meant they were close enough to see the car. Close enough to know Noor and Driver weren't in it.

Eighty-nine. Ninety-four.

Noor closed the notebook and slid it back into their sock. They palmed the folding knife and stared at the screen, willing the last files through. The wind shifted, carrying a faint smell of cigarette smoke from below—tobacco and sulfur, human and recent.

One hundred percent.

The confirmation icon appeared. Noor killed the laptop immediately, snapped it shut, and stuffed it into the go-bag. They didn't celebrate. They just rolled left, away from the crest, and dropped three feet down the far side of the ridge into a gully hidden from below. The go-bag went over first, then Noor followed, landing soft, knees absorbing the impact. They pressed their back against the earth and listened.

Driver's footsteps had stopped somewhere above. Noor couldn't see them, couldn't call out without giving away their own position. They just gripped the knife and waited, lungs burning, counting seconds. One. Two. Three. At thirty, if no one had fired, Noor would move again—north by the stars, toward the interstate, toward the nearest pay phone or patrol station or 24-hour diner with a wifi signal and a wall at their back. The story was out now, alive in the wires. The only thing left was to make sure Noor lived long enough to see it published.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I land next to Noor, panting. "What was that? What's going on?"*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't answer. They were already scanning the ridgeline above, then the dark throat of the gully below. The cigarette smoke had come from the west, which meant at least one searcher on the slope they'd just abandoned. The gully ran north-northeast, carved between granite ribs, choked with deadfall but descending toward the interstate corridor. Noor had memorized the topography in the seconds before triggering the transmission.

They grabbed the go-bag and rose into a crouch, the knife still open in their shredded palm. "Follow," they breathed. "Step where I step. Don't speak."

Noor moved up the gully, not down, hugging the eastern wall where the shadows pooled deepest. After twenty meters the gully bent sharply left, and Noor froze, shoulder pressed to stone. Voices now—two of them, muffled, from somewhere near the abandoned car. Male. One laughed, a short, clipped bark that carried no humor.

Noor dropped to one knee. Their free hand swept the gully floor until fingers closed around a fist-sized rock. They tucked it into the go-bag's side pocket, then found a smaller stone for their jacket. Improvised noise makers. They kept moving.

The gully shallowed into a field of broken shale. Above, the clouds had torn enough to reveal the North Star. Noor oriented themselves and struck out across the shale, rolling heel to toe, keeping the stones from chattering. Their palm burned. Their thighs shook. They ignored both.

At the far edge, a dirt track appeared—two ruts running straight toward the distant sodium glow of the interstate. Noor hesitated. Too exposed. But to the left, a quarter mile down, a structure sagged against the dark: a collapsed barn, its roofline broken like a rotted tooth. Beyond it, a telephone pole sagged, wires catching the starlight.

Noor turned their head toward Driver, close enough to smell the adrenaline sweat on their own skin. "See that pole?" they whispered. "Means a road. Means people." Noor didn't wait. They stepped onto the dirt track and ran low, keeping to the drainage ditch, the go-bag hammering against their hip. They had transmitted the files, but the story still needed a witness. Noor intended to survive to be that witness. The barn meant cover. The pole meant civilization. They would reach one, then the other, and they would not stop until they saw the strobing lights of a patrol car or the fluorescent hum of an all-night gas station.

Behind them, back on the ridge, a flashlight swept the crest—too late, searching empty granite. Noor didn't look back. They just ran.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I pant, trying to keep up, my own heart hammering.* "Okay, okay... lead the way." *I glance over my shoulder at the flashlight beam sweeping the ridge.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't break stride. The barn swam up out of the dark, its silhouette fractured against the sky. Noor cut left at the last moment, circling to the leeward side where the collapsed roof created a pocket of shadow against the foundation. Noor pressed their back to the rotted clapboard and slid down into a crouch, go-bag clutched to their chest. They counted to ten, listening past the roar of their own pulse. Nothing followed but silence.

Through a gap in the boards, Noor studied the road. The telephone pole sagged twenty yards ahead, wires drooping toward the gravel. Beyond it, the track met paved asphalt—a two-lane strip reflecting faint starlight. Noor's gaze tracked along the blacktop. Nothing moved. Then, a quarter-mile east, a single stationary light: not headlights, but the blue-white flicker of an LED sign. Convenience store. Gas station. Life.

Noor looked down at their shredded palm. Blood had crusted along the lifeline, but the fingers still worked. They unzipped the go-bag and pulled out the backup burner phone—battery removed, useless for tracking. They reassembled it with trembling hands, not to call, but to check for a signal bar. The screen lit. No service. They dropped it back into the bag.

The ridge behind them had gone dark again. The searchers weren't amateurs; they'd kill their lights when they realized the quarry had gone to ground. Noor needed to reach that gas station before the searchers reached the road.

Noor pushed up from the wall and moved to the corner of the barn, scanning the open ground between the structure and the telephone pole. Thirty meters of weeds and gravel. No cover. Noor's hand found the rock in their jacket pocket. They pulled it out, judged the weight, and hurled it sidearm into the darkness beyond the barn's far end. It cracked against stone. Immediately, Noor sprinted for the pole, bent double, go-bag slapping their spine.

They reached the asphalt and dropped into the drainage culvert. The concrete was dry, littered with cigarette butts and a rusted beer can. Noor crawled eastward, keeping below the grade, until the flickering LED resolved into words: OPEN 24 HRS. The gas station squatted in a pool of security light, two pumps out front, a single sedan parked by the air hose.

Noor stopped. One car. No movement inside. They checked their watch—1:17 AM. They needed a phone that worked. They needed witnesses. They needed to not walk into a trap.

Noor climbed out of the culvert and walked toward the station's glass doors, knife folded and pocketed, hands visible, shoulders squared. If death was waiting inside, they'd meet it in the light. But if salvation was there, Noor intended to buy a burner, a bottle of water, and enough time to call their editor before the sun came up.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I scramble after Noor, heart pounding.* "Are we safe now?" I ask, my voice a breathless whisper.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Eat," Noor repeated, like the word belonged to a language they'd stopped speaking. They didn't look away from the road. Headlights would show at the bend a full forty seconds before any vehicle reached the gate — Kestrel's truck, a gray Tacoma with a cracked taillight, and Noor had memorized it the way you memorize the face of someone you might have to identify later.

Nothing came around the bend.

"You're right," they said to the glass. "I know you're right." Their stomach had been a closed fist since six o'clock, but the smart move — the professional move — was to keep the machine fueled. Noor pushed off from the windowsill, let the curtain fall shut, and crossed to the cupboard. Chili, beans, a can opener older than they were. They took the chili, cracked it, and ate standing up, cold, spoon in one hand, because sitting down felt like something you did when you weren't waiting to find out if a person was still alive.

Halfway through the can, they set it on the table and woke the laptop.

"Okay," they said — to Driver, to the room, to nobody. "While we wait, we work."

The burner came out of the faraday bag first. One bar, then two, shakily. The dead-drop inbox refreshed. Nothing new since 8:47 PM — and that was the part that made Noor's skin crawl, the part they hadn't said out loud yet. 8:47 was Kestrel's all-clear. The coded check-in: *all good, see you at nine, bringing the originals.* Which meant Kestrel had been safe and talking fifty-one minutes before going dark. That wasn't the silence of someone spooked and laying low. That was the silence of someone whose phone had stopped transmitting.

Noor logged the timestamp in the notes file with steady hands and unsteady breathing, then pulled the padded case across the table and set the drive down beside the chili.

"If the drive's intact, I don't need Kestrel to hand me anything," they said. "The manifests, the convoy audio — it's all supposed to be on here. Kestrel was bringing the second half of the passphrase, but—" They stopped. Made themselves breathe. "No. There's a fallback. There has to be a fallback. Kestrel wouldn't build a dead man's switch with one door."

They plugged it in. The indicator went amber, then white. A passphrase prompt appeared, cursor blinking, patient as a held breath.

"Two wrong guesses and it wipes itself," Noor said quietly, remembering. "Two." They pulled the laptop closer, cracked their knuckles once, and started typing the first guess — the name of Kestrel's daughter, the thing they'd sworn they'd never use.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I watch them, half listening to the technical talk.* "Hey," *I say, my voice a little louder than I intended in the quiet room.* "You okay?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor's hands stopped over the keyboard. The cursor kept blinking in the passphrase field, waiting.

"Yeah," they said, and it came out flat, automatic — the journalist's reflex, the *I'm fine, keep the camera rolling* voice. They heard it, winced at it, and tried again. "No. I don't know."

They leaned back in the chair until it creaked, rubbing their eyes with the heels of their hands until colors bloomed behind their eyelids.

"It's just — sitting here feels like standing on a train platform knowing the last train already crashed somewhere up the line." They laughed once, short and ugly. "That's not — I'm not being dramatic. At 8:47 Kestrel was fine. Fine. And now it's past midnight and there's a truck in my imagination doing forty miles an hour into a culvert, and I keep making myself look at it."

They dropped their hands and looked at Driver properly for the first time in hours. The other person's face, lit blue by phone glow, suddenly looked very far from anywhere.

"I'm sorry. You drove me four hours up a mountain for a story that isn't even yours, and I've been treating you like furniture." Noor's mouth twisted. "You should go home. Seriously. If this goes sideways — if anyone comes up that road looking for me — I don't want it to be two people it finds."

Even saying it out loud, Noor knew it was half a offer. The couch was right there. The drive was right here. The second guess was in their head, the fallback Kestrel had mumbled into a bad connection in March: *if it's not her name, try the harbor. The year we met.*

Noor turned back to the laptop. Typed the daughter's name. Wrong — the prompt shook once, a small red flicker, and the counter underneath went from two attempts to one.

"One shot left," Noor whispered. Then, without looking up: "Answer me, though. Are you staying? Because if you are, I'm putting you to work. You're going to sit by that window and tell me about headlights, and I'm going to type."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look at the window, then back at Noor. I sigh and put my phone down on the cushion next to me.* "Alright, fine. What am I looking for?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Headlights at the bend," Noor said, eyes still on the screen. "The road curves a quarter mile out — nothing reaches this cabin without showing itself there first, forty seconds minimum. If it's Kestrel: gray Tacoma, cracked taillight, left side, and it flashes its highs twice before the gate. Anything else — any vehicle that slows down, any lights that just *sit* there — you say 'road' and you get your body away from the glass. Don't touch the curtain. And put your phone face-down. A lit screen in a black window reads from a long way off."

Then they stopped talking, because the passphrase field was still waiting, and the obvious answer was sitting right there: *the harbor, the year we met.* 2019. The strike at Pier 9, the woman in the yellow rain shell who'd folded a note down to the size of a stamp and pressed it into Noor's palm. Noor's fingers were halfway through spelling the year when the memory snagged like a thread on a nail.

No. Wait.

2017. The container-theft piece — the one nobody read, the anonymous longshoreman Noor had quoted saying *the numbers don't float.* Two years later, the first time they'd met in person, Kestrel had laughed at that line and said, *You quoted me before you knew I existed.* Kestrel counted everything. Kestrel would absolutely count that as *we.*

"The year we met," Noor murmured. "You meant 2017. You absolute—" They typed the name of the cannery docks, letter by letter, then the year, and hit enter before they could think better of it.

The screen went white. Then it opened.

Relief hit like a drug — two full seconds of it — and then Noor saw the file tree. MANIFESTS. AUDIO. PHOTOS. And one loose text file at the top level, modified tonight at 8:51 PM.

*READ FIRST — N.txt*

8:51. Four minutes after the all-clear. Noor opened it with a dry mouth.

*If the drive opened, you remembered 2017. Good. You listen better than you think you do.*

*I'm not coming. I know what I said. That was before I understood who was already watching the road. The all-clear at 8:47 was for them, not for you — let tonight look the way they expected it to look.*

*The manifests are the bait. Verified, damning, and they will burn whoever publishes them first. The audio is the story. Start with track 11.*

*One more thing. If a gray Tacoma with a cracked taillight comes up that road tonight — it isn't me driving it.*

Noor read the last line twice. The room got very cold, or Noor got very aware of the temperature. Three hours of watching that bend for a truck that had just stopped being a rescue.

"Change of plan," they said, voice low and level, the way you talk when raising it feels dangerous. "Forget everything I told you about the Tacoma."

They pulled up the AUDIO folder — forty-odd files, and there it was, track 11, nine minutes and change. Noor plugged in the earbuds, tugged the left one free, and held it out toward the couch.

"Come here. You asked what you're looking for." A beat. "Listen first. Then look."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor pulled the earbud back. "Okay," they said. No heat in it — and, if they were honest, a thread of relief underneath. One of them got to stay a person who just drove a friend up a mountain. That was worth protecting.

"Track 11," they said anyway, mostly to themselves. "Nine minutes."

They pressed play.

The first thirty seconds were a place: gulls, a diesel idling somewhere, a PA voice flattened by wind — *gate six closes in ten minutes* — and under all of it, the soft rhythmic rub of cloth against a microphone riding in a coat pocket. Kestrel's pocket. Noor checked the file date: eleven days ago. Pier 9. Kestrel had walked a recorder into a meeting.

Then two voices, close to each other, the recorder farther away. The first was gravel and patience, a man who'd never hurried for anything in his life. The second made Noor's jaw tighten — they knew it from a deposition video watched frame by frame last spring. Dane Renner. Meridian Logistics, VP of something called *asset integrity.*

"The shrinkage number," Renner was saying, "is whatever I say it is. That's the whole point of hiring me."

*The numbers don't float.* Noor's own headline, 2017, quoting an anonymous longshoreman. The same arithmetic, eight years apart, spoken out loud on a dock.

Then the part that mattered. Renner, unhurried: "And you're worried about the reporter. Don't be. The manifests are printed — every set, with its own mistake. Twelve sets, twelve mistakes. When a set surfaces, the mistake tells us which copy, which courier, which *friend of the court.* We don't stop the story. We let it print. Then we own everyone who touched it."

A pause. The gravel voice: "And the drive?"

"Comes to us tonight. Nine o'clock, up the mountain, in the writer's hands. We're not thieves — we're custodians. After the handoff, the story's poisoned and the writer's an accessory. Let her carry it."

"And your friend on the inside?"

"Being looked after."

Forty seconds of gulls after the men walked away. Then Kestrel's voice, barely a breath, aimed straight into the microphone: *"Eleven. That's eleven."*

The file ended. Noor sat very still. The chili had gone to cold grease in the can. The clock on the laptop said 12:31.

So that was the shape of it. The manifests were a trap with Noor's name on the trigger. The audio was the only clean thing Kestrel had ever given anyone — and the plan, as of eleven days ago, had been to let Noor *take the bait.* Kestrel had broken that plan tonight by not showing up. Which meant somewhere down the mountain, the plan's custodians were standing around a handoff point that was never going to happen, holding Kestrel's truck keys, waiting for new instructions.

Noor moved. Dragged the AUDIO folder onto the laptop — forty-one files, copying, four minutes estimated — and while the progress bar crawled, they did the math they'd been avoiding: the note was written at 8:51, four minutes after the all-clear, and the drive had been sealed in Noor's bag since six. Nothing writes to a sealed drive at 8:51 unless the drive has a way to hear. They turned the padded case over. Near the bridge, a seam no wider than a hair. Kestrel, at a diner in April, laughing over her coffee: *everything I build has a mouth.*

"Of course it does," Noor whispered, and dropped the drive into the faraday bag with the burner the second the copy finished. If it had been talking all night, it was done now.

They logged the last item from the checklist — the 8:47 message's origin tower, Dock Row, the port, nowhere near the mountain road — and closed the notes file. Then they looked over at the couch, at the blue glow.

"Renner," they said. "Dane Renner. R-E-N-N-E-R. He runs asset integrity for Meridian Logistics. If you're going to be on that phone anyway — dim it, and find out where he is tonight." A beat. "And then I'm pulling you off this couch at dawn whether you've found him or not. We're both leaving this mountain by first light. That part's not negotiable, because I just listened to nine minutes of a man explaining, very calmly, how he lets stories print so he can own the people who touched them."

Noor cracked their knuckles, opened the audio waveform, and set the playhead at the beginning.

"Track one," they said. "Forty more. Then we know everything she knew."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look up from my phone, a little annoyed at being put to work, but the urgency in Noor's voice gets through to me.* "Alright, Renner. Got it." *I start typing on my phone, already searching.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The coffee pot took three rinses before the dust stopped coming back as grit. Noor set it percolating anyway — not for the coffee, for the smell of it, which was the smell of working nights, and tonight had just stopped being an ordinary night in every way that mattered.

Back at the laptop, they sorted the AUDIO folder by date. Forty-one files, fourteen months. Nobody listens to forty tracks straight; you triage. First, last, and whatever makes the middle make sense.

Track 001, fourteen months old. Pier 9 again, but in winter — rain hammering the mic instead of gulls. The gravel voice did the talking. *"You want to know where the cargo goes, that's not the question. The question is who signs for it not existing."* And Renner, patient as arithmetic, laying out the design like an architect: *"Every set of books should tell you who's reading them."* Noor wrote it down and underlined it twice. Eight years after *the numbers don't float*, the numbers had learned to hunt.

Then the newest. Track 041, six days ago.

*Bellingham printed in March,* Renner said. *By Friday she had a correction, a retraction, and our counsel filing in three states. She'll settle. She'll never work under her own name again.* A pause. The gravel voice: *And the writer?* And Renner, unhurried: *She drives up the night before. She works off a legal pad. Two pens, no weapon, coffee she doesn't finish. We don't crowd her. We let her pack.*
