Noor sat very still. They remembered the Bellingham retraction. Everyone did — it had been more famous than the story, and Noor had filed it away as a lesson about verification. It hadn't been sloppiness. It had been a demonstration. A range test.

"New math," they said, not turning from the screen. "I told you first light. I was wrong. They watched us drive in, and the handoff they were waiting for is now four hours late. Professionals don't wait forever — a no-show triggers a protocol, and the protocol for a cabin they know ends with somebody walking up the driveway. So we leave at three-thirty. The dumbest hour there is. Nobody volunteers for a watch after three unless they're paid hourly, and paid people get slow right before shift change."

They moved while they talked. Faraday bag, charger, laptop — the notes file stayed offline and on their body. A second copy of the AUDIO folder went onto a microSD the size of a thumbnail, and the microSD went into the lining of Noor's jacket, because anything that mattered got carried where a search would have to get personal to find it. On the offline map, a logging spur behind the cabin looped nine miles west to the county road. Noor marked it. The bend cut both ways; they weren't planning to drive through it.

"Being looked after," they said once, quietly, in Renner's voice, and didn't say anything else about Kestrel. The best thing Noor could do for her tonight was make sure this audio became un-losable.

Between tracks, they checked the curtain gap. The bend was a darker shade of dark. Nothing. The absence was starting to make its own noise.

They poured two cups, carried one to the couch edge, and set it down within Driver's reach without comment.

"Status," Noor said. "What did you find on Renner — and don't just tell me where he is tonight. Tell me where he was at 8:47. If Renner was at the port when that all-clear pinged Dock Row, he was standing next to whatever's left of my source." They put the left earbud back in, playhead hovering over track 002. "And search *Meridian asset integrity* as a department, not a title. Nobody names a department that unless the asset is the story."

The coffee smell filled the cabin. Thirty-nine tracks. Three hours until three-thirty.

"Start talking. I'm listening to both of you."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I take a sip of the coffee, it's strong and hot.* "Okay, so Renner's official bio is squeaky clean, corporate ladder climber. But dig a little, and he's got ties to a few... less-than-reputable shipping companies. Shell corporations, mostly. And at 8:47 tonight, according to a checked-in flight manifest, he was on a private jet from Portland to Seattle." *I scroll a bit more.* "Meridian Asset Integrity seems to be a new division. Launched late last year. No public facing info, just a few internal memos I can find. All about 'risk management' and 'loss prevention'."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
For a moment Noor didn't move at all. Then the questions came out fast and flat, one on top of the other.

"Say the times again. Wheels-up at 8:47?" They didn't wait — they were already doing the arithmetic on their fingers against the table edge. "Portland to Seattle is fifty minutes in the air, less if he doesn't file a flight plan worth the name. So he's wheels-down by 9:40. If he drove straight here, he's been sitting at the bottom of our road since half past one." Noor checked the laptop clock. 12:43. "It's 12:43, and nothing has come around that bend. So either he's not coming — or he's already close, and he's *holding.*"

They stood up and started pacing the length of the kitchen, three steps, turn, three steps.

"Renner doesn't fly to Seattle at night for something he could phone in. He flew in because the handoff was tonight and he wanted to be in the region when it landed. The handoff died at 8:51. Which means he isn't here to watch anymore. He's here to clean up." A beat, and then the other half of it landed, and Noor stopped pacing. "Which also means he *wasn't* at the port at 8:47. The all-clear came from Dock Row. That was her. She sent it herself, standing at the water, feeding them the night they expected." Noor's breath went out slowly. "And read her note again. *You listen better than you think you do.* Nobody writes that with hands on their shoulders. She was free at 8:51. Alive, running, four hours into the dark by now — if the dark is where she went. That's the first good news since six o'clock. I'm not trusting it past dawn, but I'm keeping it."

They went back to the table, pulled the notes file up, typed fast. "Log one more thing. 8:47 twice — her all-clear, his wheels-up, same minute. Either coincidence or a clock they both work by. Write it down, don't marry it."

Then, scrolling: "Asset Integrity launched late last year. Track 001 is fourteen months old. She was recording before the department had a *name* — which means the department was never built to do the stealing. It was built to protect the stealing once it started talking. You stand up a loss-prevention unit after the losses learn to speak." Noor pointed the spoon from the chili can at the couch like a conductor's baton. "Save those memos. All of them — URLs, timestamps, everything. But not through anything with your name logged in. Clean browser, no accounts. If tonight goes right, that's evidence. If it goes wrong, it's the only copy that survives me."

While they talked, Noor scrubbed back to track 041 and let Renner's voice run one more time — *legal pad, two pens, no weapon, coffee she doesn't finish* — and this time they heard what they'd been too busy to hear.

"You don't count a person's pens from across the street," Noor said quietly. "That's a desk. That's a newsroom. That's somebody I've said hello to." The cold walked up their spine and they made it stop at the shoulders, out loud, on purpose: "Daylight problem. Goes in the file, not in my chest."

They sat back down and made the decision the way you tear off a bandage.

"New math. We're not waiting for 3:30. If his plane is still sitting on a ramp in Seattle, he's on this mountain between two and three — port stop first, then the climb. So we leave at 2:00. We roll to the gate in neutral, lights dead, engine off until we're past the tree line on the spur. They watched the road we came in on, because that's the only road a map knows. Nine miles of logging spur to the county road is where nobody's standing tonight. *Probably.* It's the best bad option we've got, and I've had worse."

Noor put the earbud back in, dragged the playhead to track 002, and ran it at double speed, hunting one word: *writer.* Ninety seconds in, the gravel voice surfaced out of the fast-forward squeal, and Noor slammed the speed back to normal to let it finish.

*"A reporter with a bad source is a weapon pointed where we want it. You don't disarm a weapon. You aim it."* And Renner, patient: *"And when it's spent?"* And the gravel voice, unhurried as ever: *"Weapons get melted down."*

Thirteen months ago. Noor stared at the waveform like it had a face.

"That's me," they said. "Thirteen months ago, I was already a line item." They flexed their fingers, cracked them once, and set the playhead moving again. "So: tail number, wheels-down, and whether that plane moves again tonight. Shell company names — every one, written down. And eyes on that window at 1:55 sharp, because at 2:00 we are two very boring people who were never here."

The coffee had gone cold in the cup. Noor drank it anyway.

"Thirty-eight tracks, seventy-five minutes. Talk to me. Wheels-down."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I'm scribbling furiously on a notepad, trying to keep up. I look up, holding the pen.* "Okay, tail number for Renner's jet: N747ER. It's still on the ground at Boeing Field in Seattle. No new flight plan filed." *I tap my pen on the pad.* "Shell companies... there's a lot. Most recent one is 'Pacific Rim Holdings.' Looks like a front for several smaller shipping ventures."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Pacific Rim Holdings." Noor said it out loud twice, tasting it, then wrote it in the notes file and starred it. "Hold that thought — Pacific Rim was the name of a terminal lease dispute in the Bellingham reporting. Buried in paragraph nineteen of the original story, the part everybody mocked. If Renner's newest shell is wearing a name from *my* retraction, that's not coincidence, that's arrogance. Or a message. Log it both ways."

But the tail number was the thing that made them stop writing.

"Still on the ground," they repeated. "No new flight plan." They looked at the laptop clock — 12:51 — and felt the math shift under their feet like a stair that isn't there. "Okay. Two readings, and they're not equal. Reading one: he landed, drove to the mountain, and the jet's just parked. Reading two—" they tapped the pen against the table, once, twice, "—he hasn't landed at *all* yet tonight. A manifest shows where a plane is, not whether it's finished. If that thing lifts off again before two, it might be coming *here* — a private strip, a county road, a flat stretch of anything. If it doesn't move, he's in a car at the bottom of my mountain right now, drinking bad coffee and waiting for a driveway report."

They let the silence sit for exactly three seconds.

"Either way, the answer doesn't change. It just means the window is the door now."

Noor stood, and for the first time all night did something that wasn't research: they got ready to leave. Boots laced tight. Jacket over the microSD. Phone, charger, burner, the chili can rinsed and set upside down on the rack — not tidiness, discipline, because a cabin that looked evacuated invited a walkthrough and a cabin that looked lived-in bought minutes of doubt. They killed the kitchen light, kept the laptop's screen glow low, and pulled the curtain back an inch at the corner — a pre-set viewing slit instead of a last-second flinch.

"New job list," they said, fast and even. "One: watch that tail number until the second we walk out the door. If N747ER files a new plan — *any* plan, even a hop to Tacoma — you say 'airborne' and nothing else, and we leave five minutes early. Two: keep pulling on Pacific Rim. I want directors' names, registered agent, anything that ties it to a human being. Shells have owners; owners have neighbors; neighbors talk." They crouched by the couch, checked their watch against the laptop clock, synchronized. "Three: at 1:55 you're off the phone, phone's off — not silent, *off*, battery out if it comes out — and you're by the door."

Noor shouldered the bag and stood there a moment in the half-dark, looking at the curtain slit, at the darker shade of dark past it. Kestrel, somewhere, alive or not. A cabin they'd never see again. A story that had just changed species — from exposé to survival — and would have to change back before anyone would print it.

"Track 041, her note, the pens, the coffee she doesn't finish," Noor said quietly, half to Driver, half to the room. "They've been reading me for months and they still got one thing wrong. They thought I'd come alone." A short breath that was almost a laugh. "You're the one variable in their math, and I intend to spend you carefully. Drive in, drive out. That's the whole job."

They sat back down at the laptop for the last hour anyway — because seventy-five minutes of audio was still seventy-five minutes, and because their hands needed work or they'd start thinking about Kestrel's hands instead.

"Track 002, double speed. Talk to me when Pacific Rim coughs up a name." The playhead moved. "And don't let me miss 1:55. On this mountain tonight, clocks are the only friend I've got."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The next hour Noor spent the way they'd spent every big story of their life — double speed, sample, scrub, log — building the gravel voice a card of his own in the notes file: *unnamed. Always Pier 9. Senior — Renner defers on numbers. Corrects tonnage from memory.* A lifer. Thirty years of signing for ships, and he had never once let a name fall into Kestrel's pocket microphone.

Track 016 was April, and it was Bellingham.

*"She retracted her own story,"* the gravel voice said, and there was something almost like pleasure in it — the first emotion Noor had heard out of him. *"Cost us a lawyer's Saturday."* Renner: *"And the editor?"* Gravel: *"Was paid to be useful. You don't buy reporters. Reporters are believers with bylines. You buy whoever stands behind them."*

Noor sat with that for a long moment, the laptop fan the only sound in the cabin. Then they typed it into the file and not the chest: *Somebody stands behind me too. Write down who knew about this cabin. Sit with it on the far side of tonight.*

Track 017 gave up a gift. Late May, dockside: *"The Pacific Rim paper is the cleanest thing we own — that's what we bought it for. The old hulls go under it by June, and after June nobody can prove which company touched what."* A pause, then: *"Voss handles the paper. Anyone asks, you talk to Voss."*

"Voss," Noor said, not turning around. "New search. Voss and Pacific Rim — might be a first name, might be a last, might be either with a bank behind it. No logins, nothing with your name on it. And whatever else you've got, tell me in the truck, because there's a clock on this now: everything prints before June, or the ghosts change their sheets and I'm holding nine minutes of two men being evil in the rain."

Track 023 was Kestrel herself, a whisper aimed into her own pocket between meetings, and it was the closest thing to a letter Noor would ever get: *"If you got this far, count backward. He prints a mistake into every set — the mistake tells him which copy, which courier, which friend. He thinks the errors are a leash. They're a map. Don't print the manifests. Print the differences."*

Noor stopped the playback. Played it again. Started laughing, quietly, horribly, into their fist.

"He built a tracker into the bait," they said to the dark window. "But a tracker reads in both directions. You can't poison twelve sets of paper without signing twelve names. He handed us the org chart and dared us to print the wrong half." They wrote it in capitals and underlined it: *PRINT THE DIFFERENCES.* Then they checked the clock — 1:41 — and started closing the cabin down. Laptop bagged. Lantern out. Curtain slit pre-set at an inch. 1:44.

At 1:47, the bend lit up.

Noor's whole body arrived before their thoughts did. Headlights, swinging slow off the curve — forty seconds, the warning they'd memorized — and the vehicle was wrong immediately. Boxy. Dark. Riding high. Not a Tacoma. It rolled to a stop perhaps a hundred yards short of the gate, beams raking the lower trees, and flashed its highs twice.

Hope arrived whole and immediate, the body's oldest reflex, and Noor put it down like something hot.

Two flashes. A long pause. Two more.

"Okay," Noor breathed, thinking out loud because thinking silently took too long. "It's either her in a borrowed car, or it's whoever emptied her pockets — and the signal stopped meaning anything the second it could be taken off her body. She knew that. She builds everything with a mouth and a lock. If she wanted to say *it's me*, she would not use the front door." Their hand found the curtain edge and held it still. "The gate stays shut. That's the only unforgivable mistake on the menu tonight. If it's her, opening it takes us both. If it's them, opening it is the trap sprung."

No sound of doors. Just an idling engine, and the beams sitting there like a held breath. Noor turned from the window, already moving. "Phone — off, battery out, in the bag, now. We're out the back. We push the car to the tree line in neutral, engine dead, then the track behind the woodshed, lights dark until the spur bends north. A car gets forty seconds of warning down there. A man on foot gets none — so if we hear a door, we drop the car and run."

The highs flashed a third time — shorter, sharper, an order this time — and then the low beams came back on, and the engine note deepened as the vehicle began to creep up the driveway.

"That's not patience anymore." Noor eased the back door open onto cold air and black trees, and held it. "Go."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I don't argue, just scramble to pull the battery out of my phone, shoving it into my pocket as I follow Noor out the back door.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The dark outside the door was a wall. Noor let the latch take the door's weight without a click and stood still for three seconds, letting their ears take over for their eyes.

The woodshed was a blacker square against the black, forty feet out. The tree line beyond it. The car somewhere left of that, where it had been parked on arrival — and Noor whispered the route over their shoulder, barely shaping the words: "Woodshed, then the car. After that we talk with hands."

At the car, they did the two things that mattered: shifter to neutral, driver's door eased open a inch at a time. The dome light stayed dead — someone had thought about that once, on some other night when it mattered — and Noor filed the small warm fact of it away and put a shoulder into the A-pillar.

The car walked along its wheels slow as syrup, steering through the open door by touch. Gravel gave under the tires in the softest possible voice. Twenty feet. Thirty. Up at the front of the property, the arriving engine settled into idle. It had reached the gate.

Then the chain — the flat rattle of a padlock being tested, carrying across the cold like it had been amplified.

Noor pushed harder. Forty feet, the first trunks standing around them like pillars—

The chunk of a vehicle door. Small. Enormous.

The rule was the rule, and Noor had made it forty minutes ago precisely so this second would contain no argument. Keys out of the ignition, into a pocket, bag strap already cinched short. They left the car standing open-mouthed at the tree line and ran — low, along the woodshed's shadow, then up into the trees where the needle duff took their boots without a sound.

Behind them a voice carried, one word, indistinct. Then light: a bloom of flashlight washing through the trunks, painting the cabin wall in slats. Noor dropped behind a deadfall, drew a breath, and held still while the beam crawled the length of the building, found the car at the tree line, and stopped on it. Voices changed register down there — quieter, then one sharp and imperative. The cabin that looked lived-in and the car that looked parked had just bought them a search that started at a locked door.

Noor moved on the beam's turn. The old skid trail climbed northwest — they navigated by bearing and ankle, counting paces in hundreds, the microSD a hard little truth riding against their ribs. At a blowdown they stopped and listened. Below, an engine idled, then died, and the silence it left was worse than the sound. Nobody leaves an engine running when the work is done. The work wasn't done. It was starting.

They found Driver's sleeve in the dark and pulled once, gently, to orient.

"New rules," Noor breathed, mouth close, voice pitched under the wind. "Step where I step. If I squeeze your arm — stop. Twice — get down. If we're separated: the spur runs northwest, then bends north. Follow it downhill to the county road and walk the ditch line, off it before first light. Sunrise is 7:12. That's not a suggestion, that's math." A breath. "If those two flashes at the gate were her, she'll have read a dark cabin and an empty drive by now and be miles gone — she didn't build all those locks to use a front door. File it. Don't carry it."

Behind and below, faint but unmistakable, came the sound of the cabin door giving way — not opening. Giving.

Noor was already moving. "Don't look back. Count my steps — at five hundred, we stop and listen to what's behind us."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, following close behind Noor, focusing on each step.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Two hundred paces in, Noor's world narrowed to rhythm: duff underfoot, breath through the nose, the car keys pressed flat inside a fist so they couldn't sing. At three hundred, sound came up the hill behind them — a vehicle door, a voice pitched to carry — and Noor knew without looking that the car at the tree line had stopped being a decoy and become a confession. *Two people, on foot, minutes ahead.* The woods would say it for them.

At five hundred, Noor squeezed Driver's arm — *stop* — and folded down behind a deadfall and made themselves do nothing but listen.

The cabin below had become a small industry. A second engine idled under the first, a radio squawked, and then came the thing Noor had been refusing to hear: a dog. One bark, high and delighted, and under it the jingle of a lead and a man's voice doing the low, eager talk of a handler whose animal had just been given a job.

"Okay," Noor breathed. "That changes the math. A dog doesn't care how many minutes we're ahead. A dog reads the ground itself." They licked a finger and held it up — wind moving upslope at their backs, carrying their scent *away*, which bought time and nothing more. "Water. It's always water."

They moved forty feet sideways to where the skid trail brushed a rock outcrop, and looked back down through the trunks.

Beams at the cabin. Men between the buildings, unhurried, methodical. And a voice rising through the cold still air in pieces — calm, patient as arithmetic — and Noor's skin knew it before their brain caught up. Nine minutes of recordings. A deposition watched at quarter speed. Renner. *Here.* On the mountain, holding the flashlight himself.

*"...if it's the writer, she'll run for water. Put the dog on the creek. Don't give her the easy crossings."*

Noor did the timeline against their will. Wheels-down in Seattle, 9:40. To be standing here by two, he'd left by eleven — not for anything he could delegate.

"He flew in to watch a handoff and stayed to walk a dog," Noor whispered. "That's not cleanup. That's *investment.* Which means the audio is worth more than I priced it." They scanned the gate once, twice. No gray truck anywhere in the beams. Either Kestrel was still breathing somewhere out in the dark, or her truck was already at the bottom of some pond, and both of those were true until one of them wasn't. File it. Noor was beginning to understand that some files don't close.

Mouth to Driver's ear, barely shaped: "He owns the crossings he can guess. So we cross where the water braids — forty yards of shallow rock — and we come out on the *upstream* side of anywhere a handler would stage. Then the spur's rocky spine. Stone keeps no prints." Noor checked their watch. 2:04. "And the math is ugly now: nine miles on this trail at night is five, six hours — dawn catches us a mile short. So we don't ride it to the end. Mile seven there's a fork on the map, and a drainage that drops to the county road early. We come out in the dark *on purpose.* Five in the morning that road runs log trucks. Two hikers, wrong turn, dead battery. Boring is camouflage. And at 7:12 I want trees over us, not sky — because first light on a mountain like this means eyes, and not all of them blink."

They found the creek at the mile mark, a black ribbon chattering over stone, and crossed it where it spread thin and braided, cold closing around their ankles like a vise. On the far bank, climbing back into the trees, Noor finally paid the toll they'd been refusing all night.

"The two flashes," they said quietly. "If that was her — borrowed car, front door, everything she taught me not to do — then she's alive and she's watching the only door she ever leaves open. The dead drop." A breath. "At the county road, the burner comes out of the faraday bag, and I put one line in the inbox: *the numbers float.* Her quote, inverted. Renner reads nonsense. Kestrel reads *me.* Then one more word — *eleven* — so she knows the audio made it out. Nothing logistical. You never put logistics in a first contact." Their jaw tightened. "If the drop's empty by noon, I stop being a reporter and become somebody's source. There are people whose entire job is catching me when I fall. I've spent six years avoiding their card." 

Noor stood out of the crouch and gave the trail back its darkness.

"You're the metronome now. Count to a thousand, whisper the hundreds — one word each. And if you hear water before I do, squeeze my arm." They started walking. "She said I listen better than I think I do. Tonight we find out if it's contagious."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, focusing on the counting. My breath comes out in small puffs in the cold air.* "One hundred."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The whispered hundreds kept arriving, steady as a pulse, and Noor ran a silent count alongside them — because a clock you can't verify is a clock you can't trust, and tonight Noor trusted nothing they couldn't check twice.

The wet from the crossing had settled into their boots and signed a lease. At the next blowdown Noor pressed their palms flat against cold stone and held them there until the shaking stopped — the last hour coming due in installments, and Noor paying it in private, the way you pay anything that would worry the help.

Past the blowdown, the dog spoke.

One bark, down at the creek — then a string of them, high and fast, the sound of an animal that had found something and wanted the world to know about it. Noor squeezed twice — *down* — and folded behind a deadfall with their ear to the open air. A flashlight washed the trunks below. The handler's voice, low and encouraging. And then, floating up over the water, patient as arithmetic, Renner.

"Cast him back to the car. The car is where the story starts. Feet are honest — give him the feet and he'll do the rest." A pause. The dog's voice cracked, went wrong, started casting. "And nobody goes up that spur ahead of me. We walk at the dog's speed. We have until the light. She doesn't — by seven she's a silhouette on a ridgeline, and I've got men who know how to read a silhouette."

Noor lay against the cold stone and felt the recognition move through them like a drafts through a room. Same math. Same sunrise. He was up there doing Noor's equation with a flashlight and a dog, and he'd gotten the same answer: *7:12.*

"He's running my homework," Noor breathed. "Which means 7:12 isn't a deadline anymore. It's his deadline too — and he's got a dog to enforce it." Below, the barking lost its certainty, scattered, turned in circles. The handler said something short. "The braid held. He can't pick a line out of forty yards of shallow water." Noor filed the win where wins went tonight — noted, not savored — because the animal would restart at the car, and the scent trail into the woods was an hour old and legible to anything with a nose. "The braid bought confusion. The spine buys silence. Move."

The skid trail climbed onto bare rock, and stone took their footsteps and gave nothing back. Noor licked a finger and held it up. The upslope breeze had gone soft. Going lazy. Dying the way mountain wind dies before dawn.

"That's the next clock," they said, mouth close to Driver's ear. "Wind dies, and the dog gets a map of everything we've touched since the creek. So the fork at mile seven stops being a plan and becomes a schedule. Road by five, before the wind quits and the net settles."

Through a gap in the trees ahead and left, faint, an engine — running slow, stopping, coming back. A pattern.

"Hear that? County road. Either the county works nights, or that's the first strand of his net on the asphalt. Doesn't matter which — I plan for hostile." Noor's jaw set. "We cross at the curve past the fork, where a slow car's headlights outrun their own beams, and we walk east, away from the junction he's watching. I'll solve the last hundred yards when I can see it. You can't out-think a road from a mountaintop."

They dug into the jacket pocket and came out with a peanut bar, tore it down the seam in the dark, and pressed half into Driver's hand without ceremony.

"You told me to eat something. We're even." A breath that was almost a laugh. "And you haven't asked one question since the gate. Most people's fear talks. Yours is doing math. Keep doing it."

Noor stood, checked the watch — 2:19 — and gave the trail back its darkness.

"When you hit a thousand, whisper *time*, and we stop and listen with everything we've got. And somewhere in the next five hundred — you had two hours on Pacific Rim before that battery came out. Did Voss surface? A first name, a firm, a registered agent, anything. It's the last name in her recordings I don't have a face for." They started walking. "Nine hundred to go. Spend them talking. I'll spend them listening — she said I was good at it. Tonight we find out."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I chew on the peanut bar, grateful for the calories.* "Yeah, Voss did surface. Julian Voss. He's listed as the registered agent for Pacific Rim Holdings. Also, he's a lawyer, specializing in maritime law. Based out of Seattle." *I whisper the details, trying to keep my voice low and steady.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor did not answer at first. The window held only their own face—pale, too alert, eyes red-rimmed from coffee and three hours of waiting. When they finally turned, their hands stayed clenched around the mug.

“I will,” Noor said. “After I know whether the source is alive.”

They crossed to the cabinet and found the food they’d already looked at twice: a sleeve of crackers, a jar of peanut butter, a spoon with the handle cracked. Noor ate four bites without tasting any of them, then set the spoon down and sat at the table. The laptop screen was dark. They woke it, typed the password, and connected the burner phone through a USB cable.

The phone records opened in a clean white window. Noor scrolled to the last twenty-four hours. The source’s number had called once at 8:56 p.m. and again at 9:04. The second call had lasted thirty-one seconds. Noor had answered. They remembered the silence, the faint sound of a car passing, then a click.

They replayed the missed-call log. No voicemail. No follow-up text.

Noor copied the timestamps into a spreadsheet, then opened the source’s last email. The message contained the expected file manifest for the encrypted drive and a single line: Don’t trust any meeting after 8:30. If I’m late, assume the cabin is already burned.

Noor’s thumb hovered over the trackpad.

“Assume,” they muttered.

They pulled the padded case closer, unzipped it, and lifted out the drive. It was heavier than it looked. Noor plugged it into the laptop and let the mounting dialog appear. They did not type the decryption password yet. First, they ran a checksum on the visible container file and compared the result to the hash in the source’s email.

It matched.

For a second, relief moved through them so sharply it hurt. The files were intact. Whatever was on the drive had not been tampered with.

Then Noor noticed the drive’s last access time.

The drive had been mounted once before. Not here. The log entry was timestamped 8:59 p.m. from a device name the source had used in the field: WIRE-4.

Noor’s breath stopped.

They opened the terminal and typed a command to list the drive’s hidden partitions. A folder appeared under a name the source had never used: SAFEHOUSE. Noor’s own name. Noor’s address. Noor’s editor’s name. The folder had been created at 9:07 p.m., three minutes after the source’s last call.

Noor closed the terminal window. Opened it again. The folder remained.

They looked down at their hands, steady now in the awful way fear made them steady. Noor pulled a notepad from the drawer and wrote three lines in block letters: DRIVE VERIFIED. SOURCE LATE. DRIVE NOT UNLOCKED. Then they wrote a fourth: CABIN MAY BE HOT.

Noor slid the laptop toward themselves, inserted the USB key that held the second backup password, and began copying the encrypted container to an external drive. Not the contents. The whole thing. If the source was dead, the password would die with them. If the source was captured, Noor would not let anyone take the evidence without a fight.

The progress bar crawled.

Noor picked up the phone they’d been avoiding for three hours and dialed the one number they had sworn not to use from this cabin. It rang once. Twice. Three times. Voicemail clicked on.

“This is Noor,” they said, voice low. “If I don’t call back by six, send the preliminary to the paper and tell them the cabin story is real.”

They hung up before the machine could ask for a callback number.

The drive copied with a soft notification. Noor ejected it, slipped it into their jacket, and zipped the padded case until the sound was a hard line. Then they stood, took another cracker from the cabinet, and ate it standing at the table like a soldier saving time.

“I’m going to check the perimeter,” Noor said, not looking away from the window. “If I’m not back in five minutes, grab the laptop and don’t wait for me.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look up from my phone, hearing the sudden change in Noor's voice.* "Whoa, hold on. Perimeter? What are you even talking about?" *I slowly put my phone down, a knot forming in my stomach.* "Noor, what's going on?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor stopped with one hand on the door. For a breath, they looked as if the fear might crack them open, but the exhaustion had hardened it into something practical instead.

“The drive was mounted at 8:59,” Noor said. “By a field computer the source used in the valley. At 9:07, after the source called me, a folder appeared on it. My name. My apartment. The editor’s name. This cabin’s address.” They said the last part quietly, as if the room itself might be listening. “Either the source knew where we were and didn’t tell me, or someone used their rig to say hello.”

Noor crossed to the cabinet and took out the flashlight, then a roll of duct tape from under the sink. They tested the light with their thumb.

“I’m going out the front. I’m not going all the way to the road. If there’s a car there, it’s waiting for someone to do exactly that.” They glanced toward the couch, and something in their face shifted. “I’m sorry I didn’t tell you this was possible before I asked you to drive me.”

Noor opened the door.

Outside, the cold was a clean, brutal thing. Noor kept the flashlight off and used the phone’s screen glow only when necessary, angling it down at the porch boards. The snow had stopped, but a thin wet layer had frozen over the steps. Near the porch rail, Noor found a boot print. It came from the road side, not from the cabin, and it stopped with the toe pointed at the window above the kitchen sink.

Noor looked up.

The window was open half an inch.

They remembered closing it. Noor’s chest tightened. They went to the side of the cabin, stepping around the back porch, and crouched beside the truck. The bed was empty. The gas cap was shut. Under the rear axle, a small black rectangle blinked red every few seconds.

Noor stared at it until their eyes burned.

A tracker. Not a professional one—magnetic, cheap, meant to be found by someone who didn’t expect to be looked for. Noor took a photo with the phone, then another with the flashlight covered by a finger so the lens wouldn’t flare. They pried it off with a pocketknife found in the jacket. The device came away with a strip of black rubber and a smear of grease. Noor dropped it into the coffee can they’d carried out, then taped the lid with two passes of duct tape. It wasn’t a Faraday cage. It was better than nothing.

Back on the porch, Noor saw the boot print had been joined by a second one. Someone had come close enough to touch the door handle. Noor took the handle in their sleeve and turned it. It was unlocked. They had locked it.

Noor stepped inside and closed the door so fast the latch slammed.

They set the coffee can on the table and looked at Driver.

“We’re leaving,” Noor said. “Right now. Not down the main road first—the logging track behind the cabin. If they’ve got someone watching the highway, they’ll see headlights coming out and think we’re stupid.” They grabbed the padded case, the laptop bag, the jacket. They shoved the jar of peanut butter into the bag without thinking, then put the cracker sleeve on top. “If someone knocks while we’re loading the truck, don’t answer it. If I’m not outside in ninety seconds, drive to the fire hall in town and leave me here.”

Noor went to the hook by the door, took the cabin keys, then stopped. The safehouse looked suddenly like a trap that had already been set. They pulled the curtains wider, checked the hallway closet, and found a heavy iron poker beside a stack of firewood. Noor took it, turned off the kitchen light, and opened the side door.

The truck started on the first turn of the key. Noor climbed into the driver’s side, put the coffee can on the passenger floor, and watched the mirrors.

“Get in,” Noor said, voice low. “We’re going to the fire hall. They’ve got cameras, radios, and a dispatcher who owes my sister a favor. We’ll call from there.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stare at Noor, my mind racing to catch up. I grab my phone, keys, and wallet automatically, shoving them into my pockets.* "Okay, okay, I'm coming!" *I scramble off the couch, grabbing the laptop bag and following Noor out the side door, my heart pounding.* "Fire hall it is. Just... tell me what's actually happening on the way, okay?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor got into the cab and shut the door with their shoulder. The coffee can sat on the passenger floor, ticking faintly as it cooled. Noor’s hands were cold, steady, and angry enough to keep them useful.

“Yes,” Noor said. “What’s happening is that someone used the source’s field computer to put our names on a drive before the source ever reached me. Then they put a tracker under the truck and left the cabin door unlocked while I was outside looking at it.”

They put the truck in gear. The engine turned over once, settled into an idle that sounded too loud in the dark. Noor kept the headlights off for the first turn, letting the snow do enough work to show the logging track.

“I’m sorry,” Noor said, not looking away from the mirrors. “I didn’t know the tracker was there when I asked you to drive me. I didn’t know the drive was already marked.”

The cabin disappeared behind the trees. Noor drove slowly, one hand at the top of the wheel, the other resting near the padded case on the bench. The external backup drive was inside it, holding a copy of the encrypted container. Noor had not opened the container. Not yet.

“Here’s the short version,” Noor said. “The source called me twice. The second call was thirty-one seconds long. At 8:59, a folder with my name, my apartment, and this cabin’s address appeared on the drive from the source’s field computer. At 9:07, the folder was created. Either the source wanted me to find it, or someone wanted me to think they could get to me before I got to the story.”

Noor’s thumb pressed hard against the wheel.

“And either way, someone else knows we’re here.”

The phone Noor had avoided for three hours buzzed in their jacket pocket. Noor pulled it out. The screen lit the cab pale blue. The caller ID said the source’s number.

Noor did not answer. They put the phone on speaker, let it ring once, then tapped it off. A text came through.

WIRE-4 WAS TAKEN. DON’T GO TO FIRE HALL.

Noor read it twice. Their jaw tightened.

They typed: Who is this?

The phone stayed silent. Noor’s breath fogged the window for a second before the cold outside swallowed it. They typed: What did you call the minister’s driver?

Three dots appeared. Stopped. Appeared again.

The reply came through: The ghost.

Noor closed their eyes for one second. “It’s them,” they said aloud, though they did not know if it proved anything. “Or someone who knows them well enough to hurt me by sounding like them.”

They typed: Where are you?

RANGER STATION MILE 7. ALONE. DRIVE IS BAIT.

Noor stared at the word bait.

They typed: If it’s bait, how do I know you’re not?

A long pause. The truck idled under them. Noor’s pulse beat in their wrists, in their throat, in the small painful places behind their eyes.

Then: You don’t. Meet at trailhead. No lights. If I see one more car, I’m gone.

Noor looked at the screen until the backlight faded. “Bait,” they muttered. “Of course it’s bait.”

They turned the phone off, then opened the coffee can and dropped it inside on top of the tracker. They taped the lid again, two hard passes of duct tape, then set the can on the bench beside the padded case.

“I’m not using this phone again until I know it isn’t a beacon,” Noor said. “And I’m not going straight to the ranger station.”

Noor pulled onto a wider logging road and killed the engine. The sudden silence was worse than the heater. Noor sat still for a full minute, watching the mirrors.

“If anyone followed us out of the cabin, they’ll think we’re stupid,” Noor said. “Let them. Stupid people live longer.”

They got out with the flashlight and the iron poker. Noor walked the rear of the truck first, checking the axle, the spare tire, the fuel line. Nothing new. Noor checked the cab, lifting the floor mats, looking under the seats, feeling along the door panels. No second tracker, but Noor did not trust the absence. They opened the padded case and ran their fingers over the seams, the zipper pull, the strap. Nothing. Still, they took the external backup drive out, put it in their jacket pocket, and zipped the padded case shut.

Back at the culvert beside the road, Noor set the coffee can in the dark water at the edge and weighted it with a stone. The phone was inside, dead now for the next few hours. Noor photographed the culvert anyway, then returned to the truck.

They climbed in, hands stiff. The peanut butter jar and cracker sleeve were still in the bag. Noor ate a spoonful of peanut butter straight, then a cracker, then wiped the spoon on their jeans. The sugar hit the hollow in their stomach and made the fear sharper, more honest.

“The source says the drive is bait,” Noor said. “That means the checksum matching doesn’t matter. They could have built a perfect container with our names in it and let me find it. If I open it, I’m walking into whatever they expect.”

Noor folded the map they had written on, tucked it into the jacket pocket, and started the engine again.

“Sleep can wait,” Noor said, almost to themselves. “Names can’t.”

They drove back toward the cabin first, then took the reservoir road in the opposite direction. Noor checked the mirrors every few seconds, counting the distance between the truck and the dark behind it. If headlights appeared, Noor would know. If nothing appeared, Noor would still know that silence could be a trap.

“If we get pulled over, we’re checking a hunting cabin for my uncle,” Noor said. “If the fire hall is dark, we don’t stop. If there’s a car at the trailhead, we don’t stop. We go to the gas station on the highway and I’ll find a landline there.”

Noor turned off the headlights once the trees closed in. The snow gave enough light to see the ruts, the edges of the road, the black shapes of pines leaning over the track. Noor’s hands stayed at ten and two.

“I’m going to meet the source,” Noor said. “But not inside. I’ll go to the trailhead with the truck. You stay with the truck. I don’t want a witness in the middle of this, and I don’t want the source to have a reason to run.”

Noor’s voice dropped.

“If someone touches me out there, I’m taking the poker. If the source lies to me, I’m taking the drive and leaving. Either way, the story doesn’t die tonight.”

They drove by the snow’s faint reflection, counting turns, checking mirrors, listening to the heater tick and the tires bite into ice. The source’s text still sat in the dead phone inside the coffee can: DRIVE IS BAIT.

Noor did not know whether to believe it.

They believed the boot print. They believed the folder. They believed the open window, the unlocked door, the tracker under the axle. They believed the fear that had gone through them when the terminal window had closed and reopened and the SAFEHOUSE folder had still been there.

At the first junction, Noor stopped and waited. Nothing came. No headlights. No engine. No sound except the wind moving through the trees and the small crack of cold metal ticking under the hood.

Noor turned toward the ranger station.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor let the truck roll without headlights, the snow throwing back just enough light to show the ruts. The cab smelled like wet wool, cold metal, and the peanut butter Noor had eaten too fast.

“On the way,” Noor said. “But you’re staying with the truck. That’s the way.”

They checked the mirrors. The logging track behind them was black and empty. Ahead, the trees leaned in like they were waiting for a decision.

“What’s happening is that I have a drive that says my name,” Noor said. “A drive that was mounted by my source’s field computer before my source ever reached me. A drive with a folder created after the source’s last call. My name. This cabin’s address. The editor’s name. If that was bait, it worked for three minutes. I believed the evidence was safe.”

Noor’s thumb rubbed a groove in the steering wheel.

“Then a text came in saying the drive is bait. That means either the source knows it’s bait, or someone is pretending to be the source. I don’t have a way to tell which yet.”

They turned the wheel slightly, keeping the truck on the softer side of the road.

“I’m sorry,” Noor said quietly. “I should have told you this could be more than late. I should have told you that if a drive says your name, it means someone looked at your name and thought you were useful.”

Noor pulled into a turnout where a fallen pine made a natural barrier between the truck and the road. They killed the engine. The silence came back too fast.

“Stay in the cab,” Noor said. “If you see headlights, do not flash them. Do not get out. Count them.”

Noor took the padded case from the bench and laid it across their knees. The laptop was in the bag. They opened it with the screen dimmed low, then plugged the original drive into a USB port fitted with a read-only blocker. Noor had carried it for months. It had saved Noor from one disaster already.

They did not type the decryption password.

Instead, Noor opened the file-system tool and mounted the visible container. The SAFEHOUSE folder sat there like a handprint on glass. Noor expanded it.

Inside were four names:

NOOR  
DRIVER  
EDITOR  
CABIN

The files were not encrypted yet. They were placeholders. Dead drops. A message written in file names.

Noor stared at DRIVER.

The cabin was too cold for the sting in Noor’s eyes, but they blinked anyway.

“They put you on it,” Noor said, almost to themselves.

Noor opened the terminal and ran a metadata check. The folder had been created at 9:07. The DRIVER file had been modified at 9:12. The CABIN file had been modified at 9:18.

Someone had been editing after the source’s last call.

Noor closed the laptop.

For a moment, they sat with the iron poker across their lap and breathed. Then they reached into the bag, found the jar of peanut butter, and used the cracked spoon to take a hard bite. It coated Noor’s teeth and made the fear more physical. Noor ate it anyway.

“Sleep later,” Noor muttered. “Names now.”

They slid the drive back into the padded case, zipped it, and placed it on the floorboard under the bench seat. Then Noor took the external backup drive from their jacket pocket and held it for a second, weighing it. It was lighter than the original, but heavier than a person should have to carry.

Noor started the truck.

“We’re not going to the trailhead yet,” they said. “We’re going to the highway. There’s a gas station with a payphone. If the source is alive, I can call them. If someone is using their number, the call will prove it.”

Noor pulled the truck back onto the logging road and drove slow enough to feel every bump through the seat. They took the reservoir road first, then swung wide through a cut where the pines opened onto a service lane. Noor checked the mirrors so often the motion became a tic.

When the gas station appeared, the lights were buzzing and half the pumps were dark. Noor parked at the far edge, under the sign, where the camera angle would miss the cab.

“Stay with the truck,” Noor said. “If I’m not back by the time the dome light goes dark, drive to the fire hall. Do not stop for me.”

Noor took the burner phone out of the padded case anyway, even though it had been sunk in a culvert. Noor had not taken it out. They had put the old phone in the coffee can. This was a different phone, a cheap one with no contacts, used only once. Noor powered it off, removed the battery, and left it on the seat.

Inside the gas station, the bell over the door sounded obscene.

The clerk looked up, startled, then looked away again. Noor did not go near the counter. The payphone sat by the door, old and gray, its cord curling into the base. Noor checked the receiver for tape, checked the keypad for a raised plastic film, checked the little glass window where coins should have been visible.

Noor dialed the source’s number.

It rang once.

Twice.

Three times.

The line clicked.

“You used the cabin,” Noor said.

The voice on the other end was not the source’s normal voice. It was thinner, scraped raw, with the edge of wind behind it.

“I didn’t send that text,” the source said.

Noor’s grip tightened on the receiver.

“Then who did?”

“The person who has WIRE-4.”

Noor closed their eyes. The payphone cord creaked.

“You’re alive.”

“Barely.”

“Where?”

“Not where you’re going to look.”

Noor looked through the glass at the dark beyond the pumps. “You told me the drive is bait.”

“I told you the drive is bait,” the source said. “Because it is. But the bait isn’t what’s on it. It’s what you’ll do when you see the folder.”

“Why?”

“Because the folder proves someone knows where you are.”

Noor’s jaw worked. “It also has the driver’s name.”

The source went quiet.

“Noor,” they said finally. “If your driver’s name is on that folder, you cannot take them to the fire hall.”

Noor’s stomach moved.

“Why not?”

“Because the fire hall is not the only place with cameras.”

Noor looked at the truck. The dome light was off. The cab was dark.

“Who has WIRE-4?” Noor asked.

“I don’t know. They took it in the valley. They used my computer to make the folder. They knew you’d verify the checksum. They knew you’d check timestamps. They wanted you to find it.”

“Why?”

“Because if you find it, you’ll bring the drive to someone you trust.”

Noor’s voice dropped. “The editor.”

“Yes.”

The payphone hummed in Noor’s hand.

“You think the editor is involved?”

“I think someone put his name on the folder because they know he is the person you will call first.”

Noor looked at the clerk, who had gone back to something under the counter. The fluorescent lights made everything look washed out, like a bad copy.

“Why did you call the minister’s driver?” Noor asked.

A long pause.

“The ghost,” the source said.

Noor exhaled. “That doesn’t prove anything.”

“What does?”

“You told me the second call lasted thirty-one seconds. I remember it. You said nothing. There was a car passing.”

“I was in a car.”

“You were in a car at nine-fourteen?”

“I was in a car at nine-fourteen,” the source said. “I told you not to trust any meeting after eight-thirty.”

Noor’s hand hurt from holding the receiver too hard.

“Why did the text say trailhead?”

“I didn’t send it.”

“Then who?”

“The person who has the phone.”

Noor looked at the dark road. If the source’s phone had been cloned, or if someone had taken the phone and learned the number, they could have sent the text. But why lead Noor away from the fire hall? Why warn against the trailhead?

“Where are you?” Noor asked.

“Not the trailhead.”

“Then where?”

“Spillway road. The old culvert under the reservoir bridge. If you come, no lights. If you bring anyone, I’m gone.”

Noor’s eyes moved to the truck again.

“I’m alone,” Noor said.

The source made a sound like disbelief. “You’re never alone.”

“I’m alone,” Noor repeated. “Answer one more question and I’ll believe you’re the source.”

“Ask.”

“What did you say when the manifest didn’t match the minister’s schedule?”

Silence.

Noor could hear the source’s breath.

“I said,” the source answered slowly, “that the files were too clean. That someone had scrubbed the meeting before it happened.”

Noor closed their eyes.

That was it. That was the line Noor had never typed into any note.

“Where exactly?” Noor asked.

“Spillway road. The culvert. If you see a white truck, it’s not me.”

“What truck?”

“The one that took WIRE-4.”

Noor hung up.

They stood at the payphone for two full seconds, then dialed the source’s number again. It rang once and went to voicemail. Noor did not leave a message. They hung up, pulled a coin from their pocket, and dropped it into the payphone slot anyway, because the sound made them feel less watched.

Back in the truck, Noor put the phone battery back in the burner, powered it on, and turned off the Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and location. Then they put it inside a small metal pouch from the padded case and zipped the pouch.

“We’re going to the reservoir spillway,” Noor said. “Not the trailhead.”

They started the truck.

Noor took the logging road back the way they had come, then turned east instead of north, toward the water. The headlights were off again. Noor drove by the snow and the faint blue glow of the dashboard.

“If the source is lying, this is a trap,” Noor said. “If the source is telling the truth, the trailhead is already watched. Either way, we don’t go there.”

Noor checked the mirrors.

“Stay in the truck when we stop,” they said. “If I go out, you do not come after me. If I say to drive, you drive. If I don’t come back by one-fifteen, take the padded case from under the seat and go to the fire hall.”

The truck slowed.

Noor turned onto the spillway road. It was narrower than the logging track, with a steep bank on one side and a chain-link fence on the other. The reservoir lay dark beyond the trees, flat and hard in the cold.

At the old bridge, Noor stopped under a stand of pines. The engine idled for a second, then died.

Noor pulled the iron poker from behind the seat.

They looked at the truck cab, then at the padded case under the bench. The external backup drive was in Noor’s jacket pocket. The original drive was still in the case. Noor took it out and held it for a second. It was still heavy. It still said too many names.

Noor opened the door.

The cold hit immediately.

The spillway smelled like wet rock and rust. The bridge was a narrow concrete span over a culvert, the kind of place engineers built so water would forget it had ever been rain. Noor kept the flashlight off and used the snow light to see the road, the fence, the black mouth of the culvert.

Halfway to the bridge, Noor heard movement.

Noor stopped.

A figure stepped out from under the bridge, hands visible, palms empty. They wore a hood pulled low and a dark jacket, but Noor could see the tremor in the person’s shoulders.

“Don’t come closer,” Noor said.

The figure stopped.

“Noor,” the source said. “It’s me.”

Noor kept the poker raised. “Show your pockets.”

The source did, slowly. No tracker. No phone. No weapon that Noor could see.

“Where’s WIRE-4?” Noor asked.

“Gone.”

“Where is it?”

“I don’t know.”

Noor looked past the source, toward the dark road, the reservoir, the trees. “Who has your phone?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then why should I believe you?”

The source’s breath fogged. “Because I’m here. Because I told you the manifest line. Because if I wanted you dead, I would have left the trailhead where it was.”

Noor’s throat tightened.

“You put the driver’s name on the drive,” Noor said.

The source looked at the truck.

“No,” they said. “I didn’t.”

“Noor’s voice went flat. “Then who did?”

“Someone used my computer after I left it. I created the folder as a warning. I didn’t know your driver was there. I saw the truck from the ridge. I saw someone in the cab. I didn’t know it was you until the folder appeared.”

Noor’s hand ached around the poker.

“You saw the cabin.”

“I saw the cabin. I saw the truck. I saw the window.”

Noor’s mind snapped back to the half-open window above the kitchen sink.

“Which window?” Noor asked.

“The kitchen.”

Noor did not move.

“The window was open,” they said.

The source went very still.

“Not now,” the source said. “That was before.”

Noor’s breath came out hard.

“You watched the cabin.”

“I had to know you were safe.”

“You didn’t tell me.”

“I was late.”

Noor took one step closer, then stopped.

“Where are the files?” Noor asked.

The source reached into their jacket.

Noor lifted the poker.

The source froze.

“Slow,” Noor said.

The source withdrew a small waterproof pouch. Inside was a thumb drive, black, unmarked, and cold.

“Second copy,” the source said. “Manifest only. Names. Dates. Bank transfers. The minister’s driver. The ghost. The editor.”

Noor looked at the pouch.

“Why did you bring it here?”

“Because if I don’t, I’m not the source. I’m just another person who knows your name.”

Noor’s jaw tightened.

“Give it to me.”

The source set it on the wet concrete between them.

Noor did not pick it up. They looked at the source’s face under the hood. The source was older than Noor remembered, or maybe fear made everyone older. There was a cut along one brow, dried dark, and the source’s left hand kept trembling.

“You’re hurt,” Noor said.

“I’m fine.”

“You’re lying.”

“I’m alive.”

Noor finally bent and picked up the pouch with two fingers. They put it into their pocket without opening it.

“Walk to the truck,” Noor said.

The source did not move.

“No,” the source said. “I’m not getting in.”

Noor’s eyes narrowed.

“Why?”

“Because if your driver is in that truck, I can’t be seen with you.”

Noor looked back at the truck. The cab was dark. The dome light was off. Noor could not see whether anyone was inside.

Noor walked backward to the truck, keeping the poker visible. They opened the passenger door and climbed in.

Noor shut the door and looked at Driver.

“The source is alive,” Noor said. “But they won’t get in. They think you’re part of this.”

Noor pulled the padded case onto their lap and opened it just enough to show the encrypted drive inside.

“Here’s what we’re doing,” Noor said. “We’re not going to the fire hall. We’re not going to the trailhead. We’re going to the train yard behind the water treatment plant. My uncle used to park there. It’s open, it’s cold, and no one will expect two people in a truck at one in the morning.”

Noor started the engine.

The source appeared at the driver’s side window. Noor rolled the window down two inches.

“You said no lights,” Noor said.

“I said if you see one more car, I’m gone.”

Noor looked past the source.

“Then move,” Noor said. “Because I’m not waiting for someone else to arrive.”

The source moved to the passenger side. Noor rolled that window down two inches.

“Talk through the glass,” Noor said. “You do not open the door unless I tell you to.”

The source nodded.

Noor put the truck in gear.

They drove slowly down the spillway road, the source keeping pace beside the cab, one hand on the mirror housing, the other pressed over their mouth as if trying to keep the cold out. Noor watched the mirrors. The road behind remained dark.

When the reservoir opened into the service lane, Noor turned off the dome light and kept the headlights off as long as the snow allowed.

“You have the manifest?” Noor asked through the window.

“Yes.”

“Did you put my name on the drive?”

“No.”

“Did you put the editor’s name on the drive?”

The source hesitated.

“I put the editor’s name on the manifest,” they said. “Because he signed the transfer that moved the minister’s files.”

Noor’s hands tightened on the wheel.

“You said he was involved.”

“I said he was on the list.”

“Those are different words.”

“Not tonight.”

Noor drove.

The train yard appeared after the water treatment plant, a maze of rusted cars, gravel, and floodlights that buzzed at intervals. Noor pulled behind a stack of freight containers and stopped.

“Stay in the truck,” Noor said.

They got out.

The source was already there, breathing hard, eyes moving to the trees, the fence, the lights.

Noor did not take the poker away.

“Show me the manifest,” Noor said.

The source reached into their jacket again.

Noor’s pulse hammered.

The source withdrew a folded paper, not the thumb drive. They unfolded it with shaking hands. The paper was cold, damp at one corner.

Noor took it.

The first line was the minister’s name.

The second line was the minister’s driver.

The third line was the ghost.

The fourth line was Noor’s editor.

The fifth line was Driver.

Noor stared at it until the letters blurred.

The fear came back, not sharp and sudden this time, but slow and enormous, like water rising under a door.

Noor looked at the source.

“You knew.”

“I suspected,” the source said.

“No.” Noor’s voice went low. “You knew.”

The source did not answer.

Noor folded the paper and put it in their pocket.

“We’re not calling the editor,” Noor said. “We’re not going to the fire hall. We’re not going to the paper.”

The source looked up.

“Noor—”

“No.” Noor’s hands were steady again in that awful way. “If the editor’s name is on the manifest, the editor may be the leak. If the fire hall is where we were supposed to go, someone may be waiting there. If the trailhead was bait, the reservoir may be watched.”

Noor looked at the truck.

“I have one backup drive,” Noor said. “I have the original. I have a manifest that says everyone I trusted was already on a list. And I have three hours before the paper’s night desk closes and the story becomes impossible to kill.”

The source said, “Then we publish now.”

Noor looked at them.

“No,” Noor said. “We verify now.”

They turned and walked back to the truck.

Noor climbed in, pulled the padded case onto the seat, and took out the laptop. They connected the source’s thumb drive through a separate port, then ran the manifest against the file names from the encrypted container.

The names matched.

All of them.

Noor copied the manifest to the external backup. Then they opened the encrypted drive again and, for the first time, typed the decryption password.

The laptop whirred.

The container unlocked.

Inside were files: bank transfers, meeting logs, audio clips, a red folder labeled DRIVER, and a final document titled IF NOOR IS READING THIS.

Noor’s breath stopped.

They opened the document.

The first line read:

If you opened this, the drive was bait.

The second line read:

I’m sorry.

The third line read:

Check the cabin’s window.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I watch Noor's face, trying to figure out what's going on. They read something, and their face just... drops. I lean forward, a cold dread creeping up my spine.* "Noor? What is it? What did you find?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor’s eyes stayed on the screen for a second too long. When they looked at Driver, the answer came out too calm.

“It says check the cabin window.”

They turned the laptop so the screen faced away. Their thumb hovered over the trackpad, trembling once before it steadied.

“The source wrote it before the meeting. If I opened the drive, I was supposed to know it was bait. I was also supposed to know the fire hall is not safe.” Noor’s voice dropped. “There’s more. The folder with my name was created by WIRE-4. The source says they didn’t make the DRIVER file. They made a placeholder. They listed everyone at the cabin because they were scared of whoever took the field computer.”

Noor looked toward the two inches of open window.

The source stood in the cold with one hand pressed flat against the door, breath fogging the glass.

“Is that true?” Noor asked.

The source’s eyes moved past Noor, toward the passenger side. “True enough.”

“True enough isn’t the truth.”

Noor turned back to the laptop and typed a command to show the document’s properties.

Created 08:55. Modified 09:19. Author: WIRE-4.

The same machine that had made the folder.

Noor’s stomach tightened. Someone had edited after the source’s last call.

They opened the next line in the document.

The window was open because I opened it. I could not get in. I left the second manifest under the storm pane. If it is gone, the cabin is hot and you are not alone in the logging track. Do not go to the fire hall. The ghost has a sheriff’s badge and a key.

Noor read it twice.

“The source opened the window,” Noor said, voice low. “They left something. If it’s gone, someone was in the cabin after we left.”

Noor looked at the source through the glass.

“Why didn’t you say that at the payphone?”

The source pressed one hand to the window. “Because the line could have been recorded. Because I didn’t know if you were alone.”

“You weren’t supposed to be late.”

“I know.”

“You watched me eat crackers and wait three hours.”

“I know.”

Noor’s hands tightened on the laptop until the hinge creaked.

They reached into the padded case, took out the iron poker, and laid it across their knees. Then they checked the truck mirrors. The train yard was empty. The floodlights buzzed, one dimming and coming back. No headlights moved down the access road.

“Verify the manifest,” Noor muttered to themselves.

They plugged the source’s thumb drive into the read-only blocker and compared hashes to the paper manifest’s scanned copy. The file names matched. The dates matched. The minister’s driver matched. The ghost matched. The editor matched. The fifth name—Driver—matched.

Noor stopped.

They looked at Driver, then at the screen, then at the source.

“You put their name on the paper too,” Noor said.

The source’s eyes dropped.

“Because I saw the truck.”

“You saw a truck. You didn’t know who was in it.”

“I didn’t.”

Noor closed their eyes. For a second, the fear became a cold, bright fact. The story had names. One of them belonged to the person who had driven Noor here without asking questions. Noor wanted to be angry. Anger would have been easier.

They opened their eyes.

“We’re going back to the cabin,” Noor said.

The source knocked once against the window.

Noor rolled it down two inches more.

“You don’t get to knock if you’re going to lie,” Noor said.

“Don’t go back,” the source said.

“Then give me a reason not to go back.”

The source looked past Noor, toward the passenger side. The source’s voice went lower.

“The note is real. I left it under the storm pane at 9:06. I didn’t go in. I didn’t touch the drive. But I saw a man on the porch after I left. He had a radio. He opened the window from inside. That means the cabin was already occupied.”

Noor’s breath stopped.

“A man,” Noor said.

“Tall. Dark coat. He knew the latch.”

“Did he see you?”

“Yes.”

Noor looked at the coffee can on the bench. The dead phone sat inside with the tracker. Noor had sunk it in a culvert. The image came back to them: the black rectangle blinking red under the axle. Someone had attached it while Noor was inside the cabin, while Driver was on the couch, while the source was late.

Noor’s hands were steady.

“Get in,” Noor said to the source.

The source shook their head. “No.”

“No is not an option.”

“If your driver is clean, I’ll wait here.”

Noor looked at Driver. The question sat between them: Is Driver clean? Noor did not know. The manifest said yes, someone thought Driver was relevant. The boot print said someone had been at the porch. The tracker said someone had been under the truck. The source’s fear was not proof, but it was not nothing.

Noor turned the laptop off.

They unplugged the original encrypted drive, slid it into the padded case, and zipped it shut. The external backup stayed in Noor’s jacket. The source’s thumb drive went into the metal pouch with the burner phone. Noor put the pouch in the inside pocket, closest to the body, and felt its weight against their ribs.

Before getting out, Noor opened the bag, found the jar of peanut butter and the cracked spoon, and ate a hard spoonful straight. Then they ate a cracker, chewing slowly because their hands needed something to do. The fat and sugar hit the hollow place in their stomach and made the fear more physical, more honest.

“Sleep can wait,” Noor said. “Names can’t.”

They got out.

The cold took the sound from the train yard. Noor walked around the truck with the poker in one hand and the flashlight in the other, still off. They checked the rear axle again. Nothing new. They checked the passenger door seam, the mirror housing, the gas cap. Nothing. They stood by the cab and listened to the heater tick and the source’s breathing.

Noor spoke through the open window.

“Here’s what we’re doing. We go back to the cabin by the logging track, not the reservoir road. I’m going to check the kitchen window. If the note is there, I take it. If it isn’t, I check the porch boards, the door handle, and the storm collar. If there’s a car, I do not knock on it. I get back in the truck and we leave.”

The source said, “If the man is still there—”

“Then we leave faster.”

Noor looked at the source’s hand, still trembling, still pressed flat to the door.

“You said no one more car. You didn’t say what to do if there’s one man.”

The source’s voice went rough. “Run.”

Noor nodded once.

They climbed back in and shut the door. The cab was small and too warm after the outside. Noor put the padded case on the floorboard and the poker across their knees. They checked the mirrors again. The access road behind them was empty. The floodlights buzzed.

“We’re going to the cabin,” Noor said. “Not the fire hall. Not the trailhead. Not the reservoir. The cabin.”

Noor’s voice dropped, not to the source, not to Driver, but to the night.

“If the note is gone, someone knows we’re still alive. If the note is there, I’m going to prove who wrote it.”

Noor started the engine. The headlights stayed off. The truck rolled forward, slow, then faster, toward the logging track and the black mouth of the woods. The coffee can with the tracker and dead phone sat on the bench, ticking faintly as it cooled.

Noor checked the mirrors every three seconds.

They did not sleep. They did not eat again. They drove, because the story had moved from a late source to a warm cabin to a name on a screen, and every name was a door someone else might open.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I'm tense, listening to everything. My eyes dart between Noor and the source outside the window. When Noor says "Get in" to the source, I almost jump. When the source refuses, and Noor looks at me, I just shake my head, my jaw tight.* "I don't know anything, Noor. I swear." *I slump back in my seat as Noor starts the engine. This is getting seriously out of hand.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor did not look at Driver. They kept their hands at ten and two, the iron poker resting on their lap, and watched the logging track unspool in front of the truck.

“I believe you,” Noor said, which was not the same as trusting them.

The words came out quieter than Noor intended. They had not planned to say that. The source’s trembling hand, the manifest, the name on the paper, the note telling Noor to check the cabin window—none of it added up. But Driver had driven Noor into the mountains, had stayed when Noor said to stay, and had not tried to take the drive, the laptop, or the poker.

For now, that had to be enough.

Noor checked the mirrors again. The source stood where they had been left in the train yard, far enough back that the truck’s taillights painted their hood a dull red. Noor had expected them to leave. They hadn’t.

The source’s face appeared at the passenger-side window as the truck slowed.

Noor rolled it down two inches.

“You’re not getting in,” Noor said.

“I’m not asking to.”

“Then stay outside and keep up. If you fall behind, I’m not stopping.”

The source nodded. They looked older in the dim glow from the dashboard, the cut above their brow dark and swollen, their jacket damp at the shoulder. Noor noticed the way they favored their left side. They noticed too that the source’s eyes kept sliding past Noor to Driver, then to the padded case, then to the road behind.

“You said the man had a radio,” Noor said.

“Yes.”

“What kind?”

“The old kind. Shoulder mic. Handheld. Not state.”

Noor’s mouth tightened. “Mercenary.”

“Private.”

“Those are the same thing tonight.”

The source pressed one hand flat against the door, knuckles white. “Noor. If he was private security, he may not have been sent to kill you.”

“Then what was he sent to do?”

The source glanced toward the cab interior, then lowered their voice.

“To move you.”

Noor’s stomach went cold.

They had not thought of that. They had been preparing for a shootout, a chase, a fire, a body. The idea that someone had come to the cabin not to burn it but to take Noor out of it made the world tilt slightly.

Noor looked at Driver.

“I’m going to say this once,” they said. “If anyone touches me, you drive. If anyone touches you, you drive. If anyone tells you to stop, you drive. You do not ask questions. You do not open the window for them. You do not let them into the cab. Do you understand?”

Driver nodded.

Noor turned back to the source.

“Get back in the truck.”

The source shook their head.

“Noor—”

“Noor’s voice was hard enough to crack frost off the glass. “I am not leaving you outside. If they’re waiting for me to bring the drive to the editor, they’re waiting for me to be alone. If they’re waiting for me to bring the driver to the fire hall, they’re waiting for you to be dead. I’m not playing their game.”

The source looked at Driver.

Driver looked at the floor.

Noor reached across and opened the passenger door.

The source flinched back.

Noor held the door open.

“I said get in.”

The source hesitated, then slid inside with the awkward, guarded movement of a person expecting a blow. They kept their hands visible. Noor shut the door before the source could speak.

For a moment, the cab was too quiet. The heater ticked. The source’s breathing came fast and shallow. Driver stared ahead. Noor stared at the road.

Noor said, “If you hurt them, I will find out.”

They did not say who “them” was. No one asked.

Noor drove.

The logging track opened into a frozen rut near the cabin’s back slope. Noor stopped the truck under the trees, engine idling, headlights still off. The cabin sat beyond the porch, dark and square in the snow, the kitchen window a black rectangle.

Noor picked up the flashlight.

“I’m going to the porch,” they said. “If I’m not back in two minutes, drive to the highway and don’t look back.”

The source turned toward them. “Noor—”

Noor looked at Driver. “If he’s lying to me, you still drive.”

Driver’s jaw tightened. “I know.”

Noor nodded once, then got out.

The cold hit their face like a slap. Noor kept the flashlight low and angled away from the cabin, moving toward the side of the porch where the boot print had pointed to the kitchen window. The boards groaned under their weight. Noor stopped, crouched, and examined the first step. The print was still there, toe aimed at the window. The edge had begun to fill with fresh snow, which meant it was old enough but not ancient.

Noor looked up.

The window was still open half an inch.

They climbed the porch steps slowly, testing each one before committing. When they reached the railing, they stopped and watched the road, the tree line, the dark spaces between the pines. Nothing moved except snow sliding off a branch.

Noor went to the window and pressed their palm flat against the storm pane.

It was loose.

They worked it up with two fingers. The pane rattled, then rose an inch. Noor slid a hand inside the gap, feeling along the sill. The wood was damp and gritty. Their fingers touched paper.

Noor’s breath caught.

They pinched the corner and drew it out. A folded sheet, sealed inside a clear plastic bag, tucked between the storm pane and the screen. The paper was dry.

Noor did not unfold it. They did not turn around. They checked the window latch, the frame, the sill, the porch boards. Nothing else. No fresh boot print on the railing. No broken twig. No smell of smoke.

They walked backward to the truck, keeping the folded paper in one hand and the poker in the other.

The source watched them through the windshield. Driver did not move.

Noor got into the cab and shut the door. The paper sat in their lap.

“It’s there,” Noor said.

The source exhaled like they had been holding their breath for hours.

Noor opened the flashlight and laid it on the bench. They unfolded the paper with steady fingers.

The handwriting was cramped, hurried, and familiar. Noor recognized the source’s odd way of crossing sevens and leaving the last line of a paragraph hanging.

The note read:

DRIVE IS BAIT.
CONTAINER IS CLEAN.
IF THE NOTE IS GONE, THE CABIN IS HOT AND YOU ARE NOT ALONE IN THE LOGGING TRACK.
DO NOT GO TO THE FIRE HALL.
DO NOT CALL THE EDITOR.
THE GHOST HAS A SHERIFF’S BADGE AND A KEY.
THE DRIVER WAS NOT IN THE ORIGINAL PLAN.
IF THEY ARE IN THE TRUCK, THEY ARE EITHER CLEAN OR VERY GOOD.
CHECK THE BACK PORCH RAIL. THIRD BOARD FROM THE END.
—WIRE

Noor read the line about Driver twice.

They looked at Driver.

Driver looked back, pale and wary.

Noor folded the note and put it inside their jacket.

“Clean or very good,” Noor said quietly.

The source closed their eyes.

Noor turned the flashlight beam toward the back porch.

“Stay here.”

They got out again.

The third board from the end had a hairline gap along one edge. Noor pressed a thumbnail into it and lifted. The board came up easily. Beneath it lay a second plastic bag.

Noor’s pulse thudded in their throat.

They opened the bag with the tip of the poker. Inside was a USB drive, black, labeled in the same cramped handwriting.

MANIFEST 2.

Noor stood there, the snow biting through their boots, and felt the shape of the night change.

The source had lied. Or the source had told only the part they thought Noor could survive.

Noor returned to the truck.

The source said, “What did you find?”

Noor held up the drive.

The source’s face went blank.

Noor got in and shut the door.

“You said you left the second manifest under the storm pane,” Noor said.

“I did.”

“No.” Noor’s voice was low, precise. “You left the note under the storm pane. You left a drive under the porch rail. That’s a different hiding place. That’s a backup.”

The source stared at the drive in Noor’s hand.
