“Noor—”

Noor held up the poker. Not threatening, not quite. Just present.

“You said the driver wasn’t in the original plan.”

The source looked at Driver. Driver looked at Noor.

Noor kept their eyes on the source.

“Why is it in the note if you didn’t make the note?”

The source’s mouth opened. Closed. Their hand rose halfway, then dropped.

“I made the note,” they said. “At the cabin. Before I left.”

“When?”

“Nine-oh-six.”

Noor’s eyes moved to the timestamp in their memory. The folder had been modified after the call. The note had said the source opened the window. The source had said they left it under the storm pane.

Noor said, “You said you didn’t put the driver’s name on the drive.”

“I didn’t.”

“Then why did the note say it?”

The source swallowed.

“Because I saw the truck.”

Noor leaned closer.

“You saw the truck. You didn’t know who was in it. So why warn me?”

The source’s voice dropped. “Because the original plan didn’t include a driver. The original plan was me, the drive, and you. When I saw someone with you, I didn’t know whether you were compromised.”

Noor’s jaw worked.

They looked at Driver.

“Did you know about this?” Noor asked.

Driver shook their head.

Noor waited.

Driver’s hands stayed in their lap. “I didn’t know your source would be watching the cabin. I didn’t know there was a tracker. I didn’t know any of this.”

Noor wanted to find the lie. They looked for it in the line of Driver’s mouth, the tension in their shoulders, the way their eyes moved. Driver looked frightened. Frightened could be real. Frightened could also be the easiest costume.

Noor turned back to the source.

“Show me the manifest on this drive.”

The source hesitated.

Noor tapped the poker against the bench. “Show me.”

The source reached for it.

Noor caught their wrist.

The source flinched.

Noor held the drive. “You touch it, I won’t. I’m not opening it in this truck with you inside.”

The source’s hand fell back.

Noor pulled the laptop bag closer and took out the read-only blocker. They plugged the new USB drive into it, then into the laptop. The screen brightened the cab, throwing sharp shadows across the source’s face and Driver’s hands.

Noor typed the source’s old passphrase—the one they had used three years ago for a different story, a different safehouse, a different life. It was the only password Noor had never changed.

The drive mounted.

Inside was a folder named SECOND MANIFEST.

Noor opened it.

The files were plain text, scanned PDFs, spreadsheets, and audio clips. Noor clicked the first PDF.

A bank transfer.

The recipient was listed under a shell company. The sender was the minister’s office. The amount was large enough to buy silence or enough to buy a gun. The date was four days ago.

Noor clicked the next.

A meeting log.

Location: parking garage below the ministry annex. Time: 22:40. Attendees: MINISTER’S DRIVER, GHOST, EDITOR.

Noor’s breath stopped.

They clicked the next.

A photograph of a car key fob. A badge. A name.

GHOST.

Noor recognized the name from a court file they had been trying to get sealed. A private contractor. A former deputy. A man who had disappeared from the state payroll the same week Noor’s first source had died.

Noor opened the next file.

An audio clip.

They pressed play.

A voice, distorted but close enough to the minister’s driver to make Noor’s stomach turn, said: “The journalist is close. We move the second meeting.”

Another voice, calm, answered: “The driver can take them. The driver doesn’t need to know.”

Noor stopped the audio.

The cab was silent except for the heater.

Noor looked at Driver.

Driver stared at the laptop screen, face drained of color.

Noor’s voice was very quiet. “Explain.”

Driver blinked. “I don’t—”

Noor raised a hand.

“Not here.”

They closed the laptop. The screen went dark, but the files did not. The evidence sat in Noor’s hands like a live wire.

Noor unplugged the drive, slid it into the metal pouch, and zipped the pouch shut. Then they put the pouch inside their jacket, against their ribs, beside the first one.

The source said, “Noor.”

Noor looked at them.

“You knew,” Noor said.

The source’s eyes were red-rimmed. “I suspected.”

“You wrote the note.”

“Yes.”

“You didn’t tell me.”

“I was trying to keep you alive.”

Noor’s laugh came out short and bitter. “By making me drive back to the cabin at midnight?”

The source looked away.

Noor turned to Driver.

“Who told you to come?”

Driver’s mouth worked. “No one. You called. You asked me to drive you.”

“No one gave you instructions?”

“No.”

“Noor’s voice dropped. “You didn’t mention the minister’s driver. You didn’t mention the ghost. You didn’t mention the badge.”

“I didn’t know.”

“You didn’t know,” Noor repeated.

They looked at Driver for a long moment. The note said clean or very good. The audio said the driver doesn’t need to know. Driver had driven Noor to a safehouse, had stayed in the truck, had not tried to take the drive, had not called anyone Noor could see. But that did not prove innocence. It only proved patience.

Noor said, “If you’re dirty, I’m going to find out.”

Driver swallowed. “Okay.”

Noor looked at the road.

The cabin sat behind them, dark and patient. Beyond it, the logging track wound toward the highway. Somewhere out there, the fire hall waited. Somewhere out there, the editor waited. Somewhere out there, the ghost had a key and a badge.

Noor picked up the iron poker.

“We’re not going to the fire hall,” they said. “We’re not going to the editor. We’re not going to the paper.”

The source looked up. “Where are we going?”

Noor checked the mirrors. The train yard was behind them. The cabin was to their left. The reservoir road was to their right. The highway was straight ahead.

Noor chose the highway.

“The gas station,” they said. “There’s a landline. If the source’s phone is cloned, the payphone is the least bad place to make a call. If the ghost is watching, I want them to think we’re stupid.”

They put the truck in gear.

The source said, “Noor.”

Noor looked at them.

“The files,” the source said. “You can’t publish from the gas station.”

Noor’s hands tightened on the wheel.

“No,” they said. “I can’t.”

“Then what are you going to do?”

Noor watched the road.

“I’m going to verify the last name,” Noor said.

The source went still.

Noor looked at Driver.

“Driver,” Noor said. “If someone asked you to bring me here, you may not have known what you were doing. But that doesn’t matter tonight. What matters is what you do now.”

Driver stared at them.

Noor said, “If you’re clean, you drive to the gas station. If you’re dirty, you try to stop me. I’ll know which one you are in the next five minutes.”

The truck rolled forward. The cabin disappeared behind the trees. Noor did not look back.

At the highway junction, Noor stopped. The crossroad was empty. The streetlights buzzed yellow over wet asphalt. Noor checked the rearview mirror, the side mirrors, the road left, the road right. Nothing.

They took the external backup drive from their jacket pocket and handed it to Driver.

“Hold this,” Noor said.

Driver took it like it might burn.

Noor looked at the source.

“You said the drive is bait.”

“Yes.”

“Then I’m going to use it.”

The source frowned. “What?”

Noor pulled a pen and a scrap of paper from the glovebox. They wrote the editor’s number, the fire hall number, the paper’s night desk number, and the source’s number. Then they crossed out the fire hall and the night desk.

Noor held up the padded case.

“The drive is bait,” they said. “But bait only works if someone expects you to bite. I’m going to call the editor and tell him I found the drive. I’m going to tell him the checksum matched. I’m going to tell him I’m coming to the paper.”

The source’s face changed.

“Noor, if he’s involved—”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

Noor’s voice went low. “Because if he’s involved, he’ll try to stop me. If he’s clean, he’ll ask for verification. Either way, I get a reaction.”

Noor turned to Driver.

“While I make the call, you keep the engine running. If anyone approaches, we leave.”

Driver nodded.

Noor looked at the source.

“You’ll sit in the cab with Driver. You’ll stay visible. You’ll say nothing unless they speak first.”

The source stared at them.

Noor said, “If you run, I leave you.”

The source’s jaw tightened. “You can’t keep me here.”

Noor held their gaze. “I can. I have the poker, the truck, and three hours until the story dies.”

The source looked at Driver, then at the padded case, then at Noor.

“Okay,” they said.

Noor opened the door.

The cold came back. The highway was wide and empty under the streetlights. Noor walked to the gas station, leaving the truck running. Their boots crunched on the shoulder. The payphone still sat under the buzzing fluorescent sign, gray and old.

Noor did not use the burner phone. They did not use the source’s number. They used the landline in the station booth and dialed the editor.

The phone rang once.

Twice.

Three times.

The editor picked up on the fourth ring. His voice was careful, too awake for the hour.

“Noor? Where are you?”

Noor stood in the booth, one hand on the receiver, the other pressed against their ribs where the drive pouch sat.

“Safe,” Noor said. “I found the drive.”

A pause. Too short. Too controlled.

“You verified the checksum?”

“Yes.”

“Any folder?”

Noor’s throat tightened.

“Yes.”

The editor’s voice softened, but the softness did not reach his words.

“Noor. Don’t open it.”

Noor closed their eyes.

“Why?”

“Because if you open it, they’ll know you have it.”

Noor looked through the glass. The truck sat at the edge of the pumps. Driver was behind the wheel. The source stood beside the cab, hands visible. Noor could not hear them through the glass, but Noor could see the way the source’s shoulders moved, the way Driver kept turning toward them.

Noor said, “Did you put my name on the drive?”

The editor did not answer.

Noor’s voice went flat.

“Did you?”

Another pause.

“No,” the editor said. “But someone close to me did.”

Noor’s breath came out slow.

“Who?”

The editor said, “The ghost.”

Noor looked at the road.

“Why?”

“Because the story is bigger than the minister.”

Noor’s hand tightened on the receiver.

“Bigger how?”

The editor’s voice dropped.

“It goes to the police. To the sheriff’s office. To the state attorney general. If you publish tonight, you won’t just hurt the minister. You’ll burn down every institution that protected him.”

Noor stared at the truck.

“Then why didn’t you tell me?”

The editor said, “Because you wouldn’t have stopped.”

Noor almost laughed.

“Where are you?” Noor asked.

“Paper.”

“Alone?”

The pause was different this time.

“Noor,” the editor said. “Come to the paper. Bring the drive. Don’t trust anyone else.”

Noor looked at the gas station clerk, who had gone back under the counter. The payphone cord creaked.

“I’ll bring the drive,” Noor said.

They hung up.

Noor stood in the booth for three seconds. Then they dialed the source’s number. It rang once and went to voicemail. Noor hung up. They dialed the minister’s driver. It rang once and a recording said the number was not in service. Noor hung up.

They walked back to the truck.

The source and Driver both looked at Noor.

Noor got in and shut the door.

“He knows,” Noor said. “He didn’t say how, but he knows the folder exists. He told me not to open it. He said if I open it, they’ll know.”

Driver said, “Who?”

Noor looked at them.

“The ghost,” Noor said.

The source made a sound under their breath.

Noor turned to them. “You knew the editor was on the list.”

“Yes.”

“You didn’t know he was involved.”

“I didn’t know.”

Noor’s hands tightened on the wheel.

“Then what did you know?”

The source looked at the padded case.

“I knew the minister’s driver was running messages for the ghost. I knew the ghost used a sheriff’s badge to move people. I knew the editor had signed a transfer that moved files. I didn’t know the editor had put your name on the drive.”

Noor stared at them.

“Why would anyone put my name on the drive?”

The source’s voice went quiet.

“Because someone wanted you to come to the cabin.”

Noor’s stomach went cold.

“To meet you?”

“To meet me,” the source said. “Or to meet whoever sent the folder.”

Noor looked at Driver.

Driver looked at the road.

Noor said, “We’re going to the paper.”

The source said, “Noor.”

Noor looked at them.

“We’re going to the paper,” Noor said. “Not because the editor is safe. Because he’s the only one who still has a reason to keep the story alive. If he’s dirty, he’ll try to stop me. If he’s clean, he’ll help me publish before they can bury it.”

Noor started the truck.

The headlights stayed off until they reached the highway. Noor turned on them then, bright and sudden, because hiding was no longer the point. The point was momentum. The point was names. The point was that Noor had spent three hours in a cold cabin waiting for a source who was already bleeding, already frightened, already lying by omission, and still came.

Noor checked the mirrors.

The road behind was empty.

Noor drove toward the city.

The source said, “If you go to the paper, they’ll have cameras at the front.”

Noor looked at them.

“Then we don’t use the front.”

The source blinked.

Noor’s mouth tightened.

“My uncle used to bring me to the loading dock when I was a kid. The paper still has a service entrance behind the bakery on Fifth. The bakery closes at midnight. The dock light stays on until two.”

Driver said, “How do you know?”

Noor looked at them.

“Because I used to hide in that dock and read the galleys before my editor found me.”

Driver’s face changed. Noor did not explain. There was no time.

The truck sped up.

Noor reached into the padded case and took out the encrypted drive. They held it in one hand. The original. The bait. The thing that had started as evidence and had become a trap.

Noor looked at the source.

“You said I should verify now.”

The source nodded.

Noor said, “We verify at the paper. Then we publish.”

The source’s eyes widened.

“Noor, the manifest isn’t enough. The drive could be fabricated. If the editor is involved—”

Noor’s voice cut through them.

“Then I’ll prove it before I publish.”

Noor opened the laptop again, but this time they did not plug in the drive. They opened a new document and began typing.

TITLE: THE CABIN FILE.
SUBTITLE: EVIDENCE, TIMESTAMPS, AND A NAME THAT SHOULD NOT HAVE BEEN THERE.

Noor typed the first line.

The source was three hours late. The safehouse was somebody’s uncle’s hunting cabin in the mountains. The coffee pot had dust on top of it.

Noor’s hands moved faster.

They typed the boot print. The tracker. The open window. The folder. The audio clip. The bank transfer. The editor’s call. The ghost. The manifest. The note under the porch rail. They typed the names, but not Driver’s yet. Not the source’s. Not their own.

Noor stopped at the last line.

They looked at Driver.

“Your name goes on the manifest,” Noor said. “If I publish it, people will look at you.”

Driver’s hands tightened around the external backup drive.

“I know.”

Noor waited.

Driver said, “Put it in.”

Noor looked at them for a long moment.

Then Noor turned back to the laptop and typed:

THE DRIVER WAS NOT IN THE ORIGINAL PLAN.

Noor hit save.

The truck rolled forward. The city lights rose in the distance, pale and orange against the black mountains. The source sat with their head tipped back against the seat, eyes closed, breath fogging the cold air in small bursts. Driver stared at the road ahead.

Noor checked the mirrors.

The road behind was empty.

For now.

Noor drove faster.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I watch Noor type my name. A shiver goes down my spine, but I don't argue. This is way beyond me now. I just hold the backup drive tight, staring at the lights of the city getting closer.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor took the last turn into the city without headlights, letting the snow do the work the road had been stolen from. The truck slid through the first two blocks under the streetlights, then Noor killed the engine behind a twenty-four-hour laundromat where the dryer vents breathed steam into the dark.

Noor sat still.

Thirty seconds.

Sixty.

The heater ticked. The city hummed beyond the trees, distant and indifferent.

Then Noor reached into the bag, found the jar of peanut butter, and used the cracked spoon to take another bite. It coated the roof of Noor’s mouth, thick and salt-sweet. Noor chased it with a cracker, chewing slowly because their hands needed something honest to do.

They pulled the second burner phone from the metal pouch and powered it on.

The screen lit blue.

Noor went straight to the message log.

One new text.

Sender: source’s number.

Time: 1:06 a.m.

Body: GHOST IS AT THE DOCK. BRING THE BAIT DRIVE.

Noor read it twice.

They opened the call history. The source’s number had called Noor’s burner at 8:56 and 9:04. No voicemail. No follow-up text. No further messages until now.

Noor looked at the source.

“You said your phone was gone.”

The source’s mouth tightened. “It is.”

“Noor held up the burner. “Then who is texting with your number?”

The source did not answer.

Noor typed a reply with their thumb.

Where are you?

The phone stayed silent.

Noor watched the three dots appear, disappear, appear again.

Then:

YOU KNOW WHERE.

Noor’s stomach went flat.

They powered the phone off, dropped it back into the pouch, and zipped it shut.

“We’re not going to the front,” Noor said. “We’re going to the service dock.”

Noor turned to Driver.

“Stay in the cab when I stop. If I’m not back by 1:45, drive to the highway and keep moving. Do not stop for me. Do not stop for anyone who says my name.”

Noor did not wait to hear whether that was a fair thing to ask. Fair had stopped being the measure at 9:07, when the SAFEHOUSE folder appeared.

Noor started the truck.

They drove the last half mile with the headlights off, turning into the alley behind the bakery where the paper’s service entrance used to be. Noor remembered this part of the city as a place that smelled of yeast and wet cardboard. Now it smelled of diesel, rust, and cold garbage.

The dock light was on.

It was a weak square of yellow above a freight door, buzzing at one corner. Noor parked behind a dumpster, engine still running, and watched.

A white utility truck sat at the dock.

It had no company lettering. No markings. Only a radio antenna taped to the rear window and a license plate obscured by a flap of black plastic. The bed was covered with a hard shell. The tires were new. The exhaust fogged in the cold.

Noor stared at it until the source’s words came back.

If you see a white truck, it’s not me.

Noor got out.

The source came around the rear of the truck, hands visible, shoulders hunched against the cold. Noor took the padded case, the laptop, the iron poker, and the flashlight. They did not take the original encrypted drive yet. They left it under the bench seat.

Noor walked toward the white truck.

The source followed three steps behind.

“Do not touch it,” Noor said.

“I’m not.”

“Good.”

Noor photographed the truck from three angles. The rear plate. The antenna. The side mirror. The dock ramp. The fresh tire marks in the snow. The source’s number text still sat in Noor’s memory. They opened the burner again and dialed it.

It rang once.

Twice.

Then the ringtone came from inside the white truck.

Noor did not move.

The ringing stopped.

A line opened.

Noor lifted the phone to their ear.

“You brought the driver,” the voice said.

It was the ghost.

Noor’s breath fogged the air. “You have the source’s phone.”

“I have what the source left in the valley.”

“You edited the folder.”

Silence.

Noor looked at the source. The source’s face had gone very pale.

“Who are you?” Noor asked.

The voice answered with a laugh that did not carry. “You already know my name. It’s on the manifest.”

“No,” Noor said. “I know what they called you. I don’t know what you’re doing here.”

“You know exactly what I’m doing.”

Noor hung up.

They powered the phone off and put it in the pouch.

Noor looked at the source.

“You knew he’d answer.”

The source’s jaw worked. “I suspected.”

“Suspected is not truth.”

“No,” the source said. “It’s not.”

Noor turned back to the truck. The cab was dark. The padded case sat where Noor had left it. The coffee can with the tracker and dead phone was on the bench. Noor opened the door and climbed in.

They took the encrypted drive from under the seat.

It was still heavy.

Noor plugged it into the laptop through the read-only blocker. The mounting dialog appeared. Noor’s thumb hovered over the trackpad.

The source’s note had said the container was clean.

The source’s text had said the drive was bait.

Noor typed the password.

The container opened.

The SAFEHOUSE folder was still there. So was the red DRIVER folder. The audio clip. The bank transfers. The meeting logs. The photograph of the badge. The final document: IF NOOR IS READING THIS.

Noor opened it.

The first lines were the ones Noor had read before.

If you opened this, the drive was bait.

I’m sorry.

Check the cabin’s window.

Noor scrolled.

There was more.

I made the folder as a warning. I did not make the DRIVER file. The ghost took WIRE-4 after I left the valley. He used my computer to reach you. He wanted you to come to the cabin. He wanted you to bring the drive to the editor. If you found the note, you are already in the trap. Do not trust the fire hall. The dispatcher is on the ghost’s list. Do not trust the paper’s main network. The editor may be involved. Do not trust the minister’s driver. He has been paid. Do not trust the source.

Noor stopped.

They looked at the source.

The source was watching the dock, one hand pressed against the window frame.

Noor kept reading.

If you are reading this in the truck, go to the service dock. The bakery closes at midnight. The dock office has a key card in the third drawer of the tool cabinet. The copy room on three has an outside line that does not log to the main switchboard. The night desk code is 2240. Use it. Upload the archive to the ombudsman’s secure server. Do not call the editor. Do not call the fire hall. Do not call anyone who can answer with your name.

Noor’s eyes moved to the last line.

If the driver is with you, do not separate them from the backup. If the backup is lost, the story dies.

Noor closed the laptop.

They sat very still.

The source spoke first.

“You opened it.”

Noor looked at them.

“You said the drive was bait.”

“It is.”

“You didn’t say it was your confession.”

The source flinched.

Noor’s voice went low. “You didn’t say the ghost was already in the building.”

The source’s eyes moved to the white truck.

“I didn’t know he’d answer.”

“You suspected.”

“Yes.”

Noor picked up the iron poker.

“Show your pockets again.”

The source did.

Noor checked the jacket, the pants, the cuffs. No phone. No recorder. No weapon. No tracker.

Noor looked at the source’s hands.

“You said you created the folder as a warning.”

“Yes.”

“Noor’s voice was almost quiet. “But you didn’t tell me the folder would include my driver.”

The source looked toward the cab.

“No.”

“Noor’s throat tightened. “You saw the truck. You saw someone in it. You still wrote that name.”

The source’s face shifted.

“I didn’t know it was them.”

“You didn’t know it was me, either.”

The source closed their mouth.

Noor turned away.

They opened the door and stepped out. The cold hit their face again, sharp and clean. Noor walked to the dock. The freight door was locked, but the side entrance had a keypad beside a scratched steel frame. Noor tried 2240.

The lock clicked.

Noor looked at the source.

“Stay with the truck.”

The source did not argue.

Noor went inside.

The dock office was a square room that smelled of cardboard and old coffee. A desk sat under one window. A metal tool cabinet stood against the far wall. The fluorescent light buzzed, then failed, then came back dim. Noor’s flashlight swept the room.

No one was there.

Noor opened the tool cabinet.

First drawer: gloves.

Second: wire cutters, tape, zip ties.

Third: a stack of press passes, a key card, and a small black notebook.

Noor picked up the key card.

It was blank except for a printed number. Noor turned it over. The number matched the source’s text.

The notebook was the editor’s.

Noor recognized the spiral binding and the coffee stain on the corner. They opened it. The first pages were meeting notes. The last page had a line written in the editor’s careful hand.

If Noor comes, send them to the fire hall.

Beneath it, in different ink:

Do not let them use the copy room.

Noor’s breath stopped.

They photographed both lines.

Noor checked the desk drawers. No computer. No phone. A wall-mounted switchboard sat beside the door, old and gray, with a paper log clipped to the side. Noor pulled the log free.

The last entries were handwritten.

12:51 — EXT 4 CALL OUT — SOURCE NUM.

1:03 — EXT 4 CALL IN — UNKNOWN.

1:06 — EXT 4 CALL OUT — NOOR BURNER.

Noor stared at the number.

EXT 4.

The dock office line.

Someone had used this landline to text Noor’s burner.

Noor opened the phone’s call log again and compared the timestamp. The text had come from the source’s number, but the route had not. Noor checked the paper’s public directory on the laptop, found the switchboard’s extension map, and matched EXT 4 to the loading dock.

This was the verification.

The phone records.

The timestamps.

The drive.

The key card.

The editor’s notebook.

All of it pointed back to one place.

Noor closed the log.

They took the key card, the notebook, and the iron poker.

Noor walked to the service elevator. The freight cage had a button for the second floor and a third that was scratched out. Noor pressed the third anyway.

The elevator groaned upward.

The copy room was on the third floor behind a set of glass doors that no longer had working locks. Noor stepped inside. The room smelled of toner and paper. A maintenance terminal sat in the corner, old and beige, with a network jack behind a plastic cover. Noor had used this room once, years ago, before the paper had installed new security and forgotten to remove the old jack.

Noor opened the terminal.

It booted.

Noor plugged in the read-only blocker, then the original encrypted drive. They did not type the password again. They opened the container’s directory and selected the archive.

The upload window asked for destination.

Noor typed the ombudsman’s secure server.

The password prompt appeared.

Noor looked at the editor’s notebook.

The last page had no password, but the first page had a phrase the editor had written years ago and never changed.

NOOR IS NOT A SOURCE.

Noor typed it.

The server accepted.

The upload bar began to move.

Noor sat back.

The files copied: the bank transfers. The meeting logs. The audio clip. The manifest. The SAFEHOUSE folder. The phone records from the burner. The timestamps from the cabin. The tracker photo. The boot print. The open window. The editor’s call. The ghost’s voice on the line. The dock switchboard log.

The bar crawled.

Noor watched it.

The fear did not go away. It only became a thing Noor carried with care, like the coffee can on the bench, like the drive in the pouch, like the poker across their knees.

The upload reached ninety percent.

The copy room door opened.

Noor closed the laptop halfway.

The editor stood in the doorway.

He looked older than he had on the phone. His coat was damp at the shoulders. His face was carefully blank. Behind him stood a man Noor had never met, but whose shape matched the figure in the white truck: tall, dark coat, shoulder mic

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor did not look at the phone light again. The word hung in the copy room too small for the night. Noor had asked once. Noor would not ask twice.

“Stay where you are,” Noor said to the editor.

The editor’s hands stayed open at his sides. Noor watched them the way Noor watched the upload bar. Ninety-four. Ninety-five. The server log window blinked with a pale cursor, waiting for the final confirmation.

Noor’s thumb hovered over the trackpad.

“You don’t know what you’re doing,” the editor said.

“I know exactly what I’m doing.” Noor’s voice was low, tired, and hard enough to keep the room from leaning in. “I’m finishing a task.”

“Don’t.”

Noor looked up.

The editor’s face was not angry. That was worse. It was careful. The face of a man choosing which half-truth would make Noor stop.

“Give me your phone,” Noor said.

The editor hesitated.

Noor lifted the iron poker two inches. Not much. Just enough to show it was real.

“Now.”

The editor drew the phone from his coat pocket with both hands, as if surrendering something fragile. Noor took it without breaking the seal on the screen. The phone was warm. It should not have been. Noor checked the battery percentage. Then the recent calls.

12:51 — outgoing — source’s number  
1:03 — incoming — unknown  
1:06 — outgoing — Noor’s burner

Noor opened the message app. The text that had reached Noor’s burner had not come from this phone. But the number it had used was the source’s. Noor checked the routing trail, the way Noor had learned to after the first story that almost got Noor fired. The message had been sent from a number registered to the source, through a gateway Noor recognized from the paper’s old dock system.

Noor looked at the editor.

“Did you send this?”

“No.”

“Did you pair your phone with a device called CABIN-TRAP?”

The editor’s face changed. Not much. A shift behind the eyes.

“I don’t know what that is.”

Noor opened Bluetooth.

A device was paired. CABIN-TRAP. Paired at 1:02 a.m.

Noor’s mouth went dry.

The upload bar hit ninety-six.

Noor did not click confirm. Not yet. Noor went back to the switchboard log from the dock office and photographed it with the editor’s phone, then used the phone’s notes app to type the timestamps beside the Bluetooth pairing. The numbers lined up too cleanly. The ghost had been close. Too close.

Noor looked at the editor.

“You told me you were alone at the paper.”

“I was.”

“You were lying.”

The editor swallowed. “Noor—”

“No.” Noor’s voice cut. “I’m not doing this while it’s still moving.”

Noor clicked confirm.

The terminal locked for a second. Then a new window opened.

UPLOAD COMPLETE.

Receipt number: 7741-DELTA-NOOR.

Noor exhaled through the nose, but Noor did not stop. Noor ran the hash check. The server returned the archive digest. Noor compared it to the encrypted drive’s local hash. Match. Noor compared the manifest file hashes. Match. The bank transfers. Match. The audio clip. Match. The SAFEHOUSE folder. Match.

Noor closed the terminal and opened the source’s thumb drive through the read-only blocker. The manifest from the porch rail matched the uploaded archive too. All of it. Noor checked every line twice, because fear made Noor sloppy and Noor could not afford sloppy.

The upload was real. The story was out.

Noor’s hands shook for the first time since the cabin. Noor set them flat on the table and breathed.

Then Noor reached into the jacket pocket, found the cracker sleeve, and tore it open with their teeth. Noor ate two crackers standing up, chewing hard because the jaw needed work. The dry crumbs made Noor cough, and the cough broke the spell. Noor washed it down with a sip from a cold cup of coffee someone had left on the copy room printer. It tasted like dust and toner. Noor drank it anyway.

“Sleep later,” Noor muttered. “Names now.”

The editor stepped inside.

Noor lifted the poker.

“One step,” Noor said.

“I’m not going to stop you.”

“You already tried.”

The editor stopped.

Noor looked at him. “You told me not to open the drive. You told me to come to the paper. You wrote the line about the fire hall in your notebook.”

“Yes.”

“You didn’t write the line about the copy room.”

“No.”

Noor held up the notebook. “Different ink. Different pressure. Someone with access to your office edited the note.”

The editor’s face tightened. “My office was unlocked.”

“Because the ghost has a key.”

“Because I gave him one.”

Noor’s breath stopped.

The copy room was silent except for the hum of the terminal and the distant clatter of the freight elevator somewhere below. Noor looked at the editor for a long, careful second.

“You gave him a key,” Noor said.

The editor’s voice dropped. “At eleven-forty. He said he needed access to the dock office. He said if I didn’t, the minister would pull the paper’s contract with the city.”

Noor laughed once. It came out flat and ugly.

“You let a man with a sheriff’s badge into a building that holds evidence.”

“I didn’t know—”

“You knew enough to write *send them to the fire hall*.”

The editor’s jaw worked. “I thought the fire hall was safe.”

Noor’s eyes moved to the receipt number on the screen. “The dispatcher is on the ghost’s list. The source said so. The note said so. If you had told me to go there, you would have handed me to him.”

The editor looked sick.

Noor did not feel satisfaction. Noor felt only the cold arithmetic of survival.

“Did you know the driver would be here?” Noor asked.

The editor blinked. “Driver?”

“Don’t.” Noor’s voice went quiet. “Don’t look innocent. You signed a transfer that moved ministerial files. You put your name on a manifest with the ghost. You gave a private contractor a key to this building. If you say *driver* like you don’t know who I mean, I will believe you are still lying.”

The editor’s hands trembled. “I didn’t know the driver was coming.”

Noor waited.

“I didn’t,” the editor said. “The plan was you, the drive, and me. The ghost said if you came to the paper, I should bring you to the fire hall. I thought he was trying to protect you.”

Noor’s stomach turned. “You thought.”

“He said the minister had a kill order on the source. He said if you published, they would trace the leak through you.”

“And through the driver.”

The editor looked away.

Noor closed the laptop. The screen went dark, but Noor did not put it down. Noor slid it into the padded case and zipped it halfway. Then Noor unplugged the original encrypted drive, dropped it into the metal pouch with the thumb drive and the burner, and put the pouch inside the jacket.

The editor watched.

“Where are you going?” he asked.

Noor pointed the poker at the door. “You’re going to sit in that corner. Hands where I can see them. If you move, I will remember that you gave the ghost a key and I will be less patient than I am right now.”

The editor sat.

Noor turned toward the phone light.

“I’m going to the truck,” Noor said. “When I get outside, I need the backup drive in my hand. Not in a pocket. Not under a seat. In my hand. If someone has offered to hold it, if someone has asked to see it, if someone has touched the truck, tell me before I open the door.”

Noor did not wait for permission. Noor moved.

The third-floor corridor smelled of cleaning fluid and old paper. Noor kept the poker in the right hand and the flashlight in the left, beam angled low. The freight elevator was still where Noor had left it, doors open, cage dark. Noor took the stairs instead. The steps echoed too much. Noor stopped on the landing and listened.

Below, the dock office door opened.

Noor did not go down. Noor took the service stair to the second floor, where the bakery-side entrance gave onto the alley. The door had a crash bar. Noor pushed it slowly.

Cold air hit Noor’s face.

The alley was empty. The dumpster. The white truck. The cab lights. The truck Noor had left running by the dock.

The source was not beside it.

Noor’s pulse jumped.

Noor crossed the snow in quick, low steps. The truck door was closed. The windows were fogged. Noor checked the rear axle again. Nothing new. Noor went to the driver’s side and rapped twice on the glass with the poker.

Inside, the dome light was off.

Noor did not open the door. Noor spoke through the glass.

“I’m going in. If you have the backup, it stays with you until I say otherwise. If someone is in the cab with you, do not move.”

Noor opened the door.

The cab was empty except for the padded case on the bench and the coffee can on the floorboard. The heater ticked. The phone light was still bright, still steady, still pointed down toward hands that had not moved to help.

Noor looked at the phone. Then at the case. Then at the alley.

The source was gone.

Noor shut the door and locked it from the inside.

The editor’s phone buzzed in Noor’s pocket. Noor pulled it out. A new text from the ghost’s number, the one Noor had just paired from the editor’s Bluetooth log.

YOU OPENED IT. YOU ARE NOT LEAVING THE ALLEY.

Noor typed, with two thumbs, fast and cold:

The archive is already with the ombudsman.

The reply came in under ten seconds.

THE OMBUDSMAN IS ON THE LIST TOO.

Noor’s stomach went flat.

Noor did not answer. Noor powered the phone off, dropped it into the metal pouch, and zipped it. Then Noor pulled the external backup drive from the padded case, checked its hash against the upload receipt stored in Noor’s jacket pocket, and compared the numbers until they matched again. They did.

Noor ate a spoonful of peanut butter from the jar, straight, because the fear had hollowed Noor out and the body needed something to keep the hands steady.

Sleep can wait.

The alley needed leaving.

Noor put the truck in gear without starting the engine, rolled backward until the tires found the edge of the asphalt, then turned the ignition. The headlights stayed off. The truck slid toward the mouth of the alley.

Noor checked the mirrors.

The white truck sat at the dock.

The bakery door was dark.

The freight elevator was silent.

Noor looked at the phone light one last time.

“If you’re going to drive tonight,” Noor said, voice low, “then drive like your life depends on it. Because mine does.”

Noor turned the truck out of the alley and onto the service road, away from the dock, away from the fire hall, away from the paper’s front door. The city lights rose ahead, pale and indifferent. Noor’s hands stayed at ten and two. The backup drive sat in Noor’s jacket pocket against the ribs. The poker lay across the lap.

Noor had one upload. One receipt. One man who might be guilty and one source who might be alive.

Noor had to reach the ombudsman before the ghost reached Noor.

Noor drove.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stare at my phone, seeing the text from the Ghost. My blood runs cold. I look up at Noor, then back at the phone, then at the empty passenger seat where the source was. My hands clench on the steering wheel.* "What just happened? Where'd they go?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor kept their eyes on the alley mouth while the truck rolled slow. The heater blew warm air across their hands, but Noor did not feel it. The source’s seat was still warm when Noor touched the vinyl. That meant less than Noor wanted it to mean.

“They were here when I left,” Noor said. “They weren’t here when I came back. That’s what happened.”

Noor looked at the passenger-side door, the mirror, the window latch. A black thread hung from the mirror housing. A thin red smear sat on the inside handle. Noor photographed all of it with the editor’s phone, then set the phone on their knee and did not unlock it again yet.

“Where did they go?” Noor repeated Driver’s question flatly, as if turning the words over for weight. “If they walked, they left their jacket. If they were taken, they didn’t have time to make a sound.”

Noor’s thumb pressed hard against the phone’s edge.

“That means one of two things. Either the source was bait and got scared, or the ghost came for them while I was inside.”

Noor did not wait for an answer. They pulled up the recent message log. The text from the ghost had come from the source’s number, but the routing metadata was still visible in the editor’s phone because the editor had kept the message thread open. Noor checked the send time: 1:17 a.m. Then the Bluetooth log. Then the call history. Then the switchboard photos from the dock office.

The numbers lined up too cleanly.

Noor opened the browser and went to the ombudsman’s public verification page. The receipt number Noor had saved—7741-DELTA-NOOR—returned a status line in plain black text:

RECEIVED. SEALED. PENDING REVIEW.

Noor stared at the words until they stopped meaning safety.

The page loaded over an https connection, but Noor checked the certificate. The issuer was wrong. Not the ombudsman’s old internal authority. Not the courthouse chain. A paper webmail certificate, still valid because someone had left the terminal open and reused the session. Noor’s mouth went dry.

“We didn’t upload to the ombudsman,” Noor said. “We uploaded to a mirror.”

The cab seemed smaller after that.

Noor reached for the padded case, unzipped it, and took out the read-only blocker and the small USB adapter they kept for phones. Noor plugged the source’s thumb drive into the editor’s phone through the blocker. The drive mounted read-only. The first folder was the manifest. The second was the bank transfers. The third was the meeting logs. The fourth was empty at first glance.

Noor checked the directory tree in the file manager. Hidden folders appeared.

IF-OMBUDSMAN-FAILS.

Noor’s breath stopped.

They opened it.

Inside were three files and a map. The map was a hand-drawn sketch of the county law library service entrance, with the time-stamp window circled in red. The first file was a PDF titled PUBLIC FILING PACKET. The second was a short text note:

If the ombudsman line returns sealed, it is not sealed. It is buried. Use the clerk desk. Ask for the red stamp. Do not use paper Wi-Fi. Do not use the editor’s phone after 2 a.m.

The third file was a photograph of a badge. Not the ghost’s. A retired clerk’s ID. The name underneath read RIVA.

Noor checked the hashes on the hidden folder. They matched the manifest paper from the porch rail. That meant the folder had been on the source’s drive before Noor ever touched it. That meant the source had planned for the ombudsman being compromised. Or it meant the source had been forced to plan it.

Noor closed their eyes for one second.

Then they opened the bag, found the jar of peanut butter and the cracked spoon, and took a hard bite. They chased it with a cracker, chewing slowly because their hands needed something to do. The sugar and fat hit the hollow place in their stomach and made the fear more honest.

“Sleep can wait,” Noor muttered. “Names now.”

Noor powered off the editor’s phone, removed the battery when they could, and slid it into the metal pouch with the burner and the source’s drive. The pouch went into the inside jacket pocket. The external backup stayed in Noor’s hand. Noor checked its hash against the upload receipt one more time. The numbers matched. The mirror had copied the files, but it had not broken them.

Noor looked at the coffee can on the floorboard.

The tape was still in place. Noor peeled it back. The black tracker inside blinked red every few seconds. Noor had assumed the phone inside was dead and the tracker was harmless. The blink proved otherwise. Noor dropped the tracker into the metal pouch, zipped it shut, and set the empty coffee can aside.

“That,” Noor said, pointing at the can, “was how they knew when we moved.”

Noor pulled the paper map from the glovebox and spread it across their knees. The city lights bled orange along the top edge. Noor’s finger traced from the alley to the river road, then east, then to the courthouse block where the law library sat behind a public parking garage. Noor circled the service entrance.

“We’re going to the county law library,” Noor said. “Not the ombudsman. Not the fire hall. Not the paper. The clerk’s desk is public, time-stamped, and stupid enough to accept a sealed affidavit before dawn if the person at the window has the right name.”

Noor looked up then, voice low.

“If you’re dirty, this is the moment I find out. If you’re clean, keep moving and do not stop for anyone who says my name.”

Noor checked the mirrors. The alley mouth was empty. The white utility truck that had sat at the dock was gone. The bakery door was dark. The dock light buzzed, then failed, then came back.

Noor’s stomach tightened.

“Take the river road,” Noor said. “Not the highway. If a white truck appears behind us, I need to know if it’s following.”

Noor folded the map and tucked it into the jacket. They opened the laptop again, this time with the screen dimmed so low it was almost useless. Noor began typing anyway, because the story had to exist in Noor’s own words before anyone else could rewrite it.

TITLE: THE CABIN FILE.
SECOND LINE: THE OMBUDSMAN MIRROR.
THIRD LINE: THE PUBLIC FILING.

Noor typed the timestamps from the dock switchboard. The Bluetooth pairing. The certificate mismatch. The hidden folder. The source’s note. The boot print. The tracker. The open window. The editor’s confession about the key. The ghost’s voice on the line. The white truck.

Noor stopped at the line about the source.

They wrote: SOURCE DISAPPEARED. UNKNOWN IF ALIVE. UNKNOWN IF COMPLICIT.

Then Noor added:

THE DRIVER WAS NOT IN THE ORIGINAL PLAN.

Noor’s thumb hovered over the trackpad.

They typed one more line beneath it:

THE DRIVER WAS ASKED TO STAY IN THE TRUCK.

Noor saved the file to the external backup, not the laptop. Then Noor copied the whole working draft onto the source’s thumb drive through the read-only blocker. If one device was taken, another would remain.

Noor checked the mirrors again.

The river road opened ahead, black and narrow, the snow gone to slush under the streetlights. Noor’s eyes moved to the rearview. No headlights. No white truck. No engine behind them.

The silence did not make Noor feel better. Silence had already been used against them once.

“The ombudsman didn’t take the story,” Noor said. “They buried it in a mirror. If we want it alive, we have to put it where someone has to sign for it.”

Noor reached into the padded case and took out the original encrypted drive. The bait. The confession. The thing that had led them from a cold cabin to a paper dock to a source who had vanished without a sound. Noor held it for a second, then dropped it into the coffee can and taped the lid again.

Not a Faraday cage.

Better than nothing.

Noor slid the can under the bench seat.

“We’re going to the law library,” Noor said. “I’m filing the manifest, the audio, the bank transfers, and the phone records. If the clerk is clean, she stamps it. If the clerk isn’t clean, she’ll try to take the drive. Then I’ll know what to do.”

Noor looked toward the front windshield, not at Driver.

“I’m not sleeping until the stamp is on the page.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, my grip still tight on the wheel. My eyes flick to the coffee can under the seat, then back to the road. This is... a lot. But I'm in too deep to back out now.* "Law library. Got it."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor watched Driver’s hands on the wheel. White-knuckled, steady, too steady for a normal person at one-thirty in the morning. Noor did not mistake that for innocence. It was only a body doing what bodies did when fear became routine.

Noor opened the hidden folder again.

The map was crude, but it matched the paper sketch from the porch rail: the law library’s service entrance behind the county parking garage, the after-hours drop box, the clerk’s window, the blue utility cart that blocked the side stair at night. Noor tapped the circled time with a fingernail.

1:35.

Riva.

Noor checked the retired clerk’s ID photo again. The name matched the manifest file. The badge number matched a footnote in the public filing packet. Noor ran the hash against the source’s thumb drive, then against the external backup, then against the bait drive still taped inside the coffee can.

All three matched.

The archive was real.

The world was not.

Noor ate another spoonful of peanut butter straight from the jar, then chased it with a cracker. The cracked spoon scraped their teeth. Noor did not care. The sugar and fat made the fear more physical, more honest.

“Sleep later,” Noor muttered. “Names now.”

Noor pulled the editor’s phone from the metal pouch and powered it on. The screen flared too bright in the cab. Noor shielded it with their sleeve and went straight to the message log.

The ghost’s last text still sat there.

THE OMBUDSMAN IS ON THE LIST TOO.

Noor typed: Then where is the source?

The reply came before the cursor finished blinking.

YOU LOOKED AWAY.

Noor’s stomach went flat.

They powered the phone off, dropped it into the pouch, and zipped it shut. Then Noor lifted the coffee can from under the bench and peeled back the duct tape. The tracker inside blinked red, patient as a heartbeat. Noor turned it over with two fingers and saw the thin Bluetooth label beneath the battery seal.

Not just GPS.

A beacon.

Noor’s breath fogged the window.

“They didn’t track the truck,” Noor said. “They tracked the can.”

Noor looked at Driver.

“I carried it into the alley,” Noor said. “I left it where I thought it was safe. I put it under the seat. I brought it here.” Noor’s voice went low, almost to themselves. “They wanted me to bring it inside.”

Noor slid the tracker into the metal pouch with the phones and drove the lid closed hard.

“We’re not going to the ombudsman,” Noor said. “We’re not going to the paper. We’re going to the law library. The clerk’s box is public, time-stamped, and stupid enough to accept an affidavit before dawn if the person at the window has the right name.”

Noor checked the mirrors again.

The river road was dark. Streetlights made the slush look like broken glass. No white truck. No dark sedan. No headlights behind them that stayed the same distance too long.

“Take the river road,” Noor said. “Under the bridge. Then the second left before the tire shop. Do not stop if someone waves.”

Noor pulled the map into their lap and traced the route with a fingernail.

The law library sat behind the county parking garage, a low concrete block with service doors that had not been painted since the nineties. Noor had used it once for a municipal budget story, when the records clerk had been a woman named Riva who still believed the public had a right to know where the money went. The source’s hidden folder said Riva was retired. The folder also said she left a stamp in the back office.

Noor did not know whether to believe it.

They believed the hashes.

They believed the timestamps.

They believed the boot print.

They believed the fear.

The garage appeared first, a squat yellow box lit by sodium lamps. The law library entrance was around the back, behind the blue cart and the chain-link fence. Noor had Driver stop under the stairwell where the cameras had a blind spot from the overhang.

Noor sat still for ten seconds.

Fifteen.

Twenty.

No headlights. No engine moving. No footsteps on concrete.

Noor checked the external backup drive in their hand. Then they checked the source’s thumb drive in the pouch. Then the bait drive inside the coffee can, still taped, still ticking with the tracker’s tiny red blink.

Noor picked up the iron poker.

“We’re not going to the front,” Noor said. “I’m going to the service door. You keep the engine on. If I’m not back in five minutes, take the coffee can to the library drop box and leave. If someone approaches the truck, drive. If they say my name, drive.”

Noor looked at Driver.

“If you’re clean, you’ll do it anyway.”

Noor opened the door before Driver could answer.

The cold outside was sharp and wet. Noor kept the flashlight off and used the garage lights to cross the gravel. The service door had a scratched steel keypad and a key card reader that had been added in the wrong place. Noor tried the key card from the dock office.

Nothing.

Noor tried the code from the source’s note.

2240.

The lock clicked.

Inside, the corridor smelled of dust, toner, and old coffee. Noor moved slowly, poker low, flashlight in the other hand. The first door was propped open with a rubber wedge. Beyond it sat the clerk’s desk, empty. A mug stood near the monitor. Noor touched the side of it.

Warm.

Noor’s pulse jumped, but Noor did not stop.

The terminal screen was dark. Noor woke it. A login box blinked.

CLERK - RIVA - OFF DUTY.

Noor did not guess the password. Noor opened the source’s thumb drive through the read-only blocker and plugged it into the front port. The hidden folder appeared. Inside was a file named LOCAL TERMINAL LOGS. Noor opened it.

The library’s after-hours system had been accessed at 12:49.

1:03.

1:11.

1:17.

Noor checked the call records from the editor’s phone against the dock switchboard photos. The times lined up. The ghost had used the library terminal to send the text from the source’s number. The ghost had been inside this room before Noor.

Noor opened the next file.

PUBLIC FILING PACKET.

It was formatted like a legal affidavit: manifest, bank transfers, meeting logs, phone records, hashes, timestamps. The first page listed Noor’s name. The second listed Driver’s. The third listed the editor’s. The fourth listed the ghost.

Noor printed it.

The dot-matrix printer shrieked to life. Noor watched the packet feed out page by page, each line a small mechanical confession. Noor stapled the pages together and placed the source’s thumb drive beside them. Noor did not leave the external backup. Not yet.

Noor opened the bottom drawer of the clerk’s desk.

A red stamp sat there, wrapped in a rubber band.

Noor took it and pressed it against the filing slip. The mark was ugly and official.

STAMPED.

Noor checked the time.

1:38.

Noor’s jaw tightened.

Late, but not impossible.

Noor smiled once, without humor.

Noor slid the packet through.

Then Noor hesitated.

Noor pulled the bait drive from the coffee can and held it. The original encrypted container. The confession. The thing that had started as evidence and had become a trap. Noor looked at the slot.

If the ghost came for it, they would have to open the box.

If they opened the box, they would have to know it was there.

Noor did not drop it.

Instead, Noor took a pen from the desk and wrote on the filing slip:

COPY OF ARCHIVE UPLOADED TO PUBLIC BOX. ORIGINAL WITH AFFIANT.

Noor photographed the slip, then left the bait drive inside the packet. Noor sealed the envelope with tape from the drawer and slid it through the box.

The slot swallowed it with a soft metal sound.

Noor stood there, breathing too fast.

Noor had just left the original drive in a public box.

Noor had just made themselves a target.

Noor had just made the story real.

Noor checked the external backup in their pocket. Still there. The source’s thumb drive had gone with the packet. The editor’s phone was dead in the pouch. The tracker was dead in the pouch. The coffee can was empty.

Noor walked back to the truck.

The alley was still empty. The white utility truck that had been at the dock was gone. The bakery door was dark. The garage stairwell cast a long black shape across the gravel.

Noor got in and shut the door.

“I filed,” Noor said.

Noor did not look at Driver. Noor looked at the mirrors.

Noor looked at the empty passenger seat where the source had been.

Noor looked at the back road.

Then Noor saw it.

A hooded figure at the side stair, moving fast, one hand pressed to their ribs. The jacket was too dark to be sure, but the way the body favored the left side matched the source. Noor remembered the cut above their brow. Remembered the trembling hand. Remembered the line: If your driver is clean, I’ll wait here.

Noor unlocked the door.

“Stay in the cab,” Noor said, voice low.

Noor got out.

The cold hit again. Noor crossed the gravel with the poker and flashlight, not shining it on the figure, not shining it at the road. Noor kept the beam angled down.

The source stopped at the bottom of the stairwell.

Their face was pale under the hood. The cut above their brow had reopened. A thin line of blood ran down their jaw. No tracker. No phone. No weapon that Noor could see.

“You followed me,” Noor said.

The source’s breath fogged. “I came back.”

“You disappeared.”

“I was being followed.”

Noor’s eyes moved to the street. “By whom?”

The source looked past Noor, toward the truck. “By the man who knows your name.”

Noor’s hand tightened on the poker.

The source raised both hands. “Noor. Listen to me. The box isn’t enough. The ghost has people at the courthouse. If they pull the packet tonight, they’ll say it was fabricated. Noor did not move.

“You said the drive was bait,” Noor said.

“It was.”

“You said the fire hall was watched.”

“It is.”

“You said the ombudsman was on the list.”

The source’s eyes flicked toward the library. “And you filed anyway.”

Noor’s voice went quiet.

“No,” Noor said. “I filed because I ran out of clean places.”

The source winced.

But Noor knew what the night wanted.

Noor knew what fear wanted.

Noor knew what a story wanted.

Noor turned back to the source.

“Get in,” Noor said.

The source shook their head. “If your driver is—”

“Noor’s voice cracked like a whip. “I said get in.”

The source looked at the truck, then at Noor.

Noor stepped closer.

“You left me in a cabin with an open window,” Noor said. “You put my name on a drive. You put their name on a manifest. You watched me wait three hours. You lied by omission, and you nearly got us both killed.”

The source’s face changed.

Noor’s voice dropped.

“But you came back.”

The source did not answer.

Noor opened the passenger door.

The source hesitated.

Noor held the door open.

“I am not leaving you outside,” Noor said. “Not tonight. Not while I still have a story to finish.”

The source slid inside.

Noor shut the door before the source could speak.

Noor looked at Driver.

“We’re going to the courthouse annex,” Noor said. “Not the fire hall. Not the paper. Not the trailhead. The annex has a public clerk, a night drop, and a filing window that opens at six.” Noor’s jaw worked. “If we can get the deposition transcript and file it before dawn, the story cannot be buried as a rumor. It becomes a record.”

Noor checked the mirrors.

The alley mouth remained dark.

Noor’s hands were steady.

They were steady the awful way they got steady when there was no other choice.

Noor reached into the padded case and pulled out the external backup drive. Noor held it for one second, feeling its weight. Then Noor placed it on the bench between Driver and the source.

“If anyone takes this,” Noor said, “the story dies with them.”

Noor looked at the source.

“You know where the transcript is?”

The source nodded. “Basement archive. Room B. The clerk keeps the old ministerial files in a red binder.”

Noor looked at Driver.

“Drive,” Noor said. “And do not stop for anyone who says my name.”

The truck rolled forward.

Noor sat back against the seat and let the heater blow warm air across their hands. The fear did not go away. It only became a thing Noor carried with care, like the drive, like the receipt, like the poker across Noor’s knees.

Noor opened the notepad and wrote:

PUBLIC FILING COMPLETE.
SOURCE ALIVE.
DRIVER UNKNOWN.
GHOST ACTIVE.

Then Noor added one last line:

SLEEP AT SIX.

Noor checked the time.

1:42.

Four hours and eighteen minutes.

Noor looked out the window at the city sliding past, dark windows, wet streets, traffic lights changing for no one. Somewhere behind them, the library drop box sat with a red stamp and an encrypted drive. Somewhere ahead, the courthouse annex waited. Somewhere out there, the ghost had a key, a badge, and a list of names.

Noor’s name was on it.

Driver’s name was on it.

The source’s name was on it.

Noor closed the notepad.

“We’re going to get the transcript,” Noor said. “Then we file again. Then we sleep.”

Noor looked at Driver.

“Unless someone decides to make it difficult.”

The truck turned onto the river road.

Noor kept their hand on the poker.

Noor kept their eyes on the mirrors.

And Noor did not look away.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I grip the wheel, my knuckles white. The external drive sits on the bench between me and the source, a silent, heavy presence. dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang pulled the earpiece from her ear and let it dangle against her coveralls. The absent humming stopped. She wiped her hands on a rag, leaving a gray smear of coolant paste, and fixed the junior officer with the flat, unblinking look she usually reserved for miscalibrated sensors.

"No," she said. "But you're clearly pleased with it, so let's take it apart before you file it."

She turned to the nearest console and slapped the atmosphere inventory up on the screen. Numbers, sharp and unromantic. "Ring habitable volume is sixteen thousand cubic meters. One standard atmosphere, twenty-two degrees Celsius, roughly nineteen thousand kilograms of gas. Nineteen tonnes. Our all-up mass is thirty-eight thousand tonnes. You are proposing to push thirty-eight thousand tonnes with nineteen tonnes of room-temperature air."

She took a grease pencil from behind her ear and did the arithmetic in the margin of the display. "Our vents are relief valves, not thrust chambers. Choked flow through a hole gives you maybe three hundred meters per second. If I machined you a perfect de Laval nozzle and plumbed it aft, the thermal energy in that room-temperature gas tops out around seven hundred meters per second, and we don't have that nozzle. Take the best case. Mass ratio is one point zero zero zero five. The natural log of that is essentially the same number. Seven hundred meters per second times zero point zero zero zero five—"

She capped the pencil. "A third of a meter per second. Less than we burn in a routine desaturation puff. You would move this ship by roughly the amount a tired tugboat nudges a barge. That is your weeks."

She leaned back, still unhurried. "Now the part you skipped. That nineteen tonnes isn't just 'air.' It's the working fluid for the entire environmental loop. Humidity recovery, trace contaminant scrubbing, thermal convection in the equipment bays that still use cabin air. You vent it, you vent every liter of water vapor we were about to condense, and you break the loop until we can repressurize, which we cannot do because the gas is in vacuum. Gone. Not recoverable. You do not get it back at the destination."

Her tone stayed level, but it did not soften. "And you do not 'wear suits for a few days.' The transit is weeks. EVA suits carry consumables for eight-hour excursions, not weeks-long coasts. The CO2 scrubbing cartridge is sized for one crew member working hard, for hours. You want them to live in a rubber suit, drinking from a straw, pissing into a bag that only functions because the suit holds pressure, all while the hydroxide saturates and their own waste heat cooks them? That is not a shortcut. That is a slower, stiffer way to die."

She tapped the schematic where the rotating ring met the central spine. "If you vent from the ring, you apply an off-axis force to a spinning structure. Hello nutation. We would burn more attitude propellant damping the wobble than your boost produced. If you try to duct it to the spine instead, you have to move nineteen tonnes of one-atmosphere gas through a rotary joint. The pressure drop alone would stall the flow before you got half of it out, and the compressor would eat the reactor margin we need for the actual engines."

Hoang set the manifold component back down on the tarp and picked up her driver. "This vessel runs on Newton's laws and a closed life-support budget, not on cleverness. We do not trade the crew's atmosphere for a third of a meter per second. If you want less transit time, bring me a burn plan with real propellant, real specific impulse, and a positive mass margin. Do not bring me a plan to suffocate everyone to move the ship less than the recoil of a docking clamp."

She glanced at the junior officer, eyebrow raised again. "Do I make myself clear? Now hand me the nine-millimeter seal driver. And next time, bring the math before you bring me a way to kill us all."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang did not sigh. She had trained herself out of sighing at junior officers sometime around her second doctorate. She set the grease pencil down on the console beside the atmosphere inventory, then turned her free hand palm-up and waited.

"Nine-millimeter," she said, mild as a coolant loop at equilibrium. "You can be earnest and still pass me tools."

She let the silence stretch for exactly one breath longer than politeness required, then lowered her hand and turned back to the schematic.

"Here is the thing you are not hearing. You keep saying 'save so much time' as if time can be bought with suffering. It cannot. Time is delta-v, and delta-v is mass expelled through a nozzle at a given exhaust velocity. You spent nineteen tonnes in your head and called it free. It is not free. It is the only atmosphere this vessel will ever have."

She tapped the numbers.

"Best case, perfect nozzle we do not possess: zero point three five meters per second. Actual case, through relief valves, off-axis through a spinning ring, fighting rotary-joint pressure drop: less, and you would burn more attitude propellant damping the nutation than the boost produced. Now trajectory. A third of a meter per second changes our arrival state by minutes. Perhaps an hour, if the geometry is generous. Weeks is three orders of magnitude away. If the nav solution said a week, the nav solution would be broken, and venting the air would not repair it."

She turned the flat look back on the junior officer.

"That is the reward. It is a rounding error. Now the cost. We already walked through the suits, but since you are attached to the idea: they are eight-hour tools, not habitats. Their CO2 cartridges, their water, their thermal loops all assume you go back inside. The transit is weeks. There is no version of 'wear suits for a few days' that becomes true because the calendar is inconvenient. You will exhaust the scrubbing capacity, then the thermal margin, then the crew. Meanwhile you have vented every kilogram of water vapor we were about to condense, killed humidity recovery, killed trace contaminant scrubbing, and killed convection cooling for half the electronics that still use cabin air. There is no make-up gas. The atmosphere goes out the nozzle and does not come back."

She shrugged, a small, economical movement.

"So no. It is not worth the risk, because there is no time to save and the price is everyone. Risk is a gamble that might pay. This is a scheduled casualty with extra steps. If you want less transit time, bring me a burn plan with real propellant, real specific impulse, and a positive mass margin. Bring me the nine-millimeter seal driver. And next time, put the rocket equation next to the big idea. If the delta-v does not survive contact with arithmetic, neither will we."

She turned back to the coolant loop and fitted her driver to the manifold bolt.

"Clear enough, or do you want it in Newtons?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I hesitate, looking down at my boots.* "No, Chief. Clear enough." *I finally spot the tool she wants.* "Here's the... nine millimeter seal driver." *I hand it over, feeling a bit deflated but also like I've learned something important.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang took the driver without looking up. She turned it once in the harsh bay light, checked the tip against the bolt head, and felt the solid click of a proper fit. The driver she had been using—an eight-millimeter, too small, would have cammed out and rounded the bolt—went back into the roll with a flick of her wrist.

"Don't look like you lost a credit chip," she said, fitting the tip into the bolt. "You brought me a number instead of a feeling. That's already better than half the bridge. The number was wrong by three orders of magnitude, but it was a number."

She jerked her chin at the console, where the atmosphere inventory still glowed. "Nineteen tonnes, and it bought us a third of a meter per second. Remember that the next time something sounds free."

She leaned her weight against the driver, breaking the seal with a sharp grunt of effort, then backed the bolt out in steady quarter-turns. Coolant paste hissed faintly as the manifold relaxed.

"Here's the useful part. You want to save transit time? Good. That's the right instinct. Aim it at something real. The propulsion section has a reaction mass budget and a specific impulse curve. Go pull the burn plan. Find me a maneuver that trades propellant we actually have for delta-v we actually need, with a positive mass margin at the end. If you can shave a day without turning the habitat into a vacuum chamber, I'll sign it and we'll run it."

She paused, glanced at the junior officer, and the corner of her mouth twitched—not quite a smile, but the absence of a scowl.

"Until then, you can hold the inspection lamp. Steady. If the light moves, I will blame you for the stripped thread, and I will be right."

She turned back to the coolant loop, driver seated, and started the slow, patient work of reassembly.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang wiped her hands on the rag until the worst of the coolant paste was gone, then took the tablet. She held it under the work lamp, thumb scrolling once, twice, and stopped at the line where the delta-v figure sat: 340 m/s.

"Three forty," she said. She did not raise her voice. She did not need to. "That is your exhaust velocity, not your delta-v. You have taken the speed the gas leaves the nozzle—or the speed of sound at the throat—and labeled it the speed the ship gains. Those are different numbers. They have always been different numbers."

She set the tablet on the console beside the atmosphere inventory and picked up the grease pencil. Under the figures she wrote:

Δv = vₑ · ln(m₀/m_f)

"Let's finish your own arithmetic. Nineteen thousand kilograms of gas. Thirty-eight million kilograms of ship. Initial mass, thirty-eight million nineteen thousand. Final mass, thirty-eight million. Mass ratio, one point zero zero zero five. Natural log of that is four point nine nine nine times ten to the minus four. Call it five times ten to the minus four. Multiply by your three hundred forty meters per second."

She capped the pencil.

"Zero point one seven meters per second. Not three hundred forty. Zero point one seven. That is the entire ship. Now your angle. If you vent thirty degrees off the thrust axis, cosine thirty is zero point eight seven, so you keep zero point one five. At forty-five degrees you keep zero point one two. You do not get to throw the gas sideways and still claim the full vector along the direction we care about. And if that vent is on the ring, we are back to nutation: you will burn more attitude propellant damping the wobble than this maneuver produces. Duct it aft through the rotary joint instead and the pressure drop at your compression ratio stalls the flow before half the gas is gone, while the compressor eats the reactor margin that runs the scrubbers."

She tapped the compression ratio field on the tablet.

"Now this. Where does the compression come from? You have no compressor train rated to move nineteen tonnes of air, no high-pressure bottles, and no thermal margin. The ring is a shirt-sleeve habitat at one atmosphere. It is not a composite-overwrapped pressure vessel. You start pumping the habitat down into a bottle, you are pulling the crew's air out of the room and spending megawatt-hours of reactor power to warm the hull. Adiabatic compression makes the gas hot, yes, and then that heat soaks into the structure and radiates away. You are burning electricity to squeeze the atmosphere so you can throw it out the back a little faster. That is not propulsion. That is a very expensive sigh."

She looked at the junior officer, flat and level.

"And it still does not change the suits. The transit is weeks. EVA suits are eight-hour tools. You have not fixed that because you found a bigger number for the gas. You have just made the suffocation more energetic."

She set the tablet down on the console, already turning to the manifold.

"Erase this before it gives somebody hope. Then go to the propulsion section. Pull the reaction mass inventory and the specific impulse curve. Bring me a burn plan that trades propellant we actually have for delta-v we actually need, with a positive mass margin. That is how you save time. Not by turning the habitat into a balloon animal."

She fitted the driver to the next bolt.

"Lamp. Steady."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little, feeling my cheeks get hot.* "Right. Exhaust velocity, not delta-v." *I grab my tablet and furiously start erasing the numbers.* "Got it, Chief. Propulsion section. Burn plan." *I hold the lamp as steady as I can, trying to make myself useful.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang did not look up at the sound of furious erasing. She finished the quarter-turn on the bolt she had started, felt the driver seat fully, and gave it a final torque. The flange relaxed another fraction of a millimeter. Only then did she shift her attention to the light.

"Down," she said. "Tilt it. There." The beam lay flat across the sealing surface, picking out the fresh seal and the machined grooves of the manifold. "Steady."

She reached for the next bolt, but paused long enough to fix the junior officer with a level look.

"You got there. Exhaust velocity is what the gas does. Delta-v is what the ship does. The rocket equation is the exchange rate between them. Burn that in, because it is the only reason you are still breathing."

She jerked her chin at the tablet.

"Scrub it clean if you want, but scrub it because it is wrong, not because I looked at you flat. Then write the correct line beside it. Nineteen thousand kilograms of atmosphere. Thirty-eight million kilogram ship. Three hundred forty meters per second exhaust, if you had a nozzle and a compressor train and a reactor with margin to spare. Mass ratio one point zero zero zero five. Natural log, five times ten to the minus four. Delta-v, zero point one seven meters per second. Before cosine losses. Before nutation eats it. Before the rotary joint stalls the flow and the compressor steals power from the scrubbers. Keep it as a warning label, not a wish."

She turned back to the manifold and fitted the driver to the next bolt.

"When this seal is buttoned up, you are done with the lamp. Go to the propulsion office. Pull the reaction mass inventory—tank by tank, not the summary page. Get the specific impulse curve for the main drive across its throttle range, and note the power draw at each point, because the reactor has to keep the scrubbers running while you are burning. Then build me a burn plan. Pick a real maneuver, departure or arrival, integrate the trajectory, and show me three numbers: delta-v gained, propellant spent, and mass margin left at the end. Positive margin. Zero is a ghost story, and negative is a murder-suicide pact with extra steps."

She leaned her weight into the driver. The bolt turned smoothly, the seal compressing with a faint hiss of coolant paste.

"If the honest plan needs more reaction mass than we have, bring me that too. I would rather look at a shortfall than sign a lie. What I will not do is trade nineteen tonnes of the only atmosphere this ship will ever have for a rounding error and a slow suffocation in a rubber suit."

The bolt seated. She backed the driver out, rolled her shoulder, and reached for the next seal on the tarp.

"Lamp steady. And junior—bring me the math next time, before you bring me a way to kill us all."

She did not wait for a reply. The coolant pumps went on humming their indifferent, life-supporting hum, and Chief Engineer Hoang went back to the patient work of keeping the ship alive.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang seated the final bolt with a controlled grunt of effort, then rolled her shoulder and reached for the next seal on the tarp. The coolant loop gave a soft, equalizing hiss as the flange drew down. She did not look up immediately; she let the silence stretch the way she let a pressure reading settle before she trusted it.

"Agreed," she said at last.

She picked up the grease pencil and tapped it once against the console, leaving a small gray dot beside the atmosphere inventory.

"You can take the burn plan forward. That is the correct instinct, and I will not pretend otherwise. But you will take it forward on my terms, because the difference between a burn plan and a casualty list is a set of conditions nobody is allowed to skip. Listen."

She held up a finger, then a second, ticking them off.

"One. Reaction mass comes from the propulsion tanks. Tank by tank, cross-checked against the propulsion chief's logs. The habitat atmosphere is not propellant, not make-up gas, and not a reservoir. The environmental interlocks stay armed. If I find a single valve on the ring cracked for your maneuver, the plan is dead and we start over with you reading me the emergency procedures."

"Two. You will pull the specific impulse curve for the main drive across its entire throttle range, and you will note the reactor power draw at every point. Then you will prove to me that life support keeps full margin for the whole burn. Scrubbers, thermal loop, water recovery. The drive does not eat the air plant's lunch. No margin, no burn."

"Three. You will sit with the navigation officer and integrate the trajectory using current mass properties. Include the ring's inertia tensor and the spin axis. Any maneuver that induces nutation beyond the attitude system's damping authority is rejected. We are not buying a shorter trip with a spin we cannot stop."

"Four. You will show me three numbers and three only: delta-v gained, propellant expended, and mass margin remaining at the end. Positive margin. Zero is a fairy tale.
