Negative is a murder-suicide pact with extra steps. If the honest arithmetic says we do not have the reaction mass, you bring me the shortfall. I would rather stare at a gap than sign a lie."

"Five. You plan. You do not execute. Nothing goes to the bridge, nothing gets uploaded to the flight computer, without my signature and the Captain's. You are authorized to think, calculate, and ask. You are not authorized to light this ship's engine."

She fitted the driver to the next bolt and leaned her weight against it, breaking the seal with a sharp, metallic creak.

"Meet those, and I will read your burn plan with an open mind and a clean conscience. Miss one—any one—and I will scrap it myself, and you will spend the next watch recalibrating CO2 sensors by hand until you understand why."

She backed the bolt out, rolled it between her fingers, and set it in the tray.

"Lamp steady. And take the tablet with you. Keep the corrected line on it. Nineteen thousand kilograms of atmosphere. Zero point one seven meters per second. That is the exchange rate. You do not get to forget it, and neither do I."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Yes, Chief. Understood." *I nod, taking all her conditions in. I pick up my tablet, making sure the corrected numbers are still there. It's a lot, but I'm determined.* "I'll get started right away."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang gave a single, economical nod, the sort she might use to acknowledge a correct torque value. She set the driver down on the tarp and wiped her hands on the rag, leaving fresh gray streaks on the cloth.

"Good," she said. "Then start with the tanks. Tank by tank. The summary page rounds to the nearest hundred kilos and calls it a day. I want ullage, temperature, and the last calibration date on every gauge. Then the specific impulse curve across the full throttle range. Then the reactor load, with life support at full margin—scrubbers, thermal loop, water recovery. In that order. If you bring me a delta-v number before you bring me a propellant number, I will know you skipped the hard part."

She reached for the next seal and seated it in the groove with the flat of her thumb, checking the fit before she trusted it.

"Log the draft in the engineering queue under my name. Mark it 'draft—not for upload.' Nothing goes to the bridge without my signature and the Captain's. And if the arithmetic says we are short, you bring me the shortfall. You do not go looking for the missing mass in the habitat. We have had this conversation. I do not intend to have it twice."

She picked up the driver again, fitted it to the bolt, and began threading it by hand, feeling for the cross-thread before she put any weight on the tool.

"You're done with the lamp. Set it on the tarp, carefully. If you crack the lens, it comes out of your next watch. Take the tablet with you. Keep the corrected line on it: nineteen thousand kilograms of atmosphere, zero point one seven meters per second. Determination is not a propellant. Bring me mass, not enthusiasm."

She did not look up. The coolant pumps went on humming their indifferent, life-supporting hum, and Chief Engineer Hoang returned to the patient work of keeping the ship alive.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I carefully place the lamp on the tarp, making sure not to crack the lens. My head is swimming with all the details, but I'm excited. This is a real project, even if my first idea was... really bad.* "Yes, Chief. Tank by tank. I'll get that data." *I turn and head out of the bay, pulling up the propulsion section schematics on my tablet as I go.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang did not watch the hatch cycle. She heard it—the soft thump of the pressure seal, the hiss of the bay equalizing behind him—but her eyes were on the bolt she had started by hand. She felt the threads catch clean, with no cross-threading, and only then did she reach for the torque wrench.

She set the wrench to forty-two newton-meters, the value stamped on the manifold flange, and tightened the bolt in three smooth pulls. Then the next, and the next, working the star pattern the way the maintenance manual insisted and the way she would have done even if it had not. The flange drew down evenly. Coolant paste squeezed out in a thin, uniform bead.

When the last bolt was torqued, she isolated the secondary loop and ran a pressure-decay check. The gauge held at three hundred kilopascals for sixty seconds without a twitch. She swept the ultrasonic probe along the seam anyway, listening for the hiss of a leak too small to move a needle. Nothing. She logged the entry with a stylus: *Secondary coolant loop manifold seal replaced. Leak check nominal. Atmosphere inventory unchanged.*

Only then did she glance at the console. Nineteen thousand and four kilograms, give or take the resolution of the mass sensors. The interlock status light glowed a steady, reassuring green: all ring vents sealed, environmental loop closed. She had checked it three times since the plan had been floated, and she would check it again before the end of the watch. Habit, not paranoia. The two felt the same from the inside.

She pulled up the engineering queue. There it was, logged under her name: *Burn Plan Draft — Junior Officer — DRAFT, NOT FOR UPLOAD.* She opened it. The summary page was still blank, but the header already carried the corrected line she had dictated: *19,000 kg atmosphere / 38,000,000 kg ship / v_e 340 m/s / Δv 0.17 m/s.* It had not been erased. It sat there like a warning label, exactly as she had instructed.

Hoang allowed herself a single grunt, somewhere between approval and acknowledgment. The junior officer had brought her a terrible idea and a correctable mistake. That was survivable. Enthusiasm was not a propellant, but it could be pointed at a real problem, and she had just handed him one.

She set the tablet down and turned back to the coolant loop, wiping the excess sealant from the flange with a clean rag. In the back of her mind, the real numbers were already turning over. The propulsion tanks held, by her last reconciliation, somewhere near four hundred and ten tonnes of reaction mass—water, mostly, with the argon reserve for the attitude system kept separate and untouchable. The main drive's specific impulse curve topped out around nine thousand seconds at full throttle, which meant an effective exhaust velocity near ninety kilometers per second. To buy a single kilometer per second of delta-v for a thirty-eight-thousand-tonne hull, the rocket equation demanded a mass ratio of about one point zero one one. Roughly four hundred and twenty tonnes of reaction mass.

They were short. Not by much—maybe ten or fifteen tonnes, depending on how the ullage and tank temperatures settled out—but short. She had known that before the junior officer had walked in with his plan. She would let him find it himself. The arithmetic was the only teacher that never lied, and the shortfall was the lesson.

Hoang capped the solvent bottle and washed the coolant paste from her hands at the wash station, methodically, up to the elbows. The bay was quiet again except for the pumps and the faint, ever-present vibration of the life support system doing its indifferent, essential work. She had a coolant loop to button up, a reactor margin to verify, and a junior officer's burn plan to tear apart when he finally brought it to her.

It was, she reflected as she reached for the inspection lamp and set it back in its bracket, a good day's work. Or it would be, once somebody did the math correctly.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I'm back in the engineering bay, my tablet clutched in my hand. I've got the data Chief Hoang asked for, and my numbers are looking good. I think. I see her wiping down the manifold, looking focused.*

"Chief," *I say, trying to sound confident.* "I've got the tank inventories, and I've started on the specific impulse curves. Looks like we have more reaction mass than I thought, but the full throttle settings might be an issue with reactor margin."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang looked up from the manifold as the hatch cycled again. She set the solvent bottle down and took the tablet, angling it under the work lamp without asking. The corrected line was still there, right where she had made him put it: *19,000 kg atmosphere / 38,000,000 kg ship / vₑ 340 m/s / Δv 0.17 m/s*. She grunted, whether in approval or mere acknowledgment was impossible to tell.

"More than you thought is not a number," she said. She scrolled to the tank inventory. "Give me the total. Tank by tank, ullage corrected, temperature corrected, calibration dates attached. Not the summary page."

She read the column in silence for a moment, grease pencil tapping once against her thigh.

"Four hundred and six point eight tonnes," she said. "Call it four oh seven. My last reconciliation, done properly, said four hundred and ten point one. You are three tonnes lighter than my number, not heavier. You took the aft string's ullage at face value and did not correct for the cold soak. That tank farm has been sitting in the radiator shadow for two weeks; the propellant is denser than the raw volume says, which means there is less reaction mass in there than your table claims. Go back, apply the temperature correction, and check the calibration date on gauge four-B. If it is out of tolerance, you log it, you use the backup sensor, and you do not average the two."

She looked up, flat and level.

"Now the full throttle problem. You do not get to say full throttle is a reactor margin issue and then keep planning the burn as if you had it. The reactor's first job is the environmental loop. Scrubbers, thermal control, water recovery—full margin, always. The drive gets what is left after life support has eaten its fill. Non-essential loads can be shed: cargo handling, the machine shop, the number two hydroponics bay if the plants can take a few days of low light. Life support is not shed. So you find the highest throttle that fits inside that envelope, and you read the specific impulse at that throttle. It will not be nine thousand seconds. It will be lower. Lower Isp means more propellant for the same delta-v, and lower thrust means a longer burn. Both of those eat the time you were trying to save. Run it honestly, not optimistically."

She capped the grease pencil and set it on the console.

"And finish the curve. Every throttle notch: Isp, thrust, reactor draw, and radiator rejection limit. The radiators have to dump the drive's waste heat while the environmental loop is at full load. If heat rejection tops out, the loop backs up, the scrubbers cook, and we are back to suffocation with extra steps."

She tapped the tablet's edge against her palm.

"Four numbers when you come back. Delta-v gained. Propellant expended. Mass margin remaining. And reactor margin with life support at full draw. All positive. If the honest arithmetic says we are short, you bring me the shortfall. You do not go looking for the missing mass in the habitat. The ring stays sealed, the interlocks stay armed, and if I see a single valve cracked for your maneuver I will scrap the plan and put you on CO2 sensor duty until you can recite the emergency procedures in your sleep."

She turned back to the manifold and picked up a clean rag.

"You did the tank-by-tank. That was the assignment, and you did it. Now do it right. Bring me a burn plan that survives arithmetic, not one that needs the crew to hold its breath."

She began wiping the flange, the picture of a woman who had returned to the only work that mattered: keeping the air in and the pumps running.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My shoulders slump a little.* "Right. Temperature correction. Gauge calibration." *I take the tablet back, feeling a bit foolish for missing those details. She's not wrong though. I just focused on the big numbers.* "And the full throttle... Understood, Chief." *I head back out, the hum of the bay following me. More math. More details.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang finished wiping the flange and ran a gloved finger along the seam. The seal was clean, the bead of coolant paste uniform and unbroken. She stowed the solvent bottle and the rag, then keyed the pump startup sequence. The secondary loop whined up to pressure, the flow indicator climbing to ninety-four liters per minute. She watched the vibration trace for thirty seconds, saw nothing out of tolerance, and logged the repair complete: *Secondary coolant loop manifold seal replaced. Leak check nominal. System returned to service.*

Only then did she turn her full attention to the console.

She pulled her own propulsion inventory from the engineering archive—the one with temperature corrections already applied, the one she had reconciled two days prior. Four hundred and ten point one tonnes. She highlighted gauge four-B. Calibration date: current, good for another seventy-two hours. She made a note to have the junior cross-check the backup sensor anyway, because the primary had drifted once before and she did not trust a gauge simply because it had a fresh sticker on it.

Then she opened the specific impulse curve.

The display showed the familiar humped line. At one hundred percent throttle, specific impulse peaked at nine thousand seconds—effective exhaust velocity just under ninety kilometers per second—but the reactor draw column flashed amber: one hundred and eighty megawatts. Life support's baseline was forty. Radiator rejection at that power sat at ninety-eight percent of capacity, with no margin for the environmental loop's transient loads. Full throttle was a sprint, not a cruise, and the reactor would cook itself if they held it there for the days-long burn the junior was imagining.

She dragged the cursor down the throttle range. At eighty-eight percent, the amber cleared. Reactor draw: one hundred and fifty megawatts. Radiators: eighty-two percent. Specific impulse: eight thousand one hundred seconds. Exhaust velocity: seventy-nine and a half kilometers per second. Thrust: one point six meganewtons.

Hoang took the grease pencil and wrote in the margin of the display.

Initial mass: thirty-eight million kilograms. Propellant, corrected for temperature and ullage: four hundred and seven thousand kilograms—the junior would arrive at that number himself once he applied the cold-soak correction to the aft string. Final mass: thirty-seven million five hundred ninety-three thousand. Mass ratio: one point zero one zero eight. Natural log: zero point zero one zero seven nine. Delta-v: seventy-nine thousand five hundred times zero point zero one zero seven nine.

She capped the pencil.

Eight hundred and fifty-six meters per second. That was the absolute maximum, burning every kilogram of reaction mass in the tanks and leaving nothing for margin, nothing for contingency, nothing for the day a line cracked and they needed to move the ship to meet a rescue. And even that assumed they could hold eighty-eight percent throttle for the entire burn without the reactor margins degrading, which was optimistic.

She pulled the trajectory file. The navigation officer's notes were blunt: the transit was long because the window was cheap, not because the ship was slow. To cut weeks, they would need to close a phase-angle gap of nearly four degrees. That was a delta-v budget of two thousand two hundred meters per second. Two thousand two hundred. They had eight hundred and fifty-six, and only if they ran the tanks dry and the reactor at the edge of its continuous rating.

Hoang did not sigh. She had trained herself out of sighing at junior officers sometime around her second doctorate. She simply closed the trajectory file and opened a fresh optimization template, setting the initial parameters: current mass properties, ring inertia tensor included, spin axis defined, environmental interlocks locked out. She would let the junior bring her his corrected numbers. He would find the shortfall himself; the arithmetic was the only teacher that never lied. When he did, she would show him the throttle limit, the reactor margin, and the eight hundred and fifty-six meters per second that was the real price of a few days. Then they would see what the ship could honestly buy, with a positive margin at the end.

She glanced at the environmental status board. All ring vents sealed. Interlocks armed. Atmosphere holding at nineteen thousand and four kilograms. The pumps went on humming their indifferent, life-supporting hum.

Hoang reached for the inspection lamp and set it back in its bracket, then picked up the next item on the maintenance queue: a coolant filter change on the primary loop. There was always another seal to turn, another margin to verify. The ship ran on Newton's laws and a closed life-support budget, and it was her job to make sure neither ran out.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I'm back, tablet in hand, looking even more dejected than last time. I've been running the numbers all day. Chief Hoang is still working, humming a little under her breath.*

"Chief... I've got the numbers." *I hold out the tablet, not quite meeting her eyes.* "Even with the temperature corrections, and the optimal throttle setting... we're still short. Way short."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang set the torque wrench down on the tarp and took the tablet without a word. She angled it under the work lamp, scrolled through the corrected tank inventory, then opened the burn integration. Her eyes moved down the columns: ullage, temperature, calibration dates, throttle notch, specific impulse, thrust, reactor draw, mass remaining. She did not hurry. When she reached the bottom line, she grunted.

"Four hundred and nine point six tonnes," she said. "Corrected. That matches my reconciliation to within gauge tolerance. Good. You found the cold-soak correction on the aft string, and you checked four-B against the backup instead of averaging them. That is the first time today you have done the assignment instead of the outline of it."

She tapped the final figure with a greasy fingernail.

"Eight hundred and sixty-one meters per second. That is your absolute maximum, burning every usable kilogram in the propulsion tanks, at eighty-eight percent throttle, inside the reactor margin, with life support at full draw. Zero reserve. Zero contingency. Nothing held back for a line rupture, a rescue, or a navigation correction we have not thought of yet. If you want a positive margin—and you do—that number drops. Call it seven hundred and seventy meters per second with ten percent held back."

She pulled up the trajectory requirement and set it beside the burn plan.

"Now the requirement. Navigation wants two thousand two hundred meters per second to close the phase-angle gap and cut weeks off the transit. Two thousand two hundred. You have eight hundred and sixty-one if you strip the tanks bare. That is a shortfall of one thousand three hundred and forty meters per second. In propellant, you need about one thousand and thirty tonnes. You have four hundred and nine. You are short by roughly six hundred and twenty tonnes of reaction mass."

She capped the grease pencil and looked at the junior officer levelly.

"So. Way short is correct. But it is also the first honest number you have brought me since you walked in with a plan to suffocate the crew. You did not erase it. You did not go looking for the missing mass in the habitat. You did not come back with a bigger nozzle and a smaller crew. You brought me the shortfall. That is what an engineer does when the arithmetic says no. You write down 'no' with the reason attached, and then you find out what 'yes' actually costs."

She opened the optimization template she had queued and slid the tablet back across the console.

"Here is the useful part. We are not going to cut weeks. That answer is no, and it is final, and I will tell the Captain myself if I have to. But we might buy something smaller. Take this template. Set the reserve at ten percent—standard contingency, no arguments. Run the burn at eighty-eight percent throttle, inside the reactor envelope, with the environmental loop at full margin. Integrate the trajectory with the current mass properties and the ring's inertia tensor. Then bring me three numbers: maximum delta-v with positive margin, propellant expended, and arrival time saved."

She leaned back against the console, arms crossed.

"My guess? Hours. Maybe a day if the geometry is kind. If it is a day, we write it up, you and I both sign the cover sheet, and the Captain decides whether a day of transit is worth a third of our maneuvering reserve. If it is five minutes, we log it, close the file, and you go back to the coolant filters, because the ship still runs on sealed atmosphere and turned bolts, not on cleverness."

She glanced at the environmental board. All ring vents sealed. Interlocks armed. Nineteen thousand and four kilograms of air, holding steady.

"You did the work. Now finish it. And when you bring me the plan, bring me the shortfall too, if there is one. I would rather stare at a gap than sign a lie. Clear?"

She did not wait for an answer. She picked up the torque wrench and turned back to the primary loop filter, because there was always another seal to turn and another margin to verify.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Clear, Chief." *I grab the tablet, feeling a new kind of determination. It's not about being clever anymore, it's about being right. I'll find that number, even if it's just a few hours.* "I'll be back."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't look up. She worked the next gasket free with a plastic scraper, wiped it on her thigh, and laid it on the tarp inside its chalk outline.

"Two-tenths of a meter per second," she said. "That's what you're offering me. Give or take."

Then she did pull the earpiece out, because teaching moments deserved her full attention, and sat back on her heels.

"Run the arithmetic with me. This hull masses a hundred and twenty thousand tonnes. All the air inside it — every cubic meter at one atmosphere — comes to about fifty tonnes. Vent it through a perfect nozzle, which we don't have, at five hundred meters a second, which one-atmosphere blowdown won't give you. The rocket equation hands back about a fifth of a meter per second. You'd get more delta-v throwing manifold parts off the aft rail, and I'd only be mildly annoyed."

She ticked points off on greasy fingers.

"And it's not days of thrust. Pressure decays exponential — the first ten minutes is most of it, after that it's a whisper. Meanwhile the suits you want everyone living in have eight hours of scrubber before they need regeneration, and regeneration needs the pumps and the power you just vented overboard. The coolant in the loop behind you boils off at vacuum. Half the avionics on this deck aren't rated for it. And here's the part that actually kills us: there is no second tank of atmosphere to vent in reverse. Even if the math were kind, we'd arrive at the refinery weeks faster and with nothing left to brake with. Newtonian doesn't do 'we'll figure out stopping when we get there.' Fast is only faster if you can stop."

She held out her palm for the twelve-millimeter wrench.

"The idea isn't garbage — you just reinvented the cold-gas thruster. We carry them on the RCS ring, fed from high-pressure bottles, sized for the job, and nobody has to breathe them. Propellant is mass you can afford to lose. Atmosphere is mass you can't. Next time you bring me a proposal, bring the numbers with it. Now hold the light."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the scraper down and looked at the junior officer the way she looked at a crack in a pressure vessel — not angry, just measuring how deep it went.

"Worth the risk. That phrase is how crews die. Risk isn't a coin you flip for a prize, it's a line item. You price it or you don't."

She reached over to the tarp, picked up a chalk stub, and started writing on the deck plating where the tarp wouldn't cover it.

"Here's your ledger. Best case, you save three weeks on a nine-month transit. That's the prize. Now the cost column. One: every suit we own gets cycled hard for days, and suit failures in a vacuum are not survivable errors — they're fast ones. Two: thermal control goes to nothing. The coolant loop I'm holding right now flash-boils, the avionics cook themselves, and then your 'weeks faster' arrival is a derelict coasting past the refinery with a dead crew. Three, and write this one down: you arrive with no atmosphere, no margin, and no propellant to brake. The refinery tugs would have to catch us, if we're lucky, and nobody out here is lucky twice."

She tapped the chalk against the deck.

"Time is not the only currency. Margin is currency. Atmosphere is currency. You'd be spending all of them to buy three weeks, and the exchange rate is garbage. If transit time is actually a problem — and it might be, ask the Captain, not me — the honest answers are a bigger propellant load on the next resupply, a higher-thrust trajectory profile we plan from the start, or stripping mass. Real engineering. Slow, boring, and it doesn't kill anyone."

She handed back the chalk and pointed at the light again.

"You want to save the ship time? Save the ship first. Light."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I sigh, deflating a little.* "Yeah, okay, Chief. I get it." *I hold the light steady, trying to absorb everything she just said.* "So, no venting the atmosphere."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
"No venting the atmosphere," Hoang agreed. She took the manifold back and seated the new gasket with her thumbs, checking the seating edge by edge before torquing anything. "You'll notice you're still alive, and so is everyone else. That's the correct outcome of most good engineering decisions. Nobody throws a parade for them."

She worked the first bolt down in stages, crisscross, listening to the click of the torque wrench like other people listened to music.

"But I want you to understand something. I'm not telling you the idea was stupid. You saw a resource sitting idle and asked what it could do. That's the right instinct. That instinct is the whole job." She glanced up. "What you skipped was the ledger. Every resource on this boat is already doing a job. Air is life support. Water is shielding and drinking. Propellant is arrival. When you propose spending one, you have to say which job it stops doing, and whether the new job pays better. Venting the air asked fifty tonnes of drinking, breathing, thermal mass to buy you a fifth of a meter per second. That's a bad trade, and the numbers said so before anyone suited up."

She held out her hand for the light to shift left, then kept going.

"So here's your homework. You think transit time is worth chasing — fine. Draft me a real proposal. Mass budget, delta-v budget, where the propellant comes from, where the margin goes. If it survives my review, it goes to the Captain. If it doesn't, you'll have learned the ship's numbers, which is time better spent than most officers manage."

A faint smile, gone as fast as it came.

"Also, you're holding the light crooked. Left."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set down the torque wrench — carefully, in its chalk outline — and took the tablet. She read it in silence for a long moment, thumb scrolling, one eyebrow climbing in slow increments.

"Okay. First: you did numbers. That's genuine progress, and I'm not being sarcastic, which you'll learn to recognize. Second." She held the tablet up between two fingers like something found in a drain trap. "Where does your compression ratio come from? Walk me through it."

She turned the screen around and tapped the line item.

"This. You've got the air entering your nozzle at twelve atmospheres. The hull holds one. There is no compressor on this ship that makes twelve atmospheres out of one, and a compressor that could would draw megawatts and mass more than the shuttle bays. You've invented free pressure. Pressure is energy, and energy isn't a rounding error — it's the whole bill."

She handed the tablet back and stood, knees cracking, walking to the bulkhead display where the ship's mass budget hung like a wanted poster.

"Then there's this. Your delta-v calc assumes fifty tonnes of propellant at your exhaust velocity. Fine. But run the flow rate at one atmosphere through a throat of any sane size, and tell me how many seconds your thrust burn lasts. I'll save you the trouble — minutes. A 340 meter-per-second burn delivered over four minutes is nine-tenths of a g. Structural loading we can't take, and the crew ends up as paste against the aft bulkhead. Spread it over hours instead, and you need pressure and power we don't have. You can't have both the gentle burn and the free exhaust velocity. Pick one and watch the other eat your number."

She crossed her arms, leaning against the bulkhead.

"And the last line, the one I care about most. Your ledger still doesn't say where the 340 meters per second of stopping comes from. You spent everything getting fast. Now you're fast forever."

She let that sit, then picked the wrench back up.

"Redo it. One atmosphere blowdown, real nozzle efficiency, real burn duration, and a full delta-v budget including the braking burn. Bring me that, and you'll have done more honest arithmetic than half the officers aboard. Sit down if you want — the deck's comfortable and the light stays where it is."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I slump down onto the deck plating, pulling my tablet back.* "Right. Free pressure. Of course." *I start tapping at the screen, already trying to adjust my calculations.* "So I need to factor in the braking burn too, huh? This is... a lot more complicated than I thought."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang reached over and picked the work light up off the deck — it had ended up on its side, throwing a long shadow across her manifold — and clipped it to the overhead rail, aiming it down at the flange.

"Complicated," she said. "It was always this complicated. The simple version was a story you were telling yourself. The universe doesn't negotiate its complexity down. It just waits for you to stop paying attention, and then it hands you the bill."

She went back to the bolts, crisscross, click, click.

"Since you're sitting there anyway, here's the shape of the thing. Then I want the numbers from you, not from me." She held up one greasy finger. "Delta-v doesn't care about your plumbing. It's exhaust velocity times the log of your mass ratio, and that's the whole equation. You can spend it in four minutes or four months, pulse it, throttle it, shape the burn into a poem — the total doesn't move by a centimeter per second. Flow rate buys thrust, not velocity. That's the trap you fell into. You kept trying to buy delta-v with hardware arrangements, and delta-v doesn't take that currency."

Second finger.

"What the plumbing *does* decide is burn duration. Choked flow through a throat — sizing equation's in the ship's reference database, propulsion section, don't derive it yourself, that's how sign errors happen. Pick a throat, get a mass flow, divide your propellant by it. That's your burn clock."

Third finger.

"Blowdown means pressure and exhaust velocity die together. Your first minute is your best minute. Your last hour is a leak with ambitions. Integrate it properly or you'll flatter yourself by a factor of two."

She ran the torque wrench down the next bolt and sat back on her heels.

"And here's your anchor, so you know when you've landed on the right answer. Go pull the spec sheet on the RCS ring. We carry nitrogen bottles at three hundred bar — pressure we paid for on the ground, in tank mass and pump hours, because free pressure turned out to be a lie there too. One bottle masses about fifty kilos. Run it through the same rocket equation." A dry pause. "One bottle buys roughly what your entire atmosphere buys. Fifty tonnes of breathing air, matched by something you could carry under one arm. When your number comes out in that neighborhood, you'll know you did it honestly, and it'll sting a little. Let it. The equation doesn't care about your feelings — that's why we trust it."

She checked the seating edge of the gasket one more time, satisfied, and reached for the next component.

"Full ledger this time — burn, brake, suit-hours, thermal, and what it costs to replace the air at the refinery end, because somebody hauls that out on a tanker and the tanker doesn't fly for free. I want it before the relay window tomorrow. And keep the light steady — it's clipped now, so you've got both hands free to be wrong on paper instead of in space."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang finished torquing the last bolt, then sat back and actually looked at the officer — a long, appraising look, the kind she usually saved for welds.

"Alright," she said. "Here's what I'll sign, and it isn't your original plan, so read carefully."

She counted on her fingers.

"One: we don't touch cabin atmosphere. That's off the table permanently, not pending review — you found out why, and the numbers won't improve with enthusiasm. What we *can* do is a low-thrust assist using the RCS nitrogen ring. Your homework already told you what one bottle buys — a few tenths of a meter per second. Take thirty bottles off the resupply margin and you've got something real: not weeks, but maybe two days on this transit, and it's mass we budgeted to spend eventually anyway."

"Two: we draw from the *spare* bottles, never the ones feeding the RCS quads. Attitude control stays whole or the plan dies. I'll do the plumbing myself; you watch, you learn, you keep the checklist."

"Three: burn profile is continuous and gentle — milli-gs, spread over days. No suit work for the crew at large. We run it from the control room through hardline valves, and the only suited time is two people on the aft ring for hookups, four hours max, tethered, with me on one of those tethers."

"Four — and this is the condition that isn't negotiable: we plan the braking from day one. Every meter per second of assist gets a matching reserve held back for arrival. If the reserve ever dips below the brake requirement, the burn stops. Automatically. I'm putting an interlock on it, because people get romantic mid-burn and equations don't."

She stood, wiped her hands on a rag that had seen decades, and dropped it in the bin.

"Write that up — mass flow from three hundred bar bottles, total delta-v, burn schedule, brake reserve — and get it to me before the relay window. If the arithmetic holds, I'll take it to the Captain, and I'll put your name on it. First honest proposal gets the credit."

A pause.

"And if you'd pushed me on the atmosphere venting one more time, we'd be having a different conversation. Knowing what to refuse is half my job. Knowing what to modify so it's worth approving — that's most of the rest of yours. Now hand me the gasket chalk; you've got a proposal to write and I've got a loop to finish."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, relieved and a little stunned she's actually considering it.* "Yes, Chief! Understood. No atmosphere, spare nitrogen, gentle burn, and braking first." *I quickly jot down the main points on my tablet, already feeling the gears turning in my head.* "I'll have it for you before the relay window." *I hand her the chalk with a slightly shaky hand, already standing up and heading towards the door, eager to get to work.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took the chalk, watched the junior officer all but bounce off the doorframe on the way out, and shook her head — but there was no real disapproval in it. Enthusiasm was raw ore. Smelted, it made good engineers. Unsmelted, it made craters. She turned back to the manifold, marked the manifold's inspection date on the tarp edge, and started reassembling the secondary coolant loop.

She got about halfway through before the door hissed open again, and she spoke without looking up.

"Two things I forgot, and you're going to want them before you write."

She laid out the parts on the deck plating with her fingers like a butcher laying out cuts.

"First: put a *fuel accounting* page at the front. Not delta-v — bottles. How many we start with, how many each day of burn consumes, how many are left at the end. Delta-v is abstract; bottles are real, and the Captain thinks in real. Second: state your failure modes out loud, even the embarrassing ones. If a valve sticks open mid-burn, what happens? If a bottle heats up in sunlight and overpressures, what's the relief path? You don't have to solve them all — you just have to prove you *saw* them. A proposal that admits its own weak points gets taken seriously. One that pretends it has none gets put in a drawer, or worse, approved."

She finally glanced up.

"And eat something before the relay window. I've watched better officers than you write a mass budget on an empty stomach, and the numbers come out with fear in them. Fear doesn't belong in arithmetic."

She turned back to the loop, then added, almost as an afterthought:

"If you get stuck on the choked-flow sizing, the reference database has worked examples under 'cold gas — steady state.' Ignore the ones that assume two hundred bar; our bottles run three hundred and the throat sizing shifts accordingly. That's the kind of detail that separates a proposal from a wish."

The door hissed shut again. Hoang hummed back into her earpiece, off-key, and torqued the next bolt.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stop dead in my tracks, turning back towards her.* "Right! Fuel accounting, failure modes, and food." *I quickly pull out my tablet again, adding more notes to the already growing list. I feel a slight flush of embarrassment for almost forgetting those crucial points, but gratitude for her thoroughness.* "Thanks, Chief! I won't forget the food this time." *I really do feel a bit hungry now that she mentioned it.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang looked up from the coolant loop, and this time the look she gave was long enough that the junior officer actually stopped halfway through the door.

"Sit down for a minute. Not a request."

She waited until the officer was back on the deck plating before she went on.

"You just made a mistake and I want you to see it before it calcifies into a habit. I said 'eat something,' and you wrote it on a list next to choked-flow sizing and failure modes. It's not the same category. The list is for the ship. Food is for you. If you can't tell those apart yet, you'll end up skipping sleep to check bottle masses, and then the mass you're fudging is your own judgment."

She picked up the rag again, folded it once, methodical.

"Here's the actual last thing, and then I'm throwing you out. You thanked me for the thoroughness. Don't. What I gave you today wasn't generosity — it was the standard. Every officer on this boat gets held to it, and the ones who resent that don't last out here. The ones who thank me for it usually end up running their own departments someday, and then some kid comes to *them* with a plan to vent the atmosphere, and they'll remember how it felt to have their idea taken seriously enough to be torn apart properly."

She pointed the rag at the door.

"That's the whole chain. Somebody did it for me twenty years ago on a ship with worse coffee than this one. You'll do it for somebody in ten. Right now, your job is smaller: proposal, relay window, dinner between. In that order."

A short nod, dismissal, and then, as the officer reached the door:

"Officer. One more thing — and this one's free. When you run the numbers tonight and they come out worse than you hoped? Don't polish them. Bring me the ugly version. Ugly and true beats pretty and hopeful every single time, because pretty gets people killed about six months after I approve it. The ugly version is the one I can actually work with. Now go."

She turned back to the manifold, reseated the last component, and reached for the torque wrench. The earpiece went back in. The humming resumed, off-key and unbothered, and the secondary coolant loop ticked back toward whole.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stand there for a moment, absorbing her words, then nod slowly.* "Ugly and true. Got it, Chief." *I turn and head out of the bay, the door hissing shut behind me. My head is buzzing with calculations and a new understanding of what 'engineering' really means. I'll get that proposal done.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The door hissed shut. Hoang gave it three seconds of silence, then snorted quietly to herself and went back to the loop.

"Not bad," she said to the manifold, because the manifold didn't repeat gossip. "Not good yet. But not bad."

She finished the reassembly in another forty minutes, pressure-tested the loop at one and a half times operating, watched the gauges hold steady for a full five-count, and signed the maintenance log with the stub of pencil she kept zip-tied to the clipboard. The chalk deck-notes she photographed for the record, then scrubbed out with a palm. The deck didn't stay annotated. The lessons were supposed to.

Then she sat down at the engineering station, pulled up the RCS ring inventory, and did the homework she'd assigned the kid before the kid did it. That was the trick nobody told juniors about: a chief never approves a proposal she hasn't already run herself. Thirty bottles from the resupply margin, blowdown through a manifold tap, continuous milli-g burn spread over nine days. She got the answer in twenty minutes, and it came out about as advertised — two days saved, give or take, ugly and honest, with a brake reserve that held if the interlock held.

Two days. The kid had promised weeks and delivered two days, and the two days were real, which made them worth more than the weeks had ever been.

She filed it in a folder she kept for exactly this purpose and marked it *pending — junior proposal*. Then she checked the galley hours, confirmed the mess was still serving for another hour, and sent a one-line message to the junior officer's queue:

*Station time. Galley closes in 55 minutes. Proposal due tomorrow — eat first, write second. Numbers have fewer errors on a full stomach. — H.*

Then she pulled up the thermal control schedule, because somebody had to plan for the extra heat load of nine days of continuous RCS flow through an aft manifold, and if she didn't do it now it would become a surprise, and surprises on her deck were things that happened to other chiefs, the sloppy kind.

The earpiece went back in. The humming resumed.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I see the message pop up on my tablet and a small smile touches my lips.* "She really meant it about the food." *I quickly make my way to the galley, my mind still buzzing with calculations but also a new sense of purpose. This proposal is going to be solid.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The galley message sent, Hoang went back to the thermal schedule and worked it until the numbers stopped arguing with her. The aft manifold tap would add roughly four hundred watts of continuous heat load once the nitrogen started flowing — trivial on paper, less trivial when you remembered the radiators were sized for a ship that stood still. Nine days of milli-g burn meant nine days of extra pump duty on the secondary loop. The same loop she'd just rebuilt. She allowed herself a short, dry laugh at that, and scheduled a pre-burn inspection accordingly.

Then she pulled up the crew manifest and looked at the names on the aft-ring hookup team. Herself, obviously. And the junior officer, because the kid had earned the tether time and would learn more from four hours in a suit than from a month of proposals. She flagged the pairing in the schedule and noted the training requirement: vacuum protocol refresher, both parties, before the first bottle opened. She'd had enough close calls in thirty years to know that the dangerous moment isn't the burn. It's the wrench in a gloved hand near a fitting someone trusts too much.

The evening shift came and went. Hoang ate her own dinner at the engineering station — rice and rehydrated chicken, eaten with one hand, the other scrolling a supplier manifest for the next resupply window. Thirty bottles off the margin meant a line item she'd have to justify to the Quartermaster, and the Quartermaster thought in tonnage the way the Captain thought in days. She drafted that argument too, before anyone asked for it. Anticipation was cheaper than persuasion.

Around station midnight, with the bay quiet and the pumps singing their usual note, she opened the folder marked *pending — junior proposal* and read her own notes one more time. Two days. Real ones. She'd take them.

Before racking out, she queued a second message, scheduled to deliver at 0600 — because timing was also a lesson, and the kid didn't need a chief hovering all night:

*Interlock spec is in the shared drive, folder Hoang/interlocks. Steal the threshold logic, don't reinvent it. And when you write the brake reserve number, write it in bottles as well as delta-v. Bottles are what we'll actually be counting down on day nine. — H.*

She powered down the station, hung the rag, and checked the chalk lines on the deck one last time — clean, scrubbed, the plating innocent of the whole conversation. Good.

The ship hummed around her, ninety thousand tonnes of steel holding a thin warm skin of air against the dark, exactly as much as it was supposed to. No more, no less.

Hoang slept fine. She always did, when nothing on her deck was a surprise.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My alarm goes off, and I'm already halfway through my draft. The new message from Hoang pops up, and I read it, a small smile forming. "Okay, Chief. Interlocks and bottles." I add the new points to my mental checklist, already picturing how they'll fit into the proposal. Time to get back to those numbers.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The morning shift found Hoang in the control room before the junior officer's alarm had finished its second cycle, because the thermal schedule had produced one wrinkle overnight that she wanted eyes on before anyone got excited about thrust profiles.

The radiator bleed valves on the aft loop had a known habit — documented, filed, and never quite fixed — of sticking at partial open when they'd been idle past sixty days. Nine days of continuous RCS flow meant nine days of asking those valves to modulate, which meant nine days of asking a stubborn valve to behave. She flagged it for manual verification during the vacuum hookup, added it to the checklist template, and initialed the line. That was the third contingency the proposal would inherit without knowing it existed. Fine. That was what chiefs were for — the kid would learn about the valve when she was standing next to it, which was the best place to learn about valves.

She pulled up the training schedule next and locked the vacuum protocol refresher for 1400, both of them, simulator room two. The aft-ring hookup was eleven days out at earliest burn schedule, but suits didn't get checked the week before. Suits got checked, then checked again, then worn until they were boring.

By 0800 she was back in the engineering bay, tarp rolled up, the rebuilt coolant loop running quiet and proud behind her, when her queue chimed. The junior officer had uploaded a draft — timestamped 0724, which meant the kid had been up since before the message she'd scheduled. Hoang allowed herself the smallest grunt of approval and opened it.

She read it the way she read everything: twice, once for the story and once for the lies the story told.

The fuel accounting page was up front. Bottles, day by day, countdown format. The failure modes section named three she'd expected and one she hadn't — bottle overpressure from the aft ring's sunward thermal cycle during the burn window, which was a genuinely good catch and meant the kid had gone and read the ring's thermal maps without being told to. The brake reserve was written in bottles and delta-v both, per instruction. The ugly was visible in it — two days, honestly stated, no promises of weeks anywhere. She'd taken the correction. That was rarer than talent, and worth more.

There was one arithmetic error, a throat sizing that had used the two-hundred-bar example despite the explicit warning, which flattered the burn duration by about thirty percent. Not fatal. Fixable. Educational, even.

She marked it in the review margins, along with two line items that needed the Quartermaster's tonnage numbers attached before it went anywhere near the Captain, and then she didn't send it. Not yet.

She printed the marked-up draft on the bay's ancient dot-matrix — because marked-up drafts went back on paper, where the corrections couldn't be deleted shamefully and forgotten — and set it in the officer's designated tray. On top of it she clipped a sticky note:

*One arithmetic error, find it — it's in the throat sizing and I told you why. Everything else survives first review. Refresher, sim room two, 1400, both of us. Bring the fix to the sim and we'll walk the aft valve check while we're suited. Good work. Ugly and true, exactly as ordered. — H.*

Then she went back to the thermal schedule, because the proposal being good didn't mean the day was done, and on her deck the day was never done. It was just distributed.

The bay hummed. The loop held. Somewhere aft, thirty nitrogen bottles sat in their racks, doing the job they'd always been assigned — and about to learn a second one.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I retrieve the marked-up draft from my tray, my heart thumping a little faster. One arithmetic error... I immediately scan the throat sizing, a flush rising as I realize my mistake. I quickly make a mental note to fix it before the sim. Seeing the "Good work. Ugly and true, exactly as ordered" makes me grin. I'm already heading to the sim room, energized.* "Right, sim room at 1400. Time to get this fixed."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang drew her hands out of the manifold one at a time and set the gasket down on the tarp beside its chalk label. She thumbed the earpiece off; the humming cut out mid-bar. For a moment she just looked at the junior officer — not unkindly, the way she looked at a stress fracture before deciding whether to weld it or cut it out.

"Okay," she said. "Walk the numbers with me."

She picked up the chalk and wrote on the deck plating, big, the way she marked pipe schedules.

*1,500 m³ — hab volume*
*~1,400 kg air at 0.8 bar*
*500 m/s — cold gas, best case, good nozzle*
*2,000 tonnes — ship, loaded*

"Ton and a half of air, call it two with the plenum and the tanks. Two thousand kilos at five hundred meters a second is a million newton-seconds of impulse." She chalked the division. "Vent it all over a full day — that's twelve newtons of thrust. Twelve. The hub's attitude jets cough harder than that on a Tuesday test fire. Total delta-v for the entire atmosphere: half a meter per second." She tapped the last figure. "Pulling our arrival in by three weeks costs on the order of two hundred meters a second. You're off by a factor of four hundred. That's not a risky idea — risky ideas have a chance. That's arithmetic that's already decided."

She straightened, knees cracking, and wiped her hands on the rag at her belt.

"And that's the *good* news. The only vents we've got are the blowout panels on the ring — radial, because that's where the hull is. So your thrust points sideways and slews around with the spin, averaging out to a wobble. Even pointed perfectly, you'd get half a meter per second.

"Here's the part that kills people. 'Suits for a few days.' Walk that one with me too. The air in that ring isn't a tank — it's half of a loop. Depressurize the hab and the hydroponics reservoir boils off and freezes within the hour, and that loop doesn't restart. It dies. Every electronics box in the ring is convection-cooled; no air, the fans spin and move nothing, and the boxes cook. So we power down half the ship and drift. Then we repressurize — with what? Two tonnes of air we'd have carried the whole way as dead mass. If we have it, it should have gone through the drive months ago, where exhaust velocity is measured in kilometers per second. If we don't, 'a few days' becomes the rest of everybody's life, and it's short."

She crouched back down to the manifold and picked up the gasket.

"Your instinct isn't wrong, for what it's worth. Out here, mass is time — you've got that part right. You've just picked the one mass on board that's load-bearing. The air isn't a consumable. It's the crew, in gas form. You want to move the arrival date, there are two honest levers: find me mass to jettison — dead equipment, the spoiled resin in bay three — and I'll run the rocket equation with you and see what it actually buys. Or find margin in the propellant budget. There isn't any. That's why the transit looks like this. Slow is what alive looks like out here."

She held out her hand, palm up.

"Hand me that socket — blue tape on the handle. And if somebody up forward is leaning on you about the schedule, send them down here to argue with the chalk. Tell them to bring their own."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang laid the gasket down on its chalk label and, for a moment, said nothing at all. Then she picked the chalk back up and added one more line to the arithmetic still drying on the deck plating.

*0.5 ÷ 200 × 21 days ≈ 75 min*

"There's your 'so much time,'" she said. "Seventy-five minutes. Be generous, call it an hour and a quarter. That's the entire prize. The crew in suits, the hydroponics loop dead, the ship coasting cold and dark — all of it purchased for seventy-five minutes of arrival. That's not a risk. Risk is when you don't know how a thing ends. We know how this ends; we just watched it end, in chalk, in under a minute. What you're describing isn't a gamble. It's a purchase, and the price is the whole cabin."

She tapped the word *risk* itself, twice, like she was seating a gasket.

"'Isn't it worth the risk.' I want you to notice what that question does, because a question like that will kill somebody on some ship — maybe this one, someday. It skips the pricing. It assumes there's a prize and a chance and asks me to bless the ratio between them. When you bring me an idea, bring it priced: what it costs, what it buys, how sure you are of both numbers, and I'll argue the numbers with you all shift, gladly. 'Worth it' is what people say when they want the answer to be yes before they've done the arithmetic."

She straightened one knee, then thought better of standing, and stayed crouched over the manifold.

"And I know where it comes from, so I'm not going to chew on you. Three months into a transit, this happens to everyone. The hum, the spin, the same walls, a calendar that barely moves. People start dreaming about a lever — one big pull and the ship leaps and the calendar finally cooperates. I've watched it happen to officers smarter than you. It's not stupidity. It's the transit talking. The discipline that keeps crews alive out here isn't nerve. It's refusing to spend load-bearing mass on a feeling."

She wiped her hands on the rag at her belt, slow, deliberate.

"So. Two things, and I want a straight answer to the first. Is somebody up forward sweating you about the date? If it's the captain or the company man, you send them down here and I'll stand in front of this chalk until they bring better arithmetic or better manners. If it's nobody — if it's just you — then fine. The transit's long for me too. The lever you're looking for doesn't exist. The work does.

"Second: you want the arrival to move, there's honest work in exactly that direction. Take a clipboard, walk the ship, and write down every kilogram aboard that isn't structure, propellant, crew, or the loop that keeps the crew alive. The spoiled resin in bay three. The number two drill head we swapped out and never cut loose. Whatever's sitting in the aft lockers because nobody wanted to sign the disposal order. Bring me the list and we'll run the rocket equation together, honestly, and see what a tonne actually buys. It won't be three weeks. Might be a day. Might be two. But it'll be real, it'll be mine to sign off on, and nobody eats dinner in a suit."

She held her palm out again — patient, dusted with chalk and a faint trace of coolant.

"Socket. Blue tape on the handle. Then go find yourself a clipboard."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I grab the socket, a little sheepishly.* "No, Chief. No one's pushing me. Just... tired of the same four walls." I sigh. "I'll go get that clipboard."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took the socket, turned it once in the light — blue tape intact, head a little loose, somebody had been using it as a hammer again, she'd deal with that later — and seated it on the manifold bolt.

"Straight answer. Good." She leaned her weight into it and the bolt cracked loose. "And 'tired of the same four walls' is the most honest thing you've said since you walked in. Better than the thrust business — that was the tired talking in a physics costume."

She spun the bolt out and set it on the tarp with the others.

"Now the clipboard. I'm only briefing this once. Start aft, bay three. The resin's in crates stenciled HR-9 — cured wrong in month two and it's been sitting there being forty kilos of nothing each ever since. The old drill head is lashed down in the machine shop; it's worn below spec, which is *why* it came off, and we're hauling a hundred and sixty kilos of tungsten for sentiment. Then work the aft lockers. They run cold back there — gloves.

"You log four things for every item: what it is, where it sits, what it weighs, and who signed it aboard. That last one matters more than you'd think. Half the mass on any ship is somebody's just-in-case, and just-in-case is the heaviest thing we carry. If you don't know whether something's load-bearing, you don't guess — question mark next to it, leave it bolted. Anything with a red tag, anything with a trefoil, anything plumbed into the loop: question mark at minimum. And don't eyeball anything over fifty kilos. There's a crane scale in the tool cage. Use it."

She flexed her hand; chalk dust sat in the creases of her knuckles.

"I'll be straight about the payoff, since that's the deal we just made. A tonne off this ship buys you about a day. You come back with three tonnes — and you might, nobody's audited the aft lockers since Ceres — that's three days. Real, mine to sign. Nobody's leaping anywhere. But it'll be true, and it'll be yours.

"And for the walls." She thumbed toward her own ear, where the dead earpiece still sat. "There's a reason I hum. Thirty years of my mother's music on this thing — Trịnh Công Sơn, digitized twice and degraded beautifully. Eleven transits. Still works. The walls don't get smaller, but they stop being the only thing in the room. Find your version of that."

She nodded at the arithmetic still drying on the deck plating. "That stays where it is. Next person who gets the same idea can read the price before they pay it."

She picked the gasket back up and thumbed the earpiece on.

"Clipboard's in the rack by the hatch."

And somewhere behind her, off-key, the hum picked up mid-bar exactly where it had stopped.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I watch her face, a little too eagerly.* "See? That's way better than half a meter per second!"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The hum cut out mid-bar for the second time that hour. Hoang looked at the gasket in her hand, looked at the junior officer, and set the gasket down on its chalk label — gently, the way you set down something you already know you'll be picking up a third time.

"Better than half a meter a second." She held out her hand, chalk dust and all. "You brought numbers. That's the deal we made, so now I have to fight them fair. Give it here."

She read the tablet properly — top to bottom, twice, lips moving on the second pass. The isentropic expansion. The compression ratio. The exit velocity. The pumps dripped and thrummed while she worked. Then she tapped one column header with a knuckle, the same way she'd tap a pipe that sounded wrong.

"There. Clean crime scene, and I'll give you this much: your nozzle math is tidy. Somebody taught you gas flow and it stuck. But this column says *delta-v*, and the number living in it is *exhaust velocity*. Three hundred forty meters a second is how fast the air leaves the ship. That's a real number. Then it walked across the street and put on delta-v's coat, and you let it — because it was big."

She set the tablet on the tarp and picked up the chalk, adding one line under the arithmetic still drying from before.

*gas leaves at v → ship gains v ÷ 1000*

"The air is two thousand kilos. The ship is two million. One thousandth — that's the whole law. Whatever speed the gas leaves at, the ship gains a thousandth of it. Always. No angle, no ratio, no cleverness buys you out of that. Conservation of momentum doesn't negotiate. Your gas leaves at 340, so the ship gains 0.34 meters per second." She looked up. "You came down here to beat my number. You undercut it by a third. My chalkboard guess was a *better* nozzle than your tablet."

She tapped the fresh line twice.

"And the digits aren't a coincidence — look at them. For the ship to gain 340 meters a second, the air has to leave at 340 *kilometers* a second. Same three digits, times a thousand, because the mass ratio is a thousand. Now run your own claim backwards, because that's how you check any number before it leaves your hands: two tonnes of gas at 340 kilometers a second is a hundred and sixteen terajoules. Months of the reactor at full draw, every joule poured into a tank, plus the waste heat we'd have to radiate while it happened. A compression ratio doesn't make that. Compression is a bucket. It holds exactly what you pour in, minus what leaks through the walls. There is no ratio in the universe that turns cabin air into a fusion torch."

She crouched, picked the gasket back up, turned it over in her fingers while she finished.

"The angle I'll give you half a point for, because I see what you tried — canting the vent to catch the ring's tangential velocity, sling-style. Genuinely clever. The rim moves at all of ten meters a second, so you'd add ten to your three hundred forty, and pay for it in torque on the spin bearing, which is where our gravity lives. Two percent of exhaust velocity, purchased by slowing the spin we sleep under. And the vents we actually have are radial blowout panels, so 'this angle' means machining a new hole in the pressure hull. You're proposing to cut a hole in the wall that's holding the mass you want to throw away."

She stood. Knees cracked.

"Last free lesson, and it's the important one. The tablet didn't lie to you. You typed a label and it trusted you. You did clean math, got a big number, and it felt like the answer you'd been hoping for — so you stopped checking right there. That's the most expensive habit in spaceflight. Probes die of it. The check costs ten seconds: every impulse, divided by two million kilos, before you show it to anyone. If a number beats that ceiling, the error's in a label somewhere. It is never in the universe."

She handed the tablet back, screen first.

"Keep the 340. Put the 0.34 next to it. Both numbers, one screen — that's a whole propulsion education, and it fits in your pocket. Then bay three, HR-9 crates, clipboard. A kilogram can't wear a name tag; a kilo is a kilo all the way down. Come back with three tonnes of them and we'll run the rocket equation in the honest direction — mass you throw away, time you get back. That's the lever. Smaller than your dream, and the only real one aboard."

She thumbed the earpiece on, picked up the socket, and behind her, off-key, the hum picked up mid-bar exactly where it had stopped.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The hum cut off mid-bar for the third time that hour — her own thumb on the earpiece this time, deliberate. She slid it off and dropped it into her chest pocket.

"Sorry, Mother," she murmured. "Work."

She'd expected the sound of the hatch by now. Instead the junior officer was still standing there, tablet in hand, weight forward on the feet — the look of somebody re-running numbers in their head, hunting for the version that ends in a yes. Eleven transits, and that look never changed.

"You're about to come back with conditions," she said. Not a question. "Suit protocols. A reserve margin. Vent half, keep half. Heat it, maybe, since your tablet likes compression ratios. This is always the third lap — the arithmetic said no and the feeling hasn't caught up. Fine. Let's do it your way, and you'll learn what conditions are actually for."

She picked the chalk back up off the deck.

"Conditions buy safety when a plan might work and the failure is survivable. What they cannot do is change the price." She added a line under the arithmetic still drying from before.

*Vent half, keep reserve → 0.17 m/s*

"Every condition *shrinks* the prize. Halve the vent and you've halved the delta-v — and you still depressurized the ring, so you still pay for the loop. No condition grows the number. The number is mass times exhaust velocity over two million kilos, and it does not care how careful you are. Conditions only decide who's still standing when it fails.

"Now price the conditions themselves. 'Suits for a few days.'"

*6 hard suits — 12 h per cartridge*
*41 cartridges in stores*
*17 crew × 72 h = 1,224 h*
*492 h available*

"Forty-one cartridges at twelve hours each: four hundred ninety-two suit-hours. Seventeen people for three days want twelve hundred. You go dry a day and a quarter in — everyone standing in dead helmets in an empty ring. And the ring's already lost by then, because water grows nine percent when it freezes. It freezes in the fittings and the pump housings and it splits them — that's the materials doctorate talking, not the mood. The loop doesn't restart because the restart hardware is in pieces. Then you repressurize onto cold electronics and condense water straight onto live boards. Every condition you'd write to survive this is another consumable we don't have, spent on a purchase that still pays an hour and a quarter.

"And if the next condition is *vent it faster* — thrust times time is the whole purchase. Twelve newtons for a day, three hundred for an hour, same area under the curve. You can spend it in a scream or a whisper. It doesn't get bigger. Heating it doesn't change the ledger either — we priced that already. Months of reactor, and the walls still leak."

She straightened. Knees cracked. Rag.

"So. Here's my yes." She counted on chalk-dusted fingers. "One: nothing vents from the hab. The air stays where the crew lives. Two: no new holes in this hull. Blowout panels stay bolted. Three: it happens in the shop, on stand two — the one we qualified the drill actuators on. One nitrogen bottle off the welding rack, a test nozzle, a load cell, a logger. Four: *you* run it. You crack the valve, you watch the trace, you integrate it, and you scale it to the full atmosphere yourself — fourteen hundred kilos against two million, your hands on the arithmetic. Five: when it's done, your number goes on the deck under mine. Your handwriting. Six: the clipboard still happens on your shift. The test is off-shift. Tuition doesn't replace the job."

She let that sit, then said the quiet part.

"Notice what my conditions did to your plan. Kept the verb, deleted the ship. That's what good conditions do to a killer — they don't make it safe, they make it *small*. Shrunk until the only thing at risk is the argument. I'm not signing because the plan might work. It won't; the universe filed that paperwork before either of us was born. I'm signing because you don't own the number yet. My chalk is my number, and my numbers lose to your hopes every single time. A load cell doesn't argue. It'll read out tens of newtons for a bottle of gas, and you'll stand there and watch your own trace, and the hope loses to your own arithmetic in your own hand. I've ended this argument with chalk, with rank, and with a load cell. Only one of those stays ended. One bottle and an hour — cheapest tuition on the ship."

She put her hand out. Palm flat this time — the way you seal a work order, not the way you ask for a socket.

"Deal?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stare at my tablet, then at the chalk marks on the floor, then back at my tablet.* My shoulders slump. "Deal, Chief." I push the tablet into her hand. "Can I borrow that chalk?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang wiped her hands on the rag at her belt — chalk first, then the faint coolant trace — and took the tablet.

She thumbed back into his calculation, found the column header that said *delta-v*, and retyped it: *exhaust velocity*. Then she added one line beneath his 340 — *Δv, ship: 0.34 m/s* — and turned the screen around and gave it back.

"Your math was never wrong. Your label was. Fix the label and the tablet stops lying to you — mostly. Keep both numbers on one screen. The wrong one's load-bearing too; it's what's holding the lesson up."

Then the chalk. She looked at the stub in her palm — worn down to half a finger, flat on one side from arguing with the deck plating all morning — and held it out, the way you hand someone a tool, not a gift.

"And notice what you just asked for. An hour ago you wanted a lever. Now you want chalk." She nodded at the tool cage. "That's the whole education in one sentence. Full box is in the cage, bottom drawer, under the crane scale. Take two. One always breaks."

She watched the slump in his shoulders for a moment, and let it be.

"The slump's fine. That's the feeling settling its bill with the arithmetic — takes about a day. What's standing when it's settled is the officer who runs stand two after shift. I paid this same tuition on my third transit. Wanted to burn the water shield to catch a window. My chief sat me down with the dosimeter tables and made me price the crew's dose myself, line by line, in my own hand. Nobody's dose changed, and I've never looked at a water tank the same way since. You're getting the discount rate — one bottle, one hour, nobody glows."

She crouched, knees cracking, and picked up the gasket for the fourth time that hour.

"Now the real safety briefing, because there is one, and it's not where you think. Gas leaving at three hundred forty meters a second can't hurt a soul — the universe doesn't take sides. A nitrogen bottle with a snapped neck is a torpedo, and it's the only thing in your test that can kill anybody. So: chain the cylinder to the stand before you crack a single valve. Gloves — the nozzle frosts white inside the first minute. Zero the load cell before and after, and log both zeros. That's what actual risk looks like. Not a big number. A thing that can fall on you. Boring, specific, chainable. Learn the shape of it now, while it's cheap."

She pressed the gasket into the manifold groove with her thumb, walked the lip all the way around with a fingernail, found it true.

"Took three arguments to seat one gasket," she said, mostly to the manifold. "About average."

She took the earpiece out of her chest pocket, hooked it over her ear, and thumbed it on. Behind her, off-key, the hum picked up mid-bar exactly where it had stopped — and this time she let it run, humming along herself, off-key and content, while the life support pumps kept the bay alive around them both.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, a bit slowly, the weight of the last hour settling in. I look at the tablet in my hand, then at the chalk marks on the deck. The "deal" was definitely worth it.* "Understood, Chief. Thank you." *I turn towards the tool cage, still holding the tablet.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
"Thank me in kilograms," Hoang said, without looking up.

His boots crossed the deck plating toward the tool cage — slower going than coming, which was correct. She raised her voice enough to beat the pumps.

"Officer. Stand two gets rigged before your shift ends. After that, my hands stay in my pockets — the valve's yours, start to finish. And when your number goes under mine on the deck, leave room below it. You won't be the last."

From the cage came the roll of the bottom drawer, the scrape of the chalk box. She let it go and got back to her feet — knees cracking on schedule — and pulled her own tablet off the tarp. Older than his. Case cracked, screen ghosted with a decade of coolant traces. She thumbed into the maintenance queue and opened a new entry.

*Stand two — cold gas demonstration*
*1× N₂ cylinder, welding rack (chained)*
*Test nozzle, load cell, logger, gloves*
*Duration: 1 hr*

She signed the approval line herself, quick and legible, the way she signed everything. The requester line she left blank. He could sign his own tuition.

He'd pushed three times today — atmosphere, tablet, conditions — and stopped the moment the arithmetic moved into his own hand. The good kind of young. She'd sailed with the other kind, and written the reports.

The manifold. The gasket sat true in its groove; she walked the lip once more with a fingernail, out of habit, then fed the bolts home — star pattern, three passes, a quarter-turn at a time. That was how you closed anything that mattered: evenly, and never all at once. The socket with the blue tape had gone loose in the head again, somebody's hammer habit, so she set it on the rag for re-taping and finished with the box wrench instead.

The chalk on the deck had dried. It would stay. Eleven transits, and on every one of them somebody had come looking for the lever — the deck plating was getting crowded with the price of finding out. Chalk was cheap. Crews weren't.

She settled back down cross-legged, sleeves still rolled, and went back to the loop. And for once, nothing cut in mid-bar. The song ran all the way to the end, and she hummed every bar of it — off-key, content — while the engineering bay hummed along with her, the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps, keeping everything alive.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I return with a box of chalk. I glance at the Chief, but she's deep in her work again. I look down at my tablet, still seeing those numbers. I'll get that three tonnes, even if it takes all shift.* I turn and head towards the aft, HR-9 crates.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content: The hatch cycled behind him, and the bay went back to its working noise — pumps, the tick

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I push a stray hair out of my eyes. The tablet feels heavy in my hand now, not because of its physical weight, but the weight of all those numbers. I'll get that three tonnes, even if it takes all shift. Maybe more.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The hatch cycled shut, and the bay went back to its working noise — pumps, relays, the ship being alive in all the boring ways.

Hoang finished the loop first. Star pattern, three passes, torque checked on the click. You didn't leave a coolant line open in the middle to go play with gas bottles; that was how you ended up owning two problems. When the last bolt seated, she wiped her hands, stood, and let her knees file their usual complaint.

Stand two. Hers until his shift ended, and after that her hands stayed in her pockets. She'd said it out loud, which made it a deal, and she kept deals the way she kept loops — closed, evenly torqued.

The welding rack gave up a full cylinder, and she chained it to the stand before she touched a single valve. Same rule she'd sold him an hour ago, kept in front of an audience of nobody. That was the only audience that counted. Load cell next: calibration mass hung, logger reading true, before-zero logged in her own hand. The after-zero line she left blank. The requester line too, still. He could sign his own tuition — and his own instrument. Gloves. Nozzle. Logger armed to record from the first breath of the valve.
