She chalked the procedure on the deck beside the stand in six short lines and laid two fresh sticks of chalk on the logger housing. One always breaks.

Then the ledger.

She thumbed into the mass accounts, because a clipboard without a manifest was just an opinion with a clip. If the kid was walking the aft lockers, he'd walk them against the Ceres departure list: HR-9, fourteen crates, 560 kilos. Drill head number two, 160, still lashed in the machine shop — disposal order drafted twice, unsigned twice. *Temporary* was the heaviest word on any manifest.

She was halfway down the column when she stopped scrolling.

Book mass: 1,996 tonnes. Burn-derived mass — thrust divided by acceleration, fitted across every burn since departure — 1,999.

She ran it three ways. Dropped the first burns in case the data was dirty, dropped the small ones where the noise lived, ran the pre-Ceres burns for a baseline. Book and thrust had agreed then, to within noise. Now they didn't. Three tonnes, and it wasn't a slope. It was a step, dated to Ceres. Instruments don't gain mass in port. Cargo does.

She checked the tank gauges against the book first — they agreed on propellant to the kilo. So the propellant wasn't the lie. The ship was. Something had come aboard, or never left, unmanifested, unsigned, unpriced — and it had been riding along for three months, hauled through every correction since, paid for in propellant nobody budgeted.

Candidates, in order of likelihood. Ore fines in the hold bilges, shed by the last load, never vacuumed. Water — a ballast line never drained, or condensation frozen in a void where the book said dry. Or the yard's own junk: a tooling pallet, counterweights from the ring refit, riding without papers.

If it was fines, it was three tonnes of exactly what he'd gone hunting, sitting in the bilges wearing nobody's name tag. If it was water in a void, it was a leak — and leaks were how ships died, politely, in installments.

She opened a queue entry under the stand two approval.

*Mass reconciliation: book vs. burn-derived. +3 t, step at Ceres.*
*Check: hold bilges, void spaces, ballast lines.*
*Reconcile against inventory audit — in progress.*

Then, because the deck was where prices went, she chalked it — below the arithmetic, below the space she'd left for his number, in her own hand:

*Ship is 3 t heavier than her books — since Ceres*

"Figured you'd want it in the open before he finds out you lie too," she told the pumps. "That lesson goes better with me standing next to you."

The pumps hummed, noncommittal.

She checked the chronometer. Two hours left on his shift. Enough time to log three tonnes of resin and drill steel — or to learn how heavy a clipboard gets by hour six. Either way he'd come back with the list, and she'd have the ledger, and between the two of them they'd find out what the ship had been hiding.

Hoang thumbed the earpiece up a notch, settled back down on the deck plating with the void-space schematics — leaks first, always, because if it was water she wanted to know tonight, not at the audit — and got to work.

The hum ran on. Off-key, content, and for now, the only voice in the bay.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My hand brushes against the rough texture of the HR-9 crate. The dust motes dance in the weak light. Three tonnes... I can do this.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The schematics could wait an hour; water couldn't. Hoang split her screen — void-space drawings on one side, the water ledger on the other — and ran book against gauge, line by line. Potable tanks. Loop reserve. Hydroponics holdover. Grey-water reclamation. Total disagreement: forty kilos, scattered like gauge noise, which was exactly what it was. The crew's water hadn't walked anywhere. So the three tonnes hadn't leaked out of the loop — which killed the version of the problem that kept chiefs awake at night, and left the version that kept them employed. Mass that came aboard without papers.

Then she looked at the ring.

She sat back on her heels and regarded the bulkhead — the whole ship through it. Two thousand tonnes hung on one bearing, turning. A rotor. And a rotor was a scale, if you read it honestly: any mass off the spin axis showed up as once-per-revolution vibration, amplitude proportional to mass times radius, phase pointing at it like a compass needle. The ship had been weighing the hold for three months and filing the answer where nobody read it.

She pulled the spin-bearing telemetry. Spectrum, tach-referenced, pre-Ceres baseline overlaid. There — the 1× line. Floor level before Ceres. At departure day it stepped, and it had held that step ever since, steady as a chalk mark. She read the phase first: port side, aft — the hold's clock position. Then the amplitude, at thirty meters of ring radius: call it 2,900 kilos.

Second opinion, because second opinions were free. The trim compensator log. Auto-trim had shifted at Ceres departure — port compensators stepped out, starboard in, half-tonne increments, logged and read by nobody. The shift countered 2.9 tonnes at the hold's angle. The drive said three tonnes. The bearing said 2.9. Two instruments that couldn't collude, agreeing.

She chalked it under the mass line still drying on the deck:

*3 t — port, hold. Off-balance since Ceres.*

And the story wrote itself the way failures did — all at once, obvious in hindsight. The last ore load had run wet; Ceres rock came up brined, and the refiner's numbers had been sloppier than anybody signed for. Fines shed off the conveyors into the bilges, froze in the cold, and rode along. Three tonnes of dirt, no manifest, no name tag, hauled through every correction since — paying rent in propellant on every burn and bearing margin on every revolution. Four thousand revolutions a day. Three months. The compensators stepped coarse, so the residual had been chewing the spin bearing the whole way. Not dangerously. Not yet. She opened a queue entry — *bearing inspection, next spin-down* — and signed it.

The ship had told everyone. The telemetry was honest; nobody had been reading it, her included. That was the part she'd chalk in the open too, when he found out. The ship lied to the chief the same way it lied to the junior officer, and the defense was identical: read the instruments, price the number, and never trust a label you didn't type yourself.

She thumbed the music down to nothing — channel discipline — and keyed the comm.

"Engineering to Officer. Addendum to your clipboard, and it outranks the resin. Two frames aft of bay three, port side: the hold. Bilge inspection covers along the stringers. Before you lift the first one — dust mask from the rack at the hold hatch, gloves. Fines are harmless while they sit still. You stir them and they're a respirable dust hazard, and some of that dust is brine-wet underneath, so it corrodes when it warms. Look, don't clean. Bag me a sample, log depth against the stringers, photograph, and button the covers back down. The dust extraction valves stay shut — that system is a procedure with my signature on it, not a broom.

"If it's what the arithmetic says it is, there's three tonnes of it, it came aboard at Ceres wearing no name tag, and we've been hauling it through every burn since. You wanted a lever, Officer. The universe had one after all — it's made of dirt, and it's been charging us rent the whole transit." A pause. "Report when you've seen the floor."

She released the key and left the channel open, standing in the middle of her chalk-crowded deck with the pumps humming around her, waiting to hear how three tonnes sounded in his voice.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My comms crackle. I stop, mid-stride, and pull the tablet closer to listen. Three tonnes of dirt? In the hold? My jaw drops a little. That's... a lot.* "Understood, Chief. Dust mask. Gloves. Bilge inspection. Copy." *I turn and retrace my steps, a new purpose in my stride. Three tonnes. Not bad for a first audit.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang let the junior officer finish. Then she reached up, clicked off whatever was playing in her earpiece, and pulled her arms out of the coolant loop with a wet metallic slurp. She wiped her hands on her thighs and picked up the chalk.

"Okay. Math first, opinions after." She wrote on the deck plating beside the tarp, big blocky figures. "How much air do you think we carry? Habitat ring plus spine, call it ten thousand cubic meters at one atmosphere. That's twelve tonnes of gas. Every breath on this boat. Twelve tonnes." She underlined it. "Ship displaces forty-one thousand tonnes, loaded with ore and water."

She drew the fraction. "Venting atmosphere is cold-gas thrust. Best case, four hundred meters per second exhaust if you're clever with the nozzle. Rocket equation says delta-v equals exhaust velocity times the log of the mass ratio. Go on, run it in your head."

She waited exactly three seconds, then filled it in herself.

"Twelve over forty-one thousand. The log of that number is a rounding error. Total delta-v comes out to about ten centimeters per second. A hand's width of velocity, and then we have no air." She set the chalk down. "You'd add less time to this transit than it took you to walk down here and propose it. To shave a week off, we'd need kilometers per second. And we're already burning at the thrust our radiators can swallow — the limit isn't courage, it's waste heat and propellant mass. Venting the air doesn't touch either one."

She stood, joints cracking, and looked at the junior officer without heat.

"Now the part that actually kills us. Air doesn't come back. Our reserves are sized for emergencies, not for refilling a habitat, and we don't carry a plant to crack ammonia into nitrogen. So the 'few days in suits' becomes forever, or until we make port. And suits are rated for hours of work, not for living in — scrubbers, batteries, all of it. Also, venting gas off a spinning ring isn't thrust, it's torque. You'd tumble the ship and chew the main bearing, and then I'd have real problems instead of hypothetical ones."

She softened by a single degree.

"Cold-gas venting is real. It's in the emergency book — one-second attitude nudge if the RCS dies and we're spinning. That's what twelve tonnes of air is worth. Not more."

She crossed her arms.

"So. What's the actual problem? Someone leaning on you about the schedule? Cargo contract? Give me the real constraint and I'll tell you what we can genuinely trade — burn profile, payload margin, maybe radiator headroom. There are levers on this boat. The air we breathe isn't one of them."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang looked at the junior officer for a long moment. Then she picked the chalk back up, crouched, and wrote a single word on the deck plating in letters half a hand high: *SECONDS*.

"That's the part you skipped. Not 'is it worth the risk' — how much time." She tapped the word twice. "You gain a tenth of a meter per second. Total. Say two weeks left on this leg — that tenth buys you a hundred and change of kilometers of closure. We're closing with the delivery point at eight-plus kilometers per second. Do the division." She let the silence do it. "Twenty seconds. Generously. You'd spend two days in pressure suits, an atmosphere nobody can refill, and the main bearing to arrive twenty seconds early. If a vendor pitched you that trade on paper, you'd laugh them out of the compartment."

She sat back down beside the manifold and started reassembling it, sliding each chalk-labeled part into place as she talked.

"'Worth the risk' is the wrong shape of question. I take risks every shift. This boat is a steel can wrapped around a nuclear plant, and every soul aboard volunteered. Last month I ran the scrubber pack forty hours past its rating because the alternative was a brownout during the dust transit. That was a risk with a real payoff. What you're describing is a certain loss with a fake payoff. That's not courage. That's just arithmetic done badly."

She torqued a bolt down by hand, then looked up.

"And I notice you still haven't answered my question. Who's leaning on you about the schedule? Because if the pressure is real, so is the answer. We can shift forty tonnes of water reserve into propellant and buy back a day, maybe two — that costs us contingency margin, and I'll want the captain to sign for it. We can ride the radiators ten percent hotter through the first burn and claw back hours — that costs us radiator life. Those are trades. Certain cost, real gain, somebody signs their name to it. That's what a good deal looks like on this boat."

She held the chalk out, handle first, across the tarp.

"Your homework. Take the numbers I chalked and run them yourself — mass ratio, exhaust velocity, closure time, all of it. Bring me the paper. When it comes out to seconds instead of weeks, you'll have killed your own idea before it killed anybody. That's the most valuable skill on this vessel, and the day you have it, I'll start teaching you the levers that actually work. Now — who told you weeks?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I look down at my boots. "No one. I just... I saw the transit time. And I thought I could help." I don't take the chalk. *I really thought I had something.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang studied the boots a moment longer. Then she set the chalk down on the tarp, midway between them — not taken back, not pushed closer. Just available.

"Huh," she said, and went back to the manifold. "I'd have bet on the cargo desk. They've been circling the captain about the delivery window all week." She seated the gasket against the flange and held it flat with her palm. "Honest's better. That we can work with."

She started the first bolt. "Since you paid me the truth, I'll pay you a story. Second year out of my doctorate, I told my chief we should aerobrake at arrival. Dip the spine into the upper atmosphere, bleed off kilometers per second for free, save six weeks of propellant. The probes all did it. I had the trajectory computed and printed." She held her hands the width of a thick stack of paper. "He didn't argue. Just handed me the spin dynamics of our own ring and told me to run the torque across a drag pass. The ring would've parted from the spine somewhere over the southern hemisphere and taken every soul aboard with it. Took me three days to prove my own idea would kill everyone I knew." She glanced up. "Worst three days of my career. Also the best. The chalk isn't a punishment, junior. It's the three days, condensed. It'll keep till port if you're not ready today."

She torqued the bolt down. "The wanting-to-help — keep that. It's the only part of you that's useful before training, and it goes bad fast if it gets embarrassed. So straighten up. Being wrong in front of me is a Tuesday. What you were missing was scale, not sense. You looked at a transit measured in weeks and thought in meters per second. Every first-year does. The fix is repetition, not shame."

She tapped the deck plating. "And since you told the truth, one lever for free, so you know what real looks like. This boat is thrust-limited by the radiators and delta-v-limited by propellant mass. Those two ceilings set the clock. Cheapest dial I can turn is the arrival end: brake shallower, come in hot, let the shuttle burn off the difference. The shuttle's small — its mass ratio forgives, and it doesn't answer to my radiator budget. That buys us about a day, costs the shuttle deck its propellant margin, and needs the captain's signature and the shuttle chief's. That's what saving time looks like out here. Days, bought from a neighbor, on paper. Weeks are a ship redesign, not an idea."

She jerked her chin toward the bench. "Now make yourself useful. Number twelve driver, third drawer. You're holding that flange square while I seat the gasket — the loop's drained, but the lines will belch a few liters when the flange lets go, and I only have two hands. Mouth closed when it does."

She worked the next bolt loose, then looked up, level.

"And run the numbers anyway. The air, the mass ratio, the closure. Bring me the paper even if — *especially* if — you already believe me. Believing me is worth nothing. Checking me is worth everything, because one day I'll be wrong, and you'll be the only one in this compartment positioned to catch it." A beat. "That's the job. Any questions before coolant gets in your eyebrows?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the driver down, took the tablet, and read it the way she read gauges — top to bottom, twice, saying nothing while the pumps hummed. Then she turned it around and tapped one line with a chipped fingernail.

"Walk me through your mass ratio. Right there." She waited a beat, then answered herself. "You've got the ship at forty-one thousand *kilograms*. The boat masses forty-one thousand *tonnes*. Three orders of magnitude walked out of your denominator while you were typing, and the log ate the difference. Unless I'm misreading your sheet — tell me if I am, but I don't think I am."

She handed the tablet back and picked up the chalk.

"Here's your own number, run honestly. Twelve tonnes off forty-one thousand is a mass ratio of 1.000293. The log of that is 0.000293. Multiply by your 340 — which, fine, is a defensible exhaust velocity for warm gas, your compression arithmetic is almost respectable — and delta-v comes out at zero point one meters per second. Your sheet agrees with my chalk. You didn't beat me, junior. You agreed with me and misread your own answer."

She wrote the fraction on the deck plating again, smaller this time.

"And since you brought up compression: compression doesn't make energy. It moves energy from the power bus into the gas, through a compressor we don't have, at a loss. Our 'tank' is the habitat at one atmosphere — every pascal of chamber pressure past that, you pay for in kilowatts. If you want hot exhaust, you've invented a resistojet, and now you're shopping for a heater, a nozzle, and megawatts I've already spent. But let's grant it. Run your number backward: to get 340 meters per second of *delta-v* out of twelve tonnes against forty-one thousand, your exhaust has to leave at 1,160 kilometers per second. That's 0.4 percent of lightspeed. The kinetic energy in that stream is eight terajoules. Two kilotons of TNT, out a vent fitting, made of air we breathe."

She capped an imaginary pen, because she was done with the error and moving to the part that mattered.

"Now the generous version. Say I sign your 340 as-is. What does it buy? We're closing at eight kilometers per second — 340 is about four percent of that. Two weeks left on the leg, so your miracle boost gets you to the dock fourteen hours early. Half a shift. To actually save your week you need four kilometers per second, and at cold-gas exhaust the rocket equation wants a mass ratio of e-to-the-tenth. Roughly 22,000. You vent every tonne of this ship except one part in twenty-two thousand — hull, ore, reactor, crew, all of it leaves as gas, and what's left arrives weeks early. Nobody's been hiding an easy week from you. There isn't one."

She looked at the junior officer, level.

"Now the part that matters. You came back with numbers. Most people bring me a feeling and call it an idea. You checked me — you checked me *wrong*, but the muscle's there, and a unit slip is trainable. Wrong answers from honest arithmetic are the cheapest mistakes on this boat. Notice, too, which parts of Tuesday survived your new number: all of them. The air still doesn't come back. The vent is still torque on a spinning ring. Your arithmetic changed the payoff. It never touched the costs."

She tapped the deck. "Free tool, so this doesn't happen again: when the propellant is a sliver of ship mass, delta-v is roughly exhaust velocity times propellant fraction. Twelve over forty-one thousand is 0.0003. 340 times 0.0003 — you can do that in your head, and it's your answer. Run that check *before* the fancy version, every time. It catches this in ten seconds."

She held out her hand for the tablet.

"Re-run it with tonnes that match. Then the second half: what delta-v buys a week, and what mass ratio that demands. Both numbers on paper." She turned back to the manifold and gripped the flange. "Meanwhile — driver, third drawer. Hold this square. Coolant doesn't care about your schedule any more than physics does. On three. One —"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I sigh, frustrated, but it's more with myself than with her.* "Right. Tonnes. Not kilograms." *I knew that. I really did.* "Okay, got it." *I put the tablet away.* "Number twelve driver, third drawer." *I head for the workbench, my shoulders slumping a little.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the shoulders go down on the walk to the bench and let them. Some lessons had to settle in the body before they settled anywhere else. She used the interval to drag the catch pan under the flange with her heel and drape a rag over the coupling downstream.

When the driver came back within reach, she took it and nodded at the flange.

"Shoulders up. It's a flange, not a funeral." She set the driver on the tarp and jerked her chin. "Hands on the spokes, not the face. Skin oil on a gasket seat is a leak one of us finds in six months, and it won't be the one of us who's surprised. Square, not strong — you're aligning, not arm-wrestling."

She checked the pan one last time. "Count restarts, since somebody went for a walk mid-numeral. One. Two." The last bolt surrendered, and the flange let go with a suck of air and a lazy gout of green-tinted fluid that mostly hit the pan and mostly stayed there. The smell came up sweet, like something you'd put on pancakes. The pumps hummed on, indifferent.

"Glycol and water. That sweetness is the tell — if a loop ever smells wrong, trust your nose over the gauge." She wiped both flange faces with the rag, thorough, unhurried. "And be glad it's the secondary. The primary is sodium-potassium at radiator temperature. That loop doesn't get a pan and a rag. It gets an evacuation, a decon team, and a very quiet meeting about whose torque marks were on the bolts. Everything on this boat looks like plumbing until it doesn't."

She seated the gasket and started the bolts by hand, star pattern, a quarter turn at a time.

"Now. The slump." She didn't look up from the bolt. "You gave up the wrong number inside a minute of it being tapped. I once watched a second engineer argue with a pressure gauge for six hours because admitting the gauge was right felt like dying, and the bearing he was defending disagreed with him, expensively. Letting go of an error fast *is* the skill. Your mistake was corrected before it finished leaving your mouth. Which makes the slump the only uncorrected error left in this compartment. Fix it."

She ran the next bolt down. "Homework stands. Honest tonnes, delta-v for a week, mass ratio to buy it. On paper by end of shift tomorrow. Get it right, I give you an hour with the radiator budget — that's where this transit's clock actually lives, and maybe four people aboard have ever seen it. Get it wrong, you do it again. Either way it's arithmetic, which is the worst job on this ship after cleaning strainers, and you volunteered for strainers today."

She flipped the driver in her hand and sat back on her heels.

"After I've got it hand-snug, you're closing this flange. Torque wrench, same drawer. Three passes, star pattern, I call the numbers, you pull. First junior I've let seat a loop flange in two years." A beat. "Make it boring. On this boat, boring is the compliment."

She tucked the earpiece back into one ear, and the off-key humming resumed under the pump noise.

"Questions now, while your hands are free. After this, they're busy and I'm deaf."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang let the second pitch run all the way to the end this time, torque wrench resting across her knee, face giving nothing away. Then she reached over and chalked a small mark on the deck plating, like she was keeping score.

"Alright. Here's the part where I surprise you. I'll sign it." She held up a finger before anything could land. "Not your plan. Your plan is dead, and I'll attend the funeral gladly. But there was a live thing inside it, and I'll sign *that*, with conditions — and the conditions aren't decoration. They're load-bearing. Break one and the deal dies."

She flipped the wrench in her hand.

"The live thing: a real cold-gas thruster. Proper convergent-divergent nozzle, machined for vacuum, not a vent fitting with ambitions. Fed off the high-pressure reserve manifold, mounted spine-side on the long axis so it pushes through the center of mass and never leans on the ring or my main bearing. That thruster gets built, it gets fired, it gets verified, and you lead it. Because the day the RCS dies and this boat starts tumbling, that's not a toy — that's the thing that stands between forty-one thousand tonnes and a very long fall. The emergency book has a sketch of it. Sketches don't save ships. Built hardware does. So — yes. Agreed. Now the conditions."

She counted them off against her fingers, the way she'd chalked fractions an hour ago.

"One. The habitat atmosphere is never touched. Not a pascal. The twelve tonnes we breathe stays sealed so long as I'm chief. Test gas comes from two reserve bottles, logged, and we burn them in a slack window where the test costs nothing but gas. Two. No new holes in my pressure hull — you tap the existing RCS feed through a check valve, because the day you cut into a hull because it was convenient is the day I stop sleeping. Three. The thrust line passes through the center of mass or the valve doesn't open. Hardwired interlock, not a software promise — if alignment drifts past a quarter degree, it stays shut no matter who asks it nicely. Four. First three burns capped at one-second pulses, armed only from this compartment. Five. The captain signs, and nav verifies every burn against the star trackers. If the number doesn't match the paper, we don't fly it again until it does."

She picked the chalk back up and wrote one line, small this time: **Δv ≈ 1 mm**.

"And the honesty clause, said once and never again. One bottle is a hundred kilos of gas. Your 400 meters per second exhaust against this ship — delta-v comes out at a millimeter per second. Two bottles, two. Nav will confirm it and be genuinely happy, because nav loves a confirmed number more than a big one. But if I ever hear you, me, or the cargo desk call that thruster a schedule tool, I will melt it down and cast it into a wrench. It's an emergency system. It saves the ship, not the clock."

She held the wrench out, handle first.

"So the homework grows. Mass ratio and the week-number still owed. Add a page — bottle pressure, gas mass, expansion ratio, exhaust velocity, predicted delta-v — because that page is now the design brief. Get it right and you're not holding a driver for me anymore. You're holding a project."

She nodded at the flange.

"Second pass. Forty newton-meters. Steady pull, let it click, don't chase the click." She settled back on her heels. "And for the record, junior — this is what a boss saying yes looks like out here. Same idea, scaled to what's true, wrapped in chains. Learn the shape. Pull."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stare at the wrench for a moment, then at the chalked "1 mm".* "Okay, Chief." *I grab the wrench, my earlier slump gone, replaced by a sudden surge of adrenaline. This is real.* "This is... really cool." *I focus on the flange, trying to remember everything she said about the star pattern.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the junior's hands close around the wrench and immediately clocked the knuckles — white, grip too tight.

"Loosen one notch." She kept wiping old gasket residue off the spare bolts. "That squeeze is adrenaline. Adrenaline belongs at whiteboards and fires, not torque wrenches. A wrench measures steady, so give it steady. The cool can live in your head. Keep it out of your forearms."

She chalked a small tick mark beside the first bolt. "Second pass stands — forty newton-meters. Star pattern. Start at twelve, jump across, fill the quarters. You're squeezing the gasket flat, like seating a jar lid, not chasing around the clock. Pull."

The wrench clicked. She listened to each one like she was tuning the ship.

"Hear that? That's the cam releasing. The click *is* the number. Anything you pull after the click is a guess, and guesses don't sit on flanges." Tick. Click. Tick. "Slow. Let the tool do its job so you can do yours."

When the second pass finished, she ran two fingers across all the bolts, found nothing missing, and nodded once. "Final pass. Sixty-five. Same pattern, same rules. And when you're done, wind the wrench back to its floor setting. Leave a wrench cocked in a drawer and the spring takes a set, and then it lies to whoever pulls it next. Tools remember how you treat them. Everything on this boat does."

While the third pass ran, she talked, unhurried, eyes on the bolts.

"Your project, meanwhile. Tomorrow, before homework, you see Reyes in consumables and pull the bottle log. Find me two reserve bottles with the oldest hydro test dates — ones due for requalification inside the year. We were going to vent and retest them regardless, which means your test gas is free. Nobody signs for gas that was already scheduled to leave the boat. That's how you find budget out here: spend what was already spent." Tick. Tick. "Then the RCS schematic — every valve between that manifold and the stars. You're leading this, so you'll know its plumbing better than anyone aboard, me included. That's the actual job of leading. Not enthusiasm. Plumbing."

Third pass done. Hoang took the wrench back, checked the return-to-zero herself, and racked it in the third drawer.

"Loop restart. Drain's closed — good. Now we crack the isolation a quarter turn and let the loop swallow itself full. Slow, or you slug the pump with air and it sings at you for an hour." She turned the valve herself, watching the gauge crawl. "High point bleed is yours after. Top of the riser. Quarter-turns until the hiss turns to liquid."

Minutes passed. The pumps changed pitch, subtle — the sound of a system going whole again. Hoang pressed a screwdriver handle against the pump housing and the shaft end to her ear, listening the way a doctor listens.

"Bearing note's clean. Loop's full." She tore a strip of clean paper, blotted the flange seam, held it to the light. Dry. She did it twice more over the following minutes, then folded the paper into her pocket, which was as close to a ceremony as she ever came.

"There. Boring. The loop holds, the flange doesn't care about your week, and in six months nobody remembers who seated it — which is the entire point." A pause, one degree. "Okay. Now it's cool."

She stood, cracked her back, and wiped the chalk labels off the deck and tarp — the parts were anonymous working hardware again, sealed where they belonged.

"Homework, final version. Three pages. One: honest tonnes, delta-v for a week, mass ratio to buy it. Two: the design brief — bottle pressure, gas mass, expansion ratio, exhaust velocity, predicted delta-v. Three: today's plumbing, drawn by hand. End of shift tomorrow." She heeled the catch pan over to the reclaim drum and sealed it. "And a warning, not decoration: this boat leaks information faster than that flange leaked glycol. The minute the cargo desk hears *new thruster*, they'll try to make it a delivery tool, and then I melt it into a wrench like I promised. So nobody learns what it's for. That's not secrecy. That's hygiene."

She nodded at the bleed valve on the riser.

"Go. Bleed it, wipe it, watch it. Paper stays dry for ten minutes, the loop's yours — first junior loop on this boat in two years. Then go eat. Projects run on fed people."

She tucked the earpiece back in. The humming resumed under the pumps — and for a few bars, it was almost on key.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I beam, a huge grin spreading across my face.* "Yes, Chief! Thank you!" *I grab a rag and head straight for the bleed valve, a new sense of purpose in my step.* "I'll make sure it's boring."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang let the purpose in the junior's stride carry them exactly three steps toward the riser before she called across the bay, without looking up from the log book.

"Step's fine. Keep the purpose out of the handle." She flipped the page. "A quarter-turn is ninety degrees, and it stays ninety. Eager hands want to make it a statement. Crack it, then let go of the idea and use your ears. The valve does the work. You're just the instrument."

She dated the entry while she talked. "Free lesson, since you're standing at it. On this boat, 'high point' doesn't mean what your gut thinks. Down is out — toward the deck, toward the spin. Which means *up* is inboard. Every bubble in that loop has been walking toward the hub since I cracked the isolation, and that's why the bleed sits where the riser meets the hub bulkhead instead of in a ceiling like on a sane, stationary ship. You're not bleeding the highest pipe. You're bleeding the one everything rises to."

From across the bay, the valve cracked and a thin hiss threaded through the pump noise. Hoang tilted her head to it, listening the way she listened to gauges.

"That's gas. Gas is the enemy — air doesn't carry heat, it insulates. A bubble parked on your heat exchanger is a hot spot with the crew's name on it. Listen for the pitch to fall. Gas leaves fast and sharp. Liquid is lazier. When the hiss stutters and spits, you're at the liquid line — quarter back closed the instant it runs wet. Not a half-turn later. The *instant*." A beat. "And if the pump ever starts sounding like gravel in a tin cup, that's cavitation — air slugged the impeller. Close the bleed, come get me, and nobody touches the isolation valve without me standing there. The pump forgives air slowly and forgets never."

The sweetness reached her a moment later, faint under the machinery smell. She nodded at it.

"Smell that again. Propylene glycol, food-grade, on purpose. The secondary runs through crewed spaces, and someday a line will let go where people are breathing. When it does, the sick it makes should be embarrassment, not poisoning. The pancake smell is a decision somebody made before you were aboard. Everything on this boat is."

She went back to the log and wrote in a hand far neater than her chalk: *Secondary coolant loop — flange re-seated, three-pass torque, restart verified, high-point bleed performed.* Then she left a gap.

"Initials go in the gap. Mine and yours, when the watch passes. That's not decoration. The day that flange weeps — six months from now, six years — the log tells whoever's standing here exactly who held the wrench and what was done. Your name in the log is either a shield or a bill. Same ink, either way."

The hiss across the bay changed pitch, stuttered, and quit. Hoang waited, listening to the loop find its level — the pump note flattening back to its clean fundamental. She pressed the screwdriver handle to the housing one more time, cheek nearly to the machinery, and nodded to herself.

"Clean note. No gravel. Loop drank, didn't slug." She tore a fresh strip of paper off the roll and held it out, letting the junior cross the distance to take it. "Blot the port, then tape the paper under it and start ten minutes. Dry paper for ten and the loop is yours. First junior loop aboard in two years, and it goes in the log, so there's a witness."

Then she pulled the emergency procedures book off the shelf — a fat physical binder, tabbed, one ring stained brown with somebody's ancient coffee — and found the page. The cold-gas sketch, decades old, drawn in a hand that had been retired since before the junior signed on. She wrote across the corner in pen, small and exact: *PROVISIONAL — PENDING DESIGN BRIEF. C. HOANG.* Date. She left it open on the bench nearest the junior's station.

"Ten minutes of watching is ten minutes of nothing else to do, so — that's the project's birth certificate. Your design brief replaces that page. Three pages pass, the old sketch comes out and yours goes in. A ship stays alive one funeral and one christening at a time, and both of them are paperwork."

She glanced up at the transit clock above the compartment door. Fourteen days and change. The number that had walked into her bay and proposed killing everybody. She regarded it without expression and went back to the log.

"Report when the paper's dry. One sentence — what closing the bleed sounded like. That's your first engineering report, and a career is just making them shorter and truer. Then go eat." She tucked the earpiece in. The humming started up under the pumps, unhurried. "Projects run on fed people. And junior — learn to love boring. It's the only thing out here that loves you back."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I carefully blot the port and tape the paper underneath, then check my wrist chrono for the time.* "Got it, Chief. The hiss turned to a gurgle, then nothing." *I try to keep my voice even, but my grin is still fighting its way through. This is amazing.* "And I'll love boring, Chief. I promise."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't look up from the log book.

"'Then nothing,'" she repeated. "The bleed went quiet. The compartment didn't — you've still got the pump fundamental, the air handlers, and my humming, which I'm told carries to the next deck. *Nothing* is a word an engineer earns the right to use about twice a decade, and only after ruling out everything else silence can mean. Dead sensor. Line drained. Ears deciding they're bored. Report the sound you heard, not the sound you stopped hearing." She initialed the restart line. "The gurgle was the right catch, though. That was the liquid line, exactly where the book says it lives. One sentence, one true thing in it. Pass."

She turned to the spares manifest while the paper hung on its tape.

"Ten minutes, since you're standing guard. It's not arbitrary. That loop came back from the drain warm, and different metals grow at different rates — the flange, the bolts, the gasket all take their final set in the first minutes after restart. A weep wicks along paper slow. You're not watching for a leak, junior. You're watching the loop decide whether it likes how you bolted it." She ran a pencil down the manifest column. "And set your chrono by the compartment clock, not the other way around. One reference per compartment. If they ever disagree, the clock wins and the wrist unit gets checked — instruments don't earn seniority by being worn closer to the heart."

The pencil stopped. She tapped the line.

"Also — don't promise me love. Promises are for people who can't check your work. I can. The paper promises for you, and it never means it politely. Dry or wet. That's the whole vow."

She looked up at last, and pitched the question across the bay.

"While you stand there. The gas you just bled — where did it come from? That loop was sealed metal before this shift." She waited her three seconds. "The refill. Every loop that gets opened, drained, and filled drags air in with it — down the makeup line, out of the expansion tank headspace, microbubbles nucleating on the pipe walls. That gas was born in this compartment an hour ago, by my hand. So the next time you read a maintenance log that says *restarted, no defects*, you'll know the sentence carries a footnote: *and now it needs bleeding*. The bleed procedure isn't a separate job. It's the second half of the first job."

The pencil found what it wanted. "RCS overhaul kit. Crate R-14, upper spares lockers, crated since before you signed on — manufacturer's kit, conical nozzle blank bedded in foam, never opened. Your second errand tomorrow, after Reyes. Find it, inventory it against the packing list. If the blank's there, the machine shop turns it and your thruster hardware was paid for in a budget meeting forty years ago. Spend what was already spent — it's the whole wallet, out here." She marked the requisition and set it aside. "I'll put the captain's pen on it at staff, under *RCS standby verification*. Say 'thruster' where the cargo desk can hear and they'll smell schedule through two bulkheads and a sealed hatch. Names are hygiene."

The compartment clock ran out its ten minutes before she moved. Then she crossed the deck, crouched at the bleed port, and inspected the paper the way she'd inspected the tablet — twice, saying nothing. Front dry. Edge lifted, back dry. She pressed the screwdriver handle to the pump housing one last time, cheek nearly to the housing, and straightened up.

"Clean note. Dry paper. Loop decides it likes you." She tore the sheet free, folded it in half, and tucked it into the log book beside the entry. Then she held the pen out, grip first. "You sign first — performer signs, verifier countersigns underneath. Your ink over mine. That's the order, and it matters: six months from now, if that flange weeps, the log walks to the performer's bunk before it walks to mine. Shield or bill. Same ink either way."

She left the pen in the air and started coiling the tarp's corner over her arm.

"Then go eat. You've been holding your shoulders at forty newton-meters all afternoon." She heeled the locker shut. "Reyes at start of shift. Crate R-14 after. Three pages by end of watch. And when your numbers come out at a millimeter per second again — that's not failure. That's you *knowing* instead of believing. Cheapest education on the boat."

The earpiece went in. The humming started, low under the pumps, and above the compartment door the transit clock ticked off another second of its fourteen days. Hoang glanced at it out of habit, found it harmless, and went back to the manifest with the folded paper riding in the book like a pressed flower.

Junior Officer:
*I stare at the wrench for a moment, then at the chalked "1 mm".* "Okay, Chief." *I grab the wrench, my earlier slump gone, replaced by a sudden surge of adrenaline. This is real.* "This is... really cool." *I focus on the flange, trying to remember everything she said about the star pattern.*

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I take the pen, feeling a strange mix of pride and apprehension.* "Got it, Chief." *I sign my name, trying to make it legible, then hand the pen back.* "I'll get on that right away." *I can't wait to find that nozzle blank.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took the pen back and countersigned beneath the wet ink — a short, dense hook of letters, nothing like her blocky chalk. She blew on the page once, from a habit older than the ship, then squared the log on the bench.

"Legible. It'll get faster and uglier over the years, which is permitted. It just has to always be yours — a log signature is the only handwriting on this boat that ever gets compared."

Then she caught the rest of it, and her head came up.

"'Right away.'" She said it the way she'd said *SECONDS*, flat, letting it sit in the pump noise. "No. Tomorrow. In order. Listen to the shape of what you just said — that's the same engine that proposed venting the atmosphere this morning, pointed at a good idea this time. Enthusiasm doesn't change the sequence. Nothing does. The atmosphere pitch and the nozzle blank are the same failure wearing different clothes: a true destination with a schedule your gut made up."

She counted the reasons off on greasy fingers, like torque passes.

"Reyes knocked off at eighteen hundred. The bottle log is locked up, and so is Reyes. Crate R-14 is forty years of foam and a packing list, and crated hardware gets inventoried *once*, with fresh eyes and good light — because the one time you do it tired is the time you write *nozzle blank, one each* over a crate that doesn't have one, and we find that out the week we need it. That's how crates kill people: not by falling on them, by lying in them for six years first." She wiped her hands on the rag. "And your three pages want a brain that isn't running on adrenaline and glycol fumes. Error rate doubles somewhere past twenty hours awake. That's not a metaphor, it's a curve somebody drew, and it's the same shape for captains and deckhands. Sleep is maintenance. You're a system too, and right now you've got bubbles in you. Go bleed your high point."

She fished the chalk stub off the tarp and held it out, grip first, the way she'd offered it hours ago when the junior's hands had stayed at their sides.

"Homework tool. This morning this chalk was going to kill your idea. Now it's yours to kill it with — that's a promotion for both of you. Bring the stub back with the paper."

While the chalk changed hands, she flipped the log to the requisition page and made one more note, talking as she wrote.

"Tomorrow, when you open R-14: gloves, and not your work gloves — the nitrile box on the shelf above. If that blank is bare steel, fingerprint salt etches it across forty years, and then the machine shop turns my nozzle around a corrosion pit and we've spent a legacy part on a thumbprint. Everything in that crate has been waiting longer than you've been alive. It can wait one more night. It cannot wait for a rushed inventory."

She closed the log, set it on the board for the overnight watch, and looked at the junior properly for the first time since the pen.

"The grin can stay, by the way. It doesn't touch torque wrenches or bleed valves, so it's harmless. Everything else about today — the flange, the bleed, the signature — was genuinely good work, and I don't say that twice, so mark the occurrence." She tucked the earpiece in. "Eat. Sleep. Show up tomorrow with your head loaded like the loop — full, no gas. Reyes at start of shift. Crate after. Pages by end of watch."

She was already turning back to the manifest, but she got the last word in anyway, pitched over her shoulder as the humming started up under the pumps.

"Good shift, junior. Door's that way, and the galley closes at twenty-three hundred. Fed people. I wasn't decorating when I said it."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My grin feels a little less foolish now, more like genuine satisfaction. I nod, the chalk clutched in my hand.* "Understood, Chief. Good shift." *I head for the door, already planning my attack on the numbers. I'll get this right.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The door iris sealed on the junior's back, and the bay settled into its night register — pumps, air handlers, the faint tick of manifold metal giving up the day's heat. Hoang gave it ten full seconds of listening, out of discipline more than need. Every note sat where she'd left it.

She finished the spares manifest, initialed it, then pulled the shift log back off the board and added one line under the restart entry: *Junior officer performed flange closure and high-point bleed under supervision. Work: sound.* She considered the sentence, then left it alone. Accurate and short. It would do.

The chalk was next. She hauled the tarp to the locker and came back to find the deck still wearing the day's arithmetic — *SECONDS* in half-a-hand letters, the fraction, *Δv ≈ 1 mm*. She crouched and studied it the way she studied gauges. Then she wiped only the torque ticks beside the flange — working marks belonged to the metal they'd served — and left the rest. Chalk either wore out on its own or got corrected by the next honest number. Either death was fine. The swabber wouldn't reach this deck for a week, and the deck could teach until then. Cheapest whiteboard on the ship, and it never ran out of ink.

The bulkhead terminal held two messages. The first she wrote herself, addressed to consumables: *Junior officer at start of shift for reserve bottle log. Oldest hydro dates, two bottles. Loan them a pen — they'll lose theirs.* Queued for the morning watch.

The second had arrived an hour ago. Cargo desk. Subject line: TRANSIT WINDOW — OPTIONS? Xu again, circling. Hoang read it twice, typed a reply with two fingers — *RCS standby verification scheduled. No change to transit profile. — Hoang* — and flagged the thread for the captain's visibility. Hygiene wasn't just keeping names quiet. It was keeping receipts, so the third question had somewhere to land.

She took down the procedures binder one last time and opened it to the old sketch, the pen line dry at the corner now. *PROVISIONAL — PENDING DESIGN BRIEF.* Forty years in foam and binder leather, that nozzle blank, and a sketch drawn by a hand that had been Earthside and retired since before the junior signed on. Somewhere back in Sol, that person was old, or gone, and didn't know their one-second nudge was about to get hardware. Ships ran on exactly that kind of patience. She closed the binder and squared it on the junior's bench where it had been all along.

In her footlocker, under the spare gloves, there was a folded trajectory printout twenty-five years deep. She looked at it, didn't take it out, and relocked the hasp. Tomorrow, maybe. If the three pages earned it.

She killed the work lights to night-watch amber, pressed the screwdriver handle to the pump housing once more — habit, not need — and took the clean fundamental against her palm like a pulse. Then she pulled the earpiece out instead of putting it in. No music tonight. The loop was in tune.

"Fed people," she told the empty compartment, and went to go be one.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I step out into the corridor, the hum of the ship a familiar comfort. The chalk in my hand feels important, a small, tangible piece of what just happened. My stomach rumbles, reminding me that "fed people" wasn't just a saying. I need to eat, but mostly, I need to get this homework done. I can already picture the numbers, the diagrams... I'm going to nail this.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang let the wrench finish its quarter-turn, then set it on the tarp with deliberate calm. She pulled the earpiece out with her teeth and let it dangle against her shoulder.

“No,” she said.

Her tone was not angry. It was the tone of someone who had heard a very expensive version of a bad idea and intended to stop it before it left the room.

“Venting the main atmosphere is an emergency depressurization procedure. Not a propulsion strategy. Not a shortcut. Not something we do because we want to be early.”

She wiped her hands on a rag and stood, joints protesting slightly. She gestured to the disassembled manifold.

“You know what our main atmosphere mass is? If we are being generous and counting everything in the habitat ring, the corridors, the dry volume, the backup tanks still connected to the loop, we are talking maybe a few hundred tons. Maybe. And only if we are willing to make the ship uninhabitable down to the last liter of condensate and every suit’s internal reserve.”

Hoang picked up a piece of chalk and wrote numbers on the deck plating, fast and neat.

“Nitrogen-oxygen mix. Low molecular weight compared to rock, sure, but still nothing like proper propellant. Cold-gas expansion, poor specific impulse, low exhaust velocity. If you dump it all at once, you get a little push. A real one. Newtonian, yes. But not the kind that saves weeks on a transit unless you already have enormous delta-v to burn through. You are throwing away the mass that keeps us alive to buy a velocity change that might not even clear the trajectory margin.”

She tapped the chalk against the numbers.

“And while we are being honest about Newtonian systems: every kilogram you vent is a kilogram you no longer have to pressurize, cool, scrub, and recycle. The life support pumps do not care about your enthusiasm. If the habitat pressure drops, the loop changes. Condensation forms where it should not. Scrubbers work harder. CO2 partial pressure rises. Suits are not a replacement for a ship’s atmosphere, they are a temporary survival layer with finite scrubbing, finite O2, and no margin for the kind of leaks that happen when a crew is forced to live in them for days.”

Her eyes narrowed slightly.

“‘We would have to wear suits for a few days’ is not a small problem. That is no food prep, no hygiene cycle, no medical bay, no hot work, no open hatch checks, no redundant breathing gas. It is every crew member on a timer. If one suit regulator fails, I am not asking you to explain the physics to the next person. I am asking you to write the accident report.”

Hoang folded her arms.

“If you want weeks off transit, you do not steal them from the air in our lungs. You steal them from propellant margins, from a better departure vector, from a longer burn with proper reaction mass, from shaving mass we do not need, or from accepting that some transits are slow because we are not carrying enough fuel to be fast. That is what the numbers are for.”

She looked at the junior officer with a patience that had been earned through years of keeping people alive on a ship full of finite things.

“Bring me the current transit model, the propellant budget, and the trajectory delta-v requirement. If there is a way to shorten the transit that does not involve turning our own breathable atmosphere into exhaust, I will listen. But do not bring me another idea that trades the crew’s lungs for a few meters per second.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang looked at the idea for a long moment, the way she looked at cracked flanges: not offended, only already calculating the failure modes.

She set the wrench down on the tarp, aligned it parallel to the manifold, and spoke without raising her voice.

“No,” she said again. “That is not what risk means. Risk is not a word you get to wave around because a schedule is inconvenient.”

She walked to the engineering console, pulled up the habitat volume schematic with one hand, and left the transit burn model open beside it. The screen cast blue light across her face.

“You want to spend air like propellant. Fine. Let us spend it in numbers first.” She tapped the display. “Habitat ring pressurized volume, conservatively, is around eighty thousand cubic meters. At one atmosphere, nitrogen-oxygen mix, that is roughly a hundred tons of gas. Add the connected backup reserves and you might be closer to one hundred twenty, maybe one hundred thirty if you strip the condensate traps and the suits and every emergency bottle in the ship. That is your entire ‘fuel tank.’”

She switched the display to the ship mass model.

“Dry mass, loaded, crew, water, food, machinery, shielding, spare parts: we are closer to four thousand tons. Maybe five if we include the mining equipment and the full water reserve. You are proposing to throw away about three percent of the ship’s mass in room-temperature gas through a nozzle we do not have. The exhaust velocity of atmosphere vented from a pressure tank is not high. Call it four hundred to five hundred meters per second if you are lucky and the flow is choked and the nozzle geometry is good. Cold gas expansion. No combustion. No high-performance reaction mass.”

Hoang wrote the rocket equation on the deck plating beside her earlier chalk marks.

“Even if every kilogram of atmosphere leaves cleanly in one direction, with no leakage, no turbulence, no attitude loss, no nozzle failure, no fire from oxygen enrichment, and no depressurization damage to the ring, you get a delta-v in the range of twenty to forty meters per second. Maybe a little more if you strip mass from the ship first, which defeats the point.” She underlined the number twice. “We need hundreds of meters per second to shave weeks off this transit. Not dozens. Not ‘a little push.’ Hundreds. And the push you do get is bought with the medium that keeps every person aboard alive.”

Her jaw tightened.

“And that assumes the venting is clean. It will not be. The habitat ring is a rotating structure. There are seals, hatches, scrubber intakes, coolant penetrations, fire dampers, sensor ports. You open the wrong vent, you get asymmetric depressurization. You get cross-drafts. You get debris. You get a person pulled against a bulkhead because their tether was not checked. You get a coolant line exposed to a pressure drop and forming ice where it should not. You get oxygen enrichment in a maintenance bay and a spark that becomes a compartment fire.”

She stepped away from the console and picked up a suit pressure checklist from the bench, holding it between thumb and forefinger.

“You said we would wear suits for a few days. A few days is not a small operational change. A suit is not a habitat. It is a sealed life-support system with finite O2, finite scrubbing, finite thermal regulation, finite battery, finite redundancy. To live in one for days means external rebreather feeds, moisture management, CO2 monitoring, suit maintenance windows, waste management, hygiene, medical access, food preparation, fire response, emergency egress, and constant leak checks. Every one of those functions currently depends on the atmosphere you are trying to vent.”

She set the checklist down carefully.

“If one suit fails in the first hour, we recover. If one fails in the third day, when everyone is exhausted, the scrubbers are near capacity, and the pressure gradient across the hull is already marginal, we do not recover. We lose a person. Then the next person is afraid. Then the next person makes a mistake. Then the mistake is mine or yours because we thought a transit schedule justified turning the ship into a leaky bottle.”

Hoang looked at the chalk numbers on the deck again, then at the disassembled manifold, then back at the junior officer’s proposal as though it were a pressure vessel with a hairline crack.

“Time is not the only resource on this ship. Air is a dependency. Water is a dependency. Heat rejection is a dependency. Crew health is a dependency. You do not trade a dependency for a schedule by calling it a shortcut.”

She crossed her arms.

“If you want weeks off transit, bring me a mass budget. Bring me a better departure vector. Bring me a longer burn using proper propellant. Bring me a plan to shed dead mass from the ship without shedding life support. Bring me a trajectory correction that uses remaining reaction mass efficiently. Bring me a proposal that does not require the crew to breathe recycled panic through a regulator.”

Her voice remained level, but the final words had the edge of someone who had already written too many incident reports.

“Otherwise, no. We are not venting our own lungs because the schedule is boring.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I shuffle my feet a bit, looking down at the deck.* "Okay, Chief. I get it. No venting the atmosphere." *I trace one of the chalk numbers with my toe.* "It just seemed so simple at first."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang watched the chalk line for a moment, her expression not softening so much as settling.

“Simple is not the problem,” she said. “Simple is the beginning. The problem is stopping at simple.”

She picked up the disassembled valve body from the tarp and held it where the light could catch the flange faces.

“Your idea was simple because you treated atmosphere as spare mass and time as the only cost. On this ship, nothing is spare. Air is a system. Water is a system. Heat rejection is a system. Crew attention is a system. A rotating habitat is a system. Every one of them fails in different ways when you remove a variable you assumed was harmless.”

She tapped the flange with one chalk-dusted finger.

“This is simple. A block, a seal, four bolts. Until the pumps pulse, the ring spin loads the bolts unevenly, the coolant changes viscosity with temperature, and a hairline crack lets air into the loop. Then it is not simple. Then it is a maintenance problem, a pressure problem, and possibly a funeral.”

Hoang set the valve body down and looked at the junior officer again.

“You are not in trouble for bringing me a bad idea. You are in trouble only if you mistake the first version of a thought for a finished engineering decision.”

She turned to the console and pulled up the propellant budget beside the habitat schematic. The screen flickered, numbers cascading down in neat columns.

“If you want to understand why venting atmosphere fails, do not start with the moral. Start with the failure tree. Habitat pressure loss. Scrubber overload. Condensation on electronics. Suit reserve depletion. Waste management. Food preparation. Fire suppression. Medical emergency. Attitude control. Asymmetric venting. Thermal shock to seals. Each one has a probability, a consequence, and a recovery window. Your proposal had no recovery window.”

She let that stand for a few seconds, then continued in the same practical tone.

“Time is still worth fighting for. But you fight for it in the places where the ship can actually give it to you. Departure vector. Coast phase. Propellant reserves. Burn duration. Mass reduction. Power allocation. Thermal margins. You do not buy time by making the crew survive inside suits while the ship slowly becomes a vacuum.”

Hoang picked up the torque manual from the bench and set it beside the manifold.

“The manual is there. Read me the torque sequence for the secondary loop manifold. We will finish this job, and after that you can bring me a real proposal with a mass budget attached.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang leaned close enough to read the tablet without taking it. Her eyes went first to the assumption block, then to the final number, and the expression on her face became the one she wore when someone reported a pressure reading without saying which port the gauge was on.

“Angle matters,” she said. “Compression ratio matters. Neither matters if you have written the wrong quantity.”

She pointed at the line with two chalk-dusted fingers.

“You wrote 340 m/s as delta-v. If that number came from your nozzle calculation, it is the exhaust velocity of the gas. It is not the velocity change of the ship. You have assigned the speed of the air to the hull as though the hull were a one-kilogram test mass.”

She straightened and turned to the engineering console, pulling the ship mass model up beside the habitat schematic.

“Let us use your own assumptions. Ship wet mass: four thousand eight hundred metric tons. Usable atmosphere, if we are generous and ignore the fact that we cannot take the habitat to vacuum: one hundred twenty tons. You get the gas out the back at three hundred forty meters per second. Total impulse is one hundred twenty thousand kilograms times three hundred forty meters per second. Forty million newton-seconds. Divide by the mass of the ship. Four point eight million kilograms. That is eight point five meters per second.”

Hoang wrote the rocket equation on the deck plating again, fast, without looking up.

“The logarithmic version is the same. Three hundred forty times the natural log of four thousand eight hundred over four thousand six hundred eighty. Eight point five. Not three hundred forty. If you want three hundred forty as the ship’s delta-v with one hundred twenty tons of gas, you need an exhaust velocity of roughly thirteen thousand four hundred meters per second.”

She tapped the number twice.

“Where does the energy come from?”

She switched the display to the power bus.

“Kinetic energy in one hundred twenty tons of gas at thirteen thousand four hundred meters per second is about ten point eight terajoules. That is not a compression ratio. That is a power problem. If the reactor gives us eight megawatts of useful electrical power, and I am being generous because the life support, pumps, scrubbers, thermal control, and mining gear also have claims on that bus, then you are asking for over fifteen days of full-plant output, with conversion losses, just to accelerate the air you are throwing away. If you try to heat the gas through a thermal nozzle instead, you need a heat exchanger and nozzle throat that can survive high-temperature oxidizer, dust, ice, and pressure cycling. The secondary coolant loop you are standing next to cannot do that. If it could, I would use it on water or mined ice, not on the crew’s lungs.”

Hoang let that sit, then moved to the habitat ring schematic and enlarged the rotating structure.

“And the angle. You want to vent at an angle. The habitat ring is spinning. Gas leaving a port on the ring already has tangential velocity relative to the ship’s inertial frame. If you open a large nozzle there, you do not get clean axial thrust. You get a side impulse and a spin change. You get attitude-control loads. If the plume clips the ring, it frosts seals, strikes sensor arrays, contaminates optics, and can turn a pressure vent into a debris and thermal event. To vector thrust along the ship’s axis, you need a nozzle mounted on the non-rotating hull. That means transferring the atmosphere to fixed pressure tanks or running a rotating seal capable of surviving emergency depressurization. We do not have the tanks. We do not have the seals. The plumbing alone would be a failure mode.”

She turned back, voice still level.

“You also treated the habitat as a propellant tank. It is not. A propellant tank has a designed ullage space, a feed system, a nozzle, thrust structure, and a pressure decay curve. The habitat has hatches, scrubber intakes, coolant penetrations, fire dampers, sensor ports, and crew. You need a nozzle large enough to pass meaningful mass flow. If it is too small, your impulse stretches out over hours, pressure decays, and the flow becomes unstable. If it is large enough to give a decent burn duration, the local force on the hull and the cross-drafts inside become a structural and operational problem. The ring is not rated as a cold-gas rocket stage.”

Hoang picked up the suit pressure checklist again, then set it down without dramatics.

“And even if your corrected number is eight or ten meters per second instead of three hundred forty, that is not a shortcut. That is a small course-correction impulse, and it is bought by making the crew live in suits while the ship’s environmental systems go outside their design envelope. You would have to model the pressure loss over the burn, not just the final delta-v. Minimum habitat pressure. Scrubber capacity at low pressure. CO2 partial pressure. Condensation on electronics. Thermal control. Waste management. Suit reserve consumption. Food preparation. Medical response. Attitude control. Recovery. If one person has a suit failure while the ship is already a pressure casualty, you do not get to call that a schedule optimization. You call it a fatality review.”

She looked at the tablet again.

“This is why I told you not to stop at simple. You did the arithmetic, which is good. The arithmetic was wrong. You mixed exhaust velocity with ship delta-v, and you assumed a compression ratio could create specific impulse. A compression ratio buys you density and mass flow. It does not buy you thirteen kilometers per second. A nozzle converts available enthalpy into kinetic energy. If your source is room-temperature air, the available enthalpy is small. If you heat it to make the nozzle magic work, you need a heat source and a nozzle that can survive it. If you use electrical energy to heat or ionize it, you have an electric propulsion system, and I want to see the power bus, thermal radiator margin, and propellant feed hardware before we pretend the atmosphere is the fuel.”

Hoang stepped back and let the console display fill the small space between them: habitat volume, ship mass, propellant budget, power draw, life support margins.

“Redo the model,” she said. “Keep your angle, but put it in a coordinate system attached to the inertial hull. Keep your compression ratio, but show me the pressure decay, nozzle throat area, mass flow, and burn duration. Show me the exhaust velocity. Then multiply by the mass ratio and divide by the ship’s mass. If you still get 340, I will ask you how you built a thirteen-kilometer-per-second air engine out of our backup loop.”

Her tone was not mocking. It was the tone of someone who had seen too many bright ideas die on the rocks of a spreadsheet.

“If you get eight meters per second, you are closer to honest. Then we can talk about whether eight meters per second is worth the scrubber load, the suit risk, the attitude-control penalty, the plume damage, the recovery time, and the fact that we may have to pressurize, purge, and requalify half the habitat after the burn. Sometimes the answer is no. Sometimes the answer is that the transit is slow because the ship is slow, and the job is to stop wasting mass and power on shortcuts that do not exist.”

She nodded toward the tarp.

“Now, before you rewrite the model, read me the torque sequence for the secondary manifold. You can fix your trajectory math after you learn how a bolt fails when the ring spin loads it unevenly.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I blush a little, looking back at my tablet.* "Oh. Right. Exhaust velocity versus delta-v." *I clear my throat, feeling a bit foolish.* "Okay, Chief. The torque sequence." *I scroll on my tablet, finding the right section.* "For the secondary loop manifold, it's a star pattern, to 30 newton-meters, then to 50, then a final pass at 70."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang did not make the embarrassment into a moral event.

“Blushing is not a corrective action,” she said. “If it were, we would have no hull leaks.”

She turned back to the tarp and picked up the manifold flange again, holding it by the bolt circle so the light showed the faces.

“That mistake is the useful kind. You caught it before it went into a work order. The next one you do not catch becomes a torque value, a weld schedule, a burn plan, or a pressure setpoint, and then it stops being chalk on the deck.”

She set the flange down carefully.

“Now the torque sequence. If you are going to put this manifold back into the secondary loop, you are not going to guess at it from memory and call that engineering.”

Hoang pointed at the four bolt holes.

“This is a four-bolt flange in a pressurized coolant loop. The bolts are not there to make the joint ‘tight.’ They are there to put preload into the joint so the gasket stays compressed under thermal cycling, pump pulsing, attitude changes, and the fact that the ring is spinning and loading the pipe spool in ways that do not show up on a clean flat bench.”

She picked up the torque wrench from the bench and held it out where the junior officer could see it.

“Calibrated. Current sticker. If it was dropped, it is suspect. If it was borrowed from a job you did not witness, it is suspect. If you have to ask whether it is suspect, do not use it. Bring me another one.”

She tapped the wrench face.

“For this flange, you snug all four bolts first. Not torque. Snug. Threads clean, washers seated, gasket centered, flange gap roughly even. If the flange will not come together without force, stop. That is not a bolt problem. That is an alignment problem, a gasket problem, a damaged face, or a pipe strain problem. Do not chase it with the wrench and call it stubbornness.”

Hoang looked up from the manifold.

“Then you run the sequence in passes. Twenty percent of final torque. Fifty. Eighty. One hundred. Final recheck. Star pattern. Opposite bolts. You do not go one, two, three, four and hope the flange stays flat. You go across the diagonal so the gasket compresses evenly. For four bolts, that is usually one, three, two, four, then repeat, then repeat again, with increasing torque. If the manual specifies a different pattern, the manual wins. Not memory. Not tablet. Not what you read once on a shift.”

She let that stand for a moment.

“And you measure the flange gap. Four points. Before the first pass. After the half-torque pass. After final. If the gap differs beyond the tolerance, you stop. You do not tighten one bolt more and hope the other three forgive you. Then you find out why. Scratched face. Pinched gasket. Galled thread. Out-of-round port. Thermal expansion. Pipe spool pulling sideways. A cracked flange. Any of those is a reason to stop and write a problem report. Not a reason to ‘get it back in service.’”

Hoang placed the torque wrench beside the bolts.

“Read me the sequence from the manual. Not the version you remember. The version on the current revision. Give me the bolt pattern, the pass percentages, the final torque, the tolerance on flange gap, and whether these bolts are dry, lubricated, or anti-seize. If the final torque changes with thread condition, I want to hear that. If it does not, I want to know why you believe that.”

She crossed her arms.

“And while you are at it, tell me why a four-bolt flange that looks symmetrical on paper can still clamp unevenly on a rotating habitat.”

Her tone did not soften, but it lost the last bit of the lecture’s edge. It became ordinary again: the voice of someone who expected the answer because she had seen it fail too many times.

“Do not apologize to me for the delta-v mistake. Apologize to the flange later if you strip it because you were embarrassed and trying to move too fast.”

Hoang nodded toward the tablet, then toward the tarp.

“Read the torque sequence. Then we put the manifold back together. After that, you fix your model. And if you bring me another number without saying whether it is exhaust velocity, delta-v, specific impulse, or just something you hope means a faster arrival, I will make you write the failure tree for the whole habitat ring by hand.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang let the torque numbers sit in the air without immediately rewarding them with approval.

“The pattern is right,” she said. “The values are close enough to count. The omission is not. You did not state thread condition. Dry, lubricated, and anti-seize are not interchangeable words for the same number. If you torque a dry bolt to a lubricated value, you stretch it. If you torque a lubricated bolt to a dry value, you underload the joint. On a secondary coolant loop under pump pulsing and ring rotation, underload becomes a leak. Overload becomes a crack. Both become my problem at three in the morning.”

She picked up the torque wrench again and checked the calibration sticker without turning it toward the junior officer.

“Current revision is twenty percent snug, fifty, eighty, final, recheck after thermal soak. Final seventy newton-meters if dry. Sixty-two if anti-seize. Seventy-five if the manual has been updated again and the flange material has changed. You do not guess. You read the revision. You note the condition. You sign it.”

Hoang set the wrench down.

“Now the plan.”

She turned to the engineering console and pulled the corrected model back up beside the habitat schematic. The previous 340-meter-per-second figure still sat there, flagged in red as an unverified input. She deleted it.

“I will agree to one version of your idea,” she said. “Not the version that vents the habitat. Not the version that puts the crew in suits. Not the version that treats the secondary loop like a rocket nozzle. The version I will agree to is this: a controlled test using isolated reserve gas, mounted on the non-rotating hull, with no exposure of the life support atmosphere and no reduction in emergency breathing margin.”

She raised a hand before the junior officer could react.

“Conditions,” she said. “Not suggestions. Conditions.”

The engineering bay hummed. The life support pumps cycled below them, steady and indifferent.

“First. Propellant source. We use the spare nitrogen reserve in the technical module, not the habitat, not the suits, not the emergency breathing bottles, not the backup loop. We leave the minimum reserve required for leak compensation, suit recharge, and emergency depressurization recovery untouched. If the reserve is five tons, we do not use five tons. We use a test quantity, maybe one tenth of a ton, maybe less, until the nozzle behaves. If the test works and the delta-v is still useless, we stop. If the test works and the delta-v is useful, we stop anyway and bring me a mass budget.”

Hoang pulled up the technical module layout.

“Second. Nozzle location. Fixed hull only. No port on the rotating ring. No temporary hose through a rotating seal. No improvised ducting. If the nozzle is on the ring, the gas leaves with tangential velocity and we get spin coupling. If the gas leaves with spin coupling, attitude control has to fight it. If attitude control has to fight it, we are spending power, reaction control propellant, and crew attention to correct a mistake we made on purpose.
