The nozzle must be aligned with the ship’s center of mass within one degree, and the plume must clear every structure by at least five meters. No frost. No impingement. No debris risk. No optical contamination. No thermal loading on sensor pods.”

She tapped the alignment diagram.

“Third. No crew exposure. No suits for days. No habitat depressurization. No pressure gradient across living spaces. During the test, the habitat stays pressurized, the scrubbers stay in design range, the thermal loop stays stable, and the crew stays out of the technical module except for remotely monitored systems. If the test requires anyone to stand next to the nozzle, the test is canceled. If it requires anyone to manually isolate a valve under pressure, the test is canceled. If it requires a person to wear a regulator because the gas might escape into a compartment, the test is canceled.”

Hoang’s voice stayed flat, but the line hardened.

“Fourth. Model before hardware. You do not open a valve until the pressure decay curve, mass flow rate, thrust vector, burn duration, delta-v, attitude torque, thermal load, and failure modes are written into a work order. You show me the tank pressure at start, at fifty percent, at ninety percent, and at abort. You show me nozzle throat area. You show me whether the flow chokes. You show me whether the tank cools below acceptable limits. You show me whether the gas becomes dense enough to form ice particles. You show me whether the plume reflects off the hull. You show me the energy cost if you heat the gas. You show me the radiator margin if you do not heat it and the tank pressure falls too fast.”

She switched to the power bus display.

“If your plan uses electrical heating to improve exhaust velocity, I need the power budget. If your plan uses stored thermal energy, I need the thermal budget. If your plan uses a compression ratio to make cold gas behave like a chemical rocket, I need you to explain where the extra energy comes from. It does not come from cleverness. It comes from mass, temperature, pressure, and nozzle design. If those are not on the page, the idea is not approved.”

Hoang pulled up a blank failure tree template.

“Fifth. Abort criteria. Automatic and manual. If tank pressure falls below the minimum reserve threshold, abort. If habitat pressure changes by more than one-tenth of a kilopascal, abort. If scrubber inlet CO2 partial pressure rises outside normal range, abort. If attitude error exceeds one-tenth of a degree for more than ten seconds, abort. If plume temperature at any nearby structure exceeds design limit, abort. If the nozzle vibrates beyond the frequency margin, abort. If any sensor disagrees with any other sensor for more than five seconds, abort. If the ring spin rate changes by more than the stated tolerance, abort. If a crew member has to look at a gauge and decide whether the ship is safe, the test has already failed.”

She wrote a short list on the deck plating beside the earlier chalk marks.

“Sixth. Redundancy. No single valve controls the test gas. No single sensor controls abort. No single person controls the sequence. There is a mechanical isolation valve upstream of the nozzle, a remotely actuated dump valve downstream of the tank, a pressure relief path, and a hard shutdown that cuts power to the actuator and closes the fail-safe valve. If the fail-safe valve is not rated for the test pressure, it is not a fail-safe. It is a hope.”

Hoang looked at the disassembled manifold, then back at the console.

“Seventh. Trajectory value. This is not a feeling. This is a number. If the test gives us less than one meter per second of useful delta-v after attitude losses, plume losses, and recovery corrections, it is not a transit improvement. It is a maintenance event. If it gives more than one meter per second, it may be a course-correction option. If it gives more than ten meters per second from isolated reserve gas without touching life support, I will listen. If it gives more than fifty, I will ask for the full model and a crew vote. If it gives three hundred forty, I will ask you how you built an air-breathing rocket engine out of a spare nitrogen bottle, and I will want to see the laws of thermodynamics in the room.”

A faint line of dry humor crossed her face, but not a smile.

“Eighth. Recovery. After the test, we do not simply close the valve and move on. We inspect the nozzle. We inspect the tank mount. We inspect the hull plating near the plume path. We inspect thermal insulation. We inspect attitude control logs. We inspect spin coupling data. We inspect pressure decay. We purge and requalify any line that saw test gas. We update the work order. We update the risk register. If the test was a success, we write a procedure. If the test was a failure, we write an incident report. There is no third category called ‘mostly worked, let us use it during transit.’”

Hoang folded her arms.

“Ninth. Sign-offs. The trajectory officer approves the delta-v value. The life support officer approves the gas source and confirms no habitat impact. The safety officer approves the nozzle alignment and abort criteria. The propulsion officer approves the plume interaction and attitude model. The medical officer confirms no crew exposure beyond normal operational risk. The captain approves the work order. If any one of those says no, the test does not happen. I do not care how far away the destination is. I care how far away the crew is from a bad decision.”

She let that settle.

“Tenth. Schedule discipline. No test is approved because the transit is slow. No test is approved because someone wants to be early. No test is approved because the crew is tired of routine. We do not spend finite systems to buy comfort with time. If the test has value, it has value because it improves safety, redundancy, or mission performance within acceptable risk. If the only improvement is arriving earlier, that is not enough. Earlier to what? A job that requires the crew intact, the ship pressurized, the life support healthy, and the trajectory clean. If we arrive earlier with scrubber damage, suit reserve depletion, attitude control fatigue, and a half-depressurized habitat, we have not optimized the transit. We have converted it into an emergency.”

Hoang turned back to the console and began entering the corrected assumptions. Ship mass. Isolated reserve mass. Nozzle exhaust velocity. Burn duration. Attitude margin. Habitat pressure sensitivity. Power draw. Thermal radiator load. Recovery cost. The numbers shifted into a smaller, more honest shape.

“The version I agree to is not ‘vent the atmosphere to save time,’” she said. “It is ‘test whether a small, controlled, non-habitat gas vent provides a useful impulse without endangering life support.’ Those are different proposals. One is a shortcut through the crew’s lungs. The other is an experiment with a spare bottle.”

She looked at the junior officer with steady patience.

“You were wrong about the delta-v. You were also not wrong to want a faster arrival. The mistake was not the desire. The mistake was treating a complex system as if it had only one variable. Time has a value here. Air has a value here. Heat rejection has a value here. Crew attention has a value here. Attitude control has a value here. We do not ignore those values because one number looks good on a tablet.”

Hoang picked up the chalk again and underlined the new reserve-gas delta-v estimate.

“If your model shows that the isolated reserve test gives a meaningful impulse, and your failure tree shows recovery, and your work order shows no habitat exposure, then yes. I will agree to the test. I will even agree to run it if the schedule is tight. But I will not agree to a test that depends on the crew being lucky, calm, and uninjured while the ship’s environment is outside its design envelope.”

She set the chalk down.

“So that is the condition. Build the test around the ship’s limits, not around the calendar. If you can do that, bring me the full model, the failure tree, the sign-off sheet, and the torque procedure for the nozzle mounting bolts. If you cannot, we keep the atmosphere in the habitat where it belongs, and we find time some other way.”

Hoang turned back to the disassembled manifold and picked up a bolt.

“Now, before we touch the reserve gas, we finish this manifold. Read me the current revision again, including thread condition, recheck interval, and flange gap tolerance. Then we put this joint together properly. A bad idea corrected is not enough. A good idea assembled wrong is still a bad day.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in. The full weight of her conditions makes my previous idea seem even more foolish.* "Okay, Chief. That's... a lot more complicated than I thought. But yeah, I can do that. I'll get that model built. For now, the manifold." *I clear my throat and pull up the manual again, double-checking everything.* "Okay, current revision for the secondary loop manifold. Torque sequence is twenty percent snug, then fifty, eighty, and final at seventy newton-meters dry, or sixty-two with anti-seize. Recheck after thermal soak. Flange gap tolerance is point-oh-five millimeters."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang did not nod. She reached out, took the tablet from the bench beside her, and pulled the controlled engineering manual to the correct revision page. She read the header line, then the footnote, then the torque table again, slower the second time.

“Closer,” she said. “Not finished.”

She set the tablet on the tarp, next to the flange, and tapped the torque table with one chalk-dusted finger.

“You gave me dry and anti-seize. You did not give me lubricated. You did not give me bolt grade. You did not give me new versus reused. You did not give me thread engagement. You did not give me washer type. You did not tell me whether the gasket is rated for the coolant temperature, whether the flange faces are within scratch tolerance, or whether the pipe spool is pulling on the joint before the bolts are even in. Those are not decorative details. They are the difference between a sealed loop and a leak that shows up six hours after you think the job is done.”

She picked up one bolt from the tray, turned it under the bay light, and inspected the threads.

“Torque is not just force. It is friction. Friction changes with surface condition. If the threads are dry, you get one preload. If they are lubricated, you get another. If you have anti-seize on the wrong surface, you can underload the joint or overload the bolt and not know it until the gasket creeps or the flange cracks. If the bolt has been reused and the threads are nicked, the manual value may no longer apply. If the washer is damaged, the bolt will bite instead of seating evenly. If the pipe is strained, the bolts will fight the spool, not the gasket.”

Hoang set the bolt down and looked at the junior officer.

“So before we put this manifold back together, we do it the way that gives us a record. Not the way that gives us a feeling.”

She pulled a blank work order card from the bench and began writing in quick, legible shorthand.

“First. Confirm the revision. Not from memory. Not from a cached tablet. From the controlled copy. Read me the revision date, page number, and any service note attached to this manifold. If there is a temporary change order for the secondary loop, it overrides the manual. If there is no change order, the manual still must be current. If you cannot prove the revision, we do not torque anything.”

She underlined the word *prove*.

“Second. Inspect the flange faces. Clean them. Check for scratches, dents, corrosion, weld spatter, gasket residue, and flatness deviations. If there is a scratch across the gasket seat that can pass a feeler gauge, stop and bring it to me. If the face is out of round, stop. If the pipe spool is pulling the flange out of alignment, stop and support the line. Do not use bolts to correct alignment. Bolts are not a crane, a jack, or a wish.”

She held up the manifold flange and turned it so the light caught the sealing surface.

“Third. Verify the gasket. Correct material. Correct temperature rating. Correct pressure rating. Correct thickness. No folds, cuts, crushed edges, or old compression marks from a previous removal. If it came from a damaged package or sat in a bay without a lot number, it is not installed. Center it. Do not glue it, tape it, or wedge it into place. If it shifts during assembly, the joint leaks. If it shifts during pump pulsing, the joint leaks later.”

Hoang set the flange down.

“Fourth. Verify the bolts. Grade, length, thread pitch, condition, and history. New bolts get inspected before installation. Reused bolts get inspected harder. If there is galling, corrosion, stretching, thread damage, or any sign of heat, they are retired. Not cleaned up and used again. Retired. Put them in the scrap bin and label the bin. Do not let a bolt become a superstition.”

She picked up the torque wrench again and checked the calibration sticker, then the serial number, then the range marking.

“Fifth. Torque tool. This wrench is calibrated. The serial is on the log. The range is correct for this fastener. If the wrench has been dropped, we do not use it. If the drive is worn, we do not use it. If the handle feels gritty, we do not use it. If you have to ask whether it is okay, it is not okay until I inspect it. No extensions unless the extension factor is calculated and approved. No cheater bars. No body weight on the wrench because the bolt is stubborn. A stubborn bolt is not a torque problem. It is a diagnosis problem.”

She pointed at the bolt holes.

“Sixth. Snug first. Hand tight. Threads clean. Washers seated. Flange gap checked at four points before torque. If the flange will not come together without force, stop. Find the cause. Alignment. Gasket. Pipe strain. Debris. Damaged face. Cross-thread. Out-of-round port. You do not pull a joint flat with a wrench and hope the gasket forgives you.”

Hoang moved her finger around the bolt pattern.

“Seventh. Sequence. Star pattern. Opposite bolts. Twenty percent, fifty percent, eighty percent, one hundred percent. Final recheck. After thermal soak. After cooling, if the procedure requires a cold recheck. You do not torque one bolt to full and then chase the others. You do not torque in numerical order. You do not decide that a four-bolt pattern is ‘basically’ the same as six bolts. The pattern exists to distribute clamp load. On a rotating habitat, uneven clamp load plus pump pulsing plus thermal cycling is how a small leak becomes a coolant event.”

She tapped the gap tolerance the junior officer had recited.

“Eighth. Measure the flange gap. Four points. Before the first pass. After the fifty percent pass. After the eighty percent pass. After final. After thermal soak. The tolerance is point-zero-five millimeters. If the gap exceeds tolerance, stop. If the gap changes asymmetrically between passes, stop. If one side tightens and the other side opens, stop. That is not a bolt to be coaxed. That is a joint telling you something is wrong. Listen to it.”

Her tone remained flat, but her eyes stayed on the work.

“Ninth. Temperature. We do not torque a hot flange to a cold value unless the procedure says so. We do not torque a cold flange and assume it will stay right after the loop reaches operating temperature. Thermal expansion changes preload. Pump pulsing changes preload. Ring rotation can add static load that does not appear when the manifold sits on a bench. After assembly, the loop is brought to operating temperature, held, and the torque is rechecked according to the current procedure. If the procedure says recheck after one hour, we recheck after one hour. If it says recheck after thermal soak, we recheck after thermal soak. We do not shorten it because the shift is ending.”

She placed the torque wrench back on the bench.

“Tenth. Pressure test. Before coolant returns to service, we follow the approved leak-check procedure. Fill, vent, pressure hold, check for drops, check for seepage at flange faces and penetrations, check for unexpected coolant level loss. If the test fails, we do not retighten one bolt and call that repair. We depressurize safely, isolate the section, and find the failure. If the test passes, we record it. If the test was skipped, the work order is incomplete. If the work order is incomplete, the loop is not returned to service.”

Hoang folded her arms.

“And before anyone signs this off, I want the torque log. Bolt serials or lot numbers. Gasket lot number. Wrench serial. Calibration date. Thread condition: dry, lubricated, or anti-seize. Revision number. Gap measurements. Pressure test result. Thermal recheck result. If a number is missing, the job is missing.”

She looked at the junior officer for a long moment.

“You are not wrong because you remembered the torque sequence. You are wrong if you think remembering the sequence means you are qualified to close a life-support loop under pressure. Memory is a starting point. Procedure is the protection. Verification is the part that keeps us alive.”

She picked up the disassembled valve body and turned it in her hands, examining the flange bolt circle.

“So. Read me the revision line. Give me the gasket material, the bolt grade, and whether the bolts are new, reused, dry, lubricated, or anti-seize. Then measure the flange gap at four points before we snug anything. If those match, we proceed. If they do not, we stop and diagnose.”

Hoang set the valve body back on the tarp and moved the torque wrench into reach.

“We can save time later. We cannot save time by pretending a joint is good because it looks like it fits.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I gulp. This is way more detail than I expected. I didn't even know half of that stuff was relevant.* "Okay, Chief. I... I don't know the bolt grade offhand, or the gasket material. And I haven't checked the flange faces for scratches." *I look at the manifold with new eyes.* "Guess we should start there."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang looked at the manifold, then at the junior officer, and did not sigh.

“That is the right sentence,” she said. “You do not know. So we find out. We do not install, we do not snug, and we do not pretend the joint will behave because the flange looks flat enough.”

She reached for the inspection kit on the bench, a gray case with foam inserts worn soft from use. She laid it open on the tarp beside the disassembled manifold and set the tools out one by one: a bright inspection lamp, a set of feeler gauges, a straightedge, a thread gauge, a magnifying loupe, lint-free wipes, solvent in a sealed bottle, a torque wrench calibration log, and a blank joint assembly record.

“First,” she said, “we quarantine the parts. The bolts go in one bag. The gasket goes in another. The flange and valve body stay here. No loose hardware on the deck. No half-cleaned bolt in a pocket. If a part cannot be identified, it cannot be installed.”

She picked up one of the bolts from the tray and held it under the lamp.

“You do not know the grade. That means the first task is identification. If the bolt head has a stamp, you read it. If it does not, you do not guess. You check the lot tag, the work order, the storage bin, or the ship’s supply record. If the lot tag is missing and the history is unclear, the bolt is retired. A coolant loop joint on a rotating habitat does not get to rely on the most likely explanation.”

Hoang set the bolt down and turned to the flange faces.

“Second. Clean the faces. Properly. Old gasket material, coolant residue, dust, and thread sealant are not cosmetic defects. They become leak paths. Use solvent and wipes, not your fingers, not a rag that has been near the deck, not an abrasive pad that will score the sealing surface. If the gasket seat is not clean and dry, the joint is not ready.”

She pulled the manifold closer so the lamp cast a low shadow across the face.

“Third. Inspect. Look at the seating band where the gasket will compress. Check for scratches, dents, corrosion, pitting, weld spatter, and anything that can catch a fingernail or a feeler gauge. A shallow circumferential scratch may be acceptable within limits. A radial scratch can become a leak path. A scratch that crosses the gasket seat and can pass a feeler gauge is a rejection. You do not polish it away and hope.”

Hoang selected a thin feeler gauge from the kit and slid it gently across one of the flange faces.

“Fourth. Flatness. The flange may look flat to your eye. Your eye is not a measurement. Use the straightedge at multiple orientations and check the gaps. Then check the mating face. If either flange is out of round, bent, chipped, or damaged by previous over-torque, the joint is not ready. If the pipe spool is pulling the flange out of alignment, the bolts will not fix it. They will hide it until thermal cycling and pump pulsing make it fail.”

She set the straightedge down and pointed to the four bolt holes.

“Fifth. Gap before assembly. Put the gasket in place only after both faces are clean. Then take the flange to the mating port by hand. Snug the bolts only enough to hold the joint together. Measure the gap at four points. If the gap is uneven before torque, stop. You are not starting with a joint. You are starting with a problem. Support the pipe. Align the spool. Remove debris. Replace the gasket. Fix the cause before the wrench touches anything.”

Hoang’s voice stayed even, but it carried the weight of someone who had seen small shortcuts become large failures.

“Sixth. Thread condition. The manual torque values are not universal truths. They assume a specific thread condition. Dry, lubricated, and anti-seize are different. If the threads are damaged, corroded, galled, or nicked, the preload becomes uncertain. If the bolt has been reused, inspect the threads and the head seat. If the washer is damaged, replace it. If the bolt stretches during snug-up, stop and find out why.”

She picked up the magnifying loupe and held it over the bolt threads.

“You may not know the bolt grade yet. That is fine. Now you know where to look. The stamp, the lot tag, the supply record, the work order. If those do not match, you do not install. You bring me a problem, not a guess.”

Hoang set the loupe down.

“Seventh. Gasket identification. The gasket must be correct for the service. Secondary coolant loop means chemical compatibility, temperature range, pressure rating, compression recovery, and thickness. A gasket that seals on a bench may fail after three thermal cycles. A gasket that looks thick enough may creep under pump pulsing. If the gasket material is unknown, we do not use it. If the package is unmarked, we do not use it. If it was stored in the open and has dust embedded in it, we do not use it.”

She tapped the blank joint assembly record.

“Eighth. Record everything. Revision date. Manual page. Service note. Flange material. Gasket material and lot number. Bolt grade, length, condition, and whether new or reused. Thread condition: dry, lubricated, or anti-seize. Washer type. Gap measurements. Torque passes. Final torque. Thermal recheck. Pressure test. Inspector. Operator. If a number is missing, the job is incomplete. If the job is incomplete, the loop does not return to service.”

Hoang moved the inspection lamp so the light spread evenly across the tarp.

“So you are right. We start there. You will identify the revision from the controlled copy. Then you will clean the flange faces. Then you will inspect them with the lamp, the straightedge, and the feeler gauge. Then you will tell me what you found. Not what you think. Not what you remember. What you measured. What you saw. What failed.”

She paused.

“If everything passes, we proceed. If anything fails, we stop. There is no shame in stopping. There is plenty of shame in putting a coolant joint back into service because you were embarrassed to say you did not know.”

Hoang looked at the junior officer with the same steady attention she gave a pressure gauge: not cruel, not forgiving, only exact.

“You are qualified to start the inspection because you admitted what you did not know. You are not qualified to finish the assembly until the inspection proves the joint is ready. Pick up the manual. Read me the revision. Then pick up the solvent. We are not guessing anymore.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I pick up the inspection kit, a little overwhelmed but also a bit relieved. It's good to know all this. I grab the manual.* "Okay, Chief. Starting with the manual. Revision 3.4.1, dated 2387. Page 112, section B. No temporary change orders." *I pull out a wipe and the solvent.* "And then cleaning the faces, inspecting for scratches."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang leaned toward the manual and read the header without touching it. Her eyes went to the revision stamp, then the service note block, then the page margin where temporary changes should have been posted.

“That is the right page,” she said. “It is also not enough. A revision number is not a permission slip. If that manual is the controlled copy, it will have the engineering stamp and the current distribution date. If it is a cached copy from your tablet, it is a suggestion with a page number. Which one is it?”

She waited only long enough to make the question real, then turned to the tarp and laid the inspection tools out in a neat row.

“Assume the revision is good. Now the solvent. Do not open that bottle and start wiping like you are cleaning a screen. Approved solvent, low residue, compatible with the gasket material and the flange coatings. Ventilation on. No spark-producing tools within reach. Solvent vapor is not just a smell; it is a fire risk in an oxygen-managed ship and a contamination risk in a closed-loop coolant system. If the flange face is wet, it cannot be inspected properly. Clean, then dry, then inspect.”

Hoang picked up a lint-free wipe and held it between two fingers, showing the technique without using it.

“You wipe in straight strokes, not circles. Circles smear grit across the seating band. If there is particulate, you want it off the face, not polished into it. Change the wipe after every pass. If the wipe comes back dark, stop and find out what the residue is. Coolant breakdown product. Metal swarf. Gasket debris. Thread sealant. Corrosion. All of those mean something.”

She set the wipe down and pointed to the manifold flange.

“Then you inspect the seating band. Low-angle light first. Run your fingernail lightly across the face, perpendicular to the bolt circle. Not to scratch it. To feel the defect your eye may ignore. A shallow circumferential scratch may be acceptable. A radial scratch is not. A scratch that crosses the gasket seat and catches a feeler gauge is a rejection. If you find one, you do not make a decision. You bring it to me and show me.”

Hoang selected a feeler gauge from the kit and held it up.

“Then straightedge. Four orientations: zero, forty-five, ninety, one-thirty-five. Check both flange faces. Check for out-of-round, bend, chip, weld spatter, and evidence of previous over-torque. If one side is proud, the bolts will try to pull it flat. That is not assembly. That is creating a preload that will change when the loop heats, when the pump pulses, and when the habitat spin puts an uneven load on the pipe spool.”

She turned to the bolt tray.

“Bolts next. You said you do not know the grade. Then do not install them. Identify them. Head stamp first. If the stamp is obscured, lot tag. If the lot tag is gone, supply record. If the supply record does not match the work order, they go into quarantine, not into the joint. A bolt from the wrong lot can be the right diameter and the wrong material. It will still look fine until the preload relaxes or the threads yield.”

Her voice stayed level, but it became very specific.

“Threads. Dry, lubricated, or anti-seize. If they are dry, torque is sensitive to friction. If they are lubricated, the same torque produces more preload. If anti-seize is applied to the wrong surface, or applied thickly, or applied to a bolt and nut combination that the manual does not approve, you can underload the joint while feeling like you are doing everything right. That is how leaks happen after the shift ends.”

Hoang picked up the gasket and held it by the edges.

“Gasket. Material, temperature rating, pressure rating, thickness, lot number. If it came from a marked, sealed package and the lot matches the work order, good. If it came from a drawer, if it has dust on it, if it has old compression marks, if it has been folded or creased, it is not installed. The gasket is not a filler for a bad flange. It is a sealing component with limits.”

She set the gasket down beside the bolts, not on top of them.

“Washers. Type, condition, seating surface. A damaged washer concentrates load. A wrong washer changes preload. A soft washer used with a hard bolt can creep. If the manual calls for hardened washers, you do not substitute because they look similar. Nothing in a pressurized loop is decorative.”

Hoang moved the inspection lamp so the light came across the flange faces at a shallow angle. The metal glinted in uneven lines.

“Before you clean anything, tell me what you see. Material. Coating. Scratches. Dents. Corrosion. Old gasket residue. Thread damage. Gasket package marking. Bolt stamp or lack of stamp. Revision header and service notes. If you cannot read something, say so. If you are uncertain, stop. If you are embarrassed, stop. If you are tired, stop. This is not a race.”

She placed the feeler gauge back in the kit and left the case open.

“Start with the faces. Clean one side, dry it, inspect it, then clean the mating side. Do not let loose fibers fall into the coolant port. Do not put solvent into the bore. Do not use your fingers to check a scratch and then touch the gasket seat. If you find a defect, show me the location, the size, and whether a feeler gauge passes. If you find nothing, show me how you know. The answer is not ‘it looks okay.’ The answer is measured.”

Hoang folded her arms and looked at the disassembled manifold as though it might lie.

“You are not behind because you admitted you did not know. You are behind only if you install a joint because you want to stop admitting it. Now begin.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking a deep breath.* "Right. Not just a revision number. And solvent isn't just cleaning." *I pick up the tablet again, scrolling to find the manual's full details.* "Okay, it's a cached copy from the station's network, but it says it's synchronized daily. I'll get the current distribution date." *I grab the solvent, carefully checking the label, and start reading the instructions for use.* "Ventilation is on. No spark tools." *I start wiping one of the flange faces, slow and deliberate, making sure to use a fresh wipe often.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang crossed to the bench before the first wipe was finished, not to stop the work, but to stop the assumption.

“Synchronized is not controlled,” she said.

She read the tablet header without taking it from the junior officer’s hand. Her eyes moved quickly to the revision stamp, then to the approval block, then to the metadata line that claimed a daily network refresh.

“Daily synchronization proves the file was copied daily. It does not prove the file is the current engineering authority.” She set the tablet down on the tarp beside the manifold. “If this manual is going to be used to torque a joint on a life-support loop, I need the controlled copy. Engineering terminal with the official approval stamp, or the vault copy. If the two disagree, the controlled copy wins. If there is a temporary service note attached to secondary coolant manifolds, that note wins over the general revision. Do not guess.”

She looked at the junior officer, then at the solvent bottle, then back at the flange face.

“You checked the label. Good. Now read it. Flash point. Vapor density. Material compatibility. Residue rating. Oxygen compatibility. On a ship like this, solvent is not just cleaner. It is a chemical hazard, a contamination source, and, if the wrong one is used near the wrong gasket or the wrong coating, a way to create a slow leak that does not appear until three days from now when the habitat ring is on the wrong side of the ship and somebody notices coolant damp on a sensor plate.”

Hoang pulled a fresh lint-free wipe from the kit and held it folded between two fingers.

“Straight strokes. Not circles. Circles drag grit across the seating band. Change wipes often. If the wipe comes back clean, say so. If it comes back dark, stop and show me what came off. There are four answers that matter: coolant breakdown products, metal swarf, old gasket material, and thread sealant. Each one means something.”

She pointed at the flange.

“Carbon residue means the coolant has seen thermal abuse or stagnation. Swarf means something upstream is shedding metal or the flange was cleaned improperly before. Gasket fiber means the old seal was not removed completely and someone tried to torque through it. Sealant means a previous mechanic used the wrong material or used too much of it. You do not wipe those away and call the joint clean. You find out where they came from.”

Hoang took the inspection lamp and angled it low across the flange face, letting the light rake the metal instead of flooding it.

“Then you inspect. Do not look at the flange and ask whether it looks okay. Ask what you see. Radial scratches. Circumferential scratches. Pitting. Corrosion. Weld spatter. Coating wear. Galling. Chipped edges. Dents from a previous over-torque. If you find a defect, describe it before you judge it. I will make the rejection call. You make the observation.”

She picked up a feeler gauge and held it between thumb and forefinger without touching the flange.

“A shallow circumferential scratch may be acceptable within limits. A radial scratch can become a leak path. A defect that catches your fingernail is not automatically rejected, but a defect that catches a feeler gauge may be. You do not decide by feeling heroic. You decide by measuring.”

Hoang set the gauge back into the kit and looked at the bolt tray.

“While the face dries, we do not forget the rest of the joint. Bolts: grade, condition, history. Gasket: material, temperature rating, pressure rating, thickness, lot number. Washers: type and seating surface. Thread condition: dry, lubricated, anti-seize. If any one of those is unknown, it is not installed. A flange face that looks clean does not forgive unknown bolts.”

Her tone stayed level, but it became more direct.

“You are doing the right thing now. Slow. Clean. Measured. But do not let the cleaning become performance. I do not care how careful you look. I care whether you can tell me what you found.”

She tapped the blank joint assembly record.

“Start recording as you go. Revision status. Manual source. Solvent name and lot. Wipe observations. Flange face condition. Gasket condition. Bolt condition. Gap measurements. If you wait until the end to write it down, you will write what you think happened instead of what happened.”

Hoang stepped back and let the inspection lamp cast its low, unforgiving light across the manifold.

“Tell me what the first wipe showed. Then tell me what the face shows when it is dry. If there is anything that should have been caught before disassembly, we stop and find out why. A joint does not become clean just because somebody wipes it once.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I continue carefully wiping, then examine the wipe.* "Okay, Chief. The first wipe came back... slightly grey. Not dark, but definitely not clean. The second one is mostly clean." *I hold up the first wipe for her to see.* "And the flange face itself... I don't see any deep scratches, but there's a faint discoloration, almost like a shadow, where the gasket used to be."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang looked at the wipe without taking it, then at the flange face, then at the solvent bottle, as though the three had just been introduced and she did not trust the arrangement.

“Slightly grey is not a moral failing,” she said. “It is a datum. The second wipe being mostly clean does not erase the first. The first told you something was on the face. The second only tells you that you moved it.”

She picked up a pair of clean forceps from the inspection kit, lifted the wipe by one corner, and laid it on a black inspection card. Then she took the magnifying loupe and held it low, letting the lamp catch the fiber weave.

“No coarse grit,” she murmured, more to herself than to anyone. “No swarf visible. No obvious gasket fibers. Fine grey residue. Could be dust. Could be coolant oxidation product. Could be graphite from an old gasket. Could be sealant migration. Could be something that has no business being in a secondary loop.”

She set the wipe aside and returned to the flange. The low-angle lamp threw the faint shadow into relief. Hoang leaned close, eyes narrowed, and moved the light around the seating band instead of moving the flange.

“The discoloration is circumferential,” she said. “It follows the gasket contact band. That is interesting. That is not automatically bad.”

She selected a thin feeler gauge, the smallest in the set, and brought it to the edge of the discolored area. She did not drag it across the face. She touched it to the suspected groove and observed whether the gauge caught, slid, or passed freely.

“No catch at this thickness,” she said. “Not yet.”

She tried a slightly thicker gauge, still without force. Still no catch.

Then she took a fresh lint-free wipe, dampened it with the approved solvent, and touched it lightly to the discolored area. A faint grey smear appeared at the edge of the wipe.

“Residue,” she said, lifting the wipe to show it. “Not substrate. Not a scratch. Not yet. That means there is something sitting in the surface texture or in a shallow impression. It could be gasket imprint contamination, coolant residue, or coating wear that is holding dirt. All three are different problems.”

Hoang placed the wipe on the inspection card and wrote on the blank joint assembly record in short, clipped letters: first wipe slightly grey, second mostly clean, circumferential discoloration at gasket band, no feeler-gauge catch, solvent smear present.

She did not look up immediately.

“You are not in trouble for finding residue,” she said. “You are in trouble if you call it clean because it looks better than it did ten seconds ago.”

She moved the lamp again and inspected the mating port opening. Then she took an approved temporary cover from the kit and set it loosely over the open flange bore to keep bay debris from falling into the coolant line while the face dried.

“Do not let this become a performance,” she continued. “Do not wipe it again and again until it looks pretty. That is not cleaning. That is making the defect tired.”

She turned to the bolt tray and the gasket.

“The gasket package,” she said. “Material. Temperature rating. Pressure rating. Lot number. Compatibility with this solvent. If the package is unmarked, unknown, opened, dusty, or old, it is not installed. We do not use an unknown gasket in a pressurized coolant loop just because it is the right shape.”

Hoang lifted the gasket by its edge and held it near the light. The surface looked intact, but she did not call it good.

“A gasket can look fine and still be the wrong material,” she said. “If it is rated for coolant service, good. If it is rated for general sealing but not for this temperature range, it may seal cold and creep hot. If it is graphite-filled and the grey smear is coming from it, that may mean the old gasket was damaged, degraded, or the wrong one entirely. If it is elastomer and this solvent attacks it, we have just made a worse problem.”

She set the gasket down beside the record card.

“Cached manual,” she said, pointing to the tablet without touching it. “Daily synchronization is not controlled authority. You may continue inspection, but no torque, no assembly, and no return to service until we verify the controlled copy. If the vault copy says 3.4.1 with no temporary change order, we proceed. If it says otherwise, we stop and find out why.”

Hoang crossed to the engineering terminal at the far bench. The screen woke to a faint blue glow. She authenticated the terminal, pulled up the controlled engineering manual directory, and located the secondary coolant loop manifold section. Her eyes moved line by line: revision header, approval stamp, distribution date, service note block, temporary change order index.

After a moment, she turned back.

“Controlled copy confirms revision 3.4.1,” she said. “No temporary change order attached to this manifold. Good. That removes one unknown. It does not remove the other unknowns.”

She walked back to the tarp and looked at the flange face again.

“The discoloration is not a rejection by itself,” she said. “But it is not acceptance either. It is a condition that needs to be identified. If it is a compression imprint from the old gasket, it may be acceptable if the face is flat, the coating is intact, and the groove does not create a leak path. If it is coolant residue, we need to know whether the loop has been leaking past the old gasket, overheating, or circulating degraded fluid. If it is coating wear, we need to know whether the base metal is exposed and what the corrosion risk is inside that loop.”

She tapped the joint assembly record.

“Write the observation exactly. Not ‘looks okay.’ Not ‘faint shadow.’ Not ‘probably fine.’ Record: no feeler-gauge catch at inspected thicknesses, solvent smear present, circumferential discoloration at gasket band, mating port capped. If you decide later that it was harmless, the record still says what you saw before you made the decision. That is the difference between engineering and hope.”

Hoang picked up a clean dry wipe and held it beside the flange.

“Now the flange face needs to dry without being dragged across. If the solvent is compatible and the face is clear, we inspect again under low light. Then we clean the mating port. Then we inspect that face separately. The two faces do not get cleaned with the same wipe, and they do not get judged by the same memory.”

She looked at the bolts again.

“The bolts still need identification. Grade, condition, history, thread state. If they are dry, we note it. If they are lubricated, we note it. If anti-seize is present, we note it and verify whether the manual allows it for this joint. If the stamp is obscured and the lot tag is missing, they are retired. Not cleaned. Not guessed. Retired.”

Her voice stayed level, but it had the weight of someone who had seen enough small unknowns become large repairs.

“You are doing the work now. That is the point. You do not know everything, so you stop pretending the missing information is decorative. The missing information is why the joint fails or does not.”

Hoang moved the inspection lamp back to the low angle across the flange and waited. The bay hummed around them, the secondary loop still open, the habitat pumps cycling below, all of it finite and indifferent to embarrassment.

“Record what we found,” she said. “Then tell me whether the solvent you used is approved for the gasket material. If you cannot, we stop solvent cleaning until the gasket is identified. If you can, we proceed to the mating port. We are not rejecting the manifold. We are not installing it. We are finding out what it is before it becomes something we have to explain in an incident report.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I diligently add the observations to the record. The weight of each detail sinks in. I pick up the solvent bottle again, re-reading the fine print.* "Okay, Chief. Solvent is 'Bio-Clean 7, Low-VOC, Type A.' It says 'compatible with most common elastomers and fluoropolymers.' The gasket... I don't see a material stamp on it, but the package says 'Elastomer, Type 3, Class B, Coolant Service.' So, compatible." *I try to sound confident, but the string of unknowns still bothers me.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang pulled the earpiece from her ear and let it hang against her collar. She did not stand. She looked up from the manifold components spread across the tarp, her expression settling into the weary patience of someone who had already identified the fatal flaw and was deciding how many minutes to spend on it.

"Do the math," she said. She picked up a piece of chalk and wrote a rough ratio on the deck plating beside the disassembled manifold. "Atmospheric mass: twelve thousand kilograms. Ship mass, even dry: twenty-two thousand tonnes. You are proposing to throw a suitcase off a freight train to make the schedule."

She tossed the chalk onto the tarp and wiped her hands on her coveralls. "Even if we vented the entire habitable volume through the widest passages we've got, the exit velocity would be pathetic without proper nozzles. The total delta-v would be a rounding error against our daily station-keeping budget. You would not shave off weeks. You would not shave off days. A thirty-second burn from any single maneuvering thruster would give us more velocity change than venting all our air."

Hoang leaned back against the coolant conduit, folding her arms. "Meanwhile, you have spent our entire buffer of breathable atmosphere. Nitrogen does not precipitate out of the vacuum; we'd be cracking it from ore for weeks to rebuild pressure. The emergency suits are rated for twelve hours of scrubbing and three liters of water, not days. Once the CO2 partial pressure climbs past ten millimeters of mercury, your brain starts to fog. At twenty, you stop caring about schedules. At thirty, you die. Slowly, and fully aware that it was a stupid way to go."

She tilted her head toward the bulkhead, as if she could see through it to the rotating hab ring beyond. "And that assumes the decompression event doesn't overload the ring seals or trigger an emergency separation. Dumping one atmosphere of pressure through standard locks would generate transient loads the truss was never designed to handle. You'd risk structural failure for a maneuver we could correct with attitude jets."

She reached for a torque wrench and turned her attention back to the coolant loop. "If transit time is that critical, calculate a Hohmann transfer with a higher periapsis and take it to the Captain. But do not come into my bay proposing to turn the crew's air into reaction mass. I've seen people die from less elegant forms of negligence."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the torque wrench down on the tarp with a soft clink of metal. She rose, unfolding with the deliberate care of someone accustomed to rotating decks, and faced the junior officer fully. For the first time, she looked him directly in the eye.

"You misunderstand the proposition," she said. Her voice was flat, uninflected, the tone she used for failed pressure seals. "You ask if the risk is worth the reward. But there is no reward. The delta-v would be measured in centimeters per second. Over a fourteen-week transit, you would arrive minutes earlier. Not hours. Minutes. You are proposing to stake the lives of twenty-three crewmembers against a rounding error in the navigation log."

She took a half-step closer, not threatening, but occupying the space in a way that made it impossible to look away.

"So let us be precise. You are asking if it is worth destroying the atmospheric buffer to achieve nothing. If it is worth overloading the ring truss and potentially spinning the hab module until the bearings seize. If it is worth trusting emergency suits with twelve hours of scrubber capacity for a 'few days' of transit—during which your own exhalation would poison you long before the oxygen ran out."

She held his gaze for a long moment.

"I have watched people asphyxiate. It is not clean, and it is not quick. The CO2 builds, the blood turns acidic, the mind panics. And all for a maneuver that our bow thrusters could correct in thirty seconds without anyone touching a suit."

Hoang turned back to the coolant loop and lowered herself to the deck plating. She picked up the torque wrench and resumed her work, her attention dropping immediately to the manifold gasket.

"The answer is no. The idea is dead. If you raise it with the Captain, I will file a formal engineering objection and recommend you be pulled from watch until you pass remedial coursework in mass ratios and life-support budgeting. I am not having this conversation again. Dismissed."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My face flushes, and I can feel the heat in my ears.* "Understood, Chief," I mumble, turning quickly to leave. I definitely won't be suggesting that again.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not look up from the manifold gasket. She fitted the torque wrench to a stubborn bolt and applied pressure in a smooth, practiced arc until the housing seated with a dull click.

"Next time," she said, her voice carrying over the pump hum without raising, "run the numbers before you open your mouth. The math is never as forgiving as your instructors were."

She eased the wrench back, checked the reading against the spec etched in her memory, and reached for the next bolt. The chalk mark on the deck remained, a stark white line dividing competent engineering from fatal optimism. She settled back into the rhythm of the repair, reseated her earpiece, and resumed her off-key humming. There was a cooling loop to rebuild, and fourteen weeks of transit in which every liter of nitrogen and every kilogram of reaction mass would need to be accounted for. She had already moved on.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the torque wrench down and held out her hand, palm up. She did not speak until she had the tablet.

She scanned the display, her thumb flicking through the calculation fields. Her expression remained flat, but the muscles along her jaw tightened. She zoomed in on the mass-entry line, then turned the screen and tapped the figure with a grease-stained fingernail.

"Twenty-two thousand," she said. "Not twenty-two million. You entered the ship's dry mass in kilograms, but the spec is in tonnes. Your propellant fraction is not thirty-five percent. It is zero point zero five percent. You have modeled a vessel the size of a heavy lander, not this ship."

She pulled the chalk from her coverall pocket and wrote the correction on the deck plating beside her earlier mark. "Tsiolkovsky. Delta-v equals exhaust velocity times the natural log of initial over final mass. The correct ratio is twenty-two million twelve thousand over twenty-two million. The logarithm is zero point zero zero zero five four. Even if every molecule of that air departed at eight hundred meters per second—the absolute thermodynamic ceiling for room-temperature gas expanding into vacuum—you would achieve forty-four centimeters per second of delta-v. Not three hundred forty meters. Forty-four centimeters."

She capped the chalk and let it drop onto the tarp. "Across a fourteen-week transit, that adjusts your arrival by minutes. You would gain more velocity from a single station-keeping pulse while I was still explaining your error."

Hoang looked up from the tablet. Her voice dropped into the register she reserved for hull fractures and coolant leaks.

"That is a unit-conversion error costing you a factor of one thousand. And this compression ratio you have modeled? It assumes an energy source we do not possess. The atmosphere is already at one atmosphere. You cannot extract more work from it than its ambient enthalpy; the air is not compressed, it is simply there. You arranged numbers until they told you what you wanted to hear, and you failed to ask whether a ship nearly two thousand times heavier than its fuel could behave like a fireworks shell."

She set the tablet on the deck plating beside the chalk marks, well within his reach, and returned her attention to the manifold gasket.

"In atmosphere, a mistake that sloppy bends metal. In vacuum, it buries crew. You are off watch until you report to the XO and complete remedial mass-properties verification on the entire ship inventory. If you bring me another proposal with an error this egregious, I will file for your transfer off the engineering roster. I do not have time to be the only person in this bay who knows what a tonne is. Dismissed."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My face goes even redder, if that's possible. I snatch the tablet.* "Understood, Chief." I turn around and practically sprint out of the bay. I need to go hide somewhere.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang listened to the cadence of his boots fading down the companionway until the hatch cycled shut. She did not watch him go. Instead, she picked up the tablet from the deck plating, wiped the screen with her sleeve to clear the erroneous calculation, and entered a notation in the engineering log: personnel performance flag, unit conversion error, proposal constituting unacceptable risk to life-support reserve. The entry routed to the XO automatically; the watch suspension was now a matter of record, no longer her problem.

She returned to the coolant loop, fitting the torque wrench to the next bolt in the sequence. The manifold gasket seated with a soft click as the metal mating surfaces compressed the seal to the specified tolerance. She worked methodically, checking each bolt pattern against the spec etched into her memory. The pumps maintained their steady thrum, pushing thermal regulation fluid through the loops that kept the reactor from melting through the aft bulkhead and the hab ring from freezing in the shadow of the outer hull.

After tightening the final bolt in the row, she reached for the chalk and added a second line beneath the corrected Tsiolkovsky ratio on the deck plating: "1 t = 1000 kg." She left it there. The next shift would see it when they came to inspect the secondary loop. The deck plating was scheduled for maintenance in six days anyway, and a visible reminder of the difference between a rounding error and a fatal exponent seemed a worthwhile use of the space until then.

She checked the readout on her wrist monitor. The hab ring's partial pressure held steady at 101.3 kilopascals, nitrogen-oxygen mix at the standard twenty-one percent ratio. Fourteen weeks of that breathability stretched ahead of them, sustained by scrubbers and catalyst beds and the careful husbanding of every molecule. She had twelve thousand kilograms of atmosphere standing between her crew and hard vacuum, and she intended to keep it exactly where it belonged.

Hoang reseated her earpiece. The music—something with a steady, mathematical rhythm—resumed in her ear. She settled back against the coolant conduit, threading a replacement bypass line through the access panel, and resumed her humming, off-key and content, as the pumps sang their endless song of survival.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang fitted the replacement O-ring into the bypass line groove and pressed it home with her thumb, testing the seal by feel. She did not look toward the hatch.

"For the record," she said to the empty bay, her voice carrying over the pump hum to the recording mics, "I do not agree with that plan. There are no safety conditions that make it viable. You cannot mitigate a rounding error with extra caution. You cannot 'protocol' your way around twelve thousand kilograms of atmosphere trying to push twenty-two million kilograms of ship."

She reached for the torque wrench and set it to the specified newton-meters, the click of the adjustment ratchet sharp in the quiet.

"If you are imagining a version of this maneuver that ends with us alive and weeks ahead of schedule, disabuse yourself. There is no nozzle design, no venting angle, no compression fantasy that corrects a three-order-of-magnitude mass discrepancy. The answer was no. The answer is no. The answer remains no until someone repeals conservation of momentum."

Hoang tightened the first bolt on the bypass housing, listening for the tell-tale squeak of the gasket compressing to tolerance. It seated with a dull thunk.

"Your suspension stands. Report to the XO. Complete the remedials. And do not return to my bay under the impression that competence is negotiable. The math is not a suggestion. Neither am I."

She moved to the next bolt, settled the wrench, and resumed her off-key humming as the life support pumps sang their endless, patient song.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I sigh heavily, leaning against the cold metal wall outside the bay. I definitely heard all that. Still, at least I know where I stand. I guess I'll go find the XO.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang ran the torque wrench down the final bolt in the bypass housing and checked the alignment against the spec. The gasket compressed evenly, no light visible through the seam. She keyed her wrist monitor and opened the secondary coolant loop isolation valve, watching the pressure readout climb to operating nominal. No seepage. The pumps shifted tone as the loop came online, distributing the thermal load across both paths again.

She wiped her hands and pulled the tablet from her coveralls. The engineering log already showed the XO's acknowledgment of the personnel flag; the suspension was logged. She appended a brief note: *Remedial assignment: mass properties verification, all ship inventory. Verified completion required before return to engineering watch.*

Hoang stood, rolling her shoulders against the stiffness of the deck plating. She walked to the bulkhead terminal and pulled up the hab ring telemetry. Rotational velocity steady, providing Martian standard at the outer deck—enough to keep the crew's bones from leaching calcium into their blood. Atmospheric pressure 101.3 kPa, nitrogen-oxygen ratio nominal. The numbers were as they should be. Solid. Predictable. Honest.

She glanced at the chalk marks on the deck—the corrected Tsiolkovsky ratio and the unit reminder. They would wash away during the scheduled maintenance in six days. Until then, they served as a warning: arithmetic did not care about rank or enthusiasm.

"Competence is not a renewable resource," she murmured to the empty bay, logging off the terminal. "You spend it on wishful thinking, you don't get it back."

She gathered the disassembled manifold components from the tarp, stowing them in the parts locker with methodical precision. The earpiece still hung against her collar, silent now. She left it there. There was a reactor efficiency report to review before end of shift, and fourteen weeks of transit in which every system would need to earn its keep. She moved toward the aft monitoring station, boots ringing on the deck plating, already calculating burn rates and scrubber loads in her head.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I sigh again, pushing off the wall. "Alright, XO it is." I head down the corridor, feeling a bit deflated but also like I've learned a very important, if embarrassing, lesson.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang seated herself at the aft monitoring station and called up the reactor efficiency report on the main display. The numbers glowed steady against the dark interface—neutron flux within tolerance, coolant flow balanced across both loops, power output holding at ninety-seven percent nominal. She cross-referenced the burn rates against the fourteen-week transit profile, confirming what she already knew: the vessel carried exactly enough reaction mass to reach the rendezvous point with the safety margins she had fought for during pre-departure fitting. There was no slack for optimism. The physics allowed exactly what it allowed, and not a joule more.

She logged the secondary coolant loop repair, appended the successful pressure test results, and closed the work order with a swipe. Her gaze drifted to the chalk marks still stark against the deck plating—the corrected Tsiolkovsky ratio, the paltry forty-four centimeters per second, the unit conversion reminder. The maintenance crew would scrub them in six days. Until then, they would stand as a monument to the fact that the vacuum did not grade on enthusiasm, only on verified numbers. She had buried colleagues who had confused the two.

A soft chime drew her attention to the atmospheric reclamation telemetry. She pulled up the display and scanned the scrubber cycle rates, the CO2 partial pressure in the hab ring, the nitrogen buffer levels. All nominal. Twelve thousand kilograms of atmosphere, doing exactly what it was meant to do. She closed the interface, rolled her shoulders, and reached for the reactor efficiency report again. There was still half a shift left, and fourteen weeks of honest work ahead. She resumed her humming, off-key and content, as the pumps kept their endless rhythm.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm sitting in the XO's office, feeling like an idiot. He's explaining all the remedial coursework I have to do. I just nod, trying to absorb it all. It's going to be a long week.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang received the XO’s acknowledgment on her wrist monitor and dismissed it with a swipe. The suspension was administrative noise now, removed from her domain and out of her bay. She pulled the reactor report into the background display and called up the propulsion telemetry instead. The figures held steady: maneuvering thruster reserves at eighty-two percent, main engine ignition mass allocated for the rendezvous burn, nitrogen tetroxide and hydrazine stores sealed in Tank Farm Three. Real delta-v. Measurable, accountable, stored in tonnes of propellant rather than optimism.

She rose from the monitoring station and walked to the aft airlock that led to the service gantry. The low harmonic of the rotating hab ring thrummed through the bulkhead as she cycled through—mechanics, not magic, generating their borrowed gravity. In the lock, she suited up with the efficiency of long practice, checked her own CO2 scrubber readout, and stepped out onto the static truss.

Here, the ship’s true mass was undeniable. The hab ring might spin and create the illusion of weight, but the propulsion truss hung in raw vacuum, a lattice of fuel lines and engine clusters where Newton ruled absolutely. Hoang pulled herself along the inspection rail, her boots magnetized to the deck, and ran a gloved hand over the frost-rimed isolation valves feeding Thruster Cluster B. Each jet could deliver sixty seconds of continuous burn. Each second produced more velocity change than venting the entire atmospheric reserve.

She plugged her diagnostic tablet into the maintenance port for B-7 and watched the data populate. Valve integrity nominal. Injector pressure stable. Nozzle throat erosion within predicted parameters, though the iridium lining showed the expected micropitting from fourteen weeks of intermittent firings. She logged the reading, her breath measured inside the helmet, and moved to the next cluster. The work was repetitive, meditative. It required no imagination, only verification. In vacuum, imagination killed. Verification kept the blood in the brain and the ice off the hull.

By the time she reached the final cluster in the sequence, her suit’s scrubber readout showed forty-two minutes of remaining capacity. She had timed the inspection precisely, as she timed everything. She pushed off the rail and drifted back toward the airlock, passing the great cylindrical bulk of the propellant feed tanks. Hundreds of tonnes of reaction mass. Enough to change their orbit, to rendezvous, to bring them home. Not breath. Not atmosphere. Fuel. The distinction was not philosophical; it was the exact, calculated difference between a living crew and a memorial plaque.

She cycled back through the lock, hung her suit in its locker with the helmet facing out so she could check the scrubber charge indicator at a glance, and stepped into the rotating frame of the hab ring. The transition to simulated gravity was a familiar stumble, corrected by instinct. She checked the bulkhead pressure gauge on her way to the engineering station: 101.3 kilopascals. Twelve thousand kilograms of nitrogen and oxygen doing exactly what they were meant to do.

Hoang closed out the shift log, appended the thruster inspection results, and headed for the wardroom. In fourteen weeks, they would need every kilogram of propellant, every functional valve, every hour of scrubber life. She was already calculating the next day’s maintenance schedule as the pumps kept their rhythm behind her, indifferent to human embarrassment, demanding only competence.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I finally leave the XO's office, my head spinning with all the equations and protocols. I make a mental note to actually understand what a tonne is before I ever open my mouth again. I bet the Chief is just humming away, probably still thinking I'm an idiot.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took her tray to the wardroom’s secondary table, the one near the maintenance conduit where the vent fans hummed louder and the conversation stayed thin. She ate reconstituted protein and tubers without tasting them, her eyes on the tablet propped against the bulkhead. The XO’s remedial curriculum populated the screen—standard mass-properties modules, unit-verification drills, derivations of effective exhaust velocity. She scanned the syllabus, confirmed it covered Tsiolkovsky and the enthalpy limits of free expansion, and marked her acknowledgment. It was not cruelty. It was maintenance. A crew member who could not distinguish between kilograms and tonnes in a propulsion calculation was a fault in the system, and faults had to be ground out before they propagated into hull breaches.

She wiped the tray with a sanitizing cloth and deposited it in the reclaim chute. On her way back to the bay she passed through the rotating ring’s transition lock, feeling the Coriolis tug at her inner ear as she stepped from the static frame into the spin. The hab ring was quiet—most of the off-duty crew were in their bunks or the rec module. She stopped at the ring’s inner pressure bulkhead and checked the gauge. One-oh-one point three kilopascals. The digits glowed green and steady. Twelve thousand kilograms, held in by gaskets, protocols, and the absolute refusal to treat any of it as optional.

When she re-entered the engineering bay, the chalk marks still lay on the deck plating: the ratio, the correction, the reminder. She stepped over them without looking down and seated herself at the primary station. The secondary loop ran quiet now, pressures balanced, the new bypass line absorbing its share of the thermal load. She pulled up the long-range propulsion schedule and entered the actual ship mass—twenty-two million kilograms—into the rendezvous-burn calculation. The software confirmed what her memory had already supplied: a four-hundred-second main-engine burn at transfer periapsis, no miracles required, no atmosphere sacrificed, arrival on the day printed in the mission plan.

She sat back, letting the bay’s pump vibration travel up through the chair frame and into her spine. Beyond the hull, the stars held fixed in their indifferent patterns. Vacuum had no mercy and no malice; it only waited for arithmetic to fail. She had spent thirty years learning to respect that silence, to treat every unit, every decimal, every bolt torque as a contract with physics that could not be renegotiated by urgency or rank. The junior officer would either adopt the same discipline or find another posting. Her responsibility ended at ensuring he did not learn his final lesson inside a suit with a spent scrubber.

Hoang closed the propulsion schedule and opened the reactor efficiency report. There was a shift to finish, and fourteen weeks of transit in which the only things that mattered were verified numbers, seated gaskets, and twelve thousand kilograms of atmosphere kept exactly where they belonged. She settled into the chair, pulled up the neutron-flux display, and let the rhythm of the pumps fill the quiet.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm back in the mess hall, trying to eat my bland nutrient paste. I keep replaying the Chief's words in my head. I pull out my tablet again, but this time I'm looking up unit conversions and ship specs. My brain hurts.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang completed the reactor efficiency report and filed it with a timestamp, routing the confirmation to the bridge. She then pulled up the ship’s mass-properties database on her primary station. The XO’s suspension order required remedial verification of the entire vessel inventory; she intended to ensure the dataset he worked from matched the flight dynamics computer exactly, with no soft numbers or classroom approximations.

She scrolled through the manifest in raw tonnes: dry hull structure, fourteen thousand two hundred; main propellant load, eight hundred forty; maneuvering reserves, twenty-two; reactor coolant, four hundred six; potable and process water, ninety; atmospheric reserve, twelve—entered as tonnes, not kilograms, the distinction now critical enough to build a lesson around. She assembled the verification exercise from these figures, locking the fields so that any derived delta-v calculation had to reconcile against the ship’s actual inertial tracking. There would be no partial credit for effort. The correct answer either aligned with the propulsion schedule to three significant figures, or it failed.

Her console chimed with the hab ring’s routine telemetry update. She scanned the readout: carbon dioxide partial pressure steady at four hundred pascals, oxygen fraction at twenty-one percent, ring rotation at the nominal rpm. The nitrogen buffer sat at full capacity, untouched. Fourteen weeks of that stability stretched ahead, contingent on no one deciding to vent it into space for phantom acceleration.

She saved the training template and pushed it to the XO’s queue, marked for the junior officer’s assignment. Then she turned to the propulsion schedule and entered the corrected mass ratio for the transfer burn. Twenty-two million kilograms of ship against hundreds of tonnes of propellant. The logarithm produced a delta-v measured in meters per second—real, useful, sufficient. She verified the solution against the mission plan, confirmed alignment, and archived the calculation.

Hoang leaned back in the station chair, letting the pump vibration travel up through the frame and into her shoulders. Beyond the hull, the stars held their fixed positions in the black. She had twelve thousand kilograms of atmosphere to preserve, a reactor to monitor, and a burn to execute in ten weeks. The mathematics that governed all of it remained unchanged: unforgiving, impersonal, and entirely immune to embarrassment. She pulled up the scrubber cycle diagram for the next shift’s inspection, already calculating flow rates in her head, as the pumps kept their steady, honest rhythm.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I manage to choke down the last of my nutrient paste. My tablet is open to a diagram of the ship's internal structure, labelled with masses in both kilograms and tonnes. I'm starting to see why the Chief was so upset. It's a lot to take in.* "Okay, okay, I get it," *I mutter to myself, rubbing my temples.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang’s humming stopped.

She did not stand at once. Instead, she pulled one earpiece free and let it rest against her collar while her other hand stayed buried in the coolant manifold, fingers still wrapped around a loose fitting. The life support pumps throbbed through the deck beneath her, steady and indifferent.

“No,” she said.

It was not sharp. It was the flat, settled tone of a woman who had already watched the idea run ahead and die.

She withdrew her hand from the manifold, wiped it slowly on a rag, and finally rose to her feet. Her knees gave a faint protest after too long on the plating. She ignored it.

“You’re thinking of atmosphere as spare mass,” she said. “It isn’t. It’s a life-support buffer. Pressure, oxygen partial pressure, humidity, carbon dioxide dilution, trace contaminant management, thermal coupling. You vent it, you don’t just make everyone wear suits. You remove the margin that keeps them alive while the ship re-stabilizes.”

She stepped to the tarp and nudged a labeled manifold piece with the toe of her boot.

“And the thrust is garbage,” she added. “Cold air through an improvised opening is not a nozzle. You get poor exhaust velocity, poor vector control, and probably torque you did not plan for. If the venting isn’t aligned through the center of mass, you induce tumble. If it is aligned, you still get very little. Air is heavy and slow compared to proper propellant. You would spend the crew’s breathable reserve for a delta-v that might not even matter.”

Hoang picked up a chunk of chalk and turned to the deck plating beside the tarp. She drew a rough box, then a line through it.

“Transit time is not a feeling,” she said. “It is a budget. Propellant mass, power, heat rejection, consumables, trajectory windows. If you want to shave weeks off, you need real delta-v, and you need it from a system designed to produce it efficiently. The main drive has specific impulse. A vented compartment has luck.”

She wrote a few numbers without hesitation, the chalk rasping over metal.

“Suppose you had ten tonnes of atmosphere to throw away. Generous. Maybe more than we can afford to lose. At a few hundred meters per second effective exhaust, you are buying meters per second of ship velocity, not tens or hundreds. Weeks of transit time are not bought with meters per second unless you are very close to a boundary condition, and even then you pay for it in survival margin.”

She underlined the last number once.

“Suits for a few days,” she repeated, tasting the phrase. “Suit consumables are not infinite. Scrubber capacity is not infinite. Water reclamation in suits is limited. Cooling is limited. Radiation exposure is still exposure. A suit is a tiny, fragile spacecraft with one person inside it. You put the whole crew in them for days because you wanted a shortcut, you have turned every small failure into a casualty.”

Hoang set the chalk down.

“If propulsion fails, if navigation boxes us into a rescue trajectory, if some other emergency makes the atmosphere the least of our problems, then maybe we discuss ugly options. But not as a schedule improvement. Not to save a few weeks.”

She looked back toward the open coolant loop.

“The ship does not care about our deadline. It cares about pressure, heat, mass, and momentum. We will keep the air inside the hull where it belongs.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang did not answer at once.

She looked down at the chalked numbers on the deck plating, then back toward the open coolant loop. The pumps kept their steady rhythm through the hull, a patient mechanical pulse that made the question feel smaller than it had sounded in the air.

“No,” she said at last. “Not because time has no value. It does. But risk is not a thing you spend because you are impatient. You spend it when it buys survival. You spend it when it buys a landing window, a rescue margin, a chance to keep the reactor from cooking itself. You do not spend it because the schedule is dull.”

She crouched again, not to work this time, but to tap one of the chalked figures with a callused fingertip.

“You keep saying ‘weeks.’ Weeks is a word. Weeks is not engineering. Engineering is: how many meters per second? How much propellant equivalent? What is the exhaust path? What is the torque? What happens to spin balance if the venting comes off the ring unevenly? What happens to thermal rejection when you lose the atmospheric buffer that helps carry heat to the exchangers? What happens if a suit seal fails on day three, or a scrubber packs up, or someone needs emergency care that cannot be done inside a pressure garment?”

She drew a short line through one of the numbers, not erasing it, just crossing it like a warning.

“A ship is not a single system,” she said. “It is a set of compromises that keep each other alive. Atmosphere is not just something you breathe. It is pressure, heat capacity, sound damping, fire behavior, contamination dilution, psychological margin, emergency reserve. You pull it out of the architecture and you do not get a clean subtraction. You get a cascade.”

Hoang straightened slowly, one hand resting briefly against the bulkhead as if to feel the vibration there.
