“If we were already committed to a hard emergency—drive failure, trajectory decay, a medical situation that could not wait—then yes, I would look at ugly options. I would look at controlled venting through proper manifolds, vector checks, mass accounting, suit rotations, consumables limits, every ugly little arithmetic item. And even then I would hate it.”

She turned her gaze back toward the junior officer’s direction, steady and unimpressed.

“But you are not proposing an emergency. You are proposing a shortcut. You are proposing that we trade the crew’s survival margin for a faster arrival time. That is not a risk worth taking. Not on this ship. Not under my systems.”

Hoang picked up the rag again and wiped a streak of coolant from her wrist.

“If the mission truly needs us there sooner, we do it the honest way. We check the drive margins. We check the propellant budget. We check the thermal limits and the power curve and the trajectory constraints. Maybe there is a higher-thrust profile we have not been allowed to use. Maybe there is a different transfer window. Maybe there is nothing at all except patience. But we will not turn the crew’s air into a poor man’s rocket.”

She nodded toward the disassembled manifold on the tarp.

“Now. Unless you have a proper delta-v proposal written out with consumables, torque limits, and failure modes, the most useful thing you can do is hand me that torque wrench before this loop decides to make the day worse.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Okay, Chief. I get it. No venting the atmosphere." *I pick up the torque wrench and hand it to her, feeling a bit deflated.* "Just trying to think outside the box, you know?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang took the torque wrench without ceremony, turning it once in her hand to check the socket fit. She crouched back down beside the coolant manifold, lined it up over a stubborn compression nut, and let the tool sit there for a moment before applying any force.

“Thinking outside the box is not the problem,” she said. Her voice had lost some of its edge, but none of its weight. “The problem is thinking the box is optional.”

She pressed the wrench over the nut and gave it a measured pull. The metal groaned faintly, then released.

“This box,” she continued, “is pressure. Oxygen reserve. Thermal buffer. Fire behavior. CO₂ dilution. Acoustic damping. Radiation shielding, however little. Psychological stability. The difference between a crew that can sleep, eat, work, and heal, and a crew that slowly dies inside their own suits while pretending they are saving time.”

The nut turned. She worked it carefully, one hand steadying the manifold with the other.

“If you want to think outside the box, fine. I want you to. But you do it where the box can move. Propellant load. Burn schedule. Power draw. Heat rejection. Trajectory correction timing. Maintenance intervals. Crew rotations. Cargo mass. Those are variables. The atmosphere is not a variable. It is a survival dependency.”

She removed the wrench, checked the thread by feel, then reached for the next fitting.

“You are not stupid for suggesting it,” she added, not looking up. “In the sims, someone always tries to use air as reaction mass. Water, waste, spare structural mass, sometimes even crew biomass if they get morbid enough. It is the natural first thought: we have mass, we need thrust, why not throw the mass away?”

A faint, dry smile touched her mouth.

“Then the instructors let the consequences run forward.”

Hoang set the wrench down and picked up a small brush, sweeping metal dust away from the mating surface.

“Mass is not just mass. Every kilogram aboard this ship has a role, even the kilograms that look useless. The air is not sitting there waiting for a better job. It is already working. It carries heat. It stabilizes temperature. It gives the scrubbers time to work. It lets us talk, hear alarms, smell smoke, move without fighting a pressure suit every second. You take that away and you do not just create inconvenience. You create a hundred new failure modes and call them progress.”

She looked up then, meeting the junior officer’s eyes with the calm patience of someone who had learned the hard way that machines did not forgive optimism.

“You want to shorten transit? Good. Ask the right question. Not ‘what can we throw away?’ but ‘what can we safely change?’”

She gestured toward the bulkhead, where the ship’s drive vibration lived as a deeper note beneath the life-support pulse.

“Can we increase main drive output without cooking the magnetic coils? Can we alter the burn schedule to take better advantage of our current vector? Can we trim nonessential mass without touching survival systems? Can we improve radiator efficiency enough to allow a higher sustained thrust? Can we accept higher crew fatigue for a shorter high-thrust window, provided radiation dose and sleep cycles stay inside limits?”

Hoang picked up the torque wrench again.

“Those are engineering questions. They have numbers attached. They have tradeoffs. They have failure modes you can list before you propose the plan. If you bring me one of those, I will listen. If it survives the arithmetic, I will even take it to the captain.”

She fitted the wrench to the next nut.

“But if you bring me a shortcut that turns the crew’s air into exhaust, I will say no. Every time. Not because I lack imagination. Because I have imagination. I can imagine exactly how it fails.”

The wrench clicked. She paused at the sound, satisfied, then moved to the next component.

“You feel deflated,” she said. “Good. That means you learned something without having to vent a compartment to find out. Do not let it make you timid. Timidity is just as dangerous as recklessness. Timidity means you stop asking questions. Recklessness means you ask the wrong ones and fall in love with the answer.”

Hoang wiped her hands again on the rag, then pointed it at the disassembled manifold.

“What I need from you is neither. I need discipline. Curiosity with a harness. You want to help the ship go faster? Help me keep the systems that let us go anywhere at all.”

She nodded toward the open coolant loop.

“Hand me that sealant kit. And while you are at it, start thinking like an engineer instead of a gambler. If you want a faster transit, write me a proper proposal. One page. Assumptions, delta-v estimate, propellant cost, thermal load, power demand, radiation exposure, crew workload, abort criteria. If it is still interesting after all that, we will talk again.”

Her expression softened by a fraction, just enough to show there was no malice in it.

“Outside the box is where improvements come from. But in deep space, the first rule is to keep the inside of the box alive.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang leaned over the tablet without taking it. Her eyes tracked down the column of figures, then back up again. The life-support pumps kept their steady pulse through the deck, a patient reminder that the ship had opinions about arithmetic whether anyone wrote them down or not.

“Three hundred forty meters per second,” she said.

Her tone was not mocking. It was the tone of someone who had just been handed a clean, shiny key and was checking whether it fit any real lock.

“That is not a trivial number. If it were real, it would be worth a conversation. If it were real, it might even be worth an emergency. But it is not real, because this calculation has left the ship behind.”

She pointed at one line on the screen without touching it.

“You have produced an exhaust velocity and called it delta-v. Those are not the same thing. One is how fast the thrown mass leaves. The other is how fast the ship changes velocity after throwing it. The difference is the mass of the ship, and the rocket equation does not let you ignore it.”

She straightened slightly, one hand resting on the bulkhead near the open coolant loop.

“Suppose, generously, that your vented air leaves at six hundred meters per second. That is optimistic for cold atmosphere through an improvised path, but I will give it to you. To get three hundred forty meters per second of ship delta-v at six hundred meters per second effective exhaust, your mass ratio must be about one point seven six. That means the propellant mass must be more than three-quarters of the remaining ship mass. If the ship after venting weighs five thousand tonnes, you need thousands of tonnes of atmosphere. We do not have thousands of tonnes of atmosphere. We have a habitat volume that keeps people alive, and a reserve that is counted in kilograms and margins, not in miracle propellant fractions.”

She let that sit for a moment.

“If you use a lower exhaust velocity, and you will, the arithmetic gets worse. At three hundred meters per second, you need a mass ratio over three. You would need to throw away more mass than the ship has left. At that point you are not designing a boost. You are designing a very slow explosion with extra paperwork.”

Hoang’s gaze flicked back to the tablet, then to the open manifold on the tarp.

“And this compression ratio,” she said. “You are treating it like a gearbox for thrust. It is not. Compression costs power. Compression creates heat. If we run compressors to raise the stagnation pressure before venting, we draw from the same power system that runs life support, thermal control, avionics, and drive support. We add heat rejection problems to a ship that already has to reject heat carefully. We add failure modes. We add contamination paths. We add rotating machinery operating near a pressure boundary. And for what? A higher number in a spreadsheet that still does not include the full mass of the vessel.”

She tapped the deck plating once with the toe of her boot.

“Then there is the angle.”

Her voice became flatter, more precise.

“This is not a non-rotating box. The ring turns. A vent fixed to the ring does not point in one inertial direction. It sweeps. If you vent continuously from one side, you do not simply get thrust. You get cyclic loading, torque, spin changes, and possibly a wobble that the attitude system has to fight. If the vent is off the center of mass, you create a moment. If the vent is not aligned through the structure properly, you put stress into frames and seals that were never designed for it. If you vent unevenly from different sections, you create pressure imbalances inside the ring. If you try to average the vector over rotation, you may get less net thrust than your calculation assumes, and you still pay the structural cost.”

She folded her arms briefly, not in anger, but in the way of someone closing a hatch against a bad idea.

“A hull opening is not a nozzle. A maintenance port is not a nozzle. An emergency vent is not a nozzle. A proper nozzle has geometry, expansion ratio, throat area, thermal tolerance, structural support, and a load path into the vehicle. Without those, you get flow separation, side loads, poor vector control, and a hole in a pressure vessel. The ship does not reward enthusiasm for holes.”

Hoang looked back at the tablet, and for the first time there was a flicker of approval in her expression, though it did not reach her voice.

“You did the calculation. That is better than guessing. I am not dismissing you for trying. But a calculation is only as good as its boundary conditions. This one assumes the atmosphere is free mass, the vent is an ideal throat, the ship is conveniently light, the vector is obedient, and the rest of the vessel will sit quietly while we turn a habitat into a cold-gas thruster.”

She shook her head once.

“On this ship, nothing sits quietly. Every system notices when another system is abused.”

She turned back to the coolant manifold and rested one hand on the torque wrench, but did not pick it up yet.

“If you want to make this proposal serious, you do it again. Use the full vehicle mass at the start of the burn. Use the actual mass of atmosphere we can vent without killing the crew or losing reserve. Use a realistic effective exhaust velocity for cold air through the path you intend, not an idealized expansion into a vacuum. Include compressor power, heat rejection, attitude-control propellant spent fighting torque, structural reinforcement mass, suit consumables, scrubber capacity, water, cooling, radiation dose, and the cost of replacing the lost atmosphere afterward if we survive long enough to need it.”

She glanced back toward the tablet.

“Then compare that to the main drive. The main drive exists to produce delta-v. It has a specific impulse, a propellant feed system, a thermal design, a magnetic nozzle or plasma channel or whatever architecture it uses, and it is mounted along a thrust structure designed to carry the load. If your atmosphere trick can beat that, even in a narrow emergency case, I want to see it. But it will not beat it as a shortcut.”

Hoang picked up the torque wrench again, then paused.

“Three hundred forty meters per second would matter if it were true. That is the point. If you ever find a way to get real delta-v from a survival system without destroying the survival part, you bring it to me immediately. But you do not bring me a number that has not been forced to carry the ship’s mass. That is not engineering. That is wishful accounting.”

She fitted the wrench over the next nut.

“Rewrite it. One page. Assumptions. Full mass accounting. Effective exhaust velocity. Duration. Thrust vector. Torque. Attitude-control cost. Thermal load. Power draw. Consumables. Abort criteria. If the number drops from three hundred forty to three or four, then you will have learned something useful. If it somehow stays high, then we will have a very different conversation.”

The wrench clicked. She gave it a small nod of satisfaction, then looked back toward the disassembled manifold.

“Now help me keep the coolant loop alive. The ship will forgive a bad idea if it stays on a tablet. It will not forgive one if we try to bolt it to the hull.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, staring at the numbers on my tablet. I thought I had it this time.* "Okay, Chief. I see what you mean about the ship's mass. And the rotation." *I swipe through a few screens, already trying to adjust my calculations.* "I'll... I'll re-run the numbers. With all the variables."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang gave a single, slow nod.

“Good,” she said. “Do not start with the number you want. Start with the number the ship will allow.”

She turned back to the coolant manifold, but did not immediately pick up the wrench. Instead, she rested one hand on the open housing, fingers spread against the metal, as if the ship’s vibration might remind her of the exact shape of the problem.

“First, use the real mass,” she said. “Not an estimate. Not a round figure from a training scenario. The current navigational mass. Structure, drive, shielding, reactors, heat sinks, cargo, consumables, crew, residue in the tanks, spare parts, dirt, water, waste, everything. If you are off by a few percent there, you are already lying to yourself.”

She glanced briefly toward the tablet, not to read it again, but to make sure the point landed.

“Second, use the atmosphere we can actually lose. Not the total habitat volume at standard pressure. The usable margin. What is the minimum safe pressure? What is the minimum oxygen partial pressure? What happens to CO₂ buildup if the scrubbers are operating at reduced efficiency? What is the reserve required for repressurization after a lock cycle? What is the reserve required for fire suppression, medical isolation, contamination control, or a hull breach that is not the one we are deliberately creating?”

Hoang picked up a piece of chalk and tapped it once against the deck plating, not writing yet, just thinking through the shape of the arithmetic.

“Third, effective exhaust velocity. Not compression ratio. Not ideal expansion. Not a number borrowed from a nozzle that does not exist. If you vent through a hatch, a maintenance port, or an emergency valve, you get a discharge coefficient, flow separation, possible icing, structural side loads, and a vector that changes as the ring rotates. If the vent is fixed to the habitat, the thrust direction sweeps. You have to integrate the inertial component over time. If it averages poorly, you get less useful delta-v than your first pass suggested. If it averages badly and asymmetrically, you also get torque, wobble, and attitude-control expenditure.”

She finally wrote a short list on the plating beside the manifold.

ASSUMPTIONS  
MASS IN / MASS OUT  
EXHAUST VELOCITY  
VECTOR INTEGRATION  
TORQUE / ACS COST  
POWER / HEAT  
CONSUMABLES  
RESTORE COST  
ABORT CRITERIA

“That is the skeleton,” she said. “Everything else is detail until those are honest.”

The chalk rasped once as she underlined RESTORE COST.

“Do not forget that one. If we survive the maneuver, we still have to replace what we threw away. Stored gas. Electrolysis capacity. Scrubber margin. Time. Power. Heat. If we are a mining vessel, we may have some elemental reserves, but reserves are not free. They have mass, power draw, and processing time. If we use them to replace atmosphere, we are spending mission capability. Maybe that is worth it in an emergency. It is not worth it to arrive early.”

She set the chalk down and wiped her fingers on the rag again.

“And suits,” she continued. “If your plan requires the crew to remain in pressure garments, put the suit consumables in the model. Oxygen bottles. Scrubber cartridges. Cooling water. Battery capacity. Humidity control. Heat stress. Work efficiency. Sleep quality. Medical access. Every hour in a suit has a cost, even when nothing breaks. Especially because something always breaks.”

Hoang picked up the torque wrench, checked the socket, then set it down again without using it. She was not finished.

“If the revised number comes back small, do not treat that as failure. That is the point. A small number tells you the idea is weak. A weak idea on a tablet is harmless. A weak idea bolted into a pressure hull is a casualty waiting for an inconvenient day.”

Her expression remained serious, but the hardness in it had eased into something more like instruction.

“Bring me three results,” she said. “Best realistic case. Worst plausible case. And the first failure mode that kills someone. If you cannot name the third, you have not finished the calculation.”

She finally lifted the wrench and fitted it over the next compression nut.

“And when you write it, write it so a tired officer at the end of a twelve-hour shift can understand it. Clear assumptions. Clear units. Clear limits. If it takes cleverness to see why it works, it probably does not work.”

The wrench clicked. She paused, listened to the coolant loop settle, then added, quieter, “You are learning. That is useful. But learning on a ship like this is not about finding the bold answer first. It is about finding the answer that lets everyone still be alive when the boldness wears off.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang studied the revised numbers for a long moment, her face unreadable. The tablet sat in her hand now, smudged with coolant and fingerprints, and the faint blue light picked out the hard lines around her mouth. The engineering bay kept its usual mechanical rhythm around her: pumps, compressors, the distant harmonic of the drive, the small metallic ticks of a ship staying alive by constant effort.

At last she exhaled through her nose.

“All right,” she said. “This is not the same idea you walked in with.”

She set the tablet down on the tarp beside the manifold, careful not to smear the chalk marks, and tapped one line with a blunt fingernail.

“You stopped treating the atmosphere as free propellant and started treating it as a survival system that can be degraded only within limits. That is the difference between a fantasy and a proposal. If the final numbers hold after I check them, and if the captain accepts the operational reason for doing this, then yes. I will not block it.”

She held up a hand before the word could become enthusiasm.

“But not as a shortcut. Not because someone is bored with transit time. And not unless every one of the following conditions is met.”

Hoang reached for the chalk and began writing on the deck plating in tight, practical block letters.

“One. Minimum safe atmosphere is preserved. We do not vent below the pressure and oxygen partial pressure required for normal operation plus emergency reserve. That reserve includes repressurization capability, lockout capability, medical isolation, fire response, and a margin for an unplanned breach. If your plan requires eating into the last breathable kilogram, it is not a plan. It is a prayer.”

She drew a short line under the word.

“Two. The vent path is engineered before it is opened. No improvised hatches. No maintenance ports. No ‘it should hold’ fittings. We use an existing emergency vent line if one can be adapted, or we build a proper manifold with a rated pressure boundary, a controlled throat, and a load path into structure. If we are making thrust, we make it through something that knows it is supposed to carry thrust.”

The chalk rasped again.

“Three. Vector control is verified. Because the ring rotates, any vent mounted off the spin axis produces a moving vector. That means either we route the vent through a non-rotating structure where the direction is stable, or we pulse the vent under attitude-control supervision and integrate the actual inertial thrust over time. No continuous blind venting. No hoping the average comes out clean. If the burn produces unwanted torque, wobble, or cyclic structural loading, we shut it down.”

Hoang glanced up briefly.

“I do not care how pretty the delta-v looks on the tablet. If it makes the ring behave like an unbalanced wheel, it is rejected.”

She returned to the list.

“Four. All crew are suited before the first gram of atmosphere is deliberately discarded. Not nearby suits. Not ‘we can grab them if the pressure drops.’ Suited, checked, leak-tested, with consumables sufficient for at least twice the planned duration. Scrubber capacity, cooling water, battery charge, comms, hydration, waste management. If someone cannot work effectively in a suit, they are not in a position where the maneuver depends on them.”

The chalk marked another line.

“Five. Life support redundancy is confirmed. CO₂ scrubbers on primary and backup. Oxygen distribution stable. Humidity and thermal control within limits. If we lose atmospheric buffer, we do not also lose the ability to handle a contaminant spike, a small fire, or a sick crew member. Medical must approve the suit duration. I want it in writing.”

Hoang’s expression tightened slightly.

“Six. Power and heat are accounted for. If compressors, pumps, valves, or attitude-control systems must run harder to support this maneuver, their power draw and heat rejection go into the plan. We do not create a thermal crisis while trying to solve a transit-time problem. If the radiators cannot carry the extra load without reducing reactor or drive margins, the answer is no.”

She wrote:

THERMAL / POWER MARGIN  
NO SINGLE-POINT FAILURE

Then she underlined it twice.

“Seven. Abort criteria are defined before we start. If pressure falls faster than predicted, abort. If oxygen partial pressure approaches minimum reserve, abort. If attitude control expenditure exceeds budget, abort. If suit consumables degrade faster than expected, abort. If any structural sensor shows abnormal loading, abort. If the thermal loop complains, abort. And if the captain, the pilot, or I say abort, then the maneuver ends immediately. No debate. No ‘just a few more seconds.’”

Hoang set the chalk down and brushed dust from her fingers.

“Eight. Replacement is planned. We do not throw away atmosphere and then discover we cannot recover it. I want to know where the replacement gas comes from, how long it takes, what power it requires, and what mission capability we lose by spending those reserves. If we are a mining vessel, we may have feedstock. Feedstock is not magic. It has processing limits. If the maneuver costs us water, oxygen reserve, or industrial capacity, that cost goes on the balance sheet.”

She looked toward the open coolant loop, then back again.

“Nine. The maneuver is only approved if it serves a real operational need. Rescue window. Medical necessity. Avoiding a worse trajectory. Preventing a consumables shortfall. Something concrete. If the only benefit is arriving earlier, then the answer remains no. Time is valuable, but it is not more valuable than the crew’s ability to survive the trip.”

Her voice softened only slightly.

“And ten. You write it so clearly that no one has to guess. Assumptions. Vehicle mass. Usable atmosphere. Exhaust model. Vector integration. Torque. ACS cost. Power. Thermal. Suit consumables. Medical limits. Abort thresholds. Recovery plan. If a single number is hand-waved, I will send it back. If a single safety condition is treated as optional, I will send it back. If someone tries to make the math kinder than reality, I will send it back so hard the tablet will need medical attention.”

Hoang picked up the tablet again and turned it so the revised calculation faced her fully.

“If all of that is done, and if the number still matters, then yes. I agree that this can be considered a controlled emergency option. Not a routine procedure. Not a clever trick. A controlled, limited, closely supervised maneuver with the crew suited, the ship monitored, and the atmosphere protected as the survival system it is.”

She handed the tablet back, but not before adding one final condition in her own voice.

“And you will not open anything until I have personally inspected the vent path. No exceptions. If I am not standing there with my hand on the structure and my eyes on the pressure sensors, nothing happens.”

For the first time since the idea had entered the bay, there was something like approval in her face. It was small, practical, and entirely conditional.

“You brought me a bad idea,” she said. “Then you did the harder thing. You let the ship correct it. That is what engineering is.”

She crouched again beside the coolant manifold and picked up the torque wrench.

“Now write the safety review. One page for the concept, one page for the conditions, one page for the abort plan. If it survives my review, it goes to the captain. If it survives the captain, it goes to navigation and medical. If it survives all of them, then maybe we talk about hardware.”

The wrench clicked once, firm and final.

“But understand me: I am agreeing to a disciplined option, not to throwing our air away because the clock is slow.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stare at the tablet, then at the Chief. My head is spinning a little, but I feel a surge of… something. Not excitement, but solid purpose.* "Yes, Chief. Understood. I'll get started on the safety review immediately. And... thank you." *I tuck the tablet under my arm, feeling like I've just been handed a monumental task, but a possible one.* "I'll make sure it's tight."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang gave a short nod, the kind that accepted intention without endorsing outcome.

“Do not thank me yet,” she said. “Thank me if the review survives. Thank me if the captain reads it and does not throw it back with questions I should have asked first. Thank me if we never need to use it.”

She turned back to the coolant manifold, but her hand paused over the torque wrench instead of closing around it.

“You have the shape of it now. The rest is discipline. Do not write what you hope will happen. Write what will happen when something disagrees with you. Hardware does not care about confidence.”

Hoang reached for a clean rag and wiped a smear of grease from the deck beside the chalked list.

“Use the current mass report from navigation. Use the atmospheric inventory from life support, not the nominal table from last month. Use suit consumable data from the actual lockers, not the manufacturer’s optimistic number. If there is a discrepancy, put it in the review and say which one you used and why.”

She glanced toward the bulkhead where the deeper vibration of the drive lived beneath the life-support pulse.

“And do not disappear into it for sixteen hours straight,” she added. “A tired engineer makes tidy mistakes. If you are still staring at the same equation after two hours, step away, eat something, and come back with fresh eyes. The ship will still be here.”

Hoang fitted the wrench over the next compression nut and checked the alignment by feel before applying any force.

“Bring me the first draft when you have the assumptions locked, not when the numbers look pretty. I would rather see an ugly page that tells the truth than a clean page that hides a bad guess.”

The wrench clicked. She listened for a moment to the coolant loop, then allowed herself a small, practical breath of satisfaction.

“Go,” she said. “And if you find yourself falling in love with the answer again, come back here and make the manifold boring before you trust it.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod again, a bit more firmly this time. The Chief's words settle in, a heavy but welcome weight.* "Understood, Chief. No pretty numbers, just the truth." *I turn to leave, already feeling the mental gears grinding.* "And I'll be back for that boring manifold if I need to."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang stood for a moment with the torque wrench hanging loose in her hand, listening to the engineering bay settle back into its ordinary noise. Pumps. Compressors. The faint electrical whine of a monitoring cabinet. The deep, almost subsonic presence of the drive through the structure. The ship did not care that someone had just left with a dangerous idea under one arm. It only cared whether the idea was allowed to touch hardware.

She set the wrench down on the tarp and pulled a battered maintenance slate from beneath a folded strap. It was older than half the crew and twice as stubborn, but it synced to the ship’s mass properties file without argument. That was all she asked of any tool.

The first thing she opened was not the vent proposal. It was the current vehicle mass report.

The number sat there, plain and unforgiving. Structure, shielding, reactor plant, drive assembly, radiator loops, propellant load, ore-processing equipment, spare machinery, consumables, crew, water, waste, fuel reserves, mining gear, contamination allowances, and the accumulated clutter of people living for months inside a closed system. The ship was not a clean textbook diagram. It was a heavy, complicated animal, and every kilogram of it had opinions.

Hoang copied the figure onto her slate, then opened the atmospheric inventory.

Her mouth tightened.

The nominal table was optimistic, as usual. The actual sensor inventory was lower. Some of that was normal leakage. Some was consumption. Some was reserve gas tied up in bottles for repressurization, medical use, and emergency response. She pulled the life-support reserve margins next and compared them against the minimum safe pressure and oxygen partial pressure required for a full crew working in a suited environment.

The difference was not large.

It was never large.

She wrote one word at the top of the slate:

USABLE.

Then she sat back on her heels and looked at it.

“Not much,” she said quietly.

The bay answered with the steady pulse of the coolant pumps.

She pulled a piece of chalk from her pocket and began drawing on the deck plating beside the manifold. Not the fantasy version. The real one. A rotating habitat ring. The central utility spine. The drive axis. Propellant tanks. Radiator loops. Attitude-control thrusters. Emergency vents. Pressure bulkheads. Suit lockers. Gas storage. Medical bay. The crew quarters. The mess. The machine shop. Every space that depended on the same thin envelope of gas to remain survivable.

She sketched a possible vent path from the habitat ring and crossed it out almost immediately.

“No,” she said.

A vent in the ring would sweep with the rotation. Even if the thrust vector looked clean for a moment, it would not remain clean in inertial space. It would become a rotating force, a source of torque and cyclic loading. The attitude-control system would have to fight it, or the ship would have to accept a wobble. Neither was acceptable as a casual trade for time.

She drew another line toward the central utility spine and paused.

That was more plausible. If there was a stable path near the spin axis, and if the gas could be routed through rated plumbing rather than improvised openings, the vector could be made less chaotic. But routing pressurized gas from a rotating section through a dynamic interface into a non-rotating vent introduced seals, valves, sensors, and failure modes. Every joint became a question. Every question became a leak path. Every leak path became a reason not to sleep.

She wrote:

ENGINEERED PATH ONLY.  
NO HATCHES.  
NO FIELD-MADE HOLES.  
RATED VALVES.  
REDUNDANT SHUTOFF.  
BURST DISK / RELIEF PATH.  
FLOW METERING.  
THERMAL CONDITIONING.  
STRUCTURAL LOAD PATH.

Then she underlined the last line twice.

A vent that produced thrust had to carry thrust. If it did not, the hull would carry it instead, and the hull had not been asked.

Hoang opened the attitude-control budget next. The ship used a combination of reaction wheels and small thrusters for trim, with the spin ring itself providing stability through angular momentum. That was fine for normal operations. It was not fine for deliberately creating an off-axis gas jet. She pulled the control authority margins and studied them with the expression of a woman who had seen too many bright ideas die in the margins.

If the vent was pulsed, the timing would have to be locked to the ring’s rotation. If it was continuous, the integrated vector would need verification. If the thrust direction changed by even a small amount, the resulting torque could cost more in attitude-control propellant than the maneuver gained in useful delta-v. And if the attitude-control system had to burn reserve propellant to keep the ship from developing a slow, irritating precession, then the “free” thrust had just spent real propellant by proxy.

She added another line to the slate:

ACS EXPENDITURE COUNTS AS COST.

Then, after a moment:

SO DOES CREW FATIGUE.

The suits were the next problem.

Hoang opened the suit locker inventory and scrolled through the status list. Some of the pressure garments were in good condition. Some had warning flags that maintenance had not yet cleared because there were never enough hours in the day. Glove seals aged. Cooling loops clogged. Scrubber cartridges had service lives. Batteries degraded. Helmets fogged. Comm units dropped out if a connector was worn. Drinking systems leaked. Waste management was exactly as unpleasant and exactly as important as it sounded.

She marked three suits for immediate inspection and one for a mandatory seal replacement.

“Medical signs off,” she muttered, writing it down. “Not a verbal nod. Written.”

If the crew had to remain suited during the maneuver, the suits became life support. That meant they had to be treated with the same seriousness as the ship’s primary systems. No one would be allowed to ride a pressure garment like it was an inconvenience. A suit was a small spacecraft. It had power, thermal control, gas supply, scrubbing, cooling, communications, and structural integrity. If one failed, the person inside it became an emergency.

She added:

SUIT DURATION × CREW COUNT.  
CONSUMABLES × 2.  
REST ROTATION.  
HYDRATION.  
WASTE.  
MEDICAL LIMITS.  
NO SINGLE PERSON ESSENTIAL WHILE SUITED IF AVOIDABLE.

The thermal problem came next.

Venting gas was not just throwing mass away. Expanding gas cooled. Valves iced. Lines contracted. Sensors drifted. If the gas was drawn from compressed storage, the pressure drop could chill fittings enough to make seals brittle or cause moisture to freeze where it had no business being. If compressors were used to raise the pressure before venting, they generated heat, and that heat had to go somewhere. The ship’s radiators were already working. They did not have infinite margin. If the maneuver pushed the thermal control system too close to its limit, the drive or reactor might have to throttle down, and then the clever shortcut would defeat itself.

Hoang pulled the radiator status curve and compared it against the projected compressor load.

She did not like the shape of it.

It was not impossible. It was constrained.

She wrote:

NO THERMAL SPIKE.  
NO RADIATOR SATURATION.  
NO REDUCTION IN DRIVE COOLING MARGIN.  
IF HEAT RISES, ABORT.

Power was the companion problem. Every pump, valve controller, sensor suite, compressor, attitude-control actuator, and suit-charging point drew from the same finite system. If the ship had to support the vent maneuver while also maintaining life support, navigation, communications, medical equipment, and drive readiness, the power budget had to close with room left for faults.

She added:

POWER MARGIN FOR FAULT CASE.

Then she sat back and looked at the list.

It was long. It should be long. Anything involving pressure boundaries and human breathing should be long.

Hoang opened a new document on the slate and began drafting the preliminary note she would send to the captain if the junior officer’s review survived first contact with her red pen.

She typed slowly, choosing each phrase as if it were a bolt being torqued to spec.

“Preliminary assessment of controlled gas venting as emergency delta-v option. Not approved. Not routine. Feasible only under constrained conditions with full safety review. Requires operational justification beyond schedule improvement. Must preserve minimum survivable atmosphere, engineered vent path, verified vector control, suited crew, verified life-support redundancy, thermal and power margin, defined abort criteria, and post-maneuver atmospheric restoration plan.”

She stopped and read it back.

Then she added:

“No implementation without Chief Engineer inspection and captain authorization.”

That was not bureaucracy. That was the hull.

Hoang set the slate aside and returned to the coolant manifold. The proposal could wait. The ship could not. She finished the compression nut, checked the adjacent fitting, and ran a gloved thumb along the seal seat to feel for imperfections. The metal was cool, smooth, and indifferent. Good. Indifferent meant it had not yet been insulted by bad decisions.

She worked in silence for several minutes, tightening, checking, rechecking. The secondary coolant loop was not glamorous. It would not shorten the transit by a single hour. It would not produce a dramatic number on a tablet. But it kept heat moving where heat needed to move, and if it failed, the crew would learn very quickly how fragile “fast” could be.

When the manifold was buttoned up enough for a pressure check, she rose again and wiped her hands.

The slate was waiting.

She picked it up and added one final section at the bottom.

FAILURE MODES THAT KILL SOMEONE.

She stared at the heading for a moment.

Then she wrote:

1. Loss of pressure below survivable reserve.  
2. Oxygen partial pressure drop during suited operation.  
3. CO₂ rise due to scrubber overload or suit malfunction.  
4. Uncontrolled torque inducing structural load or loss of attitude control.  
5. Vent path failure at pressure boundary.  
6. Thermal overload in radiator loop or drive cooling.  
7. Power shortage during maneuver preventing abort or recovery.  
8. Suit failure with insufficient rescue margin.  
9. Fire risk due to altered gas mixture.  
10. Inability to restore atmosphere before next operational emergency.

She read the list once, then again.

It was not pleasant. It was complete enough for a first pass.

Hoang looked toward the bulkhead where the ship’s deeper vibrations lived. Somewhere beyond that plating were tanks, pipes, valves, radiators, drive mounts, and the long, patient mathematics of Newtonian flight. No one got to argue with momentum. No one got to bribe pressure. The ship would not accept enthusiasm as a substitute for margin.

But it would accept honest work.

She allowed herself one small, tired breath that might have been satisfaction if it had not been so heavily conditioned.

“All right,” she said to the empty bay. “Let’s see if it survives the truth.”

Then Chief Engineer Hoang picked up the slate, tucked the chalk back into her pocket, and went to find the nearest vent line that had any business being considered for such a job, intending to stand in front of it with her eyes open and her hand on the structure before anyone was allowed to dream of opening it.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I'm still standing there, just outside the bay, my tablet clutched in my hand, lost in thought. I didn't even notice the Chief was done with the manifold until she stood up and started writing on the deck. I see her last list, "FAILURE MODES THAT KILL SOMEONE," and my stomach clenches. This isn't a game.*

"Chief... I think I just got the real definition of 'thinking outside the box' from you." *My voice is quieter now, a little humbled.* "It's about knowing the box, isn't it?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang paused with the slate tucked under one arm. She looked toward the hatchway where the junior officer’s voice still seemed to hang in the recycled air, and for a moment her expression was not stern so much as still.

“Yes,” she said. “It is about knowing the box.”

She stepped over the chalked list on the deck plating without looking down at it, as if the words had already done their work and could now simply wait.

“The box is not a punishment,” she continued. “It is the ship. Pressure. Oxygen partial pressure. Thermal margin. Power balance. Structural load. Radiation limits. Human tolerance. Every constraint that feels like a wall is usually there because the other side of it is vacuum, fire, hypoxia, or a casualty report.”

Hoang shifted the slate to her other hand. The engineering bay hummed around her, steady and indifferent, the life-support pumps keeping their patient rhythm through the deck.

“People talk about thinking outside the box as if the box is the enemy,” she said. “It is not. The box is what keeps you alive while you think. If you understand it, you can sometimes find a hinge. A place where a small, careful change opens a new option. If you do not understand it, you do not think outside the box. You just punch a hole in it.”

She glanced briefly at the failure-mode list she had written, then away again.

“That is why I gave you the conditions. Not to make the idea impossible. To make it survivable. A good engineer does not ask whether a thing can be imagined. She asks what it touches, what it stresses, what it consumes, what it breaks, and what happens when it breaks anyway.”

Hoang moved toward the open coolant loop one last time, checking the newly torqued fittings with a practiced eye. Her hand rested briefly on the housing, feeling the temperature, the vibration, the small mechanical truth of it.

“So your next task is not to be clever,” she said. “It is to be thorough. Map the box. Current vehicle mass. Actual atmospheric inventory, not the nominal one. Suit readiness by locker, not by assumption. Vent paths that are rated for pressure service. Power and thermal margins under fault conditions. Attitude-control authority. Medical limits. Restoration cost. Put every ugly number on the page before you try to make any of them do something useful.”

She picked up the torque wrench and set it back on the tarp with the other tools, aligning it neatly beside the chalk-labeled manifold parts.

“Bring me the limits first,” she said. “If there is still room inside them, then we will see whether your idea deserves hardware. If there is not, you will have learned why before anyone got hurt. That is not failure. That is the job.”

For a moment, something almost gentle passed across her face. It did not soften her voice, but it changed the weight of it.

“You are not wrong to want to find a better way,” she said. “A ship that only does what it has always done will eventually be caught by a problem it never prepared for. But improvement has to be disciplined. Boldness without margin is just a polite word for accident.”

Hoang lifted the slate again and checked the preliminary note she had drafted, her eyes moving quickly over the lines as if daring one of them to be unclear.

“Now go start the review,” she said. “And before you sit down with it, eat something. A hungry officer makes careless assumptions, and I am not signing off on careless assumptions.”

She turned toward the nearest access panel that led to the utility spine, already shifting into the next task.

“And when you come back,” she added without looking around, “bring me the number you are least proud of. That is usually the one that matters.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Right. The number I'm least proud of." *I nod, taking a deep breath. It's a lot, but for the first time, I feel like I actually understand the scope of the problem. I turn and head for the mess hall, my tablet still clutched in my hand. Maybe a nutrient paste and a long walk will help me see the box a little clearer.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang listened until the hatch whispered shut behind the junior officer, then let the silence of the engineering bay settle back around her.

Not true silence. A ship like this never had silence. It had layers. Pump pulse. Compressor cycling. Fan bearings. Relay clicks. The faint creak of structure carrying thermal stress. The deeper, almost felt presence of the drive through the keel. The ship breathed in machinery and exhaled heat. If someone ever heard real silence aboard this vessel, it would mean something had already stopped working that should not stop working.

She looked down at the chalked list on the deck plating.

FAILURE MODES THAT KILL SOMEONE.

She did not erase it. She stepped around it instead, careful not to smear the words, and went back to the slate.

The first thing she did was not calculate. She verified.

Mass properties first.

She opened the latest navigational mass report and compared it against the engineering inventory. The two did not agree. They never agreed perfectly. One came from the flight dynamics side, clean and averaged. The other came from maintenance, cargo, consumables, and the accumulated reality of a ship that had been lived in hard. Hoang trusted neither one alone. She trusted the reconciliation.

She began making a third table.

Structure. Shielding. Reactor plant. Drive assembly. Radiator fluid. Propellant load. Ore-processing equipment. Spare machinery. Water. Waste. Food. Medical stores. Mining gear. Personal kits. Tooling. Contamination allowances. Residual propellant trapped in lines. Coolant that had sloshed where the sensors could not see it. The mass of the crew themselves, not as neat averages but as bodies that needed pressure, oxygen, heat removal, and a way home.

Every kilogram had to be honest.

She copied the final number into a fresh field and labeled it:

CURRENT VEHICLE MASS — RECONCILED.

Then she paused and added beneath it:

DO NOT ROUND DOWN.

The atmospheric inventory came next.

The nominal table made her mouth tighten again. It listed storage bottles, cabin volume, emergency reserve, and repressurization margin as if they were clean blocks of capability. They were not. Some bottles were designated for medical use. Some for lockout recovery. Some for contamination recovery. Some existed because a hull patch might need pressure behind it before it could hold. Some existed because fire suppression and oxygen balance were not separate problems. The atmosphere was not a tank. It was a system.

She pulled the actual sensor readings.

Cabin pressure. Oxygen partial pressure. Carbon dioxide level. Humidity. Trace contaminants. Reserve bottle pressures. Electrolysis feedstock. Scrubber margin. Reclamation efficiency. The small, unglamorous numbers that decided whether people stayed conscious.

Hoang wrote:

USABLE ATMOSPHERE = TOTAL ATMOSPHERE − SURVIVAL RESERVE.

Then, after a moment:

SURVIVAL RESERVE INCLUDES THE THINGS YOU HOPE NOT TO NEED.

She did not allow herself to treat that as poetry. It was arithmetic.

The suit inventory took longer than she liked.

On paper, the ship carried enough pressure garments for the crew plus spares. In practice, suits were never simply “available.” They aged. Seals hardened. Cooling loops fouled. Scrubber cartridges expired. Batteries lost capacity. Helmets scratched. Glove joints weakened. Comm harnesses developed intermittent faults that behaved only when someone was already stressed and sweating inside the garment.

She opened the maintenance log and scrolled through the flags.

One suit had a cooling pump bearing warning. Another had a failed humidity sensor that had been deferred because it still passed leak check. A third had glove seals approaching service limit. A fourth had a comm drop during the last drill. None of those were dramatic. All of them mattered.

Hoang marked each one for immediate inspection.

Then she added:

SUIT READINESS IS NOT COUNT. SUIT READINESS IS DURATION UNDER LOAD.

Medical would have to sign off on maximum suited time. Not a guess. Not a shrug. A written limit based on heat stress, CO₂ exposure, hydration, fatigue, and the realities of working inside a pressure garment for longer than anyone liked.

She set that section aside and moved to the vent path.

This was the part she wanted to see with her own eyes.

She secured the slate to her wrist, pocketed a small inspection light, and left the engineering bay. The ship shifted around her as she moved toward the central utility spine. Gravity changed from the comfortable pull of the ring to the lighter, stranger feel of the hub transition. Her body knew the drill: slow the steps, keep a hand near a rail, let the inner ear stop complaining. The rotating habitat did not care about urgency. Coriolis did not negotiate.

The utility spine was colder. Quieter in one sense, louder in another. There was less ambient machinery here, but the structure carried different sounds: fluid transfer lines, rotary seals, electrical conduits, attitude-control plumbing, the faint tick of thermal expansion. The ship’s spin was still present, but closer to the axis it became a fact of geometry rather than a floor beneath her feet.

She found the nearest candidate vent line and stopped in front of it.

It was not glamorous. A pressure boundary, a shutoff valve, a manual isolation, an actuator, a sensor pack, and a short discharge path meant for emergency dumping, not sustained thrust. It had been designed to protect the hull from overpressure, not to push the hull through space.

Hoang rested her hand near the valve body, not on it. The metal was cool. Too cool.

She checked the tag number against the slate.

Last inspection: eight months ago.

Not catastrophic. Not acceptable either.

She examined the mounting brackets. Solid, but not reinforced for sustained side load. The line had a clean path outward, but it was offset from the thrust axis. Any meaningful flow through it would create a moment. Not just thrust. Torque. Bending. A force the structure would have to absorb.

She pulled up the line schematic.

The vent drew from a common emergency manifold. That manifold connected back toward habitat sections through valves that had been cycled rarely. Rarely was good for wear. Rarely was bad for confidence. Valves that sat still too long could seize. Seals that saw no motion could set. Sensors that saw no exercise could drift.

She wrote:

CANDIDATE PATH V-7.  
NOT FOR USE WITHOUT FULL TEARDOWN INSPECTION.  
BURST DISK RATING VERIFIED.  
ACTUATOR RESPONSE TIME UNKNOWN.  
SEAL CONDITION SUSPECT.  
VECTOR OFFSET FROM CENTERLINE.  
REQUIRES ACS COMPENSATION MODEL.

Then she added:

DO NOT MISTAKE EXISTING HARDWARE FOR SUITABLE HARDWARE.

The idea had one possible merit: if they ever did this, the path had to be engineered, not improvised. That meant no opened hatches. No field-cut ports. No “we will brace it later.” If atmosphere became reaction mass, it had to pass through something designed to meter it, direct it, shut it off, and survive the loads.

She moved along the spine, checking another line.

This one was worse. Closer to a rotary coupling, older insulation, a sensor harness that had been rerouted around a maintenance bracket. She marked it rejected before she finished the inspection.

The third possibility was better, but not by much.

It had a straighter path. Better structural support. A rated valve. But it drew from a section that would require pulling gas through a dynamic seal from the rotating habitat into the non-rotating spine. That seal had a service history. Hoang read it twice.

The seal had been replaced during a refit, but the test data was incomplete.

She stared at that line for a long moment.

Incomplete test data was where optimism went to hide.

She wrote:

ROTARY INTERFACE RISK.  
LEAK PATH UNDER TRANSIENT PRESSURE.  
POTENTIAL SINGLE-POINT FAILURE.  
NOT ACCEPTABLE WITHOUT FULL PRESSURE CYCLE TEST.

The ship gave her no dramatic warning. No alarm. No flashing light. Just the quiet truth of maintenance records.

Hoang exhaled slowly.

“Still not dead,” she said to herself. “But not alive either.”

That was the honest state of the idea. It had not been killed yet. It had also not earned the right to exist. It was suspended between possibility and stupidity, waiting for the numbers to decide.

She opened the attitude-control file next.

The ship’s control authority was not infinite. Reaction wheels could absorb some disturbance. Thrusters could correct others. Spin stability helped, but it did not make unwanted torque free. If the vent produced a force that swept with the ring, the control system would either have to average it, cancel it, or accept it. None of those choices were costless.

She pulled the ACS propellant reserve and compared it against the projected disturbance cases.

Best case: small trim cost.

Plausible case: significant counter-burns.

Bad case: induced wobble requiring continuous correction.

Worst case: structural coupling that made the problem worse over time.

She added another note:

USEFUL DELTA-V MUST BE NET OF ACS EXPENDITURE.

Then, because she knew how easily people forgot, she underlined it.

Power and thermal came after.

She modeled the vent not as a clean arrow of mass leaving the ship, but as a process. Gas moving through lines. Valves opening. Pressure dropping. Temperature falling. Possible ice forming at throats and seats. Sensors drifting. Actuators drawing power. Compressors, if used, dumping heat into loops that already had jobs. Radiators rejecting what they could, and no more.

The ship’s thermal system was not a trash bin for extra heat. It was a carefully balanced argument between reactors, drive, electronics, crew, and vacuum. Add load in one place and something else lost margin.

Hoang compared compressor options against radiator margin and shook her head.

Not impossible. Not clean.

If they used stored pressure only, the thrust would be brief and limited. If they used compressors to maintain flow, they bought time at the cost of power and heat. If they tried to combine both, they added complexity and failure modes. Every branch had teeth.

She wrote:

THERMAL CASE MUST INCLUDE FAULT MARGIN.  
IF RADIATORS SATURATE, ABORT BEFORE DAMAGE.  
NO BORROWING FROM DRIVE COOLING.

By the time she finished the first pass, her slate had become a dense block of tables, warnings, and red-flagged assumptions. She did not find it discouraging. She found it necessary.

The junior officer had brought an idea. The ship was now turning that idea over, feeling for cracks.

Hoang returned to the engineering bay and set the slate on the tarp beside the manifold tools. She did not sit. She pulled a fresh sheet of maintenance paper from a drawer and began writing the review outline by hand. Sometimes the act of writing slowed her thoughts enough to keep them honest.

ASSUMPTIONS  
1. Operational justification.  
2. Current reconciled vehicle mass.  
3. Usable atmosphere after survival reserve.  
4. Candidate vent path inspection status.  
5. Effective exhaust velocity, not ideal.  
6. Vector integration over ring rotation.  
7. Torque and ACS cost.  
8. Power draw under nominal and fault cases.  
9. Thermal load under nominal and fault cases.  
10. Suit readiness and medical limits.  
11. Crew workload and fatigue.  
12. Abort criteria.  
13. Restoration plan.  
14. Failure modes with casualty potential.

At the top she wrote:

IF ANY SECTION IS MISSING, THE REVIEW IS MISSING.

She looked at that line and added:

NO EXCEPTIONS FOR URGENCY UNLESS URGENCY IS DEFINED.

The hatch status board flickered as someone else moved through the ship. Hoang did not look up immediately. She was thinking about the phrase “operational justification.” It sounded tidy. It was not.

Operational justification could mean a rescue window. A medical evacuation. A trajectory correction that prevented a worse outcome. A consumables crisis. A collision-avoidance requirement. A missed transfer that stranded them.

It did not mean boredom.

It did not mean impatience.

It did not mean someone wanted to feel clever.

She had seen people die because they confused those categories. Sometimes not in dramatic ways. Sometimes they died because a margin that looked boring was spent to solve a problem that looked urgent at the time. Then the next problem arrived, and there was nothing left.

Hoang tapped the slate against her palm once.

“Write the truth,” she murmured.

She opened a new message to the captain, then stopped before typing the body.

There was a discipline to reporting dangerous ideas. If she wrote “possible,” someone might hear “approved.” If she wrote “rejected,” she might close a door that could matter in a true emergency. If she wrote “under review,” someone might think the review was a formality.

She typed carefully.

CAPTAIN —

PRELIMINARY ENGINEERING ASSESSMENT ONLY.  
JUNIOR OFFICER HAS PROPOSED CONTROLLED ATMOSPHERE VENT AS EMERGENCY DELTA-V OPTION.  
NOT ROUTINE. NOT CURRENTLY SAFE. NOT IMPLEMENTABLE WITHOUT FULL REVIEW.  
POTENTIAL EXISTS ONLY UNDER STRICT CONSTRAINTS AND VERIFIED OPERATIONAL NEED.  
I AM CONDUCTING HARDWARE AND SYSTEM MARGIN INSPECTION.  
NO CHANGES TO SHIP CONFIGURATION WILL BE MADE.  
WILL FORWARD FORMAL ASSESSMENT IF THE NUMBERS SURVIVE INITIAL REVIEW.

— HOANG

She read it twice.

Then she added one more line:

IF THERE IS NO OPERATIONAL NEED BEYOND TRANSIT TIME, MY RECOMMENDATION WILL REMAIN NO.

She sent it.

That done, she returned to the coolant loop. The manifold was buttoned up enough for a pressure check, and the ship would not wait while people philosophized about delta-v. She connected the test line, opened the isolation slowly, and watched the gauges climb. The needle steadied. No drop. No hiss. No thermal bloom on the infrared tape. Good.

She logged the result and moved to the next fitting.

Work settled into a rhythm. Check. Tighten. Test. Log. Listen. Repeat. The ship did not reward drama. It rewarded repetition done correctly. Every bolt she touched was part of the same argument: keep the inside alive. Keep the heat moving. Keep the pressure where it belonged. Keep the structure honest. Keep the crew inside the margins.

An hour passed. Maybe more. Time in the engineering bay was measured less by clocks than by cycles.

When she paused again, it was because her slate chimed with an updated file sync. The mass reconciliation had finished cross-checking against the cargo manifest. The difference was small, but not zero. It never was. She noted the discrepancy and flagged it for navigation.

Then she opened the atmospheric reserve model again and stared at the number she was least proud of.

It was not the total atmosphere. It was the usable margin.

The number was smaller than she wanted.

Not fatal. Not useless. But small enough to make the entire idea humble itself. If the junior officer had been hoping for a dramatic boost, this was where the hope went to be measured. The ship did not have endless air to throw away. It had enough to keep people alive, plus a margin that existed for bad days. If they spent that margin, they had to know exactly what they were buying and exactly what they would do when the next bad day arrived.

Hoang wrote the number in the center of the page and circled it.

Then she wrote beneath it:

THIS IS THE NUMBER THAT ARGUES BACK.

She leaned against the bulkhead for a moment, arms folded, eyes on the slate. The pumps kept their rhythm. The drive carried its deep note through the structure. Somewhere in the ring, people were living their ordinary shipboard lives: eating, sleeping, checking gauges, complaining about food, exercising against the spin, pretending the void outside was not always near. They could do that because the box held.

Her job was not to make the box exciting.

Her job was to make sure it stayed intact.

She pushed off the bulkhead and began preparing the inspection kit for the vent line. Leak detector. Thermal probe. Torque driver. Valve cycle logger. Seal inspection scope. Pressure transducer calibration check. Spare sensor pack. She laid the tools out on the tarp with the same care she gave the manifold parts.

If the junior officer returned with honest numbers, Hoang would be ready.

If the junior officer returned with pretty numbers, Hoang would be ready for that too.

She checked the inspection light, tested its beam against her palm, and clipped it to her coveralls.

The idea had earned a review. That was more than most bad ideas received. It had not earned trust. Trust would come only from hardware, margins, and the kind of boring detail that people wanted to skip.

Chief Engineer Hoang looked once more at the chalked failure list on the deck plating.

Then she picked up the slate, tucked it under one arm, and headed back toward the utility spine to look at the valves again. The numbers could wait until she had touched the metal. In deep space, metal usually told the truth sooner than spreadsheets did.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I'm back from the mess, a bland nutrient paste making my stomach feel less hollow, but my head is still buzzing with the Chief's words. I head back towards engineering, the tablet still a heavy presence in my hand. I glance at my reflection in the polished hatchway, my brow furrowed in concentration. "Least proud of," she said. I think I know what that means now.*

*When I get back to the bay, the Chief is gone, but the chalked list on the floor is still there. "FAILURE MODES THAT KILL SOMEONE." My gut clenches again. But it's not fear this time, it's a cold, hard resolve.*

"Okay, ship," *I mutter to myself, looking at the empty bay. "Let's find out what you really need."*

*I pull out my tablet and start making a new document. My fingers fly across the screen, a new energy driving them. No more hopeful estimates. Just the brutal truth.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang returned to the engineering bay with a small inspection case in one hand and a tagged actuator in the other. She paused at the hatch, eyes moving first to the chalked list on the deck plating, then to the fresh document open on the junior officer’s tablet. She did not smile at either.

She crossed the bay and set the actuator down on the tarp beside the coolant tools. It made a dull, unimpressive sound.

“V-7,” she said. “The only vent path I found that did not immediately read like a casualty report.”

She wiped her thumb along the actuator housing, checking for residue, then turned it so the tag faced upward.

“It is not good. It is merely less bad. Last inspection was eight months ago. The actuator response is slower than spec. The mounting bracket is rated for emergency relief, not sustained side load. The line is offset from the centerline, and because it sits on the ring side of the interface, any flow through it becomes a moving vector the moment the habitat rotates.”

Hoang picked up the chalk and wrote beside the earlier list, her letters tight and angular.

CONTROLLED PULSE ONLY.  
NO CONTINUOUS BURN.  
NO SCHEDULE IMPROVEMENT.

She underlined the last line once.

“If you are still imagining weeks shaved off the transit, stop. The ship has already corrected that fantasy. What remains is a limited emergency impulse. A small correction. A chance to meet a rescue window or avoid a worse trajectory if the arithmetic and the captain agree. Nothing more.”

She set the chalk down and looked toward the junior officer.

“You want the number I am least proud of? Here is its shape. The usable atmospheric margin is smaller than the nominal inventory suggests. Much smaller, once you subtract medical reserve, repressurization margin, lock recovery, fire response, contamination control, and the suit consumables required to keep the crew alive while the maneuver happens. Whatever your revised calculation used, it had better not have borrowed from those reserves. If it did, it is still pretty, and still wrong.”

Hoang lifted her slate and tapped the screen once.

“I have started the reconciliation. Current vehicle mass is not a clean number. It includes ore residue, coolant trapped in low points, spare parts, waste, water, crew, and every kilogram of dirt we have been too busy to log properly. The ship is heavier than the brochure version. It always is.”

She scrolled through a short table, then turned the slate so the junior officer could see it.

“Candidate path V-7 can provide a short, metered pulse if we replace the actuator, verify the burst disk, reinforce the load path, and phase the vent with ring rotation. It cannot provide a long, steady burn without turning into a thermal and structural problem. If you try to hold it open, the line cools, seals stiffen, valves ice, and the vector starts wandering. Then attitude control spends propellant chasing a disturbance we created ourselves.”

Her expression hardened slightly.

“That is the part people forget. A vent is not just thrust. It is a disturbance. It touches everything. Structure. Spin balance. Thermal margins. Power. Crew safety. If the useful delta-v is not larger than the cost of controlling the disturbance, the maneuver is not a gain. It is a complicated way to lose.”

Hoang crouched beside the chalked list and drew a crude diagram of the ring, the utility spine, and a short arrow from one side of the ring toward the center. Then she crossed the arrow.

“V-7 is offset. That means torque. If we pulse it, navigation must lock the pulse timing to the ring phase and confirm the integrated inertial vector. If we cannot prove the vector is stable enough, we do not use it. If the attitude-control system has to fight the vent, the cost goes into the net delta-v. Not as a footnote. As a subtraction.”

She wrote:

NET Δv = USEFUL VECTOR IMPULSE − ACS COST − RESTORATION COST − SAFETY MARGIN.

Then she looked up.

“Your review will live or die on that line.”

She rose again and moved to the tool rack, selecting a calibrated torque driver without needing to search for it. She checked the setting twice by habit, then set it on the tarp beside the actuator.

“Here is what I need from the safety review before I let it near a decision.”

She counted the points off on her fingers, each one blunt and unhurried.

“First, the operational justification. Not ‘faster.’ Not ‘better.’ A concrete need. Rescue window. Medical evacuation. Trajectory correction that prevents a worse outcome. Avoidance of a consumables crisis. If Navigation cannot define the need in terms of time, delta-v, and consequence, the answer is no.”

“Second, the real mass budget. Use the reconciled vehicle mass, not the planning figure. Include everything. If you cannot account for it, do not pretend it is harmless.”

“Third, the atmosphere inventory. Break it into categories. Habitat volume. Stored gas. Medical reserve. Emergency repressurization. Suit support. Fire response. Contamination recovery. Restoration feedstock. Then subtract everything that cannot be spent. The remainder is the only mass your plan is allowed to use.”

“Fourth, the vent model. Use V-7 only. Use its actual flow curve, not an ideal nozzle assumption. Include discharge coefficient, valve response time, pressure decay, thermal choking, ice risk, and structural load. If the flow falls off faster than predicted, the abort criteria must catch it before the atmosphere reserve does.”

“Fifth, vector integration. Because the ring rotates, the thrust direction is not a fixed arrow. Model the pulse timing, the inertial average, and the torque. If the vector efficiency is poor, say so. If the torque exceeds the structural or attitude-control budget, say so louder.”

“Sixth, suit readiness. Not the paper count. The actual condition of every garment. I already found deferred faults. Cooling pump bearing. Humidity sensor. Glove seals. Comm dropout. Those get fixed or the crew does not rely on them. Medical will set the maximum suited duration in writing. No one gets to be brave about CO₂ buildup or heat stress.”

“Seventh, power and thermal. If we need compressors, pumps, heaters, or extra attitude control, put their draw on the page. If the radiators saturate, the maneuver ends before it begins. If drive cooling loses margin, the answer is no. If the fault case leaves us unable to close the vent and restore pressure, the answer is no.”

“Eighth, abort criteria. Write them so a half-asleep officer can follow them under alarm conditions. Pressure floor. Oxygen partial pressure floor. Carbon dioxide ceiling. Valve response limit. Structural load limit. ACS expenditure limit. Thermal limit. Suit consumable limit. If any one is crossed, we stop. No debate. No finishing the burn.”

“Ninth, restoration. If we throw atmosphere away, we must know how to get it back. Stored gas. Electrolysis. Processing time. Power cost. What mission capability do we lose while we rebuild the margin? If we cannot restore the ship to a safe condition before the next plausible emergency, the maneuver is not complete. It is only the first half of a worse problem.”

Hoang stopped and looked at the chalked failure list on the deck.

“And tenth,” she said, quieter now, “the failure modes that kill someone. You saw them. You do not get to unsee them. Put them in the review. Give each one a detection method, an abort trigger, and a recovery action. If you cannot do that for one of them, the plan is not ready.”

She picked up the tagged V-7 actuator again and turned it over in her hands.

“This hardware will need a full teardown before I would trust it with pressure. Seal inspection. Seat check. Actuator replacement or recalibration. Load path review. Burst disk verification. Leak check under transient conditions. If any of that fails, we stop.”

She set it back down.

“The good news is that the idea is no longer childish. The bad news is that it is now complicated, expensive in time, and still not something we do for convenience.”

Hoang brushed chalk dust from her fingers.

“Your first page should not begin with delta-v. It should begin with the box. The constraints. The reserves. The systems that cannot be touched. Then, and only then, you ask whether there is anything left over that can be spent.”

She looked toward the open coolant loop, listening to the pumps for a moment.

“When you have the first draft, bring me the number you are least proud of. Not the one you hope will impress me. The one you are afraid will kill the plan. If that number survives my review, the rest might matter. If it does not, we will have saved ourselves a great deal of trouble.”

Hoang picked up her slate and opened a blank page, then held it ready.

“Now show me what the ship told you while I was gone.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I swallow, my fingers stilling on the tablet. The Chief's words are a cascade, each point landing with the weight of cold, hard physics. My earlier surge of purpose has solidified into something heavy, almost daunting, but clearer than before.*

"Understood, Chief," *I say, my voice still quiet. I look down at my tablet, the blank document a fresh canvas for this new, brutal honesty. My eyes flick to the chalked list on the floor, then to the actuator she just described.* "I'll start with the constraints. And that number I'm least proud of... I think I'm starting to see it already." *I take a deep breath, the smell of ozone and coolant filling my lungs. This isn't just about numbers anymore. It's about every single piece of the ship, and every person on it.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor did not turn from the window right away. Their reflection ghosted over the dark glass—hair pulled back too tightly, jaw set, the hollows under their eyes made worse by three days of bad sleep and too much caffeine.

“Later,” Noor said. The word came out rougher than intended. They softened it by adding, “I’ll eat later.”

They did not believe it themselves.

The road outside stayed empty. No headlights. No crawl of tires on gravel. No late-night delivery truck wandering up the wrong mountain by accident. Nothing but the black shapes of pines and the weak wash of moonlight over the dirt shoulder where the source’s car should have been parked by now.

Three hours and fourteen minutes.

Noor let the curtain fall back into place and finally turned away from the window. The cabin’s darkness felt thicker inside, close and stale with old woodsmoke. They crossed to the kitchen table without turning on a lamp, moving by memory and the thin blue spill of moon through the window above the sink.

The laptop sat closed. The encrypted drive waited beside it in its padded case.

Noor stared at both.

Their fingers hovered over the laptop lid, then shifted to the drive instead. They opened the case. The small rectangle inside looked harmless enough—matte black, light, no bigger than a thumb. It could contain nothing. It could contain enough to get people arrested, fired, disappeared. It could contain proof.

Noor closed the case again without taking the drive out.

Not yet.

First the phone records.

They pulled their burner from their pocket, checked the screen out of habit, then remembered it was already off. Good. They kept it off. The other phone—the one tied to the source’s first contact number—sat in a cereal box near the stove, wrapped in a dish towel because Noor had read somewhere that fabric could muffle a signal. They had no idea if that was true. It felt better than leaving it bare.

They lifted the towel, checked the phone, and saw no missed calls. No messages. No sign of life.

Noor exhaled slowly through their nose.

“Okay,” they murmured.

They sat at the table, opened the laptop, and the screen’s glow made them wince. They turned the brightness down until the display looked sickly and dim. Their fingers moved quickly after that, practiced from too many nights in too many bad rooms. Password. Decryption layer. Secondary partition. The burner Wi-Fi adapter they had bought with cash two towns back. Nothing connected to the cabin’s owner, nothing traceable to the uncle, nothing that would lead back to the person who had lent them the place out of loyalty or pity or old debt.

Noor opened the notes file first. Not the drive. Not yet. Notes were safer. Notes were just their own paranoia arranged in bullet points.

They scrolled.

Meeting time: 21:00.

Arrival window: 20:45–21:15.

Signal if delayed: one missed call from payphone, then silence for thirty minutes.

Secondary signal: text with the word “weather.”

Emergency abort: two missed calls, no message.

There had been no missed calls. No “weather.” No abort.

That was worse than a clean cancellation. A clean cancellation meant the source had remembered protocol. Silence meant either they had not been able to reach a phone, or they had stopped trying.

Noor checked the time again. 12:17.

They pulled up the call log they had copied from the first burner before shutting it down. The numbers were all there, arranged in a neat column beside timestamps. They had verified them twice already. They verified them again anyway.

One number belonged to a clinic that had been shut down after the fire. One to a church office that no longer answered. One to a prepaid account registered under a name that did not exist. The last was the source’s private line.

Noor stared at it until the numbers blurred.

They should call.

They should not call.

If the source was late because they were being watched, a call could paint a target on whoever answered. If the source had been picked up, the phone might already be in someone else’s hands. If the source was dead, the number might still ring forever in an empty room.

Noor’s thumb rested over the call button anyway.

Their stomach turned.

They lowered the laptop lid halfway, then caught it before it closed. No. They needed to work. They could not sit in the dark waiting for the road to make a decision for them.

Noor opened the lid again and pulled up the audio file from the last meeting. It was short, only four minutes, recorded without consent because consent had not been available. They put in one earbud and kept the volume low enough that the sound felt like pressure rather than voice.

The source’s words came through tinny and careful.

“If I’m not there by nine-fifteen, don’t wait. Don’t call. Move to the second drop.”

Noor paused the recording.

Nine-fifteen.

They had given the source until nine-fifteen. Not nine. Not the official time. The buffer had been agreed on because the source had family in the valley and needed an excuse to be out late. Noor had written it down. They remembered writing it down.

They checked their notes again.

There it was: 21:15.

Which meant Noor had not been waiting three hours past deadline. They had been waiting three hours past the point where the source had told them to leave.

Fear went cold through them.
