Noor looked toward the window, though the curtain hid the road. They listened. The cabin creaked. Wind moved through the pines. Somewhere in the walls, a pipe ticked as it cooled.

They pulled the earbud out.

The silence felt different now.

Noor stood, chair scraping softly against the floor. They crossed to the counter and opened the cabinet with three mugs. Inside, behind a chipped cup and a tin of ancient ground coffee, they found a sleeve of crackers. The kind that came in wax paper and tasted like cardboard and salt. They tore the package open with their teeth and ate two crackers standing up, chewing mechanically because the body needed fuel whether the mind wanted it or not.

The crumbs caught in their throat. They drank cold water from the tap, not bothering with a glass.

Better. Not good. Better.

Noor set the cracker package on the table and returned to the laptop. They opened a new document, typed the date and time at the top, then began writing in plain sentences because panic made them want precision.

Source missed secondary deadline. No signal received. Possible compromise. Do not attempt contact unless confirmed safe. Move to second drop only if drive verifies. If drive cannot be verified, destroy drive and leave.

They stopped.

Destroy drive.

The padded case sat beside the laptop like an accusation.

Noor looked at it for a long moment. Then they reached for it.

This time they opened the case and took the encrypted drive out. It was cool in their palm, almost disappointingly ordinary. They turned it over once, checked the casing for scratches, for tampering, for anything out of place. The seal they had put on the edge with a clear dot of nail polish was still intact. That meant nothing, not really. It meant only that no one had been clumsy.

Noor plugged the drive into the laptop.

The machine asked for the passphrase.

Noor’s fingers paused over the keys.

If the drive was clean, they had a story. If it was poisoned, they might already be too late. If the source had been turned, the drive could contain malware, decoys, a trap dressed up as revelation. If the source had been honest, the drive could contain names, dates, payments, enough structure to pull the thread without getting pulled into it themselves.

Noor typed the passphrase.

The drive unlocked.

A single folder appeared.

Inside were three files.

The first was named LEDGER.

The second was named VOICE.

The third was named IF YOU ARE READING THIS.

Noor’s hand stopped on the trackpad.

They did not open the third file. Not yet. They checked file sizes, dates, hashes. The ledger was large, dense with spreadsheets. The voice file was audio, seven minutes long. The third file was a plain text document, small enough to be nothing or enough to end everything.

Noor copied all three to the encrypted working partition, then ejected the original drive and shut it down. They placed it back in the padded case and zipped it closed.

Only then did they open the ledger.

Rows filled the screen. Names. Account numbers. Dates. Amounts. Some cells highlighted in yellow. Some marked with initials Noor did not recognize. It looked real. It looked boring, which was promising. Real corruption usually looked boring until it didn’t.

Noor began cross-referencing the names against their notes.

Five minutes in, they found one they knew.

A councilman who had publicly denied the land deal.

Noor’s pulse kicked harder.

Ten minutes later, they found a shell company that matched one from the clinic fire report.

Their mouth went dry.

They reached for the crackers again and ate more without tasting them. The fear had not gone away, but it had changed shape. It was no longer only waiting. It was work. It was direction. It was something they could bite into.

Noor opened the audio file next.

Before pressing play, they checked the cabin door. Locked. The back window. Latched. The curtains. Drawn. The lights. Off.

They pressed play.

The source’s voice filled the earbud, low and hurried.

“If you’re hearing this, I didn’t make the meeting. I don’t know if I’ll make the next one. The ledger is real, but it’s incomplete. The voice file is the proof, but you need the location attached to it before anyone will believe you. Don’t trust the first number I gave you. It was already burned. Use the church office after six a.m. Ask for Marta. If Marta isn’t there, abort.”

The recording ended.

Noor sat very still.

The source had known. They had known they might not arrive. They had left instructions inside the drive instead of delivering them in person.

Noor looked at the third file.

IF YOU ARE READING THIS.

Their cursor rested over it.

Outside, gravel crunched.

Noor’s head snapped toward the window.

The sound was faint, unmistakable. Tires rolling slowly over stone, cutting an engine, the kind of careful approach that did not belong on a mountain road at one in the morning unless someone meant to be there.

Noor did not breathe.

The laptop screen glowed on the table. The cursor blinked beside the third file.

Another vehicle door opened outside.

Then closed.

Noor’s hand moved before thought fully caught up. They shut the laptop lid, slid it under the tablecloth, and swept the padded drive case into their bag. The bag went over one shoulder. The burner phone went into their pocket. The cereal box phone stayed where it was.

They crossed to the kitchen drawer and opened it just enough to find the small flashlight they had brought. No beam yet. Not yet.

The floorboards settled as Noor moved toward the door, staying to the side, not in the line of the window. They listened.

Footsteps on the porch.

One set.

Maybe.

Noor’s fingers curled around the flashlight.

They did not call out.

They waited.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I'm startled by the crunching gravel. I look up, phone still in hand, eyes wide.* "What was that?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor’s hand tightened around the flashlight. They did not look toward the couch.

“Quiet,” they said, the word barely more than breath. “Don’t say anything else.”

They moved to the wall beside the front window and lifted the curtain’s edge a fraction. A vehicle sat on the dirt shoulder with its headlights off. One shape stood on the porch. Noor counted five seconds, then ten. No second shape appeared. No second voice called out. That did not make it safe.

The porch boards creaked.

Noor let the curtain fall and crossed to the table. They pulled the laptop out from under the tablecloth, tucked it under one arm, and shifted the bag higher on their shoulder. The padded case pressed against their ribs. The drive was still inside. The burner was still in their pocket. The cereal-box phone stayed where it was, wrapped in the dish towel, already feeling like a mistake.

A knock came at last.

Three soft taps. A pause. Two more.

Noor stopped.

No protocol had included a knock.

“Noor?” The voice through the door was low, hoarse, and horribly familiar from the four-minute recording. “It’s me. I had to come.”

Noor’s throat tightened. They did not answer. They moved an inch closer to the door, staying to the side, out of the direct line of the frame.

“I know you’re in there,” the source said. “I saw the curtain move. Please. We don’t have time.”

Noor’s free hand curled into a fist. They had trained themselves to distrust urgency. Urgency was how people got careless. They stared at the deadbolt and made their voice small enough to carry only through the wood.

“What was the buffer?” they asked.

A silence.

Then: “Nine-fifteen.”

Correct.

Noor’s pulse beat hard in their ears. They asked the next question before relief could turn into trust.

“If you missed it, what was I supposed to do?”

“Move to the second drop.”

Correct again.

Noor closed their eyes for half a second. Correct answers did not mean safety. Correct answers could be pulled from a phone, from notes, from a person who had already been made to talk.

“Then why are you here?” Noor asked.

The source’s breath sounded loud through the door. “The second drop is burned. I couldn’t call. They found the first phone. I need the drive, Noor. Give it to me and I can finish this tonight.”

Noor’s stomach dropped.

The recording had said: Move to the second drop only if the drive verifies. If the drive cannot be verified, destroy it and leave. It had not said hand it over. It had not said meet on the porch at one in the morning after three hours of silence.

“No,” Noor said.

The word came out steadier than they felt.

The source leaned closer to the door. The wood gave a faint creak under their weight. “You don’t understand. If you don’t give it to me now, they’ll use it to bury everyone. Including you.”

Noor looked at the bag against their hip. The drive inside had just become heavier.

They thought of the ledger. The councilman. The shell company. The clinic fire. They thought of the third file still unopened: IF YOU ARE READING THIS.

A new sound came from the kitchen counter.

The cereal-box phone, muffled by the dish towel, buzzed once. Then again.

Noor did not move at first. The source outside went still.

“Noor,” the source said, lower now. “Don’t answer that.”

That was wrong, too. The phone had been tied to the source’s first contact number. If it was the source’s line, they would not tell Noor not to answer unless they expected someone else to be using it. Or unless the person on the porch was not the only one listening.

Noor crossed to the counter in three quiet steps. They lifted the towel.

The screen glowed with a single text from an unknown number.

WEATHER.

Noor’s breath caught.

The secondary signal. The one that should have arrived hours ago.

Another buzz followed.

IF YOU ARE READING THIS, DON’T OPEN THE DOOR.

Noor stared until the words blurred. The voice outside changed, sharper now.

“Noor. Open the door.”

Noor set the phone facedown on the counter. They did not bother with the towel again. They took the flashlight from their pocket, kept it off, and moved to the back window. The yard behind the cabin was black and empty. No headlights. No shapes. Only the thin line of moon on frost.

They turned the latch with two fingers.

“Noor,” the source called from the front porch, no longer trying to be quiet. “If you walk away now, you’ll lose everything.”

Noor looked at the front door, then at the dark rectangle of the back doorway. They had spent their whole career learning the difference between a source and a lure. Tonight, the difference had teeth.

They paused just long enough to speak without turning toward the couch.

“I’m leaving. If you want to come, now. If not, don’t open that door.”

Then Noor pulled the back door open just enough for the cold to slice through the stale cabin air.

They stepped outside, pulled the door shut behind them without latching it all the way, and moved toward the tree line with the bag pressed tight against their side. The first priority was not the car. It was not the road. It was six a.m. It was the church office. It was Marta.

If Marta was real.

If Marta was alive.

Noor did not look back at the cabin. They kept low, followed the shadow of the pines, and began counting steps.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I freeze on the couch, phone still in my hand. My eyes dart between the door and Noor, who's already slipping out the back.* "Wait, what's happening?!" I yell in a hoarse whisper. My heart is pounding. I jump up, unsure whether to follow Noor or hide.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor flinched at the sound of Driver’s voice. It was too loud, too raw, too close to the kind of noise that carried through thin mountain air. They pressed their back against the cabin’s rough siding and turned just enough to speak toward the open crack of the back door.

“Down,” Noor said, barely more than a breath. “Away from the door.”

They did not wait to hear what happened next. They could not afford to.

The front knob rattled hard enough to shake the frame. Then came a heavier sound—someone testing the door with a shoulder.

“Noor.” The source’s voice had lost its careful hush. “Open the door. Please. You don’t know what you’re doing.”

Noor knew exactly what they were doing.

They moved along the side of the cabin, staying low, one hand braced against the wall for balance. Frost slicked the ground between the boards. The cold bit through their jacket and found the damp places underneath. Their bag knocked softly against their hip with every step, the encrypted drive inside it no heavier than a stick of gum and somehow more dangerous than a gun.

The source’s vehicle sat at the edge of the yard, angled toward the road as if it might leave in a hurry. The engine ticked. The headlights were still off. The driver’s side window was down two inches.

Noor counted to three.

Then they reached in.

The interior door handle was cold and greasy under their fingers. They lifted the lock, pulled the door open just enough to slide one hand inside, and found the key fob sitting in the ignition of an old truck that had probably been bought long before keyless entry was supposed to matter. Noor yanked it free.

For half a second, they considered starting the truck.

Then the passenger-side phone lit up.

Noor froze.

The screen showed a message from a number saved only as ROAD.

TEAM TWO ON RIDGE. WAIT FOR SIGNAL.

Noor’s stomach dropped.

They did not touch the phone. They did not need to. The words were bright enough, clear enough, and they rearranged the entire night in a single breath.

This was not one person trying to get the drive back.

This was a net.

Noor shut the truck door as quietly as they could, thumbed the panic button on the fob, and ran.

The truck erupted behind them—horn blasting, lights flashing, the alarm cutting through the pines like a blade. Noor heard the source shout from the porch. Heard footsteps slam against the boards. Heard the front door crash inward with a sound that made their teeth ache.

Noor did not look back.

They reached the tree line and plunged into it, keeping low, shoulders hunched around the bag. Branches snagged at their sleeves. Frost cracked under their shoes. They risked one glance over their shoulder only long enough to see the truck’s strobing lights paint the cabin walls in harsh white flashes.

Then they turned again and kept moving.

The back door was behind them. Open a crack. Dark.

Noor slowed just enough to stop at the edge of the pines. Their chest heaved. Their throat burned with cold air. They looked toward the cabin one last time.

“If you want out,” they said, voice low and sharp, “come now.”

No answer came.

Noor waited one second.

Two.

Then they turned away from the cabin and forced themselves into the trees.

The forest swallowed them almost at once. The alarm faded behind the trunks, muffled by distance and the thick stand of pine. Noor did not stop until their legs began to shake. When they finally crouched behind the fallen trunk of a dead spruce, their hands were trembling so badly they could barely work the zipper on the bag.

They pulled the laptop out, set it on their knees, and opened it only enough to let the screen glow faintly against their chest. The brightness was already turned down. Even so, the light felt obscene.

Noor opened the encrypted partition.

The folder was still there.

LEDGER.

VOICE.

IF YOU ARE READING THIS.

They clicked the third file.

The document opened instantly. No password. No secondary lock. Just plain text, white on black, as if the source had known that whoever read it would already be running.

If you are reading this, I didn’t make it clean.

The ledger is real but incomplete. The voice file has the location buried in its metadata, but it will only show if you open it with the clinic number. You know which one. Room 3, bed 7. If you don’t have it, go to the church basement, not the office. The office will be watched if they have me.

Ask for Marta. Use the word “weather.”

If she answers “cold,” trust her.

If she asks for the drive, run.

Do not open the door if I come to it.

Noor stared at the last line until the letters blurred.

The wind moved through the pines overhead with a sound like distant water. Somewhere below the ridge, an engine revved once and stopped. Noor shut the laptop and pressed both hands flat against it for a moment, as if they could push the fear back into the machine.

They checked the time.

1:27 AM.

Almost five hours until six.

Noor packed the laptop away, tightened the strap of the bag, and stood. Their legs felt hollow. Their mouth tasted like crackers and old coffee. They took the burner phone from their pocket, confirmed it was still off, and put it back.

The church was in the valley. Too far to walk quickly, not too far to walk if they had to. There would be a road eventually. A fire trail. A drainage cut. Something.

Noor chose downhill.

They moved carefully at first, using the flashlight only when the ground turned treacherous, keeping the beam cupped in their hand and pointed at the dirt. The cold sharpened everything. Every branch sounded like a footstep. Every gust sounded like a voice. They kept checking over their shoulder even after they knew it was useless.

After ten minutes, they found a shallow ravine carved by snowmelt. It ran in the right direction, away from the cabin and toward the valley. Noor followed it, boots slipping on wet stone, one hand trailing along the frozen bank.

They thought about the cereal-box phone still glowing on the counter.

They thought about the back door left open.

They thought about Driver standing in the dark, unsure whether to follow or hide.

Noor did not let themselves stop thinking about it for long. They could not afford grief yet. Grief was for later, if there was a later. Right now there was only the drive, the church, and the question of whether Marta would say “cold” or reach for the bag.

The ravine widened. Through the trees, Noor caught the faint gray line of a service road.

They crouched again and listened.

Nothing.

No headlights. No voices. No tires on gravel.

Noor crossed the road without using the flashlight and disappeared into the trees on the other side. The pines thinned gradually as the slope eased. The air smelled of frost and diesel from somewhere far below. The mountain was giving way to town.

Noor ate the last two crackers from the wax paper sleeve while walking, chewing mechanically, eyes on the dark ahead.

Sleep later.

Safety later.

Answers later.

For now, they kept moving.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor did not know what Driver did with the phone, the fear, or the open back door. What they knew was that no footsteps came after them.

That absence felt worse than a shout.

Behind them, the cabin made a new sound: the front door crashing inward, wood splitting near the lock. A man’s voice snapped something too muffled to understand. The source’s voice answered, higher now, stripped of the careful hoarseness it had worn on the porch.

Noor stopped for half a breath behind a pine, bag digging into their shoulder, fingers closed around the key fob they had taken from the truck.

They should go back.

They could not go back.

Not with the drive in the bag. Not with the ledger on the laptop. Not with the third file still burning itself into the inside of their skull.

Do not open the door if I come to it.

Noor’s thumb found the panic button on the fob. They pressed it hard.

The truck’s alarm erupted again near the cabin, horn blasting through the trees in harsh, ragged bursts. Lights flashed against the trunks. Somewhere close, a man swore loudly. Flashlight beams jerked away from the house and swung toward the yard.

Noor used the noise like cover and ran.

They did not run cleanly. They ran like a person who had spent too many nights sleeping badly and eating badly and listening for engines in the dark: uneven, stumbling, lungs dragging in cold air, one hand guarding the bag against their ribs. Branches clawed at their sleeves. Frost slid under their shoes. They went downhill because downhill was the valley, the town, the church, and because uphill was ridge lines and men waiting for signals.

The alarm faded behind them, then started again when Noor’s thumb slipped on the fob. They cursed under their breath and shoved it deeper into their pocket.

The ravine appeared through the trees like a scar. Snowmelt had cut it deep, leaving wet stones and tangled roots exposed in the dark. Noor slid into it without hesitation, catching themselves on a root that tore the skin from their palm. Pain flared bright and useful. It kept them present.

They crouched in the ditch and listened.

Above, to their left, a radio crackled.

“—back door open.”

Another voice answered, farther off. “Inside’s clear. One on the couch. No package.”

Noor’s stomach clenched.

One on the couch.

They forced themselves not to move toward the sound. The drive pressed against their side like a second heartbeat. If they went back now, they would bring the hunters with them. If Driver was still in there, the safest thing Noor could do was be somewhere else.

It was a cold calculation. It was the only one available.

Noor pressed deeper into the ravine.

The service road crossed the ditch twenty meters downhill. They reached it on hands and knees, mud soaking through their jeans, and listened again before climbing out. No engines. No voices. Only the wind moving through the pines and the distant hum of the valley waking in the dark.

They crossed the road low and fast, then dropped into the trees on the other side. Only when they were sure nothing had followed did Noor allow themselves to stop behind the concrete mouth of a drainage culvert.

They checked their inventory by touch first.

Laptop. Present.

Bag. Present.

Padded case with the drive. Present.

Burner phone, still off. Present.

Flashlight. Present.

Crackers. Gone.

Noor exhaled.

They took the key fob from their pocket and considered it. It had served its purpose. Now it was a liability, a radio signature, a thread that might lead someone back to them if they were foolish enough to keep it. Noor crawled to the culvert’s edge, wedged the fob between two stones under the lip of concrete, and pushed it until it disappeared into the muck.

Let it beep to the rats.

They pulled the laptop out next, shielding the screen inside their jacket before opening it. The battery read forty-one percent. Too low to waste. Noor turned the brightness down another notch and opened the encrypted partition.

The folder waited.

LEDGER.

VOICE.

IF YOU ARE READING THIS.

They had already checked the hashes once. They checked them again anyway, because repetition was the only prayer they knew. The ledger matched the copy on the drive. The voice file matched too. Nothing had changed while they ran. That either meant the files were clean or that whoever had poisoned them had done it before Noor ever touched the drive.

Noor opened the voice file.

It was not a normal audio file. The moment they double-clicked it, a prompt appeared: ENTER KEY.

Noor stared at the blinking cursor.

The clinic number. Room 3, bed 7.

They pulled up their notes from before the meeting, fingers stiff from cold. The clinic had been shut down after the fire. Its old administrative line had been listed in a public report Noor had saved months ago. They typed the number first.

INCORRECT KEY.

Noor closed their eyes.

They typed it again with the room and bed appended: 0307-07.

INCORRECT KEY.

Fear prickled along their scalp. They thought of the source’s voice on the recording, low and hurried. You need the location attached to it before anyone will believe you.

Room 3, bed 7.

Not the phone number.

The room.

Noor typed: ROOM3BED7.

The prompt blinked.

Then the file opened.

It was still audio, seven minutes long, but a metadata panel unfolded beside it. Noor scanned it quickly. Creation date. Device hash. A string of GPS coordinates. A note embedded in the comment field, plain as a knife:

ST. ANNE’S BASEMENT. BOILER ROOM. THIRD PANEL. ASK MARTA.

Noor copied the coordinates into their notes, then opened the offline map they had downloaded weeks ago, after the first threat had made paper feel too fragile and internet maps feel too watched. The blue dot resolved slowly on the saved grid.

Saint Anne’s.

The church was in the valley, three streets past the old rail spur, with a cemetery on the north side and a parish office set back behind the rectory. The basement entrance was under the stone steps. Noor had seen it in a photograph from a fundraising newsletter two years ago and remembered it because they remembered everything that might one day become an exit.

The coordinates matched the basement footprint.

Noor shut the laptop and sat in the dark with their arms wrapped around it.

Phone records verified.

Drive checked.

Food eaten, if cardboard counted.

Sleep later.

They told themselves they would rest for ten minutes. They set their watch to vibrate against their wrist, leaned back against the concrete culvert, and closed their eyes. Sleep did not come. Instead came fragments: the source’s voice on the porch, the truck alarm, the cereal-box phone glowing with WEATHER, the third file’s last line.

Do not open the door if I come to it.

Noor opened their eyes before the watch could vibrate.

The sky had not lightened, but the dark had thinned enough to show the shape of the town below. They packed the laptop, wiped the mud from their hands on their jacket, and began moving again.

Saint Anne’s was closer than safety.

Noor approached it through the cemetery, using headstones and bare oak trees as cover. The church was old stone, blackened by decades of weather, with a low wall around the graveyard and a wrought-iron gate that groaned when Noor pushed it open just enough to slip through. They froze, waiting. Nothing moved.

The parish office was on the east side.

Noor saw the sedan immediately.

It was parked half in the shadow of the rectory, engine off, plates obscured by dirt. Two silhouettes sat inside. One faced the church. The other faced the street. Watching. Waiting. The note had been right. If the source had been taken, or turned, or broken, the office would be the first place they looked.

Noor backed into the cemetery and circled toward the basement steps.

The stone stairwell was damp and littered with dead leaves. The basement door was painted green, chipped near the handle. Noor checked for cameras, found none, then checked again because fear had made them thorough.

They took the encrypted drive from the padded case. The case itself was too obvious, too shaped like something worth taking. Noor pried the insole out of their left shoe, slid the small black rectangle underneath, and replaced it. The drive pressed uncomfortably against their arch. Good. If someone searched the bag, they would find the padded case and the laptop and the ordinary panic of a person trying to protect their work. They would not find the thing that mattered unless they stripped Noor down to the skin.

The padded case went back into the bag with a wad of cracker wax paper inside for weight.

Noor checked the time.

5:58.

They stood in the shadow of the stone steps and waited.

At six, the church bells began to ring. The sound was louder than Noor expected, hollow and iron-heavy, shaking the cold air over the graveyard. The sedan’s passenger shifted. Noor stayed still.

A woman came around the side of the church.

She was perhaps sixty, wearing a dark green coat and a scarf wrapped twice around her neck. Her shoes were practical. Her keys were already in her hand. She did not look at the sedan. She looked at the basement door.

Noor stepped out from the stairwell shadow.

The woman stopped.

Noor kept their voice low. “Weather.”

For one terrible second, she only stared at them. Her eyes moved over Noor’s muddy jacket, their red hands, the bag clutched against their side. Then she said, “Cold.”

Noor’s knees almost gave.

They did not let them.

“Marta?” Noor asked.

She nodded once. “You’re late.”

“I know.”

“Did anyone see you come down the mountain?”

“No.”

Her mouth tightened. “That won’t stay true.”

She unlocked the basement door and held it open. Noor hesitated, looking back toward the cemetery gate, toward the sedan, toward the street where morning was beginning to gray the edges of the world.

Then they stepped inside.

The basement smelled like candle wax, damp stone, and old heating oil. Marta shut the door behind them and turned the lock. It was not enough. Noor knew it was not enough. But it changed the acoustics, made the world outside feel one layer farther away.

“Where is the office watch?” Noor asked.

“Two men,” Marta said. “They came before midnight. They asked about the food bank hours. They asked if anyone had left packages for the parish. They are not here for God.”

Noor almost laughed at that. It came out as a cough.

Marta studied them. “You have it?”

Noor’s hand tightened on the bag strap. “Depends.”

“On what?”

“Room three, bed seven.”

Marta’s expression did not change. “The clinic ward. The fire started in the east wing. They moved the patients who could still be moved. Bed seven was empty by the time the smoke reached it.”

Noor’s throat tightened. “How do you know that?”

“Because I signed the transfer forms.” Marta turned toward the back of the basement, where a low archway opened into a room full of pipes and old iron. “He said you would need that to trust me.”

Noor followed, but stayed half a step behind. “He also said if you asked for the drive, I should run.”

Marta stopped beside a massive boiler painted the color of dried blood. She looked at Noor then, and for the first time there was something like fear in her face.

“Then don’t give it to me,” she said. “Put it where he left the rest.”

She pointed to the boiler’s third access panel.

The metal was old, bolted at the corners, but one bolt was newer than the others. Its head was scratched. Noor crouched, ran their fingers along the edge, and felt the slight give of a panel that had been opened recently.

They looked back at Marta.

“If this is wrong,” Noor said, “I disappear.”

“If this is wrong,” Marta said, “we both disappear.”

Above them, somewhere in the church, a door opened.

Both of them went still.

Footsteps crossed the floor overhead. Slow. Deliberate. Not the steps of someone arriving for early prayer.

Marta’s eyes flicked upward, then back to Noor. “They’re early.”

Noor’s hand went to their shoe, where the drive bit into their foot. The laptop bag felt suddenly heavy with useless weight. The panel waited.

They pulled the bolt free.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I'm sitting on the floor, back pressed against the wall, phone still in my hand. I hear the front door crash in, and I jump, flinching. Then I hear the alarm blare again and a man swear. I curl into a ball, trying to be as small and quiet as possible.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor pulled the bolt free and slid their fingers under the edge of the boiler panel. The metal resisted, then gave with a thin rusted groan that sounded too loud in the basement. Above them, the footsteps stopped.

Noor went still, one hand braced against the boiler’s curved side, the other holding the panel just enough to keep it from clanging shut. Marta’s breath caught somewhere behind them. Dust drifted down from the ceiling beams.

For three seconds, nothing moved.

Then the footsteps crossed overhead again, slower this time. Listening. Testing the floor.

Noor eased the panel open wider.

Inside the cavity was not empty space. A flat oilcloth pouch had been taped to the inner wall of the boiler, half-hidden behind a pipe elbow. The tape had yellowed with age, but the center of it was newer, pressed down without wrinkles. Someone had opened this recently and resealed it with care.

Noor did not reach for it immediately.

They looked at Marta.

“You knew,” Noor said quietly.

Marta’s face was pale in the dim basement light. “I knew there was something. He would not tell me what.”

“Did anyone else know?”

“No one who should.”

Noor considered that. It was not a comfort. It was barely an answer.

The overhead footsteps paused again, this time directly above the boiler room. A floorboard creaked. A faint line of dust sifted down through the old joists.

Noor reached into the cavity and peeled the pouch free.

It was heavier than it looked.

They crouched lower, shielding the pouch with their body, and worked the oilcloth open with stiff fingers. Inside were three things: another encrypted drive, identical to the one hidden in Noor’s shoe; a small brass key, dull with age; and a folded square of paper covered in tight handwriting.

Noor recognized the hand.

It was the same slant as the notes from the first meetings, the same habit of crossing out words and rewriting them smaller, as if the person had not trusted the first version of their own thoughts.

Noor unfolded the paper.

If you found this, then I did not make it clean.

Marta knows the way, but not the contents. If she told you to put the drive where I left the rest, she has not been turned. If she asked to carry it for you, leave.

The drive in the panel completes the ledger. Yours has the payments. Mine has the names behind the payments. Do not connect them to a networked machine. Do not open the voice file again unless you are alone.

The office is burned. The rectory is worse. Use the coal chute behind the boiler. The alley gate sticks; lift and push left.

If you get out, do not go to the police. Do not go to the paper. Go to the rail spur at Harrow Street. Wait for the first freight after six. If Marta says cold, she can take you there.

If she does not say cold, run.

Noor read the last line twice.

Then they looked up at Marta.

“You said cold,” Noor said.

“Yes.”

“Why?”

Her mouth tightened. “Because he told me if you came looking scared and half-dead, I should say it before you did.”

Noor studied her face for any sign of performance, any flicker of rehearsed calm. There was fear there, but it looked honest. It looked like the fear of a woman who had been waiting for a knock she hoped would never come.

The paper trembled slightly in Noor’s hand. They folded it again and put it in their pocket.

Above them, a new sound came: the scrape of a key sliding into the basement door lock.

Marta’s head snapped toward the stairwell.

“They have Father Tomas’s keys,” she whispered.

Noor stood at once, knees protesting, bag sliding against their hip. “How many exits?”

“The coal chute,” Marta said. “Behind the boiler. It opens into the alley.”

“Locked?”

“From the outside, but the latch is old. You can force it.”

“You.”

Marta looked at them sharply. “You should go.”

“No,” Noor said. “You first. If there’s another way out, you’ll know it. If there isn’t, I’ll know fast.”

For half a second, Marta looked as if she might argue. Then she nodded once and moved toward the back of the boiler room, where a low iron door sat half-hidden behind a stack of folded chairs and a rusted water heater.

Noor followed, but stopped long enough to look back at the open panel.

They could close it. They could try to make it look untouched.

No.

Whoever came down here would see the missing bolt. They would see the scratched metal. They would know.

Noor reached into the cavity anyway and ran their fingers along the back wall, checking for anything else. Tape residue. A second pouch. A scrap of paper. Nothing.

They pulled the panel shut and pressed the bolt back into place without tightening it. It held enough to keep the metal from swinging, but not enough to slow anyone with a screwdriver.

The basement door lock turned with a heavy click.

Noor’s breath stopped.

The door creaked open.

A man’s voice echoed down the stairwell, low and careful. “Check the office first. Then the boiler room.”

Marta froze beside the coal chute.

Noor crossed to her in three silent steps. Their bag knocked against their hip. The laptop felt like a brick. The drive in their shoe pressed into their arch with every movement. They thought, absurdly, of the wax paper cracker sleeve still folded in their pocket.

The basement light switch snapped up.

Yellow light flooded the stairwell.

Noor grabbed Marta’s sleeve and pulled her behind the boiler just as the first footsteps reached the bottom step.

The boiler hissed.

Noor looked up. A pressure valve near the top was trembling, leaking steam in a thin white thread. They had not touched it. Neither had Marta. The building was old, and old buildings made their own warnings.

One of the men called softly, “You hear that?”

Another voice answered, “Old pipe.”

“No. Listen.”

Noor’s hand closed around the flashlight in their pocket. They did not turn it on. They did not need light to know the shape of the room now: boiler to the left, coal chute behind them, stairwell to the right, the service arch between. If the men moved around the boiler, Noor and Marta would have seconds.

Noor leaned close to Marta.

“Open it,” they whispered. “Quietly.”

Marta’s hands shook as she worked the latch on the coal chute. The iron door gave a faint metallic groan. She stopped. Breath came fast through her nose.

The footsteps in the boiler room moved closer.

Noor looked around wildly and saw a length of pipe lying on the floor near the water heater. They picked it up without thinking. The metal was cold and rough. It was not a weapon. It was a noise.

Noor placed one end against the boiler’s side and tapped it once, lightly, near the valve.

The sound rang through the iron, hollow and strange.

Both men stopped.

“What the hell was that?”

Noor tapped again, harder, farther down the boiler’s curve. The noise carried through the metal in a way that made it seem to come from the wall itself.

One of the men swore under his breath. “Check the other side.”

Their footsteps shifted away from the coal chute.

Noor did not wait.

They nodded at Marta.

She lifted the latch, pushed the coal chute door inward, and the old iron swung open with a reluctant scrape. Cold alley air rushed in, carrying the smell of wet stone and garbage and diesel.

Noor shoved the bag forward. “Go.”

Marta ducked inside.

Noor followed.

The chute was narrow and filthy, the walls slick with coal dust and old moisture. Noor’s shoulder scraped brick. The laptop bag caught on something sharp, and for one terrible second they thought it would tear open. They yanked it free and kept moving.

Behind them, a man shouted, “There! Behind the boiler!”

Noor turned just enough to slam the coal chute door shut.

It did not lock. It barely latched. But it bought them the width of a wall and the length of a breath.

Marta was already ahead of her, scrambling toward a square of gray morning light at the end of the chute. Noor pushed after her, palms slipping on coal dust, knees banging against stone. The drive in their shoe bit hard into their foot. They welcomed the pain. It kept them moving.

The alley gate was at the end of the chute, half-hidden behind a stack of rotting pallets. Marta reached it first and threw her weight against it. It did not move.

“Lift,” Noor said. “Push left.”

Marta lifted.

Noor hit the gate with their shoulder.

The gate shrieked, then gave.

They spilled into the alley in a tangle of coats and dust and fear. Morning light was thin and gray. The street beyond the alley was empty, but not silent. Somewhere in the church, a door slammed. A voice shouted from inside the basement.

Noor did not stop to listen.

They grabbed Marta’s arm and pulled her toward the far end of the alley, away from the rectory, away from the sedan, away from the street where the office watch had been parked. Their boots slid on wet cobblestones. Their breath came in ragged bursts. The bag strap dug into their shoulder like wire.

At the corner, Noor risked a glance back.

The church basement door stood open. Two men emerged into the graveyard, one already reaching for a phone. The other looked toward the alley.

Noor ducked back.

“Harrow Street,” Noor said. “Rail spur.”

Marta nodded, breathing hard. “Three blocks east. Past the old mill.”

“Then we move.”

They ran.

Not fast. Not cleanly. Noor ran like someone who had not slept, had not eaten properly, and had been carrying too much weight for too many hours. But they ran. Marta kept to the shadows between buildings, cutting through a service yard, past dumpsters and stacked crates, past a shuttered bakery with flour dust on its windowsill.

Noor’s mind worked while their body stumbled.

The ledger was incomplete.

The second drive might complete it.

The voice file had coordinates.

The note said do not connect them to a networked machine.

That meant they needed a clean system. Offline. Air-gapped. Somewhere with power and time and no one watching.

Noor thought of the safehouse.

Then they thought of the truck on the ridge, the cereal-box phone, the open back door, and the men saying, “One on the couch.”

Noor pushed the thought away before it could take root.

Marta turned down a narrow passage between a boarded-up pharmacy and a row of brick garages. At the end of it, a rusted rail spur cut across the street like a scar.

Noor checked their watch.

6:22.

Too early.

Or not early enough.

Marta stopped beside a stack of old pallets and pressed her back against the brick wall. “We wait here.”

Noor shook their head. “Not in the open.”

“There’s a signal box,” Marta said, pointing to a small metal structure half-hidden by weeds at the edge of the tracks. “It’s locked, but the key—”

Noor pulled the brass key from the oilcloth pouch.

They looked at it.

Then at the signal box.

Noor did not smile. There was nothing to smile about. But their hand steadied.

“Try it,” Marta said.

Noor crossed to the box and fitted the key into the lock.

It turned.

Inside was a narrow space, dry and smelling of grease and old wiring. A workbench. A dead lamp. A chair with one leg shorter than the others. And beneath the bench, a metal lockbox with the same kind of bolt as the boiler panel.

Noor crouched and opened it.

Inside lay a folded map, a charged power bank, a paper list of names, and a handwritten note:

If you made it this far, you have the rest of the ledger.

Do not trust the police.

Do not trust the paper.

At 06:40, the freight comes through.

Get on.

Noor stared at the last line.

Then they looked at Marta.

She met their eyes and said, very quietly, “Cold.”

Noor exhaled.

They reached into their shoe, pulled out the first drive, and placed it beside the second one on the metal floor of the signal box.

Two drives.

Two halves.

One story that could get them killed.

Noor shut the lockbox, pocketed the key, and stood.

“Then we wait for the train,” they said.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I hear the front door splinter, then men's voices. I squeeze my eyes shut, pressing myself further into the wall. My phone is still clutched in my hand, but I'm not looking at it. I hear the radio crackle. "One on the couch." My breath hitches. I want to yell, to run, but I'm frozen in place. I can't move. I can't even open my eyes.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor shut the lockbox but did not sit.

They stayed crouched with one hand on the metal lid and the other braced against the signal box wall, listening past their own breathing. The rail spur lay beyond the thin door in a gray morning stillness that felt too arranged to be safe. Tracks. Weeds. A rusted switch stand. The black mouth of the alley behind the church. Nothing moving yet.

Noor checked their watch.

6:23.

Seventeen minutes until the freight, if the note was true. If it was not, they had just traded one trap for another.

Noor looked at Marta.

She was watching the door, one hand pressed flat against the signal box wall as if she could feel the church through the brick and distance. Her face had gone the color of old paper.

“How long before they check the alley?” Noor asked.

Marta swallowed. “If they know the chute, soon. If they don’t, they’ll still find the gate.”

“Then we don’t wait here.”

Noor opened the lockbox again and took the map first. They spread it on the workbench, keeping the edges curled with their palms. The paper was soft from folding, marked with pencil lines that were not theirs and had not been made for comfort. The rail spur cut across the lower edge of the map in a dark stroke. Harrow Street. The old mill. A drainage ditch. A fence line with a gap penciled twice near the bend where the tracks curved toward the valley.

Noor tapped the gap.

“Where does the train slow?”

Marta leaned over the map. Her finger moved along the tracks and stopped just past the mill. “Here. Before the bridge. It takes the curve slow if the signal’s bad. The engineers used to complain about it.”

“Used to?”

“The line’s been cut back. Fewer trains. Fewer people watching.”

Noor memorized the shape of the bend anyway. Paper could be taken. Paper could burn. The shape had to live inside their skull too.

They folded the map and put it inside their jacket, against the laptop. Then they took the power bank and checked the charge light. One green dot. Enough to give the laptop life later, not enough to waste now. Noor plugged it into the machine anyway, leaving the laptop closed. If they had to run, the cable could be yanked. If they had seconds, seconds might matter.

The signal box smelled of grease, cold metal, and old electrical dust. Noor’s eyes moved over the workbench, the dead lamp, the chair with one short leg. Under the bench, beside the lockbox, sat a dented tin that had once held tobacco or sweets. They opened it.

Inside were three hard candies, still wrapped in crackly plastic, and a single sugar cube blackened at one corner with age.

Noor took two candies and handed the third to Marta.

“Eat,” they said.

She looked at it as if it might be a test.

“Noor—”

“Eat.”

She unwrapped it. Noor did the same. The candy was cheap lemon, sharp and sweet, and it made their mouth ache before it made their hands steadier. They let it dissolve against their teeth instead of chewing. Sugar was not food, but the body could be lied to for a little while.

Noor pulled the paper list from the oilcloth pouch and unfolded it beside the map. The handwriting was tight, slanted, impatient. Names. Some crossed out. Some circled. Some marked with the same initials Noor had seen in the ledger. They scanned fast, not reading yet, just looking for shapes they already knew.

Councilman. Shell company. Clinic fire.

There.

A name beside a date that matched the fire report. Not the councilman. Someone above him. A regional director. A signature line. Noor had seen that signature in a public filing six months ago and remembered the way the final letter hooked back like a fishhook.

Their throat tightened.

They looked at Marta.

“Do you know this name?”

Marta glanced at the paper and went very still. “He came to the parish twice. For the clinic fundraiser. He took photographs with the donors.”

“Did he speak to the source?”

“I don’t know who your source is.”

Noor believed her. It did not make them relax.

They turned the page. More names. More amounts. One line had no name, only a phone number and the words ROOM 3 / BED 7.

Noor stared at it.

The number was not the clinic’s administrative line. It had a local exchange, older, from before the valley’s numbers were consolidated. They had seen it before. They were sure of it. Not in the ledger. Not in the news clippings. Somewhere closer.

They pulled their notebook from the bag and flipped through the pages they had written in the safehouse, the cabin, the car, three towns back. Their handwriting looked like it belonged to someone who had still believed sleep was possible.

There.

The same number, copied from the first burner’s call log. Beside it, Noor had written: unanswered. No voicemail.

Now it had a place.

Room 3, bed 7.

Not just a room.

A person.

Noor closed the notebook and pressed two fingers against the cover.

The sound of an engine came from beyond the signal box.

Not the freight. Too smooth. Too close.

Noor killed the charge cable and slid the laptop into the bag in one motion. Marta’s head snapped toward the door. Noor put a hand on her arm, not to comfort, but to stop her from moving.

They listened.

The engine slowed at the end of the street. Tires rolled over broken glass. The vehicle did not pass. It idled.

Noor lifted the curtain of dust from the signal box’s narrow window and looked through the grime.

A dark sedan sat at the corner of Harrow Street and the alley road. Its headlights were off. Its windows were too clean for the neighborhood. One silhouette faced the tracks. Another faced the church.

Noor let the window go.

“They found the gate,” Marta whispered.

“No,” Noor said. “They found the pattern.”

They looked around the signal box. It had one door. One lock. One dead lamp. A place made for maintenance, not refuge. If the men walked the tracks, they would see the box. If they had keys, they would open it. If they did not have keys, they would break it.

Noor made the decision before fear could argue.

“We move to the bend now.”

Marta looked at the door. “The train isn’t here.”

“If we wait here, it won’t matter.”

Noor took the second drive from the oilcloth pouch and considered it for half a second. Then they opened their bag, shoved the padded case aside, and tucked the second drive into the lining of their jacket where the seam had already begun to tear. The first drive stayed in their shoe. The paper list went into their inner pocket. The brass key went back into their jeans, cold against their hip.

They did not give either drive to Marta.

Not yet.

“Do you have anywhere else to go if we’re separated?” Noor asked.

Marta’s mouth tightened. “My sister’s farm past the river.”

“Do you trust her?”

“I trust that she would not sell me.”

“Then if we lose each other, go there. Don’t go to the police. Don’t go to the parish. Don’t call anyone unless you know the line is clean.”

Marta studied Noor’s face. “You don’t think we’ll both make it.”

Noor did not answer that directly.

“I think the train is the only chance we have right now, and I think we need to be at the bend before it gets here.”

They opened the signal box door only enough to look out. The sedan had not moved. The men inside had not gotten out. That was bad. Waiting men meant other men were already moving somewhere else.

Noor slipped outside, staying low against the metal wall. Marta followed. The morning air hit Noor’s face like wet iron. The tracks gleamed faintly in the gray light. To the east, beyond the mill, the curve disappeared behind a line of corrugated sheds and dead weeds.

They moved.

Noor kept to the ballast’s edge, where the stones were less likely to crunch loudly underfoot. Their bag knocked against their side. The laptop charger cable trailed from the bag’s zipper, and they caught it, wrapped it once around their hand, and kept moving. The drive in their shoe bit into the same raw place it had made on the mountain. Every step sent a small bright pain up their leg.

Good.

Pain kept them honest.

At the end of the signal box, they paused and looked back.

The sedan’s driver-side door opened.

Noor grabbed Marta’s sleeve and pulled her down behind a stack of old rail ties.

Two men stepped out of the car. One wore a dark jacket. The other had a radio in his hand. They did not look like police. They looked like men who had done this before and expected the world to cooperate.

The one with the radio pointed toward the church.

The other pointed toward the tracks.

Noor’s pulse kicked hard.

“Stay low,” they murmured.

They moved along the rail ties, using the stack for cover until it ran out, then crossed the open stretch to the fence line. The gap Marta had marked on the map was real: a section where the chain-link had been peeled back and weighted with a chunk of concrete. Noor lifted it enough for Marta to slide through, then followed, catching the bag on a curl of wire and tearing the fabric with a sound that made their stomach clench.

They kept going.

The old mill rose beside them, brick walls boarded, windows dark. A loading dock sagged at one corner. Beyond it, the tracks curved sharply toward the bridge. Noor could feel the rail in the ground now, not sound yet, but a faint tension, as if the iron already knew what was coming.

Noor checked their watch.

6:31.

Too early.

Or not early enough.

They reached the bend and crouched behind a concrete switch housing. Marta was breathing hard, but she did not complain. Noor appreciated that more than they could say.

“Which side do we board from?” Noor asked.

Marta pointed to the inside of the curve. “There. If it slows, you can reach the ladder on a boxcar. Don’t try the engine. Don’t try a flatbed if you can help it.”

“And if it doesn’t slow?”

“Then you don’t get on.”

Noor looked at her. “I’m getting on.”

She met their eyes. “Then it will slow.”

Noor did not know if that was faith or experience. They decided not to ask.

They took the laptop from the bag and checked it one more time. The charge light showed a weak amber. Still not enough to trust. They closed the lid and put it back. The padded case inside the bag still held only wax paper and nothing useful. If someone grabbed it, they would get the shape of importance without the thing itself.

Noor thought of the cabin again.

The thought came without permission: the couch, the phone in someone’s hand, the front door splintering, the radio voice saying one on the couch. Noor shoved it down. Not because it did not matter, but because it mattered too much and would drag them under if they let it.

They could not go back.

They could only make sure the drive had not been carried down the mountain for nothing.

A low vibration entered the ground.

Noor looked toward the tracks.

The rails began to hum.

Marta’s hand closed around the concrete edge. “There.”

The sound built slowly, a heavy grinding rhythm from the east. The freight rounded the far curve, black engine first, then cars, metal groaning as the wheels took the bend. It was not fast. Not fast enough. Noor counted the cars with their eyes: engine, tanker, boxcar, flatbed, another boxcar. The ladder on the second boxcar swung slightly as the train slowed.

Behind them, voices shouted from the mill side.

Noor did not turn.

“Now,” they said.

They ran.

The ground shook under the train. Gravel shifted under Noor’s shoes. Their lungs burned. The bag strap slipped, and they caught it with one hand without breaking stride. Marta was beside them, coat flying, breath coming in sharp bursts.

The boxcar ladder passed within reach.

Noor grabbed it first and swung up far enough to hook an elbow over the rung. The metal jarred through their shoulder. They reached back for Marta.

Her hand found theirs.

Noor pulled.

She caught the ladder with her other hand, stumbled, caught again. The train gathered speed beneath them, not much, but enough. Noor’s bad foot slipped. Pain shot up their leg. They bit down on the inside of their cheek and held on.

The ladder climbed.

The ground fell away.

Noor shoved Marta toward the open door of the boxcar, then swung in after her, shoulder hitting the wooden frame hard enough to knock the air from their lungs. They landed on metal floor, rolled once, and kicked the bag inside before the train’s motion could take it away.

For a moment, neither of them moved.

The boxcar smelled of grain dust, rust, and old rain. Light sliced through gaps in the door, strobing across their hands. The train groaned around them, pulling away from the bend, away from the mill, away from the men who had reached the fence too late.

Noor lay on their back and stared at the ceiling.

Their chest rose and fell. Their foot throbbed. Their palm was bleeding where the ladder had torn it. They could feel the second drive inside their jacket lining and the first one under their shoe.

They made themselves sit up.

Marta was against the wall, eyes closed, one hand pressed over her mouth. Noor gave her three seconds. Then they reached into their pocket, found the last candy wrapper, and pressed the empty plastic into their palm as if it were proof they had not lost everything.

Noor pulled the laptop out of the bag.

They did not open it yet.

Instead, they took the paper list from their pocket and unfolded it again in the moving dark. The train rocked beneath them. The words swayed. Noor traced the line with the phone number and the note beside it.

ROOM 3 / BED 7.

They looked at Marta.

“Who was in bed seven?”

Marta opened her eyes.

For a long moment, she said nothing. The train wheels clicked over the rails, steady and indifferent.

Then she answered.

“A girl,” she said. “Before the fire. She was transferred out the same night.”

Noor’s mouth went dry.

“Transferred where?”

Marta’s face changed. Not fear this time. Something worse.

Recognition.

“Saint Anne’s,” she said. “The church basement. Before it was a church.”

Noor’s hands went still on the paper.

The train carried them onward into the gray morning, and for the first time that night, Noor understood they had not been running toward an answer.

They had been running inside it.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My eyes snap open at the sound of the alarm blaring again, followed by a man's angry shout. I hear heavy footsteps, then the front door splintering. My phone finally slips from my numb fingers and clatters to the floor. I hear a voice, muffled, say, "One on the couch." I press my face into my knees, shaking uncontrollably, trying to disappear into the wall. I just want it to be over. I can't move. I can't breathe.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor did not let the sentence land as fear. They made it into a task before it could become panic.

“A girl,” Noor repeated. “What name?”

Marta’s hand was still pressed over her mouth. She lowered it slowly. The train swayed beneath them, metal wheels grinding through the curve, and the sound filled the boxcar like something too large to argue with.

“I don’t know,” Marta said. “I saw the intake slip once. Before the parish took over the basement properly. There were cots down there for a few nights after the clinic fire. People who could not go home. People who had no home to go to.”

Noor’s jaw tightened. “Room three, bed seven.”

“It was not a hospital bed,” Marta said. “It was a folding cot. They numbered them with tape. The register was kept in a black binder. The parish nurse had it.”

“Where is the register now?”

Marta looked toward the slatted dark of the boxcar door, where morning light cut through in moving bars. “If it survived, it would be in the old storage room. Behind the boiler.”

Noor stared at her.

“We were in the boiler room,” Noor said.

“Yes.”

“And there was another room.”

Marta’s throat moved. “The panel you opened was not the only one.”

Noor looked down at the paper list in their hands. The handwriting seemed sharper now, less like notes and more like instructions left by someone who had known exactly how little time would remain.

The third file had said: the ledger is real but incomplete. The voice file has the location. The second drive completes the ledger.

Noor had thought completion meant numbers. Names. Payments.

They had not expected a person.

They folded the list once, then twice, and put it inside their jacket against the laptop. Their fingers were shaking again, not from cold alone. They pressed them flat against their thighs until the tremor dulled.

“Okay,” Noor said.

It was not calm. It was a container for the lack of calm.

They pulled the bag closer and took inventory again because inventory was something that could be controlled. Laptop. Power bank. Map. Padded case with wax paper inside like a joke. Flashlight. Burner phone, still off. Notebook. The brass key. The second drive sewn into the torn jacket lining. The first drive under their shoe, pressing into raw skin.

Noor reached down and pulled the first drive free. Their foot throbbed in protest. They examined the small black rectangle in the dim light. The seal was still intact. The casing was unmarked. They transferred it to the inner pocket with the second drive, then peeled off their sock enough to check the damage on their arch. The skin was scraped red and angry. They pressed the sock back down and laced the shoe tighter.

Pain was useful. It kept the body honest.

“We verify before we decide anything,” Noor said.

Marta watched them. “Here?”

“Here.”

Noor opened the laptop and immediately disabled the wireless adapter. Then they checked the network list anyway, out of habit, and confirmed nothing was searching for a signal. The screen glowed faintly against their knees. They turned the brightness down until it hurt to look at, then opened the encrypted working partition.

The power bank cable was still attached. The battery indicator climbed one weak percent and stopped.

Noor plugged in the second drive.

The machine asked for a passphrase.

They typed the one from the first meeting notes.

ACCESS DENIED.

Noor stopped.

They tried the source’s secondary phrase.

ACCESS DENIED.

The train lurched over a joint in the rail. Marta caught the wall. Noor kept their hands steady on the keyboard.

Room three, bed seven.

They typed: ROOM3BED7.

The drive unlocked.

Noor did not exhale. They copied the contents to the encrypted partition first, then checked the hashes against the list in the oilcloth pouch. The numbers matched. The second drive was not a duplicate of the first. It was its missing half.

The ledger file opened as a dense grid of accounts and dates. Noor had already seen the payments. What the second drive added was structure: a second spreadsheet with names behind shell entities, initials resolved into full titles, and a third tab locked behind another prompt.

ENTER KEY.

Noor looked at the brass key in their palm.

Then they looked at the paper list.

Beside ROOM 3 / BED 7 was the phone number they had found in the first burner’s call log. The number that had gone unanswered. The number that had belonged to no one and therefore to someone.

Noor typed the number.

INCORRECT KEY.

They typed the number followed by 0307.

INCORRECT KEY.

Marta leaned closer without seeming to realize it. “What are you trying?”

“Everything that sounds like nothing,” Noor said.

They typed the number again, but replaced the last four digits with 3707.

The prompt blinked.

Then the third tab opened.

It was not a financial sheet.

It was a patient transfer log.

Noor’s stomach dropped.

The columns were simple. Date. Room. Bed. Name. Receiving location. Authorizing signature. Disposition.

Most entries were ordinary in the way bureaucracy always was: transfers to regional clinics, discharges to family, referrals to shelters. Some lines were crossed out. Some had notes in red ink that had scanned as brown. Noor scrolled until their eyes snagged on a row near the bottom.

ROOM: 3  
BED: 7  
NAME: ELIAS VOSS  
RECEIVING LOCATION: ST. A BASEMENT  
AUTHORIZING SIGNATURE: R. HALE  
DISPOSITION: —

Noor stared at the blank cell.

The name meant nothing to them. The signature meant everything.

R. Hale.

The regional director whose signature had appeared in the public filing six months ago. The same hook at the end of the last letter. The same name marked in the paper list.

Noor copied the row into their notebook by hand, then wrote the name three times in the margin because memory could fail under stress and ink could be taken. They underlined R. HALE until the pen nearly tore the page.

“Elias Voss,” Noor said. “Does that name mean anything to you?”

Marta shook her head slowly. “No. But Hale does.”

“You said he came to the parish.”

“For photographs. For donors. He liked being near the suffering but not in it.”

Noor looked at the blank disposition field again.

A person moved from a clinic fire to a church basement. No discharge. No follow-up. No record after.

That was not an answer. That was a hole shaped like an answer.

The train began to slow.

Noor’s head lifted at once.

The change was subtle at first: the wheels losing urgency, the metal groaning less sharply as the curve widened. Through the gaps in the boxcar door, the gray morning had brightened into a thin, colorless dawn. They passed a rusted signal post, then a stretch of chain-link fence topped with dead vines. Beyond it, the silhouette of a water tower rose over low rooftops.

Marta moved to the door and looked out.

“We’re coming up on the yard,” she said.

Noor shut the laptop without closing the lid all the way. “How far to your sister’s farm?”

“Past the river. Twenty minutes on foot if we cut behind the mill.”

“If we get off here.”

“If we can.”

Noor stood and crossed to the door. They kept low and looked through the gap. The tracks were curving toward a cluster of sidings. A small rail yard spread out under the water tower: stacked containers, a maintenance shed, two parked trucks, and a single figure in a high-visibility jacket standing near a switch lever. The figure was not looking at the train. Not yet.

Noor counted the seconds between the yard lights and the slow roll of the cars.

Too many open spaces. Too many places for someone to be waiting.

They thought of the sedan at the church. The men in the basement. The radio voice from the mountain. The pattern Marta had named without meaning to: they had found the gate, but they had also found the rhythm of the night. If Noor stayed on the train into the yard, they would be contained. If they jumped too early on open track, they would be visible.

The train slowed more.

Noor looked back at the concrete switch housing they had passed, then at the water tower, then at the gravel slope on the inside of the curve. The slope dropped toward a drainage ditch and a line of dead weeds. Not cover. But better than open ballast.

“We get off before the yard,” Noor said.

Marta looked at the moving ground. “It’s still fast.”

“It’s slow enough.”

“Noor—”

“It will not get slower without putting us where they expect us.”

Noor did not wait for agreement. They moved quickly after that, because hesitation was a luxury and the train was offering them a narrow, ugly chance.

They packed the laptop into the bag with the power bank, wrapped the charger around the machine to keep it from knocking, and zipped the bag halfway. The padded case stayed inside as decoy. The drives stayed in their inner pocket. The brass key went into their jeans pocket, cold against their hip. The map stayed against their chest. The paper list stayed folded inside the jacket.

Noor checked the flashlight. Still off. Still there.

They checked the burner phone. Still dead by choice.

Then they looked at Marta.

“Stay behind me. When I say jump, jump toward the slope, not the tracks. Roll if you can. Keep the bag close.”

Marta nodded once. Her face was pale, but her hands had stopped shaking.

Noor slid the boxcar door open another foot. Cold air rushed in, carrying the smell of diesel, wet gravel, and river mud. The sound of the train changed as the gap widened: louder, more exposed, less like shelter and more like a risk being taken in full daylight.

The figure near the switch lever turned.

Noor froze.

The man looked toward the cars, hand rising to his radio.

Noor did not wait to see if he used it.

“Now,” they said.

They grabbed the ladder with their injured hand and swung out into the cold. The metal rungs bit into their palm. The ground moved beneath them in a blur of stones and weeds. The bag jerked against their shoulder. Noor hooked one leg over the lower rung and reached back for Marta without looking, because looking would cost time they did not have.

Her hand found theirs.

Noor pulled.

She hit the ladder hard, caught herself, and for one terrible second her weight dragged them both outward. Noor’s shoulder screamed. Their bad foot slipped. They bit down on the inside of their cheek again and held on because letting go was not an option.

The switch housing passed.

The water tower grew larger.

The gravel slope came up fast.

Noor looked down once.

Then they let go.

dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor hit the slope hard.

Gravel bit through their jacket. The bag slammed into their hip, and the laptop’s corner struck their ribs with enough force to drive the air from their lungs. They rolled once, twice, instinct taking over before thought could catch up, then slammed into a patch of dead weeds at the bottom of the embankment.

Marta landed beside them with a sharp cry she swallowed almost instantly.

Noor was up on one knee before the pain registered. Their left foot screamed inside the shoe. Their palm was torn. Their shoulder throbbed where it had hit the ladder or the ground or both. None of it mattered yet.

“Down,” Noor said.

They grabbed Marta’s sleeve and pulled her toward the drainage ditch that ran parallel to the tracks. The train continued past them, cars grinding around the curve, metal wheels shrieking against iron. The sound covered their movement. Noor used it. They half-dragged Marta into the shallow ditch, then pressed them both flat against the muddy bank as a flashlight beam swept the ballast above.

A voice shouted from the yard.

Another answered farther off.

Noor did not look up. They listened instead. Boots on gravel. A radio crackling. The heavy, slowing groan of the freight moving toward the sidings.

Marta’s breath came fast. Noor put one hand near her shoulder—not touching, just close enough that she would feel the warning if they moved.

The flashlight beam passed over them again.

Noor counted.

One.

Two.

Three.

The beam swung away.

The boots moved toward the train, not toward the ditch.

Noor exhaled through their nose and allowed themselves to feel the shape of their body again. Pain in the foot. Pain in the hand. Bruise forming along the ribs. Nothing broken. Nothing unusable.

They checked the bag first. Laptop present. Padded case present. Power bank present. Flashlight present. Then they checked the inner pocket of their jacket. Both drives still there. The brass key still in their jeans. The paper list still folded against their chest.

Only then did Noor look at Marta.

Her coat was torn at the elbow. Her face was streaked with dirt. She was shaking, but her eyes were alert.

“We can’t stay here,” Noor said.

“The yard—”

“Is where they’ll look first.”

Noor rose into a crouch and scanned the ditch line. It ran downhill toward a dark stand of trees and the faint metallic smell of moving water. The river. Marta had said the farm was past the river.

That was enough.

Noor moved first, staying low, one hand trailing along the muddy bank for balance. The cold seeped through their shoes almost immediately. Their injured foot left a darker print in the wet ground. They noticed it, cursed silently, and shifted their weight to the outside edge of the sole.

Behind them, the yard lights flickered over the tracks. A door opened somewhere. A man’s voice carried thin and sharp through the morning air.

Noor did not turn.

They followed the ditch until it narrowed into a concrete channel, then stopped and listened again. No engines. No dogs. No footsteps except the distant settling of the train.

Marta caught up to them. “The river’s just past those trees.”

Noor nodded. “Can we cross?”

“There’s a footbridge behind the old pump house. It’s half collapsed, but it holds.”

“Then we move.”

They moved.

The trees gave way to a gray stretch of river, low and fast from snowmelt. The pump house was a brick shell with no door and a rusted pipe jutting from its side like a broken limb. The footbridge beyond it was exactly as Marta had described: sagging, missing planks, slick with mist.

Noor tested the first board with their foot.

It held.

They crossed slowly, keeping their weight centered, one hand on the rail where there was a rail and on the air where there was not. The river below looked cold enough to stop breath. Noor did not look down longer than necessary.

On the far bank, Marta pointed toward a dark line of outbuildings. “My sister’s place. The barn is closer than the house.”

“Barn first.”

Marta glanced at them but did not argue.

They cut across a muddy field bordered by a broken fence. Dawn had fully arrived now, pale and unwilling, turning the wet grass silver. Noor kept checking behind them. The rail yard was hidden behind the rise, but the water tower still showed against the sky. If someone had binoculars, if someone had seen them jump, if someone had already traced the slope and the ditch and the pump house—

Noor forced the thought into a smaller box and shut it.

The barn was low and weathered, its doors closed, its windows dark. Marta moved toward a side entrance and lifted her hand to knock.

Noor caught her wrist.

“Wait.”

They circled the barn first, staying close to the wall. No vehicle inside. No fresh tire tracks. No light leaking from the cracks. A few chickens shifted inside a wire run. A goat lifted its head from the shadows and watched them with disinterest.

Noor returned to the side door.

“Knock.”

Marta knocked.

A pause.

Then a voice from inside: “Who’s with you?”

Marta looked at Noor.

Noor answered before Marta could. “No one who wants trouble.”

The door opened a few inches. A woman looked out. She was older than Marta by a decade, maybe more, with a weathered face and a man’s coat too large for her shoulders. Her eyes moved quickly over Noor’s mud, their torn jacket, the bag, the blood on their hand.

She opened the door wider.

Inside, the barn smelled of hay, animal warmth, and old machine oil. A lantern hung from a hook, unlit. Morning light came through gaps in the boards.

Noor did not relax.

“Phones?” they asked.

The woman’s mouth tightened. “No cell service out here. Landline’s been dead since the storm.”

“Good.”

“You brought trouble.”

“Yes,” Noor said.

The woman looked at Marta.

Marta said, “It followed us.”

Noor appreciated that more than they could say.

The woman—Marta’s sister, presumably—stepped back and pulled a blanket from a shelf. She handed it to Noor without ceremony. “You’re bleeding.”

Noor looked down. Blood from their palm had smeared the laptop bag strap. Their foot had left a faint rust-colored mark on the barn floor.

“I need water,” Noor said. “Something to wrap it. And twenty minutes where no one comes in here.”

The woman studied them. Then she pointed to a metal basin on a workbench. “Pump’s outside. Cloth’s in the cabinet. Don’t waste my water.”

Noor nodded.

They cleaned the wound quickly and badly, because thoroughness required time they did not have. The water was ice-cold and made their fingers ache. They wrapped the palm with a strip torn from an old shirt Marta’s sister provided, then tightened their jacket over it.

The foot was worse. The skin on their arch had been rubbed raw by the drive, and the jump had reopened it. Noor peeled off the sock, saw the angry red scrape, and forced themselves to look without flinching. They cleaned it as best they could, wrapped it with the last of the cloth, and put the sock back on.

Pain flared when they laced the shoe.

Good.

Pain still meant they could walk.

Noor stood and checked the barn’s interior again. Two exits. The main doors. The side door. A small window near the hayloft that looked out toward the river. No cameras. No obvious listening devices. Nothing that looked newer than the rest of the barn except a padlock on a feed cabinet.

They pointed to it. “What’s inside?”

“Feed,” the woman said.

“Anyone else know you’re here?”

“My husband went to market before dawn. He won’t be back until noon.”

Noor considered that. “If he comes back early, we were never here.”

“He won’t come back early.”

“Then we weren’t here anyway.”

Marta’s sister looked at them for a long moment. Then she went to a wooden crate near the wall and lifted a cloth-covered loaf from inside. She set it on the workbench beside a cup of water.

“Eat,” she said.

Noor had been about to say they did not have time.

They ate anyway.

The bread was dense and slightly stale. It was the best thing Noor had tasted in days. They chewed slowly, forcing themselves not to bolt it, and drank the water in three measured swallows. The food did not erase the fear or the exhaustion, but it changed the texture of both.

Noor set the cup down.

“Twenty minutes,” they said. “Marta, you sleep first.”

Marta blinked. “What?”

“You know the routes. If I fall asleep, I’m useless. If you fall asleep, I can still work. Sleep now.”

“I can’t just—”

“You can.”

She looked as if she might argue. Then her shoulders dropped. She found a pile of old horse blankets near the hayloft, sat down, and wrapped one around herself. Within two minutes her breathing had changed.

Noor envied her.

They did not lie down. They opened the laptop instead, shielding the screen with their body and the blanket Marta’s sister had given them. The cracked display made their stomach sink, but the machine still powered on. The encrypted partition still opened. The files were still there.

LEDGER.

VOICE.

IF YOU ARE READING THIS.

Noor did not open the voice file again. The note had said not to unless they were alone, and while Noor was not entirely sure Marta was safe, they were sure she was not the threat they needed to prepare for. Not yet.

They opened the ledger instead.

The second drive had completed the structure. Payments became names. Names became titles. Titles became institutions. Noor worked quickly, cross-referencing the paper list with the digital files, copying key lines by hand into their notebook because paper could not be remotely wiped.

R. Hale appeared three more times.

Once beside a land transfer.

Once beside a clinic maintenance contract.

Once beside a payment marked “disposal logistics.”

Noor stared at that last word until it blurred.

Disposal.

They pulled up the saved phone records from the first burner. The number beside ROOM 3 / BED 7 was still there, unanswered and unvoiced. Noor searched it against the scanned clinic documents they had saved months ago. Nothing at first. Then a maintenance invoice, buried in a folder they had almost forgotten: a prepaid phone purchased at the clinic gift shop two days before the fire. Purchased under a janitor’s name. Used once to call the number Noor now had.

Noor wrote that down too.

Their hand was shaking again.

They set the pen down and pressed their palm flat against the blanket until it steadied.

Then they opened the transfer log again.

Elias Voss.

Room 3, bed 7.

Receiving location: St. Anne’s basement.

Authorizing signature: R. Hale.

Disposition: —

Noor typed the name into their notes and searched the ledger for it. The result appeared in a hidden tab they had not noticed before: a list of “property transfers” disguised as medical equipment. One line read:

E.V. — ST. A. BASEMENT — HOLD UNTIL HALE CONFIRMS.

Noor’s throat tightened.

They looked at Marta sleeping in the hay.

Then they looked at the barn door.

The register Marta had mentioned—the black binder with numbered cots—could prove Elias Voss had been moved. It could prove the church basement had been used as an unofficial holding site after the clinic fire. It could connect Hale to whatever happened after the disposition field went blank.

And it was still behind the boiler.

Noor closed the laptop and leaned forward, elbows on their knees.

Sleep.
