The geometry read at a sprinter's glance: the corridor ran straight to the elevator bank *behind* the typist — call panel, steel doors, floor indicator parked on **3**. Calling it would cost a minute you didn't have. But to your left, ten feet down the wall: a gray door under a red EXIT sign, stenciled beneath — **STAIRWELL — NO REENTRY.** One-way. Down and out, wherever that went, and no way back into the building once the bar swung.

**12:12**

Behind you, the vault door began reeling itself shut on its closer — slow, hydraulic, sealing the open safe and the dead monitor and the empty foam into a room nobody would open until morning. Ahead, the typist raised the phone off their ear and held it out — toward you. Whether offering it or dialing someone new, the next two seconds would say.

**Two minutes, forty-eight seconds.** A live witness between you and the elevators. A one-way door to your left. And a corridor about to stop being empty.

The typist's mouth opened again.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I don't hesitate.* "Sorry!" *I shove past the stunned typist, making a beeline for the elevators. I'm not going through that stairwell if I can avoid it.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**12:19**

The shove was more hurry than violence — shoulder into cardigan, and the typist went sideways into the wall with a squeak of rubber soles. The phone left their hand, hit the tile, skidded — and kept talking. The call was still live, a tiny tinny voice climbing out of the speaker into the empty corridor: *"Hello? HELLO—"* Its owner dropped to their knees after it, lanyard swinging.

**12:27**

Ten feet. The call panel. Your palm hit **CALL** before you'd finished stopping — and then you saw the floor indicator, and your stomach did something complicated. Parked on **3**. The car hadn't gone anywhere. It had delivered the typist up and waited, patient as everything else in this building that ran on schedules. The button lit under your hand. The car didn't have to come. It was already here.

**12:38**

Behind you, the phone made it back to a face, and the typist's voice cracked apart into it: *"Third floor — someone's here, they were in the vault—"* The vault door finished its slow hydraulic reel and seated itself with a final clunk, sealing the open safe, the dead monitor, and the empty foam into a room with your fingerprints all over it. The elevator chimed. The doors parted on empty fluorescent light.

**12:44**

Inside. Handrail, mirror, rubber floor. You hit the bottom button — **G** — and hammered DOOR CLOSE, and through the narrowing gap you watched the typist start down the corridor toward you. Not running. Phone pressed hard to their ear, saying your location out loud to the whole building.

**12:58**

The car dropped. Three floors of lurch and cable-song, the indicator ticking **3... 2...** — and beside it, the second car's arrow, because the bank had two cars, showed *up*. Rising. Leaving the lobby at that exact moment. Somebody had answered that phone call, and they were riding toward the trouble instead of away from it. The lobby was emptying itself for you, one floor at a time. In the mirror, your own face looked like it hadn't slept since Tuesday.

**13:06**

The doors opened on the lobby: dark glass, marble-look tile, after-hours dim. The night desk sat empty — headset off its hook, chair drifting a slow half-turn, a monitor showing the third-floor corridor where a small figure in a cardigan was pointing straight up at the dome camera. At you, thirty seconds ago. The dome itself hung over the desk, unblinking. Whatever it had, it already had.

**13:13**

The exits introduced themselves fast. Street doors: floor-to-ceiling glass, mag-locked, the reader glowing its red refusal. Across the crash bar, stenciled white: **DELAYED EGRESS — ALARM WILL SOUND — DOOR RELEASES IN 15 SECONDS. LOCAL ALARM ONLY.** A corridor sign pointed to **PARKING — P1** behind a door with its own keypad and no code in your pocket. And above the elevator bank, the second car's arrow sat on **3** now. Stopped. Whatever was happening up there was happening quick.

**One minute, forty-seven seconds.** Still a choice about noise — fifteen seconds of screaming bought the street, quiet bought nothing but time, and the guard upstairs was about to spend his learning exactly where you'd gone.

The arrow twitched.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I see the **DELAYED EGRESS** sign and my stomach drops.* "You gotta be kidding me." *I hit the street door crash bar anyway, already looking for another option.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:32**

The lockpick kit came out with only the faintest scrape against the thief’s pocket. Moving to the keypad took nine seconds. Entering **8-4-7-0-0-0** took another fifteen.

The confirmation beep was short, dry, and final.

The little green light stayed dark. An amber reject lamp pulsed once beneath the number pad, then the screen cleared itself.

Wrong.

The ceiling strips pulsed—four seconds apart—and the server racks answered with a low, indifferent hum. Fourteen minutes and twenty-eight seconds remained.

The keypad waited, blank and patient. If the thief continued straight upward through **001**, **002**, and so on, each additional entry would cost at least eight to ten seconds. A full run from **000** to **999** would eat every remaining minute and then some.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**2:32**

They kept to the sequence. The pad accepted the next entry, then rejected it; accepted the next, rejected it. Eight-four-seven-zero-zero-one. Eight-four-seven-zero-zero-two. Eight-four-seven-zero-one-two.

Twelve codes. Twelve amber refusals. Each one took roughly ten seconds from press to clear, and the minutes spent themselves without drama.

The ceiling strips had pulsed thirty-eight times since the vault sealed. Four seconds each. Two minutes and thirty-two seconds gone. Twelve minutes and twenty-eight remained.

The keypad had not locked itself out. That was bad news, because it meant the only real lockout was the guard rotation. The arithmetic was plain enough: 987 combinations still lay between the next entry and 847999. At ten seconds a try, the last possible code would not be reached for well over two hours.

The only change came with the twelfth rejection.

The amber lamp lingered a half-second longer than before. The display did not snap back to blank. For a moment, a thin white line flickered along the bottom of the screen, like a log entry trying to format itself.

Then the panel cleared.

Somewhere beyond the vault door, a hinge shifted.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content:
(OOC: I'm not "they," I'm "I." Please don't write my actions.)

*I pause, my fingers hovering over the keypad.* "Did you see that? The light... and that flicker." I glance over my shoulder at the vault door, then back at the keypad. "And that sound. Someone's out there."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**2:43**

Eleven seconds passed. The thief’s question hung unanswered inside the cold vault, and the glance toward the door met only sealed steel.

The ceiling strips pulsed at **2:36** and **2:40**. The last pulse faded as twelve minutes and seventeen seconds remained.

No voice answered from outside. The hinge shift had stopped; instead, the faint scrape of a boot sole on hallway tile moved away, slow and routine, like a guard checking a closed door but not opening it.

Inside, the keypad had gone inert again. The amber reject lamp was dark. The white line along the bottom of the screen had vanished, but its absence left a faint afterimage: a horizontal seam of light, lower than the code prompt, too thin to be part of the normal display.

The numbers had not changed. **987** combinations still sat between the next entry and the top of the range. At ten seconds a try, systematic guessing was no longer a plan. It was a countdown.

The safe waited. The keypad waited. The cold hum of the servers did not care which one the thief chose to answer.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**4:11**

Eighty-eight seconds passed in the cold air. The ceiling strips pulsed twenty-two times, and the server racks hummed through every one of them.

The vault was not a cluttered desk. There was no notebook on the floor, no manila folder left on a rack shelf, no sticky note pressed to the keypad. The safe itself was brushed steel and silence, its housing clean except for the faint gray smear of a technician’s glove on the side panel.

But the vault was not perfectly empty.

Under the lowest shelf of the nearest server rack, half-hidden by a bundle of neatly tied cables, a small adhesive note had been stuck there by someone in a hurry. It had curled at the edges and gone gray at the seams. The top line was printed:

**847**

Below it, handwritten in faded blue ink, were three more characters:

**0 ? 7**

The middle digit had been ruined by a dark smear—condensation, coffee, or maybe just time. It might have been a **3**. It might have been an **8**. It might have been nothing more than an old maintenance tag for a different lock, a different rack, a different forgotten thing.

The keypad still waited. The amber reject lamp stayed dark. The safe had not locked itself out.

Ten minutes and forty-nine seconds remained.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Bingo," I whisper, a small smile playing on my lips. *I snatch the note, careful not to smudge it further.* "Okay, 8-4-7-0-something-7." I walk back to the keypad, my mind racing. "It's either 0, 3, or 8. We'll start with 0."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**4:43**

Eight ceiling pulses moved the clock from the rack to the keypad: eight seconds for the note to release, nine for the distance to close, fifteen for the digits to register.

**8-4-7-0-0-7**.

The amber lamp came on again, but slower this time. It stayed lit for two full seconds, then the screen cleared.

Wrong.

Ten minutes and seventeen seconds remained.

The keypad had not locked itself out. The safe had not sounded an alarm. But the note’s last digit had not answered the question. If the faded blue line was accurate, only **847307** and **847807** remained. If the smeared center was not a digit at all, or if the last 7 had been a maintenance mark, the range was still open.

A thin white seam flickered along the lower edge of the display. This time it held for a heartbeat, as if the panel were logging the failed attempt somewhere behind its shell.

Beyond the vault door, the external hinge settled with a small metallic tick. The scrape of a boot sole stopped just outside. Not a handle. Not a key. Just a pause.

Inside, the server hum dropped half a tone and returned. On the note, the dark smear caught the ceiling pulse from an angle that revealed a shallow curved indentation above it—part of a 3, maybe, or the top loop of an 8.

The keypad waited. The guard waited. The clock did not.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**4:45**

For the purpose of the countdown, the question cost two seconds.

The ceiling strip pulsed at **4:44**, and the cold vault clock settled at **4:45**. Ten minutes and fifteen seconds remained before the guard rotation completed.

There was no wall clock inside the safe chamber. There was no watch on the keypad, no printed time on the server racks, no digital display except the blank prompt waiting for six digits. The only timekeeper was the slow, mechanical rhythm of the ceiling lights and the quiet arithmetic of the scene.

If the question had been aimed at the safe itself, the answer was simple: the safe did not know, did not care, and did not reveal its own time limit.

If it had been aimed at the vault, the answer was colder: **4:45**.

If it had been aimed at the guard outside, the answer was worse: the boot sole had not moved away.

The pause still stood beyond the steel door, close enough that any new attempt at the keypad would make the next few seconds count more than before. The last two candidate codes, if the note meant what it appeared to mean, remained **847307** and **847807**. But the smeared center could still be a lie, and the final 7 could still be maintenance notation.

The keypad’s amber reject lamp stayed dark.

The white seam along the lower edge of the screen did not appear again.

The vault held its breath at **4:45**, and the clock did not stop for anyone.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Damn it, no time for questions." *I mutter, ignoring the question I just asked. I look at the note again, then back at the keypad.* "Okay, 8-4-7-3-0-7." *I key it in, holding my breath.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**5:10**

Six ceiling pulses carried the attempt from the note to the keypad. The entered sequence—**8-4-7-3-0-7**—was accepted by the panel and rejected by the lock. The amber lamp burned for three full seconds, longer than the previous rejection, then the display cleared itself.

Wrong.

Nine minutes and fifty seconds remained.

The hinge ticked again. The boot sole outside scraped once, not moving away, but shifting weight, as if someone had stopped directly in front of the vault door and was reading its status.

Inside, the note’s dark smear looked different under the next pulse. The shallow curved indentation was not the flat top of a **3**. It was too round, too closed—more like the upper loop of an **8**, though the ink had bled. If the note was accurate, one candidate remained: **8-4-7-8-0-7**. If it was not, the earlier arithmetic still held: systematic guessing would outlive the rotation.

The keypad stayed patient. No lockout. No alarm. Only the server hum, the four-second pulse, and the guard’s weight beyond the steel door.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My heart sinks, but then I see the smear again.* "An 8 then! It has to be an 8!" *I quickly punch in the last combination.* "8-4-7-8-0-7!"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**5:26**

The final sequence was entered, and the keypad did not reject it.

No amber lamp. No cleared display. The green light came on, small and absolute.

Three bolts retracted inside the safe with a heavy, greasy thud. The brushed steel door shifted a finger’s width open, exhaling colder air from its interior.

Nine minutes and thirty-four seconds remained.

The mechanical sound carried farther than the server hum. Outside the vault, the boot sole stopped shifting weight and began to move. A shadow crossed the narrow gap beneath the door. The external handle turned. The hydraulic seal groaned as pressure changed, and the vault door’s status light shifted from sealed red to cycling amber.

Inside the safe, on a square of anti-static foam, lay a slim black drive and a folded maintenance slip. The drive’s label was clean, factory-printed:

**847-807**

The slip, tucked beneath it, bore one line in the same faded blue ink as the note:

**PULSE = 4. FINAL CHECK AT 15:00.**

The outer handle turned again.

The vault door was about to open.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Got it!" *I grab the drive and the slip, stuffing them into an inner pocket.* "Too close!" *I scramble back from the safe, looking wildly around the vault for an exit, or a place to hide.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**5:40**

The whisper and the scramble from the safe had cost fourteen seconds. The drive and the folded maintenance slip were now concealed in an inner pocket. The ceiling strip pulsed at **5:40**, and nine minutes and twenty seconds remained before the rotation’s final check.

The vault door had stopped waiting for the schedule. Its status light cycled green now, a slow mechanical exhale running through the hydraulic seam. The external handle turned again, harder than before. The seam widened from hairline to finger-width, then to a bright edge of hall light. The panel above the frame read:

**UNSEALING — 9**

Inside, the safe stood open by a finger, its green light still burning. The brushed steel interior reflected nothing but the ceiling pulses and the dark, drive-shaped absence where it had rested.

The vault offered three answers, none of them kind.

The nearest server rack had a rear gap between cable bundles, big enough to crouch in, but a guard stepping through the door would see the gap before seeing whatever hid in it. Reaching it would take three seconds; hiding there would not hide.

Above the third rack, a maintenance hatch sat in the ceiling, its two quick-turn latches dull with dust. The latches could be turned in six seconds, the hatch pushed down in four, and the climb would take longer than the door had left. The lockpick kit’s tension bar might jam the hatch short once it was open—another four seconds.

At the left wall, under the lowest cable tray, a floor grate marked **COOLANT** was bolted down, but one bolt was already missing. The remaining three could be loosened with the pick kit in seven to nine seconds. The opening beyond was narrow, dark, and smelled faintly of ozone, but it lay outside the direct line of sight from the vault door.

The safe door could be nudged closed in two seconds, though it would not latch, and the green light would remain until the panel was reset.

The next ceiling pulse was due at **5:44**. The vault door’s seam widened by another inch, and the handle turned again.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Damn it, damn it, damn it!" *I curse under my breath.* "The floor grate!" *I drop to my knees, fumbling with my lockpicks to get those bolts out.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**5:44**

The first bolt gave after four seconds, coming free with a scrape that sounded too loud against the cable tray. The second bolt was worse. The lockpick kit was not made for bolt heads; its tension bar slipped, caught, slipped again, and released the second bolt at **5:48**.

**5:49**

The panel above the vault door read **UNSEALING — 0**.

The hydraulic seam widened from a finger’s gap to a full doorway. A boot crossed the threshold.

**5:53**

The third bolt had seized, loosened, then dropped. The floor grate fell inward on its hinge. The opening beyond was narrow, dark, and cold, breathing ozone from below the server floor.

The vault door was already open.

The guard’s flashlight did not sweep the room like a weapon. It swept like routine. It moved across the server racks, paused on the open safe, and found the empty square of anti-static foam. The safe’s green light burned. The drive-shaped absence burned beside it.

Nine minutes and seven seconds remained.

The guard’s boot shifted toward the safe, not yet toward the floor grate. The cable tray shadow covered the opening, but only partly. The guard’s hand moved toward the wall panel that would report the safe’s condition.

The next ceiling pulse was due at **5:56**.

The floor opening waited, four inches wide and dark. The wall panel waited, amber-lit and patient. The guard waited, one glance from finding the kneeling shape outside the rack shadow.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I don't hesitate.* "Hold that thought!" *I hiss, and without waiting, I squeeze myself through the grate, not caring about the scrapes.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**6:04**

The last muttered curse had cost no time; the bolts had. The grate hung open on its hinge, and the coolant channel below breathed a colder draft into the vault. The guard’s flashlight had already found the open safe, the empty foam square, and the green light that should have been reset. Then the beam slid down the wall, across the cable tray, and onto the floor.

“Control, rotation check,” the guard said into the shoulder mic. His voice was flat, almost bored, but the words cost seconds. “Vault two is unsealed. Safe’s open. I’m checking the chamber.”

The radio answered with a short static burst and a distant affirmative. That answer took three seconds. The guard turned toward the grate. His boot stopped one pace from the scattered bolts.

Eight minutes and fifty-six seconds remained.

The ceiling strip pulsed at **6:04**. The open safe still glowed green. Above the third rack, the maintenance hatch waited, its quick-turn latches dull with dust. Behind the nearest rack, the cable gap was too shallow to hide more than a shadow. The coolant opening exhaled ozone and darkness. The guard’s light hovered at the edge of the grate, not yet dropping into the gap.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I hold my breath, trying to be as still as possible in the cramped space.* "Don't look down, don't look down," *I chant silently to myself.* I can feel the cold metal of the grate against my back.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**3:28**

The keypad registered each attempted sequence with a punitive chirp and a brief red glare. 8-4-7-0-0-0 triggered a denial tone; 8-4-7-0-0-1 produced the same soft, electronic rebuff. The capacitive buttons demanded deliberate pressure, each depression emitting a distinct plastic *tick* that hung in the chilled air. The combinations climbed with mechanical inevitability through the low zero-hundreds—8-4-7-0-2-3, 8-4-7-0-2-4—each failure met by the LCD's mocking reset. The overhead light strips pulsed their slow heartbeat forty-five times during the siege, and midway through, the server fans cycled into a higher pitch before settling back to their midnight hum. Three minutes and twenty seconds drained into the dark. The lockpick kit, still in hand, remained useless against the digital panel. The hydraulic seals on the vault door behind you had cooled from their initial hiss to a patient, waiting silence. Eleven minutes and thirty-two seconds remained before the guard completed his rotation.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**7:42**

The sequence marched onward with mechanical resignation. 8-4-7-2-9-7 earned the same curt electronic chirp as 8-4-7-2-9-8; the keypad's red glare reset with metronomic indifference. The attempted combinations had climbed into the low three-hundreds, each six-digit volley consuming roughly a second and a half of the dwindling window. The overhead light strips pulsed through another sixty-three slow heartbeats, and somewhere in the server racks a cooling fan hit a transient bearing wobble before smoothing back into the midnight hum. The vault door behind you stood patient and silent, its hydraulic seals equalized to the ambient four degrees. The safe remained locked. There had been no variation in the keypad's rejections—no lag, no stutter, no telltale softening to suggest the correct sequence was near. Brute-forcing the remaining permutations would demand more time than remained. Seven minutes and eighteen seconds were left before the guard completed his rotation.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: Damn it. This is taking too long. "No tells at all?" I mutter, frustrated. *I pull out my small, flexible borescope.* Maybe I can see something inside.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**10:30**

Retrieving the borescope and threading its fiber-optic lens into the hairline seam between the keypad bezel and the cold steel faceplate consumed nearly three minutes. The probe’s LED threw a harsh white glow across potted circuitry and a tamper mesh that shimmered like fractured foil behind clear epoxy. The screen revealed no mechanical linkage to finesse, no exposed solder to bridge—only a sealed digital module staring back with silicon indifference. The locking bolts remained hidden beyond the door’s rubber seal, inaccessible to both light and reach.

While the probe was maneuvered through its slow arc, the overhead light strips pulsed their four-second heartbeat another forty-two times. The server fans in the corners hit a synchronized harmonic that made the floor thrum, then splintered again into competing whines. Beyond the vault door, the distant pneumatic sigh of the building’s HVAC switched to its night cycle, a sound felt more than heard through the floor. The hydraulic seals behind had long since equalized to the ambient four degrees; the door stood as a silent monolith. Four minutes and thirty seconds remained before the guard completed his rotation. The keypad LCD had dimmed to standby, awaiting the next input.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**13:00**

The search consumed the room with methodical slowness. You swept the safe’s perimeter first—fingers tracing the undersides of its cold steel lip, palming the wall behind it for the tacky residue of a forgotten note. Nothing. The server racks offered only vibrating metal and the mineral smell of hot electronics; no clipboard tucked between the blades, no scrawled index card taped to a cable. A recessed stainless-steel cabinet beside the door opened with a squeal that cut through the server hum, revealing a blank incident log and a tethered stylus, but no handwriting, no initials, no convenience. You crouched to check the floor seams, straightened to scan the ceiling conduit, each pass confirming the vault’s absolute sterility.

The overhead light strips pulsed their four-second heartbeat another thirty-seven times during the hunt. Somewhere in the rack arrays, a cooling fan sang a brief, high alarm before dropping back into the midnight hum. The vault door’s hydraulic seals had long since surrendered their warmth to the ambient chill; the steel stood silent and patient behind you. By the time you finished, the verdict was clear: this room kept secrets behind silicon and encryption, never ink.

Two minutes remained before the guard completed his rotation. The keypad LCD flared to full brightness, its six blank dashes waiting like a held breath.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "No luck, huh?" I whisper to myself. *I quickly check my watch, then back at the keypad.* Two minutes. This is cutting it close. "Alright, let's try something else." *I quickly pull out a small device, a frequency scanner, and hold it near the keypad.* Maybe there's an electromagnetic signature.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**14:05**

The frequency scanner’s LCD awoke with a pale green wash as its first sweep cycle started. Held an inch from the keypad’s bezel, its antenna hunted through bands in a vault saturated by server noise. The racks poured out a broadband wall of static that crowded the tiny screen into hash. The device caught only the rhythmic blip of the overhead LEDs—one faint peak every four seconds—superimposed over the denser whine of voltage regulators and spinning drives. The keypad itself offered no emission, no wireless handshake, no ghost of the final three digits lingering in the air. It remained electrically silent until touched.

The sweep consumed one minute and five seconds. During the pass, the light strips pulsed their slow heartbeat another fifteen times. Somewhere in the rack arrays, a cooling fan sang a brief high note before dropping back into the midnight hum. The vault door’s hydraulic seals had equalized fully to the ambient four degrees. The keypad LCD flared awake once more, six blank dashes waiting.

Fifty-five seconds remained before the guard completed his rotation.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**14:05**

The whisper fell into the server hum without answer. The overhead light strips pulsed their four-second heartbeat—thirteen slow throbs remaining before the guard completed his rotation. The frequency scanner still glowed pale green, its screen locked in a hash of RF noise from the surrounding racks. Fifty-five seconds of the fifteen-minute window had survived. The keypad's LCD held its six blank dashes steady against the cold steel, unblinking. The vault door's hydraulic seals had equalized fully to the ambient four degrees; the steel stood silent and waiting.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Fifty-five seconds? Are you kidding me?" *I shove the scanner back into my pack, my heart pounding.* No time for this. *I quickly put my ear to the safe door, listening intently, then start hitting random keys, trying to feel for any slight mechanical give.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**14:30**

Their ear found only the cold steel's bite and the subsonic drone of the server racks beneath it—no tick of tumblers, no scrape of bolt work, only the sealed indifference of a digital vault. Fingers skittered across the capacitive pad, hunting mechanical give that existed only in memory of older locks; each touch triggered a brief white glow beneath the digit, a flat electronic acknowledgment without travel, without resistance, without variance. A staccato cluster of random numbers flared and held for two seconds before the LCD wiped itself with a single, disdainful chirp.

Six of the overhead light strips pulsed their four-second heartbeat during the frenzy. The server fans in the corners kept their midnight hum, indifferent to the mammal panic below. The vault door's hydraulic seals had long since equalized to the ambient chill; the steel stood silent and absolute at their back.

Thirty seconds remained before the guard completed his rotation. The keypad blinked once, six blank dashes reassembling like an unspoken verdict.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Damnit, damnit, damnit!" *I pull away from the safe, breathing heavily.* "Think, think!" *I look around wildly for a second, then my eyes land on the server racks.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**14:40**

The server racks stood in their same disciplined rows, returning the thief’s frantic gaze with nothing but the amber flicker of status LEDs and the vertical wash of hot air across brushed steel. No maintenance tag, no scrawled digit, no forgotten sticky note revealed itself among the cable looms and blinking blade faces—only the same mineral reek of heated silicon and ozone they had already dismissed. The safe’s keypad sat dark and indifferent behind them, its six blank dashes dormant.

Somewhere beyond the vault door, the muffled report of a keycard reader discharged its lock in the outer corridor—a pneumatic hinge exhaled, closer than any previous sound. The overhead light strips pulsed their four-second heartbeat twice during the thief’s desperate sweep, each sterile white flash carving the vault into snapshots of black steel and shadow. The server fans crescendoed into a brief harmonic peak before splintering back into competing whines.

Twenty seconds remained before the guard completed his rotation. The hydraulic seals on the vault door stood patient and absolute, waiting for the inevitable.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "No, no, no!" *I grab a handful of cables from a server rack. My eyes dart to the keypad, then back to the cables.* "This has to work."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**14:55**

The connectors popped free from the rack in a spray of plastic clips, hot copper ends bared against the vault’s chill. A blade server flatlined behind the thief, its amber status LEDs dying in a synchronized exodus that the building’s network would already be logging as a critical fault. The keypad’s bezel remained a seamless slab of brushed steel, offering no slot or seam sufficient for the bared wires. The final fifteen seconds dissolved while the bundle found no ingress; the LCD flickered once, emitted a dry electronic cough, and went dark.

The overhead light strips pulsed three more times. The remaining server fans whined into an uneven higher register, compensating for the dead rack’s sudden silence.

**15:00**

A heavy magnetic lock discharged in the outer corridor with a sound like an industrial stapler driving home. The vault door’s hydraulic seals parted with a sustained, pressurized hiss. Rubber-soled footsteps—unhurried, methodical, and very real—crossed the threshold. The safe remained locked. The fifteen-minute window had closed. The guard had returned.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My eyes widen as I hear the footsteps. I drop the cables, heart pounding in my chest. I'm trapped.* "Crap."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The footsteps slowed as they cleared the threshold. Under the pulsing light strips, the guard’s silhouette resolved into a broad-shouldered figure in a slate-gray uniform, a baton swaying at one hip and a radio clipped to the chest. He did not reach for it immediately. Instead, he stopped three paces inside the vault, his gaze traveling from the darkened safe keypad to the butchered server rack, to the copper cables coiled on the floor like dead snakes.

The dead blade server had taken a slice of the room’s hum with it; the surviving racks sounded louder in the absence, their fans filling the vault with an uneven, accusatory whine. The ambient four-degree chill seemed to deepen, pressing against skin and steel alike.

The guard’s eyes settled on the intruder. One hand rose—not to the baton, but to the radio antenna, which he adjusted with a slow, deliberate twist.

“Rotation complete,” he said into the mic. His voice was flat, unhurried, carrying the practiced neutrality of someone who had found exactly what the schedule promised. “Vault four. One inside. Safe secure.”

He let the radio hang silent, its channel open. The overhead light strips pulsed their four-second heartbeat, casting the same slow, sterile rhythm across the scene. The safe’s LCD stayed dark. The fifteen minutes had passed, and with them, every chance. The building’s silence beyond the vault was no longer an ally, but a witness.

The guard stepped aside, clearing the doorway. “Hands where I can see them,” he said. Not a request.

The vault had kept its secrets. The heist was over.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My hands slowly raise, but my eyes dart around the vault one last time, searching for an impossible escape.* "Looks like you win this round."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**15:15**

The guard held his ground until the corridor filled with the staccato tread of backup boots. Two more uniforms appeared in the vault doorway, silhouetted against the brighter hall, their radios spitting low static. The first guard's gaze never left the thief as he reached to his belt and produced a pair of matte-black restraints.

"On your knees," he said. "Slow."

The second guard moved to the butchered server rack, muttering under his breath at the severed cables and the darkened blade. The third covered the entrance, hand resting on his baton. The vault, which had served as a silent arena for exactly fifteen minutes, had become a cramped theater of consequence. The safe against the far wall stood pristine—its brushed steel immaculate, its digital heart still locked behind the unguessed final three digits.

Overhead, the light strips continued their metronomic pulse, four seconds apart, indifferent to the shifting of human fortunes below. The building's HVAC sighed back into its night rhythm. Somewhere in the surviving racks, a cooling fan cycled down as the system finished rerouting around the dead node. The ambient chill remained absolute. The heist had ended not in alarm bells, but in the quiet, methodical machinery of capture.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I drop to my knees slowly, hands still raised.* "No need for the theatrics, I'm not going anywhere." *I eye the pristine safe one last time.* "Just curious, what was the code?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The thief drew the lockpick kit as they started across the vault floor, but the tools never left their roll. Ten seconds of soft-soled movement put them in front of the safe at **0:18**. The face was a single slab of matte-black composite: keypad, recessed LED, speaker grille. No keyway, no cylinder, no seam for a pick or a tension wrench. The lockpick kit might as well have been a brick.

They began with the sequence the source had given plus the lowest possible guess: 8-4-7-0-0-0. Six presses, each acknowledged by a muted click. A two-second pause followed the sixth digit, then the bolt motor gave one dead thump and the status LED burned red. Wrong. The pad went dark for twelve seconds, waking again at **0:38**.

The next window went to 8-4-7-0-0-1. Six presses. Two-second pause. Same dead thump, same red. Wrong. Another twelve-second timeout. The keypad went live again at **0:58**.

They entered 8-4-7-0-0-2 the moment the pad allowed. Six presses. Two-second pause. At **1:06** the LED flashed—and stayed amber. A triple-beep cut through the server hum. A small countdown ignited on the display: 30. Three failures logged; the safe’s anti-brute-force logic had escalated. The next attempt would not be possible until that count reached zero.

The ceiling light pulsed its slow four-second rhythm. The amber numerals ticked down. At **1:36** the countdown hit zero, the keypad beeped once, and the safe was ready to accept another wrong answer.

Thirteen minutes and twenty-four seconds remained until the security rotation completed and the guard’s boots returned to the vault.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**1:36**

The thief kept trying combinations. The keypad beeped once, live and waiting. They keyed in the next permutation: 8-4-7-0-0-3. Six presses. The two-second pause stretched. At **1:44** the bolt motor thumped and the status LED flashed—not the brief red of the first two failures, but a hard, pulsing amber. A new countdown ignited on the display: 60. The safe had logged a fourth failure; the anti-brute-force penalty had doubled. The pad went dark. The vault held only the server hum and the slow four-second pulse of the ceiling light. It woke again at **2:44**.

8-4-7-0-0-4 went in the moment the pad allowed. Six presses. Two-second pause. At **2:52** the LED flashed amber and the display burned 120. Two minutes. The logic was exponential now; each failure cost twice the wait of the last. The thief remained at the safe as the amber numerals ticked down. The keypad stayed dead until **4:52**.

8-4-7-0-0-5 followed. Six presses. Two-second pause. At **5:00** the bolt motor gave its dead thump and the display lit with 240. Four minutes. Six guesses were gone. The sequence had advanced only to 8-4-7-0-0-5. Nine hundred and ninety-four permutations remained. The arithmetic was brutal—the lockout penalty was growing faster than the thief could eliminate possibilities. The keypad was dead until **9:00**. The ceiling light pulsed. Ten minutes remained until the security rotation completed and the guard’s boots returned to the vault.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *Damn it!* "This isn't working. I'm wasting too much time." I look around the vault. There must be another way.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**5:00**

The curse hung in the cold air, too loud under the server hum. The thief stood at the dead keypad—its display already burning a steady amber *240*—and looked around the vault.

The room was wider than the pool of light around the safe suggested. Two rows of server racks stood to the left, three in each row, with a fourth rack set apart against the far wall. Their perforated doors breathed warm air and winking status light: greens, ambers, a few unblinking blues. Overhead, cable trays carried thick bundles of copper and fiber from the ceiling down into the rack tops. The light strips pulsed their slow four-second heartbeat. One. Another.

Directly above the safe, a narrow ventilation grille was set into the ceiling tile, its slats wide enough to admit a hand—maybe. Along the left wall at ankle height ran a conduit chase, its cover plate held by four quarter-turn fasteners that caught the pulse in faint gleams. And closest of all, rising from the base of the fourth server rack, a single black cable no thicker than a thumb ran along the floor and disappeared behind the safe’s left edge. Zip-tied to that rack’s handle was a small laminated card.

Four pulses passed—sixteen seconds gone—before the thief’s eyes adjusted enough to read the card from where they stood. *VAULT CTRL – AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY.* The same rack’s cable ran to the safe. The countdown had bled from 240 to 224.

Another twenty-nine seconds slipped away as the thief finished taking the room’s measure: the useless pick kit still rolled at their belt, no keyway on the matte-black face, the chase, the vent, the labeled rack. The ceiling light pulsed on.

**5:45**

The status display read *195*. Three minutes and fifteen seconds remained before the keypad would wake again.

Nine minutes and fifteen seconds remained until the security rotation completed and the guard’s boots returned to the vault.

The arithmetic had not improved. Six failures were logged, and the safe’s logic doubled the penalty each time. The next wrong entry—whenever it came—would carry an eight-minute timeout. If that attempt happened at 9:00, when the pad reopened, the safe would stay dead until 17:00—two minutes after the security rotation completed and the guard returned. In practice, the keypad would allow exactly one more guess before it became irrelevant.

Three avenues showed themselves from where the thief stood: the ventilation grille above the safe, the conduit chase along the left wall, and the rack labeled VAULT CTRL, whose black cable ran into the back of the target. Each would take time to reach, to open, to defeat. Searching had already cost forty-five seconds. The clock pulsed on, four seconds at a time.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**5:45**

The thief stopped. Looking for a written code was not the same as looking for a way in; it meant reading surfaces, not just shapes. That kind of care cost time, and the vault charged for it in four-second heartbeats.

The immediate area came first. The matte-black face of the safe bore no note, no taped card, no grease-pencil scrawl in the seam where it met the wall. The top surface was bare, swept clean by the rack’s exhaust. The floor at its base held only dust and the black cable running off toward the fourth rack. Thirty seconds bled away in that survey—seven pulses of the ceiling light, then part of an eighth. At **6:15** the status display read *165*. Two minutes and forty-five seconds remained before the pad would wake. Eight minutes and forty-five seconds remained until the guard’s rotation completed.

The sweep widened. Server racks to the left: perforated doors, status LEDs, no papers taped to metal, no sticky notes fluttering in the warm outflow. Cable trays overhead: bundled copper and fiber, zip-tied and labeled, nothing written on the trays themselves. The conduit chase along the left wall: its cover plate dusty and undisturbed, no notebook slipped behind it. Another forty-five seconds gone—about eleven more pulses of the light. At **7:00** the countdown burned *120*. Two minutes until the keypad reopened. Eight minutes until the guard returned.

Then the fourth rack, standing apart beneath the far wall where the black cable ran to the safe. Zip-tied to its handle was the laminated card—*VAULT CTRL – AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY*. And hanging below it from a small hook was something the first, hurried glance had missed: an aluminum clipboard, a printed sheet trapped under its spring clip.

Even from where the thief stood, the sheet was legible enough to identify: *VAULT CTRL ACCESS LOG.* Ruled columns ran across the page—DATE, TECH, ACTION, COMBO/VERIFY. Several rows held clusters of handwritten digits. Most were struck through with heavy black marker. One row partway down still showed a full sequence in the same careful hand: **8-4-7-3-8-2**, but a red stamp lay across it, the word *SUPERSEDED* clear even at a distance. Three lines below, another entry began **8-4-7** and then vanished under a dark thumb-smudge where the last three digits should have been.

The page lifted slightly in the rack’s exhaust. Reading the smaller handwriting—the dates, the crossed-out sequences, whatever lay beneath that smudge—would mean crossing to the rack and pulling the clipboard down. That would take thirty seconds at least, maybe more if the sheet had to be worked free of the clip. The thief had already spent a minute and fifteen seconds searching. The clock did not care whether the search succeeded.

**7:00**

The status display read *120*. Two minutes remained before the keypad would wake and permit exactly one final attempt. Eight minutes remained until the security rotation completed and the guard’s boots returned to the vault.

The clipboard hung thirty seconds away. The vent above the safe, the conduit chase along the wall, and the dead keypad waited with it.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *Bingo!* I move directly to the clipboard. "Let's see what we have here." I carefully unclip the sheet, trying not to disturb anything else.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**7:00**

Moving directly to the rack took twelve seconds—three pulses of the ceiling light. The thief reached the clipboard at **7:12**. During the crossing the status display bled from *120* to *108*.

Working the sheet free took longer than a simple snatch would have. The spring clip was stiff, and easing the printed sheet out from under it without disturbing the rack’s cables or the clipboard itself demanded care. Thirty-two seconds passed—eight more pulses—before the sheet came loose at **7:44**. The display now read *76*.

Beneath it, the aluminum clipboard was bare; no second page, no note stuck to the metal.

Once free, the page was a ruled *VAULT CTRL ACCESS LOG*: DATE | TECH | ACTION | COMBO/VERIFY. Rows of handwritten entries marched downward. Older COMBO/VERIFY cells held clusters of digits, nearly all struck through with heavy black marker—retired combinations. Partway down, one row showed TECH D. Ash, ACTION COMBO INIT, and the sequence **8-4-7-3-8-2**; a black bar killed the line and a red stamp cut diagonally across it: SUPERSEDED. That code was dead.

Three lines below, another entry carried a date two days earlier. TECH read R. Vega. ACTION read COMBO RESET – FIELD VERIFIED. The COMBO/VERIFY cell began with the same three digits the source had supplied—**8-4-7**—and then ran into a dark, greasy thumb-smudge where the final three should have been. The row had not been struck through. The very bottom entry, dated that morning, was an AUDIT – NO CHANGE line with an empty COMBO/VERIFY cell; nothing newer had replaced the reset row.

The thumb-smudge had soaked the ink into a black oval, erasing the last three digits. But the pen had bitten deep. In the shifting glow of the ceiling strip—another pulse of light—the pressure grooves left in the paper surfaced, legible where the ink was not: **6-2-9**.

The full combination was **8-4-7-6-2-9**.

**7:44**

The status display read *76*. Seventy-six seconds remained before the keypad woke and allowed exactly one further attempt. Seven minutes and sixteen seconds remained until the security rotation completed and the guard’s boots returned to the vault. The safe stood twenty feet away; the return walk would cost twelve seconds, and the keypad would open again at **9:00**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**7:46**

The thief’s question cut through the server hum and was gone. Two seconds passed—half a cycle of the ceiling light’s four-second heartbeat—before the answer settled. There was no wall clock in the vault, no glowing digits on the cable trays or the racks. The only time that mattered was the count since the hydraulic seal and the appointment the guard’s boots kept at the end of the rotation.

Seven minutes and forty-six seconds had elapsed since the vault door sealed behind the thief. Across the floor, twenty feet away, the status display on the safe’s matte-black face had ticked down to *74*. Seventy-four seconds remained before the keypad would wake and accept another entry—the entry now legible in the pressure grooves of the smudged log sheet: **8-4-7-6-2-9**.

Seven minutes and fourteen seconds remained until the security rotation completed and the guard returned. The return walk to the safe would cost twelve seconds; leaving the rack now would put the thief at the keypad at **7:58**, with sixty-two seconds to wait before the pad went live at **9:00**. One attempt remained before the next failure would lock the safe until 17:00—two minutes after the guard’s boots returned—but the thief no longer needed to guess.

The clipboard hung in the thief’s hand, its aluminum edge cool, the ruled page trembling in the rack’s warm exhaust. The vent above the safe, the conduit chase along the left wall, and the dead keypad all waited. The ceiling light pulsed on.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Perfect." I make sure to quickly copy the code to a small pad I have. I then walk back to the safe, ready to input the new code.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**7:46**

The thief’s satisfaction was brief. The log sheet stayed gripped in one hand while the other dug into a pocket and came out with a small spiral-bound pad and a stub of pencil. Three seconds gone.

The sheet was pressed flat against the empty clipboard still hanging from the rack’s handle. Two seconds. Then the pencil moved: 8—4—7—6—2—9. Digits and dashes, written small but clear in the wavering light from the ceiling strip. Nine seconds for the sequence, and two more to scratch a label beneath it—VAULT–SAFE—so the numbers meant something later. The thief capped the pencil, pocketed pad and stub, and let the clipboard swing back against the rack. Fourteen seconds had passed.

**8:00**

Across the room, the status display had bled from *74* to *60*. Sixty seconds until the keypad woke. The thief turned from the rack and started back across the vault floor. The return walk cost the same twelve seconds it had on the way in—three pulses of the ceiling strip, the fourth beginning as the thief stopped in front of the safe. **8:12**. The matte-black face was dark, the keypad dead. The amber countdown read *48*.

Six minutes and forty-eight seconds remained until the security rotation completed and the guard’s boots returned to the vault.

The thief was ready to input the new code, but the safe would not accept it yet. The pad was dead until **9:00**. The combination waited in the small pad in the thief’s pocket and in the pressure grooves of the smudged log sheet: **8-4-7-6-2-9**. One attempt remained. A seventh failure would carry an eight-minute timeout, sealing the safe until 17:00—two minutes after the guard returned. The correct entry would end the lockout and drop the bolt.

The thief waited. The server racks breathed warm air and winking light. The ceiling strip pulsed its slow four-second heartbeat. One pulse. Another. The countdown ticked down: *44* at **8:16**, *36* at **8:24**—six minutes thirty-six seconds remained until the rotation completed—*24* at **8:36**, and *12* at **8:48**. Six minutes twelve seconds remained. Somewhere deeper in the building, a door closed, the sound small and far away beneath the server hum.

The ceiling light pulsed on.

**9:00**

The countdown reached zero. The keypad beeped once and woke, its surface live again, the status display clearing to a faint amber prompt. Six digits waited to be entered. One attempt remained before the penalty would double to eight minutes.

Six minutes remained until the security rotation completed and the guard’s boots returned to the vault. The thief stood before the safe, the combination **8-4-7-6-2-9** ready in hand and memory, and the pad’s first key waited to be pressed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Alright, let's get this done." I punch in the code: *8-4-7-6-2-9*. My fingers fly across the pad, trying to be fast but precise.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**9:00**

The thief's finger came down on the first key—**8**. The pad acknowledged with a muted click. **4**. **7**. Those three had come from the inside source and went in without a hitch. Then **6**, then **2**, and then the final **9**.

Fingers flying, the thief managed the six presses in roughly three seconds—half the deliberate pace of the earlier attempts. There was no stumble, no double-strike; every digit landed clean. The final **9** bottomed out under the thumb at **9:03**.

Then came the two-second pause. Two seconds of nothing but the server racks breathing and the ceiling light's slow heartbeat. The light pulsed once at **9:00**, washing the matte-black face pale; it pulsed again at **9:04**, right as the silence stretched.

At **9:05**, the bolt motor answered.

It did not give the dead thump of failure. It gave a solid, heavy **clunk**—the sound of the bolt retracting, steel drawing back into the door's frame rather than slamming home against a locked cam. The status LED did not flash red. It did not pulse amber. It ignited a steady, unambiguous **green**, the first green the safe had shown since the thief entered. A single crisp beep rang from the speaker grille, clean and final, not the triple-beep of an escalation.

The keypad's brief amber prompt cleared. No countdown ignited. The anti-brute-force logic found nothing to punish: the seventh attempt had not failed. Six failures were logged; there would be no seventh. The pad stayed live, but it no longer mattered.

The bolt was retracted. The safe was unlocked.

Through the matte-black face came no further argument. The handle, previously locked solid in its housing, now sat loose—free to turn, if the thief chose to turn it. The door held its seal, cold against the wall, but nothing locked it closed any longer. It would swing on its hinges with a pull, or part from the frame with a twist.

**9:05**

Nine minutes and five seconds had elapsed since the vault door sealed behind the thief. Five minutes and fifty-five seconds remained until the security rotation completed and the guard's boots returned to the vault.

The clipboard still hung from the fourth rack across the room, the access log fluttering faintly in the warm exhaust, the smudged row with the thumbprint still legible in memory. The combination **8-4-7-6-2-9** was also safe in the thief's pocket, written small in pencil. The useless pick kit hung at the thief's belt, forgotten.

The ceiling light pulsed on: one slow four-second heartbeat, then another at **9:08**. Time was moving again, and for the first time since the hydraulic hiss at 0:00, the thief was ahead of it.

The safe stood unlocked. The door waited to be opened. The contents inside were one pull away, and **5:55** remained on the clock.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Yes!" I can't help but whisper. *Finally.* I grasp the handle and pull the safe door open, quickly scanning for the document. "Time to grab and go."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**9:05**

The handle turned under the thief’s grip with no resistance at all. The bolt was already retracted; nothing held the door but its own weight and the cold seal of the vault. It parted from the frame with a soft exhale of refrigerated air and swung inward on hinges that made no sound. By **9:07** the mouth of the safe stood open, the interior exposed to the vault’s pulsing light.

Inside, a single brushed-steel shelf divided the space. The air that breathed out was stale and dry, colder even than the room. On the shelf lay a stack of three manila folders, a small black USB drive sealed in a static-shield bag, and a 9x12 clasp envelope stamped with a red *CLASSIFIED // VAULT CTRL* band. The thief’s gaze went first to the folders—no more than four seconds of scanning—reading the top tab: *COOLANT MAINTENANCE*. The second: *GUARD ROTATIONS – Q3*. Neither was it. The third folder was plain, unlabeled. Beneath the stack, the corner of a clear plastic sleeve jutted out, a single sheet inside.

Leaning in, the thief tracked the sleeve’s edge and read the header typed in stark black across the top of the page: *VAULT CTRL – EMERGENCY ACCESS AUTHORIZATION (ORIGINAL)*. That was the document they had come for.

The ceiling light pulsed at **9:08**—one slow four-second heartbeat after the door swung wide—and again at **9:12**. It pulsed a third time at **9:16**, washing the open safe in pale light as the thief’s eyes fixed on the sleeve. The scan was complete. The target document lay identified, half-tucked beneath the plain folder, its protective sleeve catching the glow.

**9:16**

Nine minutes and sixteen seconds had elapsed since the vault door sealed behind the thief. Five minutes and forty-four seconds remained until the security rotation completed and the guard’s boots returned to the vault. The clipboard still hung from the fourth rack across the room; the smudged access log had done its work. The combination 8-4-7-6-2-9 was safe in the thief’s pocket. The pick kit remained forgotten at their belt.

No alarm had answered the opening. No bolt had slammed home. The safe stood open, the emergency authorization document waiting, and the clock pulsed on: the next four-second heartbeat would come at **9:20**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Gotcha." I pull out the document, making sure to disturb nothing else, and quickly fold it, tucking it into a hidden pocket. I then gently close the safe door, not bothering to lock it. Time to get out.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**9:16**

The thief’s satisfied whisper had hardly faded when the hand reached into the open safe. The fingers found the clear sleeve where it jutted from beneath the plain folder. Rather than take the plastic protector, the thief gripped the single sheet’s exposed corner and drew the paper free. It came out with a faint rasp, leaving the empty sleeve lying flat in its place. Neither the manila stack nor the red-banded clasp envelope shifted; the USB drive in its static-shield bag sat untouched at the corner of the shelf. The extraction cost four seconds. The ceiling light pulsed its slow four-second heartbeat at **9:20**, and the single sheet was free in the thief’s hand.

Then it was folded—once, twice, into a compact rectangle small enough to vanish. Another four seconds passed. The fold was completed at **9:24**, the pulse washing pale light across the brushed-steel shelf and the still-open door. The folded packet went into the hidden pocket sewn inside the thief’s jacket, worked down flat against the ribs. Two seconds later, at **9:26**, it was secured. Nothing else in the safe had been disturbed. The folders remained stacked exactly as they had been; only the absent sheet marked the theft, and the empty sleeve lay as if sleeping beneath the plain folder.

**9:26**

The thief turned back to the safe. The door had stood open since **9:07**, the interior exposed to the vault’s cold air. The handle was still loose, the bolt still retracted, and the keypad still held its steady green—the safe did not care whether it was open or closed, only that it was unlocked. The thief took the handle and drew the door shut. It was a gentle motion, not a slam; the heavy slab swung in and met the frame with a soft exhale of refrigerated air. Because no lock had been engaged, the bolt did not extend, the handle did not seat, and the pad gave no further command. The door rested closed, unlocked, held shut only by its own weight and the cold gasket.

By **9:30** it was shut. The thief stood before the closed safe, the document secured against the ribs, the useless pick kit forgotten at the belt. No alarm had answered. The emergency authorization sheet was out of the vault’s hands and inside the thief’s, the combination 8-4-7-6-2-9 still written small in the pocket pad, and the clipboard still hanging from the fourth rack across the room with its access log fluttering faintly in the warm exhaust.

**9:30**

Nine minutes and thirty seconds had elapsed since the vault door sealed behind the thief. Five minutes and thirty seconds remained until the security rotation completed and the guard’s boots returned to the vault.

The ceiling light pulsed on: one slow four-second heartbeat, and the next would come at **9:32**. The safe stood closed but unlocked, its face dark save for that steady green. Across the vault, roughly twenty feet of floor separated the thief from the hydraulic entrance where they had first come in; the walk back would cost about ten seconds of soft-soled movement, past the server racks, the labeled fourth rack, and the conduit chase along the left wall. Somewhere deeper in the building, a door closed, small and far away beneath the server hum.

The thief had declared it time to get out. The next move was theirs.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *Phew.* I turn and head for the vault door, keeping an ear out for any new sounds. Almost home free.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**9:30**

The vault door stood twenty feet away across the cold floor. The thief turned from the closed safe, the folded document flat against their ribs, and started back. The movement was soft-soled and quick—ten seconds of crossing, no more. They passed the fourth rack with its clipboard still hanging, the access log fluttering faintly in the warm exhaust, the black cable running from the rack to the safe; past the rows of server racks breathing warm air and winking status light; past the conduit chase along the left wall. The useless pick kit bumped once at the thief’s belt, forgotten.

Keeping an ear out, the thief listened. The server racks hummed their seven-figure drone. A single LED on the fourth rack winked amber. Somewhere deeper in the building, the memory of that distant door at **8:48** had left no echo—no new closing, no footfall, no boot heel on tile. Only the pulse of the ceiling strip marked the passage: one slow four-second heartbeat at **9:32**, washing the floor pale; another at **9:36**.

**9:40**

Ten seconds of soft-soled movement put the thief in front of the vault door. The light pulsed again at **9:40**, the third since the thief had started back, bleaching the inner face of the slab for an instant.

The door was a mass of layered steel, featureless except for its center: a recessed four-spoke locking wheel, currently rotated to the sealed position, its spokes set in a vertical and horizontal cross. The bolts were thrown; the hub’s indicator burned a steady amber. To the right of the wheel, a narrow control panel bore a single guarded button under a clear cover and a small speaker grille—no keypad, no card reader. Exit from the inside was mechanical, or it was not at all. The wheel would have to be turned and the bolts retracted before the slab could swing.

Nine minutes and forty seconds had elapsed since the vault door first sealed behind the thief. Five minutes and twenty seconds remained until the security rotation completed and the guard’s boots returned to the vault. Across the room, the target safe stood closed but unlocked, its face dark save for the steady green LED. The hidden pocket held the folded emergency authorization sheet, stolen from that safe and secured against the thief’s ribs. The combination **8-4-7-6-2-9** was still written small in the pocket pad. The clipboard still hung from the fourth rack, its access log fluttering faintly in the warm exhaust.

The corridor beyond the door was silent. No alarm had answered the theft. No boot heel had sounded in the hall. The ceiling light pulsed on; the next slow heartbeat would come at **9:44**. The thief stood before the sealed way out, the document secure, and five minutes and twenty seconds left on the clock.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I examine the door panel. "Okay, so this is how I get out." I carefully flip up the guard and press the button.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's hands came off the lid — not fast, but with the studied calm of someone who definitely hadn't been doing anything.

"Interrupt what?" Arlo said. "I'm in a staring contest with a piano. Ten minutes in. The piano's winning, which reflects poorly on my competitive background."

Then, because there'd been an actual question under the question: "It's not weird. This room is weird every day — you'd just be adding to the ambient weirdness. There's a chair under that stack of method books. It's mostly load-bearing at this point, but it's yours."

The moment before the knock — whatever it had been — got folded up small and filed somewhere behind the ribs, where it could be dealt with later, or never. Standard procedure. Six years of standard procedure.

"And of course my mom told you where I was. She keeps a registry. I'm fairly sure there's a laminated card. Possibly a map with pins."

The sign-in sheet was still clipped to the corkboard by the door, Danny's name at the bottom with a 5:40 scrawled next to it — forty minutes early. The wall clock confirmed this with total indifference. Arlo did not look at either of them. Arlo was, in fact, looking at nothing with tremendous focus.

"Fair warning," Arlo said, picking up a pencil that had been sitting on the lid for no reason and relocating it to a drawer where it would never be found again, "I've been explaining quarter notes to seven-year-olds since three o'clock, so my conversational range is currently *enthusiastic* and *counting to four*. Adjust your expectations accordingly."

It was good to see Jun. That was the complication. It was harder to sit quietly in a room with someone who'd known you back before you'd learned how to arrange your face.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at it for one second, the way you look at a picture of a house you used to live in — from the sidewalk, hands in pockets, not going up the walk.

The photo had been on that shelf for four years. Ms. Okafor had put it there — *inspiration for the kids*, she'd said, delighted — and Arlo had assembled reasons not to move it: the shelf would look bare, the kids liked pointing at it, it was probably good for enrollment. A whole file of reasons. None of them was the real one, which was that taking it down meant agreeing, out loud, in a room with good acoustics, that it was over.

"God, the hair," Arlo said. "I had a stylist back then. An actual adult whose entire job was my hair. Her name was Yelena. She cared about that hair more than I've ever cared about anything, including the hair."

They leaned back against the closed lid.

"And the fridge — yeah, I made fridge status in a minimum of four households that I know of. It's the highest honor available to civilians. Your mom kept me up there for what, two years? Long enough to get layered. First a carpet-cleaning coupon moved in, then somebody's school photo, and eventually I'm full-time behind the takeout menus. Nobody ever takes a fridge photo down. It just gets absorbed."

Arlo heard that one land somewhere it hadn't been aimed.

Jun hadn't asked anything. That was the thing about Jun — never asked, just set a thing down on the table between you and let it sit there, getting warm. Arlo had watched the photo come off the shelf and felt the room tilt, one degree, and had spent the last ninety seconds leveling it back out by hand.

Arlo crossed the room and took the photo by the corner — gently, the way you handle something that might be either evidence or yours. Paris. The Salle Pleyel, probably, or the other one; they blur. Columns of stage light. The kid at the keyboard in white tie, twenty-two, face tipped down toward the keys, not looking at the camera. Not looking at anything. The kid looked calm.

Stage light is very forgiving. It's basically a filter.

"That kid thought the hard part was the playing," Arlo said, and heard one true sentence get out through the fence, and stepped on it immediately. "Also thought gel was a personality. Limited toolset, that kid."

Arlo set the photo back on the shelf, squared it to the edge, then turned it a few degrees so it faced the wall of method books instead of the room. Housekeeping. Then back to the bench: lid up, middle C pressed once — a single round drop of sound — lid down before it finished dying.

"Still in tune. So one thing went right today."

They nodded at the shelf, the room, the whole small kingdom of it. "Anyway, this is the natural habitat. I can show you where a raisin went into the middle register in September. Never found it. At this point it's load-bearing. Like the chair."

Somewhere behind the ribs, the filing cabinet took the last two minutes, folded them small, and shoved them in. The drawer stuck a little on the way shut. It had been doing that lately.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Your mom still talks about that photo, you know." *I slide into the chair, testing how load-bearing it really is.* "She said you were born to be on a stage." I eye the flipped photo. "Seems like she wasn't wrong."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Born to it," Arlo repeated, in the tone of someone weighing a coin they'd just been paid with. "The thing about being born to something is that nobody consults the baby. You arrive, the verdict's already in. Some aunt holding your hand up to the light going, *look at those fingers, that's a pianist's hand* — which is not a diagnosis anyone should be issuing to a four-hour-old. By the time you're old enough to have opinions, the opinion's framed and hung in the hallway. And disappointing a hallway is a skill nobody teaches you."

Arlo smoothed a place on the bench that didn't need smoothing.

"And yeah, she still talks about it. In her version I'm on an extended intermission. She tells the neighbors I'm 'taking a year.' It's been six years. That is a *very* confident year." A beat. "The year is my fault, technically. It's downstream of the travel thing. I said it once at a dinner — offhand, mouth full, barely a real sentence — and it went into the family record like a notarized document. It's been load-bearing ever since. Like the chair."

Their mother, of all people, had the strongest claim on the question, and had never once gotten to ask it, because Arlo had spent six years making sure there was nothing to ask.

"As for 'wasn't wrong'—" Arlo lifted the lid and laid both hands flat on the keys. Didn't press anything. Wrists level, shoulders low, twenty years of posture aimed at nothing — a porch light on in an empty house. "The wiring was real. That's the fine print. It doesn't expire. You cancel the tours, you donate the tails, you let the agent's calls ring through until the agent retires — and the hands keep the whole inventory. Everything I ever learned is still in there. Rent-free. It's a storage unit I pay for out of guilt."

They lowered the lid slowly, the way you close a door on someone sleeping.

A real sentence had started assembling behind all of that — one with actual weight to it, the kind that changes what a room is — and Arlo stepped on it before it got anywhere near the fence. Six years of practice; they were fast. But the drawer stuck on the way shut this time, and wouldn't seat all the way, and whatever was in there was taking up more room than it used to.

"A kid asked me about that photo last month. Pointed right at it. 'Is that your dad?' No. 'Then who is it?' And I heard myself say, 'A guy I used to know.' He accepted that completely and went back to drawing a piano with eleven keys. Children have the correct amount of curiosity. It's restful."

Arlo stood, and the bench scraped, and the room went back to being a room.

"And she wasn't wrong in the way she means it, either. I'm on a stage every day. Lower ceiling. The audience draws on the pianos. Last week one of them paid me in a drawing of a cat in a bow tie, which is now the best review I've ever received, and I have received reviews."

They nodded toward the hall. "You never got your actual answer, by the way. Hanging out — not weird. It's the most normal thing that's happened in this room since September. There's a coffee machine down there with one setting, which is 'on,' and the cleanest mug in the cabinet says WORLD'S OKAYEST GRANDPA. So — stay. Tell me something normal. I've been counting to four since three o'clock. I could use the other numbers."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "World's Okayest Grandpa, huh?" *I chuckle, getting up to follow them.* "Sounds like a high bar for normal, but I'll try." I pause at the doorway, "So, how many keys did that cat-drawing kid's piano have?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Two different kids," Arlo said, locking the piano room behind them out of habit — the only thing in there worth stealing was the raisin, and the raisin had tenure. "You've merged my children. That's how legends start. Give it a year and it's one kid who drew a cat playing an eleven-key piano, and by spring he'll have a tragic backstory and a scholarship fund."

The hallway at six had its own weather — floor wax, chlorine drifting over from the pool, the particular hush of a building whose kids had all gone home. Arlo walked it like their own kitchen, straightening a crooked flyer on the corkboard in passing. SPRING RECITAL, MAY 16, glitter, and at the bottom a line that said SPECIAL PERFORMANCE: ______, still blank. Arlo's eyes went over that line the way you skip a stair in the dark. Smoothly. From practice.

"The eleven-key piano belongs to Marcus. Same kid who thought the photo was my dad — he's having a big month. I did attempt to educate him, it's my entire job, so I told him pianos have eighty-eight keys. And he looked up at me with the weary pity of someone who has seen the world, and said his piano had to fit in his backpack."

Arlo let that one sit for the length of a few floor tiles.

"Eleven keys. Fits in a backpack. He never asked whether he was doing it wrong — that didn't come up for him, not for one second. He just made the piano that fit the page, played it, and put it away."

A sentence had started assembling itself behind all of that — something about the boy never once considering not playing — and Arlo stepped on it before it got anywhere near the fence. Old reflex. Though the drawer stuck on its way shut this time, and stayed stuck a beat longer than usual, and Arlo filed that, too.

"The cat's a different artist entirely. Priya, six, works exclusively in marker. No piano in her piece — just the cat, bow tie, seated at nothing, looking at the viewer like he's about to make an announcement. Name written underneath in the handwriting of someone who just learned handwriting: KEVIN. I asked if Kevin was a performer. She said, no, he's fancy. Which is the correct distinction, and frankly more than most critics ever managed."

The coffee machine lived at the end of the hall and had been on since eight a.m., which was the only setting it understood. What it produced wasn't coffee so much as coffee's memory of coffee. Arlo poured two anyway, gave Jun the WORLD'S OKAYEST GRANDPA mug — the clean one, the honor — and kept the chipped one that said nothing at all. A mug that had given up.

Then Arlo leaned against the wall with the mug in both hands, and for the first time since the knock, wasn't managing anything. Shoulders down. The quiet in the hands was just quiet.

"Okay. Your turn. Normal — I want the boring stuff. Traffic. A sandwich that let you down. A coworker with a mug habit.
