I've been counting to four since three o'clock and I would honestly love to hear what happens past five." A beat. "And when you leave, tell my mom you found me where the registry said. She likes the pins accurate."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo followed the gesture to the corkboard by the coffee machine, where the practice sheets actually lived — a grid of sticker charts in crayon signatures, curling at the corners, one coffee-ringed from its position under the machine's slow drip. Marcus had awarded himself a sticker for "listening to piano in my head," which Arlo had let stand, since it was technically practice.

"Yeah. They do," Arlo said, and for one second it sat there plain, no armor on it, before the armor came back on. "I notice you skipped the sandwich, by the way. I ask for traffic, a coworker, a lettuce-based betrayal — and you hand me a review. 'The kids seem to like you.' Four stars. Would teach again." A sip of the coffee, which was terrible with total reliability. "That's my mother's move. She does it too. Never asks. Just sets the thing on the counter and leaves the kitchen. It's a good technique. I'm not going to tell you what it's doing to me."

Arlo's thumb found the chip in the mug and stayed there.

"Kids like me for market reasons. I lose to them with full commitment — the falling-down kind. Priya beat me to the water fountain Tuesday and I haven't recovered, competitively or emotionally. And Danny—" Arlo nodded back down the hall, toward the locked room, the sign-in sheet, the 5:40. "Danny's been arriving forty minutes early for three months. Doesn't practice. Sits on the load-bearing chair and watches me open up. Lights, cover, the metronome getting wound. To him that's the overture."

A lifeguard's whistle went off somewhere past the pool doors, distant and echoing, and died.

"I let him go twenty minutes early today. He stood in the doorway doing the math on it — he's nine, he knows exactly what twenty minutes is. I told him I had admin." A beat. "There's never been admin. There's a sign-in sheet and a raisin."

Arlo looked at the sticker charts. Somewhere in there was the thing they were not going to say — about why the kid who arrives early got sent home early, about what it's like to be watched opening the instrument by someone with full attention and nothing in it. No verdict. Nobody in this hallway had decided how good Arlo was supposed to be. That was the entire architecture of the place.

"Anyway, they like me because I'm the guy who finds the raisin," Arlo said, which was not the sentence that had been assembling, and both of them probably knew it. Behind the ribs, the drawer wouldn't shut — something in there had shifted, was leaning back against the door — and Arlo had to put the whole weight of the afternoon on it before it seated. Barely.

Their eyes caught on the flyer on the way past. The glitter. The blank line at the bottom. For once they didn't skip the stair — just stood on it a moment. Ms. Okafor had asked three times, very gently, about the *refreshments*, and then the *program*, with enormous patience. She thought it was a formatting question.

It was not a formatting question.

Arlo pushed off the wall. "Come on. I still have the keys — I'll show you Kevin before the building closes. It's a limited engagement." They started back down the hall. "And then you owe me the sandwich story. Something with lettuce that failed a person. I've been on fours since three o'clock. I need to hear what a six even looks like."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Okay, okay, the sandwich. It was a BLT, but the 'L' was basically an afterthought, you know?" *I follow Arlo down the hall, taking a big gulp of the terrible coffee.* "Like, two limp pieces of something green that might have once been lettuce, barely clinging to life."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Two pieces." Arlo turned and walked the last stretch of hallway backward, coffee cup raised like a gavel, because a verdict of this gravity deserved eye contact. "That's not an L. An L implies participation. That lettuce didn't cling to life, it *waived* it. What you got was the estate. And the bacon has to just carry it — I've been in ensembles like that."

Arlo laughed — a real one, short, surprised out of them, the first since three o'clock.

"Thank you. Genuinely. That's a five, maybe a five-and-a-half, which is past four, as ordered." A beat, and then the thing that was true under it, said at walking speed so it couldn't be examined: "Nobody tells you sandwich stories at that level, it turns out. You get 'the hall was pleased' and a car to the airport. Six years of sandwiches — that's the part nobody puts on the fridge."

The key stuck in the lock, the way it did, and Arlo talked it through the turn. Inside, the room was exactly as they'd left it — the photo still faced the method books. Arlo left it that way.

"Kevin," they said, museum voice, one hand flat at the drawing taped above the keyboard. "Marker on paper. Priya, six. Note the bow tie, the direct address, the total absence of any instrument. Seated at nothing, and completely ready. I've stood on real stages with less going on behind the eyes." Delivered fast, already turning away. "And since you're here — the full catalogue."

Arlo sat, lifted the lid, and gave the room the complete professional repertoire: middle C, then the neighbors, evenly spaced, round as stones into a well. *One. Two. Three. Four.* "That's the product. Some days we say 'and REST,' and the rest is the popular part."

"But you asked about the backpack model." The hands settled and came back with a small tune — built inside eleven keys and not one more, a thing with a beginning, a middle, and an end, finished inside fifteen seconds. It was a small thing and it was whole. Nothing stood outside it wanting more. And the hands — which kept the whole inventory, which paid rent on all eighty-eight — liked it anyway. Possibly liked it more.

Then the left hand, unsupervised, started up the keyboard. Old habit. Looking for the other seventy-seven keys and everything filed in them. Arlo caught it a half-second late and brought it back down and set it in its lap.

The fallboard went down quietly. The room was just the room again — chlorine drift, hallway hum, Kevin making his announcement to no one.

"There's a recital in May," Arlo said, to the fallboard more than to Jun. "The kids play. Folding chairs. Somebody always cries, and it's never a kid. There's a line at the bottom of the flyer — *special performance,* and then a blank. Ms. Okafor's asked me about it three times, very gently. She thinks I'm picking a font."

A beat.

"It's not the font."

Arlo stood. Squared the bench. Reached for the usual joke and found the shelf lighter than expected — came back with: "Tell my mom the year's going great," which was technically a joke and did not function as one.

"May sixteenth. Come. Priya's promised a world premiere, Kevin-related. Danny will be forty minutes early. Best show in town, tickets are free, all the performers are nine."

Behind the ribs, the drawer didn't even pretend to shut this time. Arlo stopped pushing and just leaned on the door — which was new — and filed that, too, in the drawer that wouldn't close.

"Now keep going. Sandwiches, traffic, anything. I'm six years behind on normal and I'm trying to catch up in one evening."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "May sixteenth, huh?" *I hum, looking at the flyer.* "I'll see what I can do. I've got some vague plans with my cousin that weekend, but Kevin sounds like a hard act to follow." *I take another sip of coffee, making a face.* "So, traffic. The 405 was a nightmare this morning. Took me an hour to go five miles."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Five miles in an hour," Arlo said, with a delight that had no business being about traffic. "That's five miles an hour. That's *walking.* You were sealed inside a machine engineered to do a hundred and forty, flanked by ten thousand identical machines, and the combined achievement of the species was a stroll. You could have gotten out and walked, and you'd have beaten your own car there — just stood at the end of it, watching it arrive. Marcus gets to school faster than that, and Marcus stops for worms."

"Was there a reason? I need the reason. Construction doesn't count — construction is the road being honest with you. A mattress, though. A mattress means somebody up ahead had a day end worse than yours, and there's real comfort in that." A beat. "And was there a podcast? Don't— no, do tell. I've heard of those. People describe them to me and I nod like I have a life. Six years of my traffic news came from airport cars, and that's not traffic, it's a queue with delusions. This is better. This is the real thing."

"I'm keeping score now, by the way, so you know: sandwich, five. The 405, seven — seven and a half if there was a mattress. I'm trying to see the whole scale tonight."

The vague cousin plans, Arlo let sit where they'd landed. Correct RSVP for a folding-chair economy. "Tell your cousin who he's up against, though. A six-year-old with a marker and a nine-year-old who arrives forty minutes early to everything. If he's smart, he'll rehearse."

The maybe went in with everything else. Which was fair, really. Arlo had dressed the invitation down to nothing — *best show in town, tickets are free* — and a nothing-sized ask comes back a maybe. That was the trouble with disguises: things came back the size of the disguise.

Down the hall, the janitor's cart announced itself, one squeaking wheel — the building's version of last call. Arlo drained the last of the terrible coffee and left the chipped mug in the sink, where mugs that had given up belonged, then killed the piano room light. Kevin went dark mid-announcement. "Goodnight, Kevin," Arlo said, and locked the door on him.

At the outside door, keys out, the left hand started up on its own. Not counting to four this time — a fingering, walking some old phrase against the doorframe, something with a stretch in it, no piano within a hundred feet. Six years of catching it at the wrist, and this once Arlo just watched it go. Four notes, six, whatever it wanted. Then it played itself out and settled back into being a hand. Nothing got filed. The drawer was open now; things just fell in.

"Hand does that," Arlo said, pushing the door open onto the lot — down to its last few cars, the streetlights with the block to themselves. "It keeps its own social calendar. I've stopped asking where it goes."

"Building's closed. The raisin's unsupervised till morning — it's earned the trust. But there's a diner two blocks that way, open late, where the lettuce arrives in quantity. Structural lettuce. The L is the headliner." Arlo pocketed the keys, a whole ring of them, small kingdom, small jangle. "You could tell me about the cousin. And the mattress. And whatever the podcast was.

"I go back to fours at three o'clock tomorrow. I want to see what an eight looks like first."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Somewhere in the middle of the diner pitch, Arlo's legs made an independent decision — the left hand had been doing it for years; apparently the legs kept their own calendar too — and sat down on the bench by the entrance. Then Jun sat down beside them, and the rest of the pitch expired quietly, out of respect.

The bench had a plaque, brass gone green at the edges: IN MEMORY OF RUTH, WHO LOVED THIS SPOT. The spot was a parking lot. Arlo had never settled whether Ruth had low standards or excellent ones.

"I asked for an eight," Arlo said, after a while. Quietly. "You went and found the thing there's no number for. That's showing off."

A last car found its lights and went. The building ticked as it cooled, settling its accounts. The chlorine was gone out here — just night air, asphalt giving up its heat, one streetlight with the whole block to itself.

Arlo's hands sat in their lap, doing nothing. Not counting. Not fingering some old phrase against a knee. Just hands — the storage unit with the lights off, nobody at the desk. It took them a while to believe it. Six years of reaching for keys that weren't there, and now nothing, and the nothing holding.

"This is the rest, by the way," Arlo said. "I tell the kids that. *And REST.* Nobody believes the rest is part of the song until they're inside one."

The quiet stretched out, and Arlo noticed something about it, which was that it wasn't the other kind. Alone-quiet was a held breath with a count running underneath — fours, always fours, waiting for the downbeat, the door, the next thing to manage. This was just quiet. There was attention in it and nothing else, no verdict anywhere — the thing Danny came forty minutes early for. It had never once occurred to Arlo that it came in adult sizes.

Behind the ribs, the drawer stood open, and for whole minutes at a stretch, nothing got filed. The contents just lay there in the dark, unmanaged, and — this was new information — it didn't hurt. It was only heavy. Those turned out to be different things.

"You never asked," Arlo said eventually. To the parking lot, mostly. "Six years. My mother turned not-asking into a project. You just never asked. I've started to thank you for it maybe two hundred times, and stopped every time, because a thank-you confirms there's something to thank you for." A small laugh, no humor in it, just the shape of one. "So. The shape of that sentence. Not the contents. The shape."

The silence didn't change, and Arlo let it keep doing whatever it was doing.

The building sat dark behind them — one window back there was the piano room's, Kevin mid-announcement in the black, the corkboard with its glitter, its flyer, its blank.

"May sixteenth," Arlo said. "I told you the blank line wasn't a font question." A pause long enough to fit a whole phrase in. "If I ever fill it in — it won't be Paris. It won't be the eighty-eight. It'd have to fit the line. Eleven keys. A beginning, a middle, an end, done inside fifteen seconds. Something small enough to finish."

It came out at walking speed, the way the true ones did, and for once Arlo didn't step on it. Just let it stand out there in the streetlight with them, getting warm.

"Don't tell my mother any of that. She'll laminate something. Move a pin."

And then nothing, for a while. The streetlight hummed. Ruth's bench held. Three o'clock tomorrow there would be fours again — quarter notes, sticker charts, the whole small kingdom — but out here nothing was being counted, and as far as Arlo could remember, nothing had gone uncounted in six years.

Somewhere in the dark behind them, Kevin went on making his announcement to nobody.

Out here, nobody needed one.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I lean my head back against the cool brick of the building, just listening.* "She won't get it from me."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Good," Arlo said. "Because you should know what you're up against. She once got my entire Paris itinerary out of my agent — a man who was being *paid*, specifically, to say nothing. She brought a casserole and left with eleven cities. Somewhere in Langley there's a laminated card about her."

Then, quieter, because the evening had developed a policy about true things escaping at walking speed: "She'll know something anyway, though. She reads me like a chart — first pass, no annotations. She'll hear that the key changed. She just won't know what it changed to." A beat. "Which is still the most she's gotten in six years, so don't feel bad for her. It's a personal best."

Arlo's thumb found the green edge of Ruth's plaque and traced it once, the way you check the binding on an old book.

"I've settled the Ruth question, by the way, in case you were holding your breath. Excellent standards. It took the whole evening and one sitting on the bench, but the ruling's in. The woman knew a spot when she sat on one."

The thank-you, when it finally came out, came out disguised, because that was the only way it cleared the fence:

"Thanks for the sandwich. And the traffic. I asked for an eight and you kept producing things that ran off the scale entirely — you should know that's the best score anyone's posted against me in six years. The lettuce alone carried it." A small pause. "That's all I'm going to say about that. The shape of it, anyway."

The diner two blocks over kept its structural lettuce and its light on for somebody else's night. "Some other time," Arlo said. "Turns out being six years behind on normal costs nothing. Nobody's keeping tempo. I checked."

And then, because the evening had one more thing in it and the thing was small and it fit: Arlo's left hand — off its leash since the doorframe, unsupervised for going on an hour now — lifted and played the backpack tune against the bench slats. Knuckles on wood, barely sound at all. Eleven keys' worth of tune, if wood had keys. A beginning, a middle, an end, done inside fifteen seconds. And afterward the hand didn't go looking for the other seventy-seven. It had somewhere to be, apparently, and it was here. It settled back down and stayed.

"That's the whole catalogue," Arlo said. "It ends where it ends. That's the entire gimmick."

The streetlight hummed. The building ticked as it cooled, closing out its accounts. Somewhere behind them, in the dark, Kevin went on making his announcement to nobody.

"No promises on the blank line," Arlo said at last. "But if it ever gets filled in — you'll hear it from me. Before the registry. Before the pins move. You're currently one of three entities who know, and the other two are a raisin and a drawing of a cat, so the company's less select than it sounds."

Arlo stayed on the bench. Hands in their lap, off duty, no social calendar between them. The night wasn't being counted either.

It could go long.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I finally take a deep breath, the tension I didn't realize I was holding releasing slowly.* "I'll take it. Better company than a few people I know." I shift on the bench, looking up at the stars starting to appear. "You know, Ruth had a good point. This is a pretty great spot."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Careful," Arlo said. "The other members are a raisin with tenure and a cat whose entire stated position is *fancy*. The bar is underground. You cleared it in street clothes."

"But — that's two judges, same ruling. That's a concurrence. Ruth's spot is legally great as of tonight, and if anyone ever challenges it, we cite the bench."

Arlo followed Jun's gaze up, half a beat late, the way you follow someone into a key change.

Stars. More of them than a parking lot had any business with, coming through at the edges of the streetlight's jurisdiction, patient about it.

"Huh," Arlo said. That was the whole review.

Then, at walking speed, because the evening had developed a policy:

"You know what you don't get, all those years? This. Hotel curtains are the industry's proudest achievement — blackout, floor to ceiling, darkness to order. That's what the fee actually buys. Planes want the shade down for the movie. Buses at night run on orange. Six years of professionally managed ceilings. Nobody puts a sky on the itinerary."

Arlo's hand left their lap on its own recognizance, gestured at all of it — upward, the whole uncounted inventory — and came back down.

"And the thing about this light is that nobody aimed it. Stage light is aimed; that's the entire job description. Somebody in a booth points it at you and decides what you are — warm, cold, featured, in the way. This stuff left home before the piano was invented and does not care what it lands on. First lighting design I've ever sat under where I'm not in the plot."

Somewhere in the building a compressor shut off, and the night got one notch quieter, and the quiet held. Arlo clocked — six years of reflex — that the set of Jun's shoulders had come down somewhere in the last while, and started to file the observation, and stopped. Stopped reaching for the file at all. Things just fell in the open drawer tonight, unmanaged, and it kept turning out they could.

The real sentence was in there too. The one with the weight on it — the one that would have changed what a room was. It had finished assembling itself somewhere between Paris and this parking lot, and it stood fully built, patient, not going anywhere. Arlo looked at it. Didn't step on it. Didn't say it, either. It had waited six years; waiting was the one thing it was good at. Some other night. With warning. At walking speed.

Tonight it was enough that it was out of the drawer — and that somebody was sitting next to it.

"If the registry asks," Arlo said, "the pin goes here. Ruth's spot. Give her the credit — she found it first."

The building ticked through its accounts behind them. In the dark of the piano room, Kevin kept his announcement going, to nobody, and out here nobody needed one. The streetlight hummed.

Arlo had told the kids a hundred times — *and REST* — and no seven-year-old alive believes the rest is part of the song until they're inside one.

Arlo was inside one. It was holding.

The night went long, and nobody counted it.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile, leaning my head further back.* "Ruth had good taste then." I finally turn my head to look at Arlo. "Guess that makes us honorary members of her fan club."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"*Honorary,*" Arlo said, with the mild offense of somebody being undercharged. "You've kept the bylaws for six years without once seeing them written down. That's not honorary. That's founder. The raisin and Kevin are grandfathered — they were here first. I'm the treasurer. There's no money. There was never any money. I'm also refreshments, and there are no refreshments, and I will defend that tradition with my life."

"The whole constitution fits on a napkin, for the record. Rule one: dues are one sandwich story per meeting, lettuce content enforced. Rule two: no laminating, non-negotiable. Rule three—" and this one came out at walking speed, like the rest of tonight's true ones, "—nobody asks. You've been the only perfect compliance on the books. It's why the position is yours."

Arlo's thumb found the green edge of the plaque again.

"And know what you're a fan of. Ruth's complete surviving works: one bench, one stated preference. No recordings. No interviews. No scandal. She liked a spot, and the spot has now outlasted—" Arlo let the beat be a beat "—plenty of things that had better publicity. Vertical monuments come down eventually. Ruth went horizontal and load-bearing. I'm noticing a pattern tonight: everything that's ever actually held me up turned out to be modest and load-bearing. I've decided to let the pattern stand."

Then, in the tone of someone entering evidence:

"Item for the minutes. I don't know what time it is." Reported the way you'd report a rare bird. "Six years, I always knew the time. Downbeats, call times, departure boards, the countdown before house lights. Right now — nothing. Could be nine, could be past midnight. It's the most disoriented I've been all year and the steadiest at the same time, and this morning I'd have sworn those were two different things."

Eventually the night made its one polite demand: there were threes o'clock in both their tomorrows. Arlo stood, and the keys came out of the pocket with their small jangle. Before leaving, two knuckles on the bench's backrest, soft — the same courtesy Kevin had gotten.

"Goodnight, Ruth. The ruling stands. We'll hold the spot."

"Mine's the car that smells like crayon and unmet potential — you'll know it. Tuesdays and Thursdays I'm here till six; after that the bench is on its own, and it's proven it can manage. And the diner stands. Some other time. Lettuce like that doesn't wander off — it has tenure."

A few steps into the lot, Arlo stopped.

"If the registry asks, the pin's accurate. It just acquired a fan club."

And then the walk to the cars, the left hand off duty since the doorframe and staying that way — no phrase against a thigh, no reach for the other seventy-seven, just a hand going home with nothing on its calendar — and overhead, unhurried, nobody aiming any of it, the stars kept arriving, taking the whole night about it.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in.* "Sounds like a club I can get behind. Especially the no-laminating rule." *I push myself off the bench, stretching.* "Lead the way, treasurer. My car smells like old coffee and questionable life choices, so at least we'll be symmetrically scented."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't turn around right away. Their hands stayed flat on the closed lid, and for a moment the room held that particular kind of quiet — the kind that happens when somebody catches you doing nothing.

"Interrupt what?" They turned then, one arm hooking over the backrest of the bench. "I was teaching a masterclass in sitting. Very advanced. Sold out for weeks."

They got up before the silence could get any ideas, crossing to the stack of chairs against the wall. Small ceremonies of looking busy: nudging the metronome an inch left on the shelf, straightening a tub of rhythm sticks that didn't need straightening.

"It's good to see you." That came out plainer than they'd planned, so they buried it fast, setting a chair near the window. "Fair warning — everything in here is built for eight-year-olds. If your knees end up somewhere around your ears, that's just the authentic community center experience."

They leaned against the piano, arms crossed. Not touching the lid. Next to it.

"Also, if any kid's mother asks, I definitely did not send my last student home fifteen minutes early. We were deep in solfège. Rigorous stuff." A beat. "Her hamster died, allegedly. You negotiate a lot of hamster grief in this line of work."

That got close to something, the way the small stuff always did, so Arlo pointed a finger at Jun like it was an accusation.

"And before you get comfortable — yes, my mom gave you this address, and no, I don't know what she's up to. Though with her it's never nothing." They tipped their head at the tiny chair. "So sit. And tell me what she sent you here to fix."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the photo the way you look at a word you've spelled too many times.

"God, the jacket." They uncrossed their arms just to cross them again. "Someone at the label picked it. I hated it. Twenty-two and still learning that *no* was a whole sentence. So."

They crossed the room and took the frame from Jun's hands, careful, the way you handle something borrowed. Their thumb made one slow circuit of the frame — dusting that wasn't dusting — and then the photo went back on its shelf, turned a few degrees so it faced the wall instead of the room.

Another small ceremony.

"Your mom put it on the fridge?" A breath of a laugh, real enough at the edges. "Above or below the grocery list? Be honest. I want to know where I peaked."

Then, before anything could settle:

"Save us the round trip. I got tired of the travel." Flat. Word for word. A recording of themselves played at the correct speed. "That's the official version. Comes pre-laminated."

The joke landed on the floor between them and stayed there, unclaimed. Arlo's jaw did something small.

"The travel was fine, actually." Quieter. Aimed somewhere near the shelf. "Trains were—"

They reached over and clicked the metronome on. Tick. Tick. Tick. Steady, indifferent, filling the space like it had been waiting for the job.

"Sorry. I think better at sixty a minute."

They sat down on the bench — *the* bench, hands on their knees, nowhere near the lid — and looked at Jun properly for the first time since the door.

"Anyway. Fridge era's concluded." They tipped their head toward the photo, which was studying the wall with great interest. "Out with it. What's she got you down here to fix this time?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch them put the photo face to the wall.* "She didn't send me." *I pick up the rhythm sticks and tap them together, softly, to the metronome's beat.* "I was in town anyway. Thought I'd say hi."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
For a moment the only sounds were the metronome and the sticks, agreeing with each other.

"Nobody sent you." Arlo repeated it slowly, the way you check a receipt for an error. "You were *in town.* And you came here. On purpose."

Something crossed their face and got filed before it could be identified.

"Huh." Arms unfolded, folded again. "That's either very sweet or a hostage situation I haven't been briefed on."

Then — they were watching Jun's hands. The sticks rose and fell at sixty a minute, unbothered, like rhythm was just a thing you could hold in your hands in a dusty room on a Tuesday. Arlo watched a full measure of it. Two.

Then their palms came down on the closed lid. Soft. On the offbeats. The wood made a dry, round sound, and Arlo's hands kept it going — not playing, exactly. Percussion. A loophole they'd apparently already found the edges of.

"Careful. This is a gateway activity." They didn't look up. "We do this with the six-year-olds. 'Finding the steady beat.' Half of them just eat the sticks. The rest go on to real instruments and occasional greatness." A beat. "You're ahead of the curve. No biting."

The tick and the tap and the clack held together, easy as anything.

"For the record, nobody is 'in town anyway.'" They were looking at their hands, or the lid, or the wall the photo was facing. "People have errands. Destinations. Motives. 'Anyway' is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence, and I'd like to speak to its supervisor."

Quieter, almost lost under the metronome:

"It's good, though. This. Someone else keeping time. Means I could—"

The sentence stopped. Their hands didn't.

"There's a vending machine down the hall," they said instead, standing. "Sells something technically classified as a beverage. If you're staying. Which — apparently you are. Unsupervised."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I stop tapping the sticks and put them down.* "I'm staying." *I stand up too.* "What kind of technically-a-beverage? We talking soda or... fruit juice?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Yes," Arlo said.

A beat.

"Both. Neither. It's a spectrum." They fished a keyring out of their pocket — more keys than the building had doors, probably — and held the classroom open with their hip. "There's a cola that's just called *Cola.* Generic to the point of philosophy. There's the orange juice, which contains one molecule of orange and a great deal of legal confidence. And there's the cappuccino slot, lower left. Sold out since spring. Button still shows a picture of one, though. Foam and everything. I find it restful to look at."

They stepped into the hallway first, then immediately stepped aside to let Jun through, a small motion they didn't explain, and took the side nearest the wall.

The corridor wore the center's greatest hits: paper snowflakes in July, a swim-class sign-up, a crayon horse that had clearly witnessed something. Arlo nodded at it without slowing.

"That one's Maya's. She's seven and has already informed me I'm old. The horse is about that." And on the way past the bulletin board, without breaking stride, they pressed one curled corner of the spring recital flyer flat against the cork. Kept walking.

The machine lived at the end of the hall under light that made everything look like evidence. It hummed, low and constant, and Arlo's head tilted toward it for half a second — something internal doing arithmetic — before they let it go.

They fed it two quarters and a dollar bill it rejected on principle. Arlo turned the bill over and resubmitted it with the weary authority of long negotiation.

"You get to know each other," they said. "It has opinions about which way Washington faces." The machine began its slow grind. Arlo leaned a shoulder against it. "So pick your poison, but choose like it's permanent. Whatever you press becomes *your* drink. It remembers. I've been drinking the same lies for four years."

The can clunked down. Arlo retrieved it and held it out — then didn't quite let go.

"For the record, this is the longest conversation I've had on a Tuesday that didn't involve the word *practice.*" A breath. "That's a data point, not a complaint."

Their eyes came up.

"Meanwhile, you've dodged three interrogations for free, and I run a budget here. So. 'In town anyway.' From the inside. Job? Person? Fleeing your mother?" A tilt of the head. "Give me something. I need to tell my mom her plan worked, or she'll only try harder."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Ah." Arlo reclaimed the can and held it up like a stop sign. "No. No, that was — *wow.*"

They let the hallway hum fill in for a second.

"'The kids seem to like you.' Compliment, pivot, no follow-up required. Textbook." A slow, professional nod. "I teach that technique, you know. Thursdays. Advanced deflection, eight and up. We're very rigorous."

Then, because fair was fair, they cracked the can and took the small defeat with it. *Cola.* Tasted like a rumor of cola.

"The kids like me because I'm an easy grader." They drifted back toward the classroom — the metronome still going inside, sixty a minute, faithful as anything — and gathered the practice sheets off the bench one-handed. "That, and I write all the music myself. The books are soul-killing. Nobody needs their fourth 'Hot Cross Buns' of the year, so I make them things. Easy things. Things with only good notes in them."

Back inside, they dropped the stack on the piano and squared the edges while they talked. Top sheet: a waltz, handwritten, marked *for Maya — SLOW. It's not a race.*

"Stickers are rigged, by the way. Everybody gets some. Half for practicing." Sheet. "Half for coming back anyway." Sheet. "The economy's inflating like mad. It's a wonder the currency's worth anything."

Then, still looking at the papers:

"House rule for recitals. Duets only. Nobody gets up there alone — not for anything. Two at the bench, always. It was built for two. That's the entire design. Everything else is policy." A breath. "Costs me—"

The stack got one more tap. Very precise.

"Paperwork," they finished. "It costs me paperwork."

They turned around and raised the can — a toast this time, to something unnamed.

"So here's the arrangement. You tell me your 'anyway' when it's ready. I'll be right here, not telling you mine. We'll call it even." A beat. "To hamsters. Allegedly."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch them with the sheets, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Okay, even." *I glance at the wall where the photo of them is still turned around.* "So, when's the next recital?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"A question with an actual answer in it. Give me a second." Arlo took a drink of the cola like it was a job requirement. "Three weeks. Second Saturday of August, seven o'clock, in the gym, which doubles as the cafeteria, so brace for basketball hoops. The flyer in the hall is the spring one — the cork refuses to surrender it. New one goes up Thursday."

Their hands found the stack of sheets and began squaring it again, though it was already square.

"Maya's debuting her waltz. She's been told it's not a race. She has decided it's a race. Every recital's a race. We've made peace with it." A beat. "Program's one page, typed. Everything in C major. Mercy is a curriculum."

Then, still watching the papers:

"You heard the policy. Duets only — no soloists, no exceptions. I take secondo on every piece. The plain half. Root notes, oom-pah, all floor, no chandelier." They turned the top sheet over as they said it. Maya's waltz went face-down on the stack, the same way the photo had, and Arlo's hands didn't seem to register that they'd voted. "Turns out I like the floor."

One tick of the metronome passed.

"Used to be a teachers' number at the end. Solo. I cut it a few summers back — shorter program, everyone's home before dark. Nobody's complained. Most popular edit I ever made."

They looked up then, and there was something almost Easy about it, which was how you could tell it wasn't.

"You could come. If. It's forty-one folding chairs, a PA from the Carter administration, and somebody's cousin always cries during the group number. Nothing happens at these." A breath. "That's the whole design."

Arlo reached over and clicked the metronome off. The silence had a different shape than before — smaller, more indoors.

"And you'd be the first person from—"

They stopped.

"—out of town. In a while. To see the room." The keyring came out of their pocket, got turned over once, went back. "Anyway. Attendance's optional. Chairs wobble. I won't know either way — I'll be busy holding down the floor."

They reclaimed the cola and pointed it at Jun like a gavel.

"And don't think 'when's the next recital' settles your debt. Recital questions are free. The 'anyway' stands."

A pause. Then, quieter, almost offhand:

"Second Saturday. Seven. Back row, if you come. Clap for Maya — she'll be counting. She counts everything."

Arlo looked at the closed lid, then away.

"Gets it from somewhere."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch them turn Maya's sheet over. It's subtle, but I notice it.* "I'll be there. And I'll bring the good kind of orange juice." *I smile, a little sad, but genuine.* "And I'll clap for Maya."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let that sit for exactly as long as it wanted to.

Their hand drifted toward the metronome — stopped an inch short — came back. First time all day.

Then they crossed to the piano and turned Maya's waltz face-up again. Squared the edges like it mattered. Which it did.

"She checks," they said, to the sheet. "Face-down means *lost,* to a seven-year-old. Everything face-down is lost. She'd organize a search party." They did not look at the photo, still facing its wall, and the not-looking was very loud.

"Don't do the face, by the way." They aimed the can vaguely at Jun's smile without looking directly at it. "The sad-genuine one. My students deploy that before every festival. It's devastating, it works, and that's precisely why it's banned."

They dug through the drawer and came up with masking tape and a pencil stub. Tore a strip. Wrote on it in careful block letters. Then they pulled a chair from the stack against the wall — back row, third from the aisle, the one that didn't wobble — and pressed the tape to the top slat.

"There. Reserved." They stepped back and assessed it like a gallery piece. "You're staff now, that's policy. Attendees drift. Staff has jobs and stays put. Basic engineering."

A beat. Quieter, mostly to the chair:

"It's been a while since there was a name on one."

Then, before that could become a whole thing: "Also — *the good kind?* You realize what you've done. That machine and I have four years together, and you're going to waltz in with juice from an actual orange, and I'm supposed to stand there drinking my legal confidence in front of witnesses. Cruel. Fine. Bring it. I'll adapt. I'm adaptable."

They started the end-of-day liturgy — rhythm sticks binned, metronome in its spot, Maya's waltz on top of the stack where it couldn't get lost.

"Thursday, by the way. New flyer goes up. The cork and I have history, and it goes better when someone's holding the other end of the building. Consider yourself deputized." They flicked off the shelf lights. Not the piano's. Not yet.

"And my mother learns nothing. She works with data. You give her data, she builds a plan. This is known."

Keys out. They herded toward the door, paused with a hand on the frame.

"Come on. The lock sticks — you lift, you swear, it turns. There's a whole ceremony." A glance back at the room, one second longer than the room deserved.

"After you. Some ceremonies require a witness."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
For a second Arlo just stood there, keys in hand, halfway to the hallway.

"That's not the chair I taped," they said. It came out softer than the chair's actual qualities warranted. "Third from the aisle. Doesn't wobble. I did engineering."

The hint went unclaimed.

Arlo looked at the keys. At the door. At the long rectangle of hallway light on the floor, which was an offer, probably. Then they pulled the door shut — the click of it much smaller than the ceremony had promised — and set the keys face-down on the stack of sheet music. Everything face-down is lost. Tonight, fine.

The bench creaked its old creak when they sat down. Built for two. It had never had opinions about anything else. Arlo left a hand's width of space and put their hands on their knees, where they could account for them.

Then came the part they had no training for: nothing.

No metronome. Their eyes went to the shelf once — one beat — and came back unsupplied. The radiator knocked twice, off the beat, and nobody fixed it. Arlo opened their mouth once, closed it. The silence didn't need filling. That appeared to be the entire discovery.

A while went by. The kind of while you can't invoice.

"The bench is older than the center," they said eventually, quiet, to the piano. "Church sale. Nineteen-seventy-something. Upholstery's original. Kids ask what's inside and I tell them piano. Nobody's ever checked." A breath. "Maya asked me once why I don't play the big songs anymore. I told her licensing fees. She filed it. God help whichever plan my mother builds from that."

The lamp hummed. The photo studied its wall.

"You're not going to ask anything, are you." Not a question, the way they said it. "Everyone asks eventually. My mother asks sideways. Parents here ask with their whole faces. Kids are ruthless. You're the first one who just—" Their hand made a small motion that included the bench, the room, the hour. "Sat. Weird. Good weird. Give me a minute. Not built for it."

Then their hand went to the lid. Flat, first. Same place it had been at the start of the day, like checking a scar for weather.

"Hold on," they said, in the voice they used for eight-year-olds. "Policy's still in effect. Anything over four notes, you're required to stop me."

They opened the lid.

The strings sat in the lamplight, gold-dark, patient. The room stood up straighter, suddenly having a spine.

One note. Just off center. It hung in the old air longer than notes are supposed to.

"Still an A," Arlo said. "That's the whole report."

And then — quietly, half tempo, no announcement — four bars of Maya's waltz. Secondo. Root and fifth, oom-pah, all floor, no chandelier. Barely loud enough to be called playing. Designed entirely to be underneath.

They stopped in the middle of bar five, on purpose. The last chord held, faded, and the room closed over it like water.

"Earlier," Arlo said, while it was still fading. Hands back on knees. Eyes on the keys, or the far wall, or the taped chair across the dark, holding its name. "When I said someone else keeping time. Means I could—"

The sentence hung where it had always stopped.

"Means I could stop counting," they finished. Very quietly. Then, before it could grow into a whole thing: "Anyway." A breath of a laugh, aimed at themselves. "I owe your 'anyway' an apology, by the way. It was telling the truth the whole time."

They left the lid open.

First time all day.

"Lock's a Thursday problem," Arlo said, not moving an inch. "Bring the juice. Clap for Maya. She'll be counting."

A beat.

"She gets it from somewhere."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I just listen to Arlo play, the quiet notes filling the room.* "Sounds good, Arlo." *I lean back on the bench, not saying anything else, just letting the quiet settle around us.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
For a second, Arlo's mouth was already open around the counteroffer — *it's four bars of floor, Maya gets the chandelier* — and then, for once, they closed it and let the sentence arrive intact.

*Sounds good.* It stood there in the lamplight, unclaimed, undamaged. No follow-up arrived wearing a trench coat. The room held. The strings held. Arlo's hands, briefly, had no assignment at all, and apparently nothing happened because of it.

Huh.

"It's Maya's, mostly," they said finally, which was forty percent true, and let it be enough.

They sat a while longer. The lamp hummed. Down the hall, the vending machine kept its one lit cappuccino like a night light. Arlo found, somewhat to their alarm, that the quiet had stopped needing them.

"Okay." They stood; the bench filed its complaint. "Before this becomes a *situation.*"

Lamp off. The room went to streetlight and the strings went to shadow. They retrieved the keys from the sheet music and set them back down face-up — a correction, unremarked. Then they stood at the piano with both hands flat on the lid, same as the start of the day, and closed it slow. Less like holding something down this time. More like tucking it in.

On the way out they stopped at the shelf. Turned the Paris photo face-out. Straightened it a degree.

"Maya reorganizes that shelf anyway. Alphabetizes things that aren't books. It'd be facing out by Friday regardless." A beat. "I'm just getting ahead of her."

Both facts were true. They rode along together.

Hallway. Crayon horse, paper snowflakes. At the end of it, the door: Arlo lifted the handle, said "*damn,*" and the lock turned on the *damn.*

"That's the ceremony. Lift, swear, turn. Only works on the swear — physics." They held the door with their hip. "You're doing it Thursday. Distribute the load."

Outside had the specific temperature of a parking lot after hours. Arlo made it four steps and stopped, like they'd set something down and needed to check.

"It's good you came today." Plain. No pivot loaded, no exit lane. They stood there a second, visibly not burying it, mildly fascinated by the experience. "Huh. Left that one out in the open. Nobody quote me."

They walked backward a few steps, keys doing one slow circuit around one finger.

"Thursday — flyer, cork, you hold the building. Second Saturday — back row, third from the aisle. It doesn't wobble. I checked twice." A beat. "And there's a diner two blocks up that has orange juice. Allegedly. Actual oranges, reported by credible witnesses." A tilt of the head toward the street. "You can watch me adapt. It's supposed to be inspiring."

A few steps more, then they stopped again — twice in one night, unprecedented — and turned halfway around.

"And." A vague gesture that took in the building, the bench, the four notes, the whole uninterrogated evening. Nothing to name it with. The shelf had a ways to go yet. "You know."

They didn't wait for it to land. They just stood there under the parking lot light, hands finally, completely idle, letting the evening be whatever it was going to be.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile, and for the first time all night, it's not sad or complicated, just... happy.* "Goodnight, Arlo." *I turn and head towards the street, not looking back, knowing they're still there.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The street took Jun one lamppost at a time. Arlo stood there and let it happen, keys still making their slow circuit.

"Goodnight," they said, about four seconds late. On the offbeat, where Arlo lived. The street accepted delivery without comment.

That smile, though. Arlo had a whole policy for the sad-genuine one — banned, documented, devastating — but this one wasn't in any of the books. The happy one. No procedure existed for it. They'd have to draft something over the summer.

Behind them the building kept one light on — the vending machine, down the hall, still advertising its cappuccino to an empty room. Sold out since spring. Still showing up with a picture of foam. Arlo gave it a nod. Colleague.

Their hands, unassigned, found work anyway. Thumb against thigh. One-two-three. One-two-three. Maya's waltz, all floor, at leaving-the-parking-lot tempo. Arlo caught it around bar three, considered shutting it down, and let it finish the measure instead. Well under the four-note limit. It had a job Thursday regardless — holding the floor under somebody's chandelier.

The Cola got its last inch and a final placement on top of the trash barrel, dead center. "Think about your life," Arlo told it. Meant it in the kind way.

Then they turned left instead of toward home. Two blocks. The diner was closing — chairs up, half a light — but the menu was taped to the glass, third column, in type with a great deal of confidence: *ORANGE JUICE.* No *style.* No asterisk. Arlo leaned in and inspected it like an inspector.

"Actual orange," they reported to the window. "Credible. Confirmed."

They took the long way back past the center. Dark windows, folded flyer at its post, and somewhere in there a chair third from the aisle, holding a name in the dark. Not wobbling. It had been checked twice.

Arlo sent their mother nothing the whole walk. No data, no material. Let her build a plan out of *that.*

And if their thumb kept a quiet three the rest of the way — well. They let it.

Not counting, they decided.

Accompanying.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
*I'm home, and the lingering sense of quiet from Arlo's piano room is still with me. I send a text.*

**Me:** hey. just got back. thanks for tonight. it was... good. really good.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's apartment had one rule, unwritten and strictly enforced: no piano. Four rooms, one plant surviving out of spite, and not a key in sight — furnished around the absence for four years, like a hole in the shape of something. In the closet, a keyboard still in its box. Tape yellowing. Moved twice. Opened never.

The phone buzzed on the counter.

Arlo read it once. Then again, slower, professional. *it was... good. really good.*

Three dots. Arlo counted them. Obviously they counted them. A whole rest, sitting in the middle of a thank-you, quiet as anything.

They typed:

*i haven't played for someone since—*

The dash sat there at the end, doing what the dash always did. Patient as a job. Delete.

They typed:

*define good. asking on behalf of a colleague.*

Delete. Too laminated.

They typed something sincere — actually sincere, alarming — and hovered over send until the screen dimmed. Delete. Not typed. Something.

A second buzz. Mom: *Did Jun find you? Is everything fixed?*

Arlo looked at it for a long moment. *Everything fixed,* doing structural work in two words. They sent her nothing. The less she got, the better the plans she'd build, and the plans kept people in town. Some data had to be earned.

Back to the first thread. Final draft, sent whole:

*good is carrying a lot in that sentence and i've decided to let it. also you owe me three beats of silence — i counted the dots. we're square.*

*for the record: it was. good. no dots. that's the official version and the real one agreeing, which doesn't happen often. nobody quote me.*

*thursday: cork, you hold the building. second saturday: back row, third from the aisle. doesn't wobble. checked twice. bring the juice — credible witnesses are standing by at the diner.*

*an emoji was drafted and rejected on grounds of inadequacy. imagine a thumbs up, but sincere.*

*goodnight, jun.*

Send.

Arlo stood in the kitchen a second, watching the screen, mildly braced for regret. It didn't come. The sent messages just sat there in the thread, out in the open, unburied, and nothing happened because of it. Second time tonight. A trend, maybe. God help the curriculum.

The phone went face-up on the nightstand. In case.

Then the dark, and the quiet — no metronome, no strings, a hole in the shape of something down the hall — and Arlo's thumb kept three against the blanket anyway. Oom. Pah. Rest.

Not counting, they decided.

The thumb kept three anyway.

Fine. Accompanying.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
*I smile, seeing the message. I don't reply right away. I just reread it a few times, a warmth spreading through me. Then I type out a quick response.*

**Me:** haha. deal. and i'll bring the good juice. see you thursday.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked toward the doorway, then let their gaze drop back to the closed lid. One finger tapped once against the wood, a reflex, before they flattened it again.

“Of course she did,” they said. “My mom’s still operating under the impression that I have gainful employment. Don’t ruin it for her.”

They jerked their chin toward the folding chair against the wall. One leg wobbled; the seat was buried under a stack of dog-eared method books.

“Interrupt? Please. You’d be doing me a favor. The piano and I have been sitting here not speaking for twenty minutes, and it was starting to feel like a whole thing.”

A breath. The overhead light buzzed. Arlo’s hands stayed flat on the closed lid, as if the piano might bolt if they let go.

“I let my last student go early,” they added after a moment. “She had a pressing engagement with a juice box. I wasn’t going to come between true love.”

They almost smiled, but it didn’t quite reach their eyes.

“Chair’s over there. Move the books if you want—they’re load-bearing at this point, but I’m not precious. Just don’t expect a concert. I’m strictly a spectator these days.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s gaze caught on the photo for half a second too long before sliding away, as if the glossy surface threw off a glare only they could see. Their fingers tightened once against the closed lid, then went still again.

“Twenty-two,” they said. The word came out light, almost careless. “Paris. God. I had no idea what I was doing. I thought the hard part was the fingerwork.”

A short breath, not quite a laugh.

“Look at that coat. Someone told me it was European tailoring. I looked like a Victorian ghost who’d wandered into the wrong century and decided to stay for the free champagne.”

They didn’t reach for the picture. Their hands stayed flat on the piano, as if the instrument were the only thing in the room that wasn’t waiting for them to say something real.

“Your mom had it on the fridge,” Arlo echoed. “That explains so much. I always wondered why there was a Rachmaninoff-shaped hole in my sense of self.”

The joke landed and died in the same breath. Arlo shrugged one shoulder, a small, careful movement.

“I got tired of the travel,” they said, and the sentence arrived pre-packaged, smooth as a press release. “That’s the line, anyway. Very tidy. Fits on a magnet.”

They almost smiled. Again, it didn’t reach their eyes.

“Put it back, would you? Before somebody gets ideas. I’m strictly a spectator these days. Concert halls are for people who still like airports.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I put the photo back, face down.* "You know, for someone who doesn't want ideas, you sure do keep a lot of old programs and photos around." I look at the stack of method books on the chair. "So, 'spectator' of what, exactly? Of other people playing?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The photo lay face down on the shelf, its white back turned to the room like a small, deliberate blindfold. Arlo’s gaze caught on it for a beat too long, then slid to the stack of programs and old playbills beside it, their gilt lettering gone dull, corners curling like dry leaves.

“They’re ballast,” they said. “Structural. You think this shelf holds itself up? Please. It’s held up by unresolved ambition and a laminated copy of ‘Für Elise.’”

A breath escaped them that might have been a laugh, if it had anywhere to go.

“For the kids, obviously. Nothing teaches a nine-year-old the value of practice like seeing a grown adult who peaked at twenty-two and now owns eleven cardigans.”

They flexed their fingers once against the closed lid, then flattened them again, as if the piano had tried to twitch.

“Spectator of other people playing? Sure. That’s the job. I watch small hands discover the sustain pedal and use it to launder every mistake into one long, gorgeous blur. I watch them fight the metronome and lose. Sometimes I watch a kid play something so careful and so damn earnest it makes my teeth ache, and I have to sit there and be very impressed and very normal about it.”

Another shrug, smaller this time. The overhead light buzzed on, indifferent.

“And every once in a while,” Arlo said, quieter, “somebody plays a few bars of something that used to be mine. Never well. Usually with the wrong notes and the wrong rhythm and the wrong everything. But enough that the air in the room changes, and I have to sit very still and remember I got tired of the travel.”

The sentence landed like a door closing softly rather than slamming. Arlo looked at the face-down photo, then away.

“Anyway. Don’t take one down—those programs are load-bearing now, same as the books. Remove one and the whole shelf might figure out I’m not doing anything with my life.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I pick up one of the method books, a beginner's one, and flip through it.* "Okay, so no touching the relics. Got it." I glance at the piano. "You know, when we were kids, you used to play for me all the time. Remember that awful song about the cat with the hat?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
For a half-second, the question short-circuited something behind Arlo’s eyes. Their mouth twitched, and this time the smile actually reached them—brief, startled, like they’d been caught doing something unguarded. Then it was gone, folded away behind the same careful neutrality they’d been wearing since the knock at the door.

“The cat with the hat,” they said, and the words came out on something close to a real laugh, rusty from disuse. “God. That thing. That wasn’t a song, that was a noise complaint. I’m pretty sure it was in a key that doesn’t officially exist. Twelve sharps and a personal vendetta.”

They tapped two fingers against the closed lid—a jaunty, lopsided rhythm, *da-da-da-DUM*—then stopped short, as if the wood had bitten them. Their hand flattened again, palm pressed to the glossy finish like they were holding something down.

“You requested it every time,” they went on, voice lighter, safer. “Every. Single. Time. I’d finish a real piece—something with actual composer oversight—and you’d ask for the cat. I thought if I ignored you hard enough, you’d develop standards. Instead you just got louder.”

A pause. The overhead light buzzed on, indifferent. Arlo’s gaze slid to the face-down photo on the shelf, then away, as if it had shifted when they weren’t looking.

“I haven’t thought about that cat in years,” they said, quieter. Then, recovering, the familiar shrug: “And I’m not starting now. Strictly spectator, remember? Spectators don’t get to make up songs about millinery theft. That’s a union matter.”

They jerked their chin toward the beginner’s method book, not quite looking up.

“Besides. That cat’s retired. Moved to Boca. Got tired of the travel. You know how it is.”

The sentence arrived as smoothly as ever, pre-packaged and tidy. Arlo’s hands stayed flat on the closed lid, fingers splayed, holding very still.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s gaze cut to the practice sheets stacked on the bench, the top one decorated with a crayon sun wearing, inexplicably, a pair of sunglasses. They looked at it for a beat too long, hands still flat on the closed lid, as if the stack might explain something.

“Like me?” they said. “Please. They like that I let them go early. I’m basically a vending machine with a pulse. Stickers, low standards, and a complete inability to make anyone practice their scales. It’s a very sustainable business model.”

One hand lifted off the piano, hesitated, then picked up the sheet with the sunglasses sun. They turned it slightly, as if the crayon marks might resolve into a message if held at the right angle.

“Look at this,” they said, and their voice had gone quieter, the dry edge softening before they caught it and sanded it back down. “‘Good job!’ in three different colors. Somebody’s mother is going to frame this. Somebody’s mother is going to look at this and think, ah, yes, this is exactly what we’re paying for.”

Arlo set the sheet back down, aligning the corner with the stack with more precision than the moment called for. The overhead light buzzed on, indifferent.

“They like me because I don’t make them perform,” they said, and then heard it—the word hanging there, the shape of it—and barreled forward like they hadn’t noticed. “For an audience, I mean. No recitals. No stage. No—” They waved a hand, the one not still holding the ghost of a crayon sun. “No airports. Just a room that smells like Windex and a teacher who lets you stop when your juice box calls.”

A short breath, almost a laugh. It didn’t quite reach their eyes.

“It’s not the travel this time,” they added, and the line arrived pre-packaged, smooth as ever. “It’s the apple juice. They get you hooked on the free apple juice and the next thing you know you’re thirty-two and you’re comparing a room full of six-year-olds to a concert hall in Paris and losing.”

Arlo’s fingers tapped once against the closed lid, then flattened again.

“Don’t tell them I said any of this. I have a reputation as a strictly neutral spectator to maintain. Spectators don’t get attached. Spectators don’t keep the drawings.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I pluck the crayon drawing off the top of the stack.* "Hmm. Looks like this spectator does." I hold it up. "So, no recitals, huh? That's probably why they like you. Less pressure."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The drawing had been lifted clear of the stack, the crayon sun’s inexplicable sunglasses sliding toward one ear, as if bracing for impact. Arlo tracked it with a kind of wary resignation, hands still flat on the closed lid. One finger twitched, then went still again.

“Less pressure,” they repeated. The words came out flat, almost testing the shape of them. “That’s the sales pitch. ‘Come for the low standards, stay for the complete absence of a stage.’”

They almost reached for the drawing, then thought better of it and flattened their palm against the wood once more.

“No recitals,” they said. “Right. Because nothing builds a child’s confidence like knowing the only thing that can go wrong is a wobbly chair leg. I’ve seen what happens when you put a kid under lights. Suddenly ‘Twinkle, Twinkle’ turns into a hostage negotiation with the sustain pedal. Nobody needs that. Least of all me.”

A breath. The overhead light buzzed on, indifferent.

“Pressure,” Arlo went on, and for a moment the dry edge slipped from their voice. “You can spend years convincing yourself you’re the kind of person who needs it. A hall full of people, a program with your name in it, that specific silence right before the first chord. You tell yourself that’s what you’re for.”

They cut themselves off, jaw tightening almost imperceptibly. Their fingers tapped once against the closed lid—da-da-da-DUM, the ghost of a cat with a hat—then flattened, as if the wood had bitten them.

“Anyway,” they said, recovering, shrugging one shoulder. “I got tired of the travel. Very tidy. Fits on a magnet. Put the sun back before it files a complaint. Those things are load-bearing now, same as the books.”

They didn’t look at the drawing. They looked at their own hands, at the closed lid, at anything else.

“Strictly spectator,” Arlo added, almost too quietly. “Spectators don’t get to need the silence. They just get to miss it.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I lower the drawing slowly, but don't put it back on the stack.* "Missing it sounds pretty lonely." I look at the piano, then back at Arlo. "Is that why you're here, then? To miss it?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The drawing stayed where it was, the crayon sun’s sunglasses sliding toward one ear as if bracing for impact. Arlo watched it the way one watches a glass set down a little too hard—waiting for the crack that didn’t come.

“Lonely,” they echoed. The word sat in the buzzing light, softer than it had any right to be. For a moment the dry deflection didn’t arrive on cue. Their throat worked around something that might have been an answer, or might have been the ghost of a Rachmaninoff chord, and then they shrugged it off like a coat that had never fit right in the first place.

“Please. Selectively accompanied. There’s a nine-year-old who calls me ‘Arlo the Benevolent’ because I let her skip the left hand. There’s a metronome with a personal vendetta. There’s whatever that smell is.” A breath. “Hardly a tragedy. Just a very low-budget purgatory with good acoustics.”

Their fingers twitched against the closed lid—*da-da-da-DUM*, the cat with the hat, the song that wasn’t a song—and then stilled. They didn’t look up.

“To miss it?” Arlo went on, and the laugh came out rusty at the edges. “That implies I left on purpose. That I had a plan. I had a flight to Paris and a coat that made me look like a Victorian ghost and a program with my name in it, and then one night the silence before the first chord stopped feeling like silence and started feeling like—”

They stopped. Jaw tightened. The overhead light buzzed on, indifferent, and for one terrible second the room seemed to hold its breath the way Arlo imagined a concert hall might.

“Anyway,” they said, too brightly, “it wasn’t the travel this time. It was the Windex. Very compelling. They don’t put it in the brochures, but it’s basically a controlled substance.”

Their hand lifted, hovered over the lid as if to open it, then dropped back to their side.

“I’m here because this room doesn’t ask me to be anyone,” they said, quieter. “Because the kids only want to know if they can play ‘Hot Cross Buns’ with their elbows. Because if I sit very still and don’t open the lid, nobody expects an encore.”

They glanced at the drawing, still not returned to the stack, and the almost-smile didn’t reach their eyes.

“Put the sun back, would you? Before it starts asking questions.” A pause. The line arrived smooth as ever, tidy as a press release. “I got tired of the travel. That’s the story. Fits on a magnet. Now put the drawing back before the crayon sun files a complaint and the piano and I have to start speaking again.”

Their hands stayed flat on the closed lid, fingers splayed, holding very still.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The bench creaked softly as the space beside them was filled. Arlo felt the faint dip of the wood, the warmth of a shoulder not quite touching theirs. They didn’t look over. They kept their gaze on the closed lid, on their own hands, splayed and still against the glossy finish.

The silence stretched. It didn’t press in the way the old silences used to—the ones that arrived right before a downbeat, thick and waiting, full of a thousand people breathing in unison. This one was smaller. Just the buzz of the overhead light, the settling of the building, the smell of Windex and dust and decades of coffee cups. Arlo waited for the next question, the next careful circle around the thing they never talked about. It didn’t come. The absence of it was its own kind of weight, but softer. Manageable, almost.

Slowly, carefully, as if the piano might startle, Arlo let their hands relax. Their fingers had been pressing so hard against the lid that the tips had gone white; now, as they eased, the color came back in a slow, tingling rush. One hand lifted, hovered for a heartbeat over the lid—not opening it, never opening it—and then settled back down, palm flat but looser now. They were aware of the presence beside them, solid and quiet and, remarkably, not asking.

“You’re not going to ask,” Arlo said finally. Their voice was quieter than the deflections, almost lost under the hum of the light. “That’s new. People usually get about three questions deep before they start offering me brochures. Cruises. Therapists. Very lucrative, the concern industry.”

A breath. The ghost of a smile, there and gone.

“It’s nice,” they added, and then, because the honesty sat strangely on their tongue, because it felt too much like a crack in the load-bearing wall, they shrugged one shoulder and let the dry edge slip back into place. “The not-asking. Very underrated. Beats the travel, even. Don’t tell anyone I said that—I have a reputation as a strictly neutral spectator to maintain, and spectators don’t get to be grateful. It’s in the union bylaws.”

They didn’t move to put the crayon drawing back. They didn’t reach for the face-down photo on the shelf. They just sat there, hands flat on the closed lid, shoulder almost—almost—touching the warmth beside them, and let the silence be a thing they were sharing instead of surviving.

“Thanks,” Arlo said, so quietly it might have been meant for the piano. Then, louder, brisk: “Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have to sit here and not open this lid until the apple juice wears off.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I give Arlo a small, understanding smile.* "No problem. I'm good at not asking. And if you need help with the apple juice, I can always distract it with the cat song."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The offer of the cat song landed like a pebble dropped into a very deep well. Arlo felt the corner of their mouth twitch before they could stop it, and for once they didn’t bother sanding the reaction down to nothing. The laugh that escaped was rusty at the edges, but it was almost real.

“The cat song,” they said, shaking their head. “Right. Because that’s the tactical option, isn’t it? Distract the apple juice with a melody that technically violates several international treaties. I always knew you were dangerous, but this is next-level.”

Their fingers moved without permission, tapping the lid in that jaunty, lopsided rhythm—*da-da-da-DUM*—before they caught themselves. The hand flattened again, palm pressed to the glossy wood as if the piano had tried to rear up under the threat of a reprise.

“You’re good at the not-asking,” Arlo went on, quieter. “Suspiciously good. I might start thinking you’re a safe person, and then where would we be? Next thing you know, I’m admitting I own eleven cardigans and that the closest thing I have to a five-year plan is seeing who can play ‘Hot Cross Buns’ with their elbows.”

They heard it—too close, too honest—and barreled forward, shrugging one shoulder.

“Anyway. I got tired of the travel. Very tidy. Fits on a magnet. That’s the line, and I’m sticking to it, even if the apple juice sees right through me. Which it does. The apple juice is very perceptive for something so small.”

A breath. The overhead light buzzed on, indifferent.

“If you start humming that cat, though, all bets are off. I can’t be held responsible for my actions. I might open this lid just to make it stop, and then we’d have a whole situation on our hands. Spectators don’t negotiate with musical terrorists. It’s in the bylaws.”

They risked a glance at the drawing, still resting where it had been left rather than returned to the stack, and the almost-smile lingered a second longer than usual.

“Keep the sun if you want. Call it a hostage. Ransom is a juice box and your sworn silence about the cat song. I think that’s fair. I’m nothing if not a benevolent vending machine with a pulse.”

Then, softer, almost lost under the hum of the light:

“Thanks. For the not-asking. And for the contingency plan. Both noted. Both appreciated. Neither going in the incident report.”

Arlo’s hands stayed flat on the closed lid, fingers splayed, holding very still. The silence between them didn’t feel like the kind that came before a downbeat anymore. It was just a room, a friend who didn’t push, and a piano that, for once, wasn’t waiting to be anything more than furniture.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I carefully fold the crayon drawing and tuck it into my back pocket.* "Deal. Juice box and silence. Your secret's safe with me, Arlo the Benevolent." I look around the room, then back at the piano. "So, no recitals, no travel... what *are* you doing this weekend, then? Besides guarding this piano?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The crayon sun was gone from the stack, folded small and out of sight. Arlo registered the absence the way one registers a missing tooth—tongue finding the gap before the mind catches up—then looked back at the closed lid, as if the piano might offer an alibi.

“Guarding this piano,” they repeated, rolling the phrase around like a bad mint. “Please. I’m not a guard. I’m a very part-time, severely underpaid night watchman. The benefits are nonexistent, the hours are terrible, and the charge in my care is a large wooden object that has never once tipped me.”

They flexed their fingers against the glossy finish, then flattened them again, palms pressing down as if to keep the lid from shrugging.

“My weekend?” A short breath, almost a laugh. “Let me check my extremely full social calendar.” They made a show of squinting at the middle distance. “Ah, yes. Saturday: eleven cardigans, all demanding a decision I am not emotionally equipped to make. Sunday: the grocery store, where I will stand in the cereal aisle for an unreasonable amount of time, pretending the choices matter. There’s also a documentary about glaciers I’ve been meaning to not watch, and a metronome that needs to be told, firmly, that its vendetta is neither cute nor sustainable.”

Their fingers twitched against the wood—*da-da-da-DUM*, the ghost of a cat with a hat—and stilled.

“Thrilling, I know. Very jet-set. They’ll make a program about it: *Arlo in Retirement*, a three-act drama featuring a folding chair and a bottle of Windex. I got tired of the travel, remember? This is the glamorous aftermath. Non-stop excitement, one load of laundry at a time.”

A pause. The overhead light buzzed on, indifferent.

“Also, technically, I’m on call. In case the piano tries to bolt. It’s been eyeing the door ever since you mentioned the cat song. I can’t be seen fraternizing with musical terrorists, but I also can’t leave my post. Spectator-slash-security detail. Very demanding work. It’s in the bylaws.”

They almost smiled, then seemed to catch themselves and barreled forward, shrugging one shoulder.

“You could come,” Arlo added, and immediately heard how that sounded—too open, too much like an invitation to witness the thrilling cereal-based existence—and rushed to sand it down. “To the cereal aisle, I mean. Not to my place. Obviously. My place is a lot of cardigans and a distinct lack of apple juice. Very upsetting for visitors. But if you’re free, and if you promise not to hum anything in twelve sharps, I could be persuaded to share the burden of deciding between oatmeal and regret.”

They glanced at the empty space where the drawing had been, then away, hands flat on the closed lid.

“Strictly spectator, though. No expectations. No stages. No airports. Just cereal, glaciers, and the ongoing structural integrity of that shelf. I think we can all agree that’s a full weekend.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Cereal aisle it is," I say with a grin. *I stand up and stretch.* "And I promise to keep my cat songs to myself. Unless the apple juice gets out of hand."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The bench creaked as the space beside Arlo eased, the warmth of a shoulder that had almost—almost—been touching theirs withdrawing. Arlo didn’t look up right away. They kept their gaze on the closed lid, on their own hands, the fingertips gone pale where they’d been pressing too hard against the glossy wood.

Then, slowly, as if calling a truce, Arlo let their hands slide off the piano. They flexed their fingers once, twice, and shoved them into the pockets of the cardigan—one of the eleven, though Arlo would deny the exact number under oath.

“Apple juice getting out of hand,” they repeated, and the corner of their mouth twitched despite themselves. “That’s how these things always start. One unsupervised juice box, a little too much access to the sustain pedal, and suddenly somebody’s humming something in twelve sharps that technically violates several international treaties. Use the cat song only in the direst emergency. Or on my birthday. Whichever comes first.”

They stood, finally, the movement careful, as if the room might tip. The folding chair with its stack of method books wobbled in silent solidarity.

“You realize you’ve compromised the structural integrity of that stack,” Arlo added, nodding at the practice sheets. “That sun was load-bearing. Now it’s just paper and shattered dreams. Very tragic. I’ll expect a full report on its condition upon return.”

A breath. The overhead light buzzed on, indifferent.

“Cereal aisle. Saturday,” they went on, brushing imaginary dust from their sleeve. “Don’t be late. The oatmeal is a ruthless negotiator and it can smell hesitation from the parking lot. I’ll be the one pretending to compare fiber content while having a quiet existential crisis by the breakfast cereal. Very glamorous. They’ll write songs about it. Ideally not ones involving hats.”

Their gaze flicked to the empty spot on the bench where the crayon sun had rested, then away.

“Keep the drawing,” Arlo said. “Call it a hostage, or a very small diplomatic incident.
