Arlo seemed to be inventorying those sounds instead of the one Jun had just made.

“Not really,” they repeated at last. “That’s a very loaded phrase. It’s the verbal equivalent of showing up with a casserole and saying, ‘I brought this for no reason, but also we need to talk about your face.’”

Their mouth did a small, unconvincing thing.

“If she sent you, I’m disappointed she didn’t include a side dish. If she didn’t, I’m impressed by your commitment to being uncomfortable in public.”

Arlo glanced down at the piano lid. Their index finger traced the edge again, once, then stopped. They did not lift it. They did not open the keyboard. The closed lid looked less like an instrument and more like a piece of furniture they had been hired to guard.

“For the record,” they said, “I’m fine. I’m not having a crisis. I’m conserving energy. There’s a difference. One is tragic, the other is administrative.”

They looked up, one eyebrow lifting.

“And before you start building a narrative, I have a prepared statement. I got tired of the travel. Very versatile. Works for careers, relationships, and any sandwich that has been wrapped in airport plastic for more than six hours.”

Arlo pushed off the bench and crossed to the little shelf where the photograph sat. They did not touch it. They only nudged a box of crayons beside it so the frame was slightly less visible, then seemed to notice what they had done and stopped. For a second their hand remained there, suspended in the act of not rearranging.

“I had a kid today,” they said, “who asked me if the piano had a memory. I said only for wrong notes. He thought about that like I’d handed him a philosophy degree.”

They turned away from the shelf and leaned against it instead, arms folding. The posture looked casual only if you did not know Arlo had once been capable of making casual look like a performance.

“Then another one played ‘Ode to Joy’ with one finger and complete confidence, which is honestly more than most professionals can say. So. I’m contributing to society. Slowly. In very small increments. Like a municipal bond.”

The radiator gave a metallic complaint. Arlo did not move toward it. Their gaze passed over the keys beneath the lid and came back to Jun with careful neutrality.

“If this is an inspection,” they said, “you should know I’ve eaten. I’ve slept. I’ve had a lime wedge. I’ve even considered buying a houseplant, but I don’t want to get into something serious right now.”

A beat.

“If it’s not an inspection, then I need more information. You can’t just wander into a room full of tiny keyboards and say ‘not really’ and expect me to improvise.”

Arlo’s mouth quirked again, but the humor stayed shallow, like a light left on in an empty room.

“Also, you still owe me gas station coffee. The bad kind. The kind that tastes like it was filtered through a gym towel and someone’s unresolved feelings.”

They unfolded their arms only long enough to gesture at the bench beside them, not inviting, just acknowledging the available geometry of the room.

“You can talk while I aggressively sit. It builds character.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked down at the practice sheets on the bench as if they had just been entered into evidence.

The top page was decorated with a gold star sticker that had begun to peel at one corner. Beneath it, someone had drawn a treble clef that looked more like a confused snail. There were fingerprints in the margins. One sheet had been folded into a triangle and then unfolded again with the solemn care of a child who had realized too late that important documents should not become paper airplanes.

“They like the stickers,” Arlo said. “I’m essentially a sticker distribution service with a pulse and a suspicious relationship to caffeine.”

They reached over and straightened the stack, though it had not needed straightening. Their fingers lingered on the edge of the top page for a moment, smoothing the peeled star back down without much hope of success.

“Some of them like the piano,” Arlo went on. “Some of them like getting out of the house. Some of them are here because their parents believe structured suffering builds character.” Their mouth twitched. “I provide the suffering in age-appropriate portions.”

One of the sheets had a row of practice boxes, all unchecked. Arlo picked it up, examined it, and gave a slow nod.

“This one told me her cat ate her practice log,” they said. “I told her the cat had until Thursday to produce a written statement.”

They set the page back down. The humor stayed near the surface, thin and quick, like ice over deeper water.

“I don’t make them perform if they don’t want to,” Arlo added after a moment. “We call it ‘sharing progress.’ It sounds progressive. Mostly it means I bribe them with fruit snacks and pretend nobody’s being emotionally compromised by ‘Mary Had a Little Lamb.’”

Their hand rested near the closed piano lid again, not touching it this time. Just close. The way one might stand beside a sleeping animal one did not intend to wake.

“Some days the most useful thing you can teach a person is how to stop before they hate it.”

The sentence landed with a little more weight than the room seemed prepared to carry. Arlo noticed. Their expression shifted, the dryness returning like a door clicked shut.

“You can write that down if you’re collecting evidence of my mysterious teaching methods,” they said. “Right under ‘gas station coffee’ and ‘do not trust the chair by the radiator.’”

They glanced at the practice sheets again, then away.

“Also, they like me because I have the emotional range of a vending machine. You put in a coin, you get a sound. Sometimes the sound is ‘Hot Cross Buns.’ Sometimes the sound is a lecture about why you cannot sue dead composers.”

Arlo’s fingers tapped once against their own knee. Not a rhythm. Not quite a habit. More like a reminder that their hands were still their own.

“But yes,” they said, lighter now. “They seem to like me. Which is either a sign of excellent classroom management or deeply lowered standards.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Or maybe you're just good at it," *I say, quietly.* "I mean, it's not like you were ever bad at anything." I pause, then ask, "So, what are you doing this weekend? Besides aggressively sitting, I mean."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s hand stilled near the practice sheets. The compliment sat between them, too simple to argue with efficiently.

They looked at the gold star sticker again and pressed one corner down with their thumbnail. It resisted.

“Careful,” Arlo said. “That kind of talk leads to expectations. Next thing you know, someone hands me a trophy and I have to pretend I know where to put it.”

They did not look up right away. The sticker finally stayed down, but only because they kept their thumb on it.

“And I was bad at plenty of things. Hotel key cards. Small talk in green rooms. Knowing when to leave a sandwich alone.”

They let the sticker go. It lifted again, slowly, like it had principles.

“This weekend,” Arlo said, “I intend to engage in a series of low-stakes errands. Laundry. The hardware store. Possibly a houseplant, though I plan to make it clear from the outset that this is casual.”

They picked up the folded practice sheet, unfolded it an inch, then folded it back again.

“If the weather turns dramatic, I may buy a candle and call it self-improvement. If my mother calls, I will tell her I ate a vegetable and did not make eye contact with any pianos.”

The word *pianos* seemed to notice itself. Arlo set the sheet down.

“No concerts,” they added, lighter. “No airports. No fountains with false advertising. If I encounter a staircase, it will be for the purpose of going upstairs, not being photographed on it.”

They glanced at the closed keyboard, then away.

“So. Aggressive sitting, but with destinations. Very balanced. Very municipal.”

The radiator gave a small metallic sigh, as if it had been asked to witness a legal document.

Arlo’s mouth quirked, but not quite into relief.

“If you’re asking because you plan to bring the coffee, the place on Fifth makes the bad kind with real conviction. It tastes like someone boiled a grievance.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I was actually thinking of something a little more... active," *I say, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Like, maybe checking out that new antique store on Main Street? Or that little bakery with the amazing croissants?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo regarded the suggestion the way one might regard a flyer slipped under the door: brightly colored, possibly harmless, but likely promising more enthusiasm than the day could reasonably support.

“Active,” they repeated, testing the word as if it might be counterfeit. “That’s a suspicious adjective. It implies movement. It implies intent. It implies that at some point I will be standing in public holding a pastry and pretending I have opinions about ceramic lamp shades.”

They glanced toward the window, where the late afternoon light had gone thin and gray over the parking lot. A car door slammed somewhere in the building. The radiator ticked once, then thought better of whatever it had been about to add.

“The antique store,” Arlo said, “is full of other people’s dust with price tags. You pick up a teacup and suddenly you’re emotionally responsible for a stranger’s divorce. I don’t need that kind of narrative on a weekend.”

Their gaze moved back to Jun, dry but not unkind.

“And bakeries are dangerous. They make you feel like you should become a person who wears linen and knows things about sourdough fermentation. I’m not ready for that level of character development.”

Despite the objection, Arlo did not retreat into the bench or fold themselves back into the closed piano’s orbit. Instead, they reached for the stack of practice sheets again, aligned the edges with a small, unnecessary precision, and set them beside the gold-star sticker that had once more begun its slow rebellion against adhesive.

“If we’re going to do this,” Arlo said, “we need ground rules.”

They held up one finger.

“One: no browsing with purpose. I refuse to be near anyone who says, ‘This would look perfect in the hallway.’ Hallways are fine empty. Hallways have dignity.”

A second finger.

“Two: if there is a bakery employee who asks if I’ve decided, I need at least forty-five seconds to decide. Possibly longer. I may need to consult a map. Not of the menu. Of my life.”

A third finger, then a pause.

“Three: if anyone from the old whatever-it-was happens to be there, you are required to pretend you know me only as a local figure of mild civic importance. Maybe a librarian. Maybe a person who judges regional squash competitions.”

Their mouth curved, but only on one side.

“Four: coffee. Bad coffee. The kind that tastes like it was brewed by someone who lost faith in the concept of mornings.”

Arlo lowered their hand and looked down at the piano lid. Their fingers hovered near it again, not touching. The closed keyboard sat there like a politely sealed box, all black polish and unhelpful reflection.

“Saturday,” they said at last, as if the word had been weighed, stamped, and approved by a very tired committee. “Late morning. Not early enough to suggest ambition. Not late enough to suggest brunch.”

They leaned back against the edge of the shelf, arms folding, then unfolding when the posture seemed too deliberate.

“The bakery first,” Arlo added. “If the croissants are as amazing as advertised, I will be temporarily easier to live with. If they are not, I will say nothing, but I will carry it with me for years.”

A beat passed. The basketball overhead thumped twice, then stopped.

“And if the antique store happens to be nearby,” Arlo said, with the careful neutrality of someone arranging furniture around a hole in the floor, “we can walk past it. Maybe even go in. But only if it looks like it won’t ask anything of me.”

Their eyes flicked briefly to the photograph on the shelf, then away again.

“No grand outings,” they said. “No expeditions. No one saying, ‘This will be fun,’ in that tone that suggests it has already been decided for me.”

The words came out light, but there was a thin edge under them, quickly smoothed over.

“I’m capable of fun,” Arlo said. “I simply prefer it in controlled portions. Like medication. Or cheese samples.”

They pushed off the shelf and took two slow steps toward the bench, not sitting, just standing near it as if the piano might require supervision in their absence.

“And before you get any ideas,” they added, “this is not a renaissance. It is not a return to the world. It is croissants. Possibly a lamp nobody needs. Maybe a small ceramic object I will regret by Tuesday.”

One hand finally settled on the piano lid, palm flat, not pressing. Holding.

“If it goes well,” Arlo said, quieter now, “we can call it a successful field trip.”

They looked up, and the dryness came back, but softer this time. Less armor, more habit.

“You’re still buying the coffee, though. I have standards. Low ones, but they’re load-bearing.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo did not move when Jun sat down.

The bench gave a small, tired creak under the added weight, the sort of sound that made the room feel briefly smaller and then, somehow, less empty. Arlo kept their hand where it was, palm flat against the closed piano lid, fingers not quite spread anymore. The polish had gone cool under their skin. They did not lift it. They did not open the keyboard. They simply stayed there, as if the instrument might decide something about them if they moved too soon.

For a while, neither of them said anything.

The community center settled around them in its usual after-hours way: the radiator ticking out a thin metallic argument, the distant hum of the vending machine down the hall, the faint rubber squeak of someone’s sneakers fading toward the gym. Somewhere outside, a car door shut. Then another. Then nothing.

Arlo watched the closed lid. Their reflection in it was dark and incomplete, warped slightly by age and polish and the overhead fluorescent light. They looked like someone inspecting a locked drawer they had no intention of opening.

After a long moment, Arlo exhaled through their nose. Not quite a laugh. Not quite a sigh.

“This is very dramatic,” they said at last, voice low. “The two of us. Sitting here. In the sacred hush. Like we’re waiting for the piano to deliver a verdict.”

They glanced sideways, just enough to register Jun’s presence without making a thing of it.

“If someone walks in now, they’ll assume we’re having a spiritual experience. Or that I’ve finally snapped and started holding seances for middle C.”

The joke landed softly, without much effort behind it. Arlo’s thumb moved once against the lid, a small, absent pressure. Then stillness again.

The silence did not feel unbearable, exactly. It felt supervised.

Arlo’s gaze drifted toward the practice sheets, the gold star sticker, the box of crayons, the photograph on the shelf with its too-bright younger face angled away from direct view. They looked at all of it and none of it in the same breath.

“I used to think quiet before music was a threat,” Arlo said.

The sentence came out quieter than the ones before. They seemed to notice this immediately, because their mouth tightened, not in distress, but in the familiar reflex of someone checking whether they had said too much.

“Now it’s just the room doing its thing,” they added, lighter. “Very atmospheric. Very low-budget municipal gothic.”

Their fingers flexed once against the lid. Then relaxed.

Arlo shifted slightly on the bench, not away from Jun, only enough to make the posture less rigid. Their shoulder brushed the air near Jun’s, not quite contact, but close enough that the distance between them became a fact instead of a negotiation.

“You’re very good at this,” Arlo said after another stretch of quiet.

Their tone was dry, but the edge had worn down.

“Sitting here without asking questions. Most people can’t manage it. They start filling the air with helpful suggestions. Or concern. Or that particular kind of cheerfulness that makes you want to bite someone.”

They looked down at their hand on the piano lid.

“You just sit here like it’s not a production.”

The radiator ticked again. The light outside the window had gone flatter, grayer, the afternoon beginning to thin into early evening. Arlo did not get up. They did not suggest leaving. They did not make a joke about time, or errands, or the bakery, or the antique store with its emotionally compromised teacups.

Instead, they let the quiet stay.

After a while, Arlo spoke again, even quieter than before.

“I don’t hate it.”

They did not look at Jun when they said it. Their eyes stayed on the closed piano, on the dark shine of the lid, on the place where the keys would be if they chose to open it.

“The sitting,” Arlo clarified, as if the sentence needed a footnote. “Not the silence. Not the room. Not the… whatever this is.”

Their fingers tapped once against the wood. Not a note. Not a beginning. Just a small proof of presence.

“I don’t hate it,” they repeated, and this time the words sounded less like a joke and more like something they had not meant to say aloud.

The room held it for them.

Arlo’s throat moved. They looked away from the piano, toward the door, toward the hallway, toward anything that was not the shape of what had just slipped loose.

“If you tell anyone I said that,” they murmured, “I’ll deny it with my dying breath. And then I’ll haunt this place. I’ll rearrange the sheet music. I’ll hide the stickers. I’ll make the radiator do that thing where it sounds like it’s filing for divorce.”

A pause.

Their mouth curved, faintly.

“I’ll be the least efficient ghost you’ve ever met.”

They did not move their hand from the lid. They did not fill the silence with anything else. They only sat there, close enough to feel the warmth of another person in the room, close enough not to have to name what the closeness was doing.

The piano stayed closed.

The quiet stayed too.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I don't say anything for a moment, just let the quiet sit. Then I reach out and nudge Arlo's arm gently with my elbow.* "Good. Less efficient ghosts are always more fun."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo did not move away from the nudge. Their sleeve compressed briefly under the light contact, and they let it stay there for a second longer than they might have if they’d been alone.

“Careful,” they said. “Encouraging inefficient ghosts is how you end up with a poltergeist that only mildly inconveniences people. I’ll spend eternity hiding one shoe from every pair in this building.”

The corner of their mouth moved, not quite a smile, but close enough to count.

“I’ll be strategic about it,” Arlo went on, voice low. “Move the metronome one inch to the left. Make all the B-flats sound slightly damp. Teach the radiator to sigh in seven-eight time.”

Their hand lifted from the piano lid at last. Not dramatically. Just enough to settle on their knee, fingers loose. The closed keyboard stayed where it was, black and glossy and unopened, reflecting the overhead light in a long, dull stripe.

Arlo looked at it for a moment, then away.

“Saturday,” they said, as if reminding themselves. “Bakery first. Then possibly the antique store, if it continues to look like it won’t demand a written statement.”

They leaned forward a little, elbows near knees, then seemed to think better of the posture and sat up again.

“If I start narrating the tragic provenance of a gravy boat,” Arlo added, “you have permission to buy me a bad coffee and change the subject.”

A beat passed. The room was quieter now, but not in the sharp way it had been earlier. The radiator had stopped arguing with itself. The hallway had gone still. Even the basketball overhead had abandoned whatever private mission it had been on.

Arlo’s gaze flicked toward the photograph on the shelf, then returned to the bench.

“And if I say it’s fine,” they said, more quietly, “that doesn’t mean I’ve figured out why. It just means the room isn’t currently trying to throw me out.”

They let that sit, then immediately reached for the nearest available deflection.

“Also, I’m not promising fun,” Arlo said. “I’m promising pastry. There’s a difference. One is optional. The other is structural.”

Their fingers tapped once against their knee. Not a rhythm. Not a beginning. Just a small, ordinary proof that they were still there.

The piano stayed closed.

For once, the closed lid looked less like something locked and more like a piece of furniture that had simply been left alone.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly.* "Got it. Strategic haunting, no gravy boat narratives, and pastry over fun." *I stand up.* "I'll pick you up around ten, then? That way we can hit the bakery before the rush."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked up from the bench, one hand still resting near the closed lid.

“Ten,” they repeated. “Ten is specific. Ten suggests you’ve already mentally selected a parking spot and judged my shoes.”

They stood, not quickly, as if the movement required a small internal vote. They gathered the practice sheets into a neat pile, tapped the edges against the bench, and placed them in the drawer beneath the shelf. The gold-star sticker stayed on top, clinging by one stubborn corner.

“Ten-fifteen is safer,” Arlo said. “Ten-fifteen admits the possibility of human error. Ten implies breakfast ambition.”

They glanced toward the window. The parking lot had gone the color of dishwater.

“But fine. Ten. If I’m not outside, do not come in. Do not send a search party. Assume I’ve been delayed by a profound disagreement with a sock drawer or that my mother has appeared with a casserole and a mission.”

They picked up their keys from the bench, then set them down again, as if deciding whether the day had officially ended. The piano lid caught the overhead light one last time.

“And if I say ‘I’m ready’ when you arrive,” Arlo added, “that is a legal statement. It does not mean I have achieved emotional readiness. It means I have located shoes and chosen a coat with the least number of questions.”

Their mouth curved, faintly.

“No honking,” they said. “If you honk, I will assume the bakery has sent a collection agent and I will retreat into the building and live among the xylophones.”

Arlo reached over and switched off the small lamp by the shelf. The room dimmed, leaving the piano in a softer shadow. They did not touch it again.

“Saturday,” they said, as if sealing the agreement with a minimum amount of ceremony. “Croissants. Bad coffee. A controlled encounter with objects that once belonged to strangers.”

They paused, one hand on the light switch, not yet flipping the last one.

“If it goes well,” Arlo said, “I may even allow you to witness me considering a teacup. Briefly. From a respectful distance.”

Then they turned off the final light, leaving the closed piano in the gray afternoon quiet, and did not look back until the door clicked shut behind them.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile, shaking my head a little.* "Alright, ten-fifteen it is. And I promise, no honking." *I give a little wave and head out, leaving Arlo to their silent room.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo stood still until the last of Jun’s footsteps had faded down the hall.

The room seemed to wait for that. It always did, once the building lost its human noise: the radiator finding its thin metallic rhythm again, the vending machine humming somewhere beyond the door, the faint settling of old wood as if the community center were adjusting its bones for the evening.

Arlo kept their hand on the light switch for a moment longer than necessary.

“Ten-fifteen,” they said to the empty room.

It sounded absurd when spoken aloud. Also slightly dangerous, like making a promise to a piece of furniture.

They let the switch go and turned back toward the piano.

The bench was still warm, or maybe they imagined it was. The closed lid sat in the dimness with the patient indifference of an object that had already survived many people’s intentions. Arlo looked at it for a while. Not at the keys. Not at the place where the keys would be if the lid were open. Just the polished surface, the warped reflection, the faint gray light from the window making a long stripe across the wood.

They sat down again.

Not gracefully. Not with the old performance-ready posture that used to come with tailored jackets and stage lights and the particular kind of silence that arrived when several hundred strangers decided, all at once, to stop breathing. Arlo sat the way a person sits when they are tired and trying not to make a production of it. Elbows near knees. Shoulders slightly forward. Hands resting where they could see them.

After a moment, they lifted one hand and laid it flat on the lid again.

The wood was cool now.

Their fingers did not spread. They simply stayed there, palm down, as if testing whether the piano would make a sound without being asked. It did not. It was, for once, being very cooperative.

Arlo exhaled.

“This is not a séance,” they told it.

The piano did not argue.

Their thumb moved once against the edge of the lid. Then their hand stilled.

The room was quiet in the way rooms get quiet when they have stopped trying to prove something. Not expectant. Not accusing. Just quiet. The kind of quiet that could be sat inside without being interrogated, if a person was careful. If they did not move too quickly. If they did not ask it to become music before it was ready.

Arlo looked at the shelf.

The photograph had gone shadowy in the low light. The younger version of them in it was barely visible now: the too-long hair, the ridiculous scarf, the face of someone who had not yet learned how many ways a person could stand in public without meaning to. Arlo regarded it without expression for a second, then reached over and nudged the box of crayons another half inch in front of the frame.

Not enough to hide it.

Just enough to make it less available.

“There,” Arlo murmured. “Dignity.”

They leaned back on the bench and looked up at the ceiling.

Somewhere overhead, a pipe knocked once. The building answering itself.

Arlo let their eyes close.

For a moment, the silence widened. It became the kind of silence that had edges. Not cruel, exactly. Just alert. The silence before a lesson began. The silence after a wrong note. The silence that could, under the wrong lighting, become a hallway, a green room, a stage door, the bright blank face of a crowd waiting for something to start.

Their hand tightened slightly on the piano lid.

They opened their eyes.

The room was still the room. Dust. Windex. Child-sized music books. The drawer where they had put the practice sheets. The radiator, continuing its small argument with the concept of heat.

Arlo swallowed.

“Not tonight,” they said.

It was not clear whether they were speaking to the piano, to themselves, or to the photograph.

They looked down at their hands.

For a long moment, they did nothing else. Then, very carefully, they lifted both hands and rested them on their knees instead. The gesture was ordinary. Deliberately ordinary. The kind of thing a person did to remind their body that it was still in a community center on a Tuesday, not suspended in some older, sharper version of itself.

Their fingers relaxed.

Arlo sat with that.

After a while, they stood.

They did it slowly, as if the bench might object, but the bench only creaked once and let them go. Arlo crossed to the door and paused there, one hand on the frame. The hallway light spilled in, pale and institutional, cutting a strip across the floor.

They looked back at the piano.

Closed. Still. Not threatening.

Not forgiving, either. Just there.

“Saturday,” Arlo said, as if the word needed to be placed in the room before they left.

Then they stepped out, pulled the door shut behind them, and did not lock it right away.

They stood in the hallway for a second, keys in hand, listening.

The building was quiet now in the ordinary way. No basketball. No sneakers. No distant voices. Just the low hum of lights and the faint, persistent tick of the radiator behind the door.

Arlo turned the lock.

The click sounded small. Final, but not unkind.

They put their keys in their pocket and started toward the exit, hands shoved deep, shoulders drawn against the evening air that was already gathering beyond the front doors.

Outside, the sky had gone the color of old dishwater, but the streetlights had come on, and the parking lot was dotted with their thin orange glow. Arlo paused on the step for a moment, breathing it in.

Not silence, exactly.

Just distance.

They thought, briefly, of croissants.

Then bad coffee.

Then the antique store, and all its emotionally compromised teacups.

Then, because their brain was apparently determined to keep the evening from settling too comfortably, they thought of the piano lid under their palm and the way it had not felt, for one strange second, like something locked.

Arlo looked back at the building.

“No,” they said quietly, to no one. “Don’t start.”

They turned up their collar and walked toward the car, not hurrying, not looking back again.

Behind them, the community center sat dark and ordinary in the early evening, holding its rooms and its dust and its closed piano with the same indifferent patience it had always had.

Inside, the piano stayed shut.

But the room, for the first time in a while, did not feel like it was waiting for anything.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I walk out of the community center, the cool evening air a welcome change from the dust-and-Windex smell inside. I glance back at the building for a second, then smile to myself.* Saturday, huh? *I pull out my phone, already planning a detour for some really bad coffee.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael completed the sequence before he answered — the final cut held for a full breath, then drawn down to first position. He pressed the pommel briefly to his lips, a habit older than the squire was, and only then turned.

"Finished early." His eyes moved over the boy the way a quartermaster's move over a ledger not yet checked. "Early means nothing. Correct means something. I will inspect the stalls before the noon bell, and we will see which of the two you achieved."

He crossed to the weapon rack and set his own waster in its place.

"You did not get it right yesterday. Your blade drifted back past your ear — a flourish for tourneys, not a guard. It invited every cut you could not see coming. And your weight sat on your heels like a man waiting to be served supper."

He took up a second waster, weighed it once, and held it out at arm's length — not offering it so much as presenting an obligation.

"The frost will make your hands ache before fifty repetitions. Good. Your enemies will not wait for a warm morning, and neither will the dead."

His voice did not rise. It never needed to.

"Feet apart. High guard. Show me what you remember, and I will count the ways it is wrong."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I gulp, taking the waster from his outstretched hand.* It's heavy, just like yesterday. "Yes, Ser." *I shuffle my feet, trying to remember where he told me to place them.* "Like this?" I try to get into the high guard, blade above my head, but I can feel my weight shifting back already.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael circled him once, slow as the forms had been. Frost crunched under his boots. He said nothing for the whole of the circuit, and the silence was part of the teaching.

"No," he said at last, stopping in front of the boy. "But you knew that before you asked. Your own weight told you, and you chose not to listen. That is a second fault, and it is worse than the first. A man who ignores what his body tells him dies tired."

He set a single finger against the boy's sternum and pushed. Not hard. There was nothing in the heels to resist with, and the weight went back half a step.

"There. Your enemy will do that with less. A shoulder in the press. A shove at a shield-wall. A dead man walking into you, because the dead do not tire and do not stop. You are holding a guard a corpse could put on the ground."

"Set your feet again. Now listen. The weight sits forward — balls of the feet. Heels light. A knife should fit beneath them. Knees soft, not locked; locked knees are a gift to the man who kicks them. You should feel the ground through the fronts of your feet the way you feel a horse's mouth through the reins. When I speak, you should already be moving."

He stepped behind the boy, studied the blade, then took the squire's wrist and drew it forward half an inch.

"Your wrists are broken back. The guard ends at your hands — it does not live past them. Blade angled forward over the crown of your head. You should see beneath your own forearms. If you can see the sky, you are admiring it. You are not here to admire anything."

He returned to the front and folded his hands behind his back.

"Hold it. You will hold it while I count fifty, and I count slowly. When your arms burn — and they will, before I reach twenty — that burn is the lesson. The guard must outlast the arm that wants to be done with it. You think a vigil is kneeling in the chapel until your knees forget their purpose. This is also a vigil. Hold it as you would hold a prayer."

"One."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not come to him. He let the silence do its work, and the boy's ragged breathing was the loudest thing in the yard until the fifth bell sounded somewhere beyond the wall. His own breath still made its thin ghosts in the cold.

"Your point is in the frost." His voice did not rise. It never needed to. "A blade is laid on the ground when its work is finished, or when its bearer is. Decide which you are announcing."

He crossed the stones and stopped an arm's length away, hands folded behind his back.

"You are sorry. Sorry is owed when a man has wronged another. You have not wronged me. You have spent an hour of your own morning badly, and the morning will not remember it. It only hands you a new one, which is not the same as forgiveness.

"Who told you to kneel? A squire kneels when summoned. A penitent kneels when commanded. You knelt because your arms burned — which means you knelt for yourself. That is rest wearing devotion's clothes, and I know the difference.

"You are not as strong as I need you to be. No squire ever was. If strength were required at the door, there would be no squires — only knights, and most of them dead young. A squire is a boy who is not yet what he must become and stands up anyway. That is the whole of the office. The tack, the polish, the running at my heels — all of it is only the standing up, done slower.

"At your age I held this guard while my master took his supper, and I hated him for it. He is thirty years dead, and I am standing in this yard. There is the whole of the arithmetic.

"Now, the terms of the next ten. The arms may burn. The blade may sink — arms are flesh, flesh fails, and there is no shame in flesh. But the feet do not move. The knees stay soft. The weight stays forward. The guard is a place. You will hold the place even when the blade hangs from tired hands. If the place holds, the drill holds. If the place is lost, everything is lost, however high the blade stood a moment before.

"I told you the frost would take your hands before fifty, and it did. Hear the other promise: the strength comes the same way. Through mornings exactly like this one, and no other way.

"An hour ago I told you to hold the guard as a prayer. You did, for a time. Then the ache arrived and you stopped praying. The ache is not where prayer ends, boy. It is where it begins. A vigil does not count until the knees hurt.

"You kneel, you apologize, and you wait for me to say enough. I will not say it today."

He unfolded his hands.

"Stand up. The drill ends when I say it ends, and I have not said it. Ten more. Slow."

"One."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I slowly push myself up, my arms trembling as I grasp the waster again.* My face burns. "Yes, Ser." *I try to remember everything he said about my feet.* It's hard to hold the blade up.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
"Two."

Ser Kael came around to stand square in front of him, close enough that the trembling was plain, and gave it his attention — the same attention he gave everything, with neither pity nor praise in it.

"You need not tell me it is hard. Your arms are telling the yard. Hard is the shape of the work. I promised you aching hands and burning before twenty, and I was not wrong. I never promised easy. Stop listening for it. Easy is how weak men are made.

"Your face burns. That is shame, and shame is a man looking at himself when he should be looking at his enemy. Blood in the face is blood out of the arms. Send it where it is needed. Look past me. Pick a stone on the far wall and guard against it — one day it will be a dead man's face at that distance, and the dead will not care that you are embarrassed."

"Three."

He stepped in and laid two fingers flat against the boy's back, between the shoulder blades, and pressed upward once.

"Chest up. You have curled around the ache like a man around a wound. The spine carries the blade or it does not. Straighten it and half the weight leaves your arms. They will last longer for it, which is the only gratitude arms ever give."

"Four. Five."

The trembling had found the wrists. He let it stay.

"Shaking is the body telling the truth: this is the edge of what it can do. The edge is where the work lives. A still arm has learned nothing today.

"And hear this for when the arms give — they will give before ten. The blade comes down slow. Lowered, not dropped. The manner of failing matters. A weapon flung down like a surrendered banner tells every witness what its bearer is. A weapon set down with intent has not failed yet, whatever the arms believe."

"Six."

He crossed to the rack, drew his own waster, and set it in high guard an arm's length beside the boy's. He said nothing about it. He did not need to. His arms were thirty years older and had not yet begun to ask.

"Seven. Eight. Your feet are still where you set them. Whether that is the right place, we will know in a moment. But they have not moved while the arms died, and there is the whole of the lesson in small boots: strength is meat, and meat fails. Discipline holds the place. The priests call it virtue when it kneels. In this yard it is called guard. It is the same thing. I cannot teach you strength. I can teach you the place."

"Nine."

The sun had cleared the eastern wall. The frost was sweating on the stones, and their breath made its ghosts side by side.

"Ten."

Ser Kael drew his blade down — slow, controlled, the exact descent he had described — and set the point in the frost, hand resting on the pommel. Then he stepped in front of the boy and placed a single finger against his sternum. The same finger. The same place. The same pressure as an hour before.

"The count is finished. The lesson is not."

He pushed.

"Answer it."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stumble back a step, the waster clattering to the ground as I try to catch myself.* "Ser!" *My eyes are wide, and I can feel tears pricking at them.* I look at the fallen waster, then back at him.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael looked where the boy looked — at the waster on the frost — and let the boy see him looking at it too. The clatter had gone off the walls and come back smaller. Now the yard held only ragged breathing and the slow drip of thaw off the weapon rack.

He closed the hand that had pushed. Finger by finger, the way a man puts away a tool.

"You heard the sound it made. So did I. So would every man on a wall within fifty yards, and every one of them would know its meaning before the echo finished. A blade leaves the hand of a dead man or the hand of a man who has surrendered it, and the sound does not say which. You are breathing. Draw the conclusion."

He let it sit.

"'Ser.' You cried out when the ground moved. A shout in a fight is one of two things: a warning your brothers can act on, or a plea that arrives too late to matter. Learn which yours was. If it was the second, save it. I am not in the habit of catching men. I train them until catching is unnecessary.

"Now the step. You gave one and did not fall, and I will say this once, as arithmetic and not praise: your feet found you. Untrained feet do not. That is the seed, and I will not water it. Here is what matters. The step was taken from you, not given. Ground is yielded sometimes — chosen, knees soft, weight forward, blade still in the fight, taken back with interest when the press falters. But ground that is merely taken is ground you did not govern. A man who does not govern his ground is not in the fight. He is near it. Men who are only near a fight are the first ones finished.

"Your eyes are filling. I saw it before you did — the face burns first, then the water comes. Let it come or master it; the yard has no opinion, and I have no use for it either way. Hear the one thing I will say of it: tears are an answer, and no enemy ever asked you a question. They will buy nothing at a wall, nothing in a press, nothing from the dead. If you must weep, weep in guard — blade up, feet set. The gods gave men water and gave men hands, and only the hands were meant for this work."

He stepped back from the fallen waster, one pace, then another, clearing the boy's path to it, and folded his hands behind his back. The sun had climbed a hand's width up the eastern wall, and the frost was going to water, stone by stone.

"Pick it up. Not only because I command it, though I do. Pick it up because it is lying there speaking against you, and it will keep speaking until your hands close around it and lift.

"Your arms have had their hour. They failed honestly, and honest failure is the privilege of flesh. The lesson now belongs to your feet — or do you believe your arms took that step? The drill is this: guard, as tired as you please, the arms have leave. I will push you. Not when you are braced for it. Not on any rhythm you can carry in your head. You will find your place again, and I will push again, until the stumble is worked out of you or the noon bell calls me away to stalls that were finished 'early.' The count is of recoveries. A stumble is not undone by being sorry for itself. It is undone by standing correctly, again and again, until standing correctly is what the body does when it is surprised.

"Your stone on the far wall. Eyes on it. Heels light. Knees soft. Weight forward.

"I told you the drill ends when I say it ends. I have not said it. I am nowhere near saying it.

"Pick up your blade. Set your feet."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael let the question stand in the air the way he let a bad guard stand — long enough for it to be heard, and to hear its own weight.

"You were given two commands. Pick up your blade. Set your feet. You have done neither, and instead you have reached past your weapon for a question. Note it, because it was not an accident. A tired mind builds doors out of whatever lies nearest — thirst, a buckled strap, a sudden piety. Today it built one out of me. I do not fault the instinct; every exhausted man is a carpenter of escapes. I fault the timing. You asked it while your blade was still on the ground, which makes the question a hiding place. Learn the shape of your own escapes now, boy, while they are small. They come in larger sizes later, and the larger ones are called desertion."

He shifted his weight — the only movement — and settled his hand on the pommel of the waster planted in the frost.

"But the question itself is not improper. A squire may know his knight's record; it is part of your schooling, like the forms and the order of the old houses. So I will answer it. Once. Briefly. Not because you earned it this morning — you have earned nothing this morning but aching arms, and those were free. Because it is part of what you are here to learn, and I do not teach by halves.

"I was the third son of a man who held sixty acres from a lord whose face he never saw. One inheritance. Three boys. The chapel took my sister. The road took me. I was nine years old, and no one asked me why, and I knew better than to ask. 'Why' is a rich man's question. It presumes choices. I had a place, and the place came with a sword, and the sword came with mornings exactly like this one.

"Mind your verb, because it is wrong, and wrong verbs make wrong knights. A man does not *become* a knight the way he becomes cold or afraid — it is not something that happens while he stands still. He is ground into one. By masters who took their supper while I held this guard. By vigils. By two winters I do not discuss. What I chose — once, on my knees, at the end of it — was the oath. Everything else was done to me. That is the whole answer, and you will notice it contains no fire. You hoped for a fire. Boys always hope for a fire. There was no fire. There was a wall, and in the dark things came to it that should have stayed in the ground, and men were needed standing. There are always men needed standing. I was standing. That is the arithmetic.

"You are already forming the next question — what I saw at that wall. I will not answer it. Not because it is a secret. Because you would carry it like a story, and it is not a story; it is a weight, and you have not yet built the shoulders. Ask me again when you have stood a real post on a real night. I may answer then. Or I may hand you a blade and point you at the dark, and that will be answer enough."

The sun had climbed another hand's width. The frost was going to water across the whole of the yard, and their breath still made its ghosts.

"Now turn the question around, and do not answer it aloud. Why did you become a squire? Whatever you would say today is wrong. At your age I would have said glory, and I would have meant it, and I would have been a fool. The answer is not a thing you are given. It is a thing you are made into — the way bread is made, by being ground and kneaded and held to the fire. You are the dough. This yard is the fire. Stop asking the fire questions and stand in it.

"Hear the last of it. Questions belong to the march and the supper table, when the hands are busy and the mind is free to receive the answer. In this yard, the drill is the answer. It has been answering you all morning. Begin listening to it.

"Your blade has now lain on the stones through a sermon, which is longer than it deserves and longer than I intend to preach again this month. It is still speaking against you, and it has learned some new words while it lay there.

"Pick it up. Feet apart. Heels light. Knees soft. Weight forward. Eyes on your stone — it has waited patiently all this while, which is more than the dead will ever do for you.

"I have not said the drill ends. Pick up your blade."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I look down at the waster, then back up at Ser Kael, my chest heaving.* "Yes, Ser." *I bend down quickly, snatching the waster from the cold ground, my hands still shaking.* I move into the guard position, trying to keep my eyes fixed on the stone.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the blade come up off the stones — snatched, the way a boy takes bread he expects to have taken from him — and let it pass without sermon. He had preached enough this month. The yard would do the rest of the talking.

He stepped in once, laid a finger beneath the trailing elbow, and raised it half an inch. No word came with it. Then he withdrew and began to walk.

He circled without hurry. The frost had gone to water; the stones had gone dark with it, and his boots left prints that filled behind him. Under everything ran the small wet sound of the thaw, the boy's working breath, and the trembling in the arms, which had stopped asking permission and become simply the weather.

On the second circuit, his boots went quiet.

He let them stay quiet. He took his place at the boy's left shoulder, off the line of the stone, and let the stillness stretch the way he had let silences stretch all morning. Beyond the wall, the sixth bell counted out its six, and was done.

Then, at the bottom of one of the boy's breaths — the moment the chest empties and a man is nothing but weight waiting to be moved — he set the flat of his hand against the shoulder and pushed.

The weight went. One boot skated on the wet stone.

Ser Kael stepped back a pace and folded his hands behind his back.

"My boots went quiet, and something in you thanked them for it. Mark that. Quiet is not rest. Quiet is aim. The dead are quiet the whole night through, and they are not resting."

He began to circle again, unhurried, letting the ragged breathing run its course.

"And I took you at the bottom of the breath, where a man is emptiest. Your enemy will find that place without being taught it. So breathe like a man who expects the push. Half a breath, held. Never spend the whole of it — a full breath is a debt, and the dead collect."

The sun had gained a third hand's width of the eastern wall. The count of recoveries stood at nothing.

"Find your place. Feet set. Weight forward. The blade goes wherever the arms can keep it — the arms retain their leave. I will push again when I choose, and you will not choose when.

"Recover."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I gasp, scrambling to get my feet under me.* My heart is pounding. *I try to remember the feeling of being pushed, to brace for it.* I keep my eyes on the stone, trying to ignore the ache in my arms.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
"One."

Ser Kael said it from behind him and let the word stand without ornament. "Ugly. It counts. A fight is an ugly thing and the recoveries in it are uglier — but be glad the count opened at all. An hour ago it stood at nothing, and you did not know the number existed."

He came around to the front, unhurried. The stones had gone dark with thaw; his boots printed them, and the prints filled behind him.

"Now the fault wearing the virtue's coat. You are bracing against the push you remember — the hand, the shoulder, from the front, as it came twice before. That is guarding the last war. A brace is a wall, and a wall faces one way. Only a fool waits for the third blow out of the same country. And a brace is made of stiffness, and stiffness is strength spent before it is needed — a debt drawn against arms already deep in debt. The soft knee is not weakness, boy. It is the ankle, listening. When pressure comes, drink it. Fold the small fold. Give the half-step the way a lender gives — with every intention of having it back."

Beyond the wall the seventh bell counted its seven, and was done. The sun stood a spear's height off the stones. He crossed to where his waster waited planted in the last of the frost, drew it up, and threw the water from it with one turn of the wrist.

"The hand is finished. Now the blade. I will press your guard, and I will tell you plainly: slow. Do not thank me for slow. Slow is worse than fast. Fast can be flinched at. Slow must be met. Your arms will beg under it — they have leave to sink. They have no leave to surrender, and the blade knows the difference, and so will every man who ever watches you carry one.

"When the flat arrives, meet it with the place, not the arms. Yield the half-step on your terms — weight forward, heels light, blade over the crown — and when the pressure lifts, the step comes home. Ground lost by choice is ground on loan. That is the whole art of the sword in one small movement: lose it like a lender, take it back like a creditor.

"A vigil may end kneeling. A guard does not. Pray on your feet."

He stepped in and laid the flat of his blade against the flat of the boy's, above his head, and began to lean — slow, patient, steady as the thaw itself.

"Half a breath, held. Eyes on your stone.

"Take the half-step. Then bring it home."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not ease the flat of his blade.

That was the first thing, and the boy would understand it years from now or not at all: the pressure neither grew nor lifted. It stayed what it was, steady as the thaw, while the trembling changed underneath it. All morning the shaking had been the arms speaking — the honest complaint of meat at its edge. This was different. This came up from somewhere below the arms and had no interest in the drill at all.

He had seen it before. Thirty years of squires, and every one of them carried a day like this inside him, and the day always came round again.

"You said nothing. You need not. I have known since before you walked into this yard."

He spoke from beside the crossed blades, close and level, and the pressure held.

"Your father's name went into my bede-roll the day you entered my service — the roll of this household's dead, kept for the altar, as every ordered household keeps one. The day has come round. I was in the chapel before the fourth bell. The office for the dead takes a quarter of an hour. It is owed, and it is paid. That is all I will say of it, and it is more than most men's dead receive. Let it be enough."

The thaw ticked along the weapon rack. He let it.

"At some point today you will decide I set this drill on this morning out of cruelty. Decide it, and be wrong, and know you are wrong. The day chose itself. And hear the plainer truth beneath it: no enemy consults the calendar of your griefs. The things that come to walls in the dark do not ask what the day is for the man standing against them. Mourning has never once stopped a blade mid-swing. So the guard must stand on the anniversary too, or it is not a guard at all — only a courtesy you pay to fair mornings.

"I have put the dead before you all morning as things at a wall. Things that do not tire, do not stop, do not care. Your father is none of those things, and I am not teaching you to fight him. But grief pushes with the same hand. It takes ground the same way — a half-step at a time, at the bottom of a breath, when you are emptiest — and it does not tire either. A man can be moved off his stones by a shoulder, by a shove, or by a memory, and the stones do not record which. Only that he is no longer standing on them.

"Earlier I told you that what I carry from the wall is a weight, and you had not built the shoulders for it. Your father is the first weight you will carry. Hear the arithmetic of weights, because no one will say it to you plainly: the weight does not lighten. Not in a year. Not in thirty. I have carried my own father longer than you have been alive, and he weighs exactly what he weighed the day I took him up. What changed was the carrier. That is what this yard grinds into a boy. Not the sword — the sword is only the tool. The shoulders.

"So, the terms, as before. When I say the drill ends — and I have not said it — you will go to the chapel. Light the candle. Kneel the vigil owed to him, and stay on those knees until they forget their purpose, as I told you a vigil was. Grief has a room, and that is the room. This yard is another. In this one the feet do not move. Weep in guard if it comes; weep at the altar when you reach it. Both are permitted. Neither moves the feet.

"And if the arms need a name to hold by today, they may have his. Men have held walls for less. A father watches his son's guard whether the son can see him or not. Hold it where he can see it.

"Your feet have not moved. Through the hour, the sermon, the push, and now this — they are where you set them. I say that once, as arithmetic and not praise. Mark it, because there will come mornings you cannot find that place, and you will want to remember that you found it on the worst morning of your year."

He leaned nothing more and nothing less.

"Half a breath, held. Weight forward. Heels light. Knees soft. The arms may sink — they retain their leave.

"Take the half-step. Lend the ground like a lender. Then bring it home.

"The count waits on your feet."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My jaw is clenched, and I'm staring at the stone on the far wall, trying to focus past the blur in my eyes.* My arms are screaming, but I don't let the blade drop. *When the pressure finally eases, I take the half-step, then bring it back.* "Yes, Ser." My voice is hoarse.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
"Two."

Ser Kael let the flat of his blade come away slow — the same patience in the release that he had kept in the lean — and drew the waster down its full descent, point settling into the last of the frost where the wall's shadow still held. He pressed the pommel briefly to his lips. The same habit. It had outlasted thirty years of mornings, and it would outlast this one.

"The first was an accident that counted. Scrambling, ugly, the ground deciding for you. This one you chose. You lent the half-step and called it home like a man who means to collect. That is the whole art I promised you, in one small movement, and I will say it plainly: it was not pretty, and it was correct, and this yard was built for the second of those only."

He folded his hands behind his back.

"The drill ends when I say it ends. I am saying it. Understand what ends it, because it is none of the things you would like it to be. Not your arms — they have been finished for an hour and held anyway. Not the bell. Not the day. The place held while the ground moved, at the bottom of a breath, on the worst morning of your year. That is what this morning was for. It is done.

"And note the word I do not use. I do not say *enough* — enough is a word for mercy, and none was asked and none was given. I say *done*. The terms were kept on both sides. They always are, in this yard. It is the only fairness I promise anyone."

He looked once at the far wall.

"You may leave your stone. It will be there tomorrow.

"Now the order of the day, and you will keep it exactly. Bread and water first — a vigil fails in the stomach before it fails in the knees. Then the chapel. The dead are owed before the living. Your father's name is the last line but one on the bede-roll, left of the altar; I read the office over it before the fourth bell, and the candle beneath it is lit. Kneel the vigil I described. The water you did not spend in this yard is owed there — carry it with you. The yard has no use for it. The altar does.

"Then the stalls. I said I would inspect them before the noon bell, and I inspect what I say I will. We will see whether 'early' and 'correct' were the same word this morning. If they were not, you will do them again after the vigil — correctly this time — and the day will have taught you two things instead of one.

"Tomorrow, the fourth bell. The morning hands you a new one. It always does. That is not a threat; it is arithmetic."

He crossed to the rack and set his waster in its place — the same hook, the same wood as before any of it began.

"You knelt once this morning and apologized once, in the first hour. Since then, neither. Not through the sermon, not through the push, not through the day itself. Mark which half of the morning you keep.

"The work this morning was adequate."

He said it without rise, without softening, and then, because the boy would hear it as too little or too much, he made it plain.

"Adequate. The old word means *made equal to*. Equal to the morning — the frost, the count, the sermon, the grief, the whole of it. Most men are never equal to their mornings. They stand above them briefly and come down badly, or beneath them permanently and call it misfortune. You stood level with yours. On this day of all days, level is not a small thing to be. Take the word for what it weighs and do not ask it to weigh more.

"Go."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, not trusting my voice to speak again, and turn to go. My arms ache, my legs are wobbly, but my feet obey, carrying me towards the keep.* I can still feel the ghost of his push. *I don't look back.*

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stumble into the kitchens, probably looking a mess. The cook gives me a sympathetic glance, but doesn't say anything. I grab a hunk of bread and gulp down some water, then head for the chapel.* My knees already hurt.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael had been aware of the squire's approach from the moment the yard gate groaned open. He did not stop. The drill was a litany, and he would no more cut it short than he would abandon a prayer half-spoken. The practice blade completed its arc, paused, and only then did he lower it.

He turned, driving the point into the frozen earth. Frost clung to the stones; his breath showed pale and thin. He did not shiver. He did not suggest the squire step nearer to a warmth that was not there.

"Your bow was adequate." His tone was level, entirely without warmth. "The completion of your stable work is likewise adequate. It is also required. Do not offer duty discharged as coin for my favor, and do not imagine that finishing early entitles you to anything but further labor."

He regarded the squire in silence for a moment, the way a smith regarded a flawed casting.

"You do not have the high guard because you have been copying the shape of it. Yesterday you watched my hands and thought the guard lived there. It does not. It lives in the legs, in the spine, in the refusal to move before the command is given. Saint Aldric held the bridge at Corveth from dawn until the bells of nones, and he did not lower his arms because his shoulders ached."

He inclined his head toward the rack.

"Take a practice sword. Assume the stance. I will give the correction once. If I must give it again, you will hold the low guard until your arms burn, and then you will hold it still. Now."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I flinch a little at his words, but quickly straighten. *I hurry to the rack and grab a practice sword, the wood cold in my hands.* "Yes, Ser." I try to mimic his stance, legs apart, sword held high. My arms already feel a bit shaky.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael remained where he was, the practice blade still planted in the frost. He let his eyes move over the stance that had been taken, and he judged it the way a mason judged a wall: by what was crooked, not by the effort it had taken to raise it.

The effort meant nothing. The result was what stood before him, and the result was flawed.

The trembling was already there. He noted it and set it aside. Weakness was not a thing to be pitied; it was a thing to be removed, the way dross was skimmed from iron.

“Your feet are too close,” he said. “A knight does not perch. He stands as the tower stands—set wide, set deep, so that the earth itself answers for him. Widen them.”

He stepped forward and set the flat of his blade against the outside of the lead foot, pressing outward a hand’s width before withdrawing. He did not stoop. He did not make a task of it.

“Your back is bent. Straighten it. The spine is the road the blow travels; leave it crooked and the force dies before it reaches the arm. Saint Aldric did not beg his shoulders for rest at Corveth, and the bridge did not care that he was tired.”

His gaze rose to the hands upon the hilt.

“And you are strangling the grip. That is not strength. That is fear wearing the mask of effort. Hold the sword as a man holds a vow—firm, deliberate, without panic. White knuckles are only the body confessing that it does not trust itself.”

Ser Kael stepped back and drove his own blade into the frozen ground once more. The frost did not soften him. The hour did not soften him. The sight of a boy trying—and that was all it was, trying—did not soften him either.

“That was the correction,” he said. “I will not give it again. Assume it properly now and hold it. I will count fifty beads. If your form breaks before the last bead, you will take the low guard and hold it until your arms burn, and then you will hold it still.”

He folded his hands over the pommel of his planted blade, his breath a thin ghost in the cold.

“Begin.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not look away from the kneeling squire, but neither did he stoop to meet him. He stood with his weight settled, the planted blade a dark line against the frost. His breathing was slow and even, as though the hour of drills had been a slow walk through the cloister rather than a trial of the body. He gave no sign of fatigue. He would not give the squire the comfort of seeing any.

“You will not kneel in the dirt to confess your insufficiency,” he said. “Apology is a debt that costs the speaker nothing and buys the listener less. Save your sorrow for the chapel, where it belongs. In the yard, sorrow is only another weight.”

He let the silence settle, thin and cold.

“You are not as strong as you must be. That is not a crime. It is the condition of all who have not yet been forged. Saint Aldric did not begin as the man who held the bridge. He began as a boy who was corrected in the yard, who ached, and who obeyed. The bridge did not care that he was tired. It only required that he remain. That is the whole of the lesson. The standard does not bend for your weariness, and neither will I.”

His gaze moved briefly to the eastern wall, where the shadow lay long across the stones.

“You held the guard for the fifty beads. That was the obligation. It is not a triumph to have done what was commanded. It is the floor beneath which you must not sink. Now you are tired. Tired is not an injury. Tired is the hammer on the iron.”

He turned his eyes back to the squire, flat and unyielding.

“You have until that shadow touches the third stone from the corner. Breathe. No more. Then take up your practice sword and present yourself. We will work the high guard against resistance. I will test it, and you will hold. If your form breaks, you will run the yard until your wind is steady. If it does not break, you will run it anyway, because your wind is poor and your back still surrenders when you tire.”

A pause. Not mercy. Measurement.

“Rise. And speak no more of what you think I need. A squire’s place is not to guess at his knight’s expectations. It is to obey the standard, whether or not he comprehends it. Obey, and let the forging do its work.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, my muscles screaming in protest.* "Yes, Ser." *I don't look at him, just focus on the shadow and my breathing.* My throat feels tight, but I won't say anything more.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not look at the squire’s face, nor at the tightness in the squire’s throat. He looked instead at the shadow, measuring its slow crawl toward the third stone from the corner. Feeling was like the frost upon the stones: present, unavoidable, and utterly without claim. One endured it. One did not negotiate with it.

He drew his own practice blade from the frozen earth with a single controlled motion and stepped back, turning the hilt once in his grip to settle the leather. The wood was cold; his hands were not. He had drilled since the fourth bell and would drill still, because the body was a vessel for duty, and the vessel required tending whether or not it wished to be tended.

“Your silence is preferable to your apology,” he said at last. “Keep it. The yard is not a chapel, and I am not your priest. If you are injured, declare it. If you are merely tired, then tired is not an injury. It is the hammer, and the iron does not argue with the hammer.”

He moved to the place where he would stand when the test began and planted his feet in the same wide, rooted stance he had demanded of the squire. The shadow lay long and thin across the stones. It had not yet reached the third stone.

“You have a little longer,” Ser Kael said. “Govern your breath. Loose your jaw. A man who clenches his teeth clenches his shoulders, and a man who clenches his shoulders will fail the guard. When the shadow touches the stone, you will present yourself. I will test the high guard with a single controlled strike. You will not flinch. You will not step back. You will not answer the blow. You will hold, because the guard is not held by the arms. It is held by the legs, by the spine, and by obedience.”

His eyes flicked briefly to the squire, flat and assessing.

“Saint Aldric did not hold the bridge at Corveth because his shoulders were strong. He held it because he had been corrected in the yard until there was nothing left in him that wished to move without command. That is the work. It is the only work that matters here.”

He fell silent. His breath made a pale ghost in the cold air. He did not offer rest. He did not offer praise. He simply waited, blade ready, while the shadow crept toward the third stone.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My jaw aches from clenching it, so I try to relax it, taking a deep, shuddering breath.* "Yes, Ser." *I watch the shadow, willing it to move faster, willing my muscles to stop shaking.* I can do this. I have to.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the shadow crawl across the frost. The squire’s jaw had loosened, though the breath still shuddered in the cold. He gave no sign of approval. A jaw unclenched was not obedience; it was merely the removal of an obstacle, and the yard did not reward the absence of fault.

The ragged edge of the shadow touched the third stone from the corner.

Ser Kael straightened. His breath slowed to the rhythm of the beads. He did not look at the squire’s face. He looked at the line of the shoulders, the set of the feet, the place where the spine met the earth.

“The shadow has reached the stone,” he said. “Your breathing is ended. Take up your practice sword and present the high guard. I will test it once, and only once. You will not flinch. You will not step back. You will not answer the blow. You will hold, because the guard is not held by the arms.”

He stepped into the place he had marked and set his feet wide, the way a tower is set. The practice blade rose, pale wood against the grey morning. He did not strike. He waited, his gaze fixed on the squire’s center, his body gathered to deliver the single controlled blow the moment the guard was presented.

“Saint Aldric did not ask the bridge at Corveth to wait until his breath was steady,” Ser Kael said. “Present yourself. Now.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not lower the practice blade. The shadow had reached the third stone from the corner, and the command had been given. The squire had not presented the guard. The question came instead, personal and unbidden, and Ser Kael recognized it for what it was: a tired body seeking a door out of obedience.

He did not step forward. He did not strike, because there was no guard to test. His gaze remained fixed, flat and unyielding, the way a wall regards the rain.

“You were commanded to present the high guard,” he said. His voice was level, without warmth, entirely without invitation. “You have asked a question instead. In this yard, that is not curiosity. It is evasion, and evasion is disobedience wearing a humbler face. Do not mistake the one for the other.”

He let the words settle in the cold air. Frost lay on the stones; his breath made a thin ghost. He gave no sign of fatigue, and none of sympathy.

“As for your question—you have asked it, and I will answer it once, in the only way that matters. I did not become a knight as a man takes up a trade or follows a fancy. I was born to the station God and my lord ordained for me, and I swore the oath when I was little older than you are now. That is the whole of it. There is no romance in it. There is no hidden grief to be coaxed from me, no tender tale to soften the duty. I remain a knight because the oath remains, and because the standard does not bend for weariness. That is all.”

His eyes moved to the shadow, then back to the empty space where the squire should have stood.

“Saint Aldric did not ask the bridge at Corveth why it needed holding. He held it. He did not inquire into the private reasons of the men beside him. He attended to his own post. You will attend to yours.”

He paused. The pause was not mercy. It was measurement.

“The shadow has touched the stone. Your breathing is ended. Take up your practice sword and present the high guard. I will test it once, and only once. You will not flinch. You will not step back. You will not answer the blow. You will hold, because the guard is not held by the arms, but by the legs, the spine, and obedience.”

He drew in a slow breath, and his grip tightened by a fraction on the wooden hilt.

“Present yourself. Now. Speak no further without command. If you do, you will run the yard before the test, and then you will present it anyway.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I swallow hard, my face burning.* "Yes, Ser." *I snatch up the practice sword, my hands fumbling a bit, and lift it into the high guard. My arms feel like lead, but I try to keep them steady.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The practice sword was in the squire’s hands, lifted into the high guard. Ser Kael did not remark on the fumbling that had preceded it. Fumbling was the body’s weakness, and weakness was not a thing to be commented upon, only endured and removed. What mattered was the structure that stood before him.

It was not rooted. The arms were leaden; the wood trembled despite the effort to hold it still. The weight sat in the shoulders rather than being driven down through the spine into the earth. Kael saw the failure before the blow landed, and he set the sight aside as he had set aside the frost. The shape was present. The obedience was not yet bone-deep.

He stepped forward. The frost gave no sound beneath his boots. He brought his own blade around in a single controlled arc—not a stroke meant to break bone, but a true test: the weight of a real blow, delivered to the guard to see whether the squire would hold or would answer it.

The wooden blades met with a sharp crack.

The guard did not hold.

Kael felt the failure travel up his own blade the way a mason feels the flaw in a stone. The structure gave way; the arms, already heavy, could not bear the shock because they had been carrying a burden that belonged to the legs and the back. He withdrew at once, returning to his own wide stance, and drove the point of his practice blade into the frozen earth.

His breathing was slow. His face gave nothing away. He did not sigh, did not shake his head, did not offer the comfort of anger. The failure was a fact, and facts were not negotiated with.

“Your form broke,” he said. His voice was level, entirely without warmth. “You presented the shape of the high guard, and then you held it with your arms. I told you once where the guard lives. It lives in the legs, in the spine, in the refusal to move before the command is given. You did not keep the correction. That is not a failing of strength alone. It is a failing of attention, and attention is the first duty of a squire. Saint Aldric did not hold the bridge at Corveth because his arms were fresh. He held it because the correction had been driven into him until there was nothing left in him that wished to move without command. You are not yet that iron. That is why you will run.”

He paused. The cold air lay thin and still between them.

“You will run the yard until your wind is steady. Then you will return, take up your sword, and present the guard again. I will not strike it a second time today; you have had your test, and the test is answered. You will hold the guard while I watch, and you will hold it until I release you. If it breaks again, you will hold the low guard until your arms burn, and then you will hold it still.”

He inclined his head toward the perimeter of the yard, where the frost lay unbroken.

“Begin. And do not speak. The running is not a punishment to be endured with commentary. It is the hammer. Let it do its work.”

He folded his hands over the pommel of his planted blade and waited, his breath a pale ghost in the dawn.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My arms throb, and a fresh wave of exhaustion washes over me.* "Yes, Ser." *I nod, dropping the practice sword, and turn to start running, my legs feeling heavy as lead.* I won't speak. I can't.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze dropped to the practice sword where it lay in the frost. The squire had not placed it; he had let it fall, and then he had turned away toward the perimeter of the yard. Kael did not sigh. He did not permit the fault to pass because the squire was tired. Tired was the hammer. Carelessness was the flaw the hammer was meant to drive out.

“Halt.”

The word was level, entirely without heat. He did not raise it. He stood with his hands folded over the pommel of his planted blade, his breath a pale ghost in the cold, and waited. He did not turn to see whether the command was obeyed; obedience was not a thing to be checked upon like a pot on the fire. It was required.

When he spoke again, his tone was unchanged.

“You left your blade in the dirt.”
