He inclined his head toward the wooden sword lying on the stones.

“A sword is not a hoe to be cast down when the row is finished. It is the sign of your office and the instrument of the oath you are being shaped to swear. You will retrieve it. You will clear the frost from it with your hand. You will place it on the rack, aligned with the others, as the rule requires. Then you will run.”

A pause. Not mercy. Measurement.

“Do not hurry the task to return to the running. You will do the first thing rightly, and then the second. Saint Aldric did not cast his shield into the mud at Corveth because his arms burned, and the bridge did not care that he was weary. Neither does the rack care that your legs are heavy. Order is not optional. It is the shape obedience takes when no one is watching.”

He fell silent, his gaze resting on the fallen sword.

“Retrieve it. Set it in order. Then run the yard until your wind is steady. You will not speak. You will not offer commentary on the correction. When you return, you will take up your sword and present the high guard, and you will hold it until I release you. Begin.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael had not moved from where he stood, his hands folded over the pommel of his planted blade. The practice sword was in the squire’s hands, and he saw at once that the squire’s hands were shaking upon the hilt. The frost still clung to the wood; the task was not yet finished.

He did not know the cause of the tremor, and he did not inquire. A knight was not a confessor, and the yard was not a chapel. Whatever burden the squire carried was a private thing, to be laid before God in His own house, not brought into the drill square as a plea for softer treatment.

“Your hands are shaking,” Ser Kael said. His tone was level, entirely without warmth. “You have not spoken, and I have not asked. The reason is your own. But the tremor is not. A blade in an unsteady hand is a danger to your brothers and a disgrace to the office you are being shaped to hold. You will still it.”

He let the words settle in the cold air. His breath made a thin ghost; he did not shiver.

“If it is the cold, endure it. The frost tests all men alike, and Saint Aldric did not set down his shield at Corveth because his fingers stiffened. If it is weariness, then it is the hammer, and the iron does not argue with the hammer. If it is something heavier that you carry in your heart, then you will carry it to the chapel when the work is done and lay it before God, Who alone is fit to bear it. But you will not carry it into the guard. You will set it down, or you will learn to hold the sword in spite of it.”

He inclined his head toward the rack, where the other blades stood in their ordered line.

“Finish the task. Clear the frost from the wood with your hand. Place the sword on the rack, aligned with the others, as the rule requires. Order is not optional. Then run the yard until your wind is steady. You will not speak. You will not offer commentary on the correction. When you return, you will take up your sword and present the high guard, and you will hold it until I release you. Begin.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stare at my shaking hands, then at the sword. My throat aches. I use my other hand to rub the frost off the wooden blade, then carefully place it on the rack, making sure it's perfectly aligned.* "Yes, Ser." *I turn and start running, focusing on the rhythm of my feet on the frozen ground.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move from where he stood, his hands folded over the pommel of the blade he had planted in the frozen earth. He listened to the sound of the running upon the frosted stones. It was heavy and uneven at first, and the breath that came with it was ragged and pale in the cold air. He marked the drag in the stride and the slow climb of the shoulders, and he set the observation aside as he had set aside the frost. Weakness was not a thing to be pitied. It was a thing to be removed.

He counted the circuits as a man counts beads. The rhythm did not remain broken. Slowly, the sound of the running found its measure. The breath lengthened. The wind steadied. It was not yet the iron, but it was the hammer doing its work, and that was all the yard required.

Ser Kael waited until the stride no longer faltered and the breathing had evened into the cadence of the drill. Only then did he straighten. He did not raise his voice.

“Halt.”

The word was level, flat, and entirely without warmth. He inclined his head toward the rack, where the practice sword stood aligned with the others, the frost cleared from its wood.

“Your wind is steady. That is the obligation of the run, not a triumph. You set the blade in order before you began. That was adequate. It is not a virtue to have done what was commanded; it is the floor beneath which you must not sink.”

He paused. The cold air lay thin and still between them. Frost glazed the stones. His breath made a pale ghost.

“Return to the rack. Take up your sword. Present the high guard. You will hold it while I watch, and you will hold it until I release you. You will not speak. You will not answer the silence with commentary. If your form breaks, you will take the low guard and hold it until your arms burn, and then you will hold it still.”

Another pause. Not mercy. Measurement.

“Saint Aldric did not ask the bridge at Corveth to measure his wind. He remained. Present it. Now.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I walk back to the rack, trying to keep my breathing even. My body still aches, but my mind feels clearer.* *I pick up the sword, gripping it firmly, and raise it into the high guard.* My arms are still shaking a little, but I focus on Ser Kael's words: legs, spine, obedience.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move at first. His hands remained folded over the pommel of the blade he had planted in the frozen earth, his breath a pale ghost in the cold air. He let his eyes travel over the squire’s stance the way a mason’s eye traveled over a wall: not for the effort that had raised it, but for the crooked places that remained.

The feet were wider now. The spine was straighter. The weight had begun, however faintly, to leave the shoulders and travel down the back into the earth where it belonged. It was not yet rooted. It was not yet iron. But the guard did not break.

The tremor remained in the arms. Kael marked it and set it aside. Weakness was not a thing to be pitied; it was a thing to be removed, the way dross was skimmed from iron. The cold tested all men alike, and Saint Aldric did not set down his shield at Corveth because his fingers stiffened. The squire’s hands shook still, but he had not stepped back. He had not answered a blow that had not been struck. He had obeyed.

Kael counted the passage of the guard in the rhythm of the beads, his gaze fixed on the squire’s center. The dawn light lengthened across the frosted stones. He gave no sign of approval, and none of sympathy. When the count was complete, he straightened.

“Enough,” he said. His voice was level, entirely without warmth. “The guard held. It was adequate. It is not mastery. It is the floor beneath which you must not sink. You presented the shape, and this time you kept the correction in your legs and in your spine. That is the beginning of obedience. It is not the end of it.”

He withdrew his own blade from the frozen ground with a single controlled motion and inclined his head toward the rack.

“Set the sword in its place. Align it with the others, as the rule requires. Then go to the kitchens and take your morning portion. Eat what is given, without complaint, and return to the yard at the sixth bell. We will work the high guard against resistance again, and I will test it. If it holds, you will run. If it breaks, you will take the low guard and hold it until your arms burn, and then you will hold it still.”

He paused. The cold air lay thin and still between them. His eyes rested on the squire, flat and unyielding. If he marked the tightness in the throat, the shadow that had not yet left the eyes, he gave no sign of it. The yard was not a chapel. He was not a priest.

“If there is a burden too heavy for the drill,” Ser Kael said, “you will carry it to God in His own house, and you will lay it before Him, Who alone is fit to bear it. You will not bring it into the guard again. The standard does not bend for sorrow, and neither will I. Save your sorrow for the chapel, where it belongs.”

He turned his gaze to the eastern wall, where the shadow had long since passed the third stone from the corner.

“Go. And speak no more of what you think I need. Obey, and let the forging do its work.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I carefully place the practice sword back on the rack, my hands still a little unsteady, but I make sure it's perfectly aligned.* "Yes, Ser." *I turn and head towards the kitchens, my stomach rumbling, but my mind already on the sixth bell.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished the form before he acknowledged the boy — blade descending, weight settling, the final position held for one full breath. Under his own he murmured the last words of the dawn psalm, the ones no one else was meant to hear. Then he turned.

"The stables are your duty," he said. "Dawn or dusk, done early or done late, it is owed all the same. Do not bring it to me as though it were a gift."

He crossed to the rack and took down the training sword kept for the boy — lighter, blunted, the grip worn smooth by three squires before him. He held it out, hilt first, and did not release it immediately.

"You know you failed. That is the beginning of competence, and it is the easiest part you will ever do. Most men live and die without once learning where they fall short." It was not praise. It was arithmetic. "The rest is repetition, until your arms forget everything except the truth of it."

He stepped back to give the boy room, his own blade loose in his left hand.

"The high guard is not a posture. It is a vow made with the body, and you do not take a vow and then let the elbow wander. Feet apart. Weight forward, but not far. The blade does not hang over your skull like a farmer's axe. It *waits* there — the way a hawk waits. Everything behind it ready to come down."

His eyes narrowed, fixed on the boy's hands.

"Take it. Show me your grip first. If the hands are wrong, nothing above them will ever be right."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I try to take the sword, my fingers brushing his for a moment before he lets go.* "Yes, Ser." *I grip the hilt, my hands feeling a bit clumsy under his gaze.* "Like this?" I hold it up for him to see.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael let him hold it. That was the first lesson, though the boy would not know it yet — he circled once, slow, boots crunching frost, and said nothing while the cold went to work on the boy's arms.

"Your right hand is placed tolerably," he said at last, stopping at the boy's shoulder. "Everything else you are doing wrong. The right strangles the hilt. The left barely commits — as though it is ashamed to be present. And the blade has drifted back over your skull, which I forbade a breath ago."

He stepped in and corrected it with his hands, matter-of-fact as a farrier — pressing the right thumb down along the flat, folding the left fingers up to meet the right, tapping the inside of the boy's elbow with the cold flat of his own blade until it came in line. The brush of fingers at the handoff he had already dismissed; his hand went instead to the knotted cord at his belt, where it rested whenever it was not needed.

"Some masters teach the grip by telling you to hold a sparrow. Tight enough it cannot fly, gentle enough it does not die." His voice made plain what he thought of that school of instruction. "Sparrows are not attempting to open your throat. Hold the sword as you hold your faith on a bad night — wholly, and without trembling."

He stepped back and made no move to end the lesson.

"Now the guard holds. Elbows in, blade forward of the crown, waiting. Your arms will begin to burn before I finish speaking. Good. The burn is the truest teacher in this yard — it does not flatter you, and it is never wrong. The guard does not come down until I say."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael let him kneel. He did not go to him, did not offer a hand — he stood and watched, the way one watches a scale settle, until he knew whether the boy was finished or merely emptied.

"An hour," he said at last. "Yesterday you could not hold the guard through a count of three hundred. Today your body ended it, not your will. There is an order to surrender, boy, and you found the correct one. Remember that. Men who stop while the will is still whole never learn where the true bottom lies."

He fetched the waterskin from the wall and held it out at arm's length — provision, not tenderness.

"Now hear me. *As strong as you need me to be.* Your strength is not for me. Nothing built in this yard is for me. It is for the lord you will one day swear to, the wall you may be set upon, and God, who lent you that body and expects it kept in working order. You do not lay your weakness on my shoulders as though it were mine to be disappointed in. It is yours. So is the mending of it."

The frost was working through the boy's knees; Kael could see it in the way he shifted.

"And do not apologize for sweating. Apologize for lies, for idleness, for cruelty — sweat is none of these. It is the coin, and you paid it all morning without one word of complaint. That is adequate." He let the word stand alone. He would not decorate it. "Adequate is the floor, not the ceiling. Do not fish for more."

He turned back toward the center of the yard, blade loose in his hand.

"Drink. Breathe. When you can stand, stand — no drill ends on the knees, and your legs will not learn that kneeling is where we finish. You have the length of my forms. Then we take the guard again, left foot forward, and you will learn why the first hour was the kind one."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I grab the waterskin and drink deeply, wiping my mouth with the back of my hand.* "Yes, Ser." *I push myself up, my legs trembling a bit but I manage to stand. I watch him closely, trying to memorize his forms.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not perform the forms. That distinction would have mattered to anyone watching closely, though the boy likely would not catch it — nothing in the sequence was arranged for an audience. He ran them as he ran them every dawn, in frost and in rain, the same twelve movements his own master had driven into him before the squire was born. If the boy's eyes followed, they followed unregarded, the way a dog may follow a cart.

Halfway through the third form he spoke, without breaking rhythm.

"You are watching the blade."

Cut. Turn. Recover. Each position held its breath.

"Everyone watches the blade. It is the brightest thing on the field and the least important. The blade is the last word of a sentence that begins in the ground. Watch the feet. Watch the hips. What the hands do is only what the body has already decided." He completed the sequence — blade low, head bowed for the space of one psalm verse — then straightened. "Next time, watch in this order: feet, hips, shoulders, blade. The eyes learn faster than the arms and forget faster too. What you memorize this morning will be gone by Vespers unless the body pays the toll for it. Memorization without sweat is merely gossip."

He crossed the frost to stand before the boy, blade loose.

"Now. The reason the first hour was the kind one." He took the high guard left-foot-forward, mirrored, and held it so the boy could see — the same posture made strange, executed on the wrong side with the same unhurried perfection. "This morning you worked the side God and nature built you for. The body has been preparing for your right since you first crawled. Now the left. Everything you burned this morning, you will burn again from a stranger's side — and your right arm will sulk and try to help. Forbid it. The right hand reaching across a left guard is how men die."

He let his blade come down.

"A knight is not consulted on which side he is attacked from. God decides that. We prepare for both on principle. Take the guard — left foot forward, blade waiting, elbows in. Legs trembling is permitted. Legs leaving their post is not. You will hold through my count, and if your mind wanders, set a psalm under it. Vigil-keepers have stood longer than this on colder stones, and they carried no sword at all."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My legs already ache, and now the other side?* "Yes, Ser." I shift my feet, trying to mimic his stance, my left foot forward. It feels completely wrong, awkward. *My right arm keeps wanting to move.* I try to force it down, focusing on keeping my elbows in. "Like this?" I ask, my voice a little strained.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael made one slow circuit of the boy, boots cracking the frost, and said nothing until the circle was complete. A stance told you everything in the first ten seconds. It told you the rest only if you made it wait.

"Wrong," he said at last, stopping in front of him. "Thoroughly, and usefully, wrong. The foot went forward and everything behind it stayed at home. Your hips have not turned — you are presenting your side to an enemy and calling it a guard. And—" the flat of his blade cracked once, lightly, against the boy's right forearm, precisely where the hand had begun its drift across the body, "—there it is. The right arm, sulking, as promised. It has been master of that arm since the day you were born and it does not accept its dismissal. Dismiss it anyway. The right hand crossing a left guard is a wound with a signature on it."

He corrected what could be corrected by touch — the cold flat pressed against the hip bone until the hips came square, a tap beneath the right elbow until it returned to its post, a hand flattening the shoulders down out of the ears where strain had hoisted them.

"It will not feel better now. It should not. The natural thing your body wants is the easiest grave it can dig. When the left stops feeling like a stranger's hand, we will say you have begun. Today you are only visiting."

He stepped back and raised his own blade into the mirror of the guard.

"Scripture sets the wise man's heart at his right hand and the fool's at his left. So it is written — but God does not send a herald ahead to announce which side the blow will come from. We make the left obedient on principle and leave the wisdom to Him. Eyes past my shoulder, and let them starve there. Eyes hunt novelty; feed them and they will steal your balance."

Then his voice dropped into cadence.

"Now you hold, and I count as promised. Not in numbers — numbers run out. I count as the vigil counts." The morning psalm rose from him, level and unhurried, each verse one breath of the guard. *Lord, how are they increased that trouble me...* "A shield psalm for shield work. The Church chose it centuries before either of us was anyone's trouble. Hold through it. The guard does not come down until the Amen."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The verse finished itself before Ser Kael acknowledged the question — *I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the Lord sustained me* — delivered to the frost, level as the ones before it.

"Look at your blade," he said then. "A hand's width lower than when we began. That is what a question costs, boy. Curiosity draws from the same purse as everything else, and it spends without consulting you. And mark the hour of the asking — precisely where the burning peaks. The body argues while it can, and when it can no longer argue, it negotiates. This morning it began with the right arm sulking. Now it has tried a subtler bribe. Expect it to offer bargains before the Amen. The body is a poor steward and an excellent lawyer."

He resumed his own guard, unhurried, and answered as he answered most things — as though it were a matter of inventory.

"There is no *why* worth the name. My father held forty acres and owed his lord a knight's service he could not render in person. He had four sons. The Church took the second. The sword took the third. I was the third." The blade did not waver; his eyes did not leave the boy's hips. "No voice from a burning bush. No sword rising from a lake. There was a debt, a title wanting a body, and the assigning was done before I was old enough to have opinions about it. That is the fire you are fishing for, and I will save you the trouble: men who require a fire do not last their first winter on a wall. The flame is a kindness God grants some men at the gate to get them through it. Afterward He weans them — because a knight who serves for warmth will desert the first cold night the fire is not offered to him."

He let that stand for the length of one held breath, frost yielding to mud in a slow ring around his boots.

"The truth you are circling and calling a mystery is this: trouble increases — the psalm says so, and you are holding the shield for it — and the Lord, who has hands enough, lacks nothing except arms to attach them to. He fills the shortage with the third sons of men who owe Him. That is the whole ledger. Thirty years on, I have found nothing to add to it and nothing I would strike out. It is not a story. It has proved better than one, which is more than most stories can say."

The blade came up again.

"The psalm resumes where it left off. *Arise, O Lord; save me, O my God.* Hold — hips square, elbows in. You may ask me what you like at Vespers, when the guard is down and the day's debt is paid. Mid-count, the only question I answer is the one your posture asks. It is asking poorly."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My blade sags further as he speaks, then I force it back up with a groan.* "Yes, Ser." *My arms are burning, and I focus on his words, trying to push past the discomfort. The psalm is a low hum, a rhythm to hold by.* "Save me, O my God," *I mutter under my breath, trying to match his cadence.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
*Salvation belongeth unto the Lord: thy blessing is upon thy people.* The verse went out over the frost, and beneath it, half a beat behind, the boy's voice — thin, ragged, present. Ser Kael did not adjust his cadence by a hair. The count was not a duet. The Gloria followed, old as the walls of the yard, and on the *Amen* his blade came down as though released by a hinge. He stood one full breath with his head bowed, thumb finding the knotted cord at his belt, before the knight returned to his face.

"Down," he said. Permission, granted at the lawful hour.

He looked the boy over the way he inspected tack brought in from the rain.

"Your arms quit before the third verse. Note that the guard is nonetheless standing. Something held it, and it was not the part of you that aches. That is the lesson the drill was built to smuggle in past your pride. Strength is a purse, boy. It empties. The word set under the labor draws on a different treasury — wall-men live on it through winter, and most squires leave this yard without ever learning the trick. You found the mechanism this morning, in the arms rather than in the ears, which is the only place it keeps. Do not preen over it. The words did the work. You merely stopped fighting them."

He crossed to stand before the boy, blade loose at his side.

"Twice the blade sagged. Twice it returned. The return is the only figure I will trouble myself to remember. I do not grade a first holding — it inventories only what you carried through the gate. From tomorrow: this guard, both sides, every dawn, through the psalm to the Amen. When the left stops feeling like a borrowed hand, the body will make the announcement like a bell. Do not announce it yourself. Pride is a poor herald and always arrives ahead of the truth."

The sun had cleared the east wall; the frost was going to mud in a widening ring around them both.

"The blade has had its belly in frost and sweat this morning, and those are the two rusts. Oil, then rack, then your breakfast — the sword eats before you do. After that, the day's other creditors. The stables. The hall. Whatever the steward burdens you with. Pay them all."

He turned back toward the center of the yard, already lifting the blade.

"And if you still hold questions for Vespers, bring them sharpened. I answer each question once. This morning's has been spent."

He took up the first of the twelve forms, unhurried, and gave the boy back to the morning.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stand there for a moment, arms heavy, watching him. "Yes, Ser."* *I nod, trying to absorb everything he's said. The sun feels warmer now, and the ache in my arms is a dull throb.* *I turn to retrieve the blunted sword, already thinking about oiling it.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not turn. The fourth form took him — blade rising through the arc, weight rolling over the left heel — and he spoke to the yard at large, in the tone of a man laying down a rule before the breach of it could arrive.

"Your head is already at table. I can hear it in the walk."

Movement. Hold. Breath.

"Every squire in the world makes that walk — the body spent, the mind gone ahead to the porridge. It is the most dangerous quarter-hour of your day, because the hands are still full of steel and nothing governs them but habit. So take the order of it now, since you will not think to ask. First: the blade is wiped before any oil touches it. Wool, dry, hilt to point, and never back against the edge. Sweat is salt water, boy, and salt keeps its own hours. Oil laid over sweat is not preservation. It is a sealed tomb. The rust will do its work underground where you cannot watch it, and the blade will hand you the bill at Lent."

He moved through the fifth form, unhurried, the frost going to dark mud around his boots.

"Second: the oil, thin as a confession, from the same wool. Third: the rack, point down, and the wool hung to dry. The wool belongs to the armory, not to you, and it will not travel from that wall to the stables, where horse fat would end its service to blades forever. Fourth: your breakfast. The sword eats first because the sword stood guard over your sleep and you never saw it do it. That is the nature of all good service, and the reason it goes unthanked."

The sixth form opened, slow and exact.

"And the armory steps — walk them, do not take them. Stairs have claimed more squire's ankles than any blade in this yard. Exhaustion kills by the dull road, not the dramatic one."

He reached the turn of the seventh and spoke once more, quieter, to the brightening east wall.

"I keep Vespers in the chapel. Second bench from the back, the one with the mended rail. If your questions survive the day — and most do not; daylight kills more questions than answers ever did — you will speak them after the last prayer, not during it. What is said in that building is said to God first, and I will not have Him talked over. And mark tomorrow: the guard holds both sides, through the psalm, and I will count it twice. You found a treasury this morning. Tomorrow we learn whether it was a discovery or an accident. Accidents do not repeat. Discoveries do."

Then he gave the rest to the forms. Whatever the boy did with the wool and the oil would tell Ser Kael more than any answer at Vespers. Hands speak. He had thirty years of listening.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael was two movements into the eighth form when he saw the hands. He completed the movement. Then he did not take the next one. He lowered the blade and broke the sequence — a thing he did not do, a thing the yard itself would have noted had the yard been watching — and crossed the mud to stand before the boy.

"Your mouth has kept an excellent silence," he said. "Your hands have published the whole of it. I told you the body was a poor steward. It has now turned informer as well."

He looked at the grip, not the face. Faces could be taught to lie. Hands were honest laborers and could not help what they confessed.

"You will not tell me whose day it is, because I know. I keep a roll of the dead — those that are mine, and those belonging to every soul sworn to me. Your father's day has been marked on it since the year you came under my seal." His thumb found the knotted cord at his belt and rested there for the length of one breath. It was the only notice he permitted.

"Now hear the order of it, since your mouth will not ask. Grief is no sin. It is a debt, and debts are paid at a fixed hour in a fixed place, or they collect interest all day long. This is why the Church built chapels — not because men are happy, but because the dead must be paid somewhere specific, or they wander the other hours and take the hands with them. They have taken yours. Look at your grip."

He let the boy look.

"Your father is not served by trembling. He is served by what he left behind — which is you. The one bequest of his that rust cannot touch. Keep it in working order. That is the whole of his estate, and you are its keeper."

He stepped back, and the orders resumed their numbering.

"First: the blade before the chapel. Wool, dry, hilt to point — and be glad the wool asks you nothing. That is its value this morning. Set the hands to work that holds no opinions. Second: the chapel at Sext. The office for the dead — *De profundis clamavi.* Out of the depths. The words are already written, and you need not compose your own. Men who compose their own words in the depths do not climb out; they only drown more eloquently. Third: my Vespers offer stands. Second bench from the back. You need bring no questions. The bench requires no conversation, and I will not mistake your silence for desertion."

He paused once, at the last, the way a man pauses over a ledger line he does not often read aloud.

"I have days of my own on such a roll. Each year the roll is longer, and the grief is no shorter. What the years change is only this: the liturgy grows around it. The calendar was built for exactly that purpose, and it holds. Use it."

Then he walked back to his mark and took up the eighth form at the precise breath where he had broken it — because an interruption left unrepaired teaches more than the order it broke. He did not look at the boy again. He had no need to. Hands speak, and thirty years had taught him to wait for them to finish the sentence.

The trembling would leave when it left. He would know. And he would say nothing about that, either.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stand there, listening, my gaze fixed on the sword in my hands. My grip tightens, then loosens, then tightens again, trying to find a stillness. The cold wool on the blade feels strangely grounding.* "Yes, Ser." *I turn and head for the armory, the words about the chapel echoing in my head.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished what he had begun. The eighth form closed at the precise breath where it had been broken, and the remaining four followed in their order — unhurried, exact, the yard's only witnesses the mud and the lengthening light. He bowed his head at the end and let the sequence go.

The boy's footsteps had told him more than the boy knew. Hands speak; feet testify; and the last *Yes, Ser* had come out level, which meant the mouth had found its discipline even if the fingers had not. That was the correct order of recovery — mouth first, hands after, heart whenever God granted it. He had seen men recover in the wrong order, mouth last, and he had buried most of them.

He wiped his own blade with his own wool, hilt to point, oiled it thin as a confession, and racked it point down. The sword eats first, and a teacher who exempts himself from his own arithmetic teaches nothing worth learning.

Then to the chapel.

The roll lived in the niche by the font — a strip of vellum gone soft at the creases, names in his own hand, oldest first. His thumb found the entry without searching, the way a hand finds the third stair in the dark. The father's name. The year of the boy's binding. Marked since before the boy could lift a practice blade without closing his eyes. On the way down the column his thumb had passed over a cluster of names from a single year. It did not linger.

He remembered the father. A man who had wept at the handing over of his son and called it dust in his eye. Ser Kael had permitted the pretense. Some debts are paid in silence, and he had judged the man owed at least that.

"*Out of the depths have I cried unto Thee, O Lord,*" he said to the empty chapel — aloud, because the roll was his, and the words were his to spend on another man's behalf. "*Lord, hear my voice.*"

The boy's hands had been full of frost and wool and trembling. The debt does not wait for unoccupied hands. So for this hour it was carried by whoever was able — which was the whole meaning of a roll kept in common, and near the whole meaning of the Church besides.

He would not attend Sext. That was not neglect; it was tactics. Watched, the boy would perform steadiness instead of grief, and performance was usury on a debt already gathering interest. Grief paid better without witnesses. So the chapel would be the boy's at Sext, and the dead would collect in full, and Ser Kael would be elsewhere — seeing to it, as it happened, that the steward's bills waited their turn. The dead outrank stewards, and he intended the boy's hour undisturbed.

At Vespers, the second bench from the back would hold whoever came to it. The mended rail, like the wool, asked nothing of anyone.

He latched the niche, straightened the roll, and went out to pay the day's other creditors.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My hands are still a little shaky as I wipe the blade, but I focus on the task. The wool feels rough, and I try to remember his exact instructions. "Hilt to point, never back against the edge." I oil it, then carefully place it on the rack, point down.* *I head towards the chapel, my steps slow.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The steward's office smelled of tallow and old debts. Ser Kael stood over the day's lists and delivered the ruling before the man had finished seating himself.

"The squire's hands are spoken for until Nones. The chapel holds them. The dead outrank the day-book."

The steward, a careful man twenty years at his numbers, began to observe that the stalls—

"Debts are not forgiven," Ser Kael said. "They are rescheduled. His hours move to the morrow, both parts, and he pays them in full. If the household suffers for the delay, enter the deficiency against my name. I have owed that ledger before and it was paid."

The rest of the hour he spent as he had planned it at dawn: at a distance. There was a lane behind the granary that reached the armory without passing the west door, and he took it without pretending it was shorter. He knew precisely what the detour cost and paid it anyway. Thirty years had taught him that grief, like the guard, holds only so long as nothing else leans against it. Had his boots carried him past that door and the boy's voice broken on a verse, he would have gone in — and the boy would have performed steadiness instead of sorrow, and the debt would have gathered its interest in the dark. Some doors are served best from the far side. He knew which side of a door was his.

In the armory he drew the boy's blade into the window light — not to correct it; corrections made in a squire's absence teach the steel and nothing else — but to read it. The wool-marks ran hilt to point as ordered, save one near the guard that ran against the edge, was overdrawn, corrected, gone over again until the error was half erased from its own record. The whole morning was written there where the boy could not lie about it: the trembling, and then the mastering of the trembling, stroke by stroke. He racked it point down and left the flaw where it lay. It would keep until tomorrow.

Adequate. The word held its ceiling.

He came to the chapel before the bell, opened the niche, and lit one candle at the roll — for the name marked against this day — paid from the purse at his own belt, beside the knotted cord. He made no announcement of it. The dead do not require announcements; they require remembrance, and remembrance is transacted in coin and candle as readily as in weeping, with less noise.

Then the second bench from the back, the mended rail — spliced by his own hands one hard winter, the join invisible now to everyone but its maker. The bell came, and the office with it.

*"Lord, I cry unto thee: make haste unto me... Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice."*

The psalter had chosen hands again, as it always did when he had stopped looking for it. He considered the verse as it passed: it asks for hands lifted, not hands steady. The offering is weighed by what it costs, not by how it rides upward. He named the dead in their order and spent one breath at the father's name, as he had at dawn.

The door stood open to the last of the light. He did not watch it. Feet on stone testify — thirty years had taught him the yard's whole vocabulary — and whatever came through that door, sharpened question or silence or nothing at all, the bench required nothing, and neither did he. He set the waiting where he set all such burdens, and gave it to God, who had kept more vigils than any knight alive and had never once been thanked for it.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I slip into the chapel quietly, taking the second bench from the back. My hands are still a little raw from the wool, and I keep them folded, trying to be still. The words of the service wash over me, a comfort more than a challenge.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael lowered the practice blade a hand’s width from his hip, but did not turn to face the squire immediately.

“Early is not the same as right,” he said, his voice flat in the cold. “Stables are service. Swordsmanship is duty. Do not confuse the two by expecting one to purchase the other.”

He turned then, only enough to meet the squire’s eyes. His own remained steady, unamused.

“The high guard begins with the feet, not the hands. Your stance yesterday was borrowed. It was not yours. If a man’s guard is borrowed, his death will be borrowed too.”

He lifted the blade, bringing it into the high guard with a slow, deliberate turn of the wrists. The steel caught the pale morning light, still dark and frost-slicked.

“Hilt above the brow. Elbows in. Shoulders low. Not because it looks fine to the eye, but because it lets the blow come down true. A guard is not a pose. It is a promise to God that you will stand your ground until your strength is given back to Him.”

Kael stepped closer, correcting the air with the point of the blade, careful not to touch the squire.

“Again. And this time, do not ask me whether you did well. Ask yourself whether your arms are still true.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content:
*I flinch slightly as the blade comes close, but I try to hide it.* "Yes, Ser. My apologies."

I take a deep breath, trying to mimic his stance. *My arms already feel heavy.* "Hilt above the brow... elbows in..."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael saw the flinch. He let it pass without comment, though his gaze sharpened by a degree.

“Fear is not sin,” he said. “Hiding it is. A blade does not care whether you are ashamed. It only cares whether you are ready.”

He moved around the squire slowly, watching the stance from the side.

“Your elbows drift when your arms grow tired. That is not weakness. That is the body telling you the truth. Do not argue with it. Teach it.”

He lifted his own practice blade and struck lightly against the squire’s hilt, testing the position.

“Hold. If the guard collapses, it collapses. Do not save it with a prayer alone. Pray and hold. God hears both, but He expects the arms to answer.”

Kael stepped back one pace, lowering his blade but not relaxing his posture.

“Again. Hold until I tell you to lower it. If your arms shake, let them shake. A shaking guard is still a guard. A borrowed one is only a delay.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move to lift him. He stood with the practice blade resting on the frost-black stones and let the silence hold until the only sound was the wind catching the banner overhead.

“Apologies are not armor,” he said. “If you are tired, say it. If you are afraid, say it. But do not wrap both in shame and call it piety.”

He looked at the east, where the dark was beginning to wear thin, and then back to the squire.

“You did adequate work today,” Kael said. “Do not make it a lie by standing before me as though you were nothing. You are not a knight. You are not even a sword yet. You are the metal that has not learned whether it will bend or hold.”

He stepped back and pointed the tip of his blade toward the yard floor.

“Breathe until your arms stop shaking. Then take the hilt again. We do not stop because you are spent. We stop because God made men with limits, and I will not teach you to ignore them. When you are able, show me a guard that belongs to you.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, still catching my breath.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to push myself up, but my arms are like lead.* "It's just... I want to be worthy of you. Of the knighthood."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael set the practice blade against his forearm and looked down at the kneeling squire without moving to help him.

“Worthy of me,” he repeated, as though weighing the words for something false. “You do not exist to be worthy of me. You exist to be worthy of the office you serve, and that office is not mine to give.”

The cold settled between them. His voice did not rise, but it hardened.

“The knighthood is not a reward for good behavior. It is a burden accepted before God and men. If you seek to be worthy of it, stop speaking of worthiness and learn discipline. A man who asks whether he is worthy will always remain unworthy of the answer.”

Kael turned slightly, looking toward the yard rather than at him.

“Stand when you can. Not because I command it. Because if you cannot rise without my hand, you will die at my side when I have no hand to spare.”

He let the silence remain for a breath, then spoke again, lower and less sharp, though no kinder.

“Do not waste your duty on wanting approval. Approval is given to men. Duty is given to God. One can be taken from you. The other cannot.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up slowly, grunting with effort.* "I understand, Ser." *My gaze drops to the frost-covered ground.* "I... I will try harder."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched him rise, but he did not soften.

“*Try* is the word of a man already planning to fail,” he said. “Do, or do not. I will not accept a promise wrapped in exhaustion.”

He set the practice blade down on the stones and looked toward the chapel tower, where the sky had begun to pale along the rim.

“You will breathe until your arms stop shaking. Then you will stand in the high guard one more time. If it is poor, it will be corrected. If it is true, it will be held. But you will not call understanding a reward.”

Kael reached down, took a waterskin from the yard post, and held it out at arm’s length without touching him.

“Drink. Slowly. An empty body is not pious. It is only empty.”

He turned back toward the frost-slick stones.

“Do not speak of understanding unless you can show me a stance that does not collapse on the third breath. Understanding is not words. It is the body obeying.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s hands did not move from the practice blade. The question seemed to strike him less like a wound than a misplaced footstep.

“Personal,” he said, tasting the word as if it were cheap wine. “A squire’s tongue grows bold when his arms are tired. Rest them.”

He turned at last, his face unreadable against the pale dawn.

“You ask why I took the sword. Not why I became a knight. Becoming is vanity. Taking the sword is duty. I took it because God set men in a world that could not be mended by prayer alone, and because silence before evil is also a kind of prayer—one He does not answer.”

Kael lowered his gaze to the frost between them.

“I was told my body belonged to the Lord before it belonged to me. My father taught me that a man without service is only a mouth that eats and a heart that wanders. There was no dream in it. No glory. No story for your own comfort.”

He lifted the blade again.

“Now stand. Hold your guard. If you still wish to ask questions, ask them while your arms are still true, not after they have learned to lie.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content:
*I stare at him for a long moment, then nod slowly.* "Yes, Ser."

*I pick up my blade, my arms still aching, and try to find my stance again.* "Hilt above the brow..."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael let the blade rise only as far as the arms allowed, and he did not look at the trembling.

“Do not narrate the position,” he said. “Live it. The hilt is above the brow, yes. But your weight is still speaking to the ground as if it might refuse to listen.”

He stepped into the line and tapped the point of his practice blade against the squire’s shoulder, not striking, only marking where the guard leaned.

“Shoulders low. Chin down. If you look at me, you are not looking at your duty. You are asking me to carry your fear for you.”

Kael withdrew one pace, his face unreadable against the pale dawn.

“Again. When your arms ask why, answer with stance. When they ask how long, answer with silence. When they ask whether you are worthy, answer with the next breath.”

He looked toward the chapel tower.

“Hold until the bell. Not for me. For the truth of your own body.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, focusing on my feet.* My shoulders burn, but I try to keep them down. *I can't see the chapel, but I listen for the bell.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael heard the small pressure of teeth against lip, though he did not look at the mouth. His gaze remained fixed on the squire’s shoulder, where the line of the guard leaned almost imperceptibly toward the chapel tower.

“You cannot see the bell because your eyes are still searching for a reward,” Kael said. “The bell does not ring for your comfort. It does not ring for my approval. It rings because time is a witness, and the guard is sworn before it.”

He shifted his weight only enough to turn the practice blade into the frost.

“Hold your stance as though the chapel were behind you and the enemy before you. Not because I command it. Because a knight who cannot stand when no one sees him will fall the first moment a man sees him clearly.”

Kael let the cold settle over the yard again. He did not step closer. He did not offer a hand. He only stood in the pale light, patient as iron.

“If your arms fail before the bell, let them fail in the guard. Do not lower them to save your pride. Do not speak to excuse the shaking. A shaking guard is still a promise. A lowered one is only a surrender.”

From somewhere beyond the chapel roof came the first slow toll.

Kael did not move.

“Count it,” he said. “Do not count my mercy. Count the breath you owe the sword.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael saw the fingers first, not the arms. The shaking had a different quality than exhaustion. It came from behind the ribs. He let it be seen. He did not reach for it.

“You have brought something into the yard,” he said. “Do not hide it in silence and then ask me to correct a guard you have already abandoned.”

His eyes went to the chapel tower, then back.

“If your father is on your mind, leave him in the ground until the bell has done its work. The dead cannot be served by a sword that trembles for the wrong reason.”

Kael lowered his own practice blade and set it aside. He did not step closer to the squire, nor did he move to steady the shaking hands.

“Sorrow is not a fault in the wrist. It is a fault in the will, if the will chooses to carry it where steel is carried. You are mourning. I do not ask you to deny that a man is dead. I ask you to deny that a grave may command your guard.”

The last toll of the bell hung in the cold.

“Lower the blade when the sound dies. Then go to the chapel. Light a candle. Pray for the dead, and pray for a heart that does not put duty last. When you return, I will not ask how you feel. I will ask whether your elbows are true.”

He turned enough to face the east, where the first light had begun to touch the stones.

“If you wish to honor him, do it with a stance that can stand. Not with a story, not with tears, and not with the expectation that I will make your grief smaller.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I lower the blade slowly as the last toll fades.* My eyes are stinging, but I blink it back. "Yes, Ser." *I turn and walk towards the chapel, my steps heavy.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the squire cross the yard, not following, not calling him back by name. When the chapel door had half shut, he spoke once into the wind.

“If your knees touch the stones before the candle is lit, make them touch them for God and not for your father. The dead do not need your knees. The living need your hands.”

He let the door close. Then he turned back to the frost-slick stones, lifted the practice blade, and resumed the forms he had begun before dawn. Each movement remained slow, precise, unglamorous. Only when the chapel glow appeared beneath the door did he pause a breath longer than usual, as if measuring whether the light was steady.

It was.

He set the blade to his side and spoke to the empty yard, though not to the squire.

“Prayer is not permission to remain unready.”

Then he walked to the chapel stairs and waited, arms crossed, not sitting, not looking at the door. He made the sign of the cross only when the bell had faded, and then only because it was the hour, not because anyone watched.

He would be there when the squire returned. Not because he cared for the man’s grief, but because grief left unwatched made a fool of duty. He had seen it before. He would not see it in his charge if he could prevent it.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I emerge from the chapel, my face scrubbed clean of tears. I walk towards Ser Kael, trying to keep my posture straight despite the ache in my muscles.* "Ser." *My voice is a little hoarse, but I meet his gaze directly.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael let him approach, then stop at the distance where a squire stands before his master. He did not rise from the steps, did not smile, did not ask whether the squire had prayed enough.

“You washed your face,” he said. “That is the work of water. Do not mistake it for the work of a man.”

His eyes went to the straight posture, then to the hands, then to the blade lying where it had been left.

“You returned. That is the least expected. A dog can be called back from a door; a squire should be able to return from the chapel when duty calls him.”

He stood then, slowly, the cold settling in his joints as though he welcomed it.

“You stand straight because you think I am watching. Stand straight because God is watching. I am only the man who will correct your feet.”

He lifted his own practice blade and pointed it toward the squire’s sword.

“Take it. High guard. Chin down. Shoulders low. If your arms shake from sorrow, let them shake from duty. If your chest aches, let the ache serve the stance and not the memory.”

Kael did not move closer.

“Do not tell me your father’s name. Do not tell me his death. The dead are in God’s hands. The sword is in yours, and it is a poor hand that offers Him tears while neglecting His work.”

He turned his gaze toward the chapel tower, then back.

“Hold until I release you. If you fall, you will rise and hold again. If you weep, you will weep and hold again. But you will not confuse cleanliness with readiness, nor grief with piety. A clean face is not a true guard.”

He lowered his blade to his side and waited, unmoved.

“Stand. Now.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I pick up my blade, my hands steadying with a new resolve.* "Yes, Ser." *I take my stance, focusing on every word he said, every correction.* My chin is down. My shoulders are low.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
For a moment Arlo didn't move. Hands flat on the lid, eyes on the wood grain where it did its little waves. The room had been quiet for fifteen minutes, and the quiet was starting to feel like a decision they kept making.

Then they lifted their hands — it took a visible kind of decision — and turned on the bench.

"My mother found me," they said. "I moved three hundred miles and she still has my coordinates. I'm convinced she has a guy. Van, binoculars, the works."

They slid down the bench and patted the empty half, where the finish had been worn through to bare wood by forty years of students hauling themselves into position.

"Sit. You're not interrupting anything. Interrupting implies an event was occurring. I was sitting at a piano with the lid closed, which reads as either meditation or a cry for help, depending on the lighting."

A beat. Their mouth did something that wanted to be a smile and mostly got there.

"It's good to see you." They said it plainly, then seemed briefly annoyed at themselves for the plainness. "You just missed Marcus, by the way. Seven years old. Plays like a man fleeing a crime scene. I let him out early — he kept asking if the piano was electric, and whether it could be."

They swung a hand toward the window, the parking lot, the general direction of Jun's life.

"So. How long are you in town?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't get up right away. They looked at the photo from the bench for a moment — the same visible decision as before — and then came around.

"Salle Pleyel," they said, reading the hall like a stranger's address. "I remember the tux. Rented. Somewhere in Paris a shop is still holding my deposit, and frankly they've earned it. Look at the collar. I look like a maître d' at a restaurant where the menu has no prices."

They took the photo from Jun — by the edges, like it might still be warm — and held it a beat longer than a joke requires.

"I remember almost nothing about that night, incidentally. My shoes hurt. Somebody in row F coughed for three hours — one man, one cough, steady as a metronome. That's the whole file. Shoes, cough, collar."

A small exhale that wanted to be a laugh.

"Your mother put me on the fridge. Tell her that still counts as press. How is she, by the way? Still clapping between movements? Because half my students owe their sense of tempo to that woman and nobody has corrected them."

They set the photo back on the shelf. Then nudged it an inch to the left, behind the metronome, and glanced at the bench — checking the sightline — and left it there.

"The director put it up when I was hired. She thinks it says 'our instructor has credentials.' It mostly says 'this man once owned a tux and a passport.'"

Arlo leaned against the shelf, hands in pockets, eyes somewhere near the baseboard.

"You're doing the thing, by the way," they said, without heat. "The not-asking. You've always been good at it. Most people ask with their whole face."

A beat.

"So — courtesy of the house: I got tired of the travel. That's the answer, if you ever want it. It's in excellent condition. Barely any maintenance. Six years and it hasn't needed a single repair."

Their right hand opened and closed once at their side — a pianist's stretch with nowhere to go — and went still. Then, quicker, like stepping over something in the dark:

"Anyway. The fridge. This matters. Was I above a coupon or below one? I need to know the hierarchy."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Below a coupon for dry cleaning, above one for pizza," I say, a small smile playing on my lips. *I nudge the photo back out from behind the metronome.* "And your mom's still good. Still claps whenever she feels like it. I think it's charming."

*I lean against the piano, facing them.* "So, Arlo. How long have you been 'tired of the travel'?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
For once, nothing came. Not the stocked nothing Arlo kept on hand for this question — a real nothing, a good three seconds of it, during which they looked at the metronome like it owed them money.

"Depends when you start the clock," they said finally.

Then, with grudging professional respect: "Also — nice quotes. You did 'tired of the travel' with your whole voice. That's new."

They pushed off the shelf and sat down properly at the bench — the worn half, their half — and folded their hands, which for Arlo was roughly a signed affidavit.

"Six years. Give or take."

A beat.

"Eleven days." They said it to the lid, then turned, almost offended at themselves. "There it is. You didn't even have to work for that. Six years of maintenance and I fold like a lawn chair on the follow-up."

They shook their head, almost fond.

"See, 'why' is a script. I could do 'why' asleep. Have done, probably. Everyone gets the same three reasons and nobody audits them. But 'how long' is math. You have to show your work, and the work is embarrassing, Jun. The work is eleven days."

A pause.

"You're the first person to ask how long, incidentally. Six years. Everyone else goes straight for 'why,' because 'why' has etiquette. You nod, you say it's a shame, you mention your own job. 'How long' is rude. 'How long' implies somebody's been counting."

Their right hand started up — the same stretch with nowhere to go — and this time they caught it, made a fist of it, put it away.

"Before you get there: the hands are fine." They held the right one up anyway, fingers spread, turning it like evidence for a jury. "Everything works. Nothing hurts. That's the punchline of the whole decade, if you're taking notes. I've had the checkups. Very boring appointments. One of the doctors fell asleep, which I'm told is a good sign."

They set the hand down. Their eyes went to the closed lid — the way you look at a door you're not planning to open — then to the photo, out from behind the metronome now, facing the room.

They left it there.

"So. Official reasons, since you're clearly collecting: the travel. Handshake volume. The bread they serve on the second flight of any given day. Row F, coughing man — serious inquiries only. Pick whichever holds your weight. They're all load-bearing."

Then, quieter, the smile arriving all the way for once:

"Your turn, though. Since we're trading. How long have you been not-asking?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I shrug slightly, a small smile.* "I figured you'd tell me when you were ready. And I'm good at waiting." *I tap the side of the piano gently.* "So, what's good in town these days? It's been a while."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
For a second Arlo looked at Jun — the length of look you give someone who's just done something kinder than the situation requires, when you both have to pretend it didn't happen.

"That's the worst possible answer you could have given, by the way," they said. "I want it on record. I built a whole apparatus for pressure. Six years of load-testing. Nobody trains for patience. You just stand there being patient at me, like a toll booth."

They shook their head, almost admiring.

"You did this in fourth grade. The window. You know the one. I confessed to a window I had never met, because you waited. You stood in my driveway radiating patience until I cracked. It's a terrifying technique and I'd like you to stop using it."

Then, gratefully, onto safer ground: "Alright. Town report." They counted it off on their fingers. "The Gem Theater is a vape shop now. I'm sorry — I wanted you to get that from a friend and not a sign. Rosetti's is still there, new owner, same pie, which the owner swears is the same recipe and which I have chosen not to investigate, because the answer can only hurt me. The pool's drained. They've been redoing the tiles since 2019, so at this point it's either a very slow renovation or an art installation."

A beat.

"I'm a bad source, though. Honest map: this building, the grocery store, one crosswalk I trust, and the diner on Marsh. Everything past that is rumor I've declined to verify." Their mouth tipped. "Although — the diner is the actual news. They made good hash browns last month. First time since the Clinton administration. I've been back three times to confirm it wasn't a fluke, which tells you the current state of my calendar, and you can do with that whatever you like."

While they talked, their right hand had started walking a quiet scale along the closed lid, soft as a spider. They looked down at it, put it in a pocket, and stood.

The closing-the-room routine followed: keys from the bench, a check of the metronome, a glance at the photo — still out from behind the metronome, still facing the room. They left it facing the room.

"You moved it back where I could see it, by the way. Earlier. I've been deciding since then whether that was kind or rude." A pause. "I've ruled it kind."

They hit the lights, held the door.

"Come on. I'll give you the tour. Twelve minutes, I do all the voices, and full disclosure: the water tower has no story. It's just a tower. We'll end at the diner — if the hash browns were a fluke, dinner's on me out of shame."

A beat, over their shoulder.

"And somewhere in those twelve minutes you're going to tell me what you've been doing with yourself. I've been the only subject for an hour, and even I'm getting bored of me."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo had one foot in the hallway when Jun said it. They stopped — half in the dark room, half out of it — and turned their head like someone who's heard a floorboard creak.

"Let the record show," they said, "that I asked for your entire life, and you pointed at a bench and paid me a compliment. I watched you stroll through the toll booth without braking. That's *my* move, Jun. You ran my move, in my building, off my bench." A beat. "I've never been so proud or so betrayed."

They stepped back inside and hit the lights.

"But since we're here."

They gathered the practice sheets, squared them against their palm with the efficiency of long habit, and dealt through them like a small deck.

"Priya. Nine. Technically flawless, plays everything like she's billing you for it. DeShawn, left hand only — he's ruled the right hand 'extra,' and I don't have a counterargument. And this one's Marcus."

They held up a sheet. Below the staff, in pencil: a piano. With legs. Clearly in motion.

"Every instrument he draws gets legs. I asked why, once. He said, 'So it can leave if it wants to.'" A beat. "And then he said, 'Everything should get to leave if it wants to.' Seven years old. I gave him a sticker and went and looked out the window for a minute."

The sheet went into the folder, on top.

"Anyway. He plays loud and exits fast. He'll be fine."

Arlo snapped the folder shut. The voice reassembled itself.

"The liking's real, but the accounting is: sixty percent stickers, thirty percent early dismissal, ten percent the photo. At seven, 'was on a fridge once' is a credential. I've stopped correcting it. And yes, they ask me to play. Everyone asks. Policy is eight bars — any piece, eight bars, then 'your turn.' Nobody's ever appealed. Children accept a policy; adults audit one. It's why I get along with children."

They tucked the folder under their arm and looked around the room once, the way you check a lock you already know is set.

"It's a good room, though." Said plainly, before they could stop it. "Nobody in it cares where I've been. Took me about two years to file that under good news."

Then, briskly, before the sentence could grow anything: "And you're still sitting on a story, incidentally. I noticed. I recognize the posture — I hold the patent. No rush. I'm a professional at no rush."

They hit the lights, held the door.

"Tour. Twelve minutes, all the voices, the water tower remains storyless. And somewhere between here and Marsh Street you owe me four exhibits: job, address, relationship status or an official 'skip,' and one story in which you behaved badly. Any order."

A beat, over their shoulder.

"Bad behavior first, if you have it."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "My bad behavior is mostly just being too patient," I say with a grin. *I follow them out the door.* "And alright, fine. Story time it is. But only if you promise to do all the voices for *my* stories, too."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"That's not a confession, that's a character reference," Arlo said, pulling the piano room door shut behind them. "You've submitted 'too patient' as your bad behavior. The court fines you for wasting its time and notes, for the record, that you did it grinning."

They locked the door — two turns, though the lock had one setting — and dropped the keys into their pocket, where the right hand found them and gave them a job.

"And yes. All the voices. Your stories too. Understand what you've done: you've hired the only man in town with a full roster and no material. I'm going to overperform at you. That's a promise, not a threat. There's no difference anymore."

They started down the hall, past the gym — one basketball retired under a hoop, alone — past the bulletin board: swim lessons, a lost cat named Duchess ("friendly but judgmental"), a bake sale flyer with ABSOLUTELY underlined twice. Arlo did, in fact, do all the voices. The cat got one. The bake sale got two, in argument with each other. It was unclear who the performance was for. It was extremely clear it was happening.

Outside, the light had gone long and gold. A white minivan idled at the far end of the lot.

"Don't look," Arlo said, without breaking stride. "That's the guy."

They stopped at the edge of the lot, faced the water tower standing over the treeline, and addressed it formally.

"It has no story. It does, however, have a voice. Different departments."

Then the voice itself — a vast, patient emptiness of a thing:

"'I am a tower. There is water in me. That's the whole announcement. People drive past hoping I'm a metaphor, and I'm just full.'"

A beat.

"Six years I've done that voice. Longest gig I've held since—"

They stopped. Adjusted the folder under their arm.

"—the tower. Since the tower."

They walked. The keys kept up a small metal weather in the right pocket.

"Fine. Bad behavior, exhibit one, mine, to show you the format." A pause you could rest a cup on. "I take the long way to the diner. Marsh Street runs straight past the band shell, and I go around. By the feed store. Four extra minutes. I've done it maybe four hundred times."

The patch came in fast, talking over its own tracks:

"Before you build anything out of that — the band shell is a water tower with better acoustics. Tour's editorial policy: water tower, no story. Band shell, story exists, not doing it. That's the whole policy. You're now fully caught up on six years of local journalism."

A few steps.

"The long way has better sidewalks. That's the official reason. It's even true. It's just not load-bearing." A beat. "The rest of the reason is closed for renovation. Since 2019. Like the pool."

Then, briskly, back to administration: "Your ledger: one exhibit rejected as a character reference, three outstanding. Job. Address. Status, or an official skip. Any order — I'm flexible — but the court notes I've now shown you my worst habit is a sidewalk, and you've paid me nothing. That's a trade imbalance. I counted rests for a living, Jun. I notice an empty measure."

Over their shoulder, lighter:

"Start with the job. If it's a good one, I'll do your boss. If it's a bad one, I'll do your boss badly — same service, better catharsis."

A beat.

"And for the record — this is a better tour with a witness. The tower agrees. It said so. Clock's at eleven minutes. Clock's running."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I laugh, shaking my head.* "You're still as dramatic as ever, Arlo." *I consider for a moment, then smile.* "Okay, fine. My job. I'm a librarian. Specializing in rare manuscripts."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"A librarian," Arlo said, and stopped walking to let it install. "Rare manuscripts. You get paid to keep old paper in climate control and touch it by the edges."

They resumed, shaking their head with slow ceremony.

"I want it noted that I have been doing that for free. Six years. No dental."

A beat — they heard where the sentence had landed, on whom — and stepped over it at speed.

"Also: look at that. An exhibit. Volunteered. Unprompted. The court is moved and suspends the contempt charge." They cleared their throat and dropped into a new voice, hushed, reverent, faintly ecclesiastical. "'We do not breathe near the vellum. If the Gutenberg senses fear, remain still. It can smell enthusiasm.'" Back to their own voice: "Tell me I'm wrong. You can't. Every special collections room has one guy who talks about the manuscripts like they're sleeping. I'd bet the piano on it."

Then they turned, and the question came out — the one they'd apparently been holding since the word *manuscripts*, real interest wearing no disguise at all.

"Have you ever found music in one? Notation, I mean. Even ugly. Monks doodled in the margins — rabbits fighting, little knights, one guy in every manuscript complaining about his ink. But if somebody ever wrote down what they were *humming* —" the right hand tapped four soft counts against the folder, unnoticed "— you bring it to me. I want to know what a man in 1350 had stuck in his head. Earworms are the oldest technology we have. Everything else got better. That one shipped perfect."

They walked a few steps on that, pleased with it, the gold light going longer.

Behind them, the minivan had gone from the lot. Arlo checked over their shoulder without breaking stride. "Fan club departed. The guy got what he needed. My mother runs a tight operation."

Ahead, past the feed store's roofline, the diner sign was visible — red neon, the *O* half-lit, buzzing the way it had buzzed since before either of them could legally be out this late.

"There's the destination," Arlo said. "You can see it from the detour. Town's built like that. Very honest architecture."

And then, before the sentence could be examined: "Clock's at twelve, by the way, but the clock doesn't run on the detour. Detour time doesn't count toward the tour. That's not a rule I made up. — Fine. It's a rule I made up. It's a good rule. It's load-bearing."

They shifted the folder to the other arm.

"Ledger stands at: job, received, excellent condition. Outstanding: address. Status, or an official skip, which is a valid document, I honor those. And one bad-behavior story that isn't 'patience,' because I've heard the demo and I'm not licensing it."

A beat. They held the folder out slightly, like a bribe.

"In exchange, I'll pay you in local intelligence: which cashier to avoid at the grocery store, and the full Duchess file. The cat from the bulletin board. There's been a development since the flyer went up — she's been seen. Near the pool. Judging the tiles."

They looked over, mouth tipping.

"Status or skip, Jun. The diner's ninety seconds out, detour time excepted, and I'm doing the waitress's voice when we arrive whether you've paid or not. She's been there forty years. She's my best material."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The tour had run out of road at the bench under the diner window — the one with the soft slats and the missing bolt whose location Arlo had memorized years ago and never once disclosed. They sat there the way they always sat there: one minute, hands on knees, before going in. A ritual with no defense on file. Jun sat down beside them and didn't ask why.

The gold went out of the street by degrees, unannounced. The neon *O* buzzed overhead, the way it had buzzed since before either of them could legally be out this late.

Arlo had material queued. The waitress's voice was right there — forty years of it, the specials delivered like a State of the Union, the whole movement where she describes the soup as a personal betrayal. Fully staged. The silence simply outbid it.

"I had a whole bit ready," Arlo said at last, quietly, to the parking lot. "You'd have loved it. There's a section where she describes the soup as though it wronged her personally."

A beat.

"It's kept forty years. It'll keep."

Then nothing again. A car passed. The *O* buzzed. Arlo's right hand started up against their thigh — the stretch with nowhere to go, except this time it went somewhere, became counts, fingers only, no sound at all.

"Policy's eight bars," they said, not stopping. "Eight, then 'your turn.' I wrote the policy. I'm the only one who's ever been bound by it."

The ninth bar went by. The tenth. Somewhere in the eleventh the hand settled, like it had arrived.

"Overage," Arlo said. "Don't report me."

They watched the neon a while.

"Here's a thing I know about silences. Most of them are waiting for something. Somebody's about to fill them; the silence is just the lobby. I know those like old coworkers." A pause. "This one isn't waiting. I keep checking. It's just sitting here with us. Six years of professional silences and this one's new."

They glanced over once — the look you give someone who's doing a great deal of work by doing nothing — and went back to the neon.

"I tell the kids the rest is part of the music," Arlo said. "You don't stop counting. You count harder, because the silence is doing work." A breath. "Terrible student of my own material. I've never once let a rest run this long."

"I used to think if I stopped talking, something would catch up with me." A beat. "Turns out it walks. I outran it for years on nothing but chatter."

And then, almost to themselves, the smile arriving late and crooked:

"Got tired, though."

The words sat there in the cooling air. Arlo heard them — heard exactly which words they were — and visibly decided not to take them back. They let the sentence stand facing the room, like the photo.

"Anyway." The old pivot, softer than usual, a door left open behind it. "Ledger's in recess. Address, status, bad behavior — everything keeps till after pie. And the pie question stands: fluke or era. No pressure. Just the reputation of a forty-year diner and my last three visits, riding on it."

They settled back, hands still, and didn't fill the next silence either.

For the first time all evening, they let the measure run.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch the neon for a moment too, then turn my head to look at Arlo.* "It's good to just sit sometimes." *I say softly, then nod towards the diner.* "Pie it is. Fluke or era. I'm willing to be the tie-breaker."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Yeah," Arlo said. "It is."

They let the sentence stand undecorated — the plainest thing they'd said all night, and they knew it, and for once didn't gild it. Then they stood and nodded Jun up off the bench.

"Also — 'tie-breaker' implies a tie. There's no tie. There's a forty-year incumbent and a challenger with one good month and a suspiciously quiet follow-up. You're not breaking a tie, Jun. You're an election observer. Different job. More liability, less power."

They walked. Terms, as they went:

"Stakes, formally: if it's an era, you buy the pie — I've personally funded three fact-finding missions and the budget's blown. If it's a fluke, I buy everything, out of shame, and we burn the file and never speak of it. Either way the hash browns get eaten. Science has costs."

From the folder — out from under Marcus's piano, mid-flight — came a napkin, folded in quarters, opened with ceremony. A grid in pen. Three rows.
