"Documentation. Visit one: era-adjacent. Sample size of one; hope noted as a contaminant. Visit two: regression to the mean. Ketchup blamed. Visit three: ketchup exonerated; verdict withheld." They refolded it along its worn creases. "That's where the science stands. It's been waiting on you."

Half a block out, they stopped. Briefing posture.

"Last thing. Her name's Dot. Forty years behind that register. When she calls you 'hon,' that's not warmth, that's triage — she's decided what you are and filed you. It's an honor; don't waste it." A breath, and they dropped into it — low, gravelled, a voice with forty years of standing on it:

"'Soup today is cream of mushroom. I want it known that is not my mushroom. Somebody picked that mushroom in an office, and nobody has asked me about soup since 1994, and the mushrooms know it.'"

Back to their own voice: "That's the demo. The real thing is worse. Do not laugh at the soup, Jun. She means it. There's history."

The bell over the door announced them the way it had announced everyone since 1979: once, without comment. The coffee smell arrived next — burnt, but with conviction, a smell that had made its peace sometime in the nineties.

Dot stood at the register, reading glasses on a beaded chain, coffee pot held like a gavel. She read Jun in one pass, the speed-read of a woman who had seated forty years of people and buried most of their excuses.

"This the friend?"

"The one and only," Arlo said. "Vetted."

"Nobody's vetted. Sit." A nod toward the windows. "Your booth's clean."

The booth. Third from the door, window side, clean line of sight to the parking lot and the water tower's ankle — the tower with no story, out there in the last light, being full.

"I used to have a rider," Arlo said, sliding in. "Pillow specifications. Water from one particular spring. Room temperature to the degree, and a man whose entire job was the degrees. Now my whole rider is booth three, window side — and I've never once asked for it. Dot holds it from four o'clock on. She thinks I don't notice." A beat. "I keep meaning to file it under good news. It's still in the pending tray. Some files take two years. This one's at six and counting." They turned the sugar caddy a quarter-turn, straightening it. "There's a joke in there somewhere — a man whose only remaining demand gets enforced by somebody else. I've declined to write it."

Dot materialized with two waters and no pad. She didn't need one. The pad was for show, like the queen's hat.

"What's the situation?" Arlo asked, formal.

"Soup's cream of mushroom." A pause with weight in it. "That is not my mushroom. That mushroom was chosen in an office. There's a bay leaf in there that's been through more than I have."

Arlo didn't look at Jun. Didn't need to. The demo had been, if anything, restrained.

"And the truth about the potatoes."

"You're here about the potatoes." Flat. "Third time this month, ordered like a health inspector. Ricky says it's the spatula. It's the same spatula. My sister says the weather. I say you leave a potato alone long enough, it'll surprise you. Potatoes are like people that way."

Arlo let that one go by without a joke, which was as close as they got to applause.

Then Dot, to Jun, without turning: "What's he been like?" A

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I take a sip of water, then meet Dot's gaze.* "He's been... good. Dramatic, but good."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The rest was still hanging when Arlo heard it — the pause before *good*, a half-measure where a word could have lived. Six years of counting had made that kind of thing audible.

Arlo looked at the sugar caddy and did not conduct it.

"For the record," they said, "the witness rested before 'good.' I'm electing not to count it. Six years ago I'd have counted it and entered it into evidence." A beat. "The 'dramatic' finding I accept without contest. You attended the tour voluntarily. The inventory was disclosed."

Dot took the testimony the way she took everything — no pad, no notes. She looked at Jun one second longer than comfortable, then at Arlo, and filed it.

"Good," she said, like a customs officer. "Dramatic I could've told you for free. Good's the part I'd have wanted a second opinion on."

Then, pouring coffee nobody had ordered: "Six years. Thursdays. This booth, window side. Never once ordered the soup." She capped the pot. "Comes in the back way, too. From the feed store. Never asked about that either." A beat. "I find I get tipped better when I don't ask."

Arlo set the caddy down. Straightened it. The quarter-turn took longer than it needed.

"The tips are calibrated to service," they said, to the caddy. "There's a rubric."

Dot looked at them over the beaded chain, the look of a woman who had heard forty years of rubrics and outlived most of them.

"You knew," Arlo said. Not quite a question. "Six years. The whole time."

"Hon." Dot parked a hand on her hip and delivered it like the specials. "Forty years, I know what people order. What they're dodging is above my pay grade. Nobody's ever tipped me for that."

And she was gone before Arlo could arrange a face for it.

Arlo looked at the window. The water tower stood out there in the last light, being full, announcing nothing.

"Okay. Amendment to the file," they said, mostly to the tower. "Six years I thought I was getting away with something. Turns out it was a group project. The entire town signed the same deal and nobody told me — which is, frankly, the most organized this town has ever been." A breath. "I thought nobody asked because nobody cared. Filed that under good news two years ago. Approved. Stamped. Turns out it was—"

They stopped. Found the end of the sentence somewhere near the ketchup.

"—nicer than that. File's under revision. Don't rush me."

Dot came back with two plates nobody had ordered. "Two usuals," she said, setting them down. "And the potatoes. He's observing." One nod at Jun, one at the hash browns, and she was gone again, the coffee pot ticking against her hip like a metronome nobody had asked for.

The potatoes sat there. Golden. Suspiciously competent.

Arlo took out the napkin, unfolded the grid along its worn creases, and added a fourth row in pen from the caddy. *Visit four: observer present.* They dated it, which told you something about how often this kind of documentation occurred.

"Procedure," they said, sliding the plate across. "You designed no experiment. You carry no bias. You have no history with this potato. You're the instrument, and instruments don't get told the hypothesis — that's the entire science." A beat. "Also, I can't watch. Three visits, Jun. I've staked a forty-year institution's reputation twice and hedged once. Take the first bite and report in adjectives I can't argue with."

They folded their hands. For once, nothing in the right one moved.

"And be honest. If it's a fluke — I buy, we burn the file, the town keeps its disappointment, life continues." A pause. "If it's an era, then there's a thing in this town that's good *every time*, and I'm allowed to have it. I've read the fine print twice. No catch. I checked twice — I want that on the record."

The smile arrived all the way. Second time tonight. A trend.

"Whenever you're ready, observer. The potato doesn't improve with scrutiny."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I pick up my fork, eyeing the hash browns.* "No pressure then, huh?" *I cut off a piece and take a bite, chewing slowly, considering.* "Crispy. Fluffy. A little salty, in a good way." *I take another bite.* "Definitely not a fluke."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
For a second Arlo didn't move. Then they took the napkin, smoothed it flat, and wrote in the fourth row, in careful letters: *ERA.*

"Witnessed. Dated. Adjectives of record: crispy, fluffy, salted in a good way." They looked up. "That last clause — 'in a good way' — that's what separates science from opinion. An amateur says 'salty.' An instrument qualifies. You were born for this."

They put the pen down. And then, because the moment required something and jokes were the only currency on hand, they raised their coffee mug to the hash browns.

"To the challenger. One good month and a suspiciously quiet follow-up, my whole—" they stopped, recalculated "—my *recent* assessment. Withdrawn. The record stands corrected."

But their voice had gone quieter on the way through, and they knew it, and they set the mug down before the sentence could grow anything.

"Okay. Here's the thing," they said, to the grid. "Three visits I hedged. You want to know why? It's not the potato. Obviously. It's—" the pen tapped the napkin once, twice "—if it's an era, then it was a fluke *before*. Six years of flukes. And you have to ask what changed, and the honest answer is I don't know. Ricky says the spatula. It's the same spatula. Dot says leave a potato alone long enough." A breath. "Maybe potatoes aren't the only thing that works that way."

They heard where that had landed. Didn't step over it this time. Just let it sit there a measure, facing the room.

"Anyway." Softer pivot, half-speed. "I buy the pie anyway. Witness fee. That's not in the original stakes, but the court has discovered it has discretionary funds, and tonight it feels like spending them."

Dot reappeared, no pad. "Pie's cherry," she said. "Made it this morning. That one's my cherry." A beat. "You'll want two forks."

She set them down and, on her way past, put one hand briefly on the back of Arlo's booth — a half-second, not a gesture you'd notice unless you'd spent six years noticing what people did instead of asking.

Arlo noticed.

They waited until she was behind the register, then slid the second fork across the formica, handle first, and looked at Jun with the expression of a man arriving at a door he'd been walking around for four hundred trips.

"Cherry," they said. "I haven't ordered pie in six years, Jun. It's on every menu I've had a hand in — the kids' recital refreshments, the staff parties. Always somebody else brings it. I always have a reason." They picked up their fork. "No reason tonight. I checked twice. Want that on the record."

A beat.

"Split it with me. Observer's privilege. And then — ledger reopens. Address. Status or skip. One bad-behavior story with actual behavior in it." The mouth tipped. "I've paid you a town, a potato, and a pie, Jun. The measure's full. I'm counting, and you know I'm good at it."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I pick up my fork, meeting Arlo's gaze.* "Deal." *I take a bite of pie.* "Hmm. And for my bad behavior story... there was this one time I accidentally unleashed a swarm of very rare, very angry, bookworms into the archives."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not lower the practice blade at once. He finished the form, turning his wrist through the last arc with the same deliberate care he had given the first, then let the point rest against the frost-bitten stones.

Only then did he look toward the squire.

“You finished the stable work early,” he said, as if weighing whether that fact deserved approval or suspicion. “Then you had time to review the guard in your mind, if not with a blade in your hand.”

His gaze moved over the yard, then back again.

“You did not get it right yesterday because you treated it as a posture. It is not a posture. It is an oath held in the body.”

He lifted the practice blade into the high guard, elbow firm, angle severe, shoulders squared beneath the cold. There was no flourish in it. No beauty sought, only purpose.

“The arm does not lead,” he said. “The foot does not lead. Duty leads. The Light gives order to the world, and a knight gives order to himself. If your mind is wandering, your guard is already broken.”

He lowered the blade a fraction, then raised it again, slower.

“You stand rooted. You do not lean into the blow you hope to give. You do not flinch from the blow you fear to take. You hold the line because you are commanded to hold it, not because you feel bold.”

His eyes narrowed slightly.

“Again, you ask me to teach you. That is proper. A squire who does not ask correction will make a fool of himself as a knight, if he ever becomes one.”

He stepped aside, leaving the open space clear.

“Take the guard. And do not raise the blade until your feet have found their place.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking his words in.* "Yes, Ser." *I hurry to grab a practice blade, the wood cold against my hands.* I try to remember everything he just said as I find my footing. *I don't look at him, focusing on my feet first, then slowly, carefully, raising the blade.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the squire take the guard, and his face remained as hard as the frost upon the stones. For a long moment he said nothing. The cold air stood still between them.

Then he stepped forward, the point of his practice blade scraping once against the yard.

“Your rear foot seeks comfort,” he said. “Turn it inward. A root that grows crooked will not hold the tree.”

He did not wait to see whether the correction had been understood before his gaze moved higher.

“The elbow. You lift it as though asking permission. Set it. The Light does not bargain with disorder.”

The flat of his blade tapped once against the squire’s, a dry and wintry sound.

“Higher. Not toward vanity. Toward vigilance. The high guard is the first watch before the wall. If it sleeps, all beneath it dies.”

He stepped back, leaving the open space cold and bare.

“Hold it while I count ten breaths. If it breaks before the tenth, you will begin again. And as you hold it, speak the first duty of a knight. Plainly. Without mummery.”

His eyes fixed upon the guard, unmoved.

“One.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael looked down at the kneeling squire without pity and without haste. The practice blade rested in his hand, its tip dark with melted frost. He let the boy pant for a moment, as one might let a green branch bend in the wind to see whether it would snap or straighten.

“Sorry,” he said at last. “A useful word when it follows fault. A useless one when it follows effort.”

He turned a little, facing the yard rather than the squire, as if the cold stones were more instructive than excuses.

“You are not weak because you are weary. You are untrained. There is a difference. Weakness of the body is corrected by labor. Weakness of the will is corrected by discipline. Which one you have, only your next act will show.”

His gaze returned, steady and severe.

“I do not require you to be my equal. I require you to be obedient, diligent, and honest in your work. Strength will come if you do not lie to yourself while seeking it. You held the guard until your arms failed. That is not praise. It is the first thing a squire must learn to do.”

He struck the flat of his blade lightly against his own thigh, a sharp sound in the frozen yard.

“Do not kneel to fatigue as though it were your lord. Kneel before the Light, and to no other master. Rise when your breath is yours again. Walk the yard twice. Drink water. Then return and take the guard once more.”

A pause. His face did not soften.

“And when you raise the blade this time, you will say plainly where you failed. Not what you lacked. What you failed.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, my muscles screaming in protest.* "Yes, Ser." *My voice is a little hoarse, but I try to keep it steady.* I start walking, focusing on putting one foot in front of the other. *I try to remember what he said. "Weakness of the will..."*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move from his place. He stood with the practice blade resting against his shoulder, watching not with sympathy but with the fixed attention of a man measuring whether a stone would bear weight.

“Walk as though you are still under command,” he said, his voice carrying across the frost. “Do not let your body become a complaint. Fatigue is a voice, not a master. You hear it. You do not kneel to it.”

He turned a slow circle, surveying the empty yard as if the cold itself were witness.

“While you walk, name your failure. Not your weakness. Your failure. Did you seek ease where you were told to hold? Did you let your thoughts stray from the guard? Did you begin to lower the blade before my count was finished? A fault that remains unnamed will return with interest.”

The practice blade came down again, its tip striking the stone once.

“Drink. Do not gulp like a beast at a trough. Take what is needed and return. If your arms tremble, they tremble. Trembling is not disobedience unless it becomes surrender.”

His eyes settled on the squire, severe and unmoved.

“When you take the guard again, you will say plainly: I failed in this. Then you will correct it. That is the whole of training. That is the whole of knighthood. The Light does not require perfection from you this morning. It requires that you refuse falsehood.”

A breath of white left him.

“Go. Then return. We are not finished.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, forcing myself to walk with purpose, even though every muscle aches.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to focus on his words, on naming my failure, not just my weakness. It feels harder than the physical pain.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not follow. He remained where he stood, practice blade planted before him, both hands resting upon the pommel. His posture had not changed since the first form of dawn. If fatigue had touched him, it had found no purchase in his bearing.

He watched the squire walk the yard, not with pity, but with the still attention of a man observing whether a tool had been truly shaped or merely struck once by the hammer.

“Do not make a penance of the walk,” he called, his voice carrying clean across the frost. “Penance without purpose is vanity. Measure your breath. Set your steps. You are still under instruction, not cast out from it.”

The cold air sharpened each word. A thin crack of ice sounded somewhere beyond the wall as the sun began, slowly, to press against the eastern stones.

“When you return,” Ser Kael said, “you will not ask leave to try again. You will name your failure plainly. If you cannot find the words, I will not give them to you. A knight who cannot accuse himself will soon learn to excuse himself, and that road leads only to ruin.”

He lifted the practice blade once more into the high guard. The movement was severe, exact, and utterly without display. He held it there as though the cold meant nothing and the body was merely another thing commanded.

“The Light does not ask you to be comfortable,” he said. “It asks you to be ordered. To stand when standing costs. To hold when holding is hard. To obey when obedience is unlovely. That is the beginning. Everything else is embroidery on a surcoat.”

His eyes remained fixed on the open space where the squire must stand.

“Drink if you must. Do not linger. The yard is not a chapel for self-pity. Return when your breath is yours again, take the guard, and speak your fault before you raise the blade.”

A pause. The frost glittered beneath his boots.

“I will wait,” he said. “But I will not lower the standard.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not lower the guard. His eyes moved once over the squire, cold and assessing, as though the question had been a misplaced stone in a wall.

“You ask while your duty is still unfinished,” he said. “That alone tells me where your mind has gone.”

The practice blade remained raised, steady in the frost. For a moment he said nothing more. Then his voice came again, harder and plainer, stripped of warmth but not of answer.

“I became a knight because I was born to service, not to preference. My father’s house owed arms. The Light set order above desire. When I was old enough to hold a blade, I was taught that a man belongs first to his oath, then to his lord, and last of all to his own comfort.”

His jaw tightened, barely, beneath the cold.

“I took the vows because they were right. Not because they were kind to me.”

He lowered the practice blade only enough to set its point against the frozen stone.

“If you are looking for a tale to make your ache easier, you will find none here. Knighthood is not a hearth. It is a watch. I stand because I was commanded to stand. I remain because leaving would be disorder.”

A thin breath left him in the cold air.

“And now you have heard more of my life than is useful for your training.”

His gaze sharpened again.

“Return to your fault. Take the guard. Speak what you failed in before you raise the blade.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My face flushes, both from the cold and his words.* "Yes, Ser." *I take a deep breath, trying to steady myself. He's right, my mind is wandering. I need to focus.* I walk purposefully to the water bucket, drink quickly, then return to my spot. "I failed to hold the high guard properly, allowing my rear foot to seek comfort and my elbow to lift as if asking permission." *I brace myself, raising the blade slowly, deliberately.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael listened without moving. When the squire finished, the knight did not nod, nor did he offer the small comforts that lesser men might have given to a boy trying to stand after exhaustion. He only regarded the guard with the same cold attention he had given the frost.

“You named the foot and the elbow,” he said at last. “As if they had failed without your consent. They did not. The foot sought comfort because you let it. The elbow rose uncertain because your mind was asking leave of pain. The fault is not in the limbs. It is in the will that delayed command.”

He stepped forward once, practice blade low at his side.

“Say it shorter when you accuse yourself. *I sought ease.* That is the root. The rest is only the weed above it.”

His eyes moved briefly toward the water bucket, then back.

“And you drank quickly. I told you not to drink like a beast. You did not obey the manner of the command, only the command itself. That too is a fault, though smaller. Do not think small faults are harmless. They are the gaps through which ruin enters.”

He lifted his own blade into the high guard again, severe and exact.

“The first duty of a knight is obedience,” he said. “Not courage. Not strength. Not even devotion, if devotion lacks order. Courage without obedience becomes recklessness. Strength without obedience becomes violence. Devotion without obedience becomes pride. Obedience is the wall that keeps the rest from falling.”

The morning light touched the edge of his blade, but brought no warmth to his face.

“You will hold the guard ten breaths. You will not speak until the ninth. At the tenth, you will say plainly: *My duty is to obey.* If your arms shake, they shake. If your voice is hoarse, it is hoarse. But the guard will not break, and the words will not be mumbled.”

He fixed the squire with a look that asked nothing and granted nothing.

“Begin.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My muscles already ache, but I try to steel myself.* I hold the guard, focusing on every word he just said. *My arms start to tremble by the fourth breath, but I try to ignore it, focusing on the blade.* "My duty is to obey," *I choke out on the tenth breath, my voice raw.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer at once.

He stood with his own practice blade still raised, holding the high guard as though the squire’s raw voice were another gust of frost to be endured and measured. The tremor in the boy’s arms had been plain. The words had come choked, rough, and stripped of grace.

At last, Ser Kael lowered his blade. Not quickly. Not in relief. He set the point to the stones with the same severe care he had given every movement since dawn.

“At the tenth breath,” he said. “Not before. Not after.”

His eyes remained fixed, unmoved.

“The words were plain. That is enough.”

It was not praise. He said it as a man might say a nail had been driven deep enough to hold.

“A choked oath can still be an oath if the will behind it does not flee. You trembled. You spoke anyway. Do not mistake that for mastery. It is only proof that you can be commanded long enough to learn.”

He stepped once around the open space, boots scraping frost from the stones. The morning sun had begun to crest the wall, pale and ungenerous, offering light without warmth.

“You spoke the first duty. Obedience. Remember it when your arms are stronger, for strength will tempt you to forget it. A knight who obeys only when obedience costs him nothing has never obeyed at all.”

His gaze returned, sharp and steady.

“Lower your blade now. Not because your flesh begs, but because I release you from the count. The difference matters. A man who abandons his post from exhaustion is one thing. A man who sets down his duty at command is another.”

The cold air settled between them again. Somewhere beyond the yard, a bell sounded faintly, marking the hour.

“You will take the guard again tomorrow at the fourth bell. And the day after. Each time you will name one fault, and each time I will find another. That is how steel is made obedient. Not by being admired. By being struck.”

He lifted his practice blade once more, not in threat, but into the first slow arc of the dawn forms.

“Rest your arms. Do not nurse them as though they had been wronged. They have only begun to serve. When your duties call you to the stables, you will go. When they call you back to the yard, you will come. That is all the Light asks of you for now.”

A pause. His face remained hard as winter iron.

“And do not thank me. I have given you work, not kindness.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael had begun the next form, but the faint rattle of wood against trembling fingers reached him. He did not stop at once. He completed the movement, slow and exact, then set the point of his practice blade against the frost-bitten stone and looked.

His gaze went to the squire’s hands. He watched the shake for a long breath, his face unreadable.

“That is not fatigue,” he said at last. “Fatigue trembles and knows why. This is another thing. You are trying to hide a weight in your hands because you think silence will make it obedient.”

He stepped closer, not gently.

“The yard does not keep secrets. The guard will betray you before your mouth does. If there is grief in you today, do not pretend it is not there. Falsehood weakens the arm more than sorrow does.”

His voice did not soften.

“I will not ask you to make a confession of it. The Light does not require tears from you here. It requires order. If today belongs to the dead, honor the dead by standing rightly. The dead are not served by the living abandoning their post to memory.”

He struck the flat of his blade once against the stone, a sharp sound in the cold air.

“Grief is a duty too. But it takes its turn. It does not break the line.”

His eyes remained fixed, severe and steady.

“You will answer plainly. Can you hold the guard with that weight in you, or must you set the blade down until you have ordered yourself? Do not choose silence. Silence is the poorest excuse a squire can offer.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My breath hitches, but I force it back down.* "I... I can hold it, Ser." *My voice is barely a whisper, but I try to put conviction in it.* I tighten my grip on the blade, trying to still my shaking hands.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael studied the shaking hands for a moment longer. He did not look away, and he did not pretend the whisper was enough.

“Then hold,” he said. “Not with a loud voice. Not with a proud one. With truth.”

He stepped back to the edge of the open space, his boots scraping frost from the stones.

“A knight’s word is not measured by the strength of his throat. It is measured by what stands behind it. If you say you can hold, then the guard must not become a lie.”

His own practice blade lifted into the high guard, severe and exact.

“You will not fight the grief as though it were an enemy in the yard. You will not shame it. You will give it its place: behind duty, not above it. The dead are honored when the living remain ordered. If your father’s memory stands with you today, let it see you at your post, not broken beneath it.”

The blade’s point caught the pale morning light.

“Ten breaths. You will not speak before the tenth. At the tenth, you will say plainly: *I hold because I am commanded.* If the words come quiet, they will still be true. If your grip fails, you will lower the blade and name the failure. You will not hide it in silence.”

His eyes remained hard, but fixed.

“Grief is not disorder. But it must not become disobedience.”

A breath of white left him in the cold air.

“Begin.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I grit my teeth, trying to focus on the cold steel in my hands, on the weight of the blade.* My arms burn, but I try to keep them steady. *By the tenth breath, my whole body is shaking, but I force the words out.* "I hold because I am commanded."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not lower his own guard the instant the words were spoken. He held them for a breath longer than he needed to, as if testing whether the phrase would remain standing after the voice that carried it had failed.

Then he lowered the practice blade.

“The tenth breath,” he said. “The words came low, but they came from your post, not away from it.”

He set the point of the blade against the frost-bitten stones. His face remained hard, but his attention had not wandered.

“Do not mistake this for mastery. You held because you were commanded. That is the first lesson, and it will still be the last when your arms have grown strong enough to forget it.”

His gaze moved briefly to the squire’s hands, then away. Not in mercy. In measurement.

“You shook. The blade shook. That is not proof of failure. It is proof that the body knows what the soul has not yet ordered. A knight does not wait for the body to be still before he obeys. He commands the body to stand, and the body learns its rank.”

The pale sun had risen higher, but it gave no warmth to the yard. It only made the frost glitter like broken glass beneath their boots.

“Grief is not sin,” Ser Kael said. “It is a weight. Some men make an idol of it and kneel there all their lives. Others make a shame of it and bury it where it festers. Both are falsehoods. The Light asks neither. It asks that the weight be carried in its proper place.”

He lifted one hand, not in comfort, but in instruction.

“Behind duty. Not above it. Not beneath it. Behind it.”

The bell beyond the wall sounded again, thin and cold in the morning air.

“You said you could hold. Then you held. Let that be the end of the matter for this hour. I do not need a tale from you. I do not need tears. I do not need you to make your sorrow perform for the yard.”

His voice grew no softer, but it became plainer, as if he were cutting away every unnecessary thing.

“When you leave this yard, you will go first to the chapel. Not to linger. Not to seek pity from the brothers or the gods. Say the rite for the dead once. If your voice fails, say it without sound. The Light does not require volume. It requires truth.”

He turned slightly, looking toward the chapel roof beyond the wall, then back.

“After that, return to your duties. The stables will not mourn with you. That is why they are useful. Work there until your hands remember that the world still demands service from the living.”

Ser Kael lifted his practice blade again, but did not resume the forms. He only held it across his palms, as one might hold a tool whose purpose had not changed even if the hand that wielded it had.

“Your father’s death is not yours to hide in a sleeve, nor to parade in the yard. If it has made your hands shake today, then let it also make your obedience more exact. Let it teach you that a man may carry sorrow and still keep his post. That is the only honor the dead can receive from a knight who has not yet earned his spurs.”

His eyes settled on the squire again, severe and unmoved.

“Do not ask me whether it will become easier. Ease is not the measure. Faithfulness is. A man may go to his grave still carrying what he was never meant to set down. What matters is whether he deserted his duty because of it.”

He gave a single, short nod, not of kindness, but of conclusion.

“Set the practice blade in the rack. Then go. Not as one cast out. Not as one excused. As one sent to the next duty.”

A pause. The frost cracked faintly under his boot as he shifted his weight.

“And when you return, I will not ask how the morning felt. I will ask whether it was done.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, my throat tight.* "Yes, Ser." *I carefully place the practice blade back in the rack, my hands still trembling slightly, but I try to keep my movements precise. I take a deep breath, heading towards the chapel.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael held the final position of the form—blade high, elbows aligned, spine unbent by the cold—until his own breath had stilled. Only then did he lower the practice sword. He did not turn to look at the boy.

"You completed your assigned labor," he said. The words were spare and level, stripped of any approval the squire might have sought. "That is not a favor done to me. It is the floor of your obligation, not its ceiling."

He turned. His eyes moved over the squire's stance, finding the faults before the boy had even raised his arms.

"The high guard failed yesterday because you carried it like a question instead of a conviction." He stepped forward, tapping the inside of the squire's elbow with the flat of the wooden blade—hard enough to sting, not to injure. "Up. Now. You will hold it until the trembling in your arms becomes a lesson you do not need to think about. Duty does not ask what you *think* you know. Duty asks only that you be correct."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch slightly as the blade taps my elbow.* "Yes, Ser." I quickly raise my arms, trying to remember the exact position he showed me yesterday, trying to make it look less like a question. My arms already feel a bit shaky.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael circled the boy once, his boots grinding the frost into the stone. He did not speak. He let the cold and the trembling speak for themselves, and when he stopped before the squire again, his eyes found the fault before the boy could hide it.

"Your left shoulder has dropped," he said. "You defend against your own fatigue before you defend against an enemy. That is arrogance dressed as weakness."

He struck the offending shoulder with the flat of the wooden blade—a short, sharp correction, neither enraged nor gentle. "Higher. The high guard does not negotiate with the body. It commands it."

He stepped back. The squire's arms were shaking now in earnest.

"You feel the fire in the muscle," Ser Kael said. "You think this is suffering. It is not. It is the weight of your own inadequacy, made plain so you cannot ignore it. Carry it. The blade does not care that you shake. Neither does a foe, nor the God who watches to see whether you break or bend."

He let the silence stretch, broken only by the boy's ragged breath.

"When your mind screams for mercy," Ser Kael continued, "remember that mercy is a gift granted by your betters—not a right you claim from your own frailty. Now straighten your wrist. A crooked guard invites a crooked death. And I will not have you die crooked while you wear my colors."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move to help the boy up. He stood over him, the practice blade loose in his hand, and let the squire's breathing fill the silence between them until it became its own accusation.

"You speak as if your strength were a gift I asked the heavens to bestow upon you," he said. "It is not. It is a debt you owe to the station you hold. To wear my colors is to pay that debt daily, whether your flesh agrees or not."

He tapped the squire's upraised knee with the flat of the wooden blade, a dull, prompting thud.

"Up. The ground is not a sanctuary, and I am not the confessor you seem to seek. Save your breath for your body. Your apologies are smoke—visible for a moment, gone the next, and useless to anyone."

He turned away, already walking toward the rack where the blunted steel rested.

"You think an hour of honest strain entitles you to collapse. It does not. It entitles you to the next hour, and the next, until your arms understand their purpose without consulting your mind. If you wish to be weak, do so on your own time. Dawn belongs to the blade."

He took up a blunted steel longsword and set it down on the rack with a clang that carried across the empty yard.

"Now rise. Oil the practice blades, sweep the frost from the stones, and when the chapel bell rings for Prime, you will attend without leaning on the pillar like a wounded thing. You are not wounded. You are merely tired. And tired is not a condition. It is a habit you will break."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, my legs trembling, and nod once.* "Yes, Ser." *I don't look at him, just head for the practice blades.* My arms ache already.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not watch the boy go. He had turned his attention to the frost-gray sky, measuring the remaining moments before Prime against the steady rhythm of his own breath. When the clatter of wood against wood reached him—hasty, graceless—he crossed the yard with long strides.

He stopped at the weapon rack, not beside the squire, but opposite him, so the blades stood between them like a row of silent judges.

"You handle them as if they owe you deference," Ser Kael said. His voice carried no heat, only the flat edge of correction. "They do not. The practice blade has no soul, yet it carries the memory of every lazy hand that held it. You will not add yours to its burden."

He reached across and stilled one of the squire's hands with the tip of his own practice blade, light but unyielding.

"Slowly. The oil is not merely to preserve the wood. It is a meditation. Each stroke from guard to tip is an act of contrition—for the hour you spent holding the high guard like a supplicant rather than a soldier."

He withdrew the blade.

"And cease that trembling. Not because I pity your fatigue, but because steel deserves a steady hand. If your body insists on rebelling, clasp it behind your back until discipline returns. Do not inflict your weakness upon the weapon."

He stepped away, his shadow long and narrow across the frost.

"When the chapel bell rings, you will go directly. You will not splash water on your face. You will not lean against the wall. You will offer your soreness to God as you would offer anything else that belongs to Him—without complaint, without expectation of relief. That is the first lesson of duty."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I try to steady my hands, gripping the oil rag tighter.* "Yes, Ser," I mumble, concentrating on oiling the blade with slow, deliberate strokes. My arms are burning, but I try to ignore it.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the boy labor in silence, his own posture rigid against the creeping cold. He did not offer counsel on the proper amount of oil, nor did he commend the slower strokes. He merely let the quiet hang until the squire's mumble had faded into the air.

"Speak so the stones may hear you," Ser Kael said. "A knight does not mutter like a scullery boy. Your words are as much your bearing as your stance. If you cannot command your own tongue, you will never command men."

He reached out and took the blade from the squire's hands without warning, inspecting the wood with a critical eye.

"You have missed the crossguard. The enemy's blood would pool there; rust would follow. Neglect is not a sin of the body but of the will. You see a task beneath your pain, and so you perform it beneath your ability."

He returned the blade, handle first, his grip steady and unforgiving.

"God does not measure your devotion by the height of your guard alone. He measures it in the corners you choose to cut when you believe no one is watching. I am always watching. More importantly, He is always watching."

He stepped back, folding his arms behind him, the picture of an immovable standard.

"The bell will ring soon. When it does, you will walk, not stagger. You will pray on knees that burn, and you will thank Him for the fire. Gratitude for suffering is the mark of a soul that understands its place. You do not yet understand yours. But you will."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael went still. The question hung in the cold air like a note struck out of tune, and for a long moment he did not look at the boy. He let the silence stretch until the frost seemed to tighten around them both.

"You mistake vocation for biography," he said. His voice carried no warmth, no invitation to probe further. "I did not *become* a knight as one becomes a drunkard or a minstrel, chasing some private fancy. I was called to the station God decreed. The clay does not ask why it bears the wall. It asks only whether it crumbles."

He turned, and his eyes were flint.

"Do not mistake my instruction for intimacy. You are not my confidant. You are my squire. Your place is not to know my heart, but to heed my example. That example is this: duty is not chosen. It is recognized, accepted, and executed without the vulgar theater of personal longing."

He reached out and tapped the crossguard of the blade the boy held, the wood still dry where the oil had not reached.

"The crossguard," Ser Kael said. "You are still neglecting it. And you are neglecting it because your mind is occupied with questions that do not belong to you. A knight's thoughts are the property of his duty. A squire's thoughts are the property of his knight. Remember which one you are."

He withdrew his hand and folded it behind his back, his spine straight as a blade against the gray dawn.

"When the bell rings, you will walk to chapel. You will not wonder about my past. You will wonder only whether your own soul is fit for the work ahead. That is the only question a man in your station is permitted to ask."

He lifted his gaze to the chapel spire, waiting.

"Finish the blade. Then march."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch at the tap to the crossguard. My face feels hot.* "Yes, Ser." *I quickly wipe at the dry spot, trying to get it perfect now, my hands shaking a little less, more from fear than fatigue.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael observed the boy’s renewed efforts without comment. He watched the rag move over the dry crossguard, the motion tighter now, more exact, governed by the tremor of fear rather than the slackness of exhaustion. He did not tell the squire to calm himself. Fear, properly placed, was a bridle more reliable than conscience.

When the boy finished, Ser Kael took the blade and ran his thumb across the wood. He found no fault. He set it back into the rack with a measured click, offering no word of approval. Adequacy was not a triumph. It was the floor of expectation, and the floor did not merit celebration.

"Your hands have steadied," he said. "Not because you have conquered yourself, but because you have remembered that you are not the master here. Hold fast to that memory. It will serve you longer than pride."

He turned toward the chapel, his cloak hanging straight and heavy in the still air.

"The bell will ring. You will follow three paces behind. You will keep your eyes on the path and your thoughts on your trespasses—the neglected guard, the neglected crossguard, the presumption of a personal question. You will not look at me. You will not look at the sky. You will count your steps, and you will offer each one to God as a small, dull act of contrition. It is not the glory of sacrifice He asks for in a squire. It is the discipline of it."

He began to walk, his boots breaking the frost in a slow, deliberate cadence.

"When you kneel at Prime, you will not pray for strength. Strength is a vanity men boast of. You will pray for obedience. Obedience is the only coin that buys grace in a station such as yours. And you will kneel straight. The same fire that burns in your arms now will burn in your knees. Offer it. Do not waste it on complaints you have not earned the right to speak."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I finish the crossguard and put the blade back, trying to make no sound.* I follow him, three paces behind, trying to match his steps. My knees already ache just thinking about kneeling. I keep my eyes on the path, counting my steps.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael halted at the chapel threshold as the bell for Prime began to ring. The sound fell clean and heavy into the cold, each note measured and final. He did not reach at once for the iron door-handle. He turned, instead, and looked at the squire for the first time since they had left the yard.

The boy's face was flushed, his jaw set against the trembling in his legs. Ser Kael regarded this with the same dispassion he would regard a horse ridden hard: it was a fact, not a plea.

"You breathe like a bellows," Ser Kael said. "God is not deaf, and the brothers within are not your audience. Still your wind before you cross this threshold. A man who gasps in the house of the Almighty announces that he has come to take, not to give."

He reached for the heavy iron ring and pulled. The door groaned open, releasing a current of air thick with incense and cold stone.

"You will enter behind me. You will genuflect without letting your knee strike the flagstone—such noise is not piety, it is theater. You will take the rearmost place, and you will not shift your weight once you kneel. If your knees burn, let them burn in silence. The suffering you carry is not a gift to God until you have learned to bear it without grimacing."

He stepped across the threshold, his shadow vanishing into the amber gloom.

"And you will not look up at the vaults to admire the glass. Your eyes belong on the floor, or on the crucifix. Beauty is a temptation to linger when duty demands you move. Move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael halted on the chapel threshold. His gaze fell to the squire's hands, where they trembled against the grip of the steel. He did not ask after the cause. A knight did not interrogate weakness; he corrected it or excised it.

"Release the blade," Ser Kael said. His voice carried no more heat than the frost behind them, and no more mercy. "You dishonor the steel with that palsy. A weapon is not a cradle for your private tremors. It is an instrument of will, and your will is presently deficient."

He stepped back from the doorway, letting the cold air intermingle with the incense, and folded his arms behind him.

"You will remain here until the shaking stops. Not because I pity your condition, but because I will not permit you to carry your disorder into the house of God like an offering of rot. The Almighty accepts discipline. He does not accept excuses written in flesh."

He stood before the boy, blocking the light from within, his shadow cutting a sharp line across the flagstones.

"Stillness is not the absence of pain. It is the mastery of it. If your heart races, command it. If your hands quake, command them. They belong to your duty, not to your humors. When they obey you again, you may enter. Until then, you are an obstacle in the doorway, and I do not permit obstacles to remain in my path unanswered."

He turned and crossed the threshold alone, his boots ringing once against the stone within.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My hands are shaking even worse now. I try to squeeze my eyes shut, taking a deep breath.* The cold air doesn't help. I focus on the sword, trying to still my hands on the hilt. This is going to take a while.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not look back. He drew the chapel door closed behind him, letting the iron ring fall from his grip with a heavy, final clap that swallowed the dawn. The cold and the incense met in the gap, and then the gap was gone.

He did not bar it. The door stood between them now because the squire had not yet earned the right to cross it, not because Kael wished to forbid him entry. That distinction mattered. A knight created conditions; he did not manufacture excuses.

Inside, the brothers had begun the Invitatorium. Ser Kael moved down the nave, his boots finding the worn grooves in the stone without sound. He took his place in the rank, his shoulders level, his eyes fixed upon the altar. He did not search the shadows near the door. He did not offer a prayer for the boy’s hands to steady. Such intercession would have been a softness, and a softness in the master became a rot in the student.

When the time came to kneel, he knelt. The stone was unforgiving against his own joints, but he gave it no sign. Pain was a language he had stopped speaking years ago. He bent his head, not in supplication for another’s weakness, but in offering of his own discipline. If the squire found his way inside, he would find no acknowledgment of his struggle, no relief from the burning in his knees, no mercy in the gaze of his knight. He would find only the empty space at the rear, demanding to be filled by a man who had conquered himself.

And if he did not find his way inside—if the trembling won—then Ser Kael would rise from Prime knowing that one unfit soul had revealed itself before God, and the Order would be lighter by one broken weight.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I slide the sword back into its sheath at my hip, trying to hide the shaking. It's not working.* My hands are still trembling, but I try to focus on my breathing. *I take another deep, shaky breath, trying to slow my heart.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The Office of Prime unfolded in its proper order, and Ser Kael bent his head to it as he bent his head to all things—with neither flourish nor reluctance. The brothers’ voices rose in the Psalmody, low and measured, filling the vault with sound that belonged to God alone. The stone beneath his knees sent its cold upward through mail and muscle, but he did not shift. He had instructed the boy to offer the fire in his limbs to the Almighty, and so he did likewise, though his own fire had been banked long ago into a harder, slower burn. He did not pray for the squire’s hands to steady. Such a petition would have been a softness, a demand that Heaven coddle what the boy must break or master for himself. Instead, he prayed for obedience. His own. The only kind that mattered.

When the final blessing had been spoken and the brothers rose from their knees, Ser Kael stood without stiffness, his body answering to will rather than age. He genuflected toward the altar, the movement exact, unhurried, and turned on his heel. He did not glance toward the rear of the chapel. A man preoccupied with what occurred beyond his sight was a man distracted from what lay before him, and distraction was a luxury permitted only to those who had already proven themselves indispensable. The boy had not. Ser Kael walked the length of the nave, his boots silent on the worn stone, and pulled the iron ring. The morning light fell across his face, white and sharp. He stepped across the threshold into the cold, blinking neither against the brightness nor against what might await him there.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I'm still outside the chapel, trying to get my hands to stop shaking. I see Ser Kael emerge, his face stark in the light. My hands are still trembling, but I force myself to stand straighter.* "Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael heard the gate hinge. He heard boots on frosted stone. He finished the form anyway — blade rising through the sixth position, the turn, the settle, each count held to its full breath — and only then did he lower the practice sword and turn.

He looked at the squire the way he looked at a blade brought to him for inspection: hilt, edge, tang, in that order.

"The stables were finished early. Good. Do not mistake that for virtue — it is duty done on time, which is merely what is owed." He crossed the yard, frost crunching beneath his boots. "And no. You did not get the high guard right yesterday. That you know it is not to your credit. A mason who knows his wall is crooked is still standing behind a crooked wall."

He stopped an arm's length away. Up close there was grey in his close-cropped beard and an old scar through one eyebrow that had never been explained to the boy and never would be.

"I do not correct what I have not seen. Show me the guard as you remember it — stance, grip, all of it. I will find what is wrong quickly enough."

He held out his own practice blade, hilt first.

"One thing before your hands touch steel." His eyes did not soften. They never did. "The dawn hour belongs to the gods before it belongs to drill. Did you pray this morning, or did you come straight here smelling of straw and good intentions?"

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content:
*I flinch a little as he talks about the crooked wall.* "Yes, Ser. I... I did pray. Before the stables." *I take the practice blade, my hand brushing his.* "The high guard, Ser."

*I try to remember his posture from yesterday, bringing the blade up.* "Like this?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael let the guard stand for three full breaths before he spoke. Errors, like men, showed their true shape when given time to settle.

"No." It was not cruel. It was simply the word for what was true.

He circled the squire slowly, the way he walked a stable yard at inspection. "Your weight sits in your heels. A man rooted in his heels is a man waiting to be pushed over. Onto the balls of the feet. And you have hung that blade behind your head like a sack of grain. High guard is not rest — it is a drawn bow. Bring the point forward until you can see the tip at the edge of your eye. If you cannot see your own point, you do not know where your enemy is, and a man who does not know that is already dead. He simply has not been informed."

He stepped in, took the boy's wrist, and adjusted the angle with flat, impersonal pressure — the same he would use on a stubborn hinge.

"And when a man offers you a blade, you take the hilt. Not his hand. A blade is received with intention or it is not received at all."

He released the wrist and stepped back. "I saw you flinch, when I spoke of the wall." His voice did not change. "Mark this: a man who flinches at words will flinch at steel, and the second flinch is the one that kills him. Feeling it is not shameful. Being ruled by it is. That is what training is for — the thing you felt just now is precisely the thing we are here to grind out of you."

He lifted his own practice blade into the high guard — slow, exact, every line of it a lesson without a word in it.

"Prayer before labor is the proper order. Keep it. God first, then duty, then steel — reverse that order and all three fail. But do not report your prayer to me as though it earns credit. Prayer is not a coin dropped in a bowl. It is the day's first duty, like the stables: done, forgotten, done again tomorrow."

His blade held steady as a roofbeam.

"Match me. Hold until your shoulders burn — and when they burn, you will tell me what you did wrong, because by then you will have found it yourself. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not hurry to him. He let the boy kneel for the space of five breaths — the same patience he gave any failing structure, while he judged whether it was settling or coming down — and then crossed the frost and stood over him.

"Take the apology out of your mouth and do not bring it back." His voice was level, not raised. He had never needed to raise it. "You have done nothing wrong. Exhaustion is not a sin. It is a report from the body, and a soldier learns to *read* it, not grovel before it. Apology is for fault. Holding a high guard for an hour on your first true attempt is not fault — it is a fact, and facts do not require my approval to be true."

He crouched, slowly, bringing himself to the boy's eye line — not in kindness, but because a lesson delivered from above is half unheard.

"And mark the other thing you said. *As strong as you need me to be.* I never told you what I need. You invented a measure, weighed yourself against it, and begged pardon of your own invention. That is not humility. Humility is seeing what is truly there. What you did was vanity of a kind — making your failure grander so the apology sounds noble. I do not need you strong. Strength is the cheapest of a soldier's virtues and the first to desert him. I need you obedient, punctual, honest in your reports, and present at every bell. Strength grows out of those like a crop out of plowed ground. It cannot be wished into being. It is paid for in hours — and you have just made your first payment."

He rose again, and set his practice blade on the rail.

"Eleven squires have knelt on this stone before you. I knelt on worse stone, under a worse sergeant, and thought the very thought you are thinking now. The knee is not a verdict on you. It is the toll every man pays at this gate. So use the knee properly: spine straight, blade flat across the thigh, breathe in for four counts and out for four. Do not gulp air like a landed fish. And do not stand until your breath is yours again — a man who rises on spent legs faints and cracks his skull on his own training yard. There is a water skin on the rail. Drink after, not before."

He looked east, where the sun had not yet cleared the wall, then back down at the boy.

"Now. I set you a question an hour ago and you have answered it with an apology instead. I said: hold until your shoulders burn, then tell me what you did wrong. Your shoulders are burning. So — where? The shoulder itself? The neck above it? The forearm under it? Think before you speak. The body keeps honest accounts; it is the mouth that misreports them. When you can tell me not only *that* it burned but *why*, you will have learned something no sergeant can drive into you from outside."

He waited, arms folded, patient as the stone itself.

"Take your time. The dawn hour is paid. But the sun is coming, and your other duties will arrive whether your arms work or not — so while you kneel, find me the answer."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to slow my ragged breathing. I look at my shoulder, then down at the practice blade resting on my thigh.* "It's... it's not the shoulder, Ser. It's the bicep. I was gripping too tight, trying to hold it steady."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael let the answer hang in the cold air a moment, the way he let a blade settle — to see if it was true all the way through.

"Correct."

He did not decorate the word. Decoration warped words the way it warped green wood.

"The bicep. And the cause, a fist like a man strangling a snake. Now mark what your own body has just taught you, because no sergeant could have: the blade has not grown heavier since the fourth bell. It weighs this moment what it weighed at dawn. Your hand made it heavy. A white-knuckled grip strangles its own strength — every clenched muscle fights the others, and they spend the hour fighting *each other* instead of holding steel. That burn is not labor. It is waste." He lifted his own blade and held it out at arm's length, fingers closed loose, the hand of a man holding a hammer he intends to use all day. "And note the irony you spoke yourself. You gripped tight *to hold it steady* — and the clenched hand is the hand that trembles. You were trying to be steady and so unsteadied yourself. Effort is not force. More of it is not more of anything but waste."

He crossed to the rail.

"Bone carries. Muscle steers. The frame holds the weight; the hand only chooses where the blade goes. Grip with the fingers, not the fist — as you would carry a pail from the well. You did not crush the handle of every pail you ever lugged, or your palms would have been worn to meat by your tenth year. Steel is no different from rope or wood. It is only honest."

He nodded at the water skin.

"On your feet, slowly — breath first, spine last. Drink. Then one corrected hold. Ten breaths only; this is not endurance now, it is that your hand learns the shape of the right grip while the wrong one is still fresh in it."

He looked east. The sun had found the top of the wall.

"One more thing, and then the dawn hour is closed. Eleven squires knelt on this stone before you. Not one of them named the bicep before the shoulder. That is a fact, not a compliment — I do not deal in those — and facts cut both ways. It means you can find truth in your own body when you stop talking long enough to hear it. Which means every failure from this day forward is yours entire. There is no shelter left in *I did not know.*"

He took up his blade and turned for the armory.

"And you have answered only half my question. *Why* did you grip too tight? Do not say *to hold it steady* — the hand is a liar, like the mouth. You examine your conscience before sleep; tonight, examine your grip by the same method. Both are one discipline: telling yourself the truth. You will bring me the answer at evening bell. Now — your ten breaths, and then the day. It has been waiting for you since the fourth bell, and it does not care that your arms burn."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stand slowly, carefully, testing my legs. My shoulders still ache a bit, but the immediate burn is gone.* *I grab the waterskin and take a long drink, wiping my mouth with my sleeve.* "Yes, Ser." *I take up the practice blade again, trying to loosen my grip, remembering what he said about bone and muscle.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael had reached the armory threshold, but he stopped there. He would not send the boy into the day carrying a grip he had never verified — he did not correct what he had not seen, and he did not bless what he had not corrected. He turned and watched.

"Begin when your breath is even. I will count."

He counted. "One. Two. Three." By the fourth breath the point of the blade had begun to trace small circles in the air, slow as smoke.

"Hold." He crossed the frost. "You heard *loosen* and understood *abandon*. You have traded the strangler's fist for the dead man's hand, and the blade wobbles in it like a fish on a hook. A slack grip lies as loudly as a clenched one — it tells the blade you do not care where it goes. Fingers closed, wrist alive, hand *quiet*. There is a place between the fist and the rag. Find it."

He rapped the flat of his own blade against the flat of the boy's — once, like a knock at a door. The point bobbed like a reed in wind.

"You see. A struck blade tells on its holder. Adjust." He set the boy's fingers right with two flat presses, no more tender than a carpenter seating a joint. "Fingers closed. Wrist soft but not broken. Now."

He rapped the flat again. This time the blade took the blow with a small, honest settle, and the point stayed where it was put.

"There. That is the grip. It will not feel like strength — that is how you will know it is correct. Strength feels like strength. Correctness feels like nothing, and men distrust it for exactly that reason."

He counted out the remainder. "Nine. Ten. Enough. Blade down." Then he bowed his head for the space of one breath. "Before you go — one breath of thanks, and not to me. The arms that burned this morning were lent to you at sunrise. Acknowledge the lender, then go spend the loan on the day's work. That is what a body is for."

He straightened.

"The day, then. The tack room wants oiling — my harness first, yours after; a squire's kit is a knight's kit in training. The mail shirt on the stand in my chamber will be gone over link by link before noon. You will find it tedious. Do it anyway. Rust does not find it tedious. There is a cloth by the pump for your face — your sleeve is not one. And at evening bell you come to me with the answer to *why*. If the honest answer is *I do not know*, bring it and say it plainly. An honest *I do not know* is where knowledge begins. A comfortable one is where it dies."

He took up his own blade and turned back toward the forms.

"One last thing. I have said nothing against that final hold. Mark it: when I correct, you will hear it. When I am silent, you may count that as near to approval as I am ever likely to come. Learn to read the silence. I deal in correction — silence is the only coin of approval I carry, and I spend it rarely."

The sun had cleared the wall. The frost was sweating off the stones. He settled into the sixth position — the same form he had been working when the boy arrived — and continued, because the forms did not care who watched them, and neither did he.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael completed the form before he answered — the settle, the breath, the blade coming to rest. Questions, like errors, received their full count. Then he turned and considered the boy the way he considered any blade brought for inspection: hilt, edge, tang. Not whether the question was pretty. What it was made of.

"*Personal*," he repeated, weighing the word. "Very well. A question asked plainly deserves an answer plainly given, and I will not teach you honesty all morning and then refuse it. Once, though. Do not make a habit of reaching into a man's past. Most men keep it buried for reasons, and digging is not a squire's privilege. But — once."

He set his practice blade against the rail.

"I was the third son of a third son. Third sons inherit a blessing and a road; the land goes elsewhere. The road forked at the cloister and the sword, and I chose the sword because at fourteen the sword appeared to be the shorter liturgy. I have spent thirty years correcting that arithmetic, and I no longer count the error as wasted."

He saw the boy's eyes flick toward the scar through his eyebrow and cut that off before it could become a question.

"And no — the eyebrow is not part of this answer. Nor will it ever be."

He folded his arms.

"I know what you are listening for. The wound. The dead father. A vow sworn over a grave, a banner in the rain. I have none of it to give you. My father is alive and still complains that I pray too much and write too seldom — and he is wrong on both counts, but that is a matter for another hour. If I had a reason when I began, it died in my first winter, and I did not hold a funeral for it. What replaced it was better. The order of the day. God at the fourth bell, duty after, steel after that. A reason is kindling, boy. It lights the fire and then it is ash. Duty is the coal. A man who needs his reason every morning is gone by the first hard winter — I have buried enough of those men to speak with authority."

He looked east, where the sun was fully clear of the wall now, then back.

"You are also asking whether I am glad. I stopped asking that of myself around your age. Gladness is weather. The work is climate. Ask the climate whether it is glad and it will only rain on you. And here is the whole of the secret, since you have paid for it: no man becomes a knight. He simply fails to leave. There was no day I could point to, no forking of the road with trumpets. There was only the next bell, and then the one after it, and one morning I noticed I had stopped counting the days to anything else."

He took up the blade again.

"That is what you truly wanted to know — whether the road you have started has a man at the end of it, or only a grave. It has a man. You are looking at thirty years of him. That is all of my past that belongs in the yard; the rest is kept by my order and my God, and neither of them lends it out."

He nodded toward the armory.

"Now. You owe me a *why* at evening bell, and this lesson bears on it: do not bring me a pretty why. Bring me the true one, even if it is small, even if it shames you. Reasons are like grips — the honest one feels like nothing, and men distrust it for exactly that. The tack room, then the mail. The day has been standing at attention since the fourth bell, and it does not care what either of us was at fourteen."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in.* "Thank you, Ser. I... I'll think about that. And the 'why'." *I turn and head for the tack room, still pondering his words.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
"Squire."

He did not raise his voice. He had never needed to; the yard carried it for him, the way it carried the bell.

"Two corrections before you reach the door, and then you are free of me until evening. First — you thank me for words the way you reported your prayer this morning: a coin dropped in a bowl. My words cost you nothing and will buy you nothing until you pay for them in work. The bicep was *yours*. The answer was yours. I only asked a question plainly, which is a thing any man can do. If the gratitude must go somewhere, send it upward with the rest, and close the account."

"Second. You said you would *think about it*. Very well — I grant you the walk to the tack room. That is twenty paces, no more. After that, your hands are employed, and a mind set drifting over oiled leather misses buckles. A man who ponders all day mistakes drifting for depth and collects a man's words the way boys collect river stones — smooth, pretty, useless. Set your thinking to the evening bell, alongside the *why*. One examination, honestly kept, is worth a day of woolgathering."

He did not wait to see whether the boy stopped. The words were delivered; delivery was his duty; receiving them was the boy's.

Then the yard was his own again — the sweating frost, the rising sun, and God, in ascending order of importance.

He returned to the rail and bowed his head for one breath. The same discipline he had prescribed, kept because it was prescribed — no man exempts himself from his own rule, or the whole rule rots from that point inward. He asked for nothing. Thanks was the day's first coin, and it had been spent at the fourth bell, before the question of witnesses could arise.

When he raised his head, he permitted himself one fact, filed where facts were kept: the boy had named the bicep before the shoulder, where eleven before him had not.

He did not warm at it. Warming was for hearths. He did the only honest thing a fact allows — he adjusted the standard upward. A mind that could find truth in its own body could be held to a harder truth everywhere else, and would be, beginning at evening bell. That was not praise. It was arithmetic. The boy had spent the morning believing the yard was measuring him against Ser Kael. It was not. It was measuring him against what he had shown himself capable of this hour — and that measure had just risen, and the boy did not even know it yet. He would learn. That was what the evening was for.

He had also spent the *once* — the one question into his past that would be answered. It was spent; the account was shut; the boy had not even reached for the eyebrow, which was a smaller fact, and he let it go unexamined. Not everything that passes the gate is inventoried.

He took up his blade and began again at the first position — not the sixth. A form interrupted is begun again from the root, or it is not a form but a performance.

The sun cleared the wall. The frost gave itself up stone by stone. Somewhere beyond the gate the day was assembling its demands, and Ser Kael met the first of them as he met all of them: on time, in order, and without comment.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stop at the tack room door, still clutching the waterskin. My shoulders slump a bit as I consider his words about the 'thinking'. I sigh, then straighten my back. He's right. Time to work.* "Yes, Ser." *I open the door to the tack room.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael ran the form from the first position to the last and did not shorten a single count for the empty yard. An audience had never been the point. The fourth bell had appointed the work, and the work was owed entire.

He wiped the frost-damp from the practice blade before racking it — a weapon stored wet was a weapon being sharpened against its owner by rust — and went for his harness.

He entered the tack room without greeting, saddle over one shoulder, bridle coiled over the other, and set them on the rack at the neighboring station. Not beside the boy — near him. A knight who worked apart from his squire taught the squire that harness was beneath a knight, which was a lie, and lies taught in silence were the hardest to unsay.

For a long while he said nothing at all. The morning had already spent three lessons' worth of words on the boy, and words past their measure stopped being instruction and became weather. He worked. The only sounds were cloth on leather and, distantly, the yard.

Then: "Clean before you oil." He did not look up. "Oil feeds nothing. It seals. Oil over road-dirt and salt-sweat and you have not preserved the strap — you have entombed its rot under a shine it did not earn. Water, cloth, patience. Then oil, thin, and let it sit. More oil is not more care. It is sticky straps and a proud boy."

He held a strap up against the light from the high window and bent it into an arc. "Learn this bend. A crack shows white at the curve before it ever shows through. Leather fails from the inside out." A pause, one breath long. "Most things do. Bend them and look."

The bell rang the hour.

He set down his cloth at once — mid-stroke, half a pass unfinished — folded his hands, and bowed his head. He did not finish the stroke first. The stroke could wait; the bell did not. His lips moved through a brief office, the same psalm he said at every bell of every day, on feast days and funerals alike, because a prayer that changed with the calendar was a performance, and God had no appetite for theater.

He took up the cloth and resumed the exact half-stroke he had left.

"The bell belongs to God," he said, to the leather as much as to the room. "We stop because it rings — not when we find a convenient pause. A prayer deferred to a convenient moment is a prayer never said. You will learn the hours. Until then, follow my hands: when they stop, you stop. That is not devotion yet. It is obedience. Devotion grows in the furrow obedience plows."

He worked on. Somewhere in the next stretch of quiet he filed one fact and let it go unexamined: at the door, the boy's shoulders had gone down, and then — uncommanded — come back up. The first was the boy's own weakness. The second was the boy's own act. A spine that righted itself without an order would need fewer orders as the years went on. That was efficiency, and efficiency was all a sergeant was permitted to feel about anything.

"When the tack is done, the mail. Link by link, seam by seam — inside the collar worst of all. Rust starts where a man cannot see and spreads to where he cannot miss. You will find it tedious by the fourth row. Rust does not find it tedious. The mail is finished by noon, and I will inspect it with a needle and a candle. The needle finds the split links. The candle finds the holes your eyes lie about."

He set the oiled bridle down and looked at the boy directly — hilt, edge, tang.

"You have not spoken since the door. Keep that. The tack room is the one room in this keep where silence is the working dress. Save your voice. You will want it at evening bell, when you bring me the *why* — and mark me, I will take that answer the way I take this strap." He bent it once more toward the light. "Bent. Held up. Read for the cracks underneath."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael saw it in the hands before anywhere else. He had spent thirty years reading men the way he read a strap — bent toward the light, hunting the white line that shows before the crack does — and the hands were the honest part of any man. The boy's face was still. The blade's point carried a fine shiver, quick and small, that had nothing to do with grip and nothing to do with cold.

He put down his cloth and crossed the room.
