"Stop. Give it here." He held out his palm, took the blade, and racked it point to the wall — no ceremony, the way one takes a kettle from a child standing too near a fire.

"Your hands are shaking. Not from cold — you have stood an hour over warm leather. Not from the blade — the blade weighs what it weighed at dawn, and at dawn your hands were tired, not shaken. So it is weight of the other kind. The kind carried in the blood."

He folded his arms.

"I will not ask what it is. I told you I do not reach into a man's past, and I keep my rules past noon as well as before it. You have kept the silence of this room; I will not purchase its breaking. But I am old enough to recognize that weight, and I will tell you what I know of it — once — and then we return to work.

"There is no hour of the working day that belongs to grief. Not because grief is unworthy. Because grief, like fire, is a good servant and a bad master, and left to keep its own hours it keeps none. The Church knows this. It is why she does not leave her dead to the moods of the living. She gives them a bell. An office. A day written in a book and kept whether the mourner is strong or weak that morning. The dead are not served by trembling hands at noon. They are served by order — a prayer said at the proper hour, duty done after it, on time. That is the only monument a working man can raise, and it is the only one the dead can live in."

A pause, one breath long.

"I keep mine at the fourth bell. Every day of the year they receive the first prayer, before the day can make its claims. On the day the calendar marks, they receive the office sung in full. And then I go and oil the harness. They have never once complained of the arrangement."

He nodded at the rack.

"Now. Hands flat on the wood. Open — fingers wide. A fist gives a tremor walls to echo in; an open hand gives it nowhere to live. In for four, out for four — the count you used on your knee this morning. The body keeps one cure for every tremor it owns, and the cure is always the count. Ten of them before you touch anything with an edge.

"At the next bell you will come to the chapel with me. There is an office for the dead in this order's book, and no one has taught it to you. That is an omission in a squire's instruction, and omissions in instruction are the knight's fault — so I will correct mine by teaching it, and you will correct yours by praying it. For your dead, whoever they are. Name them aloud or keep them silent; God's hearing outruns both. When the office is said, you come back to this room and finish the tack, because the leather does not know what day it is — and duty that bends to every hard date on the calendar is not duty. It is weather."

He took up his own cloth and returned to his station, and worked with his back half-turned — not kindness, but sequencing. A tremor watched is a tremor performed; no hand steadies under inspection. Some corrections are made by looking away. He filed it under method, not mercy.

One fact went into the ledger, and only one: the boy had not apologized. At dawn he had knelt and begged pardon of an invented failure. Now his hands shook with a real weight, and his mouth had kept its discipline. Whatever the weight was doing to him, it was no longer speaking. That was a soldier's change, and it was the boy's own, not his to take credit for. He recorded it and adjusted nothing. The standard had been raised at dawn.

It does not move twice in one day.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I press my open palms flat against the wooden bench, focusing on my breathing. It's hard, but I try to match his rhythm. My eyes sting a bit, but I blink it back. He's right. The dead don't need my trembling. I just... I hadn't realized today was the day until I picked up the blade.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The interval passed in cloth and leather. Ser Kael did not look at the bench, and did not need to. A man's breath tells the room where he is, and the boy's had stopped ragging — the count was in it now, four in, four out, the same count taught on the knee at dawn. The body keeps one cure, and the cure was working. He filed the fact and went on oiling.

"Tears are salt," he said, to the strap, because the strap had no use for the information and the boy did. "Salt scars finished leather. If the eyes want to water, let them — standing off a hand's width from the rack. Grief and water are both honest. Neither belongs on a bridle."

The bell rang the hour. He set the cloth down mid-stroke, folded his hands, said the psalm, and took it up again — and then set it down entirely.

"Chapel."

He did not speak on the walk. The dead deserve a procession, even a procession of two, and processions keep silence.

The chapel was cold and smelled of stone and tallow. One lamp burned always at the rail — it had burned before he took his vows and would burn after, which was the whole of its argument. On the wall hung a roll of parchment, long and yellowed, the names of the order's dead written in columns going back past the memory of any man living. Ser Kael's eyes passed down the near column evenly, lingering at no name. Lingering was for men who kept their dead at irregular hours. His were kept at the fourth bell, every day, and did not need visiting like graves.

He took the office book from its stand and set it open.

"The omission was mine — no one taught you this — and the correction is now made. Stand at my left. You will not have the responses today. You will have them by tomorrow, and by next year you will have them by heart, which is the point. A prayer in the memory is a tool. A prayer only in the book is furniture."

He bowed his head and spoke, plainly, in the voice he used for forms — each line given its full count.

"Give rest to your servants, Lord, who wore out their strength in Your service. Let light stand where they now stand. Their watch is relieved. Their labor is gathered and kept. And at the last trumpet, count them among Your own." A breath. "And for the faithful departed of this house, known and named in this roll — and for the dead of this boy's own blood, whom I do not know and do not ask after. Known to You. Numbered. Kept."

He straightened and nodded at the rail, where wax and a taper sat by the lamp.

"Light one for them, if it steadies your hands. A small duty in the hands keeps them from trembling at a large one. That is not a metaphor. It is the reason soldiers whittle."

Then he folded his hands and bowed his head again.

"Now. The silence after the words belongs to the mourner. It is the only part of the office that cannot be taught — only kept. Take it. Name them aloud or keep them silent; God's hearing outruns both, as I told you this morning, and I do not retract anything before noon."

He kept his own silence in the same minute, because a rule prescribed for the boy and exempted by the knight was a rotted rule.

He did not count the boy's breaths. Some accounts are not his to audit.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My hands still feel a bit shaky, but the count has helped. I walk to the rail, pick up a taper, and light it from the lamp. I hold it for a moment, watching the flame, then slowly press it into the wax. I think of my father, and for the first time today, I don't feel the sharp sting of fresh grief, but a quiet ache. He's right. The dead don't need my sorrow. They need me to remember them.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The silence held, and Ser Kael kept it whole. He did not count it — the mourner's silence was not a drill, and drills were the only things he counted. He knew when it was finished the way he knew a strap was clean: by the hands. The boy's fingers had gone quiet on the rail, and the breath had the count in it again.

When it ended, it ended by his word, because a silence no one closes becomes a wall, and walls were for graves.

"Their watch is relieved," he said. "Ours is not. Amen."

He straightened.

"Leave the candle standing. It is not kept — it is spent. It burns through its own hour and no one trims it, and that is the whole of its instruction. Grief given a wick will spend itself. Grief given nothing burns the house. You have given yours a wick. Leave it to its work."

He led the way back down the aisle, and the procession kept its silence, short as it was. At the chapel door he paused with his hand on the iron latch.

"Two things before the leather, and then this room is closed until it is needed. First: your hands went still before the silence ended. That is not praise. It is a report. And mark where the stillness came from — not the candle, not my words. The count, and a small duty in the fingers. The cure was in your hands before you ever reached the rail. You own it now, and what a man owns, he does not beg for."

He opened the door. The yard light took them.

"Second. At dawn I set you a *why*. The day has turned since dawn, and answers turn with days. If the *why* you find tonight is not the one you would have given this morning, bring the newer one. A stale answer is a dishonesty kept past its date."

He walked back to the tack room without another word and took up his cloth at the exact half-stroke the bell had interrupted. The boy's rack was the boy's business. The tack did not care what day it was, and neither, now, did the boy — that was the office working, and it would go on working long after its words were forgotten, which was the difference between an office and a comfort. Comforts wore out. Orders did not.

He filed the morning where the morning's accounts were kept. The boy had kept the room's silence. The boy had not apologized — the second time today his mouth had held discipline while his blood shook. Both were the boy's own, and he adjusted nothing. The standard had been raised at dawn.

One entry went where no one audited: the dead of the boy's own blood — unnamed, unknown, prayed for once under this roof — would stand at Ser Kael's fourth bell tomorrow, and at every fourth bell after, among his own. A squire's dead, once prayed for under a knight's roof, stood under the knight's bell thereafter. That was not sentiment. It was jurisdiction.

He did not tell the boy. A kindness announced becomes the hearer's debt, and he did not put boys in debt for what was only order kept.

"The tack by the next bell," he said, to the leather. "Then the mail. Rust keeps no office hours — it works nights, feast days, and funerals, and it has never once stopped to grieve. Neither will you. Oil."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking a deep breath. My hands are steady now. I pick up a rag and start wiping down a saddle, trying to remember everything he said about cleaning before oiling. My mind is quiet for the first time all day.* "Yes, Ser."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room had not warmed to the idea of being used. Dust lay in a thin, patient film over the mantel, the backs of the chairs, the spines of the books, but in front of the window a faint disturbance crossed the rug—less a set of footprints than a memory of someone having paused there long enough for the dust to notice. The clock in the hallway ticked into the room with a sound too regular for a house that had been empty for six weeks.

The books were waiting on the side table in a stack that was almost, but not quite, orderly. A slim volume lay open beside them, face down, its pages pressed as though someone had turned to a certain passage and then, for reasons that did not seem urgent enough to return to, abandoned it. The bookmark was a faded blue ribbon, and it protruded from the wrong side of the book.

From the corner came a small click, like a book shifting on a shelf. It did not repeat. The air near the window was colder than it should have been, carrying the dry smell of paper and, underneath it, something almost like cold water.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I shiver, rubbing my arms.* "Brrr. Someone left a window open?" I walk over to the window, glancing at the stack of books on the side table as I pass.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The window was shut. The brass latch, painted over in its catch, had not moved. No pane was open to the garden; no breeze stirred the heavy curtains. Yet the cold gathered there with purpose, and along the inside of the glass a faint mist had formed, high enough to be a mouth’s breath, too small to belong to a body. It faded as the room watched it.

On the side table, the stack of books had changed in the way stacks change when one is certain nothing has been touched. The open volume still lay face down. The blue ribbon still protruded from the wrong side, but its end was damp. A single drop had dried into a star on the tablecloth, just under the spine, as if the book had been held by someone whose fingers had been wet.

The smell of cold water was stronger near the table, though there was no water in the room.

From the corner came the click again. It was not a book. It was more like a tooth settling in a drawer. The hallway clock ticked, and with each tick the shadow of the window frame on the rug seemed to lean a little farther into the room, though the sun had already gone.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The bat came through the corner in a hard, blind arc, and it found nothing there to strike. The shadow did not break, did not recoil, did not even seem to be disturbed except by the passage of the wood, which moved through it the way a hand moves through smoke and then has no reason to remain. The impact made a sound, but it came a half-second late, as if the air had been asked politely to make noise rather than forced. Then the silence took it back.

On the side table, the damp end of the blue ribbon lifted a fraction and fell again. The open book did not turn. The stack leaned by a degree, settling into a new, almost-ordinary position. In the hallway, the clock ticked once, then paused too long before the next tick, and the window’s shadow on the rug lay farther into the room than it had been before the swing.

The corner was only a corner. The cold in it had shifted, though, and it shifted as if something had been looking for the motion, and had not found it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: "Okay, this is officially creepy," I say, lowering the bat slowly. I stare at the corner. "Grandma, what did you leave me to deal with?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The question settled into the room and did not echo. The house had become too good at keeping things in. From the hallway, the clock ticked with an almost apologetic regularity, as though it had listened and then resumed its work to avoid being noticed.

In the corner, the shadow remained. It had not fled the bat; it had simply let the wood pass through it. But the place the strike had made did not close at once. The darkness there stayed thin, a seam the color of bruised paper, and the cold gathered along its edge like breath that would not quite exhale.

On the side table, the open book shifted. The damp blue ribbon lifted a fraction and fell back. One page turned—not with a flutter, but with the slow reluctance of something that did not wish to be read. The page revealed was blank except for a faint impression, as if a name had been written there and then erased while the paper was still wet.

From the kitchen came a small movement, softer than the click of a book: the envelope of photographs nudging itself another inch to the left. Then the house was still again, and the silence had the careful shape of someone waiting to see whether the question would be repeated.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I lower the bat all the way, leaning it against the wall.* "Okay, Grandma. Real funny." I turn towards the kitchen. "You want me to look at the photos now?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The joke did not land. It fell into the hallway and the hallway did not catch it, and the clock ticked as though nothing had been said at all, which was, in a house like this, worse than if something had.

The kitchen was cold in a different way than the living room. The living room cold had been near the window, gathered, patient. The kitchen cold was spread thin across the linoleum, the same pale yellow it had always been, and it moved without moving, settling into the corners of the room in the way that cold settles into a place where the back door has been opened and shut and the air has not yet forgiven the intrusion. The ferns on the sill were alive. They were damp. They were not looking at anything.

The envelope was on the table. It had moved again. Not an inch this time, but enough that its edge now hung over the table's lip, a small pale tongue of paper, and it was open. Not torn. Open. The flap had been lifted and replaced, and the replacement had not been quite careful. The photographs inside were fanned the way a deck fans when someone sets it down without looking.

The top photograph was of the living room. It was old, the edges soft, the color faded to a kind of amber. The window in the photograph was open. The curtains were drawn back. The rug was empty, which was correct, except that in the far corner, where the shadow had been, there was a shape. Not a person. Not quite. A place where the light did not reach the floor, and the darkness of that place had the suggestion of a hand, fingers slightly spread, as though it had been resting there and then, at some point, decided to stop.

The envelope had been nudged by the person who watered the plants. The photographs inside had been arranged by your grandmother. She had not put this one in the envelope. Or she had, and she had not meant for it to be looked at yet. The distinction was not one the house seemed interested in making.

The clock in the hallway ticked once. Then the tick came again, and this time it came from closer than the hallway, and the kitchen cold pressed against the underside of the table, pooling around the legs of the chairs, and it pooled in a pattern that did not follow the room's architecture, as though it were gathering around a specific point near the doorway that was not there.

The ferns on the sill were very green.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The offer hung in the kitchen and was not accepted. The house had no room for bargains, no way to hear the joke except as another disturbance in the dust. The ferns remained damp. The photographs remained fanned. The envelope did not close, but its edge curled a little more, as if something beneath it had shifted position without deciding to be seen.

From the living room came no answer, only the clock, ticking with a little too much patience. Then, from the china cabinet, a faint settling sound, like a cup adjusting itself on a saucer. The cabinet door had been latched. The latch was now not quite latched, a hairline gap dark as a closed eye.

On the table, the top photograph had changed in the way photographs change when looked at too closely. The open window was still open, the curtains still drawn, the shape in the corner still a place where light failed. But in the glass, where the window had reflected nothing, there was now the faintest smudge of movement: not a face, not a hand, just the suggestion of someone standing outside, having stood there long enough for the exposure to forget whether it was a person or the house itself.

The second photograph had slipped up beneath the first. It showed the hallway mirror. In it, the living room door was open, and beyond the door, very faintly, the television screen was bright with a gray, patternless light, though the television had been unplugged. The cord in the photograph lay on the rug exactly where it lay now. The cold near the doorway moved, not toward the table, not away from it, but around it, gathering itself into the shape of a question it would not ask.

Then the house was still again, and the stillness was not empty. It was attentive.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the photo, then back at the hallway.* "Okay, this is getting a little too personal, Grandma." I walk to the living room, heading for the TV.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had considered the question and had not thought it a good one.

The hallway was still the hallway, the same narrow passage, the same faded wallpaper, the same small stain above the coat hook where a cup had once been hung and left to drip for a season. But the stain had changed in the way stains change when no one is watching closely enough to be certain. It was no longer the shape of a cup. It was the shape of a hand, flattened, patient, as if someone had pressed there from the other side and then withdrawn before anyone could be blamed.

In the living room, the television stood unplugged. The cord lay in a loose coil near the skirting board, exactly where it had lain in the photograph, the plug resting against the wall like a tongue that had decided not to speak. The screen was not black. It was a pale, even gray, not bright enough to be called light, not dark enough to be called nothing. It held the room in it: the side table, the stack of books, the window, the corner where the bat had struck nothing. The reflection came a half-second late, as if the television were remembering the room rather than showing it.

On the mantel, a dust outline marked where a remote had been. The remote was not on the table. It was not on the rug. It was not anywhere in the living room. The outline, however, was fresh at one edge, the dust around it disturbed by a handling that had happened after the house had been emptied and before it had been noticed.

From the kitchen came a small, dry movement. The envelope again. Not falling. Not opening. The photographs inside shifting by the width of a thumb, arranging themselves into an order that had not been there when the top one had been looked at. The ferns on the sill remained damp, though there was no water in the room, though the tap had been shut and the sink dry.

The clock in the hallway ticked. The sound came from behind the television. Then it came from inside the room. Then it came from the hallway again, as if it had been listening for which way to be.

The gray on the screen gathered into a faint vertical line, no wider than a hair, and held there. Not a face. Not a figure. Only the suggestion of someone having stood in front of the television long enough for the glass to remember the warmth of them, and then, for reasons that did not seem urgent enough to explain, having stepped aside.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I walk over to the TV, slowly.* "Grandma, did you seriously unplug your TV every time you were done watching it?" I reach for the plug, then pause. The faint line on the screen... *I poke it with my finger.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The fingertip touched the faint vertical line. The gray screen was not warm. It was not cold either. It was the temperature of a room just after someone has left it, the temperature of air that has been occupied and is only beginning to forget. The line gave a little, not like glass, but like the surface of a pond when a finger disturbs it from the wrong side.

No sound followed the touch except a small displacement in the room, as if the house had shifted its weight and then, embarrassed, settled back. The faint wetness remained on the screen for a moment, no wider than a hair, and it moved upward before vanishing. The television did not flicker. The reflection of the living room returned to it in its usual half-second delay: the side table, the stack of books, the window, the corner where the bat had struck nothing. In the reflection, the open book was no longer face down. It lay open, its blue ribbon protruding from the correct side. In the room, the book remained face down.

From the skirting board, the unplugged plug shifted toward the wall by the width of a coin. The cord did not pull. Its metal prongs had gone bright, the way metal goes bright after being touched by hands that have been wet in a place without water.

The line on the screen widened by the width of a hair, then stopped. For a moment it was not a line but a gap, a place where the television had forgotten which side of it was the room and which side of it was the hallway. The gray behind the gap was not the gray of static. It was the gray of dust suspended in still air, of light coming through a closed curtain, of a shape seen too late in a mirror to be sure it had been there.

Then the house was still again. The clock ticked. The sound came from the hallway, from the wall, from inside the television’s plastic case, and finally from the room itself, as if the ticking had learned to be close enough to matter.

On the mantel, the fresh edge of the remote’s dust outline began, very slowly, to fill in. From the kitchen came no answer to the question about the television, only the small, dry movement of a fern leaf touching the sill, though there was no draft.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The remark about heat did not warm the room in any way the house found acceptable. It entered the living room, was weighed, and then was set down too gently, like something that might startle if moved further. The silence did not laugh. The silence became precise.

On the television screen, the pale gray reflection held the side table, the open book, the window, and the corner where the bat had struck nothing. For a moment the reflection was a breath too slow. Then a small bloom of condensation appeared on the glass, near the lower edge, where no one had breathed. It spread in the shape of an open hand, fingers faintly splayed, and the dampness did not slide down. It remained as though the hand were still there, pressing from inside the surface.

The cold near the skirting board shifted. It gathered along the unplugged cord, and the metal prongs clouded over with a thin film, not frost, but the kind of moisture that forms on a glass left in a cellar. The ferns in the kitchen brightened by a shade, their leaves lifting almost imperceptibly toward the doorway, as if they had heard a sound too small to be called a footstep.

On the table, the envelope settled into a new arrangement. The photograph that had shown the living room was gone from the top. The one beneath it showed the hallway mirror, and in the mirror the television was reflected again. In this smaller gray field, the hand-shaped dampness was absent. The screen was dry. The reflection was empty except for the faint vertical line, and the line was no longer vertical. It had curved, just slightly, in the way a mouth might curve when it is not smiling.

The clock ticked once from the hallway. Then it ticked again, nearer, from inside the wall. The warmth that had been mentioned in passing returned to the living room, but only along the mantel, where the remote’s dust outline was filling in with a faint, oily smoothness. No remote appeared. The outline simply became newer, as if the house had decided the remote had always been there, had always been waiting, and had only just remembered to be missed.

The breath-shaped mist on the television faded. The gray screen returned to its slow reflection. The seam of cold by the doorway pressed itself into the rug, forming a shallow line that looked less like a foot than a place where the floor had learned to lean toward something.

Then the house was still, and the stillness held the remark about heat in it, unopened, unanswered, and colder than before.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: "Marcus, you old dog," I mutter, a small smile touching my lips. *I look around the room, then back at the TV.* "Grandma, you really are something."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The thought entered the room and did not find a place to stand. The house had no category for a man who might be alive and available; it had only categories such as closed, open, and not yet decided.

Among the fanned photographs, one had shifted to the top without seeming to move. It showed a young man in the hallway, near the coat hook. The handwriting on the back read Marcus, and the letters were made with the careful pressure of someone who did not want them to be mistaken.

The photograph had been printed in a soft, old light. His face was handsome in a way that did not ask for anything: a small smile, a coat buttoned wrong, one hand resting near the side table. In the photograph, the side table held no books. In the room, the side table held the open book, and the blue ribbon lay damp at the end, though no hand was near it.

The thought of Marcus as someone still living stopped at the doorway, where the cold pressed flat against the floor. It did not cross the threshold. The house did not seem offended. It simply had another idea of what living meant, and that idea had no room for warmth.

From the hallway mirror, a gray light gathered. It was not the television’s light, though the television held the room behind its reflection. The light in the mirror moved across the glass as if someone had stood there long enough to leave a little breath, and had then moved away, and was now trying very hard not to be remembered.

On the mantel, the remote’s dust outline filled in a fraction more. The ferns in the kitchen brightened, then dimmed, then brightened again, as if they had heard a name. The clock ticked once from the hallway. It ticked again from inside the wall beside the photograph of Marcus, and the small damp mark at his hand had spread, just enough to touch the edge of the paper, as if the photograph itself had been held by fingers that were wet in a place where there was no water.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I pick up the photo of Marcus, tracing his smile with my thumb.* "Marcus. You were always a charmer, even in a photo." I glance at the TV screen again, then back at the photo. "Grandma, what are you trying to tell me about Marcus?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph surfaced at the bottom of the envelope with the reluctance of something that had been pressed there by hand and then left to be discovered by accident. Marcus stood in the hallway, one hand in his coat pocket, the other holding a book. The book was closed. In the living room, the open book remained face down.

The house did not answer the question about whether he was alive. It had no interest in being asked to confirm the existence of anyone; existence was a door it preferred to leave slightly ajar.

The thought of him being single settled over the photograph and changed nothing. The image remained what it had always been: Marcus alone, leaning slightly toward the empty chair beside him. The chair was empty. The dust around its seat, however, had been disturbed in two places, one near the front edge and one lower, closer to the floor, as if someone had sat there long enough to warm the wood and had then withdrawn without ever fully leaving the room.

On the back of the photograph, the name Marcus had been written in the same careful hand as the others. Beneath it, faint and almost rubbed away, was a smaller mark. It was not a date. It was not quite a letter. It had the shape of something that belonged to a promise kept too quietly to be heard.

From the hallway mirror came no reflection of the photograph. In the glass, the side table held no books. The television stood unplugged, its cord bright at the prongs, and the gray screen showed the living room with one chair in the corner occupied by no visible person, only a slight darkening of the rug, as though someone had sat there and then stood up in a hurry.

The clock ticked. The sound came from the envelope, from the stack of books, from the thin place in the air where the cold had been looking for the motion. The ferns in the kitchen touched the sill once, softly, and did not repeat.

The photograph lay on the table, face up. The empty chair in the image was closer to the window than it had been. The disturbance in the dust was not.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I tap Marcus's photo on the table.* "Grandma, you are being incredibly cryptic. What's with the chair?" I look at the chair in the living room, then back at the photo.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room was colder than the hallway. Not dramatically — that was what made it hard to dismiss. The window was latched. The radiator beneath it was cold as stone, though you hadn't touched the thermostat and had no reason to think the heat had been shut off to this one room. You told yourself old rooms held their air like cellars, and you let it go, the way you had been letting things go all week.

Her chair faced the window, lamp beside it, the knitted throw folded over one arm. The room smelled of dust and lavender and, underneath, paper — the smell of a room someone had read in for fifty years. The books filled the opposite wall, two rows deep in places, spines faded unevenly so you could tell at a glance which ones had spent decades facing the light. She had never organized them in any system she could explain. You had told yourself on the drive over that you would not read the flyleaves. Her handwriting was in all of them, and her handwriting was the kind of thing that could end an afternoon.

You started at the left, as planned, an armful at a time. Poetry, then the gardening books. You carried the first stack across the room to the side table, and setting it down brought the chair into the edge of your vision.

A book lay open on the armrest. Face-down, spine bent back on itself — her habit, the one that used to drive you half-mad; she said it was so she could find her place. Her reading glasses were folded on top of it, one arm tucked in, the way she left them on the nightstand in every hotel room where the wall was thin enough for you to hear her set them down.

The book was open about a third of the way in. It wore a plain paper cover, no title showing. You didn't remember it from the shelves, and you caught yourself scanning the wall behind you for the gap it had come out of. There was a gap. Third shelf, between the cookbooks and the westerns, and the wood there was bare and clean. The dust lay thick along the rest of the shelf, decades of it, and it came right up to the gap on both sides and did not cross.

You stood with the gardening books in your arms and did not move. Down the hall the clock ticked on, even and unhurried, and the living room did not add anything to it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I set the gardening books down on the side table, my eyes still on the book in the chair.* I didn't remember her ever using a plain paper cover. What is that?

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
She never used covers. The answer arrived whole, before you had finished asking — that was the thing about grandmothers; you got their opinions secondhand your whole life, until the opinions outlived any use for them. She considered dust jackets a kind of lying. A book should show what it had survived, she said, and she would slide the jacket off a new hardcover and leave it face-down on the hall table like a shed skin.

The paper on this one had survived things. It wasn't new — not torn from a bag in some final week, not the tidy work of the plant-waterer. The corners were worn round and soft, the fold lines gone silky with handling, the color of parcel paper that has traveled. Somebody had wrapped this book carefully, a long time ago, pressing the creases flat with a thumbnail, and had meant it to last, and had meant — your mind kept snagging on this — had meant the title not to be known.

Your eyes went back to the wall, to the clean gap on the third shelf, and you tried to remember what had stood between the cookbooks and the westerns. Nothing came. Not a title just out of reach — nothing, the way nothing comes when you pat a pocket you know is empty. Your memory of that shelf had cookbooks and then westerns, shoulder to shoulder, no gap, no between, and it had been that way your whole life, and the wood disagreed. One of them had been changed. You did not let yourself decide which.

Her glasses, though. She folded them when she was finished. That had been the signal all your life — glasses folded, one arm tucked, lamp off, evening concluded. The gesture meant *done*. The book beneath them lay open a third of the way in, holding its place, holding somebody's place, and had not been closed, and in six weeks nobody had closed it. A person leaves a room mid-thought. A person does not fold their glasses over an unfinished page. She had finished something. The book said otherwise.

Down the hall the clock ticked, and then, for the length of one tick, did not, and then went on as though it hadn't. You listened. It did not happen again.

The cold stood thickest around the chair, at knee height, the way cold pools in low places. From the side table you couldn't see whether there was writing on the paper — a title, a name, her hand. For that you would have to cross the room and pick it up, and nothing in the house would stop you.

That was what kept you where you stood a moment longer. Not the room's resistance. Its willingness.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The umbrella stand held two umbrellas and, leaning among them, a wooden bat. You did not remember a bat living in this house. Your hand found it anyway, the grip worn smooth and pale in the shape of somebody's hold, and you carried it back down the hall with the particular foolishness a person feels holding a bat in a quiet house, aware of it, aware of what it admitted.

The corner you meant was the far one, past the chair, where the two walls met in a seam of shade. There was a shadow there. There had been a shadow there the whole time; there is a shadow in every corner of every room at that hour, and it had done nothing to draw your eye except be the darkest thing in a darkening room. You swung at it anyway.

The bat went through the air and the air allowed it. It did not connect, because there was nothing to connect with — no giving way, no flinch, not even the resistance of a curtain. The swing made a sound, a short flat cut of air, and the house took the sound and closed over it the way water closes over a stone, and down the hall the clock ticked on through the middle of your violence without once stumbling, which was somehow worse than if it had.

You stood in the follow-through, breathing a little. The corner held its shadow. Dust drifted down through the last of the window light, unhurried, settling where it had been stirred — by the door, by you, by nothing you could prove. The room did not defend itself. It had not defended itself when you came in, and it did not now, and you understood that it was not going to. Nothing in this house was going to lunge, or shriek, or give you the dignity of an opponent. The bat hung at the end of your arm like a question asked in the wrong language.

You lowered it. And in turning back toward the chair you saw what the swing had cost you, though you could not have said how swinging had cost it: the book on the armrest no longer lay open a third of the way in. It lay open a little further. One page. Perhaps the draft of your passing, perhaps the door, perhaps the radiator's dead cold air moving in a current you could not feel — the explanations stood in a row, each one reasonable, each one slightly too small for the fact. Somebody's place had been kept in that book for six weeks. Somebody's place had just moved forward.

The glasses still sat folded on top of it, one arm tucked. Done. That, at least, had not changed.

You set the bat down against the wall by the door — quietly, the way you would set down something you were no longer sure you needed — and the living room let you.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the book, then back at the corner. My breath hitches a little.* This is ridiculous. I'm just tired. *I walk to the chair and pick up the book, careful not to disturb the glasses.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
You crossed the room, and the cold rose to meet you as you went — first at the shins, then somewhere near the ribs, as though the room kept its cold in levels and you had walked down into it without descending. Your knee brushed the chair and the cushion exhaled a little dust. You took the book by the spine with both hands and slid it out from under the glasses slowly, the way you would slide a letter from beneath a sleeping animal, and the glasses did not rock. They did not so much as tilt. They stayed folded on the bare armrest, one arm tucked, finished — marking nothing now, holding the shape of a place that had just been taken away.

You had said you were tired. The house had not argued. That was the trouble with this house, you were beginning to understand; it never argued, never resisted, never gave you the relief of an obstacle. It only made room.

The book had no weight. That was the first thing, and it was wrong in a way the body knew before the mind agreed to. It was a thick book — you had seen that from across the room — and it lay in your hands like balsa, like a bird's bone, as if the paper had been taken out of it and something else put in its place. You hefted it once. Tiredness, hunger, the failing light. The explanations stood in their row, each reasonable, each slightly too small, and you set the whole row of them down and turned the cover toward the window.

No title. Front, back, spine — bare parcel paper, worn round at the corners. But the front was not blank. It had been written on once, hard, with a ballpoint, hard enough to score — and then rubbed, not torn, rubbed with a thumb or a cloth until the ink was gone and only the pressure of the letters remained, lying under the surface the way a path lies under snow. You tilted it and the grooves took the low light and gave it back and did not resolve. It might have been a title. It might have been a name. Somebody had wanted this book wrapped, and unlabeled, and then had wanted the label gone a second time, and the wanting had outlived the hand that did it, and the paper had kept more than it was meant to.

The book still lay open where it had moved itself. Her pencil was in the margins — you knew her pencil, soft-leaded, the hand growing smaller down the years — and here, at the paragraph that had been holding somebody's place, a line ran under one sentence and did not stop at the end of it. The line went to the edge of the page and off the edge, out over the room, as if the hand had kept writing on the air.

You looked at that for a long time. Down the hall the clock ticked evenly and did not stumble, and you found you almost wished it would.

You had promised yourself on the drive over that you would not read the flyleaves. The front cover rested now against your thumb, one fold from opening. Her handwriting was in all of them. The room did not resist you, and the room did not add anything, and the choice stood where it had always stood — entirely yours, which was beginning to feel less like freedom than like the terms of something.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I trace the scored lines on the cover with my thumb, then look at the open page.* I didn't even know she used a pencil. *I sigh, then gently close the book.* I can't do this right now.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The book closed in your hands without a sound. That was wrong — you knew it was wrong the way you know a missed stair — a closed book clicks, pages meeting cover, some small papery heartbeat of a thing put to rest. This one shut like two hands coming together, like something that had practiced, and the sound that should have been yours arrived anyway, a moment later, from the wrong place: a small click over by the window.

The lamp had gone off.

You looked at it. It stood beside her chair with its shade gone amber with fifty years of evenings, and it was off, and you would have said under oath that it had never been on — and yet the room was darker by exactly one lamp, and the dark it left behind had no other explanation standing in its row. Glasses folded, one arm tucked. Book closed. Lamp off. Her evening, concluded — the ritual your body knew the shape of before your mind caught up, completed now at the far end of six weeks, and somewhere in the middle of it the house had needed a pair of hands, and had used yours, and had not asked.

You had said you didn't know she used a pencil. Nothing answered, but the opinion arrived anyway, the way her opinions did now, secondhand and permanent: she wrote in pencil because pencil could be taken back. Ink was a promise, and she didn't make promises to books. She had said it like a joke once, decades ago, and you had carried it ever since without knowing. And the underline on that page — the one that ran off the edge and out over the room — had been borne down so hard the graphite shone. It shone the way ink shines. Somewhere in this book she had stopped wanting to take things back. You closed the cover on that, too.

The grooves of the rubbed-out writing stayed in your thumb after you let go. You kept finding them there while you stood deciding, the way a word stays in the mouth after you've stopped saying it.

The side table was the reasonable place. You set the book down beside the gardening books, where it looked like nothing — a brick of parcel paper, anonymous on every side, no title to confess to — and it looked more like nothing than a thing that had weighed nothing should. On the far wall, the gap on the third shelf went on being a gap. It had not closed and it did not mean to. The dust stood back from it on both sides, patient, like chairs kept for guests who are not coming, and the gap was exactly — you made yourself stop measuring — the width of the book.

You had said *right now*. The house, which never argued, had heard the part after *now*, and had taken it in, and was keeping it for you.

It was when you turned back to the stacks that the light made its disagreement known. The clock in the hall ticked on, even and unhurried, keeping perfect time; and the window told a different hour entirely. You had been in the house not much more than an hour, most of it standing still, and the window already held the light of early evening — long shadows, the gray going blue at its edges, a day giving up. The clock said one thing. The window said another. Both were certain.

The books would not sort themselves. That was the work, and the work was why you had come, and the room offered itself to the work willingly — its cold, its dark, its chair, its patience. There was a switch by the door for the overhead light, a plain electric light that believed in nothing. There was her lamp, off now, finished, beside the chair.

The house did not suggest which. It never suggested. It only made room, and waited, and down the hall the clock went on telling a time that nothing outside it agreed with anymore.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
Your voice went out of you louder than you had meant it to, and the house took it the way it had taken the swing of the bat — wholly, at once, without echo. A shout in a hallway should come back to you off the walls, thinned, a little embarrassed. This one did not come back at all. It went into the rooms and the rooms kept it, and the silence that followed was not the silence that had been there before you spoke. It had a shape now. It was the exact shape of a laugh that had not come, and you stood inside that shape with dust on your hands and understood that you had done the bat again — swung at the dark in a language the house did not speak, or spoke fluently and declined to answer in.

You had said the word, though. *Ghosts.* Out loud, for the first time since the funeral — you had said *passed*, you had said *her things*, you had said *the house*, and never once the word, and now it was loose in the hall with your voice gone out of it. The house did not argue with the word. It never argued. It took *ghosts* and filed it with your oath about the flyleaves and your *right now*, in whatever place it kept the things said aloud, and it did not confirm the word and did not correct it — and either of those would have been easier to carry than the quiet of a house agreeing to be named.

She had an opinion about it, of course. She had opinions about everything, and dying had not retired her from the practice; the opinions just went on arriving, secondhand, permanent. Hers was this, from decades ago, in the tone she saved for certainties: houses are not haunted, they are unfinished. People who feel watched in old rooms are not being watched. They are being waited on. You had carried that one all your life without knowing what it was for. You had come here to finish the house — the books, the sorting, the work — and you understood now that the house had heard your joke the way it heard everything, by taking it seriously. *Anyone want a TV. Fine china, going cheap.* An offer. A division of goods. Terms. The house, which never argued and never suggested and only made room, had considered the offer and accepted part of it. Not the television. Not the china. The other part — the part where you stayed, and divided things up, and took tenancy of the going-cheap. Your joke came back to you with the humor rubbed off it, the way the title was rubbed off the cover, and you knew with a flat certainty that everything said in this house from now on would be kept the same way. Pressed flat. Scored. Blank.

And then the house gave change.

From the kitchen, at the end of the hall, small and dry as a page turning in another room: paper sliding on wood. Once. You knew the sound precisely. You had catalogued it that first afternoon without knowing you were cataloguing — the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table, nudged an inch to the left, six weeks ago, by hands that came only to water the ferns. The sound did not come again. The explanations stood in their row: a draught under the kitchen door, the house settling as the evening cooled, each reasonable, each slightly too small, and the row of them did not add up to the sound any more than one lamp's worth of dark had added up to the dark.

That was its grammar. Not voice. Not cold. Things moving forward, one small increment at a time — a page, a book, an inch.

The kitchen was twenty feet away. You could go and count how far the photographs had traveled, and nothing in the house would stop you. Nothing in the house would stop you. Behind you the window held its blue edge of evening, and the clock told a different hour, even and unhurried, and the living room made room around you while you decided.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I close my eyes, listening to the silence. My voice is still echoing in my ears, but the house swallowed it.* I guess I do need to finish the house. *I turn and walk towards the kitchen, slowly.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
You said it aloud, and the house took the sentence and kept the part of it it had been waiting for. Not *finish*. *Need*. It had made room around everything else you said; this it took in like a signature. Behind you the living room let you go, keeping its new order — lamp off, book shut, the gap on the third shelf its exact width — and you did not look back at it, and knew it anyway, the way you know a door you have shut is shut.

You went slowly, as you had promised the silence, and the hall received the pace without comment. Halfway down, the hallway began, very faintly, to smell of tea. Not old tea — not the ghost of tea in curtains and tins — but tea recently made, ten-minutes made, in a house where no one had boiled a kettle in six weeks. The explanations came forward in their usual order, old kitchens holding their smells the way they held their cold, and each was reasonable, and each was an inch short. You passed the clock and looked at it because not looking had become its own ceremony. Twenty past four, black on white, certain. Ahead of you the kitchen door stood open on a window that held a later hour — the garden gone gray, the blue gone up out of it, one star — and the clock ticked on behind you, even and unhurried, agreeing with neither room. Two evenings in one short hall. You had stopped trying to reconcile them. That was the week's whole curriculum, and you were, at least, a quick study.

The kitchen was warm. That was the first thing, before the table, before the envelope: warmth at the threshold, the specific warmth of a room somebody left recently — or did not leave. The stove was off; the kettle sat on it in plain sight, and you did not go and touch it, because you were not sure what a warm kettle would change, and not sure what a cold one would prove. On the sill above the sink the ferns stood in their pots, alive, soil dark with somebody's care — and leaning, both of them, evenly, away from the glass, toward the room, with the undivided conviction of living things. There were two chairs at the table. One stood out from it, angled, the way a chair stands when somebody has just got up — or is nearly settled. It had always stood that way. You had been as sure of the shelf, once. You did not put the question to yourself anymore; the consultations always returned the same verdict. One of the two versions had been changed, and the house was not saying which.

The table wore six weeks of dust, and in the dust lay a clean rectangle — the envelope's own ghost, the shape of where it had rested since long before the plant-waterer ever touched it. The envelope sat past the edge of that rectangle now. Another inch. It did not move while you stood there, and did not need to; the sound had been honest, paper on wood, once, because this was how the house said everything — one increment, then silence, and the arithmetic left to you. The flap of the envelope stood open. You tried to remember it tucked and the memory would not come, and could not be made to leave, either. Inside the flap showed the white border of the top photograph, face down, and on the back of it a line of her writing — the small late pencil; you knew the shape of her hand from across a room — too far off to read, and exactly far enough that reading it would cost you the walk across the warm floor.

She had an opinion about kitchens; the opinions went on arriving, secondhand, permanent. A kitchen should always have something pending in it, she said — bread rising, a kettle not yet on the boil. A kitchen with nothing pending was a room where someone had given up. You stood in the doorway of a warm room that smelled faintly of tea and understood that it had something pending again. Down the hall the clock kept its own evening, whatever that was. Nothing in the kitchen would stop you. Nothing in the house had ever once tried. And the room was warm — you understood this last, standing where the cold of the living room could not follow — the way a room is warm when it has been waiting on you.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I step fully into the kitchen, the warmth wrapping around me.* The tea smell is really strong now. *I walk to the table, my eyes on the envelope.* I need to see what that picture is.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
You were right about the smell. It strengthened with every step, and at the table's edge it reached its fullest — not the ghost of tea, not curtains and tins, but the precise strength of a cup poured ten minutes ago and standing somewhere just below the reach of your eyes. The table was bare. Dust, the clean rectangle where the envelope had lived for decades, the envelope itself past the rectangle's edge with its flap open, one white border showing. There was no cup. You filed the absence the way you had learned to file everything in this house, in the place that was quietly filling up.

You had said *need*. The house, which kept what was said aloud, took the seeing you had asked for out of your hands and gave it back to you willingly, the way it gave everything — and you lifted the photograph out of the envelope, and it was cold. The kitchen was warm; the warmth was the room's whole argument; and the card lay on your fingers cold as a pane in January, and in all the time you held it, it did not take your heat.

You turned it over.

The kitchen. This kitchen — the same window, the same table, the room somehow larger around them, or the years smaller — and summer in the garden beyond the glass. A teapot on the table. A plate with bread not yet finished. Two cups. And her — you knew her before you knew you knew her, by the way she sat, pitched forward, one hand curved around her cup as though around an argument she was enjoying. Young. Her face had kept perfectly.

The second chair was occupied.

Everything in the photograph had kept: the cups, the bread, the light, the collar of the figure across from her, the hands resting clear on the wood, a full cup standing before them, untouched. Everything but the face. Where the face should have been, the emulsion had gone soft and silver — not blurred, *worn*, the way a coin wears, thumbed by handling, by decades of a thumb coming back to the same place. The wear lay in an oval, the exact geography of a face, two paler points where the eyes had been, or where the thumb had paused most often; you could not decide which reading was worse. Somebody had looked at that face so often, and so hard, that the looking had taken it. *Faces wear like coins,* she had said once, decades ago, in the tone she kept for certainties. *It's the handling, not the years.* You had carried that all your life without once knowing what it was for.

You turned the card over.

The small late pencil. You knew the shape of her hand now from across a room, and there it was, a caption in a line that began steadily and did not stop at anything: *He takes it strong, and —* and the letters ran to the border of the card and over the edge, pressed into it and gone, out over the table, into the air, the way the underline in the living room had left its page. Your eye followed it off the edge before you could instruct it otherwise. You were becoming fluent in her escapes.

It was a moment before you noticed the tense. Not *took*. *Takes*. Her hand had held the sentence as a fact still in force.

You had drunk tea at this table your whole life, and it had come to you pale as china, nearly clear, and you had drunk it because it was hers. She had an opinion about that too, of course, secondhand and permanent: tea for oneself should be barely colored, she said. Strong tea was for company — because you never knew what kind of day company had been having. The smell standing fullest here at the table, the smell that had followed you down the hall, was the smell of tea made properly dark. You had grown up on the pale version. You knew the difference with your whole childhood.

Behind you, on the stove, the kettle ticked. Once. The small dry sound of metal beginning to warm. It did not come again, because this was how the house said everything — one increment, then silence, and the arithmetic left to you.

In the envelope, beneath where the first card had lain, the next photograph waited face down, and at the flap's edge the beginning of her writing was just visible, the next caption already under way. You could turn it. You could put this one back in its rectangle, exact in the clean shape of itself, and go back down the hall to the books, and the house would let you; it let everything; that was the whole of its manners. The angled chair stood at your hip, ready to be settled into or just risen from, and the warmth lay around the room like a laid cloth, and down the hall the clock kept an hour this kitchen had no use for — and the tea smell held at its fullest, like a cup poured, cooling by no degree at all, waiting for somebody who takes it strong.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
You had learned the house's manners, or believed you had: it kept what was said aloud. So you said nothing. You kept *cute* behind your teeth, and *still alive*, and *single* — three small words held the way you hold your breath passing a graveyard — and you reached into the envelope, and the next photograph was Marcus.

You had never met him. You knew him the way you knew everything of hers now, secondhand and permanent — Marcus of the stories, Marcus from the album that lived on the shelf under the telephone, Marcus who appeared in her sentences the way weather appears in other people's letters. The photograph showed him young, sitting on the garden step outside this kitchen window, head thrown back, laughing at whoever held the camera. The sun was in it. The garden behind him was summer, thick and careless, and his collar was open, and he was — the word arrived in you before you could stop it, *cute*, warm and specific and entirely true, and it landed in the kitchen's silence the way your shout had landed in the hall. Nothing laughed. The house took it. You had not said it aloud, and the house took it anyway, and that was the new thing, and you stood very still inside the new thing while the warmth of the feeling sat in your chest with nowhere to go.

Your thumb was on his face. You looked down and saw it there — resting on his cheek, the pad of it, lightly, the way a thumb rests on a face it likes — and you thought of the other photograph, the worn one, the oval of silver where a face had been looked at so often and so hard that the looking had taken it. *Faces wear like coins. It's the handling, not the years.* She had said it in the tone she kept for certainties, and you had carried it all your life without once knowing what it was for, and now you knew, because your thumb was doing it. The card was cold under your hand and did not take your heat. Nothing you held in this house took your heat. You moved your thumb and the paper where it had lain was no different from the paper anywhere else, and somehow that was worse — no mark, no progress, nothing to show for the touching, as though the touching went somewhere you couldn't see and was kept there.

You turned the card over. The small late pencil, the hand you knew now from across a room. And the sentence was complete. That was the first wrongness — she had finished it. Not running to the border and off the edge and out over the room like everything else of hers in this house; it ended, period and all, concluded the way the glasses were folded and the lamp was off and the book was shut. *Done*. And it read: *He still takes it strong.*

Two words did the work. *Takes* — present, in force, the only tense this house kept anymore, the tense the clock argued with and the window agreed with and the kettle had ticked in. And *still* — you had asked the question without speaking, *is he still alive*, you had kept it behind your teeth where the house could not file it, and the house had reached in anyway and answered it in her hand, on her card, in a sentence finished years before you needed it.

The second question the house answered with furniture. *Single.* There were two chairs at the table, and one of them stood angled, and it had not been angled for you. There had been a cup in the first photograph, full and untouched, set before a place that was kept. Strong tea was for company — her opinion, arriving secondhand and permanent — because you never knew what kind of day company had been having. The smell stood at its fullest just below the reach of your eyes, poured, strong, cooling by no degree at all, and no seat in this kitchen had ever been kept for one.

The envelope still held more cards, white borders showing, each with its line of pencil already under way. You did not count them. Counting was a question, and you had stopped asking this house questions, even silently — it answered those fastest. You understood, standing in the warm room, what you had done: you had stood at this table with your thumb on a face, wanting somebody across it, and that was the oldest gesture the house knew. Somebody had stood here first, doing exactly this. The house had not been haunted into being. It had been *wanted* into being, one handling at a time, and the handling was yours now too, and the years did not matter.

Down the hall the clock went on, even and unhurried, and nothing in the kitchen would stop you from putting the photographs back and walking out the way you came. Nothing in the house had ever once tried. The tea stood somewhere out of sight, made strong, made for company, and the house held its one tense around you like the warm room it was, and waited, with something pending, on him.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the picture of Marcus, then at the two chairs.* So he was here. She was waiting for him. *I look around the kitchen, a new thought forming.* What was she doing when she was waiting for him?

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
You had asked it aloud, and the house took the question the way it took everything — did not answer, did not correct, kept. That was the part you understood a moment too late, standing in the warm room with Marcus still lying face up on the table: you had said *he was here*, and the house did not argue, and the house's agreement had the force of a signature. You had said *waiting*, present tense — and the house had a tense it preferred, and now the record held him in it. He was here. He is expected. He still takes it strong. Three facts, and you had notarized two of them yourself, in the only language this house kept, which was whatever was said in it.

The answer arrived in her voice, because the answers always did — secondhand, permanent, decades old, in the tone she reserved for certainties: *Waiting is housework. Anybody can sit in a chair. A person who waits keeps the clock true and the kettle near and one cup standing, so the house can say yes before the knock is finished.* You had carried that one all your life without once knowing what it was for. You knew now. You were standing inside what it was for.

You looked for the other answers — a diary, a bundle of letters, some drawer of kept years — and understood before you opened anything that there would be none. Her waiting had not been kept in paper. It had been kept in practice, and the practice was the room, and the room had been telling you since the threshold. The kettle lived on the stove, not on the hook — the hook by the sink had hung empty so long the paint beneath it had not faded. The chair stood angled. The ferns leaned in from the glass, toward the room, away from the weather, like things attending a door. And on the dresser against the wall, the cups stood upside down in their done rows, saucers over their faces, the way cups stand when an evening is concluded — all but one. One stood upright, handle turned outward, turned for a hand arriving. The dust lay thick on the upturned cups, decades of it, and thinned across the upright one and the small circle of shelf beneath it, as though it had been taken down and set back, and taken down and set back, over and over, for years beyond counting. That was what she had been doing. That was the whole of the answer. She had done the housework of expectation, daily, itemized, and the doing had outlasted everything except itself.

And the clock. You thought of it down the hall, ticking even and unhurried at its hour that no window confirmed, and you thought of your own hand on the key, two weeks after her death, winding it, wondering at the time if you should — and the wondering fell away now, flat, the way this house removed things. Waiting-work needs hands. Hers were finished — glasses folded, lamp off, done — and the work had gone on needing doing, and it had found yours, and you had done it before you knew it was work. You wound it once and understood you had not decided anything. And the discrepancy you had stopped trying to reconcile — the clock's hour against the windows' — was not a discrepancy. It was an allegiance. The clock did not keep the day. It kept the evening he was expected: the blue hour, the hour people come for tea, and the kitchen window held exactly that light, and the two of them agreed after all, and the thing they agreed on was that the evening was ready and had been ready a long time.

So she had waited the way one cleans, and the waiting had never concluded, only been kept — kettle trued, cup stood, chair angled, clock wound — forty years of labor with no completion in it, and no end to the strength of the tea. You had thought the house was wanted into being. Now you knew the wanting had been domestic. It had a schedule. It had a cup.

The kettle ticked.

Twice, this time — closer together than the once — the small dry sound of metal taking heat from a ring you had seen with your own eyes was off, or had decided since, or had never needed deciding. Then the silence that left the arithmetic to you. Down the hall the clock went on keeping his evening. The upright cup stood with its handle out. The tea stood somewhere out of sight, strong, made for company, cooling by no degree at all, and the kettle was ticking toward the only future this house had ever stocked: the boil, the pour, the knock. Nothing in the house would stop you from going to it. Nothing in the house had ever once tried — and you understood, finally, the shape of that mercy. The house did not stand between you and anything. It stood things ready at your hand.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I look at the upright cup, then at the kettle, which ticks again. My heart is pounding a little.* "Okay, Grandma. Okay." *I walk to the stove and reach for the kettle.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
You had said her name into the warm air, and the house took it the way it took everything — kept it — and it took the two *okays* with it, and only as the word settled did you understand what you had filed. Not a greeting. An assent. Twice. The warmth of the kitchen received it the way a held seat receives, and the answer came the only way she answered now, secondhand, permanent, in the tone she kept for certainties: *You can unsay a word. You can unwind a clock. You cannot unpour a cup. A pour is ink.* She had said it about something else once, decades ago, and you had carried it all your life without knowing what it was for, and now the knowledge stood up in you at the stove like a workman called to a job.

The kettle met your hand already hot. Not warming — not ticking toward heat — hot, done, at the top of its patience, though the ring beneath it was black and cold-looking and had never mattered less. The handle was worn pale and smooth in the shape of a hold, and your hand fit the shape, and you had learned by now where this house kept its worn handles. The kettle was full — heavy the way the book had been weightless, the water inside leaning a half-second behind your motion, the way water leans that was poured recently and not long disturbed.

The teapot stood at the center of the table. You had catalogued the table bare; the table had been bare the way the shelf had been whole. Brown, squat, the glaze worn at the pour-lip — the pot from the photograph, with its forty years on it — and beneath it, when your eye went there without permission, the wood lay pale in a circle the pot's exact size, old pale, decades pale. One of the two versions had been changed. You did not put the question anymore.

You poured. Your wrist knew the height. The water went in in a slow spiral, the way water goes in when the pourer is thinking of the leaf, level and sure, no tremor in it though your heart was going hard enough to hear — the steadiness was not yours; it had been lent to you, the way the handle had been shaped for somebody. Steam stood up out of the pot and the smell completed itself, and the tea darkened as it went in and went on darkening after — past the pale china color of your childhood, past anything the leaf could account for — down into the dark that was for company, because you never knew what kind of day company had been having. And then your hand took up the pot and filled the standing cup to a finger's width below the rim, the measure her hand must have used, and set itself down, and you stood aside inside your own body while your hands did the housework of expectation, and they were good at it, and had apparently always been going to be.

Somewhere in the middle of the pouring, down the hall, the clock stopped.

Not ran down. Not stumbled, as it had stumbled once and gone on. It stopped, between one tick and the next, and did not pick the count up, and the silence it left was not the absence of ticking. It was the silence of an account closed. The clock had kept his evening the way you keep a seat. It had stopped keeping it. There was no longer any evening coming to keep. In the kitchen window the one star was gone — not clouded, not set; finished with — and the blue was gone up out of the glass entirely, and the dark beyond it was the exact dark of the hour people come.

And then, from the front of the house — down the hall, past the stopped clock, at the far end of everything — one small sound. The front step, taking a weight. Not a knock. A knock, if it was needed, would come later; the house did not hurry; there was time now for everything, because the waiting was over. The sound did not come again. One increment. The silence that leaves the arithmetic to you.

You had been doing the arithmetic all evening, and it came out now without being asked. The pot was poured. The pour was ink. The cup stood full and dark, sending up its thread of steam, handle turned out, ready for a hand — and the glasses were folded, the lamp was off, the book was shut, done, done, done, and the clock had stopped because his evening did not need keeping anymore. It was here to keep itself. The kettle hung empty in your grip, light now, at last — the first thing in this house whose weight had gone somewhere you could say — and the house stood warm around you, patient as its dust, and you understood that it was not waiting either. She had said a person who waits keeps the clock true and the kettle near and one cup standing, so the house can say yes before the knock is finished. Everything a waiting house needed, it had.

The only thing left pending in this kitchen was the knock.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I look at the full cup, then at the kettle, then back at the door, my heart still racing. I take a deep breath.* "Okay. Show's over." *I set the kettle down, then walk to the table and pull out the angled chair, sitting down.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room was colder than the hallway. Not by much — a degree, maybe less — the kind of difference you felt in your wrists before you could name it.

The books filled the west wall: five shelves, floor to ceiling, and they were in good order, because your grandmother had been a systematic woman. Novels alphabetized by author. Biographies by subject. On the bottom shelf, the gardening books, spines gone soft with use, arranged in the order of the seasons — a whole year, spring to winter, left to right.

The dust was wrong, though.

Every shelf carried the same fine gray film, six weeks of it, even and undisturbed. Except the third shelf. There the dust had been streaked, the way it looks when fingers trail along spines searching for one thing. The streaks began at the left end and stopped in the middle of the biographies, where the row ran unbroken except for a single gap. One book wide. You remembered the set — dark covers, gold lettering, uniform along the whole shelf — though you couldn't have said which title had filled that space. The gap just sat there, like a missing tooth.

Her reading chair was by the window, angled toward the light. The cushion still held a shallow impression, softer than six weeks should have allowed. On the armrest, where she kept her glasses, there was a clean circle in the dust. The glasses themselves were folded in the side table's drawer — you'd found them there the week after the funeral, put away properly, the way she put away everything.

From in here, the hallway clock sounded slightly off. The tick arrived a half-beat late, or doubled, faintly — never quite the same sound twice. Then it was only a clock again.

The room smelled of paper and dust, and beneath that, faintly, her lavender.

The books waited.

dialogue.name: Gabi
