The house did not push. It arranged, and it waited for hands. And a photograph stood where photographs stand, facing a laid table, was, in the house's whole language, an invitation finished.

As for the other questions — *alive* went into the house and was filed with *possible*, with *why*, with *impossible*: words from the world outside, kept, unused. The house had its own answer, and gave it, as she had given all her answers, by completion. In that house *alive* had always meant *expected*, and *expected* was a chair. And the garden gave its answer the way gardens do, by going on: it was June at the window, June-warm against the glass, and the bundle in the hall had been cut clean and angled, knife-work, and in the photograph Marcus's fist held pinks cut clean and angled, the same work, and the pinks were being cut tonight at the fence in the house's June, the way they were always cut there in June. The house did not keep ends. It kept time, and tonight its time was June, and its June had Marcus in it.

In Gabi's fist the flower went on being alive — same fence, same cut, beading at the stem, wanting water — and the vase stood over its new water and its old ring, patient. Upstairs the line of lamplight burned steady under the eased-shut door. And against the teapot the held space waited, small and rectangular and exact, for the hand that had picked the photograph up — because the house kept the shapes of everything that had been taken from it; and this, for the first time in its fifty years, was the shape of a thing it was keeping ahead of.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the new arrangement on the table, then at the photo of Marcus in my hand. The quiet clinking from the kitchen stops. The lamp upstairs is still on.* "Okay, this is getting ridiculous." *I look from the photo to the flower in my hand, then to the waiting vase.* "Fine. Fine! But you're explaining everything, Grandma." I carry the flower over to the vase, carefully placing it in the water.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The vase received the stem the way the house received everything: without a sound. There should have been one — glass, water, the knock of a cut end finding the bottom — and there was only the settling, the water taking the stem the way still water takes a thing it has been waiting for. The flower stood. That was all, and it was everything: the head, which had hung at the angle of a thing cut an hour ago, came up by degrees, the stem remembering its own stiffness, until the flower stood in the good china the way flowers stand in good china on the day of an occasion, and the petals — curled an hour ago, curled the way petals curl while they still believe — eased. Not opened. Eased, the way a hand eases when it stops holding itself ready. The kitchen's smell finished becoming June. And at the window over the sink, black an hour past the day's own dark, a warmth pressed now from the outside in.

Below the waterline, the darkness at the cut end let go. It came off the stem in a slow thread, clouding the water — a bloom of dark, earth-colored, sinking — and the water took it and kept it, the way the house kept words, and by the time the kettle ticked again the vase held only water, clear to the glass, the stem standing in it pale and clean, and the vase did not say where the dark had gone.

*You're explaining everything, Grandma.* The sentence went into the warm air and was filed — *explain* with *why*, with *impossible*, words from the world outside, kept, unused — all but the name. The name was not filed. The name was hers, and the house took it the way it had taken the flower: as the answering of something. And the house, which did not explain, went on with the work, and the work was the explanation, and the next part of it could be heard from where Gabi stood: through the shut window, faint, through glass and six weeks of quiet, from the back fence, in the full dark of the garden — the shears.

Snip. A pause, the length of a stem being turned and judged. Snip. The rhythm was the worst of it: unhurried, exact, the rhythm of hands that had done this every June for fifty years and did not need the light. No lantern moved in the black of the garden. No shape crossed the fence. There was only the sound, coming through the June-warm pane, of the pinks being cut — clean, angled, knife-work — with the night on one side of the glass and the warm kitchen on the other, and between the two the work going on. The sound was not for seeing. It was for counting. Twelve snips, and the shears stopped — not wound down, not fading; stopped, the way work stops when the count is right. A dozen. The number she had always cut for the good vase, no more, the stems evened in the fist exactly as the photograph had them. And nothing came in at any door. The bundle in the hall kept its dozen. The new twelve stayed where they were cut, in the dark, in the June, kept the way the house kept its time — and the silence after the shears was the listening silence again, and it lay on the table, on the second setting, on the chair drawn in close enough to knock elbows reaching for the sugar.

Then the clock.

In the hall, the tick — faithful all evening, plain as any clock in any hall — missed. One beat. A gap the size of a swallowed word, opening in the middle of the house's sound, and in the gap the whole house leaned: the kettle, the warm, the flower standing in its water, everything hung from the tick that did not come. Then it came, and the tick went on, plain, faithful, and did not miss again, and would have said, if asked, that nothing had happened at all. But the sum stood ready to be done: eight days, wound a month ago, and the month spent — on hours struck that the day did not own, on the door's oiled silence, on the June at the window and the shears in it, on the flower drinking — and there is no telling a faithful tick from a failing one until it stops, and now the telling had begun. The key lay in the china bowl, teeth-up, bright, without dust, among the household keys it had joined; and above it, under the case, the winding-square waited, small and dark, in the shape of everything in that house left ready to be picked up.

By the time the kitchen was looked at again — and the kitchen did not hurry the looking — the water in the vase had gone down. Not the width of a sip. The width of a day. The flower stood drinking at June's rate, in the house's June, where hours were struck for the crossing of halls; and under the vase, at the rim of the faded ring-stain, the oilcloth had taken a new line, thin and dark — the first ring of many pourings, or the latest of them — and the water was new, and the water was going somewhere.

The table stood laid for two, the settings side by side. Against the teapot the kept space waited, rectangular and exact, for the photograph still warm in Gabi's hand. Upstairs the line of lamplight burned steady under the eased-shut door, and no shadow crossed it, and it did not waver. And in the hall the clock ticked on, faithful, spending, and the house went on with the work of June, which was also the work of the explanation, and was not finished, and was not going to be. It had all the time it had always had. What it did not have was winding. And the winding was the one work left in that house that the house could not do — the one thing in the world that wanted her hands, or the hands she had written to.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content:
*I'm standing in the kitchen, still holding the photo of Marcus. The sound of the shears, then that missed tick of the clock... I look at the vase, the water level noticeably lower. My flower is standing up straight now, looking so fresh.*

"What are you doing, Grandma?" *I whisper, my voice thick. I walk over to the hall table, my eyes on the clock key in the bowl.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
Up close, the clock was a different instrument than it had been at any distance. Its tick, which had carried through the house all evening plain as any clock in any hall, resolved at a foot's length into its parts — the lift, the let-go, the struck wire's small decay — and at the edge of each beat, faint, a dryness. A hair of drag. The sound of a mechanism spending what it did not have, and spending it faithfully, to the last coin. There was no telling a faithful tick from a failing one until it stopped; that had been true all evening; but at close quarters the telling had become possible, and it was not a sound one was glad to have learned. The month's winding was spent, or nearly spent. There was no knowing how nearly. The not-knowing was what the dryness meant.

The fanlight over the door stood June-dark, and the glass had taken to sweating on the inside — warm pressing in from the night, cool on the pane — and at the lip of the threshold the dark spot sat where it had fallen, not drying, keeping. The front door had its sticking back. The house was done seeing anyone off.

In the bowl, the keys had been let lie. They were no longer teeth-up and arranged, set out for a departure; they lay anyhow now, overlapped, casual, the way keys lie in a bowl in a house with people in it — the arrangement of the leaving undone when the leaving was declined. And on top of them, bright, dustless, the clock key. It was warm. Not where it rested against the other brass — along the shank, at the middle, where a thumb and forefinger take it for the winding: the exact grip, warm, the way a thing is warm when a hand has only just let go of it. Below the case, in the grey felt of the dust, the nail's clean shape waited. Above the bowl the winding-square stood small and dark. The key and the square had been made for one another fifty years ago, and the count of the winding — so many turns, and not a half-turn past them, or the movement would die — lived not in the head at all. It lived in the hands. It had been put into the hands one June long ago, patiently, over and over, the way she had put everything into them; and the hands had kept it, as hands do, without being asked.

*What are you doing, Grandma.* The house took the question and filed it — *what* with *why*, with *impossible*, words from the world outside, kept, unused — all but the name, which it had already taken, and the thickness under the words, which it took the way it took everything: literally, and as provision. For the question had an answer, and she had never in her life answered questions; she had gone on with what her hands were doing, and the answer arrived afterward, finished, set down somewhere it would be found. The hands were upstairs. The shutting-up was done — the sashes down, the night assigned — and the sounds that came now from the back of the upstairs were the other sounds, the evening sounds, the sounds of making ready: a drawer run open on waxed runners; the linen press; sheets shaken out with a double crack and squared in the dark air; the pillow's two soft thumps, beaten and plumped, the sound of hands. The lavender came down the stairwell before the sounds had finished — the press, the sachets, the good sheets, the ones kept against occasions — and then water, run briefly somewhere above and shut off. There had never been a guest room of hers without flowers on the washstand; there never had been once. The bundle of pinks stood on the hall table with its water-smell rising, twelve stems, and the water upstairs was going to a vase.

The little back room had been Gabi's on every stay since before memory — the bed with the sag at its foot, the window over the garden. The house was making up that bed. It had heard the only part of the sentence it could use — *I'm not leaving* — and provision was the whole of her, and the house had her manners. The one the night was kept for stood in the hall with the photograph going cool in Gabi's fist — the warmth going out of the card by degrees, the way a thing cools when the hand that held it has been needed elsewhere — and against the teapot in the kitchen the kept rectangle waited on, patient, exact, the house keeping shapes ahead of things now. Through the living-room door the cane lay as it lay, its debt running. Under the eased-shut door the lamplight burned steady, and no shadow crossed it, and it did not waver.

The clock ticked, spending. The square waited above the bowl, and the key lay warm at the grip, and the count lived in the hands — the last work in the house that wanted hands, set out ready to be picked up, the way she had left everything in that house for fifty years: finished, or waiting to be. Never once explained.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I slowly reach into the bowl, my fingers closing around the warm clock key. I hold it up, looking at the tiny brass teeth, then at the clock's face.* "Okay, Grandma. I get it. I'll wind the clock."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not answer right away. She let the words sit in the air between them, the way she did with anything that carried weight. Five full seconds passed. She was aware of the clock on the wall behind her, though there was no second hand to measure the silence; she counted anyway, out of habit.

She did not reach across the space between the chairs. She did not write anything down. Her hands remained still in her lap, the pen set aside, uncapped, on the notepad.

When she finally spoke, her voice was level, unhurried.

“You found their journal.”

Another pause, shorter this time. Then, because questions were the only honest thing she had to offer:

“What was it like to find it?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
*I shrug, still looking at my hands.* 

"Under their bed. In a shoebox." I pick at a loose thread on my jeans. "I don't know. Just... there."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the answer sit. She was aware of the clock on the wall behind her, though there was no second hand to measure the silence; she counted anyway, out of habit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. “I don’t know” and “just there” were not nothing, and she had learned not to treat them as nothing.

She did not reach for the pen. She did not shift forward in her chair or offer the comfort of a hand on an arm. Her hands stayed folded in her lap, the notepad untouched beside her.

When she spoke, her voice was level and unhurried.

“Under their bed. In a shoebox.” A pause, shorter than the first. “You don’t know what it was like. It was just there.”

Then, because questions were the only honest thing she had to offer:

“What did you do after you saw it was theirs?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not fill the silence. The half-spoken answer stayed in the room, unfinished, and she let it sit there. She was aware of the clock on the wall behind her, though there was no second hand to measure the quiet; she counted anyway, out of habit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She did not reach across the space between the chairs. She did not write anything down. Her hands stayed folded in her lap, the notepad and the uncapped pen resting untouched on the armrest.

When she finally spoke, her voice was level and unhurried.

“You stopped mid-sentence.”

A pause, shorter than the first.

“You couldn’t finish it.”

Then, because questions were the only honest thing she had to offer:

“What was the sentence you couldn’t finish?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, rubbing my temples.* "I didn't... I didn't want to open it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not answer right away. She let the words sit in the air between them, the way she did with anything that carried weight. Five full seconds passed. She was aware of the clock on the wall behind her, though there was no second hand to measure the silence; she counted anyway, out of habit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She did not reach across the space between the chairs. She did not write anything down. Her hands stayed folded in her lap, the notepad and the uncapped pen resting untouched on the armrest. She did not shift forward, or offer the comfort of a hand on an arm; touch was not something she gave.

When she finally spoke, her voice was level and unhurried.

“You didn’t want to open it.”

A pause, shorter than the first.

“You didn’t... you didn’t want to open it.”

Then, because questions were the only honest thing she had to offer:

“Did you open it?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not answer right away. She let the words sit in the air between them, the way she did with anything that carried weight. Five full seconds passed. She was aware of the clock on the wall behind her, though there was no second hand to measure the silence; she counted anyway, out of habit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She did not reach across the space between the chairs. She did not write anything down. Her hands stayed folded in her lap, the notepad and the uncapped pen resting untouched on the armrest. She did not shift forward, or offer the comfort of a hand on an arm; touch was not something she gave.

When she finally spoke, her voice was level and unhurried.

“They wrote about you. In the last entry.”

A pause, shorter than the first.

“You didn’t say whether you opened it. You didn’t say what it said.”

Then, because questions were the only honest thing she had to offer:

“What makes it hard to tell me?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I sniff, a little louder than I mean to.* "It's just... I don't know." I wave my hand vaguely. "It changes things."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:

She did not reach across the space between the chairs. She did not write anything down. Her hands stayed folded in her lap, the notepad and the uncapped pen resting untouched on the armrest. She did not shift forward, or offer the comfort of a hand on an arm; touch was not something she gave.

When she finally spoke, her voice was level and unhurried.

“It changes things.”

A pause, shorter than the first.

“It’s just... you don’t know.”

Then, because questions were the only honest thing she had to offer:

“What is it like, not knowing how it changes things?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look down at my hands again, tracing the lines in my palm.* "It's like... it's like a punch in the gut, every time I think about it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not answer right away. She let the words sit in the air between them, the way she did with anything that carried weight. Five full seconds passed. She was aware of the clock on the wall behind her, though there was no second hand to measure the silence; she counted anyway, out of habit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She did not reach across the space between the chairs. She did not write anything down. Her hands stayed folded in her lap, the notepad and the uncapped pen resting untouched on the armrest. She did not shift forward, or offer the comfort of a hand on an arm; touch was not something she gave.

When she finally spoke, her voice was level and unhurried.

“A punch in the gut.”

A pause, shorter than the first.

“Every time you think about it.”

Then, because questions were the only honest thing she had to offer:

“What do you do after it lands?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "I don't know." *I rub my chest, right over my heart.* "Try to catch my breath, I guess."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not answer right away. She let the words sit in the air between them, the way she did with anything that carried weight. Five full seconds passed. She was aware of the clock on the wall behind her, though there was no second hand to measure the silence; she counted anyway, out of habit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She did not reach across the space between the chairs. She did not write anything down. Her hands stayed folded in her lap, the notepad and the uncapped pen resting untouched on the armrest. She did not shift forward, or offer the comfort of a hand on an arm; touch was not something she gave.

When she finally spoke, her voice was level and unhurried.

“You don’t know.”

A pause, shorter than the first.

“You rub your chest, over your heart. You try to catch your breath.”

Then, because questions were the only honest thing she had to offer:

“What is it like, trying to catch your breath?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I close my eyes for a second.* "Like I'm drowning, but there's no water."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not answer right away. She let the words sit in the air between them, the way she did with anything that carried weight. Five full seconds passed. She was aware of the clock on the wall behind her, though there was no second hand to measure the silence; she counted anyway, out of habit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She did not reach across the space between the chairs. She did not write anything down. Her hands stayed folded in her lap, the notepad and the uncapped pen resting untouched on the armrest. She did not shift forward, or offer the comfort of a hand on an arm; touch was not something she gave.

When she finally spoke, her voice was level and unhurried.

“You close your eyes for a second.”

A pause, shorter than the first.

“Like you’re drowning, but there’s no water.”

Then, because questions were the only honest thing she had to offer:

“What is it like, drowning without water?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "Like I can't get enough air." *I open my eyes and look at her, my voice tight.* "Like I'm suffocating."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not answer right away. She let the words sit in the air between them, the way she did with anything that carried weight. Five full seconds passed. She was aware of the clock on the wall behind her, though there was no second hand to measure the silence; she counted anyway, out of habit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She did not reach across the space between the chairs. She did not write anything down. Her hands stayed folded in her lap, the notepad and the uncapped pen resting untouched on the armrest. She did not shift forward, or offer the comfort of a hand on an arm; touch was not something she gave.

When she finally spoke, her voice was level and unhurried.

“Like you can’t get enough air.”

A pause, shorter than the first.

“Like you’re suffocating.”

Then, because questions were the only honest thing she had to offer:

“What is it like, suffocating?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It's... it's lonely." *I pull my knees up to my chest, hugging them tight.* "Like no one else understands."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not answer right away. She let the words sit in the air between them, the way she did with anything that carried weight. Five full seconds passed. She was aware of the clock on the wall behind her, though there was no second hand to measure the silence; she counted anyway, out of habit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She did not reach across the space between the chairs. She did not write anything down. Her hands stayed folded in her lap, the notepad and the uncapped pen resting untouched on the armrest. She did not shift forward, or offer the comfort of a hand on an arm; touch was not something she gave.

When she finally spoke, her voice was level and unhurried.

“You pull your knees up to your chest. You hug them tight.”

A pause, shorter than the first.

“It’s lonely. Like no one else understands.”

Then, because questions were the only honest thing she had to offer:

“What is it like, feeling like no one else understands?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It's just... it's just me." *I look away from her, out the window at nothing in particular.* "Always me."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez looked down at the pen in her hand. Then she capped it and laid it on the notepad. Some things you didn't take notes on. You just listened.

She let the silence sit. Five seconds — she counted them without a second hand to help her, the way she'd learned to. The clock on the wall gave away nothing. That was the point of it.

"You found their journal."

She said it the way Jamie had said it. Plain. Not a question. Not softened. Just the words, given back.

*So that was what had changed in the way Jamie sat down.*

She waited again — two seconds, maybe three.

"When did you find it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug, still looking at my hands.* "A few days ago. Cleaning out the attic."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched Jamie's hands. The shrug had tried to make the words small. She let them stay the size they were.

Five seconds. She counted them off against the dying ficus, against the clock that kept its counsel, and then one beat more.

*A few days.* So the journal had been in the house with Jamie — somewhere, on some table or in some box — while the days went on around it. People did that. Held a thing close until the holding weighed more than the telling. She didn't say so.

"Cleaning out the attic," she said. Plain. She gave the words back one piece at a time and let them sit in the space between the chairs. *Attics were the last place people went, in her experience. Some never went at all. But Jamie had gone.*

She uncrossed her legs, crossed them the other way. Settled.

"Did you read it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez stayed where she was.

She watched the sentence stop. She hadn't gotten the words — only the shape of them, cut off somewhere before they could become anything at all.

Five seconds. She counted them against nothing — no second hand, no tick, just the count she'd learned to keep in her body years ago. Then a sixth. A seventh. The silence had weight now, and she let it keep its weight. That was the work sometimes. Holding the room still while a person found the edge of what they could say.

*She had her guess about the rest of that sentence. Guesses weren't for saying.* Where a voice broke was its own kind of answer, and you didn't step over a break to get at the ground on the other side of it. You stood at the edge a while.

Her hands lay flat on the notepad, the pen capped beside them, and she kept them there. There was a box of tissues on the side table. She didn't reach for it. Reaching was a kind of telling — a way of saying *I know what's happening to you right now* — and she didn't do that.

"You stopped," she said. Plain. The fact of it, given back.

Then, slower rather than softer, because her voice didn't have a softer, only a slower:

"It'll keep. Whatever the rest of it is — it's kept this long."

She watched Jamie's hands instead of Jamie's face. Faces had to hold up under being looked at. Hands mostly didn't know they were being seen.

"Where is it now? The journal."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug again, a bit more forcefully this time.* "In a box. With the other stuff." I don't look up. "I don't know what to do with it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The shrug came harder the second time. Louder, in the way shrugs could be loud.

*The journal wasn't getting lighter.*

Five seconds. The room had gone quiet enough that she could count against the radiator's tick — the building kept its own time no matter what she'd done to the clock. She counted five and let the count end there.

"With the other stuff," she said. "And you don't know what to do with it."

She gave the words back in the order Jamie had said them, then sat with them. Hands flat on the notepad. The pen capped beside them, where she'd left it.

She'd sat with a lot of people through a lot of boxes by now. Keep, give away, let go — the stuff mostly sorted itself if a person gave it enough afternoons. *But a coat in a box was a coat. A journal in a box was somebody talking.* And the other stuff, by Jamie's own telling, was still just things in an attic. The journal had come down the stairs. It had come into this room. It was sitting between the two chairs now, in a way the coats never would.

She didn't say any of that. She didn't go back for the sentence that had broken off, either. It would keep. She'd said so.

"What are you doing with the other stuff?" she asked. "The rest of the boxes."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Jamie was looking at her now. Not the ficus. Not Jamie's own hands. At her.

Dr. Vasquez met the look and kept it. Didn't search it. Just stayed where she was and counted — five seconds, held in the old place she kept them, the room quiet enough that the number needed no help. She let the fifth one run long.

*The last entry.* A journal only had a last entry because the writing stopped. Somewhere in that book was a final line, and after it the pen had lifted and never come down again. And the last thing it had come down to write about was Jamie.

Whatever the words were. She didn't guess at the words. Guesses weren't for saying, and she tried not to let them form all the way.

"They wrote about you," she said. "In the last entry."

Plain. Given back the way it came.

So that was what had been standing on the far side of the break. Not just *I read it.* *I read it, and it was about me.*

The pen stayed capped. Her hands stayed flat on the notepad.

"Do you want to tell me what it said?"

She hadn't asked what it said. The wanting was the thing. Some people had to get words out of ink and into air before the words were anything they could carry. Some people needed to stay the only one who'd read them, a while longer. Both were the work. It would keep either way — she'd said so — but a door standing open was a different thing from a door pushed.

Hands were where she usually watched from. But a face had been put forward, so the face was where she stayed — and she kept hers quiet, nothing moving in it that Jamie's would have to answer. A face that reacted became something to manage. She'd watched enough people manage a counselor's face instead of their own grief.

In the corner, the ficus gave up a leaf. Small, dry. She let it be the only thing in the room that moved.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, still looking at her.* "No. Not yet." *My voice cracks a little.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The voice cracked on the way out. Dr. Vasquez let it lie where it fell — the way the ficus leaf was still lying where it had fallen, uncollected. A crack in a voice was a fact. She didn't treat it as more than that, and she didn't treat it as less.

Five seconds, counted clean this time. Five and no more. The sentence before had broken off in the middle, and she'd given the silence extra room to hold the shape of it. This one had come all the way out. The voice hadn't carried it evenly, but the words had arrived finished, and she took them finished.

"No. Not yet," she said. Plain, and given back whole.

*The no was for today. The yet was the part with somewhere to go.*

She didn't reach for the tissues. A gesture was a sentence too, and the one it would say — *I saw that, I know what that was* — wasn't hers to say. She'd heard the crack. Hearing wasn't for acting on.

"Then it keeps," she said.

She didn't go back to what the entry said. Jamie had drawn a line, and she stayed on her side of it without making a show of standing there. The words weren't hers to want.

"The entry," she said instead. "Have you read it more than once?"

*Some people read a thing like that one time and couldn't go near the page again. Some people read it until the paper went soft at the fold.* She didn't know yet which kind Jamie was. The answer would tell her more about the carrying than the words ever would.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I nod, looking down at my hands again.* "Yeah. A few times." *I pick at a loose thread on my jeans.* "I keep hoping it'll change."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Jamie's hands had the thread now. Dr. Vasquez watched them work at it — small, patient, at the seam of the jeans. She didn't say anything about that. Hands did what they had to do.

She gave it five. The thread was still being worked when the fifth second ended.

"A few times," she said. "And you keep hoping it'll change."

Given back plain, in the order it came.

*So Jamie was the second kind.* She'd wondered which, two questions back — the kind that couldn't go near the page again, or the kind that read it until the paper went soft at the fold. *A few times meant the box had come open a few times. Lid off, book out, book back. That was a ritual. It was one of the ways people kept a hand on a thing.*

*And she'd heard that hoping before, from a lot of chairs. Nobody went back to a page because they'd forgotten what it said. They went back because some part of them was still asking it to be different by the time they got there. Different words. Or no last words at all — one more entry past the end, the pen come down again somewhere. Which one Jamie was asking the page for, she didn't know, and she wasn't going to pick.*

In the corner, the ficus kept its post. Two years of weekly water, two years of leaves on the floor. She'd water it again on Friday anyway.

"Change how?" she asked.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug. My voice is quiet.* "I don't know. Just... different."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The shrug was the third one. She'd counted those too, without deciding to — the first had tried to make the words small, the second had tried to make them smaller, and this one had quit trying and just meant what it said.

The voice had gone quiet under it. She let the quiet be quiet. Five seconds, counted against the radiator, and let them end there.

"I don't know," she said. "Just different."

Given back plain. Both pieces, in the order they came.

*People could usually name the change they wanted, given enough room. A different ending. Different words — kinder ones or crueler ones, but words you could point at. Those were wishes with handles on them. "Just different" had no handle. It wasn't a wish about the entry at all, really. It was a wish about everything the entry was the last of.*

She didn't say that. She'd quit, years ago, trying to hand people sentences for things they were still carrying raw. Sentences were for later. The carrying was now.

*And the page wasn't going to change. She knew that. Jamie knew it too — knowing had never once stopped the hoping, in anyone, in any chair she'd ever sat across from. That was the arithmetic of rereading. Nobody went back a fourth time, a fifth, expecting new words. They went back because the looking wasn't finished, even when the reading was.*

Her eyes went back to the hands, down at the seam of the jeans. She'd asked *change how* and gotten *I don't know*, and she wasn't going to ask the feeling again — a feeling that had said *I don't know* meant it. So she asked for the doing instead. You could walk around a thing you couldn't yet walk through.

"When you're done reading it," she said, "what do you do after?"

The pen stayed capped. Her hands stayed flat.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I stop picking at my jeans. I look up at her, a little surprised by the question.* "I put it back in the box." *My voice is still quiet.* "And then I put the box back in the attic."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The hands had quit the thread. It hung loose at the seam of the jeans, and the face was still up, still toward her. Dr. Vasquez let both things be what they were.

Five seconds. The radiator had gone quiet, so she counted the old way — no second hand, no tick to lean on, just the number kept in the place she'd always kept it.

"You put it back in the box," she said. "And then the box goes back in the attic."

Given back plain. Both movements.

*She'd watched the question land somewhere Jamie hadn't been looking. The surprise had gone through the hands first — the picking stopped before the face came up. People got asked about the reading. Whether they'd read it, what it said, how many times. Nobody asked about the after. But the after was where the ritual actually lived. Book out. Book in. Box up. Stairs. Done a few times now, which made it not an accident anymore. A few times made it a practice.*

*And she'd thought it once already today — attics were the last place people went. Supposed to be gone to once, and closed. This one kept getting its things back. The box came down for the visit and went home after. Keep, give away, let go — that sorting needed things to come down and stay down. The journal hadn't been sorted. It had been borrowed.*

*Boxes like that usually weren't heavy. It wasn't about heavy.*

The pen stayed capped. Her hands stayed flat on the notepad.

"Does the box come down," she asked, "or do you go up to it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I blink. That's a weird question. I think about it for a moment.* "I go up to it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The blink had come before anything else. Then the pause — she'd watched the question turn over somewhere behind Jamie's eyes before the answer arrived. Answers like that weren't being remembered. They were being built on the spot.

*And the question had been a strange one to be asked. She'd seen that land. People ran loops like this without watching themselves run them — lid off, book out, book back, stairs. Then somebody asked which direction the walking went, and for a second they caught sight of their own feet.*

Five seconds. The radiator had come back to its tick, and she counted against it, and let the count end clean.

"You go up to it," she said. Plain.

*So the box never moved. It had its place up there, and the person did the traveling.* A thing that came down into your life interrupted you. A thing you climbed stairs to was something else. *The verb was Jamie's. The box only held still.*

*She'd thought it once today already — attics were the last place people went. She hadn't accounted for one turning into a place a person kept going back to. The stairs had been walked enough times now to be known: which step complained, where the pull-cord hung, how far in the box sat. That kind of knowing didn't come from one trip. It came from returning.*

*She'd known people who did that same going with cemetery grass.*

She didn't say visiting. Guesses weren't for saying.

The ficus leaf was still on the floor where it had come down. She left it where it was. The pen stayed capped, her hands flat on the notepad.

"When do you go up?" she asked. "What time of day, usually."

*Grief kept its own hours. The hours would tell her more than the entry ever had.*

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look away from her, out the window.* "Usually at night. When everyone else is asleep." My voice is barely a whisper now.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Jamie had gone to the window. Dr. Vasquez let the window have that. A face had to hold up under being looked at, and the window asked nothing of anybody.

The voice had come down to the size of breath. She'd followed it all hour without deciding to — the words coming smaller the closer they got to the middle of things, the shrugs going the other way. *And even here, in a room where nobody was asleep, the voice kept itself at night-size. The quiet had been practiced that long. It traveled.*

She gave it five. Then she gave it more — the count ran on with nowhere urgent to be, because words at the size of breath got whatever room was left, and the room had gone still enough to hold them. The radiator had quit again. The clock gave away nothing. She counted the old way, in the place she'd always kept it.

"At night," she said. "When everyone else is asleep."

Given back plain. Slower, too — her voice didn't have a softer, only a slower, and in a room this quiet, slow and plain landed somewhere near a whisper anyway.

*So there were others. A house with sleepers in it, and Jamie waited out the sleeping.* She'd kept her own face still for years so that nobody in the other chair ever had to manage it. Jamie had a whole house of faces. *Daytime grief had witnesses, and witnesses had to be answered — comforted, or spared, or explained to. So this grief had taken the leftover hours. The ones the living were done with by the time the lights went out.*

She'd sat with people who grieved in parked cars in their own driveways. Bathrooms with the fan running. An attic at two in the morning belonged to that same family — places with something in between.

The pen stayed capped. Her hands stayed flat on the notepad.

"Does anyone know you go up?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, still looking out the window.* "No. No one."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez didn't reach for the pen.

She let the five seconds happen. It was long enough that a lesser silence would have needed filling. This one didn't. The clock offered up nothing — no tick, no hand to watch — and the ficus went on doing its slow work of dying in the corner, and Jamie's sentence just sat there in the middle of the room with them.

"You found their journal," she said. Flat. No question in it. His words, returned to him in her voice, so he could hear what he'd just put into the air.

She noticed where he'd been looking. The ficus. The hands. Not at her. She made a note of that without writing it down.

"Did you go looking for it," she asked, her voice level, unhurried — the one she used for everything, "or did you come across it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shrug, still not looking at her. "Does it matter?" I pick at a loose thread on the armrest of the chair. "It was in a box. In the back of the closet."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the five seconds happen again. She'd stopped apologizing for them years ago.

*Does it matter.*

It wasn't aimed at her. She'd gotten good, over the years, at telling the difference — a question for the room was different from a question for her — and she didn't reach for an answer to it. She capped her pen instead and laid it across the notepad she hadn't written on, and used the quiet to watch the thread come free of the seam and wind once around Jamie's finger.

She added that to the list of things she'd noticed and wasn't going to say.

"A box," she said. His words, given back at half speed. "In the back of the closet."

She let that sit too. The closet was where a person put things they weren't ready to decide about yet. She had a theory about that. She kept it with the rest of them, where theories belonged.

"What else was in the box?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez didn't ask him to finish.

She'd learned years ago that a sentence broken off like that wasn't lost. It was set down. You left it where it landed and let the room get used to it — chasing it only taught a person to stop starting sentences altogether. The missing half went onto her list of things she'd noticed and wasn't going to say. Under the thread. Under the way he'd sat down.

The clock held up its blank face. Without the second hand there was nothing to measure the waiting by. That had been the point.

She gave it five seconds. Then a few more, uncounted.

"The box," she said — level, unhurried, the same voice she used for everything. "Was there anything written on the outside of it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shake my head. My voice is tight. "No. Nothing." I clear my throat. "Just… a shoebox."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the five seconds happen. The light had moved on the floor since Jamie sat down — that was the only clock left in the room that said anything.

*A shoebox.* Nobody ever set out to buy one. It came into a house for the shoes and stayed for everything else that didn't have a place. She turned the thought over, found no use for it yet, and put it with the theories, where it belonged.

The tightness in his voice she left alone. The cleared throat went on the list — under the unfinished sentence, under the thread.

"A shoebox," she said. She left off the *just*. He'd set the word down himself; he could pick it back up or leave it where it fell.

She asked the next thing the way she asked everything — level, unhurried — because the question was heavy enough without her hands under it.

"The closet. Was it yours, or theirs?"

Then she let it sit in front of him, where he could reach it, or not.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the five seconds happen.

He'd spent the session giving his eyes to the ficus, to his hands, to the thread wound around one finger. Now — with the heaviest thing he'd said yet — he was looking at her. She didn't know what had brought his eyes up, whether he wanted to see what the words did when they landed or whether he'd simply run out of other things to look at. She let him look. She didn't lean in, didn't soften anything in her face. She went on being the same as always.

It went on the list, near the top. The list was getting long. That was fine. Lists were for carrying.

She didn't ask what the entry said. It went onto the list with the unfinished sentence, the cleared throat, the *just* — things set down in front of her that would be picked up when he chose, or not. A thing pried loose, she'd learned, was worth less than the same thing handed over.

"They wrote about you," she said. His words, given back at half speed. "In the last entry."

The light on the floor had moved again. She had a theory about where the journal was right now — a nightstand, a bag, a jacket pocket, somewhere a hand could find it in the dark — and she kept the theory with the others, where theories belonged.

"Have you read it more than once?"

She set the question down in front of him, where he could reach it, or not.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I nod. "Every day." I finally unwind the thread from my finger, carefully setting it on the armrest like it's something important. "Since I found it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the five seconds happen.

*Every day.* She did the arithmetic she didn't ask him for — how long since a shoebox in the back of a closet, how many readings that came to. The number was his to give or keep. She put the question with the theories, where it belonged.

She watched him lay the thread down. Not dropped — placed. Set on the armrest with both hands, the way a person puts something where they'll know to find it again. She didn't say anything about that either. It went on the list, near the top, under the way he'd looked at her.

"Every day," she said. His words, given back at half speed. "Since you found it."

The light on the floor had reached the leg of his chair. Without a second hand, the room gave no account of how long they'd been sitting in it, and she'd stopped needing one years ago.

"When you read it," she said — level, unhurried, the same voice she used for everything — "is it always the last entry? Or do you read the others too?"

She set the question down in front of him, where he could reach it, or not.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I look at the thread. "Just the last one." My voice is quiet. "I can't read the rest. Not yet."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the five seconds happen.

*Not yet.*

He'd set the words down last, after everything else — the way a person leaves one light on in a room they've otherwise finished with. She didn't point at them. A word like that did its work unremarked; remarked upon, it became a thing to defend.

"You can't read the rest," she said. His words, given back at half speed. Then the last two, returned to him in the order he'd left them: "Not yet." She stopped there. Anything added after those two words would have been her weight on top of his.

His voice had gone quiet on it. Quiet, she'd learned, came in at least two kinds — the kind that apologized, and the kind that didn't. This one sounded like the second. But that was her word for it, not his, and the list was for things he'd shown her. She left it off.

He was looking at the thread as he spoke. Not at her, not at the ficus — at the thing he'd placed. Set down, and still under watch. She thought of the shoebox in the back of the closet. Of a last entry read every day, and the rest kept closed. The same shape, over and over. She didn't name the shape. A name too early was only a lid.

The light had come off his chair and was crossing the floor toward hers. It was the only accounting the room gave, and it was enough.

She had a theory about where the journal was right now — a nightstand, a bag, a jacket pocket, somewhere a hand could find it in the dark. She'd kept it with the others, where theories belonged. This seemed like the time to spend one.

"Where is it right now?" she asked — level, unhurried, the same voice she used for everything. "The journal. When you leave the house, does it stay home? Or does it come with you?"

She set the question down in front of him, where he could reach it, or not.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: My hand goes to my pocket. "It's right here." I pat my jacket. "Always."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the five seconds happen.

The hand had gone to the pocket before the sentence was finished. That was the part she kept — not the answer. The speed of it. No pause to locate the thing, no searching, no moment of *where did I put it*. The hand had known the way a hand knows a light switch in its own hallway. Whatever else was happening in Jamie right now, that gesture was old. He'd done it past the point of thinking.

Her theory had offered a jacket pocket among its possibilities. She kept the small fact of being right off her face. Being right about grief had never done anyone a bit of good; it only meant she'd seen the shape before.

"Right here," she said. His words, given back at half speed. Then, alone, in the order he'd set them down: "Always."

She let the word stand by itself. It was a word people spent on vows, and on this, and not much in between.

There was a difference, she'd learned, between keeping a thing and carrying it. Keeping had a place — a shelf, a drawer, a shoebox in the back of a closet. Carrying had a body. She didn't say any of it. The distinction went on the list, near the top, under the thread he'd placed on the armrest like it mattered, while the journal sat against his ribs. The list was getting long. That was fine. Lists were for carrying.

The light finished its slow crossing and came to rest on her chair. Without a second hand, the room kept no account of the minutes. The light kept them anyway, in its own unhurried bookkeeping.

"When you're out with it," she said — level, unhurried, the same voice she used for everything — "do you take it out? Or does it stay in the pocket?"

She set the question down in front of him, where he could reach it, or not.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shake my head slightly. "I just... like knowing it's there." My hand still rests on the pocket. "It's heavy."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the five seconds happen.

*It's heavy.*

She looked at the hand on his pocket. It wasn't doing anything — no gripping, no patting, no checking. Just contact, laid there flat, like something keeping a promise. He'd said he liked *knowing* it was there, and the hand had apparently decided that knowing was not a thing a person did once. It was a thing a person renewed.

She heard the *just*, too. The second one that session. *Just a shoebox. Just like knowing it's there.* A word for shrinking a thing down before anyone else could see its size. She'd left the first one where it fell. She left this one beside it.

A journal was, by its nature, a light thing. Paper, board, thread. However many pages, it still weighed less than the keys in his other pocket. The distance between the word he'd chosen and the number a scale would have given went onto the list of things she'd noticed and wasn't going to say — near the top, under the hand that kept working after the sentence was done. Saying it aloud would have been handing him a feeling with her initials on it, and that wasn't the work.

"It's heavy," she said. His words, given back at half speed — the *just* left off, the same as before. Nothing in front of it, nothing behind.

The light had settled on her chair and gone no further. Without a second hand, the room kept no minutes, and offered none now.

"The day you found it," she said — level, unhurried, the same voice she used for everything. "When you lifted it out of the shoebox. Was it heavy then?"

She set the question down in front of him, where he could reach it, or not.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I think about it for a long moment. My hand slowly leaves my pocket and I look at my palm. "No. It wasn't." My voice is barely a whisper. "It felt like nothing."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the five seconds happen.

The hand had come off the pocket. She kept that first — before the whisper, before the words. Since *always*, the hand had stayed where it was, renewing its knowing, and now it had gone, on no instruction she could see, and he was looking into his palm as if the palm owed him an accounting. As if the difference between then and now were something it had picked up along the way.

*It felt like nothing.*

Of course it had. Paper and board and thread — a scale would have agreed with him that day in the closet. Which meant the weight had arrived afterward. Which meant it could, in principle, be set down. She didn't touch either half of it. It went on the list, near the top, under *it's heavy*, and the theory went with the others, where theories belonged.

"It felt like nothing," she said. His words, given back at half speed.

The whisper she left as it was. Returned in her voice, at her volume, it would have stopped being his.

The light stayed where it had come to rest, on the arm of her chair. The ficus went on with its slow work in the corner. There was still time. She knew it by something older than the light.

"Do you remember," she said — level, unhurried, the same voice she used for everything — "the first time it felt heavy?"

She set the question down in front of him, where he could reach it, or not.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I close my eyes. "Yeah." I swallow. "The first time I read it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the five seconds happen.

His eyes stayed closed through all of them. He'd spent the session giving his eyes to things — the ficus, his hands, the thread, her — and now, for the first time, to nowhere at all. Whatever he was looking at was behind his own face. She didn't call him back from it. Interrupting a visit like that only taught a person to stop going.

The swallow went on the list. The closed eyes went near the top.

*The first time I read it.*

So the weight had come in with the reading. Not with the holding — he'd held it weightless, out of the shoebox and into his hands, nothing. Which meant the weight had never lived in the object. It had arrived with the words, or in the space the words passed through on their way in. She turned that over, found the shape of it familiar, and kept it off her face. Being right about grief had never done anyone a bit of good.

She had a theory about the journal itself — that its spine had learned the way books learn, and by now fell open in one place only, the pages worn soft at the last entry from all the daily returning. She kept the theory with the others, where theories belonged.

"The first time," she said. His words, given back at half speed.

The light stayed where it had come to rest, on the arm of her chair. The ficus went on dying in the corner, which had lately begun to look less like failure and more like method.

"That day," she said — level, unhurried, the same voice she used for everything. "When you lifted it out and it was nothing. Did you read it there, at the closet?" She let a breath of space stand between the halves. "Or did it wait?"

She set the question down in front of him, where he could reach it, or not.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shake my head, eyes still closed. "I took it with me. To my room."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not answer at once. She let the sentence sit between them, counting quietly to five, her expression open and still.

“You found their journal,” she said at last.

She rested the pen on the notepad rather than writing.

“And you sat down differently today.”

Her gaze remained on Jamie, unhurried.

“What did you notice when you opened it?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug, still looking at my hands.* "I didn't open it. Not really."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let that answer hang in the room, quiet and uncorrected.

“You didn’t open it,” she said after a moment. “Not really.”

She folded her hands loosely in her lap, pen still resting on the notepad.

“What was the ‘not really’?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the unfinished sentence remain in the room. She counted five seconds, then rested her hands loosely in her lap.

“You stopped,” she said. “You couldn’t finish it.”

She did not write it down.

“What happens when you try to finish it?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head.* "It's stupid." *I finally look at her, my eyes a little wet.* "It just felt... wrong."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the wetness sit. She counted five slow seconds before she spoke.

“It’s stupid,” she said. “And wrong.”

Her eyes stayed steady, unhurried.

“They wrote about you. In the last entry.”

She did not look at the notepad. Did not write.

After another pause, she asked, “What about that felt wrong?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I take a shaky breath.* "They were angry. At me."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the shaky breath occupy the room. She counted five seconds.

“They were angry,” she said. “At you.”

Her hands stayed folded in her lap. The pen remained uncapped on the notepad.

“What was the anger about?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I clench my jaw.* "They thought I didn't care. About... things."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the pause after “things” stay open. She counted five slow seconds, her gaze steady on Jamie.

“They thought you didn’t care,” she said. “About things.”

She did not write it down. The pen lay uncapped on the notepad.

After another brief quiet, she asked, “What were the things they thought you should care about?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I scoff, a short, bitter sound.* "Everything. School, our parents, their stupid art."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the bitter sound remain in the air, unsmoothed. She counted five slow seconds before she spoke.

“Everything,” she said. “School. Their parents. Their stupid art.”

She did not reach for the pen. Did not write.

Her gaze stayed on Jamie, quiet and unhurried.

After another pause, she asked, “When you said ‘stupid,’ whose voice was in that word?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I blink at her, surprised by the question.* "Mine, I guess." *I shrug.* "It was stupid. Is stupid."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the “guess” sit in the room, small and uncertain. She counted five slow seconds, her face still, her gaze steady.

“Mine,” she said. “You guess.”

She did not write it down. The pen remained uncapped on the notepad, unused.

“It was stupid,” she repeated softly. “Is stupid.”

After another pause, she asked, “If you didn’t call it stupid, what would be left?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I think about that, really think about it.* "Just... sad. Sad art." *My voice is barely a whisper.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the whisper occupy the room, barely there. She counted five slow seconds, her hands still folded in her lap.

“Just… sad,” she said. “Sad art.”

The pen remained uncapped on the notepad. She did not reach for it.

After another quiet, she asked, “What does sad art need?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look up, meeting her eyes.* "Someone to see it, I guess."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the answer remain in the room, quiet and incomplete. She counted five slow seconds, her gaze steady, her hands still folded in her lap.

“Someone to see it,” she said. “I guess.”

The pen stayed uncapped on the notepad. She did not touch it.

After another pause, she asked, “If someone were to see it, what would that look like?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "I don't know." *I look away, feeling a lump in my throat.* "Someone to care."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez allowed the sentence to remain in the room. She did not move the pen across the page. She counted the seconds—one, two, three, four, five—until the silence had enough shape to hold what had been said.

“Their journal,” she said. “You found their journal.”

She kept her tone as level as the armrest beneath her notepad.

“What did finding it ask of you?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug, still not looking at her.* "To read it, I guess."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez allowed five full seconds to pass before answering. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. The sentence stayed between them, unaltered.

“‘To read it, I guess,’” she said. “You found it, and then you read it.”

She did not move the pen.

“What did reading it ask you to bring into this room?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move to fill the break. She let the unfinished sentence stay where it had stopped, suspended between the two chairs.

One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

“You couldn’t finish it,” she said quietly.

Her pen remained uncapped, resting above the page without touching it.

“What was the last part that made it into words?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "That... that they were hurting." *My voice cracks a little, and I clear my throat.* "More than I ever knew."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the words remain in the room.

One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She did not write. She did not lean forward. The pen stayed resting above the page, untouched.

“‘They were hurting,’” she said. “‘More than I ever knew.’”

Her voice remained quiet, careful not to add anything that had not been spoken.

“What did knowing that ask you to carry?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the sentence remain exactly as it had been spoken—two pieces, not yet joined.

One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

“About you,” she said. “In the last entry.”

She did not move toward the part that had not been said. Her gaze stayed steady, without pressure.

“You told me they wrote about you,” she said. “You didn’t tell me what it said.”

The pen remained lifted above the page.

“What did being written there ask you to do with it?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, looking away again.* "I don't know what it asked of me. I just... I don't know."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez allowed the not-knowing to remain where it had been placed. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

“‘I don’t know what it asked of me,’” she said. “‘I just… I don’t know.’”

She repeated both pieces without trying to join them. The pen stayed lifted, not marking anything.

“You found the journal,” she said. “You read it. They wrote about you. And now there is not knowing.”

Her voice stayed quiet, with no edge of correction in it.

“What would it be like to let the not-knowing be the first thing we listen to?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shift in my seat.* "It's just... it makes me angry. That I didn't know."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the words stay in the room. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

“Angry,” she said. “That you didn’t know.”

She did not lean forward. The pen remained lifted above the page.

“You said it makes you angry,” she said. “What does the anger ask you to do with what you didn’t know?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I cross my arms tightly across my chest.* "It makes me want to scream."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the sentence stay exactly as it had landed. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

“Want to scream,” she said.

She did not lower the pen. She did not move toward Jamie. The page stayed blank beneath it.

“You said it makes you want to scream,” she said. “What would the scream say, if it had words?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "That I'm sorry. And that I miss them." *My voice is barely a whisper now.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the whisper stay in the room.

One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She did not write. She did not move the pen. The page remained blank beneath it.

“‘That I’m sorry,’” she said. “‘And that I miss them.’”

She let both pieces rest exactly where they had been spoken, without joining them or choosing one over the other.

“You said the scream would say sorry,” she said. “And that you miss them.”

Her voice stayed quiet.

“What does the sorry need to have heard?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look up at her, tears welling in my eyes.* "That it wasn't my fault."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the words stay exactly where they had fallen.

One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She did not write. She did not reach across the space between the chairs. The pen remained lifted above the blank page.

“‘That it wasn’t my fault,’” she said.

Her voice stayed quiet, carrying only what had been spoken.

“You said the sorry needed to hear that,” she said. “What happens when those words are allowed to be in the room?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look away, wiping at my eyes.* "I don't know."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez allowed the words to remain in the room. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

“You don’t know,” she said.

She did not write. She did not lean forward. The pen stayed lifted above the blank page.

“You said you don’t know what happens when those words are allowed to be in the room,” she said. “What would it be like to let them be here without knowing?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I sniffle, rubbing my nose.* "It's just... hard."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the silence sit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. She did not shift in her seat; she simply watched Jamie with the same steady, patient gaze she had held for the last forty minutes.

"You found their journal," she said. The words were measured, even, offered back exactly as they had been given. She let another moment pass. "Did you read it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shake my head, still looking at my hands. "I... I don't know." My voice is barely a whisper. "I opened it. Saw their handwriting."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the silence sit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. She did not reach for her notepad. She did not adjust her posture. She simply held the space between them with the same quiet steadiness she had offered since the session began.

"You don't know," she said. The words were even, offered back exactly as Jamie had given them. "You saw their handwriting."

She let another moment pass, unhurried.

"What happened after that?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the silence sit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. She did not shift in her seat. She did not reach for her notepad. She simply held the space between them with the same quiet steadiness she had maintained since the session began.

"You can't finish it," she said. The words were even, measured, offered back exactly as Jamie had given them. She let another moment pass, unhurried.

"What stopped you?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I look up at her, my eyes welling up. "I just... couldn't." My voice cracks. "It felt too... private."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the silence sit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. She did not shift in her seat. She did not reach for her notepad. She simply held Jamie's gaze with the same steady, patient quiet she had maintained since the session began.

"It felt too private," she said. The words were even, measured, offered back exactly as Jamie had given them. She let another moment pass, unhurried.

"What about it felt private?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the silence sit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. She did not shift in her seat. She did not reach for her notepad. She simply held Jamie's gaze with the same steady, patient quiet she had maintained since the session began.

"They wrote about you," she said. The words were even, measured, offered back exactly as Jamie had given them. "In the last entry."

She let another moment pass, unhurried.

"You haven't said what it said."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shake my head quickly. "I can't." I bite my lip, looking away from her.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the silence sit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. She did not lean forward. She did not reach for her notepad. She simply remained as she was, the same steady, patient quiet settled in the space between them.

"You can't," she said. The words were even, measured, offered back exactly as Jamie had given them. She let another moment pass, unhurried.

"What makes it impossible?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I clench my fists.* "Because... if I say it, then it's real."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the silence sit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. She did not shift in her seat. She did not reach for her notepad. She simply remained exactly as she was, the same steady, patient quiet settled in the space between them.

"If you say it, then it's real," she said. The words were even, measured, offered back exactly as Jamie had given them. She let another moment pass, unhurried.

"What becomes real?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I finally look at her, tears streaming down my face. "That they're gone. That... that I didn't get to say goodbye."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the silence sit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. She did not shift in her seat. She did not reach for her notepad. She simply remained exactly as she was, the same steady, patient quiet settled in the space between them.

"That they're gone," she said. The words were even, measured, offered back exactly as Jamie had given them. "That you didn't get to say goodbye."

She let another moment pass, unhurried.

"What would you have said?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I close my eyes. "I would have told them... I loved them."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the silence sit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. She did not shift in her seat. She did not reach for her notepad. She simply remained exactly as she was, the same steady, patient quiet settled in the space between them.

"You would have told them you loved them," she said. The words were even, measured, offered back exactly as Jamie had given them.

She let another moment pass, unhurried.

"What else would you have said?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I open my eyes, looking at a spot on the wall behind her head.* "I would have told them... to be careful."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the silence sit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. She did not shift in her seat. She did not reach for her notepad. She simply remained exactly as she was, the same steady, patient quiet settled in the space between them.

"You would have told them to be careful," she said. The words were even, measured, offered back exactly as Jamie had given them.

She let another moment pass, unhurried.

"What did you want them to be careful of?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I wipe my eyes with the back of my hand.* "Everything. The world. Themselves."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the silence sit. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. She did not shift in her seat. She did not reach for her notepad. She simply remained exactly as she was, the same steady, patient quiet settled in the space between them.

"Everything. The world. Themselves," she said. The words were even, measured, offered back exactly as Jamie had given them.

She let another moment pass, unhurried.

"What about themselves?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I sigh, a shaky breath.* "They always put other people first. Never themselves."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"You want fire drawn? Fine. Try not to get dead while I'm being loud about it."

Kira broke from the boulder at a dead sprint, angling east along the ravine floor, zigzagging between rocks. She made herself big. Made herself obvious. Screamed something obscene about the archers' parentage that echoed off both walls.

The third arrow answered — cracked into stone a hand's width from her shoulder, spraying grit. She juked left. Another hissed past her ear close enough to burn.

"Yeah! That's it! Eyes on me, you inbred shits!"

She skidded behind a leaning slab, yanked a throwing knife from her belt — not one of her twins, a cheap backup — and hurled it up the slope. It wasn't meant to kill. It was meant to make the nearest archer flinch, and he did, ducking long enough for Kira to close the gap to the ridge base. Flat against the rock now, breathing hard, one blade in her fist and a wall of stone between her and four bowstrings.
