"Cap!" she shouted over the din. "Two broke off the west rim — climbing down, not shooting! Could be flanking your push, watch your ass!" An arrow shattered overhead, raining shards of rock. "And I've got four up here who really, *really* hate me!"

Then — a boot scrape above her. Someone picking their way down the talus for a better angle.

Kira spat a strand of hair from her mouth and grinned, all teeth.

"Never mind. Company."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood, Kira. Hold them there!" I bellow, pushing forward with my polearm. I see the two figures scrambling down the west ridge. "Vanguard, form up! Push the flankers!" *I jab my polearm towards the descending figures, ready for a fight.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The scrapes above her grew louder. Loose stones ticking down the talus. Whoever was up there wasn't being quiet about the descent — confident, or stupid. With archers it was usually both.

Kira flattened against the slab and went still. Not frozen — coiled. Counting his steps while he committed his weight to the climb. They always slung the bow for the last stretch. A bow was a worthless club at knife range, and every one of them learned that lesson exactly once.

A shadow spilled over the slab's edge.

She came up fast and mean, shoulder into his leading knee before his foot found its next hold. He made a sound like a startled goose and went backward down the slope, bow clattering off stone, plowing into the legs of a second archer near the rim. Both vanished below the lip in a hiss of scree.

"Special delivery, east ridge!" Her voice came out shredded. "No returns!"

Arrows answered — two of them slamming into the slab hard enough to shudder the stone against her spine. She rolled to the next rock, then another, because standing still was just dying with extra steps. One shaft sheared the edge of her hood and kissed her ear hot enough to sting.

"Shit— okay. Fine." She spat grit. "Cap! One off my ridge, maybe two — heard something break that wasn't mine! Call it three shooters left up here!"

Steel was ringing off the west wall now, shouts tangled in with it.

"Sounds spicy your way — hope that's your steel doing the singing!"

She risked a lean around cover. The rim was nearly clear, one silhouette dropping flat behind a rock.

"Also — you said hold 'em, so I'm holding. But there's a goat-track up this spine, and I can see it. Give me the word and sixty seconds, I go up their backs and end the shooting for good. Your call, Cap."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Movement on the west rim — a figure stepping off a ledge, unhurried, bow coming up. Drawing down on the knot of steel and shouting below that had to be Captain.

Kira's stomach dropped through the ravine floor.

"*CAP! WEST RIM — ARCHER ON YOU—*"

The words couldn't cross the gap faster than an arrow. Steel could.

She came off the slab already throwing — her left twin, the one with the worn grip, the one that fit her hand like it grew there. A throw twice her range. She put everything into it anyway — shoulder, hip, something tearing in her back that she'd be invoicing someone for later — and the knife tumbled across the ravine, a flicker of grey on grey.

It caught the archer at the top of his draw. Punched into the meat of his bow-arm. The string sang anyway — loosed wild, the shaft sailing off to bury itself in the far wall a country mile from anything that mattered — and the man folded back off the ledge with a shriek that echoed beautifully off both sides.

"YOU'RE WELCOME!" Her voice came out destroyed. "THAT'S MY BEST THROWING STEEL — SOMEBODY'S BUYING DRINKS!"

No answer from Captain. Too busy. Fair enough.

Kira rolled her screaming shoulder once and eyed the goat-track.

"Don't answer? That's a yes, Cap. Rim's mine in sixty."

She went up the spine fast and ugly, hands and boots, scree hissing loose under her. The track wasn't built for people in a hurry. She took a stitch of rock across the palm for it and kept climbing. Halfway up, an arrow skipped off stone a foot from her knuckles — "shit, *shit,* okay—" — and she hugged the rock face tighter, breath sawing, waiting out the twang of the next draw before she moved.

From the height, the whole ravine opened up under her. Steel still singing on the west side. And there — a lone figure breaking from cover, sprinting for the far mouth of the ravine, bow slung, running like a man carrying news.

"RUNNER!" she bellowed down. "Far end, making for the mouth — he's fetching friends or running home, your call if it matters!"

Then the crest. The last flat-hiding shooter popped up right in front of her, eyes going wide, fumbling for an arrow he'd never nock in time.

Kira grinned, all teeth, and drew her remaining twin.

"Hi. Remember me?"

She went to work.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Runner sighted! Let him go! We've got bigger problems!" I yell, parrying a blow from one of the flankers. Kira's doing good work up there. This fight is far from over.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The archer never got the arrow nocked. He got half a scream out instead, and then Kira's twin took that from him too — a short, ugly business on the flat of the crest, and then it was over and she was kicking his bow off the edge for spite, watching it pinwheel down into the ravine.

"East ridge is *dark!*" she rasped down, voice wrecked. "Copy on letting the runner trot — wasn't gonna chase him anyway, I don't do cardio."

Then the rest of it landed. *Bigger problems.*

She straightened slowly at the crest, and the whole board opened up under her. Below, the vanguard was a knot of steel shoved against the west wall, the two flankers in tight and giving as good as they got. She picked out the glint of Cap's polearm at the center of it and made herself stop looking there — he had his work, she had hers.

Hers was the road.

The runner scrambled up the far bank at the ravine mouth, cresting onto the trail — and behind him, low and fast and growing, a plume of dust. Riders. Too far to count. Not too far to worry about.

"Shit. *Cap.* Bigger problems confirmed — your runner's leading a parade. Dust on the road past the mouth, mounted, moving quick. Can't get a number from here but it's more than we've got."

She spat over the edge, watching the drop.

"So. Two doors. One: I break this ridgeline loose on top of your dance partners — flankers solved, one landslide, no refunds. But rock doesn't pick sides, so give me a clear fall line and get your people out from under it before I pull. Two: we don't stay boxed at all. Mouth's about to be crowded, but the way we came in is open now my ridge is quiet. Loud either way."

While she talked she'd wedged her boot under a knee-high slab at the crest's lip, working it loose in its bed with her whole weight, breath sawing.

"I'm down to one blade and whatever geology this ridge donates, so it's your call. Word and I bring the mountain down — or word and we run. Either way, word *fast.*"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The slide was already in her legs before the thought finished forming — because below, the two flankers broke off the vanguard. Both of them. Not retreating. Pivoting along the west base, angling toward the lone figure cut off past the gully.

Toward Cap.

"*CAP! Two peeling off — they're on your side of the floor and closing!*"

Her voice wouldn't cross the ravine with anything useful in it. Steel could. Except hers was down to one blade and a hundred feet of vertical between them.

She looked at Cap's position. Looked at the fall line. Looked at two idiots obligingly stepping into it.

The math was ugly, but it was short.

"ANYTHING UNDER THE EAST WALL — OFF THE BASE! PULLING THE RIDGE! *OFF THE BASE!*"

Then she threw her weight on the wedged slab.

It went with a crack like the world's spine giving out, and the whole lip of the crest followed it — and Kira went with *that*, because once geology starts moving you either ride it or end up under it. She half-surfed, half-fell, boots skating stone that had no business still holding shape, and hurled herself off the moving edge onto old talus as an entire ridgeline came down behind her. The roar swallowed everything. Steel. Shouts. Probably her own screaming. Hard to say.

Then dust. White, choking, total. The ravine stopped existing.

"*Cough* — okay," she rasped to nobody. "That was the loud part."

She gave it three heartbeats, eyes streaming, reading shapes through the haze. The slide had piled a rubble dam clean across the west base — the flankers were under it or sealed behind it, and the one scream she'd heard through the thunder said at least one was the former. Cap's ground sat clear of the fall line. She'd aimed it. Rock didn't pick sides, but she did.

And the fresh talus — the slide had built her a ramp.

"CARDIO AFTER ALL," she snarled, and went down it in a controlled crash, boots hammering, using the settle of rubble like stairs built by a drunk god. Across the floor. Up the west side. One blade out, dust boiling around her, coughing hard enough to taste copper.

"Cap!" His silhouette was resolving out of the murk ahead — and there, glinting in the settling grey beside the gully, a familiar worn grip standing up out of a dead archer's arm. "East ridge is down, flankers are buried or boxed, and that dust cloud is working for *us* now — riders can't see the ravine any better than we can."

She staggered the last few feet, wheezing, holding her side.

"Two plays while the screen holds. We ghost out the back way blind and clean. Or we let their horses funnel into this soup single-file and murder the first three in the choke — mounted men in a filled ravine are just targets with opinions." She spat dust. "Dust won't last, they will. Call it."

A cough. Then, pointing with her chin at the corpse:

"Also if that's my left steel in that guy — mind grabbing her? She's got seniority and I've got nothing left to throw."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Grab it!" I yell back, already moving toward the dead archer. "They'll be here soon. Let's make them regret it." *I retrieve Kira's blade, checking the edge.* "You ready for a close-quarters fight, Kira?"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira took her twin back from Cap's hand like a reunion — spun it once, tested the bite against her thumb, rolled her shoulders until the torn something in her back crackled a complaint she ignored.

"Hey, gorgeous. Missed you." Then, to him, one side of her mouth pulling up: "Ready for close quarters? Shit, Cap, close quarters is the *only* quarters I've ever been good at. It's all the far ones I keep failing at today."

She dropped her voice to a rasp — for once, quiet was the job.

"Shape of it: dust blinds horses worse than riders. First one through will balk at the rubble and the blood-stink — horses are smart about places things die. That's our door. I take the first man off his saddle before his eyes finish watering. Body drops, horse spooks back out, second horse piles into the first, and the whole parade becomes a traffic accident. We murder into the pileup." She tipped her chin at the invisible mouth of the ravine. "I'll take the lip of the slide — drop angle's better. You want the floor. Whatever leaks past me is yours."

She climbed the fresh talus and settled onto a waist-high slab, back to stone, both blades loose in her fists. Her palm throbbed where the rock had opened it. Her back had opinions too. She told them both to wait their turn.

Hooves.

She held up a hand, pointless in the murk. Listening. Echoes off two walls, doubled, lying to her — but—

"Four in the lead," she breathed. "Walking pace. They think the mountain got us." The sound swelled. "More behind. Muffled. Can't count the muffled."

The first shape swam out of the grey at the choke — rider hunched, reins short, spear across his lap. Somebody out there had a brain.

Too bad for him.

She came off the slab on the drop, weight down through both daggers, and hit him like the landslide's little sister — one blade hooking rein and collar, the other punching up beneath the jaw before his eyes cleared the dust. He was dead before he knew he'd arrived. She shoved the body off sideways, slapped the horse's flank hard, and it screamed and bolted back into the grey, into its friends.

Beyond the mouth: animal shrieks. A crash. Men shouting over each other.

"PILEUP!" she rasped, delighted—

Then stopped.

The hooves weren't scattering. They were *slowing*. Beyond the crash and the chaos, more of them — many more — pulling up in good order. Circling.

"Cap." All the delight had drained out of her voice. "Good news, the first two were garbage. Bad news — that wasn't the parade. Those were the scouts. The parade's *parking* outside."

Dust swirled. A second rider came through the choke at a canter, visor down, already shouting something back over his shoulder.

"Yours!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I nod grimly.* "Understood. The scouts are down, but the main force is here. We're still in a bad spot." *I tighten my grip on my polearm.* "Let's make them earn every inch."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The second rider's charge broke apart somewhere in Cap's lane — steel, a scream, the crash of a man and his opinions leaving the saddle. Kira gave it half a second of professional respect and kept her eyes on her own side of the grey.

Movement. Low. Two shapes at the choke — on foot now, shields up, feeling along the toe of the slide where horses couldn't follow. Spear-points over the rims. Somebody out there was done feeding riders into the grinder.

"Footmen! Two, on your— no. Mine. *Mine.*"

The spear was the problem. Reach murdered dagger-work; she'd buried enough sellswords to know. So she refused him the reach. Let him plant and thrust, came off the slab on the drop, slapped the shaft wide with her left blade, and stepped *onto* his shield as he flinched it up — rode it down into him, hooked his ankle, and opened the back of his knee as he folded. Loud. Done. She was moving before he finished being surprised.

The second squared up fast, shield tight, better trained. Didn't matter. Shields were slow and she wasn't. Inside his guard before his feet caught up with his plan — two short strokes under the rim — then she shoved the body back down the rubble to be somebody else's problem.

"Two down! Somebody over there's having a *terrible* afternoon!"

Then the horn. One flat note beyond the mouth.

And the sky started hissing.

Arrows — blind, arcing, a dozen — came whistling down through the murk, thudding into rubble and stone the length of the ravine. One punched into the talus a hand from her boot. Another kissed sparks off rock near where Cap stood. They weren't aiming. They were plowing the whole ravine on a timer.

Kira flattened small against the slide, ears working through the racket.

There. *Behind* them.

Hooves. Shod, several, trotting up the trail from the way they'd come in.

"Cap!" Gravel voice, barely carrying. "We're being boxed for true — detachment's rounding on the near mouth, and they're already firing the dust blind. That murk bought us minutes, not the day. When it settles, they stop wasting arrows and just walk in."

She rolled upright, blades low, coughing copper.

"So — now or never. Near end's the only door that isn't a meat grinder, and the lid's coming down on it. If we run, we run *through* them up the near trail, hard, before they dismount and set. Or we sit in this fishbowl and buy every foot with blood." A ragged breath. "For the record, I'm leaking from three places and my back's filing a grievance. Love this decision quick."

Behind them, the hoofbeats weren't slowing.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Through them it is!" *I adjust my grip, preparing for the charge.* "Vanguard, form up! We're breaking out the way we came!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Through them. Great. Running *at* things — that's cardio again, isn't it."

Kira took her spot on the left point, half a length ahead of the vanguard's edge, blades low and reversed in her fists.

"Rules!" she rasped back along the line. "Nobody stops in the middle. Standing still in a cavalry fight is volunteering to be a speed bump. Blades moving, feet moving — horses won't ride into steel that's *coming at them*, but they'll happily trample a man having second thoughts. We punch through and keep going. Bleeding gets sorted later."

The trail curved, and there they were — six, seven, strung across the narrow ground where it climbed away from the ravine, half-dismounted, spears still coming down. Not set. Seconds left in that.

"MOVE YOUR ASSES, WE'RE COMING THROUGH!"

The charge hit their seam.

First man had a spear and too much of it. She didn't argue with reach — slapped the point wide as it dropped, got inside it, put her left twin through the meat above his knee and *pulled* as she passed, dragging him off his horse and into his friend's way. Didn't stop. Didn't look.

Second rider came down the trail, sword high. She ducked under the swing — inside the horse's eye-line, where it couldn't see to kick — and put one short stroke through the girth strap. One. The saddle, and the man attached to it, departed leftward without her involvement.

Third tried to ride her down outright. She went flat against the trail, let the hooves go over her, came up and opened his hamstring on the way past. He stayed in the saddle exactly as long as it took to not.

Behind — hoofbeats from the far mouth, and the hiss of a fresh volley arcing over the settling dust. It came down into the melee blind, screaming off stone, hitting anything.

"THEIR OWN VOLLEY! It doesn't pick sides — *go, go, they'll stop loosing when they start skewering friends!*"

Then the trail tipped downhill and the ravine was behind them, and they were through.

Kira staggered down to a walk, coughing copper, back seizing properly now — and risked a look back.

The detachment was re-forming. Wheeling. And at the center of it, a man on a grey horse with a brass horn, waving it in circles, sorting riders into pursuit order like a shepherd with terrible intentions.

"Cap!" Hoarse. Nearly gone. "Their drover — grey horse, horn. Kill him and this parade turns into fifty lost sheep. He's got two bodyguards and thirty feet of open ground, so it'll cost. I can pay it — but I'm three leaks and a bad back past my best day."

She wiped her blades on her thigh, one, then the other.

"So. Buy the shepherd, or spend the legs and outrun the flock? Legs are cheaper. Shepherd's permanent. Call it."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Shepherd it is, Kira. I'll take point." *I adjust my grip on my polearm, my eyes fixed on the man on the grey horse. This would be a bloody one.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Point's yours. I'll pay for the door."

Kira ran the geometry one last time while her legs filed their complaint. Grey horse, center of the wheel. Horn man standing in his stirrups, waving riders into order like the world's worst dance instructor. Lance-guard on his right stirrup, couched, forward in the saddle — the dangerous kind of bored. Shield-guard on his left, big, patient, riding loose.

"Right one's mine. Left one's yours to trip for two heartbeats — I'll finish him if you're slow." She rolled her neck until it cracked. "Thirty feet. I go when your line goes."

The vanguard's war-cry went up and Kira went with it — out of the settling dust, into the open, thirty feet of ground her legs swore they'd already spent. World narrowed to stirrup height and closing.

The lancer saw her late. Wheeled, dropped his point. She didn't argue with reach — never had — slapped the shaft wide as it came on, got inside the horse's eye-line, and put her right twin through the wrist holding the couche. Lance and hand both quit the argument. He folded off the far side and she was already past him.

The shield-guard turned fast. Good man. The shield's edge caught her across the ribs on the backswing — a hit she took instead of dodging, because dodging cost the window — and it spun her down to one knee, white noise across her vision, breath gone somewhere expensive.

"*Four,*" she snarled at nobody. "Four leaks. The invoice is going to be *historic.*"

She came up inside his next swing — everything slow, everything predictable, big men always were — hooked his elbow with one blade, opened the underside of his arm with the other, and shoved him off his horse's blind side. He'd live. He wouldn't lift anything heavy for a season. She didn't stay to admire the work.

The grey horse was turning. The shepherd's eyes went from her to the charging line to the space where both his guards used to be — and did the math faster than she liked. Then his hand dropped to the horn at his belt.

No. *No.* If that note went up, thirty riders wheeled as one and this whole suicide became a footnote.

She had one throw left in her and it was one of her twins, and she'd already donated her left once today — but a horn was worse than a knife gone, so her arm was already cocking—

Then she saw the better option. The thirty feet of open ground, and the one man in the world with the reach to cross it faster than a note could travel it.

She threw anyway — not at the man, at the *horn*, close enough to smack the metal and sting his hand wide of it — and screamed through a throat that had nothing left:

"WINDOW, CAP! *GO!* He's fumbling and I'm out of gifts!"

Behind her, shouts. The column noticing. First wheelers coming around.

The shepherd reached for the horn again.

Kira put her head down and ran anyway, because backup plans were just prayers with footwork.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I see the opening, a brief moment of hesitation from the shepherd.* "For the Company!" *I roar, launching myself forward, polearm leading the charge. This was it.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The world ended for one man on a grey horse, and Kira heard it rather than saw it — a grunt, a scream that wasn't human, something heavy coming off a saddle and hitting the dirt the way heavy things do. The horn itself skipped loose across the stones, spun twice, and lay still against a rock.

Unblown. Still full of its one flat note.

The flock felt it instantly. The wheel fell apart mid-turn — riders checking, shouting over each other, one spurring forward, two hauling back, horses bumping haunch to haunch in the settling grey. Thirty men who'd been one animal a minute ago were suddenly thirty opinions with no shepherd to herd them.

She allowed it half a heartbeat of satisfaction.

Which was when a wheeler found her — sword up, cutting across her lane — and she had one blade, no legs, and no clever left. Just the math she'd been running all day. The horse saw the slide first. Rubble, bodies, the whole reek of a bad afternoon. Horses were smart about places things die — she'd *said* so — and the animal balked hard, chest-height, warring with its own reins. She took the rider off on the way past. Short. Ugly. Didn't stop.

Didn't stop at the grey horse either, except to snatch her right twin out of the dirt where it had fallen. The man beside it was face-down and not asking questions anymore, and she gave him the courtesy of not looking closely.

"NO SHEPHERD, NO FLOCK!" she rasped, tearing past the vanguard's edge, voice down to gravel and blood. "They'll chase in *trickles* now — nobody's worked together a day in their lives!"

Out the far side, the open ground. Behind them: hoofbeats in ones and twos, ragged, each rider his own general. Exactly like she said.

She risked her one backward glance. Riders streaming from the ravine mouth — then *bunching*, gait shortening. Blown. They'd double-timed it into the killbox and now their horses were paying for it.

"Cap — listen! They can't sustain it!" Every word cost her. She paid anyway. "Blown horses, no order, no horn. Quarter mile of hard ground and the chase dies on its feet — but it has to be *hard*. Scree, water, anything that unlevels the odds. Point me at a horizon, Cap. Any horizon."

She spat copper, wiped her blades on her thigh without breaking stride.

"Fair warning — I've got maybe a quarter mile of fast left in these legs, and then it's all slow and bitter. Also my invoice is now four leaks, one bruised everything, and *twice* today my steel's gone travelling." A ragged breath. "Somebody's buying the whole damn tavern or I'm Unionizing."

She didn't look back again. Looking back was for people with legs to spare.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I glance back at Kira, a grim appreciation on my face.* "Understood, Kira. Ahead, towards the river! We can lose them in the rapids!" *I push the vanguard forward, polearm still at the ready.* "Unionizing sounds fair."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The quarter mile spent her down to the studs.

Kira ran on hatred and momentum, boots hammering scrub, ribs filing addenda to the invoice with every stride. Behind her the chase was audibly dying — hooves shortening, a man swearing at his horse, another hauling up entirely. She didn't look back. Looking back was for people with legs left.

Two sets of hooves stayed in it. Fresh. Angry. The kind that had a name to avenge.

The river announced itself as spray and thunder before it showed — the bank dropping away to black boulders, white water braiding between them. Fast. Deep-looking. Loud enough to eat a shout whole.

She skidded down the shingle at the tail of the vanguard and gave the water three seconds of professional respect.

"Read! They won't ride this — no horse alive swims rapids on purpose. They'll need a ford, that's a mile-plus downstream, so we're buying hours." Already tearing a strip off her cloak with her teeth, hands shaking too hard for buckles. "But the water's honest about two things. It's cold enough to stop a heart, and it *wants my steel.*"

She lashed both twins to her wrists, hilts up, tight enough to bite.

"Nobody separates me from my girls twice in one day."

The two riders broke the scrub behind them as the first of the vanguard waded in. One pulled up hard at the rim — sensible man, sensible horse — and wheeled along the bank hunting an angle.

The other wasn't sensible. He came down the shingle at a gallop, straight into the shallows after them, sword high. For two strides it nearly worked.

The river took his horse's footing on the third. Animal went sideways, screaming, and the rider went with it — sword gone, armor dragging, a thrashing blur sucked downstream into the white. A boulder or two later, he wasn't doing anything at all.

"Water doesn't pick sides either," Kira rasped. "Everything I like about geology, I like about hydrology."

The smart one on the bank watched his friend teach the lesson, then wheeled and galloped off upstream. Toward the ford, no doubt. Carrying the news.

*Clock started.*

She went in after the last of the vanguard. The cold hit like a slap — knocked her breath sideways, turned every cut on her body into a single screaming compound instrument. Mid-river the current shoved her feet out from under her and for one ugly heartbeat it had her, spinning, blade-hilts jammed hard against her palms because the lashings held, and then her boot found a submerged rock and she clawed back upright and *kept going*, because stopping was just drowning with patience.

For once, somebody else was doing the cardio.

She came out the far side shaking, blue-lipped, water running off her in pink sheets, and stood there while her legs remembered their job.

"Cap." Gravel, barely. "Status. Chase is dead on this side. But the smart one's alive and he knows the ford — that means their whole flock converges on one crossing, maybe an hour back. Maybe less." She wrung out her cloak one-handed, teeth chattering through the next part. "So my professional recommendation is we don't stop until dark. Dark hides, cold trails, and they've got blown horses to argue with."

She started walking. Talking cost extra, but she paid.

"Also — collective bargaining agreement, article one: the *entire* tavern. Article two: a fire, a needle, and a healer who doesn't giggle. Article three's a bath, and I'll die before I drop it."

A shiver, halfway to a laugh.

"Your march, Cap. I'll keep up. Complaining the entire way. But keeping up."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I look back at Kira, a wry smile touching my lips despite the grim situation.* "Agreed on all counts, Kira. Especially the bath. Let's push for the old hunting lodge, it's a day's march but we can get a fire going there." *I turn and gesture the vanguard onward, my polearm acting as a walking staff now.* "And I think we can stretch the company's budget for that entire tavern."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Draw their fire," Kira muttered. "Of course. Six bows up top, and my job's to stand in front of them. Fucking wonderful." She spat into the dust and moved.

No point in quiet now. She broke from the boulder at a dead sprint, boots kicking gravel, and made herself big — arms wide for one stupid heartbeat before tucking low. The volley came down hard. Two arrows sparked off stone behind her. A third split the air close enough to feel it drag past her ear.

She hit the next rock shoulder-first and rolled behind it, lungs working. Listened.

Six bows loosing together. Reloading together. That wasn't bandit work — bandits shot when they had a shot. That was drill. Somebody was paying for this ambush, and paying well.

"Cap!" she shouted, loud enough to bounce off both ravine walls. Loud was the point. "They're volleying — disciplined! Four, five seconds between shots! If you're pushing, push the gap!"

Behind her, steel and boots were moving west. Good. She counted the next volley down by sound — the creak of strings, the scrape of boots shifting on the ridge — then broke cover again.

Rock to rock. Never more than three breaths in the open. On the fourth sprint an arrow punched into the dirt a hand's width from her boot — someone up there had gotten impatient, snapping a shot instead of waiting for the volley. Good. Impatient archers aiming at her meant fewer arrows falling on the push.

She risked a glance up. Five shapes on the ridgeline.

The sixth was gone.

There — movement on the scree below the east wall. A man descending fast, blade out, cutting for the ground between her and the western advance.

"Cap, one's off the ridge on your side — coming down the scree, sword out!" She reversed her grip on her right dagger and cut the angle, planting herself in his path. "I've got this one. Don't get shot."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood, Kira. Hold the line!" I bellow, pushing forward with my polearm. *These disciplined bastards...* I spot the gap Kira mentioned and surge through it, my vanguard close behind.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
He hit the flat ground at the bottom of the scree and the loose rock betrayed him one last time — a stagger, boots skating — and Kira spent those two heartbeats reading him.

Brigandine, not patched leather. Proper boots. A dark green tabard under the plate, some white device stitched on the chest. Paid men. Somebody with real coin wanted them dead in this exact ravine.

Then he was set and swinging, a big overhand cut meant to end it in one. She gave ground instead of a parry — her daggers didn't argue with swords, they murdered them up close — and let the blade pass through the space her skull had just left. The wind of it stirred grit off her cheek. He recovered slow. Heavy blade, and he trusted it.

He was better than his recovery suggested. His second cut was a feint — low, then a rising diagonal that snatched a line of fire across her left forearm before she found the angle. "Fuck—" She hissed it through her teeth and kept giving ground, two steps, three. Let him believe she was breaking.

He stepped in to finish it. That was the mistake.

She caught the cut on her left dagger, angled to slip it wide rather than stop it, and was inside his arm before the blade finished its arc. This close his sword was just a bar of steel and she was already working — right dagger across the inside of his wrist, and his hand opened. Left into his thigh, deep, on the pull. He folded with a sound like a dropped grain sack, and she ended it through the throat, stepping back so the spray went the other way.

He settled into the dust and stopped being a problem.

Forearm was bleeding, shallow — it'd keep. She listened. The volleys had stopped. Of course they had; nobody loosed into their own man's melee. But the ridge wasn't quiet. Boots scraped up there. Gravel trickled. They were moving — and not toward her.

"Cap!" She turned toward the push — steel ringing on steel somewhere past the boulder field, shouts she couldn't parse. "Arrows stopped! They're repositioning along the ridge — sounds like west! They'll try to catch your flank from the high ground! Watch your right!"

No answer she could hear over the fighting. Fine. He'd caught it or he hadn't.

*Hold the line.* She looked at the scree, at the shapes shifting along the ridgeline — five of them, maybe four, hard to count through the dust — and did the arithmetic. The line she'd been given was the ground between this dead man and the western advance, and the only way to hold it was to make those archers worry about something other than the Captain's flank.

She started up the scree, daggers low, picking her footing between the loose stone.

"Drawing fire," she muttered. "Again. Godsdamn job."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The scree fought her for every foot — two steps up, one sliding back. She was maybe halfway when she clocked it: one shape on the ridgeline that had stopped moving west. Planted. Bow canted down toward the push.

Drawing on the Captain.

No time to climb. No time to shout anything that'd matter. Kira quit worrying about footing, set her boots, and threw her left dagger the way she'd thrown ten thousand of them at wine-soaked boards in training yards — uphill, into the light, thirty yards of ugly angle.

It took him high in the back, under the shoulder blade. The string ripped loose from his fingers and the arrow went nowhere, snapping off stone somewhere down the western slope. He folded sideways off his aim, one hand clawing behind him for the hilt, screaming a warning down the ridgeline.

She was already climbing, scree avalanching under her boots, half-running the last stretch. He got a short blade out by the time she reached him. His swing was all panic — she slipped inside it, hooked his collar with her free hand, and dragged him down onto her right dagger, up under the ribs. Held it there while he stopped.

"Goddamn job," she breathed, and let him fold.

She wrenched the thrown dagger free and wiped both blades on his tabard. Dark green, and the white device on the chest was clean enough to read now — some herald's crosswork, nothing she knew. *Somebody* knew it. Somebody with coin, who'd paid for disciplined volleys and proper boots and an ambush in this exact cut of rock. That thought was going to matter later, if there was a later.

Boots hammered the ridgeline to the west. A shout answered the dead man's. She risked a look — three shapes, maybe four, fifty yards and closing on the ground above the push. One of them had already turned back toward her. Bow coming around.

"Cap!" she roared downhill, not caring who else heard. "One down on the east ridge! Three or four still moving for your right flank — but they know I'm behind them now! They split to deal with me, your flank clears — they don't, I'll be on their backs inside a minute!"

Whatever he did with that was his call. She was already moving, daggers low, eating ground along the ridgeline, the cut on her forearm turning her left grip slick — she swapped the dagger to her right hand and back, shaking blood off her fingers.

The one who'd turned was younger than the rest and faster. He gave up on the bow at twenty yards — no shot at a moving target closing this quick — and dropped it, drawing a long knife and a hand axe instead, setting his feet square across the ridge like he'd been taught.

*Drilled. All of them drilled.*

"Come on, then," Kira said, and gave him something to worry about.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I hear Kira's shout about the archers splitting up. Good. That buys us time. "Fan out! Don't let them flank us!" I bellow, pushing my polearm into the gut of a mercenary who got too close. This fight isn't over yet.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
He came on like the drill yard had built him — measured steps, axe high, knife low, nothing wasted. Young, but nobody had paid to teach him bad habits.

Kira gave ground. The ridge ran maybe four paces wide here, scree-shouldered, and footing was a weapon if you knew it was one. He didn't. Yet.

The axe came down and she slipped it — and the knife was already riding behind it, chasing the axe's recovery line. A taught pairing. She caught it on her right dagger barely, steel ringing, impact buzzing up her wrist. *Fast. Faster than the one on the scree.* Drilled and young and quick. Wonderful.

Then he did the smart thing, the thing that turned her stomach: his eyes dropped to her left arm. To the blood slicking her grip.

The axe hooked — beard of it catching her guard — and he wrenched. The wet grip betrayed her and the left dagger tore free, skipping end over end across the stone. "Fuck—" She gave ground, one blade left, and he grinned like the fight was already over.

"Come get it," she said, and kept backing. Left and toward the lip, where broken ground went to outright treacherous. He followed. Planted his feet square — exactly like they'd taught him on some flat yard somewhere — and lunged for the finish.

The scree avalanched under his planted boot.

Half a heartbeat was all she needed. She stepped inside the lunge, drove her dagger up under his jaw, and let his own momentum carry him past her off the lip. He was dead before the fall could argue about it. Green tabard, white crosswork — same livery, third man running. A whole company of somebody's coin, and that thought could wait.

She scooped the lost dagger, swiped both on her thigh, and looked west.

Two shapes left on the ridge above the push. One had turned — sword out, cutting back toward her, close enough now to hear him breathing. The other had planted his feet and drawn his bow to the ear, aimed down at the vanguard spreading out below.

"Cap! Archer high on your right — he's drawn, loosing any fucking second!" She broke into a dead sprint along the ridgeline, boots hammering loose stone, daggers low. The swordsman squared up in her path. Fine. He was between her and the bowman, and the bowman was the one killing her Captain's people.

She intended to go through him.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The veteran didn't chase. That was the problem.

She gave ground and he just came on — measured steps, point low, holding the ridge at exactly his blade's length. Grey in his stubble. Scarred knuckles. He'd watched young men die on daggers before, and he wasn't going to be one. Her feints did nothing. He read them and waited, letting her bleed grip into her boots one exchange at a time.

Then, over his shoulder, she saw it.

There he was. Across the cut, high on the west slope — polearm out, unmistakable. Alone. *Fuck.* The vanguard had been shoved back down into the boulder field, pinned under fresh shooting from the west ridge. And coming off that same ridge toward the Captain, easy and unhurried, like they'd been told exactly where he'd end up — three men in dark green.

Her chest went tight enough to hurt. She put the fear somewhere it could be spent.

"Cap! Three off your ridge, coming down—" The veteran's point caught her mid-shout and she gave ground she didn't have, steel opening a hot line along her ribs. Shallow. Fine. She was done being patient.

She threw the left dagger at his eyes.

Wine-soaked boards. Ten thousand of them. He threw his guard up — had to — steel ringing a hand's width from his face, and in the half-second his line broke she was already through it. Right dagger up under the sternum. Shove, twist. His counter dragged along her hip on the way down, an afterthought. She rode him to the stone and let him stop being a problem, then wrenched her blade free and scooped the thrown one off the scree.

The last archer stood at the ridge's end, drawn to the ear. Not on the vanguard. On the lone man across the cut.

She ran. "CAP— BOW—" Her roar beat her there by half a second, and the string ripped loose early, rushed and wild, the shaft sparking off rock a long stride wide of its mark. Then she was inside his arms before the bow could come down. A bow is a club at that range, and she had two knives. Green tabard, white crosswork — fifth of that livery she'd put down today. A whole contract company in this cut of rock. That thought could keep.

The east ridge was hers. Five of them dead between here and the scree slope — and if there'd ever been a sixth, he'd decided the pay wasn't worth it.

She picked up the dead man's bow.

Not her weapon. She knew enough to loose at a doorway, not enough to brag about it. But the quiver was full, and across the cut the green-tabs were eating ground toward her Captain.

Kira moved to the lip, nocked, drew — the grip finding every cut on her forearm and introducing itself — and loosed on instinct and a prayer. The shaft took the lead man through the back of the thigh and put him down screaming. Her second went wide on purpose, and the next man hugged his rock like it owed him money. One left, moving cover to cover, still closing.

"Cap!" She nocked again, scanning the slope. "East ridge is clear! One hunter down, one pinned, one still coming at you — vanguard's stuck under the west ridge, and I can't cross before he reaches you! I can keep heads down from here, or I try the crossing anyway! Your call — and don't get shot!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Kira! Cross the ravine! I can handle this last one!" I yell, spinning my polearm. I've faced worse odds. I need her here.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Handle him. Sure." Kira muttered it at the ridge, at the dust, at the general state of her life. "Famous last words, Cap."

Then she moved. She slung the dead archer's quiver across her back, kept the bow in her left fist, and took the east scree down in a controlled avalanche — boots surfing the same loose stone she'd just bled climbing up, daggers sheathed so her hands could work. The ravine floor opened below her: fifty yards of boulder field that had been a shooting gallery since the first arrow. Five of the shooters were her kills now. The rest held the west ridge, and she was about to cross under every one of them.

She hit the flat and sprinted.

The first shaft sparked off a boulder a stride to her right — the pinned one had found his nerve. The second dragged the air past her ear. *Asshole.* She bent lower and gave him targets made of rock instead of meat, cover to cover, the cut on her ribs tearing wider with every stride. Above her, up the slope, steel rang on steel somewhere she couldn't see — the Captain and his last one. She didn't watch. He'd said he had it. She'd left men in ditches who'd said that.

At the base of the west slope, the thigh-shot man was still dragging himself toward a fallen sword. She put her boot on the blade and skated it down the scree, out of the argument, and kept climbing while he screamed at her back. His own wound would finish him slower than she would, and she was in a hurry.

The pinned archer had quit shooting. She came around his rock low and fast, both daggers out, and found him waiting anyway — knife up, feet square, drilled to the last. He lunged. She slipped it down her left blade and opened his forearm on the pull, and his knife rang away off the stone.

The horn went off the west ridge while his blood was still in the air.

Two notes, low, carrying. Every bow on that ridge went silent at once — and the shapes up top started pulling back over the crest, unhurried, like tradesmen knocking off at dusk. The pressure on the vanguard quit with them. Below, the boulder field filled with regathering noise, someone down there bellowing assembly.

Her man looked at the ridge. At his arm. At her knives. He did the arithmetic and went to his knees.

"Yield. Yield—"

"Smart." She kicked his knife down the slope and put a point under his jaw until his hands locked behind his head. "Move and you're the sixth of that pretty tabard today." She trussed his wrists with his own belt, then cut a strip off his hem and wrapped her forearm with it. "Seemed fair," she told him. He didn't argue.

The last of the Captain's fight ended while she climbed — steel, then something heavier, then nothing. She hadn't looked up. Looking up on scree is how you die on scree. She marched the prisoner over the last shelf and found it finished: the last dark tabard flat in the dirt, white crosswork staring up at the sky, the Captain still on his feet.

"Cap." She was winded and bleeding from three places she could count without looking, and none of them were the problem yet. "East ridge clear — five down by my hand. This slope's clear. One prisoner, one bleeder down there his own people left him, and the west ridge just sounded recall. That's not a rout, Cap. They came off in good order. Somebody's cutting losses — and whoever holds the purse still holds it."

She toed the dead man's tabard flat.

"Proper boots. Drilled volleys. A whole company sitting in this exact cut of rock, waiting for us to walk into it." She looked up at the empty ridgeline. "Somebody told them where we'd be. That's the part I don't like."

Below, the vanguard was climbing out of the boulder field, wounded and whole mixed together, someone already counting their dead.

"Prisoner's yours — question him, keep him for the column to drag, or put him in the ground. Your call. If you're thinking chase, I'll say it once: I don't love running drilled men over a ridge they picked. Also your call." She rolled her shoulders and felt every cut report in. "So. What are we doing?"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I examine the dead merc, then turn to the prisoner, a grim expression on my face.* "They knew we were coming. No doubt about it. We'll question this one. See what he knows." I glance at the west ridge. "No chase today. We'll tend to our wounded and move out. Something isn't right."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"No chase." Kira said it like a verdict. "Smart. Smartest order anyone's given all day."

She hauled the prisoner up by his collar and marched him the last few yards, dropping him to his knees beside the dead man in the green tabard. Let him get a good long look at the white crosswork staring up at the sky. Let him do that arithmetic on his own time.

"Before you start asking — know what he's worth." She crouched and cut his purse off his belt, weighed it in her palm. "He's a ranker. Rankers know their sergeant, their pay, and where they slept last week. Contracts run client to broker to captain, and the only man who ever hears a name is the broker. So don't burn time on who. Ask where they mustered, when they were paid, and what they were told about us. That's where the rot is."

She spilled the purse into her hand. Good silver, every coin off the same die, edges still sharp. "Paid inside the week. Contract's fresh." She looked up. "Meaning whoever sold your route did it recent."

The prisoner's eyes hadn't left the dead man. "Waymeet," he said, when she put a point against his jaw to hurry the conversation along. "Mustered at Waymeet, ten days back. Half pay up front, the balance on completion. We're the White Cross — and you don't quit the Cross with the second half outstanding. So I'm talking, aye? I'm talking."

"What were you told about us."

"Route. Day. Hour. That you'd take the ravine by midday." His voice thinned. "And the contract didn't name the column. It named the man. The one who carries the polearm, leads from the front. The rest of you were — cheaper by the head. By-catch."

Kira sat back on her heels. "That's why three of them peeled off that ridge straight for you and nobody else, Cap. You weren't in the way. You were the job."

"And the horn," she said to the prisoner. "What's the horn?"

"Standing orders. Hold the ridges till the horn, then pull off clean. No pursuit past the crest. Even mid-kill." He swallowed. "Even mid-kill."

"So somebody sat on a hilltop and watched the whole thing," Kira said, mostly to the Captain. "Decided the price had gone up and cut losses. That somebody still holds the purse — and he knows the product's still walking." She stood, rolling the shoulder that had stopped being hers an hour ago, and gave the Captain the rest.

"Your bleeder down-slope is still leaking. Strap that thigh inside the hour or he's a corpse — second prisoner or a grave, your call. Their kit's worth a month's pay, boots alone, and dead men don't invoice; I'll have the vanguard strip them if you want it done. And somebody needs to stitch my arm before we march, because I'm down to a grip and a half."

She toed the dead man's tabard flat one more time.

"Here's the part I actually don't like. Route, hour, your face. That's not scouts, Cap — that's someone who eats at your table or marches in your column." She wiped both daggers and sheathed them. "So. Where are we moving — and are we moving like hunted people, or like people who haven't figured it out yet? Because we're the first ones." A breath. "And don't get shot."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I stare at the prisoner, then at Kira, a cold fury rising within me. My grip tightens on my polearm.* "Someone in our ranks. A traitor." *I nod to the vanguard, already gathering below.* "Strip the dead. Tend to the wounded. We march immediately. Double time. We're not hunted, Kira. We're hunting."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Hunting," Kira said, flat, like she was checking the word for cracks. "Aye. One trouble with that, Cap — hunting needs a scent, and the only one we've got is down there forming ranks in our colors."

She hauled the prisoner up by the collar and shoved him downhill toward the vanguard. "Walk. Fall behind and I save somebody the rope." To the first pair of soldiers reaching the slope: "Cap's orders — strip the green tabs. Boots and quivers first. Every purse goes in one bag, sealed, for his eyes only." Not because she figured the vanguard for thieves. Because one of them might be worse.

Then she sat on a stone, found the stitcher, and had the forearm done — six ugly loops, no wine. Somewhere below, someone was still counting their dead, and the number was already ugly. "Quick and crooked," she told the stitcher through her teeth. "Matches the rest of me."

She stood, rolled the shoulder, and gave the Captain the rest, low enough the ranks wouldn't carry it.

"Here's how you hunt a man in your own column. You don't — not out loud. You go roaring 'traitor' down the line, and he either buries himself so deep you'll never dig him out, or he slips camp tonight and sells everything he knows to whoever holds the purse. So far as the column hears, nothing's changed. We're angry. We're marching double time because we're angry. That's the whole story."

"But tonight, when we camp — you feed him. Three sergeants, three routes, each told quiet and separate it's the real road and to keep it shut. North track, river crossing, whatever else you like. Then you wait. Whatever the next ambush smells like, that's the mouth the coin came out of. You don't catch a leak by staring at the bucket, Cap. You pour water in and watch where it runs out."

"And if you want a scent that walks — Waymeet. They mustered there ten days back, half pay up front. Coin changed hands in that town inside the fortnight, and coin leaves marks. Somebody remembers a face, a name, a purse too heavy for its owner. That's where hunting starts. This road's just where we walk."

She glanced at the empty ridgeline, then the sky. "One more thing. Double time throws a dust column every watcher on any hill can read for two miles. Whoever blew that horn might still have eyes on us, and right now we're telling him where we're going and how spooked we are. Could be a lie worth telling for free — angry men charging straight down the road, too furious to think. Or we swallow the pace and take broken ground. Your call which story he gets."

"Prisoner walks tied between two men — he's seen the White Cross captain and whoever held the pay at muster, and that's worth the drag. The bleeder won't keep at this pace; shield-drag or a grave, pick before we step, because I'm not hauling either one." She flexed the stitched arm, testing the grip. It would do.

"Meantime, I'll be walking the line watching for the man who's too calm. Whoever sold the route knew the ravine was hot — he had time to pick his rock before the first arrow flew." She settled the dead archer's bow across her back with the quiver. A knife-fighter with a bow was a liar at thirty yards, but a liar with options.

"So — where do you want me? Point, rear, or the shadows?" A breath, almost a grin. "And Cap — try not to get shot. Apparently you're worth more than the rest of us."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Point," I say, without hesitation. "Your eyes are better than anyone's. And keep an eye on the prisoner. He's our only lead." I turn to the waiting vanguard, my voice ringing with authority. "Move out! Double time! We have a traitor to find!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The secret lasted exactly as long as it took the Captain to empty his lungs.

*We have a traitor to find.* Kira watched the words travel down the forming ranks like a dropped torch — face to face, each man checking whether his neighbor had heard it, then checking whether his neighbor was checking *him*.

She swung in close to the Captain as the column started to move, voice pitched under the noise. "That was the one thing I asked you to keep behind your teeth, Cap." She let it sit for one stride. "Done's done. Salvage: a flushed bird still flies where you can see it. A man who knows he's hunted runs tonight, turns loyal enough to make your teeth ache, or does something stupid and fast. First one names himself if you've got quiet eyes on the picket line — get two men who know how to watch without being seen watching. I'll find the other two walking your line."

She tipped her chin at the vanguard. "And look at them. They're not watching the road, they're watching each other's hands. That's a slower wound than anything the Cross bought today. Work them till they're too tired to think, or somebody settles an old grudge tonight and half the column calls it justice."

Then she moved up the line to take point. The bleeder was already strapped to a shield-pole, cursing at two men who ignored him professionally. The prisoner walked tied between a pair of spearmen; she stopped long enough to look him in the eye. "You heard the man. You're the only lead we've got, which makes you the second-most expensive thing in this column. Try not to die of anything stupid." To the spearmen: "He talks to anyone but me or the Cap, I want to know who."

Then she ran.

Point at double time meant holding sixty yards ahead of the first rank and hating every stride. The ravine spat the road out onto a long downslope of open scrub, sun hammering the scree. Her body kept an honest ledger — stitches pulling at every arm-swing, the rib-cut burning with sweat in it, the hip only reporting on uphill. The dead archer's bow slapped her back every second step. A knife-fighter carrying a bow: a liar at thirty yards and a joke past it.

She looked back once. The column's dust stood up against the sky like a banner. Every eye on every hilltop for two miles could read their pace, their numbers, their fury. She'd said as much. She'd been overruled. Filed, kept running.

The road ran clean for two miles and she read it the whole way — shoulders, high ground, dead ground, every place she'd sit if she still held the purse. At the far end of the open stretch the land pinched again: the road bent down into a dark belt of pine where the hills came close enough to whisper. She'd have bet the dead man's purse there was a second contract in those trees, or would be by tomorrow.

And there was the watcher. A smudge of dust on the far ridge track, north side, a mile off. Moving when the column moved. Stopping when it stopped. Not hunting. Counting.

She held the pace a quarter mile, memorizing the shape of the hills around that smudge, then dropped back and fell in at the head of the column.

"Point report, Cap." Winded, flat, economical. "Two miles open behind us, then the road drops into a pine cut — close walls, dead ground, exactly where I'd sit if I still held the purse. I want to clear it with my own eyes before the column's committed, or we camp short and take it at first light with rested legs. Your call, but decide before the trees decide for you.

"Second — we've got a shadow. One rider, far ridge, keeping our pace. He's not hunting us, he's counting us. Somebody wants to know where you sleep tonight. Now they will.

"Third — the line's rotten with staring. Work them hard tonight or somebody gets a knife between friends over a card hand."

She rolled the stitched arm, testing the grip, and gave him the last of it.

"And here's what's been chewing on me since the prisoner opened his mouth. They didn't hire six archers for you, Cap. They bought a company — drilled volleys, proper boots, recall on a horn. That's not head-hunter coin. That's war coin. Nobody pays company rates for one man unless the man's worth more than a head." She glanced uphill at the dust smudge, still keeping pace. "So chew on this while we march: who hates you enough to buy a whole war for your name? Because somebody out there already decided you're worth it — and I'd rather hear the name from your mouth than find it stitched on the next green tabard."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
I listen to Kira, my face grim. "War coin, you say?" I look at the distant smudge. "Send two of our fastest scouts to shadow that rider. See where he goes, who he meets. And yes, we'll take the pine cut at first light. We'll make camp just before it."

I look at the column, then back at Kira. "As for who hates me... there's a long list, Kira. A very long list."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"A long list," Kira said, and gave the words the weight of a coin she suspected was shaved. "Good news, Cap — a long list means steady work. Bad news: hate's the cheapest currency on any road. Every man you've ever beaten carries it, and beggars carry the most. Nobody bought the Cross with hate. Muster pay, half up front, proper boots, recall on a horn — that's a treasury, not a grudge. So take your long list and cross off every name that can't sign for a company's muster. I'd wager you're down to a handful. *That's* the list I want. And I want it away from the fires — names travel down a column faster than orders. Tell me tonight, or sleep on it and hand me three names at dawn."

Then she dropped back down the line at a jog, bow slapping her back, cuts keeping their honest ledger with every stride, and found her two — Harl, a dispatch-runner with ten years of road in his legs, and Tench, hill-born and quiet, the kind who noticed things for a living.

"Far ridge, north side, that dust smudge keeping our pace. One rider, counting us. You two are going to count him back. Low ground only — never crest a skyline he can see. Half a mile back, more if the ground gives it to you. I don't need him followed to his grave. I need to know where he lays his head tonight and who comes to share his fire. If he makes you — and a man paid to watch will — break off clean and bring me his heading. That alone's worth the shoe leather. You report to the Cap or to me. Not your sergeant, not your mates, not over supper. Nobody. Go."

They peeled off the column's rear and cut downslope through the scrub, and were gone.

She fell back in at the head of the column, breathing easy, voice low. "And there's the shape of the problem, Cap. I just sent two men I can't vouch for to shadow a man I can't read, out of a column with a hole in it. There's no clean fucking test for it either — the leak fought like everyone else today, because that's the whole trick of being a leak. If one of them's dirty, the rider learns we're hunting the hunter. If they're clean, we learn where the purse sleeps. Either way beats marching blind."

"We'll camp short of the trees like you said, and I'll walk the ground before the first tent goes up — backs to a rise, water inside the picket if there is any, no dead ground within a long bowshot, fires dug in and small. I'll work the column till they're too tired to stare at each other's hands. Tired men sleep. They don't settle grudges over card hands."

"Here's the ugly arithmetic for tonight, though. The leak heard 'traitor' same as everyone. Running's a bad trade for him — leaves a trail, forfeits his balance of pay. His cheapest move is one quiet knife, and the target isn't you. It's the *prisoner*. Dead men don't describe the Waymeet muster or the broker's face." She rolled the stitched arm, testing the grip. "So the prisoner's bait whether we planned it or not. He sleeps inside my reach — close enough I hear him roll over — and anyone who walks near my fire tonight explains their business to me at knife-length. If our bird does something fast, that's where he does it."

She glanced once at the far ridge, at the smudge still keeping pace, then back.

"So. When we camp, walk the picket with me, out past the fires, and give me the names of men rich enough to buy the Cross and mean enough to want you under it. Whoever holds that purse already knows your route, your hour, and your face, Cap. Time we returned the favor — I'd like to know *his* before the next green tabard gets close enough to read."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Agreed," I say, a grim set to my jaw. "The prisoner is bait, and your fire is his cage tonight. As for the names... I'll tell you tonight, Kira. Every last one of them." I quicken my pace, the polearm feeling heavy in my hand. "Let's make sure our shadows don't get too comfortable."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Shadows don't get uncomfortable, Cap — that's the whole trade." Kira dropped back toward the head of the column. "Worry about the ones we haven't seen yet."

The march burned the afternoon down. She ran point and fell back and ran point again, reading the road the whole way — and the smudge on the far ridge read them right back. Moving when they moved. Halted when the column balked at a washed-out culvert. When they finally came off the road a half mile short of the pines, on the rise she'd marked, the smudge stopped with them, patient as a creditor. Paid by the day, not the mile.

She walked the ground twice before she let a tent stake bite. Granite at their backs, a spring seeping into a rock fold inside the picket, no dead ground inside three hundred yards on any bearing. Fires went into pits small enough to cup in both hands. Then she worked the column — ditch, picket, wood detail, again — until the staring died the only way staring ever dies: of exhaustion. By dusk the men were too busy hating her to wonder about each other's hands. Old trick. Reliable one.

The bleeder made camp alive. The stitcher gave him until morning and wouldn't swear to that.

The prisoner sat tied within her reach, bow across her knees, and somewhere in the third hour of watching fires he spoke without being asked. "The paymaster at Waymeet. Kept his hood up. Never spoke to us — only the captain. But he counted the coin out himself, piece by piece. Soldier's hands." A pause. "Ring on the left thumb. Silver, worn shiny."

"Noticed a lot for a ranker who wasn't supposed to."

"Rankers notice everything. That's why rankers live." He shut up after that.

She filed the ring away. Soldier's hands, silver thumb-ring. Men who paid companies out of hoods kept paying until the job was done.

Here was the joke of the evening: nobody else came within ten feet of her fire. In a column that had heard *traitor* shouted down its own length, the prisoner was the one man nobody could afford to be seen looking at. One boy tried — cook's helper with the ration — and she had steel out before his third step. He nearly gave the bowl to the dirt. Sergeant's orders, prisoner needs feeding, *gods, lady.* Fine. She took the bowl herself and noted his face anyway. Habit.

So the Captain's roar had garrisoned the bait. Nobody was knifing the prisoner tonight — and nobody was springing the trap either. Alive and useless in one breath. She'd call it even and adjust.

Then dusk proper, and up on the far ridge, in the exact place she'd last marked the smudge, a fire kindled. Small. Deliberate. In the open, where the whole camp could see it.

She stood at the picket line and looked at it a long moment. "Well, shit." Either the rider wanted to be seen — *still counting, sleep well* — or that fire wasn't for them at all. A signal for eyes she hadn't met yet. Both readings stank.

No sign of Harl or Tench by full dark. Tench was hill-born and wouldn't cross a skyline at dusk with his mother's life staked on it, so *careful* was the cheap read. She kept the expensive one in her boot.

When the camp had settled into snoring and small fires, she found the Captain out past the light, where names couldn't travel, and fell in on the picket walk.

"Report first, then you pay what you owe me." Her voice stayed at knife-length. "One — your speech garrisoned my bait. Nobody goes near the prisoner, so he lives and my trap's dead. Call it even. Two — the rider lit a fire on the ridge, in the open, where we'd all see it. Either he's telling us he's still counting, or that fire's a signal for somebody we haven't met yet. Both are bad. Three — scouts aren't back. Careful, or caught. I'll know by midnight, or I'll know it's gone wrong. Four — I watched the line all day. I've got three faces that never once spent the march staring at anyone. Could be steady men. Steady men exist. I'll point them out quiet when we pass the fires, and you tell me if any of them eats at your table."

She rolled the stitched arm — itching now, which the stitcher called healing and Kira called spite — and gave him the last of it.

"Five — the prisoner gave up a freebie. Paymaster at Waymeet kept his hood up, but he counted the coin himself, and he wears a silver ring on his left thumb, worn shiny. Soldier's hands. That's a thing you can check at Waymeet — and a thing I'll be checking on every left thumb in this column between here and the pine cut. Six — tell me you fed the three routes. Three sergeants, three roads, each told his is the real one and to keep his mouth shut. If that's not done, tonight's the last cheap night to do it."

She let a stride pass. Two. Out past the fires the night was big and cold and full of things that watched.

"Now the other half of what I'm owed, Cap. You said every last name. So walk and talk — who's rich enough to sign for a company's muster, and mean enough to want you under it?" A breath, almost a grin. "And while you're at it — tell me which of them wears a ring."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I walk in silence for a moment, listening to Kira's report, my gaze fixed on the distant fire. "The ring... that's new. A good catch." I sigh, the cold air misting my breath. "As for names... There's Marcus. Always had more coin than sense, and a grudge going back to the White Pass. And Elara, but she's more subtle than this. Then there's the Iron Hand, though I thought he was across the Dragon's Tooth by now."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the words sit where Jamie had left them, in the air between the two chairs. Five seconds. She counted them privately — the clock on the wall offered no seconds to count anymore; she'd seen to that years ago.

She capped her pen and set it down on the armrest, beside the notepad.

"Their journal," she said. Just the two words, given back unchanged.

A small pause.

"When did you find it?"

She left the question out there with room around it, the way she left all of them. The pen stayed capped. Whatever came next, she had the sense, wasn't for the page.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "Last night." My voice is flat. I pick at a loose thread on the armrest of the chair. "In the old chest in the attic."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched Jamie's fingers work the thread, around and around. She didn't say anything about it. Hands often got somewhere before words did.

Five seconds. She let them run their full length.

"Last night," she said. "In the attic."

She left the pieces where Jamie had set them, unhurried. Then she put her question down beside them, the way she might set a cup of water within someone's reach — there if they wanted it.

"Did you read it?"

No lean forward. No change in her voice. If the answer was no, that would tell her one thing. If it was yes, another. Either way, the journal had come down from the attic this morning, and she suspected it had been in the room since before Jamie sat down.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez didn't fill the silence. She had learned long ago that a sentence breaking off in the middle was often more complete than one that reached its period — the person had arrived somewhere and couldn't yet look at what was there.

She let the unfinished thing hang. Five seconds. Then five more, because the second five belonged to Jamie, not to her.

"You stopped," she said finally, not as an accusation. As an observation, the way one might note where a path ends at a cliff's edge.

She uncrossed her ankles. Set both feet flat on the floor.

"Where were you, just now? When the sentence wouldn't go on."

She wasn't asking about the journal anymore. Not directly. The journal was a door, and Jamie had walked through it last night, and something in that attic had followed them down. But doors could be approached slowly. She had time, and this hour, and the room.

The ficus dropped a yellowed leaf onto the carpet. Neither of them moved toward it.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shrug, still looking at my hands. *My throat feels tight. I can't look at her.* "I don't know."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the shrug have its say. It didn't take long. She gave it five seconds anyway, and then a sixth, because the sixth was where the honest things sometimes started.

"I don't know," she echoed, in the same level tone she gave everything. "That's all right. Not-knowing is a place too. You can stand there as long as you need to. This room doesn't require anything of you."

She didn't ask Jamie to look up. She had noticed — the flatness at the edges of the voice, the eyes still fixed on the hands — and she kept the noticing where she kept most of it: behind her teeth, in the notepad she wasn't writing on.

"I'd like to take my last question back," she said. "The one about where you went. It doesn't have to be answered today. It can wait on the carpet with the leaf."

A pause, brief and deliberate.

"Here's a smaller one instead. It only asks about the chest. Nothing about you." She tipped her head a fraction, toward the door, toward last night. "When you opened it — was the journal sitting on top of everything? Or did you have to dig for it?"

It was a small question with a large answer folded inside it. Whether Jamie had gone looking, or merely stumbled. Whether someone had left it where it could be found. But Jamie didn't need to know any of that yet.

She hadn't touched the pen in a while.

She didn't touch it now.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez didn't look away. Jamie had finally raised their eyes, and she received the look the way she received everything in this room — steadily, without reaching for it. Whatever Jamie was searching for in her face, she made sure of one thing only: that nothing in her flinched, and nothing leaned.

Five seconds. Then five more, because a first look deserved its own measure of time.

"They wrote about you," she said. "In the last entry."

She gave the words back unchanged. Same weight, nothing added.

The last entry. Last things written were rarely written by accident. But that was a thought to keep behind her teeth, where she kept most of them.

"You've told me what it's about," she said. "You haven't told me what it says." A pause. "You can keep that as long as you need to. The room doesn't require it. It never has."

She let one breath pass.

"Here's a smaller one. It doesn't ask what they wrote. It only asks what you did." Another breath, set carefully between the two halves of it. "Did you read it more than once?"

The pen stayed capped on the armrest. The leaf stayed where it had fallen. She had told Jamie earlier that things could wait on the carpet, and she meant this room to be a place where that was true — where nothing had to be picked up before its time, and nothing was.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shake my head slowly. "No. Just once." *But I remembered every word.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the head shake and the words both have their five seconds. She counted them privately. The clock on the wall offered no help with that. It never did.

"Just once," she said, and gave the words back exactly as they had come — no weight added, none subtracted.

Jamie had looked at her when they said it. The first time all hour their eyes had come up and held. She received the look and did nothing with it. Didn't warm it, didn't weigh it. Some looks were load-bearing. You didn't test them. You let them hold.

She used their name aloud for the first time that hour. The question had earned it.

"Jamie. Where is the journal right now?"

Not the entry. Not what they'd written. The book itself — the paper, the cover, the spine. *Right now* doing quiet work, asking about this room, this hour, the space between the two chairs, and leaving the attic where it lay.

She didn't glance at the places a book might be — the chair's edge, a bag, a coat pocket. Her eyes stayed where they belonged. The question would do that work on its own.

Because there were two answers. If the journal was back in the chest, under whatever it had lain beneath all these years, then Jamie had climbed up, opened it, read themselves inside it, and returned it to the dark. And if it was here — within reach of the carpet where the leaf was waiting — then some part of them had already decided something, whether or not the rest of them knew it yet.

The pen stayed capped.

She had told Jamie that things could wait on the carpet. But some things came down from attics, she knew, because they were done waiting.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It's in my bag." *I gesture vaguely to my backpack slumped beside my chair.* "I brought it with me."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the words have their five seconds. She didn't look at the bag. It sat slumped beside Jamie's chair, and it could stay slumped — her eyes had no business over there yet. Jamie had gestured at it vaguely, without turning to look at it, and she filed that away with the rest.

"In your bag," she said. "You brought it with you."

The words went back unchanged. Then she let the fact of them stand in the room on its own for a moment. Last night the journal had been in a chest, in the attic, in the dark, under whatever it had lain beneath all these years. This morning it was an arm's length from her chair. She didn't say any of that aloud. Some distances did their own talking.

"Here's a smaller one," she said. "It only asks about the bag. Nothing about the entry. Nothing about you." A breath set between the halves, the way she'd been doing all hour. "Is it zipped in deep — or in a pocket? Somewhere your hand would have to go looking for it. Or somewhere it could reach it without deciding to."

She heard the question do its quiet work and left it alone. Buried or reachable. Kept, or ready. She didn't name those possibilities any louder than that, even to herself.

"For the record," she added, settling back a fraction, "nothing in this room is reaching for that bag. The pen is still capped. The journal stays wherever you keep it — zipped in, pocketed, or out on the carpet with the leaf. There's room there, if it ever wants it. But that part is yours. It doesn't become the room's until you make it so."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I finally look at the bag, really look at it. "It's... right on top. Just tucked inside the main compartment." *I hadn't realized how accessible it was until now.* "I guess I didn't zip it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let it have five seconds. Then a sixth, because all hour Jamie had handed her facts — flat, finished, set down like stones on a table — and "I guess" was the first thing that had arrived still warm, still deciding what it was.

"Right on top," she said. "Tucked in. Not zipped."

The words went back the way they'd come. Then she allowed herself one observation, stated plainly and left where it fell.

"Earlier, you pointed at that bag without turning your head. Just now, you looked at it." A beat. "I'm not going to tell you what the difference means.
