In this room, meanings are made by the person carrying them. I only wanted to say it out loud — so it could exist outside your head for a minute, where you could look at it too."

She let that sit. Then she reached for the smaller question, the way she'd been reaching for smaller ones all hour — each one a step to the side rather than a step forward.

"This one only asks about this morning. Nothing about why." A breath set between the halves. "When the journal went into the bag — did the zipper close and then come back open? Or did it never close at all?"

She knew the shape of both answers before they came. A zipper closed and reopened meant a hand that had gone back — a decision made twice, the second time against the first. A zipper that never closed meant the journal had never really been put away at all.

Only carried.

She kept all of that under the surface, where she kept most things. Out loud there was only the question, resting on the carpet beside the leaf.

She tipped her head toward the clock on the wall — the one with nothing moving on its face.

"We have time," she said. "I took the second hand out of that clock years ago. It doesn't get to hurry anyone in this room."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I blink. *My mind is racing, trying to recall that moment.* "It... it never closed at all. I just put it in there." I look down at my hands again. *That's new information to me, too.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let it have five seconds. She didn't count them this time. Some silences counted themselves.

"It never closed at all," she said. "You just put it in there."

She gave the words back at half speed, because they weren't the same words anymore — not for Jamie. She'd seen the blink. The slow kind, the kind that happens when something inside rearranges and the eyes need a moment to let it settle. And then the hands again, arriving somewhere before the words did, the way they had all hour.

"I want to say one thing out loud, and then I'll leave it alone." She waited a beat, not for permission — just to let the sentence find its footing. "Every answer you've given me today arrived finished. Flat. Set down like stones on a table — decided long before I ever asked. That one wasn't finished. That one arrived the way answers do when a person hears them for the first time in the middle of saying them."

A breath.

"I'm not going to tell you what it means. Meanings are made by the person carrying them — I've said that before, and I mean it more now. I only wanted it out in the room. Some things get lighter the second someone else has heard them. I'm not promising that one will. I'm only setting it on the table with the stones."

She picked up the notepad from the armrest and moved it to the side table, out of her own reach. The pen went with it, still capped. Some hours were for the page. This one wasn't.

"Here's the smallest question I've asked you yet." A beat. "Now that you know it's lying there on top — do you want to zip the bag, or leave it open?"

She let the question stand in the open, then added the railing to it.

"There's no right answer. You're not deciding forever — the zipper will wait for you whenever you want it. I only ask because an hour ago you didn't know it was open, and now you do. And once we know a thing, leaving it or closing it stops being an accident." A pause. "I'd rather it be yours than an accident."

Then she did the thing she was best at, which was nothing, on purpose, for a long time.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I look at the bag, then back at Dr. Vasquez. My hands are still in my lap. "I want to zip it." My voice is a little stronger now. "I want to close it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let it have the five seconds. This silence had a different job than the others. All hour they'd been for holding things — the unfinished sentence, the not-knowing, the entry neither of them had opened. This one was for letting something stand up straight.

"You want to zip it," she said. "You want to close it."

She gave the words back at the strength they'd arrived — a little stronger than anything else all hour, and she didn't soften them to fit the rest of it. Words that came in stronger deserved to stay that way.

"You said it twice. I heard it twice."

Then she set the observation down, plainly, where Jamie could look at it too.

"Everything you've given me today arrived in past tense. Found. Brought. Read once. Never zipped. All of it finished before you ever sat down in that chair." A beat. "That was the first *I want* of the hour. The first thing you've said that points forward instead of back." A pause. "I'm not going to tell you what that's worth. I only wanted it out loud — so it could be true in two heads instead of one."

She didn't reach. Didn't nod toward the bag. Didn't make her stillness into a nudge.

"It's an arm's length away. If you want to do it here — now, with a witness — nothing in this room is in your way. If you'd rather do it later, somewhere that belongs only to you, that counts too. The zipper doesn't care where it happens." A breath. "The deciding is the part that matters, and you did that part out loud, here, where I could hear it. The hands can catch up whenever they're ready. There's no deadline on this carpet. There never has been."

On the side table, the pen lay capped, out of her own reach, where she'd moved it. The leaf still held its patch of carpet. All hour, things had been waiting down there — questions, sentences, meanings — and now, for the first time, something wanted to be picked up. She thought that, and kept it. There was a difference between what a counselor thought and what she said, and most of the job lived in the space between.

She didn't watch the bag. Bags don't need witnessing.

And then she waited. Not for the sound of a zipper — for Jamie. All hour, the hands had been getting somewhere before the words did. This was the first time the words had gone ahead.

She wanted to see what the hands would do with that.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I reach for the bag. My fingers find the zipper and I pull it closed with a soft *zzzip*. I don't look at Dr. Vasquez, but I can feel her presence. *It's done.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the sound have the room first. The zipper ran its short track and stopped, and the small click of the pull settling against the bag was the last of it. All hour, the only sounds in here had been made by voices. That was the first one neither of them had to say.

Jamie hadn't looked over while doing it. She was glad of that, in the quiet way she was glad whenever a true thing got done without an audience.

Five seconds. She gave them all the way to the end. This silence didn't need to hold anything, or carry anything, or let anything stand up straight. It only needed to let a finished thing come to rest.

"Closed," she said. One word, set down flat, the way she set everything down.

Then, plainly:

"For the whole hour, your hands have been ahead of your voice. The thread on the armrest. The zipper you didn't know was open. Just now, for the first time, the words went first and the hands followed them." A beat. "I'm not reading anything into that. Order is a fact. Facts can sit out in the open where both of us can look at them."

She let one breath pass.

"One more fact, and then I'm done laying them down. Last night, that journal got closed inside a chest, in the dark, under everything it had lain beneath for years. A few minutes ago, it got closed in daylight, in this room, by your hand." A pause. "Two closings. I'm not going to tell you the difference between them. I only wanted them spoken in the same room, side by side, where you could stand them next to each other."

She reached for the smaller question, the last one she had in her for now.

"It only asks about tonight. Nothing about the entry. Nothing about what any of it means." She let the breath fall where the two halves met, the way it had all hour. "When the day is done and the bag gets set down somewhere — where does the journal sleep? Back in the chest, in the dark where it's always lived? Or somewhere it hasn't lived before?"

She added the railing to it, because she always did.

"There's no right answer. The chest kept it safe for a long time. Maybe it should again. And you don't have to answer now — that one can lie down on the carpet with the leaf. It'll keep."

Then she leaned back a fraction, and gave the last of her words for a while.

"One more thing. You carried it down from the attic. You brought it into this room. And not one word of it was read aloud here — the entry is still only yours. I want you to know that counts. It came, and it traveled in a bag that wouldn't zip, and it's leaving zipped. All of that is real whether or not a single word of it ever reaches me. Not everything that comes into this room is required to be said in it."

She didn't look at the bag. It had done its work for the day.

On the carpet, the leaf still held its ground, patient in the way that only fallen things are patient. It could wait. Everything in this room had learned how.

Across the room, the ficus went on dropping its leaves at its own pace, in its own season. She had stopped trying to hurry it years ago.

It had taken her longer to stop trying to hurry herself.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I nod slowly, taking it all in. *I didn't realize how much I needed to hear that.* I look at the ficus, then back at the bag, then finally at Dr. Vasquez. "Thank you."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn’t argue. Orders were orders, and if the east ridge wanted a target, she’d give them one.

She dropped lower and moved fast toward the open slope, boots skidding on loose scree. Daggers out. Shoulders tight. Every step made her feel like a bug on a table, but that was the point.

The first arrow came again too close.

“Shit—” She twisted hard behind a sandstone outcrop, stone chipping above her head. A second arrow thudded into the crack where she’d been standing a half-second before.

She used the cover, then broke from it, angling toward a cluster of rocks that gave her only a few feet of shadow. Too visible. Too slow. Not dead yet.

“Hey, you ugly bastards!” she called up the ridge, flashing one dagger low and moving. “You shoot like farmers throwing rocks!”

More movement above. Two figures shifted left. One stayed right.

Kira counted. “Five clear on east ridge,” she muttered, mostly to herself. “Maybe six if that ledge holds someone.”

She feinted right, then ducked left, drawing a volley that kicked dust into her face. One arrow grazed her shoulder, tearing cloth. She snarled and shoved behind the rock, breathing hot and fast.

From the west, something shifted—movement, noise, pressure. Good.

She stayed low for three heartbeats, then rose just enough to throw a stone at the nearest archer’s perch. Not to hit. To irritate. To make them look at her.

“Cap,” she said, voice tight between gritted teeth, “east ridge is splitting. If they turn, we can push under the rocks before they reset.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Understood, Kira. Hold them there."

*I nod to the vanguard, then charge the west ridge myself, polearm sweeping wide.* "For the Company!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira exhaled through her teeth. “Hold them there. Right. Because nothing makes archers forget their job like being insulted.”

She rose enough to draw a second look, then dropped before the arrow came. It bit into the rock where her head had been, sending a shower of grit down her collar. She spat, wiped her mouth with the back of her hand, and shifted low and hard toward the nearest cluster of boulders.

Up on the east ridge, one of the archers moved sideways—out of sight behind a slab, but not far enough. Kira heard the scrape of his boot on loose stone. Another turned his head west. That was what she wanted. That was what she was supposed to buy with her own skin.

She pulled a small stone from her belt and hurled it upward. It skipped off the rock face and made the exposed archer flinch. Not a hit. Just enough to make him look.

“Over here, cowards!” she shouted, then immediately winced at how stupid it sounded. “Yes, me! The one who can’t pay for armor!”

Two more arrows came at once. They sparked against the boulder and sent stone chips stinging across her cheek. Kira pressed flat behind the rock, daggers up, one hand clamped over her mouth. Her breath came fast and angry. She hated being bait. She hated being shot at. But she did it.

From the west, the ravine noise changed.

Kira risked a glance around the rock. Movement along the ridge line—shadows shifting, the sound of bodies hitting stone, the brief flash of steel against the high sun. Good. Bad. Too many directions to watch at once.

She heard a bowstring above her left. Not east ridge. Lower. Someone had started down the slope toward the vanguard’s path.

“Cap,” she said, voice low and urgent, “one of them’s breaking east. He’s coming down the west shoulder. If he reaches the ridge line, he’ll get a clear shot on the flank.”

She didn’t wait to see if the warning had been useful. She couldn’t. The archer on the east ridge shifted again, and Kira had to choose: stay pinned and let him climb to a better perch, or make herself the ugliest target on the slope.

She chose ugly.

Kira burst from cover and ran toward the nearest scree slope, boots kicking loose stones down the ravine wall. A volley cracked after her, one arrow thudding into the dirt just behind her heel. She didn’t look. Looking meant stopping. Stopping meant dying.

She reached the loose rocks, grabbed a fist-sized chunk, and shoved it down the slope with her foot. The scree went with it in a rattling cascade.

Above, a man swore.

Kira grinned, all teeth and dirt. “That’s right, you ugly bastard. Come get me.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw it before the warning could be useful—a shape on the west shoulder, bow arm already level, string drawn back toward the ravine. Her stomach turned. That line wasn’t aimed at her.

“Cap, high right!” she barked.

She didn’t wait. Kira snatched a loose stone and hurled it at the archer’s head. The man flinched, draw breaking. The string snapped, but the shot went wide, sparking off stone. Kira used the second. She came from cover in a low sprint, both daggers out, and closed the last few feet before the archer could nock another arrow. He swung the bow. She sidestepped, took it on her shoulder, and drove her point into his neck. The archer crumpled.

For one bad heartbeat she stood exposed, chest heaving, blood hot on her wrist.

Then the east ridge remembered her. Arrows bit the ground near her feet. Kira swore, grabbed the archer’s quiver, and threw it downhill toward the ravine floor where her own cover waited. Not because it would hit anyone. Because it would make them look.

She ducked back behind the boulder, teeth clenched. “Cap,” she said, voice low and fast, “west shoulder’s down. One less flank. East ridge still pinned me. I can keep them here, but if that ledge on our left is manned, I’m going to need a different plan.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I bring my polearm around, sweeping it into the chest of a man trying to scramble down the rocks.* "Good work, Kira! Get to that ledge, clear it if you can."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn’t waste breath on a reply. If the Captain wanted that ledge cleared, she’d clear it or die trying.

She shifted along the boulder’s shadow, boots silent against the stone, daggers low and ready. The east ridge still held too many bows, and the sun was high enough to make the scree glare. That meant she couldn’t climb straight up. Not without becoming target practice.

“Damn it,” she muttered, scanning the wall.

A narrow crack ran upward between two fractured sandstone shelves, half-hidden by a dead shrub and a spill of loose rock. It wasn’t clean. It wasn’t safe. But it gave her cover from the ridge line for the first ten feet, and above that, the ledge cut into the ravine like a shelf.

Another arrow struck the boulder behind her, sending a chip of stone into her cheek.

Kira hissed through her teeth and moved.

She hit the scree slope at a crouch, boots slipping, daggers tucked close. One hand went to the crack for purchase, the other stayed free. She climbed fast, not gracefully, hauling herself up by the stone shelf while her shoulder burned from the earlier graze. A shout came from above—east ridge, one of them seeing her go.

She didn’t look up. Looking up meant slowing down.

A stone kicked loose from the ledge and skittered down her forearm. Kira grunted, shifted higher, and finally risked a glance.

Two men were on the ledge. One was turning, bow half-raised, the other had a short sword drawn but no quiver on his back. Not a mixed pair. Probably one to hold the perch, one to shoot the flank if the vanguard pushed too hard.

Kira spat blood from a bitten lip.

“Company,” she said under her breath. “I hate this job.”

The archer saw her. He started to draw.

Kira went faster.

She pulled herself over the ledge with a snarl, both daggers out, and drove one knee into the stone to stop her slide. The archer’s string snapped back. The arrow punched into the dirt inches from her hip. Before he could reach for another, Kira was on him.

He swung the bow like a club. She took it on her forearm, bone jarring hard, and came in inside the arc. Her left dagger caught his wrist, opening a line of red across the skin. The bow clattered. He stumbled back, shouting, and Kira followed, not giving him space to breathe or aim.

The second man came in from the side, sword low, trying to cut off her retreat.

Kira saw the shadow before she saw the steel.

She dropped. The sword passed over her head, close enough to stir the hair at her temple. Kira drove upward with the right dagger, catching the man under the arm and into the side. He grunted hard, stumbling, and she kicked his knee out from under him.

For one bad second, she stood over them both, chest heaving, daggers slick.

Then east ridge arrows came biting into the ledge behind her.

Kira swore and threw herself flat against the rock wall.

“Cap!” she shouted down into the ravine, voice rough but clear. “Ledge’s mine! East ridge still has shooters, but they can’t see the west flank from here anymore. Tell me that’s enough.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw the gap widen between them—the ravine floor a broken line of scree and shadow, with the far side too exposed for her to cross. She crouched on the ledge, daggers still in her hands, blood cooling on her wrist.

“Cap, I can’t reach you!” she shouted, voice rough. “The ledge covers the west flank, but the east ridge is still live. They’re turning bows this way.”

She glanced at the dead archer’s bow. It was a mess—loose string, wrong grip, arrows fletched badly. Still, arrows were arrows.

Kira grabbed the bow and a handful of shafts. She rose just enough to see the east ridge, then dropped as an arrow sparked off the ledge.

“Shit. Fine. You want loud? I’ll be loud.”

She nocked one, half-drew, and fired. The arrow went wild, thudding into sandstone a yard left of the nearest archer. It wasn’t a kill. It wasn’t even close. But the man flinched.

Kira grinned despite the ache in her shoulder. “That’s two on me now. Maybe three.”

She looked down at the ravine again. The east ridge archers were adjusting. If they reset, the ledge wouldn’t stay hers. If she stayed, she could buy minutes. If she moved down, she’d be cut in half before she reached the floor.

“Cap,” she called, keeping her voice low between shots, “I can pin their eyes up here, but I can’t cross. If you need me to keep them looking at me, say the word.”

She threw a stone at the ridge, then another, making the scree rattle like footsteps.

“Come on, you ugly bastards,” she muttered. “The real target’s over there. But I’m still meaner.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Keep them busy, Kira! We're almost through here!" *I parry a wild swing from a bandit and push him back into another, creating an opening.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira caught the order, rough and urgent, across the ravine. Her jaw tightened. Almost through meant almost safe, and almost never stayed still long enough to matter.

She checked the dead archer’s bow. The string was wrong. The grip was sticky with his blood. It was still a weapon.

“Fine,” she muttered. “Bad shot. Loud shot.”

The east ridge shifted above her. One archer ducked behind a sandstone lip, another stood too long in the open. Kira nocked a shaft and fired. The arrow went high, thudding into rock above the ridge and sending a crack of stone down the slope.

The exposed archer flinched. Good.

“Over here, you ugly bastards!” Kira shouted. “You’re paying to look at me, not him!”

She grabbed another arrow and fired into the scree beside the man’s perch. This one missed the body but hit loose stone. The cascade rattled down the wall. The archer lost footing, slid a few feet, and swore at the ledge.

Kira grinned through the grit on her teeth. “That’s one shooter off the line.”

She looked along the ridge, counting shadows. The west shoulder was clear now, but the east ridge was learning her pattern. Two archers behind the boulder had stopped aiming at the ravine floor and were adjusting toward the ledge. The third was out of sight, probably crawling for a better angle.

“Cap,” she called, voice low and sharp, “east ridge is resetting. They’re getting the ledge’s blind side. If I stay up here, I can keep their heads turned, but not forever.”

Another arrow sparked off the shelf. Kira swore and flattened against the rock wall. The sounds below were still thick with stone and steel, but she couldn’t see enough of it to help. That was the worst kind of waiting.

She popped up, pulled a stone from her belt, and hurled it at the archer behind the boulder. It skipped off his cover and struck the ridge with a sharp crack.

“Come on!” she snarled. “Is that all you got? My grandmother shoots better from her grave!”

The ridge answered with two arrows at once. They bit into the sandstone inches from her hip. Kira dropped behind the bowstring crack and breathed through her teeth. Her shoulder throbbed. The blood on her wrist had gone tacky. She hated that feeling. It meant the body was already thinking about weakness.

She nocked another arrow and fired without looking. It went wild. That was the point. Wild meant confusing. Wild meant they couldn’t tell if she had support, if the ledge held more people, or if she was just one stupid sellsword with bad aim and a bigger mouth than sense.

A voice shouted from above. Then movement. The archer who had slid was trying to climb back to his perch. The other two were shifting left, trying to line up the ledge edge.

Kira saw the pattern and moved before fear could finish the thought.

She ran low along the shelf, boots scraping loose chips, daggers bouncing at her hips. She stopped at a narrow cleft where the ledge narrowed into rock, just enough to break the archers’ straight shot. From there, she leaned out and fired another bad arrow into the ridge line.

“West shoulder’s down!” she shouted. “East ridge still live! Ledge still mine!”

She grabbed a fist-sized stone and threw it again. This time, she hit the edge of the boulder the nearest archer was using for cover. The impact made him jerk. His bowstring sang. The arrow went wide, punching into dead scrub.

Kira laughed, harsh and ugly. “There it is.”

Then the east ridge got angry. Three arrows came at once. One struck the wall above her, one skipped off the ledge, and one buried itself in the dirt beside her boot. Kira swore and dropped flat, heart hammering.

“Shit,” she hissed. “Shit, shit.”

She stayed down for three heartbeats, counting. The ridge was louder now. They were scrambling, trying to get a better angle. That meant they weren’t steady. That meant they weren’t watching the west shoulder as closely.

Kira rose just enough to see.

“Cap,” she called, voice tight, “they’re coming off the ledge line. If you’re pushing through, that’s the window.”

She nocked one last arrow and fired into the open, not at a body but at the loose scree above the ridge. The shaft sparked off stone and kicked a small cascade down the slope. The archers flinched again.

Kira pressed her back to the rock and smiled, all teeth and blood.

“Still ugly bastards,” she muttered. “Still looking at me.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood, Kira! Fall back when you can!" *I kick a stunned bandit off the cliff edge and signal for the company to push through.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the order and swore under her breath, though she was already doing it.

“Almost through,” she muttered. “Almost doesn’t pay my wages.”

She crouched behind the ledge, fingers closing around the dead archer’s bow. The wood was ugly, the string stiff, the balance wrong. She had maybe six arrows left in the quiver, and not one of them felt steady in her hand. The east ridge was still live, still turning toward her like a mouth opening, and every second she spent up here meant someone below wasn’t getting shot in the back.

That was the whole job. Make them look at you. Make them hate you enough to aim at you.

She nocked an arrow, rose just enough to draw, and fired toward the nearest archer’s perch. The shaft went high and wide, cracking off a sandstone shelf above the ridge. Dust rained down.

“Is that all you got?” Kira shouted, voice raw. “I’ve had better shots from a drunk man throwing bread!”

A volley answered. Two arrows sparked against the ledge. A third thudded into the dirt beside her boot. Kira dropped flat and rolled her shoulder, hissing through her teeth. The old graze had torn open again, sticky and hot under her sleeve.

She ignored it.

From the west side of the ravine, noise still carried—shouts, the bark of stone under boots, the ring of steel she couldn’t see. It was enough to tell her the fight hadn’t died down. It was also enough to tell her she couldn’t leave the ledge yet. If she broke cover now, the east ridge would remember that she was the only obvious target up here.

Kira counted archers again. The first was behind a low slab, half hidden. The second was farther left, trying to crawl toward the blind side. The third was still pinned, but moving. The fourth was gone from view—probably looking for a better angle down the slope.

“Four visible, maybe five,” she said to herself. “Maybe six, because nothing in this damn ravine is ever simple.”

She grabbed two stones from the ledge and threw them hard toward the ridge. They skipped off the wall and rattled down into the scree like footsteps. The first archer flinched. The second turned his head, trying to spot movement that wasn’t there.

“Over here!” Kira barked. “I’m the one you want! The one with the daggers and the big mouth and the bad attitude!”

She popped up, fired another wild arrow, then dropped back before the ridge could answer. The bowstring sang almost immediately. An arrow struck the wall above her head, showering her hair with grit.

“Fuck,” she muttered, wiping her eyes. “They’re learning.”

The ledge had bought them time, but it was becoming a cage. The east ridge was no longer aiming blindly at the ravine floor. They were adjusting for elevation, for angle, for the way she moved. If she stayed, she could still draw them. If they sent someone down to flush her, she’d have to fight it out on narrow ground.

Kira looked toward the west shoulder. It was still clear. Good. Bad. Too clear meant they might try to circle back once they realized she was alone.

She crawled along the ledge to the narrow cleft where the rock broke her silhouette. From there, she leaned out and threw a stone at the archer on the low slab. It missed him but hit his cover hard. He jerked back. His bowstring snapped without an arrow.

“Come on!” she shouted, grin sharp and mean. “Shoot something! Shoot *me*! Don’t waste arrows on the rocks, you cheap bastard!”

More movement above. The crawling archer on the left shifted higher. He was trying to get behind her. If he found the right angle, he could put an arrow into the ledge while the others kept her pinned.

Kira’s stomach tightened.

She grabbed the bow and a handful of arrows, moved low along the shelf, and kicked a pile of loose stones down toward the slope. They went clattering over the edge, making the scree hiss. It sounded like someone climbing down.

The east ridge reacted at once.

Three arrows came down toward the falling rocks. Kira threw herself sideways behind a broken slab. One arrow punched through dust. One sparked off stone. One buried itself in the ledge where she’d been standing.

“Too slow,” she snarled.

She rose and fired again. This time the arrow went low, skittering off the ridge and sending the crawling man swearing as a stone chip grazed his leg. He dropped behind the rock.

Kira laughed, though there was no joy in it. “There it is. That’s the noise I like.”

She checked the quiver. Four arrows left. One of them was cracked. She tossed it aside and took a bad arrow from the dead archer’s belt instead. It was crooked, but it would still fly if she pulled hard enough.

Across the ravine, the fighting sounds had changed. Not ended. Changed.

Kira pressed her back to the ledge and breathed slow. Her shoulder throbbed. Her mouth tasted like dust. The sun was too high, the walls too exposed, and the east ridge was too smart for its own good.

She called down toward the west side, voice tight but carrying.

“Cap, I’m still drawing them, but I’m running out of arrows and patience. If they send someone around to flush me, I’ll have to go loud. If you need me to fall back, say it before I’m up here with a bow and a mouth and no cover.”

She nocked another arrow and fired toward the ridge, missing on purpose. The shaft hit a slab with a sharp crack.

“Hey!” she shouted. “You forgot me! Come back and look at me!”

The ridge answered with two arrows.

Kira ducked behind the stone and waited, daggers close, breath rough, watching the ledge for movement. She couldn’t cross the ravine. She couldn’t reach him. But she could still make the east ridge remember her name.

For now, that was what the job was.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood, Kira! Fall back now!" *I bellow, seeing the rest of the company is clear.* "We're pushing through!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn’t wait for the order to be repeated.

“On my way!” she shouted, though it came out ragged.

She pulled back the dead archer’s bowstring one last time and fired at the nearest east-ridge cover. The arrow struck stone and exploded into chips. It was enough. The man behind that slab ducked lower.

She checked the quiver. Three arrows. One good, two crooked. The bow was still slick with the archer’s blood, and her shoulder screamed when she raised it. She ignored it.

“Fall back. Fall back. Right. Because open ground is my favorite.”

She grabbed the quiver, shoved the remaining arrows into it, and tossed it down the slope. It rattled like someone moving. Then she kicked a pile of loose stone off the ledge. The scree hissed after it.

From the ridge, a voice shouted.

Kira used the distraction.

She dropped backward over the ledge lip, boots finding the crack she had climbed earlier. Her weight jerked on her wounded shoulder. She bit a curse back into her teeth and slid down the scree, heels braking, hands scraping against rough sandstone. Daggers stayed out, points low.

Above her, the east ridge started firing.

An arrow punched into the wall inches from her hand. Another struck the ledge where she had been. She twisted, shoved her back against a boulder, and breathed. The ledge was gone. The open ravine floor was twenty yards below. Twenty yards of bad stone, dust, and line of fire.

“Cap,” she called down, voice tight, “I’m coming down the ledge. East ridge has shooters on the shelf line. One might be moving off the slope.”

She couldn’t see the whole ridge from here. That was bad. She could hear them, though—boot scrape, bowstring creak, a man swearing when a stone rolled under his foot. That meant they weren’t all dead. That meant they were still aiming.

Kira counted cover. Three boulders between the ledge base and the ravine floor. A dry channel under the wall, shallow and useless against arrows. A cluster of dead shrubs that might hide a dog, not a woman with daggers.

She nocked one of the crooked arrows and fired up toward the ridge without standing fully. The shaft wobbled and struck a slab high on the wall. The noise was wrong, but the movement was visible. The archers flinched, just enough.

Kira ran.

Her boots kicked loose scree. Every step sent small stones skittering downhill, making the whole slope sound alive. An arrow thudded behind her. Another sparked off the first boulder. She hit the boulder hard, shoulder and hip against stone, then pushed on.

“Come on!” she snarled. “Shoot me, not your own feet!”

She reached the second boulder and slid behind it. The east ridge was resetting. She could hear it—the scrape of arrows being nocked, the soft creak of bows. Four, maybe five shooters still active. One was moving. She looked down the slope and saw a shadow break left, away from the ridge line, trying to get a lower angle.

“Shit,” she said.

If that man got below the ledge, he could cut across the ravine and put arrows into the retreat path. She couldn’t let him.

Kira rose with the bow and fired at the moving shadow. The crooked arrow flew wide, but it forced him behind a rock. She grabbed a stone and threw it at the scree above him. The cascade broke loose and sent him sliding backward. He swore loudly.

She didn’t stay to see if he got up. She ran again.

The third boulder was close. Too close. The ravine floor opened beyond it, a broken lane of sand and stone. She could hear movement ahead—boots, voices, the clatter of gear—but not enough to see. Not enough to know if she was running into cover or straight into another killzone.

An arrow struck the boulder just above her head. Stone chips cut her cheek. Kira ducked, hissing, and pressed flat against the hot rock. Her breath came short and sharp. Blood ran down her jaw. She wiped it away with the back of her hand and left a smear of red.

“Almost there,” she muttered. “Don’t be a stupid corpse yet.”

She counted heartbeats. One. Two. Three. Then she burst from the boulder.

The east ridge fired.

She ran low, arms pumping, daggers catching light. An arrow punched through the air close enough to make her hear the split. She twisted, and something sharp bit into the side of her thigh. Not deep. Not fatal. It made her stumble, and she caught herself with a snarl and a bloody hand on her knee

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I whirl, seeing Kira stumble, an arrow in her leg.* "Kira! Down!" *I charge back, polearm ready, trying to draw fire.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the order and obeyed it before pride could argue. She dropped hard behind the boulder, thigh screaming as the arrow shaft ground against muscle. The impact shook dust from the ledge. Above, a bowstring sang. The arrow punched into the boulder’s edge and sent a splinter into her cheek.

“Down, down, I’m down!” she hissed, pressing her back to stone.

She looked at the shaft. It had gone in shallow, through cloth and meat, not bone. Pulling it would bleed. Leaving it would slow her. She chose leaving it, for now, and braced one hand against the rock while the other kept her dagger raised.

The east ridge was still alive. She could hear boots shifting, a man talking to himself, another cursing as loose stone slid under him. One shooter had moved left. One had stayed high. The third might be trying to circle down behind her—bad, very bad.

“Cap,” she called, voice tight, “I’m behind the third boulder, thigh’s hit but not done. If you’ve got any cover left, I can move to it. If I try to run this open lane again, they’ll put another one in me before I clear the slope.”

She grabbed a fist-sized chunk of sandstone and hurled it not at the ridge but at the scree above her left. The rocks went down with a sharp hiss. The ridge flinched. A shot came, wide, striking the boulder behind her.

Kira laughed, ugly and breathless. “That’s it. Keep aiming at the rock. It shoots back better than I can right now.”

Her leg throbbed. She tested the arrow. The shaft wobbled. She swore and shifted lower.

“East ridge still has at least two shooters high, maybe one moving to the lower slope. If they get a line on the retreat path, we’re boxed again.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Kira, cover fire! We'll clear that lower slope!" *I signal the company to form a skirmish line and lay down suppressing fire on the east ridge.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the order and barked a curse through her teeth.

“Cover fire. Right. With one bad bow, a leg full of arrow, and the personality of a wet rock.”

She shifted behind the boulder, jaw clenched, and looked at the shaft in her thigh. Pulling it now would make her bleed faster. Leaving it would snag on every step she tried to take. She chose the ugly option and snapped the exposed shaft.

Pain hit like a hammer. Kira spat once, hard, and kept her breathing down.

The east ridge was moving again. Two shooters still held the high line, heads low behind sandstone slabs. One had broken off and was working down the slope, trying to get an angle on the retreat path. Kira caught the flick of his sleeve as he slid behind a fallen boulder.

“There,” she muttered.

She nocked the last good arrow, rose just enough, and fired.

The shot was bad. It struck the slab above the moving archer and exploded into white chips. He jerked back, swearing, and ducked.

Kira grabbed two stones and threw them hard at the scree above his cover. The cascade went down with a sharp hiss, like boots moving fast. The archer stayed behind the rock.

“Lower slope shooter’s pinned,” she called, voice rough. “Not dead. If he gets to the channel, he can put arrows into anyone trying to clear him.”

An answer came from above. An arrow sparked off the boulder edge and bit into stone near her hip. Kira dropped lower, daggers up, breath hot and angry.

She couldn’t see the whole fight, but she could hear it. The ridge was learning the rhythm of the ravine floor. That was bad. It also meant some of the east shooters were turning away from her.

Good.

She still had to keep them looking.

Kira rose, fired the cracked arrow into open scree, and shouted, “East ridge! You missed! My dog shoots better than that, and he’s dead!”

Two arrows came down fast. One struck the wall above her head. The other punched into the boulder and sent a shard of stone across her forearm.

“Fuck,” she hissed.

She used the moment. The ridge shooters were ducking, resetting, aiming by sound instead of sight. Kira slid low along the rock, boots scraping loose chips, and stopped behind the next boulder in the line.

“Cap,” she called, breath ragged, “I’m moving down the boulder line. If the lower slope’s clear, say so. If not, stay where you are and keep them busy. I’ve got one crooked arrow, two stones, and a leg that’s starting to swell.”

She checked the dead archer’s quiver. Still too few. Still too ugly. She took the last bad arrow, snapped the ruined fletching, and nocked it anyway.

It wasn’t a weapon. It was noise.

From the ridge, a figure stood too long behind a slab. Kira fired. The arrow skipped off stone and struck the man’s boot. He stumbled, dropped behind cover, and yelled at the ledge.

“That’s right,” Kira muttered. “Stay down.”

Then movement below and left caught her eye.

Not ridge movement.

A shape broke from behind a fallen boulder, low and fast, moving toward the open lane between the third rock and the ravine floor. No bow on his back. Sword in hand.

Kira’s mouth tightened.

“Flanker,” she said, too quiet for the order to matter.

She had no arrows left worth firing. The man was too close for a bad shot, and she couldn’t throw her daggers without being unarmed.

She waited until he passed the gap, then rose and charged.

Kira hit him sideways, shoulder into chest, daggers low. He gasped, stumbled, and swung. She took the blow on her forearm guard, gritting against the impact, and drove her left dagger into his hip.

He howled.

Kira kicked him down the slope and grabbed his sword before he could rise. For half a second she stood over him, thigh arrow grinding, breath tearing out of her.

Then she turned to the ridge.

“Still here!” she shouted, waving the stolen sword badly. “Still looking at me!”

She tossed the sword down the slope toward the open lane and slid behind the boulder.

“Cap,” she called, voice rough, “lower slope’s not clear. I took one with a sword, but the archer behind the slab might be moving again. If the lane’s open, I can drop to the floor. If it isn’t, I’m staying here.”

She nocked the last crooked arrow.

“Tell me which way I’m not dying.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Hold, Kira! Hold!" *I yell, seeing the flanker Kira took down was the one I'd been trying to pin. My polearm sweeps, knocking aside another bandit trying to reach the opening.* "One more minute! Then clear!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn’t wait for the lane to be confirmed. Waiting got people killed, and her thigh was already telling her she had made too many mistakes in one day.

She pressed her spine against the hot sandstone and looked at the broken arrow shaft in her leg. The cloth around it was dark, stiff, and sticky. She gritted her teeth, tested the angle, and hissed when the shaft shifted. Not deep. Not clean. Bad enough.

The east ridge was still moving. Too much noise for dead men, too little for a full charge. One of the archers had gone quiet behind the slab, and the lower-slope shooter was shifting again, trying to find a line on the retreat path. Kira caught the scrape of his boot before she saw him.

“Not there,” she muttered.

She nocked the last crooked arrow and fired without standing fully. The shaft wobbled, struck the rock face above the lower-slope archer, and exploded into chips. He flinched back behind cover, swearing at the ledge.

Kira grabbed one of the stones from her belt and threw it hard at the scree beside his perch. The cascade went down with a sharp rattle. The man ducked again.

“Good,” she snarled. “Stay low.”

She used the bow as leverage to rise, jaw clenched, thigh screaming. The open lane beyond the boulder line looked like a death sentence. The ravine floor was closer now, but not close enough. The fallen slab to her left gave her a few more feet of shadow, and the dry channel beyond that might break a shooter’s line if she could reach it.

Kira moved low along the rock, daggers up, one hand brushing stone. The ridge answered with an arrow that sparked off the slab above her head. Stone chips cut her cheek. She spat blood and kept moving.

“Still here!” she shouted, though the words were half curse, half warning. “Still ugly! Still looking at me!”

She reached the fallen slab and dropped behind it, breathing hard. The lower-slope archer was still pinned, but the east ridge was learning the angle. If they shifted left, they could catch the retreat lane. If they shifted right, they could catch the ledge line. Either way, she was exposed.

Kira checked her remaining stone. She checked the crooked arrow still in her quiver. She checked her leg.

“Cap,” she called, voice rough, “I’m behind the fallen slab. Lower-slope shooter’s still pinned, but not dead. If that lane’s open, I’m moving. If not, I’m staying here and making them waste arrows.”

She pressed her back to the stone, daggers close, breath hot and angry.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Fall back, Kira! Now!" *I shout, seeing a clear path. The last of the ambushers on my side are falling or fleeing.* "We're clear!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira spat a curse and shoved off the boulder. "East ridge—copy that." The scree slope offered shit for cover, but that was the point. She needed eyes on her, not west. She broke into a sprint, boots sliding on loose shale, daggers held tight against her forearms to keep the blades from catching light.

An arrow punched into the ground a handspan from her ankle. Another whistled overhead, close enough to ruffle her hair. She jinked left, then right, keeping her center low. "Yeah, that's right—look at me, you shitheads!" she shouted up at the ridge.

She spotted a half-buried pillar of weathered stone ten yards ahead and dove for it, hitting the dirt hard. Pebbles tore at her cheek. From the new angle, she could see two archers clearly—dark leather, drawn bows, tracking for her head. There were more shapes moving behind them, silhouetted against the sky.

"Four confirmed east, maybe five!" she yelled. "They're adjusting—if you're moving, move now before they split their fire!"

She grabbed a fist-sized rock from the rubble and hurled it upslope, clattering against the ridge face. The sound drew another arrow instantly, striking wide. She grinned, nasty and sharp. Good. They were angry. Distracted.

She edged around the pillar, daggers ready, looking for a path up.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I nod, a grim set to my jaw.* "Alright, vanguard, you heard the lady! Push hard!"

*I surge forward, polearm held ready, eyes scanning the western ridge for movement.* "Stay low, keep moving!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the shift in the valley before she saw it—shouts rising from the west, the rhythm of the ambush faltering. The archer above her leaned out, attention pulled toward the noise, and his next shot went wide of her pillar by a full yard. They were dividing their focus. Good. But if they reoriented completely, she'd lose her window and end up hugging this rock while the real fight happened without her.

She needed height, now.

A vertical seam split the ridge face ten feet to her left, choked with dead brush and loose scree—a chimney, steep as hell and offering shit for cover, but it led to the archers' blind side. "Fuck me," she muttered. She sheathed her left dagger, kept the right bare, and launched from behind the pillar.

Arrows punched into the ground where she'd been, kicking up dust. She hit the chimney and climbed, fingers clawing into cracks, boots scraping for purchase on crumbling stone. Halfway up, a sentry appeared at the ridge lip, spear leveled down at her. He drew breath to shout.

Kira hurled her dagger. The blade caught him in the throat, silencing the cry before it left his lips. He toppled backward and disappeared.

She didn't slow. Her shoulders burned as she hauled herself over the edge, gravel tearing at her palms. Three archers stood in a loose line not twenty feet ahead, bows drawn, firing down into the ravine. Backs turned.

One started to turn.

Kira yanked her second dagger free and charged.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn't slow. The turning archer managed half a step before she drove into him, slamming her dagger deep into his side. She rode his body down, yanked the blade free, and surged toward the second bowman.

That one had his string drawn, arrow angled down toward the valley. Toward Captain.

"Fuck that," she snarled.

She threw herself across the last few feet and hit him shoulder-first. The bow discharged with a sharp snap, the arrow punching into the scree at the ridge's lip. They crashed sideways into the third archer. Kira came up slashing, fast and ugly, and felt her blade catch the second man high in the chest. He gurgled and folded.

The third man scrambled back, ditching his bow and hauling out a hatchet. Kira squared up, dripping dagger loose in her hand, and spat blood onto the stone. "Your turn, you shithead."

She kept low, watching his wrists, waiting for the opening. The east ridge was hers for the moment, but she couldn't see the west ridge anymore, couldn't tell if the fire had shifted off Captain's team. All she could do was keep these bastards busy and hope it was enough.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I parry an arrow with my polearm, the shaft splintering.* "Looks like Kira's making good time on the east. Let's not be outdone!"

*I push harder up the western slope, looking for their archers.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn't wait for the hatchet-man to set his feet. She darted left, baiting another overhead swing, then slipped right and sank her dagger into the gap between his neck and shoulder. She twisted, kicked his legs out, and let him fall. "Stay down," she growled.

Breathing hard, she swept her gaze along the ridge. Four hostiles down, no more bows drawn on this side. The immediate threat on the east was dead. But the valley still echoed with combat—shouts and ringing steel from the west, muffled by the ravine walls. She couldn't see who was winning, and that gnawed at her.

"East is clear!" she shouted, raw-throated, hoping the words carried. She retrieved her thrown dagger from the sentry's throat, wiped the blade on his tunic, and spotted a coil of hemp rope piled near a dead campfire—these bastards' climbing gear. She cut a length and lashed it around a waist-high boulder. If anyone needed to get up here in a hurry, they had a line.

A sharp horn blast cut through the noise from the west. Three short notes. Enemy signal? Withdrawal? She couldn't tell. She gripped her daggers tighter, eyes scanning the ridgeline for movement, ready for whatever came over the crest. She needed orders, or she needed another target. Sitting still made her itch.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira spotted Captain across the ravine, isolated on a scree shelf halfway up the west wall. The vanguard had vanished into the dust and noise below, and above him, she counted at least three hostiles picking their way down through the brush beneath a jagged overhang. They had the angle. They had the patience.

"Son of a bitch," she spat. The gap was twenty feet of empty air at best, the walls sheer and crumbling. No crossing. Not from here.

She grabbed a loose stone from the ridge floor and hurled it across the chasm. It struck the west wall above the hostiles with a sharp crack, echoing through the ravine. Another followed, wider, splintering dead brush. Noise was all she could send him.

"Hey! Over here, you shit-stained cowards!" she roared.

She didn't wait to see if they took the bait. Kira sheathed her daggers and snatched up the coil of rope she'd lashed to the boulder, slinging it over her shoulder. She ran north along the ridge edge, boots skidding on loose shale, eyes raking the ravine below. The walls slumped closer a hundred yards ahead where the stream had undercut the stone. Maybe a ledge. Maybe a trunk wedged in the narrows. Maybe a way down that didn't break her legs.

Another horn blast sounded from the west, deeper in the valley, long and mournful. She pressed against a tilted slab, chest heaving, and checked the west wall again. The hostiles above Captain had frozen in place, hugging the overhang. Not advancing. Not retreating. Holding.

"Cap, three hostiles above you, using the overhang!" she shouted, her voice tearing raw across the stone. "They're holding position—looks like they're waiting on you to move. I'm looking for a crossing!"

She scanned the drop below her boots. Nothing looked friendly. Every second she spent searching was a second she wasn't there. It gnawed at her gut.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood, Kira! Keep looking!" *I see the three hostiles above me, but I'm more focused on the archer I'm currently fighting.* He drops his bow and draws a short sword. *I grin. This is more my style.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw Captain turn to face the archer across the gap, the two of them closing on the scree shelf in a brutal, distant struggle she couldn't touch. Then movement snapped her eyes back to the overhang. The three hostiles above Captain had begun to move, creeping down the scree while his back was to the slope.

"Shit," she hissed. Distance was going to kill him if she didn't close it.

She tore her gaze away and ran. The ridge narrowed ahead, the ravine walls drawing closer as the stream cut deeper. Thirty yards on, a vertical gully spilled down to the water—a channel carved by runoff, choked with dead brush and loose stone. No gentler path offered itself.

Kira didn't slow. She looped the rope around her forearm, gripped the rock lip, and dropped into the gully. Her boots skidded on gravel, and she slid half the descent, catching herself on snarled roots and stone outcrops. A branch raked her forearm. She barely felt it.

She hit the ravine floor ankle-deep in the stream, icy water shocking her legs. The west wall loomed, sheer and rotten. But twenty yards south of Captain's position, she spotted a diagonal seam in the stone—a series of broken ledges climbing toward the overhang from below. It was a shit climb. It was the only climb.

Kira splashed toward it, daggers bouncing at her hips, and grabbed the first handhold. "Hold on, Cap," she breathed, hauling herself up. "Just hold on."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I parry a wild swing from the archer, disarming him.* "Looks like you picked the wrong fight, friend." *I glance up to see Kira beginning her ascent. Good. Just a little longer.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira's fingers found the next ledge, and the stone groaned under her weight, grit raining into her eyes. She blinked it away and hauled herself up another foot. The seam was worse than it looked from below—crumbling, shallow, and stinking of rot and birdlime. Her left boot slipped on moss-slick rock and her knee slammed into the wall hard enough to make her vision swim. "Fucking—" She bit the curse off and kept climbing.

The broken ledges offered barely enough room for her toes. Fifteen feet up, she caught the scuff of boots on scree directly above. The overhang jutted out like a broken tooth, and beneath its shadow she saw the legs of the three hostiles. They'd stopped creeping. One of them crouched at the lip, arm drawn back, readying a jagged chunk of stone.

No time for stealth. Kira reached up, snatched a loose rock from a crevice, and hurled it at the nearest man's knee. It struck with a wet crack. He cried out and buckled, skidding on loose shale. The other two whipped around, faces pale and angry in the dim light beneath the rock.

"Up here, you cowards," Kira snarled.

She lunged, catching the ledge lip with her left hand. Her right dagger cleared its sheath. The closest hostile stabbed downward with a shortsword, and she twisted her shoulders hard, letting the blade spark off the stone beside her ear. The impact shuddered through her forearm. She swung her body inward, kicked off the wall, and hooked her elbow over the edge. For a heartbeat she hung there, exposed, before she drove her dagger into the man's thigh.

He screamed and staggered back. Kira hauled herself onto the shelf, rolling into a crouch. Two hostiles still standing, between her and the drop. She kept her center low, daggers up, breathing ragged. "Alright," she spat. "Who's next?"

Steel rang somewhere below the overhang, echoing off the ravine walls, but she didn't dare look down. The two remaining swordsmen crowded her, trying to pin her against the long drop at her back. She circled left, boots scraping on treacherous scree, watching their wrists. The footing here was shit—first misstep meant a long fall. But at least the bastards on this slope had their eyes on her now, not the shelf below. She feinted high, dipped low, and waited for one of them to overreach.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I finish off the archer, kicking his body away from me.* "Good riddance." *I see Kira engage the hostiles above me. She's a force of nature.* "Show 'em what you're made of, Kira!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard Captain’s voice rise from the shelf below, raw and carrying, but she didn’t have breath to answer. The swordsman on her left took the bait—lunging low, blade slicing for her ribs. She slipped inside his reach, gravel spraying under her boots, and drove her right dagger up under his jaw. The blade punched deep. She twisted, yanked it free, and shoved him backward. His heel caught the lip of the shelf and he vanished over the edge, stone crunching in his wake.

The second hostile screamed something wordless and swung overhead, a two-handed chop meant to split her skull. “Fuck off,” she snarled, dropping to one knee inside his arc. The sword whistled past her ear. She rammed her left dagger into his groin, then her right into his side as he doubled over. He staggered, and she kicked his legs out from under him, sending him crashing onto the scree. A quick slash across the throat ended it.

Silence on the shelf, except for her own ragged breathing and the distant clash below. She rose, spitting blood—must have bit her cheek somewhere in the scramble. Her shoulder throbbed where she’d slammed the wall. She wiped her blades on the nearest corpse and scanned the overhang. Nothing but dead men and circling dust.

She edged to the drop and risked a look down. The scree shelf below was too blind from this angle to see clearly, but the archer lay motionless. “Overhang is clear!” she shouted, her voice cracking across the ravine. “West ridge hostiles are down!”

She kept low, daggers bare, eyes tracking the ridgeline above for any new silhouettes. The rope she’d dropped dangled in the gully, useless unless someone needed a fast exit. “Standing still up here feels like begging for an arrow,” she muttered. She needed to know if the valley was secure, or if there was another target to kill. “Cap, status? Give me something to do.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Looks like the vanguard's got 'em routed! Fall back to the ravine floor, Kira! We'll regroup there." *I sheath my polearm, a satisfied grin on my face.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn't need to be told twice. She spat to clear the blood from her bitten cheek, sheathed her daggers, and turned toward the gully. The rope she'd secured earlier still hung against the stone, the knot at the boulder holding firm. She grabbed the line, looped it around her forearm for control, and kicked off the shelf. Her boots scraped and bounced down the crumbling wall, grit showering the stream below.

She hit the water hard, ankle-deep and splashing, and pressed her back against the ravine wall. The shelf above was silent now, nothing shifting up there but dust and settling pebbles. She moved south along the stream bed, keeping low, her hand never straying far from her dagger hilts. The valley still carried the sound of steel and shouting, but it had thinned—broken into isolated pockets further down the pass, growing quieter by the breath.

Kira reached the designated regroup point, a cluster of weathered boulders at the ravine's belly, and tucked herself behind the largest one. From there she had eyes on both slopes. The east ridge was clear, and the west overhang was dead. But the ravine walls still loomed thirty feet high on either side, and anyone with a bow and patience could pin them down again if they lingered.

"High ground is ours for now," she called out, her voice rough from shouting. "But this place is still a fucking deathtrap. We need to move before someone else decides to occupy those ridges." She wiped grime from her neck with a bloody sleeve and checked her daggers, making sure the edges hadn't dulled on stone. Her shoulder throbbed where she'd slammed into the wall, and the cut on her forearm had soaked her sleeve dark. She'd live. She kept her eyes up, scanning the ridgelines, waiting for the others to close in.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Agreed, Kira. Let's not linger in this cozy little ambush spot." *I stride over to the cluster of boulders, surveying the surroundings.* "Is everyone accounted for?"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira straightened from the boulder, her shoulder throbbing as she did a quick headcount through the settling dust. Four of the vanguard were upright, though one dragged a bad leg and another clutched a bloody rag to his scalp. A fifth lay facedown near the stream, half-submerged, armor catching the dim light. She didn't see the young spearman who'd been flanking east.

"Four standing that I can see," she said, her voice raw. "One down by the water, not moving. Missing the kid with the red scarf—if he's still up on that ridge, he needs a rope or a grave." She kept her eyes pinned to the ridgelines above, watching for any shift of silhouettes against the sky. The horn notes still itched at her spine. "That signal didn't sound like panic. Sounded like coordination. Whoever they are, they might be regrouping."

She spat to clear the copper taste from her bitten cheek and tested her weight on her bruised knee. It held. "This ravine is still a fucking deathtrap. We need to move the wounded out before whoever blew that horn comes back with numbers." She drew her right dagger, checked the edge with a bloody thumb, and shoved it home. "I can scout ahead up the ravine, or I can watch our six while the vanguard hauls the injured. Your call. But sitting here inventorying bodies feels like asking for a second volley."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Damn. Alright, Kira. You scout ahead. Take point. Vanguard, get the wounded moving. We're not leaving anyone behind." *I turn to the men.* "Anyone seen the kid with the red scarf?"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira jerked her chin in acknowledgment. "On it," she said, and broke for the ravine's east wall where the shadows ran deepest. She kept low, boots testing each step on the loose shale before committing her weight. Her daggers stayed bare in her hands, blades angled downward so they wouldn't flash in the dim light. Every few yards she paused, shoulder pressed to the cold stone, eyes raking the ridgelines above and the tumbled boulders ahead.

The ravine pinched narrower fifty yards up, the stream vanishing beneath a choke field of house-sized rocks. Kira cursed softly. Natural fortification. If anyone held those boulders, the whole ravine became a shooting gallery. She scanned the gaps between the stones, watching for bowstrings or the shift of a silhouette. Nothing moved, but the silence felt brittle, stretched too thin after the fighting behind her.

She spotted a glint of metal near the base of the boulder field. A spear—snapped near the head, the haft splintered. Red wool tangled around the break. Blood darkened the fabric, though not enough to mean death. The scree around it showed scrape marks, shallow but clear, cutting west toward a narrow cleft in the ravine wall. A gap barely wide enough for a man to pass through sideways.

"Fuck me," she muttered.

She crept closer, staying below the ridgeline sightlines, and knelt beside the broken spear. The drag marks led into that cleft. Shadows swallowed the gap entirely. She couldn't see more than three feet inside.

Kira straightened, keeping her center low, and swept her gaze across the boulder field above the gap. No movement. No sound except the distant shuffle of the vanguard behind her and the thin trickle of water. Her gut churned. "Found the kid's spear," she called back, keeping her voice tight and pitched to carry. "Broken, blood on the scarf, but not much. Looks like he was dragged into a cleft in the west wall. Could be a prisoner, could be bait in a fucking trap." She shifted her weight, daggers loose in her grip, and studied the dark opening. "I can check it, but if they've got a blade to his throat in those shadows, I need numbers, not stealth. Your call."

She edged another step toward the boulder field anyway, positioning herself where she could dive for cover if the cleft spat out arrows. Her shoulder throbbed against her leathers. She ignored it and watched the gap, waiting.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "A trap, you say?" *I grip my polearm, my eyes narrowing at the cleft.* "Alright. Vanguard, leave the wounded for a moment. With me! We're going in." *I nod to Kira.* "You lead the way, Kira. We'll be right behind you."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira gave a short, sharp nod.

“East ridge. Fine. Try not to get me killed while I’m making noise.”

She didn’t wait for anything else. One hand snagged a loose stone from the dirt, and she hurled it hard against the rock face farther down the ravine. The crack echoed, sharp and convincing. Then she broke from the boulder in a sprint, staying low, boots scraping over gravel as she angled toward the eastern wall.

“Come on, you ugly bastards!” she shouted, slashing one dagger across a stone as she ran. Sparks jumped. “Shoot at me, or are your mothers ashamed?”

Arrows snapped after her. One sparked off the rock near her shoulder. Another punched into the ground at her heels. She cursed through her teeth and twisted her path, using broken cover—slabs, dead scrub, a shallow wash where the shadows lay thick.

On the east ridge, shapes shifted. Archers leaned from cover, bows drawn, attention dragging toward her.

“Six visible,” Kira called out, breath tight but steady. “Two more behind that split boulder. They’re repositioning south. If the west push stalls, they’ll enfilade it.”

She dropped behind a fallen chunk of cliff face as another volley hissed down. Stone chips sprayed her cheek.

“Fuck,” she muttered, wiping grit from her face. “They’ve got range, but the angle’s bad once they move south. Keep them pinned and they’ll have to expose themselves.”

One dagger stayed ready in her grip. The other she reversed low, blade out, waiting for the next opening.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I ignore Kira's colorful commentary, focusing on the western ridge.* "Alright boys, let's clear these rats out!" I bellow, pushing forward with the vanguard. My polearm is ready, its tip glinting in the limited light of the ravine.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the captain’s bellow roll down the ravine and bared her teeth.

“About damn time,” she muttered.

She surged up from behind the fallen slab and ran hard toward the east ridge, keeping her shoulders hunched and her stride uneven. Another arrow hissed past her ribs. She flinched but didn’t slow, boots skidding on loose scree as she slid behind a cracked spur of rock.

“Over here, you blind bastards!” she shouted, rapping one dagger against the stone. The sharp clang carried up the ravine. “Or do you need me to draw you a picture?”

The east ridge answered with movement. Two archers rose from behind a ledge, bows lifting. A third appeared farther south, trying to angle around the split boulder she’d marked earlier.

Kira’s eyes narrowed.

“They’re committing south,” she called toward the western side of the ravine. “Two moving to flank. If your push stalls, they’ll get arrows into your flank before you’re halfway up.”

She couldn’t spare a glance to see how the vanguard was faring. All she had were sounds: boots on rock, shouted orders, the rasp of steel, the heavy echo of the captain’s advance. Her job was simpler and stupider: keep the east ridge looking at her.

She grabbed another stone and hurled it wide, then broke cover again. The trick worked. One archer tracked the movement and loosed too early. The shaft slammed into the dirt behind her. Another snapped against the rock at her hip height, sending a sting of grit across her thigh.

“Fuck

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
“—fuck!” The word ripped out of Kira as she saw one of the east-ridge archers shift his aim away from her. The man’s shoulders set. The bowstring came back to his cheek. The line of the arrow pointed toward the captain.

Kira broke from cover without waiting for a better plan.

“Archer!” she roared. “High right—draw on you!”

She snatched a loose stone from the ground and hurled it hard toward the ledge. At the same time, she raked one dagger across the rock beside her, sending a bright spray of sparks jumping into the gloom. The noise and flash were cheap, ugly, and exactly the sort of thing that made a man flinch if he wasn’t disciplined.

The archer flinched.

His release spoiled. The arrow snapped loose with a harsh twang and whipped into the ravine wall, striking stone somewhere above the floor with a sharp crack.

Kira didn’t stop to enjoy it. She was already moving, boots sliding over scree as she cut sideways toward a shallow wash. Another shaft punched into the dirt behind her. A second hissed past close enough to tug at her sleeve.

“Shit,” she breathed, shoulders hunching as she dropped low behind a broken slab. “They’re getting pissed.”

She risked a glance upward. The east ridge was stirring now. Two more shapes shifted near the split boulder, trying to work south along the lip. Their bows were up, but the angle was tightening. They would have to lean out to keep her in view, and if the western push kept pressure on them, they would have to choose between shooting her or holding their cover.

“South pair’s still loose!” Kira shouted toward the captain’s side of the ravine. “If you take the lower shelf, they’ll have to expose themselves to track you. Don’t let them settle!”

Another arrow sparked off the slab above her. Stone chips rained down into her hair.

“Come on, then!” she snarled, slapping her dagger against the rock. “Look at me, you half-blind bastards!”

She rose just enough to be seen, then dropped again as two more shots snapped toward her position. Her heart hammered, but her breathing stayed controlled. She had their attention. Now she just had to keep it without getting herself full of arrows.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
(OOC: I didn't see the archer target me directly, my bad.)

*I parry an incoming arrow with my polearm, the shaft splintering against the steel.* "Focus on the west, Kira! We'll handle the south flank." I yell, pushing harder up the slope.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the order and didn’t waste breath arguing.

“West it is,” she muttered, teeth bared. “I’ll keep the east honest.”

She shoved off the slab and ran in a low, broken sprint, dragging one dagger’s point along the rock as she moved. The scrape rang out, harsh and ugly, and a shower of sparks skipped into the dimness. Another arrow struck where she’d been half a heartbeat before, biting into the dirt with a dull thud.

“Over here!” she shouted. “Come on, then!”

She cut hard toward a shallow wash, boots skidding on loose stone. A shaft snapped past her shoulder. Another clipped the edge of a dead scrub and sent dry branches rattling. Kira dropped into the wash, shoulder slamming into the bank, and cursed as gravel rained down on her.

Above her, the east ridge was waking up properly now. She could hear them moving, boots grinding on rock, low voices snapping back and forth. Two shapes stayed near the split boulder. Two more had shifted farther south, trying to get a better angle without silhouetting themselves against the sky.

Kira snatched up two stones, then rose just enough to be seen.

“Hey!” she yelled, and hurled one stone wide to the left. It cracked against a slab and echoed sharp. At the same time, she slashed the other dagger across the bank beside her, throwing more sparks.

One archer loosed at the sound. The arrow went wide. The second hesitated.

Good enough.

She dropped again and scrambled along the wash, staying below the sightline. Her breath came harder now, but her hands were steady.

“South pair’s still loose!” she called toward the western side of the ravine. “They’ll have to lean out to track anything moving low! If they settle behind that cut, they’ll get clean shots!”

Another arrow thudded into the bank above her. Dirt spilled over her hair.

“Fucking hell,” she hissed, wiping grit from her mouth.

She risked a quick look up. The southern archers were edging along the ridge, bows half-drawn, trying to find something worth shooting. The angle was bad for them, but only as long as they stayed cautious. If they got bold, they’d start finding gaps in the cover below.

Kira reversed one dagger, kept the other ready, and measured the distance to the next slab.

“Don’t let them settle,” she growled, more to herself than anyone else. “Keep their heads down, or they’ll make a mess of the west side.”

She slapped her blade flat against the rock once, hard, then broke from the wash in another sharp sprint.

“Come on, you cowards!” she shouted. “Look at me!”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira’s boot checked on the gravel as she came up from the wash and the shape of the fight turned ugly.

Across the ravine, the vanguard’s line had stretched too thin. The captain was no longer shoulder-to-shoulder with the shields, no longer folded into the push. There was open stone around that position, too much of it, and Kira was on the wrong side of the killzone with arrows still coming down from the east.

“Fuck,” she hissed.

The distance might as well have been a

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I curse under my breath as an archer on the western ridge gets a clear shot.* I deflect the arrow with my polearm, but it stings my arm. "Hold the line!" I yell, trying to rally the scattered vanguard.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw the western archer settle into a clean line and her gut went cold.

From where she was, there was no way across the ravine in time. No route. No cover that would hold. No chance of putting a blade into that bow before the shot came. All she had was noise, movement, and the east ridge still trying to pin her.

“West bow! Clear line!” she roared, the warning tearing out of her.

Then she threw herself out of the wash.

Not toward safety. Across it. Low, fast, ugly. Both daggers came down hard on the rock as she ran, scraping a shriek of steel that bounced off the ravine walls. Sparks spat into the gloom. She kicked a loose plate of shale and sent it skidding and cracking across the stone.

“Here!” she shouted. “Look here, you shit-eating cowards!”

The east ridge took the bait.

A bowstring twanged. An arrow slapped rock beside her hip. Another hissed past her jaw close enough to make her teeth ache. Kira twisted, dropped a shoulder, and came up behind a narrow spur of stone with her breath burning.

Good. Let them waste shafts on her.

She risked a glance upward. The two archers by the split boulder had leaned out too far, eager for a clean kill. The southern pair were still edging, trying to find the western fight, but their heads were turning toward her noise now.

“South pair’s still loose!” Kira called toward the far side. “They’ll settle if the pressure drops!”

She yanked one dagger free and jammed its point into a crack in the cliff face, hauling herself up a few feet. Boots scrabbled on stone. She made herself a hard, moving target, just enough to look like she meant to climb.

An arrow punched into the rock beneath her boot. Stone bit her knuckles.

“Fuck!” She dropped back down and rolled behind the spur as two more shots came in quick succession.

Her heart hammered. Her palms were slick. She wiped them on her sleeve and gripped the daggers again.

She couldn’t reach the far side. Couldn’t take the western archer. But she could make the east ridge stupid.

Kira snatched another stone, hurled it wide, then slapped her blade flat against the rock.

“Come on!” she snarled. “Shoot at me, you useless bastards!”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I see Kira making herself a target, and it makes my gut clench.* "Push! Don't let them pin her!" I bellow, parrying another arrow. The vanguard needs to advance, or Kira's sacrifice will be for nothing.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The shout from the far side reached Kira through the ravine’s echo, thin and hard against the rattle of falling stone.

She did not waste breath answering with comfort.

“Then keep them frightened!” she yelled back, even though the walls chewed her words into noise before they could carry far.

Kira surged up from behind the spur and made herself ugly to look at. Not a clean target. Not a brave one. She ran bent low, shoulders rolling, boots sliding over gravel as she dragged both daggers along the rock in a ragged, shrieking scrape. Sparks spat up in short orange bursts. Loose chips flew. The sound was enough to set teeth on edge.

Two bows answered from the east ridge.
