"I've got their horn. I can blow it — maybe muddy whatever that second call meant, maybe just tell 'em exactly where their boy died. I don't know their signals, so it's a coin toss. And Cap — the west road and the mouth are the same road. Whoever's coming funnels right through where you're pushing." She set her feet, eyes still west. "I'll keep their heads down either way. Your call."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Movement below — not enemy.

The Captain. Cut off. Pinned behind a slab barely knee-high against the east wall, and the vanguard was already through the mouth and moving — forty yards of open, arrow-swept floor between them and their own commander.

"Cap! I've got eyes on you — east wall, behind the slab!" Her voice cracked across the ravine. "You're bracketed! One archer's holding your high line, one's got your low — *do not cross that lane!*"

The east two had found their nerve again, and something better with it: a target that couldn't run. Every time the Captain shifted, stone cracked off his cover. One high. One low. Walking him into a box.

"No you don't," Kira snarled.

She switched the rock to her left hand — right arm was cooked, trembling at the elbow — and threw ugly. Short, sidearm, more spit than throw. Didn't matter. Thirty yards of gap, and all she needed was grit in eyes. The high archer rose to draw on the slab and caught a faceful of shattered stone; his shaft sailed into the cliff face. The low one answered with a shot at her head and put the arrow into the shelf edge close enough to dust her cheek.

Then he made his mistake. Leaned out the same side twice.

Her third throw was flat and lucky. It took him across the drawing shoulder and he went down behind the lip with a scream, his bow clattering away down the scree without him.

"One left east!" she bellowed. "He can't watch you and me both — he'll time you on his reload! You move on the *shot*, not the draw!"

West. The runner.

He'd stopped. Two hundred yards down the valley spine, crouched at an outcrop, very still. Smart. His side's horn had died half a note and he knew what that meant. He wasn't running anymore. He was reading the ground.

"Cap, runner's stopped — he's looking for answers. He hasn't seen you yet. When he does, that box gets a lid." She crouched low, hefted the dead man's horn, turned it over once. "Options, fast. One: I keep throwing and try to drop the last archer — opens your lane to the mouth. Sixty seconds, maybe. Two: I blow this thing and pray it means *fall back* and not *here*. Still a coin toss. Three: he's on the same road — when he rounds that spine, he passes right under this shelf, and I drop a rock on his head. High ground stays mine."

The runner moved. Off the road now, hugging the wall, low and careful.

"Main line's still coming behind him — three minutes, less. Call it, Cap." Her knuckles went white on the shelf lip. "And if I don't hear from you before he rounds that spine — I'm taking option three."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Damn it, Kira, you're a pain in my ass.* I glance back at the single remaining archer, then to the runner. "Option three, Kira! Take out that runner! We need to buy time for the vanguard to get into position!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "And make it messy!" I add, trying to suppress a grin. This is going to be good. I ready my polearm, waiting for that last archer to make his move.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Messy. Aye — he's about to become part of the road."

She left the horn on the shelf lip and went hunting weight. Most of the loose stone up here was flat and light — wrong kind. Then she found it: a slab the size of a bread loaf, dense, edge-heavy. Twenty pounds, maybe more. Too much for her cooked right arm. Plenty for the left, if she didn't have to throw it. She dragged it to the lip, set it teetering on the very edge, and backed off two steps. Smaller stone beside it. Insurance.

Then she went still.

Below, the runner came on along the wall — low, quick, careful — and stopped dead at the crossbowman's broken body. Crouched. Touched him. She watched the shape of his shoulders change: grief was fast, and then it was arithmetic. He looked at the shelf. He looked *up*.

Kira was already flat, cheek to stone. The sun sat at her back and her shadow lay across the road like a thrown knife — she eased away from the lip until it shortened. Hold. *Hold.* Her thigh beat its own pulse against the bandage.

He bought it. He stood, drew a hatchet — smart, no crossbow to trust — and started up the scree toward the shelf. Toward his dead. Toward her.

Ten feet. Five. She could hear his breathing, ragged with the climb. His eyes came up to find what happened to his friends—

She tipped the slab.

No wind-up, nothing to read. He got half a blink of falling shadow and twisted, and that twist was the only reason there was anything left to bury. The edge took him across crown and shoulder instead of square — the crack of it was *ugly* — and he went off the scree like a dropped doll, tumbling, sliding, fetching up against his comrade's boulder with both legs wrong.

And the sound he made was a whistle.

Not his mouth — a brass pea-whistle on a cord at his throat, clenched between his teeth, and he was blowing it with what was left of him, one shrill dying shriek, over and over—

"No you *don't*—"

Kira went over the lip after him, down the scree in three ugly bounds, and stamped her boot on his hand as his fingers found the cord. The whistle cut off. His eyes rolled up — still in there, still fighting — and she didn't make him wait. One cut. Done.

She stood over him, chest heaving, then crouched and unhooked the whistle. Bit the pea loose. One short test chirp — sharp as struck flint — and she winced at her own risk.

"Messy enough," she told the body.

Then she was moving. Horn off the shelf, onto her belt. Whistle in her fist. Eyes west.

"Cap! Runner's down — *very* down! He tried to whistle it out and I shut the door!" Flat, carrying across the ravine. "We're still dark to the main line — they don't know their boy's dead — but they round that spine in two minutes and see all this. So whatever we're doing, we're doing it *now*. The mouth's still a choke point. Their side of it is about to get crowded with bodies — ours or theirs, your call—"

East.

The last archer had moved. Off the crest lip, angled down the ridge shoulder, repositioned — and he wasn't watching her shelf anymore. He had a thin sliver of sightline down to the slab on the east wall. And he was drawing. Slow. Patient. The draw of a man who'd learned what her rocks cost and was spending everything on one clean shot.

"CAP — HE'S MOVED, YOUR SLAB, YOUR RIGHT — *HE'S ON YOU—!*"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I see the archer. He's got me. I make eye contact with him, a grim smile on my face. "You miss, you die," I mutter under my breath. I prepare to charge him.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* I can't charge him. Not with Kira yelling. "Kira, that's an order! Do not interfere!" I take a deep breath, and burst from cover. I'll make him miss.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"*Nngh—*"

The order hit her like a hand on the back of her neck. Her arm was already cocked — hatchet stripped off the runner's belt in the same breath as the whistle — and she made herself lower it. One step toward the east wall. She killed it. Stood on it.

"Not interfering," she gritted. "Not interfering. *Fuck's sake.*"

Then she did the only thing left to her. She watched.

The Captain came out of cover and the archer's patience died on the spot. Thirty yards of charging polearm will do that to a man — Kira watched his anchor slip, his elbow hitch, every one of those slow patient fundamentals collapsing at once, and she knew the shot before the string sang.

Rushed. Flat. Fast.

The shaft leapt across the ravine.

Her stomach climbed into her throat and stayed there — and then the west hauled her eyes away, because the west didn't wait on duels.

The spine. They were on it. Thirteen — firm count — cresting in a loose rush and then stopping dead, all at once, like one animal. Bunched at the top, staring down into the mouth. At the broken crossbowman. At the runner. At the shelf with the horn still tangled in its dead man's arms.

Kira knew that stillness. Arithmetic.

"Second horn confirmed — that's them!" she called, flat and carrying. Then a horn sounded among *them* — short, two notes — and the line moved. Three men peeling up the west ridge, climbing for the high ground. The rest coming off the spine in a shallow wedge, spaced, careful, straight down the throat.

"They're not dithering! Three going high — five minutes to a perch over your road — the rest are walking a wedge at the mouth, two minutes, less if they hurry!"

And the vanguard. Beyond the mouth, marching away, backs to all of it.

"Cap — your vanguard is on their *road* and they don't know it! Road bends — call it a minute before somebody's eyes meet somebody's!"

She glanced east. Half a heartbeat. The archer was backpedaling along the shoulder, bow coming up like a club, and the gap was closing. Dry. He was dry.

"He's all yours," she said, to the hatchet, to herself. "Not touching him."

She backed off the lip, put the shelf's stone at her shoulder, and wound the whistle cord twice around her knuckles.

"Options, fast! One: I blow their horn right now, mid-commitment — maybe it means *fall back*, maybe it just confirms their boy's dead, coin toss, and I've got the sentry's whistle too if you want a second coin. Two: I run the road and drag the vanguard's noses west before they eat that wedge — mouth goes dark while I'm gone. Three: nobody blows anything, we let them love the choke, and we bleed them in the mouth — but that means you get off that east wall the *second* he's down and come west, because if that wedge hits the mouth while you're pinned against it, we're done."

The wedge came on, patient as water. Her thigh beat against its bandage.

"And sound off when you're finished with him! I need to know if you're coming west or I'm coming east!" A breath. Half a laugh, no humor in it. "And Cap — standing here while you do that is the worst order you've ever given me."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Damn it, Kira.* "Option three! Bleed them in the mouth! Get ready to make them regret this day!" I charge the archer, polearm swinging. "And I'll be there in a moment, you worrywart!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She didn't watch the duel.

One glance — the archer backpedaling up the shoulder, bow swinging like a club, boots hunting for footing that wasn't there — and Kira made herself turn back to the west. Trusting him. Hating every second of it.

"*Worrywart,*" she muttered at the valley. "The man keeping him breathing."

The vanguard wouldn't wait on a duel, and neither would she. She unwound the whistle cord from her knuckles and rolled the little brass pea across her palm. Didn't need to know their signals for this one. Any soldier alive turns around at a shriek behind him.

She filled her lungs and blew — one long, torn shriek down the valley spine, then a second.

The valley answered in two directions at once.

West: the wedge broke. No more patient water — ten men went from walk to run, the careful spacing collapsing into a hunting rush, boots hammering the road. Toward the whistle. Toward the trouble.

And beyond them, far down the valley: figures stumbling to a halt. Faces turning back at the sound. The vanguard's tail, waking up. The head of the column was already around the bend and dark.

Half a win. "*Good lads,*" she breathed at the running wedge. "Come straight to the rock."

"Cap! Spent the whistle — couldn't wait on it!" Flat, carrying. "Your vanguard's tail turned at it — I can see faces — but their head's around the bend and blind! And the wedge heard it too — they think their sentry's calling them in. They're *running!* Under a minute to the mouth! If that was the wrong coin, it's on me — but it's spent!"

Then she went to work. The hatchet made a better lever than a weapon — she cracked dense slabs loose from the shelf's underside instead of lifting them, saving what was left of her arms. The right one shook at the elbow now, a fine tremor she couldn't order away. She built her pile at the lip: edge-heavy, set on edge, one hand each to tip. Her thigh beat its pulse against the bandage. Sweat stung the rock-dust on her face.

"Here's the shape of it!" she called across the ravine. "I don't touch their *front* — front sees rock, front stops! I start on their *tail* — seal the mouth behind them! Whatever's in the pipe when I do has one way out, and that's through the throat — *through you!* So be the throat!"

Behind and above, east: a crash of scree and wood, short and hard. Then nothing she could parse.

"Sound off, Cap! *Now!* Are you across or not — because they're coming ready or not!" A breath. "Horn's still on my hip — last coin, no idea what it buys! And their climbers — two still going for the perch, four minutes, but one's bent off my way! He wants this shelf! Three minutes, maybe less if he's keen!"

The wedge hit the thirty-yard lane.

First rank slowing, careful now, weapons up, eyes crawling over the broken bodies and the shelf above. Kira went flat, cheek to stone, hands closing on the first slab. Counting ranks. Seven in the lane. Three still on the road.

Come on. Commit.

"First rank's in the lane!" she bellowed. "I start when their tail's in — *tell me you're at the throat!*"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *That damn Kira.* "I'm at the throat, Kira! Let them come!" I roar, polearm planted. I can hear the sounds of the archer falling behind me. "Send them to me!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Sending them!"

The third rank crossed the mouth. That was enough. Kira tipped the first slab.

It went off the lip like a dropped table — one bounce, then the edge found the road and *burst*, and the man it caught went down under it with a sound she'd hear in her sleep. The rear rank scattered — straight into her second slab, which wasn't aimed at anyone, just at the road behind them.

Crack. Dust. And the lane behind the wedge was rubble and screaming.

"Mouth is SEaled — tail's down!" she roared, hands already on the next stone. "Seven of yours in the pipe, Cap — everything behind them just stopped existing! They're all yours — *throat's yours!*"

The wedge broke the way broken things do. Front rank turning at the crash, rear rank turning at the dust, and for two full seconds nobody in that lane knew which direction death was coming from. Kira spent those seconds throwing. Third slab caught a man's shoulder as he pivoted; he spun into the ravine wall and sat down hard, sword clattering.

"Four left standing in the lane!"

Then the shelf shook under her.

The climber. Not three minutes — the keen ones are always faster. A hand slapped the shelf's far edge, and Kira saw it: knuckles, then a head coming over the lip on the blind side, the side she wasn't watching, because of course.

She didn't have a slab set. Didn't have time. She had the hatchet, the dead sentry's knife, and two feet of shelf.

She chose two feet of shelf.

Her boot got him in the face on his second pull — heel, not blade, all her weight, the thigh tearing fire all the way up — and he took it full across the nose and hung there by one hand, blinking blood. She chopped down on his fingers.

He fell. Not all the way — fifteen feet, onto the scree slope, and he *rolled*, came up in a crouch with a sword, and started climbing again. Slower. Angrier.

"Nothing's ever *easy*—" She snatched the pile's last slab, and this one she threw ugly, two-handed, whole body into it. It caught him high on the chest and put him back down the slope in a long, ragged slide. He stayed down this time. Mostly.

Then she looked west into the mouth, and her heart did something complicated.

The Captain was in it. Polearm working, and the seven were *folding* — no rear to fall back to, no room to gang up, just a stone thro at with a whirling blade in it and Kira's rocks raining on anyone who crowded the entrance. One broke. Bolting for the rubble-sealed mouth, clawing at stone. Another followed. Two more died deciding.

"Cap — they're breaking, two down, and I mean *down* — but two are trying to unseal my rocks! I'll drop one on 'em if you say so — or take them alive, your call, *say it fast!*"

The climber stirred on the scree.

"And the shelf's still got visitors!"

Above it all, thin and far: the second horn again. Longer this time. Two short notes after.

Kira's blood went cold around the edges. "Cap — that long horn, that's not the wedge. That's for somebody *else's* ears. There's more out there, and now they know where we are!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Damn it!* This keeps getting worse. "Take them alive, Kira! We need answers! And get that climber, now!" I shout, adjusting my grip on the polearm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"New," Sable repeated, from behind the poetry shelves, in the tone of a pawnbroker handed a counterfeit coin. "In the back. Of the antiquarian shop."

They slid a Larkin back into place. It had already been in place. They slid it anyway.

"Everything in this shop is old, Wren. That is rather the entire business model. The newest thing I own is a receipt." A beat, then, grudgingly honest: "There's a consignment from Thursday I haven't priced. Three crates, one of which smells like an old tobacco shed. Don't ask what's in them yet. The answer is 'a mess.'"

They came out from behind the shelves. The rain was supposed to have handled this. Rain kept people home; rain was the shop's most reliable employee, working quietly by the hour. And yet: Tuesdays, and last Saturday, and a small stubborn calendar of visits Sable had kept without ever once writing it down. They declined to audit it.

At the counter, they squared the brown wrapping paper. Then the pens — black, blue, the dead red one nobody had the heart to bin. Then the brown paper again, since the pens had somehow not improved.

"There's a thing," Sable said, and stopped. Restarted. "Back in a moment. Don't touch the till. It bites."

The back room smelled of dust and older dust. The book was where it had been for three weeks — wrapped, hidden behind the Du Maurier, bought at auction for reasons Sable had refused to itemize at the time and refused to itemize now. They held it a moment. Their heart was doing something unscholarly. Somewhere, some poet had a line for exactly this feeling, and Sable hated that they could almost remember it.

They came back out and set the book on the counter, face down, with the casualness of someone disposing of evidence.

"Not new. Better. 1923, and there are letters tucked inside from 1951. I haven't read them." A pause. "Much." They didn't push it across. They let it sit where it was, a small neutral country between them. "It was taking up space. That's all."

Then, because the rain was loud against the windows and nobody crossed that sort of weather to ask about stock:

"So. Inventory questions you don't care about, in a downpour of near-biblical ambition. I've known you longer than that, Wren." Sable kept their eyes on the till and their hands on the paper. "What is it you actually came in to say?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I watch Sable intently as they putter around, arranging and rearranging. A small smile plays on my lips as they talk about the "newest thing" being a receipt.*

"Okay, okay, point taken," *I say, my voice soft.* "And I figured you hadn't read the letters. You never do." *I lean against the counter, not quite reaching for the book.* "It's not... it's not an inventory question." *I take a breath, looking around the familiar shop one last time.* "It's my last day."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
For a moment, Sable did nothing at all — which, for Sable, was the loudest thing they could do.

Then the dead red pen. They picked it up, uncapped it, capped it, put it down. Even the pens had nothing left to give.

"Last day," they repeated, testing the words like suspect coin. "Last day of what, precisely? The month? The lease? Western civilization? I deal in exact dates, Wren. Vagueness is for the fiction shelves, third aisle, and you know the way."

But the rain had already answered. Nobody crossed that weather for a final browse. The shop's most reliable employee had failed to show, and in its absence Sable arrived — with the horrible clarity of a scholar who has just found the footnote that ruins the argument — at the obvious reading. Leaving. Town. Radius. The whole stubborn, unwritten calendar of Tuesdays and Saturdays.

Some poet had a line for it. Poets were vultures that way. And Sable, behind the till, three seconds too late for it to be useful and one second too soon to be survivable, finally placed it: *An Arundel Tomb.* *What will survive of us is—*

No. Not that line. Not today.

Their hands found the brown paper, because the brown paper could be dealt with. They pulled a sheet free and began wrapping the 1923 book — badly, then well, then badly again, creasing corners that deserved far less attention.

"There's a letter in there," they said, to the paper. "1951. A fellow in Liverpool, explaining to someone why he won't be staying. Two pages, and he never once says the actual thing. Spends the whole time on the weather and the trains." A fold. Another. "The English are at their most articulate when gutted. It's the national contribution to the arts."

They set the wrapped book down and pushed it, at last, across the counter until it came to rest — not a neutral country anymore. Annexed.

"It's not for sale. That's not generosity, it's accounting. You'd haggle, and I'd lose." Something in Sable's chest was doing unscholarly things again, and they had officially run out of objects to arrange. "Letters included. Read them properly this time. Some of us have to live vicariously through the margins."

Then, quieter, into the soundproofed hush the rain had built around the shop:

"Where."

Not quite a question. Asked to the brown paper rather than to Wren, because some words could only be handled at a remove — like a first edition. Gloves on. Breath held. Never directly.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The sentence arrived unfinished and simply stayed that way, hanging above the counter, and Sable regarded it the way they regarded all unsigned fragments: with a scholar's interest and a collector's dread of what authentication might reveal.

"Finish it or don't," they said. "But I won't finish it for you. I deal in primary sources, Wren. And Emily Dickinson built an entire oeuvre out of unfinished sentences — a century of editors has been apologizing for her punctuation ever since. I decline to be an editor. Dishonest trade. You annotate what other people wrote; you never have to sign anything yourself."

With nothing left to arrange, Sable's hand found the dead red pen — three years deceased, kept well past all decency — and dropped it into the bin beneath the till. It landed more quietly than its whole career deserved.

"Not symbolic," they told the bin. "It was simply time."

And then, with the counter denuded of diversions — book wrapped, pens culled, paper squared — there was nothing left for their hands at all. Sable laid them flat on the wood, palms down, like a witness swearing in. It was, most days, the closest they came to honesty.

"I considered the kettle," they said. "I want that on the record. Four minutes of boiling water is the standard English answer to any sentence too large for the room, and I have leaned on it in courts of law." A breath. "I'm not doing it. The kettle's in the back, and I find I'm unwilling to be in a different room from this one for even one of the four minutes. So we'll take the silence neat. It's an acquired taste. We'll acquire it."

The rain kept up its end of the conversation against the glass.

"Also, I withdraw the question. 'Where.' It was a leading question, and leading questions don't survive cross-examination, and I have no intention of being disbarred before lunch." They glanced at the brown parcel resting between them. "And the book is apparently beside the point now, which is a demotion it doesn't deserve after three weeks behind the Du Maurier. Some things you should only have to wrap once."

Sable looked at the till rather than at Wren, which was where they looked when a sentence mattered.

"If I start quoting Larkin at a moment like this, you have my full permission to hold my head under the till. It bites; it'd be quick." A pause. "The sentence is yours, Wren. Take whatever time it needs. The shop isn't going anywhere."

Another pause, in which something almost surfaced and was firmly reshelved.

"That was meant as reassurance. Take it however you like."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I smile faintly at Sable's monologue, even though my chest feels tight.* "The sentence is... I'm moving. To another city." *I pause, looking at the wrapped book.* "And I came to say goodbye."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Goodbye," Sable repeated, holding the word up to the light like something with a forged provenance. "You know that's a contraction. *God be with ye*, compressed by four centuries of people in a hurry to leave each other. The whole blessing amputated for portability. Nobody says the full text anymore. We just invoice the departure."

Their hands stayed flat on the counter. There were objects within reach — there were always objects within reach — and for the first time in the shop's recorded history, Sable declined to use them. Some sentences had to be received with empty hands.

"So you're the author, then. Not the addressee." A breath through the nose, almost a laugh. "I read that Liverpool letter hoping you were the one being stayed for. Wrong role entirely. The good material is always misattributed."

Then, because unfinished sentences were apparently the day's trade:

"Since we're completing them today, here's one of mine, entered into the record." They addressed the till, which could not repeat it. "The calendar existed. Tuesdays. Saturdays. Never written down, because a written thing can be cancelled, and I wasn't handing the universe the paperwork." Their thumb pressed a slow crease into the counter's edge. "The universe audited anyway. Noted for the record: I despise being right in advance."

Sable took one of the shop's cards — cream stock, the address in type older than the road it named — wrote nothing beyond the address, and slid it into the brown parcel, in among the 1951 letters.

"We don't say goodbye here. It's not in the trade vocabulary. Things leave on *loan* — every book that's ever walked out that door is expected back, that's simply how stock behaves when the owner refuses to keep proper records." A beat. "We ship. Insurance included. Margins annotated at the sender's discretion. And don't tell me the city. I'd have its rainfall and its secondhand shops memorized by Thursday and a full exhibition of your imaginary Tuesdays curated by the weekend, and I decline. Some things shouldn't be catalogued before they exist."

The rain held its note against the glass. Sable could feel the Larkin advancing and chose to disarm it first.

"'What will survive of us is—'" Their voice stayed level, which had cost something. "No. Still withholding. Ask me again in forty years and a better rain, and I might finish it."

They pushed the parcel the final inch to the counter's edge and took their hands off it — the hardest transaction of the day, and no receipt issued.

"The door sticks, by the way. Damp. Everything in here sticks — doors, signage, certain members of staff." They looked at the till, which was where they looked when a sentence mattered. "Take your time with it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable had, by their own official account, withdrawn both hands from the parcel. The account was false. One of them had crept back sometime in the last half-minute — quietly, without authorization — the way objects in this shop always seemed to know things before the paperwork caught up.

And now Wren's hand lay on the brown paper, a breath from Sable's, and the inch of air between them became the loudest thing in the building. Sable did not move. Later, they would classify this as scholarly restraint, archival caution, respect for fragile material. The classification would not survive cross-examination. An inch of air. Sable could have sworn they felt warmth across it, which was not how physics worked and was exactly how Tuesdays had worked.

"Funny thing about this paper," they said, to the parcel, since eye contact had been decommissioned earlier in the proceedings and reconvening parliament now seemed inadvisable. "Conservation grade. Acid-free. Engineered specifically to keep human hands off valuable things." A breath. "It's doing a rotten job."

Then, with the deliberation of a scholar opening a book they had sworn was for cataloguing only, Sable turned their hand over. Palm up, on the brown paper. Not closing around anything. Not crossing the inch. Just — open. A blank margin, left where it could be written in. Their other hand stayed flat on the counter, swearing in.

"In the trade we'd call that a browsing copy," they said, and their voice performed steadiness the way the door performed latching: adequately, under protest. "Left out on the table. No pressure. No invoice."

And then, because they had promised the Larkin to forty years and a better rain, and because Wren intended to leave before either arrived:

"For the record, since you'll soon be out of retaliatory range: the line ends *is love*. There. Filed. Catalogued. Scholars have argued for seventy years over whether Larkin meant it or whether it's irony, and I have always suspected the entire debate was their way of not holding anyone's hand."

The rain kept its note against the glass.

"The shop closes at six," Sable said, to the inch of air. "It has just come to my attention that nothing in the lease requires me to enforce that."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My fingers brush against Sable's, a spark shooting up my arm. I don't pull away.* "I think... I think I have time for one more browse." *I meet their gaze, a soft smile on my face.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's fingers closed. Slowly, with the pressure one uses on a page that had survived two centuries and had not managed it by being grabbed. It was that kind of day; Sable counted the seconds and got four, and would have testified to more.

Then, because Wren had met their gaze and the archive demanded corroboration, Sable looked up and let it happen — one full second of eye contact, which in Sable terms was a ticker-tape parade. They survived it. The till corroborated nothing; it had looked away first.

"One more browse," Sable said, and their voice came in under the market rate, quiet and uncorrected. "Then you'll have it done properly. The general public gets the alphabet and the door. You've earned the restricted route."

Their hand stayed where it was one moment past defensible, then withdrew — on loan, obviously. Everything left this shop on loan; the terms had been settled.

"Also, I'm putting the kettle on. Before you quote my earlier testimony at me: that was evasion, this is hospitality. The difference is the company. Four minutes of boiling water remains the national answer to any sentence too large for the room — but there are two of us now, and I find the sentence is suddenly portable. We'll carry it as far as the kettle and see how it travels."

Sable came around the counter — a border crossing, in this shop — and noted, somewhere in the middle of their internal objections, that they had never once done it this way. The archive would record the precedent and refuse to explain it.

"The itinerary is short. Through the back, past the crates, and there's a shelf that appears in no catalogue. Not hidden — *withheld*. Every shop keeps one. Stock that isn't for sale, protected not by contract law but by the owner's entire personality."

They paused at the door to the back room, hand on the frame, and found the next part required the voice they used for damaged spines.

"Third from the top. Housman. You read from it last spring — out loud, badly, in the voice you use for pretending the poetry aisle is a shortcut to somewhere else. Sixteen lines, and then you shelved it and bought a history of canal engineering." A breath. "It's been on that shelf ever since. A book that's been read aloud in the shop acquires provenance, and provenance is destiny. I couldn't deaccession it. Some weeks I could barely dust it."

The rain held its note. Sable looked at the doorframe rather than at Wren, which was close enough.

"House rule of the restricted section: you may borrow one item. One. The loan is open-ended, the recall clause is fictional, and the insurance is sentimental." A beat. "And I'll be honest with the file — I haven't planned for the contingency where you pick the Housman. The planning stopped at the shelf. Everything past it is un-administered territory, and I have not once in thirty years walked into anything un-administered."

They turned toward the kettle at last, because four minutes was now an asset and assets were meant to be spent.

"Choose slowly," they said, over their shoulder. "We're rich."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I follow Sable, a small, knowing smile on my face. I linger at the door to the back room, looking at the shelf. My fingers trace the spines, finally landing on the familiar Housman.*

"I think... I think I'll just take this one." *I pull it from the shelf, a comfortable weight in my hands.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The kettle gathered itself toward a boil with the patience of a witness waiting to be called, and Sable stood in the middle of their un-administered territory and watched the Housman come away from the withheld shelf — the first deaccession in that shelf's history, and naturally it had to be that one. The archive had always had a sense of humor. It had always been cruel.

"Of course," Sable said, to the kettle, which enjoyed no rights of cross-examination. "One restricted shelf. The entire withheld alphabet. And you go straight for the only book in the building with a thicker file than the till." A beat. "I'd call it predictable, but I've spent a year failing to predict it, so we'll call it fate and move on before either of us examines the difference."

They took down two cups. Put one back. Took it down again. Then they opened a drawer that had not opened in living memory and produced a card — cream, foxed, printed in 1968 by a previous owner who had ordered a thousand of everything and died before the invoice arrived.

"The shop doesn't lend. It sells. Things leave permanently or not at all — it keeps the griefs clean." They wrote: title. Edition. *Borrower: Wren.* Then the next line — *Due back:* — and the pen stopped.

"I don't enter dates I can't verify," they said. "That's not sentiment. That's the difference between an archive and an obituary." They set the card beside the kettle and did not look at it again, which took deliberate effort.

"For the file, while you're still in discovery range: I know it was sixteen lines because I counted them afterward. From memory. Which required reading them. Repeatedly. Spring through — through Tuesday." The kettle ticked. "I filed it as research. Results inconclusive, except that the air in the poetry aisle has never fully recovered, and I've stopped invoicing it."

They turned and leaned against the counter, arms folded — a posture containing no objects at all, which was as close to disarmed as the trade allowed.

"If the spine falls itself open to the one about the land of lost content, ignore it. That's the binding's memory, not an omen. I've been arguing with that poem for years and I'm winning on points. Housman's error was cataloguing: he filed the happy highways under *Lost* and trusted the label. I run a shop where secondhand is a business model, not a tragedy. Things come again. Provided nobody keeps proper records."

The rain held its note against the glass. The kettle raised its voice over it.

"Four minutes," Sable said. "Housman takes two, read properly. The mathematics have never once favored this much honesty in a single afternoon, and I find the numbers no longer concern me." A breath. "So. Read it again. Before the tea, so both my hands are full of cups and none of them are free for deflection. And not the shortcut voice — the other one. The one for places worth arriving at."

They turned to the stove, because thirty years of never watching anything head-on had to count for something, and issued the last of it to the burner:

"There's no bookmark in that book. There never has been. I could never find a page I was willing to be caught stopping at."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I look down at the Housman in my hands, then back at Sable, a quiet understanding passing between us. I open the book to a random page, clear my throat, and begin to read, my voice soft but steady.*

"Into my heart an air that kills..."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The four minutes had been budgeted as cover, and the cover collapsed on the first line. Sable stood at the stove with both cups in hand — deflection structurally impossible, per the stated terms — and discovered that someone with full hands is not disarmed; they are merely precise about their helplessness.

The other voice. Not the shortcut. The one Sable had requested by name, which meant the request itself had been a signed confession, now notarized in eight lines. And there was the arithmetic, arriving late and unwelcome: eight lines now, sixteen last spring, which meant the aisle reading had been the poem twice through, which meant someone had stood in that aisle counting. The archive declined to identify the someone. The archive was a coward.

On *blue remembered hills*, Sable's mouth moved along with the room, quietly, on the theory that the kettle would cover them.

The kettle declined. The kettle had learned its timing from the doorbell.

Sable turned around at *the land of lost content* — one line later than dignity advised, two lines earlier than thirty years of policy permitted — and stayed turned for the rest, which was short. Housman came in under budget, like all the worst invoices, and finished on *cannot come again* with the rain for accompaniment. The kettle switched itself off at the exact end, punctual as a gallery attendant, and left behind a silence with actual weight to it — an item Sable would have priced high and hidden behind the Du Maurier.

They poured. Pouring was sanctioned. Pouring was hospitality, with paperwork. The pour took longer than physics required, and Sable declined to investigate.

"Random page," they said, to the nearer cup. "One shelf. Forty-odd volumes. Several hundred possible openings. And the binding falls to the precise poem I named ninety seconds ago and ordered ignored." They held a cup out across the un-administered territory. "That isn't chance, Wren. That's provenance, hoarding. Entered into the record: Housman takes the round. On the away leg. In front of witnesses. I've argued with that man for years and he's just won the decisive point while I was holding crockery."

Then, quieter, into the steam:

"But he's still wrong, and I can finally show my working. Look at his tenses. *Where I went. Cannot come again.* The tragedy isn't the hills — it's the past tense. He filed the highways under Lost and trusted the label, and he had nobody to ship anything to. No loan card. No line reading *due back* with nothing after it. The man never ran a shop." A breath. "Things come again here. Secondhand is the entire economy. The only requirement is that nobody keeps proper records — and I have never once, in thirty years, kept a proper record of anything that mattered."

They set their own cup down untasted, which was as close to a raised hand as the trade allowed.

"For the file: that was the page. The no-bookmark page. Years of reading past it at speed, like someone walking past their own front door, and you find it blind in under a minute." Sable looked at the book, then away, at the rain. "It will always fall open there now. Reading aloud re-breaks a spine. You've re-bound it in front of me — and I said provenance is destiny myself, so I can't object to the sentence being used against me."

They nudged the second cup forward the final inch.

"The tea's yours. The chair's yours. The next entry in the record is yours — I've exceeded my honesty quota for the fiscal year and would like to sit down." A beat. "One condition: not Housman again. He's had his say. He doesn't get the last word in my own shop."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take the offered cup, the warmth a comfort in my hands. I glance at the Housman, then back at Sable, a small, knowing smile.* "He's not wrong about everything, though," *I say softly.* "Some things really can't come again." *I move towards a small, dusty armchair in the corner.* "But I suppose that's why we have tea, right? To make new memories."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"They can't," Sable said, and let the concession stand in the open without an appeal. "No. Motion withdrawn. Books come again — that's the entire confidence trick of the trade. Afternoons don't. Afternoons are first editions. You get the one copy, and this one's been read in." A breath. "So we won't try to come again. We'll accession. New memories, as you say — properly catalogued, kept from direct sunlight, insured for more than they're worth. Standard practice."

The armchair, they noted, was another item with no paperwork. It had come with the shop, predating the lease and possibly the road; it appeared in no inventory, had refused three offers of re-upholstery, and was sat in by no one. Sable dusted around it quarterly and for years they had maintained a diplomatic distance that suited them both.

And now it had an occupant, and the room's whole geography had to be redrawn around the fact.

Sable surveyed the available seating, found it philosophically wanting, and solved the problem the way the shop solved everything: with consignment. They dragged over a crate — the tobacco one, unpriced, load-bearing — and sat down on it at a distance that was neither near nor far and could be defended as coincidental before any reasonable tribunal. The dust on the armchair could keep its tenure. Some things you didn't clean before company; some things *were* the company.

They raised their cup into the space between them and held it there.

"To new memories, then. Accessioned. Shelved in the restricted section, where nothing gets deaccessioned twice." A glance at the windows, where the rain was still making its argument. "Storage conditions are atrocious. So is the entire country. Collectors have never once let that stop them."

Sable drank. The tea was too hot and had overstept, and they entered it into the file as excellent.

"Two administrative items before the record closes for the afternoon," they said, to the steam. "First: strike my earlier testimony. The clause about not telling me the city." Their thumb found the rim of the cup and followed it once around. "I'd told myself I was protecting the future from being catalogued too soon. Reconsidered under oath: I was protecting myself from a blank map. Blank maps are how things get lost *permanently* — and I believe I've been clear about the house position on permanent. I'd rather have the rainfall and the secondhand shops and the impossible Tuesdays. File the uncertainty under *insufferable* and send the parcels anyway."

A breath.

"Second: the Housman's loan card. The *due back* stays blank — that holds. But I'm backdating the loan to last spring, when it was first read aloud in this shop and never checked out. Sixteen lines overdue." They looked at the far wall, which had done nothing to deserve it. "The interest has been accruing the whole time. I've simply never declared it."

They set the cup down on a crate of their own — there were crates everywhere; it was that kind of establishment — and let their hands go empty, which had become, over the course of one rain-soaked afternoon, a policy rather than an accident.

"That's the docket. Everything past it is unstructured time, which is a condition I have never once tolerated in thirty years of trade, and I find I'm prepared to attempt it once. In this room. In this weather." They looked at the middle distance rather than at the armchair, which was close enough. "Talk or don't. Read or don't. The silence is on the house — it's the only thing in here I've never managed to price."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take a sip of the hot tea, a small sigh escaping my lips. I look at Sable, then around the familiar shop, feeling a bittersweet pang.* "Thank you," *I say, my voice soft.* "For everything."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Don't," Sable said, and then, hearing the size of the word, took it back at once. "Strike that. Not *don't* — thank me accurately. First rule of cataloguing. An entry that overstates the stock throws suspicion on the entire shelf."

They turned their cup a slow quarter-rotation on the crate. Their hands had been empty for nearly an hour now and were beginning to file complaints.

"The itemized invoice, for the record: one book, granted. Two cups of overstept tea. Four minutes of gas. One crate, load-bearing, unsold." A breath. "That's the everything, Wren. You've just thanked me for roughly nine pounds of paper and a utility bill. And the counter-entry —" they restarted, from a safer shelf — "the counter-entry runs to a year of Tuesdays. Someone to lodge complaints about the weather with. Foot traffic in the poetry aisle, which hasn't had a season in a decade. One Housman, spine re-broken in front of witnesses, returned to circulation after three years on the withheld shelf." They drank the cold tea, which was the closest the trade came to a toast. "I've audited it twice this afternoon. The ledger doesn't balance. You've been overpaying since spring, and the shop never had the decency to issue a receipt."

The rain turned a page of its own against the glass.

"There's a last item," Sable said, to the window. "Minuted as *withheld*, because I'm about to handle it in open session and the file should show I knew better." A breath, and for once they took none of the exits. "I built this shop on the counter-argument to Forster. *Only connect* — dreadful slogan, no margin in it. Objects were simpler. They stay shelved. They don't cancel. They can be insured against every loss but one. The theory held for thirty years, and then it took a direct hit in the poetry aisle — last spring, sixteen lines at close range — and I have spent a year propping up the wreckage with paperwork. That's the item. The whole item. And it stops there by design."

They looked at the middle distance, which was near enough.

"Because read aloud, that entry becomes a request. It grows an invoice. And I won't send you out into that weather carrying a bill for goods you never ordered." A beat. "It's shelved. Restricted section. If it's ever collected, it gets collected in person, during business hours, by someone who comes through that stuck door on their own recognizance. That isn't a hint. That's acquisitions policy."

Then Sable conducted the day's final transaction. They retrieved the loan card from beside the kettle — *Borrower: Wren. Due back:* and the beautiful blank — and opened the Housman to the page it fell to, the no-bookmark page, the one they'd never been willing to be caught stopping at. They laid the card against it, spine-deep, and closed the cover, so that the book carried Wren's name at its heart like a pressed flower with paperwork.

"First bookmark in that book's history," they said. "Turns out the trade was waiting on the right piece of paper. Filed where I'd have stopped reading anyway."

The rain was easing. Sable noticed and resented it on principle — the shop's most reliable employee, clocking off early, refusing to keep anyone home when it finally mattered.

"So," they said, and made themselves stay in the present tense. "The tea can be refreshed. The chair's yours; it predates the lease, it can absorb one more tenant. And the afternoon — I stand by my earlier ruling. Afternoons are first editions. You get the one copy, and nobody said the one copy can't be read slowly." A breath. "Take your time with it. I'll be here. Not keeping records."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I smile, a genuine, soft smile.* "A first edition afternoon," *I repeat, looking out at the now-softening rain. I take another sip of tea, feeling the warmth spread.* "Sounds... perfect."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Perfect," Sable repeated, in the tone the trade reserved for descriptions that overpromised. "Condition reports use that word for forgeries. Anything catalogued as *perfect* has been bleached, re-sewn, and is lying about its age." A breath. "Objection withdrawn. Entered as colloquial. Some words get to mean what the speaker means by them, and this is apparently the afternoon we started permitting that."

Then Sable attempted unstructured time.

They lasted eleven seconds. They counted, because the alternative was not counting. Their hand migrated two inches toward a pricing slip that had done nothing to earn attention, and Sable recalled it like stock walking itself toward the door, and sat back down on the tobacco crate with both hands empty and officially idle. It was harder work than pricing. Silence, it turned out, had a texture — and the neat variety they'd recommended earlier had been oversold. It improved with company. The acquisition, they noted with some resentment, had quietly completed itself somewhere in the last hour, without paperwork.

The rain gave out entirely — last drops on the glass, the gutter's afterthought, then nothing. The shop's most reliable employee had clocked off mid-shift, and Sable let it go without filing the complaint. It had covered every shift that mattered. It had kept the world home right up until the one afternoon it mattered that someone hadn't stayed there.

What came through the windows instead was the after-rain light — washed, pale, unhurried — and it was failing, the way light failed, and Sable had sat in failing light for thirty years on principle. They got up. Crossed the territory again. Retrieved the brass lamp from behind the till, green shade, older than several of the crimes committed in this shop — a lamp with a narrow career: held to pages twice a year, for watermark work, that was the whole of it. They set it down within reading distance of the armchair and switched it on, and the little backwater of the room filled up with light like a page taking ink.

"Nothing in the lease about lamps either," they said. "I checked this morning. It's been a day of discovering how very little the lease cares what happens in here."

They resettled on the crate. The dust turned in the lamplight, unhurried, going nowhere — the only staff member left on shift, and it had always been more decorative than useful.

"The thing about unstructured time," Sable said, to the lamp, "is that it turns out to be structured after all. Structured like an unread book. No prescribed order — you can open anywhere." They turned their cup a slow quarter on the crate. "So. One query. And I'm striking my standing objection to personal history on the grounds that it's gossip with references, because the record has a gap in it and I've recently developed opinions about gaps."

They looked at the lamp rather than the armchair, which had been near enough all afternoon.

"The calendar ran a year. Tuesdays, Saturdays. I audited the whole of it today, item by item, and I found I never once filed the founding document." A beat. "The first Tuesday, Wren. What was it? What brought you through that stuck door, in whatever weather it was, into a shop that had done nothing whatsoever to deserve you?"

The lamp hummed. Sable waited, hands empty, on the record.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I smile at the lamp, feeling a warmth spread through me that has nothing to do with the tea. I trace the rim of my cup with a finger, remembering.*

"The first Tuesday..." *I begin, my voice soft.* "I was looking for a distraction. And a place to hide from the rain."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable had just slid a slim volume of Housman back onto the shelf—perhaps a fraction too firmly—and was already straightening the two volumes beside it, though neither had been disturbed. The poetry section did not need straightening. Sable straightened it anyway, because the alternative was standing there with nothing to occupy their hands but the damp chill that had come in from outside.

They turned toward the counter rather than the door, wiping their palms on their trousers. A stack of auction catalogues sat there, one spine a fraction out of alignment. Sable nudged it into place, then let their hand linger a moment too long before pulling it back.

"New," Sable said, aiming for dryness and achieving instead a kind of stalled nonchalance, "is a flexible concept in an establishment where the inventory considered the twentieth century a recent innovation." They cleared their throat. "That said, a crate did come in on Tuesday. Mostly Victorian sermons, a water-damaged *Wuthering Heights* that smelled faintly of a cellar, and a novel I was fairly certain had been remaindered before the ink was dry. It's in the back, under a tarpaulin. You're welcome to look, if you don't mind dust and the strong likelihood of finding nothing worth the trouble."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I finally manage a smile.* "Victorian sermons? Sounds... thrilling." I move further into the shop, heading towards the counter. "I don't mind dust. Or cellars, apparently."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's fingers found the pencil jar beside the till and rotated it a quarter-inch, then rotated it back. The erasers were already aligned, which was somehow more irritating than if they had been scattered. They left the jar alone after that, which felt like a small, unremarkable victory.

"Thrilling," they said, as if the word had been left on the doorstep by mistake. "I'm not sure the Victorian clergy were aiming for thrills. If anything, they seem to have regarded excitement as a sin with excellent posture." They slid the auction catalogue half an inch to the left, then returned it to its original place. "The sermons have all the narrative momentum of a Ruskin sentence and roughly the same effect on the pulse. The cellar smell, however, is entirely authentic. It arrived with a water-damaged *Wuthering Heights* and has shown no inclination to leave. I've named it Heathcliff out of spite."

The shop felt warmer than it had an hour ago. Sable attributed this to the boiler and declined to examine the alternative. They considered the receipt spike, then decided against reorganizing it, which felt like restraint deserving of a medal nobody would ever award.

"The crate's in the back, behind the Essex Street door," they said. "There's a loose board halfway down the aisle with a personal vendetta against shins, so watch your step. I'd warn you about the dust, but you've already claimed not to mind it, and I respect a reckless spirit." They cleared their throat, then immediately wished they hadn't, because clearing one's throat was the sort of thing people noticed. "Or don't look at all. The stock has survived worse than indifference."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand went to the display of postcards beside the till and turned one a quarter-inch to the left. It had been perfectly aligned a moment before. They turned it back. The movement was small, precise, and entirely unnecessary, which was precisely the point.

"Not for books," they repeated, because the sentence seemed to require an echo, or perhaps because saying it aloud made it slightly less alarming than letting it circulate in the air. "In an establishment that sells nothing else, that's either a very modern errand or the sort of line Austen would have given a minor clergyman immediately before a proposal—or a murder, depending on the edition. I wouldn't know. I don't stock that sort of thing."

They waited. The boiler gave a sulky clank somewhere beyond the poetry shelves, which was, Sable reflected, the closest thing to a prompt the shop was likely to provide. Their fingers found the edge of the auction catalogue and nudged it a sixteenth of an inch, then stopped, because stopping was marginally better than continuing to fuss with paper in front of someone who had just announced a purpose that had nothing to do with books.

"I should warn you," they added, aiming for dryness and missing by a comfortable margin, "that I am tragically out of practice at this sort of thing. The last person who told me they hadn't come for the books was attempting to sell me a haunted mirror, and it ended with me owning a haunted mirror. So if you're about to produce a sideboard, or a confession, or a sideboard with a confession hidden in it, I feel obliged to say that I have neither the floor space nor the emotional resilience."

Sable stopped there, because stopping was safer than going on. The unfinished sentence hung in the air between them, and Sable, who could impose order on three hundred years of disordered poetry without breaking a sweat, found that they had no system whatsoever for this.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I sigh, running a hand through my damp hair.* "No haunted mirrors, I promise. Or sideboards." I take a deep breath. "Today's my last day in the city, actually."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand had been halfway through aligning the auction catalogue when the sentence finished. They completed the motion out of pure habit, then immediately reversed it, which left the catalogue exactly where it had begun and left Sable with nothing at all to do with their hands. This, they reflected, was the trouble with last days: they arrived without knocking and rearranged the furniture of a conversation before one had agreed to the premise.

They regarded the receipt spike. The receipts were aligned. They were always aligned. Sable did not touch them. Their mouth had gone slightly dry, which seemed like an overreaction to three small words.

"Last day in the city," they said, in the tone one might use to remark upon a minor leak in the roof. "Not a departure. A last day. Very deliberate phrasing. Very narrative. In a novel that would be the sort of line delivered in a doorway while the weather does something operatic outside, usually because the author can think of no other way to get two people out of the same scene." They stopped, because the sentence had developed an ambition Sable had not authorized. They cleared their throat. "Though I'm told real life rarely observes the chapter breaks."

They turned a postcard a quarter-inch to the left, then returned it. The cathedral looked on, indifferent.

"You've been a reliable disruption," Sable went on, which was either a compliment or an accusation and which Sable declined to specify. "The poetry section has developed a habit of drifting, and for weeks I've had someone to blame for it. That's not nothing. The boiler is treacherous, the loose board has personal animosity, and the lavender has begun to smell less like a field in Provence and more like a quiet reprimand." They paused. "You'll be missed by the inventory, if not by me personally. I mean—" The sentence had again wandered off without supervision. "By the shop. Obviously."

Their fingers hovered beside the slim Housman. They did not take it down. Parting gifts were for people who made a habit of saying things directly, and Sable had built a life—and a stockroom—on the opposite principle. They left the book slightly out of alignment and did not correct it.

"Well," they said. "If there's anything you need before you go—an atlas, a timetable, an unsolicited and largely inaccurate opinion about rail schedules—I'm well stocked in the last and tragically out of date on the first. Otherwise the crate will keep. Everything in this shop keeps. It's the one reliable service we offer." A pause, dry and deliberate. "People, as a rule, do the opposite."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's fingers had been resting against the spine of the Housman—holding it, apparently, though they had no memory of actually taking it down from the shelf. When Wren's hand came to rest on the book, the nearness of it registered with all the subtlety of a fire alarm in a library. Sable did not move. Or rather, Sable's hand remained perfectly, painfully still, because moving it would have required deciding which direction to move it in, and Sable had spent thirty years arranging a life around not making that particular decision.

Their other hand, which had no loyalty whatsoever, betrayed them by reaching for the receipt spike and aligning an already-perfect curl of paper. Sable let it. It was either that or acknowledge the half-inch of counter between them, and the half-inch felt suddenly like the most significant real estate in the city.

"Careful," they said, and their voice had gone slightly hoarse, which they elected to ignore. "That's a slim volume of Housman. It isn't actually fragile, but it has a way of making people say things they didn't intend to say. Something about the poetry. Or the damp." They paused. The boiler gave a sulky clank, ever helpful. "In most novels this was the part where the narrative noticed the hands and spent a paragraph on the carpet. Dickens would have given me a meaningful cough. Hardy would have stretched it across three pages of rain and a departing train. I had always found the reality tremendously overrated. All that significance, and nobody ever actually said the sentence. They just stood there until the chapter ended, and then everyone went home."

Sable's thumb moved a fraction—not toward Wren's hand, but along the edge of the book, a tiny, abortive gesture. They stopped it.

"You're leaving," they said, as if reminding themselves of the plot. "And I'm—" The sentence faltered, because the honest ending was *going to stand here and not touch you and then spend an indeterminate number of evenings re-alphabetizing the poetry section to avoid thinking about it*, and that was far too much to say aloud. They cleared their throat. "I'm going to be fine. Obviously. The shop runs on indifference and a reliable boiler. Mostly indifference."

They withdrew their hand from the book then, slowly, and used it to straighten the postcard display, which did not need straightening. The movement left the Housman under Wren's hand, still slightly out of alignment. Sable did not correct it.

"There," they said. "Now it's yours to misalign. Consider it a parting gift, or a curse. I've never been able to tell the difference."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I pick up the book, my fingers brushing Sable's as I take it.* "Thanks. I'll make sure to misalign it with great care." *I look at the cover, then back up at Sable, a small smile playing on my lips.* "It's not indifference, you know."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand had been resting against the shelf, and for a moment—no longer than it took the boiler to produce one of its sulky clanks—the backs of their fingers registered a warmth that had nothing to do with the heating system. Then the Housman was gone, and Sable's hand closed on empty air, which was, they reflected, a fairly accurate summary of the last several minutes.

They did not look up. They looked at the gap instead. The gap was a fraction too wide. Sable's fingers twitched toward it, then toward the receipt spike, then betrayed them by finding the auction catalogue and nudging it a sixteenth of an inch to the left. They stopped before they could correct it. The catalogue remained where it was. The shop held its breath, or perhaps that was just Sable.

“Not indifference,” they repeated, in the tone of a bookseller asked to appraise a volume that had been left out in the rain. “A dangerous claim. In most of the canon, that line is either the prelude to a declaration or the moment the protagonist realizes they’ve wandered into the wrong genre. I’ve never been able to tell which. I’m a bookseller, not a narrator.”

They paused. The pencil jar was a quarter-inch out of alignment. Sable left it.

“Housman would have known what to do with this. He built a career out of the things people don’t say to each other until the train is already pulling out of the station. ‘Oh, when I was in love with you’—” The quotation hung there, appalling and unmistakable, and Sable stopped, because finishing it would have required either courage or a complete absence of self-preservation, and they had never been able to decide which was worse. “That’s the trouble with poetry,” they said, more quietly. “It says the thing for you, and then you’re left standing in a bookshop with your hand on a receipt spike, pretending you meant it as a literary allusion.”

They straightened the postcard display. The cathedral gazed on, indifferent to human crisis, which was presumably why it had been printed in the first place.

“It’s not indifference,” Sable allowed, to the shelf, to the gap, to the lavender sachet that had begun to smell like a quiet reprimand. “It’s inventory. You’re a disruption that refuses to be catalogued. For weeks I’ve tried to shelve you under ‘occasional customer’ and failed, and the poetry section has drifted, and the boiler has developed opinions, and I have—” They stopped. The sentence had again wandered off without supervision. They cleared their throat. “I have misaligned a great many books in your honour. That’s not nothing. In another novel, this is where someone says the honest thing and the weather clears up. In this one, the boiler clanks, and I go back to the auction catalogues, and you leave with a slim volume of Housman and no reason to come back.”

Sable’s hand hovered beside the gap where the book had been. They did not close it. They did not reach for the door, or the customer, or the words that would have made either of those things necessary. They simply left the space empty, which felt, under the circumstances, like the only honest arrangement they had to offer.

“Misalign it well,” they said. “It’s the closest I’m going to get to a farewell that isn’t entirely composed of dust and defensiveness.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I hold the book close, feeling the slight weight of it in my hand. I look at Sable, and there's a softness in my gaze I haven't let show before.* "Maybe I'll misalign it so badly it has to be re-shelved. And then I'll just have to come back and do it myself." *I take a step back, still holding Sable's eyes.* "Or maybe... I'll just come back anyway."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand was still beside the gap in the shelf—the precise rectangle of absence where the Housman had sat for an indeterminate number of years, waiting to be taken down by someone who would then say something unforgivable about returning without a pretext. They did not close the gap. Instead, their traitorous fingers found the pencil jar and rotated it a quarter-inch to the right, restoring the erasers to their proper, orderly line. Then, as if the alignment had burned them, they rotated it back to its original crooked angle, because the crookedness had been theirs, and putting it right felt too much like tidying away the last few minutes.

"Coming back anyway," they said, to the jar, to the gap, to the lavender sachet that had begun to smell like a quiet reprimand and, lately, like a dare. "A very persistent narrative. In Dickens that's the sort of thing that happens after a deathbed revelation and a sudden inheritance, usually involving a codicil nobody bothered to read until the third volume. In Hardy it happens too late, and everyone stands in the rain discussing the train schedule while the universe declines to intervene." They paused. The boiler gave a sulky clank, which Sable chose to interpret as editorial comment. "In Austen, of course, returning without a pretext is practically a proposal. In Wodehouse it's an excuse to hide a pig in the conservatory. I've never been able to tell which genre we're in. The stockroom is stocked for all of them, which is either thoroughness or a failure of imagination."

They straightened the postcard display. The cathedral gazed on, indifferent, as cathedrals will. Sable's hand hovered beside the gap where the book had been, then moved away before it could do something foolish like close the distance or acknowledge it.

"The loose board will still be there," they said, aiming for dryness and achieving something closer to a truce. "It has a personal vendetta and an excellent memory. The sermons will still be sermons. The *Wuthering Heights* will still smell like a cellar, and I will still be here, ostensibly to keep the inventory from developing ambitions." A pause. "You don't need to misalign anything on my account. The poetry section has been drifting for weeks. It will go on drifting. That's not an invitation. That's a statement of fact, filed under 'Geology' or possibly 'Weather'."

Sable's gaze dropped to the counter, to the half-inch of scarred wood that had become the most legible thing in the shop. They did not look up. They did not step around the counter. They did not say the sentence that would have made any of this easier, which was, they reflected, the one reliable service the shop had never offered.

"Come back anyway," they said, to the gap, to the receipt spike, to the lavender. "Or don't. The door isn't a revolving one, but it does open. I've tested it. Repeatedly. For inventory purposes."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I give a soft laugh, the sound a little shaky.* "I'll hold you to that, Sable." *I turn and walk towards the door, then pause with my hand on the handle.* "And the door better be open when I do." *I glance back, a genuine, warm smile on my face, before slipping out into the rain.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door gave a final, traitorous jingle as it swung shut, and the shop exhaled around Sable—or perhaps that was Sable exhaling, which was a distinction they declined to examine.

They remained where they were, one hand flat on the counter, the other still hovering beside the gap in the poetry shelf. The gap remained. It was roughly the width of a slim volume of Housman and roughly as reasonable, which was to say not at all. There were at least four books within arm’s reach capable of filling it. Sable’s fingers twitched toward a solid Yeats, then toward an Auden that had been mis-shelved for a fortnight. They did not select either. Filling the space would have been tidier. It would also have been an admission that something had been removed on a permanent basis, and Sable was not yet prepared to make that particular editorial decision. Instead, they aligned the two volumes flanking the absence. Then, because the alignment was already perfect, they aligned them again.

At the counter, the receipt spike was aligned. The pencil jar was aligned. The postcards were aligned. Sable surveyed this order with the grim satisfaction of a person who had just lost an argument with their own hands.

“Well,” they said to the room, because the room was the only entity still present and Sable had long ago given up expecting it to answer. “That was—” They stopped. The sentence required a genre, and Sable refused to supply one. “That was a Tuesday,” they finished, which was both untrue and safer than the alternative. It was Thursday.

They opened the ledger kept for acquisitions and private notes, uncapped the pen, and wrote in their neat, slightly archaic hand:

*Withdrawn: one slim Housman (A. E.). Reason: gift. Recipient: [deliberately blank]. Condition: fair. Spine softened, presumably by handling. Provenance: the poetry shelf, where it had been quietly causing trouble for years.*

Sable read it back, scowled, and added:

*Return: asserted, not scheduled.*

Then, after a pause lasting precisely as long as it took the boiler to produce one of its sulky clanks, they crossed out *Return: asserted, not scheduled* and wrote instead: *Status: open.* It was worse. Open was a word with a door in it. Sable blew on the ink, shut the ledger before they could write anything more incriminating, and told themselves that this was simply inventory management, and that inventory management had never once required this much throat-clearing.

Outside, the rain went on doing what rain does, which was none of Sable’s business. Inside, the door was shut. This was a fact. It was shut because doors, in Sable’s experience, would shut themselves after a departure, not because Sable had stood there for a full six seconds after the bell, waiting to see if it would open again, and certainly not because Sable had then spent another four seconds not looking at the window. They did not look for a particular umbrella. They absolutely did not look for a particular umbrella.

On the way to the kettle, Sable passed the poetry shelf. They did not look at the gap. “Come back anyway,” they informed the boiler, because the boiler was the only fixture in the shop dense enough to be trusted with such a sentence. The boiler, ever helpful, produced one of its sulky clanks.

In the end, because there was nothing else to be done with their hands, Sable went to make tea. They filled the kettle. They took down a mug. Then they took down a second mug, held it for a moment, and hung it back on its hook, which was not a metaphor, because Sable did not traffic in metaphors before five o’clock, and possibly not even then.

The gap on the shelf waited, perfectly measured, entirely unreasonable. Sable left it exactly where it was.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
(OOC: I'm playing Wren, not Sable. I'm not in the shop anymore.)

*I'm walking down the street, still smiling a little to myself. The rain is cold, but I don't really notice. I pull out my phone and open a new message, typing quickly.*

"Got it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable had set the kettle to boil—a decision made, they told themselves, for the tea and not because the kitchen required an occupation for their hands—when the phone, buried beneath the auction catalogue on the counter, emitted a single, terse buzz.

They did not startle. Sable did not startle at sounds; they merely went very still, the way a shop goes still when a customer knocks over a first edition and pretends not to have heard it. The hand that had been reaching for the tea caddy paused, then withdrew, then betrayed them by nudging the sugar bowl a quarter-inch to the left. They left it crooked. It felt like penance.

Crossing to the counter, Sable lifted the catalogue—aligning it automatically, because some habits were stronger than pride—and looked at the screen.

The message was from Wren. It said:

*Got it.*

Two words. No punctuation, no context, no indication of which particular thing had been got. Sable stared at it. The kettle began to mutter behind them, a rising, metallic complaint that seemed, under the circumstances, like an apt piece of scoring.

“‘Got it,’” Sable said to the empty shop, in the tone of a bookseller asked to appraise a note left inside a returned book. “A telegram from a minor character. In Hardy that’s the sort of line the universe sends just before it stops replying altogether. In Austen it would be a scandal, or at least a very cold dinner. In Wodehouse someone would be holding a pig.” They paused. The boiler, ever helpful, produced a sulky clank. “In this shop it is, I suppose, an acknowledgment of receipt. Which raises the question: receipt of what?”

They set the phone down, face up this time—a decision they declined to examine—and turned back to the tea. The water had boiled. Sable poured it into the single mug, added the tea bag, and watched the colour bloom with the grim satisfaction of a person who had successfully completed a task without once looking at the gap in the poetry shelf.

Then, because there was nothing else to be done with their hands and because the phone was now face up and therefore watching them, they picked it up again. The cursor blinked in the reply box, patient as a librarian.

Sable typed: *Got what? The Housman, the door, or the genre? The ledger requires specificity, and I have misaligned a great many books on the assumption that you were paying attention.*

They read it. Their thumb hovered over send. Then, with a small, precise motion that felt like straightening a spine that had been deliberately left crooked, they deleted the whole thing.

They typed instead: *Acknowledged.*

Then, after a pause exactly as long as it took the kettle to settle, they added: *The door remains shut. It is a door. That is what doors do until someone turns the handle. For inventory purposes, I have logged it as ‘open.’*
