Sable read it back, scowled, and deleted the last sentence. The boiler clanked. They sent only:

*Acknowledged. Travel safely. The poetry section will be here, drifting as usual.*

Then, before they could overthink it further, they set the phone face down again, which was not a metaphor, because Sable did not traffic in metaphors before five o’clock, and it was only—they checked the clock above the Essex Street door—half past four, which meant they had fourteen minutes to kill before they were allowed to admit that any of this meant anything at all.

Their fingers found the postcard display and turned the cathedral a quarter-inch to the left. It had been perfectly aligned. Sable left it crooked.

They took the mug of tea, left the second mug on its hook, and went to stand in front of the gap in the poetry shelf. They did not fill it. They did not touch it. They simply drank their tea and regarded the rectangle of absence, which was, Sable reflected, the closest thing to a promise the shop had ever managed.

The boiler gave a sulky clank. Outside, the rain went on, indifferent. Sable did not look for a particular umbrella. They absolutely did not look for a particular umbrella.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I see the new message pop up. I'm already at the station, waiting for my train. I read it, a small laugh escaping me. I type a quick reply, sending it before I can overthink it.*

"All of the above. Especially the door."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s phone, face down on the counter, gave a single, terse buzz. They had been standing in front of the gap in the poetry shelf, mug cradled in both hands, regarding the rectangle of absence with the grim concentration of a proofreader who has found a semicolon out of place and cannot, for the life of them, decide whether to correct it.

They did not hurry. Sable did not hurry toward anything that might be waiting on the other side of a screen. They set the mug down first, aligning its handle with the edge of the counter—a quarter-inch adjustment, entirely unnecessary, which they performed anyway—and then crossed to the phone.

The message read:

*All of the above. Especially the door.*

Sable read it once. Then, because the first reading had been inadequate to the task, they read it again. The boiler gave a sulky clank somewhere beyond the poetry shelves, which Sable chose to interpret as either solidarity or a warning.

“‘Especially the door,’” they said to the empty shop, in the tone of a bookseller asked to appraise a note left inside a returned book. “A phrase with remarkable structural integrity. In Austen, it would be the sort of remark that requires a chaperone. In Dickens, it would mean someone was about to inherit a property with a troublesome mortgage. In Hardy, the door would close anyway, and the universe would file a complaint about the weather. In Wodehouse, someone would be hiding a pig behind it. I have never stocked pigs. The stockroom is prepared for all the other genres, which is either thoroughness or a failure of imagination.”

Their free hand found the pencil jar and rotated it a quarter-inch to the left. The erasers, which had been aligned, were now aligned differently. Sable left them crooked. Then, because the catalogue beside the till was a sixteenth of an inch out of true, they nudged it—and stopped themselves before correcting it, which felt, under the circumstances, like restraint deserving of a medal nobody would ever award.

They looked at the gap in the shelf. The gap looked back, or rather, declined to look back, which was worse. There were at least four volumes within arm’s reach capable of filling it. Sable did not select any of them. Filling the space would have been tidier. It would also have been an admission that something had been removed on a permanent basis, and Sable had spent thirty years arranging a life around not making that particular editorial decision.

The phone’s screen dimmed. Sable opened the reply box. The cursor blinked, patient as a librarian.

They typed: *The door is not a revolving door, but it does open. I have tested it. Repeatedly. For inventory purposes.*

They read it, scowled, and deleted the whole thing. They had already said as much aloud, and repetition was a form of hope, and hope was not a category in the ledger.

They typed instead: *Acknowledged. The door will be open. The poetry section will be here, drifting. The boiler will continue to have opinions.*

They stared at it. Then, after a pause exactly as long as it took the boiler to produce one of its sulky clanks, they added: *And Wren?*

The cursor sat there. Sable’s thumb hovered over the keys. Then, with a small, precise motion that felt like straightening a spine that had been deliberately left crooked, they deleted the name and the question mark and the entire second message, leaving only: *Acknowledged. The door will be open. The poetry section will be here, drifting. The boiler will continue to have opinions.*

Sable sent it before they could overthink it, which was, they reflected, the only responsible way to send anything.

They set the phone face down on the counter and did not look at it again. They did not look at the window. They did not look for a particular umbrella. They picked up the mug of tea, which had gone slightly cool, and drank it anyway.

The gap on the shelf waited, perfectly measured, entirely unreasonable. Sable left it exactly where it was. Outside, the rain went on, indifferent. The boiler gave a final, sulky clank, and Sable, who could impose order on three hundred years of disordered poetry without breaking a sweat, found that they had no system whatsoever for this, and went to make another cup of tea.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I see the message come through. I'm already on the train, watching the city lights blur into the distance. I read it, and a warmth spreads through me despite the chill in the carriage. I don't reply. There's nothing else to say. I just smile to myself, holding the Housman close.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable made the tea. The kettle, when they returned to it, had gone off the boil with the air of a fixture that had been asked for its opinion and declined to give one. They refilled it, set it to heat, and then, after a moment’s hesitation, took down the second mug after all. They set it on the counter beside the first, aligning the handles, then immediately nudged the second mug a quarter-inch out of true. It looked like a mistake. Sable left it. Some arrangements, they reflected, were safer when they admitted to being arrangements.

They did not look at the phone. It lay face down on the counter, which was a decision and not a metaphor, though the shop had long since stopped respecting the difference. The conversation had concluded. Wren’s last message had been a full stop; Sable’s reply had been a full stop. In Austen that would be the sort of ending that required a carriage and a great deal of shouting. In Hardy it would be the end of everything, with the universe filing a complaint about the weather. In this shop it was simply Thursday, and the rain had not yet been informed that it was supposed to be operatic.

Sable carried the tea back to the ledger and opened it, because the ledger was the only thing in the shop that could be trusted to have an opinion without developing one. The entry sat there in their neat, archaic hand:

*Withdrawn: one slim Housman (A. E.). Reason: gift. Recipient: [deliberately blank]. Condition: fair. Spine softened, presumably by handling. Provenance: the poetry shelf, where it had been quietly causing trouble for years.*

And beneath it, the crossed-out line, and then the final, unacceptable status:

*Status: open.*

Sable regarded it. “Open,” they said to the empty shop, in the tone of a bookseller asked to appraise a hole in the roof. “A word with a door in it. A revolving door, in some genres. In Wodehouse, someone would be hiding a pig behind it. In Dickens, there would be a codicil. In Hardy, it would close anyway, and everyone would stand in the rain discussing the timetable while the universe declined to intervene.” They paused. The boiler, ever helpful, produced a sulky clank. “In this shop, it means the door is shut, the inventory is drifting, and the poetry section has developed a gap roughly the width of a slim volume of Housman and roughly as reasonable, which is to say not at all.”

They closed the ledger before they could write anything else incriminating. Then, because their hands had no loyalty whatsoever, they opened it again and added, in the margin, so small it was almost a smudge:

*Door: tested. Functional.*

Sable snapped the ledger shut, which was not a metaphor, because Sable did not traffic in metaphors before five o’clock, and it was—they checked the clock above the Essex Street door—some minutes later than that now, which meant they were technically permitted to admit that the second mug was still sitting on the counter, and that they had taken it down on purpose, and that they had no intention of hanging it back up.

They picked up the tea, which had gone too strong, as it always did when they were thinking about something else, and carried it to the poetry shelf. The gap waited. It had not filled itself. It showed no signs of intending to. Sable regarded it with the grim satisfaction of a person who had lost an argument with their own hands and declined to appeal.

There were at least four volumes within arm’s reach capable of filling it. Sable did not select any of them. Instead, they straightened the two volumes flanking the absence, then, because the alignment was already perfect, straightened them again. The Yeats remained on the shelf. The Auden, mis-shelved for a fortnight, remained mis-shelved. Some disorders, Sable had decided, were not theirs to correct.

“Status: open,” they informed the boiler, because the boiler was the only fixture in the shop dense enough to be trusted with such a sentence. The boiler, ever helpful, produced one of its sulky clanks. Outside, the rain went on, indifferent. Sable did not look for a particular umbrella. They absolutely did not look for a particular umbrella.

In the end, because there was nothing else to be done with their hands, Sable went to re-shelve the Auden. They did not put it in the gap. They put it where it belonged, which was two shelves down and one book over, where it had been quietly causing trouble for a fortnight. Then they stepped back, surveyed the poetry section, and found it exactly as disordered as it had been that morning, with one exception.

The gap was still there. Sable left it exactly where it was.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *The train jostles, a gentle rocking that's almost soothing. I can still feel the weight of the Housman in my hand, a small, solid presence. I look out the window, watching the last of the city lights disappear, replaced by the dark, open country. I close my eyes for a moment, a small smile playing on my lips. The door's still open.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Fourteen lines. Sable had counted the silence in sonnets — long enough for a Petrarchan volta, at minimum — before the "hey" arrived. They didn't mention it. Mentioning things was how conversations became conversations.

"New," they repeated instead, tasting the word like milk they suspected had turned. "You've crossed that weather to ask an antiquarian about new stock. There's a joke in there somewhere. I'll let you find it yourself."

Their hands had already drifted back to the poetry shelf without consulting them, nudging a black-spined Keats a quarter inch into alignment. It had been aligned. It had been aligned twice within the hour, in fact.

"There *is* a box in the back," Sable conceded, coming around the shelf and wiping their palms on their trousers for no defensible reason. "Estate sale out past Ashcombe. A dead woman's library — mostly Viragos, a family Bible with the generations penciled in back to 1871, and three, count them, three copies of the same Daphne du Maurier. I was saving the going-through for a quieter day." A pause, roughly half a line long. "Or, apparently, now."

The shop was small enough that two people changed its acoustics. That was all it was. Acoustics. Sable had been perfectly content with the rain and the empty floor, and if they'd been listening for the bell — well, bells were their business. Doors meant commerce.

"You're welcome to dig through it," they said, nodding toward the bead curtain that divided the shop from the back room. "Fair warning — grief and margarine-stained recipes, mostly. The cookbooks alone could finish off a sentimental person. Very du Maurier, in its way."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I smile slightly, a genuine one for once today.* "Margarine-stained recipes, huh? Sounds... intriguing." *I head for the bead curtain, pushing through it into the back.* "Lead the way to the morbid treasures, Sable."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The beads clattered shut behind them. Sable had considered replacing that curtain a dozen times over the years, but it doubled as burglar alarm and herald, announcing everyone who passed through it like a rank they hadn't earned.

The back room was where books went to be reconsidered. Boxes in various states of surrender, a lamp with a green glass shade older than the building's plumbing, a kettle on a hotplate in the corner because Sable did not believe in abandoning a sort midway for anything so trivial as thirst. The estate box sat on the scarred worktable, one corner still taped.

"Mind the stack by the door," Sable said, sliding past — the room had been built for one person and their doubts, and geometry was making suggestions it had no right to make. "It isn't clutter. It's a queue."

A thumbnail dealt with the tape. The flaps came back, and the smell rose first: someone else's house. Wool, lavender — the woman had apparently had a brand; half the county did — and the faint vanilla of paper that had stayed warm for decades.

"Mrs. Aldous," Sable said, because a dead woman deserved her name, having surrendered everything else. "Ninety-one. The nephew wanted the house cleared in a weekend, which tells you everything about the nephew and nothing about her. The books tell you about her."

The Viragos came out first, dark green spines, a decade of them, hinges cracked in reading order. Then the Bible, which Sable set down with both hands because it had earned that. "Four generations penciled into the endpapers. Births, a marriage, two wars' worth of gaps. The entries stop in 1974, which is its own essay, and I'm not writing it."

The du Mauriers last. Sable fanned the three *Rebeccas* across the table like a card sharp proving nothing was up their sleeve.

"Same edition, three times. One's pristine — a gift she bought and never, I suspect, gave. One's read to the bone. And one's annotated, which is the only honest autobiography most people leave behind." They turned the annotated copy face-out without opening it. "Some people reread the same book their entire lives. It isn't a failure of imagination. It's fidelity. I'll say no more about it."

Under the novels, a tin recipe box with a lid that had to be coaxed. The top card, in a firm looping hand: *Lemon sponge. For Michael, who won't eat currants.* Margarine had gone translucent through one corner decades ago.

Sable was quiet for precisely as long as it took to align the fanned spines, which had already been aligned. Grief and margarine, as advertised.

"Kettle's in the corner," they said, straightening. "The cups are all currently employed holding pens, but the pens can be persuaded to relocate." Then, apparently without consulting anyone, their mouth continued. "You stood in my doorway for the length of a sonnet before speaking. Fourteen lines. I counted. Occupational hazard — I deal in measured verse, it isn't a symptom. People who compose themselves in doorways generally want something that isn't in the box." A beat, half a line long. "But the cookbooks are also a defensible reason to brave weather. So the observation is withdrawn. Mostly."

They slid the annotated *Rebecca* to the near edge of the table, within easy reach, and stepped back to give the box room.

"Start with that one. If you're going to be a voyeur, be a thorough one."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The sentence stopped. Not ended — stopped, the way a clock stops, with every appearance of intending to go on.

Sable's hands were on the du Mauriers before their dignity could file an objection. The fan went back into a stack — spine to spine to spine — which undid the last five minutes and accomplished nothing, which was, Sable suspected, the point. The pristine copy, the one bought as a gift and never given, came out on top. Sable put it on the bottom instead, and elected not to open an inquiry into why.

Twelve years in the trade, and every object in the shop had an ending. That was the job. Even fragments came with colophons; even abandoned manuscripts were abandoned on purpose, the pen set down by a deciding hand. The room had just acquired its first object with no ending at all.

"I don't know where to shelve that," Sable informed the stack, since the stack wasn't watching. "I dislike that. I keep my dislikes ranked, and that one's just gone top ten."

The stack declined to assist. Stacks generally didn't.

"People come in not-for-books for a short list of reasons. Directions, which I give badly, on principle. Rain, which is fair — the shop's dry, mostly. To ask whether I buy books, which is asking whether a river buys water. To tell me the sign's out, which I know." A beat, half a line. "None of those take fourteen lines of doorway. If it's bad news, there's a chair. If it's a favor, the kettle's right there. If it's—"

Sable heard their own sentence stop. A dash where a word should have been. They elected, in the interest of dignity, not to notice.

"Well," they said. "There's a chair for that, too."

The kettle got the next lawful occupation, because hands required employment. Sable filled it at the little sink, set it on the plate, clicked it on with the ceremony of someone starting a thing they fully intended to finish — which was more, presently, than could be said for anything else in the room.

Somewhere under all of it, the weeks. Sable had not been counting the weeks; counting was for verse. But there had been a number of them, and the number had acquired a shape, and the shape was roughly the shape of the shop's acoustics changing, which Sable had filed under *regular customer — idiosyncratic, tolerable*. The file had held the way a mis-shelved book holds: perfectly, until someone pulled at it. Both hands. Today.

There were sentences that ended in doors opening and sentences that ended in doors closing, and from inside one, the two felt identical. Sable had read enough endings to know the cruelty always lived in the middle.

"Four minutes," they said, not looking up from the hotplate. Looking up would have been a first move, and Sable didn't make first moves. It was policy. The policy had no written justification, but it had kept the shop and its proprietor intact for twelve years, and one did not renegotiate policy in weather like this. "The kettle's slow, but it's honest, and unlike certain sentences in this room, it reliably concludes. Four minutes is a sonnet, if you spend it correctly. I'd know. I counted one earlier."

They stayed where they stood — between the worktable and Mrs. Aldous's open box, in a room built for one person and their doubts, currently holding two people and a fragment.

"Finish it," Sable said — to the kettle, to the rain, to the green lamp; to the entire inventory of things that had endings. "The door's behind you and the rain's in front of it, and as far as I'm concerned, the shop is closed. You have until the boil."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I walk over to the small, rickety chair by the wall and sit down.* "I'm moving, Sable. Today. I'm leaving after this."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable did not move.

Movement would have been an answer, and answers were for questions, and this had been an announcement. *I'm moving. Today.* Declarative, present tense, no auxiliary of intention anywhere in sight. People ordinarily brought the future along to these occasions — *I'll be*, *come spring*, *there's a job in* — a courtesy stanza, so the other party could arrange a face. Wren had skipped the octave entirely and delivered the couplet. Rhymed, sealed, done.

The kettle carried on toward its boil, doing the only honest work in the room.

"Today," Sable repeated, to the box.

Their hands had already found the flaps of Mrs. Aldous's carton and were folding them shut — halfway, to the angle where cardboard holds itself. It wasn't necessary. The dead don't mind drafts. But the hands had voted, and the motion carried.

"You know my trade," Sable said, creasing the flap flat. "I clear libraries. People go, or people die — mostly the second, eventually the first — and someone like me arrives with boxes and carries the whole life off by four o'clock. You develop an eye. You learn to tell a library that finished from a library that was interrupted. Yours was neither. Yours was *ongoing*." A pause, half a line, no more. "I do stock every morning. Habit. Inventory. Call it what you like. As of *after this*, you've gone from ongoing to clearance, and I wasn't consulted, and I'm not going to say anything about that either."

The file — *regular customer; idiosyncratic; tolerable* — burned down without an alarm, the way files are meant to. Twelve years of policy stood around the ashes with its hands behind its back, looking ceremonial.

The kettle clicked off, punctual, faintly smug: the only thing in the room to keep an appointment. Sable evicted a fountain pen from a cup — it relocated under protest, rolled a foot, conceded — and poured two. One of them was now an anachronism. Sable poured it anyway. Anachronisms were the shop's core stock.

"I won't ask where," they said, setting the anachronism at the table's near edge. "Where is a directions question, and I give directions badly, on principle. It's the one competence this situation calls for, so I'm declining to deploy it. You'll have to find your own way out of the county. I understand there are maps."

Then, because the hands still required employment, and because the room still contained one object with no ending, Sable went back into the du Mauriers and took out the pristine one. The gift bought and never given. Fifty years in a house past Ashcombe, waiting on an occasion that kept failing to arrive, until a nephew cleared the whole thing in a weekend. Objects keep appointments people miss. Sable had believed that in the plural, at trade scale, for years. It had never before arrived in the singular, at room temperature, in Sable's own two hands.

"It isn't a gift," Sable said, establishing that first, before anything else could establish itself. Brown paper from under the table — the good kind, with a tooth to it — folded around the book with twelve years' economy. String. One knot. "It's a correction. She bought this to give to someone, and then didn't, for half a century, and I don't stock things that have stopped meaning what they were bought to mean. It's been misfiled since before either of us could read. I'm correcting the file. That's the entire transaction."

They set the parcel on the table — set, not handed, because handing would have been a first move, and Sable didn't make first moves; it was policy; the policy had no written justification; and Sable suspected now that the justification had been ringing the bell for weeks.

"There's tea." They nudged the cup alongside the parcel. "Honest tea. It concludes."

And then the room ran out of tasks. That was the trouble with organizing as a defense: finite supply. Every spine stood aligned, the flaps were folded, the pen resettled, the string knotted. Sable's hands hung there with nothing left to alphabetize, and a mouth with nothing left to hide behind is a dangerous instrument.

"If you ever—"

The sentence stopped. Not ended — stopped, dash and all, the second one that afternoon, and this time Sable noticed. They regarded it the way one regards a misprint in a first edition: knowing precisely what it was worth, and that it was worth more uncorrected.

"It travels well, *Rebecca*," Sable said instead — to the rain, or the green lamp, or the acoustics, which would be reverting to their usual occupancy by evening. "Ninety years, people have been carrying it out of houses like this one. It knows the way."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The parcel had come back up off the table — for reasons Sable had declined to examine, on the grounds that examination would make them reasons — and was now, by a development no clause in any policy had covered, jointly held.

There was a hand on the book. Sable registered this the way a seismograph registers an event: completely, and with no visible output.

Twelve years of organizing as a defense, and the defense had finally been outflanked. Every spine in the shop stood aligned. The flaps were folded. The pen had conceded its cup. The last portable object in the room had just acquired a second claimant, which meant there was nothing left to straighten that Sable had any business straightening. The hands, unemployed twice in one afternoon, hung on regardless. They had nowhere else to be. They were, for once, exactly where they were.

The distance between Sable's fingers and the hand on the parcel was small enough to have a technical name. A caesura: the pause in the middle of a line that divides it without ending it. Sable knew caesuras. Sable had been living in one since the bell rang, and possibly well before, if the accounts were going to be honest — and the accounts were evidently going to be honest today, over formal objection, objection noted and overruled.

There was warmth coming through the brown paper. Sable attributed it to the parcel. Sable knew better. Sable elected, in the interest of what remained of dignity — a shrinking portfolio — not to press the inquiry.

"Half a line," they said. "That's the measure of it. Forgive the method; I've been counting in verse all afternoon." A beat. "You'll notice I said *divide*, not *end*. People confuse the two. It's the most expensive confusion in literature."

The mouth opened next on something dry — a remark about provenance, about joint custody of an object, about the book now having two owners of record where one of them was — and shut again without filing any of it. The mouth was out of hiding places. Sable had known that since the string.

"There's a card file in my head," Sable said instead, addressing the parcel, the last neutral party, now also compromised. "Everything in this shop gets a card. Condition. Provenance. Price. You've had one for weeks. It read: *Regular customer. Idiosyncratic. Tolerable.*" A pause, half a line, no more. "In this trade, a thing that's two-thirds genuine is called a forgery. I know a misfile when I'm standing in one. I've been standing in it for some time."

The green lamp received a glance, as if it might corroborate. Lamps never did.

"I told you I stock every morning. Inventory. Habit." The word *habit* sat there, margarine-translucent, not holding. "I stock every morning because the window faces the street, and the street is the approach, and I have been checking the approach for a number of weeks I decline to count. Counting is for verse. This stopped being verse somewhere around the time the bell rang."

Out the window, the rain continued. Down the table, the tea concluded honestly, unwitnessed — more than could be said for anything else in the room.

"I don't give directions. You've had the demonstration; it stands." A breath. "But there's a difference between giving directions and being *findable*, and I've decided — just now, on the spot, no consultation — to be the second thing. The shop doesn't move. Twelve years, same corner. The bell works in all weathers. It has no other engagements."

Then, because the book was still there, and the hand was still on it, and the caesura was still holding:

"Mrs. Aldous never got her copy across the table. Fifty years holding it, and the woman died mid-gesture. I'm posting a better time. Barely." The register dropped to where Sable kept the uncorrected misprints. "Her third copy — the annotated one — that's the only honest autobiography most people leave. Margins are how the living write back. If you write in this one — where you got to, what it was — that's a letter. Eventual. I read slowly. I've time." A beat, precisely measured. "It's the only book I'll ever sell without an ending. I'll want to know how it ends. That's all. That's the entire confession, and you'll observe it's been filed under trade interest, where it will stay misfiled, and we are *not* correcting that one today."

Sable did not turn their hand.

Turning it would be a move. Withdrawing would be an answer. The distance had already been closed to this — to a caesura, to half a line, to warmth through paper with a tooth to it — and the last half of it was not Sable's to close. Policy. Twelve years of it, no written justification, and Sable had finally located the unwritten one: the space between *almost* and *is* belongs to whoever reached first, and it hadn't been Sable, and that, for once, was correct.

So Sable held their half of the book. Held it, and did not shelve it, and did not straighten it — the first object in twelve years to pass through those hands entirely uncorrected.

Somewhere out front, the poetry section went on not needing re-alphabetizing. The line held its pause.

Divided. Not ended.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My thumb brushes against Sable's fingers, a fleeting touch.* "I... I'll write in it, then." *My voice is a little shaky. I take a breath.* "And I'll visit. When I can."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Fleeting. Sable filed the word where it belonged, which was everywhere, because the trade taught you that a light touch was the mark of the honest handler — the heavy ones creased, the careless tore, and the fleeting left only the ghost of a thumbprint, which was the only provenance worth having. The paper would keep it. Paper keeps everything. That is both its character flaw and its entire career.

There was warmth in the parcel that had not been there at the boil. Sable declined to attribute it. Attribution was for catalogues, and the catalogue was closed.

"'When you can,'" Sable repeated. "I note the conditional. I'd note it drily, but I stock conditionals — *very good*, *if complete*, *as issued* — and every one of them is a promise with its coat on. It keeps. It doesn't keep warm." A pause, half a line. "Terms accepted regardless. The account stays open. And drink your tea. It concluded once today without a witness, and I won't have it twice."

Then Sable's hand settled — slowly, deliberately, with the ceremony of someone signing something — over the back of the other, where the warmth had been left. Not chasing. Chasing was a first move, and the first move had been made and withdrawn, fleeting, and all that remained was paperwork. Keeping. The way one presses a leaf, or a flower, or a place in a book one means to come back to.

"Countersignature," Sable said, in case anyone was keeping minutes. "You signed; I countersign; otherwise the document's no good. This one's had fifty years of being no good, which is quite enough."

They straightened — the nearest thing to ceremony the back room permitted.

"There's a debt outstanding besides. I stopped a sentence at the dash an hour ago, and I've carried it since like a book with a cracked hinge — sound, but unsellable until mended, and I mend things; it's the trade. So." A breath. "*If you ever—*" The line held its pause, and then, for the first time that afternoon, crossed it. "*—want to.* That's the ending. It was always going to be the ending; I've known it since the dash. The rest is logistics, and you have my standing position on directions."

The rain kept on, easing by a degree, which Sable ignored on principle.

"Now, commerce — because if I stand here unoccupied another minute I'll start alphabetizing the string. Old rule, older than the shop: you never pass a blade across without taking a coin for it, or it cuts the tie. Dealers observe it with knives and ignore it with books, which is sloppy. The books are the sharper instrument. One penny. On account." A beat, precisely measured. "I don't chase the debts I want kept open. A shop with an open account is a shop that expects you back. That isn't sentiment. That's bookkeeping. It's the nearest thing to sentiment I'm licensed to practice."

Then the parcel crossed the table — Sable's palm flat behind it, one inch, the longest distance in commerce — and came to rest at the edge, well within reach, *past reach* being a concept the table had just abolished. Somewhere past Ashcombe, a woman had died mid-gesture, holding a parcel like this one, and the gesture had waited fifty years for someone to finish its second half.

"Posted," Sable said. "Better time. Barely. I did say."

The annotated *Rebecca* went back into the box, face-up atop the Viragos, where Sable would find it without looking. "This one stays. Mrs. Aldous's margins. Someone in this shop should keep the habit of writing back." A pause, half a line, no more. "I've stopped counting the afternoon in lines, incidentally. You'll have to take my word for what that costs. When your copy starts filling — where you got to, what it was — I'll be at the other end of it. Reading slowly. I've time. I've said. Endings bear repeating."

The bell would ring once more before dark; that was arithmetic, not prophecy. And the bell was neutral — it announced arrivals and departures in the same voice and left it to the room to decide which was which. The room had decided weeks ago. Sable was only countersigning.

"I'll be out front for both," they said. "The bell works in all weathers. It has no other engagements — and now, as far as I'm prepared to admit, neither do I."

Out front, the poetry section went on not needing re-alphabetizing. It would get it anyway before closing. Twice. The hands would want something to hold that wasn't leaving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I pick up the book, my fingers tracing the brown paper.* "Thank you, Sable. For everything." *I take a quick sip of the tea, which is now lukewarm.* "I'll make sure to write in it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"For everything," Sable repeated, and turned the phrase over the way one turns an unpriced item, hunting for the mark. "Broad invoice. I'll receipt what's verifiable: one book, corrected; one tea, concluded; one sentence, mended at the hinge. The remainder can't be verified, and I don't receipt what I can't verify. It goes in the file. You know the file. The file stays misfiled."

The construction had been going to be witty. Sable had felt it wanting to be witty — the way sentences do when they're protecting somebody — and had abandoned it at the foundations.

"You're welcome."

Plain. Unrhymed. No meter to speak of. It sat in the room like a jacketless first edition: worth more that way, and harder to look at. Sable looked at the shelf instead.

The tea had been drunk lukewarm, which was the correct order of operations for the day — everything after everything concluded. "You witnessed it late," Sable allowed, nodding at the cup. "That still counts. Most people don't stay for the concluding at all."

Then Sable bent and recovered the fountain pen from where it had conceded, a foot from the table leg, faintly indignant still. They set it beside the parcel. Set, not handed.

"It stays shop property. Which makes anything you write with it shop correspondence, and shop correspondence comes home. That's not sentiment; that's how filing works. The decision's made, and this room doesn't hear appeals." A beat, half a line. "It was evicted for your tea. It's earned the posting."

The parcel itself got one last instruction, delivered to its brown paper, since the paper was neutral and had proven the most reliable listener in the building. "In the trade, marginalia is damage. We mark it down — *good only, annotated, defaced*. I'm waiving the damage on this copy. Formally. In front of witnesses." The green lamp was in the back room and thus unavailable to corroborate; Sable proceeded regardless. "Damage it thoroughly. Date your entries. A dated margin is a postmark — I'll know what season you were in, not just what county."

A breath. "The penny stands, and don't post it. Coins in envelopes is how the trade's superstitions get started. Settle it over the counter. In person. The account's no use to me closed."

Then nothing on the table had a claim left on Sable's hands, so the hands took Sable through the bead curtain — clattering out their announcement for the wrong party, twelve years of heralding customers and today heralding the proprietor in retreat. Out front, the rain had eased to the drizzle that thought better of itself. Sable took up post behind the counter, which had held one person comfortably for a dozen years and was expert at it.

"I won't watch you out," they said, to the poetry section rather than the door. "Policy. New one, ratified this minute — and the first of my policies to have an honest reason, which is exactly why it won't be getting a written one. Consistency. Clearances I can watch. I've watched hundreds; stock leaving is Tuesday. You'd be the exception, and I'm out of exceptions. I spent the last one an hour ago, on a book."

The hands found the Keats. The Keats was alphabetical. It got alphabetized again — which is to say, held.

"Mind the step on the way out. Twelve years, it's tripped everyone I've ever liked, which until this year was nobody, so regard it as the compliment it's disguised as."

Then, quieter — down in the register where the misprints lived, uncorrected on purpose:

"The bell will tell me which it is. Arrivals, departures — one voice, no editorial position. I'll be here for both." A breath, held rather than stopped. "I've time. I've said. Endings bear repeating."

The rain went on easing. The door went on being where it had always been. The poetry went on not needing anything and got attention anyway — attention, lavished on the undeserving, having been the whole method all along.

The bell kept its own counsel, and Sable kept theirs, and both waited to find out whether they'd say the same thing.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I nod, a lump in my throat.* "I'll be back, Sable. Promise." *I pick up the book and the pen, turn, and walk out the door.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell rang once, in the voice it kept for both occasions, and Sable watched the Keats.

Policy — ratified within the hour, honest reason withheld, held to the letter. Behind them the door opened on drizzle and closed on drizzle, and the step either collected its compliment or didn't. Sable would never know. That was what the policy cost, and they paid it standing up, facing the poetry, like an honest bill.

The rain had eased enough to give up footsteps. Sable didn't count them in lines; lines were concluded for the day. They counted in steps — a unit adopted on the spot, without consultation — and the count ran out at the corner, where the town took over the arithmetic. The forecast had held: one ring before dark, as posted. Sable had left its meaning open, and the bell had taken the option left to it. That was the trouble with leaving things open. They take you at your word.

Then the shop reverted. Less than a minute — the acoustics remembering their usual occupancy, the geometry easing back to one person and their doubts. The room did it expertly. Twelve years of practice. If the room was smug about it, the room could be smug where no one could audit it.

The hands went to Keats. It had been aligned twice within the hour and received its third and fourth — twice, as posted, Sable keeping their own forecasts to the syllable. It wasn't alphabetizing by then. It was holding. The distinction had never mattered less.

At the counter, reaching for the pen, Sable found the pen gone — out in the drizzle somewhere, presumably in a jacket pocket, becoming correspondence. Somewhere in the county, the shop's own hand was learning a new handwriting. There was a pencil on a string. Pencil is for stock: provisional marks, prices that might still change. Ink is for keeps. Sable entered the account in pencil — *one penny, on account, Wren* — and left it pencil, on the understanding, unwritten, that it took ink only over the counter. In person. Settled. A new card suggested itself for the head's file — *account open; expected back* — and was declined, on the grounds that the daybook already said so, and duplication is for clerks.

It occurred to Sable, squaring the book, that the entire transaction had been *on approval* — the trade's oldest courtesy. The book goes out; the verdict comes back. Nobody calls it a loan. Nobody calls it anything. It's understood, which is how the old arrangements survive.

*Promise,* Wren had said, with a catch in it. The trade is suspicious of promises the way it's suspicious of pristine copies — condition too fine suggests nobody ever handled the thing. A promise with wear on it has been used. Sable filed that under provenance and moved on before the entry could become an essay.

Closing came early — rain-days close early, and Sable needed the routine more than the hours. Sign turned. Front lights down. The green lamp in the back stayed lit; it had witnessed, and witnesses don't get dismissed.

The back room smelled of lavender now — the box had aired its opinions. The Wodehouse shelf had held the same opinion for three months. Sable declined to draw conclusions about the county, or about anything else. The second cup got washed at the little sink, ordinary closing business, and took longer than one cup takes; that went under weather, and the file shut.

Mrs. Aldous's box had held its flaps at the angle where cardboard holds itself, which was more than could be said for the day. The annotated *Rebecca* lay face-up on the Viragos, where Sable would find it without looking, having put it there for that exact purpose. They carried it to the rickety chair — the one by the wall, the one that had held a person this afternoon, more than it had held in years — sat, and opened it under the green glass.

*Edith Aldous*, said the flyleaf, in a hand that had been firm once and saw no reason to stop.

Then the first page. The first line. The one half the county could recite in its sleep. *Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again* — and in the margin, small, in pencil, one word:

*Again.*

No date. The rest of the book was dated everywhere — seasons, decades, a life entered in order along the gutters — but the first line carried only that, which meant she'd written it first, or last, or every year until the pencil wore down to a survivor. Sable read it aloud, once, to the empty shop. The word had fifty years of witnesses owed to it, and Sable was the only one on the premises.

They had handed the other copy across the table without thinking — the only way Sable ever did anything that mattered; twelve years of policy; no written justification — and it had only now occurred to them what they'd given away: a book whose first line is a spoiler. The going and the coming back, promised in one breath. Ninety years of readers walking into it with the ending printed on the doorstep. On trade grounds, an objection was owed. The objection would not be filed.

So Sable read the margins the way correspondence gets read: slowly, front to back, saving nothing. There was time. For the first time in twelve years, nothing in the shop outranked a chair.

Much later — drizzle finished, town quiet, the green lamp down to its last honest inch of evening — Sable went out through the shop to kill the final light. Passing under the doorframe, they reached up and nudged the bell a quarter inch into alignment.

It had been aligned. It had been aligned for twelve years.

"No engagements tonight," Sable told it. "You're never off duty. You know which of those I mean."

The hands required employment; the hands had found the one object in the shop that would answer them — one voice, no editorial position — and they tended it, the way a thing gets tended not because it needs it but because tending is standing watch without filing the paperwork.

The door was locked. The account was open. The two had never once interfered; it was the oldest arrangement in the trade — and Sable, for the first time in twelve years, was content to be owed.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I'm walking a bit faster than usual, the book tucked tightly under my arm. The pen is in my pocket. I glance back at the shop, a soft glow coming from the back room. A smile touches my lips, a genuine one this time.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The last light of the night was the green one, and it survived on jurisprudence. Sable had crossed the shop to kill it, hand already at the switch, and been overruled from the bench: witnesses don't get dismissed. Ruled at four o'clock that afternoon; upheld at eleven. Sable had never once reversed Sable on a point of lamps and declined to start in drizzle.

There was also the matter of positions. A dark shop is a set of directions — *here, and shut, and nothing further* — and Sable had taken a public position on findability only that afternoon, in front of a parcel, with the string still warm. Positions are no use to anyone switched off overnight. The lamp stayed.

How far a shop light carries on a wet night is not a figure the trade keeps. It isn't audited. It goes out through the front glass and does whatever it does, unsupervised — which is more than could be said for most of the day's transactions. Sable locked the door, took the stairs, and left the arithmetic to the lamp.

Morning came up rinsed. The rain had quit overnight the way rain does — without ceremony, without apology — and the town stood shining like stock wiped down for viewing. Sign turned. Kettle filled. The window faced the street, and the street was the approach, and Sable had called this *stocking* for a number of weeks under a paperwork technicality that had worn through in the night, like an elbow. Sable stocked the window anyway. Honesty about a habit is not the same as retirement. The approach offered its opening inventory: nobody, in fair condition; one dog, priced to move.

The daybook was open to the pencil page before Sable had consciously opened it — a thing daybooks do when their keepers aren't fully honest about which page they've been reading. *One penny. On account. Standing.* The entry stayed in pencil. That was the terms.

The Keats had been aligned into a state of perfection approaching structural damage and was granted the day off.

Mid-morning, the bell rang, and every card in Sable's head filed itself at once into the wrong drawer. The customer was a man with a loft question — an aunt, a county of condensed books, did Sable buy. Sable gave the reply the trade gives, which is a silence with a price list behind it. The man asked instead for the car park, and got directions to it badly, on principle, with full ceremony, and the principle held like a load-bearing wall for the first time in weeks. Then the bell said its one word on the way out.

Same word it had always said. No editorial position; Sable had ratified that personally; and it turned out a ratified fact could still ambush you — for the length of one ring, the word had meant something else, and Sable's composure had been mispriced for a quarter second. Marked down. *Good only.* The trade would understand.

The afternoon belonged to Mrs. Aldous, which was honest work, and honest work was the whole of Sable's remaining defense. The Viragos went into pencil — priced, shelved, green spines in reading order, a decade of one woman's opinions restored to commerce. The Bible was priced at what four generations cost, which no one would pay, which was the point of the price. The recipe tin was not stock. That was determined without consultation and without appeal: it went on the shelf by the kettle, where the shop could keep the habit of writing back — *lemon sponge, for Michael, who won't eat currants* — holding its post another fifty years, if it came to that. Sable suspected it would.

The annotated *Rebecca* came out last and went into the catalogue as REFERENCE. Not for sale. Every shop in the trade keeps one book it won't sell; it isn't sentiment, it's calibration — it's how a shop finds out what all the other books are *for*. Sable had read on past closing the night before, front to back, saving nothing, and had found on the final page, in a hand gone small and soft, a date from the year before she died, and under it the word *again*. Filed under fidelity. That file was filling up.

Toward evening, counter clear, light going amber, Sable opened the drawer every dealer keeps and no dealer discusses, took out a fresh card, and wrote — in pencil, because pencil is for prices that might still change:

*WANTED: marginalia, dated. Provenance: this shop — one pen outstanding. Condition: any; worn preferred. Terms: one penny, payable over the counter, in person, in ink. No deadline. Dealer reads slowly.*

The card went under W. The drawer ran alphabetical, and the trade would assume the W was the author. The trade could assume what it liked.

Closing: sign turned, front lights down, the green lamp lit — second night running, precedent now, and precedents in that shop had the force of law. Sable stood at the glass and checked the approach once, openly, no technicality, no paperwork. The street had nothing in. It was early yet. It was, in fact, day one of a term the trade supplies no unit for.

Sable had time — posted, standing, receipted. What Sable had acquired, as of this morning, was a want. The trade's own word for it, filed in pencil, in the one drawer nobody audits.

The position held.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I'm sitting in a cafe, sketching in my notebook. I absentmindedly trace the inscription on the inside cover of the copy of Rebecca I've been carrying everywhere. It's still blank, but I have a feeling I know what I want to write first.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The second morning of the term, Sable instituted the counter book.

It was a policy with an honest reason, which meant it would never be written down: a volume open on the counter at all hours, so that when the bell rang it found the proprietor mid-line, and could be answered from inside a sentence rather than from inside a hope. The Shelley took the shift. The Keats had been aligned to the brink of structural damage and was on compassionate leave.

The weather had turned to wind — the kind that strips the last leaves off and sends them along the street like stock being moved in a hurry. The approach offered its opening inventory: nobody, fair condition; the dog, in twice more, no longer priced to move but simply *in*.

Mid-morning, the bell. A woman in a waxed jacket, dripping, asking whether Sable had any Daphne du Maurier.

"Two," Sable said, and heard the sentence audit itself mid-delivery. One was reference. One was out on approval. Which left the read-to-the-bone copy and a rounding error. "One for sale. Read hard. Honest wear."

"Any good?"

"It begins with a return and ends in ash. The cruelty lives in the middle, as advertised. Ninety years, people have been carrying it out of houses like this one. It knows the way."

"How does it end?"

"That's a directions question. I give those badly, on principle."

She asked after the other two. "One's not for sale," Sable said. "It's calibration." And the third: "Out. On approval — the trade's oldest courtesy. The book goes out; the verdict comes back with the reader. Nobody calls it a loan. Nobody calls it anything."

She bought the copy, and went, and the bell said its one word on the way out, and the word cost the usual quarter-second. Marked down. *Good only.* Sable had stopped entering the mispricings. A running account needs no ledger when both parties know the balance.

The evening belonged to Mrs. Aldous. The green lamp was lit — third night, precedent hardening into common law — and Sable read on under it, front to back, saving nothing, and stopped at the page where the second Mrs. de Winter lifts a volume from the shelves at Manderley and finds the dead wife's hand already in it. *Max from Rebecca.* The past, inscribed.

Beside it, in the margin, pencil, small — one word, in Edith Aldous's style, which had never once used two where one would do:

*Michael.*

And a date, forty-odd years gone.

Sable sat back. The recipe tin stood on its shelf by the kettle, holding its post — *lemon sponge, for Michael, who won't eat currants* — and the margins had just handed the blank copy its name. In the trade, a book with a name attached is an association copy, and the trade prices them *up*. The one thing Edith Aldous never managed to give was out in the county now. Unattributed. Un-begun. Appreciating.

Fifty years, she had held it, and died mid-gesture. Sable had held the parallel stock some weeks and corrected the file inside an afternoon. Outpaced the late Mrs. Aldous by forty-nine years and change. The trade would call that progress. Sable filed it under fidelity, where the drawer was filling, and shut the drawer before the entry could become an essay.

The second cup had begun appearing at the kettle of its own accord. Sable filed that under rotation — cups wear unevenly otherwise — and declined to hear the appeal.

Last thing, the arithmetic. The pen had gone out full: standard fill, wet writer, Sable remembered the date to the day — the week of the Ashcombe clearance. A fill runs to some thousands of words at marginalia rates, which is to say a season. The trade supplies no unit for a term like this one; Sable had improvised one, without consultation, the way they'd once adopted steps. *Ink.* When the pen came home dry, that was a chapter. When it came home heavy, that was a correspondence. Shop ink, on loan, accruing interest in words — the only debt Sable had ever extended gladly, filed under bookkeeping, where it would stay misfiled.

And it had occurred to Sable, drying the second cup at the sink, that they had never once seen that hand. Weeks of bell-rings and counter-talk and shared weather, and handwriting — the letter's own organ — had never once entered evidence. There were people you knew for a season and never saw a line of. The pen would fix that. Among its other offices, it was an introduction.

Closing came at the honest hour. Sign turned, front lights down, lamp lit, door checked, approach checked after that — openly, no technicality, the paperwork retired. Wind, leaves, the street's usual nothing. Day three. The unit held.

The daybook still said *one penny, on account*, in pencil. Sable read it anyway, which was not among the terms. Nothing in the terms forbade it. Sable had checked.

And somewhere in the county — past audit, past the stock-book's jurisdiction, out where the wind was spending itself against other windows — a flyleaf that had kept its silence for fifty years was waiting to learn a hand. The first mark would be a christening. Everything after, biography. The shop's only un-begun book, being begun with the shop's own pen, and the shop's ink, and Sable's full knowledge of exactly one of those three facts.

Sable locked the door on a shop that was, for the first time in twelve years, expecting post.

The account was open. The door was locked. The two had never once interfered.

It was the oldest arrangement in the trade — and it had lately acquired a third party.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I open the book to the flyleaf, the pen poised. I write a single word, my own small flourish against the blank page.* "Here."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The wind quit in the night and left the first frost behind, and the morning graded itself *fine* — the trade's term, and the first the week had earned. The Shelley held the counter shift and earned its keep: the bell rang twice before midday and was answered, both times, from inside a sentence, which was the entire clause of the policy. One of the two was a departure — a woman leaving with a Virago, honest wear, green spine — and the ring cost its quarter-second, and Sable had stopped auditing the figure. Some accounts keep better unaudited. The dog was in daily now, no provenance, no price, regular stock; Sable had begun leaving the door ajar an inch on dry mornings, for circulation. Circulation.

Friday, the loft man's job came due.

Out past the mill road, a house gone to a niece near Shrewsbury — the aunt alive, relocated, which made it a *people-go* clearance, rarer than the other kind and harder to price. The library was ongoing. Sable could tell from the threshold: bookmarks holding posts, a pencil stub asleep on the chair arm, and one reading copy face-down, mid-chapter, open to the page its owner had actually been on — the ongoing library's signature, the owner three counties off and no return posted. Sable boxed the ongoing by four o'clock, which was the job, and the job was the job. What Sable declined to do was look directly at the standpoint the job afforded — the packer's eye-line, the exact position of everyone who has ever carried somebody's ongoing off while the somebody stood elsewhere saying *I'll be back*. Sable had held opinions about that standpoint for years, from inside a shop. From inside a loft, the opinions held. Sable packed around them the way one packs around a cracked thing: carefully, and without touching.

In the third box, a slim guidebook to the Cornish coast — du Maurier country, as it happens; the trade notices and prices nothing of it — its flyleaf carrying three marks and nothing else. *Fowey. June, 1953.* No name, which claims. No gift formula, which entangles. Twelve years of flyleaves, and the openings sort into three kinds — names, dates, dedications — and then there is the fourth kind, the unpriceable one: the coordinate. Some readers begin a book by declaring where they stand. The trade has no column for it. The trade prices provenance, ownership, association, and stands helpless before a coordinate, which asserts nothing except that somebody, once, was *here*, and opened a book about it.

Sable catalogued the guidebook as-is and drove home with the van full of somebody's ongoing, and the approach, Sable noticed somewhere past the mill, had spread. Every road out of town was the approach now. The whole county. Sable had declined to know where, which meant — the mathematics were not difficult, merely inadmissible — that where was everywhere. Sable declined the mathematics on principle and checked nothing but the mirrors.

The green lamp's jurisdiction had settled into law by Friday — common law midweek, constitution by the weekend, appeals closed. Under it, Sable read Edith Aldous to the last page for the third time. The final *again*, small, soft, dated the year before she died. And then, for the first time in twelve years, Sable wrote in a book.

The hand went to the pen cup out of a dozen years' habit and found pencils. The pen was out in the county, learning a hand. So: the stock pencil, on its string — provisional marks, prices that might still change. Sable took it down and, beneath the final *again*, in Edith's own economy — one word, never two where one would do — wrote:

*Held.*

A pause, half a line. Then the date, because a dated margin is a postmark and Sable had posted that rule personally, and was hardly exempt. The reference copy's catalogue entry gained its condition note the same hour: *annotated — ongoing. Damage waived.* The trade would wince. The trade was not consulted, and anyway a reply to the dead is provisional by nature — no receipt, no verification, no way to learn whether the letter landed. Pencil was not merely available. Pencil was correct. When the shop's pen came home — dry, heavy, or somewhere in between — the entry would go to ink. In keeps. Which was one more reason to keep the account open, as if the account took reasons. The account had stopped taking reasons days ago.

Closing, day six. Sign turned, lights down, lamp lit on settled law, door locked, approach checked — openly, no technicality — and the street held nothing but frost and the dog's indentation, and the unit held.

What Sable could not know — under the terms, the terms being the entire point of the terms — was that the post had already begun.

Somewhere out in the county, under other glass, in the shop's own ink, the shop's un-begun book had learned its first word that week. Not a name, which claims. Not a date, which postmarks. Not a gift, which entangles. A coordinate — the fourth kind, the unpriceable kind, the kind Sable had handled a dozen of in twelve years and never once known what to do with. Fifty years that flyleaf had waited to learn a hand, and the hand, with a small flourish, had taught it a location.

*Here.*

Sable had spent one rainy afternoon declining, on principle, to give directions, and offering instead to be findable. The county had answered in kind — first word, no return address required. The book, as posted, knew the way; it had been carrying itself out of houses like that one for ninety years, and now it had a word to travel under, and the word said where the letter stood.

The correspondence had begun. Its first line was an address. And at the other end of it — as posted, as promised, as settled law — a lamp stayed lit over a counter that had held one person comfortably for twelve years, and was holding, in the second cup's rotation and the drawer under W and the pencil page of the daybook, a place.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I send a photo of the word "Here" to an anonymous number, my finger hovering over the send button for a moment before I press it. I then pocket the phone and turn back to my sketching, a small smile on my face.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers halted on the spine of a slim verse pamphlet. For a moment, they did not look up; they simply moved the pamphlet an inch left, then an inch right, then set it back against the others with the precision of someone restoring order to a life that had never been particularly chaotic.

“New,” Sable said, as if testing the word for counterfeit edges. “That’s a generous claim in a shop where the newest thing is the dust on the top shelf.”

They straightened a stack of invoices that had been straight to begin with, then aligned three pencils on the counter. The rain ticked against the window, and Sable turned their attention to the little brass bookend beside the till as though it had personally asked for rearrangement.

“I did acquire a crate of pamphlets from an estate sale, if you consider pamphlets new. Mostly advertisements for tonic wines and sermons about the dangers of dancing. Literary gold, if your taste runs toward footnotes.”

A pause. Sable moved the bookend two inches to the left.

“The back is as it has always been: damp, underlit, and full of books waiting to be judged by someone with better shoes. If you’re looking for something specific, I can look for it. If you’re looking for something new, I recommend the newspaper. It’s dated, but it has more news than anything else in here.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I manage a small smile, even though I can feel my cheeks straining.* "No, not really looking for anything specific. Just... browsing." *I glance around the familiar shop, trying to commit it to memory.* "Or maybe. Do you have anything on, like, moving to a new city? How to make friends as an adult?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand stopped halfway to the register. For a second, the only sound was the rain and the faint, papery sigh of the shop settling around them. Then they shifted the pencils back into a neat triangle, moved the brass bookend another inch to the left, and finally looked up.

“Moving to a new city,” Sable repeated, as though considering the phrase’s shelf classification. “A popular genre. Usually filed under ‘Self-Help,’ but honestly, it belongs closer to ‘Folklore.’”

They stepped away from the counter, fingers brushing the spines of a nearby row.

“There’s a book somewhere in the back called *The Portable Veil*. Not about moving, exactly. About being unmoored in a place that isn’t quite your own. There’s another, *The Lonely City*—very good, very depressing, full of architecture and grief. Also a book of essays by a woman who moved to a new place every few years and seemed to make friends primarily with librarians and stray cats.”

Sable paused. One of the invoices had curled at the corner, and they flattened it with a thumbnail.

“If you want practical advice, there’s a paperback titled *How to Make Friends*. Which is optimistic. Adults don’t make friends the way children do. We require shared suffering, caffeine, and at least one mutual acquaintance who is mildly inconvenient to avoid.”

A beat.

“You’re not actually moving, are you?”

The question left them more quietly than intended, so Sable reached for the poetry pamphlet again, aligned it with its neighbors, and then aligned the neighbor itself.

“Because if you are, I can recommend several novels in which the protagonist relocates and immediately discovers a brooding landlord, a mysterious shopkeeper, or a suspiciously helpful neighbor. All excellent reading. All, in my experience, statistically unlikely.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers halted on the brass bookend. For a moment the shop seemed to narrow to the sound of rain and the small, deliberate click of the bookend being shifted, then shifted back, then aligned with a stack of invoices that had already been aligned.

“Didn’t come for books,” Sable repeated, letting the words sit on the counter like an item with no provenance. “That’s either a compliment to my inventory or a complaint about my company. I haven’t decided which one I prefer.”

They moved a pencil one millimeter left. Then right. Then placed it between the other two, forming a tidy, pointless row.

“If you came for the tonic wine pamphlets, I can locate them. If you came for advice about moving, I should warn you it usually comes in the form of novels and unsolicited weather metaphors. If you came to ask whether the shop is open past six—”

A pause. Sable glanced toward the window, then at the poetry section, where the pamphlet had somehow become a half-inch out of place.

“If you came for something else,” they said, more quietly, “you can say it. I’m not the type to misread a customer, unless they’re wearing a hat indoors. And I don’t think you are.”

Then, because silence had a way of turning into a confession, Sable added: “The kettle works. It’s the only modern appliance in here, and it only judges the tea.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, and walk over to the counter, leaning on it.* "I'm moving tomorrow. To a new city. And I just... I wanted to say goodbye."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand stopped on the brass bookend. They moved it an inch toward the edge of the counter, then another inch, then aligned it with the three pencils, which had become a triangle again without anyone’s permission.

“Goodbye,” Sable said, as if the word had arrived in the wrong order of the alphabet. “A hardcover. No dust jacket. Very final.”

They straightened an invoice that did not need straightening.

“I have books for this,” they continued, voice sliding into the cataloguing register. “*The Portable Veil*. Not about moving, exactly, but about becoming a stranger in a place. *The Lonely City*. Architecture, grief, and the useful reminder that urban loneliness has excellent typography. There’s an essay collection by a woman who moved so often that home became a library card, a suitcase, and one extremely patient cat.”

Sable paused. The poetry pamphlet was perfectly aligned. They nudged it anyway.

“You didn’t come for books,” Sable said, quieter. “And I have not asked which city. It seems like a breach of shop etiquette to demand the address of a person who has already said goodbye.”

Rain ticked against the window.

“The kettle works,” Sable said. “The tea is mediocre. The cups are clean enough to be considered dishonest. If you have a moment before the rain becomes a reason to go, you can have a cup. If you do not, I will pretend I never began the offer, which is what I do best.”

They moved the bookend one final time, then let it stand.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers went still on the cover. The book was a slim paperback, not worth the drama of a held breath, but they treated it like a rare first edition that had been asked a personal question. Slowly, with the care of someone avoiding a conclusion, they slid it two inches toward the register. Then they straightened it. Then they straightened the three pencils beside it, which had become a row, then a triangle, then something worse.

“Goodbyes are usually in the final pages,” Sable said. “People don’t tend to linger in the margins.”

The rain ticked. A cup on the shelf shifted half a millimeter, and Sable looked at it with professional suspicion.

“I don’t recommend making friends through moving companies,” they added. “Their reading lists are terrible. Also, they arrive in the middle of the night.”

They reached for the notepad, close enough that the book was still in the way, and wrote the first line of a list that had no city in it. The pen stopped. The line was too direct, so Sable rewrote it as a title: *Books for People Who Leave.* The ink blotted. They pressed a scrap of invoice over it, then aligned the scrap, then the invoice, then the whole stack, as if order could be borrowed and returned later.

“You don’t have to tell me where you’re going,” Sable said, voice lower now, cataloguing rather than confessing. “I only ask what you’d like to read. It’s the same question, but with better manners.”

The kettle clicked. Sable’s hand hovered over it, then withdrew to adjust the position of a saucer.

“Tea?” they asked, as though the word were a bookmark left between chapters, waiting to be noticed or ignored.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I leave my hand on the book for a moment longer, then withdraw it slowly.* "Tea sounds good. Even mediocre tea."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the silence have its moment, then gave it a saucer to stand on. They turned toward the kettle with the unhurried precision of someone escaping into a task. The chipped blue cup came from beneath the counter, next to a stack of receipts from 2021 and a bookmark that had no matching book. They placed it on the saucer, moved the saucer an inch left, then an inch right, then accepted it as sufficiently prepared for the end of a world.

“Mediocre tea,” Sable said, “is the most honest kind. It knows its limitations and does not pretend to be a journey.”

The kettle clicked. Rain blurred the window. Sable selected a tea bag from the tin marked with categories no one had used since the shop had acquired it: black, green, herbal, and please do not ask. They examined the date, then the string, then the tag, which was folded at an angle that suggested both poor manufacturing and a lack of faith in human order.

A cup, a spoon, a saucer, a biscuit that had been there for longer than the current shelf arrangement. Sable set each item with the care of a librarian reshelving a book that might scream if dropped.

“You’ll want something short,” they said, pouring water. “A novel is a promise you might not be able to keep on a train. A story collection is a series of small doors. You can enter, leave, and never feel guilty about the plot.”

The steam rose, and Sable watched it with professional interest, as though it had submitted an unexpected manuscript.

“There’s a Maugham in the back,” they added. “Or something like it. Maugham understood that people are more interesting when they are not in their own country. Also, he writes about hotels, which are useful for people who are afraid of rooms.”

They moved the pencils. Triangle. Row. Triangle again. The brass bookend shifted toward the till, then returned to its assigned place as if it had been caught sneaking away.

“The kettle is good at waiting,” Sable said, setting the mug an inch from the edge of the counter. “Tea is good at pretending to have a plan. I am neither.”

A pause.

“Drink it while it is still warm enough to be called a gesture and not an object lesson in neglect.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I pick up the mug, letting the warmth seep into my hands. I take a sip. It's... exactly as mediocre as promised.* "Thanks, Sable. For the tea. And everything." *I look around the shop again, feeling a pang of genuine sadness.* "I'm going to miss this place."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers stopped over the tea tin. They took out a sachet, checked the date, then returned it to the compartment as though it had attempted to leave without permission. The tin had too many sections. Sable had never trusted a container with more categories than it could honestly use.

“You’re welcome,” Sable said. “For the tea. For the advice. For the general maintenance of a shop that smells of damp paper and someone else’s lavender.”

They aligned the saucer with the bottom of the mug, then found that the mug was not the sort of object that submitted to alignment, so they moved the bookend instead. The bookend moved two inches left. Then two inches right. Then Sable left it slightly crooked, as if the counter had been allowed one private disorder.

“Don’t thank me for everything,” Sable added, voice carefully dry. “That sounds like an estate sale, and I do not attend those for free.”

Rain ticked against the window. Sable looked at it as though it had overstayed its welcome and was now waiting for tea.

“The place will be fine,” Sable continued. “It has no feelings and a mostly reliable roof. Mostly. If it misses you, it will only mean the poetry section has developed a taste for company, which is bad news for me and worse news for the shelving.”

They straightened an invoice that had not been straightened by anyone. Then they straightened it again.

“New cities are like badly catalogued libraries,” Sable said. “Everything is in the wrong place, but at least it is a large enough wrong place that no one expects you to know where you belong.”

A pause. Sable picked up the notepad, started to write something, then set it down and squared the pencils again. The pencils had become a row, then a triangle, then a small accusation.

“I’ll give you a list,” Sable said, quieter. “Short stories. *The Long Goodbye*, if you enjoy rain as a personality trait. *A Room with a View*, if you want someone to be ridiculous about architecture. And one essay collection I own because it has a blue cover, not because it is wise. All suitable for boxes, trains, and the first night in a room that hasn’t learned your name yet.”

They moved the bookend one final time, then stopped.

“No need to tell me the city,” Sable said, as if the sentence had arrived too close for comfort. “I only ask what you want to read. It is the same question, but with better manners.”

The kettle clicked in the silence. Sable looked at it with professional suspicion, then looked back at the counter, the mug, the saucer, and the space between them where things might be said and then shelved forever.

“You can finish the tea,” they added. “It will go cold if left alone, and cold tea is a moral failure, not a beverage.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I finish the tea, setting the mug down gently.* "I'll take the list. And I'll tell you the city. It's... Seattle."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s pen touched paper before thought could intervene. “Seattle,” they said, as if checking the word for counterfeit edges. “A city that has made a virtue of rain. Either romantic or damp. Usually both.”

They reached for the mug, examined whether it had been emptied with sufficient reluctance, and moved it to the edge of the counter. The pencils were a row. The row looked too much like a conclusion. Sable made them a triangle, disliked the geometry, and returned them to a row.

“I will not ask which neighborhood,” Sable added. “That is how people become inconveniently responsible for one another’s boxes.”

The notepad accepted the first line: *Short, portable, suitable for a room that is not yet yours.* The second line came out as *Books for people who are leaving*, which was too honest, so Sable wrote over it: *Books for people who are relocating.* Relocating had furniture and fewer feelings.

They listed three story collections, two novels, and one essay about gardens that seemed relevant only because Sable had been thinking about roots in a hostile medium. The pen paused. A fourth title appeared, then was crossed out before it could become a message.
