"The shrine offers a middle road. The Commander demands a leash. The Treasury demands a price." Her gaze settled on you and did not waver. "Consider what my oversight must mean, Ambassador, for the word to carry any weight at all. Your patrols, sworn to my law. Your captains surrendering themselves to my justice if they break faith on those roads — no appeal to Velheim, no shelter behind your seal." A beat, cold and precise. "The Priestess's icons would witness it. The Commander's officers would enforce it. Daven's ledgers would record it. Tell me plainly — does your proposal survive that meaning? Because if it does not, we are all of us wasting candlelight."

The Herald did not strike his staff. There was no one left to announce. The floor was yours again, and this time the silence had a shape — it was a question, and it carried your name.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For the space of three heartbeats, nothing in the throne room moved. Then somewhere in the gallery a lord coughed and strangled it halfway out of himself.

The Herald's staff came down like a headsman's axe. "The Ambassador will address the throne, and only the—"

Two fingers lifted from the armrest. That was all. The Herald's voice stopped as though a hand had closed over it.

"The court," Queen Isara said, "will hear the Commander's answer."

Commander Ash had gone still in a way parade rest was never built for. When he spoke, he looked past the throne, past the protocol, directly at you.

"Six weeks." He made no attempt to deny it, and the denial's absence moved through the hall like a cold draft. "Six weeks of Velheim hulls running dark past the quarantine markers with steel in their holds and no manifest to name it. Steel bound north, Ambassador — to the clans that bleed my garrisons on the very passes you're so eager to reopen." His thumb traveled along the pommel, slow, like a man sharpening something. "My ships stopped them. That is what garrisons are for. Shall I read the cargo lists into the record? Some of your merchants were less careful with their paperwork than you have just been with your protocol."

The staff cracked, salvaging what ceremony remained. "The court recognizes Lord Daven of the Treasury."

Daven rose from the gallery without his usual leisure. "Cargo lists. Yes, Commander — let us have them, every page." A thin smile, precise as a ledger entry. "Because lawful interdiction is adjudicated in prize court. Seizures are assessed, filed, and their proceeds recorded in the Crown's accounts. Six weeks of seizures, and the Treasury has received not one crown. Not one filing. Not one page." He turned his open palms toward the throne, reasonable as arithmetic. "Either the seizures never happened, and the Commander has slandered Velheim before his Queen — or they happened, and an entire season of cargo has vanished between the northern coast and this room. The Treasury is genuinely curious which."

In her alcove, the prayer beads clicked.

"A soldier's oath binds him to his sovereign's word," Priestess Yuna said, to the icons rather than the court. "A commander who acts on his own authority keeps no oath the icons can witness. And cargo taken at sea without warrant or adjudication—" a bead turned against its neighbor "—the old word for that is piracy." Her gaze drifted, mild and terrible, across the hall. "Though if those holds truly carried steel, then Velheim's merchants have broken faith of their own. The icons keep both accounts open. Both."

"Commander." Queen Isara's voice dropped into the hall like a stone down a well. "By whose order?"

"Standing authority, Majesty. The security of the northern approaches—"

"I do not recall granting it."

The hall did not breathe. And for the first time since you had entered the throne room, Commander Ash's hand fell away from the sword pommel and hung empty at his side — a statement with nothing left to state.

Whether the fault lay in his memory or in hers, no one in that hall could have said, and that was plainly the point. The Queen had neither pardoned the blockade nor claimed it. She had set it down at Ash's feet like an unpaid debt, and stepped back to watch him carry it.

Then her gaze came to rest on you, and stayed.

"You came with terms in one hand, Ambassador. It appears you carried a knife in the other." Something crossed her face that a generous man might have mistaken for approval. "The court notes the breach and will not extend the courtesy twice. The blockade will be examined. The prize court will convene. The Commander's authority will be weighed — and if his holds contain what he claims, Velheim's merchants will be weighed beside them. You have purchased the court's full attention. Consider carefully whether everything it now sees flatters you."

She settled back against the marble.

"The terms. Again. And this time, Ambassador — account for the knife."

The Herald struck his staff once, and the sound was almost gentle. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim."

The floor was yours. The silence had changed shape once more: no longer a question but an open blade laid on the table between you and the throne — and the whole court waited to see who would be first to reach for it.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *My jaw tightens. They had me. I take a slow breath, gathering myself.* "Your Majesty. The knife is a response to the threat. Velheim's merchants have acted to defend themselves against piracy." *I let the word hang in the air for a moment, meeting Ash's furious gaze.* "As for the terms, they stand. Joint patrols, joint oversight, and a new tariff structure."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The word *piracy* struck the hall and stuck there, glittering, too sharp for anyone to swallow. The Herald's staff rose halfway — then settled. The letter of the law had been kept: the words went to the throne. Only their aim had been elsewhere. In the gallery a chair creaked as someone leaned forward, and no one told them to sit back.

Commander Ash's hand found the pommel again. Not a statement this time. A need.

"The court recognizes Commander Ash, Lord of the Northern Garrison."

"Piracy." He said the word like a man tasting something spoiled. "Majesty — the Ambassador has just told this court his merchants carried that steel *deliberately*. There is the confession, wearing better clothes." His voice dropped, which was worse than shouting would have been. "The first dark hull I logged ran iron north four months before my ships ever stopped a single one. What were they defending against then — the winter?" He let it land. "I welcome the prize court. I will stack the seized bars on this marble myself and let the icons count them. And if running war iron to the clans is Velheim's idea of defense, then the document in the Ambassador's sleeve is not a treaty. It is a supply schedule."

"The court recognizes Lord Daven of the Treasury."

Daven rose without leisure, with the speed of a man reaching a fire before it spreads. "The court is trying the past. The treasury bleeds in the present. Piracy, smuggling, warrantless seizure — these have a legal home, and it is the prize court Her Majesty has already ordered. Let both accounts be weighed there, side by side, under one law." He turned, deliberately, to include you. "What remains in this room is *tomorrow*. So — arithmetic. Velheim's patrols march under Crown law, as the Commander demands. Velheim's captains swear before the icons, answerable to Crown justice without appeal, as Her Majesty defined and the shrine requires. In exchange, Velheim retains one share in three of the route tariffs, seven years, funding its patrols from that share alone. The Crown's coffers untouched. The roads open." His eyes found yours for the space of a blink — long enough to say *I am buying you out of the fire, and you will owe me.* "If the Ambassador can live with a third for seven years, let him say so plainly. Candlelight is not free."

The prayer beads clicked.

"Half an answer has been given," Priestess Yuna said to the icons, not the court. "The Ambassador calls iron a shield. The icons do not hear what men call things. They hear what men swear." A bead turned against its neighbor. "Let both ledgers be weighed — the Commander's seizures, the merchants' steel. Whoever broke faith, on either side, stands before the icons and answers. No treaty signed above an unweighed crime. A house built on ice holds very well. Until spring." Another click. "The Treasury's arithmetic, with oaths on both ends of it — that much the shrine can witness."

Queen Isara let the last click fade before she spoke.

"You were asked to account for the knife, and you accounted for it by renaming it a shield. Your merchants armed themselves against a piracy that began, by your own telling, only when ships stopped them — for carrying arms. The circle is elegantly tailored, Ambassador. The court has seen the stitching." Her fingers tapped the armrest once. "You were also asked whether your terms survive my meaning of oversight. You did not answer. The Treasury answered for you. Perhaps wisdom. Perhaps a man watching someone else pay his debts."

She straightened against the marble.

"Here is what the court will do. The blockade, the seizures, and the steel go to the prize court — both accounts, as the shrine requires. The treaty goes forward on the Treasury's arithmetic: Crown law over the patrols, captains sworn and answerable without appeal, one share in three, seven years. That is now the meaning of your terms, whether you meant it or not. So the court asks one final time, and will accept no word besides: *yes, or no.*"

A beat, cold and total.

"And understand what your answer buys. Sign, and the roads open under oath. Refuse, and they stay closed — and the prize court weighs your merchants' steel either way. The treaty buys trade, Ambassador. It does not buy absolution."

The Herald struck the floor once. "The court will hear the Ambassador of Velheim."

The silence had found a third shape: a scale, balanced and patient, with your yes on one pan and your neck on the other.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *My gaze flickers to Daven, a silent acknowledgment of the rescue, then back to the Queen.* "Yes, Your Majesty. The terms are accepted." *I offer a slight, almost imperceptible nod.* "Velheim agrees."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The word was small. The hall received it as though it were not.

The Herald's staff struck the marble once, clean and final. "So entered. The Ambassador of Velheim accepts the terms of this court. Let the rolls record it, and let no man present claim he heard otherwise."

The silence found its fourth shape: a ledger closing.

Queen Isara did not smile. Smiling, you suspected, was among the many things she had declined to bring into this room.

"Then the court has its treaty." Her voice carried no warmth, but it carried weight, and in that hall weight was worth more. "The instrument will be drawn by the Treasury and sealed before the shrine. The oaths will be sworn at the icons — captains and officers both, and the Ambassador's own hand upon the parchment, since he has proven so fond of holding two things at once." A pause, surgical. "The roads open on the seventh day. Or they do not open at all."

Then she turned her head, and Commander Ash learned what it was to be looked at the way you had been looked at.

"Commander. The blockade ends before this court adjourns. The seized cargo passes to the prize court under Treasury seal — inventoried, weighed, and entire. If a single bar is missing when it arrives, the court will remember precisely which coast it vanished on." Her fingers tapped the armrest once. "And no ship under your command will stop a hull on the northern approaches without warrant from this throne. The standing authority you remember so fondly — consider it forgotten."

"The court recognizes Commander Ash, Lord of the Northern Garrison," the Herald said, and for once the announcement sounded almost like mercy.

Ash bowed his precise half-inch. His voice, when it came, was level in the way of ice over deep water.

"As my Queen commands. The bars will be counted in the open, every one, and the cargo lists read into the record — including the four manifests bearing a countersignature." His eyes found yours across the hall and settled there with the patience of a siege. "The prize court will ask whose hand holds the pen that signs Velheim's shipping papers, Ambassador. Merchants carry steel. Someone sells it to them. I intend to read that ledger all the way to the top."

"The court recognizes Lord Daven of the Treasury."

Daven rose without leisure, with the crisp economy of a man closing accounts. "The Treasury will draft the instrument within three days and deliver it to the shrine for sealing. Tariff shares as ruled: one in three, seven years, patrol costs drawn from the Velheim share alone." He inclined his head toward the throne — then, deliberately, toward you. "The Treasury also notes that the Ambassador and I have arithmetic to discuss before the seventh day. The roads, Majesty, will open on schedule."

The glance he gave you lasted a blink. It said: *the fire is out. Now we discuss the price of the water.*

In the alcove, the prayer beads clicked.

"The shrine will receive the oaths at dawn on the seventh day," Priestess Yuna said, to the icons, to the hall, to no one. "Both ledgers travel together — the Commander's seizures and the merchants' steel — and both will be weighed before a single signature dries." A bead turned against its neighbor. "Bring your captains, Ambassador. Bring clean hands. The icons will know the difference, and they have never been skilled at pretending otherwise."

Queen Isara rose, and the hall rose with her in a rustle of silk and steel.

"You came for roads, Ambassador. You leave with roads, a treaty, and a trial. Few envoys depart carrying so much." She descended the dais without hurry, passing close enough that her final words belonged to you alone. "Do not mistake the weight for a gift. Candlelight was spent on you tonight — the Treasury's, the shrine's, mine. Weight is what a man owes." She did not look back. "The court is adjourned."

"The court is adjourned!" The Herald's staff struck the floor a last time. "All honor to Her Majesty, Queen Isara, and to her court!"

The doors swallowed the Queen. Then the hall loosened, precedence dissolving into motion. Commander Ash came down the aisle first, and he did not alter his path by a single step — he passed close enough that his words needed no volume at all.

"Forty-one letters, Ambassador. I write them well now. Pray the prize court never asks me to write to Velheim." He was gone before the words finished cooling.

From the alcove, one final click of beads — Yuna's gaze resting on you a moment, mild and bottomless, before the attendants began snuffing candles around her.

Lord Daven descended from the gallery at an unhurried amble, all his leisure returned now that it cost nothing, and stopped before you with his hands folded like a man presenting a bill.

"You said yes with admirable speed," he said. "Now walk with me, Ambassador. The treaty was the easy arithmetic. What you owe me for the fire escape is the harder sum — and I prefer to collect debts while the ink is still wet."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I glance at Daven, then back to Yuna.* "These are your ledgers, Priestess. Velheim's counter-claim."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The beads stopped.

All through the hearing they had measured the court's silences — click, turn, click — a small sound that had somehow become the metronome of the hall. Now it ceased, and the cessation was louder than the Herald's staff had ever been. The attendants froze mid-snuff around the alcove, tapers hovering, and the last departing lords stopped pretending to leave.

Priestess Yuna did not reach for the papers eagerly. She received them the way the shrine received everything: as a weight, to be carried before it was understood. An attendant brought the taper close.

"The court is adjourned," the Herald said, recovering his ceremony. "Nothing presented after adjournment enters the record of the court."

"No," Yuna agreed, mild and bottomless. "It enters the record of the shrine." A beat. "That record is longer."

She read without performance — no gasp, no widened eyes — and the absence of theater became a theater no one in the hall could look away from.

"Orders of the northern fleet," she said at last, to the icons rather than to anyone living. "Instructions for the stopping of Velheim hulls — and the quiet sale of what they carried. A southern port. No filing. No entry in the prize rolls. Proceeds to an account named by cipher alone." A page turned with a sound like a small bone settling. "Dated three days before the first hull was stopped." Another page. "The counterseal of the Northern Garrison rides every sheet. The hand is not the Commander's."

She closed the folio and held it flat on her palms, the way one holds a sleeping thing that might wake.

"So the ledgers open wider. The Commander's steel is real; the graves are owed. The piracy is real; the seizures were priced before they were justified. And beneath both, a third hand — one that sells the iron, stops the ships, and keeps the difference." A bead turned against its neighbor, slow as a verdict. "The icons will hold all three accounts open until the seventh day."

Lord Daven had gone very still — the stillness of a man watching arithmetic change shape in front of him. When he spoke, his leisure was gone, and his voice had the clipped cadence of an auditor who has found the discrepancy.

"You gave the shrine a knife before your ally saw its edge," he said, without heat — he was too busy thinking to be insulted. "Noted, and filed. Now. The Commander spoke tonight of four manifests bearing a countersignature. If that countersign and this cipher resolve to the same account, then someone has been selling iron north and confiscating it south, billing both kingdoms for the privilege of being robbed." He stepped to the edge of the alcove, close enough for the taper to find his face. "The Treasury knows every numbered account in this realm and several it politely pretends not to. Give me the cipher and three days, and I will hand you its owner. But understand the cost of the asking: the Treasury cannot pull a thread without the thread feeling the tug. Somewhere south of here, a man still believes those orders are exactly where he left them. You have seven days — or fewer, once he begins to wonder. Paper travels slower than fear."

His gaze drifted toward the doors Ash had gone through, and something cold and practical moved behind it.

"And consider the Commander. His counterseal. Another's hand. That makes him the crime's author, its instrument, or its careless landlord — and Lord Ash strikes me as a man who would burn the coast down to learn which. Whoever you tell first, Ambassador, and when, will decide whether he arrives at that prize court as your accuser or your witness. Her Majesty, you will notice, had already quit the hall before these surfaced. With that woman, nothing is ever only coincidence."

The taper's light steadied. Yuna let the folio rest on her palms a moment longer — then, for the first time since the adjournment, she aimed her voice at you, and the difference was like a lens taking the sun.

"These will be weighed at dawn on the seventh day, with both ledgers, before the icons, as I promised." A pause. "But the icons weigh more than paper. They will weigh how it crossed your hands, Ambassador. Orders intercepted are still intercepted. Stolen truth is still truth — and it is also still stolen. The Queen asked you to account for one knife tonight. I am asking you to account for the hand that caught this one." Her gaze rested on you, mild and bottomless as ever. "Where did Velheim's fingers close on the Crown's orders, and who watched them do it? Answer plainly. The icons are listening, and they have never been skilled at pretending otherwise."

Down the long aisle the last candle went out, and the dark came up the marble toward the alcove like a tide. The Herald's staff struck once — "The hall closes, honored guests" — and Daven stood waiting at your shoulder with his hands folded, patient as an unpaid bill.

Somewhere in the dark, the beads began to click again.

The silence had found its fifth shape of the night: a confession, waiting to see who would claim it.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *My eyes meet Yuna's.* "A Crown officer, Priestess. Disgusted by the corruption. He sends regular reports to Velheim." *I hold her gaze.* "He will testify, under oath, at the prize court."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The beads turned once more, then were still.

"A Crown officer," Priestess Yuna said, to the icons rather than to you. "Then the shrine holds a fourth ledger tonight. The Commander's seizures. The merchants' steel. The cipher's hidden hand. And now an oath, sworn to the Crown and kept instead by Velheim." The taper's light crossed her face and found nothing there to read. "Disgust writes one letter, Ambassador. Regular reports are a correspondence. The icons will not weigh which of those he kept — not until he stands before them and names it himself."

She rose, the folio still flat on her palms, carried the way one carries a sleeping thing.

"Bring him whole on the seventh day. The icons weigh the dead as honestly as they weigh the living — but they cannot make a dead man swear." A bead turned against its neighbor. "And carry this back to him from the shrine: they heard his first oath when he made it. They will hear his answer for it. No man should swear a second oath unless he is prepared to pay for the first."

An attendant preceded her with the lamp. The dark took her a step at a time, and the beads went on clicking somewhere down the colonnade long after the light was gone — a small sound, keeping its own record.

"The hall is closed," the Herald said, recovering what ceremony the evening had left him. "Honored guests will conclude their honors in the outer corridor, where the candles are humbler and the echoes are loyal." His staff struck once — a formality now — and he conducted you out through the western doors at the pace of a man closing accounts.

The corridor ran cold, night air pooling on the flagstones, guards posted at even intervals like fence posts. Through the seaward arches the harbor lay black — except for three lamps burning at the mouth, where the blockade still held its line.

Lord Daven stopped at the window and looked at those lamps for a long moment before he spoke.

"A Crown officer. In Velheim's purse." He said it the way he said numbers. "You told that to a priestess and a treasurer in the same breath, so I'll assume it was deliberate — the alternative obliges me to think less of you, and I'd rather not." He turned. "Understand what you spent tonight. That fact is currency, and you paid it out twice. Very well. My advice, which is free and therefore should alarm you: do not tell me his name. I can be compelled. Her Majesty compels. The Commander compels. The owner of that cipher can simply purchase. Names are for the seventh day and the icons. What I want is what he *knows* — the cipher, the southern port, the broker who moved the iron. If your man can put a face to that account, I close this ledger in three days instead of hunting it for thirty."

His knuckle tapped the sill, once, toward the window.

"And then get him out alive. Consider his position. He lives inside the machine he intends to condemn. The moment those orders are read at dawn — the moment, Ambassador — the cipher's owner counts his secrets and finds one missing. Meanwhile the Commander will already be tearing his own garrison apart hunting the hand that forged his counterseal. Two hunts, one warren, one rabbit — and the rabbit reports to you." A nod toward the lamps. "She ordered the blockade ended before adjournment. The court adjourned a quarter hour ago, and the ships are still out. Either the tide is against him, or Ash is deciding how literally he obeys. Your officer lives under that man's flag. Weigh what that is worth."

"Ambassador." The Herald had followed after all. He stood at formal attention, hands empty, voice pitched for a corridor. "Before Her Majesty departed the hall, she left an instruction with me. Should any matter arise tonight that did not enter the record of the court, the Ambassador of Velheim was to be told: Her Majesty will receive him at the ninth hour tomorrow." A pause, and then, because he was a precise man and precision was its own message: "The instruction was given before the court adjourned."

He bowed the exact depth protocol required and withdrew.

Daven went still. Then, softly, with something that was almost admiration: "Before the paper existed in that hall, she had already priced it. Or she simply assumes every ambassador carries a second knife — which, in fairness, is sound fiscal policy." He folded his hands. "So. The morning is hers. The night is mine. I need two answers before the ninth hour, Ambassador: what your officer knows of the cipher, and how Velheim means to keep him breathing long enough to swear it. Because whatever you tell me tonight, you will be telling her a version of it by daylight — and I prefer to know which version before she does."

Below, the blockade lamps burned on against the black water. The silence had found its sixth shape of the night: a fuse, quiet and patient, laid all the way to the ninth hour — and the match, as it had been all evening, was yours.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet Daven's gaze, a cold certainty in my eyes.* "The officer's name is Lieutenant Valerius. He knows the cipher, and the southern port. He's also aware of a ledger maintained by the broker, detailing every shipment." *I pause, a subtle challenge in my voice.* "Keeping him breathing is your problem now, Lord Daven. He serves the Crown, not Velheim."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For the space of a breath, Lord Daven said nothing at all. Then he laughed — once, softly, with no humor anywhere in it.

"I told you not to give me the name." He said it the way he noted discrepancies: without anger, with finality. "And you handed it over anyway, in a corridor, with guards at every post. So either you stopped listening halfway through my advice — and I don't believe that — or you wanted it sitting in my hands." His eyes narrowed, running sums. "A name shared is a chain shared, Ambassador. If Valerius burns, my hands carry the same smoke as yours. You have just promoted your ally into your accomplice. The most expensive gift I have received all year, and you gave it freely." He inclined his head a precise inch, ceremony worn as mockery. "Noted. Filed. It will appear on the bill."

Then the rest of it caught up with him, and his voice changed — the auditor finding the master page.

"A ledger. Kept by the broker. Every shipment." He turned from the window as though the harbor had stopped mattering. "Do you understand what you described? The Commander's seizures, the merchants' steel, the cipher's account — all three of tonight's books are abridgments of that one. Whoever keeps it isn't a thread in this, Ambassador. He's the loom." A pause, and something moved behind his eyes like fish under ice. "Bring me that ledger, or bring me Valerius sworn to what's in it, and the Treasury will owe you a favor. There is no rarer coin in this city, and none harder to counterfeit."

He spread his hands — reasonable, precise, merciless.

"As for whose problem his breathing is. The Treasury does not keep men alive; it keeps them solvent. Breathing is done with soldiers, and tonight there are exactly two sets of soldiers in reach: the Queen's guard and the Commander's. So follow the arithmetic. Your rabbit goes to ground under the shrine's lamp, where the Priestess weighs his first oath the moment he's warm. Or into Her Majesty's hand at the ninth hour, where you will ask our Queen to shelter a man who serves her Crown's uniform and Velheim's interests at once — and the Priestess named that one exactly: disgust writes one letter, yours keeps a correspondence, and Her Majesty will want the dates." A thin smile. "You handed me the problem. Accepted — at interest. But the problem has two doors, and you are standing in front of both."

The smile thinned further.

"Which brings us to the version. She will ask what you gave me tonight — the instruction was left before adjournment, so she already knows you carried a second knife; she merely lacks its shape. Decide now, in this corridor, whether the name Valerius crosses your lips in that room. If you speak it and I deny it, we are both dead in different ways. If you withhold it and she compels me later, I will name you as the hand that gave it to me — without apology, without hesitation. I keep my ledgers balanced, Ambassador. Even the ones written in blood."

Below, the outermost lamp at the harbor mouth went dark. Then the second. The third burned a moment longer, as if considering, and followed.

"So," Daven murmured. "He obeys." He watched the black water. "A man who obeys that literally will hunt the same way. No doors kicked in. Every door, in order, with paperwork."

Footsteps then — a runner came down the corridor at a pace no court had taught him, a Treasury boy with ink on his cuffs, and pressed a folded note into Daven's palm. Daven read it once. His leisure died a second death that night.

"I keep a clerk on the garrison gate. Old habit." He refolded the note along its crease. "The Commander has recalled every commissioned officer of the northern fleet. Muster at the garrison hall at first bell — logs, seals, and correspondence laid out for inspection. He is hunting the hand that forged his counterseal, and he means to have it before the prize court does." A beat. "First bell, Ambassador. Her Majesty receives you at the ninth. Your lieutenant stands in that hall with his papers in three hours — or he is absent, and in the Commander's arithmetic, absence is a signature."

Somewhere down the colonnade, faint and indifferent, prayer beads clicked twice — the shrine, keeping its own record of the hour.

The silence found its seventh shape of the night: a snare, set quiet between two bells — first bell on one jaw, the ninth hour on the other — and the rabbit, as it had been all evening, was yours.

"Where," Daven asked, very quietly, "is Valerius sleeping tonight?"

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *My jaw tightens. I look at Daven, then out at the now-dark harbor.* "He's at the Red Dragon Inn, room seven. But he won't be there for long." *I turn back to Daven, a desperate edge to my voice.* "We need to get him out *now*."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
"We," Daven said.

He turned the pronoun over once, like a coin of doubtful mint. "You said 'we,' Ambassador. That word has ruined better men than either of us. Noted. Filed." Then he was moving. "Pell — paper, seal, the traveling inkstand. We are being informal tonight."

The Treasury boy produced all three from inside his coat with the speed of a man who had been cold and ready for hours. Daven braced the page against the seaward arch, the night wind riffling it, and wrote standing, fast, in a hand that looked unhurried even at speed.

"By order of the throne, given this night at adjournment: the seized cargo of the northern fleet passes to the prize court under Treasury seal, to be inventoried, weighed, and entire." The pen scratched. "To that end, the Treasury requisitions one officer of the northern fleet, versed in manifests, for inventory duty — detached from all other duty, effective this hour." The pen stopped above the line for exactly one heartbeat. Then it wrote: *Lieutenant Valerius.*

"There," Daven said, quieter. "Now my name burns in the same fire as yours."

He pressed his signet into the wax and kept talking, because the ledger in his head never closed.

"Understand the trick, so you can defend it at the ninth hour. You don't pull a rabbit from a warren — you paper over the warren's door. At first bell the Commander counts his officers. One man absent, and his hunt ends before it begins; absence is a signature, he told us so himself. But one man *detached on Treasury business under the Crown's own adjournment order* — that man is not absent. That man is furniture." He folded the writ with clean, exact creases. "He hunts with paperwork, Ambassador. Very well. Tonight the paperwork hunts for us. Pell lodges a copy at the garrison gate within the hour — he knows which window never closes — filed in order, door by door, exactly where a man like Ash expects paper to be. He will read it. He obeys literally, but he reads everything, and he is not stupid: he'll know what this writ is the instant he sees the name. What he cannot do is break it. Not without a warrant from the throne, and the throne wrote the order it stands on. This buys the letter of the law between your rabbit and his commander. It buys no blindness. Six days, if we spend them well."

Through the seaward arches, the black harbor had begun to fill with returning lamplight — the fleet coming home with the tide, every hold a locked box of evidence, every lamp a man who had sailed the seizures and knew what the holds weighed.

"He goes to the prize-court stores. The cargo comes off Ash's ships tonight, and your lieutenant will inventory it — six days of honest work, counting the bars that will hang his betters, sleeping behind the one door in this city no one may lawfully open before the prize court convenes. Not the Commander. Not the cipher's owner, unless he hires a man too stupid to read seals. He becomes inventory, Ambassador. Crown-sealed, weighed, entire. Her Majesty will appreciate the bookkeeping."

He held the folded writ up between two fingers — and did not hand it over.

"The price. If the words 'Valerius' and 'Daven' are ever read in the same sentence by the wrong eyes, this page is my confession. So: when the broker's ledger surfaces — and it will, your man knows where it sleeps — the Treasury reads it first. Before the throne. Before the shrine. Before the prize court. Whatever it proves, I read it while the ink is wet. That is the mortgage, and it is cheaper than it sounds. Or dearer. We'll know when we see the numbers."

Then he set the writ on the cold stone of the sill, where the torchlight and the harbor lamps disputed over it.

"Last door, and it's yours. Pell can carry this to room seven — clean, boring, deniable. A Treasury summons at midnight is strange but lawful; the cargo lands tonight, the inventory is urgent, no one questions urgency." A pause. "But Pell is a stranger, and frightened men open dockside doors at midnight expecting knives. Your rabbit doesn't know Pell's face. He knows yours. So — send the paper, or bring the face. I cannot; the Lord of the Treasury does not visit dockside inns at this hour, and I decline to learn why. First bell is in three hours. And you told me he won't wait — which means, Ambassador, that the race is already run on his legs, not ours."

Pell vanished down the corridor toward the garrison gate at a dead sprint, ink cuffs flapping. Somewhere deep in the palace, far off, prayer beads clicked once — the shrine, keeping the hour.

The silence found its eighth shape of the night: a race, run in the dark between a room and a bell — and the rabbit, for the first time all evening, was not waiting to be caught.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I grab the writ off the sill, my fingers closing around the stiff parchment.* "I'll go. He'll recognize me." *I don't look at Daven, already turning towards the corridor.* "Just make sure Pell does his part."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Daven watched you take the writ the way misers watch coins leave the vault — no protest, just inventory.

"Pell does his part the way ink dries: without opinion, without witnesses. The gate is what I cannot vouch for. If his copy isn't through that window within the hour, the page in your coat is paper with my name on it and nothing else." He was already giving you the route, fast, like dictation. "Seaward stair, not the postern — the postern's sergeant logs faces. Rope Street, past the fish market, dock side of the chandlers. The sign's dragon lost its wings some winters back; you'll know it by the door that doesn't quite close. And, Ambassador — if room seven is already empty, you come back. A rabbit lost is a cost. An ambassador lost is a scandal, and scandals are the one line item the Treasury has never once budgeted."

He folded his hands, all his leisure gone somewhere to wait for morning.

"Ninth hour. Whatever the night does to you, be washed by the eighth."

The seaward stair carried you down off the hill, and the palace let you go a candle at a time — windows dying above you as the snuffers worked through the wings. One window stayed lit, high in the western tower, small and steady. Whoever owned it was awake, and pricing things. Somewhere in all that dark behind you, prayer beads clicked once — the shrine, keeping its own record of the hour.

Then the city had you.

The route Daven chose ran out along the quay, and the quay was anything but asleep. The fleet was coming home with the tide — lamps multiplying on black water, anchor chains groaning, boats thick across the harbor mouth where three hours ago the blockade's lights had died one by one. The seized cargo was already moving ashore: Treasury porters and fleet sailors wrestling crates down the gangplanks, wax seals pale and fresh on every lid, a clerk counting each crate aloud the way a man counts sheep he has been warned will be stolen.

Past the garrison wall, the yard was lit like a feast day and was nothing of the kind. Officers arrived out of the dark in twos and threes, dragging document chests — logs, seals, correspondence — to trestle tables set under lamplight. At the gate's lamp, a boy with ink on his cuffs was passing folded paper through a window that never closed, and it went in without slowing.

At the head of the tables stood a silhouette you knew — parade rest abandoned, bent over the first chest, already reading. Commander Ash had not gone to bed and did not mean to. He read the way he obeyed: literally, and in order.

Rope Street narrowed around you until the overhangs nearly met overhead, and the fish market's smell arrived before the market did. The Red Dragon's sign hung from one chain — a dragon that had lost its wings to weather and its fire to time — and the door, as promised, did not quite close.

The common room was low and tallow-smoked, half full of fleet sailors spending their first un-blockaded night on dice and worse wine. Nobody marked you but the innkeeper, a woman with forearms like mooring line, who looked up from a barrel she was not polishing and went back to it.

One man marked you anyway, without appearing to. Corner table, back to the wall, alone — a cup gone cold hours ago, boots too clean for Rope Street at this hour. His gaze crossed you once, found nothing, and moved on. A man paid to notice is practiced at not seeming to.

The stair was narrow and honest; every step announced you. At the end of the corridor, under door seven, a candle burned, and a shadow crossed it twice, fast — the shadow of a man packing with the discipline of flight.

Then the door opened from the inside.

Plain wool over an officer's frame. A sea bag on one shoulder. A knife held low and correct in the other hand — a soldier's way of opening a door he meant to leave through at speed. He was half a step into the corridor before his eyes came up, and the knife came up with them — and then recognition arrived and stopped everything but his breathing.

"Ambassador." Barely a sound. His gaze went past your shoulder, swept the corridor, came back. He was young in the jaw and old around the eyes, and the eyes held no sleep and expected none.

"They recalled the officers. Muster at first bell — logs, seals, all correspondence laid for inspection." A soldier's bitter precision. "I've run musters, sir. I know what inspection finds. I know what I've been sending out twice a month for a year." He shouldered the bag tighter. The knife stayed where it was.

"And there's been a man on my stairs since dusk. *Dusk* — before the Queen's court ever sat, before tonight started handing out reasons. Whoever he answers to knew to watch this door before any of this happened." His voice dropped further. "You want the broker's ledger. I know where it sleeps. If that man downstairs belongs to who I think he does, it will be sleeping somewhere else by morning."

From below came the rattle of dice and a burst of laughter — the sound of a world that did not know. Out across the water, a ship's bell counted off an hour you could not spare.

He stood with one foot still in the room and the rest of himself aimed at the corridor window — a man holding two doors open at once, able to afford neither.

"First bell is less than two hours off. I have one set of legs and no trust to spare." The knife turned once in his grip — not a threat; arithmetic. "So talk fast, Ambassador. Why did you come through that door — and where does the other one lead?"

The silence found its ninth shape of the night: a knife in a lieutenant's fist, still deciding what it wanted to be.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *My eyes lock on his, my voice low and urgent.* "Valerius. The Crown knows. Queen Isara, Lord Daven, Priestess Yuna. They know it all." *I push the writ into his hand.* "This is your protection. Treasury business. You're to inventory the seized cargo."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
A ripple ran through the assembled courtiers at the word *terms* — and died the instant Queen Isara lifted a single finger from the arm of the throne.

"Patience," the Queen repeated, as though tasting the word for spoilage. "Velheim asks for this court's patience. Curious. Velheim's last petition asked for our timber, our grain, and our silence regarding certain ships in the Bay of Merrows. It received two of the three." She let the silence do its work. "State your terms, Ambassador. The court will listen. Whether it agrees depends on what follows."

Commander Ash spoke before the echo faded. "Your Majesty — with respect — the northern routes run through waters my soldiers bleed to patrol. Every Velheimish clause I've read came sheathed in courtesy, and every one of them cut. I ask that the garrison's objections be heard before the crown binds itself to anything."

"You will be heard, Commander. *After*." Queen Isara did not turn her head. "This court does not decide from fear, and fear always speaks first."

Ash's knuckles whitened on his sword pommel, but he stepped back to parade rest.

From the gallery, Lord Daven descended — uninvited, yet not forbidden — and halted at the proper distance from the dais. "Your Majesty. These terms will touch Threeford Harbor and the tolls of the Gray Span, both under my stewardship. I request leave to advise the court as they are read."

The Queen considered him a heartbeat longer than courtesy required. "Leave granted. *Advise*, Lord Daven. Do not advocate. There is a difference, and I will know if you forget it."

In the alcove, Priestess Yuna spoke for the first time that session — quietly, yet the whole court leaned in to catch it. "The Flame teaches that a bargain struck in haste burns twice. Yet one weighed forever never warms at all." Her mild gaze settled on you. "The court has been asked for its patience. I find myself wondering whether Velheim carries any of its own."

The Herald's staff cracked against the marble. "The court has heard the Ambassador's request. The Ambassador will now state the terms of Velheim — fully, and in the court's hearing."

Every eye in the room returned to you. Queen Isara's fingers steepled beneath her chin. Waiting.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
*I meet Priestess Yuna's gaze, a small, knowing smile playing on my lips.* "Velheim has always had patience, Priestess. Especially when dealing with... *delicate* matters."

*I turn back to the Queen, my smile fading to a more formal expression.* "Your Majesty, Velheim proposes a new treaty. One that ensures safe passage for *all* merchant vessels through the northern routes, not just our own."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The word *all* landed in the throne room like a coin dropped on marble — a small sound, and every head turning to see where it would roll.

Queen Isara let it roll. "All," she said at last, tasting this word as she had tasted *patience*. "An expansive choice, Ambassador. Velheim's last petition taught this court caution with Velheim's expansiveness. So I ask plainly: does 'all' mean ships that *are* merchants? Or ships that merely borrow merchant colors?" Her eyes narrowed by a degree — with her, that was a full strike. "The Bay of Merrows saw vessels flying trade flags that no harbormaster could account for. Would your treaty make them unaccountable by law?" She did not wait for an answer. "But there is a larger absence. You have told the court what Velheim asks of us. You have not said what Velheim surrenders. The crown does not purchase a promise with a promise."

Commander Ash stepped forward without waiting to be recognized — deliberate, this time, in his breach. "And there's the second blade, Majesty. Passage guaranteed is search forbidden. Today a grain hull sails through unboarded. Tomorrow a hull rides low in the water under the same flag, and my soldiers stand on the quay with a treaty in one hand and no right in the other. Someday someone must put a boarding party on one of those ships. I would hear now which of us that someone is meant to be."

"You are ahead of the articles, Commander," Queen Isara said, without heat. "I permit it once, since the article itself invites the question. Sit down in your boots."

Ash held his ground a moment, then returned to parade rest.

Lord Daven inclined his head from his place at the proper distance. "A point of stewardship, Majesty, offered strictly as advice. Threeford Harbor lives on anchorage dues. The Gray Span takes toll from every keel that passes beneath it. If this treaty's guarantee outranks harbor law, both revenues die in the same hour — and the crown inherits the cost of patrols with nothing left to pay them. I advise the court to ask precisely which laws fall silent when this treaty speaks." A pause, perfectly measured. "Not advocacy, Majesty. Arithmetic."

In the alcove, Priestess Yuna's voice came soft as ash settling. "The Flame teaches that a gift is weighed by what it costs the giver." Her gaze had not left you since your smile. "The Ambassador speaks of delicate matters, then offers protection — protection bought with other men's patrols, in other kingdoms' waters. I observe only that the hand offering warmth has opened nothing of its own."

The Herald's staff cracked against the floor. "The crown has posed its questions. The court will hear the Ambassador's answers."

Queen Isara settled back against the throne, fingers steepling beneath her chin once more. "Answer plainly, Ambassador. And begin with the question you like least: what is Velheim prepared to *lose*?"

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For the space of one breath, the throne room forgot to breathe with it. Somewhere in the gallery a fan stopped mid-wave. This was not how petitions were conducted. This was how wars were begun — in small rooms, years later, by people who remembered exactly this moment.

Commander Ash turned toward you the way a siege engine turns: slow, unhurried, meant to be watched. His hand did not go to his sword. He had been offered an insult in open court, and he paid it the courtesy of his silence — for exactly as long as it took the Herald's staff to crack against the marble.

"The Ambassador will address the throne," the Herald began. "Questions to the crown's officers are put through—"

Queen Isara raised one finger. The Herald's voice died in his throat.

"No, Herald. Let him keep the question he aimed so carefully. I find I want to hear the answer myself." Her eyes left you only once — deliberately — and settled on her Commander. "You have been accused before this court, Commander. Answer as befits an officer."

Ash came to attention — not parade rest; *attention* — and spoke to the space between you and the dais. "Six weeks, Majesty. Every keel out of Velheim. By your writ, sealed and dated, after three hulls ran the strait at night — dark lanterns, no pilot, Velheim colors at the mast — and no harbormaster in Velheim would name them. Your Majesty's writ closed the strait until someone did." He let that sit. Then his eyes found yours. "You asked who would explain my blockade, Ambassador. I don't explain it. I enforce it. The explanation belongs to whoever flew your flag over ships no one will claim."

"Stewardship, Majesty," Lord Daven offered from his proper distance, smooth as poured wine. "Purely arithmetic. Six weeks of closed strait, and the Gray Span has taken toll from supply keels and little else. Threeford's anchorage dues run a quarter of the season's norm — and the patrols the Commander enforces are paid from that same shrinking purse. I advise the court to remember that a wall has two sides, and the wind bites both. Nothing further."

From the alcove, Priestess Yuna's voice drifted down like smoke. "The Flame does not ask whose hand struck the flint. It warms, or it burns, all the same." Her gaze moved between you and the Commander with something like sorrow. "Two fires burn in this court now. I am watching to see which one is fed."

Queen Isara rose, and the court rose with her — not quickly; queens of her make never moved quickly.

"*Or shall I*," she repeated, tasting the words as she had tasted *patience*, as she had tasted *all*. She descended one step. "You were given a choice of speakers, Ambassador. Not of targets. The writ that closed the strait bears my seal and my hand. The blockade is not my Commander's to explain. It is mine to answer for — if anyone present has the standing to ask."

A second step. Her eyes did not blink.

"So. Withdraw your question, or put it to me. Both are permitted." A pause, thin as a blade's edge. "Only one is wise."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *My gaze doesn't waver from the Queen's, even as she descends.* "Your Majesty," *I concede, a slight inclination of my head.* "The blockade is an act of war, by any other name. A direct response to merchant vessels that were, in fact, registered and accounted for."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The word *war* left your mouth, and the temperature of the throne room changed — not dramatically; nothing in this court did anything dramatically. But the gallery rustled like a field before rain, and somewhere a fan closed with a soft click.

Queen Isara completed her descent. Unhurried, step by step, until she stood on the marble floor itself — level with the court, level with you. No one could say afterward that she had loomed over the accusation. She had made certain of it.

"*War*," she said, tasting it as she had tasted *patience*, as she had tasted *all*. "You have chosen that word in open court, Ambassador. Not interdiction. Not lawful closure. War. Understand what you have done — a crowned court does not hear that word and forget it. It is now a matter of record that Velheim's ambassador called my sealed writ an act of war, beneath my own banner. Whatever follows, that word belongs to you."

A pause, thin as a blade's edge.

"But you said something *else*. You said the vessels were registered and accounted for." Her head tilted by a fraction. "Commander Ash named three hulls that ran the strait by night under your colors — hulls no harbormaster in Velheim would name. You now stand in my court and claim they *can* be named. So I will answer your question after all, since you have finally found the standing to ask it. My writ closes the strait against *unnamed* ships. The day those ships are named, the writ is waste paper. Name them, Ambassador. The three vessels, their masters, their home ports, and the seal of whichever harbormaster accounted for them. Do that, and the blockade dies by nightfall."

Commander Ash did not wait for recognition, and this time no one moved to stop him. His hand had left his sword pommel; this was a quarrel of papers now, and he knew it. "Majesty — soldier's terms. My watch logs name the nights, the tides, the headings, the lantern-light on all three hulls. Lay Velheim's registry beside them. If the papers match, I'll cast off the picket lines myself." His eyes came to you, and there was no heat in them at all, which was somehow worse. "Name the ships. It is all anyone has asked of you for six weeks."

"Stewardship, Majesty," Lord Daven offered, smooth as poured wine. "Two sets of paper have now been promised this court — the crown's watch logs and Velheim's registry. Paper is patient. I advise that both be fetched and laid together, rather than that men go on guessing at one another across a throne room. I note further, as arithmetic, that the word *war* stops every keel, closes every toll, and empties every harbor from here to the Merrows. The word *registry*, properly read, opens them again. I advise the court to prefer the second word. Nothing further."

From the alcove, soft as ash settling: "The Flame argues with nothing placed upon it. It burns away what is false, and what is true stands in the ashes after, unashamed." Priestess Yuna's gaze had not left you since your smile. "You bowed as a guest and accused as a plaintiff in a single breath. Both offerings were seen. If the registers exist, the Flame is not their enemy. My alcove will hold them in neutral keeping, until they can be read aloud."

The Herald's staff cracked against the marble. "The Ambassador of Velheim has claimed before the crown that the vessels in question were registered and accounted for. The court requires the names of the three vessels, their masters, and the harbormasters who accounted for them — spoken now, or shown by paper, as the crown directs."

Queen Isara remained standing on the floor of her own court, which she had not done in living memory, and regarded you the way an apothecary regards a sealed vial of unknown provenance.

"The tide turns in six hours, Ambassador. So does my patience. The court waits."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, a flicker of surprise perhaps crossing my face at her sudden, direct challenge.* "Your Majesty, the identities of those vessels are part of the new treaty. A treaty that ensures *all* ships are accounted for, not just those your Commander deems suspicious."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The silence that followed had a different texture than the ones before it. Not shock — calculation. Half the court had done the same arithmetic in the same instant: the Ambassador was not refusing to name the ships. He was pricing them.

Queen Isara let the silence do its arithmetic too.

"*Part*," she said at last, tasting it as she had tasted *patience*, as she had tasted *all*, as she had tasted *war*. "You fold the only proof in this room into an annex, to be unwrapped upon signature. Do you understand what you have just told this court? Let me tell you what it heard. It heard that the ships *can* be named. Mark the record, Herald — Velheim concedes the three hulls are claimable and known to its registry. It declines only to name them now." She let that settle. "That is no longer a mystery, Ambassador. That is merchandise."

She descended no further, but her voice did. "And mark the shape of the treaty as you have described it. It accounts for every ship that comes *after*. It says nothing of three that came *before* — except, I think, to pardon them. Your first article is amnesty, and the price of it is amnesia. The crown does not sign blind for the privilege of forgetting. You have aimed at my Commander twice in one session, which tells me anger is your instrument. Very well. But anger at the shape of a treaty is not the same as blindness to it."

Commander Ash spoke to the dais this time, not to you — the lesson had landed somewhere. "Majesty. A soldier's answer to the word *suspicious*. Suspicion is what I felt on the first night. Logs are what I kept for the six weeks after. Suspicion can be wrong. Tides, headings, and lantern-light cannot." His eyes crossed to you once, flat as slate. "The moment your paper leaves your coat, Ambassador, one of us is mistaken, and I have already agreed to be the one who casts off the lines if it's me."

"Stewardship, Majesty," Lord Daven offered, smooth as ever, though his fingers had gone still against his belt. "The court now holds two promises of paper and one offer of keeping. As arithmetic: a registry placed under seal in the Priestess's alcove costs Velheim nothing until it is read, and buys the crown a reason to keep listening. Paper promised in six weeks proves nothing. Paper surrendered by the tide proves the hand that surrendered it. I advise the court to set a clock rather than a condition. Nothing further."

"The clock is already set," Queen Isara said. "The tide set it."

From the alcove, soft as ash: "The Flame asks no dowry and no delay. Wood placed upon it warms. Wood promised burns nothing." Priestess Yuna's hands folded within her sleeves. "My alcove has held neither this crown's papers nor Velheim's. It can hold a seal — unopened, unread, until the court itself orders the wax broken. The Flame does not need to see the wood to keep it from rotting." Her mild gaze rested on you, patient as her order. "I am still waiting to learn, Ambassador, what you found worth smiling at."

The Herald's staff cracked against the marble. "Velheim has made the names of three vessels a term of treaty. The court will hear the crown's terms for the same."

Queen Isara finally returned to the first step of the dais and turned.

"Then here is the crown's answer to your annex. Before the tide turns, a sealed registry — the three vessels, their masters, their harbormasters — reaches the Priestess's alcove. Sealed, if you insist. Unread, even. If the wax breaks true when this court orders it broken, my writ dies that night and the crown hears your treaty article by article, including the one called *all*. If the tide turns on an empty alcove, the writ stands, the word *war* remains in the record under your name, and Velheim may treat with my Admiral. She is less patient than I am."

Her fingers steepled once more.

"You have kept your card, Ambassador. This is how the crown plays with an open hand. Show it, seal it, or lose the table. The alcove, Ambassador. The tide does not extend its courtesy twice."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The packet crossed the marble floor like a verdict in search of a courtroom. Oilskin, tied with waxed cord, the fold cracked from travel — and every courtier watched not the papers but the *hands*. You walked past the dais. Past Commander Ash. Past the throne itself. And you laid Velheim's proof in the palms of the one person in the room who wanted nothing from it.

The gallery did not gasp; this court had been trained out of gasping. But the fan in the third row opened again, slowly, like something deciding to watch.

Priestess Yuna descended from her alcove — the first time she had left it all session — and received the packet with both hands, the way one receives something that might still be alive. She weighed it. She turned it once.

"The wax is broken," she said, aloud, for the record. "It reached me already split. The Flame can witness what is written on this wood. It cannot witness what was done to the wood before it arrived." Her gaze lifted to the dais. "My alcove keeps, Majesty. It does not decide. The court must order it read."

"Intercepted." Queen Isara stood on the first step of the dais and tasted the word as she had tasted *patience*, as she had tasted *all*, as she had tasted *war*. "Mark it before any ink is read, Herald. *Intercepted.* The crown will come back to that word. The crown always comes back to that word." A beat. "You hand papers in my court to my Priestess and not my throne, Ambassador. You were offered that alcove within the hour. I will allow that you listened." One finger rose. "Read, Priestess. Aloud, all of it, in the court's hearing. Paper read in my presence belongs to my record. Paper withheld belongs to whoever holds it."

"Majesty," Commander Ash said, flat as slate, "orders are *written*. Before one line is read, I'd have the signature. Someone gave these hulls their heading."

"The Flame reads whole, Commander," Yuna said mildly. "Signatures come last for a reason."

She broke the cord.

"'To the masters of the *Kindly Tide*, the *Sable Gull*, and the *Fair Return* — hulls registered and flagged out of Whiteharbour, masters bonded to silence —'" she read, and the names fell into the throne room one by one, six weeks late and heavier for the waiting. "'Show Velheim colors at the mast. Dark lanterns. No pilots. The strait by night. The harbormasters are paid to forget you. If pressed, show this pass.'" A pause. "'Countersigned under the eel and the trident.'"

Yuna turned the final page outward and held it high, so the whole court could see the seal pressed into the leavings of broken wax: a coiled eel about a broken trident.

Commander Ash crossed to within arm's reach of it and went very still. "I know that mark, Majesty. Freeporters. The Merrow syndicates stamp their charter-men with it so their knives can never be traced to a harbor that owns them." His voice did not rise; it dropped, which was worse. "Six weeks I've held a strait against what I took for Velheim's blades. The blades were *borrowed*. I said I'd cast off the lines if paper proved me wrong. This paper proves I had the right guns aimed at the wrong ships — and that someone dressed them in Velheim's colors to make certain of it."

"Stewardship, Majesty," Lord Daven said, though his fingers had gone quite still against his belt. "As arithmetic: my toll books at the Gray Span name every keel that passed beneath it, night or day. Laid beside the Commander's logs and these orders, the dates will either agree or they will not. Paper alone persuades no one. Three papers agreeing persuade everyone."

"Ledgers will be fetched," Queen Isara said. "You will carry the order yourself, Lord Daven — and you will not read them on the way."

He inclined his head and withdrew up the aisle at a steward's unhurried pace.

Isara descended the final step and stood on the marble before you once more.

"Registered, yes," she said. "*Accounted for* — the paper itself confesses no harbormaster ever did, only that they were paid not to. Mark the distinction; the record marks everything else. And the word *war* stays where you put it, Ambassador — though it would seem it was never aimed where you thought. This court once asked Velheim's silence regarding certain ships in the Bay of Merrows." Her eyes narrowed by a degree. "It appears the Bay has stopped asking and started answering."

She let the silence arrive at its own conclusion.

"So now the crown has one question that outranks all others, and you will answer it before the tide turns. Where, Ambassador? In whose water did Velheim's hand close around Merrows correspondence?" Her voice softened into something colder than shouting. "Mind your chart before you answer. If that paper was caught off *my* coast, then Velheim has been hunting in my waters longer than six weeks — and this session changes shape entirely."

The Herald's staff cracked against the marble. "The court waits on the Ambassador's answer."

Behind you, in the alcove, Yuna's voice drifted down, soft as ash. "So the smile was not for me."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I take a breath, meeting the Queen's gaze evenly.* "The correspondence was intercepted in international waters, Your Majesty. Off the coast of the disputed Southern Reach." *I don't look back at Yuna, though her words sting.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your answer crossed the throne room like a keel into unfamiliar water — and half the court reached for the charts they kept behind their eyes. Old men in the gallery leaned together. Somewhere near the doors, a page slipped out at a whispered word, no doubt sent running for the sea-atlas.

The Herald's staff cracked against the marble. "The Ambassador names the place of interception: international waters, off the coast of the disputed Southern Reach. So entered."

"*International*." Queen Isara handled the word as though it had been left out in the rain. "There is no such water, Ambassador, and there never has been. There is water too far from any coast to defend. Everything else the phrase has ever meant was written by chancelleries, and I would wager Velheim's held the pen. Mark the record, Herald — the Ambassador claims the sea itself as his warrant."

She let that settle before she returned to the second half of your chart.

"But it is the other word I thank you for, since you gave it under seal of record. *Disputed.* The Southern Reach is disputed between my navy and the eel, and by no one else alive. There is no third chart — until this morning. You stood in open court and named the Reach as Velheim's hunting ground, and a nation that hunts in a water is a nation that claims an interest in it. Enter that also, Herald. Velheim has joined the dispute by naming it."

A pause, and then, cold as fair dealing: "And you steered wide of my coast. Well sailed. I said the answer would be minded, and it was — the paper was not taken off my shore. I will say so aloud, once, because this court punishes badly aimed words and honors well aimed ones. Which brings us to the question your answer was built to outrun."

Her voice dropped to the register she reserved for verdicts.

"You have named the prey. Three hulls, dressed in your colors, bought and bonded. Now name the hound, Ambassador. The vessel that made the interception. Its name, its master, the papers it sails under. And understand the fork before you step into it. Name a hull of Velheim's navy, and Velheim's fleet has hunted in disputed water wearing a trade embassy for a coat — war by another name, and this time the word will fit. Name a merchant hull, and Velheim's merchants carry dark lanterns and a taste for other nations' letters. That is the same confession at a cheaper price. Either way, the crown will have the name before the tide turns."

Commander Ash spoke, and the Queen did not stop him, which from her was permission. "The Reach is three days south of my pickets, Majesty. Hulls that drill dark-lantern work there are rehearsing for straits." His eyes crossed to you, flat as slate. "I'll have that hunting hull's headings as well, when they come. Practice leaves wakes."

From the alcove, soft as ash settling: "The Flame keeps no charts. It has never once refused to burn because the wood lay across a line drawn in water." Yuna's hands were still folded around your oilskin packet. "In the Reach there is a shrine. My order keeps the lamp there. Fishermen of the crown's coast and Velheim's and the eel's have burned offerings at it for nine generations and never once disputed it. It is only ashore that the lines are drawn." A beat, and the needle came gentle as her order's patience. "And I note, Ambassador — this time you answered the question you liked least before the court had to set a snare for it. The Flame marks the difference."

The doors opened. Lord Daven crossed the marble at a steward's unhurried pace, a satchel in both hands, his own wax unbroken on the clasp.

"The Gray Span's toll books, Majesty, as ordered. They did not leave my hands on the way."

"Then they may leave them now," said Queen Isara. "Read."

Daven opened the ledger and delivered it like a merchant delivering sums. "As arithmetic, Majesty. The night the Commander's watch logged three hulls running dark, my clerk below the Span entered three keels southbound on the same tide — the *Kindly Tide*, the *Sable Gull*, the *Fair Return* — spaced a quarter-hour apart. Each paid the night toll. None paid in Velheim silver. All three paid in merrow-silver, and my clerk, who marks his payers by habit, chalked the coiled eel beside every entry." He closed the book with care. "The tolls on ships dressed as Velheim were collected for the syndicate that dressed them, Majesty. I advise the court to weigh that the disguise was worth paying for. Nothing further." A pause, perfectly measured. "Save one thing. There is a fourth entry. The eel's chalk again — on a night when the watch logged no keel at all, and the toll column is struck through in another hand: *waived*. No order named. I advise the court to wonder what paid for nothing."

"The ghost in the ledger will keep," Queen Isara said. "Ledgers do not have tides. You do."

She turned back to you, standing on the marble of her own court, and the last of the daylight through the tall windows lay across the floor between you like a line neither of you had drawn.

"The hound, Ambassador. Name it."

The Herald's staff cracked a final time. "The crown requires the name of the intercepting vessel, its master, and the papers it sails under. The court waits — and the tide does not."

Beyond the windows, far below, the river gleamed flat and silver, already beginning to think about turning.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *My eyes dart to the ledger in Daven's hand, a brief, calculating flicker. Then back to the Queen.* "The vessel, Your Majesty, was the *Sea Serpent*. A Velheim merchant ship, captained by Elara Rostova." *I hold her gaze, daring her to question it.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For the second time that session, you handed the court a proper noun — and this one you served with your chin up, daring the throne to knock it from your hand.

The Herald's staff cracked. "The Ambassador names the intercepting vessel: the *Sea Serpent*, a merchant hull of Velheim, master one Elara Rostova. So entered."

Queen Isara regarded your daring the way she regarded all freight offered too boldly — to be weighed, not accepted. "Save the stare for the sea, Ambassador. On this floor it is only posture." Then she took up the name and tasted it as she had tasted every word you had given her tonight. "*Sea Serpent*. A serpent hunting eels. At least the bay has a sense of humor." The tasting ended; the verdict began. "Mark the shape of your choice, Herald. The Ambassador stepped into the cheaper tine of the fork, whose price the crown named in advance — so there is no surprise in it, and I will pretend none. A Velheim merchantman carries dark lanterns and a taste for other nations' letters. That is not war. That is piracy with a chancery's manners. And it is a confession Velheim can survive, which is why you chose it." A pause. "You also answered before the snare closed. This court honors well-aimed words. Two questions remain. What papers does the *Sea Serpent* sail under — Velheim's registry, or a charter she has not confessed? And where does the crown find her?"

"Logs first, Majesty." Commander Ash spoke to the dais, having learned where his voice was permitted. "Six weeks of watch, and no hull named *Sea Serpent* appears in them once. Not northbound, not southbound, not hailing, not running dark. Every Velheim trader I've ever logged crosses this strait — that's where the trade *is*. A merchant that never touches merchant water isn't a merchant. She's a hound that hunts from a kennel." His eyes crossed to you, flat as slate. "So give me the dispatch brig, and I'll carry your order south myself, Ambassador. I should like to see with my own eyes whether your Rostova heaves to."

"Stewardship, Majesty." Lord Daven turned the ledger's clasp once in his fingers. "As arithmetic: the *Sea Serpent* appears nowhere in the Gray Span's books either. I caution the court against weighing that heavily — my Span taxes the river, and a sea-coaster bound for southern water need never pass beneath it. Absence from my ledger proves a ship takes the long way. It does not prove she is a lie." A measured beat. "One further sum. If the hound obeys the Ambassador's order to heave to, the crown has proven Velheim rules its merchant marine, and this session was worth the candles. If she does not, the crown has proven who truly owns Velheim's colors — which is worth more. A rare question, Majesty: both answers feed it. Nothing further."

From the alcove, soft as ash settling: "There is a third paper in this matter, and it holds no politics." Yuna's hands were still folded around your oilskin packet. "The shrine at the Reach keeps a lamp-book, Ambassador. Nine generations of fishermen — the crown's, Velheim's, the eel's — have signed or paid oil there, and my order records every hull that waters at the Reach, with dates and headings, written for the Flame and no throne. If your *Sea Serpent* ever drank at the Reach, the ash remembers. The book can be fetched under my seal." A pause, and the needle came gentle. "Twice now you have answered well when the snare stood in plain sight. The Flame begins to wonder what answers you keep for snares it has not shown you."

Queen Isara ascended one step — the first ground she had given back all session — and the court understood that something had been decided.

"On the wax: it reached the alcove broken, so the letter of my terms was never met." She let the gallery hold its breath. "But the substance stands corroborated from an unprompted source — the eel's chalk beside three hulls on the very night of the Commander's logs, paid in merrow-silver, in my own toll books. This court rules on substance. The writ does not die tonight. It *hangs* — and the rope is the hound's to cut."

Her finger rose. It did not point at your throat. It pointed at your hands.

"Before the tide turns, you will dispatch your order to the *Sea Serpent*: Elara Rostova to heve to at the Reach anchorage, under the shrine's lamp, for inspection by this crown's officer — hull, papers, and master. The crown's brig sails with your dispatch to witness delivery; the Commander carries it. Send the order under the crown's eyes, and the writ dies at the anchorage and the treaty called *all* is heard, article by article. Send it sealed against the crown, or decline to send it, and the naming of the *Sea Serpent* is entered as fiction, the word *war* keeps the seat you gave it, and my Admiral reads the whole file by morning."

The Herald's staff cracked a final time. "The court waits on the Ambassador's order to his hound."

Below the tall windows the river had gone from silver to pewter, and the first boat-lamps of the evening watch were coming out along the quay. The tide would stand only a little longer — and the one man in the room who could shorten the waiting stood on the wrong side of it.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I look at the Queen, then at Commander Ash, then back to the Queen.* "I will dispatch the order. But Commander Ash will not be carrying it. He will send it." *I pause, a subtle challenge in my eyes.* "He has, after all, proven rather skilled at sending things."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The insult crossed the throne room at the speed of arithmetic — every courtier running the sum of *skilled at sending things*, arriving at six weeks of blockade, and deciding, in the same instant, not to look at Commander Ash. Two young officers in the gallery developed a sudden fascination with the rafters. The fan in the third row did not move at all, which was its own kind of applause.

Ash considered the jab the way he considered weather, and answered the dais, not you.

"Granted, Majesty, and without cost. Six weeks I've sent logs, patrol reports, and one closed strait. Everything I ever sent arrived." His eyes crossed to you, flat as slate. "The order goes by the *Wren* — the courier brig. She's faster than my hull, and I'll not slow her with my shadow. My letter will beat me to the Reach by a day." A beat. "I will not. I find I want to see that anchorage with my own eyes, Ambassador. Not to carry your order. To count masts."

The Herald's staff cracked. "The Ambassador moves that the crown's dispatch be sent at the Commander's command, and not carried in his person. So entered."

"*Send*," Queen Isara said, tasting it as she had tasted *patience*, as she had tasted *all*, as she had tasted every word you had fed this court since the doors opened. "A session spent handing me proper nouns, and now you hand me a verb and an insult, and ask the court to weigh them together. Very well. Mark the count, Herald — three times this session the Ambassador has drawn on my Commander, and three times the shot has cost the shooter more than the target. I said once that anger was his instrument. I amend the finding. Instruments are held. Before this court rises, I will learn who holds the other end of him."

She let that settle into the record like a stone into a well.

"And yet the motion is granted — and mark the reason, since reasons are the only coin this floor honors. My terms required the order sent *under the crown's eyes*. They did not require it from the crown's hand. The Ambassador found the seam in my sentence, and a seam honestly found is honestly earned. Note it." Her eyes narrowed by a degree.
