Queen Isara’s gaze returned to the clause. “Define the hours. Define the writ. Define who signs the compensation.”

Commander Ash’s voice dropped. “No foreign officer signs a crown writ.”

Lord Daven said, “No foreign officer signs a crown writ. The writ is signed by crown officers under joint inspection. Velheim signs only the manifest.”

Priestess Yuna said, “That is a smaller door. Smaller doors are easier to lock.”

Queen Isara’s fingers tapped once against the throne’s arm. “The clause remains under consideration. The court recognizes the Ambassador for amendment.”

The Herald struck the floor, softer now. “The court recognizes the Ambassador.”

Lord Daven leaned toward the rail. “The gallery hopes the amendment is as precise as the clause.”

Commander Ash’s hand rested on his sword pommel again. “The fleet hopes the amendment is not a trap dressed as ink.”

Priestess Yuna looked at the sealed exhibit. “Ink is often where traps begin.”

Queen Isara’s voice cut through the room, cool and final. “The temple will witness. The gallery will speak when recognized. The Commander will remember that this is a court, not a bridge.”

Ash bowed his head, but the motion carried resentment like a drawn blade.

Queen Isara’s eyes stayed on the center of the room. “Amend the clause.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I nod, a thoughtful expression on my face.* "Indeed, Your Majesty. The writ of release will be issued by the Crown, as is proper. However, the clause will specify that said writ must be issued within 24 hours of a satisfactory joint inspection, countersigned by a representative from Velheim to confirm the inspection's completion."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The amendment left your voice clean and narrow, as if a door had been fitted with both a lock and a window.

Queen Isara regarded it the way a surgeon regards a stitch: useful, but still blood. “A writ within twenty-four hours,” she said. “The Crown’s hand signs. The foreign hand countersigns. The Crown’s delay becomes a debt.”

Commander Ash moved one step out of stillness. “A countersignature is not a witness. It is a seal.”

The Herald struck the floor once, a precise note of interruption. “The court recognizes the Commander for procedural objection. The objection is recorded.”

Lord Daven’s eyes brightened from the gallery, ambitious and careful. “The objection is narrow. The amendment is narrower. Velheim does not ask to release a prisoner. It asks to confirm that the inspection was completed.”

Priestess Yuna, standing by the sealed exhibit, let the pause settle before she spoke. “A completed inspection may be false. A false completion signed by two hands is called agreement.”

Queen Isara’s fingers moved along the throne’s arm. “The temple will not amend the clause.”

“The clause amends itself,” Yuna said, “when it trusts the hand.”

The Herald turned toward the alcove. “The temple would witness within bounds.”

Yuna inclined her head. “The bounds were noted.”

Ash’s voice hardened. “No Velheim representative enters a customs house to inspect manifests. That is not joint inspection. That is occupation by paperwork.”

Daven smiled, thin and edged. “The Commander fears a pen because a pen can make his seizures legible.”

“The Commander speaks for the fleet,” Ash replied.

“The fleet speaks for itself when it signs,” Daven said.

Queen Isara lifted one hand. The room stilled.

“The Crown will accept the twenty-four hours,” she said. “The Crown will not accept a foreign countersignature as authority. The Velheim representative may confirm that the inspection was conducted, that the manifest was examined, and that the document was delivered. The confirmation will carry no power to release, detain, accuse, or interpret.”

Ash bowed his head, but his jaw did not soften. “That is manageable.”

Lord Daven’s smile warmed by only a degree. “The gallery accepts manageable.”

Priestess Yuna touched the edge of the sealed exhibit, not lifting it. “Manageable is what a wound says before it remembers pain.”

Queen Isara’s gaze returned to you, cool and unblinking. “The clause is provisionally accepted. The court recognizes the Ambassador for the second clause.”

The Herald struck the marble once, formal and soft. “The court recognizes the Ambassador for continuation of negotiation.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "Thank you, Your Majesty." *I acknowledge the provisional acceptance.* "Now, for the second clause, Velheim proposes a joint naval patrol along the northern routes, with shared command and equal representation."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The second clause moved through the throne room like the first crack in an ice bridge.

Queen Isara did not look at the papers, did not look at the sealed exhibit, did not look at Lord Daven’s eager gallery or Commander Ash’s rigid hand. She looked only at the center of the marble, where the proposal you had offered now waited for judgment.

“A joint naval patrol,” Queen Isara said, each word measured as if it had to be paid for separately. “Shared command. Equal representation. These are pleasant phrases, Ambassador. Pleasant phrases make good wine talk and bad sea law.”

Commander Ash answered before the Herald could gather his staff for a warning. “The fleet is not a partnership. The fleet is a crown instrument under one flag. A foreign officer does not stand on the bridge of a crown warship.”

The Herald’s staff struck the floor once, sharp and formal. “The court recognizes the Commander for procedural objection. The objection is recorded. The court recognizes Lord Daven.”

Lord Daven lifted both hands from the gallery rail, palms open, as though the room’s anger were a bird he might coax onto his wrist. “The Commander objects to a foreign officer on a bridge. Let us not be dramatic. Velheim does not ask to steer the crown’s ships. Velheim asks to be seen in the patrol’s record.”

Queen Isara’s gaze shifted to Lord Daven. “The gallery is fond of records.”

“The gallery is fond of allies,” Lord Daven replied, with a bow so slight it barely disturbed the air. “Allies require records. Enemies require only borders.”

Priestess Yuna spoke from beside the evidence table, her voice low enough to draw every head toward her. “A shared patrol is not shared peace. It is shared responsibility for future storms.”

Commander Ash turned toward the alcove. “The temple should not twist weather into policy.”

“The temple should not,” Priestess Yuna said. “The temple should remember what weather did before men learned to call it policy.”

The Herald shifted his weight. “The temple would witness within bounds.”

Priestess Yuna inclined her head. “The bounds are remembered.”

Queen Isara lifted one finger. The room tightened.

“Commander Ash,” Queen Isara said. “Explain the objection without raising the sword.”

Ash’s jaw moved once. His hand remained on his sword pommel, though the motion had changed from threat to habit. “A joint patrol means shared signals. Shared signals mean divided authority. Divided authority means confusion in fog. Confusion in fog means ships lost.”

Lord Daven smiled, thin and quick. “And a blockade in fog means cargo seized.”

Commander Ash’s eyes narrowed. “The gallery mistakes law for weather.”

“The gallery mistakes weather for command,” Lord Daven replied. “The fleet chose the storm. The fleet also chose the cargo it detained.”

The Herald struck the marble twice. “The gallery would confine its remarks to the clause.”

“The clause,” Lord Daven said, “is the storm.”

Queen Isara’s fingers closed once around the arm of the throne. “Enough.”

The word did not rise. It fell. The room bent beneath it.

Queen Isara looked at the evidence table, then at Commander Ash, then at Lord Daven, and finally at the center where the hearing continued.

“A joint patrol may be discussed,” Queen Isara said. “Shared command may not. The crown does not divide its flag. If Velheim requires presence, Velheim may require liaison, not command. If Velheim requires equal representation, Velheim may require equal notice, not equal authority.”

Commander Ash bowed his head. “That is acceptable.”

Lord Daven’s smile cooled. “That is not what the clause said.”

“The clause will be amended,” Queen Isara said, “or the clause will end.”

Priestess Yuna’s eyes remained on the sealed exhibit. “A clause amended by threat is a clause prepared for breaking.”

The Herald turned toward the alcove. “The temple would not counsel the court.”

“The temple counseled nothing,” Priestess Yuna said. “The temple observed the counsel’s shape.”

Queen Isara’s gaze returned to the evidence table, and something like warning passed over her face. “The temple will return to silence unless recognized.”

Priestess Yuna folded her hands. “Silence was already recognized.”

The Herald’s staff trembled faintly in his grip, as if formal authority had to be reminded of its own limits.

Commander Ash moved half a step toward the throne, not enough to break formation, enough to make the movement mean something. “If Velheim liaison officers are aboard crown ships, they will not be permitted into the chart room.”

Lord Daven answered before the Herald could decide which rule had been violated. “Velheim will not ask for charts. Velheim will ask for logs.”

“Logs can be altered,” Ash said.

“Seals can be forged,” Lord Daven replied.

The room’s attention shifted, sharp and sudden, toward the intercepted orders resting under the court’s seal.

Queen Isara’s expression did not change. “The exhibit is not precedent.”

Lord Daven bowed his head. “The gallery would never suggest otherwise.”

Commander Ash’s voice hardened. “The fleet does not take instruction from a gallery that trades in accusations.”

Lord Daven’s smile went thin as wire. “The fleet does not take instruction from a gallery that trades in results.”

Priestess Yuna said, softly, “A gallery that trades in results is only a court that has not yet been forced to keep receipts.”

The Herald’s staff struck once, too quickly. “The temple would witness without interpreting.”

Priestess Yuna looked toward the throne. “The temple would witness without forgetting.”

Queen Isara lifted both hands now, palms down, and the room became still in a different way. Not a silence waiting for permission, but a silence listening for command.

“The second clause may continue,” Queen Isara said. “But the crown’s conditions are these. One flag. One flagship. One crown officer in command of the patrol’s movement. Velheim liaison may observe, may report, may countersign patrol logs, and may request investigation of any incident. Velheim liaison may not issue orders, may not alter course, may not command crown vessels, and may not be placed aboard any ship in active pursuit.”

Commander Ash exhaled once through his nose, satisfied but still wary. “That is sovereignty.”

Lord Daven leaned forward. “That is a beginning.”

Priestess Yuna said, “A beginning is often the first place a wound is dressed.”

Queen Isara did not look at the temple. “The clause requires precision. If Velheim can define the liaison’s role within the crown’s conditions, the court will hear it. If not, the second clause will be tabled and the first clause will be reopened.”

The Herald struck the floor once, softer now, but with clear intent. “The court recognizes the Ambassador for amendment within the crown’s conditions.”

Commander Ash’s hand remained on his sword pommel, no longer quite a statement, no longer quite a threat, but a man’s first thought returning to his first weapon.

Lord Daven’s eyes brightened from the gallery, ambitious and careful, as if he could see the shape of leverage forming.

Priestess Yuna touched the edge of the sealed exhibit once, then withdrew her hand, as if the papers had remembered her.

Queen Isara waited, cold and calculating, her gaze fixed on the center of the room.

The throne room held the second clause between them like a blade laid flat across the negotiation, ready to be claimed, refuted, or broken.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I consider her terms carefully, a slight frown creasing my brow.* "Your Majesty, Velheim will accept a liaison's role under those conditions. However, the liaison's report of an incident will automatically trigger a joint investigation, with findings binding on both parties."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The word *binding* moved through the throne room like a blade drawn slowly from its sheath.

Queen Isara’s eyes narrowed by the smallest possible amount. “A joint investigation,” she said, “with binding findings.” The phrase seemed to cool on her tongue. “Velheim asks the crown to accept a verdict before it has chosen the judge.”

Commander Ash stepped forward without being summoned. His voice was clipped and hard. “No Velheim report decides what the fleet must do. A crown officer answers to the crown, not to a foreign ledger signed in the same hour as the incident.”

The Herald’s staff struck the marble once, sharp and precise. “The court recognizes the Commander for procedural objection. The objection is entered. The court recognizes Lord Daven.”

Lord Daven rose from the gallery rail with the easy grace of a man who had been waiting for this opening since the first word of the clause. “The Commander objects to binding findings,” he said, “because he fears a finding may bind him. Let us be honest in the throne room. If the inspection is joint, then the investigation must be joint. Otherwise, the word *joint* is only decoration.”

Priestess Yuna, still standing near the sealed exhibit, spoke without lifting her voice. “A joint investigation may be a shared shield,” she said. “Or it may be a shared net. The question is who is caught when the net is drawn.”

Queen Isara turned her gaze toward the alcove, cold and unyielding. “The temple does not counsel the clause.”

“The temple counsels nothing,” Priestess Yuna replied. “The temple names the shape of what is offered.”

The Herald shifted toward her with formal displeasure. “The temple would witness within bounds.”

“The bounds have been heard,” Priestess Yuna said. “The bounds were noted. The bounds were remembered.”

Commander Ash’s hand tightened at his side. “Findings are not weather. Findings are orders.”

Lord Daven smiled without warmth. “Then let the orders be written by both hands. If the fleet fears a foreign pen, it should fear less a blank one.”

“Blank pages are not safe,” Ash said. “They are invitations.”

The Herald’s staff cracked against the marble. “The Commander would confine his remarks to the clause.”

“The clause is the remarks,” Lord Daven said.

Queen Isara lifted one finger, and the room fell still again.

“The crown will not accept an automatic trigger,” she said, “based upon a Velheim report alone.” Her voice remained smooth, but the edge beneath it was unmistakable. “A report may initiate investigation. It may not bind judgment. If Velheim wishes a joint investigation, then the investigation must begin only when a documented irregularity exists in the manifest, the seal, or the inspection log.”

Commander Ash inclined his head. “That is manageable.”

Lord Daven’s eyes brightened, though his smile remained thin. “Then let the irregularity be defined.”

Priestess Yuna looked at the sealed exhibit, then back to the throne. “Definitions are the first lock placed upon a door,” she said. “Or the last key left in it.”

Queen Isara did not look away from the center of the room, where your clause still waited. “The court recognizes the Ambassador for amendment within the crown’s condition.”

The Herald struck the floor once, softer now. “The court recognizes the Ambassador.”

Lord Daven leaned forward, ambitious and careful. “The gallery hopes the amendment is not a door with no hinges.”

Commander Ash’s voice dropped low. “The fleet hopes the amendment is not a trap dressed in procedure.”

Priestess Yuna folded her hands near the evidence table. “Traps are often dressed in procedure,” she said. “That is how they remain clean.”

The Herald turned toward her sharply. “The temple would witness without interpretation.”

“The temple would witness,” Priestess Yuna replied, “and the temple would remember.”

Queen Isara lifted one hand, and the silence gathered itself around her like a cloak.

“The crown’s condition stands,” she said. “A documented irregularity. No automatic judgment from a single report. If Velheim can define the irregularity, the investigator, the timeline, and the authority that binds the findings, the second clause may be amended.” She paused, letting the weight of her gaze settle. “If not, the clause will be tabled, and the exhibit will be examined before the hearing continues.”

Lord Daven’s head tilted slightly, as though the queen’s warning were music he could still dance to. “Then the clause must name what counts as irregularity.”

Commander Ash answered at once. “A missing seal.”

“A wrong seal,” Lord Daven corrected.

“A delayed seal,” Priestess Yuna murmured.

The Herald struck the floor once, warningly. “The court recognizes Her Majesty for clarification.”

Queen Isara’s fingers rested upon the throne’s arm. “An irregularity shall be one recorded in the joint manifest: a missing seal, an unverified cargo entry, a discrepancy in inspection time, or a refusal of inspection by either party.”

Ash’s jaw tightened, but he did not speak out of order.

Lord Daven bowed his head. “That is a door with hinges.”

Priestess Yuna said, “A door with hinges is still a door. It may open, or it may shut.”

Queen Isara’s gaze returned to you, cool and patient. “Define the investigator,” she said. “Define the timeline. Define the binding authority. The crown will not enter a joint investigation with no judge and no hour.”

The Herald’s staff touched the marble again, formal and soft. “The court recognizes the Ambassador for continuation of amendment.”

Commander Ash’s hand rested on his sword pommel, no longer a threat, but a habit of hostility.

Lord Daven waited with the stillness of a man who had already calculated three moves ahead.

Priestess Yuna touched the edge of the sealed exhibit once, then withdrew her hand as if the intercepted orders had grown warm.

Queen Isara watched you, cold, calculating, and utterly unwilling to be hurried.

The second clause hung between the throne and the marble floor, waiting for the next line of ink.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, meeting her gaze steadily.* "Very well, Your Majesty. The investigator will be a neutral arbiter, mutually agreed upon. The investigation will conclude within 72 hours. The binding authority will be this very treaty, signed by both Crown and Velheim."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald did not strike his staff again; he simply retreated a half-step into the column's shadow, his face returning to the mask of ceremony.

You felt the silence turn ponderous as the court waited upon the Queen's pleasure.

Queen Isara's finger tapped once against the arm of her throne, a sound too faint to carry yet somehow louder than the herald's staff. "Terms," she said, drawing the word out as though tasting it for poison. "Velheim has offered terms before, Ambassador. They expired at the border, choked by the same blockades your ships now claim suffocate commerce. What flavor do these new terms carry?"

Commander Ash's gauntlets scraped against his sword pommel as he shifted. "The only terms worth hearing come at sword's point," he said, his voice carrying the rough edge of a man more accustomed to drill yards than diplomacy. "Northern trade routes feed northern raiders. Your ledgers and your blades share the same blood, whether dressed in silk or steel."

Lord Daven leaned forward against the gallery rail, his smile thin and patient. "If blood is the Commander's only currency, no wonder his accounts remain so empty," he called, the words oiled and deliberate. "Her Majesty, I submit that an Ambassador who bows to the exact degree of protocol does not come to bluster. Let the terms breathe before we suffocate them with old grievances."

Priestess Yuna's beads clicked against the stone alcove, a single dry note. "The icons do not speak of swords or silk," she said, her voice carrying the flat neutrality of ritual. "They speak of rivers that find the sea by winding. Hostility is a stone. Patience is the current that wears it smooth. The court rushes toward judgment as though judgment were a virtue."

"The court rushes toward nothing without the Crown's leave," the Herald intoned, his staff snapping against the marble with a crack that scattered the murmurs. "The word belongs to Her Majesty. The rest is wind."

Queen Isara's gaze remained fixed upon you, unblinking and surgical. She raised one hand, and the quarrel died unborn. "The Ambassador requested patience," she said, the chill of her tone frosting the air between the thrones. "Patience shall be granted. Precisely enough to lay these terms bare before the court. Then Commander Ash may answer with his steel, Lord Daven with his schemes, and Priestess Yuna with her parables. The Crown shall decide which cuts the deepest. Speak, Ambassador."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "Thank you, Your Majesty." *I keep my voice even, despite the obvious tension.* "Velheim offers a new charter, opening three northern ports for unrestricted trade, with reciprocal access to our southern docks." *I pause, letting that sink in.* "In exchange, we ask for a neutral arbiter for all disputes, chosen by both kingdoms."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You felt the silence fracture along predictable lines, each shard reflecting a different hunger.

Commander Ash’s gauntlets scraped against his pommel again, a sound like teeth grinding stone. “Unrestricted,” he said, spitting the word toward the foot of the throne. “You throw open three gates and call it commerce. I call it a landing ground. Every hull you smile at carries a hold deep enough for axes, and every ‘neutral’ eye you propose is a blindfold we would tie ourselves.”

Lord Daven spread his hands upon the gallery rail, the picture of reason. “The Commander’s war never ends, not even in peacetime,” he called, the observation light and lethal. “Yet I have seen the ledgers. Our granaries know no politics when they stand empty. Reciprocal access is not charity—it is a leash with two ends. If Velheim’s southern docks welcome our colors, their northern waters welcome ours. The arbiter is the wager, and wagers require two bettors.”

Priestess Yuna’s head tilted, the beads at her waist shifting with a sound like dry rain. “Two currents forced together do not mix,” she said. “They carve a channel. The stone placed between them wears smooth, then it wears thin. Who replaces the stone when it grinds to dust? The river does not pause to mourn the bridge.”

“The court does not deal in dust,” the Herald announced, his staff rigid at his side. “It deals in decree. The Crown alone weighs the wager.”

Queen Isara had not moved, yet the stillness of her body seemed more terrible than any gesture. Her gaze pinned you to the marble. “Symmetry is a pretty lie,” she said, her voice low and precise as a surgeon’s stitch. “Your southern harbors swim in calm seas. Our northern shores bleed. You ask for a key to three wounds and offer in return a key to a pantry. And this arbiter—” her lips thinned, “—chosen by both kingdoms. Tell me, Ambassador, when wolf and shepherd choose the fence together, who picks the gap?”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
A murmur rippled through the gallery, then died as though cut by a blade. Every eye in the chamber turned first to Commander Ash, then to the throne, waiting to see which protocol would shatter harder—the Ambassador's breach of order, or the Queen's silence.

You felt the temperature of the room drop, though the braziers burned as before.

Commander Ash's hand closed around his pommel, knuckles whitening beneath the steel. "Explain?" The word came out edged, a blade drawn half from its sheath. "I sleep poorly when merchants weep. Six weeks of steel in the water, and your hulls still tried to run it. I answer to the Crown, not to ledger-men who dress their greed in diplomacy's silks."

Queen Isara's eyes narrowed, the only crack in her glacial composure. "The Ambassador forgets the aisle's order," she said, each syllable dropping like frost. "This court is not a barracks where any voice may bark at any other. Yet—" and here her finger lifted from the arm, pointing not at you but through you, "—the Commander's blockades answer to the Admiralty, and the Admiralty answers to the Crown. You presume much, Ambassador, to wield another man's secrets before they are confessed."

Lord Daven's laugh was quiet, a single note of genuine delight. "Oh, well thrown," he murmured, just loud enough to carry. "The wolf complains of the trap's teeth after he has already stepped inside. Commander, if your fleet prowls northern waters without the court's leave, that is one sin. If it prowls with leave, it is another. Which ledger shall we open first?"

Priestess Yuna's hands folded within her sleeves. "A stone thrown into still water does not choose the ripples," she intoned. "It chooses only the splash. The Ambassador has disturbed the surface. What rises from the depths is not for the thrower to command."

The Herald struck his staff once, a sharp report that sealed the chamber. "The word remains with Her Majesty. The Ambassador spoke out of turn. The Commander answered. The Crown weighs both."

Queen Isara settled back, her spine finding the throne's edge with deliberate care. Her gaze pinned you to the marble, unblinking and surgical. "You stand in my house, break my order, and demand confession from my Commander," she said. "Bold. Or desperate. The distinction matters only to the headsman. Speak your explanation then, Ambassador. Since you have already taken the liberty of asking the question, you may finish the accusation. But know—" her lips thinned, "—accusations are doors that open both ways."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "Your Majesty, I merely offered the Commander a chance to explain Velheim's current proposal's context. Our ships were blockaded *before* these terms were offered." *I let my gaze sweep to Lord Daven, then back to the Queen.* "I assure you, I am not desperate."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You felt the weight of the Queen's scrutiny press against your shoulders like a physical hand, testing the strength of your claim.

Commander Ash's jaw tightened. "Context," he said, the word rough as a file against iron. "You paint six weeks of interdiction as a surprise, as though your hulls did not sail under sealed orders of their own. Velheim's merchants carry more than grain. They carry charts, tides, and harbor depths. My blockades answer to the Crown's security, not to your convenience."

Lord Daven's fingers drummed once against the gallery rail, his smile sharpening. "Security is a cloak that fits any shoulders," he observed. "Yet the Ambassador speaks chronology, not conspiracy. If the iron was placed in the water before the olive branch was extended, we must ask whether the hand that offers peace is the same hand that closed the fist. Or—" his gaze slid toward the Commander, "—whether the fist closed without the Crown's full knowledge of what it gripped."

Priestess Yuna's eyes remained fixed upon the icons behind the throne, her voice carrying the hollow resonance of the alcove. "The tree does not argue with the axe," she said. "It only counts the rings. Before and after are marks in the wood. The forest judges not which blow fell first, but whether the trunk yet stands."

"The court does not count rings," the Herald intoned, his staff snapping against the marble with a crack that scattered the echoes. "It counts commands. The Crown commands the chronicle."

Queen Isara's finger returned to the arm of her throne, tapping a slow, deliberate rhythm that matched the pulse in your throat. "Assurance is a cloak worn thin by those who shiver," she said, her tone clinical, dissecting. "You assure me you are not desperate. Yet desperation wears many masks—pride among them. If your ships were seized before your parchment was inked, you invite me to believe that Velheim offers ports not from strength, but from the weakness of a blade already at its throat." She leaned forward by a fraction, no more than the width of a hair. "I do not purchase what is already mine by right of pressure. Convince me this is not ransom dressed in silk, or let the Commander keep his blockades and his explanations both."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "Your Majesty, Velheim is not so easily brought to its knees." *I meet her gaze directly.* "The blockade is an inconvenience, not a surrender. These terms are an offer of mutual prosperity, not a plea."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You felt the temperature of the Queen's interest shift, as though your defiance had struck a flint against her composure.

Queen Isara's finger stilled upon the arm of the throne. "Inconvenience," she said, letting the syllables collapse one by one. "You name six weeks of interdiction an inconvenience. You name the closing of waters a stubbed toe. Either your treasury is inexhaustible, Ambassador, or your definition of prosperity does not require commerce. Which fiction shall the court entertain?"

Commander Ash's gauntlets scraped against his pommel, the sound a warning. "Strength does not bargain," he said, his voice carrying the rough edge of the parade ground. "It conquers. You stand in the wolf's den and claim you are not bleeding. I see the posture. I know the wound beneath the silk."

Lord Daven's smile remained, but his eyes had grown sharp as awls. "The Ambassador's spine is admirably straight," he called from the gallery. "Yet straight timber catches the wind, and the wind here blows cold. Your Majesty, if Velheim suffers merely inconvenience, then these terms are generosity indeed. But generosity untested is either saintly or suspicious, and saints rarely sit at council tables."

Priestess Yuna's hands folded within her sleeves, her gaze still lifted toward the icons. "The oak calls the storm inconvenience," she intoned. "The reed calls it music. Both are tested. Only one remains to speak of the weather."

"The court does not listen to trees," the Herald announced, striking his staff once against the marble. "It listens to the Crown. The word is Hers."

Queen Isara leaned forward by the breadth of a hair, her eyes unblinking and surgical. "Then hear the Crown," she said, the frost in her tone deepening. "You deny desperation. You dismiss blockades. You speak of mutual prosperity while clutching your purse to your chest. I am left to wonder, Ambassador—if this costs you nothing, why offer it at all?"

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You withdrew the sealed packet from within your coat and crossed the last few steps to the observer's alcove, extending the orders to Priestess Yuna before the throne could demand them. The parchment felt heavier than its weight, as though the ink itself carried the mass of fleets.

The Herald's staff struck the marble with a crack that shattered the chamber's held breath. "The court tenders all proof to the Crown! The observer's alcove is no vault for the Ambassador's stratagems!"

Commander Ash's blade sang a finger's breadth from its scabbard, though his hand stayed the draw. "A forger's cowardice," he said, his voice carrying the rough edge of the drill yard. "You duck behind ritual to peddle fiction. Seals can be lifted, dates can be dried by candlelight, and a priestess's blessing does not make lies holy."

Lord Daven gripped the gallery rail, his smile bright and predatory. "Oh, but the Ambassador has read the room's geometry with admirable precision," he called, the words oiled and swift. "Priestess Yuna owns no fleet, no grudge, no ledger stained by these waters. If the seals are false, she is the only witness whose word cannot be bought by either crown. Let the icons judge the ink, Commander—unless you fear what they will see."

Priestess Yuna received the packet in her weathered hands, her gaze meeting yours for a single unreadable moment before she broke the wax. The beads at her waist clicked against the stone, a dry rhythm beneath the murmurs. "The scroll does not choose the hand that bears it," she intoned, her voice carrying the flat neutrality of ritual. "Only the eye that reads chooses whether to look away." She scanned the lines, her expression blank as the icons behind her. "These orders carry the Admiralty's mark. They command the northern interdiction to hold regardless of embassy or parley. They were issued twelve days before the Ambassador entered our waters."

Queen Isara had not moved upon her throne, yet the air around her seemed to compress, cold and clinical. "You bypass my seat to deposit truth in an observer's palms," she said, each syllable dropping like frost. "You trade insult to the Crown for the illusion of fairness. A calculated gamble. Let us discover whether Priestess Yuna's neutrality repays your investment, or whether you have merely purchased a share in her silence."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I turn back to face the Queen, my expression calm.* "The truth speaks for itself, Your Majesty. I believed Priestess Yuna's impartiality would best serve this court."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You felt the chamber's atmosphere compress, as though the very air had crystallized around your gamble.

Queen Isara's finger lifted from the throne's arm, the gesture small and surgical. "You mistake this court for a temple of truth," she said, each syllable dropping like ice into still water. "You deliver stolen parchment into an observer's hands and call it transparency. But transparency is a window, Ambassador, and I now see through it clearly. These orders bear the Admiralty's seal. They were not lost to the wind. They were intercepted." Her gaze remained unblinking, calculating. "Velheim does not merely seek open ports. It has already opened the Crown's own mail."

Commander Ash's blade scraped an inch from its scabbard, the steel singing against leather. "A confession wrapped in a lie," he said, his voice the rough bark of the drill yard. "You wave stolen orders and demand justice. I wave a sword and demand a cell. Espionage is not diplomacy's shadow—it is its replacement."

Lord Daven leaned further over the gallery rail, his smile sharp enough to draw blood. "Oh, but the Ambassador has shown us the depth of the board," he called, the words oiled with ambition. "If Velheim's fingers can pry open sealed Admiralty commands, then the blockade is not a wall—it is a curtain. Her Majesty, one does not hang a thief who reveals where the vault is cracked. One hires him to guard the next."

Priestess Yuna's hands folded the parchment with deliberate care, her gaze lifting to the icons above the throne. "The mirror shows the stain without judging the cloth," she intoned, her voice carrying the flat neutrality of ritual. "But the stain remains. Truth has been spoken. The manner of its arrival speaks also. Two voices now echo where one stood before."

The Herald struck his staff against the marble, the crack scattering the rising murmurs like birds. "The court stands upon the threshold of accusation," he announced. "The Crown alone holds the key. All other words are wind against the lock."

Queen Isara leaned forward by the breadth of a hair, her stillness more terrible than any shout. "You offer ports and arbiters," she said, the frost in her tone deepening. "You offer mutual prosperity. And in the same breath, you demonstrate that Velheim already possesses the keys to my kingdom's sealed chambers." Her lips thinned. "I am left to wonder what else your fingers have touched, and whether any arbiter you propose would sit to judge disputes, or to count the silver while your agents empty the vault." She settled back, her spine finding the throne's edge with deliberate care. "Speak, Ambassador. The court has heard your proof. Now let it hear your explanation for how it came to rest in an enemy's coat."

You felt the marble beneath your boots seem to tilt, the room's geometry rewriting itself around your revelation. The path you had chosen had carried you past the blockade, only to deposit you at the edge of a sharper precipice.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I hold the Queen's gaze, a slight smile playing on my lips.* "Your Majesty, I merely demonstrated that Velheim is capable of protecting its own interests. A demonstration, not an admission."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You felt the stillness in the chamber crystallize around your smile, as though the air itself had paused to measure the audacity of your distinction.

Commander Ash's gauntlets scraped against his pommel, the sound like a whetstone against nerve. "Capability," he said, the word rough as broken gravel. "You name theft capability. You name trespass protection. I have seen wolves dress in such logic before they lunged for the throat."

Lord Daven's laugh was a single, bright note that rang against the marble. "And I have seen kingdoms fall for lack of it," he called, his hands spread upon the gallery rail. "Her Majesty, the Ambassador does not beg—they display. A merchant shows his gold to prove he can pay. Velheim shows its reach to prove it can defend. The sin is not in the demonstration. The sin would be in discovering our seals are soft and doing us the courtesy of silence."

Priestess Yuna's beads clicked against the stone alcove, a dry counterpoint to the tension. "The thunder does not ask the mountain's permission," she intoned, her voice carrying the flat neutrality of ritual. "Yet the mountain does not thank the thunder for the crack. A demonstration is still a breaking. What is broken must be mended, or the next storm enters through the same wound."

"The court does not mend," the Herald announced, his staff snapping against the marble with a crack that scattered the echoes. "It decrees. The Crown alone names the breaking."

Queen Isara's gaze remained fixed upon you, unblinking and surgical. The corner of her lip did not rise, yet something in the calculus of her eyes shifted—a reassessment, cold and rapid as an abacus. "A demonstration," she said, drawing the word out until it frayed. "You stand in my house and prove you can pick its locks. You offer this as courtship." Her finger tapped once against the arm of the throne. "Very well. You have demonstrated your reach. Now demonstrate your restraint." She leaned forward by the width of a breath. "Return to me the method by which these seals were broken. Name the hands that touched my Admiralty's commands. Do this, and your 'demonstration' becomes a gift of security. Refuse, and it remains what it is—an act of war wearing a diplomat's smile."

You felt the weight of her offer settle upon your shoulders like a yoke forged in ice, the room's geometry narrowing to the space between your next breath and the Queen's patience.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I maintain my calm demeanor, though my smile fades slightly.* "Your Majesty, Velheim does not betray its own. The method, and the agents, remain our secrets. Consider it part of our 'capability'—a deterrent, if you will."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You felt the Queen's patience snap shut like a sprung trap, though no muscle in her face moved to announce it.

Queen Isara's finger stilled upon the arm of the throne. "A deterrent," she said, the word falling flat and heavy as a lead ingot. "You enter my house, display my own secrets as trophies, and then declare you shall keep the lock-picks hidden behind your pride." Her gaze remained fixed upon you, unblinking and surgical. "Pride is a luxury of the untested, Ambassador. You have tested me, and now you refuse the remedy. That is not diplomacy. That is occupation wearing courtesy's mask."

Commander Ash's blade cleared its scabbard by a hand's breadth, the steel singing against leather in a sound that silenced the gallery. "The remedy is steel," he said, his voice carrying the rough edge of the drill yard. "A foreign hand pries open sealed commands and calls it statecraft. I call it infiltration. I call it cause. The cells beneath the Admiralty are deep enough to drown secrets and the men who keep them."

Lord Daven gripped the gallery rail, his knuckles whitening as he leaned forward. "Her Majesty, the Ambassador's folly is not in the knowing, but in the telling," he called, the words swift and oiled. "If Velheim wished us harm, the proof would not rest in an observer's palms. It would rest in ash. They show us the crack in our foundation not to watch us fall, but to bargain for the scaffolding. The method is their final coin. Would we strip a man naked and then ask why he shivers?"

Priestess Yuna's hands released the parchment, letting it rest upon the stone alcove like an offering. "A secret kept is a wall maintained," she intoned, her voice carrying the flat neutrality of ritual. "A wall maintained is still a wall between. Two kingdoms cannot dine at the same table if one hides the recipe for the bread and the other hides the knife. The icons watch. They do not hunger. The court hungers enough for all."

"The court does not hunger," the Herald announced, his staff snapping against the marble with a crack that scattered the murmurs. "It decrees. The Crown alone names the trespass."

Queen Isara leaned back, her spine finding the throne's edge with deliberate care, yet the space between you seemed to shrink, compressed by the calculus of her regard. "Then hear the Crown's decree," she said, the chill of her tone frosting the air between the thrones. "Velheim has shown its capability. Velheim has shown its reach. And Velheim, by its own admission, holds agents within my kingdom's marrow who can touch sealed Admiralty commands." Her lips thinned. "The northern ports remain closed. The blockade remains. And you, Ambassador, remain in this court not as a guest of negotiation, but as a witness to consequences." She raised one hand, the gesture small and surgical. "You have until the sun crosses the spire to produce the method and the names. After that, your 'deterrent' becomes the justification for whatever answer the Crown deems fit to send northward. The court is not a marketplace for threats dressed in silk. It is the anvil. And your hammer has struck its final blow."

You felt the marble beneath your boots grow cold, the room's geometry rewriting itself until the aisle behind you seemed longer than it had been, and the space before the throne seemed to hold no quarter.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, a cold calmness settling over me.* "As the Crown wishes. But know this, Your Majesty: an anvil can break a hammer, but a hammer can also reshape an anvil."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You felt your words settle into the chamber like stones dropped into deep water, the ripples invisible but the weight unmistakable.

Commander Ash's blade cleared its scabbard another inch, the steel gleaming in the torchlight. "You threaten the Crown in its own house," he said, his voice dropping to a growl that scraped the marble. "I should end this parley now and carry your head to the parapet as a warning to the next fool Velheim sends south."

Lord Daven's knuckles whitened on the gallery rail, his smile vanishing. "The Ambassador speaks of metallurgy, not malice," he called, though his voice carried an edge of urgency beneath the oil. "A hammer knows its own weight. Her Majesty, this is the voice of a kingdom that believes itself cornered. Cornered beasts do not bark—they bite. The question is whether we wish to bleed, or to step back from the hounds."

Priestess Yuna's head turned slowly, her gaze descending from the icons to fix upon you with the flat gleam of ritual. "When anvil and hammer quarrel," she intoned, "the forge is silent. No plow is shaped. No bell is cast. Both lie broken in the ash, and the smith weeps for tools that forgot their purpose."

"The court does not permit threats to reshape its geometry," the Herald announced, his staff striking the marble with a crack that scattered the echoes like frightened wings. "The Ambassador overreaches. The Crown alone speaks of breaking."

Queen Isara rose. It was a small movement, no more than the shift of a statue settling on its pedestal, yet the air in the throne room seemed to flee before her. Her gaze remained pinned upon you, unblinking and surgical, and when she spoke, her voice carried the low, precise chill of a blade drawn across velvet. "You mistake this court for your forge," she said. "You mistake my patience for brittleness." She descended one step, then stopped. "The sun climbs. Your hammer remains raised. But consider, Ambassador—every anvil in this kingdom is crowned, and every hammer that struck it has been melted down for scrap." Her hand opened, palm up, in a gesture that offered nothing. "You have until the spire. Use it to choose whether Velheim's next embassy arrives with terms, or with mourning colors."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet her gaze, unflinching.* "The sun will set, Your Majesty. And Velheim will still stand." *I turn, and without waiting for dismissal, begin my walk back down the aisle.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You felt the marble stretch beneath your stride, each step echoing in the sudden vacuum of the chamber. The distance to the threshold seemed to lengthen, measured not in yards but in the held breath of the court.

The Herald's staff struck the marble with a crack that chased your heels. "The audience is not concluded! The Ambassador withdraws without the Crown's leave! Let the record mark the breach!"

Commander Ash's blade sang fully from its scabbard, the steel flashing torchlight across the aisle. "You turn your back on the Queen," he said, the words a rough snarl that filled the space behind you. "Guards! Seize the—"

"Let him walk," Lord Daven called, his voice cutting through the command like oiled silk. "Her Majesty gave until the spire, not until the cell. The Ambassador leaves with the Crown's deadline, not against it. To arrest him now is to admit the bargain frightened us."

Priestess Yuna's beads clicked against the stone, dry as winter leaves. "The arrow does not call back the bowstring," she intoned. "It flies toward whatever mark the archer chose. To strike it from the air changes nothing. The target still waits."

Queen Isara did not raise her voice. She stood upon the step, her figure framed by the throne's shadow, and when she spoke, the frost in her tone stopped the guards before their hands could close upon your shoulders. "Let the wolf return to his pack," she said, each syllable precise and glacial. "Let him carry the Crown's mercy and the Crown's warning in the same mouthful." Her gaze remained upon your back, unblinking and surgical. "When the sun kisses the spire, Ambassador, the threshold you now cross will become a wall. And Velheim will discover whether it stands upon stone, or upon the ash of its own pride."

You felt her words settle between your shoulder blades like the touch of a blade not yet drawn, the court's eyes upon you as you continued down the aisle.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I continue my measured walk, not bothering to look back.* "We shall see, Your Majesty. We shall see."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The precision of your bow did not escape Queen Isara. Her gaze lingered on the angle of your spine as though she could measure intent by geometry alone. When she spoke, her voice was cold and unhurried.

"Patience, Ambassador, is a debt this court does not extend lightly. You have our attention. Spend it wisely."

Commander Ash's laugh was short and humorless. "Attention? The last Velheim envoy had our attention too — right up until his 'trade routes' became a march on Kessir's Ford." His hand flexed against his sword pommel. "Terms. The word wears thinner every time your people say it."

The Herald's staff cracked against the marble once, sharp enough to silence the murmur before it could form. "The Commander will confine himself to the matters of war when the court sits in peace." The Herald's tone was courteous, but it carried the weight of law. "The Ambassador of Velheim holds the floor. Her Majesty will recognize commentary in its proper order."

Priestess Yuna's fingers traced a small sign against her palm. "Words spoken here are woven into the tapestry, Ambassador. Not even queens may cut the thread." Her eyes were unreadable, calm as the icons behind her. "Speak what is true, or speak not at all."

From the gallery, Lord Daven inclined his head — first to the throne, then to you. "Your Majesty, the Ambassador has come unarmed and without threat, bearing a sealed proposal. That alone distinguishes this embassy from its predecessors." He let the faintest smile touch his mouth. "I would hear the terms before I sharpen my tongue."

Queen Isara's fingers stilled against the armrest. "A rare indulgence, Lord Daven — but not an unwise one." She turned her gaze back to you, and the weight of the throne seemed to press behind her stare. "You asked for patience. You shall have it — until you give this court reason to withdraw it. Read your terms, Ambassador. Every clause. Then we will judge whether Velheim's friendship is worth its price."

The Herald raised his staff slightly, not to strike, but to signal.

"The court will hear the articles of the proposed northern trade accord, as spoken by the Ambassador of Velheim."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, holding it just long enough before turning to the court.* "Thank you, Your Majesty. And I thank the court for its... attention." *My voice is steady, betraying none of the irritation Commander Ash's comment sparked.* "The terms are simple, and I assure you, entirely focused on trade."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The echo of your last word faded into the vaulted silence of the throne room. Somewhere above, a banner stirred in a draft that did not reach the floor.

Queen Isara did not blink. Her fingers, pale against the dark wood of the throne, tapped once against the armrest — a slow, deliberate rhythm.
"Assurances are not articles, Ambassador," she said, her voice as cold and unhurried as a winter stream. "You came to this court to read terms. 'Simple' and 'focused on trade' are not clauses. They are prefaces. The court did not grant its patience to hear a summary. Read the first article."

Commander Ash's boots shifted against the marble, the only sound he permitted himself. "A summary is all we ever get from Velheim," he growled. "They summarize their way across a border and then act surprised when the garrisons mobilize. Focused on trade. Ha. The road to Kessir's Ford was focused on trade until the wagons started carrying spears instead of salt."

The Herald's staff came down — not a crack this time, but a firm, resonant thud that cut through the Commander's scorn.
"The Commander will confine his tongue to the armistice," the Herald announced, and his formal tone brooked no argument. "The Ambassador holds the floor. The court will not be provoked into disorder by ghosts of campaigns past. Ambassador, the throne requires the first article of the accord."

From her alcove, Priestess Yuna's voice drifted down, quiet but somehow carrying to every corner. "A promise spoken beneath the icons is a stitch in the tapestry, Ambassador. You began to sew. The pattern will show whether the thread is silk or serpent's tooth." Her fingers traced that same small sign against her palm. "The gods are patient. The weave is not."

Lord Daven rose halfway from his seat in the gallery before he caught himself and settled back, and his ambition wrestled with protocol. "Your Majesty," he called, inclining his head with polished grace, "the Commander's vigilance is the crown's shield, and the Priestess's wisdom its soul. But we cannot judge the weave until the first thread is laid. Let the Ambassador speak the article. If the terms are poison, we will taste it soon enough — and Lord Daven's own spies will have read the antidote in Velheim's ledgers." He offered a thin, shark-like smile. "Read, Ambassador. I am listening."

Queen Isara's gaze never left you. The tapping of her fingers ceased.
"You have your opening, Ambassador," she said, and there was an edge beneath the ice now — a warning dressed as permission. "The Herald has called for the first article. Commander Ash will hold his peace, and the Priestess will count your stitches. Do not make this court ask twice. Begin."

The Herald raised his staff slightly, and the signal was clear.
"The court is in silence. The Ambassador of Velheim will now read the first article of the proposed northern trade accord."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your question shattered the silence the Herald had just declared. Leveled at Commander Ash rather than at the throne, it ignored protocol as blatantly as it ignored the command to read the first article. Somewhere in the gallery, a councilor's breath hissed between his teeth.

Commander Ash went rigid. His hand clenched on his sword pommel until the leather creaked, and for a moment it seemed he would step forward and answer with steel rather than words. “You dare—” he began, voice low and thick with fury.

The Herald's staff cracked against the marble, the sound sharp as a whip. “The Commander will hold his tongue,” the Herald announced, formal and unyielding. “The Ambassador of Velheim holds the floor. Her Majesty has not recognized the Commander. Ambassador, you were commanded to read the first article. You have not read it. You have instead hurled a question across this chamber. The court will not be governed by ambush.”

Queen Isara raised one pale hand, and the Herald fell silent at the gesture. “No,” she said, her voice colder than the draft above the banners. “The Ambassador has thrown a stone into a deep well. I would know what it strikes before I judge the throw.” Her eyes slid to Commander Ash, and the weight behind them was absolute. “Is it true? Have our ships closed the northern routes to Velheim merchants for six weeks? Answer, Commander. Fact, not fury. You have the court's leave—briefly.”

From the observer's alcove, Priestess Yuna's voice drifted down, quiet and inexorable. “A blockade is a border drawn upon water, Majesty. The tapestry records it whether the thread is pulled in peace or in war.” Her fingers traced the small sign against her palm. “Let the question be answered. The pattern will show whether this is quarantine or conquest.”

Lord Daven rose from the gallery, his ambition barely leashed by courtesy. “Your Majesty,” he said, inclining his head, “the Ambassador's method was irregular—I will not pretend otherwise. But if the northern routes are closed, then every clause of this accord is built on a foundation the court cannot see.” His gaze flicked to you, brief and sharp as a knife-edge. “I beg you, let the Commander's answer stand before the first article is read. We cannot weigh Velheim's price while Velheim's merchants rot at anchor.”

The Herald struck the floor once more, but this time the blow was a formal signal, not a rebuke. “The throne recognizes Commander Ash to respond to the Ambassador's question. The Ambassador will hold the floor thereafter to read the first article, as commanded.”

Commander Ash's jaw worked as though the words tasted of ash. He dragged his hand from his sword and stood at rigid attention, though his eyes never left you. “Six weeks,” he bit out. “The northern straits are closed to Velheim hulls—by order of the crown. Not blockade. Quarantine.” The word was a shield and a snarl. “Your merchants were running steel to the highland clans. Salt on top, spears beneath. We searched three hulls and found iron enough to arm a rebellion. Warning was given. It was ignored.” He straightened, hostility radiating from him like heat. “So answer me this, Ambassador: if your trade routes are so innocent, why does every Velheim ship we stop carry more weapons than wool?”

A murmur ran through the gallery, quickly stifled. Queen Isara's fingers tapped once against the armrest, then stilled. She turned her gaze back to you, and the edge beneath the ice was bare now. “You have your answer, Ambassador,” she said. “The straits are closed. Whether it is quarantine or blockade is a question for this court to unravel—later. But you were commanded to read the first article, and you have not. You ignored my order once. Do not make me repeat it.”

The Herald raised his staff, signaling that the floor remained yours. “Read, Ambassador. The first article. Now.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I meet Commander Ash's gaze, a slow smile spreading across my face. "Quarantine? Interesting choice of word, Commander." *I turn back to the Queen.* "Your Majesty, the first article of the accord is as follows: *All blockades and quarantines of Velheim shipping are to be immediately lifted, and free passage guaranteed through all northern trade routes.*"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The words left your mouth, and the silence that followed was heavier than the one before. It was not the expectant hush of a court waiting to be impressed; it was the stillness of a snare drawing tight. Somewhere behind you, a scribe's pen scratched against parchment, recording the demand exactly as you had spoken it.

Queen Isara's eyes narrowed, just slightly—the first true crack in the ice. "You have read your first article," she said, her voice a study in cold control. "And in it, Velheim does not ask for the restoration of trade. It demands the crown dismantle a measure taken for the security of this realm, effective immediately, with no offer of recompense, no provision for inspection, no acknowledgment of the steel we found beneath your salt." She leaned forward a fraction, and the throne seemed to lean with her. "That is not an article, Ambassador. That is an ultimatum wrapped in the language of commerce."

Commander Ash shot forward, his face dark with fury, his mouth already opening to snarl—

The Herald's staff cracked against the marble like a whip. "The Commander is not recognized!" the Herald announced, his formal tone brooking no argument. "The Ambassador has the floor until Her Majesty sees fit to open the court to response!"

Queen Isara raised one pale hand, and the Herald broke off, though his staff remained half-raised. "Speak, Commander," she said, her voice as cold as the draft above the banners. "But confine yourself to the article, not the Ambassador's throat."

Ash dragged in a breath, his hand flexing at his side as though he wished it were your neck. "The article is surrender!" he bit out, his voice harsh. "Your Majesty, they want the roads open so the next three hulls can carry swords instead of plowshares. You heard him—lift everything, guarantee passage. What do we get? Nothing but the privilege of being stabbed in the back with Velheim steel! The iron we found wasn't a mistake. It was a shipment. And now they demand we forget it ever happened."

Priestess Yuna's voice drifted down from the alcove, soft but inexorable as the toll of a distant bell. "The tapestry drinks the thread, Majesty," she said, her fingers tracing that same small sign against her palm. "The first stitch is bold—perhaps too bold. It seeks to unravel a knot tied in blood and iron without offering a new strand to replace it. A demand for peace must be woven with the silk of concession, or the tapestry will show only the shape of a noose." Her eyes were calm, unreadable, fixed not on you but on the empty air where the weave was imagined.

Lord Daven was already rising, his ambition burning through the thin veneer of his courtesy. "Your Majesty," he said smoothly, inclining his head first to the throne and then, briefly, to you, "the Commander's vigilance does the crown credit, and the Priestess's metaphor is as ever illuminating. But we are judges of an accord, not executioners of a single clause. The Ambassador has done what was commanded—the first article is read. Is it harsh? Yes. Is it the whole of Velheim's intent? We cannot know until the second thread is laid." He paused, and his smile was thin and sharp. "Surely the court is not so fragile that one bold article sends us reaching for our swords. Let the Ambassador continue. If the next clause offers inspection, or recompense for the seized hulls, then the quarantine may yet become a treaty."

The Herald struck the floor with his staff, the signal that order had been restored. "The first article of the proposed northern trade accord has been spoken and recorded," the Herald intoned, his voice filling the vaulted space. "The court awaits the second article, as spoken by the Ambassador of Velheim."

Queen Isara's fingers tapped once against the armrest—the same slow, deliberate rhythm as before. "You heard the Herald," she said, her voice dropping to that cold, unhurried register that had opened this hearing. "The first article is heard. It has sharpened every tongue in this room and drawn a line beneath Commander Ash's accusations. Now unblur it. Read the second article—and take care that it does not sound like the first. This court's patience is not a bottomless well, and you have already thrown a great many stones into it."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, my expression unreadable.* "Your Majesty, I assure you, the subsequent articles are far more... accommodating." *I take a breath, preparing to speak.* "The second article states: *In exchange for the lifting of the aforementioned quarantines, the Kingdom of Velheim agrees to regular, scheduled inspections of all Velheim vessels traversing the northern trade routes, conducted by agents of this court.*"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The second article settled into the throne room like a blade returned, at last, to its sheath. The words you had spoken did not erase the tension so much as reshape it; the scribe’s pen scratched as the clause was recorded, and somewhere in the gallery a councilor let out a long, quiet exhale.

Commander Ash’s hand had gone to his sword the instant the word inspections was spoken, but the rest of the sentence robbed him of the outrage he had been nursing. His fingers spasmed against the pommel. “Inspections?” he repeated, voice thick. “By our agents? In our ports?” He took a step forward, boots striking the marble. “That is not concession. That is a serpent offering its throat to the knife so the court will not look at its tail!”

The Herald’s staff cracked against the floor. “The Commander is not recognized!” the Herald announced, formal and unyielding. “The Ambassador of Velheim holds the floor. Her Majesty will decide when the court responds.”

Queen Isara raised one pale hand, and the Herald broke off. “Speak, Commander,” she said, cold as the draft above the banners. “But answer the article, not the Ambassador. If Velheim yields to inspection, say why that is a snare rather than a safeguard.”

Ash’s jaw worked. He did not look away from you as he spoke. “Because it is revocable!” he bit out. “The first article says the straits open now. This one says Velheim will allow inspections—until Velheim decides otherwise. Once the hulls are through, who drags them back to harbor? Who boards a Velheim ship in Velheim water? The clause has no teeth, Majesty. It is a promise written in smoke.”

Priestess Yuna’s voice drifted down from the alcove, calm and inexorable. “The second thread is cut from a different fleece, Majesty,” she said, fingers tracing the small sign against her palm. “It does not unravel the first; it binds it. But the pattern asks whether the knot is tied by both hands or only one. An inspection granted is a stitch. An inspection withdrawn is a tear. The gods will see which the weave is made to bear.”

Lord Daven rose from the gallery, ambition barely leashed by courtesy. “Your Majesty,” he said smoothly, inclining his head first to the throne and then, briefly, to you, “the Commander’s suspicion is the crown’s armor, and the Priestess’s metaphor its mirror. But armor must not become a tomb. The Ambassador has done what the court demanded—the second article answers the first. It offers process where before there was only demand. Surely that is the shape of a treaty, not a trap.” His smile was thin and sharp. “I would know the mechanics before I render judgment. But let us not pretend the clause is nothing. It is something. And it deserves the third article to complete it.”

Queen Isara’s fingers tapped once against the armrest, then stilled. Her gaze never left you. “You have conceded a point, Ambassador,” she said, her voice dropping to that cold, unhurried register. “Do not think the court does not mark it. But concession without enforcement is pageantry. You offer inspections by agents of this court. Who selects them? Where do they board? What penalty falls on a Velheim hull that refuses the search once the straits are open? The first article demanded immediacy. This one offers machinery. Machinery can be stalled as easily as a gate can be barred.” She leaned forward a fraction. “Answer the question of enforcement. Then read the third article. Take care that it does not sound like the second’s shadow.”

The Herald struck the floor with his staff, the formal signal cutting through the murmurs that had begun to rise. “The second article of the proposed northern trade accord has been spoken and recorded,” the Herald intoned. “The throne has put a question to the Ambassador of Velheim regarding enforcement. The floor remains with the Ambassador to answer, and thereafter to read the third article, as commanded.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The folded packet passed from your hand into Priestess Yuna’s before the Herald’s staff could crack again. It was not a tidy thing: the wax seal had been torn open, the ribbon cut, the edges creased as though the orders had been carried in a saddlebag rather than a courier’s case. Yuna received it with both palms, her face as calm and blank as the icons behind her, though her fingers traced that small sign against her flesh.

The Herald’s staff came down hard. “The Ambassador will not bypass the throne!” the Herald announced, formal and unyielding. “All proofs are laid before Her Majesty! The court does not receive evidence through the observer’s alcove!”

Queen Isara lifted one pale hand, and the Herald broke off mid-breath. Her gaze had gone to the torn seal, and something almost like interest flickered behind the ice. “Hold,” she said. “The Ambassador has chosen a strange custodian for this proof. Priestess Yuna is bound to the icons, not to my crown nor to Velheim’s ledgers. If the thread is to be judged, let the neutral hand hold it first.” Her eyes slid to Yuna. “Read, Priestess. Aloud. Every line. If this is forgery, let it burn in the light of the tapestry. If it is true…” Her voice dropped. “…then we shall see what manner of quarantine the Commander has been keeping.”

Commander Ash was already moving, boots striking marble, his face dark. “That packet is stolen!” he bit out. “It bears my seal—or the crown’s—and it was taken from a northern courier by Velheim knives! You expect this court to believe a thief’s proof? I never—”

The Herald’s staff cracked between them, a whip of sound. “The Commander is not recognized!” the Herald intoned. “The Priestess holds the floor for the reading. You will hold your tongue, or you will be removed from this hall.”

From the gallery, Lord Daven rose, ambition and delight barely leashed by courtesy. “Your Majesty,” he said, inclining his head, “the Commander calls it theft; the Ambassador calls it proof. The distinction matters less than the words themselves. If Velheim stole the orders, let that be answered in its turn—but a stolen truth is still a truth. Let the Priestess read. The stone has been thrown into the well; we must all hear the splash.”

Priestess Yuna did not look at any of them. She unfolded the parchment, her fingers tracing the small sign one last time before she read. Her voice drifted down, quiet and inexorable.

“These are orders,” she said, “issued to the captains of the northern fleet. They are dated eleven days before the first Velheim hull was searched. They are signed by Commander Ash, and countersigned by the royal chancellor.”

She paused. The silence was absolute. Then she read on:

“‘The straits shall be closed to Velheim shipping for a period of no less than six weeks. No vessel shall pass though it carry only wool. Should inspection find no contraband, the iron shall be placed in the hold and the discovery logged as found.’”

Yuna’s eyes lifted, calm and unreadable. “The royal seal is stamped at the foot, Majesty. The wax is broken, but the die is clear.”

Commander Ash went rigid. “That is a lie!” he snarled. “That is not my hand! That is Velheim forgery from the first stroke to the last! I ordered searches because we found steel, not—”

Queen Isara’s fingers tapped once against the armrest, then stilled. “You told this court it was a quarantine, Commander,” she said, her voice colder than the draft above the banners. “You said your ships searched three hulls and found iron beneath the salt. The orders read by the Priestess say the straits were closed before the search, and that iron was to be placed if none was found. Which is the forgery, Commander—the paper, or the tale?”

Lord Daven’s smile was thin and sharp as a knife. “If the seal holds, Your Majesty, then the Commander did not discover a smuggling ring. He manufactured one. And the first article begins to look less like an ultimatum and more like justice.”

The Herald struck the floor once, but not in rebuke; it was the formal signal that order held. “The intercepted orders have been read into the record,” the Herald intoned. “The throne retains the document for verification. The floor returns to the Ambassador of Velheim.”

Queen Isara’s gaze settled on you, heavy as the throne behind her. “You have thrown your proof into the well, Ambassador,” she said. “It is either the salvation of your embassy or the rope that hangs it. The court will examine that seal, and the Commander’s signature, and the royal counter-sign. If it is true, the quarantine is worse than a blockade—it is a lie dressed as law. If it is false, you have brought forgery into my hall, and no article will save you.” Her eyes did not blink. “You were commanded to answer the question of enforcement and read the third article. You have done neither. Now you will do both. Explain how you came by these orders. Then read the third article—and pray it does not sound like the second’s shadow.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I smile, a genuine, if slightly grim, smile.* "Your Majesty, the orders were... acquired through means necessary to protect Velheim's interests. As for enforcement, the third article addresses it directly." *I clear my throat, my voice steady.* "The third article states: *Any agent of this court found to have violated the terms of inspection, or to have fabricated evidence of contraband, shall be subject to immediate dismissal and criminal prosecution within their own jurisdiction.*"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The moment the word *prosecution* left your lips, the great hall seemed to draw a collective breath and hold it. The grim smile you wore did not falter, though the steadiness of your voice made the clause sound less like a concession and more like a sentence. Somewhere in the gallery, a scribe’s pen snapped under a tightening grip.

Commander Ash did not shout. He went utterly, dangerously still, his chest rising once as if he meant to inhale the fire in the room. Then his voice came, low and rough with a fury he could barely leash. “You expect this court to try its own commanders?” he bit out, his gaze locked on you. “You bring stolen paper and whisper of treason, and now you demand my officers stand in chains if they defend this realm? This is not an accord, Majesty—it is a purge!”

The Herald’s staff cracked against the marble, a sharp, commanding report. “The Commander is not recognized!” the Herald intoned, his voice formal and unyielding. “The Ambassador of Velheim holds the floor until Her Majesty surrenders it! You will not threaten this envoy, nor this court, with the language of rebellion!”

Queen Isara raised one pale hand, and the Herald broke off, though his staff remained half-raised. The Queen’s eyes were fixed on you, cold and unblinking, but her words were addressed to the hall. “The Commander speaks of purge. I hear enforcement.” Her voice was frost over deep water. “Ambassador, you have admitted these orders were acquired by ‘means necessary.’ That is a confession of espionage within my borders, and I do not mistake it for innocence. Nor do I mistake your third article, which places the agents of this court—my agents—under the threat of criminal prosecution for fabricated evidence.” She leaned forward a fraction, and the throne seemed to lean with her. “You have answered my question of enforcement. But you have aimed it like a crossbow at the heart of my own authority. If the seal is true, Commander Ash stands condemned by your very clause. If it is false, you have brought a lie into my hall and demanded I hang my own officers upon it.”

From the alcove, Priestess Yuna’s voice drifted down, quiet and inexorable. The intercepted orders still rested in her palms, her fingers tracing that same small sign against her flesh. “The third thread is spun from iron, Majesty,” she said, her eyes calm and unreadable. “It binds the hand that holds the knife as well as the throat it is pressed to. The tapestry does not favor the inspector over the inspected; it records the pull of every thread. But the weave is not yet set. A seal broken can be remade in truth or in treason. Until the wax is tested, the iron thread hangs loose—waiting to snare the guilty, whichever side of the loom they stand upon.”

Lord Daven rose from the gallery, his ambition burning bright through the thin veneer of his courtesy. He inclined his head first to the throne, then gave you a nod that was almost approving. “Your Majesty,” he said smoothly, “the Commander’s outrage is the shield of a guilty man, or the vanity of an honest one—we do not yet know which. But the Ambassador has done precisely what the crown demanded. The provenance of the proof is stated, however uncomfortably. The third article provides the teeth this court required. It punishes corruption on *both* sides of the dock. If Commander Ash’s men are blameless, this clause is their protection against Velheim’s slander. If they are not, then the crown should welcome the pruning of its own rotten branches.” His smile was thin and sharp. “I move that the articles be accepted as read, and that the seal be delivered to the royal chancellor for verification this very hour. Let the truth of the thread be proven before we judge the weaver.”

Queen Isara’s fingers tapped once against the armrest—the same slow, deliberate rhythm—then stilled. “So moved,” she said, though her gaze never left you. “The third article is heard. All three articles now stand before this court. Priestess Yuna will deliver the intercepted orders to the royal chancellor, and the seal tested against the die in the crown’s archive. Commander Ash, you will surrender your northern fleet’s logs and the names of every inspector who boarded a Velheim hull in the last two months. You will do it without your sword.” Her eyes flicked to Ash, and the ice in them was absolute. “If the orders are true, you will answer for them under the laws of this realm—and perhaps under the third article of this very accord, should it ever be ratified. If they are false, Ambassador, you will answer for theft, espionage, and forgery, and no clause will shield you.”

She leaned back, though the weight of the throne did not seem to ease. “You have fulfilled the commands laid upon you, Ambassador—barely. You confessed to acquiring stolen orders by ‘means necessary,’ and you have aimed your enforcement at my own officers. Whether that was brilliance or suicide depends entirely on the wax.” She paused, and the edge beneath the ice was bare now. “If there are further articles to this accord, speak them now.
