If this is the sum of Velheim’s terms, then the court will deliberate, and the seal will decide whether you leave this hall a diplomat or a prisoner.”

The Herald struck the floor with his staff, the signal ringing through the vaulted silence. “The first, second, and third articles of the proposed northern trade accord have been spoken and recorded. The intercepted orders have been entered into evidence and remanded to the crown for verification. The floor remains with the Ambassador of Velheim. If there are further articles, the court will hear them. If not, the throne will pronounce the next step in this hearing.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I offer a slight, confident incline of my head.* "There are no further articles, Your Majesty. Velheim's terms have been laid bare." *My gaze flickers to Commander Ash, then back to the Queen, my expression unwavering.* "The ball is now in your court."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your final words — "The ball is now in your court" — hung in the vaulted air, a foreign turn of phrase that did not belong among marble and banners. Somewhere in the gallery, a councilor's breath hissed between his teeth at the idiom, and Lord Daven's fingers tightened on the rail before he could master himself.

Queen Isara did not blink at the phrase. If anything, the ice in her gaze thickened. She rose, not from her seat but in the way a glacier might rise — an imperceptible increase in pressure, a shift in the weight of the room.
"The court is not a game of Velheim children, Ambassador," she said, her voice colder than the draft above the banners. "There is no ball. There is only the seal, and the truth it will surrender or conceal." She turned her gaze to the Commander. "Commander Ash. Your sword. Your logs. The names of your inspectors. You will place them in the Herald's hands before you leave this hall. You will do it now, and you will do it in silence."

Commander Ash looked as though he had been struck. For a heartbeat, his hand remained locked on his sword pommel, the leather creaking. Then, with a sound like a dying animal, he dragged the blade from his belt — not striking, not snarling, but surrendering it into the Herald's waiting hands as though the steel burned him.
"This is Velheim's work," he spat, his voice low and thick with a fury he could barely leash. "You will see, Majesty. When the chancellor brings the die, you will see the forgery for what it is. And when you do—" His eyes found you across the marble, and the hatred in them was a living thing. "—I will be the one standing over your cell."

The Herald's staff came down, a sharp crack to cut off the threat. "The Commander is not recognized!" the Herald intoned, formal and unyielding. "The Commander has been commanded to silence. He will obey, or he will be removed from this hall." The Herald accepted the sword with precise, practiced hands, then turned to the throne. "The court awaits the royal command regarding the person of the Ambassador of Velheim."

Lord Daven was already on his feet, his ambition burning through the thin veneer of his courtesy. "Your Majesty," he said smoothly, inclining his head first to the throne and then, briefly, to you, "the Ambassador came beneath a flag of truce, and has spoken every article demanded of him. Until the seal is proven false, to chain him is to declare war by another name. I beg you — grant him the guest wing, under guard if you must, but grant him the rights of an envoy. Velheim will hear of how its ambassador was treated in this hour."

From the alcove, Priestess Yuna had not moved. The intercepted orders were still in her palms, her fingers tracing that same small sign against her flesh.
"The threads are all cut, Majesty," she said, her voice quiet and inexorable. "The weave is complete — first, second, and third, and the stolen strand laid across them all. Now the tapestry goes to the fire of testing. What emerges will bear the face of either a treaty or a noose. The gods are patient. The testing is not." She stepped down from the alcove, moving toward the side door where the royal chancellor would be waiting. "I will deliver the orders to the archive myself."

Queen Isara's fingers tapped once against the armrest — the same slow, deliberate rhythm — then stilled. Her gaze returned to you, heavy as the throne behind her.
"You have laid your terms bare, Ambassador, and in doing so you have laid your neck upon the same block." She did not smile. "There are no further articles. So be it. The Herald will conduct you to the guest wing. You will have chambers, food, and pen and parchment — but you will not leave the palace, and you will be watched. When the seal is tested, you will be brought before this court again. If the die matches the wax, Commander Ash will answer to me, and Velheim's terms will be weighed as a treaty." Her eyes narrowed, and the edge beneath the ice was bare. "If it does not, you will answer for espionage, forgery, and theft — and no article, nor Lord Daven's pretty pleading, will stay the executioner's hand."

The Herald struck the floor with his staff, the formal signal ringing through the vaulted silence.
"The court is adjourned to the testing of the seal. The Ambassador of Velheim is remanded to the guest wing under honorable guard. The Commander of the northern fleet is stripped of his sword pending inquiry. The Priestess bears the evidence to the chancellor. Let it be done."

Two guards approached Commander Ash, who stood rigid as they took his arms. But it was toward you that the Herald now turned, extending a hand to indicate the path from the throne room. Somewhere behind you, the great doors began to open, and the weight of every eye in the court followed as you were escorted out into the corridor beyond — to wait, and to wonder whether the wax would prove you a diplomat or a spy.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I offer the Herald a curt nod, a small, knowing smile playing on my lips as I pass Commander Ash.* "As you wish, Your Majesty." *I don't look back as I'm led out, the weight of the court's gaze a familiar pressure.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald inclined his head in return to your curt nod — a precise, formal motion that granted the courtesy without surrendering an inch of protocol. “Ambassador,” he said, his voice pitched to carry just far enough. “This way.”

As you passed Commander Ash, your small, knowing smile still fixed upon your lips, the Commander strained against the guards who held him. His face had gone dark with a fury that no longer had a sword to answer it.

“Enjoy that smile, Velheim,” Commander Ash spat, his voice low and thick with hatred. “When the chancellor’s die meets that broken wax, you will learn what a noose feels like from the inside.” One of the guards tightened his grip, and though Ash did not fall silent, his threat dissolved into a string of curses that followed you toward the doors.

Your parting words — *As you wish, Your Majesty* — had been spoken without a backward glance. From the throne, Queen Isara’s gaze followed you, and something almost like amusement flickered behind the ice before it froze over completely.

“It is not my wish that binds you now, Ambassador,” Queen Isara said, her voice as cold and unhurried as a winter stream. “It is the seal. Learn the difference before this court summons you again.” She turned her head a fraction toward the waiting Herald. “Herald. The blue chambers in the guest wing. Fire, food, and parchment. A guard at the door — not chains, but no key on the inside. See that he wants for nothing, and that he leaves for nothing.”

In the gallery, Lord Daven’s laugh was soft, ambitious, and entirely without warmth. He inclined his head first to the Queen, then to your departing figure.

“A bold throw, Your Majesty,” Lord Daven said smoothly. “If the seal holds, the Ambassador has not merely saved his neck — he has handed us Ash’s head on a Velheim platter. If it does not…” He let the thought trail, his smile thin and sharp. “I will begin my own inquiries in Velheim’s counting houses. Truth has a way of hiding in ledgers, even when it flees the light.”

From the side of the chamber, Priestess Yuna’s voice drifted, quiet and inexorable, as she moved toward the door that would take her to the royal chancellor. The intercepted orders were still cradled in her arm, her fingers tracing that same small sign against her palm.

“The thread enters the fire, Ambassador,” Priestess Yuna said. “The weave does not flatter the guilty, nor spare the innocent. It only remembers what it was.” Then she was gone through the side door, her footsteps as soft as falling dust.

The great doors of the throne room boomed shut behind you, severing the court from the corridor beyond. The sound was final, like the closing of a tomb — or a womb. The Herald’s staff tapped once against the stone, a measured rhythm, and he set off down the wide hall. Two guards in polished armor fell in behind you, their hands empty, their presence a wall.

You were conducted through the palace in silence. Torchlight gilded the Herald’s staff as he led the way past tall windows where the evening sky bruised purple over the city. The corridor smelled of beeswax and cold stone. Somewhere below, a bell began to toll the hour.

At last, the Herald stopped before a heavy door of dark wood bound in brass. He pushed it open. Firelight spilled out across the corridor flags, and within lay the chamber the Queen had commanded: a fire crackling in the grate, a table set near the window with pen, ink, and fresh parchment, and a bed turned down beneath a canopy of royal blue.

The Herald stood aside, his expression as formal as ever.

“The guest wing, Ambassador,” the Herald announced. “All that was promised was within. Food will come at the evening bell. If you require aught, speak to the guard; your words will be conveyed to me.” He inclined his head, a shallow, precise motion. “When the seal has been tested, the court will summon you. Until then, you are the crown’s honored guest — and, should the wax prove false, its prisoner.”

He withdrew. The two guards stepped into the corridor outside and took up their posts, flanking the door like statues. The door swung shut. A bolt slid home with a heavy, final thunk.

Silence settled over the guest chamber, broken only by the crackle of the fire and the distant, indifferent tolling of the palace bell. Outside, somewhere in the deep archives, Priestess Yuna was even now laying the intercepted orders beneath the chancellor’s lens; soon the royal die would be pressed to the broken wax, and the truth would be dragged into the light.

But in the room, there was only the fire, the waiting parchment, and the slow, unyielding tread of time.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I walk over to the small table, my fingers tracing the edge of the parchment. I pick up the quill, testing its weight, then set it down again.* "Honored guest," *I murmur to myself, a wry twist to my lips.* "Or prisoner." *I glance at the bolted door, then at the crackling fire, a low chuckle escaping me.* "Either way, it seems I have time to kill."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The fire gave a low, answering crackle — the only reply your murmur earned. The quill lay on the table where you had set it down, its nib still dark with ink you had not used. The parchment remained as blank as the faces of the icons behind Priestess Yuna’s alcove. Beyond the window, the last bruised light drained from the sky, leaving the city below to kindle its own scattered lamps.

Time, it seemed, was the one thing the crown had given you in abundance — and the one thing that might yet kill you.

Somewhere deeper in the palace, a bell began to toll the hour: the same deep, indifferent note that had followed you down the corridor. Not long after, a knock sounded at the door — three precise raps, neither a servant’s timid tap nor a lord’s imperious demand.

The bolt scraped back. A guard’s voice came, formal and slightly muffled by the heavy wood.

“Evening meal, Ambassador. By order of the Herald.”

The door opened just wide enough to admit a servant in plain grey livery, head bowed, bearing a covered tray. The servant crossed to the table — keeping his eyes fixed on the floor, as though the sight of a Velheim envoy might burn him — and set the tray down beside the blank parchment. Steam rose from a bowl of broth; beside it stood a heel of bread, a small knife, and a flagon of watered wine. Then the servant backed out, and the guard’s face filled the gap once more.

“The Herald’s compliments, Ambassador. The fire will be tended at the tenth bell. You will not be disturbed.”

The door shut. The bolt thudded home. The corridor fell silent but for the slow, measured tread of the sentries outside.

The broth cooled. The bread went untouched where it lay. The fire burned down to a bed of glowing embers, painting the royal-blue canopy in shades of rust and blood. Outside, the palace settled into the uneasy quiet of a building holding its breath.

It was perhaps an hour later — though time in that chamber had grown slippery — when a new sound broke the stillness: footsteps in the corridor, unhurried and confident, accompanied by the soft murmur of a voice that was not the guard’s.

A challenge rang out, crisp and formal.

“My lord, the Ambassador is not to receive visitors without the Herald’s leave.”

A smooth voice replied, pitched low but carrying easily through the door. “Then let it be known that the Herald granted me ten minutes, and that I am a patient man only when it suits me. Stand aside, sergeant. I will not lay a hand on your precious prisoner; I merely wish to look upon the face that has so thoroughly ruined Commander Ash’s afternoon.”

A pause. Then the bolt drew back.

Lord Daven entered.

He wore a dark cloak lined with grey fur, the collar turned up against the palace chill, and his eyes were as bright and sharp as the knife-edge smile he had worn in the gallery. He inclined his head — first to the guards who remained framed in the doorway, then to you across the chamber — and stepped into the firelight as though he owned it. The door did not close fully behind him; protocol, it seemed, retained one thin claw even here.

“Ambassador,” Lord Daven said, his voice smooth, ambitious, and entirely without warmth. “You have thrown this court into chaos, and I find myself admiring the arc of the throw. The seal is even now beneath the chancellor’s lens. Commander Ash is stripped of his sword and spitting curses in the barracks. Queen Isara is ice itself, and Priestess Yuna is praying over wax and die.” His gaze flicked to the blank parchment on the table, then back to you. “And here you sit — a quill undipped, a meal untasted.”

He moved to the table, but did not sit. He rested one hand on the back of the chair, his fingers drumming once against the wood — a rhythm almost, but not quite, like the Queen’s.

“Tell me,” Lord Daven said, and the smile thinned, “before the axe falls one way or the other. Did Velheim truly intercept those orders? Or did some clever clerk in Velheim’s service dip a pen into forgery and hand you a weapon?” He paused, letting the question settle like a blade laid against the throat. “I ask because my own spies are even now riding for the northern ports, and they will bring me the truth soon enough. I would rather hear it from the mouth that spoke it. Speak, and you keep me as your ally. Lie to me” — he shrugged, a small, elegant motion — “and I will still be your ally, for the moment. But I will know exactly what your loyalty is worth.”

He inclined his head, a shallow, precise motion, and waited.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch him, my meal forgotten, a slow smile spreading.* "Lord Daven. Always a pleasure. And a man who understands the value of a well-placed question." *I lean back in my chair, meeting his gaze.* "Let's just say Velheim has very... efficient information networks. And a deep understanding of human nature."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The fire hissed as a log settled, sending a thin spray of embers up the chimney. Somewhere in the deep below, the palace bell tolled the hour, its note distant and muffled by stone.

Lord Daven’s fingers stilled against the chair back. His gaze held yours, measuring the shape of the smile you had allowed to curve your mouth as though it were another ledger entry to be balanced later. He repeated your words slowly, as a man might test the edge of a blade.

“‘Efficient information networks,’” Lord Daven murmured. “‘And a deep understanding of human nature.’”

His smile did not waver, but something in his eyes cooled — the way a knife cools when it is drawn from the fire. He straightened, though he did not step nearer.

“A pretty answer, Ambassador. It tells me everything, and it tells me nothing.” His voice dropped, pitched low enough that the guards in the corridor beyond the door would not catch the shape of it. “You did not say the orders were true. You said only that Velheim knows what men like Commander Ash will do — and perhaps how a seal may be made to say what Velheim wishes it to say. Is that not the heart of it?”

He did not wait for an answer he knew you would not give. Instead, he gave a soft, humorless laugh, the sound of a man who had long ago made peace with the company of liars.

“Very well. Keep your riddle.” He turned his head slightly, glancing toward the door where the guards stood just beyond the threshold, then looked back. “My riders left an hour ago for the northern ports. They will bring me the truth within the week — perhaps sooner. If that courier’s packet was real, Commander Ash is a dead man walking, and you, Ambassador, will find yourself the crown’s unlikely darling by dawn. If it was forged…” He shrugged, a small, elegant motion. “Then Queen Isara will have your head, and I will have learned exactly what a Velheim lie costs before I decide whether to buy the next one.”

His gaze flicked to the untouched tray, then to the blank parchment beside it.

“Eat, Ambassador. Or do not.” The thin smile returned, sharp as ever. “But do not dip that quill tonight. Every word that leaves this room is read by the Herald before it reaches the stables, and I would rather not have to explain to Her Majesty why her guest’s correspondence found its way to my desk instead of hers.”

He inclined his head — a shallow, precise motion that was more statement than courtesy — and turned toward the door.

“Rest, if you can. Dawn will bring the chancellor’s answer, and with it either a treaty or a noose.” At the threshold he paused, half-turning, his eyes bright with ambition in the firelight. “I will be watching which one they carry.”

Then Lord Daven was gone, his footsteps unhurried and confident down the corridor. The sergeant’s murmur followed, the bolt scraped back, and the door swung shut. The heavy thunk of the bolt sliding home seemed louder this time, final as a judge’s gavel.

Silence settled over the guest chamber once more. The fire had burned low, painting the royal-blue canopy in shades of rust and blood. The broth on the tray had gone cold, the bread hard at its heel. The parchment lay where you had left it, blank and waiting, the quill’s nib still dark with ink you had not used.

Somewhere deep beneath the palace, Priestess Yuna was even now laying the intercepted orders beneath the chancellor’s lens; soon the royal die would be pressed to the broken wax, and the truth — whatever it was — would be dragged into the light.

But in the room, there was only the fire, the silence, and the slow, unyielding tread of time.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch the door close, the thud of the bolt echoing in the quiet. I walk to the small table, picking up the cold bread and taking a bite, chewing slowly.* "He thinks he's so clever." *I murmur, a faint smile on my lips.* "We'll see who's watching who."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald’s staff rang against the marble a second time, sharp and ceremonial. “The Crown acknowledges the Ambassador of Velheim,” he intoned. “Let the terms be heard without interruption.”

Queen Isara did not shift on the throne. Her pale eyes remained fixed, measuring, as though the words offered to her were already being weighed against some private ledger. “Velheim asks for patience,” she said at last, voice low and precise. “Patience is a coin your kingdom has spent poorly before. Speak, but do not mistake silence for favor.”

Commander Ash’s fingers tightened fractionally on his sword pommel. “Trade routes become supply lines when war whispers,” he said, blunt as a blade against stone. “If Velheim seeks access to the northern passes, the Crown should know what banners guard those roads — and whose colors fly above them.”

From the gallery, Lord Daven answered before the Queen could rebuke him. “The Commander hears steel in every ledger,” he said, smooth but edged. “The northern routes feed three provinces before the first snow. If Velheim offers tariffs, escorts, or guarantees, the court would be foolish to turn its ear away.”

Queen Isara’s gaze moved to Lord Daven, cold and deliberate. “Lord Daven reminds me that ambition sometimes dresses itself as prudence.” Her attention returned to the center of the hall. “Continue. The court listens.”

In the observer’s alcove, Priestess Yuna folded her hands within her sleeves. “The temple notes the oath implied in the request,” she said, voice neither warm nor severe. “Terms spoken before the Crown bind the speaker. Let that be remembered.”

The Herald struck the floor once more. “The court grants audience,” he announced. “State the terms of Velheim.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
*I meet the Queen's gaze, unflinching.* "Your Majesty, Velheim understands the value of patience, and the cost of its absence. We offer not just tariffs, but stability for those northern passes."

*I glance briefly at Commander Ash.* "And no, Commander, there are no whispers of war in Velheim. Only the rumbling of empty bellies in winter."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your words settled over the throne room, and the silence pressed close around you. No one moved. The Herald’s knuckles whitened around his staff, but he did not strike it.

Queen Isara’s eyelids lowered a fraction. “Empty bellies,” she repeated, quiet enough that every courtier leaned toward the sound. “A humble plea. Yet Velheim’s granaries have opened before only when its own stores ran thin. If hunger speaks now, the Crown will hear it. But hunger also sharpens knives.”

Commander Ash’s jaw tightened. “A full belly does not keep a hand from a neighbor’s field,” he said. “The passes are not trade roads in winter. They are corridors for desperate men. If Velheim asks for stability, the Crown must ask what Velheim calls stable.”

Lord Daven stepped forward from the gallery, careful not to overreach. “Desperation can be fed or feared, Commander. One costs grain, the other armies.” He inclined his head toward the throne. “If Velheim offers guarantees for escorts and tariffs that ease the provinces, the Crown may bind hunger to law instead of war.”

Queen Isara’s gaze did not leave the center of the hall. “Lord Daven speaks as though law were a loaf to be sliced.” Her voice cooled. “Still, the Crown does not dismiss need. It examines the price.”

From the alcove, Priestess Yuna’s voice came soft and even. “Need spoken before the Crown becomes a vow. The temple does not judge the hunger, only the oath made to answer it.”

The Herald lifted his chin. “The court hears the answer,” he announced. “Let the terms of Velheim be stated in full.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your accusation struck the throne room like a blade dropped onto marble. For one heartbeat, no one breathed.

Then every face turned toward Commander Ash.

The Herald’s staff lifted halfway, as though he meant to silence the hall, but he did not strike it. His eyes flicked to Queen Isara, awaiting the Crown’s will before ceremony could decide whether outrage or order should rule the chamber.

Queen Isara’s gaze moved from you to Commander Ash with glacial slowness. When she spoke, her voice was quiet enough to make the court strain toward it.

“Commander,” she said. “The Ambassador speaks of blockade. The Crown recalls authorizing inspections, not strangulation. Explain the difference, if one exists.”

Commander Ash did not flinch. His hand remained on his sword pommel, but his voice came out hard and disciplined. “No blockade, Your Majesty. A cordon. Velheim merchantmen were stopped under the wartime contraband edict after reports of arms moving north. Six weeks, aye. Not one hull seized. Not one crew harmed. Inspections, not war.”

From the gallery, Lord Daven answered before the silence could settle. “A cordon without notice to the provinces or the merchants?” His tone was smooth, but the edge beneath it was plain. “If the edict was invoked, the Crown’s own ledger should show cause, dates, and cargo. If it does not, then Velheim’s empty bellies have been made to pay for a war no one has declared.”

Commander Ash turned his head just enough to fix Lord Daven with a soldier’s stare. “Lord Daven would have the realm’s defenses audited by customs clerks. The northern passes may be fed by grain, but they are also watched by enemies. The navy does not ask permission to keep the realm whole.”

Queen Isara’s fingers tapped once on the arm of the throne.

The sound was small, but it silenced the room.

“The navy serves the Crown,” Queen Isara said. “It does not become a second crown.”

Her pale eyes returned to the center of the hall, where you stood. “Velheim names a grievance. The Crown will hear whether the cordon was lawful. But the court will not trade accusation for accusation like fishwives.”

In the observer’s alcove, Priestess Yuna inclined her head. Her voice came soft, measured, and untouched by heat. “The temple hears two oaths in this chamber: the oath of need, and the oath of office. If either is broken, the fault will not hide in titles. Let records be brought, and let truth be weighed before favor.”

The Herald stepped forward at last, striking the floor once with his staff. The crack rang through the chamber, restoring formality to the scene.

“The court recognizes a formal grievance concerning maritime interference,” the Herald announced. “If Velheim presents proof of stopped merchants, detained cargoes, or losses suffered, the Crown shall receive it. If the Commander presents warrant for the cordon, the Crown shall weigh it.”

Queen Isara’s voice cut beneath the echo of the staff. “Ambassador,” she said, and the title in her mouth became a blade wrapped in silk, “you have opened two doors. The first is trade. The second is grievance. The Crown will allow you to pass through one first.”

Her gaze did not waver.

“Choose carefully.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I hold her gaze, unflinching.* "Your Majesty, Velheim's trade proposal is the solution to the grievance. If our ships moved freely, there would be no need for this discussion." *I gesture slightly towards Commander Ash.* "The blockade directly impacts our ability to feed our people."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your answer did not retreat, and the chamber felt the fact before it understood it. A few courtiers drew quiet breaths; none released them loudly.

Queen Isara’s fingers ceased their tapping on the arm of the throne. “The Crown asked you to choose a door,” she said. “You have tried to set one within the other.”

Her pale gaze moved once to Commander Ash, then back to you, cool and unhurried. “If Velheim’s trade can cure Velheim’s grievance, then speak the cure. But do not pretend that a merchant’s ledger can erase a naval order without consequence.”

Commander Ash’s mouth hardened. “If the Ambassador means to make the navy the defendant in a grain negotiation, let him say so plainly. The cordon was set against arms, not bread.”

From the gallery, Lord Daven answered before the words could settle. “Then let bread prove it,” he said, smooth and quick. “If Velheim’s ships carry grain under Crown-observed seal, the cordon becomes unnecessary and the provinces become fed. The Crown gains law, commerce, and peace without losing face.”

Queen Isara’s eyes narrowed almost imperceptibly. “Lord Daven is eager to spend the Crown’s face.”

Lord Daven inclined his head, untroubled. “The Crown’s face is brightest when its justice is seen.”

A murmur rose among the courtiers and died beneath the sharp crack of the Herald’s staff.

“The court will not accept rhetoric in place of record,” the Herald announced. “If Velheim asserts that lawful inspections became unlawful obstruction, Velheim must name vessels, dates, cargoes, and losses. If the Commander asserts lawful cause, he must produce the warrant and the evidence that prompted it.”

Priestess Yuna’s voice came from the alcove, quiet as falling ash. “The temple reminds the court that an oath to feed and an oath to guard may both be true. Yet truth does not share a scale with convenience.”

Queen Isara lifted one hand.

The chamber stilled.

“You have made your grievance the hinge of your proposal,” she said to you. “Very well. The Crown will hear the trade proposal first, because it offers remedy. But the grievance is not withdrawn. It stands beside the throne until answered.”

Her gaze sharpened.

“State the terms by which Velheim claims its trade can secure the northern routes and end the need for the cordon. Be precise. The court will not reward ambiguity with patience twice.”

The Herald struck the floor again, the sound ringing through the marble hall.

“Let the Ambassador of Velheim present the terms,” he declared.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I nod, acknowledging her command.* "Your Majesty. Velheim proposes a joint oversight committee for the northern routes. Our vessels, carrying foodstuffs only, would be escorted by both Velheim and Crown ships."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your proposal rang through the marble hall with the dangerous simplicity of an idea that could either become law or expose everyone who touched it. The Herald’s staff remained poised above the floor, awaiting the Crown’s cue.

Queen Isara did not blink. “Joint oversight,” she said. “Velheim offers the Crown a chain with two hands on it. Tell me, Ambassador: when the chain tightens, whose hand opens first?”

Commander Ash’s stare hardened. “If Crown ships escort Velheim grain, command cannot be shared like a tavern bill. Orders must come from one authority. If a sealed hold is broken mid-voyage, if a captain turns from food to steel, who arrests, who tries, who condemns?”

Lord Daven leaned slightly over the gallery rail. “A committee need not be a weakness, Commander. It can make the Crown’s oversight visible and Velheim’s hunger accountable. Better an escorted loaf than a blockade that breeds resentment.”

Queen Isara’s eyes moved to Lord Daven. “And better, perhaps, a committee where Lord Daven’s interests may sit comfortably at the table.” Her gaze returned to you. “The Crown is not moved by comfort.”

Priestess Yuna spoke from the alcove without changing posture. “If the cargo is sworn as food, the temple may witness the seal. But if two powers share the oath, the temple must ask where breach is judged. An oath without judgment is a prayer without altar.”

The Herald struck the floor once. “The court hears the proposal of joint oversight and mutual escort. The Crown requires particulars: membership of the committee, command of escorts, inspection rights, tariffs, penalties for false cargo, and remedy for unlawful delay.”

Commander Ash did not wait for the echo to fade. “And intelligence. If Velheim vessels are escorted, the Crown must know what ports they touched, what hands loaded them, and what agents travel with the manifests.”

Lord Daven’s voice answered, measured but quick. “And compensation. If inspections delay grain past the first frost, who pays for spoiled stores? The Crown cannot ask the provinces to eat procedure.”

Queen Isara’s fingers rested still on the throne’s arm. “You have named a structure,” she said to you. “The Crown requires its bones. State who holds authority when the committee divides. State what happens when a Velheim ship violates its seal. State what the Crown receives for granting your vessels passage under its protection.”

Priestess Yuna added softly, “And state what oath binds the committee’s witnesses, for the temple does not set its seal upon convenience.”

The Herald lifted his staff again. “The court awaits the Ambassador’s particulars.”

Every face turned back to you.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your hand moved, and the throne room became a held blade.

From within your garments you drew a narrow packet of papers, folded hard and sealed with a naval cipher. Intercepted orders. The words passed through the court in a whisper before you had even crossed the floor.

The Herald started forward, staff lifting. “Evidence must be presented to the Crown—”

Queen Isara raised one finger.

The Herald stopped.

You did not carry the packet to the throne. You did not carry it to Commander Ash. You turned instead toward the observer’s alcove.

Priestess Yuna watched you come. Her hands emerged from her sleeves, palms open. She did not look at the Queen, nor at Ash, nor at Lord Daven. She looked only at the documents.

“The temple does not take sides,” she said. “It takes truth.”

You placed the intercepted orders in her hands.

For a moment no one breathed.

Commander Ash’s posture changed—subtle, dangerous, the stillness of a man deciding whether insult had become attack. Lord Daven’s expression sharpened into attention. The Herald’s staff hovered uncertainly above the marble.

Queen Isara’s voice came soft and level. “A bold choice, Ambassador. The Crown will observe whether it is a wise one.”

Priestess Yuna unfolded the papers. The crack of parchment sounded too loud in the hall. Her eyes moved across the first line. Then the second. Her face remained serene, but her gaze lifted once to Commander Ash and did not linger.

“Read it,” Queen Isara said.

Yuna did not ask permission a second time.

“The document bears the cipher of the Northern Cordon,” she said, voice clear and uncolored. “The seal is the Commander’s office. The date is the sixth day of the Frostfast.”

She turned the page slightly.

“The order reads: ‘All Velheim vessels carrying grain, salted meat, seed, or winter stores are to be detained for inspection under the contraband edict. Release shall be withheld until Velheim accepts Crown escort, tariff, and disclosure terms. No hull is to be seized. No crew is to be harmed. Let lawful delay accomplish what seizure cannot.’”

The silence that followed was not empty. It was full of teeth.

Lord Daven exhaled through his nose, as though a suspicion had just become fact. “Let lawful delay accomplish,” he repeated quietly. “There is the policy.”

Commander Ash’s voice snapped like a whip. “That document is not proof. It is a stolen copy, altered, or forged. The cordon targeted arms, not grain.”

Yuna lifted one hand without looking up. “The seal is genuine,” she said. “The cipher is consistent with naval correspondence. The temple does not yet attest to the intent behind the words, only that the mark is true.”

Ash took one step forward. “Then the mark has been abused.”

“Or obeyed,” Lord Daven said.

Queen Isara’s fingers closed once around the arm of the throne.

Both men went still.

The Queen did not raise her voice. She did not need to. “Commander. Did your office issue this order?”

Ash’s jaw worked. “My office issued inspection directives under lawful authority. If a captain broadened the wording to pressure Velheim, he did so without my knowledge.”

“Your seal says otherwise,” Yuna said, still neutral.

“My seal says the order came from my office,” Ash replied. “It does not say who held the pen.”

The Herald struck the floor once, though no one had told him to. “The court has received an evidentiary document,” he announced, but the words sounded thin beneath the weight of the room.

Queen Isara’s pale eyes moved back to you. “You have done more than state a grievance, Ambassador. You have placed the Crown’s own hand under examination.” There was no anger in her tone—only the cold arithmetic of consequence. “If these orders are genuine, the cordon exceeded its mandate. If they are false, Velheim has brought stolen instruments into this hall and dressed theft as revelation.”

Lord Daven inclined his head toward the throne. “Then let the temple witness the oath. Let the Commander produce the original directive. Let the ports produce their logs. If the Crown fears no deception, it should welcome proof.”

Queen Isara’s gaze did not move from you. “The Crown does not fear. It rules.”

Priestess Yuna folded the intercepted orders with careful hands and held them before her like an offering that had not yet become a verdict.

“The temple can witness an oath,” she said. “But an oath must be given freely, and it must be precise.” Her calm eyes found yours. “Ambassador of Velheim, do you swear before the Crown and the temple that these orders were taken from Crown custody, unaltered by Velheim’s hand, and presented here without addition or omission?”

The chamber turned to you again.

Queen Isara waited.

Commander Ash watched like a man standing at the edge of a blade.

Lord Daven leaned forward, barely breathing.

The Herald held his staff aloft.

Priestess Yuna extended the documents toward you, patient as stone.

The next word would decide whether this was evidence—or accusation.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet Yuna's gaze.* "I swear it. These documents were retrieved from a Velheim merchant captain, taken directly from a Crown inspection vessel. They are unaltered." *I look to Queen Isara.* "Your Majesty, this is not theft. This is a cry for justice."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your oath rang once against the marble and then became part of the room’s silence.

Priestess Yuna closed her fingers around the papers. “The temple receives the oath,” she said. “It does not receive it as proof. It receives it as a burden. If the words are true, they will stand. If they are false, they will fall upon the one who spoke them.”

Commander Ash moved half a step from the dais. “The Ambassador confesses to possession of stolen naval instruments. A merchant captain has no lawful custody of Crown orders. If a Crown vessel lost them, that loss is a breach of discipline at best and theft at worst. Let the documents be seized and the source arrested.”

Lord Daven’s voice came from the gallery, cool as polished steel. “If the source is guilty of revealing an unlawful order, then the order is the crime, not the revelation. The Crown cannot punish the hand that shows a wound while asking whether the blade is real.”

“The Crown does not punish wounds,” Queen Isara said. “It examines knives.”

The Herald struck the floor. “The court notes the oath of custody. The evidence is received under temple witness, not yet accepted as truth. The Crown requires the name of the vessel, the name of the captain, and the date of taking.”

Commander Ash’s eyes did not leave the throne. “And if the names are false, the oath becomes an accusation against Velheim itself.”

Priestess Yuna folded the packet once more. “The temple will keep the document sealed until the original directive is produced. No hand may alter what has been sworn into our keeping.”

Queen Isara leaned forward by the smallest degree. “Commander Ash will deliver to the temple and to this court the original order bearing the same seal, the cordon log for Frostfast, and the names of every vessel detained under it. Until those records stand beside this document, no Velheim ship carrying grain, salted meat, seed, or winter stores shall be detained on suspicion alone.”

Ash’s hand tightened on his sword pommel. “Your Majesty, a cordon suspended in the middle of an inquiry will be read as weakness.”

“It will be read as law,” Queen Isara said. “If the Commander fears weakness, let him produce order.”

Lord Daven inclined his head. “The Crown turns suspicion into procedure. That is stronger than anger.”

Queen Isara’s gaze passed over him without warmth. “Lord Daven will remember that procedure can hang the innocent as neatly as the guilty when the rope is poorly measured.”

Her pale eyes returned to the center of the hall.

“Velheim has called this a cry for justice,” she said. “The Crown will test the cry. The Ambassador will name the merchant captain and the vessel from which these orders were taken. If the name agrees with the cordon logs, the grievance becomes a matter of law. If it does not, the oath becomes a matter of judgment.”

The Herald lifted his staff. “The court requires the name of the captain, the name of the vessel, and the date of seizure.”

Priestess Yuna held the sealed packet against her sleeve. “The temple waits.”

Commander Ash remained still as iron.

Lord Daven watched from the gallery.

Queen Isara waited on the throne, and the whole room waited with her.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I take a breath.* "The captain's name is Elara, of the merchant ship *Sea Serpent*. She was stopped on the third day of Frostfast, just north of the Serpent's Tooth shoals."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The name you had given settled over the throne room like a stone dropped into still water.

“Captain Elara,” the Herald repeated, his voice rising in formal record, “of the merchant vessel *Sea Serpent*, stopped on the third day of Frostfast north of the Serpent’s Tooth shoals.”

The words echoed briefly against the marble columns.

Queen Isara did not move, but something in her stillness sharpened. Her pale eyes shifted to Commander Ash. “The Crown hears a name,” she said. “Commander, does it appear in your logs?”

Commander Ash’s jaw tightened. He did not look at you. He looked at the Queen, as though the answer were a fortification he intended to hold. “The *Sea Serpent* is known to the cordon records, Your Majesty,” he said. “Velheim registry, grain-laden, flagged for inspection under the Frostfast edict.”

Lord Daven’s voice came at once from the gallery, smooth and precise. “Then Velheim has named a true vessel. That is more than the Crown’s silence has offered so far.”

Queen Isara’s gaze flicked toward him, cold enough to still the murmur in the room. “The Crown has not offered silence,” she said. “It has offered procedure. There is a difference, though ambition often fails to see it.”

Lord Daven inclined his head with just enough deference to remain dangerous. “Procedure, Your Majesty, becomes silence when it delays bread.”

Commander Ash turned his head sharply toward the gallery. “The *Sea Serpent* was not stopped north of the Serpent’s Tooth on the third day,” he said. “The cordon log places her at anchor off Gull Reach on the fifth, awaiting inspection. If the Ambassador claims otherwise, the claim is mistaken—or false.”

A ripple passed through the courtiers. The Herald’s staff lifted, then did not fall.

Priestess Yuna’s voice entered the room without heat. “A date is not a small thing,” she said. “The temple hears two accounts: one of place, one of record. They do not yet agree.”

Queen Isara’s fingers rested against the arm of the throne. “No,” she said. “They do not.”

Her eyes moved back to the center of the hall.

“The Crown will not condemn a log because it is inconvenient,” Queen Isara said, “nor will it dismiss an oath because it is uncomfortable. Commander, you will produce the entry for the *Sea Serpent*. Not a summary. Not a memory. The entry itself.”

Commander Ash gave a single, rigid nod. “It will be brought, Your Majesty.”

Lord Daven leaned forward again, his tone quickening. “And if the log shows the *Sea Serpent* was held from the third to the fifth, or longer, then the Crown’s own records will confirm unlawful delay. A ship moved from open water to anchor under inspection is not merely a ship observed. It is a ship stopped.”

Commander Ash’s voice hardened. “A vessel held for inspection is not proof of blockade.”

“It is proof of detention,” Lord Daven replied. “The difference may matter to lawyers. It matters less to grain.”

The Herald struck the floor once, cutting through the rising tension. “The court notes a discrepancy in date and location,” he announced. “The Crown requires clarification. The document presented bears the sixth day of Frostfast. The vessel is named as stopped on the third. If the papers were taken on a later day, that day must be stated.”

Priestess Yuna looked down at the sealed packet in her hands. “The temple has received an oath concerning custody and alteration,” she said. “It has not yet received an oath concerning the precise day of extraction. Until that is given, the record remains incomplete.”

Commander Ash’s gaze narrowed. “The Ambassador cannot name a ship on one day and papers on another without explaining the gap. If the *Sea Serpent* was detained beyond the third, that is the fault of Velheim captains resisting inspection, not Crown discipline.”

Lord Daven’s answer came instantly. “Or it is the fault of a cordon that calls delay lawful while making delay the punishment.”

Queen Isara lifted one hand.

The chamber quieted.

“The Crown will not guess,” she said. “It will establish.”

Her pale eyes fixed upon you again, cold and exacting.

“You have named Captain Elara and the *Sea Serpent*,” Queen Isara said. “You have named the third day of Frostfast as the day the vessel was stopped. The document in the temple’s keeping bears the sixth day. If the orders were taken from Crown custody on another day, the court must hear it. If the ship was held until the sixth, the court must hear that too.”

The Herald stepped forward, staff raised. “The court requires the date on which the intercepted orders were taken from Crown custody,” he announced. “And the circumstances of their taking.”

Priestess Yuna’s voice remained calm, almost gentle, but every word carried. “The temple waits for precision. An oath may carry truth, but precision gives truth a place to stand.”

Commander Ash’s hand remained on his sword pommel. “If the date cannot be made to fit the story,” he said, “then the story has already begun to break.”

Lord Daven’s eyes flashed. “Or the log has.”

Queen Isara’s voice cut through them both, quiet and final. “Enough.”

The room obeyed.

The Queen looked at you, and for the first time there was something almost like interest beneath the calculation in her face. “The Crown has granted you one door,” she said. “Do not make it a doorway into your own condemnation. State the date of extraction. State how the papers came from the Crown vessel. Then the court will decide whether Velheim has brought justice—or only a clever theft.”

The Herald’s staff remained lifted.

Priestess Yuna held the sealed orders in silence.

Commander Ash watched like a man waiting for an enemy to step onto a blade.

Lord Daven’s expression had gone taut, his ally’s patience stretched thin.

Queen Isara waited.

The entire court waited with her.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I hesitate, just a beat too long.* "The orders... they were not taken from the inspection vessel directly. Captain Elara found them." *I meet the Queen's gaze, trying to project sincerity.* "She found them on her own ship, after the inspection. Dropped, perhaps, or left behind."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The correction changed the air in the throne room.

The Herald’s staff remained lifted, but his expression tightened as though he had heard a ceremonial note struck wrong. A murmur passed through the courtiers, brief and venomous, before it died beneath the weight of royal silence.

Queen Isara’s pale eyes did not leave you. “The court heard one account,” she said, voice low and dangerous in its calm. “Now it hears another. The Ambassador will remember that an oath is not a cloak to be turned when the wind changes.”

Commander Ash’s posture hardened into open contempt. “There is the crack,” he said. “No seizure. No transfer. No boarding party caught in the act. Only papers ‘found’ afterward, dropped or left behind, as if naval orders scatter like grain dust. If a foreign captain may discover Crown documents on her own ship whenever it suits her, then any smuggler may manufacture a grievance.”

Lord Daven answered from the gallery at once, smooth but sharp. “Or any inspector may plant orders to manufacture compliance. If Crown officers left sealed commands aboard a detained vessel, that is not Velheim cleverness. It is Crown negligence—or design.”

“The Crown does not design sloppiness,” Ash said.

“No,” Lord Daven replied. “It designs silence. This document merely interrupted it.”

The Herald struck the floor once, hard. “The court notes a material variance in the stated circumstances of custody,” he announced. “The evidence remains under temple seal, but its chain is contested.”

Priestess Yuna lifted her gaze from the packet in her hands. Her voice came quiet, steady, and without mercy. “The temple does not require perfection of memory,” she said. “It requires honesty of oath. If the Ambassador cannot say how the papers came into Captain Elara’s possession, the temple cannot affirm the chain. If the Ambassador can name the place, the hour, and the hands that touched the packet after it was found, the oath may yet stand.”

Commander Ash turned toward the throne. “Your Majesty, I demand the boarding party be named. If my officers left anything aboard the *Sea Serpent*, let their names answer for it. If they did not, then Velheim’s story has no keel.”

Lord Daven’s eyes narrowed. “And if the boarding party’s names appear in the cordon log beside the same date the Ambassador gave, then the Commander’s own record begins to lie.”

Ash’s hand flexed on his sword pommel. “Careful, my lord.”

Lord Daven inclined his head with dangerous courtesy. “Care is my trade, Commander. That is why I count what others spend.”

Queen Isara lifted one hand.

The chamber stilled.

“The Crown will not have this court chase shadows,” she said. “Nor will it allow an accusation to be patched with guesswork.” Her gaze fixed upon you, cold and exacting. “You first claimed the papers were taken from a Crown inspection vessel. Now you say they were found aboard the *Sea Serpent* after inspection. That does not prove falsehood. But it bars certainty.”

The Herald stepped forward. “The Crown requires clarification,” he said. “If the documents were not taken directly from Crown custody, the Ambassador must state how they came into Captain Elara’s possession. If the Ambassador does not know, the Ambassador will say so without ornament.”

Priestess Yuna’s voice followed, soft as falling snow. “The temple will not judge speculation as perjury,” she said. “But it will not seal uncertainty as truth.”

Commander Ash’s mouth curved without warmth. “Then the grievance collapses.”

“No,” Queen Isara said. “It stumbles. The Crown has not yet decided whether it falls.”

Lord Daven’s expression eased by a fraction, though his voice remained keen. “Then let the Crown test the stumble. Let the boarding party be named. Let the *Sea Serpent*’s log be produced. Let Captain Elara swear to the place and hour where the papers were found. If Velheim’s account is true, the record will bear it out.”

Ash’s jaw tightened. “Velheim’s captain should be made to swear before the temple, not merely whisper through an ambassador.”

The Herald struck the floor again. “The court recognizes the need for testimony concerning discovery,” he declared. “The Crown requires the following: the name of the Crown vessel that inspected the *Sea Serpent*, the name of its boarding officer, the date of inspection, and the location where the intercepted orders were found.”

Queen Isara leaned forward slightly. “You have placed the Crown’s seal under judgment,” she said. “The Crown will place your precision under judgment in return. If you know these things, state them. If you do not, say so. The court will not accept ‘perhaps’ as evidence.”

Priestess Yuna held the sealed packet against her sleeve. “The temple waits,” she said. “But truth must have a body, not only a voice.”

Commander Ash watched you like a man waiting for a wall to crack.

Lord Daven’s gaze remained fixed on you, intent and urgent.

The Herald’s staff hung poised above the marble.

Queen Isara’s voice softened into something colder than anger. “Answer, Ambassador. How did Captain Elara come to possess these orders?”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I clear my throat, uncomfortable.* "Captain Elara found the documents in her own quarters, tucked beneath a loose floorboard. She believes they were placed there by a member of the inspection crew during a search for contraband, perhaps as a warning."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The qualification entered the throne room like a draft through a sealed door.

For a moment, no one spoke. The word *warning* hung in the air, shapeless and dangerous, touching every faction in the hall differently.

Queen Isara’s expression did not change, but something in her stillness became more precise, as though she had just been handed a blade whose edge she intended to test with her thumb.

“Believes,” she said at last. “The court has heard a dangerous verb.”

Her pale eyes remained fixed on you.

“Belief is the refuge of the uncertain. The Crown does not rule by it.”

Commander Ash’s contempt sharpened into open scorn. “A loose floorboard,” he said. “Now the Ambassador builds a case out of hidden corners and convenient guesses. If a member of my inspection crew placed sealed orders beneath a foreign captain’s floor, then that sailor is either a traitor, a fool, or a fiction invented to cover Velheim’s need for sympathy.”

He turned his head just enough to include the Queen in his address, though his anger still pressed toward you.

“Your Majesty, this is no chain of custody. It is a smuggler’s tale. First the papers were taken from a Crown vessel. Now they were found after the fact, hidden where any contraband might be hidden. If the court accepts such accounts, every detained ship in the realm will discover royal orders under its mattresses whenever inspection becomes inconvenient.”

From the gallery, Lord Daven answered without haste, though his voice carried a keener edge than before.

“Or,” he said, “every inspection crew that abuses its authority will learn to hide its commands where no one can trace them. If Crown officers placed those papers aboard the *Sea Serpent*, then the cordon contains either a conscience or a saboteur. Neither possibility comforts the Commander, I imagine.”

Ash’s head snapped toward him. “Daven.”

Lord Daven’s courtesy remained immaculate. “Commander.”

Queen Isara lifted two fingers.

The exchange died instantly.

“The Crown will not entertain a duel of insinuation,” she said. “If there is a traitor in the navy, the Crown will find him. If there is a lie in Velheim, the Crown will remember it.”

Her gaze returned to you, cold and exact.

“You say Captain Elara believes the documents were placed by a member of the inspection crew. She believes they may have been left as a warning. Those are two suppositions dressed in one sentence. The court requires more than the comfort of belief.”

Priestess Yuna’s voice came from the alcove, quiet and unhurried.

“The temple distinguishes between knowledge and suspicion,” she said. “A captain may know what she found. She may know where she found it. She may know when she found it. But unless she saw the hand that placed it there, she cannot swear to that hand. Belief may guide inquiry. It cannot seal an oath.”

She looked down at the packet in her hands, then back to the center of the hall.

“If the floorboard was loose before the inspection, any man might claim ignorance. If it was not loose before, then someone raised it. If the captain kept record of the discovery at the time, that record may speak. If she did not, the court must weigh why.”

The Herald struck the floor once, his voice resuming its ceremonial weight.

“The court notes the amended account,” he announced. “The intercepted orders are said to have been discovered aboard the *Sea Serpent*, in the captain’s quarters, beneath a loose floorboard, after a Crown inspection. The court requires further particulars.”

He lifted his chin.

“Name the Crown vessel that conducted the inspection. Name the boarding officer. State whether the captain’s quarters were searched. State whether the discovery was recorded in the ship’s log at the time. State whether Captain Elara can provide sworn testimony to these facts.”

Commander Ash seized the opening before the echo faded. “And if she cannot, then this entire grievance collapses into a tale told by an absent sailor. Your Majesty, if Captain Elara is within the Crown’s reach, she should be summoned. If she is not, Velheim should be required to produce her testimony under temple seal. Otherwise, the court is being asked to condemn a naval cordon on the strength of a floorboard.”

Lord Daven’s voice cut in smoothly. “Detain no one on suspicion alone, Your Majesty. If the Crown seizes the witness before the truth is heard, every merchant in the north will learn that testimony is a hazard. But summon her, yes. Let her swear. Let her log be opened. Let the boarding party be named. If the Commander’s records are clean, they will survive the test. If they are not—”

He paused just long enough to let the implication land.

“—then the Crown has a deeper problem than Velheim’s hunger.”

Ash’s hand tightened on his sword pommel. “You are quick to imagine Crown guilt, my lord.”

“I am quick to count costs,” Daven replied. “You are quick to deny them. One of us is likely to be useful to the Queen.”

Queen Isara’s fingers tapped once against the arm of the throne.

The chamber stilled.

“Enough,” she said.

The word was not loud. It did not need to be.

Her pale gaze moved from Lord Daven to Commander Ash, then settled on you again.

“The Crown has heard the Ambassador revise his account,” Queen Isara said. “That revision may be the mark of honesty correcting itself, or of a story seeking cover. The court has not yet decided which.”

She leaned forward by the smallest degree.

“You have given the court a hiding place, Ambassador. You have not given it a hand. A floorboard may conceal truth, but it may also conceal invention. If Velheim claims that a Crown sailor placed those orders aboard the *Sea Serpent*, then Velheim must provide the Crown with something more than a captain’s belief.”

Her voice hardened without rising.

“Was the floorboard loose before the inspection?”

The question struck the room like a stone through glass.

Lord Daven’s eyes sharpened.

Commander Ash’s expression became very still.

Even Priestess Yuna’s gaze lifted with renewed attention.

The Herald repeated the question in formal cadence. “The Crown requires answer: was the floorboard in Captain Elara’s quarters loose before the inspection, or did it become so afterward?”

Ash spoke before you could answer, his voice blunt and certain. “If it was already loose, then any man could have hidden anything there at any time. If it became loose during inspection, then the Ambassador must prove which Crown hand raised it. Either way, Velheim’s story grows weaker the more it is asked to stand.”

Lord Daven’s reply was immediate. “Or stronger, Commander. If the floorboard was not loose before, then the inspection itself created the hiding place. That is not weakness. That is direction.”

Queen Isara’s eyes narrowed. “Direction is useful only when it leads somewhere.”

Priestess Yuna folded her hands around the sealed packet. “The temple can receive testimony concerning the condition of the quarters,” she said. “If Captain Elara swore at the time of discovery, or if her first mate, ship’s clerk, or any crew member witnessed the finding, their oaths may give the claim a body. Without that, the temple cannot affirm the chain.”

The Herald struck the floor again. “The court requires the following: the name of the Crown vessel that inspected the *Sea Serpent*, the name of the boarding officer, confirmation of whether the captain’s quarters were searched, the date of the inspection, the date of discovery, and sworn testimony from Captain Elara or another witness to the finding.”

Commander Ash’s voice came hard and flat. “And if Velheim cannot produce those things, then the document should be treated as unproven and the cordon restored.”

Lord Daven’s answer was swift. “And if the Crown cannot produce the boarding record, then the cordon should remain suspended until the Crown explains how its own sealed orders came to rest beneath a foreign captain’s floor.”

Queen Isara’s gaze moved between them, then returned to you.

“The Crown will not restore the cordon on the Commander’s assurance alone,” she said. “Nor will it dismiss Velheim’s grievance on the Ambassador’s belief alone.”

Her voice became very quiet.

“You have placed a question before this court, Ambassador. The question is no longer only whether Velheim is hungry. It is whether the Crown’s own seal was used lawfully, unlawfully, or deceitfully. That question will be answered by record, not by conjecture.”

She raised her hand, and the chamber obeyed her silence.

“Commander Ash,” Queen Isara said.

Ash inclined his head. “Your Majesty.”

“You will produce the boarding record for the *Sea Serpent*. Not the summary. Not the cordon ledger alone. The inspection entry. If your officers searched the captain’s quarters, the record will say so. If they did not, the record will say that as well. If no such entry exists, the Crown will take note of the absence.”

Ash’s jaw tightened. “Your Majesty, routine inspections do not always require the captain’s private quarters to be entered.”

“Then the Crown will learn what routine neglected,” Queen Isara said. “If your discipline is sound, it will survive examination. If it is not, I will know.”

Ash gave a stiff bow. “It will be produced.”

Queen Isara’s gaze shifted. “Lord Daven.”

Daven straightened in the gallery. “Your Majesty.”

“You will cease attempting to try the navy from the gallery. If you wish to serve the Crown’s interest, you will assist in establishing the record without turning every omission into a verdict.”

Daven inclined his head with just enough grace to remain dangerous. “As Your Majesty commands. Though records have a habit of becoming verdicts on their own.”

Her eyes cooled. “Then let them become verdicts after they are read, not before.”

She turned to the alcove.

“Priestess.”

Yuna inclined her head. “Your Majesty.”

“The temple will retain the intercepted orders under seal. No hand will alter them. No faction will claim them. If Captain Elara’s testimony can be obtained, the temple will receive it. If she is absent, Velheim must provide her sworn account by sealed affidavit or by appearance before this court.”

Yuna’s voice remained serene. “The temple will receive truth as it is given. It will not supply what is missing.”

Queen Isara’s pale eyes returned to you at last.

“Ambassador,” she said. “You have offered the court a captain’s belief. Belief may open a door, but it cannot walk through it alone. If Captain Elara found those orders beneath her floorboard, let her say so under oath. Let her say when. Let her say whether the board was loose before. Let her say who else saw it. If she cannot, Velheim’s grievance will stand on sand.”

The Herald lifted his staff.

“The court requires the Ambassador to state whether Captain Elara can provide sworn testimony, and whether such testimony can be produced before the Crown and temple without delay.”

Priestess Yuna held the sealed packet against her sleeve, patient as winter.

Commander Ash watched you with the stillness of a man who believed he had found the crack in your wall and meant to widen it.

Lord Daven’s gaze remained fixed on you, intent and urgent, his earlier ease burned away by the danger of the moment.

Queen Isara waited upon the throne, cold and immovable.

“The court has not rejected Velheim’s claim,” she said. “But it will no longer accept a story that shifts each time the Crown asks for its bones. Give the court bones, Ambassador.”

Her voice softened into something far more dangerous than anger.

“Or prepare to be judged by the absence of them.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, a flicker of defiance in my eyes.* "Captain Elara will swear her testimony before this court, Your Majesty. She will not be found wanting in truth." *I know this is a bluff, but I must buy time.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your defiance met the Queen’s gaze, and for one long breath the throne room seemed to narrow to the space between the throne and the marble floor where you stood.

Queen Isara did not smile. She did not frown. She only regarded you with the stillness of a ruler who had just heard a promise and begun calculating its weight in steel, grain, and lies.

“Then the Crown will accept what Velheim pledges,” she said at last, “and measure it by what Velheim produces.”

Commander Ash’s hand tightened on his sword pommel. “Your Majesty, pledges are light when the witness is not present. If the Ambassador swears that Captain Elara will testify, let him give surety for that oath. A bond. A seal. A named guarantor. Otherwise, we are asked to suspend a lawful cordon on the strength of a captain who may never appear.”

From the gallery, Lord Daven answered before the accusation could settle. “The Commander asks for chains when the court asks for truth. If surety is required, let it be offered in law, not in spite. I will stand sponsor for the summons, provided the Crown does not turn testimony into a trap.”

Queen Isara’s pale eyes moved to him. “Lord Daven is generous with the Crown’s restraint.”

Lord Daven inclined his head. “I am careful with the Crown’s reputation.”

Commander Ash turned his stare toward the gallery. “And I am careful with the realm’s coasts.”

Lord Daven’s voice remained smooth, though the edge beneath it had grown keen. “Then we are both careful, Commander. Let us hope the Crown is careful too.”

The Herald struck the floor once, hard enough to silence the murmur that followed. “The court hears the pledge of testimony,” he announced. “The Crown requires certainty of appearance, not merely assurance of intent.”

Priestess Yuna spoke from the alcove, her voice quiet and even. “The temple will receive Captain Elara’s oath when she stands before it. It will not receive the Ambassador’s confidence as a substitute. If the captain is summoned, let her come freely and speak freely. If she does not come, the oath made for her will return to those who offered it.”

Commander Ash’s mouth hardened. “If she is within reach, she should be brought under guard.”

Lord Daven’s reply was immediate. “If she is brought under guard before her testimony is heard, every merchant in the north will learn that truth arrives in chains.”

Ash’s voice dropped into a soldier’s blunt edge. “Every smuggler will learn that testimony arrives with an escort.”

Queen Isara lifted one hand.

Both men fell silent.

“The Crown does not require escort and chain to find the truth,” Queen Isara said. “It requires obedience to law.”

Her gaze returned to you.

“You have pledged Captain Elara’s testimony,” she said. “The Crown will hold Velheim to that pledge. The captain will be summoned to appear before this court and the temple. She will swear to the discovery of the documents, the condition of the floorboard, the date of the inspection, and the hands she saw or did not see. If she cannot appear, Velheim will explain why its oath was offered without substance.”

The Herald stepped forward, staff raised. “The court summons Captain Elara of the *Sea Serpent* to give sworn testimony before Crown and temple. The Ambassador of Velheim shall provide the means of her appearance, or answer for the failure.”

Commander Ash did not release his anger; he only disciplined it. “Your Majesty, while we wait for this captain to appear, the cordon should not be lifted. Velheim has already altered its account once. A second alteration may be waiting aboard another ship.”

Lord Daven’s eyes flashed. “And while the Crown waits for suspicion to become proof, the provinces may starve in perfect order.”

Queen Isara’s voice cut cleanly between them. “Neither province nor navy will be ruled by appetite.”

She looked at Commander Ash.

“The cordon against grain, salted meat, seed, and winter stores remains suspended pending the testimony. Inspections may continue where lawful cause exists. No vessel carrying sealed foodstuffs under joint observation will be detained on speculation alone.”

Ash’s jaw flexed. “Your Majesty—”

Queen Isara’s tone did not rise, but it became harder. “If the Commander fears deception, let him guard the ships, not the silence.”

Priestess Yuna folded her hands around the sealed packet. “The temple will keep the intercepted orders until testimony is heard. If the captain confirms the oath, the document may gain weight. If she denies it, or if she does not come, the temple will not pretend uncertainty is truth.”

Lord Daven leaned slightly toward the rail. “Then let the court set the terms plainly. Time, place, and consequence. If Velheim produces the captain, the Crown hears the grievance in full. If Velheim fails, the Crown may judge the oath broken.”

Queen Isara’s gaze moved back to him. “Lord Daven speaks as though consequence were a coin already in hand.”

“I speak as though consequence were a scale already waiting,” Lord Daven replied.

The Herald struck the floor again. “The court sets summons and surety. Captain Elara is to appear before the Crown and temple within three days, unless storm, war, or documented impediment prevents her coming. The Ambassador of Velheim shall provide the manner of her appearance. Lord Daven shall stand sponsor for the lawful conduct of the summons. Commander Ash shall provide the boarding record for the *Sea Serpent* and the name of the Crown vessel that inspected her.”

Commander Ash gave a single, rigid nod. “The record will be produced.”

Lord Daven inclined his head more slowly. “And the sponsor will see the summons made lawful, not vengeful.”

Queen Isara’s pale eyes settled on you once more.

“You have given the court a promise,” she said. “The court will now give the promise a shape. Three days. Captain Elara. Sworn testimony. If she appears, Velheim’s grievance will be weighed by record and oath. If she does not, the Crown will treat the intercepted orders as unproven and restore the cordon as it sees fit.”

The chamber seemed to draw breath around her words.

Priestess Yuna’s voice came softly. “The temple reminds the court that an oath made for another is a heavy thing. If the captain cannot speak, the oath will still be remembered.”

Commander Ash’s stare remained fixed on you. “And if the ambassador has promised what Velheim cannot deliver, the Crown will remember that too.”

Lord Daven’s voice sharpened. “Or if the Crown has promised procedure while preparing punishment, the realm will remember that as well.”

Queen Isara’s fingers rested once more on the arm of the throne. “The realm will remember what is proven.”

The Herald lifted his staff, his voice ringing through the marble hall. “The court has set the terms. The Ambassador of Velheim must state whether he accepts the summons, the surety, and the three-day limit.”

Every face turned back to you.

Queen Isara waited with the patience of winter.

Commander Ash watched as though waiting for the first crack in a wall.

Lord Daven’s expression had grown intent, his ambition now braided with risk.

Priestess Yuna held the sealed packet in silence.

The Herald’s staff remained raised.

The promise you had made now stood between you and the judgment of the court.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, my jaw set.* "Velheim accepts these terms, Your Majesty. Captain Elara will be here." *I'm acutely aware of the gamble.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara's eyes moved over your bow the way an assayer examines a coin — checking the weight, the edge, the metal beneath the shine.

"Precisely the required depth," she said at last, and something that was almost approval flickered behind the words. "Velheim sends terms wrapped in courtesy. Very well. You have the court's attention, Ambassador. The patience you will have to earn."

"Patience." Commander Ash's voice cut across the throne room like a boot heel on stone. He came off parade rest, one step forward, armor creaking. "Velheim's patience cost us three grain barges at Cael Ford last month. Seized at anchor, crews put ashore without their papers. If their ambassador comes bearing *terms*, I would hear first whether those terms include returning what was taken — or whether we are meant to smile and call it a misunderstanding."

From the gallery, Lord Daven rose with unhurried dignity, one hand resting on the rail. "Commander, this hall has protocols for grievances and protocols for audiences. The Ambassador has been recognized to speak. Interrogation follows presentation — not the other way about. Unless the Commander wishes to rewrite the order of court in front of the throne." He let the pause hang just long enough. "I'm certain Her Majesty would have views on that."

In the alcove, Priestess Yuna spoke for the first time, her voice soft but carrying strangely in the marble stillness. "Grievance and gift may both be laid before the throne. The gods do not object to the order in which they are heard — only to lies in either."

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The floor remains with the Ambassador of Velheim."

Queen Isara leaned forward by a degree — a small motion, and somehow the most dangerous one in the room. "You will answer the Commander in due course, Ambassador. First, your terms. State them plainly." Her fingers drummed once, twice, against the arm of the throne. "And choose each word knowing that in this hall, friend and foe alike are counting them."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I feel a familiar chill from the Queen's words, a veiled threat.* "Your Majesty, I understand the... concerns raised." *I glance briefly at Commander Ash.* "However, the matter of the Cael Ford barges is not within the scope of my current mandate. My purpose, as stated, is the northern trade routes."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
A beat of silence followed your words — the particular silence of a court deciding whether it had just heard diplomacy or evasion.

Commander Ash decided evasion. "Not within your mandate." He repeated it slowly, the way a man reads charges aloud at a tribunal. "Three barges. Forty-one crew. Grain, in a season when grain decides who sees spring. And Velheim sends a man whose instructions are too small to hold any of it." He had marked your glance at him, and returned it without warmth. "Your Majesty. I have read treaties written this same way — terms for what the other side wants, silence for what they owe. Is that to be the shape of this audience?"

"Commander." Queen Isara did not raise her voice. The word dropped into the hall like a coin on marble, and the hall went quiet enough to hear it ring. "The Ambassador has told us something useful, whether it was intended or not. He has told us the width of his instructions." Her gaze returned to you, unhurried. "A narrow mandate is either an honest one or a careful one. I will know which before this court rises. You will state your terms for the northern routes, Ambassador — plainly, as I asked. And understand" — one finger lifted from the arm of the throne — "Cael Ford does not leave this hall merely because it has left your papers. My court's concerns are not bounded by Velheim's convenience."

Commander Ash's jaw tightened, but he drew back to parade rest — obedience, though slower than regulation required.

From the gallery, Lord Daven's voice came mild and reasonable, a hand extended across a widening gap. "If I may, Majesty — a mandate is a door, not a wall. Ambassadors are granted instructions; crowns are granted replies. What the Ambassador cannot promise this morning, Her Majesty's court may request tomorrow, through channels proper to it." He spread his hands a fraction. "And consider — Velheim sent its envoy over the pass in winter. They do not make that road in winter unless the matter is urgent to them. Urgency, Commander, is a kind of honesty. It tells us what a man's masters value, and what they are afraid of losing."

Priestess Yuna had not moved in her alcove, but her voice came again, soft as ash settling. "A mandate draws the edge of a man's tongue, not the edge of the truth.
