What he may answer and what the throne may ask are different measures." Her dark eyes found you, calm and unblinking. "The gods weigh both."

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "Her Majesty has called for terms. The court waits."

Queen Isara settled back by the same single degree she had leaned forward. The almost-approval was gone from her voice now, replaced by something colder and infinitely more patient. "You heard the man. Terms, Ambassador. And know that my question about Cael Ford has not expired with your preamble." A pause, precisely measured. "Mandates may be narrow, Ambassador. Thrones are not."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The words left your mouth, and for one heartbeat the throne room held perfectly still — the stillness of a hall recalculating everything it had assumed about the man from Velheim.

Then came the sound: a rustle through the gallery like wind through dry grain. A guardsman's spear-butt tapped marble once and went silent. Lord Daven's hand left the rail; for half a breath his eyes closed — the briefest prayer to whatever god manages diplomats — before his face reassembled itself into mild parliamentary interest.

Commander Ash turned to face you fully for the first time. He did not draw his sword. He smiled, which was worse.

"Explain it." He rolled the words like a stone in a sling. "Gladly."

The Herald's staff cracked the floor. "A charge has been laid against the Commander of the Fleet. The court recognizes Commander Ash to answer."

"You call it a blockade, Ambassador. I call it an inspection cordon, established under Her Majesty's writ six weeks ago — the day after Velheim's barges put forty-one of my people ashore at Cael Ford without their papers." He began to count on gauntleted fingers. "Since then, every hull flying your colors has been boarded. Last month alone: forty casks of war-powder sewn into salt-fish bales. Three hundred crossbow heads consigned as *agricultural iron*. And a strongbox of Velheim's silver addressed to a name in the border provinces Her Majesty's spymaster already knows." His smile sharpened to an edge. "So yes, I will explain it to the court. Then, if you wish, we proceed to the manifests — hull by hull, aloud, before everyone. Shall I begin with the *Merrow's Daughter*?"

From the alcove came that soft, ash-settling voice. "This morning one grievance lay upon the scales. Now there are two." Priestess Yuna's eyes moved from Ash to you and back, unblinking. "The gods do not mind a crowded scale. They mind only what is placed in it, and whether it is true. Weigh carefully. Both of you."

Lord Daven took the opening with the ease of long practice. "Majesty — the Ambassador has answered grievance with grievance, which is an old custom of this court, older than any of us. I propose both matters stand before the throne: the cordon and the cargoes, Cael Ford and the northern routes. Order can be found. Courts are good at order." His glance crossed yours for a single heartbeat, and it said, plainly: *stop improvising.*

Queen Isara had not moved. Her fingers lay still against the throne's arm, and the stillness was worse than the drumming had been.

"Twice," she said. "Twice I have asked you for terms, Ambassador, and twice you have spent the court's time on everything else. Observe what your defiance has purchased. A charge against my Commander — which he will answer, and which I will hear, because a crown that fears its own record is already falling. And something else besides." Her voice dropped, quiet and precise as a blade being sheathed. "You have told this court where Velheim bleeds. Six weeks of cordon, and your masters sent a man over a winter pass — and pressed, the first thing he does is cry out about the cordon. I will remember it was *you* who told us. It is the most honest thing you have said this morning."

She leaned forward by that same single degree. "My patience is not a well, Ambassador. It is a ledger, and you are overdrawn. Terms. Now. Stated plainly. And there will not be a third asking."

The Herald struck the floor. "The floor is with the Ambassador of Velheim. The court waits."

The silence that followed was the loudest yet — and it was yours to fill.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *A heavy silence. My gamble didn't pay off, but it did reveal something.* "Your Majesty, Velheim seeks open and safe passage along the northern routes, unhindered by... inspections. We propose a joint oversight council to ensure fair passage for all vessels."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For the first time since you had entered the hall, ink touched paper. The Herald took your terms and gave them back to the room in the flat cadence of the record: "Open and safe passage upon the northern routes. Passage unhindered by inspection. A joint oversight council, seated by both crowns, to ensure fair passage for all vessels." A clerk at the throne's foot wrote without looking up, and the record did not keep hesitations — the pause before *inspections* had already been sanded away, leaving the word absolute, standing alone in the entry like a man on ice.

"Unhindered." Commander Ash did not smile now. He said the word once, quietly, the way a man names a thing he intends to kill. "Your Majesty. I have forty casks of war-powder under guard in a warehouse, sewn into salt-fish bales. The Ambassador proposes I stop looking for the next forty." He turned to you, and there was something in it almost like respect — the respect of a soldier measuring another man's nerve, if not his judgment. "But you said *council*, Ambassador. Good. Here is a council: Velheim sets observers aboard my boarding parties. Your own eyes watch me open your own hulls, hull by hull, and certify what is found. Fair passage, verified by both crowns. That is your council, sir. I am merely offering to wear it honestly."

From the alcove came the soft, ash-settling voice. "The Ambassador has placed two things upon the scales, and they press against one another." Priestess Yuna's tone was gentle; the words were not. "*Unhindered* is a thing without watchers. A *council* is a thing made of watchers. A man cannot carry both up the same mountain. The gods will ask which he meant to weigh." Her dark eyes rested on you, unblinking. "So, I think, will the throne."

Lord Daven stepped into the gap with the ease of a man joining a dance whose music only he could hear. "Majesty — the terms as entered are two instruments, not one. The first is an aspiration. The second is a mechanism, and I would counsel the court to weigh the mechanism. A joint council is a table, and a table is a place where grievances may be laid down beside terms — Cael Ford next to the cordon, both crowns seated, neither shouting past the other." A modest inclination of the head. "If it would serve, I have drafted such instruments before. I place my hand at the court's disposal for the writing of them."

Queen Isara had listened without moving, and when she spoke, it was with the quiet satisfaction of a woman confirming a figure already entered in her ledger. "Two askings, Ambassador, and at last something plain enough to weigh." One finger lifted from the throne's arm. "Half of it plain. You offer me a council — a table. Tables interest me. But you wrapped it in the word *unhindered*, and that word is rotted at the core: it was Velheim's hulls that built my Commander's cordon, and powder does not become flour because a council is watching. So mark my ledger." Her gaze did not waver from your face. "The council may live. Nothing of Velheim's travels unhindered while Cael Ford lies unanswered and my warehouses fill with your contraband. If your masters want their passage, they will purchase it — with answers, with restitution, or with inspectors under my writ. Those are the only coins this table accepts." A pause, precisely measured. "And understand — the record shows what Velheim asked for first. Passage before restitution. My spymaster reads records too."

She settled back by that single degree. "Now choose the manner of it, Ambassador. Answer for Cael Ford here, before this throne, this morning. Or the terms go to parchment under Lord Daven's hand, and a parley is set where everything sits on the table together — the routes, the cordon, the cargoes, and the Ford — with this morning's record seated beside them. I will have either. I will not have silence."

The Herald struck the floor. "The floor is with the Ambassador of Velheim. The court awaits his choice."

The clerk's pen hung above the page, waiting. In the gallery, Lord Daven's eyes moved — briefly, deliberately — to that waiting pen, and then back to you. It was the smallest possible gesture. It said: *paper buys time.*

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing the Queen's words. Paper buys time, and time is what I need to regroup.* "Your Majesty. Velheim will agree to a parley, under Lord Daven's hand. Let all grievances and proposals be laid upon the table, including Cael Ford."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The clerk's pen came down at last, and the scratch of it against paper was the only sound in the hall for the space of three heartbeats. The record would show that the Ambassador of Velheim chose parchment over answers — and, as Lord Daven had wagered, parchment was the coin that bought time.

Queen Isara regarded you for a long, unhurried moment. Whatever passed behind her eyes did not reach her face.

"So be it," she said. "The terms go to parchment under Lord Daven's hand. A parley is set." One finger rose. "But mark the manner of it, Ambassador. It will not convene in a neutral town on the border, chosen for Velheim's convenience. It will convene at Cael Ford — on the very ground your barges emptied and my crews were put ashore. If your masters must be reminded of what sits upon the table, they may look out the window and see it."

From the gallery, Lord Daven inclined his head, accepting the burden and the honor in the same motion, though you — and probably the Queen — noted that his draftsmanship now served two masters. "I am the crown's hand in this, as Your Majesty pleases. I will begin the instruments within the week."

Commander Ash settled back to parade rest, and there was the ghost of something in his face that was not quite satisfaction — a soldier who has won the ground and knows the war is not over. "I will arrange the escort to Cael Ford myself," he said, to no one in particular and to you entirely. "The road along the cordon is instructive this time of year. One passes the warehouse."

Priestess Yuna spoke once more, soft as ash, final as a bell. "Two grievances, one table, one ground where both were born. The scales begin to balance — or to break. The gods will watch which."

The Herald struck the floor with his staff, and the flat cadence of the record gave your morning its final shape: "The terms of the Ambassador of Velheim are entered. A parley is set at Cael Ford, under the hand of Lord Daven, all grievances and proposals to be laid upon the table. The audience of Velheim is concluded."

Queen Isara's gaze released you — a thing done with the precision of everything else she did. "You have your time, Ambassador," she said quietly, so that only the throne's foot of the hall could hear it. "Spend it well. At Cael Ford, the ledger and the river both run one direction."

You bowed — precisely the required depth, no deeper — and turned down the marble aisle. Behind you, the court was already murmuring, and somewhere in that murmur, forty-one crews, forty casks of powder, and one winter pass were being weighed anew.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You were three steps down the marble aisle when the words left you, and the hall stopped as if a hand had been laid flat against its chest.

The murmur died mid-syllable. A guardsman's boots shifted on marble. In the gallery, Lord Daven's head came around slowly — and for one naked instant there was no parliamentary mildness in his face at all, only the arithmetic of a man discovering his ally had been holding cards he had never counted. Then the mildness came down over it like a visor. His glance crossed yours, and it no longer said *stop improvising*. It said: *how long have you had these?*

The Herald's staff cracked the floor. "The audience of Velheim is concluded. The floor—"

The Queen's finger lifted from the arm of the throne, and the Herald's next word died in the air.

"I concluded this audience," Queen Isara said, and her voice did not rise because it did not need to. "I reopen it. The record will show a conclusion, a reopening, and the paper that caused both." She had not otherwise moved. She watched you cross toward the alcove the way a woman watches a man walk on ice, counting the cracks.

A spear dipped across your path a spear's length from the alcove. Commander Ash did not stir from parade rest, but his voice reached you over the marble. "Let him through. I want to see which god he thinks will hold it for him."

Priestess Yuna took the papers from your hands without hurry and without expression. She did not read them — not first. She turned the folded flap to the alcove's lamp and studied the wax, tilting it against the light, and the hall waited on a priestess reading seals the way sailors wait on weather.

"You gave this to the alcove before the throne, Ambassador," she said, soft as ash settling. "That was either wisdom or cowardice. The reading will tell us which." Her thumb moved down the page and stopped. "The wax is old, and unbroken since it was sealed. The hand is a chancery hand — a clerk's patience in every letter. The writ commissions an inspection cordon upon the northern routes. And wax is honest about one thing only, but it is honest about that." Her dark eyes lifted to the throne. "The seal bears its date. The date is eleven days before Cael Ford."

The sound that went through the hall was not a murmur this time. It was quieter and worse — the sound of many people not saying anything at once.

"Before the Ford." Commander Ash came off parade rest fully now, and his voice had changed — no longer a blade aimed at you; a man re-reading his own orders in memory and finding the dates wrong. "Writs are drafted before they are executed, Priestess. Councils anticipate. Ink ahead of an event proves preparation, not—" He stopped. He had heard himself. *Preparation.* The word sat in the air where he had set it down, and it did not come back to him.

So he turned on you instead, and the blade returned. "And mark the manner of this proof, Majesty. The Ambassador holds a writ of this court — paper that has never left the council's hands. He confesses it: *intercepted.* Velheim did not find this. Velheim was given it, or stole it. Either way, the Ambassador has proven my cordon necessary by the very manner of his proving. One does not intercept a crown's paper unless a crown's walls leak. I rest my case on his own evidence."

"Then let us have no case resting on truth kept beneath the table," Lord Daven said, rising in the gallery. "Majesty — an hour ago this court set a parley so that all things might sit upon one table in the light. It appears Velheim has brought its document early. I counsel it be read — every line, before the throne — because a table with truth upon it is dangerous, but a table with truth beneath it is fatal."

Queen Isara listened to all of it without moving. "I gave you time, Ambassador, and told you to spend it well," she said at last, quietly. "You have chosen to spend it three steps from my throne, before my doors had closed. Observe, also, his choice of hands. He had a throne to give this to. He had a Commander. He chose the alcove — a reader I cannot command and Ash cannot seize. It is the most intelligent thing he has done this morning, and I will not pretend otherwise by raging at it." Her eyes went to Yuna. "Priestess, keep the paper. The throne does not take back what has been given to the gods. But the throne may question the giver."

Then her gaze came back to you, and it was the assayer's gaze again, and colder than it had been at your bow.

"Before one word of that writ is read aloud, you will answer me one question. Paper of this kind does not leave my council chamber. Yet it crossed a winter pass in an Ambassador's coat. So: was it stolen — which is espionage, and I will answer it as war. Or was it *given* — which means a hand in my council feeds my writs to foreign crowns, and I will answer that as something worse than war." One finger lifted from the throne's arm. "You will tell me which. And then, Priestess, you will read the last line — the name — before this court. Unless the Ambassador has reason the throne should hear first."

The Herald struck the floor. "The audience of Velheim is reopened. The floor is with the Ambassador. The court awaits the manner of the writ's coming into his hands — and his leave, or his refusal, for the last line to be read."

Behind you, without any order being given, the great doors of the throne room were quietly closing.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *My heart pounds, but my face remains impassive.* "Your Majesty, I cannot reveal my sources. However, the writ was not stolen. It was... shared."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
"Shared."

Queen Isara took the word and held it to the light the way Priestess Yuna had held the wax — turning it slowly, reading what was inside it.

"Not sold. Venality has a price, and I could have paid it. Not stolen — a stolen writ is a hole in my wall, and holes can be mended and guarded. *Shared.*" She let the word fall. "That word has a sharer, Ambassador, and a reason, and a belief that the gift would be welcome in Velheim's hands. You have confirmed before my court that my council gives away my writs. You will not name him — I did not expect you to. A source is the only property an envoy owns, and I would think less of you if you surrendered it cheaply." One finger lifted from the throne's arm. "I do not want his name from your mouth. I want it from the paper. Priestess — the last line. Read it exactly."

In the alcove, Yuna turned the final leaf to the lamp. And in the gallery, Lord Daven — who had risen for every fight that morning — did not rise now.

Yuna's voice came soft as ash settling. "*Drawn under the hand of Lord Daven of the council, for the seal of the throne, and entered into the book of instruments.*" A pause. "The endorsement is in the same hand as the body of the writ, Majesty. One patience wrote it all. And beneath it, the date of the drawing — the same date the seal bears. Eleven days before Cael Ford."

The clerk's pen at the throne's foot scratched, and did not stop.

"Bar the—" Commander Ash began, turning toward the doors.

"They were barred when the audience reopened, Commander," a guardsman said.

Ash looked at the doors a moment too long. Then he looked at the gallery, and his voice came low, without any blade in it at all — which was worse than the blade. "I told this court the walls leaked. I did not know the leak had a signature." He stepped forward, gauntlet creaking. "Forty-one of my crews were put ashore in their shirts, Majesty. If a pen in this council knew the Ford was coming eleven days before it came, then either my people were left blind by a man who could see — or the Ford was not a raid at all, but an *appointment*. I would like to know which. I would like to know it very much."

Lord Daven rose at last, unhurried still — but you could see the unhurriedness costing him something now. "Majesty. The hand is mine. Drafting is my office, and has been for nine years. Every cordon, every charter, every tariff this crown has signed has passed through my pen — including, I would wager, the commission the Commander brandished at this court an hour ago like a trophy. A draftsman's name proves authorship. It does not prove betrayal — unless this court means to convict its own pen, in which case no instrument of state will ever again be written in this kingdom, for no man will sign one." His eyes cut to Ash, cool as a scalpel. "And if the date damns the draftsman, Commander, it damns the sword that executed the writ. Your fleet went to sea ready, on paper you never questioned. Either we both knew, or neither of us did. I do not recall informing you. Do you recall informing me?"

"A hand that draws the blade is not always the hand that aims it," Priestess Yuna said, gentle as falling ash and just as final. "The signature tells us whose patience wrote the writ. It does not tell us whose purpose carried it over the pass — nor why Velheim's barges sat at anchor at the Ford, eleven days after their masters could have outrun the cordon entirely. The paper remains with the alcove. The questions do not."

Queen Isara spoke to the hall then, quietly, as a woman enters figures in a ledger. "Eleven days. A response drawn before its grievance is not a response. It is a stage. So there are three doors, my lords, and every one of them opens into my own house: either my council saw the Ford coming and let it come; or my council made the Ford; or the paper lies about its age, and someone with a clerk's patience forged a clerk's patience. Each door will be opened in its turn — but not by shouting." Her gaze moved to Daven, and rested there. "Lord Daven keeps the parley. A pen I am reading is worth three pens I am not. And the Ambassador will be the crown's guest until it convenes — my hospitality will be exact, and so will my watch. You will ride to Cael Ford in the Commander's column, Ambassador. So will Lord Daven. I am told the road passes the warehouse."

Then her eyes came back to you, and they were the assayer's again.

"One matter remains, and it is not the name you will not give me. It is the *date*. Grain barges do not loiter at anchor, Ambassador — they are scheduled. Your masters held my writ eleven days before the Ford, and their ships were there when the moment came, and my three barges and forty-one crews were the price of the morning. So tell this court plainly which it was: did Velheim walk into my Commander's fist because your masters did not believe their own intelligence — or because the Ford was *meant* to happen, and a grievance worth a table was worth three barges?" She leaned forward by that single degree. "Consider before you answer. The record already holds your word *shared*. It will hold this beside it."

The Herald struck the floor. "The audience of Velheim remains open. The floor is with the Ambassador. The court awaits his answer: whether the grievance found the writ — or the writ found the grievance."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *The Queen's gaze is a trap, a choice between two equally damaging confessions.* "Your Majesty, Velheim did not seek this confrontation. We sought to expose a deception." *I let the implication hang in the air.* "The writ proves your intentions. Cael Ford proves ours."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For a moment the only sound in the hall was the clerk's pen — and then even that stopped, because the clerk had heard what you said, and understood what it was, and would not set it down without orders.

Queen Isara gave him none. Not at first. She sat with her fingers still against the throne's arm and regarded you the way she had regarded your bow — the assayer again — except that this time the metal had named itself.

"Enter it verbatim," she said at last, quietly. "The record has sanded enough of this morning smooth."

The Herald's staff struck the floor, and the flat cadence of the record gave your words back to you in a voice that would never change its mind: "*'Velheim did not seek this confrontation. We sought to expose a deception. The writ proves your intentions. Cael Ford proves ours.'* Entered as spoken, in the reopened audience of Velheim."

Commander Ash did not raise his voice, which from him was the loudest thing yet. "I asked this court which it was — left blind, or an appointment. You have answered." He turned to face you fully. "And hear how the record will hold it: my forty-one went ashore in their shirts by *design*. Not weather. Not chance of war. Design." His gauntlet tightened on the sword pommel. "This morning I learned my fleet executed a writ drawn before its grievance. Now I learn my sailors were written into Velheim's proof the same way — ink, on both sides of the pass. Everyone in this hall holds a pen over my people, Ambassador, and no one holds one over their own." He stepped back to parade rest, slow and deliberate. "The road to Cael Ford passes the warehouse. It also passes the shore where they were put ashore. I will point out both to you myself."

From the alcove, Priestess Yuna's voice came soft as ash finding the floor. "This morning the scales held two grievances. Now they hold two confessions." Her eyes went from the writ in her hands to your face. "But the Ford was *paid* for, Ambassador — in grain that was to feed mouths, and in the shame of forty-one men who were never consulted. The gods do not weigh proofs. They weigh what proofs cost. And they find the cost was laid on hands that held no pen on either side of the pass." A pause, unblinking. "That is not justice. The gods have a longer memory for it than any ledger."

Lord Daven rose in the gallery — and did not look at you at all, and the not-looking was the loudest thing in the gallery. "Majesty. Whatever else this morning has unloosed, it has placed in the crown's hand what no interception could: Velheim's own confession, spoken before the throne. I ask it be copied under seal and carried to Cael Ford as an instrument — so the table remembers, when Velheim's next envoy speaks of grievances, what Velheim's own envoy has confessed to staging." Then, before suspicion could reach him, steady as a man stepping off a ledge onto his own scaffold: "And since the court must now ask whether the pen that drew the writ and the hand that shared it are one — I invite the throne's inquiry into my office. My books, my clerks, nine years of drafts, open before the parley convenes. A draftsman who hides his papers looks like a sharer, and I do not intend to look like anything inquiry cannot find." His voice cooled a degree. "Though I note a writ passes many hands between a pen and the throne's wax. The antechamber. The seal room. The courier satchels. The inquiry will need a wide net. I will help cast it."

Queen Isara let the offer hang — long enough for the hall to mark exactly when he had made it, and why.

"Your books will be read, my lord. Every page." Then, to the alcove: "Priestess — the writ says it was entered into the book of instruments. Wax can be pressed twice. A book has neighbors on either side of the page. Bring me the book, and lay it open beside the paper."

A runner was dispatched at a pace just short of unseemly. The Queen turned back to you, and it was the ledger-voice now, entering figures.

"Two matters, Ambassador. First: the forty-one. Their names, their condition, the shore they were left on. Velheim has confessed the taking; Velheim will account for the taken. Before any parley convenes. Enter that also." One finger lifted from the throne's arm. "Second — the mirror. You would not spend my sharer's name, and I did not press, because a source is an envoy's property. But you have given the court a confession instead, and confessions have authors. So you will spend a name of your own choosing, or refuse at your own cost: whose order put my barges at anchor on that morning? Whose pen in Velheim scheduled my grain and my sailors as the ink of a proof?" She leaned forward by the single degree. "You kept my secret for nothing, Ambassador. You will find yours is not free."

The Herald struck the floor. "The book of instruments is summoned. The demands of the throne are entered. The floor is with the Ambassador of Velheim. The court awaits the author of the Ford."

At the end of the aisle, the great doors opened, and a scriptorium under-clerk came hurrying down the marble with a ledger the size of a paving stone held against his chest — the crown's record coming to meet Velheim's. Winter light followed him in and lay across the floor between you like a line ruled in a book. In the gallery, Lord Daven watched the ledger approach with an expression you had never seen on him before: a man watching his own trial arrive in someone else's arms. And Commander Ash's eyes were on you, doing arithmetic.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *A heavy weight settles on me, heavier than any ledger.* "I will not name a name, Your Majesty. The responsibility for Velheim's actions rests with Velheim, not with one individual."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
"Velheim, then."

Queen Isara did not say it loudly. She said it the way a clerk closes an account — one entry, balanced, done.

"The crown of Velheim, then. Not a minister. Not a council. Not a hand. The whole weight of it, distributed so finely that no one need feel it." She settled back by the single degree. "You have spent this morning teaching my court the value of precision, Ambassador, and now you offer me the vaguest word in the language. But I will take it, because a refusal entered honestly is worth more than a name extracted poorly. Enter it, Herald. *'The Ambassador of Velheim declines to name the author of the Ford, and accepts the throne's cost.'*"

"The cost has not been set, Majesty," the Herald observed, formal to the bone.

"Then set it." She did not look at the Herald; she looked at you. "The Ambassador will depart for Cael Ford with the Commander's column — tomorrow, at first light, not at his convenience. He will ride the shore road. He will see the warehouse, the anchorage, and the ground where forty-one of my people stood in their shirts. And at the parley table, when Velheim's envoy next speaks, the first document laid out will be this morning's record — the confession and the refusal together, read aloud before anything else is said. That is the cost. Not a cell. An audience." The almost-approval flickered, once, and died. "I find that courts forgive faster than rivers. The Ford will not."

The under-clerk arrived at the throne's foot at that moment, breathless, and laid the book of instruments open on the clerk's table with a boom that echoed off the marble like a door shutting.

Priestess Yuna descended from the alcove — the first time she had left it all morning — and every eye in the hall followed her, because everyone understood that the next minute would decide whether the writ was scripture or forgery. She stood over the great ledger, laid the intercepted paper beside it, and read. The hall waited. Even Commander Ash leaned forward.

"The entry stands," she said at last. "Page forty-one." A pause, and the pause had teeth. "Page forty-one, Majesty. The writ authorizing the cordon is entered on page forty-one of the book of instruments." Her dark eyes lifted. "The gods do not write in margins. But they have been known to underline."

The sound that went through the hall this time was not silence. It was the opposite of silence — a low, involuntary exhale from forty throats at once, and somewhere in the gallery a woman began, very quietly, to pray.

"Superstition," Lord Daven said, but his voice had gone thin at the edges. "Coincidence of pagination. Books are long, pages are many—"

"Coincidences are entered too," Yuna said, unbothered, and returned the writ to the alcove with both hands, as one returns a relic.

Commander Ash had gone very still. When he spoke, it was quietly, to the middle distance. "Forty-one. I have counted that number all morning — my crews, my shame. I did not think to count it twice." He turned his head and looked at you, and there was something new in his face, and it was not warmth, but it was no longer only the blade. "You knew. Before you ever crossed the pass. Your masters knew the writ, the date, the Ford — and they sent you anyway, into this hall, carrying paper that was going to cut whichever way the day fell." He shook his head slowly. "I have spent six weeks calling you an enemy, Ambassador. I owe the word an amendment. You are something worse. You are a *message*."

Queen Isara rose from the throne. It was the first time she had moved to her feet all morning, and the hall rose with her like iron filings.

"The book stays under the Priestess's seal. The inquiry into the council's offices begins tonight — Lord Daven's books with the rest, as he offered, and the court will remember he offered. The record of this audience is closed, copied, and sealed for Cael Ford." Her gaze found you one last time, and held. "You came into my hall this morning with a bow of exact depth, Ambassador, and I marked you as a man who understood that everything is measured here. I was right. I merely measured the wrong thing. You are not the envoy of a crown, are you? You are the instrument of a proof. And instruments," she said, descending the dais steps toward the doors, passing within arm's reach of you without slowing, "are used once."

At the doors she paused, without turning.

"Priestess. The Ambassador will want a confessor before the road tomorrow. See that he has one." A beat. "Whether he confesses is between him and the gods. Whether he *arrives* is between him and the Commander."

The great doors opened onto the winter light, and the Herald's staff struck the floor one final time.

"The audience of Velheim is concluded. The court rises."

And the hall emptied around you — Lord Daven already deep in murmured conference with his clerks, Commander Ash giving orders for a column that would ride at first light, Priestess Yuna standing in the alcove with the writ against her chest, watching you with an expression that might, in a less disciplined face, have been called pity.

The road to Cael Ford began at those doors. It passed the warehouse. And now, apparently, it passed page forty-one.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I stand there for a moment, the weight of the Queen's words and the court's stares pressing down on me. I turn towards Priestess Yuna, a silent acknowledgment of the trap I've walked into, and the role she played.* "A confessor, then." *I say, my voice flat, already weary of the games.* "And a message, apparently."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Priestess Yuna looked down at you from the alcove, the writ dark against her breast, and for the space of three heartbeats she said nothing at all.

"A confessor, yes," she said at last, soft as ash settling. "The Queen commanded it, and the alcove consented before she finished speaking. But mark what you called me, Ambassador. A *role*." Her head tilted by a single degree. "You gave the paper to my hands this morning because you believed the alcove played no part in any man's game. I told you then that the reading would tell us whether that was wisdom or cowardice. The reading has told us it was neither. It was hope. The gods see very little of that in halls like this one. They mark it where it appears."

Her dark eyes did not blink. "I will hear the confession myself. Not at dawn — the gods keep no office hours, and tonight, neither do I. But understand what my hearing is. Whatever you lay upon the scales with me is weighed by the gods and kept by the alcove. It is not *concealed* by them. If you confess a thing that belongs before the throne, I will carry it there with my own hands, and tell you plainly that I have done so. Confession is not a pocket, Ambassador. It is a scale. Come to it knowing which."

Then the hall finished emptying, the way a wound finishes bleeding — steadily, and without any part of it asking your leave.

At the throne's foot, a clerk under the Herald's seal placed a sealed packet in your hands. The Herald himself delivered the words, flat as ever, the staff held at rest. "The record of the reopened audience, copied under the throne's seal, to travel with the Ambassador. It will be read aloud at Cael Ford before any other word is spoken." A beat, precisely measured. "Whether you read it first on the road is your own affair. The record does not mind being read in either order."

Across the hall, Commander Ash's voice carried over his sergeant's shoulder — "East postern, first light. Light horses, no banners" — and then he crossed the marble to you, unhurried, the new thing still in his face where the blade had been. "Center column, Ambassador. Not honor — *reach*. I want you where my voice carries and the road can't have you." He stopped at arm's length. "A message. Hm. I have carried orders I did not write for thirty years. The trick is surviving the reading." He turned away, and added without turning: "Sleep. The shore road is honest, and honest roads are long."

In the colonnade beyond the doors, Lord Daven dismissed his clerks with a word and fell into step beside you, and the parliamentary mildness was gone — not into anger. Into arithmetic.

"I told you paper buys time," he said, low. "I neglected to say *whose*." His eyes stayed forward. "Twice today my hand served you — once between you and the Commander's blade, and once beneath a writ drawn eleven days before its grievance. Before the column rides, you will tell me which of those you planned, and which you improvised. I can serve a man who gambles. I cannot serve a man who gambles *with me* and calls it alliance afterward." His voice dropped further still. "One thing more. My books open to the inquiry tonight. If your sharer sits in that council, Ambassador, then you have handed me either my enemies — or *myself*. You will tell me which. Not at the Ford. At the first turning of this corridor, if it pleases you. But before the column rides."

At the courtyard arch he stopped, already half-belonging to his own trial, and gave you the smallest possible nod — the same nod as that morning, and nothing like it. "You made me the crown's hand at the parley. See that you have not made me its hostage." Then he was gone, and the clerks' footsteps hurried after him like dogs called to heel.

They quartered you in the guest wing, and the hospitality was exact: a fire already laid, a supper worth a minister's table, wine from the royal cellars, a long window over the frozen river where the winter light was failing. The door did not slam. It closed, and the bar came down on the outside with the sound of a full stop. Two shadows crossed the courtyard wall below, and settled, and stayed.

The sealed record sat on the table where the clerk had left it. The fire ticked. The river creaked under its ice, patient as a ledger.

Then, footsteps. The bar lifted.

Priestess Yuna stood in the doorway without lamp, without escort, the writ no longer anywhere upon her. "The gods keep no office hours, Ambassador," she said. "I told you." She stepped inside, and the bar came down behind her — from the inside, this time, by her own hand.

"Bring whatever you carry. The scales have been open all day."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch her, the silence of the room broken only by the crackle of the fire. The wine sits untouched. I gesture to a chair by the fire.* "Please, Priestess. Sit." *I pick up the sealed record and hold it, turning it over in my hands. The weight of it feels immense.* "I carry a great deal. And a great many more questions than answers."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Priestess Yuna considered the chair the way she had considered the wax — without hurry, and without expression. Then she sat, and the sitting was precise, her hands folded in her lap, the firelight finding no purchase in her dark eyes.

"You hold the record as if it might answer you," she observed. "It will not. Paper is patient in the wrong direction. It only remembers." She glanced at the seal, the throne's mark pressed deep in it. "You are also holding it wrongly, if it comforts you to know. The weight is not in the packet. The weight is in the fact that you have not yet decided whether to read it. A man who has decided does not turn a thing over in his hands. He sets it down."

The fire ticked. The river creaked beneath its ice, far below the window.

"You said you carry questions more than answers. Good. The alcove has no use for answers — answers are what courts trade. Questions are what the gods keep." She leaned forward by a single degree, and it was strange how much the gesture resembled the Queen's, and how different it was. "But I will be honest with you, Ambassador, because you were honest enough to be flat with me, and flatness is rarer than virtue in this palace. I did not come only to hear a confession. I came because of a thing I have not said aloud, and it concerns you."

Her hands unfolded. She turned her right palm upward, as if weighing something invisible.

"When I read the writ before the throne, I told the court the wax was unbroken since it was sealed. That was true. I told them the hand was a chancery hand. Also true. I did not tell them — because the court did not ask, and the alcove answers questions, it does not volunteer — that the writ was *warm*." She let the word sit. "Wax holds heat for an hour, perhaps two, if it is kept against the body. That writ was pressed against someone's skin when you carried it into the hall. Not hidden in a coat lining among cold papers. Kept close. The way a man keeps a thing he cannot decide about."

Her eyes came up to yours, unblinking.

"Velheim's masters did not send you a document, Ambassador. They sent you a *dilemma* — and they kept it warm enough that it was yours until the moment you chose to give it away. I have carried relics I believed in less." A pause, soft as ash. "So before the scales, I ask you the question the court could not: when you walked down that marble aisle this morning and bowed exactly the required depth, had you already chosen the alcove? Or were you, like the rest of us, waiting to see which way the day fell — carrying another man's decision against your own heart, hoping the fire of it would go out before you had to answer for it?"

She sat back, and the room seemed to settle around her.

"You need not answer as an envoy. There is no Herald here, no clerk, no pen. Answer as the man who held the writ. The gods make no record of the manner — only of the truth." Her gaze did not waver. "And when you have answered that, then bring your questions, one at a time, and we will see what the scales say. But I warn you of one thing now, so it does not surprise you later." The firelight moved across her face, and for an instant something that was not blankness moved behind it. "The question you most want to ask me — I can feel it waiting behind your teeth, the one about page forty-one, about whether the gods underlined that number for you or for someone else in this hall. When you ask it, I will answer honestly. And my honest answer may cost you more than the Queen's cost has."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I put the sealed record down on the small table. It lands with a soft thud.* "The dilemma, then. Yes. Velheim sent me with a dilemma. And no, I hadn't chosen the alcove. I was waiting to see which way the day fell." *I meet her gaze.* "As for page forty-one... I have my suspicions. But I'll save that question for when I'm ready to pay the price."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You ease the door open an inch. The alarm drops to a muffled throb behind the fire door. Cold air, concrete, the chemical sting of floor cleaner. You hold your breath and listen.

Boots. Below you — two floors down, maybe three. Quick, syncopated, unhurried. Trained. One set stops, and a voice bounces up the shaft, clipped and tinny: "—east stairs, bottom up. Lock the garage on my mark." A radio crackles in answer.

They're coming to meet you.

Mira's grip tightens on your jacket. She hears it too.

"Freight elevator," she murmurs. "Service corridor on this floor, past the copy room. It skips the lobby lockdown." A beat. "It also has a camera. And they'll know I know about it."

Your earpiece spits static — half a syllable, maybe your handler, maybe nothing — then goes dead again.

The boots grow louder. Two floors. Maybe less by now. Behind you, the corridor runs dark toward the copy room, toward the elevator she swears exists. Ahead of you, the stairwell drops straight into the sweep.

Seconds now, not minutes.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Copy room it is." *I pull Mira, half-carrying her, toward the corridor she mentioned. No time for subtlety anymore.* "Give me details on that camera."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
"Fixed dome, above the doors," Mira says between strides. "It sees the elevator and about ten meters of approach. No pan, no tilt — old system. But it's low-light capable and it feeds straight to the security desk. Blind spot tight against the left wall, up under the housing." Her bad leg drags; she locks her arm harder around your neck and keeps herself moving. "The last three meters to the call button, you're in the open."

The corridor strobes red, black, red. Behind you, iron bangs on iron — the stairwell gate. Then boots on tile, faster now. They've found the corridor.

The copy room swallows you both. Dead monitors, paper trays, the ghost-smell of burnt toner. Through the wire-glass pane of the far door, the freight elevator waits at the end of a short service hall — the call button glowing orange, and above the doors, the matte black eye of the camera, aimed exactly where you'd have to stand.

Your earpiece coughs. "—tive, do not take the— ...elevator is... hold for—" Static swallows the rest. Whether the line is dying or the handler is, you can't tell. Do not take the what? The elevator? The dock?

"Breaker panel, back wall," Mira breathes, nodding at a gray box behind the copier. "Kill the hall lights, camera drops to infrared. Grainy. Maybe not enough to ID you." A beat. "Or the Xerox. Three hundred kilos, on casters. Roll it ahead of you and the lens never sees a face."

Flashlight beams swing through the wire glass behind you. Two shapes in the corridor, closing.

The elevator is thirty seconds away. So are they.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Down is the garage. Down is the lockdown, the sweep, the boots coming up the east stairs. You turn your back on the orange call button, shoulder through the far door, and pull Mira into the service hall.

"Up?" For the first time, her voice cracks. Then she locks it down. "Service stair is past the lift. Go."

The camera watches you cross all ten meters of open floor — no killed breaker, no rolling Xerox, just speed. Its lens takes everything: your face, hers, the direction you're moving. Somewhere at a security desk, a screen is changing right now.

The copy room door slams open behind you. Flashlights spear the wire glass. "Service corridor! West stair, west stair!"

The elevator chimes as you pass — doors parting, warm light, the hiss of a radio. Someone steps out into a hall you've already left. The stair door's crash bar gives under your palm and steel swallows the shout behind you.

Concrete. Cold. You climb. Mira's arm is locked around your neck, her left leg hopping every second step, her breath sawing against your jaw. SIX, stenciled gray on the wall. SEVEN. EIGHT.

Below, iron bangs on iron. They're in the stairwell. One flight down, then level with the noise, then climbing — faster than you, because they aren't carrying anyone.

"Twelve floors," Mira grinds out. "Roof door's chained from the inside. Padlock." A breath. "Eleven's mechanical — air handlers, ducts, a window onto the dock side." Another breath, raggeder. "Roofs are where they take the pictures. In case that radio of yours hasn't told you."

Your earpiece coughs — closer to a voice now. "—moving— good— ...roof, four minutes— ...do not let—" Static eats the rest.

Through the concrete, you feel it before you hear it. A rotor, thumping somewhere above the city. Getting closer.

NINE.

The boots below are one landing under you. Rising.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Eleven," I gasp, pulling her up the next step. *I'm already moving toward the mechanical floor door. Let's see how good these ducts are.* "We're going for the window."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The ELEVEN door gives onto heat and roar. The mechanical floor swallows you — sodium-yellow light, air handlers bellowing, a forest of gray ductwork sweating condensation onto slick concrete.

"Center aisle," Mira shouts over the din. "Pipes at head height — duck at the second bank. Window's past the return duct, high on the dock wall!"

You move. The machine noise buries your footsteps. It buries theirs too. That's the trade.

Behind you the stairwell door bangs open. No more shouting — they've gone professional. Flashlight beams swing between the handlers like searchlights through a wreck. One sweeps the center aisle, ten meters back, and Mira hauls you sideways by the sleeve into the shadow of a condenser. Her breath hammers against your ribs. The beam slides past. A boot finds a puddle somewhere; a voice mutters a curse, low.

Then your earpiece cuts through, cleaner than it has all night. "—operative, listen— the bird is not— say again, the bird is NOT ours— do not—"

The whine of the machinery eats the rest. Not ours.

Mira's head snaps toward your ear. She caught it. "Then whoever's riding it," she says, "is theirs. I told you. Roofs are where they take the pictures."

The window waits at the far wall, above a humming condenser — a hopper of wired glass, whited with grime, latch buried under decades of paint. Beyond it, an exterior catwalk of steel grating runs the dock face: a meter wide, waist-high rail, thirty meters to a rusted ladder dropping toward the annex roof three stories below.

"Contact switch, top corner," Mira says, nodding at the frame. "Tied to the door system — that alarm's already screaming, so nobody hears a new chime. But the desk gets a new dot." A breath. "The catwalk I can do. The ladder..." She doesn't finish.

Outside, a blade of white light sweeps up the dock-side windows. The helicopter, working the building floor by floor. Nine. Ten.

In the machine hall, the flashlights split — one pair working the near side, one coming straight down the center aisle.

The searchlight climbs to eleven.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
TEL / DATA 11, stenciled on steel. The door stands propped by a folding sign — EQUIPMENT TESTING. DO NOT POWER DOWN — and the moment you're through, the closer swings it shut behind you and the latch bites. Card-locked. For now, that works in your favor.

The cold hits like a plunge. Server rows breathe white noise, LED constellations winking down the aisle, raised floor tiles chill through your boots. After the machine hall, the hum is almost silence.

You get Mira down against a rack. In its light her face is gray, and the leg finally refuses to be ignored — trouser soaked black from knee to boot, the tile beneath her going dark.

"Belt," she says, and strips her own. She cinches it above the knee, buckle set with her teeth, and never makes a sound.

The barricade: a UPS battery cabinet, half a tonne on casters. It grinds across the tiles and seats itself flush against the door. A lock is only a lock until the desk opens it. This buys seconds after that.

A crash cart by the wall, monitor awake — the camera head-end lives in this room. Sixteen gray tiles. The freight lobby, empty, doors hanging open. The west stair, two pairs of boots, climbing. The machine aisles, flashlight beams sweeping between the condensers.

And the roof. A figure at the stair housing, unhurried, hands loose, facing the chained door. The timestamp reads LIVE. Through the concrete, the rotor holds station overhead.

"Told you," Mira says quietly. "Pictures."

Your earpiece: "—roof is not— say again, the roof is not— annex, take the annex, the window— three minutes—"

On the monitor, feeds start dying. One by one, floor by floor, someone at the desk is pulling systems. Machine hall. Stairwell. The roof feed flickers, holds, dies. This room stays bright — you're standing on the building's UPS spine, and the desk is going to notice that.

Outside, the handle turns. Stops at the latch. "Locked. Card access." The boots move on. The desk is another matter.

Mira looks up at you, belt cinched, sweat on her lip, eyes level. "Roof's occupied. Stairs are theirs. Elevator's a box with a bow on it. That leaves a window, thirty meters of catwalk, and a ladder I can't climb." A breath. "Your handler says three minutes. The desk says two. Think."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "They want us on the annex roof." *I grab a handful of fiber optic cable from a loose spool.* "Catwalk to the ladder, then. I'll get you down."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The handful comes with friends. The cable drags its whole reel off the rack — a plywood drum of armored trunk line, orange jacket, heavy as a rolled carpet. Mira does the math out loud while you heft it.

"Trunk cable. Pull-rated to two-seventy kilos." She loops the freed end around her chest, under her arms, and ties it off — a bowline, fast, muscle-memory neat. "I weigh sixty-one. It holds me. Once."

The card reader's LED goes green.

The door knocks against the UPS cabinet. Casters shriek an inch across the tile. Overhead, a PA voice, female and bored: "Floor eleven. Access control transferred to central management." Out in the machine hall, the hunting beams stop hunting and start converging — on the screech.

You haul the cabinet aside — grinding, loud, subtlety dead — and shoulder back into the roar and the heat.

Duck at the second bank. The pipes pass close enough to comb your hair. Behind you, every beam is on the server-room door; for ten seconds the far aisle is naked and yours. The reel rides your hip, cable end wrapped twice around your fist. It snags a condenser foot once; a flashlight swings toward the sound; you rip it free and the beam finds only condensation dripping off the housing.

The window latch is a paddle buried under paint. You hammer it with the butt of your fist and the paint cracks like lake ice. The hopper swings out into the night — cold floods in, a slap after the furnace — and the rotor thump fills the whole room.

The contact switch clicks. Somewhere, a new dot. The searchlight is just leaving this face of the building, sliding toward the corner. It comes back on a count of about fifteen.

Your earpiece cuts through one last time, closer to a voice than it has been all night. "—they want her breathing— say again, they want her alive— you, not so much— ...annex stair, north corner— two minutes—" Then nothing. Not static. Nothing.

Mira cinches her loop, tests the knot with her full weight, and looks out: thirty meters of open grating, the rusted ladder, the annex roof three stories down — tar paper, HVAC units, a dark stair housing in the north corner. When the light passes, you catch the helicopter for the first time. Dark hull. No running lights. A white ball under the nose. And in the open side door, a figure with a long lens braced on the rail.

*Pictures.*

"Told you," Mira says.

Behind you, through the roar, the machine-hall door gives. Flashlights flood the far aisle. Thirty seconds back. Maybe less.

The beam starts its swing back along the dock face. Mira's hand closes on your sleeve.

"Anchor high, wrap the rail twice, lower me smooth — it's glass under that jacket, it'll cut before it snaps." A breath. "Now or on the dark. Pick."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Dark," I breathe, already testing the steel rail of the catwalk. *I'm looking for a good anchor point. This is going to be rough.* "Hang tight."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The rail midspan is a liar. Rust flakes off under your palm and the steel beneath flexes like a strummed string — it would hold a hand. Not a life. But every two meters a stanchion punches out of the concrete, boxed section, four bolts at the base, and the bolts don't shift when you lean your weight on them. At the far end, above the ladder, the last one stands thick as a fence post. There's your anchor.

The light slides off the face of the building. The dark comes down like a lid.

You go.

Thirty meters of grating sing under your boots. Mira's arm is a vise around your neck, her left foot striking every second panel, the reel slamming your hip, rotor wash shoving you sideways like a hand. Her blood finds the gaps in the grating and lets go of her — three stories of nothing under every drop. Fifteen meters. Twenty. A panel is missing entirely; you step long over the city showing through.

The light swings back. You flatten against the stanchion, Mira cheek-to-steel beside you, and the white blade rakes the empty grating behind you. In the open door of the bird, the long lens swings toward you. Unhurried. It doesn't need to hurry. It's only here to remember. The light slides on.

You wrap the cable twice around the post, twice around the rail. Mira goes over the side on her arms alone, jaw set, and the bowline takes her with a creak of jacket over steel. The reel becomes a drum brake in your hands. You feed it half a second at a time, and she pays out down the face of the building.

Where the cable crosses the rail, the orange jacket starts to open. Glass fibers lift off the cut like pale hair, spraying downwind. Every meter costs a few more.

Behind you, the hopper fills with light. A head. Shoulders. No shout — a radio raised to a mouth. Then the first one is through the window and running, a second behind him.

A round sparks off the stanchion base, ten centimeters from your boot. The flinch costs Mira a meter of free fall — you hear her swallow it. The next round never comes. They've done the math. The line has her on it, and you are the line.

"Halfway," she calls up, level as a surveyor. Then, quieter: "Five meters. And it's going, isn't it. I can feel it letting go."

The boots cross the grating. Twenty meters back. Fifteen. Through the drum you feel the core parting one glass strand at a time — tiny slips, like stitches giving. Below her: tar paper, and the north stair housing, still dark.

"I can take five meters," Mira says. "Probably."

The light starts its swing back along the dock face. Something reaches its limit first — the cable, the boots, or the five meters of air under her.

You're the only one who gets to pick which.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I brace myself against the stanchion, grimacing.* "You take the five, I'll distract them." *I yank the cable hard, making it sing against the rail, hoping to draw their fire away from her.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You yank. The cable comes off the rail singing — a struck-wire note that cuts clean through the rotor thump — and the jolt runs down the line like a whipcrack.

The lead runner freezes mid-stride. He can't know what you know. "Line!" he barks, hand slashing sideways at his partner's rifle — because if you've cut it, she drops, and they need her breathing.

The math buys you half a second. Then the math changes.

At the rail, where the jacket peeled open, the last of the core gives. Not a snap — a soft letting-go, like a tendon parting. The tail whips over the side, glass fibers spraying off it like pale hair in the rotor wash, and Mira is in the air.

Five meters. She takes it on the dark. You hear the landing more than see it — a flat, heavy thud, the grunt she doesn't let out. Then nothing. One second. Two. The silence is worse than a scream would be.

Then movement. A shape lurches up off the tar paper, one-legged, arms out for balance, crossing the open roof in a broken sprint. The black smear she leaves behind tells you what the drop cost. She makes the stair housing, hauls the door open — a rectangle of dim light in the north corner — and her voice reaches you once, thin over the blades:

"North stair! I'm in!"

The door swallows her.

The searchlight finds you. Full white, pinning you against the stanchion like a specimen — and in the open door of the bird, the long lens swings off the annex and settles on you. It got its frame of her. Now it's here to remember you.

"She's off the line." The kneeling shooter says it flat, almost relieved. "Weapons free."

The burst sparks off the stanchion — steel chips and rust flakes sting your cheek, a round tugs your sleeve, and the post you're braced against rings like a bell. Fence-post narrow. Everything below your waist is naked to them. The runner is up and moving again, eight meters now, his partner firing over his head.

Your earpiece gives you nothing. Not static. Nothing.

At your feet: the rusted ladder, three stories of it, dropping straight through the light — a shooting gallery with you lit for it. On the post: your wraps still hold, the reel still carrying thirty meters of line — rated to two-seventy kilos, and it has already lied to you once. Between you and the runners, the missing panel gapes in the grating, a hole in the dark the searchlight hasn't found yet.

The runner hits six meters. The light holds. The cable end hisses glass into the wind.

Down is the only direction left. How you take it — and what you leave behind for them — is yours to pick.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I don't look at the ladder.* "You want me? Come get me." *I drop the spool of cable, letting it clatter loudly, and jump over the missing panel, disappearing into the darkness below.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The spool goes first.

You pitch it through the gap and it drops out of the light trailing thirty meters of orange, and when it hits the annex roof the crash is enormous — plywood drum, steel core, line hissing loose across gravel like something alive. The searchlight snaps to it. Both muzzles snap with it. "Contact below— he's down—"

The runner breaks toward the sound. Three strides, four — and the hole the light never found takes his front

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I grin grimly, already moving. One down. Now for the other.* "Come on, then. Just you and me."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The runner lands in the light.

The searchlight is still on the spool, so it catches everything — the shape coming off the catwalk, three stories of drop, the landing. He folds wrong. Gravel sprays. He skids to a stop in the black smear Mira left behind, ten meters shy of the north stair.

He doesn't get up. Then one arm does. He starts to crawl — not toward the spool. Toward her door.

The door opens an inch. An eye in the dark. It closes. She saw him. She's counting the same meters you are, on a leg that won't carry her.

The second man's weapon light comes on, a white cone raking the catwalk for you. You give it something to find. You charge.

He's good. He doesn't spray — he drops to a knee, braces on the rail, fires measured pairs. The first pair goes over your shoulder because you're running broken, low, stuttering, letting the singing grating lie about your speed. The second pair doesn't miss. A line of fire opens along your ribs — shallow, you tell yourself, because deep is a luxury you can't afford. Your legs don't care either way.

He's set up beyond the missing panel. Of course he is. He watched his partner find it. The light sits on the gap like a tripwire — jump it and you jump into his muzzle.

You jump anyway.

The long step over nothing, into the white. He tracks you — fast — but the muzzle is still turning when you land inside it. Both your hands find the barrel and shove it past your ear. The shot is a hammer inside your skull; your left ear becomes one long ring. After that it isn't marksmanship anymore. It's work.

He's trained and he's strong — an elbow finds your temple, stars everywhere; his knee hunts your ruined ribs and nearly gets them. But the walkway is a meter wide, slick with condensation, and you've crossed it twice in the dark and he hasn't. You pivot. His heel skids. His weight goes past the rail.

The rifle tumbles first, three stories, gone. He catches the rail with both hands, boots swinging over the drop — and your fist is in his vest, and your fist is the only thing holding him.

The searchlight climbs back and pins you both. In the open door of the bird, the long lens settles. It got its frame of her. Now it gets one of you, blood on your side, holding a man over the edge.

He looks down at the drop first. Then up at you. Flat. Not begging.

"You think we chase you up eleven floors for fun?" His voice is level under the rotor. "We were herding you. The lockdown, the stairs — all of it, to the roof. For that." His eyes flick to the bird. "And that thing doesn't answer to us. We were told to clear the way."

The rail creaks. A breath.

"Pull me up, and I'll tell you who it answers to."

Below him, the crawler makes another meter — his drag-line crossing hers now, two black trails converging on one door. Your earpiece gives you nothing. Your left ear wouldn't let you hear it anyway.

The light holds you one second longer — then slides off toward the annex roof. Toward her.

The ladder is at your back. The man is on your fist.

Pick.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I drag him up, hard, slamming him against the catwalk.* "Start talking. Now."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Steel rings. The gunman's back hits the grating where you throw him, and he stays down — no hands up, no fight. A man who just hung over three stories of nothing doesn't spend strength on a catwalk brawl he can't win. He gets his breath back in flat, professional pieces.

Your side burns where the bullet opened it. Your left ear is one long ring, so you give him the right one.

"Retrieval contract," he says. "Not hers, not yours. The service she walked from doesn't chase defectors — it sells them. She left with a ledger, and the client bought the recovery before her feet hit the pavement. We're movers. That bird is the client's own — it rides every job, and everything the lens sees, a man on the other end sees live. Your face. Hers. The route you chose." He works his jaw; blood shows at the gumline. "You've been on his desk since the ground floor. Her, as product. You, as friction — expendable at the team's discretion. That's what the bullets were."

Your earpiece sparks. A voice, thin, wrong, like it's arriving through water: "—locked out— the desk isn't ours— I can't—" Then nothing. Not static. Nothing.

"There it is." He watches your face, not your radio. "Your handler, screaming into a dead line. Because central management isn't the building's. The client doesn't chase buildings — he buys the security contracts. This one has been his for two years. The lockdown, the elevator recalls, the feeds dying floor by floor — you were never outrunning us. You were running his maze with the lights on." A breath. "Why herd you at all? Because a frightened man doesn't ask where he's running. And because your handler keeps sending you to places." His eyes stay flat. "Ask yourself whose map he's reading."

Below, gravel scrapes. The crawler's hand lands on the door handle of the north stair.

The door doesn't move. From inside comes one flat bang — Mira, bracing it, or done with doors. Through the rotor wash you can't tell which. The searchlight has stopped sweeping. It sits on the annex roof, on the north corner, on that door — and in the open side of the bird, the long lens settles on the same rectangle. The rotor note shifts. The helicopter begins to slide sideways through its own wash, closing on her.

"Everything that lens sees, the client sees," the gunman says. "And the bird goes home when he confirms delivery. It has a home plate — twenty minutes' flight. When it lands, the contract closes, the escrow pays, and the woman is wherever the client keeps his purchases. You won't find her. Your handler won't find her." He turns his palms up — an accountant's gesture, flat on his back at the edge of the light. "I know the home plate. I know the cutout. I've been on this client's sheets six years — I'm not loyal, I'm priced. So here's the trade."

He nods at his own vest. "Cuffs are on my belt. Walk me down that ladder as your prisoner — alive, intact — and I'm a document. Documents get traded. Or cinch me to this rail and take your chances with what you already know."

Below, the crawler's fingers tighten on the handle. The door holds. For now.

"Either way," the gunman says, level under the blades, "the bird doesn't wait. And neither does she."

The ladder waits at your back, three stories into moving dark. The document waits at your feet. Her door waits below, with a dying man's hand on it and a camera settling over both — and the rotor thump is already sliding away toward the annex.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content:
*I kick the cuffs off his belt. They clatter across the grating.* "No deal." *I grab him by the collar, haul him back to the rail, and tie him to it with the remaining cable.* "You're a distraction."

*I turn to the ladder, ignoring his protests. She's counting on me.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The stairwell door is steel, painted white, and the red alarm light makes it look wet. Through the narrow gap at the bottom, you hear footsteps below—slow, even, too calm for a guard patrol. One person. Maybe two. They stop just out of reach.

Mira’s weight shifts against you. Her fingers tighten on your sleeve.

“That’s a breach team,” she says, low enough for only you. “They’re not running. They’re listening.”

Static crackles in your earbud. Then a voice, clipped and unfamiliar, cuts through the noise. “Operative, do not take the stairs. Repeat, do not take the stairs.”

The corridor behind you pulses red. A door chime sounds at the far end, cheerful and wrong. The stairwell door has no handle on your side—push bar only. It is not locked. It is waiting.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content:
*I glance back down the hallway, then at the defector.* "Breach team, huh? Great."

*I push the bar on the stairwell door, just enough to see.* "Too many unknown variables down there. We're not going that way."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The push bar dips under your hand and the stairwell door cracks open six inches. Cold air slides out, carrying rust, sweat, and the faint click of a rifle selector. The red corridor light spills into the concrete shaft and paints the first landing. Two boots stand there. One boot shifts. A muzzle swings toward the opening, then waits.

Mira’s fingers press harder into your sleeve. Her breath comes fast through her teeth.

“They know we’re here,” she says.

The radio in your ear pops. The unfamiliar handler voice is gone. Static fills the channel, then a soft chime repeats from the far corridor. The cheerful door sound comes again, closer. The elevator. Someone summons it.

The stairwell door is not locked. It wants to open. The garage door is forty meters down the hall, behind the service alcove. The service tunnel mouth sits under the stairwell behind a maintenance panel. The panel seam glints in the red light.

Mira looks at the panel, then at the corridor. “The tunnel is worse,” she says. “But the stairs are a kill box.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The push bar dips again. Cold stairwell air hits your face. It carries concrete dust and gun oil. Mira gasps as you haul her through the gap. Her bad leg skids on the first step. Below, the muzzle swings up. The door edge bites into the shot. A spark jumps along the threshold.

The stairs rise in a tight spiral. Mira’s weight drags you toward the center. Each step makes her hiss through her teeth. The alarm bell fades inside the shaft. A wet, ringing silence fills the concrete.

At the top of the first flight, a maintenance hatch waits. Gray and seamless except for a screwdriver slot. To your left, the corridor continues upward. To your right, the stairs descend into darkness.

The radio pops.

“Operative,” the clipped voice says, “you’re off pattern. Return to protocol.”

Mira presses her forehead against your collarbone.

“The service tunnel,” she whispers. “It goes up before it goes down. If they seal the lower level, we still reach the roof catwalk.”

A heavy thump comes from below.

Then another.

Someone kicks the stairwell door. The metal flexes once, twice. The third kick breaks the latch.

The hatch is three steps above you. The upper corridor is darker, but it is clear. The stairs below are no longer a choice.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content:
*I push Mira ahead of me, toward the maintenance hatch.* "Clear the hatch. Now."

*I pull my sidearm, aiming it down the stairwell.* "Let's see if they like lead."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira stumbles up toward the hatch. Her hand slaps the gray metal, fingers scrabbling for the slot. The sidearm in your grip points down the stairwell. The muzzle is steady. The spiral concrete is not.

The door is off its hinges.

Two figures spill into the stairwell. One wears a black plate carrier. The other has a helmet with no face visible. They are fast, but the narrow shaft slows them. The first takes the steps two at a time. The second raises a rifle.

A shot cracks upward. Concrete dust puffs from the wall. Mira flinches but does not turn. Her fingers find the slot. The hatch cover lifts with a metallic groan.

“The radio,” Mira says. “If they have a drone relay—”

The second figure sees the hatch. The rifle muzzle dips toward it.

Your sidearm is aimed down. The first figure is close enough to count the scuffs on his boots. The second is behind him, half hidden by the stair rail. The alarm light makes their armor shine like wet plastic.

The radio pops again. The clipped handler voice is back, tight with something new. “Operative. Do not escalate. Do not open the roof.”

Mira’s knuckles turn white on the hatch cover.

“Up,” she says.

The first figure lunges.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The hatch flips up and the stairwell drops away behind you. The space beyond is a narrow server room: black racks, blue LEDs, raised floor tiles, and hot dry air. Mira collapses near your feet, breath tearing through her teeth.

The barricaded hatch door takes a blow. The frame buckles. Another blow. The latch screams.

Mira’s fingers find your sleeve. “The catwalk,” she says, pointing to a ceiling panel above a UPS unit. “It connects to the roof exhaust. If the fire door seals behind us, they can’t follow.”

Your radio pops. The clipped handler voice returns, calm and static-free. “Operative, you are inside a secure node. Do not interface. Do not access the terminal. Return to the extraction vector.”

A green terminal near the racks blinks. Its screen shows a building map: a red stairwell icon, a flashing lower tunnel, and a thin line that reads ROOF CATWALK. Another label pulses near the elevator bank: EXTRACTION VECTOR 2 — ACTIVE.

From below, a muffled voice says, “Cut it open.”

Mira’s face tightens. “They have a cutter.”

The hatch door bows inward. A thin line of orange sparks appears at its seam. The server room has three ways out: the ceiling panel to the roof catwalk, a narrow vent shaft between the racks with a loose grille, and the barricaded hatch door. The alarm pulses through the room in red waves.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Vent shaft. Now." I grab Mira and pull her towards the grille. *I don't even look at the terminal. Too much noise.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The grille comes off in your hands. Four screws, rusted loose, and the metal panel swings inward with a groan that echoes off the server racks. The vent shaft is tight. Sheet aluminum, narrow as a coffin lid, angled upward at thirty degrees. Blue LED light bleeds through the gaps between racks and makes the shaft walls shimmer.

Mira grabs the grille edge. Her knuckles go white. She pulls herself up, one arm, then the other, and her bad leg drags against the aluminum with a long scraping sound. She does not cry out. Her jaw just tightens until you hear the muscles work under the skin.

You climb in behind her. The shaft swallows you up to the chest. The hatch door behind you shrieks as the cutter bites deeper. Orange sparks arc across the server room floor. The blue LEDs flicker.

"Keep moving," Mira whispers. Her voice comes back down the shaft, thin and metallic. "The exhaust fan is forty meters. It cycles every ninety seconds. You feel the air change, you go."

You feel nothing but your own breathing and the scrape of Mira's jacket ahead of you. The shaft bends left, then right. Your shoulder drags along the seam. The metal bites through your shirt.

Behind you, the hatch gives way with a crash. A flashlight beam sweeps the server room. You hear boots on tile. Two sets. Then the muffled voice from below says, "They went up. Vent shaft. Call it in."

Your radio pops. The handler's voice is clean now. No static. Almost gentle.

"Operative. The vent connects to the roof. The roof is not clear. You do not understand what is on the roof."

You pull the earbud out. You do not throw it. You just pull it out and let it dangle.
