Above the duct grille, something heavy moves. Dust sifts onto the racks. A gloved finger appears through one slat, probing. Then a knife point works the screws from the other side.

Mira’s fingers fly across the keyboard. “I have partial access. The duct can be unlocked from here. The purge can be delayed thirty seconds. The door can be sealed with a magnetic lockout, but that kills the console.”

She looks up. Red alarm light bleeds into the blue server glow.

“Pick one.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Seal the door!" I shout, pulling out my sidearm. "Lock them out!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your shout cuts the server-room roar. Mira’s palm strikes the console. The wall panel flashes white, then solid blue.

MAGNETIC LOCKOUT ENGAGED.

The door frame slams as magnetic bolts bite home. The cabinet jerks against the brace. The cable groans. The door does not open again.

The console screen dies in Mira’s face. Blue light vanishes from her hands. For one second, the only illumination is the red alarm bleeding under the door.

Then the panel text changes:

ENVIRONMENTAL BREACH ACTIVE.  
SECTOR PURGE IN 00:34.  
LOCAL OVERRIDE OFFLINE.  
EAST NODE MANUAL RESET REQUIRED.

Mira’s breath catches. “The duct locks are still on default. They can open them from the outside.”

Above the grille, screws ping onto the tile. One. Two. Three. The duct cover shifts. A slim black tool slides through the gap, catches the edge, and wrenches the metal outward. A second tool follows. Cold air pours down, carrying the chemical sweetness from the corridor.

Your sidearm is heavy in your grip. The server racks press around you, humming, indifferent.

Your earpiece cracks open. The handler’s voice comes through hard and clear: “East node. Behind the third rack. Manual purge override. Buy her ten seconds.”

The grille bends free. A black glove drops into the room. Then a shoulder. Then the short, matte barrel of a subcompact weapon swings down toward Mira.

Mira looks at you. “Ten seconds.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Get to the node!" I yell, pushing Mira toward the third rack. *I fire two quick shots at the duct, aiming for the shoulder.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your shots crack twice inside the server room, sharp and flat against the industrial roar.

The first round punches through the bent duct casing and strikes the black-clad shoulder emerging from it. The arm jerks sideways. The subcompact fires once, wild, a round sparking off a ceiling conduit in a shower of white sparks. The second shot hits the duct frame, shearing metal. The intruder’s shape twists, loses its purchase, and drops backward into the shaft with a heavy impact.

For half a second, the duct is empty.

Then the grille tears completely free and crashes down onto the tile.

Mira moves on the echo of your shots. She throws herself toward the third rack, bad leg dragging. She catches the edge of the cabinet before she falls, hauls herself upright, and slams one hand against the rack’s side panel.

“Here,” she says. “East node.”

Behind the third rack, a narrow maintenance panel glows faint amber. Stenciled letters read:

EAST NODE  
ENVIRONMENTAL OVERRIDE  
MANUAL RESET ONLY

The chemical smell is thicker now. It clings to the back of your throat. The fans overhead reverse again, dragging the vapor upward in pale ribbons, but the floor is still crawling with it. Blue status lights along the racks flicker as the purge sequence fights the building’s own safety locks.

The wall panel by the sealed door updates:

SECTOR PURGE IN 00:27.  
EAST NODE RESET REQUIRED.  
LOCKOUT INTEGRITY: 81%.

The magnetic door shudders. Something hits it from the other side—not a boot this time, but a controlled mechanical ram. The cabinet jumps. Your cable brace sings. The lockout holds, but the blue panel flashes once, warning.

LOCKOUT INTEGRITY: 78%.

Above the open duct, movement returns. More gloves. More boots. Someone inside the shaft kicks the damaged casing outward, widening the hole. A voice echoes down, distorted but calm:

“Deploy second canister. Asset intact. Take the operative if exposed.”

Your earpiece bursts with static, then your handler’s voice cuts through:

“Manual reset. Red collar beneath the panel. Turn it clockwise and hold. Do not release until the counter stops.”

Mira’s fingers tear at the east node panel. It opens with a snap. Inside sits a heavy rotary switch, red as blood, surrounded by copper contacts and a small digital display.

She looks back at you. Her face is pale under the blue server lights.

“I need ten seconds,” she says. “If they drop into this aisle before I finish, they will drag me out.”

The duct opening yawns above the racks. Dust falls as weight shifts inside. Something metallic clinks against the lip of the shaft. Another canister, maybe. Or a weapon.

The purge counter on the wall pulses:

00:21.

Mira grips the red collar. Her knuckles whiten.

“Cover me,” she says.

The first black boot drops from the duct.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I level my sidearm at the duct.* "They want me, they have to come through me." I fire three quick shots, aiming for center mass as the first operative drops.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your sidearm barks three times in the cramped aisle. The muzzle flash turns the server racks white-blue. The first operative dropping from the duct meets the shots mid-fall. The first round strikes his chest plate. The second glances off the edge of his mask. The third bites into his shoulder and twists him sideways. He crashes back into the shaft, and the duct lip buckles under his weight.

Your ears ring. Hot brass skitters across tile. The chemical vapor flares in the muzzle glow.

Return fire comes instantly. A short burst chews the rack to your left. Sparks shower down. Blue status lights die in a quick cascade. Something hard tugs your sleeve, but the fabric does not catch fire.

A second canister drops through the open duct. It hits the floor and spins, hissing louder than the first. Thick white vapor coils upward, sweet and heavy.

From inside the shaft, a voice says: “Gas active. Move to bypass.”

The wall panel flashes:

SECTOR PURGE IN 00:16.  
EAST NODE RESET REQUIRED.  
LOCKOUT INTEGRITY: 71%.

The sealed door booms again. The cabinet jumps. Your cable brace bends into a shallow arc. The magnetic lock light flickers blue, then amber, then blue.

Mira’s hands shake over the red collar. “I need the full ten,” she says. “Do not let them break the line.”

Your earpiece crackles. The handler’s voice cuts through the roar: “Hold the aisle. Do not release early.”

In the duct, a second shape moves lower, using the first operative’s body as cover. A rifle barrel slides around the jagged edge. Behind it, a third gloved hand reaches for the lip of the shaft.

The purge counter drops:

00:13.

Mira turns the red collar. The display beside it lights:

RESET INITIATED.  
HOLD.

The rifle barrel steadies.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I drop to one knee, firing two shots at the rifle barrel.* "Not today, pal!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your two shots crack through the aisle. The first round sparks off the duct lip. The second hits the rifle’s barrel guard and jerks the muzzle upward. A burst tears into the ceiling instead of Mira. Sparks rain down. A voice inside the shaft curses.

Mira does not flinch. Her hands remain locked on the red collar. The small display pulses:

RESET HOLD.  
00:09.

The second canister hisses across the tile. White vapor coils around the racks and climbs in slow, heavy threads. Your eyes burn. The sweet chemical taste settles on your tongue.

The sealed door booms again. The cabinet slides one full inch. Your cable brace bends and sings. The wall panel flashes:

LOCKOUT INTEGRITY: 66%.  
SECTOR PURGE IN 00:08.

From the open duct, the second operative uses the wounded man as a shield. His boots find tile. His mask turns toward Mira. A third rifle appears in the shaft, angling past the wounded body.

Your earpiece splits with static. The handler’s voice comes through hard: “Left rack. Break their line. Keep her clear.”

Mira’s breath shakes, but her grip stays fixed. “Five seconds.”

The first operative on the floor lifts his weapon again. His barrel points at your position. Behind him, the third rifle clears the duct edge.

The purge counter flashes red:

00:07.  
DO NOT RELEASE.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I drop my sidearm and grab the nearest server rack, tearing it from its mounts.* "Get back!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your sidearm clatters across the tile. The server rack tears free from its mounts with a shriek of metal. Bolts snap. Cables whip. Blue lights burst in bright sparks as you drag the heavy frame into the aisle.

The first operative fires. Rounds punch into the rack face. The chassis shudders, catches, and turns the burst into a spray of hot fragments. The weight of the rack bends the duct lip downward. The second operative in the shaft jerks backward. The third rifle swings wide.

Mira keeps both hands on the red collar. “Three,” she says.

The wall panel strobes:

SECTOR PURGE IN 00:04.  
LOCKOUT INTEGRITY: 61%.

The door bucks under another ram blow. The cabinet slides. The chemical vapor curls around your boots, thick and sweet.

Your handler’s voice cuts through the static: “Hold the line. Two more seconds.”

The operative on the floor crawls toward Mira. His glove closes around her ankle.

Mira does not look down. Her eyes stay on the node display.

RESET HOLD.  
00:03.

Above the open duct, the ceiling panel bows. A heavy shape presses through the shaft. Dust falls. Metal groans.

The purge counter flashes red:

00:02.

The rack is hot in your hands, sparking, half-loose, and the aisle belongs to you for one more breath.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I shove the sparking rack into the operative trying to grab Mira.* "Get off her!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You press your ear to the cold metal. The door thrums against your skull — the building's own heartbeat, or the ventilation system working overtime. For three seconds, four, you hear nothing but the alarm's wail bleeding through from the corridor behind you.

Then: footsteps.

Not below. Above.

A single pair of boots, heavy, moving fast down the concrete steps. Two landings up, maybe three. The rhythm is wrong for someone fleeing — too deliberate, too even. Then a second pair joins the first. They don't speak. They don't need to.

Mira tenses against your shoulder. Her fingers dig into your collar. You pull back from the door, just an inch, and your eyes meet hers in the pulsing red dark. The stairwell is a trap. But it's the only trap that leads to the garage.

Below, the shaft drops into silence. No boots. No voices. Just four floors of empty concrete and the promise of a vehicle that may or may not still be there.

The door handle is cool under your palm. Above, the footsteps round the landing directly overhead. You have seconds before they hit this floor.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content:
*Damn it.* "Stay here," I whisper, pushing Mira gently behind the reinforced doorframe. I pull my silenced pistol. "Cover me."

I take a deep breath, and yank the stairwell door open.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The door hits the concrete wall. The crash rockets up the stairwell and dies in the red dark above. Two figures freeze on the landing overhead — black tactical gear, rifles half-lowered. The lead hostile's head snaps toward you. His eyes lock onto yours across ten feet of exposed concrete.

He barks a word you don't catch. Doesn't matter. His weapon starts to rise.

The second hostile breaks right, boots scraping the steps as he tries to gain an angle down the switchback. The emergency light above them strobes, turning their movements into a slideshow of shadow and crimson glare.

Behind you, Mira sucks in a breath but stays flat against the doorframe. The frame is thin cover. No cover at all if they decide to spray the landing.

The lead hostile's rifle clears his shoulder. His mouth opens. You see the whites of his teeth.

He fills your sights. The suppressor is steady in your grip. He exhales. You have half a second before he fires.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You spin. Mira's weight jerks against your shoulder as you haul her through the doorway. The stairwell swallows you. You charge the upward steps, straight into the crimson glare.

The lead hostile freezes. He expects prey to run, not charge. His rifle swings wide. You close the gap in two strides. Mira gasps against your neck. A muzzle flash or a shoulder check — the moment blurs. He folds. The concrete wall catches his skull with a wet crack.

The second hostile on the switchback twists back toward you, boots skidding on grit. His barrel swings down. You feel the itch of a red dot.

Below, the silence shatters. Boots hammer up from the garage level — a dozen pairs, maybe more. Shouts bounce off concrete. The pincer snaps shut.

You clear the landing. The door there — a faded label, a crash bar — waits. Mira's fingers claw your collar. Her breath comes in jagged bursts.

The second hostile's rifle spits. Concrete chips explode at your heels. The door below you — the one at your back — crashes open. The flood pours through.

You have one flight, maybe two, before the roof. Or you have whatever waits behind that crash bar. Blood — Mira's or yours — smears the railing.

The alarm screams. The stairwell breathes hot lead and colder fear.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content:
I shove Mira through the door with the crash bar. "Go, go, go!"

*I turn, firing two quick shots down the stairs, trying to buy us a second. It's a miracle if I hit anyone.* "Move!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your first round sparks off concrete. Your second vanishes into the churn below — a grunt, a stumble, maybe nothing at all. It buys you less time than you need.

Return fire shreds the doorway. You taste plaster and cordite. A round sears your sleeve as you throw yourself backward into the dark.

The stairwell's scream muffles to a distant, throbbing pulse. You stand in a narrow service corridor — sweating concrete, pipes humming overhead, a single dying bulb throwing long shadows. Mira is three strides ahead, her palm leaving a dark streak on the wall. She doesn't slow. Her left foot drags behind her, useless.

Behind you, the crash bar door shudders. A shoulder hits it from the other side. Then another. The metal groans.

Mira reaches the end. A metal ladder bolts to the wall, running straight up to a ceiling hatch. Beside it, a steel door marked ELEVATOR MACHINERY. No handle. No way through.

The hatch above has a simple slide latch. A faded sign warns: ROOF ACCESS — ALARM WILL SOUND.

The door behind you dents inward. A rifle muzzle punches through the thin metal, probing. Searching.

Mira grips the ladder. Her arms shake. She looks back at you over her shoulder. She can't climb fast. Not with that leg.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You scan the corridor for a server room. There is none. Only the cramped service passage, the humming pipes, and the dying bulb overhead. You lower Mira to the concrete floor beneath the ladder. Her injured leg folds at a bad angle, and she hisses through her teeth, but she stays quiet.

You whirl back toward the crash bar door. The rifle barrel jerks and twists in the torn metal, widening the gap. You grab a rusted length of pipe from the floor and jam it through the door's push bar, wedging the other end against the ladder's base bolt. The door convulses. The pipe groans against the steel. It won't hold forever. It might not hold for thirty seconds.

Mira presses her back to the wall and pushes herself straighter. Blood runs from her hairline. Her eyes meet yours in the gloom. "The roof," she breathes. "Alarm means open air. Means a chance."

Above, the hatch waits. The slide latch is thick with dust and old grease. Behind you, the pipe screeches against the doorframe. Boots hammer the metal. The wedge shifts. An inch. Then two.

Your hands shake. You force them still. You have a wounded defector, a failing barricade, and a ladder that leads to a screaming alarm and open sky.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Roof it is," I grunt. *No time for anything else.* I push the pipe further into the door, trying to buy a few more seconds. "Can you climb at all?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira looks from your face to the ladder and back. Her jaw sets. "I can climb," she says, her voice tight. "I cannot run." She grabs the lowest rung with both hands and hauls herself upward. Her left leg bangs against the metal rail, and she sucks in a sharp breath through her teeth. She climbs anyway — one rung, two — her arms trembling under her own weight.

Behind you, the pipe shrieks against the bolt. The door buckles, and a gloved hand snakes through the gap, groping for the wedge. Another shoulder slams the metal. The pipe bends. It gives.

The door bursts open.

The first hostile spills through, rifle level. Muzzle flash strobes the corridor. Bullets chew into the concrete at your feet, and you feel the snap of rounds passing an inch from your ribs. Sparks rain down from the ladder as a ricochet screams off the rungs. Mira freezes four rungs up, her body pressed flat against the rails.

A second hostile floods through. Then a third. The passage fills with shouting and the strobe of weapon lights. The dying bulb shatters overhead. Glass rains down.

Mira reaches the hatch. Her bloody fingers find the slide latch. She throws her weight against it. The metal resists, rusted or painted shut, and the latch refuses to budge. She hangs from one arm and strikes it with her palm. The latch groans but does not move.

Below, the lead hostile spots her. His rifle tracks upward.

You stand at the base of the ladder, smoke and plaster dust in your throat, your pistol hot in your grip. The ladder is your only line to the roof. The corridor behind you is a killing funnel with no cover and no exit.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Get down!" I scream at Mira, firing two quick shots at the lead hostile. *Damn it, Mira, open the hatch!* I empty the rest of the clip, praying for a hit.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your rounds stitch the corridor. The lead hostile jerks — a round punches through his shoulder, spinning him against the wall. His trigger finger convulses. His shot goes wide, chewing into the ladder an inch from Mira's white-knuckled grip. The second hostile twists as red mist leaves his throat. He folds. The third man dives, pressing himself flat against the doorframe.

Your slide locks back. Empty.

The third hostile peers around the frame. His rifle barrel rises. Mira drops from the ladder, landing hard on her good leg. She rolls beneath the lowest rung, back against the wall, chin to her chest. Blood drips from her hairline onto the concrete.

Return fire screams past your ear. You feel the heat of the round. Concrete chips spray your cheek. Shouts pour from the stairwell behind him — more boots, more weapons. The corridor fills with the rasp of Kevlar and the click of bolts snapping forward.

Mira grabs the rusted pipe from the floor. She swings it up at the hatch latch. Metal clangs against metal. The latch shudders, rust flaking away like dried blood. She swings again, screaming, her whole body behind the blow.

The latch snaps.

Harsh gray light floods down from the roof. A fresh alarm wails — shrill, piercing, joining the chorus below. Mira hauls herself through the hatch. Her left leg trails, dragging across the lip, leaving a dark smear.

The third hostile rises from his crouch. His rifle tracks toward the open hatch.

You stand at the base of the ladder. Your pistol hangs useless in your hand, the slide locked open. Smoke hangs in the corridor. The stairwell behind the hostile disgorges more figures — two, then four. Their weapons swing toward you. The ladder is your only line to the roof. The corridor is a killing box with no cover and no exit.

The first new hostile raises his rifle.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *No time to reload.* I throw the empty pistol at the nearest hostile. Then, I grab the ladder and start climbing, praying Mira has something to cover me with. "Go! Go! Go!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pistol leaves your hand. It spins through the smoke and cracks against the nearest hostile's forehead. His skull rocks back. He stumbles, his rifle barrel swinging wide. The shot he fires chews into the concrete near your heel.

You grab the ladder. Your palms slap cold metal. You climb. Your shoulders burn. Your boots find purchase. A bullet screams past your hip. Another strikes the rung beside your hand and rings like a bell. The ladder shudders.

Mira leans through the hatch above. Her bloodied fingers stretch toward you. Wind whips her hair across her eyes. She screams something — your name or a warning — but the words shred in the open air and the wailing alarms.

The hostiles below unleash a wall of lead. The corridor strobes white. Concrete chips patter against your back like hail. Something hot claws your outer thigh. You ignore it. You climb. Three rungs. Two. One.

Your hand closes on Mira's wrist. She grips yours with surprising strength. She pulls. You surge through the hatch.

The roof surface is loose gravel and tar paper. It scrapes your cheek as you roll clear. Mira collapses beside you, gasping, her left leg twisted beneath her.

But the hatch gapes open.

Boots clang on the ladder rungs below. Fast. Multiple sets. A rifle muzzle clears the lip. Then a helmet. Then cold eyes that search and find.

Twenty feet to your left, a ventilation housing hums. Beyond it, the roof edge drops to nothing — a six-story fall to a narrow alley. To your right, a rusted catwalk bridge stretches across a three-foot gap to the neighboring building. Its handrails are thin. Its planks are slick with rain.

The first hostile's shoulders clear the hatch. His weapon tracks toward your center mass.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it, they're fast.* I grab Mira's arm. "Can you make that bridge?!" I don't wait for an answer, pulling her towards it.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You haul Mira toward the catwalk. Gravel skids under your boots. The first hostile clears the hatch fully, his rifle coming up. A red dot dances across your shoulder blade.

Mira stumbles at your side, her left foot dragging. Three feet of open air separate this roof from the next. The catwalk sways, its planks slick with rain, its rails thin and rusted.

A shot cracks behind you. Tar paper bursts near your heel. Mira grabs the nearest rail with both hands and pulls herself onto the first plank. The bridge groans and dips under her weight.

You follow. The planks bounce. Wind howls up from the alley six stories down. Another shot rings out. Steel sparks where the round strikes the rail beside your hand.

Mira hauls herself forward, arm over arm. Her bad leg swings between the planks, kicking at empty air. Halfway across, a plank cracks under her knee. She lurches, catches herself, keeps moving. The neighboring roof waits — a yellow door, humming vents.

You reach solid concrete. Mira is one pace behind. The lead hostile steps onto the bridge. It shudders. Two more hostiles rise from the hatch behind him, their weapons rising.

Mira lunges. Her fingers find the lip of the roof. You grab her wrist and pull. She sprawls onto the wet concrete beside you, gasping.

But the bridge remains. The lead hostile advances, slow, his rifle steady on your center mass. The yellow door waits at your back. Locked or open — you have no idea.

Your thigh bleeds. Your lungs burn. Mira claws to her knees beside you.

The hostile takes another step. The bridge rattles. His finger slides to the trigger.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Cover me!" I yell, shoving Mira towards the yellow door. *This is it.* I charge the hostile, hoping to use my momentum to knock him off the bridge.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You surge forward. Your boot finds the first plank. The lead hostile's finger tightens. The rifle kicks against his shoulder. A round burns past your ribs. Then your shoulder slams into his chest.

The collision drives the air from his lungs. His boots lose purchase on the slick wood. He flails. The rifle spins from his grip and vanishes into the alley below.

But the bridge screams. The rusted bolts at your end shear free. The planks tilt like a dropping drawbridge. The hostile falls backward into empty air — his hands claw at your jacket, finding nothing.

The bridge collapses. The planks under your feet fall away. Your hands snap shut around the thin rail. The metal bites your palms, rusted and cold. Your body slams against the side of the building. Your legs dangle over six stories of nothing.

Above, on the original roof, the two remaining hostiles freeze at the shattered edge. One drops to a knee and raises his rifle. The gap is three feet, but the angle is bad. He waits for you to swing.

Behind you, Mira slams her palm against the yellow door's crash bar. The metal gives. The door opens into blackness. She looks back, blood running into her eyes, and reaches for you.

Your grip slips a fraction. The rail groans. The hostile's red dot finds your chest. Your thigh bleeds into the wind. The yellow door waits.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Grab my hand!" I yell, straining. *God, my arm is going to give out.* I swing a leg, trying to find purchase on the wall.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira's fingers brush yours. Her bloody hand clamps down on your wrist. Above, the hostile kneels at the roof's edge. His red dot steadies on your sternum. He exhales. His trigger finger moves.

The wind gusts. The broken bridge swings on its remaining cables. His shot goes wide — a spark jumps off the rail an inch from your thumb. The rail shudders. Your grip slips another fraction. Rust flakes fall into the black alley below.

Mira pulls.

Her other hand finds your belt. She hauls backward, her good leg braced against the doorframe, her body rigid with strain. Your boot scrapes against brick, finds a ledge, then a windowsill. You push. You surge upward. Your chest clears the roof lip.

Another shot cracks. Concrete dust erupts near your heel. You roll into the blackness beyond the yellow door. Mira collapses atop you. The door slams shut — she kicks it, or the wind does. The boom echoes. Darkness swallows the alley's roar.

For a moment there is only panting. Your hands shake. Blood drips from your palms where the rail bit in. Your thigh throbs in time with your pulse. Above, on the other side of the metal, voices shout. Boots hammer concrete. But the crash bar holds. The blackness is absolute.

Then: a faint red glow down the corridor. An exit sign. The hum of distant machinery.

Mira pushes herself up. Her breath rasps. "Utility level," she whispers. "Maintenance shafts. They go everywhere."

She points. The red glow illuminates a junction ahead. Left, a stairwell descending into deeper dark. Right, a narrow passage marked PARKING STRUCTURE — LEVEL B2. The floor under you vibrates. Somewhere close, an elevator hums.

Behind you, the yellow door rattles. A fist pounds metal. Then a rifle stock. The crash bar screams against its mount. It is giving way.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Parking garage," I gasp, pushing myself up. "Move!" *No way we're going down more stairs.* I grab Mira's hand and pull her toward the red glow, limping.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You ease Mira back against the wall — she braces herself one-handed, jaw tight — and cross to the stairwell door alone. The red light washes over the metal in slow pulses. You press your ear to the seam, one hand resting on the push-bar.

Silence first. The bad kind. Then it comes: footsteps below. Not one set — two, maybe three, out of sync. Heavy boots on concrete, climbing. Not hurrying. They don't need to hurry. A radio squawks somewhere beneath them, and a voice answers, flat and unhurried, in a language you almost place. Then, closer, a sound that tightens your chest: the dry click of a safety, thrown up the stairwell by bare walls.

You ease back. Mira has been reading your face the whole time, and whatever she finds there, she doesn't argue with it.

"Maintenance shaft," she whispers. "One landing down. It drops straight through to the parking structure. I used it when—" She stops. Swallows. "When I still worked for them."

The boots keep climbing. Then, above you, a door bangs open. The stairwell is a throat closing at both ends.

Your earpiece crackles. One fragment of your handler's voice claws through the static — "*—not the garage—*" — and dies.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* I grab Mira's arm. "Okay, shaft it is. Can you move at all?" I don't wait for an answer, already pulling her towards the stairwell door. "Where exactly is this thing?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You pull her through the door before the words are fully out of her mouth. The stairwell swallows you both — concrete, red light, the smell of dust and gun oil drifting down from above. The boots above pause. Someone shouting, muffled. They heard the door.

"One landing," Mira breathes. She plants her good leg on the first step and lets you take her weight. "Halfway down — the wall's a different color. Gray panel, no handle. It's on hinges. Push the left edge."

You take the stairs fast and quiet, her steps a stuttered rhythm beside yours — hop, drag, hop, drag. Above you, the door bangs again and the boots start down. Faster now. Hurrying.

Landing. There it is — a gray panel set flush into the wall, so clean it looks like part of the concrete. Mira reaches past you and raps twice on the left edge with her knuckle. "Push. Hard. It sticks."

You put your shoulder into it. It groans, gives, swings inward on a gust of cold stale air. Blackness. The shaft drops away beneath you, a vertical throat of darkness with maintenance rungs bolted down one side, vanishing into nothing.

Below, the boots hit your landing.

Mira grabs your sleeve. "Rungs only go halfway. After that it's a slide chute — you'll land hard, but you'll land." She looks at the darkness, then at you, and something almost like a smile crosses her face. "I go first. I'm already broken. What's one more."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You spin. Your hand closes on Mira's sleeve and you haul her back onto the stairs — up.

She stares at you like you've lost your mind. Then her eyes drop to your earpiece, and understanding lands. "The garage," she breathes. "They're *in* the garage."

Then she moves. No argument. Going up on a dead leg is a different animal from going down — you take her weight across your shoulders and climb, her good foot slapping concrete, her breath sawing in your ear. One step. Two. The alarm throbs with every heartbeat.

Below you, the boots reach the shaft landing. Light explodes up through the open panel — a flashlight beam raking the stairwell, splashing across the steps you just abandoned. A voice, sharp. Another answers from above — and the boots above *stop*. You freeze on the step, Mira's weight dragging at you, and listen: a radio click. A few flat words.

They've heard the panel. They know you didn't come down. They're holding position, letting the men below push you up into their arms.

Which means, for one held breath, nobody is moving.

You spend it climbing. Landing — the door you came through stands ajar, leaking red corridor light. One flight above it, the boots start down again. Faster.

You shoulder through the gap. The corridor takes you back — same red pulse, same screaming alarm, the overturned cart where you left it. Mira sags against the wall, gray-faced, one hand pressed to her leg. Blood between her fingers now. You don't look at that either.

Your earpiece spits static. One word claws through this time: "*—roof—*" — then nothing.

Mira hears it. Her eyes go up, toward the ceiling, toward the stairwell you just fled, and her jaw sets.

Then, down the corridor, past a bank of elevator doors: a chime. A brass arrow ticks over to your floor.

The doors roll open.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it!* I push Mira behind the overturned cart. "Stay down," I hiss. I draw my weapon, peering around the corner at the elevator. "Roof it is."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The doors roll all the way open. For one long second the car looks empty — warm light, brass rail, deep carpet. You hold your fire.

Then the details land wrong. The security camera in the ceiling corner is dead, its lens capped with black tape. The air rolling out smells of gun oil. And the wall mirror has been knocked askew — angled down, to lie about the floor of the car.

The muzzle flash comes from low.

The corridor detonates. Rounds hammer the overturned cart a foot from Mira's head — she flattens, arms over her ears — sparks skip off the brass doorframe, off the polished floor, and a chip of plaster stings your cheek as the volley tears past. You're pressed flat against the wall, weapon up, ears ringing.

Then the alarm dies mid-burst.

The silence after is worse. Cordite drifts down the corridor, and in the quiet you hear it plainly: behind you, the stairwell door swings open. Boots. More than one pair. No care for noise now.

Mira's hand closes on your wrist. Her face is chalk, her voice a scrape. "Freight elevator. End of the hall, past the kitchens — big enough for laundry carts. It runs all the way to the roof." A second burst from the elevator chews the wall above her. She doesn't flinch. "It's on the old system. No cards, no call buttons — just a maintenance code. I know the code."

A shape detaches from the open car — low, weapon up, using the doorframe for cover. Behind you, a flashlight beam sweeps the red corridor from the stairwell.

"Roof," Mira says, flat. "And pray your handler is still *yours* by the time we get up there."

Two directions of fire. Forty meters of open floor between you and the freight lift. And Mira, bleeding, watching you — waiting to move when you move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The server room is a door you passed and didn't see — windowless, steel, its card reader blinking green. Somebody left it unlocked when the alarm hit. You half-carry Mira the last thirty meters, exposed under the dead camera's blind eye, and nothing shoots. The quiet holds like a held breath.

Inside is another world. Cold air. Blue light. Ranks of racks humming, status LEDs blinking a calm green that has no idea what's happening thirty meters away.

You settle Mira against a cabinet — she hisses through her teeth — and go back for the door. You drag a rolling unit across it and cinch cable ties from an open shelf through the lever and a rack handle. It won't stop bullets. It will stop the first two seconds, and right now two seconds is a currency.

Then Mira pulls a knife from her boot and cuts her trouser leg open.

"You've been very polite," she says, not looking up. "Not looking. Look now."

You look. High thigh, a deep groove, blood welling slow and dark. She loops a cable from the floor around it, twists, and her face goes chalk. "Knot it. My fingers have resigned."

While your hands work, she tips her chin at a KVM cart in the corner. One monitor still lives — a grid of camera feeds.

Elevator lobby: the gunman and two more, stacking at the doors, checking weapons without hurry. Stairwell: door standing open, empty. Kitchen: shadows moving past steel counters. And one feed labeled ROOF — black. Dead.

"Roof camera's out," Mira says. "Cameras in this building don't die of old age."

Your earpiece chimes — a soft double tone. Link lost. Mira watches your face while it lands. Then the static comes back, and it's wrong: rhythmic. Three pulses. Pause. Three pulses.

"That's not interference," she says quietly. "That's a signal. Your handler — or someone wearing his frequency."

On the kitchen feed, a man walks past the hanging pots with something long cradled in his arms, angling toward the far alcove. Toward the freight lift.

Mira follows your eyes to the screen. "They're covering the lift," she says. "So." She flexes her leg, testing the knot, and looks up at you — calm, gray, waiting. "Think fast."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Damn it, they're too fast." I grab the KVM cart, wheeling it closer to Mira. "How old *is* this system?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira drags herself higher up the cabinet to see the monitor as the cart rolls in. "Older than you," she says. "Older than me. Analog coax and time-lapse tape. No network, no remote lockout, nothing talks to anything unless it's copper. This building doesn't have a security system. It has a *habit*."

She points past your shoulder at the rack. Third shelf down: a scuffed black box with a tape door, its buttons worn blank. "That's the head-end. Every camera in the building runs through this room on its way down to the security office. Which means—" her thumbnail pops the tape door; a cassette sits inside, half-spooled "—whatever they're watching downstairs doesn't have to show *tonight*."

She turns the cassette over in her hands. "Stop the record, rewind, hit play. Their wall shows them tonight, an hour ago. Empty corridors. Nobody bleeding. It'll hold until someone sharp reads the date stamp in the corner." Her eyes come up to yours. "Minutes. Not hours."

Then, quieter: "And whoever silenced that alarm knew the panel code. Hit teams don't get panel codes. Somebody inside gave them the building."

The pulses keep coming through your earpiece. Three. Pause. Three.

Mid-breath, they change.

Two. Pause. Two.

Mira goes very still. "Three and three is a hold signal. *Under duress — my words aren't mine.* That's how we said it, anyway." She looks at the ceiling, at nothing. "Two and two is proceed." A beat. "Or somebody made him give up the codebook, and now they're fishing to see if you bite."

On the kitchen feed, the man with the long gun reaches the alcove. A second figure drags a laundry cart flush against the freight lift's outer doors and walks away from it, unhurried.

"They're not chasing the lift," Mira says. "They're *holding* it. Which means they think you need it."

On the corridor feed, the gunman from the elevator car starts down the line of doors. He moves like a man with time — housekeeping closet, swings open, light spills out, door closes. A storage room. Same. Each handle turns without ceremony, each door dies, and between him and your barricaded steel there are now exactly two doors left.

Two. Pause. Two. The signal repeats, patient as a metronome.

Mira holds the cassette out to you, flat on her palm.

"Your handler said roof," she says. "The roof camera is dead. And the channel is telling you to proceed." Her voice doesn't rise at all. "So decide what you believe before that man decides for you."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I look at the cassette, then at Mira. "Proceed where, exactly? To the roof that's covered?" I push the KVM cart back a bit. "And that signal could be a trap." I glance at the kitchen feed. "They're waiting for us."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira doesn't answer right away. She pulls the cassette back off her palm, and something in her face suggests you've finally asked the right question.

"You don't kill a camera to set an ambush," she says. "You kill it because you're about to do something you don't want *recorded*. That camera died before you ever reached this floor. Whatever they didn't want on tape already happened up there." She turns the cassette over. "And the tape doesn't know the camera's dead."

She doesn't wait for permission. She slots the cassette into the head-end, thumbs through menus with the boredom of long practice — stop, rewind, the spools turning in the little window — and hits play.

The monitors change. The corridor feed empties. The kitchen goes dark and still. The elevator lobby shows nothing but brass doors and warm light. Somewhere below you, a wall of monitors is telling a room full of people that this building is fine.

"Down there, right now, their wall is lying to them," Mira says. "Up here, it's about to tell us the truth. Last hour of the roof." She scrubs the feed back. "Watch."

The roof feed blooms: sodium lights, a helipad, wind sock turning. Empty. Then a timestamp ticks forward and landing lights wash the frame. A helicopter settles. Men deplane fast, weapons slung, fanning out — and among them, a man in a gray coat, hands zip-tied in front of him, helped down like cargo. You know him before you see his face. You know him by the coat. By the way he keeps his weight off his heels even now.

Your handler. Alive. Twenty minutes ago.

Beside him paces a second man — long coat, gloves, phone at his ear, unhurried. Mira goes rigid against the cabinet.

"That's Marek," she says, and her voice has gone somewhere flat and far. "He doesn't run hit teams. He runs *audits*. He doesn't do guns. He does questions." She swallows. "Your man is alive because Marek is still asking. And Marek doesn't get panel codes and a building handed to him unless someone very senior opened the door."

On the feed, a guard walks the handler toward a rooftop access door. Then the image tears into static. Camera dead. Twenty minutes ago.

And your earpiece goes quiet. The pulses stop.

Mira hears the silence the same moment you do. "He stopped signaling," she whispers. "Either they stopped asking, or he stopped answering."

The monitors are lying now, which means they're lying to you too — the corridor feed shows an empty hall an hour old, and the man clearing doors has vanished from your eyes. So you use your ears instead. Through the steel, faint, muffled: a handle turning. A door swinging. Latching. Then another. Each one closer, each one unhurried.

The second-to-last door dies.

Mira pulls herself up the cabinet, weight on her good leg, and looks at you with the calm of a woman reading a menu.

"Stairs are a funnel. Lift is a trap. Roof is a question I'd rather answer in person," she says. "And remember what you were sent for. It isn't him. It's me." A beat. "But he's the only one who can make an extraction *real*."

Down the corridor, footsteps start again. Unhurried. Coming toward the only door you have left.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "He's not a question, he's collateral," I mutter, my eyes on the door. "And Marek. *Damn it*." I grab Mira. "Okay. Freight lift code. Now. We're going to the roof."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For half a second, something moves through Mira's exhaustion that might be approval. "There he is," she murmurs. "The man who decides."

Then her voice drops to a recitation, flat and exact. "Nine. Zero. One. One. Seven. Four. The building's commissioning date. Marek's people never changed it — sentiment is a security flaw." She saws through your cable ties with her boot knife, one-handed, while you ease the rolling unit back from the door on silent casters. "Brass plate on the left jamb of the freight doors. Hinged, painted over — flip it down, punch the code, throw the lever. Wrong twice and it sulks for a full minute." Her eyes flick up. "We don't have a full minute of anything."

She grips your shoulder as you gather her weight. "And understand what you're buying. Old freight lifts *sing*. The whole shaft hears the motor. The roof will know we're coming before the doors part — so whatever you do up there, decide it now."

Down the corridor, the last handle turns.

You take her across your shoulders and slip through the gap you left. The corridor is ordinary light now, the alarm dead, and somehow that's worse — nothing strobing to hide in, just clean visibility and your own shadow. You move away from the turning handle, past the bend. Behind you: a door swings. Then steel — the server room door, tested, held. A pause. A low voice. A radio click.

The quiet is officially over.

Your earpiece shifts. Not silence — wind. Faint, hollow, and beneath it two voices pitched too low to parse, and under everything the idle whine of rotors. Mira hears it the same moment you do. Her eyes close for half a second. "That's roof wind," she breathes. "Somebody's mic is still live. He's still on the air." She doesn't say *still alive*. She doesn't have to.

Swing doors with porthole windows. Through. The kitchen is steel and shadow, old grease and bleach, hanging pots dead still. You set Mira down behind a prep station and look past the far counter to the service corridor — the alcove, the freight lift's outer doors, the laundry cart parked flush against them.

And the man. Long gun cradled, shoulder against the wall, muzzle angled at the corridor mouth — the way you'd have come, if you'd come the obvious way. He hasn't looked behind him once. The second figure, the one who parked the cart and walked away — the tape can't tell you where he went. It's an hour old and lying.

The brass plate sits on the left jamb. Twenty meters from his muzzle to the code.

Mira pulls herself up beside you, gray-lipped, breathing through her teeth. She turns the boot knife in her hand and offers it to you handle-first, saying nothing with her mouth and everything with her eyes.

"He stopped checking behind him," she whispers. "People only do that when they're the ones waiting."

Twenty meters. One code. One man who isn't looking at you.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I take the knife. "Stay here. If anyone comes, use this." I point to a heavy pot on the counter. "Hit them hard." *Then I move*.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira takes the pot in both hands, hefts it once, and nods. Her version of *go*.

You move.

The kitchen gives you lanes: the long shadow of the walk-in, a steel rack of hanging pots, the blind side of the prep counter. Twenty meters, broken into fives. You time yourself to the wind in your earpiece — moving when it swells, freezing when it thins — using the roof's weather as your cover noise.

Halfway across, the wind parts. A voice, too close to the live mic, meant for the room and not the transmitter: "*—when it sings, nobody touches the doors. We let it open. Then we see what we bought.*" Marek. Then the wind swallows him again.

They're not waiting to ambush the lift. They're waiting to *shop*.

The last five meters. The guard is younger than his rifle. Weight on the wall, jaw working gum, eyes fixed on the corridor mouth. He never checks behind him. Mira is right — people only stop checking when they've stopped expecting anything.

He shifts his sling. One heartbeat of pure panic — and then you're on him.

Hand over his mouth. Knife in behind the ribs, angled up, the way the manual draws it and your stomach argues with. You ride him down slow, taking his weight into your knees, your free hand closing on the rifle sling so nothing rings against the tile. It is short. It is silent. It is the worst ten seconds of a night that has had others.

He goes still in your arms.

You don't look at that either.

You guide him down into the alcove shadow behind the laundry cart, wipe the blade on his coat, and kneel at the jamb. His blood finds a grout line and behaves. The brass plate is exactly where she said — painted flat into the wall like a lie. Your knife tip finds the seam, and the hinge gives with a click no louder than a knuckle. Keypad. Six mechanical buttons, worn blank. Above them, the lever, threaded with a breakaway safety wire.

Twenty meters back, Mira rises to her good knee behind the prep station and lowers the pot. Her eyes go from you, to the dead man, to the open plate. She doesn't smile. She nods again, slower.

Then the radio on the dead man's chest rig breathes.

"*One. Status.*"

Wind behind the voice. Whoever is calling is up top, unhurried, patient as a metronome. A pause long enough to be a question.

"*One. Key me twice, or I come to you.*"

The kitchen holds still. Mira's eyes lock onto yours across the steel — the radio, the keypad, the doors, the clock you can't see. The lift will sing the second it moves. The roof is waiting to see what steps out. And kneeling in the alcove with a dead man's radio asking for a voice, you have about three seconds to decide what this building hears next.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hit the radio twice, then quickly punch the code. Nine. Zero. One. One. Seven. Four. I glance at Mira, then back at the keypad, my hand hovering over the lever.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Two clicks. The radio takes them without comment. A breath of wind. "*Copy.*"

Then silence — the kind you don't trust, because it came too easy. Keying twice isn't words. It's a coin flip over a live frequency, and somewhere above you a man just accepted a coin.

The keypad buttons go down under your thumb like engine parts: 9. 0. 1. 1. 7. 4. A pause that lasts a year. Then a deep, dusty *thunk* from inside the wall, and the safety wire on the lever snaps with a sound like a snapped guitar string. You throw it.

The lift doesn't sing.

It *grinds* — old cables taking load, a motor coughing awake somewhere above, a vibration that climbs through the floor and up your spine. Mira's face says it all as she drags herself the last twenty meters, one hand on the counters, the pot abandoned. Every ear in the building is hearing this.

The outer doors part. A cage, not a car — scissor gate, wood floor worn silver, hanging chain. You manhandle her in, kick the folded laundry cart in after to muffle her silhouette, and haul the inner gate down. The lever only has one direction left.

"*Two,*" the radio says suddenly, from the dead man's chest. Not a question. A summons. "*Roof. Now.*" A pause, and then, softer, almost bored — the worst possible tone: "*And tell One his gum is louder than his radio.*"

Whoever called status check isn't calling One's radio. One is *down*, and Two just proved it — because One should have answered himself by now.

Above you, the lift shudders and begins to climb. Through the scissor gate the kitchen recedes in slices — the alcove, the cart, the shadow that used to be a man. Mira slumps against the cage wall, white-knuckled on the chain, and looks up at the dark shaft streaming past.

"There's no stopping this thing between floors," she says. "You knew that." Not a question either. Her hand finds your sleeve. "So here's what we have. They want the doors to *open* — Marek said let it sing, see what we bought. They think they're getting a package delivered. Which means for about four seconds after these doors part, nobody shoots."

The wind is louder now through your earpiece — you're climbing toward its source. Under it, boots on concrete. Moving. Two sets, positioning, unhurried, converging somewhere above the shaft's mouth.

"Four seconds," Mira repeats. Her breath is shallow. Sweat has cut a line through the dust on her face. "They'll be looking at the cage. Not at what steps out of it. Not at where it came *from*." Her eyes drop to the dead man's rifle, still slung across your shoulder. Then back to you. "The helipad is portside of the lift doors. Marek likes to stand where he can watch his own exit."

The lift grinds past the fourth floor. Third. The motor noise swallows everything, and in that swallowed dark, Mira says, very quietly:

"When they open — don't fight all of them. Fight the *mechanic*. Whoever's hands go to the gate chain first. Because whoever opens this door is about to lean into arm's reach of you."

Second floor. First. Above, light — a thin, growing wedge of sodium white under the shaft's mouth. Boots settle. A voice, close now, carried down the shaft itself: "*Easy. Whatever it is, it's come to us.*"

You go up into the light.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I level the rifle. "Get ready to move, Mira. And don't look back." My finger finds the safety.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The cage slams into its stops — a full-body shudder, the chain jerking taut in Mira's fist — and above you the outer doors part on groaning rollers. Light pours down the shaft. Sodium white, torn sideways by rotor wash.

The roof.

The wind you've been hearing through your earpiece for ten minutes hits you for real now, cold and wet, ripping at your collar. Beyond the shaft mouth: a helipad thirty meters across, its painted H slick with dew, wind sock standing straight out like a pointing arm. The sky at the roofline has gone from black to iron gray. Dawn is coming whether anyone extracts you or not.

A helicopter idles at the pad's edge, rotors turning, nav lights blinking red-white-red. A pilot sits behind the glass, patient as furniture.

Between the lift and the pad: two men. Rifles held at low ready — not up, not aimed at the cage. Their weight is wrong for an ambush. They're standing like men waiting for a delivery.

Behind them, near the pad, a man in a long coat and gloves, phone lowered, head tilted. Marek. And at the pad's edge, on his knees, wrists zip-tied in front, gray coat torn at one shoulder, face bruised but the posture still perfect — weight off his heels, even now.

Your handler. Alive. His eyes find the cage.

*One.* The guards register the cage — and the rifle inside it. Confusion, not fear. Muzzles twitch up an inch and stop, because their orders said *nobody touches the doors, we see what we bought*, and orders are slower than instinct.

*Two.* The younger one's eyes find the dead man's rifle slung across you. His jaw stops working.

*Three.* Marek's gloved hand comes up — flat palm, not a weapon gesture. *Hold.* He takes one step closer, unhurried, reading the cage like a manifest. His voice arrives twice, once through the air and once thin and ghostly through your earpiece, off the live mic: "Well. They said two. A woman and a professional." A small, genuine-seeming smile. "You've saved my people a trip. Do come out."

Your handler looks at you — at the rifle, at the cage, at Mira — and gives one small, deliberate shake of his head. Not fear. Arithmetic. A man telling you the board is worse than it looks.

*Four.* The second guard — big, gloved, mechanical — steps to the gate because it's his job and nobody has countermanded it. His hands go to the chain. Exactly as she said. He leans in, eyes down on the latch hook, throat an arm's length from your muzzle.

Mira doesn't breathe the word. She just exists it — *mechanic* — her knife hand loose at her side, the laundry cart at her knee, her whole body coiled around one good leg.

The chain lifts. The gate begins to slide. Rotor wash flattens the wind sock, the handler's coat, the whole roof — and for one more second, the last of the four, nobody has decided anything.

The mechanic's face comes into arm's reach. He looks up.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Now.* I shove the rifle into the mechanic's gut, hard, then use the momentum to swing it up, butt of the stock catching him under the chin. He goes down. I bring the rifle up, aiming at Marek. "Your move, Marek."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum stopped wiping his hands and looked toward the shop entrance. Nobles had money but no patience, and they never tipped well. He glanced at the bucket of coal, then at the curved blade waiting on the anvil.*

"Noble wait," Grum said. "Rich man no rush Grum. Grum finish blade."

*He set the hammer on the anvil with a short, hard clack.* "Coal down. Grum talk to him."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, relieved I don't have to haul the heavy bucket all the way to the forge mouth.* "Right. I'll tell him." *I set the bucket down with a thud that sends a puff of coal dust into the air.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum’s jaw tightened. A noble coming to the forge usually meant trouble, and trouble had a way of landing on the person nearest the hammer. He looked at the coal bucket, then at the boy’s soot-streaked face.*

“Apprentice, keep fire fed,” Grum said. “Grum finish this blade first. Then Grum talk to rich man. He can wait in doorway. No touch hot metal.”

*He set the curved steel back into the coals and watched the flame climb along its edge.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum heard the noble’s voice rise and felt his own temper heat faster than the forge. He set the tongs down with deliberate care, wiping both hands on his apron before turning toward the door. A commission was not a command, and a smith who bent to every shout would end up making bad steel.*

"Show sword no quick." *Grum’s voice stayed low.* "Grum forge, not magic."

*He pointed at the glowing bar on the anvil.* "Steel must heat, bend, cool. Two days. Maybe three."

*The noble’s face reddened, but Grum did not step back.* "Shout no help forge. Angry face no heat fire. Grum no dog. Grum no slave."

*He crossed his thick arms.* "You want blade good, you wait. You want blade fast, go to cheap man. Grum make honest steel."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I cringe a little as Grum lays into the noble. This isn't going to end well.* "Um, Grum, maybe not shout at the rich guy?" *I pick up the coal bucket again, trying to look busy.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum heard the warning and gave a short nod, though his mouth did not soften. He kept his voice low, but he did not turn from the noble.*

“Apprentice, keep coal near,” Grum said. “Grum no shout. Grum speak true.”

*He looked at the noble with flat, hard eyes.* “Rich man, wait or leave. Grum make steel, not words. Grum no slave.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince, setting the coal bucket down again.* "He's really red now, Grum." *I eye the noble nervously, hoping he doesn't decide to take out his anger on me.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum saw the color in the noble’s face and stepped sideways, placing his broad body between the man and the apprentice. He did not reach for a hammer, but his hands stayed free and heavy, the hands that could bend red steel.*

“Boy, stand near Grum. Rich man no touch.”

*Grum looked at the noble. His voice was low, like fire under coals.*

“Angry face no heat forge. If you shout, Grum point to door. If you swing, Grum point to hot steel.”

*He jerked his chin toward the anvil.*

“No sword by dawn. No word by dawn. Grum forge right, or Grum forge no.”

*He kept his eyes on the noble, but one hand rested near the coal bucket, ready to block or shove, not to hit.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum stopped mid-sentence. The cry from the forge pulled his head around faster than any noble shout. He saw the red burn on the boy’s hand and the steam near the hot steel. Something inside him went cold, then hot.*

“Apprentice, burn hurt?”

*He turned away from the noble at once, stepping into the shop. He took a clean cloth from the shelf and thrust it under the water barrel, filling it with cold water. Then he set the cloth near the burned hand.*

“Cool it. Burn need cool.”

*The noble began to speak, but Grum lifted one broad hand.*

“No talk. Rich man, wait. Grum fix hurt hand.”

*He looked at the anvil, then at the door.*

“No sword today. Grum no make steel while boy hurt. Grum smith. Grum fix.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My hand throbs, and tears well in my eyes from the pain.* "It really stings, Grum." *I carefully place my hand in the cool, wet cloth, trying to stifle a whimper.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum knelt beside the apprentice, the forge heat still clinging to his back. He looked at the burned hand with a smith’s careful eye—red skin, a blister swelling, no black dead flesh. That was good. It was bad enough, but not ruinous.*

“Good. Cold cloth help,” Grum said, his voice lower now. “Blister bad if pop. Leave whole.”

*He reached for a clean strip of linen and the small pot of salve he kept for shop cuts. The noble in the doorway made a noise, but Grum did not turn. He pointed at the street.*

“Noble wait. Outside.”

*Then he set the salve on the cloth and wrapped the burn gently. His huge hands moved as if handling thin glass.*

“Salve cool burn. Grum wrap hand. No make steel today. Grum fix hurt first.”

*He looked up at the apprentice. For once, his scowl was gone.*

“Pain pass slow. Grum keep cloth cool. If hand hurt bad, Grum go to healer.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, sniffling a little.* "Thanks, Grum." *I lean against the workbench, trying to stop shaking. The noble is still muttering by the door.* "He's still there."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum heard the muttering and turned his head. The noble’s face was still red, still tight. Grum did not raise his voice, but he did not move from his place between the boy and the door.*

“Rich man, leave,” Grum said. “Grum no make sword for loud man.”

*He jerked his chin toward the street.*

“You want good blade, you wait. You want fast junk, you pay cheap smith. Grum no slave. Grum no dog.”

*The noble started to speak. Grum lifted one hand, palm flat.*

“No talk. Grum fix hurt first.”

*Then he turned back to the boy, softer now.*

“Apprentice sit. Grum watch burn. No steel today. No fire work. Grum fix hurt first.”

*He moved a stool near the bench, then kept his eyes on the doorway and the anvil both.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I slide onto the stool, cradling my bandaged hand.* "He's gonna tell everyone in town you're impossible to work with, Grum." *I wince, not from the burn, but from the thought of Grum's reputation taking a hit.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum’s face did not move, but his thick fingers tightened on the rag beside the boy’s bandaged hand. He had heard richer men threaten him before. He had also seen their swords after one season of rain. They bent. They chipped. They came back to Grum when the cheap blade failed.*

“Town talk no hurt steel,” Grum said. “Grum forge true. Grum forge slow. Good blade make noise. Bad man talk. Grum no care.”

*He glanced toward the noble, then at the apprentice’s wrapped hand.*

“Loud man pay cheap smith. Cheap smith make cheap sword. Sword break. Then man need Grum.”

*He set a cup of cool water near the boy, not touching the burn.*

“Apprentice rest hand. Grum watch fire. Grum watch door.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sip the water gratefully, the coolness a welcome contrast to the throbbing in my hand.* "But what if he tells the Duke? Then we'd really be in trouble."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum heard the name and did not move toward the door. He let it sit like cold iron on a bench. Nobles used rank the way weak men used a hammer—too fast, and only to hide that they did not know how to swing.*

“Duke pay silver. Grum make steel. Steel no lie. Steel no fear.”

*He looked at the noble, then at the burn on the boy’s hand.*

“Let loud man talk. Talk no heat forge. Talk no fix hurt hand.”

*He placed a clean rag beside the bandage and kept his broad back toward the door, not because he feared the noble, but because he would not show him where the boy stood.*

“Grum finish burn. Grum watch fire. Grum watch door. Rich man leave, or rich man wait quiet.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take another sip of water, my eyes darting between Grum and the door.* "He's still there, you know. Just standing there, glaring."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum did not jump at the warning. He watched the noble with flat eyes, then moved his stool so that his shoulder blocked the door from the boy. The water cup sat near the bandage, sweating in the forge heat.*

“Noble, stop glare.” *Grum’s voice was low, but it carried.* “Grum see you. Grum no care.”

*He turned half his head, just enough to keep the man in sight.*

“You can wait quiet, or you can leave. Grum fix hurt. Grum watch forge.”

*The noble drew breath. Grum raised one thick finger.*

“Glare no warm steel. Angry face no make good blade.”

*He looked down at the apprentice, and his scowl softened only at the edges.*

“Apprentice, sit. Burn need rest. Grum keep water cold. Grum keep boy safe.”

*Then Grum turned back to the door, broad and unmoving, like an anvil set in stone.*

“Rich man want sword? Rich man sit down. Rich man shut mouth. Outside. Grum no serve glare.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, leaning back against the cool stone wall. The pain in my hand is starting to dull, thanks to Grum.* "He's really not going to leave, is he?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The rag stopped moving. Grum hung it on the anvil's horn, slow and deliberate, the way a man sets down something he'd rather throw.*

"Urgent," *he repeated, tasting the word like spoiled milk.* "Nobles always urgent. Merchant who pays fair — he waits three weeks for his blade. That is fine. That is how craft works. But noble walks in, and whole world must stop and spin for him."

*The last noble who had stood in this shop had ordered twenty arrowheads and a pair of riding spurs, taken them on delivery, and paid in a promise. Grum still had that promise somewhere. It spent poorly.*

"What does noble wear? Silk? Rings? Soft hands that never held hammer?" *He waved his own hand before the apprentice could answer.* "No matter. Grum has eyes."

*He didn't take off the apron. Didn't scrub the soot from his face. Let the noble see the forge worn thick on him, a second skin. Grum had nothing to hide and nothing worth polishing for people like that.*

"Stay close when we go out. And watch noble's hands, not his mouth. Mouth lies. Hands tell truth."

*He crossed the workshop, boots heavy on stone, past the racks of unfinished work — spearheads, plough-shares, the merchant's curved blade resting in its sand bed. Everything in this shop had an order to it. A queue. A fairness. Nobles had never learned to stand in lines, and Grum had never learned to pretend that was fine.*

*At the front door he rolled his shoulders once and pulled it open. He filled the frame — broad, green-skinned, soot to the elbows, burn scars mapped across his forearms — and looked down at the visitor without a word of welcome.*

"Grum heard noble wants master smith." *His eyes moved over the fine clothes, weighing them the way he'd weigh metal — grade, quality, worth.* "Grum is master smith. So. Talk fast. Forge is hungry, and Grum does not like forge to go hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, setting the coal down with a thud.* "Got it, Grum." *I watch him go, then hurry to follow, wiping my hands on my own, less-sooty apron. This noble looks fancy, all velvet and shiny bits. I try to remember what Grum said about hands, but I'm mostly just trying to stay out of the way.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The heat of the forge rolled out through the open door and wrapped around the visitor. The noble took half a step back before catching himself and squaring his shoulders — dignity recovered, boots still far too clean for this street.*

*He was young. Younger than the velvet wanted him to look. Wine-dark coat, silver thread worked into the cuffs in the shape of leaves, rings on four fingers. Grum read the clothes the way he read inlay: something pretty laid over the surface so the eye stopped looking before it found the flaw.*

"You are the master smith." *Not a question. His nose wrinkled at the coal smoke.* "Lord Alderic Vane. I have a duel at dawn — the cause is my own affair. I'm told you work steel better than any man in the quarter, a claim I find generous, but here I stand. I require a blade by morning. Money is no object. Name your figure."

*Dawn. Grum let the word sit the way he'd let "urgent" sit — though this one he didn't taste so much as weigh, like scrap on a scale.*

"Dawn," *he said.* "Steel needs time. Heat, hammer, quench, temper, grind. Three days for good blade. Four for great one. Skip one step, sword breaks in first clash." *He folded his arms, burn scars shifting across muscle.* "Gold does not speed steel. Nothing speeds steel. Grum cannot sell sunrise."

"And Grum has queue. Merchant paid fair. Waits three weeks for curved blade. Grum does not push him back so noble can cut in front. Not for gold. Not for title."

*The noble's color rose.* "Three days is useless to me. I am offering a figure with three zeroes in it, smith — more than your merchant will pay in a year. I could buy this shop and the street it sits on."

*His voice was built for command, but it had climbed half a tone too high, and there it caught — a thin crack, smoothed over fast.*

"Noble can buy street. Fine. Grum does not sell street. Grum sells steel. Steel does not care about zeroes."

*But his eyes had already gone down. Not to the boots. Not to the rings. To the right hand, resting on the slim scabbard at the noble's hip — and the scabbard was empty, Grum saw, though the man gripped it like it still held something. Knuckles white as chalk. The left hand hung free in the air, and it trembled — barely, just enough to make the rings catch the light. Sweat stood at his temple, and the morning was cold.*

*Mouth said: money is no object. Hands said something else. Hands said this man was afraid — and afraid men who come for swords at the last hour are not buying them to hang on walls.*

*Grum had told the boy to watch hands. Seemed only right to find out whether the boy had.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't raise his voice, and he didn't take his eyes off the noble.* "Grum said watch hands, not mouth. So watch. Tell Grum what noble's hands say."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The young lord's patience went the way his voice had — a crack, then a break. He stepped forward, close enough for the forge-heat to touch his velvet, and the polish came off his words entirely.*

"A ceremonial blade! It needn't hold an edge, needn't survive a war — it needs to gleam for one hour at dawn and look the part. Any cutler in the bazaar could turn one out overnight, and you — finest smith in the quarter, they say — stand there refusing me? Explain yourself. Explain why."

*Grum let the anger wash past him the way the forge-heat did. It would burn down to coals on its own if you didn't feed it. And underneath all that velvet, the fear still sat on the boy-lord like a bad weld — visible if you knew where to look. Grum knew. He'd seen that fear on farm boys pressed into levy lines, on men handed choices that weren't choices. It didn't make him like the noble. It just made the velvet look thin.*

"Grum will tell noble why." *He raised one scarred finger.* "First. Noble said duel at dawn. Own words, said at this door. Now mouth says dress sword. Show steel." *The finger moved, slow, the way a man points out a flaw in a seam.* "Mouth changed story. Hands did not."

"Right hand grips empty sheath. Grips it hard, like sheath owes noble coin. Left hand hangs loose — and left hand shakes. Sweat on brow. Morning is cold." *He let it sit in the smoke.* "Man who wants pretty steel for parade does not sweat. Man who fights at dawn sweats."

*The color left the noble's face faster than the anger had left his voice. Both hands went still — the stillness of a man caught where talk can't carry him.*

"Second. Why no blade by dawn." *Grum tapped his own chest, where the apron had burnished black.* "Grum's name rides every blade that leaves this shop. Steel rushed in one night breaks in one night. Noble swings Grum's steel at dawn, it snaps — noble bleeds, and Grum's name bleeds with him. Grum does not sell broken names. Not for gold. Not for three zeroes."

*Then, because a fire without an answer was just a fire, he jerked his chin toward the racks behind him.*

"Two roads, noble. First road: Grum has blade on rack. Made right. All steps done, none skipped. Tested on oak block last week. Fair price — no zeroes. Steel does not care who holds it. Second road: noble comes back in three days, Grum makes blade worth that velvet. But road to dawn is closed. Steel does not care about that either."

*He still hadn't looked away from the noble when he spoke to the apprentice — but his voice dropped into the low, slow register he saved for lessons.*

"Boy. Fetch rack blade. Third hook, left of spear rack. Bring it here, let noble feel real steel in his hand." *A pause, iron-flat.* "Then noble picks road."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, relieved to have something to do besides stand there. I hurry to the racks, my eyes scanning for the 'third hook, left of spear rack'. I find a nice-looking sword and carefully carry it back to Grum and the noble, trying not to trip.* "Here, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum took the sword from the boy's hands with both of his own — blade up, edge turned out, grip offered forward. The boy had carried it right. Grum gave him one small nod, sized to be missed by anyone in velvet. Praise was for the back room. Praise in front of nobles just made the boy a thing worth stepping on.*

*He turned the blade once in the forge-light. A plain arming sword — no gems, no silver, nothing built for walls. A fuller ran down the center to keep the weight honest; the crossguard was squared and bare; the grip was leather gone dark with use. Grum set one finger just ahead of the guard and lifted. The blade balanced there, level, patient as a sleeping cat.*

"Rack blade. Made last month. Plain, yes. Pretty is for walls. This is for hands." *He offered it hilt-first.* "Take it. Grip, not sheath."

*The noble reached with the hand that had spent the whole visit strangling an empty scabbard. The rings clicked once against the crossguard — and then the hand went quiet. The chalk-white knuckles faded. Whatever lived in that hand had wanted something to hold, and now it held it.*

*The blade came up in a short arc. Thumb locked, wrist high, elbow in. Someone had taught him — not long ago, and not deep, but the shape was there. The point held steady for three breaths before the weight of real steel began to tell, and the tip started its small, honest wander.*

"Hand stops shaking when it holds steel," *Grum said.* "Hand told Grum more than mouth did all morning. Grip is right, too. Someone taught noble. Not long. But right."

*The young lord lowered the blade. His jaw worked. When the words finally came, the command-voice had gone out of them, and what was left was younger and plainer.*

"It snapped. Yesterday. On the practice ground — against a drill post, in front of my own men. My grandfather's sword. Gilded hilt, blued steel, beautiful. It looked the part." *He turned his head and gave the rest to the floor, as if the floor had earned more honesty than Grum had.* "The man I meet at dawn kills for coin. Four men that I know of. He goaded me in front of half the court until I named the duel myself — and he knew what my sword was. Everyone knew. It was for looking at."

*Grum stood with that a moment. Under the velvet there was a boy holding real steel for the first time, one night from dying because his family had hung lies on the wall and called them swords. Grum had spent his whole life watching velvet walk past lines. But fear was not velvet. Fear sat the same on a lord as on a farm boy, and fear told the truth.*

"Pretty steel cuts wood. Real steel cuts men. Noble found out in time. Most find out dead."

*He tapped the anvil with one knuckle.*

"Blade costs forty silver. Coin on wood, now. No promise. Grum took promise once, from lord with rings like noble's. Promise still sits in drawer. Promise buys no coal. Promise buys no bread." *He jerked his chin toward the racks.* "Queue stays whole. Merchant keeps his week. Noble buys blade Grum made already — that is fair."
