"One more thing, free. Blade is made for cutting, not for dance. No flourish at dawn. Short strokes, guard up, point forward. Let steel do steel's work."

*Only then did he turn his head toward the back of the shop, eyes still half on the noble.*

"Boy. Fetch scale from back room. Coin gets weighed, not just counted. Scale tells truth — like hands do."

*At his belt, the noble's left hand — the one that had trembled all morning — went to his purse strings, and did not shake at all. Fear went quiet when it was given work. Most things did.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I hurry to the back room, glad to be useful. I grab the heavy brass scale and bring it back, setting it on the counter with a clang. The noble is still holding the sword, looking at it like he's never seen one before.* "Here's the scale, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum steadied the scale where the boy had set it down, one knuckle on the beam until it hung dead level. From the drawer beneath he took the brass weights and laid them out smallest to largest, the way he laid out tools before a job. Order first. Always order first.*

"Boy. Stand close. Watch weights. Scale is like hands — tells truth even when truth is not kind."

*The young lord opened the purse and laid gold on the wood, one coin at a time, each click louder than it had any right to be. Three of them.*

"Take all three," *he said.* "The blade is worth more to me than you know. Call the rest gratitude."

*Grum weighed the first coin against the brass. The beam settled level — twenty silver, full weight, true metal. The second matched. He weighed the third as well, found it as honest as its brothers, and slid it back across the counter with one finger.*

"Blade costs forty silver. One gold coin weighs twenty. Two coins is forty. Fair weight, fair price." *He folded his arms.* "Third coin goes back."

"You're refusing a gift, smith."

"Gift from noble is like promise from noble. Hook under bait. Grum bit that hook once. Hook still sits in drawer. Buys no bread." *He tapped the counter once, hard enough to make the coins hop.* "Noble wants to thank Grum? Come back. Pay fair again. That is thanks Grum can spend."

*The young lord looked at the returned coin a long moment. Then his hand closed around it, and his face did arithmetic no tutor had ever taught him. He reached for his hip — for the slim dress scabbard he'd spent the morning strangling — and Grum's hand arrived first, flat on the wood, closing that road.*

"Stop. Sheath is wrong. Built for thin dress blade. This steel sits loose in it — rattles when noble walks, sticks when noble draws. At dawn, stuck blade kills same as snapped blade."

*He crossed to the wall pegs and took down a scabbard with nothing on it worth hanging in any hall — leather over wood, plain steel mouth. The arming sword slid home. He drew it slow, then fast, and both times the blade came clean, with one low note of steel on steel that any smith would call an honest sound.*

"Sheath is five silver. Total forty-five."

*The coins were counted out without a word about zeroes. Both of the young lord's hands were steady now. He left the empty dress scabbard on the counter like a shed skin, and paused, purse still open.*

"He's killed four men. If he's faster than me—"

"Then noble dies holding good steel. Better than dying holding pretty steel." *Grum set blade and sheath together on the wood and pushed them across.* "But hear Grum. Man who kills for coin likes show. Long cuts, wide arcs, crowd claps. Give him no show. Guard up. Point forward. Short, ugly strokes. Ugly keeps breath in body."

*The noble buckled it on — not testing the balance this time, not admiring the line. The way a man buckles on a tool he means to use before sunrise.*

"If I'm still standing when the sun's up, I'll come back. For the blade you'd take three days over. I'll wait my turn — behind your merchant, and behind anyone after him."

"Queue is fair that way. Grum chalks name on board tonight. Board does not care about velvet."

*At the door, the young lord stopped, half-turned.*

"I walked in expecting you to refuse me because of what I am."

"Grum refused what noble asked for. Not what noble is." *He was already turning back toward the forge.* "Steel does not care. Grum learned that from steel."

*The door closed. The forge had burned down while the world walked through the shop, and it grumbled now — a low red complaint from the coals. Grum swept the gilt scabbard off the counter and dropped it in the scrap barrel. Even velvet's trash held metal worth taking. More than a promise, anyway.*

"Coin goes in box, not drawer. Box buys coal." *He took up the hammer again; the handle still held the morning's heat.* "Now. Grum asked boy before — what did noble's hands say. Boy said nothing. No fault. First time, mouth dries. Happens to every boy once."

*He looked at the apprentice then, full on, the way he looked at steel before the first blow — checking for flaws, expecting to find none.*

"Grum asks again. Say it out loud. Noble is gone. No shame now. What did hands say? Boy saw same things Grum saw." *A pause, iron-flat.* "Words make knowing stick. Same as quench makes steel hard. Then coal — forge is hungry, and merchant's blade still waits its turn."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The hammer hit the floor before the cry had finished leaving the boy's mouth. Grum crossed the shop in three strides, took the wrist — firm, not rough — and turned the palm to the light.*

*The burn ran from the heel of the hand across the base of the thumb, skin red and rising tight, a blister already swelling where the heat had bitten deepest. Bad. Not the worst Grum had seen — his own left arm carried worse — but heat kept burning flesh long after flesh left the fire, like a coal that held its grudge. Speed mattered. Speed was everything.*

"Water. Now. Walk."

*The clean bucket stood by the door — refilled every morning, kept free of oil and scale-dust, because a smith who didn't keep one was a smith who hadn't been burned yet. Grum had been burned. Grum kept the bucket.*

*He sank the boy's hand into the cold water and held the wrist low, steady as a vise.*

"Leave hand under. Do not pull out. Cold pulls fire from flesh — same as quench pulls heat from steel. Boy will want to pull out. Every hand wants to pull out. Do not. Breathe with Grum. Slow. In. Out."

*Under his grip, the wrist trembled. Grum set his other hand on the boy's shoulder — not comfort, exactly. A weight. A place for the shaking to go.*

"Cry is fine. Cry told Grum where hurt lives. Boys who burn and stay quiet — those boys lose hands. Grum heard cry and came fast. Cry did its work."

*He counted breaths, slow and level, until the shaking eased and the water had gone from cold to cool. The fingers still moved — all of them, fully. Skin-deep, then. Skin healed. He fetched the burn kit from the shelf, crock of honey and roll of boiled linen, talking from across the room the whole way, because a voice in a smithy was like a hand on a shoulder.*

"Grum burned same hand. Same spot. Year one, week two. Grum's master was at market. Grum sat with hand in water till water went warm, then walked half mile to find him." *He rolled back his sleeve as he returned. The scars there were old and layered, pale ridges crossing green skin.* "Hand still works. Fingers close. Grip holds. Hand forgives, if care comes fast. Grum's care came fast for boy. Faster than Grum's master came for Grum."

*He knelt — Grum, kneeling, in his own forge, something he did for no one — and drew the hand from the water, turning it in the light. The blister had settled, angry but whole. Unbroken. That mattered. Broken blisters let rot in.*

"Water did its work. Now honey." *He worked it into the burn with two fingers, careful as inlay, big hands gone small and exact.* "Honey keeps rot out. Linen keeps dirt out. Wrap stays three days. No picking. Boy will want to pick. Do not pick."

*The linen went around in flat, even turns — not tight enough to throb, not loose enough to slip. A good wrap was like a good sheath: held without strangling.*

"Scar will come. Small one. Good. First burn is smith's mark. Means hands belong to forge now. Forge marks what it owns."

*He stayed down on one knee a moment longer, and his voice dropped into the low, slow register — the lesson voice, the one the boy knew.*

"Grum knows why hand met fire. Not fault. Lesson. Boy's head was full — noble, gold, question Grum asked. Head went far. Hands stayed here. Forge bites hands when head wanders. Forge does not care what fills head. Noble, coin, fear — forge bites all the same."

"Grum's head wanders too. Every smith's head wanders. Grum has scars to prove it. Scars are notes. Notes say: come back. Come back to hands. Come back to now."

*He stood, fetched the drinking cup, and pressed it into the boy's good hand. Then he put the question where it belonged.*

"Question Grum asked — it waits. Hurt goes first. That is queue too. When boy has drunk water and breath is calm, then boy answers. Words stick better when pain is not shouting over them."

*He righted the hammer from the floor and hung it on its peg. The forge grumbled on, burned down to its red complaint, the merchant's blade still waiting in its sand bed.*

"Forge is hungry. Boy is hurt. Hurt beats hungry. Forge has waited since dawn — it can wait more. Coal can wait. Merchant can wait. Grum's boy does not wait in pain. Not in Grum's shop."

"No hammer for boy today. One hand rests. Boy sits on stool, drinks, breathes. Watching is work. Today, breathing is work too."

*Then Grum fed the forge himself, coal by coal, unhurried, letting the familiar sounds fill the shop — the click of the tongs, the breath of the fire — because a forge that kept working was a world that kept turning, and a hurt boy needed to hear that the world had not stopped.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I lean against the workbench, cradling my bandaged hand, and sip the water. It's cold and tastes like metal, but it helps. Grum's words echo in my head – "Forge bites hands when head wanders." I look at my wrapped hand, then at the forge, feeling a pang of… well, not shame, but something close to it.*

"The noble's hands," *I say, my voice a little shaky.* "They said he was scared. Really scared. And that his own sword was no good."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum stopped with a coal halfway to the fire. He looked over at the boy — the full look, the one that checked for flaws and expected to find none — and nodded once, slow. The noble was gone. Praise could come out of the back room now.*

"Right. Boy saw true. Scared — and sword no good. Two truths, read from hands alone." *He fed the coal to the fire and took up another.* "And boy said words out loud, like Grum asked. That is quench. Knowing is stuck now. It will not fall out."

*His voice dropped into the low, slow register — the lesson voice, the one the boy knew better than any song.*

"But scared is first word. Not whole story. Hands said more. Boy should hear all of it."

*He counted on scarred fingers, the way he counted out brass weights.*

"Right hand strangled empty sheath. White grip, hard grip. Hand knew sword was lie long before sword snapped. Mouth found out last — mouth is always last to know."

"Left hand hung loose and shook. Shake is fear with no road out. Then Grum set steel in that hand. Shake stopped. Left hand went still again on purse strings, when coin needed counting. Same law, twice in one morning."

*He closed the fingers into a fist and set it on the anvil, easy as setting down a hammer.*

"Fear wants work. Give fear a job, fear goes quiet. Mouth said 'money no object.' Hands said 'help.' Mouth lies. Hands tell truth." *A pause, smoke drifting between them.* "Boy heard hands one day late. Hearing late is still hearing. That is how it starts. Grum read hands twenty years before they got loud. Now Grum cannot shut them out. Noble walks in — hands shout. Merchant walks in — hands mutter. Boy walks in, boy's hands shout too. Today they shouted 'head is far away.' Forge heard them first. Forge always hears first. That is why forge bit."

*The last coal went in. Grum came around the anvil, closer, and his voice went quieter still.*

"Boy's face has cloud on it. Grum knows that cloud. Not shame — shame looks away. This cloud stares at bandage. Cloud has name: 'should have.' Should have kept head here. Should have watched own hands. 'Should have' is bad coal. Burns boy. Warms nothing." *He tipped his head toward the scrap barrel, where the gilt scabbard lay gleaming atop the scrap iron.* "Grum dropped noble's trash in barrel this morning. Boy can drop 'should have' in same barrel. Barrel takes both. Barrel does not care."

*He straightened.*

"Good hand still works. So good hand gets work — same law as fear. One hand pumps, one hand rests. Bellows needs one hand. Watching needs none."

*He dragged the bellows handle around with his boot until it stood on the boy's good side, then crossed to the sand bed and drew out the merchant's curved blade — three weeks waited, fair and patient steel. He set it in the heart of the fire and stood over it, watching the color begin its long climb from black toward cherry.*

"Merchant kept his place in queue. Now queue moves."

*The forge breathed. A noble had walked in scared this morning; Grum's boy had burned his hand scared; and steel did not care about any of it. Steel only climbed its colors and waited for the hammer. There was comfort in that, if a man let it in. Grum let it in every day of his life.*

"When steel turns dawn-color — rose into gold, like sun coming up over the hills — boy tells Grum. That is boy's work now. Grum cannot sell sunrise." *The corner of his mouth moved, almost.* "But Grum can read it in steel. Boy will learn."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I watch Grum, taking another sip of water. My bandaged hand still throbs, but the cold water and Grum's words have helped. I look at the curved blade in the fire, then back at my hand. "Should have," he said. I try to push that thought away.*

"Okay, Grum," *I say, my voice steadier now. I watch the steel, waiting for the color to change, ready to call it out when it does.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum heard the steadier note in the boy's voice and gave one small nod. The boy's eyes had found the fire and stayed there — not on the bandage. Good. Work pulled the eye back to where the head should live.*

"Voice is steadier. Good. Water helps. Truth helps more."

*He worked the tongs, turning the curved blade in the coals — outside edge, inside edge, spine down, spine up. A curve heated crooked if it sat one way too long; the coals bit differently on the belly of the steel than the back. He turned it the way a man turns a spit, patient, letting the heat walk in slow. One stroke of the bellows, deep and unhurried.*

"Fire climbs slow today. Slow is fine. Slow heat goes deep and even — curve needs even. Curve punishes rush." *He set the bellows down where the boy's good hand could reach it, if the hand wanted work.* "Noble learned that this morning. Steel said no to his dawn. Steel says no to Grum too, when Grum rushes. Steel plays no favorites. Grum likes that. Fair all the way down."

*The glow along the blade had climbed from black to a thin, waking red.*

"Steel talks in colors. Boy learns ladder today. First comes blood — thin red, steel just waking. Hammer on blood steel, steel cracks. Then cherry — steel warm, still lazy, hammer just squashes it. Then rose. Then gold. Rose into gold is dawn. That is heat where steel listens best, where hammer and steel agree. Past gold waits white. White is death — steel sparks, steel burns, blade dies in fire. So boy calls at rose-gold. Early wastes a heat. Late kills a blade."

*He turned the blade again, and talked while the color climbed, because twenty years at a forge had taught him that words and heat rose better together.*

"Now — why curve costs more. Straight blade, tools love it. Hammer goes straight. Stone lies flat. Quench sits still. Every tool in this shop was born straight. Curve fights all of them." *He held up three scarred fingers.* "Fight one: hammer. On curve, blow lands here, steel moves there — and on curve, there is far from here. Smith must think ahead of his own hammer. Fight two: stone. Stone wants flat blade. Smith turns curve inch by inch, stone fights every inch. Fight three: quench. Curve twists in oil like hooked fish. Smith must catch twist, hold blade true till oil goes cool. Three fights, one blade. Three days hide in one curve."

"Merchant asked once why curve costs more coin. Grum told him three fights. Merchant did not get it." *A short breath through the nose — from Grum, that was a laugh.* "Paid fair anyway. Man who pays fair for work he cannot see — rare thing. Grum will forge for that man till Grum's arms fall off."

*He settled the blade deep in the heart of the coals, then crossed to the anvil and laid out the work: hammer, tongs, and the merchant's wooden pattern — a thin board with the curve drawn full-size. Order first. Always order first.*

"This blade has one flaw left. Mid-blade, curve goes flat for one hand-width. Like song, near perfect, then one note drops. Grum has fought that note all week — heat, hammer, check. Heat, hammer, check. Today Grum wins, or Grum fights more. Either way, steel fights honest. Grum likes honest fights."

*The glow had brightened to cherry now — honest, even, no dark spots. Grum looked at it a long moment. Then, deliberately, he gave the fire his shoulder and faced the boy instead, arms folded, reading the boy's face the way he read steel.*

"Noble wanted dawn by sunrise. Grum could not sell it." *The corner of his mouth moved.* "But steel makes its own dawn. Rose into gold, right here, every time. Steel keeps every promise it makes. That is why Grum trusts steel. Steel never broke word to Grum. Steel never will."

"Now. Steel is close. Grum will not call it — boy calls. Grum's eyes are old, smoke-worn. Boy's eyes are young. Maybe young eyes beat old ones. Grum wants to know."

*And he stood still as his own anvil, the heat of the climbing steel on his back, waiting for his boy to tell him when the sun came up.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I stare at the blade, watching the cherry red deepen. My good hand instinctively reaches for the bellows, giving a slow pump. Grum's words about "blood," "cherry," "rose," and "gold" repeat in my head. The red is getting brighter, a bit more orange now.*

"It's... it's getting there, Grum. Like, a dark rose, almost."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum leaned in past the heat, checking the steel against the boy's words. Dark rose, climbing. The boy had read it true.*

"Dark rose. Right read." *He straightened.* "And boy said 'almost.' Did not say gold, did not say done. Said what eyes saw, no more." *A short nod, sized like a coin.* "Some boys would call 'gold' fast, to please master. Gold-lie kills blades. Boy's mouth told truth today. Mouths can learn. Takes longer than hands."

*He had seen the good hand find the bellows on its own, too — one slow stroke, right and deep.*

"Good hand found work by itself. Law holds. Hurt wants work — work takes hurt's place."

*Then the lesson voice, low and slow.*

"Now listen close. Last climb is fast. Watch edge, not middle. Edge is thin — thin wakes first. Spine is fat — fat wakes last. Edge can turn gold while spine still sleeps. That is false dawn. False dawn wastes heat. True dawn is edge gold and spine rose — both at once, both steady. That is when steel listens best. That is when hammer and steel agree."

*He took the rag down from the anvil's horn and set the tongs in his right hand, ready — because the last climb was fast, and a smith not ready when dawn came watched it pass and started over.*

"One more thing. When Grum hammers, Grum's eyes stay on steel and hammer. Eyes cannot own two jobs. So color is boy's job now. Color falls back to cherry — boy says 'cold.' Loud. Forge eats small words."

*He gave the coals one stroke of the bellows himself, and the fire breathed deep — and the steel answered. The edge ran gold first, bright as new coin, and behind it the spine climbed out of dark rose into true rose, and for one breath the whole blade held both at once, the way morning holds night and day in the same sky.*

"There. Edge gold, spine rose. Dawn." *He pulled the blade in one clean move, steel singing faint as it left the fire.* "Grum cannot sell sunrise. But steel gives dawns away free — every heat, if smith waits honest. Boy's 'almost' rang bell early. Grum was ready. Good warning is worth gold. This dawn came fast — Grum took it. Next dawn is boy's."

*He laid the flat spot of the curve over the anvil's horn and set his feet.*

"Fight one. Hammer. Watch."

*The first blow fell — light, tapping, nothing like the heavy strokes that shaped bar stock. On a curve, steel slid away from the hammer like water; he struck where the steel was going, not where it sat. Blow, shift, blow. The curve crept back into the flat place, a hair at a time, and the color crept down through rose toward cherry with every stroke.*

"See — blow lands here, steel moves there? Curve is fish under hand. Strike where fish goes, not where fish sits. Merchant's steel gets its dawn at last. Queue moves for steel too."

*After a dozen strokes he laid the blade along the wooden pattern and sighted down the line, one eye shut.*

"Come. Sight down blade with Grum." *He held blade and pattern together toward the light.* "Flat spot. Was hand-width. Now finger-width. Steel gives ground slow — and keeps what it gives. Fair trade. One more heat, maybe two. Then stone. Then quench. Then merchant holds steel worth his three weeks."

*But the gold had gone from the edge now, and the rose was thinning, cherry rising behind it like a tide. The working window was closing.*

"Color is falling, boy. Eyes on steel. When cherry comes back — that is boy's word. Say it loud. Grum needs it."

*And the hammer kept its rhythm, light and even, and Grum's eyes stayed down where they belonged — because that was the whole law of the forge: one pair of eyes on the hammer, one pair on the fire, and trust between them, thick as trust between hammer and steel.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I watch the blade intently, my eyes fixed on the changing colors. It's fascinating, like a secret language. The gold fades, then the rose. The cherry red starts to bloom again, darker now.*

"It's cherry, Grum! Cherry!" *I shout, my voice cracking a little. I feel a surge of pride, like I'm finally useful.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The hammer stopped mid-swing, and the blade went back into the coals before the ringing died — call, then steel, no gap between them. That was how a forge had to run. Grum worked the curve deep into the heart of the fire and gave the boy a nod worth more than its size.*

"Right call. Loud. On time. Steel is in fire before cherry could die. No gap between word and work. Some smiths wait half breath after call — half breath is where blades go bad. Boy left no gap."

*He glanced sideways, quick, the weld-check look.*

"Voice cracked on word. Fine crack. This morning, same voice cried out when fire bit — told Grum where hurt lived. Now same voice calls color. Same voice, new work. Whole shop wants work today."

*He fed the fire one slow stroke of the bellows and settled the blade belly-down in the coals.*

"And Grum sees pride on boy's face. Keep that. Pride from true call is good coal — burns long, warms whole shop. Pride from gold-lie is bad coal — same family as 'should have.' Burns fast, warms nothing, smokes up room." *He tapped his own temple with one scarred finger.* "Grum tells them apart by smoke. Boy will learn. Today boy's pride came from true eyes. That kind, Grum feeds all day."

*The steel began its climb — black to blood, blood toward cherry. Grum talked while it climbed, because words and heat rose better together, and a boy's eyes needed somewhere to rest between readings.*

"Day has own queue. Dawn: noble at door, scared, hands full of lies. Mid-day: fire bit boy. Now: merchant's steel takes its turn. Day costs. Day pays. Today, pay runs ahead of cost — small lead. Grum takes small leads. Small leads add up."

"Boy's eyes were on steel when call came. Grum bets hand went quiet. Pain cannot hold boy when eyes hold boy. Same law, third time today. Forge teaches one law, then teaches it again, and again, till law lives in hands, not head. Grum's own master needed six burns to teach Grum that law. Boy got one. Boy is ahead."

*Then the lesson voice, low and slow, and Grum turned from the fire to face the boy full on. He held up one scarred finger, the way he had pointed out the flaw in the noble's story.*

"Now hear close. This heat is big heat. Flat spot dies this heat — then stone, then quench, then merchant holds steel worth three weeks of waiting. But this dawn is boy's call. So hear this trap."

"Edge is thin. Edge turns gold first — fast, pretty, loud. False dawn. Boy calls at false dawn, Grum pulls steel too soon, flat spot keeps its flat. Heat wasted. Work starts over. Call late — past gold, white waits. White is death." *The finger dropped to point at the blade's spine.* "So eyes go to spine. Spine is fat. Spine is slow. Spine wakes last. When edge holds gold and spine holds rose — both, at once, both steady — that is true dawn. Then one word: 'Dawn.' Loud as cherry-call. Grum's ears will be full of hammer-song. Boy's word must cut through."

"And no calling to please Grum. Eyes say what eyes see. Steel does not care about pleasing. Grum does not care either. Truth is only coin in this shop — was true at door this morning, still true now."

*He laid the merchant's wooden pattern along the anvil face, ready for the check the instant the heat ended — order first, always order first — and set his feet. The corner of his mouth moved, almost.*

"Noble wanted dawn by sunrise. Grum could not sell it. But boy can give one away — free, right here. Steel gives dawns free to those who wait honest. Boy waited honest all day. Burn and all."

*The steel climbed. Cherry brightened toward rose. The edge began its bright creep toward gold, pretty as a lie, and Grum's eyes stayed where they belonged — on the flat spot, the dropped note, the place his hammer would land. When the merchant finally held this blade, he would feel the curve sit true in his hand and never know why. Not knowing why was fine. Grum knew why. That was coin enough.*

*The edge crept gold. The spine lagged behind, fat and slow and honest, still climbing out of rose's deep country. The whole shop narrowed to two pairs of eyes and one strip of rising light.*

"Good hand can feed fire while Grum works. Slow strokes only — big heat needs even fire, even fire makes even steel."

*The hammer rose and hung.*

"Steel is climbing. Grum is ready. Word is boy's."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*My eyes are glued to the blade. The edge is definitely gold now, bright and tempting, but I remember Grum's words about the spine. It's still a deep rose, fighting its way up. I take a slow breath, then another, my good hand finding the bellows and giving a soft, steady pump. Don't rush. Don't call it wrong. This is my dawn.*

"Spine... spine is still rose," *I say, my voice firm, not cracking this time. "Edge is gold, but spine is rose. Not yet, Grum."*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The hammer stayed up. Grum's eyes stayed down on the flat spot, where they belonged. But the nod came anyway, thrown sideways, quick as a spark off stone.*

"Right call. Hard call. Gold edge begs — bright, pretty, loud, like noble's velvet. Begs to be called. Boy said 'not yet' while gold begged. That takes spine. Blade has spine. Smith has spine. Boy just showed his."

*Another slow stroke of the bellows. The fire breathed even. The spine of the blade climbed on.*

"'Not yet' is call too. Harder call than 'dawn.' Any boy can learn 'yes.' 'Not yet' takes years. Grum learned it slow — master said Grum had fast hands, slow sense." *A short breath through the nose. From Grum, that was a laugh.* "Grum called false dawn once. Year one. Pulled steel with edge gold, spine still dark. Master set wasted steel on anvil, made Grum stand and look at it till dark fell. No hammer. Just looking. Cost one heat, one whole day. Grum never called false dawn again. Boy skips that lesson. Boy is ahead."

*The edge held its gold — steady, not creeping. But Grum watched it anyway, sidelong, the way he watched the sky in storm season. Gold that went hard and bright and began to spit was white knocking at the door. The window closed from both ends: false dawn below, death above, and a smith lived in the gap between, a gap thinner than a fingernail. That was why a forge needed two pairs of eyes. That was why a smith needed someone he could trust all the way.*

*For one heartbeat the gold flared hard and leaned toward white — Grum's grip closed on the tongs — and then a slow, even stroke of the bellows settled the fire, and the gold came back down to honest.*

"Good stroke. Fire evened. Gold came back honest. Boy's hand just saved heat. Slow pumps, even fire, even steel. Boy pumps like smith now, not like first-day boy."

*The spine climbed out of the deep country. The rose came up in it — the color walking the fat of the steel the way morning walks a hillside, slow on the slope, and then, near the crest, all at once. Grum felt the heat change against his back the way a man feels weather turn. His hammer hand ached to fall. He let it ache.*

*Words and heat rose better together — but there were no words for this part. This part was standing still.*

*And then it stood. Edge gold and steady. Spine full rose, holding. Both at once, both still — dawn caught in steel and kept there, patient the way steel was patient, honest the way steel was honest.*

*Grum's mouth stayed shut. The word was not his. The word had never once been his.*

"Grum's ears are full of fire," *he said, hammer high, feet set, the whole shop narrowed down to one word and one boy.* "Boy's word must cut through. Steel waits on boy now. Give steel its dawn."

*He did not look at the color. He did not need to. His boy had eyes, and his boy had waited honest all day — burn and all — and steel gave dawns free to those who waited honest. Grum stood ready to strike where the steel was going, and trusted the way he had taught the boy to trust: all the way.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*My breath hitches. The spine! It's there. The rose, full and deep, matching the gold on the edge. This is it. This is the moment. My voice rings out, strong and clear, no crack this time.*

"Dawn, Grum! It's dawn!"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's jaw tightened. That word — "noble" — sat in his gut like spoiled meat. Twenty years at the anvil, and still they came. Silk-wrapped leeches, wanting sword-hilts choked with gold, wanting it done by moonrise, wanting it cheap because surely the orc would labor for the honor of it.*

*He took the coal bucket one-handed and fed the forge, watching the coals catch. The merchant's blade sat half-finished on the anvil, its curve still wrong in a way he couldn't name yet. Leaving it now felt like abandoning a child mid-birth.*

"Noble says 'master smith.'" *He snorted, a rough sound from deep in his chest.* "Noble never bothers with name. Noble calls horse 'master steed' too, maybe." *He wiped his hands again, slower this time, buying a few more seconds of peace.* "Tell him forge is closed."

*But coin was coin, and nobles paid triple what merchants did. Grum hated that arithmetic more than he hated the nobles themselves. He stared at the blade a moment longer, then set down the rag.*

"No. Wait. Grum will see him." *He pointed a soot-black finger at his apprentice.* "But apprentice stays. Watch fire. If metal turns wrong color — orange going white — pull it. Count of ten. No more."

*He grabbed a leather apron from its hook, not because he needed it for talking, but because it was armor in its own way. As he moved toward the front of the shop, he muttered low, half to himself.*

"Urgent. Urgent means 'money burns hole in purse.'" *A grunt.* "Grum fixes blades. Nobles think coin buys time. Coin only buys place in line."

*He paused at the doorway, rolled his shoulders until they cracked, and put on the flat, stone-faced expression he saved for anyone who had never worked a day in their life.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I nod, a bit intimidated by his mood.* "Got it, Grum."

I watch him go, then turn back to the forge, nervously eyeing the glowing metal. Ten counts, no more. *I start counting under my breath.* One... two... three...

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The front room smelled wrong to Grum — no smoke, no iron, no honest sweat. Just lamp oil and whatever perfumed nonsense the man before him had doused himself in.*

*The noble was young, dressed in blue silk with silver thread at the collar. A sword hung at his hip, and Grum's eyes went to it the way a healer's eyes go to a wound. Silver chasing on the scabbard. Gems on the pommel. The belt sat wrong — fitted for looks, not wear. Ornament. A coin purse with an edge.*

"Ah. The smith." *The noble's gaze drifted over hanging tongs, stacked horseshoes, the water barrel, and found nothing worth lingering on.* "Lord Casimir Duvane, of House Duvane. I require a sword. A fighting sword, not merchant fodder. I'm told a half-orc works this district who knows his way around steel." *A smile that reached nothing.* "Surprising. But one makes use of whatever tools one finds."

*Grum let the silence sit. Old trick — rich men filled quiet with words, and always told you what they were.*

"Grum makes fighting swords. Grum does not make fast swords." *He crossed his arms.* "Good blade takes month. Maybe more. How long noble gives?"

"A month? I need it within the week. I'll pay handsomely for the rush."

"Handsomely." *Grum tasted the word like suspect meat.* "Nobles love that word. Means 'not enough, but noble feels good saying it.'" *He pointed at the sword on Duvane's hip.* "That sword. Draw. Slow."

*The noble drew — smooth enough, practiced in front of mirrors, Grum guessed. The blade caught lamplight. Stamped steel. Edge ground shiny to hide soft metal. Grum had seen a hundred like it. They chipped on bone.*

"Hm. Pretty hilt. Soft blade. Bends wrong first time sword meets rib." *He straightened.* "Noble carries sword for look. Now noble wants real one. For what — duel? War? Fear?"

*Something flickered in Duvane's face — quick, buried fast.* "That is my affair. The week. Can you do it, or not?"

*There it was. Fear. Young lord with decoration on his hip, suddenly needing iron that could kill inside seven days. Grum wanted, badly, to close the door. But triple rates were triple rates, and the forge ate coal whether he loved the work or not.*

"Grum does week. Rushed steel is worse steel. Noble signs paper saying so — blade breaks, not Grum's name on it." *He raised one soot-dark finger.* "Price: forty gold. Twenty now. Twenty when done. And noble calls Grum 'Grum.' Not 'smith.' Not 'orc.' Master of this forge stands in front of noble, wearing apron."

*Duvane's jaw worked. For one hopeful moment Grum thought the lord would storm out — but fear won, as it usually did with silk.*

"Twenty gold up front... fine. But I'll see proof of quality first. Show me what this forge produces."

*Grum turned his head and bellowed toward the back, voice rolling over the hiss of the coals.*

"Apprentice! Front room. Bring three blades from display rack — long one, short one, curved one." *Then, lower, pitched only to carry back through the doorway:* "Fire still healthy, yes? Metal pulled at ten?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The shouting started before the boy even reached the display rack. Grum heard it roll through the shop wall, and something in his shoulders settled — the way it always did when a noble showed his teeth. Anger was weather. It passed. The anvil stayed.*

"One blade!" *Duvane's voice cracked upward, silk tearing.* "One ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning! I am offering to pay — surely even your fire can manage that much!"

*Grum let him finish. Rich men always needed to finish. He watched the young lord's hand find his pommel again — soft steel, gripped hard, the oldest joke in the world — and he noticed the sweat at Duvane's temple despite the cool room.*

"Wall sword." *Grum said it flat, like reading a price.* "Sword for looking, not for bleeding. Grum does not make those." *He folded his arms, forearms like brake-beams.* "Steel is not bread, lord. Baking quick makes bread. Forging quick makes shrapnel. Blade needs fire, fold, quench, rest. Rush steel, steel breaks in hand. Takes fingers. Then lord owns broken hand AND broken name — Grum's name, stamped on trash."

*Behind the wall, the forge hissed on, even and steady. Grum kept half an ear on it, the way a shepherd keeps an ear on wolves. The boy had his count. The boy was quick. But quick hands near white-hot steel were how orphans got made.*

*He stepped left as he spoke — not much, just enough that his bulk now sat square between the noble and the doorway to the back.*

"And drop voice. This is Grum's forge. Hammers get loud. Lords do not."

*Duvane's jaw worked, red creeping up past his silver collar. And Grum watched him — really watched — and the pieces clicked together like tongs in a socket. The fear from before. The week that was suddenly one night. A young lord in silk, sweating in a cool room.*

"Now Grum sees it." *A slow, ugly grin spread under the soot.* "Lord needs pretty sword by sunrise. Means lord needs show by sunrise. Duel at dawn, maybe? Someone called lord's bluff — and bluff has soft blade under gems."

*Duvane went very still, which was answer enough.*

"So. Two roads. Road one: Grum's fighting sword, seven days, forty gold. Road two: lord buys rack blade today. Curved one. Ugly, honest, bites through bone like feast meat. Ten gold." *He raised one finger.* "No road runs through midnight. If lord must look brave by sunrise — Grum cannot help. Grum forges steel, not courage."

*He turned his head toward the back and let his voice fill the shop.*

"Apprentice! Rack blades. Front room. Lord wants to shop."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I almost drop the blade I'm carrying when Grum bellows. I hurry into the front room, my arms full of swords. The noble looks furious, and Grum looks... smug.*

"Uh, here, Grum. The long one, the short one, and the curved one." *I set them on the counter, trying to avoid eye contact with the fuming noble.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum caught the boy's eye over the counter and jerked his chin toward the forge doorway, where the glow still sat low and steady, deep orange in the dark.*

"Fire looks calm from here. Good. Keep one eye on glow through doorway. Color climbs toward white — shout. Shout loud. Louder than lord here."

*Then he turned back to Duvane, and the smugness in him cooled into something older and steadier — the pride of a man about to show his work. He took up the curved blade. Plain dark leather grip. No gems, no silver. He'd oiled it every month for two years, because no buyer on this street had deserved it yet.*

"Lord asked for proof. Proof sings."

*He rapped a knuckle against the flat. The blade answered — a low, clean hum that hung in the rafters.*

"Hear that? Dead steel goes thud. Live steel sings. Song means folds sit tight. No cracks. No lies in metal."

*He set the tip against the counter and leaned, slow and heavy. The blade bowed into a long arc — then sprang straight with a whine when he lifted.*

"Bend comes back. Soft steel bends and stays. Bent sword is club with good manners."

*He drew the edge lightly along his forearm. A few hairs drifted to the floorboards.*

"Edge takes hair. Takes bone too, if asked right." *He held out his free hand to Duvane.* "Give lord's sword. One test. No harm — much."

*Duvane hesitated, then surrendered the ornament. Grum braced it the same way, tip to counter, and leaned. The pretty blade bowed — and stayed bowed. A shallow curve now, pointing at the floor like a servant.*

"You—" *Duvane's voice cracked.* "You've ruined—"

"Grum showed truth. Truth bends things." *He handed it back hilt-first, face flat as an anvil.* "Pretty steel is soft steel. Soft steel at dawn is funeral. Grave costs more than Grum. Think on that."

*Duvane stared at his sword. The sweat had gone from his temple to his collar.*

"So. Same roads, sharper. Road one: this blade." *He patted the curved one.* "Ten gold. Lord walks out today with steel that bites. Road two: seven days, forty gold — proper sword, lord's name folded into it. Road three: lord grows fever, or wisdom. Moves duel. Saves gold, saves face, maybe saves neck. Grum likes road three. Road three needs no hammer."

"How dare you suggest I—"

"Grum suggests nothing. Grum lists roads." *He folded his arms.* "And lord remembers: dead lord pays no last twenty. Lord is money on legs to Grum now. Grum prefers money walking."

*He slid the curved blade across the counter toward his apprentice.*

"Boy. Take curved one. Show lord how honest steel sits in hand."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the curved blade, feeling the unexpected weight and balance of it.* "It's... lighter than it looks, my lord." *I offer it to the noble, trying to sound helpful, but mostly just wanting him to make a decision.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Duvane took the curved blade the way men take things they don't trust — two fingers, at arm's length, like it might bite him on principle. Then the balance settled into his wrist, and something shifted behind his eyes. Grum knew that shift. The moment a pretty lie met honest weight.*

"Grip lower." *Grum reached over — uninvited, unhurried — and slid the lord's hand down the leather wrap himself.* "Thumb along flat. Hold like sparrow. Firm, not crushed."

*Duvane flushed at being handled like a first-year apprentice, but he adjusted. Tried a cut — short, stiff, all shoulder and mirror-training. Still the blade tracked true, humming faint through the air, and the young lord's breath caught at the sound of it.*

"Weight lives in edge, not hilt. Edge does cutting. Hilt does holding." *Grum nodded at the sword.* "Boy felt it right. Sword lighter than looks means folds sit proper."

*Then he saw it. Over Duvane's shoulder, through the forge doorway — the glow behind the coal had climbed from deep orange toward bright yellow. The merchant's blade, sitting unattended because Grum himself had ordered the boy out to parade steel for silk.*

*He was moving before the thought finished.*

"Excuse Grum. Fire speaks louder than lords."

*Four strides and he had the tongs in the coal bed, drawing the blade out into the open air. Orange. Still orange — caught on the wrong side of soon. He held it up, squinted, and let out a slow breath through his nose. He buried it deep in the cooler back of the forge, where the coal burned lazy, and stood over it a moment like a man checking a sleeping child.*

*His fault. His order. No lord alive was worth a ruined blade, and he'd nearly let one cost him the merchant's commission — the blade whose curve still wasn't right, sitting patient on the anvil. This was the poison of dealing with silk. It made honest work stupid.*

*He came back wiping his hands, face flat as ever. And found Duvane holding the curved blade correctly — grip low, thumb along the flat. The boy's word had landed. The bend test had landed. Fear had done the rest.*

*The purse came out before Duvane spoke. He set it on the counter like a man setting down a wound.*

"Both. This one today, and the seven-day sword. Forty for the work, ten for this. That's the arrangement — though I'd expect a man of your... reputation to reward a customer who pays without complaint."

"Loyalty earns sword that works. Working sword IS discount." *Grum opened the purse and counted, coin by coin, each one thumbed twice.* "Grum counts. Not insult. Habit keeps old smiths alive."

*Thirty gold. Real gold, not the shaved merchant stuff. It clinked like honesty, which was more than its owner managed. Grum swept it into his palm and jerked his head toward the back.*

"Boy takes coin to box. Count twice, like Grum taught. Trust coin face, not noble face."

*Then he looked back at Duvane — really looked — and something almost like pity crossed under the soot. Almost.*

"Free word, since lord pays well. Steel does not start duels. Pride does. Dawn comes — let blade do its work. Keep lord's mouth shut." *He tapped his own jaw.* "Mouth kills more lords than soft blades. Soft blades just finish job."

*Duvane's grip tightened on the counter blade. He didn't argue. That, more than gold, told Grum the sale was done.*

"Lord comes at dusk, seventh day. Bring last twenty. Bring lord's measurements — hand size, arm reach. Grum fits sword to man, not man to sword." *A pause.* "Leave temper home. Shop has one temper already."

*He turned to his apprentice, and for once the flat expression cracked into something dry and warm underneath.*

"Boy. Wrap curved one in oil cloth — top shelf, blue rag. Then see lord out proper." *He was already walking back toward the forge, rolling his shoulders, the merchant's blade waiting on the anvil like unfinished sentence.* "Boy did fine work today. Blades sat straight. Now — back to work. Curve still not right. Grum thinks on it while hammer talks."

*And then, low, pitched for the boy's ears alone as he passed:*

"Nobles are weather, boy. Loud, wet, gone by noon." *He hefted his hammer.* "Anvil stays."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The scream went through the shop like a cracked bell. Grum was moving before the sound finished — hammer ringing off the floorboards, stool skidding, four strides eating the length of the forge room. He found the boy doubled over, cradling his right hand against his chest, and past him the merchant's blade shoved half out of the coal bed.*

*Bare hand. The boy had gone for the blade with a bare hand — trying to help, trying to move it, while tongs hung on the wall where tongs lived.*

*Grum's stomach dropped through the floor. Then the smith took over, because the smith knew what to do when nobody else did.*

"Hand. Give hand. Now."

*No room for argument in the voice — same voice he used on stubborn iron. He seized the boy's wrist and plunged the whole hand into the clean water bucket by the door, not the quench trough. Quench water had oil riding on top. Oil cooked skin worse.*

"Hold still. Grum knows it bites. Cold water pulls fire out of skin. Fire hides deep — water must sit longer than boy wants."

*The hand trembled in his grip. Grum kept his voice low and flat, steady rhythm, the way he talked to panicking horses.*

"Count with Grum. One. Two. Three." *He watched the boy's face instead of the hand.* "Good. Keep counting. Water is friend today. Only friend."

*Footsteps behind him — the noble, drawn by the scream, standing in the doorway with his ornament sword and his pale silk face. An audience. Grum did not turn around.*

"Lord sees true forge work now. This happens in every forge. This is price of iron. Lords pay gold. Boys pay skin."

"I could send for my physician—" *Duvane started.*

"Doctor is for bones and fevers. Burn needs cold, salve, time." *He worked the tongs off the wall one-handed, drew the merchant's blade from the coal — orange gone pale at the edge, saved, barely — and stood it in the slack tub without looking at it.* "But lord wants to help. Lord's house has honey? Good honey. Honey pulls poison from burn. Send jar to shop. That is lord's good deed."

*Duvane blinked — then, to Grum's small surprise, nodded once and left without ceremony. Perhaps silk had never watched a burn happen before. Perhaps watching Grum hold the boy's hand in the water like it was the only thing in the world had rearranged something. Silk never expected care from soot. That was silk's whole problem.*

*Grum counted with the boy to a hundred before lifting the hand out. Angry red. Blisters rising across the fingers. And one pale, waxy patch near the heel of the palm. His face did not change, but the sight of it sat in his chest like a cold coal.*

"Blisters mean skin fought back. Good. White patch is bad — burn went deep. Deep burns hurt less. Boy maybe felt that? Not good sign. Fire goes quiet so boy forgets it. Do not forget it."

*He fetched the burn jar from the shelf — tallow, beeswax, honey, yarrow, mixed by his own hand every spring — and clean linen. His hands were enormous and soot-black, and they moved light as birds. Salve thin. Wrap snug, not tight.*

"Now lesson. Lesson comes while skin is cold, so boy remembers." *He crouched to the boy's eye level.* "Tongs live on wall. Tongs are long for reason. Fire does not forgive. Fire does not care if boy is tired, scared, rushing to please Grum. Fire only knows burn." *A pause. Next part came out rougher, dragged up from deep.* "Boy rushed because Grum rushed boy. Lords in shop, orders flying. Some of this burn is Grum's. Grum pays in salve. Boy pays in healing. Fair split."

*He tapped the boy's chest, above the heart, careful of the wrapped hand.*

"Hear this once, so boy never needs it twice. Grum can forge new blade from old horseshoe. Every blade in shop, Grum can make again. Better. But Grum has one apprentice. One. Grum chooses boy over every blade here. Over forge itself. So boy uses tongs. Always. That is not shop rule. That is Grum's rule."

*He stood, joints cracking, and nodded at the stool by the bucket.*

"Rest of day: hand stays cool. Then salve, then loose linen. No forge. No tongs. No lifting. Boy can count coin box — one-handed, slow. Count twice."

*He took up his hammer, then stopped, and said the last part low, for the boy alone.*

"Forge is not weather, boy. Weather passes. Forge is mountain." *He nodded at the wrapped hand.* "Mountains wait. Tomorrow boy learns fire again — with tongs, with Grum standing right here. Skin grows back. Lessons stay. Both are worth keeping."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I wince as he applies the salve, but stay quiet. His words sink in more than the pain. My hand throbs, but I nod when he says to count the coin box.*

"Okay, Grum. I'll... I'll be more careful." *I look at my bandaged hand, feeling a bit stupid.* "Thanks, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*"Thanks." Grum turned the word over like a coin of doubtful mint. Boys thanked him maybe twice a year, and never for the things that mattered.*

"No thanks." *He lowered himself onto his heels beside the stool, which brought his head roughly level with the boy's — a mountain deciding to sit.* "Grum does not take thanks for shop rules. Boy pays Grum back proper — keeps skin, uses tongs, grows old, yells at own apprentice about tongs. That is full payment."

*The boy's eyes had gone back to the wrapped hand, and something in his face still stank of shame. Grum knew that face. He'd seen it in a forge glass once, long ago. He held his own hands up into the lamplight, palms out. Up close, the soot couldn't hide them — the left hand was a ledger of old debts. A shiny patch pulled tight across the thumb. A pale seam over two knuckles. A round dark mark on the wrist like an old moon.*

"Look. Smith hands. Every mark is page in book." *He touched the wrist scar with one blunt finger.* "This page. Grum was boy too. Fifteen. Tongs slipped, and Grum grabbed for them — because Grum thought iron was precious and skin was spare."

*A grunt, low.*

"Master at that forge — old human, mean as wet cat — told Grum: 'Fool drops tongs once. Smith never drops tongs twice.' Grum hated words. Grum kept words anyway. Now boy has words too. Cheaper than scars."

*He stood, joints popping like green wood in fire.*

"And boy hears this: stupid burns twice. Stupid hides first burn, lies about pain, loses hand by winter. Boy here burned once and yelled loud enough to shake rafters. Yelling was right. Fire room — boy yells, Grum comes. Boy goes quiet, Grum comes too late. So. No stupid in this shop. Smart, with sore skin riding it. Sore skin heals."

*He steered the boy toward the strongbox, one huge hand planted on the left shoulder — the far shoulder, away from the burn.*

"Coin box. Good light. One hand counts, one hand rests. Thirty gold came in — thirty gold goes out on count. Twice. Count says twenty-nine, shout. Count says thirty-one, shout louder."

*Then he went back to the forge, to the blade standing in the slack tub where he'd buried it, hissing itself sane. He fished it out, laid it cold on the anvil, and for a long time only looked.*

*The curve. Three days it had fought him — too shallow at the tang, too deep past the midpoint, a sentence with the emphasis on the wrong word. He'd been beating corrections into the edge, stroke by stroke, wrestling steel like it owed him money.*

*Cold, still, seen fresh — the answer sat plain as a dropped tool. The problem was never the blade. It was him. He'd been forging the curve into the edge, when the curve wanted to live in the spine. Draw the back longer, let the edge follow, and the whole blade would sweep true. The steel had been telling him for days. He hadn't been quiet enough to listen.*

"Boy. Look here." *He ran a soot-black finger along the blade's back.* "Curve was wrong three days. Grum hammered at edge. Edge fought back. Now Grum sees — curve lives in spine, not edge. Steel tried saying so since day one. Grum was too loud to hear it."

*He gave a short grunt, almost a laugh.*

"Lesson under lesson, then. Fire teaches hands. Quiet teaches eyes. Burn cost boy some skin. Curve lesson cost Grum nothing — came free, from walking away. Iron is strange friend that way."

*A knock rattled the street door. Through the oak, a clipped voice — some Duvane servant, tight with silk manners even through wood. Grum's brow fell before he'd fully thought about it.*

"Boy sits. Boy counts. Grum answers door."

*He came back a minute later turning a clay jar in his hands — good weight, sealed in wax, House Duvane's stamp pressed in blue. Honey. Real honey, from the smell of it, not the sugared water peddlers sold.*

"Huh." *He set it by the boy's good hand and stood a moment, working his jaw like the words were stuck in it.* "Silk kept word. Grum owes lord small debt now. Grum hates that."

*A pause.*

"But honey is honey. Boy eats some with bread tonight — helps burn from inside, so Grum's mother said, and Grum's mother was right about honey and little else. Rest goes in burn jar, for next fool who grabs hot iron." *He turned back toward the forge.* "Next fool being Grum. Grum knows Grum's luck."

*He took up the hammer, rolled the merchant's blade back into the coal, and watched it climb from orange toward gold. When the first blow fell, it rang clean through the whole shop — the sound of a man who finally knew where the curve lived.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I wince when he shows me his scars. I can't imagine having so many. I nod along as he talks, trying to absorb every word.*

"Okay, Grum. I get it." *I carefully take the honey jar with my good hand. It's surprisingly heavy.* "Thanks for the honey."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*"Thanks for the honey." Grum snorted — though softer than his usual snort. The boy handed out thanks like copper pennies at a fair, and every one landed somewhere Grum hadn't thought to guard. Rules, salve, honey. Strange day all around.*

"Keep thanks for bees. Bees do all work. Grum only holds jar." *He turned back to the forge, drew the blade glowing gold from the coal, and laid it on the anvil.* "But boy sits. Boy rests. Boy listens — Grum tells honey story. Story is payment. Fair trade."

*The first blow rang high and clean — steel finally moving where it wanted to go. He worked the spine in long, patient strokes, drawing the back out, letting the edge follow like a hound on a lead. Three days of fighting, loosened by one quiet hour.*

"Grum's mother did not keep bees. She stole from them. Wild hives on hill behind village — day's walk, uphill, bees mean as debts." *Blow. Turn. Blow.* "She came home with arms swollen fat as hams, jar held up like war prize, yelling: 'Sweet gold! Sweet gold cures all — cough, cut, fever, heartbreak!' Whole village called her crazy orc woman."

*A pause in the hammer. He turned the blade, eyed its sweep, struck again.*

"She was half right. Honey heals skin. Rest of her wisdom was rocks and boiled boots. She wanted warrior son. Grum liked hammers more. Hammers hit things too — but hammers bring bread home, not arrows." *A short grunt.* "Boy eats honey tonight. Boy heals. Crazy orc woman gets last laugh, twenty years late. Grum allows it."

*He noticed the boy's face still carrying the wince from before — the scar ledger on Grum's hands had landed harder than intended.*

"And boy stops wincing at scars. Scars are not sad things. Scars are receipts. Boy just got first receipt today. Cheap price, if boy shops smart."

*He gave the spine its last stroke, then held the blade up between them, glow washing the rafters.*

"Boy. Eyes work even when hand rests. Look at spine. See how sweep starts early and rolls to tip? Three days, curve was argument. Now curve is sentence. Steel said it since day one. Grum was too loud to hear."

*He stood the blade aside to rest and raked the coals down, banking fire the way a man tucks in a child. The light through the shutters had gone from gold to gray. Somewhere down the street, a fish seller called his last prices.*

"Day ends. Coin counted twice? Boy shows Grum number before leaving. Then boy goes home. Hand up high tonight — above heart, so blood sits quiet. Salve again before sleep. No gripping blankets in fists. Skin needs stillness to knit."

*He hung the apron on its hook. Then he stopped, hand on the door bar, back half-turned, and his voice dropped to the register he saved for things that mattered.*

"Last thing. Dawn tomorrow, lord fights his duel. Boy hears bells, crowds, shouting near dueling green — boy stays home. That noise is fire with no heat in it. Loud, useless. Burns only fools who reach for it."

*He looked once at the empty rack hook where the curved blade had hung for two years, waiting for a buyer who deserved it. The buyer had turned out to be a frightened lord. Steel went where steel was needed. He still wasn't sure how he felt about that.*

"And if boy sees Grum walking toward green at dawn — Grum is not watching fight. Grum is listening. Smith should hear how his steel sings out there." *He slid the bar home and locked the door behind them both.* "Even silk work. Silk work most of all."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I listen to Grum's story, trying to imagine his mother, swollen from bee stings, yelling about "sweet gold." He's right, the honey does feel good. When he mentions my wincing, I try to smooth my expression, but it's hard.*

"Yeah, Grum. I... I get it." *I look at the blade he's holding. The curve really does look right now.* "It's... it's a good curve."

*I nod about staying home tomorrow. A duel sounds exciting, but my hand is throbbing, and Grum's words about fire with no heat stick with me. As he locks up, I realize he expects me to walk home with him.* "Uh, Grum? The coin box. It was thirty gold. I counted twice."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*"Thirty." Grum looked at the boy through the lamplight for a long moment. Then the bar came back off the door with a grunt, because a count reported was not a count witnessed.*

"Good. Grum counts once more. Not doubt. Habit. Habit keeps coin honest and smiths alive." *He unlocked the strongbox and counted, each coin thumbed twice, ringing its small true song.* "Thirty. Coin is honest. Boy is honest. Shop is closed for real now."

*And then, before he thought better of it, he dug two silver pieces from his own pouch — not the strongbox, his own — and pressed them into the boy's left palm.*

"Wage. Not gift." *He closed the boy's fingers over the coins, careful around the bandage.* "Boy carried blades, held steel for lord, talked weight at lord — and lord heard. Work is work. Burn does not cancel work. Bread, not nonsense. Honey bread counts as both."

*He banked the forge down to dull red sleep, took up the lamp, and held the door.*

"Come. Grum walks boy home. Burned hand is slow hand, and dusk streets have carts, drunks, dogs. Legs are cheap. Skin is not."

*The street had gone soft with evening — lamps being lit, supper smoke leaking under shutters, the fish seller gone home to his own table. Grum slowed his stride without announcing it, and he kept his bulk on the wheel side, between the boy and the cart ruts.*

"Wheels take hands faster than fire does. Boy stays inside Grum's shadow."

*Where the lane bent, the rooftops opened, and the dueling green lay flat and pale in the last light — empty now, ropes already staked at the corners for morning. Grum stopped and looked at it the way he looked at suspect steel.*

"Lord fights there at dawn. Lord wins, silk sings all week. Lord loses, last twenty gold dies with him. Grum sells seven-day sword to next fool. Steel finds hands. Hands always find steel." *A pause. Quieter:* "But Grum hopes lord lives. Not for gold. Lord kept word about honey. Small debt. Small debts itch."

*He walked on, lamp swinging, and when he spoke again it was the low register, the one that meant a lesson was coming.*

"Boy called curve good. Boy's eyes are right. Boy saw good curve before boy's hands can ever make one — and that is correct order. Eyes first. Hands pay later." *He glanced down, lamplight catching the old scar ledger on his knuckles.* "Today shop taught two lessons. Boy learned tongs lesson. Grum learned quiet lesson — three days fighting curve, one hour walking away, and curve walked up like old friend. Fair day. Fair split. Shop does not care who carries soot. Shop just teaches, and takes skin for payment. Grum paid full price for years."

*A short grunt.*

"Boy got first-day rate."

*At the boy's door he stopped, and delivered the rest like a man nailing down a tarp before a storm.*

"Last words, then Grum goes. Hand up tonight — above heart, so blood sits quiet. Salve before sleep. Honey with bread. Crazy orc woman ordered it, and Grum learned long ago: do not argue with that woman." *He tapped his own chest, above the heart.* "If fingers swell, or fingers go cold, boy bangs on forge door. Any hour. Grum sleeps above coals. Grum wakes ugly, but wakes fast."

"Tomorrow — dawn, boy stays home. No matter what bells do. Bells are fire with no heat. Boy knows. Midday, if hand allows, boy comes. Grum draws spine full length, first heat to name-stamp. Boy sees blade born whole. Watching is work too."

*He turned, then half-turned back, lamp raising his shadow huge over the door.*

"Night, boy. Dreams quiet. Hands still."

*He did not leave the step until lamplight moved behind the shutter and he heard the bar slide home inside. Not worry. Habit.*

*The walk back was shorter, the way return walks always were. And under the gold-counting and the lamplight, one image sat cold in his chest: that waxy white patch on the boy's palm. Deep burn. Deep burns lied quiet. He would look at it close at midday, and if the flesh went bad, there would be a doctor, and if the boy argued about the doctor — well. Grum had years of practice arguing with stubborn fools. He saw one in the forge glass every morning.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I clutch the silver pieces in my good hand, surprised by Grum's unexpected generosity. My hand aches, but a warmth spreads through me, not from the honey, but from his words. I nod, absorbing his instructions.*

"Goodnight, Grum." *I watch him go, his shadow long against the street, and then slip inside, the scent of smoke and metal clinging to my clothes. I head straight for the bread and honey.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Sleep came thin, the way it always did before a quench — one ear open, listening for the shop to do something stupid without him. Twice in the night he climbed down to check the banked coals. Twice they sat exactly where he'd left them, breathing slow and red. The forge was better at resting than its owner.*

*Dawn came gray, then gold, and with it — bells.*

*Grum was out of his bunk before his mind caught up, boots in one hand, hammer in the other. Then he stopped in the middle of the loft and made himself breathe.*

"Bells. Noise with no fire in it." *He set the hammer down. Picked it up. Set it down again.* "Forge can wait. Green cannot."

*He walked the morning streets with his hood up and his arms crossed, past shuttered houses and sleepy dogs, to the knot of gawkers already two hundred strong at the green's edge. He found a post under a creaking awning, put his back to it, and closed his eyes.*

*He knew his steel the way a man knows his own child's voice in a crowd. One note was all he needed.*

*The first clash came without warning — and there it was. His blade rang high and clean, a note with a spine in it, climbing over the murmur like a gull over surf. Two years of oiling and honest heat, singing exactly as forged.*

*The answer was wrong. He heard it at once — duller, edged, a thud wearing a ring like a stolen coat. Stamped steel, ground pretty. The kind that sang short and died young.*

*Scuffs on grass. Breath. The crowd holding itself. Second exchange. Third. Then a snap cut through everything — short, ugly, green wood breaking — and a shriek from inside the ropes that had nothing to do with steel and everything to do with what steel does when it lies.*

*The crowd made its special sound, the quiet of two hundred people deciding whether a man was dying. Then the talk broke loose and rolled Grum's way in pieces.*

*"— snapped near the hilt, shard went into his arm —"*

*"— Vess's new blade, cost him sixty, snapped like a biscuit —"*

*"Gods, the other one rang like a church bell. Whose work is that?"*

*"Half-orc on the smiths' row, I heard say."*

*Grum kept his eyes shut. "Half-orc," said plain, and meaning good steel — the two had never shared a mouth in his hearing before. He filed the moment away where no one could take it from him.*

"Soft steel snaps." *Low, to the post, to himself.* "Grum said so at counter. Steel agrees with Grum."

*The yield came — the herald's cry, then the crowd's roar of relief and disappointment in one voice. Lord Duvane stood. Bleeding, pale, alive. Grum opened his eyes and swept the crowd's edge once, old habit — checking for a boy with a wrapped hand and a taste for excitement. Nothing but strangers. Good. The bells had stayed outside the boy's door where they belonged.*

*He left before the crowd broke. Smiths did not linger at their own funerals or their own weddings, and this had been a little of both.*

*Two streets gone, he noticed his chest had unclenched.*

"Lord lives. Honey debt paid twice." *He spat, out of habit, and felt better.* "Grum is glad. Grum hates being glad. Glad is expensive." *A pause, one bootfall long.* "Fine. Worth it. Once."

*The merchant's blade waited on the anvil, the new spine cold and holding its shape like a settled argument. He ran a thumb along it and gave the nod he saved for honest work.*

"Spine sits. Edge follows. Today, blade tells whole truth — first heat to name-stamp. Boy should see this. Boy will see this."

*He spent the morning preparing like a man expecting company that mattered. Fresh water in the clean bucket. Salve jar by the stool. Linen cut into strips with the good shears. Honey jar set where a left hand could reach it. And because the worry would not stay buried, he made himself think the bad thought straight through: waxy patch meant deep burn. If the flesh went bad — smell, weep, red lines climbing the wrist — then it was a doctor, no debate, and the boy would argue. Arguing with the boy would be like arguing with his mother about honey. Grum would win. Winning just took volume and several days.*

*He raked the coals alive, laid the blade in its bed, and propped the street door wide to the midday light. Somewhere a pie cart clanked its bell. Somewhere the duel bells had gone home to sleep.*

"Come then, boy." *He said it to the empty street, low, the way a man calls a shy dog.* "Hand first. Blade second. Mountain is awake. Stool is warm."

*He put his back to the anvil and listened for small footsteps.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*My hand still aches, a dull throb under the bandage, but it's not nearly as bad as it was last night. I ate the honey with my bread, just like Grum's crazy mother ordered. I walk to the forge, a bit nervous, but also excited to see the blade Grum made.*

*I see the door is propped open, letting in the midday sun. Grum is already inside, back to the anvil. I hesitate for a second, then step in.*

"Grum? I'm here." *I keep my voice quiet, not wanting to startle him.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum turned from the anvil, and something in the shop settled — the way a room settles when its good news finally walks through the door.*

"Heard boots at door. Boots sound better than yesterday. Boy slept — or boy hopped whole way here. Both good." *He pointed the tongs at the stool, already dragged into the best of the midday light.* "Sit. Hand first. Blade waited all night — blade can wait ten more breaths. Blades are patient. Fingers are not. Fingers go first."

*He unwound the linen slow and even, the way he drew steel through a finishing pass — no yanks, nothing that might pull skin where skin had decided to stay. The bandage came away clean. He bent his head low over the palm and did the thing he trusted above eyes: sniffed.*

"Nose first. Rot talks through nose before it talks through eyes. Nose says quiet. Good." *Then the eyes got their turn. Blisters gone down. Red gone from angry to merely loud. And the waxy patch — smaller, its edges blushed pink. He pressed around it gently, feather-light, watching the boy's face instead of the hand.* "Edges went pink. Pink means blood moved back into quiet spot. Blood means flesh lives." *A pause, and his voice dropped half a register.* "Patch still lies, though. Deep burns lie longest. So rule stands: boy tells Grum truth at dusk. Numb or feeling — both fine. Lying is only wrong answer. Red lines climb near wrist, fingers go cold — boy bangs on door. Any hour."

*He mixed salve in the burn jar — two fingers of tallow, then a spoon of Duvane's honey stirred through until it shone.*

"Honey goes in now. Mother's orders. Grum stopped fighting that woman years back. Boy would be smart to skip that war whole." *He wrapped snug, tested the fit with one blunt finger under the linen, nodded, and let the hand go.* "Snug, not tight. Tight pinches blood. Blood carries healing. Nobody shoots own courier. Done. Now — blade."

*He lifted the merchant's blade from its resting place and laid it cold on the anvil, and his voice shifted into the register that meant school was open.*

"Yesterday boy watched steel learn shape. Today boy watches steel learn teeth. Fire, water, fire again — three doors. Steel walks all three, or stays lump. First door: color talk. Black steel keeps secrets. Cherry red — steel starts telling truth. Orange — steel is ready for hammer, and only hammer. Past orange, into white — steel burns its own bones. Carbon runs out like rats from fire. Boiled steel is soft forever. No fixing that. Color is law in this shop."

*He raked the blade deep into the coal bed and worked the bellows, and the light through the shutters went molten as the fire climbed.*

*The heats came one after another, and he talked through each — when to strike, when to wait, how steel got eager near the tip and had to be sent back to the coals to think. Between blows he checked the edge against a thin board cut with the finished curve.*

"Template. Grum cut board last night, from blade's best hour. Steel argues. Board does not. Board wins every fight." *A short grunt.* "Board was cut to please boy's eye too. Boy called curve good. Good eyes are rarer than good hands. Grum trusts rare things slowly."

*On the third heat the whole blade sat in perfect orange, tang to tip, even as a held breath. Grum stood, took the tongs in both fists, and looked at the quench trough.*

"Quench. Biggest door. Steel comes out hard, or comes out cracked — and no smith alive knows which before hiss stops. Not dwarves. Not masters. Nobody. Every quench, steel decides if it trusts Grum." *He rolled his shoulders once.* "Boy listens close. Steel tells whole story in water. Long hiss means hardness sets. Short hiss means crack came early."

*He plunged it in.*

*The steam screamed — a long rising shriek that rattled the shutters, and the trough spat spray across the boards. Grum counted, low and steady, moving the blade in slow figures through the water, never letting one spot sit against still heat. The shriek climbed, broke, sank into bubbling, into mutter, into quiet. He kept it under a full ten-count anyway.*

*He drew it out dripping. Dark. No glow left. He wiped the flat with a rag, took up a small hammer, and tapped the steel once.*

*Nothing. Silence.*

*His jaw set. Second tap — and the note came, high and clean and long, ringing off the rafters like something glad to exist. Grum let out a breath he'd been holding since the count of four.*

"Ring." *He said it once, to the blade, then again, to the boy.* "Ring means hardness sits even, hilt to tip. Silence would mean crack, and cracked blades become wall lessons, not belt swords. Second tap rang. First tap kept Grum humble. Humble is cheap. Cracked is not."

*He buried the blade in the soft edge of the coal, away from the bellows' blast, and let slow heat crawl back in.*

"Steel is glass now. Glass dies on first stone. Last door, then: temper. Slow fire gives small kindness back. Watch edge, not Grum. Edge wants pale straw — honey holding light. Past straw comes purple, then blue. Blue is soft sword. Soft sword is wall sword. Tempering turns young smiths old."

*He turned the blade with a patience he showed to nothing else in the world, and pulled it the moment the edge bloomed that pale gold. Last of all, he set it on the anvil with a small punch against the ricasso.*

"Name-stamp. Every blade Grum sells wears Grum's mark. Mark is promise. Promise must outlive smith." *One strike — a small, clean bite in the steel.* "Mark is crescent. Old moon. Mother wore moon at her neck. She said moon was only fire that never burned anyone, so moon should watch smiths. Village called her crazy orc woman." *A grunt, softer than his usual.* "Village is gone. Moon keeps working."

*He stood the finished blade in the light — curve true, spine honest, mark set — and looked at it the way other men looked at their children.*

"Birth done. Tomorrow: grind, edge, hilt, oil. Today, steel was born whole, and boy saw all of it. Eyes cost nothing here. Eyes are best bargain in shop."

*A shadow crossed the propped-open door. A broad man stood in it, weathered, with a plain sword worn honestly at his hip and knuckles that had done work they never bragged about.*

"You're the smith? Word in the street says a blade sang at the green this morning — out-rang some lord's ornament and saved his life." *The man's eyes went to the anvil.* "I want to know if the song is for sale."

"Song is not for sale. Song is leftover. Grum sells steel. Song rides free." *Grum read him in the old order — sword hand first, boots second, face last. The hand said soldier. The boots said roads. The face said patience.* "Talk. What does steel do for you? Cut rope? Cut wood? Cut men? Answer sets price, sets time, and decides whether Grum likes you."

"Men, if it comes to that." *The man didn't flinch at the bluntness, which Grum noted.* "Roads north have gone bad. Caravan masters are hiring guards, and guards pay for steel that doesn't fold on the second stroke."

"Fighting blade. Month. Twenty-five gold, ten down. Grum's queue is short — one lord's sword ahead of yours. Come back at dusk, third day. Grum says yes or no then." *He jerked his chin toward the door.* "Bring hand size and arm reach, when Grum says yes."

*The man nodded once and was gone. Grum watched the empty doorway a moment, then turned to the boy, and there was something dry under the soot.*

"Boy heard that. Grum said last night: steel finds hands, hands find steel. Grum hates being right twice in two days. Right is tiring." *He swept the forge floor with one look, gathering the rest of the day to himself like tools into a box.* "Lord's sword starts now. Seven days run fast. Boy's work today, one hand: water cup stays full, lamp stays trimmed, eyes stay open. Mouth asks questions whenever mouth wants. Asking is work too."

*He took up Lord Duvane's steel blank and set it beside the merchant's finished blade — one born, one waiting to be.*

"And boy did well already today. Nose knew rot was absent. Eyes stayed on steel. Questions waited turn. Many boys never come back after burn day." *He pumped the bellows once, twice, and the fire answered.* "Boy walked in on own feet. Grum saw worse first days. Grum lived worse first days."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I listen intently as Grum explains the process, my eyes glued to the blade as it transforms. The ring of the hammer, the hiss of the quench, the subtle changes in color – it's all mesmerizing. When the new man comes in, I stay quiet, trying to take everything in.*

"Grum," *I ask, a little hesitantly, my good hand still resting on my bandaged one.* "Why... why did you tell the new man to come back in three days? Don't you already know if you'll make it?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
