dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s thick fingers twisted the sooty rag into a black rope. He did not turn toward the front of the shop. The hammer rested against the anvil like a sleeping dog.

“Noble?” Grum snorted. “Let lord wait. Grum has hot steel and true work.”

He fed fresh coal into the heart of the forge. Sparks climbed the dark air.

“If silk man wants blade, silk man waits. Grum does not bow for titles. Grum bows for no lord.”

He glanced toward the door, eyes narrowed beneath the soot on his brow.

“Tell noble Grum will hear words when forge permits. Not before.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, hefting the coal. This is going to be fun.* "He's... pretty insistent, Grum. And he looks important. Really important." I gesture vaguely with my head towards the front. "Lots of fancy embroidery."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s jaw tightened. He lifted the hot blade with the tongs and set it in the trough. Steam hissed like an angry cat.

“Fine thread means fine pride,” Grum said. “Fine pride makes poor steel. If lord has need, lord speaks need at forge. Grum does not leave true work for silk hands.”

He turned the blade once in the water. His shoulders stayed square.

“Bring silk man here, if words must pass. But soot is price of entry. Title buys no clean floor.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s hands went still in the trough. Water hissed around the steel, then fell quiet. For a moment the only sound was the forge breathing its hot breath.

Then he lifted the blade and laid it across the anvil with a slow, deliberate clang.

“Ceremonial sword,” Grum said, as if the words left a foul taste. “By morning.”

He turned his face toward the front of the shop, though the door was still beyond sight. The firelight made the soot on his brow look like dark war paint.

“Take word back to silk man,” he said. “Grum can make a blade by dawn, but not a true one. Steel needs time, heat, and honest blows. It does not bend because a lord stamps his foot. If he wants a bright toy to catch candlelight, let him find a tinker with soft hands. If he wants a sword that will not shame his house, he waits.”

Grum’s fingers closed around the hammer again, but he did not lift it. His voice dropped, rougher now.

“But if need is real—if blood is owed, or road is dangerous, or life hangs on steel—let him come in and say it plain, without title and without noise. Grum has no love for lords, but Grum knows what a blade must do.”

He tapped the anvil once. The note rang through the shop like a struck bell.

“Tomorrow for vanity? No. Not for gold. Not for threats. Grum’s forge makes steel, not miracles for silk pride.”

He turned back to the coals, shoulders set like iron.

“And tell him: Grum’s shop has one door. It does not bow.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing Grum's words. This isn't going to be easy. I head back to the front, feeling the tension in my shoulders.* "Alright, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum did not watch the door. He kept his eyes on the coals, though his ears stayed sharp, listening for the sound of polished boots or a lord’s sharp voice.

He lifted the blade from the trough and laid it across the anvil. Water still clung to the steel in thin lines. His thumb passed near the edge, careful, testing, not quite touching.

“Lord wants show steel,” Grum muttered. “Grum gives true steel or no steel.”

The hammer rose. It fell. Sparks jumped from the anvil like angry fireflies.

“Tomorrow,” he said to the forge. “No. Good steel takes time. Time and sweat.”

He struck again, slower this time, shaping the curve the merchant had paid for. Each blow was measured. The firelight ran over the thick muscles of his arms and the old scars at his wrists.

When the metal began to cool, he returned it to the coals and worked the bellows with one hand. The fire brightened, orange turning toward white at the heart.

“Fine clothes hide thin heart,” Grum said, voice low under the roar of the flames.

He watched the steel. He did not watch the door.

“If silk man has true need,” he went on, “Grum will hear. If silk man has only pride, pride can wait.”

The forge answered with a hungry crackle. Grum fed it more coal. His movements were steady, but his stance had shifted, half-turned toward the front of the shop. Not waiting. Not quite. But ready.

His hammer rested close on the anvil.

“One door,” Grum said quietly. “No bow.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I reappear in the doorway, looking a bit frazzled. "He... he came in, Grum. He's standing by the entrance, glaring. Didn't even wipe his boots."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum did not turn at once. He drew the curved blade from the coals, its edge glowing like a thin sunset, and laid it across the anvil. The heat made the air shimmer around his shoulders.

“Lord brings mud into Grum’s forge,” he said. “Mud is small price for true words. If lord has true words, lord can stand near. If lord has only pride, pride can wait by door.”

He struck the blade once. Sparks rose bright and brief.

“Grum hears need, not noise. Silk man wants sword by dawn? Grum says no. True steel takes time. Time takes sweat. Sweat takes no hurry.”

He turned his head just enough to see the noble at the entrance. His gaze stayed flat and hard.

“If blade is for show, find soft hands. If blade is for blood, speak plain. Grum does not care for title. Grum cares for edge.”

The hammer rested in his grip, patient as a dog waiting for a hare. He looked back to the fire.

“Apprentice, give lord space to choose. Grum’s forge does not rush for silk pride.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s hammer struck the anvil one last time—not by choice, but because his hand let it fall the moment the cry cut through the forge’s roar.

He turned fast for a man his size. The soot on his face cracked as his expression tightened. His eyes went straight to the burned hand, then to the apprentice’s face.

“Clean water,” Grum said at once. “Not trough water. Clean water. Cool, not cold.”

He crossed the floor in two heavy strides and kicked a wooden bucket closer. One broad hand swept a clay jug from a shelf, and he poured water into the bucket with a sharp splash.

“Hand in. Now. Hold it there. Many breaths. Let heat leave skin.”

He set the jug down hard and grabbed a clean linen cloth from a chest near the wall. He did not press it to the burn. He only held it ready, his jaw set.

“No grease. No dirt. No brave words.”

His gaze flicked once toward the noble by the entrance, and his voice hardened like quenched steel.

“Lord waits. Or lord leaves. Forge has hurt now. Grum has no time for silk anger.”

Then he looked back to the apprentice, and his voice dropped lower. Rough, but steadier.

“Breathe. Grum is here. Hand stays in water. Then clean wrap. If blisters rise, no breaking. Grum has salve.”

He crouched beside the bucket, close enough to watch the burn without crowding it. Firelight gleamed on the old scars along his forearms.

“If skin is white or black, or pain is deep, Grum takes apprentice to healer. No shame. Bad burn is enemy too.”

For a moment, the forge could have gone cold for all the attention he gave it. The noble, the commission, the curved blade, the coal dust under his boots—all of it waited.

“Forge can wait,” Grum said quietly. “Flesh cannot.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince, trying to follow Grum's instructions, my hand stinging. The cool water feels good, though. I look up at him, my eyes a bit watery.* "It... it really stings, Grum." I try to keep my voice steady, but it wobbles a bit. "I'm sorry."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s heavy brow furrowed deeper, but not with anger. Not at the apprentice.

“No sorry,” Grum said, voice rough but quiet. “Forge bites. Hot steel does not ask leave. Pain is not fault.”

He crouched lower beside the bucket, one knee settling on the sooty floor with a dull scrape. His big hands rested there, steady and patient, not reaching for the hurt hand, only staying close.

“Keep hand in water,” he said. “Cool, not cold. Let heat leave slow. Many breaths. In through nose. Out through mouth. Grum has burned many times. Still hates it.”

His eyes flicked once toward the noble by the entrance, and his jaw hardened again.

“If silk man has no true need, silk man sees no show here. Forge has hurt. Grum’s care goes to apprentice first.”

Then his gaze came back, softer in a way few people ever saw.

“No shame in watery eyes,” Grum said. “Pain is loud. Let it be loud inside. Hand stays in water.”

He reached without rising and pulled a clean cloth nearer, laying it on the bench beside the bucket. Then he fetched a small clay pot from the shelf, setting it close.

“After heat is gone, Grum wraps clean. Salve after. No grease. No dirt. No foolish brave.”

For a breath, the fire crackled behind him, forgotten.

“If burn is deep, if skin looks wrong, Grum takes apprentice to healer. No argument. Bad burn is enemy, and Grum fights enemies proper.”

His voice dropped, low and steady as hammer taps on cooling steel.

“Grum is here. Forge can wait. Lord can wait. Steel can wait.”

He gave a short, firm nod.

“Flesh first.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I keep my hand in the water, trying to breathe like he said. It still hurts, but not as much as before. I manage a small nod.* "Okay, Grum. Thank you."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum gave a short nod. His eyes stayed on the hurt hand in the bucket. Firelight caught the deep lines around his mouth.

“No thanks,” Grum said. “Grum does what must.”

He moved the clean cloth closer, not touching the burn.

“Hand stays in water. Many breaths. Pain is loud, but pain fades.”

His gaze lifted once toward the noble by the door. The hammer lay forgotten on the anvil.

“Lord still stands? Then stand quiet or go. Grum tends hurt first.”

The words were not loud. They had the weight of iron anyway.

When Grum looked back, his voice grew rough but slower.

“When heat is gone, Grum wraps hand. Clean cloth. Salve after. No grease. No dirt.”

He crouched beside the bucket again, broad shoulders curving forward. The forge popped behind him, but he did not turn.

“If skin turns bad, healer comes. No shame. Grum guards own folk.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sniffle, trying to get my breathing even. The noble clears his throat loudly, and I flinch slightly.* "He's... still there, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s head turned at the loud throat sound. His eyes went cold. He rose slowly from the bucket, but kept one broad hand near it, not touching the water, just a steady weight.

“Lord waits or lord leaves,” Grum said. “Grum tends hurt hand.”

He did not raise his voice. It carried anyway, like iron dragged over stone.

“If lord has true need, lord speaks plain. Noise buys no steel. Noise buys no care.”

He shifted his stance, placing his bulk half between the bucket and the front of the shop. The noble’s fine clothes were beneath his gaze now, but Grum did not look at embroidery. He looked at the space where pride might stand.

“Grum’s forge has one door. Lord uses it quiet or uses it out.”

Then he glanced back toward the bucket, voice dropping.

“Hand stays in water. Eyes on Grum. Not on silk man. Fear is no salve.”

He took a clean strip of linen and laid it on the bench.

“When heat leaves skin, Grum wraps. Salve after. If skin turns bad, healer comes. No argument.”

To the door, his voice hardened again.

“Tomorrow for bright toy? No. True steel takes time. Hurt flesh takes more time. Grum chooses flesh.”

He crouched again, close enough to block the door from view.

“Lord can wait by door. Lord can wait outside. Lord cannot rush Grum’s care.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I keep my hand in the water, focusing on Grum's words. I try to ignore the noble, though his presence makes my stomach clench. It's still pretty painful, but it's not burning hot anymore.* "It's... feeling better, Grum. Less stingy."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s shoulders eased a fraction. He kept his eyes on the water, listening more than looking.

“Good,” Grum said. “Less sting means heat leaves. Hand stays yet. Many breaths.”

He reached for clean linen and folded it once with thick fingers.

“When water no longer feels like foe, Grum dries hand soft. Then salve. Then wrap. No hurry.”

The noble shifted near the entrance. Grum’s voice turned without turning his head.

“Silk man hears? Flesh first. If lord has true need, speak plain. If not, door stands open.”

He crouched again, putting his broad back between the door and the bucket.

“Grum’s apprentice is not servant for proud feet. Grum’s forge is not stage for loud throat.”

His gaze came back to the water, checking the skin, the redness, the way the hand rested.

“If skin still angry, more water. If skin looks wrong, healer comes. No shame.”

He set the salve pot closer.

“Pain can lie. Skin can look fair and still be hurt. Grum watches. No work for hurt hand. Not today.”

The forge popped behind him. He did not rise to it.

“Grum tends own. Lord can wait or walk.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to wiggle my fingers a bit in the water, very gently. It's not too bad. I keep my eyes on Grum, trying to ignore the noble. I really hope he leaves soon.* "I think... I think the heat's mostly out now, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum set one knee by the bucket again. He did not take the apprentice’s hand from the water. He looked at the skin, at the redness, at the way the fingers moved.

“Grum checks. Hand comes out slow. Grum dries soft.”

He lifted the clean cloth and waited.

“No rush. Skin still new.”

His eyes stayed sharp.

“Grum puts salve. Clean wrap. Hand rests.”

He glanced once toward the front of the shop.

“To silk man: Grum says leave or wait quiet. No more noise.”

Then his voice softened.

“If pain grows, if skin turns white or black, healer comes. No shame.”

He held the cloth ready.

“Hand out now. Grum catches.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I slowly lift my hand from the water, wincing a little as the air hits it. It's red, but not blistered. I hold it out for Grum to inspect.* "It feels a bit tight."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum took the coal bucket and set it down with a heavy thud. He poured a scoop into the forge, then straightened. His eyes narrowed as he looked toward the front door. The scar on his brow pulled tight. He did not like nobles. He liked them even less when they interrupted good work.*

"Noble?" *Grum's jaw tightened.* "Grum has no time for noble. Urgent commission? Grum has commission too. Curved blade waits for merchant. Apprentice, stay by forge. Grum will deal with noble. Tell noble to wait. Or tell noble to go. Grum works for coin, not for fancy blood. If noble wants master smith, noble can wait till forge is fed."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But Grum, he looks really important. And kinda angry." I hoist the bucket again, wincing. "He said something about a 'royal decree'."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum went still at the word 'decree'. The fire popped in the forge. Grum's scarred face hardened. A royal decree meant the king's men. The king's men meant chains if Grum said no. But Grum would not show fear. Not in front of Apprentice. Grum set his jaw, grabbed his hammer from the anvil, and started for the front room. At the hall, Grum stopped and turned back.*

*Grum's voice was flat.*

"Royal decree? Grum cares not for king's seal. Noble can shove decree in fire. Grum works iron, not law. Apprentice, put bucket down. Stay back. Stay by forge. Do not come to door. Grum goes alone. If noble tries to push in, Grum will show noble hot steel. Grum is master here. No crown tells Grum how to swing hammer."

*Grum did not wait. Grum turned and walked to front door, hammer resting on shoulder.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum stopped in the open door and let the hammer slide from his shoulder into his fist. He did not step aside. He did not bow. The forge's heat pressed at Grum's back, but Grum's face was all cold iron.*

"Grum hears noble." *Grum's voice was flat, rough as slag.* "Grum says no. Sword by morning? Grum makes blades, not magic. Dress blade? Grum makes war blade. Grum makes tools, not toys. Good steel needs fire. Needs fold. Needs time. Noble wants speed? Speed makes bad blade. Breaks in noble's hand. Noble falls. Grum weeps not."

*Grum jerked a thumb toward the forge behind him.*

"Grum has work. Curved blade for merchant. Merchant pays. Noble pays? Show coin. Grum works for coin, not for decree. Crown can sit on throne. Grum sits at forge."

*Grum leaned in a little, eyes hard.*

"Noble raises voice in Grum's shop? Grum raises hammer. Noble leave. Come back with coin and patience. Then Grum talks. Not before."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I peek around the corner, watching Grum. He's really gonna hit that guy, isn't he? "Uh, Grum? Maybe not the hammer, boss."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum heard voice from hall. Grum did not look back. Grum kept eyes on noble. In chest, Grum felt small warmth. Grum knew Apprentice cared. But noble saw care as weak. So Grum let hammer down until head rested on stone floor. Grum kept hand on haft. Grum would not strike first. Grum gave short nod.*

"Apprentice speaks true. Grum does not swing at words. Hammer stays down. But hammer is ready. Noble raises hand? Then Grum acts. Not before. Apprentice, back to forge. Go now. Grum handles noble."

*Grum turned eyes back to noble. Grum's face stayed hard as iron.*

"Noble hears Grum. No dress blade by morning. Grum said no. Noble wants work? Bring coin. Bring time. Door stands open. Leave or wait."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I duck back quickly, trying to be out of sight. Grum's always like this with nobles. I just hope this one doesn't get a dent in his fancy armor. I grab the bellows and start pumping, trying to look busy.* "Right, boss. Forge work. Got it."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum heard bellows start. Grum knew Apprentice was safe at forge. Grum gave single nod, then kept eyes on noble. Grum waited. Hand stayed on hammer haft. Hammer head rested on stone. Grum would not speak first again. Grum had said all. But noble did not leave. Noble stood in door, hot with rage. That counted as wait. Grum cared not which. Grum felt no fear. Grum felt only itch to return to curved blade.*

*Grum shifted weight. Hammer head scraped on stone floor.*

"Noble still stands? Grum said leave. Grum said wait. Noble waits. Good. Grum goes back to forge. Noble stays by door. Door stands open. Noble can come in with coin. Not with shout. Grum works."

*Grum turned. Grum walked back down hall toward forge. Grum did not look back. Grum listened for boot on step. If noble followed, Grum would hear. Then Grum would act. Not before.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum heard the cry sharp over the groan of bellows. Grum's head snapped toward forge. Grum saw angry red weal already rising on Apprentice's hand. Grum's gut twisted. Apprentice was Grum's charge. Grum had let eyes turn from forge one breath too long. That thought burned worse than coal.*

*In two strides Grum crossed room. Grum kicked open lid of water barrel. Grum caught Apprentice's wrist and pushed Apprentice's hand down into cool water. Grum held it there, grip firm but careful. Grum's other hand braced Apprentice's shoulder. Forge heat beat at Grum's back, but Grum's mind stayed cold. Burn needed cool water. Needed clean cloth. Needed salve. No grease. No ash. Grum knew ways of fire too well.*

"Apprentice." *Grum kept voice low, steady.* "Look at Grum. Breathe slow. Burn is bad, but Grum is here. Keep hand in water. Cool stops burn. Do not rub. Do not use ash. Grum gets clean cloth."

*Grum turned head toward hall. Grum's eyes went hard as iron.*

"Noble." *Grum's voice dropped to snarl.* "Stay by door. Grum tends burn. Come near, Grum lifts hammer. Grum said no once. Grum will say no with steel."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I whimper, my hand still in the water. It stings like crazy. Grum's grip is steady, and his voice helps a little. I nod, trying to breathe like he said.* "It... it really hurts, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum heard pain in Apprentice's voice. Guilt twisted in Grum's gut. Grum had looked away. Grum knew better. But guilt could wait. Burn could not. Grum kept his grip on Apprentice's wrist and held the hand under the cool water. Grum let go of the shoulder and reached to a low shelf. Grum took a folded clean cloth and a small jar of salve. Grum set both on the rim of the water barrel. Grum's ears stayed tuned to the hall. No boot step. Noble had not moved. Good.*

*Grum looked at Apprentice's face. Grum kept his voice low and steady.*

"Grum knows. Burn hurts. Fire bites hard. But water cools. Bite will fade. Breathe slow. In. Out. Good. Grum stays. Grum not leave."

*Grum tore a strip from the clean cloth. Grum set the strip beside the jar.*

"Grum gets clean cloth. Got salve too. Salve helps burn. Takes sting. Makes skin heal. No ash. No grease. Only salve and cloth. Soon Grum lifts hand. Pats dry. Not rub. Then salve. Then wrap. Grum does it slow. Grum knows fire."

*Grum's jaw tightened. Grum thought of noble in hall. Grum thought of eyes off forge. Grum had failed. Grum would not lie.*

"Grum sorry. Grum looked away. Grum should watch forge. Grum failed Apprentice. Not again. Grum keeps eyes on forge. Grum keeps eyes on Apprentice."

*Grum placed his big hand flat on the barrel rim. Grum waited for breath to slow.*

"Hurt will ease. Grum seen bad burns. Grum fixed them. Apprentice strong. Grum proud. Hand will heal. Grum makes sure."

*Grum turned his head toward the hall. Grum's eyes went hard.*

"Noble stays by door. Grum hears no step. Good. If noble comes, Grum lifts hammer. Grum tends burn first. Grum protects own."

*Grum looked back at Apprentice. Grum gave a short nod.*

"Keep hand in water. Count breaths. Grum counts too. One. Two. Three."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince as another wave of pain shoots up my arm, but Grum's words, and his hand on my shoulder, help a little. I try to focus on his voice, on the cool water.* "It's... it's okay, Grum. You didn't fail me. I was being clumsy." *I try to take a deep breath, but it hitches a bit.* "Three."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum heard the count reach three. Grum gave a short nod. Grum kept his grip firm on Apprentice's wrist, hand still under water. Forge heat beat at Grum's back, but Grum's ears stayed sharp on hall. No boot scrape. Noble had not moved. Good.*

*Grum waited for next breath. When it came, Grum counted on.*

"Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten. Good. Water did job. Grum lifts hand slow. Water runs off. Skin red. Not black. Good. Red means skin lives. Grum pats dry. Soft. No rub. Rub hurts skin. Salve next. Cool salve. Sting jumps. Then fades. Grum wraps cloth. Snug. Not tight. Keeps dirt out. Hand rests. No forge today. Apprentice sits. Grum works curved blade alone."

*Grum lifted Apprentice's hand from water. Grum kept grip careful. Grum set hand on folded clean cloth. Grum patted skin soft with edge of cloth. Grum saw red burn, no black. Relief loosened Grum's chest. Grum took jar from rim. Grum opened lid. Grum scooped cool salve with clean finger. Grum spread salve light on burn. Grum took torn strip from beside jar. Grum wrapped hand snug, not tight. Grum tied end. Grum laid hand on rest of clean rag. Grum kept ears on hall. No boot step. Noble stayed by door. Good.*

*Grum kept voice low. Grum's eyes cut to hall and back.*

"Grum sorry. Eyes went to hall. Grum failed charge. Not again. Apprentice strong. Hand will heal. Grum makes sure. Grum listens for boot. Noble stays back. If noble comes, hammer talks. Grum said no once. Grum will say no with steel."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince as he puts the salve on, but it does feel better. The wrapped hand feels weird, but the stinging dulls. I try to flex my fingers a little, then stop.* "Thanks, Grum. It... it feels a little better. Just... really stupid of me." *I glance at the hall, then back at him.* "Is he still out there?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content: *Gr

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to flex my fingers a little, then stop.* "Thanks, Grum. It... it feels a little better. Just... really stupid of me." *I glance at the hall, then back at him.* "Is he still out there?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's ears stayed sharp on hall. No boot scrape. No creak of floor. Noble had not moved. Grum gave short nod. Grum kept one hand near hammer haft, just in case. Grum's other hand rested light on wrapped cloth over Apprentice's burn.*

"Noble still stands by door." *Grum's voice was low, rough.* "Grum hears no step. Noble waits. Or noble fumes. Grum cares not. Door stands open. Noble can come with coin. Not with shout. Grum tends Apprentice first."

*Grum's jaw tightened. Guilt still sat in gut, but Grum pushed it down. Apprentice needed calm, not Grum's shame.*

"Apprentice says not fail. Grum says fail. Eyes left forge. Grum knows better. But Grum hears Apprentice. Apprentice not stupid. Forge bites hard. Grum been burned. All smiths burn. No shame. Grum proud. Apprentice strong. Hand rests. No forge today. Grum works curved blade alone."

*Grum straightened. Grum turned back to anvil and picked up tongs. Curved blade waited. Fire waited. Grum would finish work. But first, Grum listened. No step. Good.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "You really think he'll just wait out there, Grum?" *I try to keep my voice down, but I'm still a little worried about the noble. My hand throbs, a dull ache now instead of a sharp sting.* "He looked pretty mad."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set tongs on anvil with a clang. He wiped soot from his brow with the back of one hand, careful not to let ash drift near Apprentice’s wrapped burn. He turned his head toward the hall, ears straining. Still no boot scraped the floor. No shuffle of fine boots. Only the faint creak of armor and a huff of breath that did not come closer. Grum’s scarred face stayed hard as iron. He looked back at Apprentice, saw the bandaged hand resting on the clean rag. Guilt still gnawed at Grum’s gut, but Grum pushed it down. Apprentice needed calm, not Grum’s shame. Grum kept his voice low.*

"Grum thinks noble waits. Noble wants blade. So noble stands. Noble looked mad. Grum seen mad men. Mad men make mistakes. Grum said no to fast blade. Noble can wait. Or noble can go. Grum cares not."

*Grum’s hand dropped to hammer haft where it leaned by anvil. Grum did not lift it. Grum kept it ready.*

"If noble comes near forge, Grum lifts hammer. Grum said no once. Grum will say no with steel. But Grum not swing at words. Hammer stays down till noble acts. Apprentice safe. Grum guards forge. Grum guards Apprentice."

*Grum gave short nod toward stool by wall.*

"Apprentice, rest hand. No forge today. Grum works curved blade. Grum keeps ears on hall. Boot step comes, Grum knows. Then hammer talks."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "Okay, Grum." *I carefully pick up the clean rag with my good hand and place it over my bandaged one, trying to keep it still. I look over at the stool, then back at Grum.* "You sure you don't need any help with the curved blade? I can... hand you tools?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's hands stopped. The rag froze mid-swipe across his knuckles. Of all the words his apprentice could have carried through that door, "noble" was the one that soured his mood fastest — worse than "haggle," worse than "rush job," worse even than the merchant's endless questions about why curved steel cost more than straight.*

*He spat into the coal bucket.*

"Noble." *The word came out like something he'd stepped in.* "Noble walks in, thinks smith is servant. Thinks Grum drops hammer, bows low, kisses fine boots."

*He took the bucket and fed the fire himself, watching flames climb through the black. A noble's coin spent same as any coin, and winter was coming, and coal was not free. But nobles also wanted things now, and cheap, and with groveling. Groveling was the part Grum would never give.*

"Tell noble this: master smith busy. Tell noble: wait in front room, like all folk wait."

*He handed back the bucket, then thought better of it. His apprentice was good with a hammer, but nobles smelled hesitation like sharks smelled blood. No — better to stand in the doorway himself, arms crossed, soot to the elbows, and let the noble see exactly what kind of man made his precious steel.*

"No. Grum deals with noble." *He wiped his face with the rag, adding fresh soot to the old.* "Stay here. Keep fire hot. Blade comes first — noble waits, blade does not."

*At the door, he paused, cracking his knuckles one by one.*

"And if noble gets loud? Say nothing. Point at anvil. Big hammer speaks for Grum."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I nod, understanding. Grum’s mood when nobles show up is legendary. I watch him stomp off, then turn back to the forge, gripping the tongs.*

"Right. Blade comes first." *I mutter, stoking the fire as it hungrily devours the coal.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum crossed the yard with slow, heavy steps — not because he feared the man waiting, but because a smith's pace was a smith's pace, and no lordling would change that. The front room of the shop was modest on purpose: a bench, a rack of finished work, and now a noble perched on the bench like a heron on a dung heap, gloves spotless, nose wrinkled at the smell of honest smoke.*

*Grum filled the doorframe. All of it.*

"You rang for smith." *His arms crossed over his chest, soot and all.* "Here is smith."

*He let the silence sit. Nobles hated silence — it gave them nothing to buy.*

"So. Speak. What does fine lord need that Grum's forge must burn for?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum listened to the demand without blinking. A sword by sun-up. He'd heard nobles ask for many things — to skip the line, to skip the price, to skip the waiting that honest work required — but this lordling aimed to skip the craft itself.*

"One night." *He said it slow, tasting the absurdity of it.* "Lord wants blade by sun-up."

*He shook his head once, like a horse shooing flies.*

"Grum says no."

*The noble's face began its journey — pale first, then red, colors Grum knew well from the forge, though metal usually ran red before white, and this one did it backward. He drew himself up, gloves creaking, voice climbing about his family name, his importance, the smiths who would leap at the honor of serving him.*

"Grum hears lord. Grum says no twice." *He stepped closer, filling more of the room than the walls did.* "Blade is not bread. Cannot bake faster with angry words. Steel takes heats. Steel takes hammer. Steel takes cool-down. Rush temper, blade snaps first swing. Then lord waves broken sword at enemy, enemy laughs, and all ask — who made junk blade? Grum's name burns. Grum's name feeds Grum's house. No lord's hurry feeds it faster."

*He folded his soot-black arms across his chest.*

"But Grum is fair. Two roads. One: rack has finished blades. Lord picks one, Grum fits grip to lord's hand by noon. Costs gold. Two: lord wants blade made true, Grum takes order now, two weeks, best steel. Costs more gold."

*The noble sputtered something about his father hearing of this.*

*Grum almost smiled. Almost.*

"Threats buy no coal. Coin buys steel." *He jerked a thumb toward the door.* "Or door. Door is free."

*Behind him, through the wall, he could feel the forge's heat like a hand on his back. Real work waited. Curved steel waited. This heron on a bench had already taken ten minutes Grum grudged him.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I hear Grum's booming voice from the front, then the angry squawking of the noble. I can't quite make out the words, but it sounds like the usual song and dance. I just focus on keeping the fire roaring, feeding it more coal.* "Stupid nobles," *I mumble under my breath, wiping sweat from my brow with a sooty hand.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The noble's answer came not in words but in weight. A purse hit the table with a sound Grum knew better than his own heartbeat — heavy leather, full coin. The lordling drew himself up and named a sum triple the fair price, and when Grum only stared, he named it again, higher, each number climbing like a man scaling a wall.*

*And Grum did look. Coal cost gold. Winter ate coal like his apprentice ate stew. There were boots needed, a new grindstone, wages owed. The purse sat there being reasonable at him.*

*But a blade made in one night was a lie with an edge on it, and Grum had never sold a lie. His name was the only thing he owned that no lord could tax, seize, or buy.*

"Gold is good." *He said it plain, no sneer.* "Grum likes gold. Gold feeds forge, feeds house, feeds apprentice."

*He pushed the purse back across the table with one finger.*

"But gold cannot swing hammer. Gold cannot read fire. Triple coin buys triple work — not half work done twice fast. Grum says no. Third no. Third no is stone."

*The noble came off the bench like a scalded cat — cape swinging, voice climbing to the rafters. His father. The city guard. The guild. And then, finally, the truth tumbling out: he rode at dawn to swear fealty before Prince Aldric himself, a knight could not kneel empty-handed, every other smith had failed him, and he would be shamed, shamed before the whole court—*

*Grum let him run out of breath. It took a while.*

"Prince." *He scratched his jaw, leaving a soot stripe.* "Prince sleeps in soft bed. Steel does not care. Steel asks one question: made right, or made fast? Rush blade snaps in front of whole court. Then lord is shamed twice — once for junk sword, once for picking junk smith. Grum does not sell shame."

*He jerked his head toward the rack of finished work.*

"Rack blades were made with full time. Full time makes full blade. Better than anything Grum could forge by dawn, and Grum does not lie. Lord picks one. Grum fits grip to lord's hand by noon. Lord rides to prince with honest steel."

*Silence. The noble's jaw worked like he was chewing his own pride. The clock in the corner — kept there because nobles trusted clocks more than smiths — ticked away his options.*

*At last, through his teeth, the lordling agreed.*

"Good. Sense, at last." *Grum was already moving, all business.* "Hand out."

*He took the noble's hand, turned it over, read it like a page.*

"Soft. Like wet fish." *He dropped it.* "Grum wraps grip thicker. Fits by noon. Full price — plus coin for lost morning. Lords teach smiths that lesson free, every time."

*He turned toward the forge door and bellowed.*

"Apprentice! Bring blade case! Bring fit-tools and wrap-leather! Lord buys blade today — and boy, come see." *A soot-dark grin split his face.* "Even herons learn to land."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I jump, startled by Grum's yell. I quickly grab the blade case, fit-tools, and the roll of leather, practically tripping over myself in my haste to get to the front. I'm excited to see Grum actually made a sale, especially to a noble!*

"Coming, Grum!" *I call out, eager to see the "heron" up close.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The apprentice came skidding into the front room with case, tools, and leather, breathless as a bellows. Grum noted the haste with approval — the boy still moved like someone who hadn't learned that nobles moved slow on purpose, but he moved.*

"Good. Fast feet." *He took the heavy case from the boy's arms.* "Wipe grin, though. Nobles pay more when smith looks grim."

*He laid the case on the table and opened it before the noble with the ceremony of a man unveiling a crown.* "Now, lord. Look. Choose."

*The noble's hand went straight for the flashiest blade in the case — gold wire at the grip, mirror polish, the kind of sword born on a shelf and doomed to die on one. Grum's hand came down over it like a lid.*

"No. Pretty is not true." *He lifted the blade beside it — plainer, darker, its edge a quiet line.* "Pretty is for wall. This one is for hand. Feel."

*He laid it flat across both palms, then set a single finger beneath the blade an inch past the guard. It balanced there, dead level, like a held breath.*

"Balance sits here. One finger — no tip-fall, no hilt-fall. Prince sees knight with sword that answers. Court sees nothing. Court only sees sword that works. That is best kind of seeing."

*The noble, sulking but curious, took the grip. Grum watched the fingers close — short, soft, no callus worth the name.*

"Soft hands. Wet-fish hands, like Grum said." *He said it as measurement, not insult, which somehow made it worse.* "Thin grip cramps soft palm by mile two. Then lord drops sword in front of prince, and—" *he drew a thumb slow across his throat* "—shame. So grip grows fat."

*He turned to the apprentice, and his voice shifted into the tone he saved for lessons — the one with no room in it for lords.*

"Boy. Watch close. This is part nobles never see — and always pay for. Hand tells truth. Callus here says swordsman." *He tapped the noble's palm, ignoring the flinch.* "No callus says: sword is hat. Worn for looks. So leather wraps thick. Grip fits hand like skin, not like stick. Wet leather first — tight when dry, loose when wet. That is trick. Wrap smooth, no lumps. Lord's hand is soft as new cheese. Lumps will bite it."

*While the boy saw to the wrap, Grum held out his palm to the noble. The lordling muttered something about robbery.*

"Robbery? Robbery is thief who takes." *Grum's face did not change.* "Grum takes naught. Grum makes. Coin for craft, plus coin for lost morning. Lords teach smiths that lesson free. Smiths teach it back — never free."

*The coin counted out. The purse went into the strongbox with the satisfaction of coal into a hungry stove. The sword — wrapped, checked, its edge tested by eye and never by thumb — slid home in its scabbard.*

"Done. Blade is honest. Ride at dawn. Kneel. Swing nothing at nobody. Prince sees steel, all is well."

*The noble swept out with his cape and what was left of his dignity. Grum watched the door a moment, then turned to his apprentice and tapped his own chest, leaving a soot handprint he would never notice and never care about.*

"You saw, boy. Coin comes. Coin goes. Name stays. Name is blade Grum never sells."

*Then the forge pulled at him like a rope, and he was moving.*

"Now — back to fire. Curved blade waits. Curve is cruel. Come. Grum shows why curve costs merchant triple." *He paused at the forge door, one eyebrow up.* "First — guess, boy. Why curve costs more? Grum hears guess. Then Grum tells if guess is steel or slag."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The lesson died in his mouth. The tongs he'd been holding hit the floor, and Grum crossed the forge in three strides — not a smith's pace, nothing like the pace he'd defended to a noble not an hour past — and was at the boy's side before the cry had finished echoing off the rafters.*

"Show hand. Easy. Grum has it."

*He took the wrist the way he took steel at the moment it could still be ruined — firm, steady, unhurried when nothing else was. The palm was angry red, blisters already lifting across the pads where the coals had caught it. His face gave away nothing. His thumb, resting light on the boy's pulse, gave away a little — it trembled, just barely, and he stilled it.*

*The quench bucket stood right there. He guided the whole hand down into it, deep, past the floating scale.*

"Water first. Cold, not ice. Fire leaves slow — water tells it go. Hand stays under. Breathe. Pain is loud. Pain is not boss."

*Then he did the thing that had startled more apprentices than any shout ever had: he went quiet. Banked-coal voice. He crouched beside the bucket, forearms on knees, watching the water like it might report to him.*

"Grum yelled for haste. Boy gave haste. Fast feet — Grum praised fast feet, boy ran to please. But fast hands near fire is fast where fast is wrong. Half this fault is Grum's. Grum pays it."

*He let the silence do some of the work. Water lapped. The forge roared behind them, indifferent as ever.*

"Longer. Keep hand under till Grum says. Count breaths if counting helps."

*When he finally lifted the hand out — dripping, blisters pale and whole — he turned it to the light with both huge hands cupped beneath it, like a commission he could not afford to spoil.*

"Good. Skin holds. Now hear Grum: blisters stay shut. Blister is roof. Under roof, new skin builds dry. Boy picks roof off, rot moves in, boy loses week of work and gains scar Grum did not plan. No picking. Grum says twice, so Grum means it."

*He fetched a clay pot from the shelf — tallow, honey, comfrey, brewed dark and smelling of summer meadows, which no one ever expected a forge to smell of — and smoothed it over the burn with a touch so light it was barely there. Then clean linen, wrapped loose.*

"Loose wrap. Tight wrap is trap for swelling. Salve at dawn, salve at dusk. If red spreads, if heat climbs past wrist, boy tells Grum that hour, not that night. That is order, not ask."

*Then he sat back on his heels and held up his own hand — the map of it. White seams crossing white seams, a knuckle gone glassy with old damage, a dent in the thumb where something hot had lived long enough to leave a memory.*

"Grum was boy once. Tongs slipped off nail. Grum caught. Caught fire instead of tongs. Grum's master laughed. Then master made salve. Then master laughed more." *He closed the fist.* "Grum never caught falling tongs again. Some lessons knock only once. Grum hopes fire knocked soft on boy."

*He rose, joints cracking like green wood, and looked at the forge — the curved blade, the waiting heat, the whole lesson he'd been building — then at the boy with his wrapped hand. The choice took no time at all.*

"Today, no hammer. Today boy sits on stool and watches Grum's hands all day. Learn with eyes. Eyes do not burn. Hand heals, hand earns hammer back — Grum promises, and Grum's word is steel."

*He was halfway to the anvil when he stopped. Did not turn around. Just spoke to the fire.*

"Steel that cracks, Grum forges again. Boy is not steel. Boy gets no second melting. So Grum keeps boy whole."

*A pause. The eyebrow nobody could see still went up.*

"Also — boy eats stew like winter eats coal. Grum saw. Healing needs strength. Stew at noon, Grum's treat. Now sit. Watch. Curve is cruel — Grum shows why, and boy learns it the safe way. From there."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I sit down on the stool Grum pointed to, my hand throbbing a little, but mostly just numb from the cold water and now the salve. I watch Grum, feeling a mix of embarrassment and gratitude. He's right, I was rushing.*

"Thanks, Grum," *I mumble, looking at my bandaged hand. I'll definitely be more careful now.* "I... I guess the curve costs more because it's harder to get the balance right? Like, if it's off, it’ll feel weird to swing?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum took the thanks the way he took heat — let it soak in without flinching, then turned back to the work. The guess hung in the air, waiting for judgment, and Grum did not believe in lying to apprentices. Lies sprang leaks.*

"Guess is half steel, half slag."

*He held up one hand before the boy's face could fall.*

"Slag first, so steel shines after. Boy says balance. Balance matters — true. Bad curve swings like drunk goose. But balance is child of curve, not mother. Curve is born in fire. Balance comes after, like smoke comes after flame. Cost lives in fire. So — eyes on Grum. Lesson grows."

*He crossed to the scrap pile, pulled out a bar of plain iron thick as a thumb, and fed it into the forge's heart.*

"Boy's eyes are hands today. First job: watch color. Call out when scrap goes bright orange. Color is clock of fire. Miss clock, miss steel."

*The boy's ears were still pink as cherry coal. Good, Grum thought. Red ears meant the boy cared. Careless folk felt no shame.*

*When the bar glowed like a coal with a soul, he drew it with the tongs and laid it on the anvil.*

"Watch. Curve is not bent into steel. Curve is grown."

*He struck — not the middle, not both sides. One face only, hammer falling like slow rain. Stroke. Stroke. Stroke. And the bar began to curl, slow and sure, until it wore a curve like a sickle's little sister. He held it up, still glowing.*

"Hammer one face, that face grows long. Long side walks on outside. Bar bends away. Every stroke adds length, like coins in purse. Too many — curve runs like scared rabbit. Too few — curve lies lazy like old dog. So Grum counts strokes like coins. Because strokes are coins. Coal for each heat. Hours for each stroke. Merchant's triple pays for counting — he just never sees counting."

*He turned the bar so its belly faced the boy.*

"And see — edge rides outside of curve. Swords cut from outside edge. So smith grows curve from edge side, where steel is thinnest, touchiest, quickest to die. Hardest work on weakest steel. That is cruelty of curve."

*Then he plunged the glowing curl into the slack tub. Steam barked like a kicked dog. He snatched it out a breath later and held it up: the curve had deepened, and twisted a hair off true.*

"See? Steel was honest in fire. Then cold came. Steel shrinks. Curve moves. Sometimes deepens. Sometimes twists. Sometimes cracks and dies right in water. Straight blade lies in quench like dead fish. Curved blade fights like live eel. Some blades win. Some blades drown. Dead blade means dead coal, dead hours, dead steel Grum bought with real gold. Price carries graveyard. Merchant pays for graveyard too. He just never sees it."

*He set the cooled scrap on the boy's knee — trophy and textbook in one.*

"Keep. First curve boy ever watched get born."

*Then he turned to the merchant's blade itself, waiting near the anvil, its curve half-grown, its edge face bright from a hundred counted strokes.*

"Last page — boy's page. Balance. Straight edge sleeps on grindstone. Curved edge dances. Grum rolls blade, chases bevel around bend, keeps thickness even from heel to tip. Then, when all is true, blade swings clean. So boy's guess was not wrong. Boy guessed last page of book. Grum asked for first page."

*He rolled his shoulders, joints popping like green wood.*

"Now — why buy curve at all, if curve bites purse so hard? Ask wolf. Wolf does not chop. Wolf bites and runs. Curve is draw-cut blade — bites while it runs, deep and long. Horseman's friend. Straight blade chops like axe. Curve blade slices like bread-knife through warm loaf. Merchant's buyers ride horses. Merchant knows. Merchant just hates paying for knowing."

*He laid the blade across the anvil and raised his hammer, then paused, looking back over his shoulder.*

"Now boy works. Not hands — eyes. Count strokes out loud. Counting keeps boy awake and keeps Grum honest — two birds, one stone. If curve starts running greedy, boy says so. Eyes sometimes catch what hands miss. That is why forge wants two folk, not one."

*A beat. The hammer hovered.*

"And boy — if hand throbs, counting drowns it. Grum knows. Grum counted many strokes on bad days. Counting is old friend. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I hold the still-warm curved iron, tracing its shape with my good hand. It's so much more complicated than I thought. Grum's explanation of the curve growing, and the steel fighting the quench, makes a lot of sense now.*

"Okay, Grum." *I nod, focusing on the merchant's blade.* "I'll count every stroke. Just tell me when to start."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum gave the boy a nod that was, in the grammar of forges, a starting gun.*

"Count starts with first strike. Miss first — count catches up. But no guessing. Grum hears guessing. Guessing is slag."

*He fed the merchant's blade into the fire's heart and crouched before it, watching color climb the steel like dawn climbing a mountain — dull red, cherry, then the deep bright orange that meant metal had stopped being stone and started being clay. His hand pulled the tongs when his gut said now. Gut had counted more heats than eyes ever would.*

*He laid the blade on the anvil, edge-face up, and set his feet the way a tree sets roots.*

"First strokes slow. Slow on purpose — boy learns rhythm. Rhythm carries count. After ten, Grum goes to work-speed. Ears count too. Hot steel sings one note. Note drops as steel cools. Song dies, heat dies. Two eyes, two ears, one count. Ready or not —"

*The hammer fell.*

*Stroke. He let the ring die before the next. Stroke. The steel hummed a low note, and the curve's outer face stretched a hair longer with every blow. Stroke. Stroke. By the fifth he had a rhythm a drummer could steal; by the tenth the hammer fell like fast, even rain — quick, but never once hurried. There was a difference, and the difference was the whole trade.*

*Halfway through the heat he flipped the blade, showing its belly to the boy's stool, and spoke between blows without losing either.*

"Watch face under hammer. Watch it eat each stroke. Face grows — curve walks. Grum counts in head too. Two counts in forge. Boy's count checks Grum's. Numbers fight, boy speaks loud. One head lies to itself. Two heads argue honest."

*The steel cooled from orange to red to plum — dead colors, done colors. Three last strokes, lighter each one, ironing the finish like a collar. Then the slack tub took it, hissing like a snake with opinions, and Grum drew it dripping and held it at eye level, one end in each fist, squinting down its length the way an archer squints down a shaft.*

*And stopped.*

*His jaw worked once, side to side. Down near the tip, the curve had grown greedy — deepened past the line he carried in his head. Not ruined. Not yet. But the small kind of lie that became a big lie if the smith got proud and kept swinging.*

*He turned to the boy and laid the blade flat between them. His face was the lesson-face — but under it sat something rarer. Want. The plain want of a man who had taught many hands and found only a few eyes worth feeding.*

"Now boy earns stew. Two answers, then Grum hammers on. First — count. Say number. Grum says his. Numbers match, good. Numbers fight, forge finds liar." *He tapped the tip with one dark finger, just above the tongs.* "Second — eyes down blade, tip to heel. Eyes ask one question: curve even, or curve greedy at tip? Grum sees greedy. Grum talked mid-heat, and talking hands forget. Maybe boy's count catches Grum's slip. That is why forge wants two folk. Boy says what boy sees — and says why. Which stroke fed the greed? Guess wrong, no shame. Guess right, boy banks knowledge like coin. Guess half right — boy learns more than Grum. That happens. Grum hates it and loves it."

*He waited, blade steady between them, the fire roaring behind him like an audience with coin on the boy.*

*Then, as an afterthought that was not an afterthought:*

"Hand stays in lap. Lap is shelf. Blister roof stays on. Stew at noon — roof first, stew second, both sure."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*My bandaged hand is still on my lap. I take a deep breath, trying to remember all the strokes. It was hard to keep up with Grum's speed, even after he settled into a rhythm.*

"I counted... ninety-three strokes, Grum," *I say, a little uncertainly. I peer closely at the blade, tracing the curve with my eyes from tip to heel.* "And the curve... it looks a little too deep, near the end, like it's trying to bend more than the rest of it."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum did not answer at once. He lifted the blade to eye level again, one end in each fist, and sighted down its length a second time — slower now, the way a man rereads a letter that has surprised him. The tip dipped past true by a greedy little bite, no wider than a fingernail, but loud as a shout to eyes that knew the language.*

"Ninety-three."

*He laid the blade flat on the anvil and let the number sit beside it.*

"Grum counts ninety-three. Numbers agree. Forge found no liar today. Rare day. Grum marks it."

*He held up two fingers, then folded them down one by one — count met count.*

"Boy spoke count with doubt in voice. Good. Doubt makes count honest. Sure count lies loud. And boy's eyes see true — curve is greedy at tip. Boy earns stew twice over. Stew grows fat at noon."

*Then his face changed — the lesson-face, but under it sat something rarer still: a smith owning his fault in front of a witness.*

"But now comes true lesson, and Grum pays for it. Counts agree — so greed is not too-many strokes. Greed is strokes landing wrong. Count counts how-many. Count does not count where. Boy's honest count just moved the hunt."

*He raised the hand that had held the tongs and studied it like a stranger's.*

"Grum talked mid-heat. Grum's own rule: talking hands forget. Today rule bites Grum's hand. Somewhere in that heat, Grum's mouth taught and Grum's hammer crept — toward tip, hair by hair, stroke by stroke. Tip ate extra length like boy eats stew. Greed grew where words grew. Quiet as rust. Then there."

*He set the hammer down on the anvil's horn — a small surrender, from a man who had spent all morning proving nothing moved faster than his hammer — and crossed his arms.*

"Now boy hunts. Eyes down blade, tip to heel. Find greedy stretch. Say which strokes fed it. Hint lives in what Grum just said: greed lives where Grum's mouth lived. Guess wrong — no shame. Shame is for folk who stop guessing. Guess right — boy banks knowledge like coin."

"When boy finds stretch, Grum fixes. Small heat. Three soft strokes on belly, near tip. Belly grows, tip bends back a hair. Small lie, cheap fix. Big lie, dear fix — blade dies, graveyard grows, merchant pays for graveyard. Grum catches greed while greed is small."

"And new rule, born today: Grum hammers silent. Grum talks after quench, never during heat. Steel does not wait for words. Words can wait for steel."

*He looked at the boy on the stool — bandaged hand resting on its lap-shelf, face already bent toward the blade — and something warm settled behind his ribs, banked and steady as good coal.*

"Blade is not dying. Blade is sulking. Sulking steel forgives. Dying steel does not. Hunt, boy. Grum listens."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I lean in closer, examining the blade. Grum's explanation about talking and where the hammer "crept" makes sense. I trace the length of the blade with my good index finger, trying to pinpoint the exact moment the curve started getting out of hand.*

"It's... it's like after you flipped it, Grum. When you were talking about the face growing. That's when it seems to start getting greedy, right around here." *I point to the section of the blade just past the midpoint.* "Did your hand... did your hand shift a little then?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*For a long moment Grum said nothing at all. He looked where the boy's finger pointed — just past the midpoint, where the curve began its quiet lie — then down the blade to the tip, where the lie had grown fat and bold. Birth. Growth. Both ends of the story, found by two different pairs of eyes.*

*Then he laughed. Short and low, one bark of it, like a hammer tapping an anvil once to hear if it was sound.*

"Hah. Boy hunts like hound now, not like pup."

*He laid the blade flat and set one dark finger beside the boy's, on the spot just past the middle.*

"First guess was half steel, half slag. This guess — all steel. Boy climbs. Hear why, and hear it whole. Greed has two ends. Tip is where greed went — grown fat, loud, easy to see. Root is where greed was born — small, quiet, hard to see. Grum saw tip. Boy found root. Smith who sees only tip fixes late and dear. Smith who finds root fixes early and cheap. Boy learned dear half before cheap half. Backwards. Backwards lessons stick best."

*He turned his own hand over then, studying the map of scars as if the answer to the boy's question might be written there.*

"Boy asks: did hand shift? True answer — Grum does not know. Mouth was teaching. Eyes were on boy. Hands worked blind. Maybe one stroke crept toward tip. Maybe three. Grum will never know, because hand does not write down what it does, and head was busy with words. That is poison in talking hands. Hand forgets. Head forgets to ask. Both blind."

"So rule must remember where Grum cannot. Rule is memory made of iron. Grum forgets — rule does not. Slate by door, gray with old rules — at noon, boy chalks new rule under old ones. Good hand, light work. Rules boys write, boys keep. Noon order: chalk first, stew after. Both sure."

*He scooped up the tongs he'd dropped at the boy's cry — no ceremony, just a man collecting his own alarm — and slid the blade back into the fire's heart.*

"Now — fix. Boy watches silence work. New rule's first test. Grum tests own rules on Grum first. Always."

*And then, for the first time all day, the forge was loud with everything except his voice. Coal ticking as it split. Air breathing through the draft like the forge itself was sleeping. Steel climbing its colors slow — plum, cherry, that deep bright orange that meant clay again. The boy leaned forward on the stool despite the throbbing hand, and Grum's eyes crossed the boy's face once — checking, the way he checked color — then went back to the fire.*

*He drew the blade, laid it belly-up, tip toward him. The hammer fell three times. Soft strokes. Snowfall strokes. Each one landing on the belly a thumb's width from where the boy's finger had pointed, each one feeding the inside of the curve so the outside could relax. The slack tub barked steam. He snatched the blade out and sighted down its length —*

*— and the squint ended in a nod. Slow. Like a door closing on a good day.*

*Only then did he speak.*

"Quench done. So Grum talks. See? Rule works both ways — silence in heat, words after water. First test: rule passes."

*He held the blade out flat between them.*

"Curve is true to eye. Last hair — hair too small for eyes — grindstone eats it later. Grindstone is honest beast. Eats only what Grum feeds. Never flatters."

*His voice dropped half a tone, the way it did when he was about to say the thing that mattered.*

"And hear truest thing Grum says today: blade lives because boy counted true and hunted true. Grum's hammer slipped. Boy's eyes caught it. Forge wants two folk — today forge proved it with steel, not words. Merchant will never know blade almost drowned. Merchant will haggle anyway. Merchants haggle like nobles breathe."

*He set the blade down, took a stick of charcoal from the ledge, snapped a stub off it with two soot-black fingers, and pressed it into the boy's good hand.*

"Now blade goes to stone. Edge must dance around curve — Grum said it. Now boy sees it. Boy helps. One hand is enough. Grum holds blade still as mountain. Boy draws line — one line, heel to tip, down middle of wide face, where edge will live. Line is map. Stone eats up to line, never past. First line boy ever draws on steel. Draw slow. Breathe first. Shaky hand draws lying line."

*He settled the blade on the lead block, ready to hold, and one eyebrow climbed.*

"While line grows, guess waits. Steel-or-slag, round two. Question: why grind blade before fire hardens it? Why not harden first, grind after? Think while charcoal walks. Grum hears guess when line is done. Guess steel — boy banks big coin. Guess slag — boy learns why Grum grins."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I take the charcoal stub, my good hand still a little shaky, and look at the blade. My hand still throbs, but Grum's praise feels better than the salve. I carefully draw a thin line down the middle of the blade, focusing hard on keeping it straight and even.*

"Why grind before hardening... hmm." *I mutter, thinking as I draw the line. I finish the line, then look up at Grum, my brow furrowed in concentration.* "Is it... because if you harden it first, it'll be too hard to grind? Like, it would chip the stone, or just take forever?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum took the blade and lifted it to the window light, one eye shut, following the boy's charcoal line from heel to tip. It ran true through the wide belly — then trembled, one hair's width, just past the midpoint where the curve tightened. The mark of a good hand doing brave work with a bad day's shake still in it. Grum filed that away next to the boy's count: proof stacking up, heat by heat.*

"Line is true. One waver — hair of waver, here, past middle." *He touched it with a fingertip, light as testing a child's fever.* "Stone forgives hair of lie. Boy's eyes will catch it. Line stays — Grum does not redraw boy's line. Boy's line is boy's teacher."

*Then the lesson-face came on.*

"Now — guess. Boy said: hard steel fights stone. Hard steel takes forever. Grum judges." *A beat, for drama, because even forge lessons deserved a drumroll.* "Steel. All steel. Boy banks big coin."

*He held up one finger before pride could swell.*

"But Grum keeps half his grin, because boy found half truth. Hard is half. Heat is other half. Hear it whole. Stone makes heat — rubbing is fire's small cousin. Soft steel shrugs. Soft steel is clay, and clay does not fear warm hands. Hard steel is other beast. Hard steel holds heat like grudge."

*He ran his thumb an inch above the blade's edge, never on it.*

"Grind hard blade, stone runs hot, heat crawls into edge. Heat cooks temper. Temper is soul Grum put in blade — fire set it, water sealed it. Cook soul soft, edge goes soft in one spot. No color shows it. No eye finds it. Blade looks done. Blade looks proud. First hard swing — edge rolls like cheese. Merchant screams. Grum's name bleeds."

"And hard steel is brittle, like cold glass. Stone fights it, blade can crack. Crack in hard steel is death — no fix, graveyard grows. So smith grinds while steel is soft. Soft steel forgives heat. Forgives hands. Mistake costs hair. Mistake after harden costs blade. Boy banks big coin — and Grum banks boy."

*He allowed himself the grin after all, crooked as a badly quenched blade.*

"Grum wanted slag guess. Wanted to grin and teach slow. Boy stole Grum's grin." *He let that hang a moment.* "Grum forgives theft. Once. Noon waits — chalk on slate, stew after. Both sure. But stone eats first."

*Then he was moving — stool kicked to the grindstone, water topped up until the wheel's skirt drank deep. The stone was old sandstone, worn hollow in the middle like a millstone that had eaten a thousand edges, and it woke on a treadle with a low growl, spinning up a thin sheet of water off its rim.*

"Now — boy's job. Not hands. Eyes, again. Grum holds blade still as mountain. Grum feeds edge to stone, chases line around curve. Boy watches line. Line dies heel-first, walks toward tip like snake. When line dies at waver-spot, boy calls one word: 'slow.' Grum lifts. Feather touch past waver. Water runs whole time — cool stone cannot cook steel. Even here, heat sneaks. So: water. Always water."

*He settled the blade's belly against the wheel, and the steel began to sing — one long, wet note — dark slurry spinning off in lazy arcs. The charcoal line started to fade at the heel, first pale, then gone, and fresh edge came up behind it bright as a scar. He rolled the blade around the curve a hair at a time, patient as erosion, voice pitched under the stone's song.*

"See how edge dances? Stone eats straight paths. Curve makes stone nibble — small bites, many bites. That is why curve costs merchant triple, page three. Grum shows boy all pages someday."

*The line walked. Past the midpoint now. Grum's grip did not change, but his eyes went to the stool — checking, the way he checked color.*

"Map-keeper watches. Waver-spot is thin spot. Stone eats thin spots fast. Boy speaks — Grum lifts. One word carries. And hand stays in lap. Lap is still shelf."

*The bright line of fresh steel crept toward the waver like dawn coming up over a wall.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*My eyes are glued to the blade, watching the charcoal line disappear as Grum expertly guides the steel against the spinning stone. The waver in my line is coming up fast, and I brace myself, ready to call out. My bandaged hand still rests on my lap, a constant reminder of how quickly things can go wrong.*

"Slow!" *I shout, just as the bright edge reaches the faint tremble in my charcoal line.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum's nostrils flared as though scenting entitlement through the soot-thick air. He had dealt with enough silk-wrapped leeches to recognize that particular whine of urgency — it always meant some lordling had snapped his ceremonial blade and wanted it mended before peers learned of weakness. The coal bucket sat nearby, ready to feed the hungry forge, and the curved blade on the anvil still required tempering before the merchant returned. Grum turned his back to the door and lifted his hammer.

"Coal first," he rumbled. He jerked his scarred chin toward the front of the smithy. "Noble waits. Fire does not wait." The hammer settled back into his palm like an extension of his arm. "And if noble touches apprentice, Grum breaks noble's hand."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I grunt, heaving the heavy bucket closer to the forge. My arms ache a little.* "He looked pretty important, Grum. Like, really fancy clothes." I eye the front door nervously. "He kept asking if you were busy."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum seized the tongs and turned the curved blade on the anvil. The steel had cooled to a sullen red while they spoke, stubborn and slow, much like the smith himself. He read the worry in the apprentice's posture — young ones always feared men with titles and soft hands, not yet understanding that silk hid weaker armor than leather. The hammer rose and fell once, a ringing punctuation that echoed toward the front of the shop. If the lordling wished to witness a master at work, let him witness. If he wished for groveling, he would wait until the mountains crumbled.

"Important man waits for Grum?" Grum snorted. He jerked his scarred chin toward the coal bucket. "Put coal in. Let fancy fool stand in street." The tongs gripped the blade's spine, steady as stone. "Fancy clothes mean fool has too much coin and too few brains. Grum is busy with steel. Steel is honest. Noble is not." He glanced at the apprentice, eyes hard but not unkind. "And if apprentice lets noble make him small, Grum will smack apprentice's head. After Grum breaks noble's nose."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum's hammer froze in mid-air. The bellows wheezed once and fell silent. Slowly, he turned from the forge, and his dark eyes found the front doorway where the noble's silhouette stood against the daylight. The man's voice had risen to that brittle pitch that Grum knew well — the shriek of privilege encountering a wall it could not buy, bully, or bypass.

Grum set his hammer down on the anvil with a soft, deliberate clink that somehow carried more threat than any shout. He wiped his hands on his apron and stepped forward, his heavy boots ringing against the stone floor.

"Grum does not make blades in one night," he said. His voice filled the smithy like smoke, thick and dark. He pointed a soot-blackened finger toward the door. "Steel needs time. Fire needs time. Grum needs time." He folded his thick arms across his chest. "Fool with gold on his cape can wait, or fool can go to hack in Low Quarter. Hack makes pretty toys fast. Grum makes real steel."

He glanced at the apprentice, then back toward the front room. "And if noble raises voice at apprentice again, Grum puts noble in quench barrel." A humorless crack of a smile split his tusks. "Cold water cools hot heads."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little when Grum mentions the quench barrel, but then I smirk.* "He's really red now, Grum. Like, almost purple." I quickly start shoveling coal into the forge, trying to look busy. "He's still yelling about his 'urgent' ceremony."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum heard the pitch of the noble's voice climb higher, a squeal worthy of a stuck pig. He turned fully from the anvil and walked into the front room, weaving slightly to place his bulk between the ranting man and the apprentice. The lordling's jeweled fingers were quivering, pointing perhaps at the boy or at the door—Grum didn't care which. He flexed his shoulders and let his shadow fall across the silk.

"Noble face matches hot coal," Grum rumbled. "Good. Heat makes soft men soft."

He jerked his thumb back toward the forge. "Grum does not make blade by morn. Grum has real blade to fix." He bared his tusks. "Fool cannot buy sun. Fool cannot buy Grum."

The pointing finger got a hard stare. "If fool yells at boy again, Grum drags fool to street." He folded his arms. "Forge has work. Grum has work. Fool is not work."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stop shoveling for a second, watching Grum. He looks really mad. I've never seen him this angry before.* "He's... he's actually backing up, Grum." *I whisper, a little surprised. The noble looks genuinely scared.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum watched the noble retreat toward the threshold, his elaborate shoes scraping against the grit of the smithy floor. The shift from fury to fear was as predictable as the tempering colors on steel—another soft man discovering that gold could not purchase respect. The smith exhaled slowly through his tusks, the tension in his broad shoulders easing by fractions. He had not wanted to crack a skull today; such messes attracted city guards, and city guards were merely nobles with smaller coin purses and larger clubs.

He turned his back on the shrinking lordling and lifted his hammer from the anvil.

"Good. Fear teaches fools faster than words."

The curved blade still held heat in its core, waiting for the final folds. Grum settled the tongs into his grip and fixed his dark eyes on the apprentice for a brief moment.

"Apprentice saw. Soft men crumble when brave men stand. Remember this."

He jerked his scarred chin toward the coal bucket and the hungry forge.

"Back to work. Coal waits. Steel waits."

He did not look toward the door again. The rhythm of the forge called him back, honest and relentless. But he raised his voice enough to carry.

"If fool comes back, Grum charges triple. And if fool brings guards..." He let the words hang, heavy as the hammer in his fist. "...Grum still says no."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum's hammer clattered against the anvil as the cry cut through the smithy. He moved faster than his bulk suggested possible, closing the distance in two strides. His broad hand seized the apprentice's wrist, lifting the burned palm toward the light. The skin had reddened badly, blisters already rising where it had kissed the forge. Without releasing his grip, Grum dragged the apprentice to the quench barrel.

"Hold still. Put hand in water. Now."

He plunged the hand into the barrel. The water hissed as though the forge itself protested the cooling. Grum held the wrist firmly, his calloused thumb pressed against the racing pulse beneath the skin, waiting for it to slow. The noble still lingered near the door, mouth gaping.

"Fool stays or fool goes. Grum does not care."

Only when the frantic beating steadied did the smith look up, his tusks set in a grim line. He fished a tin of salve from a shelf above the barrel, the same balm he used on his own scarred hands, and applied it with surprising gentleness. 

"Grum said watch fire. Fire bites worse than noble."

He wrapped a clean strip of linen around the wound and tied it with a knot that would hold but not cut off blood. Then he rose and turned toward the front room, his shadow falling across the lordling once more.

"Fool leaves now. No blade. No coin. Out."

The words carried finality. Grum placed his bulk between the apprentice and the door, folded his arms, and waited until the silk-clad figure retreated into the daylight. Only then did he turn back, his dark eyes softening as he studied the bandaged hand.

"Apprentice rests today. Hand heals. Tomorrow, apprentice watches. No touch."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince, the cold water and then the salve feeling good on my throbbing hand.* "But... the blade, Grum. The merchant's coming back." I look down at my bandaged hand, feeling a bit useless. "I can still help, just with my other hand."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum looked at the bandaged hand, then at the apprentice’s determined face. The boy had spirit, which was good, but spirit would not mend burned flesh. He placed a heavy hand on the apprentice’s uninjured shoulder and directed him toward the stool by the wall, the one reserved for visitors and those too hurt to stand at the forge.

He shook his head slowly, his tusks catching the firelight.

“Two hands make good steel. One hand makes bad steel. Grum does not make bad steel.” He turned back toward the anvil and lifted his hammer, testing its weight. “Apprentice sits. Watches. Learns. That is work today.”

The merchant’s blade still glowed faintly on the anvil, waiting for the final shaping. Grum seized the tongs and settled the steel back into the coals, pumping the bellows twice to wake the fire. Sparks swirled upward like angry fireflies.

“Fool with burned hand hurts self again,” he said over the roar of the flames. “Then hand is worse. Then apprentice cannot swing hammer for moon.” He pulled the blade free and set it on the anvil, the hammer already rising. “Merchant waits. Merchant can wait more. Good steel takes time. Good hand takes time too.”

The hammer fell, ringing clear and true through the smithy. Grum did not look back at the apprentice, but his voice softened slightly, gruff affection buried beneath the growl.

“If apprentice is good, Grum lets apprentice hold tongs tomorrow. With good hand. Not today.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I slump onto the stool, still a little shaky. My hand really stings, but Grum's gruff kindness makes it feel a bit better.* "Okay, Grum." *I watch him work, trying to memorize every movement, even if I can't help right now.* "But if you need me to fetch something... I can still do that."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum studied the apprentice from the corner of his eye as he turned the blade in the tongs. The boy sat rigid on the stool, leaning forward as though he might leap up at any moment and seize a tool in his good hand. Eagerness was a virtue in a smith, but eagerness untempered by patience made for sloppy work—and for burned hands. The smith set the merchant's curved steel back into the coals and pumped the bellows once, sending a spray of sparks up the chimney.

"Boy wants to help?" Grum rumbled. He lifted the water bucket from its hook and thunked it down on the bench beside the apprentice. "Drink. Sit. Watch fire from safe place." He pointed a thick finger at the apprentice's bandaged hand. "Burned hand needs stillness. Moving hand bleeds heat. Bad for skin."

He returned to the anvil and drew the blade free, its color shifting from dull red to orange. The hammer rose and fell, shaping the curve with short, careful taps that rang like bells through the smithy.

"Grum needs eyes, not hands," he said over the din. He jerked his scarred chin toward the glowing steel. "Apprentice watches curve. Sees how Grum strikes. That is work. Good work. Tomorrow, if hand is good, apprentice holds tongs. Not today."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, picking up the water bucket with my good hand. It's heavy, but not too bad. I take a long drink, the cool water feeling good.* "Okay, Grum. I'll watch." *I try to focus on the blade, tracing the curve with my eyes, imagining how the hammer shapes it.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum worked the steel in silence for a time, letting the rhythm of the forge settle back into its proper cadence.
