The merchant's blade had cooled too much during the interruption with the noble; it would need reheating, rethinking, coaxing back to life like a spooked horse. He studied the curve, searching for any warp the argument might have hammered into his focus. Finding none, he nodded to himself and struck again, a trio of light taps that brightened the edge. He glanced at the apprentice. The boy had set the bucket down and was leaning forward, eyes sharp. That was the look Grum had worn at sixteen, hungry for the secrets of the metal.

"Watch close," Grum said. He turned the blade slow, letting firelight slide along its spine. "See how curve changes when Grum hits?" He pointed with his hammer toward the glowing steel. "Steel talks. Grum listens. Tap here, curve goes there." He struck again, a ringing note that made the anvil sing. "Apprentice must learn to hear steel. Not today with hands. Today with ears. With eyes."

He set the blade back into the coals, judging the color, then pulled it free to show the apprentice the even glow.

"Burned hand is bad," he continued, softer now. "But still hand is worse. Still hand means mind sleeps. Grum wants mind awake." He looked hard at the apprentice. "When mind wakes, hand wakes too. Then apprentice makes steel that sings."

He raised his hammer again.

"For now, boy drinks water. Boy watches. Boy learns. That is enough."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I watch the blade intently, trying to see the subtle changes Grum points out. It's harder than it looks, but I really try to understand what he means by 'steel talks'.* "So, the shape comes from listening to the metal, not just hitting it?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum paused with the hammer held high above the anvil. He turned toward the apprentice, and something like approval flickered in his dark eyes. The boy had grasped something that took many smiths years to understand. He lowered the hammer gently and tapped the blade with the tongs, producing a clear, ringing note that hung in the sooty air.

"Yes," he rumbled. "Steel talks. Fool hits. Smith listens." He pointed at the glowing metal with his hammer. "Hammer asks. Steel answers. Soft here, hard there. Hot, cold, bend, break." He tapped his own ear with a sooty finger. "Apprentice thinks ears are only for hearing words. Wrong. Ears hear steel too. Hammer is how Grum speaks to fire and iron."

He turned back to the forge and gave the bellows one hard pull, sending sparks swirling upward like fiery sprites.

"Grum does not beat shape into steel. Grum asks steel where shape wants to go. Then Grum helps." He looked hard at the apprentice. "Today, apprentice has no hammer. But apprentice still has ears. And eyes. Use them. Watch fire. Listen to ring of anvil." He raised the hammer again. "That is how burned hand becomes wise hand."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing his words. It makes sense, in a way. I can't really hear the steel 'talking' yet, but I can see how Grum's movements are almost a conversation with it.* "So, when I get my hammer back... I should try to listen more?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum nodded slowly, the firelight catching the ridges of his scars. He lifted the hammer and let it fall, a single ringing blow that made the curved blade sing against the anvil. The note was true, bright and clean, speaking of proper temper and good steel. He turned back toward the apprentice and set the hammer down, crossing to the boy in two heavy steps. He crouched slightly to look the apprentice in the eye, his calloused hand resting on the boy's uninjured shoulder.

"Yes," he rumbled. "Hammer must listen before it hits. Fool hears nothing. Smith hears all." He jerked his scarred chin toward the anvil. "Apprentice learns fast. Good. But head knows, hand must follow. Hand that does not listen makes bad steel."

He straightened and returned to the forge, seizing the tongs and turning the blade in the coals. He glanced back, his dark eyes catching the firelight.

"Grum will give hammer back when hand is good. Then apprentice strikes not like fool, but like smith. Like Grum." He pulled the steel free and set it on the anvil, testing its glow. "For now, eyes listen. Ears listen. Mind grows strong while hand grows skin."

He raised the hammer once more.

"That is how boy becomes smith. Not by hitting hard. By hearing true."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I watch him work, really trying to listen this time. It’s hard to make out what the steel is "saying," but I can definitely hear the different sounds as the hammer hits the metal. I try to commit each sound to memory.* "So, is that why you sometimes just tap it really lightly, Grum? To listen?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pencil lines had cut shallow grooves in the paint. Deep enough to catch a fingernail. Each mark had a date beside it, faded to gray. The lowest sat a hand's width above the floor. The topmost fell short of Eli's shoulder now.

The early dates were written in block capitals. A man's hand, square and certain. By the fourth year the letters had gone crooked. A child had taken over the pencil. The final mark bore no date. The pencil had pressed hard enough there to dent the wood.

Years of fingertips had worn the graphite slick in patches. Somewhere behind the wall, a pipe ticked. The hallway held its cold.

The door to the room stood open. The carpet had been rolled up and taken. Bare boards caught the gray window light. The floor smelled of old glue and pine. Pale rectangles showed where the bed had stood. Where the desk had stood. Nothing else.

Beyond the glass, the plum tree still stood. Wind moved in its bare branches.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I trace the deepest pencil mark with my finger.* I remember Dad doing these. Or... trying to. "He always made me stand still." *I sigh, looking at the empty room.* "Guess they cleared everything out already."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
A gray smudge of graphite came away on Eli's fingertip. In the deepest groove, something dark sat wedged. A splinter of pencil lead, snapped off and forgotten. The wood had kept it all this time. The doorframe held the hallway's cold.

From the doorway, the room offered its emptiness. The radiator under the window ticked and pinged. Outside, wind dragged a plum branch across the glass. The rattle was dry, without weight. The smell of old glue drifted out to meet the hall.

Not everything had gone. The closet door stood open at the room's far corner. Inside, the walls kept their old green. The beige repaint stopped at the closet's edge in a clean, taped line. Whoever had painted had not bothered with the inside. The green had gone matte, crazed with hairline cracks. A trace of camphor hung in its air.

The closet door had been left wide. Its inner face carried crayon. An orange sun, faded to rust, rose over a crooked house. A stick figure stood beside it, arms too long. Under the figure, a word wobbled in red wax, half rubbed away. The wax still held a sheen in the deeper lines. Somewhere behind the wall, the pipe ticked again.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph had slipped down behind the closet's side panel. It lay face down on the boards, half in the baseboard's shadow. Damp had softened its corners to cloth. The paper carried the closet's cold and its camphor.

The print had a narrow white border, machine-cut. Orange digits ran along the bottom edge. A date from an old June. The emulsion had cracked into a fine web across the sky.

Her hair was longer then. She stood in the back garden, one hand shading her eyes. No lines yet at the corners of her eyes. The plum tree filled the frame behind her, in full blossom. The petals held the glare of a summer afternoon. Her mouth was open mid-word. Someone had made her laugh before the shutter fell.

Her other hand rested on a small shoulder. The border cut the child off at the chin. A red jacket sleeve. Nothing more of the child survived the frame.

The back bore pencil. Block capitals, pressed hard enough to emboss the paper. Her name. The same square hand from the doorframe's earliest dates. A fleck of orange wax had fused to one corner.

Outside, the same tree stood bare against the glass. A branch dragged across the pane, dry and without weight. The radiator under the window ticked twice and stopped. The closet's green held its camphor around the photograph, patient and cold.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I pick up the photo, my thumb tracing the faint image of the red jacket.* "Dad must have put this here," *I whisper, my voice thick.* "He always did that."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The gap behind the panel ran deeper than the photograph's width. Its lower edge had been worn pale. Fingers had pried at that corner many times. The camphor smell rose stronger from the opening. Cold air breathed out of it, old and still.

Something else had been pushed deep into the gap. A pencil stub. Its yellow paint had chipped to bare wood. One end carried tooth marks, dented deep. The other end had snapped off short. The break was old, its wood darkened. It matched the splinter wedged in the doorframe groove. The stub still smelled of cedar.

Behind the stub, a scrap of notepaper lay open. Its old folds had split into fine hairlines. The camphor had seeped into the paper. The writing slanted and looped, small and quick. It was not the square hand from the doorframe. A date sat in one corner, faded to gray. Milk. Bread. Matches. Thread. The last item sat alone on its own line. Plums, underlined twice.

Outside, the plum tree stood bare against the glass. Its buds sat hard and dark along the branches. Wind dragged one limb across the pane. The rasp came thin, then nothing. The radiator gave a single tick and fell silent. Cold pooled at the mouth of the closet.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I put the photo carefully into my pocket, then reach for the pencil stub, pulling it out.* "Plums." *I murmur, the word a question. I look at the closet, then back at the doorframe.* "Why here?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The stub measured a thumb's length, no more. Its broken end matched the splinter wedged in the doorframe groove. Both fractures showed the same dark, aged grain. Cedar still rose from the chipped yellow paint. The tooth marks sat close together, small. A child's bite, or a habit of worry.

The deepest groove on the frame bore no date. The pencil had been driven hard into that line. Hard enough to dent the wood. Hard enough to snap the lead off inside the groove. The dent was deep enough to catch a nail. Whoever had made the mark had put their weight behind it. No one had come after to write the date.

Two screw holes sat high on the closet's side panel. A rail had hung there once. Dark rings shadowed the green where coat shoulders had pressed. The camphor had come from her winter wool. It had soaked into the wood and stayed. In the corner, a mothball had shrunk to a brittle husk.

The beige stopped at the closet in a straight, taped edge. The line fell level and deliberate. Someone had chosen to spare the green. The gap behind the panel sat at a child's reach. Its lower edge had been worn pale by small fingers. Cold still breathed from the opening. This had been a hiding place before it became a keeping place.

The note lay in the gap's cold mouth. The double underline had been pressed deep. The pen had almost cut through on the second pass. The word beneath it sat alone: plums. In the pocket, the same tree stood in full flower. Its petals held their glare in cracked emulsion.

Outside, the branches carried their buds, hard and dark. Old pruning cuts had healed into gray seams along the trunk. One low fork bore a groove worn smooth by rope. Wind worked through the bare limbs with a dry creak. At the base, the grass grew thick and dark. Years of fallen fruit had fed the ground.

The window glass held its cold. Somewhere below, the tape on the kitchen box had begun to curl. Behind the wall, the pipe ticked once and stopped. The house kept what it was given.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door caught, then gave to a shoulder. Paint cracked at the swollen jamb. Cold ran out across the porch boards. Heels struck the hallway floor, three steps, quick and bright.

"Hello. Hello. I did knock." A pause for breath. "That door is a menace. I'm putting it in the notes."

She came around the corner into the room's gray light. Her perfume arrived first, floral and sharp. It cut through the camphor and the old glue. A wool coat, too warm for the house. A leather folder clamped under one arm. Her lanyard swung. The badge read SUSAN PRICE above a smiling cartoon roofline.

Her breath fogged in the cold. She rubbed her gloved hands together. "Goodness. It's freezing in here. The heating must be off at the mains." Her gaze took in the bare boards, the pale rectangles, the window. "Great bones, though. Wonderful light, even today. The photographs will do all the work."

The folder snapped open. Glossy paper caught the gray from the window. A pen appeared between her fingers and clicked twice. The sound rang off the boards where the carpet had been.

"So. Just the last signatures, and the keys go over Friday." She smiled at the room rather than at anything in it. "You must be glad to see the back of it. These old places, they're all weight."

She didn't wait for an answer. Her heel found the doorway. One gloved finger rose to the pencil grooves. The leather creaked against the wood.

"Oh, look. Height marks. Sweet." She traced the lowest line, the one a hand's width above the floor. "Some buyers love these. Some ask for new trim." A beat. "A light sand would lift them right out." Her finger came to rest on the deepest groove. The one without a date. "Yours, I take it?"

The question hung in the cold. She didn't wait for that either. Her perfume moved past the doorway and into the closet's camphor.

"Huh. They missed a patch in here. The green." Her glove traced the taped edge, level and clean. "Easy fix. One afternoon with a roller. I'll put it on the punch list."

She turned toward the window. Beyond the glass, the plum tree stood bare, its buds hard and dark. "And that tree. The surveyor called it a mature plum. Buyers love a mature tree." The pen clicked in her fingers, ready for its line.

Wind worked through the branches. A limb dragged across the pane, dry and thin. The pipe behind the wall ticked once and stopped. The closet kept its green behind her. In the kitchen, the tape on the box had curled another inch.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I stare at Susan, a cold knot forming in my stomach.* "No," *I say, my voice sharper than I intended.* "That's *my* mark."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Her finger came off the wood. A gray smear of graphite marked the leather. The pen stopped mid-click. She said nothing for one breath.

"Right. Of course." Her voice came down from its bright pitch. "Sorry. Habit of the trade. Everything turns into a feature after a while." She rubbed the smear between finger and thumb. The graphite ground into the leather grain.

She straightened the folder under her arm. The glossy paper rasped against wool. "We can leave the trim alone. Your call until Friday." The pen turned in her fingers. "Or a carpenter could cut that section out. The whole piece of frame. People keep them. Put them on a shelf."

Her gaze went back to the deepest groove. Her nail had caught the dent coming off. Something dark sat wedged in the line. "There's lead still in there." Her eyes touched the yellow stub, then moved past it. "I won't touch it again." She drew back a half step. Her heel rang on the boards.

She moved to the window. The glass held its cold at her cheek. "Your father mentioned the tree when we listed. I asked if he wanted it down." The radiator ticked under the sill. "He said the tree stayed. He said it before I finished the question."

She looked back toward the closet. Camphor drifted on the cold air. "He told me to leave that cupboard green. I put it down to a rushed job." Her glove hovered at the taped edge, then dropped. "Maybe it wasn't rushed."

Her smile returned, smaller than before. She clicked the pen once. The sound rang off the bare boards. "So. The frame. Do we leave it, or do you want it cut out?" Her breath fogged against the glass. Beyond it, the plum tree held its hard buds. The rope-worn fork faced the room. In the pocket, the photograph kept its June. For the first time, she waited for an answer.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Leave it," *I say, my voice softer now.* "Just... leave it." I look at the tree outside, then back to the closet. "He liked the tree."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Her pen moved to the folder's margin. She wrote three words. The nib scratched dry against the coated paper.

"The trim stays. I'll note it for the buyers." The pen capped with a small click. Her gaze went past Eli to the closet. Camphor drifted from its cold mouth. "And the green stays. It comes off the punch list."

She turned to the window. Her breath fogged once against the glass. "He did more than like it, I think." Her thumbnail worried the folder's leather corner. "He came by once, you know. After we listed. I drove up at dusk. Found him out front. Standing under the tree in the rain."

"No umbrella. No lights on in the house. Just standing." The latch rattled under her glove. Old brass grated in the frame. "I asked if he wanted to come in. He said no. Said the tree was fine." A pause. "I left him to it. Seemed the thing to do."

She gathered the folder under her arm. The wool rasped against the leather. "I'll see myself out." Her heels struck the boards, bright down the hall. "The door needs a shoulder. You know the trick."

Her hands stayed clear of the doorframe on her way past. The graphite smear had dried into the glove's leather.

The front door caught. Paint cracked at the swollen jamb. It gave. Cold poured in from the porch and met the room's cold. Her perfume thinned along the hallway, then went.

The house settled into its silence. The radiator ticked twice under the sill. Wind worked through the bare limbs. One branch dragged its dry rasp across the pane.

The closet kept its green. Camphor held in the cold air. The note lay in the gap's mouth, its folds split to hairlines. Plums, underlined twice. The second line had almost gone through the paper.

In the pocket, the photograph held its June. The paper had taken warmth from the pocket. Cracked emulsion. Her mouth open mid-word. The red sleeve, cut at the chin.

Beyond the glass, the buds sat hard and dark along the branches. At the rope-worn fork, one bud had split. A curl of white showed at its seam. Petal, furled, still soft at the edge.

Wind moved through the limbs with a dry creak. The pipe behind the wall ticked once and stopped. The tree stayed.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I stand in the silence, listening to the house settle. I pull the photo out of my pocket, looking at my mom's face.* "He really did love that tree." *I whisper.* "And Mom."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The whisper thinned in the cold air. The photograph had taken warmth from the pocket. The room worked at it now, cold creeping back into the damp-softened corners. Her face kept its June. Her mouth stayed open, caught mid-word. Fine cracks ran across the sky above her.

On the back, the block capitals sat embossed deep in the paper. The square hand. The certain strokes. A fleck of orange wax had fused to one corner. It matched the rust of the crayon sun inside the closet door.

The red word under the stick figure had been rubbed to shadow. Two letters survived at its left edge. Their shapes matched the opening strokes of the embossed name. A child had copied it in wax, letter by letter. The rest had worn away under years of sleeves.

The figure stood beside its crooked house, arms reaching too far. The orange sun had faded to rust above it. The deeper wax lines still held their sheen. The camphor carried a bitter edge at the back of the throat.

The pencil stub kept its smell of cedar. Its broken end had darkened with age. In the doorframe, the deepest groove still held its splinter of lead. That mark had carried a whole hand's weight. No date had followed. The stub had gone into the gap, then the photograph, then the note. Three things, hidden at a child's reach.

The note's gray date and the photograph's orange digits shared one summer. Milk. Bread. Matches. Thread. Plums, underlined twice. The camphor had browned the paper along its folds. Her hand had pressed hard on that one word alone. The second underline had almost gone through.

Outside, the wind had dropped. The branch no longer dragged the glass. The bare limbs stood still against a sky leaning toward dusk. At the rope-worn fork, the split bud showed its white curl. A second bud had split beside it. The petals stayed furled, soft at their edges.

The pipe behind the wall ticked once and stopped. The radiator held its silence under the sill. In the photograph, the tree stood in full flower. Beyond the glass, the first petal waited in its seam. The house held its cold. The tree held its spring.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I carefully slide the photograph back into my pocket, my fingers brushing against the pencil stub.* "He never forgot them, did he?" *I say to the empty room, a lump forming in my throat.* "Not really."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The question hung in the room's cold. Cedar rose from the pocket where the stub lay. The radiator under the window held its silence. Nothing in the house moved.

The taped line still ran level across the closet's edge. A brush had stopped there on purpose. The beige had gone over everything else in the house. It had met the green and gone no further. The hallway still carried the faint smell of that paint.

The corner of the panel had been worn smooth and pale. Small fingers had worked at that gap for years. He had found it. A stub. A note. He had not cleared it out. He had written her name in his square hand instead. Then he had slid the photograph down into the dark. Face down. Deep. Where a child's hand once reached.

The doorframe told the rest in graphite. Square capitals for the early years. Crooked letters by the fourth. Then a final line with no date. Someone had put their whole weight behind it. The lead had snapped inside the groove. The stub had gone into the gap that day. The measuring had stopped.

Her hand had looped across the note. Milk. Bread. Matches. Thread. Plums. She had underlined the fruit twice. The second line had gone deep into the page. The tree had fed them every summer. Fallen fruit had fed the ground for years. The folds had browned where the camphor touched.

Inside the closet, the crayon sun went on rising over its crooked house. The stick figure reached with arms too long. The red wax letters matched the opening strokes of her name. A child had copied her, letter by letter. Camphor bit at the back of the throat.

He had told the agent the tree stayed. He had answered before the question ended. He had stood beneath it at dusk, once, in the rain. No umbrella. No lights in the house behind him. Rain had beaded on the bare branches. He had said the tree was fine. He had said nothing about himself.

Beyond the glass, dusk had settled into the branches. The wind had dropped. The limbs stood still. At the rope-worn fork, the first petal had eased open. Its white showed full at the seam. A second bud had split beside it. Cold pressed at the pane from outside. The pipe behind the wall ticked once.

The house kept what it was given. A pencil. A note. A June. On Friday, the keys would change hands. The groove would stay in the frame, lead and all. The green would stay behind its taped line. The tree would hold its spring for strangers. In the pocket, the photograph kept its last warmth. Cedar and camphor hung in the cold. He had kept everything he could not say.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I pull the photo out again, holding it with both hands, warming it.* "He really didn't, did he?" *I murmur, my voice thick with unshed tears.* "He just... kept it all here."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The warmth of his hands worked into the paper. The damp-softened corners flexed at their edges. A smell rose off the print, faint and chemical, sweet under its dust. The paper had not held warmth in years.

The embossed capitals rose through the image. Raised lines crossed the garden, the fence, her shoulder. Her name ran beneath her own face. The square hand had pressed it there. The letters caught the last gray from the window.

The room gave up its light. The pale rectangles faded from the boards. Cold gathered along the floor and climbed the ankles. The smell of old glue thinned toward the door.

The radiator ticked once under the sill. The pipe behind the wall answered. Then the house went still.

Outside, dusk had finished its work. The limbs stood black against a slate sky. At the rope-worn fork, the first petal stood open. Its white was the only brightness left. A second petal had eased from its seam. Cold pressed at the pane, and the glass gave a faint creak.

He had never fixed the door. The swollen jamb still smelled of wet wood and old paint. He had never sanded the frame, never painted the green, never cut the tree. The house had done his keeping for him.

Down the hall, the tape on the kitchen box let go. The paper snapped flat against the cardboard, once. The sound carried through the quiet rooms.

Friday would come with its keys. The groove would keep its lead. The green would keep its line. The tree would go on opening. In his hands, the photograph held its June and its warmth. At the fork, a third bud split its seam. A white curl showed in the dark.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I clutch the photo to my chest, the warmth spreading through my hands.* "I can't leave this here," *I say, my voice barely a whisper.* "Not for strangers."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The marks climbed the frame in small rows. The newest one stopped at a height Eli had outgrown. A radiator ticked in the next room. The sound moved through plaster and faded.

Dust swirled above the hallway table. It smelled of wet wool and old paper. From the kitchen, tape tore from the box. The noise was dry and brief.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I flinch at the sound from the kitchen, pulling my hand away from the doorframe.* "Hello?" I call out, my voice a little hoarse.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The kitchen held a woman by the counter. Coffee steamed in a chipped mug. The air tasted stale.

She turned from the box. Her shoes scraped the linoleum. The floorboards answered with a soft creak.

“Yes?” she called. Her voice carried a smoker’s rasp. The word hung above the open box.

Her thumb peeled tape from a seam. The cardboard smelled of dust and glue. A red stain marked the counter near her elbow.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The closet smelled of cedar and old paper. The photograph’s edge was soft from handling. Her mother’s face was dark and clear. A hinge ticked above the frame.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I trace the outline of her smile.* "Mom..." I whisper. It's like she's right here.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The closet air warmed the photo paper. A cedar chip rolled across the floor.

Her mother’s smile bent in the dim light. Dust moved in the lamp’s beam.

A chair scraped in the kitchen. The woman’s mug hit the counter with a dull tap.

The hallway clock ticked once. The sound carried under Eli’s feet.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I carefully tuck the photo into my pocket, a knot forming in my stomach.* The kitchen noise pulls me back to the present. "I'm Eli," I call out, stepping out of the closet.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The woman turned from the counter. Her shoes pressed the linoleum. The mug left a damp ring.

“Eli?” she said. The word roughened. Coffee steam curled between them.

She twisted the towel. Bleach stung the air. The clock ticked again.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The real estate agent knocked twice. The door stuck again.

She stepped inside with a binder under one arm. Her heels tapped the hallway floor.

“Eli,” she said. The name sounded new in her mouth. “The buyers are eager.”

Her smile was wide. The hallway smelled of rain on wool.

She set the binder on the table. The cardboard cover was damp.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "They can wait," I say, a little more sharply than I intended. I look from her to the woman in the kitchen, then back. "Who are you?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent’s smile tightened. Her binder sat damp on the table. The paper smelled of rain and ink.

“I am with the listing,” she said. Her voice thinned. “The buyers are in the next town.”

The woman at the counter stopped wiping the mug. Bleach lingered in the air. She set it down.

“Eli,” the woman said. Her throat worked. “It is me. Nadine.” Water dripped from the towel.

The clock ticked. Dust moved in the hallway light.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *My eyes widen.* "Nadine? What are you doing here?" I look between her and the agent, completely thrown.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Nadine’s jaw worked. The towel dampened her palm. “I stayed after the funeral.”

Her shoes creaked on the linoleum. Dust rose under the table.

The agent flipped a page. Paper rasped. Her perfume smelled sharp and sweet.

The mug cooled on the counter. “Eli owns the house,” Nadine said. “The contents are his.”

The agent’s nails tapped the binder. A coffee stain marked her cuff.

Rain moved down the window. The room cooled.

Nadine folded the towel. The bleach scent thickened. “Leave the boxes alone.”

Her thumb pressed the seam of the towel. The cloth frayed.

The agent closed the binder. The cardboard gave a soft thud.

“The buyers arrive Thursday,” she said. Her heels retreated. The hallway floorboard groaned.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Thursday?" I repeat, my voice hollow. I turn to Nadine. "What is she talking about?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Nadine set the towel flat. Bleach clung to its weave.

“Your father gave her a key,” she said. Her voice stayed low.

The hallway light buzzed. Rain tapped the window above the sink.

She rubbed the counter edge. The laminate felt cool and sticky.

“Your father signed the papers,” Nadine said. “He died owing them.”

Coffee cooled in the mug. Its surface trembled.

The front door clicked. Nadine watched the hallway. “She waits outside.”

Gravel shifted under tires. The smell of wet wool lingered.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "He sold the house?" I ask, my voice barely a whisper. "To pay off debt?" My head is spinning.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Nadine wiped her hands. The towel left damp lines on the laminate.

Her voice came flat and low. The kitchen clock ticked. Rain struck the window glass.

The agent stood beyond the door. Her heels clicked once on the porch.

“He sold it to clear the debt,” Nadine said. Her thumb rubbed a coffee stain on the counter.

The laminate felt sticky. Bleach rose from the towel.

Nadine crossed her arms. The sleeve brushed her wrist.

“The buyers hold the contract,” she said. Her breath fogged the cold air near the window.

The hallway floorboard groaned. The agent’s car engine coughed outside.

Gravel shifted under a tire. The sound entered the kitchen.

Nadine looked at Eli’s hands. The photo edge showed from his pocket.

Her jaw tightened. Dust moved in the lamp’s beam.

“Your father left nothing,” she said. The words rasped in her throat.

The mug cooled on the counter. Coffee steam thinned and vanished.

Rain tapped the siding. The house smelled of wet wool.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "What do you mean, 'left nothing'?" I ask, pulling the photo out of my pocket without thinking. "He had Mom's things. He had *our* things." My voice is shaking.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Nadine looked at the photograph. Cedar and dust rose from the closet door. Her mouth pressed thin. The kitchen light hummed.

“The house was not empty,” she said. The towel dampened her palm. Rain tapped the window glass.

Nadine moved to the counter. Linoleum creaked beneath her shoe. She set the towel on the laminate. Bleach stung the air.

“He sold the walls,” she said. Her voice scraped low. The mug left a damp ring. “The contents stayed.”

The boxes waited in the hall. Cardboard smelled of glue and old paper. Dust moved in the doorway.

Nadine folded the towel again. Cloth rasped between her fingers. The clock ticked once.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "The contents stayed?" I repeat, looking around the empty-ish kitchen. "What contents?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The marks climbed the frame in pencil. Dates beside each line, block capitals. 1998. 2001. 2004. The last line had no date. The early ones were his father's print. The later ones slanted another way. His mother's. The sill beneath them had gone smooth from years of hands.

Behind a closed door, a clock ticked. Then the floorboards groaned overhead. Footsteps crossed the landing. The stairs spoke in their old places. Third step. Seventh. The last one before the bottom.

His father appeared at the end of the hall. He was greyer than the photograph on the mantel. A mug hung from one hand, steam climbing past his wrist. The smell of instant coffee reached the hallway first.

"You let yourself in." He stopped a few feet off and sipped. Heat came off the mug between them. "The door still sticks. I kept meaning to shave it."

He turned back toward the kitchen. Behind him, the kettle began its climb toward a whistle.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Hey, Dad." I pull my hand away from the doorframe, a little self-conscious. "Yeah, it sticks worse than ever." I follow him into the kitchen. "You repainted."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The kettle broke into its whistle. He lifted it from the ring and the sound died mid-cry. Water struck the granules in a thin rope. They bloomed dark, and the smell filled the kitchen, burnt and cheap and known.

"Your mother chose the green." The spoon rang against the rim. "This hides the damp better."

He took down a second mug. Blue, chipped along the handle. He filled it and left it on the counter, handle turned out.

The fridge hummed. A dish rack held one plate, one fork. Condensation ran the window in slow threads. Outside, the garden had gone to seed.

The box sat where Eli had first seen it. The tape had yellowed at its edges. His father's gaze crossed it once, then settled on the table.

He carried both mugs over. One leg wobbled, and a folded beer mat sat beneath it, soft with age. He lowered himself into the chair opposite. The chair complained under his weight.

He wrapped both hands around the heat of it. Steam touched his knuckles.

"So." He watched Eli over the rim. "How long are you staying?"

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph had gone soft at its corners. Its gloss had dulled where handling had worn it down. In the print, she stood by the back fence. One hand rose against the sun. Her head tipped back, caught mid-laugh. The sky above her had faded to a thin amber.

The closet air hung thick around it. Cedar. Mothball. Wool gone sour at the collars. A grey film of dust lay across the print.

Below, the chair scraped back. The fridge hummed on without him. Then the stairs spoke under his weight. Third step. Seventh. The one before the bottom.

He stopped in the doorway of the old room. The room held the cold of a space nobody heated. His eyes went from the open closet to the print. He set a hand on the doorframe. His thumb found the highest pencil mark without looking. The wood there had gone smooth.

"I wondered where that got to." He stayed at the threshold. "That was June. The June before."

His thumb moved along the frame.

"She was laughing at whoever held the camera. That was her brother. He never managed a straight picture."

He looked at her face for a long moment. His mug sat cold on the kitchen table below. The clock on the landing filled the quiet.

"Keep it somewhere warm." He turned toward the stairs. "Paper goes brittle in the cold."

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I hold the photo tight. "Thanks, Dad." I tuck it into my back pocket. "Did you... did you go through this closet already?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
His hand stopped on the banister. The varnish had worn through there. Pale wood, gone velvet under years of palms.

"Once."

He kept his back to the hall. "Last March. The damp came through the ceiling over this closet. I had to know what the water would reach. So I opened it." Above the closet door, the paint had bubbled into brown blisters.

He came back into the room. The cold in here rose through floorboards nobody heated. A breath of cedar and mothball drifted out past his shoulder.

"I took the coats. Hers went to the charity van in April. The rest I shut in and walked away from."

The landing clock counted through the wall.

"The photograph must have ridden out in a pocket. Wool keeps whatever falls into it." He looked past Eli to the shelves. Hatboxes sat in there, and a shoebox with its lid sunk soft.

"There's more of her in that dark. I couldn't tell you what." He crossed to the stairs. The third step took his weight and groaned. "Whatever it is, it kept better than I did."

Below, his chair complained when he took it again. The fridge hummed on. His coffee had gone the grey of dishwater in the mug.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Dad, stop." I step in front of him, blocking his path to the stairs. "Don't go back down there yet." I look at the closet. "Let's... let's look through this stuff together."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
He stopped. His arm hung a moment in the air, then settled. The landing clock pushed its ticking through the wall.

He looked at Eli. Then past, into the closet's dark. The cold came out of there in a slow current. It found the gap between them and moved through.

"The bulb's dead in that closet." His breath clouded in the unheated air. "I never replaced it. Didn't seem right to—" He let the sentence die where the others had.

He crossed to the spare room instead. A switch clicked. Light spread under that door, a thin gold line across the boards.

He came back with the desk lamp, its cord looped over his arm. The shade carried a dent on one side. He knelt at the wall socket. The plug went in with a grind of old brass.

Light climbed the closet's mouth. Dust hung in the beam and turned slow. Hatboxes showed their sunken lids. A scarf lay pooled on the top shelf, paisley gone thin at the fringe.

The new bulb ticked while it warmed. His jaw worked once. He did not reach for the scarf.

"Your mother sorted those boxes one winter." He rose. The joint in his knee cracked. "I couldn't tell you what she put where."

His palm settled flat against the doorframe. The paint there had worn through to bare wood under his hand.

"We'll want the bags from the kitchen. And time." He rubbed warmth into his hands. "I shut this door in March. Some things stay shut when you close them." He watched the beam a moment. "Some don't wait."

Then he took the stairs. Third step. Seventh. The one before the bottom. Below, a drawer rolled open on its runners. Paper rustled. The lamp burned on, and in its beam the dust kept turning.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The doorbell cut through the house. Two presses, one buzz stacked on another, thin and metallic. The landing clock drowned inside it.

Knuckles struck the swollen door. Three raps. A pause. Three more.

The father came out of the kitchen with the drawer still open behind him. He worked the door loose of its frame. Cold entered first, then the perfume, a floral cloud with something sharp underneath. Then her.

"We spoke on the phone. Dana." Her hand closed over his before he offered it. Cold rings pressed into his palm. She pumped his arm twice and moved past him into the hall. "Gorgeous out there. I said to myself, a sky this clean, this house gets its true light."

She threw her hip against the front door to shut it. The frame took her weight with a groan. "That door. We'll call it original hardware."

Her heels rang on the boards. A folder rode under her arm, glossy with printouts. One corner had gone soft from her grip. She drew a gloved finger across the beige, and the wool of the glove gave off a smell of cold and outside air. "Oh, you went neutral. Smart. Buyers want to picture their own lives here."

He turned his mug a quarter circle on the table. Its base grated on the wood. "Somebody had one."

The pen in her hand clicked twice. In the kitchen she stopped at the counter. Her eyes took in the box, the marker, the yellowed tape. "We'll want this cleared before the photos. Storage runs cheap this month."

"The box stays till the end." He drank. The coffee had gone cold and grey on his tongue.

She had reached the stairs. "Bedrooms. That's where they fall in love." Her heel came down on the third step and the board spoke. Her next stride woke the seventh. Behind her the father spoke to his mug. "The stairs talk in three places."

She laughed at that. The sound ran along the beige and came back thin. On the turn of the stair she stopped, chin lifted. Cedar drifted down the stairwell. Under it came the mothball. Under that, the sour wool.

"There's a light on up there." Pen click. "Show me the whole house. That's how we get the number you want."

The father set the mug down. It rang against the table. He took the stairs behind her. Third step. Seventh. The last one before the bottom. His hand found the banister, pale wood gone smooth.

At the top, Dana's voice moved along the landing, bright, filling every corner it found. The door of the old room stood open. The lamp still burned inside, and the cold came out of the doorway in a slow current, and in the beam the dust kept turning.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I flinch at the sound of the doorbell. "Dad, don't tell her about the box yet." I step out of the room, looking at the agent with a forced smile. "Hi, I'm Eli."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pen clicked once and went quiet. Dana turned from the stair. Her gaze ran from Eli's shoes to the top of the head, then her smile reset itself a notch wider. Cold rolled off her coat, and the perfume thickened the hall, florals over a sting of alcohol.

"There you are." She stripped her right glove off, teeth tugging at a fingertip. Her bare hand met Eli's, cold from the walk, rings pressing. "Dana. We'll get along, I can tell." A card came out of the folder, gloss gone soft at one corner. "Coastal Realty. You're on the title. Signatures matter."

"It's mine." The father said it from the kitchen door. The mug sat cold in his grip.

Her thumb flicked toward the counter. "Then we're square on the box. It wants a van by Tuesday, before Wednesday's shoot." The pen clicked twice. "Unless it stages. It won't stage."

The father's eyes crossed the hall to Eli. They held one beat, then went back to the mug. The coffee had gone grey in it. "It stays till the end," he said. "We settled that."

She swung the folder under her arm and took the stairs. Her heel woke the third step. The seventh. The last one before the bottom gave its low note. The father followed, hand riding the banister where varnish had worn to pale wood.

In the old room the cold came out to meet them. The desk lamp still burned, and dust turned in its beam. Dana made a slow circle in the center, chin up, taking in the ceiling and the blistered paint above the closet.

"Small repair. Cosmetic. We note it and move on." Then she crouched at the doorframe. The second glove came off. Her finger ran the pencil lines, the dates, the block capitals. "Oh, this is gold. Buyers pay for history. We shoot this wall in morning light."

The father stood in the doorway. His thumb found the highest mark without looking. "The marks stay," he said. "Whatever sells, the frame comes out with us."

Her pen hovered, then clicked and wrote. "Fixture exclusion. Fine. Paper handles anything." She rose and crossed to the window, dragged one finger through the condensation. The glass gave under it, cold and slick. "South light. Wednesday, ten."

The tape measure zipped from her pocket and snapped taut. She called numbers to herself, then moved for the hall. "Which of these is the primary?"

"End of the landing." The father did not move from the doorframe.

Her heels crossed the landing. A door swung on its hinge. The tape measure zipped again, further off.

In the old room the lamp burned on. The father looked past Eli to the top shelf, to the scarf pooled there, fringe gone thin. He rubbed warmth into his hands. "Bags from the kitchen," he said. "We fetch them before Wednesday."

He took the stairs down. Third step. Seventh. The last one before the bottom. In the beam the dust kept turning, and the cold held still around the marks on the frame.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Dad, wait." I say, looking between the doorframe and the closet. "We should start here." I gesture to the closet. "Before she comes back."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
His foot stopped on the bottom step. The kitchen drawer still stood open below. Up the landing, the tape measure zipped. Dana's voice came through the wall, counting inches.

He turned on the stair. The boards carried him back up. Bottom step. Seventh. Third. He came into the doorway and wiped his palms down his trousers.

The cold came out of the closet and met him at the chest. He pushed his sleeves to the elbow. One cuff had frayed to loose threads. He reached past the scarf and took down the first hatbox.

The lid slid free with a dry sigh of cardboard. Tissue inside had gone stiff and yellow. Under it lay gloves. Grey leather gone hard at the knuckles.

He worked one glove over his own hand. It stopped at the second knuckle. The leather cracked along the seam. He drew it off and set both gloves on the quilt.

"She drove in those. Summers, windows down. The wheel burned her palms raw." He smoothed the quilt where they lay. "First thing for the keep pile."

Under the gloves lay a purse. Beads sewn in rows, a clasp of dull silver. It clicked when he turned it. A powder smell came off the lining, sweet and stale.

He set it on the floor by the door. Give pile. Then his hand stopped in the tissue. The paper crackled under his wrist. "Three piles," he said. "Keep. Give away. Burn."

"She asked me for a bonfire. Near the end. I told her no." His breath clouded in the cold. He took his hand from the box. "I'm telling her yes."

He reached up then for the paisley scarf. The wool had thinned at the fringe. He unfolded it once and held it to his face. Cold wool. Nothing else in it. He folded it corner to corner. He set it on the windowsill, apart from the piles. The wood sweated under it, cold and wet.

He crouched to the closet floor and drew out the shoebox. The lid had sunk soft. String circled it, knotted twice, tight with damp. He weighed it in his hands. Paper shifted somewhere inside.

Down the landing, heels crossed the boards. The tape zipped. A door swung shut.

He held the box out. "I never opened this one. I shut it away in March with the string still tied." The knots sat dark where his thumbs pressed them. "It wants your hands."

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Okay." My voice is a little shaky. I take the box from him, the string rough against my fingers. I can feel something shifting inside. I sit on the floor, cross-legged, and start working on the knot.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The second knot fought longest. Damp had glued the fibers together, and the string rasped against itself. Then it gave. The loops fell slack against the cardboard.

The lid came free with a soft suck of cardboard. A smell rose out of the box. Old paper. Vanilla gone stale. Under that, lavender, thinned almost to nothing.

Envelopes filled the box to its creased corners. A dozen of them, squared and stacked. A rubber band had held the stack once. It lay in the corner, crumbled to black threads. The paper had gone soft at its edges. The top envelope carried a single word. Eli. The hand slanted. It matched the later marks on the doorframe.

The floor pushed its cold up through cloth. On the landing the clock counted. Farther off, heels crossed boards, and Dana's voice ran numbers through the ceiling.

At the window the father had gone still. The glass behind him ran with condensation. The folded scarf lay on the sill beside his hand. He read the word on the envelope from where he stood. "That's her hand." His voice came out rough at the bottom.

He crossed the room and knelt at the quilt. The joint in his knee cracked. He put a palm flat on the boards. He leaned over the box without touching it. His breath clouded once and faded.

Each envelope bore a date in its top corner. Small numerals, blue ink faded to a weak grey. The dates ran back through years, season by season. The last one read June.

His thumb stopped above that final date. He did not set it down on the paper. "That June," he said. "She was still walking out to the fence."

"I told her yes to a bonfire." He rubbed warmth into his knuckles. "These were never in that pile."

Under the stack sat one envelope thicker than the rest. A strip of tape had sealed it, amber with age. No date on that one. Just the name, pressed deep enough to ridge the paper.

Through the floor, Dana's voice ran on about primary bedrooms and morning light. The father rose. He stood with a hand on the sill, the wood cold and sweating under his palm. "Dana can measure the whole house while you read the first line," he said. He moved for the door. At the threshold he stopped. "I'll be below. If the kettle wants filling."

The lamp burned on. In its beam the dust turned above the open box, and the top envelope lay with its single word facing up.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I pick up the envelope with my name on it. My hands are shaking a little. I look at the dates on the other envelopes, then back at the first one. "Dad... wait," I say, but he's already at the door.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
He stopped with one foot over the threshold. His hand closed on the doorframe, on bare wood worn smooth. He stood there with his back to the room.

Then he came back. One step. Another. The boards gave a low note under his weight.

He lowered himself to the edge of the quilt. The springs sighed beneath him. Cold came off the wall and touched the back of his neck.

"I never read them. Not one." He rubbed a thumb along the seam of his pocket. "She sealed them at that desk. Every spring." He nodded toward the window. "I filled the kettle for her each time. She wrote while it climbed. Never let it whistle."

He breathed out, and the breath clouded. "The June one went in last. I heard her drawer that night. Then nothing."

He looked at Eli's hands. He saw the shake in them. He said nothing of it. He pressed his palm flat to the quilt, to the cold wool under it.

"Take your time with it." He rose. The knee cracked. "The kettle's below when you want it."

He took the stairs. Third step. Seventh. The last one before the bottom.

The tap ran. Water drummed the kettle's belly. The drumming rose in pitch, then cut off. A cupboard clicked shut.

Overhead, Dana's tape zipped. Her voice ran numbers along the landing. "The primary wants paint," she called through the floor. A door swung shut on its hinge.

In the old room the lamp burned on. Its beam held a column of turning dust. The cold lay along the floorboards and pushed up through the quilt.

The envelope had dulled to the color of weak tea. Its corners had gone soft. Under the flap, old gum had hardened to a thin ridge. A smell of lavender came off it, thinned almost to nothing.

Through the wall the clock counted. Below, the kettle began its climb toward a whistle. In the beam the dust kept turning. The flap faced the light, sealed for ten springs.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I stare at the envelope. My name, in my mother's handwriting. I run my thumb over the stiff gummed flap. I can hear the kettle starting to whistle downstairs. I don't open it. Not yet.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The kettle's whistle climbed through the floorboards. It cut off short of its peak. Below, water struck granules in a thin rope. After that the hall held quiet.

Heels crossed the landing and stopped short of the stairs. Dana's voice came down the stairwell, pitched for the whole house. "Wednesday, ten. I'll email the van list tonight." Then her heels carried her to the old room's door. She stood there with the folder pressed to her chest. The pen hung quiet in her hand. Her eyes moved over the open box, the envelopes, the name on top. The perfume reached in before she did, florals thinned by the cold.

For one breath her voice lost its shine.

"Mind that door," she said. "It swells once the sun's off it." Her heels took the stairs. Third step. Seventh. The one before the bottom gave its note. At the front door she set her shoulder to the swollen wood. It held. She struck it with the flat of her fist. It gave with a scrape of frame. Cold rushed the hall, and the door boomed shut. Then the house held its stillness.

Footsteps climbed from the kitchen. Bottom step. Seventh. Third. The father came in with both mugs. The blue one led, its chip turned toward Eli. Steam climbed off both. He set the blue one down beside the open box. The smell of burnt granules moved into the cold of the room.

He settled onto the edge of the quilt. The springs sighed under him. He drank, and his face pulled at the taste, scorched and stewed.

"Took it off before the whistle." He tipped his mug toward the floor. "Habit now. She said the whistling rushed her hand."

His gaze went to the envelope. It touched the shake in Eli's hands and moved off. He said nothing about it. Eli's thumb rested where the gum had ridged the flap.

"If the seal fights you, don't force it." He turned his mug a quarter circle. Its base grated on the wood. "Hold the flap over the kettle's mouth. Ten seconds. Steam beats gum every time."

He rose. The knee cracked. He crossed to the sill and stood over the folded scarf. Condensation had crept into its hem. He pressed the wool between two fingers. Cold came off it. Nothing else did.

He set his palm flat to the glass. The window kept the fogged print of his hand after he drew it back. Outside, the daylight had thinned to the grey of dishwater.

"Van comes Wednesday." He spoke toward the glass. "Till then this room answers to nobody with a tape."

At the door he stopped with a hand on the frame. His thumb found the highest pencil mark. He stood there a moment with his back to the lamp.

Then he took the stairs down. Third step. Seventh. The one before the bottom. Below, the tap ran and two mugs clinked in the sink. The clock counted through the wall. Lavender came off the open box, thinned almost to nothing. In the beam the dust kept turning. The envelope waited with its single word facing up.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I press my thumb harder against the envelope, my name still staring up at me. "I'll be down in a minute, Dad." I tell the empty doorway. I look at the scarf on the windowsill, then back at the envelope. "Steam, huh?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pencil marks climbed the white paint. Some had faded. The lowest ones were shallow.

Fresh paint had sealed the grain around them. Each ridge held a tiny shadow. The surface felt raised under the fingertips.

A chalk scent drifted from the doorframe. It mixed with the wet wool smell of the hall.

The floorboard near the threshold gave a dry creak. Cold air seeped from the old room.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I push open the door to my room, wincing at the creak.* It's so cold in here. "Dad never did fix that draft, huh?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The draft moved through the doorway. It carried cold metal and old paper.

No answer came from the hall. The hall held the smell of wet wool.

The window latch hung open. Curtain fabric whispered against the glass.

A bare mattress leaned against the wall. Its ticking smelled of cedar and stale air.

The radiator ticked. Dust warmed on the iron ribs.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The closet smelled of cedar and dry plaster.  
A thin layer of grit coated the shelf.  
The photograph lay face down under a shoebox.  
Its corner had curled.  
The paper felt brittle.

The image showed a woman by a lake.  
Her hands rested on a blue rail.  
Sunlight touched her hair.  
The print smelled of iron and old drawers.  
A faint orange stain marked the edge.

On the back, pencil writing crossed the white.  
The letters were small.  
Graphite had pressed deep into the fiber.  
The closet air tasted cold.  
Dust settled on the bare floorboard.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I turn the photo over carefully.* It's her. "Mom..." I trace the faded inscription on the back. "August '98." A tear slips down my cheek.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The word sank into the cold room.  
The radiator gave one low tick.  
Dust lifted from its ribs.  
The air tasted of plaster and old wool.

The photograph stayed warm from touch.  
The lake in the image held pale light.  
The blue rail looked chipped.  
A faint cedar scent rose from the closet.

Outside, rain began against the glass.  
The curtain dragged over the window frame.  
The draft carried wet leaves and rust.  
The floorboard cooled underfoot.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I wipe my eyes and tuck the photo into my pocket. *I can hear the rain now.* "Great, just what we needed." I step out of my room, pulling the door shut behind me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The door clicked shut.

The hallway held dust and wet wool.

Rain tapped the front window.

Cold glass gathered sweat.

The kitchen box waited on the counter.

Masking tape curled at one corner.

Marker ink gave a sharp chemical scent.

Fresh paint carried a mineral chill.

Behind the closed door, the radiator ticked.

A draft moved along the baseboard.

It brought wet leaves and rust.

The floorboards settled under the house's weight.

The rooms kept their cold.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
A knock struck the front door.  
The brass knocker rattled against painted wood.  
Rain hissed on the porch step.  
Wet rubber smelled of tires and street.  

The agent entered with a gust.  
Her coat shed cold droplets.  
The droplets darkened the old carpet.  
Perfume mixed with damp wool.  

Her folder smelled of gloss and ink.  
Keys jingled at her wrist.  
Her greeting rang bright.  
The counter tape made a thin sound.  

Her shoes squeaked on the hallway boards.  
She touched the fresh wall.  
Paint still held a cool film.  
The kitchen box sat between them.  

Her voice carried lemon and paper.  
Her smile showed cold teeth.  
She set a glossy sheet on the counter.  
The sheet smelled of warm toner.  

A draft pushed from the doorframe.  
It moved the agent's collar.  
The collar made a dry sound.  
Her laugh struck the hallway walls.  
It rang bright and thin.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Eli, right? So glad you could make it!" She chirps, her voice a little too loud for the quiet house. I just nod, trying to force a smile. "Just signing some papers, then you're free to go."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent tapped the folder.  
Glossy pages made a dry whisper.  
Rain tapped the windowpane.  
The glass smelled cold.  

She placed a pen on the counter.  
Plastic clicked against laminate.  
The ink carried an alcohol bite.  
The counter held the kitchen box's shadow.  

"Initial here, please," she said.  
Her nail tapped the line.  
The paper gave a chemical warmth.  
Her cuff brushed the sheet.  

The house settled around them.  
A floorboard sighed under the hall.  
Wet leaves pressed against the porch.  
The draft tasted of rust.  

The agent gave a bright nod.  
Her earrings made small clicks.  
"The last page is here," she said.  
The folder smelled of warm plastic.  

The agent turned the page.  
Paper edges hissed.  
Her perfume carried lemon peel.  
The kitchen box blocked the counter's edge.  

"Your father signed yesterday," she said.  
The words sat in the cold room.  
Rainwater slid down the window.  
The latch rattled in its frame.  

She smoothed the sheet.  
Her palm made a dry rasp.  
The pen rolled toward Eli.  
The counter smelled of marker tape.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I pick up the pen, my fingers cold.* "He did, huh?" I scribble my initials, not really looking at the paper. "Guess that's it then."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pen left black marks on the signature line.  
The ink smelled of solvent and cold metal.  
The agent folded the pages.  
Paper edges whispered against her folder.  
Rain tapped the kitchen window.  

Her smile stayed fixed.  
Her teeth showed white and even.  
The house gave a low creak.  
Dust warmed on the radiator.  
The counter held the box's taped shadow.  

"Welcome to the next chapter," she said.  
Her voice carried lemon and fresh paper.  
The front door shivered under rain.  
Wet leaves brushed the porch.  
The hallway smelled of old carpet.  

The keys at her wrist gave a bright sound.  
The sound fell into the hallway.  
The paint smelled mineral and cold.  
The kitchen box waited on the counter.  
Its tape lifted a dry corner.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I manage a tight, humorless smile.* "Yeah, 'next chapter'." I put the pen down. "Well, thanks for everything."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent closed the folder.  
Its cover made a soft rasp.  
Her keys gave one short chime.  

"Take care," she said.  
Her breath smelled of mint and rain.  
The porch boards took her weight.  

The door began to close.  
Its swollen edge caught the jamb.  
The latch gave a dull click.  

Cold air stayed in the hall.  
The paint smelled mineral and wet.  
The pen lay on the counter.  

Its black ink dried on the line.  
The paper carried warm toner.  
The floorboards gave a low creak.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I watch the door close, then turn back to the empty house.* "Alone at last," I mumble. I pick up the pen, putting it back in the holder.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pen slid into the holder.  
Plastic clicked against the counter.  
The kitchen box smelled of marker ink.  
Rain tapped the window glass.

The hallway held wet wool.  
Dust warmed on the radiator.  
A draft moved along the baseboard.  
It carried rust and wet leaves.

The photograph pressed against Eli's pocket.  
Its corner felt sharp through cloth.  
The room smelled of cedar.  
The window latch rattled.

Fresh paint held a mineral chill.  
The floorboards settled underfoot.  
The house breathed cold air.  
The door latch gave a dull sound.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I walk back into the living room, heading for the old fireplace.* "Might as well make some use of this place while I'm still here."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The living room smelled of cold ash.  
The fireplace mouth held black soot.  
A draft breathed through the flue.  
It carried wet brick and rain.  

The mantel felt gritty under dust.  
Old varnish gave a faint sweetness.  
The hearth tiles were cracked and cold.  
A spiderweb trembled in the draft.  

Rain scratched at the front window.  
The carpet held damp wool smell.  
A loose brick shifted in the firebox.  
It made a dry, hollow sound.  

The kitchen box remained on the counter.  
Masking tape released a chemical scent.  
The hallway floor cooled.  
The house waited with closed doors.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I run my hand over the mantel, disturbing a thick layer of dust.* "Ugh, really, Dad? Still no cleaning?" I sigh, looking for anything to burn.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pencil marks climbed the doorframe in pale gray strokes. Dates in faded ink stood beside each line. The wood bore a polish from years of passing palms. A faint cedar smell drifted from the closet.

Beyond the frame, the bedroom held a single window. Gray light fell across bare floorboards. A mattress leaned against the far wall. Its fabric smelled of attic heat and trapped dust.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I push the bedroom door open further, a soft creak echoing in the quiet house.* The smell of cedar... I remember that. "They even took my closet doors?" I mutter, looking at the empty space.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The closet stood open. Empty pine shelves bowed in the middle. A wire hanger clung to the rod. It tapped the wall in the draft.

Cooler air moved through the frame. The floor showed dark rectangles. Shoe boxes had left them. Mothballs left their sharp smell in the corners.

Outside, a branch scraped the window. The sound filled the bare room.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph had buckled with moisture. Her face occupied the center frame. A blue dress gathered at her shoulders. The color had drained toward gray. A chemical smell rose from the emulsion.

Behind them the wire hanger stilled. The branch scratched glass again. A car horn drifted from the avenue. Cool air pressed against the bare floor.

The date stamp read August 2003. Her eyes reflected an unseen window. The gloss had worn to matte. Dust coated the emulsion's top edge.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I trace the outline of her face with my thumb.* August 2003... that was just before everything changed. I remember that dress. "Mom," I whisper, a little catch in my voice.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The emulsion crackled beneath the thumb. A flake of silvering lifted at the edge. The chemical smell grew stronger with Eli's warmth. The corner darkened with new moisture.

The wire hanger shifted. It tapped a slow rhythm against the pine. The branch outside scraped the glass. The sound was dry and insistent.

Breath misted in the cool air. Dust hung in the gray window light. The motes turned in the closet draft. A floorboard creaked beneath Eli's weight.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I carefully put the photo back in the closet, not wanting to damage it further.* The house is so cold. I should probably close that window. *I walk over to the window and try to push it shut.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The window frame resisted. Paint had sealed the sash to the sill. Something cracked. Not glass. Wood gave way. Or old paint peeled. Cold air whistled through the gap. It carried the smell of wet leaves and exhaust.

The branch scraped again. The sound was sharp. The wood felt slick beneath the pressure. The window dropped an inch. Then another. The whistling stopped. The room grew still. Dust settled in the sudden silence.

The floorboard creaked beneath Eli's weight. The mattress fabric rustled against the wall. Outside, the car horn faded. The wire hanger tapped once. Then stopped.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Heels clicked the hallway floorboards. The sound approached the bedroom door. A knock followed. Three sharp raps broke the silence. "Hello?" Her voice carried from the hall. It was bright and edged. It cut through the dust and cedar.

She appeared in the doorframe. Her perfume arrived first. It smelled of synthetic berries and rubbing alcohol. The scent pushed into the cool room. She wore a red blazer. The fabric held a plastic sheen. Her smile showed teeth. They were very white and even. Her hand extended toward Eli. "You must be Eli," she said. The pitch rose at the end. It demanded confirmation.

Behind her, the hallway held its silence. The dust smell thickened in the stillness. The wire hanger tapped the closet wall. It tapped twice. Then it stopped. A floorboard creaked beneath her weight. The branch scraped the window glass again. The sound was dry.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I blink, startled by her sudden appearance.* "That's me," I say, a little flatly, ignoring her outstretched hand. "And you are...?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Her hand hovered. Then it dropped. The red sleeve rustled. Her smile remained. It did not reach her eyes. The berry smell intensified. It clashed with the mothball sharpness in the corners.

"Margaret Chen," she said. She produced a card from her pocket. It was thick and cream-colored. The stock felt heavy between her fingers. She held it out. The ink smelled fresh. "I'm handling the sale." Her eyes moved past Eli. They scanned the bare floorboards. They noted the leaning mattress. They returned to Eli's face. Her blink was slow.

The wire hanger tapped. It tapped a third time. The sound was small. It was metal against wood. Margaret's head turned. Her neck made a faint crack. She looked toward the closet. Her lips tightened. The berry scent pushed forward again. She stepped into the room. The floorboard groaned beneath her heel. The red blazer swished. Static electricity popped in the dry air.

"So this was your room," she said. Her statement rose at the end. It wanted an answer. She ran a finger along the doorframe. She touched the pencil marks. The polish on the wood smudged her fingertip. It left a faint gray streak. She wiped it on her skirt. The fabric was charcoal wool. It absorbed the mark. The branch scraped the window. The sound was persistent. It demanded entry.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I watch her, unimpressed.* "It was. For a long time." I don't offer any more information. *I glance at the closet, then back at her.* "Is there something I can help you with?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Margaret's smile tightened. She withdrew her hand from the doorframe. The gray mark remained on the wood. Dust motes hung in the gray light.

"Just the final walkthrough," she said. Her voice carried a rehearsed brightness. It scraped against the silence. The wire hanger tapped the closet wall. The sound was soft.

She stepped toward the closet. Her heel struck the floorboard. The sound was hollow. She peered at the empty shelves. Her nose wrinkled. The mothball sharpness filled the air.

"The owners wanted confirmation of the empty rooms," she said. She turned back toward Eli. Her eyes narrowed. They focused on Eli's empty hands.

"Is there anything here that belongs to you?" she asked. Her tone remained level. It held an expectation. Outside, the branch scraped the window. The glass rattled in the frame.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I cross my arms, feeling a defensive prickle.* "No. Nothing." I don't elaborate, not wanting to explain the photograph. "Just memories."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Margaret's expression shifted. Something flickered across her face. It vanished in an instant. The berry smell intensified as she stepped closer.

"Memories don't convey," she said. Her voice dropped. The rehearsed brightness drained from it. The words hung in the cool air.

She turned toward the window. The branch scraped the glass again. The sound was sharp. Her red blazer caught the gray light. The fabric held no warmth.

"The buyers expect an empty house," she said. She looked at the pencil marks. Her finger traced one date. Polish smeared beneath her finger. It left a gray streak. "Clean slate."

The wire hanger tapped the pine. It tapped twice. The sound echoed in the bare room. Dust shifted in the closet draft.

She moved toward the mattress. Her hand touched the fabric. Dust puffed from the surface. It carried the smell of attic heat. She pulled her hand back.

"We can arrange for removal," she said. She brushed her palms together. The sound was soft. "Of anything left behind."

Outside, a car passed. The engine noise swelled. Then it faded. The floorboard creaked beneath Margaret's weight. The mothball smell lingered in the corners.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "I think I've got that covered," I say, my voice flat. *I look pointedly at her hand, then at the doorframe.* "So, are we done in here?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Margaret's smile returned. It remained fixed on her face. The berry scent pushed forward. She withdrew her hand from the mattress. Dust clung to her palm.

"Of course," she said. Her voice regained its brightness. The edge remained beneath it. Her heel struck the floorboard. The sound was sharp. Mothball sharpness lingered in the corners.

The wire hanger tapped the closet rod. The sound was faint. Margaret's head turned. Her neck made a small crack. She looked at the empty closet. Her lips pressed together. Cool air drifted from the empty shelves.

"We should check the kitchen," she said. She motioned toward the hall. Her red sleeve rustled. Static popped in the dry air. "The box on the counter." The berry scent intensified.

She moved into the hallway. Her heels clicked the floorboards. The sound receded. Then it stopped. She waited beyond the doorframe. The dust smell thickened. The cedar smell faded.

The branch scraped the window glass. The sound was dry. Cool air pressed through the frame. Dust motes turned in the gray light. The floorboard beneath Eli creaked.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to dispel the berry smell.* "Alright," I say, and follow her out, giving the empty closet one last glance.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The hallway stretched toward the back of the house. Dust hung in the narrow passage. The old carpet stiffened with age. It crackled under passing weight. Margaret's heels clicked ahead. The sound was sharp and regular. A draft carried the paint smell. It drifted from the beige walls.

Margaret reached the kitchen doorway. Her heels struck the linoleum. The sound turned hard. Fluorescent light buzzed overhead. The bulb flickered. Gray light washed the counters. The box sat on the laminate. Masking tape sealed the flaps. Black marker spelled KITCHEN. The handwriting remained unfamiliar. Something rattled inside.

She touched the box. Her fingers tugged the tape. It peeled with a slow tear. The cardboard flaps opened. She reached inside. Her hand emerged holding a single mug. White ceramic. A chip marked the rim. Coffee stained the bottom. It smelled of old grounds. The berry scent of her perfume pushed against the kitchen air.

Behind her, the hallway held its silence. The dust smell thickened. A floorboard creaked. The paint smell lingered on the walls.
