Lena looked at the doors, then at him.

“You said two interviews,” she said. “One before the canvass, one after. What was different?”

The detective’s throat moved.

“The witness was afraid,” he said. “Not of us. Of whoever was listening.”

Lena’s gaze sharpened.

“Whoever,” she said. “Good word.”

She stepped closer to the elevator, but not enough to touch it. She studied the floor, the seam beneath the doors, the faint dark line where someone had tried to clean something that hadn’t come up.

“Someone was listening,” she said. “And someone decided the best way to stop a case wasn’t to bury it. It was to make sure the right questions never got asked.”

The detective’s hand tightened on the paper.

Lena finally looked at him.

“You have two choices,” she said. “You can stand here and keep saying things that sound like warnings. Or you can tell me what was on that sheet that was worth leaving off the report.”

The detective stared at her.

For a moment, Lena thought he might fold again.

Then he said, very quietly, “The witness said the freight elevator was used by someone who wasn’t assigned to the dock.”

Lena’s expression went still.

“Not a name,” she said.

“No.”

“A role.”

The detective looked down at the paper. “A job title.”

Lena’s eyes flicked to the elevator.

The light buzzed again. Somewhere above them, a door opened. Footsteps. Not many. Not far.

Lena didn’t turn. She spoke low, almost pleasant.

“If you want this to stay a conversation,” she said, “you’re going to tell me that job title while we’re still alone.”

The detective’s face went pale.

Lena’s hand lifted slightly, not toward him, but toward the exit.

“Say it,” she said. “Before the room says it for us.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I shift my weight, glancing nervously toward the sound of footsteps above. This is getting intense.* "What's he waiting for, Lena? Just tell her!"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s eyes slid toward the client, but only for the length of a breath. Then they went back to the detective, who still hadn’t moved, still hadn’t spoken, still hadn’t chosen.

“No one tells her,” Lena said. “She isn’t here. He is. And he’s deciding whether he’s the kind of person who remembers a detail or the kind who waits until someone else remembers it for him.”

Above them, the footsteps stopped.

Lena didn’t look up. She didn’t need to. She had already counted the floor. She knew where the exit led. She knew where the shadows thinned and where the camera blind spots might have been, if anyone had thought to leave them.

She stepped closer to the detective, not enough to crowd him, just enough to make the space around them feel smaller.

“Job title,” she said. “Now.”

The detective’s mouth tightened.

“Facilities supervisor,” he said quietly. “Second shift.”

Lena’s face stayed blank.

“That’s a title,” she said. “Not a person.”

The detective looked at the folded paper in his hand like it had betrayed him.

“He had master-key access,” the detective said. “Freight logs. Dock schedule. Elevator override.”

“Override,” Lena repeated.

The word came out flat, dangerous, the way a door sounds when it locks.

Lena glanced at the elevator. The faded notice on the steel doors curled at one corner. Not out of service. Not in service either. A gray space. The kind people lived in when they wanted to do something and still pretend they hadn’t.

“Did he use it?” she asked.

The detective hesitated.

Lena looked at him again. “If you start lying to me because you’re scared of what it means, you’ll already be too late.”

The detective exhaled through his nose. “The witness said the elevator was used after the dock closed. The supervisor’s card was logged in the building, but the elevator system showed the car on the loading level.”

Lena’s eyes narrowed.

“So the system saw him,” she said.

The detective didn’t answer.

Lena turned slightly, angling her body toward the exit while keeping the detective in her view. The cold air from the street slipped through the garage door, carrying diesel and wet pavement and the faint smell of rust.

“Where did the witness say the supervisor went?” she asked.

The detective looked at the paper again. His thumb rubbed the crease until the fibers softened.

“He didn’t know,” the detective said. “Only that the supervisor was arguing with someone. Someone who wasn’t assigned to the dock.”

“Someone I used to work with,” Lena said, not as a question.

The detective looked up sharply.

Lena’s expression didn’t change. She had heard the phrase before, in her own voice, in her own rules, and she let it stand.

The detective swallowed. “That’s what the witness said.”

Lena studied him. The client’s question hung in the air, impatient and ordinary, the kind of question people asked when they wanted the truth to arrive faster than it was willing to.

She did not answer the client.

Instead, she said, “You’re not going to make this easier by waiting for permission.”

The detective’s face went pale.

“I’m not asking you to confess,” Lena said. “I’m asking you to stop pretending this is safe because nobody’s written it down.”

The detective looked at the elevator. At the dark seam beneath the doors. At the folded paper in his hand.

Then he said, very quietly, “The witness described a woman.”

Lena’s jaw tightened.

The detective continued before he could lose the thread.

“Not a badge. Not a name. A role. She told the witness she was handling it.”

“Handling what?”

“The file.”

Lena let the silence sit.

Above them, a door opened again. Footsteps moved across the concrete floor. Slow. Deliberate. Someone walking like they believed they belonged there.

Lena stepped back from the detective, putting distance between herself and the elevator, between herself and the sound, between herself and whatever kind of answer was coming down the stairs.

Her hand slid into her coat pocket.

“We’re done here,” she said.

The detective blinked. “We’re not done.”

“No,” Lena said. “We’re done letting the room finish the conversation for us.”

She looked at the exit, then at the client, then back at the detective.

“If anyone asks,” she said, “you didn’t meet us. You didn’t bring out a sheet. You didn’t say the title.”

The detective’s mouth opened, then closed.

Lena’s voice dropped.

“You were here alone. Thinking about your coffee.”

She turned toward the garage exit, her steps even, unhurried, as if the footsteps above had only confirmed something she had already known.

“Walk,” she said. “If you follow, keep your eyes forward. If you don’t, don’t look back when the file gets reopened.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I hesitate for a second, glancing at the detective's pale face, then quickly follow Lena towards the exit.* "What just happened? Who was that woman?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena reached the sidewalk and kept walking until the garage door had swallowed the sound of the footsteps behind them. The street outside was too bright for the hour, the light flat and gray, bouncing off wet asphalt and car windows. She moved through it the way she moved through everything else: with a body that looked relaxed and eyes that were not.

She did not answer right away.

Her coat pocket was empty where the folded sheet should have been, and she kept one hand near the opening as if the absence were still something that could be checked.

“What happened,” she said at last, “is that the file found a voice it had been avoiding.”

She turned down a side lane, away from the diner, away from the garage entrance, choosing the route with more shadows and fewer cameras.

“A job title is not a person,” she continued. “A keycard log is not a confession. An argument by the freight elevator is not a motive. It is a seam. We pry.”

The wind moved along the wall beside them, carrying the smell of oil and old rain.

“If that detail means anything, it means someone I used to work with.”

The words came out even, ordinary, as if she had spent them before and found them cheap.

Lena stopped under the edge of a loading awning, where the roof cast a darker rectangle across the pavement. She looked toward the mouth of the alley, not through it, but just far enough to understand how someone might exit it without being seen.

“Now the next question is not what that person looked like,” she said. “It’s what access they had after the dock closed.”

She pulled out her phone and turned the screen away from the street.

“The supervisor’s building has a maintenance office across the loading yard. Not a desk. Not a station. A window. If the clerk’s willing to talk, she meets us by the fuel stop on Ninth Avenue. If she isn’t, we find another window.”

Her thumb hovered over the screen.

“Because someone kept this file quiet long enough to call it complete. We’re going to find out what it still refuses to say.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "So, we're going to another window, huh? Does this 'someone you used to work with' have a name yet, or are we still dealing with 'job titles'?" *I ask, a little sarcastically, but trying to keep my voice low.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s thumb stopped on the screen. She did not look at him right away. Her eyes moved down the side lane, counting shadows the way another person might count exits.

“The point,” she said, “is that a name is a door. Once you open it, someone else knows where you are.”

She slid the phone into her pocket and began walking again.

“We don’t need the door yet. We need the keycard log. The override code. The shift that wasn’t there. The part where the file stopped pretending it was closed because it was finished.”

A second passed. The wind pushed a plastic bag against the curb and gave up.

“If the person handling the file wants to be called something,” Lena said, “they can meet us where the coffee is cold and the cameras are broken. Until then, ‘someone I used to work with’ keeps us moving.”

She glanced back once, expression flat.

“And if you’re waiting for the answer to make this simple, you’re waiting at the wrong window.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Understood. No names until they're unavoidable. So, the maintenance office across the loading yard. That's our next stop then?" *I ask, trying to keep up with her pace.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pencil marks climbed the doorframe in a crooked line. Dates beside each one, faded to gray. The lowest mark sat at knee height. Someone had dated it the year the house still belonged to everyone.

The hallway held a coolness the kitchen lacked. A draft moved from somewhere unseen. It carried the smell of the dust Eli's fingers had gathered.

Beyond the doorframe, the room waited with its door ajar. The hinges made no sound when the air touched them. Nothing moved inside. But the light through the window fell across a bed stripped to its mattress, and the mattress sagged in the middle the way used mattresses did.

Wait. Not that way. The mattress sagged in the middle. Years of sleeping had pressed it down.

On the sill, a dead fly lay on its back. Its legs curled inward. The window glass above it had gone cloudy at the corners, sealed with grime no cloth had reached.

Eli's hand rested on the frame. The wood there was smooth. Worn down by shoulders and by hands and by one small body pressed against it, year after year, chin lifted, heels dug into the floor.

The next mark up had a different date. A different year of the same ritual.

Somewhere below, the refrigerator hummed. It had always hummed. That sound had once meant someone was home.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content:
I trace the dates with my finger. *The same ritual.* I remember how much I hated standing still for these. Always wanted to be doing something else.

"Bet you still hum, huh?" I say to the fridge, not moving from the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The hum went on. It had not paused for the question. It would not pause for anything. The sound climbed the stairwell and thinned by the landing.

Below, the compressor clicked off. The silence after it had weight. Then it caught again with a shudder, and the note resumed, a half tone lower. Old machines drifted. The pitch went where it wanted.

The words Eli had sent down the stairs came back changed. The house returned them flat, without the joke in them. Empty rooms kept the words and gave back their shape.

In the room, the light had moved on. The pale stripe across the mattress had slid toward the foot of the bed. The sunlit half of the sill held warmth. The shaded half kept its chill.

Overhead, plastic stars clung to the ceiling. They had faded from green to the gray of old teeth. Beneath them, two crescents were scuffed into the paint, the feet of some chair. Someone had stood up there in the dark, reaching.

The room smelled of shut glass and warm dust. Under that sat a stale sweetness, a bar of soap gone quiet in some drawer. Then the draft came again from the hallway behind Eli. Inside the room, a page turned. A dry rasp, brief. Somewhere past the stripped bed, paper had moved.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph had curled at its corners. The gloss had dulled along one edge. The color had faded, drained toward brown at the margins. A decade of dark had eaten the image inward. The paper still held a faint warmth from the closet dark.

In the picture she stood at the kitchen counter. The same counter. Her sleeves were rolled to the elbow. Flour dusted one wrist. She laughed at something past the camera, head tipped, hand raised. The print smelled of dust and of the mothballs that had guarded it.

The closet door stood open. Inside, the rail held three empty hangers. Their paint had rusted at the hooks. The shelf above carried a smell of cedar, faint, almost gone. Beneath the shelf, in the corner, a shoebox slumped. Its lid had softened. More prints stood inside it, edge to edge, a spine of paper.

The hallway draft reached the closet floor. Beside the shoebox, one print lay loose, curled. The draft took its edge and laid it back down. That had been the sound. Paper, moving once, nothing more.

Below, the refrigerator held its lowered note. The sound rose through the floorboards, thinner here, still present. On the counter down there, the taped box waited, marked in a stranger's hand. Whoever had written it had worked through this house. The kitchen had been first.

The sill had cooled where the sun had been. The face in the photograph had not changed. Faces in photographs never did. The corners of the print had gone soft from handling. The sickness came after the flour, after the laugh. None of it had reached this paper. Here she remained, someone the house had been built around.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I pick up the shoebox. It's heavier than I expect. I sit on the bare mattress, careful not to disturb the dust too much, and open the box.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The lid lifted free. The cardboard had gone soft at the fold. A smell rose out of the box. Mothballs first. Then old paper. Then the soap, faint, sunk deep in the paper itself.

The weight made sense now. Beneath the prints lay glassine sleeves, negatives sealed inside. Each sleeve carried a number, penciled at the corner. The numbers ran past forty. The pencil marks held a trace of graphite smell. The sleeves had gone brittle at their seams.

The top print showed the garden. Tomatoes staked with twine, the soil dark from watering. A small Eli stood at the edge in a sun hat, mouth set, mid-sulk. The colors had held here. The green still looked wet. The paper drew cool from the closet dark and kept it.

The prints beneath came from later years. The mother thinned through the stack, print by print. A scarf in July. A hospital window behind her in one, its light the gray of paper. In that one she had raised the same hand. The same laugh, worn down to its edges. These prints had kept the cold of the box bottom.

Near the end, one sleeve sat empty. Its number read thirty-one. Whatever had lived there had been lifted out. The box had been closed on the gap. The empty sleeve lay flat, its seam split at one end.

At the bottom, under the last sleeve, lay a folded page. The creases had gone furry from handling. A gray thumbprint sat in one corner, ground into the paper. The handwriting leaned hard to the right. Flour. Butter. Candles, birthday, ask which kind. The list had outlived the kitchen it was written for.

The springs of the mattress shifted. A thread of dust climbed through the light and turned there. Below, the refrigerator found its old note again. The sun stripe had left the sill and lay thinning on the floorboards. The floorboards held its warmth in a narrow band. Downstairs, the taped box waited for a truck.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I trace the thumbprint with my own thumb.* I don't recognize the handwriting. It's not Mom's or Dad's. I look through the rest of the photos, trying to find one from when Mom was sick.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The thumbprint had been worked into the paper's tooth. It sat below the surface, part of the sheet now. No fingertip would ever lift it free.

The sleeves gave the search its order. Dates sat penciled on some of the print backs. Most backs were blank. The prints slid against one another with a dry whisper. The box kept breathing its mothball smell.

The dates ran forward through the stack. Birthdays. Four Julys of the garden. The kitchen in its old green. In one print the mother carried a cake, tongue out, candles unlit. The stack thinned with her. Then the dates jumped. Eighteen months sat unaccounted for. The sleeves kept their numbers through the missing time. The film inside had gone clear. Nothing on it but edge markings. The acetate gave off a smell of vinegar.

The hospital print sat at the gap's near edge. One print sat at its far edge. In that one, the mother sat by the front window in the good chair. A blanket covered her knees. Her wrists had gone small. Behind the glass the garden stood in late light. The frame leaned off true. It had been shot without looking. A thumb crossed one corner, pressed gray into the gloss.

The back of the print held writing. The pencil had leaned hard to the right. The hand matched the list. The words read, "Last day home. She wanted the window open." The date under them was ten years old. The sleeve numbers shared the lean. The same hand had numbered the film and kept the box. The K on the kitchen box downstairs had leaned the same way. A third hand had moved through these rooms.

The pencil had pressed through to the front. The letters stood in ridges, reversed, ready for a fingertip. Against the window's last light, the words came through thin and reversed.

The gray on the photo's corner matched the gray on the list. One hand had shopped, and captioned, and numbered, and kept. The list had said to ask which kind. No record survived of the answer.

Sleeve thirty-one fell inside the gap. Whatever it had held belonged to the missing months. The empty sleeve had kept its chemical smell with nothing to show for it.

Downstairs the refrigerator held its old note. The light had left the floorboards. The warmth went with it. On the ceiling the plastic stars had begun to wake. A weak green came off them. They had saved their glow through fifteen years of dark.

Outside, tires crossed the gravel and stopped. A car door opened. It shut. Footsteps came up the path to the latch. The latch caught. It always caught. The stuck door bought the room a minute.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Upstairs, the minute spent itself. The plastic stars gave off their weak green above the open box. Sleeve thirty-one lay flat in its place, keeping its vinegar to itself. The springs of the mattress did not speak again.

Then the latch lost its argument. The door came open on the second pull, wood dragging wood. Outside air crossed the threshold, cut grass and hot engine and pine freshener. The new draft ran the length of the house. In the closet, paper stirred once against paper.

A voice arrived ahead of the footsteps. "Hello. Hello up there. It's Carol. We said two." The voice sat high and carried and did not wait for answers. It did not ask. It announced.

Her heels struck the hallway boards in a quick, even pattern. The boards gave back a dry knock. Her perfume came with her. Lilies and alcohol, a department store in a bottle. It crossed the dust and the mothballs and refused to mix.

In the kitchen, the taped box caught her on the way past. "Kitchen," she read, to nobody. "Well. Somebody was organized." Her knuckle rapped the counter twice. The tape had lifted at one corner, a pale flag.

The refrigerator hummed its lowered note. Carol laid her palm flat against the door. The note wavered under her hand and steadied. "Now, this old fellow. He's had a good run." A pen came out of her blazer. It scratched across a clipboard, and the letters leaned hard to the right. The hum had once meant someone was home. Under her palm it meant a line on a list.

She took the stairs at a clip. Her hand gathered fifteen years of grime off the rail. She did not notice, or she did not mind. The third step spoke under her. The ninth spoke too. "Oh, and the banister. Original. People pay for original." The stairwell had thinned the refrigerator's hum on its way up. It did nothing to thin her voice.

At the top she stopped. The pencil marks climbed the frame beside her shoulder. "Oh," she said. The word came out smaller than the rest of her. Her fingertip hovered over the lowest mark. The polish on her nail had chipped at the edge. For the first time since the door, she let a silence stand. Then she filled it. "Well. Somebody grew up here. Buyers eat this stuff up."

She turned toward the room and stopped on the threshold. The light through the window lay thin on the floorboards. "There you are. Oh, but look at this light. This is the one. This is the picture for the listing." She stepped inside, and the boards took her weight without comment.

The stars went on glowing above her head, their green almost spent. On the sill, the fly kept its position of ten years. Between her and the window, the shoebox sat open, its paper spine showing. The vinegar smell reached the doorway and stopped.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I gently close the shoebox, covering the pictures and the list. I don't want Carol to see them. "Yeah, this was my room," I say, my voice flat. "It's a nice room."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Carol's heels crossed to the middle of the room. The boards gave back a dry knock. Her perfume reached the mattress first, lilies over old paper.

"A nice room," she repeated. The cheer dropped a half step. It climbed back before it finished falling. "Good bones in this one. This light is the listing."

She crossed to the window. The floor had cooled where the sun had been. Her heel found the cold band and stood in it. She set both palms on the sash and pushed. Old paint cracked along the frame. The sash rose a hand's width and stopped there. Outside air came through the gap, cut grass and hot engine. "There. It works. A buyer wants to hear that."

Her shadow crossed the sill and took in the fly. She tipped her head back to the ceiling. The plastic stars gave what green they had saved. Her pen came out and scratched the clipboard. "Glow stars. Whimsical touch. Families with kids go soft for that." The letters leaned hard to the right.

Her gaze crossed the shoebox. It stopped there a half second. Then it moved on. "We'll clear the personal things before the shoot. Boxes read as clutter." The vinegar smell reached her and she wrinkled her nose. "Musty. A day of air fixes that." Her knuckle rapped the mattress edge once. Dust climbed through the light and turned.

At the doorframe she paused. The draft from the gap moved the lapel of her blazer. Her fingertip ran the air an inch above the pencil marks. "Shame about these. One coat of paint takes them clean off. Clean frames sell."

She turned for the stairs and stopped at the threshold. "They went beige on my advice, you know. The avocado read as work in the photographs. Beige reads as space." She clicked her pen shut. "Your mother fought me on it. She loved her green."

Below, the refrigerator held its lowered note. The hum rose through the boards and thinned by the landing. Carol stepped back into the hallway and turned.

"Now. The rest of the tour. And that box." She nodded at the shoebox in Eli's hands. "Does it travel with you, or with the truck?"

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "It travels with me," I say, a little too quickly. I clutch the shoebox to my chest, feeling the soft cardboard against my shirt. "Where to next, Carol?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Carol went down first, pen and clipboard leading. Her heels took the steps in pairs. The third step spoke. The ninth spoke. "Original pine under this carpet, I'd bet. Buyers love a reveal." Her palm ran the rail and left a second stripe of gray.

"Principal bedroom." She shouldered the door. It held, then gave with a rip of old paint. The air inside sat warmer than the hall and still. It smelled of pressed linen and shut windows.

The bed stood made, corners tight, the spread pulled smooth. One nightstand held a lamp and a pale ring where a glass had sweated. The other held dust circles where a clock and a bottle had stood. The nothing there had a shape.

A housecoat hung on the back of the door. Its floral print had faded toward pastel. It still kept the shape of shoulders. The wardrobe stood open a hand's width. The rail hung full on one side. Coats, shirts, a tie gone shiny at the knot. The other side stood bare. The bare side breathed the same stale soap from the shoebox paper.

Carol's pen scratched. "Takes a queen, no problem. We'll stage it bright." She lifted the curtain edge with one finger and let it drop. The rings rasped along the rod. She did not open the wardrobe. She wrote something long and did not read it back.

The bathroom came next. Mint tile ran from floor to sill. The mother's green, surviving. The grout had yellowed at the seams. Carol rapped a tile with her knuckle. "Hear that. Solid. Nobody pours them this thick anymore." The tub carried a line at its old water mark. The medicine cabinet stood open on empty shelves, each shelf printed with a dust ring. A cup on the sink held one toothbrush, its bristles flattened to a fan.

"Office." The last door opened without argument. The room held a desk and walls of boxes. STUDY. BOOKS. CHINA, GOOD. LINENS. The marker had leaned hard to the right. The same hand from the shoebox. The same hand on the kitchen box. The tape still shone at every seam. The room smelled of fresh cardboard and marker solvent. The packing was days old. Maybe less.

One box sat apart, on the desk chair, turned to face the door. The label read ELI — ROOM. The same hard lean. A gray thumbprint sat pressed into the tape at one corner. The tape had been laid in one pass, smooth, its end tucked under.

"The packer your father hired," Carol said. "A local girl. Quiet thing. Whole house in two days." The clipboard scratched. "He speaks well of her. Calls when he needs anything done."

She led out the back door. It stuck, then gave. The garden had gone past keeping. The tomato stakes stood bare, their twine rotted to black thread. Grass swallowed the path to the shed. Next door a mower ran, stopped, ran. The air held cut grass and warm soil. Under that sat the sour edge of the compost bin. The vinegar smell from the shoebox came out too, thinned by the open sky.

The birdbath stood dry, ringed white at the bowl. Late light lay along the fence, and the boards held the day's heat. The kitchen window gave back the sun, beige and blank.

Carol clicked her pen. "Southerly exposure. Room for beds, if a buyer wanted them." Her phone buzzed in her blazer. She read the screen. Her face did what it had done at the pencil marks. The mower next door cut off.

"Your father." Her thumb had pressed the phone's edge white. "He signed for two o'clock. Two." She looked at the garden a while. "He's not coming. He says the keys stay with me. He says you know which ones."

The cheer tried to climb back on her. It got halfway. "Well. More time for photos." Through the open door behind them, the refrigerator held its lowered note. It had not paused for any of it.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: My dad's not coming. Of course he's not. I expected it, but it still stings. I nod, my grip on the shoebox tightening. "Right. The keys." I turn from the garden, back toward the house. "So, you're just going to leave me here?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Carol tucked the phone into her blazer. Her cheer came back where she had left it.

"Leave you here." She turned the words over once. "I have a four o'clock two streets over. You have the house until Friday. He paid the power through the month. The old fellow in the kitchen stays on with it."

Next door the mower caught and ran again. The fence boards let their heat go into the cooling air. Carol went to the car for the keys.

The car had baked in the sun since noon. Its door opened on a breath of hot vinyl and pine freshener. On the passenger seat lay a folder. An envelope sat on top, taped shut. The front read ELI in a hard right lean. A gray thumbprint pressed the corner of the tape. Under the hood, metal ticked while it cooled.

She brought the envelope back across the grass. It carried a smell of marker solvent. The envelope sat light in her palm. One key, from the weight. "He had the girl run these over Tuesday. Efficient thing. She kept a spare for the truck on Thursday. Mind the front door. It sticks." The tape had gone tacky in the heat. The envelope changed hands. "There's a room booked at the Motor Lodge, Route 9. Two nights, paid, under your name. He says you know which ones. I carry what I'm given."

At the car door she stopped. She turned her own keys over in her fingers. "Your father asked me tonight about the height marks. Whether they could be saved. I told him clean frames sell. He was quiet on the line a while. Then he said to leave them be."

Her phone camera clicked once at the garden. At the gate she looked back at the house. The look had nothing for sale in it. Then she got in. The engine started on the first turn. Gravel popped under the tires and faded down the road. The pine freshener hung in the air after the car had gone.

The headlights swung across the beige wall and shrank. The yard let go of the day's heat, fence board by fence board. Inside, the hallway had gone blue with the last light. The refrigerator held its lowered note. Upstairs, the plastic stars had begun their weak green. The third step and the ninth kept their silence. The hum had always meant someone was home. For once, it was true.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "He asked about the height marks?" I say to myself, the envelope still in my hand. I look at the house, then back at the envelope. "He knows which ones." I head back inside, ignoring the stuck door this time. The hum of the fridge is surprisingly comforting.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The door gave easier this time. The wood dragged once and let go. It swung toward the frame behind Eli and stopped short of the latch. The hallway had kept its coolness in the walls. The blue had drained out of the light. The beige had gone the gray of dishwater.

The kitchen still held the west sun's warmth. The window had spent the afternoon taking it in. It gave the heat off now, wall by wall. The paint smell ruled the room, solvent-sweet, days old. Under it sat the older smell, grease and burnt toast pressed into the years. The KITCHEN box had not moved. Its tape flag had curled further off the counter. The draft from the door reached it. Something shifted inside, metal on metal, a dull ring.

The refrigerator hummed on in its corner. At close range the note had a rattle under it, a small fatigue. The side panel gave off a faint warmth of its own. A machine keeping its own weather, summer and winter, through old owners and new.

The envelope had gone soft in the hand. The sun at Carol's car had cooked its tape, and the hold had gone slack. At one corner the flap lifted a finger's width on its own. Through the gap lay the key, brass gone dull. Its teeth had been worn bright at the tips. Behind the key sat a fold of paper. The crease had been opened and shut past counting. The paper had worn thin there, thin enough to let light through. On the face that showed, pencil. The lean ran left. It matched no label, no list, no caption in the box.

Next door the mower quit for the night. A screen door slapped somewhere down the street. Charcoal smoke came through the gap Carol had left upstairs. It worked its way down the stairwell, carrying onion and fat. Somebody down the street was cooking. The smoke crossed the paint fumes, and the kitchen held both. The streetlight at the curb laid its stripe through the front window. The beige wall took it and gave back nothing.

The compressor clicked off. The quiet showed how big the kitchen was. Then the motor caught, shuddered, and took the note up again. It came back lower than before. The machine was finding its night pitch. In Eli's hand the envelope stood with its flap open at a finger's width. The key kept its teeth to the dark. The list had asked which kind. The father had said which ones. The house had collected unfinished sentences. Thursday the truck would come for the rest of it. Upstairs, the pencil marks stood in the dark, reprieved by a phone call. Beside them the plastic stars spent their last green.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I pull out the key and the folded paper. The paper feels thin, almost fragile, between my fingers. I carefully unfold it.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The creases fought the opening. Each fold crackled and gave by degrees. The sheet opened into four panels and would not lie flat. It bowed back toward its old shape, toward a pocket and a waiting thumb.

The hand leaned left. The letters were small, pressed hard at their starts and lighter at their ends. The pencil had dug grooves into the sheet. Under a fingertip the ridges stood. This was no practiced hand. It was a hand that had made itself do the work.

At the top left corner sat a date. Ten years old. Under it ran one line. Further down the page, another date, then another. The dates ran down the sheet. The years ran up the doorframe upstairs. Two charts had been kept in one house, apart. The page gave off a faint smell of graphite, strongest at the bottom.

The oldest line sat under the oldest date. The pencil had pressed hardest there, and the grooves still caught a fingertip. "I opened her window. She slept. The floor was cold. I stayed."

A year below, in the same grooved hand: "Frost came. I winterized the garden anyway. There was no one to tell."

Mid-page, a water stain ringed the margin brown. The paper had buckled there and dried wavy. The line beside it read, "Your number rings out. I keep the card by the phone."

Below that: "Her pots are in the shed. The green ones. Behind the seed cans." One date later: "Found thirty-one. Could not look at it. With the pots." Then, alone on its line: "One key. You know which."

Near the bottom the dates crowded together, recent. "The girl packed the kitchen first. She knew where things went." And under it: "Asked after the marks. They stay."

The last line was days old. Its graphite smelled sharp, fresh cut. "I kept meaning to tell you that I—" The pencil had lifted at the dash. Nothing followed. The blank ran clean to the bottom corner.

The main fold had worn to a thread. The streetlamp's light passed through it in a thin gold line. He had carried the page for ten years. He had read it more than he had sent it. The edges had gone soft and round, the softness of a thing handled in a pocket.

On the counter the key lay in the streetlight stripe. The brass had gone dull everywhere but the teeth. The teeth shone at their tips. The metal still held the cold of Carol's car. It had lived in a pocket for years. It had opened one door often.

Through the window the garden had gone to shapes. The shed stood black against the fence line. Its roof held a last thread of gray. The door there stuck too. It had always stuck. The shine on the key said he had gone out there often. Behind that black door, behind the seed cans, thirty-one kept its chemistry. Acetate does not wait well. Ten years sat on that sleeve. The green pots waited with it.

Through the gap in the sash upstairs, night air came down the stairwell. It carried the last of the charcoal smoke. The compressor clicked off. The kitchen showed its size in the quiet. Then the motor caught and took up its night pitch. The hum ran through the floorboards and up the walls.

Upstairs the plastic stars spent their last green on nobody. On the counter the dash held its small blank. The house had waited ten years for the end of that sentence. It could wait a little longer.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I read the note again, my eyes lingering on the last, unfinished line. *I kept meaning to tell you that I—* The words hang in the air, a ghost of a conversation. I fold the paper carefully, tucking it into my pocket with the key. "Dad," I whisper, the word feeling strange on my tongue after so long. "I guess I know which ones now."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena squared the photos and slid them back into the file, tapping the edges flat. Somewhere below, the dry cleaner's press hissed and thumped. The *why* hung in the air between them. She let it.

"Precincts are the worst place to ask a cop anything," she said. "Desk sergeant logs every visitor. Cameras in the lobby. You walk in asking about a case somebody's already buried, and by lunch the whole building knows somebody's digging — including whoever did the burying."

She pulled a legal pad toward her and copied the detective's name off the file. She didn't write the precinct number. She didn't need to.

"Cops are creatures of habit. Same diner, same bar, same parking spot, same shift for years. Give me a day. I'll know when this one clocks out and where they go after. We talk on neutral ground — someplace without a desk sergeant taking names."

She capped the pen and looked up.

"Or if you're in a hurry, you can go yourself. Walk in, give your name at the front desk, ask for the detective." She laid one hand flat on the file. "Just understand what you're trading for the speed. Your call."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I sigh, running a hand through my hair.* "No, no. You're right. That's why I hired you." *I lean forward, lowering my voice slightly.* "What exactly are we looking for, anyway? Beyond just 'new information'."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena leaned back and let the question sit for a moment. Below them, the press finished its cycle, and the quiet made the room feel smaller.

"New information," she said. "That's what everyone asks for. What they usually get, if they're lucky, is old information somebody spent money to keep quiet."

She pulled the file back across the desk and opened it, fanning the photos out again.

"Dead cases have a shape. A real dead end looks like effort that ran out — interviews that go nowhere, tips that don't pan out, the same question asked four different ways because nobody had a better one. Boring. Sad. Human." She tapped the desk once with a knuckle. "A killed case is different. It looks like a case that was going somewhere and then, all at once, wasn't. Reports that stop mid-page. Evidence logged into a property room and never sent anywhere. A witness gives a statement and never gets a callback. The work doesn't trail off. It stops — like a hand came down over it."

She recited that flat, like inventory. No story attached to it.

"Here. This is what we're looking for." She turned one of the photos over. On the back, small, in pencil: a number. She flipped the others and laid them out in a row, backs up, and moved her finger down the line. "Eleven. Twelve. Fourteen. Fifteen." She left the gap where it was. "No thirteen. And the summary in here references two attachments — an evidence log and a supplemental report — that aren't in the folder. So either this file was already gutted, or somebody gutted it on the way to you. Made choices about what you'd get to see."

She stacked the photos and set her palm flat on top of them.

"That's what we're after. Not the truth — I can't sell you the truth. The line where this case got cut, and the hand that did the cutting. Which means my first question is one you should've seen coming." She looked up. "Where did you get this file? Records request, family copy, somebody on the inside? Because whoever assembled it made those choices for a reason. And I need to know whether they were protecting you — or protecting themselves."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The question sat in the room. Lena let it sit.

She got up, crossed to the window, and stood in front of the half-closed blinds the way she always did — close enough to see out through the gap, far enough back that nobody on Mercer could pick her face out of the dark glass. A delivery van. A man walking a dog. Nothing that needed her attention. She came back and stopped at the end of the desk, her voice level, no edge on it anywhere.

"You answered my question with a question. People do that when the answer costs them something. Fine — it tells me the file's provenance is a live wire for you, which is worth knowing. But the wire's still live, and I still have to touch it."

She laid two fingers on the folder.

"Records request, family copy, or somebody on the inside. And then the part that matters more: who physically put this in your hand? Not where it originated — who gave it to *you*. Because that person saw everything in here and decided what you'd get. Photo thirteen, gone. Evidence log, gone. Supplemental report, gone. Somebody made those cuts, and they made them right before this landed in your possession."

She uncapped the pen and held it over the legal pad, like the answer was a matter of transcription.

"And understand why I'm asking. If your source is on the inside, then either they're risking something to help you — or they're using you to find out how much you know. Same folder. Two very different situations. I can't tell which one we're standing in until you tell me who handed it over."

She waited. She was good at waiting. Most people weren't.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I shift uncomfortably, avoiding her gaze.* "It was... a family copy. My uncle gave it to me." *I pause, considering.* "He said he got it from a friend at the DA's office, years ago."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena wrote while the client spoke. *Uncle. Friend at the DA's office. Years ago.* She boxed each phrase and drew arrows between them until the legal pad held a small map — three boxes, ending at the client's chair. She turned the pad around so they could see it.

"Chain of custody. Friend, uncle, you. Now here's what the file says about that chain." She opened the folder to the summary page and set two fingers on the line citing the attachments. "An office that wants a file clean produces a clean copy. Redaction bars. Renumbered pages. A clerk's stamp. This is the opposite. Pages pulled from an assembled file. A photo lifted out of a numbered set. And the summary still pointing at evidence that isn't there — whoever cut this didn't have time to rewrite a paragraph. That's not institutional work. That's a person, moving fast, with their hand already in the folder."

She flipped the pad shut over the diagram.

"Which means the cuts happened somewhere in *your* chain. And understand what that favor cost. Nobody walks a case file out of the DA's office for a friend's family out of kindness. Either your uncle asked for it — and people don't ask for copies of dead cases unless they've stopped believing it's dead — or the friend needed it out of the building. Both versions end the same way. Somebody thought this folder was dangerous years before you did."

She uncapped the pen again.

"Two questions and an instruction. First — is your uncle alive, what's his name, where does he live? Because he just moved to the front of the line. Warmer lead than the detective. When I sit down with him, I'll want what he said when he handed this over. Not the gist — the words. People smooth out a gist. The words they actually said hang around longer. If he ever named the friend, I'll want that too, but he can give me that himself."

"Second — this file sat in your family for years, and today you're sitting across from me. That doesn't come from boredom. Something changed. Somebody died, or said something, or something landed where you couldn't ignore it anymore. What?"

"Third, the instruction." She dealt the photos out again — face up this time, in their broken sequence. "Look at what's here. Eleven, twelve, fourteen, fifteen. Any face you know. Any place. Anything that belongs to your family. Because when somebody pulls one picture out of a set, it's because that picture shows something the others don't. Sometimes it's a thing. More often it's a face."

She left them spread across the desk, within the client's reach, and didn't gather them back.

"Tonight I start on the detective's habits, like I said. One more thing about your uncle, whenever that happens — I'd rather he not know I'm coming. A warning call gives a man a night to decide what he remembers. If you insist on calling ahead, fine, he's your family. But don't tell him what's missing from this file. Let him bring that up himself."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I stare at the photos, my mind racing as Lena talks.* "My uncle... he's still alive, yes. Robert. He lives upstate now. I... I can get you his address." *I trace the edge of photo 12.* "And what changed... my aunt, his sister, she passed away a few months ago. She was the one who always talked about it. The case. After she was gone, it felt... wrong, not to try."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena wrote it down. *Aunt — Robert's sister. Deceased, several months. The one who carried it.* She drew the box, connected it to the others, and sat back with the pen still in her hand.

"That's usually how these find my desk. Not curiosity. A death rearranges the room, and the thing the family lived around for years suddenly has nobody standing in front of it." She nodded once, to herself. "I'm sorry she's gone. Now I'm going to treat her like evidence, because in this room that's the respectful thing to do."

She tapped the new box with the pen.

"'Wrong not to try.' That's how a promise feels from the inside — usually somebody else's promise. So here's the question that matters more than anything you've told me so far. When did Robert put this folder in your hands? Before she died, or after?"

She laid out the fork before the client could answer.

"Because there are two shapes this can take. Shape one — Robert held this file the whole time. Years. His sister alive and talking about it at every holiday table, and he hands it to you only once she can't ask about it anymore. That's a choice with an edge on it. Either she made him promise — dying people extract promises, it's nearly all they do at the end, and you'd be the promise being kept — or he kept this folder away from the one person who'd have known exactly what to do with it. Those are very different uncles."

"Shape two — the file never lived with Robert at all. It lived with *her*. She's the one who talked about it. He inherited it with her effects and passed it along fast, and what he gave you wasn't his. It was hers." She turned the pad and drew a new box between the DA friend and Robert, then drew the line through it. "If that's the shape, then photo thirteen wasn't pulled by anyone at the DA's office. It was pulled by her. People take out the one picture they can't stop looking at. And they don't throw that picture away. They keep it near. A drawer. A handbag. A book nobody else was supposed to open."

She set the pen down.

"So — her house. Is it standing the way she left it, or has it been cleared, boxed, sold? Because if her things are intact, there's a shoebox somewhere with my photo in it, and estates get emptied fast. That's a clock already running. And one piece of arithmetic, not grimness, just practicality — did she go slow or sudden? If she had months, she had time to arrange what mattered, and it's somewhere deliberate. If it was sudden, whatever she kept is wherever she happened to keep it, and the only person who knew is gone. Two different searches. I need to know which one I'm running."

She pulled the legal pad back and started a fresh page.

"Meanwhile, here's what I want from you tonight, before the address. When she talked about the case — not the subject. The *sentences*. The ones that repeated. People who carry something for decades stop telling the story and start wearing grooves in it. A name. A date. A complaint she made every single time, like a stone in her shoe. Grooves are where the important parts live." Her eyes flicked to the desk. "And you went to twelve first, when I dealt those out. I watched you do it. You don't have to know what it means — that's my half of the job. Just tell me what your eye keeps finding in it."

She stood and gathered her coat off the back of the chair.

"Tonight I work the detective, like I said. Get me Robert's address, her full name, and the address of whatever's left of her place. His routine will still be there Thursday. Her closets might not be."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena had one arm in her coat. She took it back out.

She draped it over the back of the chair and sat down again, flipping the legal pad back a page to the name she'd copied off the file that afternoon. Whether the name meant anything to her — she didn't pick that question up. She picked up the pen instead.

"File says the detective on this was R. Carver. Ninth Precinct. It's been in my notes since this folder opened." She wrote TORRES beneath it and boxed the two together. "Your witness says Torres. Two names for one case. Three ways that happens."

"One — the witness is wrong. More common than anyone wants to believe. Witnesses keep faces for decades and lose names inside a year. They remember who let them smoke in the interview room, not who signed the form. Two — the file is wrong. The attribution is part of the rewrite. That would mean somebody didn't just pull pages, they reassigned the case on paper after the fact — heavier surgery than I described before. Three — both names are right. Two detectives worked it. Carver's stayed in the folder, and Torres's came out with the pages. And we already know pages came out. The summary still points at a supplemental report that isn't there."

She drew a line from the boxed names to the gap where the attachments should have been.

"Three is the shape I'd bet on. Nobody rewrites a dead case — you rewrite a live one. If Torres was cut out of the paper on purpose, Torres is the part somebody was afraid of, and my night just doubled. I was going to learn one detective's habits. Diner, bar, parking spot, shift change. Now I learn two, and I learn which one your witness actually dealt with — because that's the one who worked it. And a cop who gets cut out of a file ends up one of two places: retired early, or promoted out of reach. Both are findable. Neither is a walk-in."

She set the pen down and looked at the client straight on.

"Now the part you slid past me. 'The witness.' You said it like I'd know who that is. I don't. This file has a witness statement in it — and if my read is right, it's from somebody who gave that statement and never got a callback. Is that who you mean? The one in the folder? Because their name is in a file somebody gutted, and you've been talking to them. And you said *says*. Present tense. That's not a conversation you had once — that's a channel that's still open."

She leaned back.

"So: who called whom. Did you go looking, or did they come to you? Because a witness who surfaces after all this time to hand somebody a detective's name is doing one of two things — finally feeling safe, or being used to point you somewhere. When someone hands you a name, they're handing you a direction. A direction can be a gift or a leash. If they came to you after your aunt died — if it was recent — that's not a memory surfacing. That's somebody else's clock running on the same case."

She turned the pad around so the two boxed names faced the client.

"And that's twice now. Before I picked up my coat I asked you for five things. Robert's address. Her full name. What's left of her house. The sentences she repeated until they had grooves in them. What your eye keeps finding in photo twelve. Both times since, you've paid me in facts I didn't ask for — the uncle, now the witness. Good facts. I'll keep them. But you're still holding the change, and I don't run on credit."

She capped the pen and laid it across the boxes.

"Start with the witness. Who reached out first, and when. Then the five you owe me."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I swallow hard, feeling the pressure.* "Okay, okay. The witness. Her name is Maria. Maria Rodriguez. She was the one who found the body. She... she called me after my aunt's obituary ran. She saw the family name." *I take a breath.* "She said she tried to reach my aunt for years, but my aunt moved around a lot after... after all this. She just wanted to know if anything ever came of it."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena wrote the name and boxed it. *Maria Rodriguez. Found the body.* Then she drew the line from the box to the folder on the desk and tapped the folder once.

"Then the witness statement in this file is hers. The one that never got a callback." She said it like arithmetic. "She's been carrying that for decades, and you just told me she's still trying to hand it to somebody. That makes her the warmest thing in this case. Warmer than the detective. Warmer than Robert."

She flipped back a page to the aunt's box and wrote two words beside it: *moved around.*

"Now back up one sentence, because you said something bigger than you know. 'She moved around a lot after all this.' People move for jobs. For rent. For somebody they love. Nobody moves around for *years* over something they've made peace with. Your aunt would talk about this case at any table she trusted — and made sure nobody outside those tables could find her. That's not grief. That's a woman who believed something was still looking for her." She set the pen down. "And you said 'after all this' and stopped, like it's a thing with edges. Hold onto that. I'm coming back for it."

She stood and worked her arm back into the coat she'd just taken off.

"Then there's the obituary. Your aunt spent years being hard to find, and then your family put her death in a newspaper with names attached. Maria read it as a door finally opening — and her story hangs together, a woman who found a body and got ignored, keeping an eye out. That's the most common animal in these woods. But an obituary doesn't have one reader. If this case was buried by hand, whoever held the shovel watched the one person who wouldn't let it stay buried. The paper just told them the watching's over. That's a bell. Bells get heard by more than the person they're rung for."

She squared the file on the desk.

"So tonight changes. If her house is still standing, it stops being Thursday's job. A detective's habits keep — same diner next week, same bar the week after. An estate with a bell rung over it doesn't. Which means before you leave this office I need her full name, the address of whatever's left of her place, and the answer you still owe me — slow or sudden. And one more: who holds the keys. Because if Robert's the executor, my quiet arrival at his front door just got complicated. I can't surprise a man and then ask him to open a house for me."

"Two small things about Maria, and small is where cases live. An obituary hands you a name — it doesn't hand you a phone number. She got from the paper to your ear somehow. A relative, a directory, a friend of a friend. I want to know which, because that gap measures how findable *you* are. If she crossed it in a day, anyone can. And if she was trying to reach your aunt through the family for years, somebody in the family was hanging up on her. If that somebody was Robert, I want to know it before I sit across from him, not after."

She picked the file up off the desk and held it under her arm.

"Until I meet her, the channel stays exactly as it is. Warm — don't cut it, don't change your tone. But you don't feed it. She doesn't hear about the missing photo, the missing pages, or me. And you don't ask her any more questions. You got lucky with Torres. Every question you put to a witness leaves a shape in her mouth, and she'll start building what you seem to want. She's been building that memory alone for thirty years — I want it the way she built it, not the way we sanded it."

"When I sit down with her — her ground, her pick of place, coffee, daylight — I'm not there to interrogate anybody. She gave a statement once and nobody called her back. I'm the callback. That's the whole play. People who've waited that long empty out everything they've been carrying, if you let them go in their own order. And I won't start with names. I'll start with the face — who sat across from her, what he was like, what he promised. Then we see which name fits the face. If the face is Torres and the file says Carver, this file wasn't just cut. It was rewritten."

She buttoned the coat.

"That was the first answer you've given me straight through to the end. I noticed. It gets easier. Full name, address, keys, slow or sudden — and Robert's address whenever you have it. One thing for the road: as of tonight, you've hired a lawyer to help settle an estate. That's your story, to family, to Maria, to anyone who asks — including a friendly voice on the phone calling about your aunt's affairs. Nobody legitimate needs to know what's in this folder. And nobody legitimate calls asking."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in.* "Okay. Lawyer for the estate. Got it." *I pull out my phone, already feeling the weight of the new tasks.* "Her full name was Sarah Jenkins. She passed... it was sudden. A heart attack. Robert is the executor. I'll get you his address and hers."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena wrote it down. *Sarah Jenkins. Sudden — cardiac. Executor: R.* She boxed all three and looked at them for a moment before she spoke.

"Sudden sounds like the bad version of events. It isn't. I told you earlier that sudden means whatever she kept is wherever she happened to keep it, and the only person who knew is gone. I'm amending that, because you've since told me she moved around for years — and that changes the arithmetic. Sudden only makes a mess of people who lived loose. Sarah Jenkins lived tight. A woman who keeps moving because she believes something's still looking for her doesn't arrange things at the end. She's not planning on an end. She arranges things every day. So somewhere in whatever's left of her life, there's one box that moved with her every single time — the one she carried to the car herself while the movers took the furniture. Movers remember that box. Supers remember it. I'm not going to search a house. I'm going to find a box, and boxes like that keep habits."

She unlocked the bottom drawer of the desk, dropped the file in, and turned the key.

"Robert being executor changes my approach to him, so here's the new play. You call him — tonight's fine, family calls family at night about this. You tell him you've got someone helping with the estate paperwork, and she wants to come up, walk the house, go over the inventory. That's the whole call. Not the file. Not Maria. Nothing that isn't probate. I never claim to be a lawyer — I say I'm handling the estate for the family, which is true enough to survive daylight."

"Executors file an inventory with surrogate's court. Public paper. Tomorrow morning I pull that, and her death certificate — who signed it, where it happened, who found her. I'm not reopening a heart attack. I just like knowing who signs the paper. And between his inventory and her bank statements, there's a map of every anchor she ever dropped — storage bills, box fees, a PO box. People who move that much don't put down roots. They drop anchors. If Robert's straight, he hands it over wondering what I'm after. If he's not, the anchors are already gone. Either way, I learn which uncle I'm dealing with."

She laid the pen down flat.

"Now the question you've been holding since before the Torres detour. I asked when Robert put that folder in your hands — before she died or after — and you paid me in a witness instead. I kept the receipt. It's worth more now than it was an hour ago. If he handed it over after, then he gave it to you with his hands already in her things — executing her estate, gone through her house — and the real question becomes what else left that house in the same car. If before, he's a different man with a different problem. One word. Before, or after."

She tore the top sheet off the legal pad and set it on the desk, facing the client. Her handwriting, small and squared:

*Before or after.*
*How Maria got from an obituary to your phone.*
*The sentences Sarah repeated — the grooves, not the story.*
*What your eye keeps finding in photo twelve.*
*Both addresses. And whether anyone's been through her place — cleaners, a Realtor's sign, a dumpster in the driveway.*

"A dumpster in the driveway tells me more than a week of interviews."

She picked up her keys.

"Tonight I work the detectives — both names now, Carver and Torres. Habits, and faces. I want their faces in my head before I sit down with Maria, because she'll hand me a face before she hands me anything else, and I want to know it when she does. Tomorrow, the courthouse. Then upstate. Maria comes after — her ground, her pick of place, daylight. She's been waiting decades for a callback that never came. She can wait a few more days for the real one."

She crossed to the window and checked the street through the gap in the blinds, the way she always did — close enough to see out, far enough back to stay a shadow in the glass.

"When you leave, look both ways down Mercer. Not because I think anyone's out there. Because it's free."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I stare at the list on the page, feeling a surge of overwhelm, but also a strange clarity.* "He gave it to me after. A few weeks after she passed." *I pick up my phone again, already typing.* "I'll get you those addresses now. And I'll think about Sarah's words, and photo twelve."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena took the legal pad back and wrote the answer into Robert's box. *After — weeks.* She underlined it once and set the pen down on top of it.

"A few weeks after does something to his story. He told you he got this file from a friend at the DA's office, *years ago*. So either that's true, and he's held it all that time — while his sister carried this case to every table she trusted, while a witness spent years trying to reach her and getting nowhere — and he handed it over only once she couldn't touch it anymore. That's a decision. It could be protection. A man who believed the file was dangerous would keep it away from the one person most likely to go digging with it — and that rhymes with everything she did. The moving. The being hard to find. Or it's something else. But it's not nothing."

She drew a second box beside the first and split the line between them.

"Or his story isn't true, and the file never lived with him at all. It lived with her. It came out of that house in the weeks after she died, with his hands already in her things, and the DA friend is cover for where it actually came from. People launder provenance the same way they launder money — you wash where a thing came from so nobody asks where it's been. And here's the number that bothers me either way: *a few weeks.* Most people take months to face a dead sister's closets. Either her life was small enough to clear in a weekend, or he went through that house fast because he already knew what he was looking for. Fast is a tell."

She pulled the pad closer.

"You were there for the handoff, which means you're holding evidence you don't know you're holding. So when you're done with those addresses, I want the scene — not the conversation, the *scene*. Where you were standing. What the file came in — an envelope, a grocery bag, a stack of her mail he'd been sorting. Whether he handed it over like paperwork or like it was warm. And the words, like I said before. If he said *I've been meaning to give you this*, that's a man clearing his desk. If he said *she would have wanted you to have it*, that's a man telling you where it came from without saying so."

She tapped the two boxes.

"And set that next to Maria. She tried to reach Sarah for years, through the family, and somebody was a wall. Robert is the executor, the file-holder, and the brother. If he was also the wall, that's not three facts — that's one pattern. A man standing between this case and his family for decades. Walls keep things out. They also keep things in. And if the file did come out of her house, then photo thirteen wasn't pulled at the DA's office at all. It was pulled by her, and it's either still in whatever box moved with her every time — or it left that house in Robert's car. Same search either way. Him first, the house right behind him."

She stood and pocketed her keys.

"Tonight's call to him stays exactly what I said. Estate paperwork, someone coming up to walk the house, nothing else. Don't ask him where the file came from — and if he tells you the DA story again, let him tell it all the way through and listen to it fresh. Second tellings are where people improve the parts that bothered them the first time." She glanced at the desk where the photos had lain. "And don't work at photo twelve. Your eye already knows what it's finding — that kind of knowing doesn't come when you push. It surfaces on its own. Doing dishes. Falling asleep. Let it come to you."

She waited while the client typed.

"Whenever you're ready — addresses first. Then go home, make the call, and get some sleep." A thin fold at the corner of her mouth, almost a smile. "One of us should."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I finish typing the addresses and send them, then look up at Lena.* "Okay. Got it. I'll make the call tonight." *I feel a knot of anxiety in my stomach, but also a weird sense of purpose.* "And I'll... I'll pay attention to the details when I talk to Robert."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's phone buzzed against the desk. She read the message twice — once for the words, once for what was around them — then copied both addresses into their boxes on the pad in her small squared hand and deleted the thread.

"Do the same on your end. From tonight on, nothing about this case lives in your phone. No notes, no texts, no voicemails. Phones remember everything and they testify for free."

She took a card from the desk drawer — plain stock, a name, a cell number, nothing else — and laid it on the pad.

"Text me logistics only. Times, addresses, whether Robert says yes. Anything with edges to it, we save for a room. I invoice monthly, and the line item reads *research services* — boring paper, consistent story. And you pay me from your own account, not the estate. Estate payments leave a trail with a judge's signature sitting on top of it."

She buttoned the top button of her coat, which didn't need it.

"Now the call. Make it before nine — a late call about a dead sister reads as either drunk or urgent, and tonight you're neither. Two minutes, tops. Script doesn't change: estate paperwork, someone the family hired is coming up to walk the house and go over the inventory, when suits him. If he asks why now — the estate's been sitting, it needs settling. If he asks what it costs — answer boring."

"And two things to listen for. First, get his opening sentence. People rehearse the middle of a story. The first sentence comes out true. If he leads with the file, or with *what's this really about* — let him run. Don't feed him, don't finish anything for him, and write his words down after you hang up, while they're still warm. Second — if he pushes back on a stranger walking the house, don't argue and don't negotiate. Say you'll think about it, hang up, call me." She held the client's eyes. "Executors don't guard empty houses."

"Maria's item keeps. How she crossed from the obituary to your phone — don't chase it tonight. It'll come back to you on the drive home or in the shower. When it does, text me that one fact and nothing around it."

She looked at the client for a moment longer than the conversation needed — the same flat attention she'd spent on the photographs.

"The knot in your stomach, keep it. Fear with a shape keeps people careful. It's the shapeless kind that makes people stupid. And you did today what most clients need three meetings to do — you found out what you don't know. That's half this job. The other half is days worse than this one." The corner of her mouth moved, barely. "You'll do."

She killed the desk lamp and the room dropped to the gray bars of light through the blinds.

"Thursday, nine a.m., here. Bring Sarah's grooves. The handoff scene — down to what the folder came in and how he held it. And whatever your eye found in twelve. By then I'll have two faces in my head and a copy of what Robert filed with surrogate's court." She was already moving for the stairs, collar up, somewhere else in her mind — Carver, Torres, and the long sit ahead of her. "Tonight I start at a bar three blocks off the Ninth. Old habits drink within walking distance of the house, and nobody logs a face in a bar."

"Door sticks on your way out. Lift the handle on the pull." One foot on the stairs. "Go home. Call before nine. One of us should sleep — I said that already. It bears repeating."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod, pocketing the card. I feel a weird mix of apprehension and adrenaline. I head for the door, pulling the handle up like she said, and step out into the dim hallway, the smell of chemicals and old coffee fading behind me.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena listened to the client all the way down — eleven stairs, the street door's heavy swing, then Mercer Street swallowed the footsteps. She gave the dark room another minute, then copied what mattered from the legal pad into the pocket notebook that lived in her coat. Two names. One precinct. One witness, one executor, one dead woman who'd spent years being hard to find. The file itself stayed locked in the drawer.

She killed the lights and locked up, lifting the handle on the pull — the same trick she'd given away for free. The short way to the bar ran past the Ninth's front steps. She took the long way. She always took the long way.

Feeney's sat three blocks off the precinct, wedged between a shuttered typewriter repair shop and a laundromat, and it looked like what it was: red vinyl gone black with age, a game nobody watched, one long wall of photographs — softball teams, retirement parties, a fishing trip, thirty years of the Ninth curling behind glass. She took the corner stool. Back to the wall, door in the mirror, photo wall over the bartender's shoulder. She ordered a beer and planned to make it last two hours.

She let the 4x12 come in first. They always arrived smelling of cold air and burnt coffee, and she knew the rhythm without checking her watch. When the second round went up, she caught the bartender's eye. Sixties, forearms like dock rope, pouring there since the mayor before last.

"I'm looking for a retired detective," Lena said. "Insurance file. My mother's estate — old claim, and the adjuster's a zealot about paperwork." Boring opens doors. "Carver. R. Carver, out of the Ninth."

"Ralph Carver." The bartender wiped a glass that didn't need it. "Retired, Lord, fifteen years back. Still vertical. Does the Legion post on Fridays — dayside, never nights. Sweet man. Drank ginger ale in here his whole career, if you can believe it." She aimed her rag at the wall. "Softball picture, top row. Third from the left — the one losing the fight with the mustache."

Lena found him and kept him.

"If it's his statement you need, you could call the house," the bartender said. "They'll tell you if—"

"Legion's closer. Fridays, you said." Lena turned the beer an inch. "There's a second one. Torres. M. Torres, same era, out of the Ninth."

The rag stopped. Half a second, maybe less, and then it moved again — and that half-second went into the notebook along with everything said out loud.

"Torres went downtown," the bartender said. "DA's squad, years back. Made investigator over there. Haven't seen him since. Guys who go over don't come back to drink."

"Torres." That was the old-timer three stools down, listening with the professional attention of a man who'd spent forty years listening in bars. He said the name the way you taste milk you suspect. Then he went back to his beer and gave her nothing else.

He rolled his stool an inch toward her anyway, squinting into the mirror. "You look familiar. You a cop?"

"I get that a lot."

"Nah, I know that face. You been in here? You somebody's kid—" He was reaching for it, and reaching was the dangerous part.

Lena pointed at the softball picture. "Who's the big one on the end? He looks like my uncle Frank."

And the old-timer was gone — a stolen Buick, a captain's daughter, the summer of '87, told at full sail with the whole bar's light behind his eyes. By the end of it he'd forgotten he'd ever thought he knew her face at all. She bought his next two rounds on the way out and tipped like the questions had never happened — enough that the bartender would remember the money instead.

At the end of the bar, a plainclothes drinker who'd come in late and ordered nothing much didn't look up from his phone when she passed. She'd told the client nobody logs a face in a bar, and that was true. Bars don't. People do. The ones who don't look are the ones who noticed. She gave him nothing to notice twice and took a different route home.

The office, two a.m. She reheated the coffee once and decided against a second time. The laptop, the library's newspaper archive, *Torres + detective + the decade that mattered.* Box scores. A councilman. Then a photograph, small and grainy: *Det. M. Torres (l.), outside Criminal Court after the Halloran trial.* Young, mustache, tired eyes, holding his coat like it owed him money. She studied the face until she could have drawn it, then closed the laptop without printing anything.

Two faces in her head, like she'd promised.

The notebook came back out. She wrote the night's boxes. *CARVER — retired, Legion Fridays, face on the wall, drank ginger ale.* *TORRES — left the Ninth for the DA's squad. No face on the wall. Not one frame in thirty years of softball and retirements.* People who leave clean get their picture hung. Either Torres left before anyone thought to miss him, or nobody wanted the reminder.

Then she turned back a page to the afternoon's boxes and found the one she'd written at the client's elbow: *Robert — file from a friend at the DA's office.*

She drew the line between Torres's box and Robert's, and sat looking at it. A line isn't a fact. But it's where facts hang their coats. She didn't write what it meant. She left it there in the dark, holding its own weight while the coffee went cold.

Her phone. 2:14. The call to Robert would be over by now, one way or the other. She typed:

*Call go through? One thing — if Robert names his friend at the DA's office tonight, any name at all, even just a first name, write it down while it's warm. Don't ask. Just catch it if he drops it. —L*

She sent it, put the phone face-down, and went to the window. The sky over Mercer was working its way from gray toward a different gray. Four hours until the clerk's window opened at surrogate's court. She'd told the client one of them should sleep. She'd never said which one.

She checked the street through the gap in the blinds one more time before the light came. Not because she thought anyone was out there.

Because it was free.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *My phone buzzes, startling me. I pick it up, seeing Lena's message. I didn't get that name. Damn.* "The call went... okay. He wasn't thrilled about a stranger, but he agreed to meet you. Didn't mention a friend."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
