Lena squared the photos against the edge of the desk and slid them back into the folder one at a time, like she was dealing herself out of a bad hand.

"Because the detective who closed a case doesn't want it reopened — and that goes double when the person reopening it collects fees in cash." She leaned back, chair springs complaining under her. "Walk into the Ninth with those photos, you'll get an hour of coffee and courtesy and leave knowing exactly nothing new. Except now they know somebody's still pulling at it. Cops close ranks fast. By lunch, the whole floor's heard your name and mine."

She got up and went to the window, parting the blinds with two fingers. Below, a woman was feeding quarters into the dry cleaner's change machine like she was mad at it.

"So we don't go in. Nobody goes in." She let the blinds drop. "Detectives are creatures of habit. Same coffee, same exits, same smoke breaks. Marsh steps outside that building around four, four-fifteen, and for ten minutes they're just a person on a sidewalk. Off the floor, off the record. That's when people actually talk."

She came back around the desk and pulled a legal pad toward her, uncapping a pen.

"The paperwork side's yours — records request, case number, the boring things they'll hand a family member without blinking. The sidewalk conversation is mine." She glanced up. "But not yet. First I want to know Marsh. Age, how long at the Ninth, what they look like. Anything in that file with a name on it besides the victim's?"

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking all that in.* "Okay, that makes sense. Cops closing ranks... I hadn't thought of that." *I tap my chin.* "Marsh, huh? Let me see." *I dig through my bag, pulling out a smaller folder.* "I did some digging before I came to you. Just basic stuff, you know. Here's his photo, and a few articles mentioning him."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena set her coffee down and took the smaller folder with both hands — a small ceremony, like the contents outranked the drink.

She studied the photo first, holding it up near the desk lamp, tilting it against the glare.

"Marsh." She said the name like she was checking its weight. "Fifty, give or take. Twenty years in, minimum — look at the shoulders. A man who stopped standing at attention sometime around his tenth anniversary." Her thumbnail tapped the corner. "And it's a press shot. He handed this out himself, which means he likes being quoted. That's useful. Men who like the camera come down to the sidewalk."

She spread the articles and read fast, finger walking the columns.

"He's quoted twice in the closure piece. Same phrasing both times — *'the evidence was consistent with'* — verbatim. That's not a man talking, that's a statement being recited." She looked up over the top of the page. "Comfortable detectives don't reopen anything. But proud ones will correct the record if you poke the right spot."

She squared the pages and slid the folder back across the desk.

"Two things. One — you're done digging. Grieving family member, that's your lane now. Grief doesn't get flagged; investigating does." She capped her pen. "Two — before you came here, did you talk to anyone at the Ninth? Anyone at all?"

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's pen stopped over the legal pad. Half a second — the hum of the dry cleaner's machinery downstairs filled it — and then the pen started moving again, like nothing had interrupted it.

"You didn't answer my question." She wrote in small block letters, no flourish. "Ninth Precinct, before you walked in here. Did you call? Stop at the front desk? Talk to anybody wearing a badge or sitting behind glass?"

She reached for her coffee, found it cold, drank it anyway.

"It matters because precincts are small towns. Everything travels by end of shift. If someone's already been poking at a closed case, then Marsh steps out to that sidewalk at four o'clock already braced for it — and a braced man gives you nothing but his press voice." She turned Marsh's photo face-down on the desk, a small, tidy gesture, and squared it with the edge. "I'd rather know what's coming than guess at it."

She looked up.

"So. Who'd you talk to, and what exactly did you say?"

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "No, no one at the Ninth," *I say quickly, holding up my hands.* "Just... a records clerk at City Hall, for the old newspaper articles. And the library, of course." *I pause, thinking.* "And an old friend of my mother's who used to work there, but she's been retired for years. She just gave me Marsh's name."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena slid Marsh's face-down photo aside to clear room on the desk and wrote three lines on the legal pad in block letters — CITY HALL. LIBRARY. FRIEND. — then boxed the last one, pressing hard enough to dent the page.

"The first two are noise. To a records clerk you're a form number with a name typed on it. The library keeps better records on overdue books than on who sat in the reading room. Nobody calls either of them back." She rapped a knuckle against the box. "The friend is a live wire. Retired doesn't mean gone. Those retirees run a precinct of their own — Thursday coffee, birthday lunches, a phone tree that moves faster than any duty roster. Whatever you told that woman is already working its way back through the building."

She uncapped the pen again, held it over the pad without writing.

"Here's the part I want you to actually think about. A name, volunteered or asked for — those are two different women. If you asked who handled the case and she answered, she's a directory. Useful once, forgettable. If she handed you Marsh's name on her own, unprompted, then she's carrying an opinion about how that file got shut. Nobody volunteers names for cases they believe were closed right. A retired employee with a doubt is worth more than every clipping in that folder."

She finally wrote one word under the box — VISIT — and circled it.

"Until I say otherwise, that woman's cold. No calls, no stopping by, no checking in on her. When I'm ready, I'll knock on her door myself, and you'll be somewhere else."

She looked up.

"So. Three answers. Where did she work — City Hall, or the Ninth? Did she give you Marsh's name, or did you ask? And what exactly did you tell her. All of it, word for word as close as you can get."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "She worked at the Ninth, back in the day, before Marsh was even on the force." *I think hard.* "I... I think I asked who worked the case originally. And she said Marsh. I told her I was just trying to understand what happened." *I wince a little.* "Not that I was hiring a PI, obviously."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena wrote a fourth line on the pad — PRE-MARSH — and boxed it harder than the others.

"'Before Marsh was even on the force.' That changes her from a directory into a history book." She circled it once. "She doesn't just know who caught the case. She knows who ran that floor when the file was fresh. Who taught Marsh the job, whether he was ever actually good at it, whether he got careful or lazy on the way up. That's worth more than his press clippings. I'll use it later. Slowly."

Her pen moved back up the page.

"Now the critique. You gave her two sentences. The second one — 'trying to understand what happened' — that's grief talking. Nobody flags grief. A woman who sat behind that glass for twenty years has heard a hundred versions of it and hands out a name the way she'd hand out tissues. That sentence is why you're probably safe."

She held up one finger.

"The first one. You asked who worked the case *originally*." She let the word sit. "That tells a listener there's an originally and a later, and you're weighing one against the other. Most retirees let it slide. A sharp one files it. Nothing to do about it now except know it's in the air."

She turned the legal pad sideways and sketched the block in quick strokes — coffee cart on the corner, parking-garage mouth on the side street, bus stop with a clean line on the front steps. She drew it fast, from memory, and didn't say whose.

"Your week. Case number and closure date, off the letter they sent your family. Records request by mail, not in person. File copy to me when it lands — I want *both* names off the cover, because files from that building carry two signatures and your friend gave you one. Could be memory. Could be she gave you the name that's safe to give." She capped the pen. "The friend stays cold either way."

She looked up.

"Last thing, and be exact. What day did you talk to her? Three days ago, we work like the building's already warm. Three months, we've got breathing room. The date decides how careful I am."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena set the pen down.

"Torres." She said it once, flat, the way she'd said *Marsh* an hour ago — checking its weight. Then she was already moving, pulling the case folder back across the desk and flipping through it page by page, fast, like she was counting.

"Not in here." She closed it. "Two articles with Marsh's name in the headlines. A closure statement with Marsh all over it. Not one line of Torres anywhere in what you handed me. So either your witness is wrong, or your folder is missing the most interesting name in this case."

She reached for her coffee, found the cup empty, and set it back down in its own ring.

"And back up a step. *The witness.* There's no witness in anything you've given me. Which means one of two things — this came from your before-Lena digging and you've been sitting on it, or you talked to somebody after I told you your digging days were over." Her eyes came up off the folder. "Those are very different problems. Be precise."

She uncapped the pen again and wrote TORRES on the legal pad, boxed it beneath VISIT.

"Here's the version where nobody's lying yet. I told you files out of that building carry two signatures. Marsh catches the case, Torres rides second — the one who sits in the passenger seat, does half the work and none of the quotes. Your friend remembered the name that made the newspaper. That's the boring answer, and the boring answer wins most days."

She tapped the box once.

"Here's the version where I earn my fee. I told you your friend might've given you the name that's safe to give. Now a witness hands you a different one. If those records come back and the cover page says Marsh, Marsh, and only Marsh — while somebody's out there swearing it was Torres — then a name got left off a closed file. And names don't fall off covers by accident."

She looked up.

"Three things, and take your time. Who is this witness — family, neighbor, out of the original file, from where. When did you talk to them — before me or after me. And did they hand you the name Torres on their own, the way your friend handed you Marsh." She capped the pen. "Because once is memory. Twice is a message."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I shift uncomfortably in my seat.* "It was... an old neighbor of my family. Mrs. Gable. She said she saw Torres at the scene more than Marsh, and that Torres was the one who seemed to be in charge. I talked to her after I met with you, Lena. She brought up Torres' name on her own." *I try to meet your gaze, a little sheepishly.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn't pick the pen back up.

She let the silence make a full lap of the office — the dry cleaner's hum through the floor, a bus hissing past on Mercer — and she held the client's gaze the whole time, without softening it.

"I told you your digging was done. And somewhere between that sentence and this one, you walked up to a neighbor's door." No heat in her voice. Something flatter than heat. "Understand what that actually costs. It's not that you hurt anything yet. It's that every door you open ahead of me is a door I can't open clean. If I knock on Gable's porch next week, I'm the second person asking — and seconds get polite answers. You've been spending my work before I've done it."

She turned the legal pad a quarter inch, unnecessary, precise.

"For what it's worth — you could've buried Gable in a list of errands and I'd have found out a week from now. You put her on the table. That's the only reason this is a warning and not a refund." She picked up the pen. Punishment was a luxury; information wasn't. She wrote GABLE under TORRES and boxed both. "And while we're counting what you owe this desk — you still never gave me the day on the friend. You're quick at stepping around dates. I'm quicker at noticing them."

She tapped the box twice.

"Now the part that matters. What you bought with that mistake is good. Neighbors watch — they don't know they're doing it, but they clock who stands where. Who the uniforms look at when a call has to be made. Who talks to the family and who talks to the radio. A woman who watched that scene from her window will tell you who ran it without ever using the word. Paper says Marsh. Her eyes say Torres. I believe eyes over paper most days — paper gets written by whoever signs it." A short pause. "And notice what she did. Your friend was *asked* — that's a directory. Gable volunteered. Unprompted names come from people carrying an opinion. She's been waiting years for somebody to climb her steps and ask."

She looked up.

"Three answers, straight. One — *when*. The day decides how far this has already traveled. Two — what you told her about yourself. Grief only, or did the words *hired someone* come out of your mouth? Because if they did, that's not a name drifting through a coffee circle anymore. That's a flare. Three — Gable herself. Age, does she drive, does she go anywhere. Church, senior center, a card table. Names travel from mouths to rooms, and I want the map of where hers goes."

She capped the pen.

"Then the rule, and it's not negotiable. Gable's mine now — I knock, you're elsewhere. And from today, nobody gets a word from you without that name landing on this desk first. You go around me again, I close the file and you can explain to whoever comes after me why the building was warm." She turned Marsh's photo face-up, studied it a moment. "You got lucky. Luck isn't a method. Talk."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I wince, but nod, taking her words in.* "Okay. Understood. No more digging. I won't go around you again, Lena. Promise." *I take a deep breath.* "Mrs. Gable... I talked to her yesterday. And I just told her I was still trying to understand what happened to my family. No mention of a PI." *I try to remember more about Mrs. Gable.* "She's in her late seventies, maybe early eighties. Doesn't drive anymore, but her daughter takes her to church on Sundays. And she plays bingo at the community center on Tuesdays and Thursdays."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena pulled the legal pad back and drew seven small boxes in a row across the top of the page. In three of them she wrote: SUN — CHURCH. TUE — BINGO. THU — BINGO.

"'Yesterday.'" She set the word down like it was hot. "That's the third date you've stepped around at this desk. I need days of the week, not directions. Look at the map you just handed me — bingo twice a week, church once. Depending on which day yesterday was, the name Torres has either already made a lap around a card table, or it makes one inside of forty-eight hours." She tapped the boxes. "Those are different problems. If a lap's already happened, I'm not just asking Gable what she saw at that scene. I'm asking her what came *back* to her afterward. So — which day."

She uncapped the pen and wrote GRIEF SCRIPT beneath the calendar.

"The sentence held. No flare, no hired-man smell on you. One note, though — you've now said nearly the same words to two different women. It's a good sentence, don't retire it. But vary it. If the friend and Gable ever land at the same table, matched wording reads as rehearsed. Rehearsed reads as lawyer."

She turned Marsh's photo face-up again, studied it a beat.

"Now the part I keep turning over. Scenes carry two kinds of men — the one who talks to the family, and the one who owns the paperwork after. Sometimes it's the same man. Sometimes the one everyone remembers isn't the one who signs. Gable's eyes say Torres ran that street. The file says Marsh. Both can be true and still be boring — senior man shows, handles the cameras, hands the file off, goes home. Or both are true and nothing about it is boring. The records copy settles the signature. Gable settles the street. I don't need them to agree yet. I need them both clean."

She squared the pad against the desk edge.

"And understand what you actually bought on that porch. A woman pushing eighty who watched that scene from her window and never moved is a camera that's been recording the block for twenty years. She didn't just see who was in charge that night. She saw who came back the following week. Who parked with the engine running. Whether anyone from that building ever knocked on her door again. That last one is mine to ask her — because if somebody else has been up those steps over the years, we're not the first ones pulling at this."

She capped the pen.

"Orders. Records request in today's mail — I want the postmark before sundown. The friend stays cold. Marsh stays untouched — a proud man gets one poke, and I don't poke until the file copy tells me what I'm poking at. Gable's mine, and I move ahead of whatever church or bingo session comes next. You'll be somewhere that isn't her street."

She looked up.

"Three things. One — the two days. Friend, Gable. Weekdays. Two — does Gable still live on the same street she lived on then? Because people who stay are watching. People who moved right after were watching something that scared them. I want to know which one she is. Three — the daughter. Does she live with her, or just drive? Porch conversations get edited when there's family standing in the room."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay, the friend... I talked to her last Tuesday. Mrs. Gable, yesterday was a Wednesday." *I think about the rest.* "Yes, she still lives on the same street, same house even. And her daughter just drives her, she doesn't live with her."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena went back to the row of seven boxes. In the second she wrote TUE — FRIEND. In the third, WED — GABLE. Then she set the pen tip down on the fourth box, the empty one, and left it sitting there.

"Today's Thursday." She said it the way other people announce a fire. "And from a Thursday, 'last Tuesday' means nine days. If you meant two days ago, stop me now, because the math changes everything." She watched a beat, then went on. "Nine days. Your friend has had a week and a half to feed the word *originally* into whatever circle she keeps. That's not warm, not cold — one lap at coffee-and-bingo speed. Retired precincts move slow." She tapped the empty fourth box twice. "Except today. I told you they run a Thursday coffee. Gable runs a Thursday bingo. The whole retired shift clocks in this afternoon, and both of your conversations are on the agenda whether we like it or not."

She pulled the legal pad around, tore off a fresh sheet, and slid it across with the pen.

"Same house, same street, twenty years — that's the good answer. She stayed because the block is hers and she never stopped minding it." She capped the pen. "It also means I don't drive there. A woman who's watched one street for two decades knows every car on it by engine sound. I walk in from a few blocks out, up the side where she can see me coming, empty-handed, unhurried. Watchers trust what they watch arrive."

She reached for the coffee cup, remembered it was empty, and ignored it.

"Daughter drives but doesn't live there — porch stays unedited most hours. Except the hours she's standing on it. Thursday she comes to collect Gable for bingo, and once that car pulls away, Gable's off the board until tonight. So — what time's the pickup? If you don't know, say you don't. I'll read it off the porch myself."

She tapped the blank sheet.

"Now your morning, in order. You write the records letter on that page — by hand, plain words. However you're related to them, say it in the real word. Then: *I'd like a copy of the closed file, case number's on the closure letter you sent us. My address is below. Thank you for your time.* Nothing else. Sign it, fold it, and take it to the post office counter — not the corner box. I want today's date stamped on it while a clerk is watching. A handwritten note from a grieving relative is furniture. Anything typed is a flashlight."

She stood and took her coat off the hook, working the buttons while she talked.

"While you're at that counter, I'm on her step. If I beat the daughter there, Gable hears a version from me, and tonight's bingo table gets a boring story. If the daughter beats me, I don't chase the car — I come back here and we let bingo test the water for free."

She parted the blinds with two fingers and checked the street.

"Bottom of the sheet — Gable's address, and the pickup time if you have it. Then you're a man mailing a letter, and that's the whole day. Write."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I quickly write down the letter on the fresh sheet.* "I don't know the exact pickup time for Mrs. Gable, but I think it's usually around two." *I push the paper back across the desk.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena picked the sheet up and read it standing — the letter first, twice through, then the address line at the bottom.

"Letter's clean. Furniture, like I said." She set it on the bare corner of the desk, away from the folders. "Return address stays your home. And when it lands — city offices run two weeks if they love you, six if they don't — you don't open it at your kitchen table. You bring it here sealed. Envelopes talk. Whether a flap's been steamed and re-stuck, whether a corner got thumbed in transit. I read the envelope before anybody reads the file."

She pulled the legal pad back and filled today's box — THU: PORCH — then the evening one: THU PM — BINGO TELLS ME. Under tomorrow, one line: FRI — QUIET OR LOUD.

"'Around two.'" One corner of her mouth moved, which was as close as she came to laughing before noon. "You and 'around' — I'll bill the two of you separately. Doesn't matter. I'm on that block by one. Porches keep better schedules than people do."

She capped the pen.

"I knock as myself. Not a survey, not a census — a woman who's watched one street for twenty years smells a pretext before the door finishes opening, and a burnt pretext burns the whole block. The family hired someone to sit with her. That's the whole story, and if it travels to bingo tonight, it's a boring story. Families hire listeners. Nobody pulls a file over listening." She tapped the evening box once. "By her second card, my visit is old news at that table. Tomorrow I find out whether the name Torres came back quieter or louder overnight — and that answer's worth the trip even if she tells me nothing."

She slid both folders to the client's side of the desk.

"Leave these. Everything with a name on it. Today you're a man who mailed a letter, and a man like that carries keys, a wallet, and nothing that reads."

She checked her watch, then the street through the blinds, parting them the same two-fingered way.

"Eleven-twenty. That's a slow walk and a slower look at the block, and I'll still beat your 'around' with room to spare." She let the blinds drop. "Orders. Counter, postmark, home. You don't call me today — I call you. You don't drive past her street, not once, not to *just look*. Be back here at six. Six, not five-fifty — I hate stepping over people camped on my stairs. If I'm not here at six, you go home, you eat something, and tomorrow you answer your phone like a man with nothing on his mind. I don't send distress signals, and I don't lose fights on porches."

She held the office door open and nodded at the letter waiting on the desk corner.

"That's your whole day. Go be boring."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I gather my things, feeling a strange mix of relief and nervous energy.* "Got it, Lena. Boring." *I make sure to leave the folders on the desk, then head out, the dry cleaner's chemical smell still faint in my nostrils.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The stairwell gave the client back to the street, and Lena watched through the blinds until he turned the corner — keys, wallet, nothing that reads. Then she spent her hour with Marsh's photo face-up and the recited sentence *the evidence was consistent with*, and wrote nothing new under TORRES, because there was nothing to write until a file or an old woman said otherwise.

At ten past one she came into Gable's block from the east, at the pace of a woman with sore feet and nowhere urgent, and let the street look at her for a full block before she climbed the steps. Gable opened the door on the second knock with her reading glasses already up.

"You police?"

"Family."

A long look over the glasses. "Family sends flowers. Come in before the heat gets out."

Lena gave the version she'd promised — hired by the family to sit with the people who were there that night, listen, write it down so nobody had to keep asking. Then she listened for forty minutes and interrupted twice.

"Two of them, that night," Gable said. "The talker walked my fence line three days running — little book, wrote like a minister. The tall one in your pictures stood by the car trunks, made two calls from Paynes' corner, and left before I'd straightened my curtains." She never used a name. She'd already spent that name; what she'd been saving was different.

"Did anyone from that building come back? Any time at all, after?"

"Nobody. First week, then nothing, going on twenty years." A pause — watchers pause before the part that matters. "Once."

A car, that autumn. Forty minutes across from the hydrant, engine running at dusk. "Too far to swear a face. But he sat the way the talker sat. Like the seat was borrowed."

Then she went to the kitchen and came back with a church bulletin folded in quarters, and in the margin, a plate number in square handwriting, a date beside it. "You watch a street long enough, you keep score." She handed it over like returning a borrowed book. "Take it. It's waited long enough for somebody to ask."

At the door, the old woman squinted. "You've done this before."

"I drink a lot of coffee."

"Mm." Gable shut her door on that, the way you do on a door you already know is shut.

The daughter's car turned the corner at quarter to two, right on the hour of *around*. Lena was three blocks gone, bulletin inside her coat, before bingo got its boring story.

---

The stairwell creaked at six sharp. Lena squared the legal pad and didn't look up.

"Door's open. Sit."

She let the client get seated, then set the folded bulletin on the desk between them.

"Grading today in two parts. One — Gable's clean. I was off her step before the daughter arrived, and that woman will feed bingo something duller than what I actually said. Old watchers bore people on purpose."

"Two." She unfolded the bulletin, turned it around. "Twenty years, nobody from that building ever went back up that street. Except once. A car, forty minutes, engine running at dusk — and Mrs. Gable writes down what matters. Plate, and the date, in her own hand, kept in a drawer because nobody ever asked her." She let that sit. "The plate goes to a man at an insurance desk in Rahway. He's slow and honest, which is the only combination I'll pay for. Two days, maybe three. And she *dated* it — so when your records copy lands, we see how far that date sits from the official closure date. Distance between dates is a story too."

She leaned back.

"Your half. The letter. Show me the receipt."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod, impressed.* "Wow. Mrs. Gable sounds incredible." *I reach into my pocket and pull out the post office receipt, sliding it across the desk.* "Here you go. Got it stamped just like you said."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena closed the file and pushed it back across the desk. "The Ninth Precinct is a fortress with bad lighting. Nobody gets answers inside unless they're wearing a uniform or holding a subpoena."

She scribbled a name on her notepad, tore off the sheet, and held it out. "Third floor. Ask for Detective Marchetti. Tell him I want the supplementary file—the one that didn't make the official log." Her gaze stayed level. "He'll refuse at first. Then mention that I know about the witness he failed to sign in back in March. He'll find a photocopy room real fast."

She stood and moved to the window, pulling the blinds aside just enough to watch the street below. "You go. I'll wait here. Call me when you're heading back, and don't let anyone walk you out through the side door. That's not hospitality. That's an interview tactic."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I stare at the note, then back at her.* "You want *me* to go? To a precinct you just called a fortress?" I pocket the note. "Fine, but if I end up in a holding cell, you're bailing me out." *I head for the door.* "And what exactly did Marchetti do in March?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena let the blinds fall shut but stayed by the window, her silhouette sharp against the gray light. "He left a witness sitting in a hallway for six hours. Never signed him into the log. By the time Marchetti got around to the paperwork, the man had already taken a bus to Baltimore." She paused. "That's the leverage. Nothing else."

She pushed off from the wall and returned to the desk, though she didn't sit. She picked up her cup, felt the weight of cold coffee, and set it down again untouched. "Wait until he refuses you. Then mention March. If he asks you to sit in a room with no windows, leave. That's not bureaucracy. That's him buying time to call upstairs."

Her gaze cut toward the door, then back to the file on the desk. "You won't see a holding cell. Arresting a civilian inside a precinct generates paperwork nobody wants to explain."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena crossed the room and held out a slim digital recorder. "Take this. Start it in the lobby—New York's a one-party consent state." Her gaze dropped to the file still open on the desk, then back to the client. "When you see Marchetti, watch his left eye. It twitches when he's lying. If it moves when he says the supplementary file doesn't exist, mention March again and don't blink."

She stepped back, putting the desk between them, and folded her arms. "Call the office line when you're outside. Not my cell. And if anyone offers you coffee in an interview room, decline. They didn't make it for you."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I take the recorder, turning it over in my hand.* "Wow, you really know the drill, don't you?" *I start for the door again, then pause.* "Okay, one more thing. What exactly am I looking for in this 'supplementary file'?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena drummed her fingers once against the file. "Discrepancies. A second timeline, a witness statement dated after the case was marked closed, photographs that never got an evidence sticker."

She withdrew one of the photos from the spread and studied it under the desk lamp, though her focus seemed to drift past the image itself. "Marchetti's predecessor documented everything. Then he tried to carve out the pieces that didn't fit the theory. The supplementary file is what's left of the carving."

She set the photo down. "Look for a folder that isn't blue. Gray, brown, maybe unmarked. Inside, you'll find a secondary location—somewhere the official report says nobody visited. If there's a vehicle description or a partial plate, memorize it. Don't write anything down while you're inside."

She nodded toward the recorder. "If he steps out for more than five minutes, check beneath the folder. Someone I used to work with used to tape duplicates to the underside when they didn't trust the filing clerk."

She moved back to the window, her posture rigid. "Forty minutes. His shift supervisor does a walk-through at quarter past. Be gone before then."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking all of that in.* "Got it. Different color folder, secondary location, vehicle info, no notes, check the underside." *I glance at my watch, then back at her.* "You really think this Marchetti guy will just... hand it over to me?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's gaze stayed fixed on the street below, tracking something beyond the glass. "He won't hand it to you. He'll leave it on the corner of his desk and find a reason to check his email, or he'll slide it across and call it a photocopying error." She let the blinds snap shut. "What he won't do is let the March story reach his lieutenant. He's got four years until pension."

She turned then, leaning against the windowsill with her arms crossed tight. "If he brings anyone else into that room—a uniform, a clerk, anybody—you get up and walk out. Two people means he's building a witness, and you're the one being witnessed."

She nodded at the recorder still in the client's hand. "Keep that running the whole time. If he asks why, tell him you're hard of hearing. Don't smile. Don't thank him on the way out. Gratitude makes him reach for the phone."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena went still by the window, her fingers resting on the blind cord. For a moment the gray light seemed to sharpen against her face. Then she turned back to the room and gathered the photos into a neat stack. "Torres logged evidence in blue ink. If you see his initials on anything Marchetti hands you, check the color of the date stamp. Black means it was re-filed under new management."

She slid the file into a manila envelope and left it on the corner of the desk. "You should move. Marchetti takes his break at half past, and his desk goes cold for twenty minutes after that."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod, processing all this new information about Torres.* "Okay, blue ink, black date stamp. Got it." *I glance at my watch again.* "Right. Break time. Wish me luck." *I head out the door, recorder already on.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena threw the deadbolt behind the client and listened to the footsteps fade down the narrow stairwell. The dry cleaner's steam press hissed through the floorboards below, steady as a heartbeat. She returned to the window and eased the blinds apart with one finger, watching the corner of Mercer until the client rounded it and disappeared toward Houston.

She went back to the desk. The photo she'd set aside earlier still sat beneath the lamp, and she picked it up, studying the background edges where the shadows pooled. Her thumb traced the corner without seeming to realize it. Then she set it down, reached into the pencil drawer, and retrieved a prepaid phone she hadn't used in three months.

"The diner across from the Ninth," she said when the line clicked. "North window. If you see a gray sedan leave the lot with two in the front seat, text this number. Nothing else."

She hung up, set the phone on the windowsill, and checked her watch. Thirty-five minutes. She moved to the radiator, retrieved the magnetic case from behind it, and checked the load on the revolver by feel. The action was smooth, well-oiled. She slipped it into the holster at the small of her back and returned to the desk chair, turning it to face the door. The cold coffee sat untouched. She left it that way and waited in the half-light.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *My heart is pounding as I walk into the precinct, the recorder buzzing softly in my pocket. It smells like stale coffee and something vaguely metallic. The front desk sergeant barely looks up as I ask for Detective Marchetti. I'm directed to the third floor, and the elevator ride feels like it takes forever.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The burner phone on the windowsill rattled against the wood. Lena crossed the office in two strides and thumbed the screen. The message was spare: *In.* She typed back, *Sedan?* and set the phone face-up, screen glowing dull against the gray light. 

She checked the wall clock—twenty-six minutes since the client had disappeared around the corner toward Houston. Marchetti would still be at his desk for another four minutes, maybe five, before he stood to stretch his legs and complain about the break-room coffee. That was the window. 

Lena returned to the desk and turned the photo facedown, not wanting to look at the blurred figure in the background anymore. Her hand drifted to the small of her back, confirming by feel that the holster was seated and hidden beneath her jacket. The office line remained silent. She pulled the manila envelope closer and memorized the case number written inside the flap, in case the client had to read it back over a bad connection or through a cracked line. 

Then she sat back in the chair, kept her breathing even, and watched the door, listening to the empty conveyor belt of the dry cleaner click through its rotation one floor below.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I step out of the elevator onto the third floor. It's quieter up here, the fluorescent lights humming over a long, empty hallway. I spot a desk with a nameplate, "Det. Marchetti." He's there, hunched over some papers. I take a deep breath and walk toward him, trying to look confident.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena sat in the half-light, the revolver’s weight a familiar pressure at the small of her back. The office line stayed silent. She picked up the photo again and studied the background margins where the shadows bled into the asphalt. Under the desk lamp’s glare, she caught a reflection in the chrome of a parked car—a fragment of a green street sign, white lettering. She retrieved a jeweler’s loupe from the pencil drawer and held it over the glossy surface.

Hester Street. Or enough of it to matter.

She set the loupe down and pulled a folded borough map from the bottom drawer, spreading it across the desk. Her finger traced the grid near the East River, finding the intersection where Hester crossed beneath the old viaduct. The secondary location. It wasn’t in the official report because Torres had photographed it three days before the crime scene unit logged the primary.

She circled the block in pencil, then folded the map away. The burner phone on the sill remained dark. She checked her watch—eighteen minutes gone. Marchetti would have looked up from his paperwork by now, would have heard the client’s footsteps on the linoleum. She turned the chair to face the door and listened to the dry cleaner’s belt click through another empty rotation, her hands folded loosely in her lap, ready.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I clear my throat as I approach Marchetti's desk.* "Detective Marchetti? My name is [Client's Name]. I'm here regarding a cold case, the one involving... the incident from [year]." *I try to keep my voice steady, remembering to watch his left eye.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The wall clock ticked past the half-hour. Lena had not moved from the chair, her posture deceptively relaxed, her eyes fixed on the office door. The burner phone on the sill remained dark. No gray sedan. That meant the threat, if there was one, was still inside, breathing the same stale air as the client.

She slid the remaining photographs from the manila envelope. The fifth in the stack caught her—not the subject in the foreground, but the reflection in a sidewalk puddle behind it. A green-and-white striped awning, and beneath it, a fragment of an address painted on brick. Numbers. Hester Street, but farther east than she'd circled, closer to the river.

She wrote the digits on her palm with a ballpoint, the ink stinging slightly against the skin. Someone she used to work with had always checked the reflections first, before the body, before the weapon. She had never disagreed with the logic.

Below, the dry cleaner’s radio played a tinny melody that seeped through the floorboards. She shut it out. The office line stayed silent. She kept her breathing even, her hands loose in her lap, and watched the door, waiting for the sound that would tell her whether the client was returning with a folder or returning with a story about a room that had no windows.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *Marchetti finally looks up, his left eye twitching almost imperceptibly. He gestures to the chair opposite him.* "Take a seat. What cold case are you talking about? I've got a dozen open files on my desk right now." *I sit, trying to remember everything Lena said. This is it.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena checked the wall clock. The minute hand had slipped past the half-hour, which meant Marchetti would already be reaching for his jacket, eager for his break. If the client hadn't laid down the March card by now, the detective would offer a chair in the windowless room and disappear for twenty minutes. It was a stall, not a courtesy.

The office line stayed silent. Lena pushed away from the desk and went to the window, pulling the blind cord to widen the gap. She studied the corner of Mercer, then the distant traffic moving east. No sign of the client. No gray sedan creeping against the curb.

She retrieved the prepaid phone from the sill and thumbed another message to the diner contact: *Still eyes on?*

Then she slipped the photo and the folded map into her inside jacket pocket and checked the revolver by feel, ensuring the holster sat flat and hidden beneath her coat. If the office line didn't ring within the next few minutes, she would head down to the Ninth herself. Not through the precinct doors—she didn't do that—but close enough to read the body language of whoever walked out, and whether they walked out alone.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "I'm here about the case of Elias Thorne," *I say, trying to sound calm even though my heart is hammering.* "The one from '98." *I watch his left eye. It twitches again.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s fingers paused on the edge of the file. She lined the photos up again, one by one, as if the answer might be hiding in their order.

“Because the Ninth isn’t a place I can walk into,” she said. “Not for this. Not for anything.”

She pulled the desk phone closer, but didn’t dial yet. Her thumb rested lightly over the receiver.

“If a detective touched it, then there’s paperwork. There’s memory. There’s someone who noticed who asked questions and who didn’t. We call first. If that gets us nowhere, we find them outside the building. A coffee shop. A car. A stoop. Somewhere with no desk sergeant and no cameras in the lobby.”

Her gaze lifted briefly, then settled back on the closed file.

“And if it turns out the only way to get what we need is through that precinct door, then you’ll be the one walking through it.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I lean forward, intrigued.* "So you've got history with the Ninth, huh? I figured as much. What's the story there?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn’t take the bait.

She turned the top photograph a quarter inch until its edge aligned with the desk blotter, then tapped one corner of it with her fingertip.

“The story,” she said, “is whether that detective still has the file, who else has looked at it since, and whether your name has already been attached to it.”

She slid the phone off the hook one inch, then stopped.

“Twenty minutes away doesn’t matter. Precincts keep their own weather. We don’t go in there to ask favors. We find out who the detective is, where they take coffee, what shift they work, and whether they’ll talk without a notebook in front of them.”

Her gaze lifted to the blinds, where the afternoon light cut thin yellow stripes across the floor.

“If you want this done clean, you let me choose the door. And the Ninth isn’t a door I use.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena let the question pass without picking it up.

She turned the top photograph over. Blank. She checked the next, then the next. Nothing on the backs but fingerprints and the faint chemical smell rising from the desk.

“The name isn’t here,” she said. “That means whoever gave you these either didn’t know it or didn’t want it written down.”

She opened the file again and scanned the margins, the stamps, the faint pencil marks near the staple line. Her voice stayed flat, practical, as if the earlier question had been a wrong number she was already forgetting.

“We need the detective’s habits, not a history lesson. Where they take coffee. Whether they still have the file or passed it on. If a phone call gets us anything, we use it. If not, you go to the counter and ask for records. I wait outside.”

She pulled the phone closer and dialed from a creased card tucked behind her license, not from the file.

“The Ninth stays where it is. We work around it.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I sigh, frustrated, but I can tell she's made up her mind.* "Alright, fine. So who are you calling?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena held up one finger while the phone rang.

“Someone who works near the Ninth,” she said. “Not inside it.”

The line clicked open. Street noise came through faintly — the hiss of a milk wand, cups knocking against a metal counter, a register beeping somewhere in the background.

“It’s Lena,” she said. “I need a name, but I need it from the sidewalk. A detective from the Ninth has been carrying a file that matches what I’m looking at. Maybe recent, maybe reopened. I don’t need the official version. I need habits. Coffee order. Where they sit if they stop by before shift. Whether they keep the folder in a bag or under their arm.”

She listened, her eyes on the photographs again. One showed a doorway. Another, a blurred street corner. The third had a crease across the corner, as if someone had folded it in a hurry.

“If they paid cash, I want to know,” Lena continued. “If they talked to anyone while they were waiting, I want to know that too. And if someone else looked over their shoulder at the file, I want the description first.”

Her gaze shifted to the window, to the thin bars of light still striping the floor.

“No,” she said, softer. “I’m not coming in. I won’t be anywhere near the front steps. If you see them again, you call me. If they ask about me, you never heard the name.”

She let the silence on the other end settle for a beat.

“That’s right,” she said. “I’m asking as a favor. Not as anything else.”

Lena covered the receiver with her palm and looked back at the client.

“A coffee cart two blocks from the Ninth,” she said. “The people who work there see more than the detectives ever notice. If your detective has a routine, that’s where it starts.”

She uncovered the phone again.

“Start with the last week,” she told the voice on the line. “Anyone from the Ninth who looked tired, careful, and like they were carrying something they didn’t want to leave in a desk drawer.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing all this.* "Okay, so we wait for this coffee cart person to call back, then what? We can't just ambush them."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena listened for another moment, then ended the call and set the receiver back in its cradle with deliberate care.

“We don’t ambush anyone,” she said. “Ambushes make people stupid. Or brave. Both are bad for us.”

She gathered the photographs into a neat stack, squared them against the desk, and slid them back into the file.

“When the cart calls back, we ask one thing at a time. Did the detective come alone. Did they carry a bag. Did they look like someone guarding a secret, or someone tired of carrying one. If the answer is useful, we make contact soft.”

She opened a drawer, took out a small notebook, and wrote the time beside the word *coffee* in tight, slanted letters.

“No cornering. No blocking their route. We pick somewhere public. Daylight. Enough noise that nobody feels trapped. You sit. I stay close, but not beside you. If the detective comes to you, you talk. If they don’t, you leave. That’s not failure. That’s information.”

Her pen paused over the page.

“If they do talk, you don’t push for the file. You ask what they remember. What bothered them. What didn’t fit. People protect paper. They’re looser with impressions.”

She closed the notebook and set it on top of the file.

“And if they tell you to go to the Ninth, you smile, thank them, and walk away. You don’t argue. You don’t follow them inside. You call me from the street.”

Lena glanced toward the blinds again, where the light had gone thinner and more gray.

“If they want to help, they’ll give us a place outside. A bench. A car. A doorway. If they only want to know why we’re asking, then we’ve learned something too.”

She tapped the file once, lightly, as if sealing the plan into it.

“So we wait. But we don’t wait here doing nothing. You think about who gave you these photos. What they said. What they didn’t say. I’ll think about why a detective from the Ninth would keep a file close enough to remember, but not close enough to solve.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena did not answer at once.

Her thumb rested on the corner of the file, pressing just hard enough to whiten the skin beneath the nail. Outside, a bus sighed to a stop on Mercer, then pulled away, leaving the room quieter than before.

“Torres means we stop working with shadows,” she said at last. Her voice stayed level, but the name sat between them like something metal and cold. “It doesn’t mean we start trusting what we’ve been handed.”

She opened the notebook again and wrote *M. Torres* under the earlier line. The pen made a dry sound against the paper.

“A name can be a clue. It can also be a fence. Somebody puts it in front of you so you spend your time looking at the person instead of the hand that passed it over.”

She underlined the initial once, then set the pen down.

“If Detective Torres worked the case, we find out whether they still think about it. Coffee cart first. Habits. Whether they mention the file, carry it, leave it alone, or come back to the same corner like they’re waiting for someone to ask. We don’t go near the precinct with the name in our mouths.”

Her eyes moved to the phone.

“When the cart calls back, I’ll ask if Torres has been by. If the answer is yes, we learn how they’ve been moving. Alone. Hurried. Looking over a shoulder. If the answer is no, we ask who from the Ninth has been asking after old paperwork. Either way, we stay outside the walls.”

She looked back at the file, not at the client.

“And if the name makes someone nervous, we don’t push it in the open. We let it sit. Nervous people repeat themselves.”

A beat passed. The blinds ticked faintly as the light outside shifted.

“The witness gave you Torres. That’s useful. It’s also the first thing I’d want checked. Did they say it like a fact, or like a warning? Did they know the initial, or just repeat it? Did they look relieved when they said it, or like they’d just handed you a key they didn’t want back?”

Lena closed the notebook slowly.

“For now, it means we’re careful. We don’t walk into the Ninth calling for Torres. We don’t let the name get into any room before we know what it’s carrying.”

Her gaze settled on the desk phone.

“If Torres is the answer, we’ll meet them somewhere with daylight and noise. If Torres is the trap, we’ll spring it from far enough away that nobody gets a clean look at us.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I chew on that, a little unnerved by her intensity.* "The witness... he just said the name. Like he was trying to be helpful. Didn't seem like a warning. But he did say 'M. Torres' specifically." *I pause.* "So, if Torres is the detective, and they're still at the Ninth... how are we even going to get a message to them without going through official channels?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s eyes left the file and moved to the window. The street had gone quiet in that late-afternoon way, sounds arriving separately: a horn, a cart wheel, the dry cleaner’s door chime below.

“The initial helps,” she said. “It narrows without making noise. It also means your witness either read a nameplate, heard it in passing, or was told exactly what to say. We don’t know which yet.”

She opened the bottom drawer and took out a blank white card, the kind that might have come with a bouquet or a cheap box of stationery. She placed it in the center of the desk.

“We don’t send Torres a message,” she said. “Not the way you’re thinking.”

Her fingers rested on the card as if measuring it.

“Official channels are counters and logbooks. You ask for a detective by name, and the request starts traveling before you’ve left the lobby. It goes through a sergeant, maybe a partner, maybe somebody who remembers the file and somebody else who wishes nobody did. We don’t need it traveling. We need it sitting still until Torres decides whether to pick it up.”

She uncapped her pen but did not write yet.

“The coffee cart is the first door. If Torres stops there, the vendor can slide a card across with the change. No envelope. No name. No case number. Just enough to make a person who’s been carrying that file stop stirring their coffee.”

The pen touched the card. She wrote in small, slanted letters:

*You kept a file close. Someone else has the photographs. If you want to know who, call once.*

Beneath that she wrote a number from memory, then looked at it for a moment as if checking whether it still belonged to her.

“It rings at a message service on Canal,” she said. “They don’t know me as Lena. They know me as a voice that pays monthly. If Torres calls, they give another number. If someone else calls, they say the line’s been disconnected.”

She set the pen down.

“If the cart worker won’t pass it, we don’t push. We watch. We learn whether Torres comes out alone, whether they look for the same faces, whether they take calls by the car or step into the deli across the street. If the cart fails, we use the neighborhood. A delivery runner. A parking attendant. Somebody who can get close without ever walking through the precinct door.”

Her gaze returned to the client, steady and unreadable.

“You don’t mention the Ninth. You don’t mention the witness. You don’t say Torres unless Torres says it first. If the message works and a call comes back, you listen. You don’t bargain. You don’t explain. You give them a public place and a time, and you let them choose whether to be brave.”

She turned the card over, blank side up, as if the blankness mattered more than the words.

“The trick isn’t getting a message inside. It’s making the message look like something only Torres would recognize. Detectives get asked for favors all day. They don’t often get asked about the thing they never stopped thinking about.”

The phone sat between them, silent for now.

“So we wait for the cart to call. If Torres has been there, we move soft. If Torres hasn’t, we start looking for the person at the Ninth who has been asking about old files. Either way, we stay outside the walls.”

She tapped the card once, lightly.

“And if somebody thinks they can use Torres as bait, they’ll find out we don’t bite where we can’t see the hook.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I stare at the card, then at Lena.* "That's... bold. You really think a detective would respond to something like that? It sounds like something out of a movie."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena looked at the card for a long moment, not offended by the comparison.

“Movies make it look bold,” she said. “Because they skip the boring parts. The waiting. The bad coffee. The way people decide whether to trust a stranger based on one sentence on a piece of paper.”

She turned the card over again, blank side up, then slid it a half inch to the left.

“A detective won’t respond because it’s dramatic. They’ll respond because it names something they can’t let go of. If Torres kept that file close, then somewhere along the line it stopped being paperwork and started being a loose thread. People ignore a lot of things, but a loose thread in their own memory? That pulls.”

Her eyes moved to the phone.

“And if they don’t call, that tells us something too. Maybe they’ve moved on. Maybe they’re scared. Maybe somebody told them to stop thinking about it. Silence is still an answer.”

She leaned back slightly, chair creaking under her.

“The card isn’t a trick. It’s a test. It gives Torres a chance to reach out without walking into a room full of witnesses. No desk, no sergeant, no form to fill out. Just a choice.”

One finger tapped once against the desk, quiet and deliberate.

“People in that job learn to be careful. But careful doesn’t mean curious isn’t still there underneath. If the case mattered, this will itch. If it didn’t, we’ll know by tomorrow.”

She looked back toward the blinds, where the light had gone thin and gray.

“And if it sounds like a movie to you, that’s fine. Movies end when the audience gets bored. We don’t have that luxury. We keep moving until something real happens.”

Her gaze returned to the card.

“So yes. I think someone might respond. Not because it’s bold. Because it’s small enough to be safe, and specific enough to matter.”

She set the card beside the file, squared its edge with the photograph stack, and let the quiet sit for a beat.

“Now we wait for the coffee cart.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I pick up the blank card and turn it over, looking at the message again.* "Okay. So, what do I do while we're waiting? Just... sit here?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena watched the card in the client’s hands without trying to take it back.

“You don’t sit,” she said. “Sitting makes you feel like the case is happening to you. We need you useful.”

She pulled the notebook closer and opened it to a fresh page. The paper made a dry rasp in the quiet office.

“Write down everything you remember about the witness. Not impressions first. Facts. Where you met. What time. Whether he chose the place. Whether he faced the street or the wall. Whether he touched the photos, or wouldn’t touch them.”

She turned the page slightly so the blank space sat directly under the client’s line of sight.

“Then write every word he used around the name. Did he say ‘detective’ first, or only the name? Did he give you the initial before you asked? Did he say Torres like he’d been carrying it, or like he’d just learned it?”

Her fingers rested on the edge of the desk.

“Memory isn’t soft. It’s a scene. Put yourself back in it and tell me what’s in the corners.”

She glanced at the phone, then back.

“After that, you check the photographs again under the lamp. Not the pictures themselves. The edges. The backs. The staple marks. If there’s a lab stamp, a date code, a smudge from a printer, a crease that came from a wallet or an envelope, I want it separated. We don’t need the image to tell us where it’s been.”

Lena opened the top drawer and took out a clean envelope. She set it beside the file.

“Anything you find goes in here. Not your pocket. Not your bag. Not your memory. Paper forgets less badly than people do.”

Her gaze returned to the card.

“When you’re done reading that, put it face down on the desk. It doesn’t leave this room. It doesn’t get copied. It doesn’t get repeated out loud anywhere but here.”

She leaned back just enough for the chair to creak once.

“If the phone rings, let it ring twice. If it’s the cart, I answer. If it’s the message service, I answer. If it’s anyone else, we let it stop. You write down the time either way.”

The light through the blinds had gone paler, thinning toward evening.

“And if you need to make a call, you use your cell, not this line. Not yet. We don’t know who’s been near this case, so we don’t give them a sound to follow.”

She tapped the notebook once with the back of her pen.

“Start with the witness. Then the photos. Then every person who knew you had either. If we’re going to meet Torres, we meet clean.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I pick up the notebook she offered.* "Okay, got it. Witness first, then the photos. So, the witness... his name is George. George Miller. He looked nervous, kept looking at the door." *I start writing.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena listened to the name without reaching for it too quickly.

“George Miller,” she said, once, as if setting the name on a scale and watching the needle move. “Common enough to forget. Specific enough to write down. Keep going.”

She shifted the desk lamp a fraction to the left, pulling more light over the photographs without letting it spill toward the window. The chemical smell from below still clung faintly to the room, mixed with the stale bitterness of the coffee she had stopped drinking an hour ago.

“Nervous is an impression,” she said. “I need the pieces that made it. Did he sit facing the door? Did he choose the seat, or did he wait for you to choose first? Did he keep his coat on? Hands on the table, or out of sight?”

Her eyes moved from the file to the notebook, then back again.

“If he kept looking at the door, write down what made him look. Every time. Was it the stairwell? The street? The dry cleaner’s bell? Did he check the room before he said Torres, or after? Did he lower his voice when he said it, or did he say it like he wanted someone else to hear?”

She tapped one fingertip against the desk, slow and deliberate.

“People don’t just hand over a detective’s name. They hand over what the name cost them. Maybe it cost him nothing. Maybe it cost him sleep. Maybe he was afraid of you. More likely, he was afraid of being seen giving you anything at all.”

The phone sat between them, dark and patient.

“Write whether he had a phone out. A wallet. Keys. Did he carry an envelope, or did the photos come loose? If he touched them, how? Like evidence, or like something he wished he hadn’t touched?”

She paused, listening less to the room than to the shape of what had just been said.

“Miller may have been trying to be helpful. Helpful people often give too much or too little. They don’t give clean facts. They give facts wrapped in apologies, or facts they think you want. I want the wrapping too.”

The desk phone rang.

Lena’s hand moved toward it, then stopped.

One ring.

Two.

She lifted the receiver on the third.

“Go ahead,” she said.

The voice on the other end was low, nearly lost under the hiss of steam and the clatter of cups. Lena’s expression didn’t change, but her shoulders went still in a way that had nothing to do with patience and everything to do with attention.

“When?” she asked.

A pause.

“Alone?”

Another pause.

Lena’s gaze dropped to the card on the desk. The message she had written sat there in small, slanted letters, waiting.

“What did they order?” she asked. “Did they drink it?”

Her thumb pressed lightly against the receiver.

“Did they have the file?”

The answer came quick this time. Lena’s eyes narrowed, not with surprise, but with the quiet satisfaction of a line pulled taut.

“Under their arm,” she repeated. “Or in a bag?”

She listened.

“Cash,” she said. “Did they say anything to you?”

The voice on the other end grew a little longer. Lena didn’t interrupt. Outside, another car passed on Mercer Street, tires whispering over damp pavement.

“Did they ask if anyone had been asking?” she said.

This time the silence lasted longer.

Lena’s jaw tightened.

“Anyone in particular?” she asked. “Description. Coat. Age. Did they look like they worked nearby, or like they were waiting?”

A beat.

“No name,” Lena said. “Good. If they come back, you don’t know me. If they ask about anyone asking, you say there’s been too many people in too much of a hurry and you can’t keep faces straight. You understand?”

She listened for another moment, then hung up without saying goodbye.

For a few seconds, she didn’t move. The office seemed to contract around her, smaller and quieter than before, the blinds cutting the fading light into thin gray lines across the floor.

Then she looked back at the notebook.

“Torres was at the cart,” she said. “Recently. Alone. Carried a folder under one arm, not in a bag. Paid cash. Didn’t drink the coffee.”

She let that sit for half a breath.

“And asked whether anyone had been asking about them.”

Her fingers rested near the card but didn’t touch it.

“That changes the temperature. If Torres already knows someone’s moving around the edges, then this card isn’t just a message anymore. It’s confirmation.”

She leaned back just enough for the chair to creak once.

“It also means we don’t rush to hand it over. A person who asks whether someone’s been asking is a person who’s already decided they’re being watched. We need to know whether they want to be found, or whether they’re trying to find whoever’s behind them.”

Her gaze sharpened.

“Miller’s name just got more important. If he knew Torres was still carrying the file, then he’s closer to this than he looked. If he didn’t, then somebody gave him just enough to point you in the right direction without telling you what you’d walk into.”

She pushed the envelope a little closer across the desk.

“Finish writing what you remember. Every detail. Then check the photos again. If there’s anything on the backs, even a mark that looks like nothing, I want it noted.”

The phone remained silent now, but it had the look of something that might not stay that way.

“And if Miller gave you a number,” Lena added, “don’t call it. Not from here. Not from your cell. Not yet. If he’s nervous, his phone may be the first place someone looks when they want to know who he’s been talking to.”

She looked toward the blinds, where the street had begun to darken at the edges.

“We’re not going to the Ninth. We’re not standing on the steps waiting for Torres to come out. If Torres is moving, we let the movement bring them somewhere we can see them without being seen first.”

Her eyes returned to the card.

“For now, we keep the card. We keep the name. And we find out whether George Miller was trying to help you, or whether he was trying to see how far you’d go once you had a name to follow.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I gulp, suddenly feeling the weight of all this.* "George didn't give me a number. He just... gave me the name and the photos, said he'd heard things. But he did say 'M. Torres' like he was sure of it, not guessing." *I start writing down everything else I can remember about George, my hand shaking slightly.* "He wore a dark blue jacket. Kept looking at the stairwell, not the street. And he didn't touch the photos at all."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena listened without interrupting. Her eyes stayed on the notebook page, on the words forming in uneven lines, and when the pen trembled she didn’t tell the hand to steady.

“Dark blue jacket,” she said. “Write whether it was new enough to remember or old enough to disappear into. Nylon, wool, canvas. Did it zip or button? Was there a logo on the chest, a stain on the cuff, a tear near the pocket? If it was too warm for the room, he wore it because he needed the pockets. If it was too thin, he left somewhere fast.”

She tapped one fingertip against the desk, slow and deliberate.

“Stairwell, not street. That’s the detail. He wasn’t watching traffic. He wasn’t worried about faces behind glass. He was listening for footsteps inside the building. That means the thing he feared had already gotten close enough to use a door.”

Her gaze moved to the photographs, still stacked neatly beside the file.

“He didn’t touch them because he wanted them to stop being his. Or because he’d already handled them too much and knew it. Either way, he passed them over like something that had started burning his hands.”

She let the silence sit for a beat.

“But the initial is what matters. M. Torres. He didn’t say ‘a detective named Torres.’ He didn’t guess. He gave you the initial like someone who had seen it written somewhere, or heard it used by people who didn’t waste words. That means access. That means somebody close to paperwork, or close to the people who make it.”

She reached for the card she had written, then stopped herself and left it where it lay.

“We don’t move it yet.”

The phone rang.

One ring.

Two.

Lena lifted the receiver on the third.

“Go ahead.”

The coffee cart came through the line again — steam, cups, the low murmur of people in a hurry. The voice on the other end was lower this time, tighter.

Lena’s shoulders went still.

“They came back?” she asked.

A pause.

“Alone?”

Another pause.

Her eyes moved to the client’s notebook, to the words *dark blue jacket* and *stairwell*.

“Did they ask anything?” she said.

The answer came quick.

Lena’s jaw tightened.

“About a man?” she asked. “Description.”

She listened.

“Dark blue jacket,” she said quietly. “Nervous. Looking at the stairwell.”

Her gaze lifted to the blinds.

“Did they use a name?”

A pause.

“No name,” Lena said. “Good. Did they have the folder?”

Another pause.

“Under their arm,” she said. “Not in a bag. Which way did they go?”

The voice on the other end grew longer. Lena’s eyes narrowed.

“Not toward the precinct,” she said. “That’s useful. Any car waiting?”

A beat.

“Color?”

She listened.

“Gray,” she said. “Don’t try for the plate unless you can do it without leaving the cart. If it comes back, call me. If anyone else asks about me, you don’t know the name. If anyone asks about the man in the jacket, you saw too many people and not enough faces.”

She let the silence settle.

“That’s right,” she said. “You’re doing yourself a favor by forgetting.”

She hung up.

For a moment, the office felt smaller than before. The chemical smell from the dry cleaner below seemed to thicken, mixing with the old coffee and the dust warmed by the lamp. Lena looked at the card on the desk, then at the file, then at the notebook where the client had written George Miller’s name.

“Torres just went looking for a man in a dark blue jacket,” she said.

She didn’t raise her voice. She didn’t need to.

“That means your witness either got himself noticed, or somebody used him as a flag to see who would move.”

She picked up the card, read the message once, then set it face down.

“If Torres is hunting Miller, this card becomes a threat. If Torres is trying to warn him, it becomes a lifeline. We don’t know which yet, so we don’t send it into the world blind.”

Her fingers rested on the edge of the desk.

“It also means Miller may not be safe just because he walked away from you. People who give names get remembered. People who hand over photographs get noticed. And people who look at stairwells usually have a reason to keep looking at them.”

She pushed the notebook a little closer, but didn’t take it from the client.

“Finish what you have. Then add every place Miller mentioned, even if it seemed useless. A street name. A bus route. A bar. A church. A building with a stairwell he knew too well. Did he say where he came from? Did he say where he had to be? Did he mention a job, a neighborhood, a train line? Even a complaint about the weather can put a man somewhere if you listen hard enough.”

Her eyes moved to the window, where the last of the daylight had gone thin and gray.

“We need to find George Miller before he tries to find us. And we need to know whether Torres is looking for him to protect him, pressure him, or shut him up.”

She looked back at the desk, at the file, at the card turned face down like something waiting to be judged.

“So tell me where you met him. Did he choose the place? Was it near his home, near his work, or halfway between nowhere and nowhere? And when he said ‘M. Torres,’ was he looking at you — or at the stairwell?”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *My hand is shaking more now, the pen scratching nervously on the page.* "We met at the diner on 3rd. He chose it. Said it was 'neutral ground.' He was looking at me when he said 'M. Torres,' but he kept glancing at the door after he said it."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Stew is what's hot, and lucky for you it's the only thing worth ordering anyway. Venison, rosemary, root vegetables. Old Pell makes it, and he'll tell you it's nothing special, and he'll be lying through what's left of his teeth."

Maren reached beneath the bar with her left hand and came up with a deep clay bowl. She ladled a full portion without consulting the traveler further — anyone road-worn enough to ask for 'whatever's hot' wasn't in the mood for reciting a menu. A thick slice of dark bread went on the side.

"Room's four coppers. Six with breakfast, and you want it with breakfast, because Pell's honey porridge is worth the difference on its own and I don't haggle before people have eaten."

She set the bowl down in front of the stranger, then paused, rag still draped over her left forearm. Her eyes went, briefly and without apology, to the pack — settled down careful as a sleeping infant. She'd watched merchants handle ledgers that way. Couriers with letters that could start small wars. One woman with an egg she swore was a dragon's, which had turned out to be a very committed fraud and a very ordinary goose.

She didn't ask. Asking was the fastest way to get lied to, and the stew was getting cold.

"There's a hook under the end of the bar if your pack would rather sit up straight. Spoon's beside the bowl. Ale's local and honest — wine's imported and a crime against your coin, so I'll pretend I didn't offer."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod, a small smile touching my lips at her description of the stew.* "Sounds perfect. And the room with breakfast, then." *I glance at my pack, then shrug and leave it on the floor. I pick up the spoon.* "Ale, then, if it's honest."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Honest as anything that's been fermented," Maren said. "Which is to say it tells you the truth the next morning whether you asked for it or not."

She took a tankard down from the shelf with her left hand and pulled the tap on the local cask. The ale came out amber and unbothered, a modest finger of foam at the top — poured properly, because she'd served enough soldiers to know the difference between generous and sloppy. She set it at the traveler's right side, then cut a second slice of the dark bread and slid it onto the board without being asked. People who ordered 'whatever's hot' were always hungrier than they admitted.

"Six coppers for room and breakfast. Pay me when it suits — before you leave, ideally. I've held a cloak or two as collateral in my time and only ever had to sell one, so we can be civilized about it."

Down the bar, the dwarf folded his letter, unfolded it, and read it a fourth time. Maren noted it the way she noted everything, and let it go.

"One thing I will need from you, and it isn't your story or your destination. It's a name for the ledger. First name's plenty if you're particular about the rest." She tapped the tally sheet with two fingers. "I write 'traveler' too many nights running and Pell starts mixing up the rooms, and then I've got a tinker sleeping in the dyer's bed and two very unhappy craftsman come sunrise."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The plate arrived on Maren's bar trailing the smell of the sea, and she regarded it the way she regarded all gifts that came unasked: with courtesy, and from a short distance.

"Well now." She did not reach for it. Her left hand kept up its slow work at the far end of the counter. "Tell Lord Havel I'm obliged, but I don't care for seafood. Never have. Couldn't acquire the taste."

She caught the eye of Bram, the younger of her two servers, and tipped her chin at the plate. "Take that back to the gentleman's table with my compliments, and wipe the bar where it sat. Crab and my stew don't share a counter. Pell would take it personal."
