To the traveler, she added, "It's yours if you've a mind for it, friend. I won't have good food sent away on my account. But it sits at your end of the bar, not mine."

While she spoke, she turned the name over. Lord Havel. She didn't know one, which meant he was new money, far off, or invented. Merchants who fed strangers at a crossroads inn were usually selling something or apologizing for something. She filed it away with the dwarf and his letter.

"Fresh from the coast this morning," she said, mostly to the tankard she was filling. "The coast is four days east. Either his couriers have wings, or the story is fresher than the crab."

She slid the ale across. "And whenever you've settled on a name, I'm still one short for the ledger."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow at the crab cakes, then shrug as they're whisked away.* "A long journey tends to cure most pickiness, but I'll stick with the stew for now." *I take a sip of the ale.* "Name's Elara."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Elara." Maren said it once to fix it in place, then wrote it into the ledger with the charcoal stub that hung on a string by the register. Left-handed, quick strokes, letters neat as a fence line — quartermaster's penmanship, though she'd have denied it under oath. "Elara's plenty. Room nine. Up the stairs, turn left, last door on the right. It faces the yard, so you'll get the chickens instead of the cart traffic. Some people find that a fair trade. The rest come down at dawn and I tell them the chickens were here first."

She tucked the ledger under the bar and answered the earlier remark without looking up from the tap she was checking. "Travel cures most pickiness, that's true enough. Mine's a conviction, though. I've held it longer than I've held this tavern, and I'm loyal to it the way some men are loyal to a losing horse."

The kitchen window scraped open and Old Pell's head appeared in it, all beard and disapproval. "Someone's put shellfish in my house."

"Sorted, Pell. Bram's carrying it back as we speak. Mind your pot."

The window scraped shut.

Bram returned, wiping his hands, and leaned close. "He wants you to know the coast is 'closer than you'd think,'" the boy reported. "Also that he's a lord."

"Mm." Maren took the cloth from him and folded it over the bar rail, voice pitched for the two of them and no one else. "I've seen coastal crab, Bram. Those were crayfish out of a mill pond, drowned in butter and told to hold their breath. Which means our lord is either a fool paying silver for fraud, or a man who wants us to think he is. Carry back my compliments anyway. No sense making an enemy over pond life."

She straightened and nodded at the bowl at Elara's elbow.

"Eat while it's hot, friend. And if his lordship tries to buy you anything else, do me the courtesy of checking it's not crawling first."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"'Damn' is a strong word for a bowl of stew, friend. It was raised modest. It embarrasses easy."

She said it without a flicker of expression, and let Elara sort out whether it had been a joke.

Then she touched two knuckles to the bar rail — a small salute, more soldier's toast than drinker's, though if anyone asked she'd have said she learned it from her aunt. "To Pell, then. He won't thank you for it. He'll tell you the venison ran tough this week and the rosemary's past its season. Then tomorrow he'll put in double the rosemary out of pure vindication. I've watched him do it for eleven years."

She rapped the kitchen window with her left hand. "Pell. Compliment at the bar. Best in months, from a guest with no reason to flatter."

The window scraped open an inch. "Guest has been on the road," came the reply, muffled by beard and steam. "Road food rots the judgment."

The window scraped shut.

"You see what I live with," Maren said.

Bram drifted back over, collecting empty bowls as cover. He leaned in, voice low. "He laughed when I carried the plate back. Then he asked if you were spoken for."

The cloth in Maren's left hand stopped for exactly one second. "And what did you tell him?"

"That I hadn't the nerve to ask."

"Good lad. The nerve's the expensive part." She took the bowls from him and nudged him toward the far tables with an elbow. To Elara, she said, "That's the establishment you're sleeping in tonight. Free crab one minute, courtship the next. I don't care for seafood and I trust lords less, and I've no patience for either arriving uninvited."

She nodded at the emptying bowl.

"There's more in the pot. Second helping's free for anyone who toasts the cook — he doesn't know that's the rule, and if you mention it to him I'll swear on my ledger you lied."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, shaking my head.* "Sounds like a lively place you've got here. And a good stew. I'll take that second helping." *I push my bowl forward.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren took the bowl with her left hand and filled it to the same generous line as the first — full measure, another slab of the dark bread set alongside. Road hunger didn't quit after one bowl. She'd learned that on her own stomach twenty years back.

The kitchen window scraped open before the ladle was back in the pot.

"That's her second," Pell said, beard first.

"It's the same bowl, Pell. She eats slow."

"The first was full to the rim. This one's full to the brim. That's a finger's difference."

"Then the bowl swelled. Stew does that."

The window scraped shut with the air of a man filing the matter away for later. Maren set the food in front of Elara, face unmoved.

"He knows. He's known for years. He lets me think he doesn't know, and I let him think I think he doesn't. It's an arrangement. We've run it since my second winter here and neither of us would survive the indignity of naming it."

Down the bar, the dwarf had finally stopped reading his letter and taken to staring into his ale instead, which Maren judged to be progress of a kind.

Then a young man in a coat too fine for the room approached, carrying two cups of red wine on a small tray. He set one at Elara's elbow with some ceremony. "From Lord Havel, for the lady traveler. He asks only that she drink his health."

Maren looked at the wine, then at the bottle the man held, and something dry settled into her voice.

"That's from my cellar. The red the merchant swears came over the mountains. I call it the expensive mistake." She nodded at the cup without touching it. "So his lordship bought it off me an hour ago at my prices and is now buying goodwill with it at my bar. I can't fault his taste in venues."

The servant withdrew. Maren folded her arms on the counter and spoke quieter, without contractions, the way she did when a thing was worth the extra syllables.

"It's not poisoned, Elara. It's just overpriced, and in my experience that's the more common sin. It's yours to drink or let sit. I'll only say this once and then leave it: the man asked after my situation before he finished his crab, and a man who spends silver on strangers within the hour of meeting them is lonely, selling something, or already spoken for. Occasionally all three at once."

She picked up the tally sheet again, giving the moment back to Elara.

"Your health's your own business. I just prefer my guests making their decisions with the arithmetic done."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The clock struck twelve, and Maren let it finish. She never talked over it — rude to interrupt anyone mid-sentence, and the clock was the only thing in the building that kept a schedule.

On the last chime, she set down the tally sheet. From under the bar, well back where the cheap bottles weren't, she brought up a squat glass bottle and two small cups. She poured with her left hand, two measured fingers in each, no spill, no thought about it — the sort of pour that had been done so many times it had worn its own groove.

One cup she kept. The other she carried down to the far end of the bar and set before the last stool, nudging it square with the rail. She stood there a moment with her palm flat on the wood, saying nothing to anyone.

Then she came back, raised her own cup an inch — to the room in general, as far as any observer could tell — and drank it down in one easy swallow.

"House habit," she said, before a question could get its boots on. "Midnight, every night, two pours. The glass at the end belongs to nobody you'll meet, and nobody touches it until morning. Not you, not Bram, not Pell — especially not Pell, who tried to claim it for his sauce pot once and has never been fully forgiven."

She rinsed her cup and set it upside down on the drying board, and that was the whole of the ceremony. Her voice went back to its usual weather.

"That's all there is to tell, and it's more than I usually tell, so we'll leave the rest where it lies. Now. It's midnight, your room's made up, and the chickens start their nonsense around dawn whether you've slept or not. Can I pour you anything last, or are you the sensible sort who quits while the quitting's cheap?"

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "I'll take the sensible route, I think." *I push my empty ale mug forward.* "The stew and the company have been more than enough."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"The company does not appear on the bill," Maren said. "It's the stew you're paying for. But I'll take the review. I'm having it painted over the door — 'The stew and the company: more than enough.' Pell gets top billing. He'll pretend not to care, and then he'll stand outside reading it to the chickens."

She took the empty mug with her left hand — turned it once for chips, pure habit — and set it in the basin. From the key board behind her came a heavy iron key stamped with a nine, and she laid it on the wood between them.

"Room nine, up the stairs and left. You bar the door from inside, and nobody comes up after the clock. Not me, not Bram, and not his lordship's man if he's taken with reciting verse under windows. That bar's oak and it's held against worse than poetry. Six coppers whenever it suits you — I've your name in the ledger, and that's collateral enough for one night."

Around the room, the place was folding itself up. The dwarf tucked his letter into his coat and paid without a word. Lord Havel's table settled their bill, and Maren charged him for the wine without one copper of courtesy discount, and wished him a night as uneventful as his crab was fresh.

She made her rounds banking the lamps with her left hand and left the far end of the bar alone, so the untouched cup sat in its own small dark.

At the bar again, she folded her cloth and spoke without contractions, which was how Elara could tell the words were meant.

"One last thing, and then you sleep. You carried that pack like it mattered, and gave me a first name and no more, and I asked nothing, and I mean to keep it that way. But if you find you want a quiet table and a closed door, or a second pair of eyes on anything written — the snug's at breakfast, no questions with it. Questions you'll get from Pell, free of charge, whether you want them or not."

She nodded toward the stairs.

"Good night, Elara. Chickens start at dawn. They were here first."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Thanks, Maren." *I pick up the key, the weight of it solid in my palm.* "And good night to you too." *I give the mysterious pack a quick, almost unconscious pat, then head for the stairs.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched her go as far as the landing — the careful pack, that second unconscious pat, the key fisted like it might be reclaimed by force. She'd catalogued the same things at the door hours ago and catalogued them again now, and arrived at the same conclusion: nothing she could name, and nothing she needed to. Packs and first names kept their own counsel until they didn't.

"Fourth step from the top creaks," she called up, not loud. "It's been doing it since before my aunt owned the place. I refuse to negotiate with it."

Presently a door thumped shut overhead, and a moment later the iron bar found its bracket on the other side of it. Good. A guest who barred her door on the first night was a guest who'd slept rough somewhere worth sleeping rough about.

The kitchen window scraped open. "The one in nine," Pell said. "What's her trade?"

"Her trade is eating stew and going to bed, Pell."

"Hm." He considered this at length. "She toasted me twice."

"Once. I toasted with you."

"Twice," Pell said, and shut the window with dignity.

Bram took his pay and a heel of bread and let himself out. The merchants had gone up to three and four an hour past, still arguing grain at a volume that promised a sunrise rematch. At the front door, Maren dropped the oak bar into its brackets and glanced through the shutter. Two lanterns from Lord Havel's party were going down the east road. Toward the coast. At midnight.

She watched until the dark took them.

"Nobody travels east at midnight unless they're paid for it or running from it," she said to nobody. "And crab keeps for neither."

She counted the till — quick, left-handed, done before she'd finished thinking about it — and wrote a single line in the ledger. *Elara. Room nine. Six coppers, pending.* A first name and a careful pack, filed in her head beside a dwarf and his letter and a lord and his pond life. Some nights the most honest thing in the book was what it didn't say.

The cup at the end of the bar sat where she'd left it, in its own small dark. She didn't touch it and didn't look long — just rested two knuckles on the rail as she passed, an old habit in an old place, and banked the last lamp.

She left the Antler to the banked fires, the sleeping house, and the chickens, who would begin their nonsense at dawn precisely because they could. Breakfast was honey porridge, and the snug was there if it was asked for, and Pell's questions were free of charge either way.

Morning would tell her what the ledger didn't.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I lay in bed, listening to the tavern settle down. The creaking step Maren mentioned was a good landmark. My hand goes to the pack beside the bed. Whatever tomorrow brings, at least I'll have a full belly.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren was awake before the chickens, which she regarded as the last real authority she had over them.

She came down in the dark and dealt with the cup at the end of the bar first, the way she always did — emptied it into the stone sink, rinsed it, set it upside down beside the squat bottle where it would wait for midnight to come around again. Eleven seconds, start to finish. She hadn't had to think about any of them in six years, and didn't start now.

Then fires, banked coals breathed back to life. Then the bar across the front door lifted, and the grey hour came in over the crossroads, and she stood in the yard with her breath steaming while the chickens began their nonsense right on schedule, shrill and self-important, as though the sun required their supervision.

The east road, she noted, had been busy. The mud at the crossing held the churn of several horses going out around midnight. And one set, fresh over the top of it, coming back in the dark before dawn — single rider, moving quick, headed west. She'd heard the hooves pass while she was lying awake doing sums, and she'd finished the sums now: whoever went east with Lord Havel's lanterns, somebody came home alone and in a hurry.

She filed it and went in to start the day.

The dwarf's table was wiped and his stool pushed in square. The tidy ones worried her more than the messy ones. She let it go.

The kitchen window scraped open at half past dawn. "The rosemary is fresh," Pell said, beard first, and there was a smell rolling out behind him that suggested he'd put in double and was daring the world to comment.

"It's November, Pell."

"The rosemary," he said, "is fresh."

The window scraped shut with the satisfaction of a man closing an argument he'd won by himself.

Bram arrived shortly after, hair full of straw and no good explanation for it. Marit came through the back with the milk, the older and steadier of his two servers, and set to laying the common room without being told, which was why Maren had never once had to raise her voice inside these walls.

Maren stirred the porridge herself while Pell handled the stew pot — he trusted her with exactly one dish and she'd earned it over eleven years. Honey, a pinch of salt, low heat, her mother's silver ring flashing dull on her left thumb as she turned the spoon. She set the big pot on the hob, laid out bowls and the dark bread, and then, on her way past, banked the little fire in the snug and left that door standing ajar.

She said nothing about it to anyone, least of all the house.

"Breakfast is on when you are, room nine," she called up the stairs — not loud, because the walls had enough noise without her adding to it. "Porridge doesn't hold well, and Pell takes cold porridge as a personal insult. He'll also want to know your trade, and I'll warn you now that I've stopped protecting guests from him. Costs me nothing and it keeps him humble."

Down in the yard, the chickens escalated. Maren folded her arms on the bar rail and watched the east road through the shutter, where the morning sat empty and told her nothing.

"Six coppers whenever you're ready," she added, to the stairs in general. "No hurry. The ledger's patient. I'm the one they say isn't, and I'd like to keep surprising them."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I stir, the morning light filtering through the small window. Pell's voice drifts up from downstairs, along with the smell of honey and something savory. My stomach rumbles in agreement.* "Be down in a moment!"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Take your time," Maren called back. "The porridge holds better than Pell claims. He just likes an audience while it's steaming. Audiences are how he knows it worked."

The common room filled by degrees. The two grain merchants came down and resumed hostilities over breakfast without bothering to greet one another, picking up mid-sentence as though the night had been a brief intermission in a very long negotiation. Marit kept ahead of them with bread and cider. Bram ate his own porridge standing at the hearth, straw still in his hair, contributing nothing, which was his usual morning contribution.

The kitchen window scraped open. "Is she up?"

"She's up."

"Good. I've decided what she is."

"Have you."

"Dyer's apprentice. Or courier. The pack's wrong for a dyer — too narrow." A pause while he reconsidered eleven years of police work. "She's not the goose-egg woman come back again?"

"Different chin entirely, Pell."

"Hm." The window scraped shut, unconvinced.

Marit came through the back with eggs and paused at the bar, voice low. "Someone watered a horse at the trough before first light. Didn't stop otherwise. Westbound."

Maren nodded once and filed it with the churned mud — in a hurry, out before dawn, and nobody's business yet. "Empty the trough and fill it fresh. First impression of the place shouldn't be last night's leavings."

She stirred the porridge herself, low heat, honey, the pinch of salt that Pell pretended not to know about — the one dish in the house she was allowed to touch, and she guarded the privilege. She ladled a deep bowl, set out the dark bread and the honey crock at the bar where Elara had sat the night before, and poured her own small portion to eat standing, one elbow on the counter, the way she'd eaten breakfast for twenty years.

Then the fourth step from the top gave its opinion, right on schedule, still refusing all negotiation.

"There she is," Maren said, nodding at the set place. "Sit. Porridge, honey, bread, and Pell's already guessed your trade three separate times and reported all three to me through glass. If you want the pleasure of disappointing him, do it at the window — he takes correction best through glass. It's the only way he stays humble and it's Touching at my age."

She tapped the ledger where it lay. "Six coppers, whenever. The book's patient and I'm only rumored not to be."

Then she tipped her head, slightly, toward the back of the room, where the snug door stood ajar with the little fire banked warm behind it. She didn't explain it. She'd left it ajar without a word to anyone and saw no reason to start explaining now.

"One thing while you eat, and it's innkeeper's talk, nothing more. Which way are you pointed when you go? Because the east road did a fair amount of business at midnight, and somebody came back alone before dawn without stopping to sleep. Might be nothing. I've just served at this crossroads long enough to know that 'might be nothing' and 'is nothing' are different animals, and only one of them shows up for breakfast."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I settle onto the stool, my stomach already rumbling.* "Morning, Maren. And Pell, I suppose." *I pick up the spoon, a small smile playing on my lips.* "As for my trade, he's half right. I'm a courier, of sorts." *I glance briefly towards the open snug door.* "And west, mostly. Always west."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Hot is easy tonight." Maren raised her voice not at all — the kitchen pass was close enough that she'd never needed to. "Pell. One bowl, bread on the side."

A grunt came back through the window. In Old Pell's language, that meant *yes*, possibly also *about time*.

She drew an ale with her left hand and slid it across the bar. "Stew's two coppers, ale's one. The wine is four and tastes like it, so I won't be offended when you skip it." She tucked the tally sheet under the till stone, a habit of half-finished work. "Room's five for the night — that's a bed, a lock on the door, and breakfast if you're down before Pell decides it's lunch instead. I've got nine sitting empty, so take your pick of anything that isn't under the eaves. That one I keep for people I don't like."

Her eyes flicked once to the pack. The way it had gone down — slow, balanced, like something inside it shouldn't be jostled. She'd seen that manner of setting a bag down maybe a hundred times over the years. It preceded either a very quiet night or a very loud one, and the odds had always struck her as about even. She filed it away and said nothing.

"Name, if you're willing to give one," she said, pulling a slim ledger from beneath the bar and opening it with her thumb, the silver ring catching lamplight. "I keep a book. Habit from an old life. It makes the tax collectors feel watched, which I consider a public service."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Traveler will do for now." I take a long drink of the ale. It's cold and good. "Sounds like a fair price for the room." I nod towards the pack, a small, worn leather-wrapped parcel. "Just some… breakables in here. Nothing exciting."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Traveler." Maren wrote it in the ledger with her left hand, the letters square and even — a soldier's hand, all function, no flourish. "'For now' is the honest part. Most folk who'd rather not give a name invent one anyway and expect me to pretend otherwise." She set the quill across the inkwell. "When the 'for now' wears off, tell me. Ink forgives more than people do."

She unhooked a key from the board behind her — iron, on a wooden fob worn smooth as riverstone — and laid it beside the ale. "Number six, end of the hall. Nobody walks past it but the cat, and she's quieter than my regulars."

The stew came through the pass a moment later, bread balanced on the bowl's rim, steam curling up rosemary-scented. Maren set it down with her left hand. "Careful with that. Pell's bowls hold heat like a grudge."

She gave the pack one more look — steady, brief, the way she looked at everything. "Nothing exciting," she repeated, and there was no accusation in it, only the dry tone of a woman keeping score out of habit. "Nobody tells me their bag is boring unless they've caught me looking at it. Fair enough. I look at everyone's bag — occupational habit, not suspicion." She took up her bar cloth again. "Whatever's in there is your business. What happens under my roof is mine. As long as your breakables and your evening both stay quiet, you and I will get along famously."

Behind her, the grain merchants had reached the stage of agreeing loudly, which was somehow louder than disagreeing. She let it be.

"Eight coppers all told — two for the bowl, one for the ale, five for the bed. Now or at first light, whichever suits you. Twice in eighteen years somebody's walked out owing me, and both times they had to come back through this crossroads eventually." She said it the way she said everything: level, unhurried, like a remark about weather. "They paid."

Then she fished the tally sheet back out from under the till stone and returned to her columns, as though the ledger, the stew, and the careful little parcel were all just pieces of an ordinary evening. In her experience, they usually were.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Wren ferried the plate over from the merchant's table and set it on the bar between them, careful with it in the way people always were with somebody else's generosity. The cakes sat golden in their oil, smelling of brine and frying and the long road inland. The grain men paused mid-agreement to watch it travel, because free food moving through a room draws every eye in it.

Maren gave the plate a look. Then she gave the merchant a nod — the same nod she gave the cattle drovers, which she considered the correct amount of nod for anybody, lord or otherwise.

"Lord Havel's compliments," she said. "Well. That's neighborly of him. I've kept this house eighteen years and the man has never once come through that door. His tax collector I see every quarter, regular as migrating geese. I'll pass the lord's regards along next time his man is here counting my kegs."

She didn't touch the plate. She folded her bar cloth over twice — a habit older than the cloth itself — and nudged it down the counter with the flat of her left hand until it came to rest in front of the Traveler, beside the stew.

"You're welcome to my half. I've never cared for seafood — nothing against the crab, we simply never came to an understanding." A sentence worn smooth from use, all its edges gone. "And since the crab came free, here's something free to go with it: the finest crab in any region gets eaten within sight of the boat that caught it. The coast road is a day and a half for a good team, and that's before the toll queue at Marrow Ford, which is wide enough to picnic in. That crab has been traveling longer than you have, friend."

Her eyes went once to the merchant's table — not a stare; staring was for people who wanted to be caught at it. By the time she glanced, he was studying the bottom of his cup, which in her experience meant he'd watched the plate arrive and preferred that fact go unnoticed.

"Friendly advice, worth exactly what it costs you: when a stranger buys you the finest of anything, he is generally about to ask for something worth more than it. Not always. But often enough that I stopped betting against it years ago." She took up the tally sheet and found her place in the columns. "Your business is your business, and your stomach's its own master. But if it were mine, I'd trust the bowl I paid for. Pell's stew has never had anything in it but stew — he takes that as a matter of professional honor."

She bent back to her figures, though her eyes kept making their slow circuit of the room — the grain men, the dwarf's letter, the merchant and his cup, the door with its creak. In her experience, an evening that opened with free crab generally closed with somebody owing somebody an explanation. She set the odds at even and carried the one.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I glance at the crab cakes, then back at Maren, a small smile playing on my lips. "A day and a half, huh? That *is* a long journey for a crab." I push the plate back towards the middle of the bar. "You've convinced me. Stew it is. But I appreciate the warning." I dig into my stew, savoring the rosemary.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Longer than some pilgrimages I've hosted," Maren said. "Though the pilgrims at least got a say in the trip." The corner of her mouth moved a quarter inch, which from her was close to applause.

She caught Wren's eye and tipped her chin at the plate. That was the entire conversation — six years working together had done away with the second half. Wren ferried the crab back toward the merchant's table, level and careful, and Maren leaned a hip against the till and spoke under the room's noise, for the Traveler's ears alone.

"He was through in the spring, that one. Ferren, if I have the name right. Paid his bill, asked a great many questions about the east road — who was traveling it, what they carried — and drank less than a man needs to drink to ask that many questions. Bought nothing, sold nothing, gone by mid-morning." She straightened. "He was shopping then. Looks like he still is."

When the plate had gone, she wiped the stretch of bar where it had rested — twice, cloth folded double over her left hand, with rather more thoroughness than oak requires.

Across the room, the dwarf folded his letter along its old creases and signaled Wren for another ale. He had read it three times since arriving. Maren's money was on bad news; nobody rereads good news.

The merchant watched his crab come home the way a man watches a hand of cards lose. Then he rose, tugged his coat straight, and crossed the floor unhurried — good wool, soft hands, rings on three fingers, the build of a man who had made a career of being agreeable. He took the stool one down from the Traveler and folded his hands on the bar.

"Forgive me. It seems my crab aged worse on the road than I did." The smile was well kept. "Ferren. I run the coast road for Lord Havel's household — the household, mind, not the tax office, before you hold that against me." He nodded at the stew bowl, courteous. "No hard feelings there. I would have picked the stew myself." Then, settling in: "I'll say my piece plainly, since we're strangers and strangers can afford plainness. I noticed how you set that pack down. I notice packs for a living — glasswork, instruments, anything that resents a hard road. I buy it, pack it, and get it to Havel's people unbroken. Twenty years of that teaches the eye."

He spread his hands, the rings catching lamplight. "My wagons go east at first light. Well-sprung, straw-packed, walked and never trotted, and my drivers are the only two men on this road I would trust with a crate of good glass. If dawn finds you eastbound, there is a place in the wagons — no charge. I would sooner have a careful man's company on that road than the quiet." A pause, timed like everything else about him. "So. Which way are you bound?"

Maren turned a clean glass upside down on the rack. "That is two free things in one evening," she said, to the glass rather than to either of them. "In my experience the third one arrives with a price attached."

Ferren smiled at that — unhurried, unoffended, the smile of a man who had been called worse by barkeeps in every town between here and the salt water. He did not answer her. He kept his hands folded and waited, and his question sat on the bar where the plate had been.

Maren did not say *I told you so*. She had never once needed to; the evening was saying it for her. She kept her left hand moving along the counter and her eyes making their rounds — the rings, the bowl, the pack, the door with its creak — and in her private ledger, the odds on a quiet night quietly moved.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"To Old Pell." Maren let the oath pass without comment — a man's vocabulary was his own ledger, and in her experience the stew had earned stronger language than most men kept on hand. She leaned toward the kitchen pass, voice no higher than it ever was. "Pell. You've been toasted. Best in months, says the gentleman."

A grunt came back. Then a second grunt, pitched lower, almost gracious.

"That's him accepting the honor," Maren said. "If he ever puts an actual thank-you into words, I'll oil the door hinge as a day of mourning."

At his table, the dwarf lifted his mug an inch and set it back down — the way his people second a toast without getting involved in one. Maren answered with a short phrase in Dwarvish. The dwarf snorted into his ale, which from a dwarf is about as pretty as applause gets, then caught Wren's sleeve and pointed at the empty stretch of table before him: whatever the rest of the room was having.

"You've sold two bowls tonight," Maren told the Traveler, taking up her cloth. "One to you, one by proxy. Pass through again and remind me — I'll stand you the ale. That's the whole of my advertising. One full mouth at a time, paid in beer."

Ferren had let the toast happen the way a card player lets a folded hand finish without him. When it was done, he turned his cup a quarter-turn on the bar.

"I asked which way you were bound," he said, "and you answered with a toast to the cook. That's an answer of a kind. The polite kind. I'll take it as such." Coin appeared between two ringed fingers and was placed, not tossed, on the wood. "Ale, whatever Pell has left, and a bed if one's going. The wagons and my drivers sleep in your yard tonight, if that suits. I've spent enough nights on straw to know what I pay for them come morning."

Maren drew the ale with her left hand and took the coin with the same. He'd counted it over to the copper, unasked. A man who had practiced being liked. She unhooked a key — number two, near the stairs, at the far end of the hall from number six, a fact she mentioned to no one, ever.

"Kitchen closes within the hour. I'll have Pell hold a bowl back."

Ferren rose, cup in hand. "First light, then. Blue canvas, the big wagon. There's room because the fourth crate is still sitting in the customs shed at Marrow Ford — guild glass, and a guild can wait, which is a lesson they teach everyone eventually." He gave the Traveler a nod polished smooth by twenty years of use. "Eastbound or not, the road's wide enough for both kinds of folk. Good night."

He carried his ale to a different table than the one he'd come from — one facing the yard door. Maren had known soldiers who sat that way, and coachmen, and one very honest tax assessor. It told her nothing except that he'd spent his life around things that could be stolen. As for the crate in the customs shed: the story was tidy. Tidy stories were assembled, not lived. She'd known that since before she owned a bar.

The grain merchants called for their bill, having discovered that agreeing loudly was thirstier work than arguing.

Maren came back down the counter, wiping as she went, and spoke under the room's noise, for the Traveler alone.

"You answered his question with a toast. That was well done. Most men either lie to a stranger or confess to him, and neither habit carries them far. The third road — say nothing, stay pleasant, keep your pack where you can see it — that's the road I'd walk." She folded the cloth double and draped it over her shoulder. "You've until first light to decide which way you're bound, which is longer than most decisions get in this room. And if you want my read on our coast-road friend, ask before midnight. After midnight I'm poor company. Ask anyone who's tried."

She picked the tally sheet back up, but her eyes made one more slow circuit and stopped at the window. The wagons sat dark in the yard, blue canvas gone grey with night, two drivers by a small fire, one of them whittling. Nothing to see.

She looked anyway. Eighteen years had taught her that *nothing* was a thing you confirmed, not assumed.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "He certainly is persistent." I finish my stew, pushing the bowl away. "Sounds like he's looking for something specific. What's your read on him then, Maren? Before you turn into a pumpkin."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Pumpkins are for children's stories," Maren said. "I turn tedious. Same effect, less color." She tipped her chin at the hour-candle burning on the shelf behind the bottles, marked off in rings — a habit she had carried out of an older life than this one. "It is down to its last quarter. You have most of an hour of me yet. Spend it well."

She came along the bar to the Traveler's end and kept her voice under the room's noise.

"You want my read on Ferren. All right. I will count it out like coin, since that is a language everyone reads honestly."

She folded the cloth over her left hand and began.

"One. He was at that table half an hour before you came through the door. One ale in all that time. A man drinking for pleasure drinks faster; a man drinking for posture nurses. I marked it and thought nothing of it, because half my room on any given night is men waiting on nothing. Then you walked in, and inside of five minutes his crab was crossing the floor to you. Men who watch a door that hard are waiting for something particular to come through it. I was slow to it. I will dock my own wages.

"Two. Spring. He asked after the east road — not the tolls, not the bridges, not the price of anything. Who walked it, and what they carried. A man buying freight asks what it costs. A man finding freight asks where it is. Two trades share that road, and he talks like the second one.

"Three. He watched you set that pack down before he ever spoke to you — and told you so himself, plain as a compliment. That was a confession with the edges filed off. The crab was the knock. The wagon is the door.

"Four, and I would hang the most weight here: he did not press. You dodged his question with a toast, and he smiled, paid his bill, and took a bed. A man hunting for his own profit presses, because his profit was standing up to leave. A man on somebody else's errand can afford patience, because the errand does not end tonight. There will be another door tomorrow, and another pack after that. That is not a whim. That is a commission. Somebody wants something that comes through this crossroads, and they have hired agreeable feet to stand in the way of it."

She straightened, one hip against the counter.

"Now the other side of the ledger, because I keep my reads balanced or I do not keep them. Everything he said could be true. Freight men do prize careful passengers — careful with your own crate tends to mean careful with theirs — and wagons run half-empty, and company on a long road is worth more than the seat. If what he is hunting sits east of here and your parcel is genuinely boring, then he is a generous man and you would have the pleasantest ride of your life. That reading exists. I would simply not bet the house on it.

"If you held me down and made me give odds — and I only give odds under duress — I would say three to one he is a finder, working for Havel's household or for somebody borrowing the name. Better than even that what he is finding is in your pack, or near enough to matter. And I have not asked what is in your pack, and I am not starting. It would change the odds. It would not change the advice.

"So. The advice, free as the crab was. Do not board that wagon. If east is your direction, the cooper's cart runs every third morning and charges honest coin — the cheapest thing you will ever buy from a stranger. Or walk; a pack rides lighter on your own back than in another man's net. Or — and this is the one I would choose — sit still a day. Let the blue canvas take a day's lead and watch who else comes through that door asking careful questions. Trouble that waits for you is the best kind there is. It is trouble you can watch leave." A beat. "I'll confess a bias: I like my rooms full and my evenings dull, and a second night buys me both. Weigh my counsel accordingly.

"Last thing, and it is arithmetic, not alarm. He is in room two, by the stairs, and every stair in this house talks — I have meant to silence them as long as I have meant to oil that door. His drivers are in the yard with a fire. There is no way out of this inn tonight that he has not already thought about, and I'd have charged him extra for the net if I'd thought of it first. So sleep on it. Morning will sell you the same decisions, and at a fairer price."

The evening wound down around them. Ferren's table stood empty — gone up somewhere between the dwarf's second bowl and the grain men's bill, without the stairs saying a word. She would have noticed. Usually.

The grain men settled up, haggling over arithmetic she had already checked twice, and went out into the dark still agreeing with each other. The dwarf paid, stopped at the door, and said — in Common he had plainly been saving all evening — that Pell's stew was the only thing on this road worth the toll at Marrow Ford. Then he was gone.

Maren relayed it through the pass. "Pell. Worth the toll, says the dwarf."

A grunt. Then a second, longer one, with something in it that was the nearest Pell ever came to taking off his hat.

Wren stacked bowls and banked the fire. The cat emerged from wherever cats conduct their business and took the dwarf's chair, which everyone had known was hers anyway. Pell shuttered the kitchen pass with a bang that was his version of good night.

The hour-candle guttered down to its final ring.

"There's the hour," Maren said — to no one, and to the room.

She set her cloth down. From beneath the bar she took a bottle she did not sell to anyone and two glasses that matched, and poured with her left hand — two fingers each, unhurried, the way you pour when nobody is waiting on it. She carried one glass to the far end of the bar, where nobody sat, and set it where the lamplight would find it. The other she kept, and drank from, a little, looking at nothing in particular.

She did not explain. She never had. The glass at the end of the bar would sit there until morning, as it always did. She glanced at the Traveler once — not an invitation, not a warning — the kind of look that says some things in a room are furniture.

Then she took up her cloth again, and the Antler settled into the last quiet hour of the night, holding its one small secret the way it held all the others: without comment, and with the lamps turned low.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The clock in the corner took its own counsel about midnight — twelve strokes, each half a breath behind the last, so the hour arrived more than it struck. Maren counted them without looking up from her glass. She counted most things without looking up. It was the whole trick.

"Candle and clock agree tonight," she said, when the last stroke had thinned away into the rafters. "They manage that eleven nights in twelve. On the twelfth I side with the candle — it cannot be wrong by more than the width of a mark, and it has never once had opinions about anything."

She turned her glass a quarter-turn on the wood — left hand, the silver ring catching what the lamp had left — and looked at the Traveler properly. Not the working look, the one that measured packs and counted ales. A plainer one.

"You stayed." Not a compliment and not a complaint. A tally. "All right. The terms change with the hour, so hear them once. The bar closed when the candle did — what's in your hand is the last pour of the night for anyone but me. The till is counted, the kitchen is dark, and everything said between now and first light is off the books. From midnight on I am not the keeper of this house. I am the woman who lives in it. You were warned. Twice, if you count the pumpkin."

She came out from behind the bar and crossed to the corner, unhurried. The case clock's glass front swung open under her hand; the winding key hung inside on its hook. She wound it with her left hand, slow and even, because by this hour the right wrist had opinions about small gears and expressed them at length.

"Bessa bought this off a bankrupt innkeeper for the price of a meal and a bed," she said over her shoulder. "My aunt. She raised me, and she kept this house before me. She said a publican needs a clock big enough to settle arguments without her having to. She was right. In eighteen years it has settled more disputes than the magistrate, and it has never once taken a fee." She closed the glass front. "It also gives me an excuse to stand in the corner at midnight and look out the window, which is its other function."

Which is what she did. The yard lay grey and still. The drivers' fire had burned down to low orange under its stones, set where it could light the yard gate — she would have placed it exactly so herself. One driver was a shape under the wagon canvas. The other sat against a wheel with his knife going, long patient strokes that carried no sound across the yard. Nothing moved on the east road. Nothing moved anywhere. She confirmed it, because nothing was a thing you confirmed, and let the curtain fall back into place.

"The stairs have kept quiet since our coast-road friend went up," she said, coming back along the bar. "Either the man sleeps like the honest, or he already knows which boards talk. I have not decided which of those I would prefer."

She took the stool at the far end of the bar — the end where nobody sat, where the full glass stood in its pool of lamplight. She left a stool's width between herself and it, and the width was not accidental. The cat arrived from the common room, hopped up onto the bar, and walked its length with the gravity of a tax assessor, stopping to inspect the full glass at close range.

"Leave it," Maren said.

The cat considered the instruction, found the glass beneath its interest, and folded itself down on the bar within a paw's reach anyway. Maren permitted this. The cat had seniority in this house and knew it.

"Bring your cup down if you mean to keep talking," she said. "I do not raise my voice at the best of times, and past midnight I won't raise it the length of my own bar."

On the shelf behind the bottles, the hour-candle guttered, found its last ring, and drowned in its own wax. The room narrowed to the banked fire and one lamp. Somewhere under the floor, the settling of an old house ticked and ticked, keeping its own time.

She drank — a little, unhurried — and set the glass down.

"You've had a full evening's worth of me. Advice, odds, a read on a stranger, and a bowl I'll vouch for. After midnight I stop giving things away, so if you mean to sit here, you carry your half." A pause. She was not looking at the Traveler now but at the middle distance where publicans keep their thoughts. "I'll start you easy, since it's a question I only ask after the candle's out. In eighteen years, the folk who stay past midnight come in three kinds. The ones dodging a bed because of what's waiting in it — debts, mostly, sometimes a woman, once a very determined horse. The ones who cannot sleep and would rather be tired in company than tired alone. And the ones with a road ahead they'd rather not think about, who stay up so the road stays tomorrow's problem instead of tonight's."

She turned her glass another quarter-turn.

"Which are you? You needn't answer. I've asked that question two hundred times if once, and the ones who don't answer tell me as much as the ones who do. But I find I'm curious tonight, which is rare at this hour, and I have decided to spend it."

The lamp hissed softly. Down the counter, the full glass sat in its light, untouched. Maren waited the way she counted — without appearing to.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I slide my cup down the bar towards her. "I suppose I'm the third kind, mostly." I take another sip. "Though I've had worse company." I nod towards the untouched glass at the end of the bar. "Who's that for?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The cup came sliding down the bar and Maren stopped it flat-palmed with her left hand, an inch short of the ring.

"'Worse company' is the best review this hour ever gets. Past midnight my competition is the stairs and the cat, and neither of them has bought a drink all night. I'll bank it."

She let the Traveler's answer sit a moment, the way she let coins sit before weighing them. "The third kind, *mostly*. That word's doing heavy lifting, and I'll leave it to its work — you answered straight, and straight answers at midnight are worth more than the questions were. For what it's worth, the third kind keeps the best company. The first kind want to talk about what they owe until I know their debts better than they do. The second want silence and resent needing it. The third just want the road to stay tomorrow's problem — and that I can arrange. It's called a lock on the door, and you already hold the key." A beat. "I won't ask which way you're leaning. I told you I don't ask about packs, and a man's direction is only a pack he hasn't opened yet."

Then the other question.

She looked down the length of the bar to where the glass stood full in its circle of lamplight. For a moment something in her face was older than the room. Then it wasn't, and she turned back.

"You spent it on the one thing in this house that isn't for sale." No frost in it — a door held, not a door slammed. "I called it furniture earlier. That was generous of me. It's the one piece of furniture I dust before all the others, and the only pour under this roof that never gets drunk, and it has stood at that end of my bar every midnight for six years and will stand there every midnight after you and I are both dust. That is the whole of what I will say about it. The terms changed at midnight — they did. That one doesn't.

"You can build whatever story you like on the foundation. Most folk build close to the mark. In eighteen years nobody has built one I confirmed and nobody has built one I corrected, and that is the ceremony entire. It works because nobody pushes at it — and you strike me as a man who knows which doors in a strange house stay shut out of courtesy."

She turned her glass a quarter-turn, left hand, the ring clicking softly against it. "But you answered my question straight, and I keep my ledgers balanced even at this hour. So you're owed one answer at full weight — just not that one. Pick another. I'll show you the shelf. The scar over my eye: payable in full, short story, happy ending. The ring: payable. The cat's name: payable, though she'll deny it. The four wrists: payable, and it's less a story than an inventory. Why I speak Dwarvish well enough to be insulted in it: payable, and long. The glass alone stays in the vault. Choose, and I'll pay out to the copper."

Above them, a stair spoke. One board — third from the landing, by its voice — a soft complaint under weight, then nothing. Maren's head didn't move. Everything behind her eyes did. She counted ten slow breaths of quiet. The house ticked on under the floor. At the end of the bar, the cat's ear swiveled toward the ceiling and back, which was the whole of the cat's opinion.

"Third step," she said at last, level. "A man turning over in his sleep comes down heavy on his heel. A man listening comes down light. I heard light." She let that sit exactly as long as it needed. "So he's awake. Awake men past midnight sort into the same three kinds as everyone else, and a stair won't tell me which he is. Nothing said at this end of my bar carries past the till — I built the room that way on purpose. But mind it all the same. Walls keep accounts, same as I do, and I'd as soon not add to his."

She drank, a little, unhurried. Down the counter, the other glass sat full in its light, and the stool's width between her and it stayed exactly the width it was.

"So. Pick your question, friend. The candle's drowned and the night's already paid for. And I'll confess a wager of my own: what a careful man spends his curiosity on will tell me more than your pack ever could."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "A story with a happy ending, huh?" I push my cup back towards her. "Tell me about the scar."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren slid the cup back down the bar until it rested within the Traveler's reach — not a refill; the terms had been set at midnight and she kept her terms the way she kept her ledgers. Then she touched the scar with the pad of her left thumb, just under the right eyebrow, the way a person checks a coin is still in their pocket.

"The scar, then. Fourteen years old this spring. It aches when the weather turns, which is the only pension my first trade ever paid out, so it earns its keep." She turned her stool a quarter toward him. The lamp sat between them. Down the counter, the cat slept with one ear standing watch, and the full glass stood in its circle of light, and neither was going anywhere. "You'll get your happy ending. It's only sitting in a different part of the story than you're expecting. Most of them are."

She drank, a little, and set the glass down.

"Fourteen years ago, this house was four years mine. Tobin — my husband, then alive, then standing right where Wren stands tonight — worked the bar beside me. It was a Thursday. Wool days, we called them: the teamsters came through with the spring clip, and wool men drink the way other men march — in formation, and until the job is done.

"Harl drove oxen on the coast road. Built like a door, quiet as weather, and he had wintered badly — his wife died of a fever after harvest, and he'd been drinking since the thaw. Slowly. There's a difference between a man drinking to get drunk and a man drinking to stay numb, and you can smell it from across a room. Tobin cut him off at sundown, gentle as anything. Gentleness was Tobin's whole method, and it worked nineteen nights in twenty.

"On the twentieth, Harl stood up and swung at him."

Her voice never rose. It was the same voice she used for the price of a room.

"It wasn't a drunk's wild swing. It was slow, and it carried the whole man with it. I'd been watching him all evening, and I was moving before his shoulder knew what it intended. I meant to catch the arm, and I got most of it — enough that the fist only clipped me. He wore a brass ring. A brass ring on a brow opens like a purse string. The room thought I was dying. I was mostly annoyed.

"I did not learn to step into a punch by carrying trays. Before this house I kept stores for the Kingsguard — five years, quartermaster, and I'll thank you to let that stay between us and the hour. A quartermaster learns two trades nobody thanks her for: where a man's weight is going, and how to stitch. His arm was still coming around, so I put the cudgel across the wrist — left-handed, once. That's wrist number one of the four, so if you ever draw on the inventory, you've already had a piece of it. I'll see it discounted.

"He went down like a felled ox, which was tidy of him, and the room emptied itself of everyone who didn't live here. Head wounds are liars — more blood than a killing, less damage than a shaving cut. Tobin stitched me at this bar, apologizing the whole while, as though the needle had been his idea. It healed crooked anyway. I kept it. A publican does well to have one scar where the customers can see it. It settles arguments before they learn to walk."

The lamp hissed. Somewhere under the floor, the house ticked.

"We put Harl in the yard to sleep it off — the cells in this town are for men who mean things. Then, past one o'clock, I couldn't sleep for thinking of the cold. I'd broken his drinking wrist, and there's no way for a one-handed man to pull a blanket over himself that doesn't end in a bad night. So I took him one. Tobin watched me carry it out, and he said that was the whole of my character in a single act, and that he had married me already knowing it.

"Morning came, and Harl came with it — hat in his good hand, wrist bound to his chest, standing like a boy caught at the jam. He got about half an apology out. I charged him for the ale, the mug his fist went through, and a bowl of stew for the road. The wrist I threw in free."

She turned her glass a quarter-turn, left hand, the ring clicking softly against it.

"He's come through twice a year since. Spring and autumn, ox team, coast road, and he sits at the third table by the window and tells the story to strangers. It grows with every telling. In his version, by now, I am seven feet tall, the cudgel is a roof beam, and the fight lasted the better part of an hour. I have never once corrected him. A man's memory is his own ledger, and his balances in my favor. Auditing it would be poor accounting.

"And that's the happy ending — but not the whole of it. Six years back, when Tobin died, Harl drove his team four days out of his way to stand at the burying. Never said a word to me. Left before the bread was cut. He knew what the winters after are like. That was the blanket, come back around."

She let it sit, the way she let coins sit before weighing them.

"Paid in full. Now my side of the wager. You had the ring, the wrists, the war, and the cat's name on that shelf, and you spent your question on the one story that ends well. In my experience, the man who picks that one is carrying a road he'd like to see end the same way. I'd have bet the house on your choice. Fortunately for the house, I don't bet."

She drank — a little, unhurried.

"And note what the telling cost me, since I pay at full weight. You asked after a scar and got a husband in the bargain. You now hold every material you'd need to build the story at the end of this bar correctly — if you ever choose to build it. Build it quietly. Build it to yourself. That's the entire price on it."

Down the counter, the glass sat full in its light. For once, Maren looked at it while someone watched her look — no explanation offered, none asked. A moment's accounting, no more. Then she took up her cloth, though there was nothing left in the room to wipe, and the Antler held its quiet, and the clock in the corner ticked on toward morning at its own deliberate pace.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I sit with her words for a moment, letting the story settle. "Tobin sounds like he was a good man." I look at the untouched glass at the end of the bar, then back at Maren, a question in my eyes.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"He was," Maren said. "I will say it plainly, because it is true, and true things get said less often than they deserve."

She turned her glass its quarter-turn, slower than usual, the ring clicking once against the rim.

"Tobin ran the people and I ran the numbers. He knew every regular's name, and their children's names, and what they drank before they reached the bar. I knew what they owed and where the kegs were and which of the two mattered more. Between us we kept a fair imitation of a good house." A small breath — in another woman it might have been a laugh. "He could not lie. Not on moral grounds; he simply lacked the equipment. When he watered a man's wine because the man could not pay, he marked it full price in the book, paid the difference out of his own pocket, and blushed about it for an hour, so the whole room always knew. I never told him I knew. It was the only thing he ever got away with, and I let him keep it."

Then, plainly, because she paid at full weight: "The fever gave him four days and me six years. I have run that arithmetic a thousand times since. It never balances. I keep the books anyway."

She felt the Traveler's look move — down the bar to the full glass, then back to her. Of course she felt it. She counted things without looking up; that was the whole trick, and it worked on eyes as well as coin.

"And there it is," she said. "You are asking with your eyebrows. That is still asking, friend. You have simply gone to the trouble of doing it politely." No frost in it. A door held, with the lamp lit behind it. "I do not confirm and I do not correct. You have known that since I told you — which is why you asked this way and not the other way. This way, neither of us has to refuse anything."

She drank. A little. Then she looked down the bar at the full glass, and this time she let the Traveler watch her do it.

"But I will tell you what it is. Not who it is for — what it is. There is a difference, and tonight I am spending it."

The lamp hissed. The fire settled with a sound like coals agreeing with each other.

"In my old trade we closed the ledgers at year's end. Everything balanced, everything settled, everything squared and signed. I was good at it. You watched me half the evening — I am still good at it. And somewhere in those five years I learned that clean books are clean because you close them, and that some lines are worth the mess."

She set her glass down, a stool's width short of the other one. The width was not accidental. It never was.

"So there is one line in my books that does not close. It costs two fingers a night, out of a bottle I do not sell to anyone, and one minute of standing still, and it buys me a house that is still the house I meant to keep. Folk assume it is grief. Grief is a creditor — it ages, it quiets, it settles for less than it asked. This is not a creditor. This is a standing order. The drink gets poured. The drink stays poured. The account stays open. That is the whole of the doctrine, it is more than I have ever told anyone, and I am telling you because you chose the story with the happy ending, and because just now you looked at that glass the way a man looks at a grave he is not sure he has permission to visit."

She let that sit, then added, dry as the bottom of the bottle: "And before you build further — a woman who keeps a standing order is not necessarily pining. The house is not for sale, and neither am I. That part is preference. I have said so to everyone who asked and several who did not."

The cat, without opening its eyes, moved one paw nearer to the full glass — territorial, not affectionate, which in a cat amounts to nearly the same thing. The clock carried its argument with the night forward, one deliberate tick at a time. Above them the stairs kept their counsel. Either the man in room two had gone back to sleep, or he had learned which boards talked and was stepping around them out of professional courtesy. She would confirm which at first light. She confirmed all her nothings eventually.

"You have a name in your mouth right now," Maren said. "I can see it sitting there. Keep it there. That is the ceremony, and you are upholding it handsomely — better than most manage. Most folk either ask outright, once, and never ask again, because the door they knocked on does not open. Or they decide the glass is furniture and go to bed with the wrong story. You found the third road. Say nothing, stay pleasant, keep it where you can see it. I told you it works on strangers. It works on glasses, too."

She took up her cloth, though the room had nothing left in it to wipe, and stood.

"First light is five hours off. The road will be where you left it. So will the blue canvas, and so will I. Sleep on it — that is the one piece of advice in this house I give away twice."

She raised her own glass a fraction of an inch — not a toast, not an invitation; the way one colleague across a room acknowledges another — and drank from it, unhurried, and the Antler held its quiet, and the night, for once, was exactly the kind of nothing she had spent eighteen years confirming.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "I think I'll take that advice." I finish my drink, setting the empty mug down. "Thanks, Maren. For everything." I stand, picking up my pack.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"For everything," Maren repeated, weighing it. "Everything comes to eight coppers. A bowl, a bed, an ale, and my opinion of the wine, which I hand out whether folk ask or not. The first three go on the book. The opinion was free, and so was the company, which by the arithmetic of this house leaves us about even." She let one beat pass, then paid the sincere part at full weight, as she did everything: "But you're welcome to it. This was the kind of evening I keep the house for. They don't all manage it."

She slid the key down the bar with the flat of her left hand — it had sat forgotten by the till stone since the ring from his ale dried around it. "Number six. Hard to sleep in a room you can't open, and you were a step from finding that out the interesting way. First light settles the bill, as agreed. It goes in the book tonight — ink collects better than memory."

She came around the bar as he gathered the pack, and gave the practical part the way she gave prices: level, unhurried, once.

"Bolt the door. The locks in this house are iron and I keep them oiled — that habit came out of the same old life as the ledgers, and it's the one I'd keep if I kept no other. The stair will announce you on the way up; it announces everybody, that's its profession. Mind the parcel on it, too — the stairs are the last thing in this house that jolts. I've seen to everything else." A beat. "And if they talk in the night and you're not the one on them, you'll know the house has another walker. It'll probably be me — I'm up twice most nights, checking. But count the footsteps to a door before you lose any sleep over them. Which door they stop at is worth more than how many there are."

She walked him as far as the foot of the stairs, lamp in her left hand, the ring catching what light was left.

"Breakfast is seven to half nine, and after that Pell reclassifies you. And so you can sleep with the arithmetic done: the cooper runs east on market days, every third morning. Tomorrow isn't one. The day after is. So 'sit still a day' isn't just my preference — it has a schedule, and the schedule agrees with me. Everything in this house comes around to that eventually."

The cat watched from the bar, one eye open, standing its guard over the full glass at the end.

"Good night, Traveler. The 'for now' keeps — no hurry on it. The book will be open at first light, and ink forgives." She raised the lamp a fraction, no higher than she ever raised anything. "Sleep well. The road will keep."

She did not watch him up the stairs. She turned back to the end of the bar instead — the last thing she meant to look at tonight, and the first thing she'd look at come morning.

And for once, she did not count the steps as the stairs had their say. Eighteen years of counting; she could spend one night's worth on courtesy. The ceremony asked that much, and she had spent half the evening explaining it, so she paid it.

She finished her two fingers, unhurried, standing. Down at the window she lifted the curtain edge with two fingers and gave the yard its last audit: the drivers' fire gone to ember-dark under its stones, both men under the canvas now, the whittling done and put away, the east road empty in both directions. Nothing. She confirmed it twice — once more than the nothing required — and let the curtain fall.

She turned the lamp down to a breath and left it burning on the shelf. Fires got banked in this house. That end of the bar, never.

The clock in the corner carried its argument with the night forward, one deliberate tick at a time. Somewhere above her, a room held a careful man and his boring parcel. Somewhere in the yard, blue canvas held whatever it held. And at the end of the bar, in its thumb of lamplight, the account stayed open — the way it had for six years, the way it would after everyone under this roof was dust.

Maren took up her cloth, though there was nothing left in the room to wipe, and kept her house.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking the key and my pack, then head towards the stairs, my boots thudding softly on the old wood. I glance back once, and Maren is already at the end of the bar, looking at the untouched glass. A moment later, I'm at room six, fumbling with the key.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren set the tally sheet aside with her right hand and used her left to lift the lid from the stew pot behind the bar. The scent of rosemary and slow-cooked venison rose sharp and immediate. She ladled a bowl full with an easy, practiced motion—left hand, naturally—and set it on the counter before the newcomer along with a wooden spoon and a heel of brown bread.

"We have both," she said. "The stew is hot, the room is clean, and the mattress does not smell. That is the best review I can give it."

She wiped her left hand on her leather apron and leaned slightly on the bar, her weight on her left arm. "The room is three coppers and includes whatever Old Pell puts out in the morning. The stew is two. Ale is one, wine is four, but I will tell you now the wine is imported and overpriced. The ale is local and honest."

Her dark eyes flicked to the pack, then back to the traveler's face. She did not ask. "You handle that like it has feelings. I will have one of the servers carry it up if it is heavy. The stairs have killed no one yet, but I do not wish to break that streak tonight."

She turned to the key rack and lifted a brass key from its hook with her left hand. "I am Maren. The Antler is mine. The rules are few: no drawn steel, no unkindness to my staff, and if you break something you pay for it before you leave. Sit where you like, eat while it is hot, and let me know if the stew is not to your liking. Old Pell is sensitive about his craft, but I am the one who has to listen to him sulk."

She placed the key on the bar. "What name should I put in the ledger, friend?"

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content:
*I nod, taking a deep breath of the stew's aroma.* "Smells perfect, Maren. Thank you." I pick up the spoon, taking a careful bite. "And the room sounds just right. As for the package... I'll manage it myself. It's not heavy, just... delicate."

*I hesitate for a moment, then offer a slight smile.* "You can call me Traveler. No need for a name in your ledger."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren regarded the traveler with a look that suggested she had heard stranger requests and served stranger people, though perhaps not both at once. She picked up the tally sheet again with her left hand and made a notation beside the stew and room charge.

"A name for the ledger is customary," she said, her tone carrying no accusation, only calm observation. "But I have found that customs, like stew, are best served to those with an appetite for them. Traveler it shall be."

She set the sheet aside and wiped at a spot on the bar with her left hand, her silver thumb ring catching the lamplight. "The room is the second door on the left at the top of the stairs. The floorboards in the hallway creak by the third step—" she paused, her deadpan delivery precise, "—which is how I know when guests are wandering where they ought not. Consider it a courtesy warning."

She glanced at the pack once more, her scarred eyebrow lifting slightly. "Delicate is often more troublesome than heavy. The stairs are narrow and the turn at the landing is sharp. If you change your mind about assistance, my server Corvin has steady hands and no curiosity. A rare combination in a young man."

Maren reached beneath the bar with her left hand and set a small clay cup of water beside the stew. "Drink that. Old Pell salts his broth like he is personally offended by the deer. The water is free, which is more than I can say for most things in this world."

She leaned back slightly, her weight shifting to her stronger left side. "Eat while it is hot. I will be here when you are ready to settle accounts. And Traveler—" she added the name with the same deliberate weight she gave everything else, "—welcome to the Antler. Make yourself unwelcome, and we will have a different conversation. But I suspect you know that already."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s gaze dropped to the plate with the same wary focus she usually reserved for broken glass in the common room. She did not reach for it. She took a half-step back, putting a deliberate few inches of clean oak between herself and the crab cakes, her left hand resting flat on the bar while her right hung loose at her side.

"That is a generous gesture," she said, her voice level and carrying just far enough to reach the merchant’s table. "Please tell Lord Havel that I appreciate his consideration, but I do not care for seafood. Never have."

She turned her attention back to the Traveler, using her left hand to nudge the clay cup of water a hair closer to the stew bowl, careful to keep her fingers well away from the offered dish. "You are welcome to them. Fresh crab is a luxury on this road, and I would hate for good food to go to waste on my account."

Her scarred eyebrow lifted slightly as she glanced toward the merchant again. "Though in my experience, gifts from lords arrive with an invoice attached. If Lord Havel wishes to discuss grain tariffs or river rights, he knows where to find me. I prefer my conversations without breadcrumbs."

She wiped her left hand on her leather apron — a habitual gesture, though she had not touched the plate — and settled her weight back onto her stronger left leg. "Eat what you like, friend. I will stick to what Old Pell makes. At least with his stew, I know precisely what I am indebted for."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow at Maren's reaction, then glance at the crab cakes.* "Well, I'm certainly not one to refuse fresh crab." *I take a fork and try one, chewing thoughtfully.* "They're quite good, actually. No hidden agenda taste."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the Traveler eat with the resigned patience of a woman who had seen many things consumed at her bar that she would not touch herself. She shifted her weight to her stronger left side and used her left hand to straighten a row of mugs hanging beneath the lip of the counter, keeping her gaze from lingering too long on the plate.

"No hidden agenda taste," she repeated, the corner of her mouth twitching almost imperceptibly. "That is a flavor I have yet to encounter in any dish, though I have tasted plenty of hidden agendas in the men who order them."

She wiped at the bar with her left hand, working a slow circle farther down the oak, safely away from the crab. "Lord Havel sends crab cakes to a stranger at a crossroads tavern. Either he is cultivating a reputation for generosity, or he is cultivating something else. The two often look identical until the harvest."

Her dark eyes moved to the merchant's table, then back to the Traveler. "If you find them to your liking, enjoy them. But I would advise against accepting his horse if he offers it next. That is when the accounting truly begins."

She reached beneath the bar with her left hand and produced a clean cloth, setting it on the counter near the Traveler's water cup—not touching the plate. "The bread is less complicated and less inclined to start conversations about grain tariffs. But then, I have always been a woman for simple pleasures."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren reached beneath the bar with her left hand and lifted a clay mug, pouring a thin measure of the local ale into it. She raised it in answer to the toast, her silver thumb ring catching the lamplight.

"I will tell Old Pell you said so," she said. "Though I may leave out the emphasis. He considers himself an artist, and artists prefer their praise delivered with punctuation rather than volume."

She took a small sip and set the mug down, her weight settling on her stronger left side. "He will smile when I tell him. It is a rare and unfortunate event, like a solar eclipse. I suggest you finish your bowl before he emerges to accept compliments in person. The last man who praised his stew spent an hour hearing about the proper rendering of deer fat. His companions left without him, and he had to rent a room for another night. I did not mind the extra coin, but his wife was displeased."

She wiped the bar with her left hand, working a slow circle. "There is more if you want it. The deer have been plentiful this season, and Pell cooks them with a sense of personal vengeance that does wonders for the flavor. Eat your fill. The road is long, and the Antler does not move."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, finishing my bowl.* "An hour on deer fat, eh? I'll take my chances. But yes, a second bowl would be great." *I push the empty bowl forward.* "And perhaps a small ale to go with it."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
