Maren took the empty bowl with her left hand and replaced it with a fresh ladleful from the pot behind the bar, the rich scent of rosemary and slow-cooked venison rising sharp and immediate. She topped off the clay mug with ale, her left hand steady on the pitcher, her silver thumb ring catching the lamplight as she poured.

"Two bowls and a compliment," she said, setting the mug down and sliding it forward with her left hand. "Old Pell will be insufferable by morning. I may have to charge you extra just to cover the cost of his ego."

She wiped her left hand on her leather apron and glanced at the remaining crab cakes with the wary detachment of a woman who had already categorized them as someone else's concern. "If you are finished with Lord Havel's generosity, I will have Corvin clear the plate when he makes his rounds. It is taking up valuable real estate on my bar, and I prefer my seafood at a comfortable distance."

Leaning on the bar with her left forearm, she settled her weight comfortably on her stronger side. "Eat while it is hot. The second bowl is always better than the first, because you know precisely what to expect. The ale, likewise, improves with acquaintance. Though I am told that is true of many things in life."

She straightened and retrieved the tally sheet with her left hand, making a notation beside the growing column of charges. "Your debts accumulate, Traveler. But they are honest debts, which is more than can be said for most."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The clock began to strike, and Maren stopped. She had been leaning on the bar with her left forearm, listening, but when the first chime sounded she went still. The twelfth bell faded into the rafters above, and the common room seemed to hold its breath with her.

She set down the cloth she held in her left hand. She reached beneath the bar and withdrew two clean glasses, placing them side by side on the oak. With her left hand she lifted a bottle from the back shelf — not the local ale, not the overpriced wine, but something amber and rarely touched — and poured a careful measure into each. Her right hand steadied the second glass, but the pouring, the measuring, and the intent all came from her stronger side.

She picked up the first glass in her left hand and carried it to the far end of the bar, where the hearth-light did not reach. She set it down on the worn counter with a gentleness that seemed almost out of place in her scarred grip. Then she turned her back on it and walked away.

Returning to her place before the Traveler, she wrapped her left hand around the second glass. She did not drink. She did not raise it in toast. She merely held it, her dark eyes on the liquid, until the silence became its own kind of conversation.

Then she looked up. “It is midnight,” she said. “That is the hour when some debts are settled, and others are merely acknowledged. I do not explain my habits, friend. I keep them, as I keep this tavern, because they are mine.”

She took a small sip and set the glass down. “Your account stands at five coppers. The second bowl was free — Old Pell is asleep, and I do not wake an artist to amend a ledger. Finish your ale, or do not. The room is yours whenever you wish to climb. The stairs have killed no one yet.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I watch Maren with quiet curiosity. This is new. I finish my ale, then push the glass forward.* "A fair price, Maren. And your habits are your own." *I stand, stretching slightly.* "Think I'll take that room now. Long day."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren set her glass aside with her left hand and slid the brass key across the oak with the same hand, leaving it at the edge of the counter. She gathered the empty ale mug and stew bowl with her left hand, stacking them neatly beside the wash basin.

"Five coppers now, or settle after breakfast. I am particular about honesty, not the hour of its arrival."

She wiped her left hand on her leather apron and glanced toward the stairs, then to the pack the Traveler carried.

"The room is where I said. The floorboard by the third step still creaks. If you misstep, let the pack fall. The stairs have killed no one, but a broken burden is its own kind of tragedy."

She reached beneath the bar with her left hand and produced a small candle in a brass holder. She lit it from the wall sconce with a steady left hand and set it on the counter. "Take this. The hall lantern burns low, and I do not wish to explain to the morning why a guest broke their nose on my doorframe."

She settled her weight on her stronger left side. "Sleep well, Traveler. The Antler keeps its own hours, but its guests are welcome to keep theirs. If you require anything before dawn, knock on the wall by the hearth. The boards are thin, and I hear well."

Her gaze moved briefly to the untouched glass at the end of the bar, then back to the Traveler. "And if you hear me moving about at odd hours, pay it no mind. Some debts require midnight attention. I have already told you I do not explain my habits."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I pick up the key and the candle, nodding.* "Understood, Maren. And thanks for everything. The stew really was fantastic." *I head for the stairs, my hand instinctively going to the mysterious package.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the Traveler ascend until the turn at the landing hid them from view. The third step sang its usual creak, followed by the softer press of footsteps moving down the hallway above. She said nothing further. She had offered bed, light, and fair warning. Whatever the pack contained, it was not hers to unpack.

She turned back to the common room. The merchants had departed, leaving two empty mugs and a silver coin that had not been there before—Lord Havel’s man, perhaps, settling his lord’s account. The dwarf remained, staring into his ale as if it contained a map he could not read. Maren left him to his navigation.

With her left hand, she gathered the empty dishes and set them in the wash basin. Then she walked to the far end of the bar and stood before the untouched glass. She did not pick it up. She rested her left hand on the oak beside it, her silver thumb ring tapping once against the wood, a small sound lost beneath the crackle of the dying hearth.

She stood there for a moment that measured itself in breaths rather than minutes. Then she returned to her place behind the bar, retrieved her tally sheet with her left hand, and made a final mark beside the entry she had written: *Traveler*.

She reached beneath the counter and set her oak cudgel in its customary spot, within easy reach but out of sight. The dwarf raised his empty mug. Maren took it with her left hand and refilled it without being asked.

“Long night?” he asked.

“Every night is long,” Maren said. “Some merely have better company.”

She leaned on her left arm and waited for the hearth to burn low and the last of her guests to find their way to bed.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I reach the top of the stairs, the candle flickering. The third step definitely creaked. I find the second door on the left and unlock it, pushing the door open to reveal a simple, clean room. I set my pack carefully on the small table by the window, then light the room's single lamp before blowing out the candle.* "Finally." *I whisper to myself, stretching my back with a groan. I glance at the package for a moment, a small smile playing on my lips, before turning to settle into the bed.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The dwarf drained his mug and set it down with a click that carried in the quiet room. He slid another coin across the oak and pushed back his chair.

“Quiet night,” he said.

“They usually are, once the right people leave,” Maren said.

She took the coin with her left hand and dropped it into the till. The dwarf grunted, shouldered his pack, and made his way out. Maren bolted the door behind him with her left hand, sliding the iron bar into place with a solid clunk. She turned back to the common room and began extinguishing the lamps, using her left hand to turn down each wick until only the hearth remained.

The crab plate still sat on the bar. She took a clean cloth in her left hand and lifted it by the edge, carrying it to the kitchen hatch and setting it on the shelf for morning. She did not let her fingers touch the meat. She wiped the cloth across the oak where the dish had rested, though it had not touched the wood directly.

At the far end of the bar, Tobin’s glass sat in the gloom. She did not move it. She had told the Traveler she left it until morning, and her habits required no witness and no explanation.

A floorboard overhead gave its familiar groan—the one just past the third step, outside the second door on the left. The bedframe answered with a single creak, and then the house settled into silence. Maren stood still for a moment, her left hand resting flat on the bar, her right hanging loose at her side. The old wrist injury throbbed gently, as it always did when the night’s chill crept in. She rubbed her left thumb across the silver ring on her hand.

She retrieved the tally sheet and made one final mark beside the traveler’s entry: *Settled, breakfast pending.* Then she hung the sheet on its hook and reached for the lamp behind the bar.

Before she turned it down, she glanced once at the two glasses. One held, one waiting. She extinguished the flame and let the darkness take them both.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I wake with the morning light, stretching again. My back still aches a little, but the bed was surprisingly comfortable. I can hear the sounds of the tavern below, the clatter of pots and pans, the low murmur of voices. A new day. I get dressed, taking a moment to check on the package. Still safe. Good.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren stood behind the bar in the grey morning light, her left hand wrapped around the glass from the end of the counter. The hearth had burned to ash. She lifted it—empty, as it always was—and carried it to the wash basin. She rinsed it with her left hand, her fingers working carefully around the rim, and set it on the drying rack alongside the others. She did not look at it again.

Old Pell was already at work in the kitchen. The sound of a skillet hitting the iron stove rang out like a bell, followed by the smell of frying bacon and coarse bread toasting. Maren wiped down the bar with her left hand, working a damp rag in slow circles across the oak. Her silver thumb ring caught the light and scraped faintly over a scratch some mercenary had left with a spur two winters past.

Corvin moved between the tables, setting out wooden spoons and clay cups with the careful posture of a young man who understood that curiosity was a luxury his wages did not cover. Maren watched him set a spoon straight with his elbow rather than his fingers—good—and returned to her ledger. Her left hand moved the quill across the page in short, precise strokes. The dwarf had overpaid by two coppers. Lord Havel's man had not paid for the crab at all. She made a notation to settle that debt herself rather than send an invoice up the road. Some accounts were not worth the parchment.

A floorboard overhead gave its familiar groan, the one just past the third step, outside the second door on the left. The bedframe answered with a single creak. Maren did not look up from her numbers, but she added a line beneath the traveler's entry: *Breakfast, standard.*

She set down the quill with her left hand and called through the kitchen hatch, her voice carrying just far enough to reach Old Pell without rising above the morning clatter. "One more for breakfast, Pell. And do not lecture this one about rendering. He has a long road, and I do not wish to start his day with suffering."

Old Pell's reply was lost in the sizzle of bacon, but Maren took the grunt for agreement. She straightened, rolled her shoulders, and rested her left hand on the bar. The oak cudgel sat in its place behind the counter, untouched. The common room was quiet, the shutters were open to let in the road-dust and the daylight, and the Antler had survived another night with all its debts accounted for—those settled, and those merely acknowledged.

She looked toward the stairs and waited, her weight settled comfortably on her stronger left side.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I descend the stairs, the package still clutched in my hand. The smell of bacon is intoxicating. I head straight for the bar, a small smile on my face.* "Morning, Maren. Something smells incredible."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren looked at the pack as it came down beside the Traveler, then at the careful way it had been set on the floor. She did not ask what was in it. People carried things for all sorts of reasons, and half of them were none of her business.

“You’ve got a room,” she said. “Nine are taken. Three are free. Number four’s the quietest, unless the merchants in the snug start singing again, and then no room in this house is safe.”

She turned and lifted a brass key from the hook behind the bar with her left hand, setting it on the polished wood with a soft click. The silver ring on her thumb caught the lamplight as she slid a mug from the shelf.

“Kitchen’s got venison stew, bread, and a bit of roasted turnip that Old Pell is pretending is a delicacy because it came from the garden instead of the cellar,” Maren said. “Hot enough for your asking.”

She poured the ale in one steady motion, foam just shy of the rim. Then she set the mug on the bar in front of the Traveler and folded her arms, the right one resting a little lighter than the left.

“Four coppers for the stew. One silver for the room, linens included. I’ll need a name for the ledger unless you fancy being called ‘Traveler’ all night and then wondering why the other guests are looking at you like you’ve lost a bet.”

Her voice stayed even, but her eyes flicked once toward the stairwell, checking the way people always checked when a tavern owner was deciding whether a tired stranger was trouble, trouble’s cousin, or just tired.

“Take the mug while it’s cold enough to drink,” she added. “It won’t stay that way if you keep holding it.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I pick up the mug, taking a long drink. "Traveler's just fine, for the ledger," I say, a small smile playing on my lips. "And the stew sounds perfect, even with the fancy turnips." I reach for my coin purse. "Four coppers, one silver, you said?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren accepted the answer with the calm of a woman who had spent years writing down names that meant very little. “Traveler,” she said, and the word was not mocked, only measured. “I have written worse in that ledger. Last winter a man signed as ‘Probably Honest.’ I gave him a private room. It was less expensive than arguing with him.”

She reached for the ledger with her left hand, uncapped the ink, and set the single word down in firm, unhurried letters. The silver ring on her thumb caught the lamplight as she worked. Her right hand remained at the edge of the bar, steadying the pages but doing little else, as it had for years.

“The coin goes on the wood,” Maren said. “I trust a stranger better when I can see what is being paid. Four coppers for the stew. One silver for the room. If the silver is clipped, I will notice. If it is false, I will be personally disappointed.”

She did not watch the purse with greed, only habit, then turned her head toward the kitchen door. “Pell! Venison and turnip at the bar. The traveler says fancy.”

Old Pell’s answer was a grunt and the clang of a ladle against the pot. A moment later, one of the servers set a bowl of stew on the polished wood, steam rising in a pale ribbon beside the brass key. Maren nudged the key closer, but not into the Traveler’s hand.

“Room four,” she said. “Quiet as a saint’s afternoon, unless the merchants in the snug discover harmony. Then you will learn what a true punishment is.”

Her eyes went briefly to the pack, then back to the stew.

“Eat first,” Maren said. “Ask about the rest of the world after you have been fed. It is easier to be suspicious of everything when your belly is empty.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s eyes went to the plate first, then to the steam curling off it, then to the merchant who had sent it, with the measured patience of a woman deciding whether the interruption was a gift or a headache wearing a bow.

“Lord Havel,” she said, and the name did not seem to improve the food.

Her left hand moved before her right had any reason to. She took the folded cloth from beneath the mug and used it to slide the plate a careful half-inch away from herself, not enough to insult the giver, not enough to let the smell settle into the stew.

“If Lord Havel wishes to be generous,” she continued, “he may send his compliments to Old Pell, who will thank him in the language he prefers, which is mostly grunts. He may also send the crab cakes elsewhere. I do not care for seafood.”

She said it plainly, without apology, the way one might say *I do not care for wet socks*.

The plate remained between them. Maren glanced at the Traveler only to add, “It is yours if you want it. If you do not, leave it be. Pell will scrape it into the bucket with the look of a man burying a friend.”

A pause. Then, toward the merchant’s corner, though her voice did not rise:

“And if Lord Havel expects a thank-you for sending me a plate of shellfish, he may come down from his fine room and receive it from my own hand. I will thank him for the thought. I will not thank him for the trouble.”

She set the tally sheet back in order with her left, letting the right rest at the edge of the bar, fingers curled loosely around nothing.

“Now,” she said, returning to the Traveler as if the interruption had been only a fly landing on a pie. “You said Traveler for the ledger. I have written Traveler. I have also written ‘Probably Honest.’ I trust you are less poetic.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I pick up a crab cake and take a bite, ignoring Maren's disdain. "Poetic, perhaps, but certainly not dishonest." I gesture to the plate. "These are quite good, actually."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the crab cake leave the plate with the patient horror of a woman who had seen too many well-meaning gifts.

“Then they are quite good,” she said, in the tone one might use for a horse that had kicked through a wall. “I am glad Lord Havel’s judgment is better in the kitchen than in the giving.”

Her left hand took the folded cloth and nudged the plate away from the brass key, away from the stew, and away from the edge nearest her apron. She did not touch the food itself. There was no need. The shells came apart in pieces that found their way into sleeves, and Maren had no patience for that sort of trouble, even when it arrived as a compliment.

“If you are going to eat it,” she said, “do it with a fork. I will send one. If you are going to eat it with your fingers, do not then reach for my mug, my ledger, or my coin.”

A pause.

“The coin I can forgive. It is only silver. The mug I have washed.”

From the corner, Lord Havel lifted his cup in what might have been apology or amusement. Maren returned it with a nod so small it could have been mistaken for settling a collar.

“Your stew will cool,” she said, looking back to the Traveler. “Pell will not say anything. He will simply ladle the next one thinner, and we will both know the reason.”

A grain of crab caught on the rim of the plate and slid, with fatal precision, toward Maren’s wrist. Before it could land, she drew her sleeve back with a small, sharp motion that was not quite a flinch and not quite a command. The cloth came over it. The grain vanished into the fold.

“If it is quite good,” Maren said, still looking at the Traveler as if the matter had only just become personal, “then it is quite good elsewhere.”

She lifted the key with her left hand and laid it beside the bowl, then pushed the bowl half an inch closer to the Traveler. Her right hand stayed at her side, curled loosely around nothing, as it often did when there was no need for it.

“Room four. Second landing. Left. The handle sticks. Lift it as you turn it. Do not force it. If the cat is on the bed, she belongs to the room. If she is on your pack, she belongs to the pack, and I will not mediate.”

Then, quieter, almost as an afterthought:

“And wipe your mouth before you pay. Crab grease has a way of turning my clean bar into a map of somebody else’s lunch.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren took the raised mug as evidence the stew had gone down well.

“Best in months,” she said, and the words were dry enough to start a small fire in the air between them. “That is not praise. That is an accusation against every cook you have met since then.”

She lifted her own mug with her left hand, touched it to the Traveler’s without a sound, and set it down again. Only a sip. The right hand remained near the ledger, steadying nothing that needed steadying.

“I will not drink to Old Pell while he can hear me. He starts believing he is valued, and then he expects gratitude. Gratitude makes him cook with extra rosemary, and extra rosemary makes a man feel as if he is eating a garden that has taken a personal interest in him.”

From the kitchen, a ladle struck the pot in a way that sounded suspiciously like agreement.

Maren’s mouth twitched once.

“See,” she said. “He is already claiming the compliment.”

Then she slid the clean cloth toward the Traveler with her left, while her gaze went to the crab plate as if it had begun to speak to her.

“Oh, for the love of every saint who ever stubbed a toe, that plate is closer to my apron than my patience is,” she said, not loudly, not to anyone in particular. “If you mean to toast the cook, do it with your mouth full of stew, not with crab grease on your fingers. Some generosity is merely trouble wearing better linen.”

A pause.

“And friend, praise deserves better than that word of yours. It is for lost keys and wet boots. If you must swear at the food, swear it is too good, not that it is damning.”

She gathered the tally sheet, checked the stew bowl, and nudged the brass key beside it.

“Eat slowly. Room four until noon. If you want breakfast, Pell will have porridge, eggs, and bread that has not been insulted by fancy turnips. If you want silence, do not ask for the snug, because the merchants have discovered harmony. If you want company, ask for nothing. It will find you when it has finished being expensive.”

Maren looked toward the stairwell, then back at the Traveler.

“And wipe your mouth before you pay. I am particular about my bar. It has suffered enough this evening.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I dab my mouth with the cloth. "Right. Well, I'll keep that in mind for my next meal." I push the crab plate back towards Lord Havel's table with my elbow. "And this is all yours, Lord Havel. Enjoy."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the plate slide away from the bar and judged it a better journey than most unwanted things made before closing.

“Fairly delivered,” she said, as if the Traveler had been performing a small act of courtly warfare. “If Lord Havel takes offense, let him. The Antler does not serve grudges, only stew. The stew is better behaved.”

From the corner, Lord Havel raised both hands in a gesture that might have been apology, amusement, or the particular arrogance of a man accustomed to having his gifts mistaken for obligations.

“No offense intended,” he called, voice carrying just enough to prove he had been listening.

Maren inclined her head. Her voice did not rise. It never needed to.

“None received,” she said. “Though the plate has traveled far enough for both of us. Lord Havel may keep his generosity at a respectful distance. It is easier to admire from there.”

The merchant laughed. Maren did not laugh with him. She merely looked at the bar where a few faint crumbs had survived the retreat, then reached for a clean cloth with her left hand and swept them into one small pile. Her right hand rested at the edge of the ledger, fingers loose, keeping the pages steady without asking them to do more than they could manage.

“Sela,” she called quietly toward the nearer server. “If Lord Havel sends anything else with fins, claws, or the temperament of a noble gift, place it on the side table. Do not bring it near the cook’s stew. Old Pell has enough enemies without acquiring seafood.”

The server nodded and moved to take the plate before it could become an insult with legs.

Maren returned her attention to the Traveler, and to the bar, where the brass key still sat beside the empty bowl.

“You have wiped your mouth,” she said. “That is progress. I will not ask for a written statement. I will ask for coin.”

A pause.

“Four coppers for the stew. One silver for the room. On the wood. Not in my hand. Not in your pocket. Not in a speech. I have had enough poetry for one evening, and last winter’s ‘Probably Honest’ still makes me feel as if the ledger owes me an apology.”

She left the tally sheet open. The word Traveler sat in the ledger with the quiet stubbornness of a name that had no intention of growing into anything more useful.

If the coins came, Maren would examine them without touching the Traveler’s purse. She had learned long ago that a tavern owner’s hand should know the weight of what it took, and not know the warmth of what it refused.

“Pell will hear you praised,” she added, glancing toward the kitchen door. “He will begin to believe his own legend. That is a more dangerous thing than Lord Havel’s gift. A cook who believes he is adored starts adding rosemary with intention. We will all suffer.”

The kitchen gave a grunt.

Maren gave no sign that she had heard it.

“The room is four,” she said, sliding the brass key closer to the Traveler with one steady push of her left hand. “Second landing. Left. The handle sticks. Lift it as you turn it. If the cat is on the bed, she belongs to the room. If she is on your pack, she belongs to the pack. If she is on both, she has found a strategy and I am not involved.”

Her eyes went briefly to the pack again. Still not asking. Still noticing.

“Breakfast is from dawn until the merchants remember they are hungry. Pell will have porridge, eggs, bread, and turnips that have been told to behave like vegetables. If you want something fancier, ask. If you want something imported, ask with your coin already out. If you want wine, I will tell you where to find it, and then tell you what it will cost, because I am honest and not cruel.”

The lamplight caught the silver ring on her thumb as she gathered the empty bowl and set it aside.

“You may leave your pack at the bar for a moment,” Maren said, “but not for long. This is a tavern, not a waiting room for trouble. I have seen enough waiting rooms to know what happens when a man sits too still.”

Then, quieter, with the dryness worn thin by years of use:

“Eat what is left. Pay what is owed. Room four until noon. And if you meet me after midnight, do not ask what my drink is for. I will tell you it is for the weather. The weather has been unkind for six years.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The clock struck midnight, and Maren stopped in the middle of a sentence.

It was not a dramatic stop. She did not look as if she had heard a bell from another world, only as if the hour had arrived at the exact second she had expected it and had still not been properly received.

The common room had thinned. The merchants in the snug were laughing now, one of them badly, the other worse. Old Pell’s kitchen door stood ajar, the fire banked to a sullen glow. The smell of rosemary and turnips had gone soft and late-night, and one of the servers was sweeping near the hearth with the careful boredom of a person who knew she was being watched.

Maren set down the cloth in her left hand.

“You are still at the bar,” she said.

The word came out as a fact, not an accusation, though it carried both inside it.

She reached beneath the counter with her left hand and brought out two clean glasses. They were plain, thick-bottomed, and had survived the last decade of the Antler’s better and worse evenings. Her right hand remained at the edge of the bar, near the ledger, resting there with the habitual discretion of a limb that had learned not to be trusted with important tasks.

She poured the first glass with her left hand. Pale ale, just short of the rim. She poured the second from the same jug, with the same steadiness, and set the stopper back in place without looking.

The second glass went to the end of the bar.

Not close to the brass key. Not close to the empty stew bowl. Not close to the Traveler. It was placed at the far end, in the spot that had been left unclaimed for six years, as surely as if a chair had been set for someone no one could see.

Maren left it there.

Then she took her own glass and stood at the bar, neither drinking nor setting it down. The silver ring on her thumb caught the lamplight as she slid her fingers over the side of the glass.

If the Traveler asked what the second drink was for, Maren would not explain. If the Traveler stared at it long enough to make it awkward, she would not offer the name of the dead. If the Traveler mistook the ritual for superstition, she would let them. Superstition was easier to answer than grief, and she had never been fond of wasting good breath on either.

Instead, she said, “The room is four.”

Her voice was even, as if the night had not just shifted into a different hour.

“Second landing. Left. The handle sticks. Lift it as you turn it, and do not force the poor thing into an argument it cannot win.”

A pause.

“The key is beside your bowl.”

It was. It had been there for some time, waiting with the quiet patience of brass.

Maren took a small sip of her own drink, then looked toward the end of the bar. The other glass remained untouched. The clock ticked. Somewhere above them, a floorboard settled with the particular creak of a house remembering its own weight.

“You have coin on the wood, or you do not,” she said, without rudeness. “If you do, I will leave the ledger where it is and you may take the key when you wish. If you do not, we will have a civilized conversation about trust, and I will tell you that I have seen men run from a bill for a bed and return to a bill for a horse. The horse, at least, understands debt.”

She set her glass down in front of herself, but did not move away from the bar.

The merchants in the snug raised a chorus of sorts. One of them began a tune with confidence. The next phrase arrived in a different key and with fewer apologies than it deserved.

Maren turned her head a fraction of an inch.

“Oh, for the love of every saint who ever stubbed a toe,” she said, not loudly, not with anger, but with the weary precision of a woman who had survived the same song twice before. “If the snug is to become a chapel, let it at least have better hymns.”

The chorus faltered.

Maren returned her attention to the bar.

“You may stay until the ale is gone,” she said. “You may not stay until the patience is gone. Those are not the same amount of time, and patience is the rarer vintage.”

She looked at the end of the bar again.

Her expression did not change, but something in the set of her shoulders did, very slightly. A door closed and reopened without a sound.

“If you mean to ask what the second drink is for,” she said, “I will tell you it is for the weather.”

She lifted her own glass and turned it in her left hand.

“The weather has been unkind for six years.”

No name followed. No explanation followed. No invitation to sympathy. Maren had learned that the best way to keep a private thing private was to say it plainly enough that no one wanted to ask again.

She drank.

The other glass remained at the end of the bar, pale ale catching the lamplight, waiting for morning.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "The weather is certainly a fickle thing," I say, echoing her sentiment. I push my coins onto the bar. "Six years is a long time for bad weather." I pick up the key. "Good night, Maren."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren heard the word *six years* the way one hears a door that has not quite latched.

She did not turn to the end of the bar. She kept her eyes on the coins.

Her left hand gathered them first, one by one, not touching the purse. Coppers, then silver. She thumbed the edge of the silver coin without pressing too hard; the right hand stayed near the ledger, holding it steady with the patience of a woman who had learned to let the weaker hand do the quiet, necessary work.

“The silver is sound,” she said. “And the count is correct. That makes you a rarer guest than the merchants in the snug, who paid for their room by insisting their singing was payment. It was not. The singing was worse than the room.”

She pushed the coins into a small stack with the edge of the cloth, then slid the cloth under them and tipped the stack into her palm. The motion was practiced and economical, like a quartermaster closing the day’s accounts.

Then she looked at the empty space where the brass key had been.

“Room four,” she said, as if the reminder were for the house and not the guest. “Second landing. Left. Lift the handle when you turn it. Do not force the poor thing into an argument it cannot win.”

A pause.

“If the cat is on the bed, she is older than the room and has rights. If she is on your pack, she has opinions. If she is on both, she is running the place.”

The clock ticked. The other glass remained at the end of the bar, pale ale catching the lamplight, untouched.

Maren looked at the coins in her left hand, then at the ledger, then at the second glass without quite looking at it.

“The weather is fickle,” she said at last. “Some people speak as if that explains everything. Some people say it because it is easier than explaining the storm. I am mostly the second sort.”

She did not move the second glass. She did not drink from it. She did not name it.

Instead, she set the coins away and drew the ledger shut with the back of her left hand.

“If you are going to be polite about it, do not make it a question,” she said, more to the bar than to the room. “I have had enough questions this evening to last until the next flood, and the last one came from a man who wanted to know if the stew was fit for a lord. It was not. It was fit for a man with teeth and a sense of gratitude.”

From the kitchen, a ladle struck the pot in a way that sounded suspiciously like agreement.

Maren gave the door a brief glance.

“Pell hears everything,” she said. “He pretends not to, because that is how he remains dignified.”

She lifted her own glass, but did not drink. She turned it once in her left hand, the silver ring on her thumb catching the lamplight, then set it back down.

“Good night, Traveler.”

The name was given without warmth and without sharpness. It was a word set on a shelf, measured and returned.

“If you wake before dawn, the privy is behind the stair. If you wake after dawn, breakfast is porridge, eggs, bread, and turnips with a grudge. If you wake to singing, the merchants have found harmony. Pray it is not the one from the snug. That one has fewer notes than a goose.”

She gathered the empty stew bowl, then stopped, looking down at the bar.

A faint smear of crab grease had survived Lord Havel’s generosity. Maren stared at it for a moment, as if it had personally insulted her mother, then took a clean cloth and wiped it away with the deliberate calm of a woman who had never met a stain she could not outlast.

“And if you meet me tomorrow and say something kind about the evening,” she said, “I will accept it with the suspicion it deserves. A man who is too grateful at midnight has usually had his room, his stew, and his crab cake all in the same hour. It leaves one’s standards unbalanced.”

The cloth returned to the underside of the mug. The ledger was squared. The tally sheet was folded once, twice, and left open at the word *Traveler*.

Maren stood at the bar, neither moving toward the kitchen nor toward the stairwell.

“Go up,” she said. “Do not force the door. Do not leave your pack in the hall. This is a tavern, not a waiting room for trouble.”

A breath.

“And do not ask about the glass at the end of the bar.”

She looked at it then, just briefly. The ale was still pale in the lamplight. No one reached for it. No one needed to.

“The weather is a private thing,” Maren said.

She lifted her glass at last and drank, not because she was thirsty, but because the hour had arrived and the ritual required a beginning.

Then she set it down, straightened the cloth beside the ledger, and let the house settle around her.

“Good night.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I nod once, a silent acknowledgment, and turn towards the stairs. My hand finds the key, and I start my ascent, the weight of my pack feeling a little lighter after the stew. The creaking floorboards seem to whisper Maren's words as I climb.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the Traveler climb without saying anything else. She had learned that some people were steadier after a hot bowl and a paid room than they had been at the door. The pack moved with him carefully. The key did not. That, too, was information.

When the second landing creaked underfoot, Maren’s left hand rested on the bar near the ledger. Her right stayed folded at her side, the weaker one, the one she did not ask much of when there were no witnesses.

“Room four is left,” she said, quietly, as if the stairwell had developed a tendency to forget its own geography. “The handle sticks. Lift it as you turn it. Do not make enemies of hardware. It holds grudges worse than Pell.”

Old Pell gave a single grunt from the kitchen doorway. He had been listening, which meant he had been doing nothing else for the last quarter-hour.

“I am not speaking to you,” Maren said.

“You are speaking loud enough,” Pell answered. “That is how I know.”

Maren gave him a flat look. It did not land. Men who had survived on grunts and rosemary rarely feared eyes.

The common room had gone into its late-night hum. Two of the merchants were now in the snug, their voices muffled by the door and their tune worse for the attempt at privacy. One server was wiping down the far tables with the slow, dignified patience of someone who had been told not to leave the bar cluttered unless the clutter was hers. Lord Havel had gone upstairs, crab cakes and all, though Maren suspected he had taken the plate with him. That was either good manners or good appetite. She did not know which bothered her more.

Maren turned back to the end of the bar.

The second glass waited there, pale ale catching the lamplight in a small, steady shine.

She did not move it.

Sela, the younger server, came up behind the bar with an empty bowl balanced on her hip. She was careful, as usual, though care in a tavern was mostly a way of doing things without apologizing to the floor.

“Should I take that?” Sela asked, nodding toward the glass at the end of the bar.

Maren’s left hand closed around her own mug. The silver ring on her thumb shifted with the movement.

“No,” she said.

Sela looked at her for a moment, then wisely looked at the bowl instead. “Lord Havel’s man asked if the kitchen could do eggs before dawn.”

“It can do them,” Maren said. “Eggs are simple. They do not require fancy turnips to feel important.”

Sela smiled, then stopped before it became a thing.

“Tell him the price is one copper per egg, two for a soft one, three if he wants them burned and called rustic,” Maren continued. “If he wants them fancy, he may ask the moon.”

Sela took the empty bowl and went toward the kitchen. Pell’s ladle struck the pot again, this time with what might have been approval.

Maren let the room settle around her.

The clock ticked. The fire in the hearth shifted, sending a brief orange tremor across the floorboards. Upstairs, a door opened and closed somewhere near the third landing, which meant one of the rooms had accepted its guest without a fight. That was a small mercy. Maren had seen enough doors that needed arguments.

She lifted her own glass with her left hand and looked at the other one.

For a moment, her expression did something she would not have named. It was not softness. It was closer to the way a stone looks after long rain: still stone, but changed by the water’s patience.

“To the weather,” she said, very quietly.

She drank.

The second glass did not move.

Maren set her mug down and reached for the cloth. She wiped the bar in slow, deliberate circles, starting near the place where the Traveler’s coins had been, moving toward the spot where the crab plate had lingered. Her right hand stayed at the edge of the ledger, fingers curled loosely, steadying the book when it did not need steadying. It was easier that way. The right hand liked to be useful without being trusted.

A smear of grease survived her first pass. Maren looked at it as if it had committed a personal offense.

“Oh, for the love of every saint who ever stubbed a toe,” she muttered.

She wiped it again, harder this time. The cloth came away with a faint orange stain. Maren stared at it. The stain stared back.

“You have no business being that cheerful,” she told it.

The stain did not answer. Maren was not surprised. Grease rarely was.

From the snug, the merchants began a chorus again. It started with confidence and ended in a manner that suggested confidence had been taken outside and left without its coat.

Maren did not raise her voice.

“If that becomes a hymn,” she said to the room, “I am closing the snug and calling it a chapel. If it becomes a war song, I am calling it a bad idea. If it becomes a lullaby, I am calling it a mercy and putting the whole lot of you in bed.”

The snug went quiet enough to be noticed.

Maren nodded once to no one in particular.

“Good,” she said. “Silence is the best vintage in the house. It also costs less than the wine.”

She gathered the coins she had already counted, slid them into her apron pocket with her left hand, and squared the ledger. The word Traveler sat there in firm, unhurried letters. She looked at it longer than she needed to.

Then she added, in smaller letters beside it:

Room four. Paid. No poetry.

She considered that for a moment and changed it.

Room four. Paid. Probably polite.

Maren gave the page a small, dry look.

“I am not generous,” she said to the ledger. “I am merely fair to people who do not make a mess.”

The clock ticked past the first minute after midnight. The house had shifted into its deeper hour, the hour when the beams remembered they were trees and the floorboards remembered they had once been walked on by better and worse men. Maren liked that hour less than she admitted. It made the bar feel too wide, and the empty end of it feel too narrow.

She did not move the second glass.

Instead, she walked around the bar with her left hand on the counter and her right resting lightly at her side. The cudgel leaned in its familiar place behind the shelves, oak worn smooth by years and use. Maren did not look at it directly. She did not need to. She knew where everything was in the Antler, the way a quartermaster knows a supply line before it fails.

The cat appeared from beneath the hearth bench as if summoned by a sound only cats could hear. It was a thick-tailed grey thing with the expression of a creature that had never once been asked to justify itself.

Maren looked down.

“No,” she said.

The cat sat.

“I do not care what room you belong to. That is not an argument.”

The cat blinked.

Maren’s left hand came down and scratched briefly behind its ear. The cat accepted this as its due.

“Room four,” Maren said, glancing toward the stairwell. “If you are on his pack, you are in trouble. If you are on the bed, you are in the room. If you are on both, you have chosen violence and I will not support you.”

The cat moved toward the stairs.

Maren watched it go.

When it reached the second landing, she turned back to the bar. The second glass remained. The lamplight made the ale look almost pale enough to be daylight, almost clear enough to be hope. Maren was not a woman given to either when the hour was late.

She took her cloth and wiped the last dry spot near the ledger. Then she picked up the empty stew bowl with her left hand and carried it to the kitchen pass.

Pell was already there, stirring something that had no need of further stirring. He looked at the bowl, then at her, then at the bowl again.

“He liked it,” Maren said.

“Of course he liked it,” Pell said. “He is not dead.”

Maren stopped.

Pell did not look up, but his ladle paused in its slow circle.

“I do not say that lightly,” Maren said.

“No,” Pell agreed. “You do not.”

The kitchen fire crackled. Somewhere above them, the house settled again. Maren set the bowl on the counter and wiped her left hand on her apron.

“Bank the fire,” she said. “And do not let the cat near the turnips. She has been making plans.”

“Cats do not make plans,” Pell said. “They make accusations.”

Maren looked at him.

Pell lifted one shoulder.

“I will bank the fire.”

Maren returned to the common room. The merchants had given up their singing, perhaps because they had noticed the walls were not forgiving, perhaps because they had noticed Maren. The dwarf who had been reading a letter was gone. One of the tables had a ring of spilled ale on it. Maren looked at the ring with the weary respect of a woman who had seen many rings and trusted none of them.

She wiped the table with her left hand, moving in small, patient circles. Her right hand rested on the back of a chair, doing nothing that mattered.

When the table was dry, she straightened the chair. When the bar was squared, she squared it again. When the ledger was closed, she opened it once more and checked the final entry.

Traveler.

Room four.

Paid.

Probably polite.

Maren shut the ledger.

At the end of the bar, the second glass waited.

She stood there for a moment, neither drinking nor leaving. The silver ring on her thumb caught the light as she turned her own glass a quarter-inch, then stopped.

“I am not sentimental,” she said to the room.

The room, being a room, did not contradict her.

Maren lifted her glass and looked toward the stairwell. The pack had gone up with the Traveler. The careful hands had carried it. The careful back had climbed with it. Whatever was inside it was still not her business.

She drank the last of her ale in one small, measured swallow.

Then she set the empty glass beside the full one, took the cloth from her apron, and began closing the Antler.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I finally reach room four, fumbling a bit with the sticky handle just like Maren said. The cat, a fat grey tabby, is indeed curled up on the bed. It opens one eye, regards me for a moment, then closes it again. I drop my pack by the door, careful not to disturb the sleeping feline.* "Well, hello there, Room Four security."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren heard the second landing complain before the door of room four was fully open.

She had been wiping the last stubborn smear of crab grease from the bar, her left hand working the cloth in slow, patient circles while her right kept the ledger from sliding toward the edge. When the boards above spoke, she stopped. Not because the sound surprised her, but because a tavern owner learned every creak in her house the way a farmer learned the moods of his animals. The second landing had three voices: the one near the stairs, the one near the privy, and the one outside room four that had not been properly oiled since the reign of her aunt Bessa.

Maren set the cloth down and came around the bar.

She carried no lantern. The small oil lamp on the landing had burned low but steady, throwing a square of yellow light across the hall. Her left hand rested on the banister as she climbed. Her right stayed near her side, loose and quiet, the way it had been for years. The silver ring on her thumb caught the light once, then not again.

At the doorway of room four, she paused.

She did not step over the threshold.

The cat was exactly where Maren had predicted she would be, which did not make Maren feel less betrayed. The fat grey thing lay on the bed as if it had been born in the bed and had merely been waiting for someone else to pay for the linens. One eye opened. It regarded Maren with the flat, legal certainty of a creature that had never once been found at fault.

“Room four security,” Maren said, her voice even and low enough not to disturb the merchants or the beams, “is unpaid. She does not guard the room. She rules it.”

The cat blinked.

Maren nodded once.

“That is not an argument. That is a ruling.”

Her eyes moved to the pack by the door. It had been set down carefully. Not tossed. Not dropped. Not left where a server might trip and make a scene before Old Pell had finished banking the fire. Maren noticed the care the way she noticed most things: without asking, without praising, and without forgetting.

Carrying something they were being careful with.

He had carried it up the stairs with the same care.

Maren did not ask what was in it.

She looked at the bed, then at the cat, then back at the doorway.

“If she has chosen your pack as a pillow,” Maren said, “then she has chosen your pack as a pillow. I will not mediate. I told you I would not mediate.”

The cat settled its thick tail across the bedclothes.

Maren’s mouth twitched, but not into a smile. More like a woman recognizing a rival.

“She has rights,” she said. “The bed has rights. The room has rights. You have rented the room, not the cat. If she is on your pack, she belongs to the pack. If she is on the bed, she belongs to the bed. If she is on both, she has found a strategy and I am not involved.”

A pause.

The merchants in the snug had gone quiet. Maren listened for a moment, deciding whether the quiet meant sleep or a dangerous new plan. It seemed to mean sleep. She did not trust sleep either, not when it came after singing, but it was better than harmony.

“The handle will stick,” Maren said, as if the door had personally offended her. “Lift it as you turn it. Do not force the poor thing into an argument it cannot win. Doors are like men with too much time and not enough work. They become difficult when they are given a reason.”

She shifted the cloth over her left forearm. The tally sheet was still tucked under her arm, though she had folded it once, squared it, and folded it again in the way she squared things when she wanted to keep from saying more than she meant.

“Room four until noon,” she said. “Breakfast is porridge, eggs, bread, and turnips that have been told to behave like vegetables. If you want fancier, ask before the merchants wake. If you want wine, ask after you have looked at the price and decided whether your thirst is worth the lesson.”

Her gaze dropped to the pack again. Only for a moment.

“If you need the privy, it is behind the stair. If you need anything else before dawn, knock on the stairwell and not on my door. My door is for staff, bills, and emergencies.”

She considered the word.

“A sticky handle is not an emergency. A cat on your face is not an emergency. Fire is an emergency. So is a man trying to pay with a story.”

Maren reached into her apron with her left hand and brought out a small stub of candle. She set it on the landing rail outside the door, not inside the room. She did not cross thresholds at midnight unless she meant to stay, and she did not mean to stay.

“If you need light to find the privy, use the stair lamp,” she said. “If you need light to read, use your own. If you need light to worry, I suggest porridge in the morning. Worry is worse on an empty stomach, and you have just had stew, so that is an insult to Old Pell.”

From the kitchen doorway, Pell’s voice carried low and tired.

“I hear you.”

Maren did not turn.

“You always hear me,” she said. “That is why I speak plainly.”

Pell grunted.

Maren looked back toward the stairs. The house had settled into its deeper hour, the hour when the beams remembered they were trees and the floorboards remembered they had been walked on by better and worse men. She liked that hour less than she admitted. It made the bar feel too wide, and the empty end of it feel too narrow.

“Sleep if you can,” Maren said, returning to the doorway. “If the cat leaves the bed, do not assume the room has become yours. She is merely changing tactics.”

She turned to go.

Then stopped, looking at the pack one more time.

Maren did not ask what was in it.

She said, “Whatever you are carrying, keep it out of Sela’s path. She trips with conviction. If she falls into your pack, she will apologize, and then you will have an apology with a broken wrist and a complaint from the cook.”

The cat gave a small, skeptical sound.

Maren gave the cat a flat look.

“You are not helping,” she said.

She went down the stairs slowly, left hand on the banister, right hand at her side. When she reached the common room, the lamplight had gone soft and low. Sela was wiping the far tables with the careful boredom of someone who had been told not to leave clutter unless the clutter was hers. Lord Havel’s table had been cleared of crab cakes, though Maren suspected the lord had taken the plate with him. That was either good manners or good appetite. She did not know which bothered her more.

Maren set the tally sheet on the bar and squared it.

Sela looked up.

“Room four?” she asked.

“Occupied,” Maren said.

“Cat?”

“Cat.”

Sela considered this. “If the cat is on the bed, she is in the room.”

“If the cat is on his pack, she is in trouble,” Maren said.

“What if she is on both?”

Maren picked up the cloth and wiped a spot that had already been wiped three times.

“Then she has found a strategy,” she said, “and I am not involved.”

Sela smiled, then stopped before it became a thing.

“Lord Havel asked if the kitchen could do eggs before dawn,” Sela said.

“It can do them,” Maren said. “Eggs are simple. They do not require fancy turnips to feel important.”

Sela’s smile became slightly less dangerous. “Tell him the price is one copper per egg, two for a soft one, three if he wants them burned and called rustic.”

“You are learning,” Maren said.

“I have been watching you,” Sela answered.

“That is how you learn to charge people for being disappointed,” Maren said. “It is not a virtue, but it is a trade.”

From the kitchen, Pell’s ladle struck the pot in a way that sounded suspiciously like approval.

Maren gave the door a brief glance.

“Pell hears everything,” she said. “He pretends not to, because that is how he remains dignified.”

Sela took the empty bowl from the table and moved toward the kitchen pass. Maren watched her go, then looked toward the end of the bar.

The second glass waited there.

Pale ale. Untouched. The lamplight made it look almost clear, almost patient. Maren did not move it. She did not drink from it. She did not name it.

She set her own glass beside it, then looked at the ledger.

Traveler.

Room four.

Paid.

Probably polite.

Maren stared at the last line longer than she needed to.

Then she closed the ledger.

The front door creaked somewhere above them as the wind shifted, a small sound like a house turning in its sleep. Maren went around the bar with her left hand on the counter and her right resting lightly at her side. The oak cudgel leaned in its familiar place behind the shelves, worn smooth by years and use. Maren did not look at it directly. She did not need to. She knew where everything was in the Antler, the way a quartermaster knows a supply line before it fails.

She checked the hearth.

She checked the snug.

The merchants had gone quiet enough to be noticed, and quiet enough to be believed. One of them had fallen into a chair with his mouth open and his dignity nowhere to be found. Maren looked at him with the weary respect of a woman who had seen many men surrender to bad ale and better music. She did not wake them. She merely turned the lamp down another notch and said, in a voice low enough for the walls and not the men,

“If the snug is to become a chapel, let it at least have better hymns.”

The room did not answer.

Maren nodded once to no one in particular.

“Good,” she said. “Silence is the best vintage in the house. It also costs less than the wine.”

She gathered the coins she had already counted, slid them into her apron pocket with her left hand, and squared the ledger again. Then she took the cloth and wiped the bar one last time, starting near the place where the Traveler’s coins had been, moving toward the spot where the crab plate had lingered. Her right hand stayed at the edge of the counter, fingers curled loosely, steadying nothing that needed steadying.

A faint orange smear survived her first pass.

Maren looked at it as if it had committed a personal offense.

“Oh, for the love of every saint who ever stubbed a toe,” she muttered.

She wiped it again, harder this time. The cloth came away with a faint stain. Maren stared at it. The stain stared back.

“You have no business being that cheerful,” she told it.

The stain did not answer. Maren was not surprised. Grease rarely was.

She took the cloth to the kitchen pass, where Pell was banking the fire with the grim devotion of a man performing a funeral rite.

“Room four,” Maren said.

Pell did not look up. “Cat?”

“Cat.”

“Good,” Pell said. “She has a right to the bed.”

“The traveler has a right to the room.”

“Cats do not read ledgers.”

“No,” Maren said. “But they understand boundaries better than lords.”

Pell gave her a sideways look. “You mean Lord Havel.”

“I mean the sort,” Maren said. “Lord Havel is merely the one who sent the evidence.”

Pell grunted and turned back to the fire.

“Turnips are safe,” he said.

“The cat is not.”

“The cat is always not.”

Maren left the cloth on the counter and returned to the common room. Sela had gone to the stairwell with the empty bowl, moving carefully, as if she suspected the house of trying to be in her way. Maren watched her go, then looked up toward the second landing.

The stairwell was dark, but the lamp on the landing rail still burned low and steady. The door of room four stood half open enough to suggest that the occupant had either gone to bed or had not yet gone to sleep. Maren could not see the pack from the common room, and she did not climb again.

She did not need to.

Whatever was in it, the Traveler had carried it carefully. He had set it down carefully. He had paid, wiped his mouth, and gone up without making a mess. That was not enough to earn trust. It was enough to earn patience.

Maren had plenty of patience.

She had less of it after midnight, but it was still enough.

The clock ticked. The fire shifted. Somewhere above them, a floorboard settled with the particular creak of a house remembering its own weight.

Maren stood at the bar for a moment, neither moving toward the stairwell nor toward the kitchen. The second glass remained at the end, pale ale catching the lamplight, untouched.

She did not move it.

Instead, she lifted her own glass, looked toward the empty space beside it, and said very quietly,

“To the weather.”

She drank.

The other glass did not move.

Maren set her glass down, straightened the cloth beside the ledger, and let the house settle around her. Then she turned off the last lamp near the hearth, leaving only the small light on the landing, and began closing the Antler.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I settle into the room, kicking off my boots and stretching. The cat gives a soft meow, then jumps onto my pack, sniffing around the mysterious package. I sigh, a little smile playing on my lips.* "Alright, alright, but don't get any ideas about opening that."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren heard the cat before she heard anything else.

A meow came down from the second landing, soft, pointed, and entirely too confident. It was followed by a rustle that might have been linens, or a pack being made to feel personally considered.

Sela paused with a bowl halfway to the kitchen pass.

“That is room four,” Sela said.

“It is,” Maren said.

“The cat?”

“It has chosen.”

Maren set the cloth on the bar with her left hand. Her right rested against the ledger, not helping, only present. She looked toward the stairwell. The landing lamp burned low, a small square of gold on the wall. She did not climb again. Midnight had already made one exception for the weather, and Maren was not inclined to make another for a cat that had never paid rent.

But she did raise her voice enough to reach, no more.

“If she is on your pack,” Maren called up, “do not assume she is helping. Cats do not help. They inspect, accuse, and depart.”

A pause. From above, there was no answer, only the faint creak of the bedframe settling, as if the room itself had sighed.

Maren waited one breath, then added, “If she gets hair on the linens, Sela has to wash them. If Sela has to wash them, she becomes expensive. If she becomes expensive, I become reasonable. That is a bad chain of events for everyone except the cat.”

The cat meowed again, from somewhere near the pack.

Maren nodded once, as if this confirmed a long-held theory.

“That is not a request,” she said to the room, though her gaze went up the stairwell. “That is a summons. Do not answer it like a man who has been summoned.”

Sela came back to the bar, empty bowl under her arm. “Do you want me to check?”

“No,” Maren said.

Pell’s voice came from the kitchen pass, dry and tired. “The cat will get what the cat wants.”

“The cat will get exactly what the cat wants and nothing else,” Maren said. “That is the problem. She has no imagination.”

Pell grunted.

Maren turned back to the bar. The second glass still waited at the end, pale ale catching the lamplight. She looked at it, then at the stairwell, where the pack had gone up careful and the key had been taken by a man who said he was not dishonest.

She lifted the cloth with her left hand and wiped a place that had already been wiped.

“If the handle sticks,” she called up, quieter now, “do not force it. It is old. It remembers arguments better than it wins them.”

A floorboard shifted overhead. The cat gave another small sound, more pleased than before.

Maren looked at the stairs.

“And if she is on both,” she said, “you are on your own. I told you I would not mediate.”

Sela smiled at the bar top. Maren did not look at her.

She squared the ledger with the back of her left hand. Her right stayed at her side, curled loosely, the weaker hand keeping the book of debts company while the stronger one did the counting. The coins were already in her apron pocket. The room was already paid. The name Traveler sat in the ledger with its stubborn little claim to being no one in particular.

Maren wrote beneath it: Cat, maybe.

Then she considered the line, changed it to: Cat, probably.

She gave the page a dry look.

“I am not generous,” she said to the ledger. “I am merely accurate.”

From the kitchen, the fire popped once. Old Pell had finished banking it. The common room had gone into the hour that belonged to the house itself, the hour when the beams remembered they were trees and the floorboards remembered every foot that had ever passed over them. Maren did not like that hour. It made the empty end of the bar feel less empty and the filled end feel too wide.

She looked toward the stairwell again.

“If you need the privy,” she called up, voice low and steady, “behind the stair. Do not make a mess. If you make a mess, Sela has to clean it, and Sela will do it with a face that makes men apologize to furniture.”

No answer came down. Only the small settling sound of the cat, perhaps, and the house breathing around it.

Maren took her own glass from the bar. It was empty. The other glass at the end was not. She set them side by side for a moment, then moved hers aside and left the untouched one exactly where it belonged.

“To the weather,” she said again, very softly, to no one who needed to hear it.

Then she turned off the lamp by the hearth, leaving only the small light on the landing, and began locking the front door.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Too late, Maren! She's made herself quite at home," I call back, my voice a little muffled as I pull off my traveling shirt. The cat purrs, kneading my pack. "And no worries about Sela. I'll take care of the cat hair."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Whatever's hot would be Pell's venison stew. The candle wax is also hot, but I do not recommend it."

Maren reached under the bar with her left hand, came up with a clean tankard, and drew ale from the cask. She set it in front of the traveler with a cup of well water beside it. "Pell. One stew, bread alongside." Her voice carried back to the kitchen without rising above the noise of the room.

She slid the tally sheet under the bar with her right hand and rested both hands on the counter. "Rooms I have. Five coppers for the night, two for the stew, bread comes whether you ask for it or not. You will get the room at the end of the hall. It is the only one that does not sing when the wind comes off the east road."

Her eyes passed over the pack — set down carefully, the way people set down things that mattered — but she said nothing about it. She hooked a wooden peg hanging at the bar's end and pushed it along the top with two fingers. "For the pack, if it would rather not spend the evening underfoot. Nobody in here will trouble it."

She picked up her cloth again. "Now. What do I call you, friend? Pell butters the bread for people whose names he knows."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking a long drink of the cool water.* "Traveler will do." I eye the peg. "Good offer, but it'll stay with me." *I push the pack a little closer, subtly.* "Steward sounds like a good fellow."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Traveler, then. It is not much of a name, but it is honest about its limits." Maren picked up her cloth again and worked it along the counter in slow circles, left hand steady, right hand resting on the tally sheet. "And the cook's name is Pell, not Steward. Though between the two of us, he would make a terrible steward. The man organizes his spices by sentiment, not by use."

Behind her, the kitchen door swung open and one of her servers came out with a bowl on a wooden board — the stew, dark and thick, steam rising off it, a heel of bread alongside. The server set it down in front of the traveler and disappeared back toward the tables.

Maren looked at the bread. Plain. Dry. Unbuttered.

"Hm." She said nothing about it for a moment, then leaned one forearm on the bar. "Your bread came dry. That is not an oversight. Pell butters for names, and 'Traveler' did not qualify. He is very principled about his butter. I have seen him refuse a baron."

She held out her left hand, palm up, casual as anything. "Seven coppers when you have them — two for the stew, five for the room. Key is on an antler carved from oak, so do not lose it, because I will have to carve you a new one and I am slow at antlers."

Her eyes flicked once to the pack, then back to the traveler's face. Whatever she thought about it, she kept it behind her teeth.

"House rules are short. No blades on the tables, no shouting after the eleventh bell, and if you break it, you bought it. Breakfast is at sunrise. The stew is not breakfast. The stew is never breakfast, no matter how you beg."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren's cloth stopped moving.

The smell reached her before the plate did — butter, herbs, and underneath it something briny that had no business sitting two hundred miles from any coast she trusted. She looked at the plate. Then at the merchant in the corner, who ten minutes ago had been defending a barley price like it was his firstborn child.

"Well," she said, mostly to herself. "For the love of dry land."

She did not lean toward the plate. She did not touch it. She balled her cloth in her left hand and used it to slide the plate down the bar — smooth, unhurried, a good stretch of oak opening up between it and her — until it came to rest beside the traveler's stew.

"Friend," she called to the corner, without raising her voice. "I run a house that sells food. Outside plates are how cooks' hearts get broken, and Pell sulks for a full day when it happens. But generosity is generosity, so the plate stays — down the bar, where it will do the most good and the least harm."

She rested her forearm on the counter. "One thing, though. You were arguing over a half-copper in barley when I lit the lamps tonight. Now you are sending coastal crab across my floor. Either your fortunes improved considerably in the last hour, or somebody wants to be seen being generous. I do not mind which. But tell Lord Havel, from me, that the coin for those cakes would have bought ale for the whole room and made him twenty friends instead of two."

Then, to the traveler, in the same flat tone she used for quoting the price of a room: "I do not eat seafood, myself. Do not care for it. Never have. They are all yours, Traveler. I can vouch for the stew. The crab and the lord, you are on your own."

She wiped the spot where the plate had sat, folded the cloth dirty-side inward, and dropped it into the wash basin beneath the bar. A fresh cloth came up in its left hand. Anyone watching closely might have noticed the sequence. She was not explaining it.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I look from the plate of crab cakes to Maren, then back at the crab cakes. I pick up a fork and spear one, taking a bite.* "These are pretty good, actually. You sure you don't want one?" *I offer her the plate, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Maybe just a little bite?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren looked at the fork. Then at the smile behind it. Then she raised her left hand, palm out — the same flat-palmed gesture that had stopped drunks, tax collectors, and one very determined goat in her years behind this bar — and waited.

"Oh, for the love of every saint who ever burned the porridge," she said, quietly, mostly to the countertop.

Then she straightened and gave the traveler the same tone she used for quoting room prices. "Traveler. I am going to say this once, plainly, so we can both get on with our suppers. I do not eat seafood. I do not eat it in small portions. I do not eat it to be polite, and I do not eat it to prove a point. A little bite of a thing I do not eat is still, by every measure I know, a bite."

She had not touched the plate — not with her hand, not with the cloth — and she did not start now. Instead she picked up the water jug with her left hand and topped off the traveler's cup, unhurried, as though the matter had already been filed and shelved.

"Now." The jug went back on its shelf. "You have a look about you. The look of a person tapping a lock to see whether it turns. Save yourself the tapping. What that lock guards is old, it is dull, and it is mine. As for the cakes — you were a stranger when that plate arrived, and generous lords do not generally feed strangers. Chew slowly. Mind the road you leave by."

From the kitchen, a pot lid came down on the stove with slightly more force than any lid strictly required. Pell had seen the plate.

Maren nudged the stew an inch closer with two fingers on the board. "That does not wait. Cold venison is an insult to a good deer, and Pell takes insults personally."

She went back to wiping the counter in slow left-handed circles. Three seconds later, without looking up: "And if you mention the butter to Pell after this, he will not butter bread in this house until spring. I have watched it happen. It is not a thing you want to live through."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren set her cloth down and rapped the bar twice with her left knuckle — the house's answer to a toast, this side of dark.

"He cannot hear you through a wall, but I will carry it." She lifted her voice just enough to clear the kitchen door. "Pell. The stranger says the stew is the best he has had in months."

The kitchen went quiet. Then the door swung open and Pell filled it — broad, grey-bearded, forearms like proving dough, a towel over one shoulder. He looked down the bar at the traveler. Then, briefly and without affection, at the plate of crab cakes.

"Hm," said Pell.

"That is his standing ovation," Maren said. "You will not get more out of him before midnight."

Pell leveled a thick finger at the traveler's bread board. "You ate the bread dry."

"It arrived dry," Maren said. "You sent it out that way on purpose, and we both watched you do it."

Pell grunted — a sound with a great deal of history in it — and withdrew. The door had barely settled on its hinges when one of the servers slipped out of the kitchen and set a second board beside the stew: bread, split, and buttered all the way to the crust.

Maren looked at it. Then at the kitchen door. Then she leaned her forearm on the bar and lowered her voice.

"In fourteen years I have never seen that man reverse a butter ruling. It has now happened once, and we will not speak of it again, because if he remembers tomorrow that he did it, the whole thing unravels and I am back to dry bread like everyone else."

She picked up her cloth again, left hand working slow circles, right hand resting flat on the counter. "One small note, since we are trading words tonight. That word you spent — 'damn' — is a coin with no face on it. It spends anywhere and stands for nothing. Pell hears 'good' from a hundred mouths a week. What he can use is detail. What it tasted like. What it reminded you of. He will pretend not to listen, and he will keep it until spring."

Then, quieter still, with the smallest tip of her chin toward the corner: "And while you chew. The gentleman who sent your cakes has looked over here four times since you took the fork. Not at you. At the plate. Generosity that counts its own swallowing is not generosity, friend. It is a ledger entry. Eat what you like — it is your stomach, and it seems to be holding. But I would want to know what the entry buys before I put my name to it."

She left the bar then, unhurried, and drifted down to where the two merchants sat. Whatever she said to them was too low to carry, and it took about the length of a swallow. When she came back, the taller one had returned to his grain prices with the diligence of a man who had been advised.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I take another bite of the stew, savoring it.* "Well, Pell, it tastes like my grandmother's cooking. And that's high praise, indeed." *I watch the merchant. Then I pick up another crab cake, take a bite, and offer it to the small dog that has wandered over to my feet, giving me hopeful eyes.* "Want a piece, boy?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The kitchen went quiet.

Not the ordinary quiet of a simmering pot — the particular, offended quiet of a large man holding very still so he could listen better. Then the chopping resumed, slower, with the care of someone working out a feeling with a knife.

"He heard that," Maren said, not looking up from the counter. "Grandmother's cooking. You have just spent the highest coin in this house without knowing it was currency. That man has spent thirty years trying to recreate his grandmother's gravy. You are now a person of interest."

Then she looked down.

The dog had taken the crab cake with the delicacy of a pickpocket, swallowed it whole, and was now sitting at the traveler's boot with one ear up and the gravity of a tax assessor.

"Her name is Turnip. She came in under a wool cart three years ago, and the cart left without her. She has held the grudge against carts ever since, and against the rest of us she has simply declined to accept that she does not live here." Maren tipped her chin at the hopeful stare. "Do not read gratitude into that face. She would eat a boot if you buttered it."

Across the room, the grain argument stopped mid-word.

The tall merchant's head came around — not to the dog, Maren noted, but to the plate. And the quiet one, who had not spent a word all evening, set down his tankard, stood, and went out the front door with the unhurried step of a man who very much wished to be seen leaving for ordinary reasons.
