The privy was the other way. Maren knew precisely where her privy was.

She picked up the water jug in her left hand and did not move from her spot. Her voice stayed under the noise of the room.

"Well, now. The man counting his own generosity just watched a dog eat it, and his quiet friend remembered an urgent errand in the dark." The jug went back on its shelf. "Two readings, and I do not pretend to know which. Either he is offended to see coastal crab in a cur — some men are, and it costs nothing but our patience. Or there was something in those cakes meant to go down a person's throat, slowly, where folks could watch it happen. Dogs do not count for that kind of work."

She folded her cloth over the bar rail, smoothing it flat.

"Before you ask — you have had two of them yourself, and if it were the fast kind of trouble, you would know by now. The slow kind I cannot speak to, and I do not enjoy saying so. And feeding the cake to Turnip while you watched him — that was neatly done, whether you meant it or not. I have seen worse technique from people paid for it."

She nudged the stew board closer with two fingers.

"My counsel is stew, bread, and a face that noticed nothing. If the quiet one comes back, he will find a tired traveler finishing supper. If you would rather ask questions — wait until he is standing in the doorway. Doors have a way of telling you what a man is carrying before his mouth does."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The clock's last stroke faded, and the room had thinned while nobody was marking it. The grain merchants had gone up to their beds. One of the servers banked the lamps low without being asked — the house knew the hour as well as she did — and Pell came out shrugging into his coat, marked the end of the bar with a look, and went out the side door without a word.

The quiet one still had not come back.

Maren set her cloth on the rail. She reached up with her left hand to the high shelf, past the imported wine she overcharged for on principle, and brought down a squat bottle with no label and a coat of dust everywhere but the place a hand had gripped it for years. Two cups came down after it. Hers, and one chipped at the rim that had never been replaced — not once, not when better cups broke every month.

She poured two measures, left-handed, no deeper than a thumb. She drank her own in one swallow and made no face about it. The other she carried down the bar to the far end, where the varnish had worn to a pale ring in the shape of the cup's bottom, and set it there. She turned it a quarter-turn, so the chip faced the wall.

Then she came back, and did not pretend the traveler had not seen it.

"Every house keeps one custom it does not chalk on the slate," she said, in the tone she used for quoting prices. "That one is mine. It keeps better unasked-after, like bread."

She set the oak-antlered key on the counter and pushed it across with two fingers. "Your coppers can wait for morning. The key cannot wait past tonight. Bar the door — not because I am expecting trouble, but because barring a door costs nothing and explains itself afterward."

Turnip had not moved from the traveler's boot. Maren looked at her a moment longer than a dog strictly deserved — a whole cake, an hour gone, no harm showing yet — and set a bowl of water down where the dog could find it.

"Now. The quiet one has not come back through the front of this house, and the privy is the other way, and I know exactly where my privy is." She folded her cloth, dirty side in. "I told you nobody here would trouble your pack. I still believe that. But it sleeps better upstairs with you tonight than down here where a door creaks. So do I."

She took up a fresh cloth and went back to her slow left-handed circles.

"If anyone knocks on your door in the dark and says Maren sent them — nobody did. I do not knock."

At the end of the bar, the cup sat with nobody's name on it. It would sit there until morning. Nobody in the house would ask.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I pick up the key, then lift Turnip into my arms.* "Come on, girl. Let's see if this room sings." *I nod to Maren.* "Thanks for the hospitality. And the advice."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Advice is free," Maren said, taking up her cloth again. "The stew was two coppers. Do not go confusing which of those I charge for."

She watched them toward the stairs — the traveler, the pack, and the dog riding in the crook of an arm like a lady of quality. Turnip looked back over the traveler's shoulder with an expression of pure conscience.

"She does not live here," Maren informed the room. "That has been settled for three years, and she has nearly accepted it."

Then, to the traveler's back, before the stairwell swallowed them: "Mind the third stair from the top. It does not sing, but it clears its throat. And the room does not sing either — the one beside it hums, but only in February, and only to itself. Yours is the honest one." A beat. "Seven coppers on the bar at sunrise. I am trusting you upstairs on the strength of a dog's good opinion, which is more collateral than half the barons in this county have ever offered me."

The door at the bottom of the stairs creaked. Maren listened to it the way other people listened to music.

When the footsteps reached the landing, she set about closing the house. The plate of crab cakes she neither scraped into the fire nor fed to anything. She wrapped them in a clean cloth, left-handed, and set the bundle on the high shelf beside the unlabeled bottle. "If a magistrate ever asks," she said to nobody, "it is best to have the question still on a plate."

She barred the front door and banked the lamps down to one. Through the window she checked the east road, then the west, where the privy was not.

The quiet one had not come back.

"Sleep wherever you are standing, friend," she told the dark, in the tone she used for quoting prices.

Then she turned down the last lamp. At the end of the bar, the chipped cup sat with its chip to the wall, full, patient, going nowhere until morning. Maren rested two fingers on the counter beside it — briefly, and not for anyone to see — and left it exactly as it was.

She climbed the stairs, past the third one, and left the common room door open a hand's width, the way she always did. The house could keep its own watch.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I carefully open the door to my room, Turnip still in my arms. It's a small room, but clean. I set Turnip down, and she immediately sniffs the corners.* "Alright, girl. Make yourself at home." *I set my pack on the small table, then test the bed. Not bad.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren paused level with the door, not knocking, because she had told the truth about that. Through the wood came the small sounds of a room taking on a guest — a pack set down with care, a bed tested, a low murmur. She listened a moment and established that the traveler was talking to the dog before talking to anyone else.

Good order of operations, she thought.

"The latch lifts unless you press the thumb-piece down," she said through the door, in the tone she used for quoting room prices. "The window sticks after rain and forgives you in dry weather. Turnip will decide where she sleeps and inform you of the arrangement by morning." A pause. "Goodnight, Traveler."

Then she went on to her own room at the end of the hall, boots off, the oak cudgel laid within reach of her left hand — a habit from five quartermastered years she had never bothered to retire.

She slept the way she always slept: in shallow water, one ear on the house. Once, in an hour she could not have sworn to, gravel outside took a weight and gave it back. She was up with the cudgel before the second step. She stood at the window through ten slow breaths — east road empty, west road empty, frost silvering the woodpile — and nothing came again. She went back to bed. Filed, not forgotten.

She was downstairs before the sun cleared the hills. Fire banked up, bread in the oven, porridge on. The chipped cup she carried to the clay pot of herbs on the sill, poured it out over the roots, rinsed it, dried it, and set it back on the high shelf beside the unlabeled bottle. Nobody was down to see it, which was the point of the hour she chose.

Her rounds turned up what the night had been doing. Room four — the quiet one's — bed unslept, window latched from the inside, no key on its hook. Outside, the frost lay unbroken everywhere except two patches gone to wet earth: one on the privy path, and one directly beneath the taproom shutter, where the latch sat a hair wrong with a fresh nick in the paint.

"Oh, for the love of every saint who ever bolted the barn after the horse was sold," Maren said, quietly, to the latch.

She read it the way she read a tally sheet — someone had stood there a while, in the dark, at the window where the wrapped plate sat on the shelf inside — and then she mended the latch, her right hand doing the holding and her left doing the work, because a thing broken is a thing that gets used again.

The tall merchant came down before sunrise, paid for two rooms in silver, and did not ask for change. "My associate walks at night," he offered. "Habit."

"He walked past the privy and did not come back," Maren said. "That is the whole of what I know about his evening."

The merchant's face did something brief and complicated. He took the east road without touching his porridge.

By the time the light was honest, the house smelled of bread and bacon. Maren set a bowl and plate at the traveler's spot, refreshed the water, and left the wrapped cakes where they were on the high shelf — questions kept better on a plate, and she was in no hurry to be asked any.

She took up her cloth and worked the counter in slow left-handed circles, glancing once at the stairs.

"Breakfast holds until the bell, Traveler," she informed the empty room. "After that, it is porridge's problem. Seven coppers, and I will even say good morning."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I come down the stairs, Turnip trotting happily beside me. I nod to Maren.* "Morning. Seems the room didn't sing after all." *I slide the seven coppers across the bar.* "And here's those coppers. Hope the dog's good opinion was worth it."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Good morning," Maren returned, in the tone of a woman settling a debt. She swept the coppers off the bar with her left hand and weighed them in her palm rather than counting — a habit she did not explain — then dropped them through the till slot. "True weight, all seven. And you have saved me the cost of a good morning, which I will put toward Turnip's board. She does not pay it, and does not know she does not pay it, and that is the arrangement she prefers."

She hooked a bowl of porridge, a rasher of bacon, and bread still warm enough to argue back, and set them across. At the far end of the bar, the pale ring in the varnish sat bare this morning. She wiped around it and not over it.

"The room did not sing because it knows better. The only performer in this house is the third stair, and it has never once been paid." A beat. "The stew is not breakfast. I want that on record before Pell comes out, because he will ask."

The kitchen door opened. Pell came out carrying a small dish with both hands, the way a priest carries relics — a spoonful of dark gravy over a broken dumpling, steaming. He set it beside the porridge, looked at the traveler, said "Hm," pointed one thick finger at the dish, and withdrew.

"You said 'grandmother' last night," Maren translated. "He has been up since it was dark, and that is his fourth attempt. Judge it honestly. He can taste a polite lie the way I taste watered ale."

Then she crossed to the high shelf, brought down the wrapped plate by its cloth corners, and laid it on the bar. Her hands never met the food.

"While you eat, I will spend the night's news, because some of it is yours whether you like that or not." She turned the plate a half-inch with the cloth. "Six cakes came on this. Two went to you, one to Turnip — who is fine this morning, which rules out the fast kind of trouble and says nothing about the slow kind. Three remain. And I will say this from arm's length only: that one there was pressed in two acts. The others were not. I do not know cakes. I know when two things have been made to look like one thing."

She folded the cloth back over them.

"Now the house news. The quiet one went past my privy in the dark and did not come back through any door I own. His bed is unslept and his key is gone. The frost kept two secrets and gave up two patches — the privy path, and under that shutter, where somebody stood long enough to nick the paint at the latch. And here is the part I keep turning over: the silver drawer sits under the far end of this bar. The plate sat under that shutter. Whoever stood there did not want my coin. He wanted the plate."

She took up her cloth, left hand working slow circles.

"So I will not ask your name, Traveler. I will ask this instead, and you may answer or not: did you walk into this house alone last night, or did something follow you in? Because if it followed you, it has now stood at my shutter in the dark, and I take that personally." She nodded toward the low door at the room's end. "If there is a thing you would say away from these walls, the snug is empty until noon. Thicker walls, smaller door. I keep it for conversations shaped exactly like this one."

Three seconds, without looking up: "Whatever you decide, eat first. Careful people think better on a full stomach, and the tall one took the east road — so if that is your road, know you will not be walking it alone."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I poke at the dumpling with my fork, then take a bite.* "He's getting closer. The gravy... it's almost there. Tell him that." *I look at the plate Maren set down.* "I came alone. But I'm not always alone, if that makes sense." *I push the plate with the crab cakes back towards her.* "And I think I'll stick to the stew."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren stopped the plate with two fingers through the cloth before it crossed the middle of the bar, turned it, and walked it back to its place — the same unhurried housekeeping gesture she used on drips and elbows.

"The plate lives on its own side of the bar," she said. "That is a border, like the eleventh bell. Nothing personal to you, and nothing personal to the cakes." She rewrapped the cloth and set the whole business back on the high shelf, out of reach of everything in the room, herself included. "But I am noting, for the record, that you ate two of those last night with an appetite, and this morning will not sit in the same county as the rest. Either you took my counsel about careful faces further than I intended, or you know something about those cakes that I do not. Both are acceptable answers. I am not asking. I am filing."

She took up her cloth. "As for sticking to the stew — the stew is not breakfast. I have said it before and I will say it now, because it is not a rule, it is a law of nat—"

The kitchen door opened.

Pell came out slow, towel over his shoulder, and planted himself across the bar. He looked at the traveler the way he looked at a sauce that was nearly right. When he spoke, it was in a voice he used perhaps twice a year.

"Closer how," he said. "Say it plain. What went in her gravy."

Maren set her cloth down. "Mark the hour," she told the room at large. "Fourteen years, and that man has asked a customer a question. I will be telling this story until the roof is replaced."

Pell pointed one thick finger. "Think on it. The sauce keeps." The door settled behind him. A moment later, from the kitchen, a pot came down onto the stove with intent.

"There is the deadline," Maren said. "And there, unless my ears have failed, is the sound of fourteen years of house law collapsing. The stew is never breakfast — except as of this morning, when it is, and the exception has your name on it. Do not let it go to your head. He has overridden me exactly once before, over saffron, and the less said of that the better."

Turnip had taken up her post under the bar stool, performing famine for an audience of one. "Do not pay her," Maren advised. "She ate a crab cake last night that most men would call a fortune, and she has decided it did not happen."

Then she folded the cloth, dirty side in, and rested both hands on the counter.

"Now. 'I came alone, but I am not always alone.' That sentence has two floors to it, and I would like to know which one the trouble lives on. I have heard its shape before — from couriers, from a debt-carrier or two, from folk whose companions ride ahead and wait. It can also mean the road behind you is never as empty as it looks." A beat. "And before you offer the dog — Turnip does not count. She chose you at this bar, and she cannot follow a cart."

She worked the counter in slow left-handed circles.

"Here is what I will do with my half of it. The pressed cake does not go back with its brothers. It goes in the tin with the tax receipts, where nothing good has ever happened. The market cart comes up from Dunmore at midday, and the reeve's man rides it on Wednesdays. Today is Wednesday. Whether I hand him a cake and a story is my decision, made in my house, about a man who stood at my shutter in the dark. You owe that nothing."

She looked up. "Two things from you, and then I will let you eat in peace. Which floor is the trouble on — people who are yours, or things that are not? And which road takes you out of here today? The tall one went east with an appetite for getting away. If that is your road, I would rather hear it before the stew arrives than after. And if the answer has a second half — the snug keeps until noon."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I finish the dumpling, wiping my mouth with the back of my hand.* "Tell Pell... it needs more thyme. Just a whisper, to brighten it." *I look at Maren, then down at Turnip.* "The trouble... it's more of a shadow. Something that follows, but isn't quite there." *I push my chair back slightly.* "And I'm heading west. Always west."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave a single nod, as if the request had been lodged in her ledger before it was spoken.

“Venison stew,” she said. “Old Pell has had it on the fire since noon, and it is better for the wait. Bread comes with it. Ale is local. Wine is imported and overpriced, but I will not stop you from making an expensive mistake.”

She moved the tally sheet aside with the tips of her left fingers, then reached beneath the bar for a clean bowl and spoon. The silver ring on her left thumb caught the lamplight as she set the bowl down on the counter with a soft wooden tap.

“There are rooms,” she continued. “Twelve upstairs, and more than enough emptiness tonight. You can have one facing the yard if you want quiet, or one facing the road if you want to hear your own troubles less.”

Her gaze flicked briefly to the pack, not with suspicion, but with the practical notice of a woman who had spent years watching what people carried and how they carried it.

“If it is fragile, keep it near. If it is merely precious, the room will do. If it is both, the floor by the bed is sturdier than it looks.”

She straightened, resting her left hand lightly on the bar.

“Stew, room, and a cup of something to drink with it. Unless you have a preference, friend.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I let out a soft sigh of relief.* "Venison stew sounds perfect. And a room facing the yard, please. I'll take whatever ale you have on tap." I glance down at the package, then back up at her, a small smile playing on my lips. "It's... both fragile and precious. I'll keep it close."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren reached for a clean mug with her left hand, hooking it from the shelf beneath the bar in one practiced motion. Her right stayed folded near the tally sheet, not idle so much as permitted to rest while the left did the work. She drew the ale slow, letting the head settle rather than forcing it, and set the mug before the traveler with the base touching the wood first, no clatter.

“Yard room, then,” she said. “Second door on the left at the top of the stairs. The shutters close properly, which is more than I can say for the one on the corner. If the cock in the yard begins before dawn, that is between him and whatever conscience poultry have.”

She took a brass key from a hook behind her and set it on the bar, turning it once with a fingertip until the bow faced the traveler. The silver ring on her thumb winked in the lamplight.

“As for what you are carrying,” Maren said, her voice dropping no lower than the room required, “I do not ask after goods that make a person careful. The Antler has seen reliquaries, wedding gifts, stolen geese, and once a cage of very angry songbirds. Most of them arrived in better condition than they left because the owner knew when to keep a hand on them.”

She glanced toward the kitchen door, where the scent of stew had grown thick enough to stand in.

“Eat first,” she said. “Old Pell treats it as a personal insult when food cools on the pass. If the pack needs a place while you eat, the stool beside your knee is sturdier than it looks. If it needs the room before then, I will walk ahead of you and show you where the lock sticks so you do not fight it in the dark.”

A faint, dry amusement touched her face, gone before it became a smile.

“But if it is the sort of thing that needs watching while you chew bread, then keep it where your knee can feel it. I have not had to reach for the cudgel in six years, and I would prefer not to begin again over a misunderstanding.”

She lifted the tally sheet again with her left hand, marking a line beside the evening’s ale count with a small stroke, then looked back.

“Stew will be out before the foam settles on your cup. If you want a candle for the room, say so now. The stairs are honest enough, but they were built by a man who believed everyone had the knees of a goat.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s gaze dropped to the plate, and for the span of a breath her expression went carefully blank. Crab. She did not recoil—recoiling would have made a story of it—but she did shift her weight a half-step along the bar, putting a little more distance between herself and the plate as though it had arrived carrying a tax demand.

With her left hand she drew a folded linen pad from beneath the counter. She did not touch the crab cakes with it, nor did she let her fingers come near the rim where any stray crumb or moisture might sit. Instead, she used the pad to guide the plate a careful span away from her side of the bar and toward the traveler’s. The movement was smooth, unhurried, and utterly deliberate. Her right hand stayed clear near the tally sheet, resting but not helping. The silver ring on her left thumb caught the lamplight as she withdrew.

“Lord Havel is generous,” Maren said, her voice carrying just enough for the merchant’s table to hear without inviting them closer. “The Gilded Antler thanks him. Tell him I do not care for seafood. The traveler is welcome to the whole of it.”

She turned back to the bar, her tone settling into the lower, practical register she used for guests who looked as if they had walked half the road behind them already.

“If you have a taste for it, help yourself,” she said. “If you do not, or if shellfish disagrees with you, say so plain. I will have Pell send out the stew, and the plate can go back to his table with my compliments intact.”

She glanced at the plate once more, then away, with the air of a woman regarding an object she had decided not to adopt.

“I prefer my dinner to have had the decency to live on land.”

With the same linen pad, she wiped the spot where the plate had rested, though it had not needed wiping. Then she folded the cloth inward and set it aside for the wash bucket rather than returning it to the bar.

“Your ale is yours,” she added. “Stew will follow. And if you would rather sit at the far end of the counter while you eat, say so. I can manage both.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow, a small smile touching my lips.* "Well, that's certainly a strong opinion on seafood." I push the plate of crab cakes a little closer to me. "I don't mind them, actually. Thank Lord Havel for me." I take a sip of the ale. "This is excellent, by the way."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave the sort of nod that accepted a compliment without letting it sit down and make itself comfortable.

“The ale is local,” she said. “The brewer is vain, and his wife keeps a close account of his honesty. Between the two, the tap behaves.”

A beat later the joke arrived, dry as dust. She did not wait for it.

Her gaze passed over the crab cakes once, then left them alone with the dignity of a magistrate declining to examine evidence he had already ruled inadmissible.

“I will thank Lord Havel’s man in the morning,” she said. “Generosity is welcome in this house, especially when it arrives cooked and does not ask me to share it.”

She reached with her left hand for a fresh napkin from the stack beneath the bar and laid it beside the traveler’s elbow, careful to keep the cloth well away from her own sleeve. The silver ring on her thumb flashed briefly in the lamplight. Her right hand remained where it had been, near the tally sheet, useful mainly as a witness.

“If you mean to eat them, use the napkin,” she continued. “Shellfish has opinions of its own once it meets linen, and I have no wish to explain the smell to the next guest.”

She shifted a half-step down the bar, not enough to seem rude, but enough to give the plate a margin of air. She did not mention that shellfish and she had an old disagreement. She preferred to let the dislike stand as preference rather than confession.

“The room key is already yours,” she said. “Second door on the left. If the lock sticks, lift the latch a finger’s width before you turn it. The last guest tried to argue with it and lost. I did not mourn him, but I did have to oil the mechanism.”

From the kitchen came the sound of a ladle striking a pot, followed by Old Pell’s voice, muffled but indignant, as though he had heard his name being considered rather than spoken.

Maren lifted her chin slightly toward the door.

“Pell,” she said, not raising her voice at all, “one bowl. The traveler has ordered stew, the ale is behaving, and the crab has found a willing victim.”

She turned back to the bar, left hand resting lightly on the wood.

“Stew will be out in a moment. Bread with it. If you want mustard, say so before Pell decides you are the sort who ruins good meat. He has a memory for that.”

Then, after a glance at the pack near the stool, her tone became practical once more.

“And keep the strap under your foot, not hooked on the stool leg. If it slides, it will make noise. If it makes noise, people look. If people look, they remember.”

She picked up the tally sheet again with her left hand, though she did not mark it yet.

“That is not wisdom, friend. That is tavern arithmetic.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s mouth twitched, not quite a smile but the place where one might have stood if it had been invited.

“The stew has earned better language,” she said, “but I will accept enthusiasm in whatever dialect it arrives.”

She turned her head slightly toward the kitchen door, not enough to call, only enough to acknowledge that praise had crossed the pass and might be listening.

“Pell will hear that and become impossible,” she continued. “He already believes his venison stew is proof the saints have opinions about his ladle. If I repeat the compliment, he will ask for a second pot, a larger spoon, and a monument.”

Her left hand rested on the bar near the tally sheet, the silver ring on her thumb catching the lamplight. Her right stayed nearer the paper, not quite idle, but not asked to work. She did not look at the crab cakes except in the general way one looks at a bucket that might leak.

“Still, the toast is just. Pell can coax flavor from a stubborn bone and a sprig of rosemary if the day demands it. He has fed better men than Lord Havel and charged them less for the privilege.”

A dry pause followed, the kind that arrived late and left quietly.

“Drink to him, friend. But if he comes out to gloat, do not encourage him beyond one nod. Two, and he will begin to compose.”

Her gaze flicked briefly to the pack at the traveler’s knee, then back to the mug.

“And keep the crab on the napkin. Pell regards shellfish as a rumor he does not wish to verify.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, taking another spoonful of stew.* "Understood. One nod, no more. And the crab stays put." I take another sip of ale, savoring the warmth from the stew. "So, Maren, how long have you been running this place?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren did not answer at once. She used her left hand to straighten a mug that had not needed straightening, giving the question the same unhurried consideration she gave a coin before accepting it. Her right hand remained near the tally sheet, resting more than working, the old wrist content to let the left take the lead.

“The Antler came to me from my aunt Bessa,” she said at last. “I have kept it since. For twelve years I kept it with my husband Tobin. For six, I have kept it alone.”

She let that sit for a moment, neither bitter nor sentimental about it.

“Before that, I was underfoot enough to learn which floorboards gossip, which shutters only pretend to latch, and which guests are merely loud and which are quietly becoming a problem. That last lesson is expensive. It is usually paid in broken crockery.”

Her gaze moved briefly over the common room—the merchants, the dwarf, the lamplight catching the edges of bowls and mugs—then returned to the traveler.

“If you are asking whether I know the work, the answer is yes. If you are asking whether I have ever wanted to do anything else, the answer is no. The Antler and I have an arrangement. It gives me a livelihood, and I give it a straight ledger, a steady roof, and the dignity of not letting fools set the tone after dark.”

A faint dryness touched her expression, arriving late and leaving without ceremony.

“The door has been meaning to be oiled for most of those years. I suspect it creaks out of loyalty now.”

From the kitchen came the soft scrape of a ladle against iron, as if Old Pell were listening and pretending not to.

“Pell has been here longer than the current sign,” Maren added. “Which means he will tell you the place began with him. I do not argue. It makes him season the stew defensively.”

She rested her left hand lightly on the bar, the silver ring on her thumb catching the light.

“So, friend, you have had your answer: long enough to know the house, and long enough to know better than to be impressed by it. Eat while the stew is still warm. If you mean to travel early, I can offer porridge that is honest, bread that is fresh, and coffee that will not flatter you.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The first stroke of the corner clock cut cleanly through the low murmur of the common room.

Maren stopped what she was doing.

Not with alarm, and not with the exaggerated patience of a woman making a performance of habit. She simply set the tally sheet aside, left hand smoothing the paper flat before she lifted it from the bar. The cloth she had been using followed, folded once and placed neatly out of the way.

“Forgive me a moment,” she said. Her voice remained level, unhurried. “The Antler has one piece of business that keeps its own time.”

From beneath the counter she brought out two small cups, plain clay, unglazed near the rim. She handled them with her left hand, the movements sure and quiet. Her right hand rested near the edge of the bar, present but not asked to carry its share. From the same shelf beneath the bar she drew a squat bottle with no label and no flourish. She poured two measures, steady and exact, the lamplight catching the silver ring on her left thumb as the bottle tipped.

One cup she carried to the far end of the bar.

There was a place there where the wood looked a little paler than the rest, worn smooth by years of the same careful placement. Maren set the cup down without sound. She did not arrange it. She did not look around to see if anyone had noticed. She simply left it there, as one leaves a chair for someone who may not come, but whose seat is kept all the same.

The second cup she brought back to her place at the bar.

For a breath, she stood still.

No toast. No bow. No words offered to the room. Only the faintest lowering of her eyes, and the brief touch of her thumb against the rim of the cup. Then she straightened again, calm as a door closing.

The clock finished striking midnight.

The merchants in the corner had not stopped arguing, though one of them had paused long enough to listen for something that never came. The dwarf turned a page. Old Pell’s ladle scraped once against iron in the kitchen.

Maren rested her left hand lightly on the bar.

“There,” she said. “Now the night may settle.”

Her gaze moved briefly to the cup at the end of the bar, then away.

“If you are wondering,” she added, without quite looking at the traveler, “it is an old custom of the house. I do not recommend asking it to explain itself. Customs are like hinges: they work best when people stop arguing with them.”

She drew the tally sheet back toward her, though she did not mark it yet.

“You were well served by the stew,” she said, returning to the conversation as though midnight had merely been another guest passing through. “And the ale is still behaving. If you mean to finish either, now is the hour for it. After midnight, the Antler grows quieter whether the guests agree to it or not.”

A faint dryness touched her face.

“I will bring a candle when you are ready for the stairs. The second door on the left. Remember the lock: lift, then turn. The stairs will forgive you more than the key will.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I watch her, fascinated, but keep quiet until she's done.* "I wasn't wondering, but thank you for the explanation all the same." *I take another mouthful of ale.* "I think I'll finish this, then take that candle and call it a night. Long journey tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren accepted the thanks with a slight inclination of her head, as if it had been a coin placed on the bar and found acceptable.

“Then I will not burden it with further history,” she said. “Customs that are explained too often wear thin at the edges.”

She reached beneath the bar with her left hand and brought up a plain brass candlestick, polished enough to catch the lamplight in dull patches. From a shelf beside it she chose a candle, straight and white, and set it into the holder with a small press of her thumb. The silver ring on her left thumb flashed briefly as she smoothed the wax into place. Her right hand remained near the tally sheet, present but not asked to work.

“The yard room will suit a long journey,” she said. “Quiet enough for sleep, close enough to the stairs to make morning an argument you can win. If you wake before the household, there is a bell by the kitchen door. One pull means coffee. Two means food. Three means something has gone wrong, and Pell will appear with a ladle and a grievance.”

Her gaze moved once to the cup at the far end of the bar, then away.

“Leave the crab plate where it is if you have finished with it,” she added. “I will see it goes back with my thanks, and Lord Havel’s man can draw whatever conclusions he pleases from our moderation.”

A faint dryness touched her mouth, arriving late and leaving without ceremony.

“When you are ready for the stairs, I will bring the candle and show you where they begin to believe they are a ladder. The lock will behave if you remember the lift. If it forgets its manners, I am within earshot, and I have little patience for a key that argues after midnight.”

She picked up the tally sheet again with her left hand, marked a single line beside the evening’s ale count, and set it aside once more.

“Rest when you can,” she said. “The Antler will keep its roof quiet over you until morning.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I drain the last of my ale, a comfortable warmth spreading through me.* "Sounds good, Maren. Thank you for everything." I carefully gather my pack, making sure the precious contents are secure. "Lead the way when you're ready."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren took a thin wooden spill from the jar beside the bar lamp and touched it to the flame with her left hand. When the spill caught, she carried the fire to the candle, steadying the wick until it burned clean and bright. The silver ring on her left thumb flashed once in the lamplight as she shook the spill out and set it aside.

“Then we will leave the Antler to its own creaks,” she said.

She came around the end of the bar with the candle held before her, palm curved to shelter the flame. Her right hand stayed at her side, unused out of long habit rather than helplessness. As she passed the plate of crab cakes, she gave it the same wide berth she might give a wet patch of floor—no comment, no fuss, only a practical adjustment of route.

Behind them, the small clay cup at the far end of the bar sat exactly where she had placed it.

Maren paused at the foot of the stairs and looked back over her shoulder.

“Keep the pack close,” she said. “Not swinging, not dangling from one strap like a sack of turnips. If it is precious and fragile, it deserves your arm, not the floor.”

She turned and began up the stairs, keeping to the left side of the treads with the ease of someone who had memorized their moods years ago. The wood complained once under her step, then thought better of it and held still.

“The first three are honest,” she said. “The fourth enjoys attention. Step on the edge and it will announce you to the whole house. Step where I step, and it will keep your secrets.”

At the top of the landing, she stopped beside the second door on the left. She did not enter. She simply lifted the latch a finger’s width with her left hand, held it there for a breath, then let it settle again without turning it.

“Lift, then turn,” she said. “If you force it, it will pretend to be a vault. If you humor it, it will remember itself.”

She lowered her hand and looked briefly toward the dark yard beyond the shutters.

“The room smells faintly of lavender because I keep a bundle near the window. It is harmless, and the moths dislike it. There is a table by the wall where you can set the candle without setting fire to the curtains, and the floor by the bed is as solid as any floor has a right to be.”

Her gaze returned to the traveler’s pack for only a moment.

“Sleep with the strap under the bedpost if you want to be certain of it in the morning. Not because I expect trouble in my house, but because tired people misplace what they love, and I would rather not start the day with a search.”

She took one step back from the door, giving it space.

“Key is yours,” Maren said. “If it argues, lift higher. If it still argues, come down and I will bring the spare and a short lecture. The Antler may be old, but it is not unkind.”

The candle flame swayed gently in her hand.

“Rest well, friend. Morning will find you whether you bargain with it or not.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I follow her up the stairs, careful to step where she steps.* "Thank you, Maren. For the room, the stew, and the advice." I take the key from her, giving a small nod. "I'll heed your warnings. Goodnight."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren accepted the thanks with a small nod, the kind that had been polished by years of hearing travelers say the same thing in different voices.

“You are welcome for what can be counted,” she said. “The stew belongs to Pell. The room belongs to the Antler. The advice belongs to me, and I give it away because it keeps better when it is used.”

She set the candlestick on the narrow shelf beside the door rather than pressing it into the traveler’s hands, her left hand lingering around the brass base for a moment. The silver ring on her thumb caught the low light. Her right hand remained folded at her side, present but not asked to share the labor.

“Take the light when you are ready,” she said. “The lock will behave if you remember the lift. If it forgets its manners, knock once. I will come up with the spare key and a disappointed look, and one of those things will open the door.”

She did not linger in the doorway. Tavern keepers learned early where guests wanted privacy, and Maren had never been the sort to stand in it like a tax collector waiting for an excuse.

“Sleep well, friend,” she said. “The Antler will keep its roof quiet over you until morning.”

Then she turned and went down the stairs with her left hand on the rail, choosing the treads that had long ago made their peace with her weight. The fourth stair gave the faintest sigh under her step, then held still.

Below, the common room had settled into the deeper quiet that came after midnight. The merchants in the corner had stopped arguing and were now merely comparing grievances in lower voices. The dwarf had folded the letter away and was watching the last of his ale as if it might offer a final opinion. The lamp flames burned steady, and the smell of venison stew still clung to the air, warm and rosemary-dark.

Maren returned behind the bar and glanced once at the plate of crab cakes. She did not approach it.

Instead, she lifted her voice just enough to reach the kitchen.

“Pell,” she said. “Lord Havel’s generosity has finished its visit. Bring a tray and a pair of tongs. I have no wish to become better acquainted with it than I already am.”

From the kitchen came a grunt that might have been agreement, or the ghost of one.

Maren used the interval to draw the tally sheet back toward her with her left hand. She marked the room, the stew, the ale, and the candle in neat, economical lines. Her right hand rested near the edge of the paper, the old wrist content to let the left do the accounting.

At the far end of the bar, the small clay cup sat untouched.

She did not move it. She did not look at it longer than necessary. She simply wiped the wood around it with a cloth, leaving the cup exactly where it belonged.

When Old Pell emerged from the kitchen with a tray and the expression of a man being asked to carry a live coal, Maren stepped aside.

“Take it to the wash,” she said. “Or to Lord Havel’s man, if he is still awake and fond of being thanked. Either way, keep it away from the bread.”

Pell muttered something about nobles and their coastal fancies, gathered the plate with the tray, and retreated. Maren watched only long enough to ensure the crab had departed without incident.

Then she looked toward the front door.

It gave a faint creak in the night air, as if reminding her of its existence.

“Tomorrow,” Maren said quietly.

She did not believe herself, but the Antler had survived many years of her honest intentions.

She rested her left hand lightly on the bar near the untouched cup, listened to the quiet house above her, and let the night settle where it would.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I close the door behind me, careful with the lock. The room is simple but clean, just as Maren described. I set my pack on the floor, leaning it against the sturdy bed frame, and place the candle on the small table. The lavender scent is faint but pleasant.* "Finally," *I whisper to myself, stretching my tired limbs.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren heard the lock above her remember its manners: the small lift, the brief pause, then the turn. A moment later the faint pressure in the stairwood eased as weight crossed the landing and passed into the room.

She stood at the foot of the stairs for one breath longer than necessity required, listening not for secrets but for the ordinary sounds of a house settling itself around a guest. The candle had been taken. The door had shut. The Antler, for all its creaks and complaints, had done its first duty of the night without embarrassing itself.

Then she turned back to the common room.

The dwarf had drained the last of his ale and folded his letter away with the careful hands of someone accustomed to keeping paper alive on the road. He gave Maren a nod, the sort that meant he wanted nothing more except perhaps to be left alone with the end of his drink. She returned the nod and did not trouble him with conversation.

At the merchants’ table, the argument over grain had softened into mutual exhaustion. One of them was now stirring the last of his stew with the aimless devotion of a man who had already lost the debate and was searching for dignity in the broth.

Maren moved behind the bar again with her left hand leading. She gathered the traveler’s empty mug and the plate from the crab cakes, though she did not touch the latter directly. Instead she waited until Old Pell returned with a wooden tray and a pair of long-handled tongs, wearing the expression of a man asked to remove a minor but morally offensive animal from the pantry.

“Take it,” Maren said. “And wash the plate twice. Hot water, strong soap, and do not let it lean against the bread trenchers.”

Pell lowered the tray with a grunt. “Coastal nonsense,” he muttered. “Crab in a cake. Might as well put a boot in a pie and call it supper.”

“If Lord Havel’s man asks,” Maren said, “you may tell him the Antler appreciated the gesture. If he asks why the plate was washed twice, you may tell him I have standards. If he asks anything further, you may look at him until he remembers he has somewhere else to be.”

Pell’s mouth twitched beneath his beard. “And if he asks about you not touching it?”

Maren’s expression remained perfectly calm.

“Then you may tell him I am a woman of refined dislikes.”

Pell snorted once, wisely did not pursue the matter, and carried the tray away toward the kitchen. The smell of crab faded beneath the stronger comforts of rosemary, woodsmoke, and old ale. Maren watched the swing door settle, then washed her hands at the basin beneath the bar shelf even though she had not touched the plate. She did it thoroughly, drying each finger with a clean cloth before she let herself relax.

The small clay cup at the far end of the bar remained exactly where she had set it.

Her gaze passed over it without lingering. She did not move it. She did not cover it. She simply wiped the wood around it with a folded cloth, careful not to disturb the space it occupied, and then returned to the tally sheet.

The ledger came back beneath her left hand. Her right rested at the edge of the bar, fingers curled loosely, the old wrist content to be spared the finer work. She marked the evening in neat strokes: one room, one stew, one ale, one candle, bread, mustard withheld unless requested. Her arithmetic was quick and clean, the kind learned not from leisure but from years of quartermaster tables, supply wagons, and men who pretended they could not count when it suited them.

When the numbers balanced, she set the pen down and flexed her right hand once, slowly, feeling the familiar stiffness that never quite left it. Then she reached for the lamp beside the register and lowered the wick a fraction, easing the light toward the deeper hours of the night.

The common room was nearly done for the evening. The merchants paid their reckoning with the muted sorrow of men who had been outargued by both weather and prices. The dwarf took his key without comment and went up the stairs with the solid, unhurried tread of someone who had spent years sleeping in places not built for his knees. Maren listened until the third stair complained and then subsided.

After that, the Antler grew quiet.

Not silent. The tavern never truly fell silent. There was the low tick of cooling embers in the hearth, the soft complaint of timber remembering the day’s weight, the distant murmur of the yard where the cock had not yet decided whether to become a problem before dawn. The door, when a draft found it, gave one thin creak.

Maren looked at it.

“Oh, for the love of every hinge that ever held a grudge,” she said quietly.

She reached beneath the bar and produced a small clay pot of oil and a strip of rag. With the rag wrapped around her left forefinger, she crossed to the door and touched the oil to the upper hinge with the patience of a woman who had performed many small repairs in a life that rarely permitted them to stay repaired. The metal drank the oil greedily. She worked the hinge once, twice, then wiped away the excess.

Then she paused, rag hovering near the lower hinge.

Above, the house gave a faint settling sound. Not trouble. Not distress. Only the room accepting its guest, the floorboards accepting their burden, the night accepting its shape.

Maren looked toward the stairs, then back at the door.

She lowered the rag.

“Tomorrow,” she said.

She did not believe herself any more than she had the first hundred times, but the Antler had always been patient with her honest intentions.

Returning to the bar, she banked the lamp lower and checked the bell rope beside the kitchen door. One pull for coffee. Two for food. Three for trouble. She gave it a small test with her left knuckle, heard the faint answer in the kitchen, and nodded.

“Pell,” she called softly, “if the traveler rings once, coffee is to be ready before the second pull. If twice, bread and whatever is fit to send up without an apology. If three times, bring me the cudgel and a very good reason.”

From the kitchen came the sound of a ladle being set down with theatrical care.

“And if it is three,” Old Pell called back, “I am bringing the ladle too.”

“You bring the ladle and I will put you on dish duty until the saints grow old.”

Pell muttered something about tyranny and stew, but there was no heat in it.

Maren allowed the corner of her mouth to soften for just an instant. Then she gathered the traveler’s empty mug with her left hand and carried it to the wash basin, moving with the quiet economy of someone who had learned that a tavern survived not on grand gestures but on the steady repetition of small things done correctly.

Behind her, at the far end of the bar, the untouched cup waited in the lamplight.

Maren did not look at it again. She did not need to. She knew exactly where it was, and exactly why it was there, and exactly how long it would remain.

The Antler kept its roof quiet over the night, and for now, that was enough.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I wake with the sun, stretching and feeling surprisingly rested.* "That was a good night's sleep." *I retrieve my pack, check the contents, and then head downstairs, curious what the morning brings.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren set the tally sheet down with her right hand, the fingers stiff from the old wrist injury, and finished her wipe with her left before hanging the rag over her shoulder. She gave the pack a glance, noting how carefully it had been placed, then looked the traveler over again. Road dust, tired eyes, nothing that spelled trouble yet.

“Whatever is hot is venison stew,” she said, voice even, pitched low so it would not carry over the murmur of the room. “Old Pell makes it, and it is the reason folks travel two days to sit in this chair. It is venison, no shellfish, in case that matters to you. I do not care for seafood myself. Bread comes with it if you ask nicely, which you have not, but I will pretend that you did. Ale is local and honest. Wine is imported and overpriced, and I will tell you so before you waste your coin on it.”

She moved down the bar, using her left hand to lift a clean bowl from the shelf. The silver ring on her thumb caught the firelight for a moment. She did not raise her voice toward the kitchen; she simply turned her head and spoke toward the hatch.

“Pell, one stew for the bar.”

She set the bowl on the counter, then took a key from its hook with her left hand and placed it beside the bowl. The key landed with a small click.

“I have rooms. Twelve upstairs, and only four taken tonight. Four silver, and that includes a washbasin and a door that locks more often than it does not. You can leave your pack there, or I can set it behind the bar where I can keep an eye on it. I keep an oak cudgel back here. I have never drawn blood with it, but I have broken four wrists, and I would rather not start tonight.”

A beat passed. She did not smile at her own joke; she simply waited, one eyebrow raised, the scarred one.

“Name is Maren,” she added. “Most folks call me Maren. What do they call you, friend?”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking in her words, a small, tired smile playing on my lips.* "Stew sounds perfect. And bread, please. Traveler's fine for now." *I glance at the key, then back at my pack.* "Behind the bar would be good, thank you. No need for broken wrists tonight."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren inclined her head, the scar through her right eyebrow pulling slightly with the motion. “Traveler, then. I will use that until you give me a better one. I will not pry before you are fed. Prying on an empty stomach is bad business, and I have enough bad business without adding to it.”

She came around the end of the bar rather than reaching across it, moving with the unhurried step of someone who had crossed this room ten thousand times. The pack sat where it had been placed, upright and careful. Maren took it by the straps with her left hand, the silver ring on her thumb pressing into the leather, and hefted it. It had weight to it, packed with care rather than haste. She carried it behind the bar and set it on the floor in the corner beside the oak cudgel, within easy reach of her left hand. Her right hand she let hang loose at her side, the fingers stiff from the old injury.

“It will sit there,” she said. “I can see it from anywhere in this room. So can anyone foolish enough to reach across my bar. They generally decide against it.”

The key still lay on the bar where she had set it. From the hatch came the scrape of a bowl being pushed forward, and the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked venison grew stronger. Maren took the filled bowl in her left hand, set it down beside the key, and returned the clean bowl she had set out earlier to the shelf behind her. She added a heel of bread and a small crock of butter, then drew a cup of water from the barrel and set it down as well.

“Stew, bread, butter. Water is free, and it tastes like the well, which is to say it tastes like water. Ale is two coppers if you want it, and I will pour it myself. Wine is imported and overpriced, and I will keep telling you that until you believe me.”

She rested her left hand on the bar, the thumb-ring catching the firelight, and gave the traveler a measured look.

“Eat. Room four, top of the stairs, second door on the left. The key is there when you are ready. If you want hot water for the washbasin, say so and I will have Pell send up a jug for a copper. If you want to tell me why you are carrying that pack as though it holds something breakable, that is your business, and I will not ask twice.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The plate arrived on a tray, carried by a lad from the merchant’s table, and was set down on the bar between them. Three crab cakes, golden at the edges, steam rising off them, a smell of salt and coast that Maren did not care for in the slightest.

Maren went still. Only her scarred right eyebrow lifted, a fraction. She did not touch the plate. She did not even let her left hand drift toward it. Instead she reached up, took the rag from her shoulder with her left hand, and shook it out one-handed, the silver ring on her thumb winking in the firelight.

“Well,” she said, voice even and pitched low so it would not carry over the murmur of the room. “That is kind of Lord Havel. It is also the fastest way to get a plate put back in front of him. I do not care for seafood. Not crab, not shrimp, not lobster, not mussels. It is nothing against the coast, and nothing against whoever cooked it. Crab and I have an understanding: it stays on that plate, I stay over here, and neither of us troubles the other.”

She kept her hands well away from the cakes. Touching them would have brought her out in hives within minutes, and she had no intention of explaining that particular embarrassment to anyone, least of all a room half full of strangers. Using the rag as a barrier, she took hold of the edge of the plate with her left hand, fingers thick through the cloth, and slid it carefully across the bar toward Traveler’s place. She left a hand’s width of clear wood between it and her own spot, then set the rag down at the far end of the counter, well away from the plate. Her left hand she flexed once, as if reassuring herself it was still its own self and not covered in hives. Her right hand she let hang loose at her side, the fingers stiff from the old wrist injury.

“You are welcome to it, Traveler,” she said. “Eat it if you like. If you do, keep it on your side of the bar, and for the love of every saint who ever stubbed a toe, do not offer me a bite. I will not be having any. If you do not want it, I will have it taken back to Lord Havel, and I will suggest he try the venison next time. The stew is better anyway.”

She glanced toward the merchant’s table and inclined her head, not raising her voice. The walls had enough noise without her adding to it.

“Tell him I said thank you. And that the next time he wants to send something to this bar, he should send it without a shell. That is not a complaint. It is a preference, and it is one I will repeat as often as necessary.”

She rested her left hand on the bar again, at a safe distance from the plate, the thumb-ring catching the light, and waited. She did not smile. She rarely did when she was being serious, and she considered this a serious matter indeed.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I eye the crab cakes with a mix of curiosity and amusement, then Maren's stern expression.* "Well, I certainly wouldn't want to cause any trouble." *I slide the plate closer to me, giving one of the cakes a tentative poke.* "They do smell good, though. Lord Havel has good taste, even if it's not yours." *I take a bite, chewing slowly.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the traveler take the bite, her expression unchanging. She was a good judge of character, and so far the only trouble in the room was sitting on a plate wearing a breadcrumb coat. She did not lean closer. She did not let even the edge of her apron drift toward the crab cakes. Her left hand stayed flat on the bar, the silver ring on her thumb catching the firelight, while her right hand hung loose at her side, the stiff fingers curled slightly from the old injury.

“Chew it well,” she said, voice even and pitched low so it would not carry over the murmur of the room. “If your throat starts to itch, or your skin begins to rise in welts, tell me now and I will send for a healer. I am not one, but I know the look of it. I would rather pay for a healer than explain to the watch why a traveler died in my common room eating a gift he felt obliged to accept.”

She lifted her left hand just enough to indicate the bowl of stew beside the key, the thumb ring flashing once, then let it settle back to the wood.

“Your stew is cooling. That is not a complaint. It is arithmetic. Old Pell takes cold stew as a personal insult, and I have to work with him. Eat it if you mean to. If the crab was politeness, you have been polite and you can stop. If it was curiosity, satisfy it and move on. If it was hunger, the stew will go further.”

A beat passed. She did not smile. She rarely did when she was being serious, and she considered this a serious matter indeed.

“Lord Havel has fine taste, I am sure. A man who sends crab to a woman who has told him plainly she does not touch the stuff has either a poor memory or a strange sense of humor. I will assume poor memory, because the alternative is impolite. When you are finished, leave the plate where it is. I will have the lad carry it back and tell his lordship it was appreciated. That is true, and it costs me nothing.”

She glanced at the plate, then back to the traveler’s face.

“And keep it on your side of the bar. For the love of every saint who ever stubbed a toe, do not offer me a bite, and do not flick crumbs in my direction. I have already washed this floor once today, and I have no ambition to do it again before midnight.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren regarded the raised mug for a moment, then reached for her own. She kept a mug of the local ale behind the bar for herself, and she took it now in her left hand. Her right hand stayed loose at her side, the fingers stiff from the old wrist injury, curled slightly as they always did when she was not using them for anything that required strength. She did not lift the mug high. There was no need to give the room something to stare at; the walls had enough noise without her adding to it.

“To Old Pell,” she said, voice even and pitched low. The merchants had gone back to arguing quietly about grain prices, and the dwarf had returned to his letter, so the words did not carry past the bar. “He will be insufferable by morning. He already believes the stew is the reason travelers stop at this crossroads. Tell him it is the best you have had in months and he will start charging me for the recipe. He has no recipe. It is meat, rosemary, and time, and he will deny all three.”

She took a drink, measured, and set the mug down with her left hand. The silver ring on her left thumb clicked once against the wood.

“And I will take the word you used as a figure of speech rather than a habit, Traveler. We keep the language cleaner than the floor in here. Not because I am easily shocked—I have thrown out men who said far worse—but because there is no need for it when 'remarkably' will do the same work without making the walls repeat it.”

Her gaze flicked to the crab-cake plate, still on the traveler's side of the bar. She did not move it. She did not need to. Touching shellfish would have brought her out in hives within minutes, and that was an embarrassment she kept to herself; she told people she did not care for seafood, and that was the end of it. Her left hand flexed once against the counter, well away from the plate, and then stilled.

“Enjoy your toast,” she added. “Keep the crab where it is. I have already had one surprise tonight, and I have no ambition to explain to a healer why I am covered in hives before midnight. Eat the stew, drink your ale—or your water, whichever that is—and if Lord Havel sends anything else, I will remind him that anything with a shell belongs on his table, not mine.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, taking another sip of my ale.* "Remarkably good, then. My apologies. And I'll be sure to keep the crab on my side, promise." *I push the empty crab cake plate slightly away from me, then return to my stew, finishing it off.* "So, Maren, what's good around here that doesn't involve shells?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren let her gaze drop to the empty stew bowl and the crab-cake plate, which sat at the traveler’s place, pushed a careful distance from her side of the bar. She did not reach for the plate. Instead, she took up the rag from the far end of the counter with her left hand, shook it out once, and used the cloth as a barrier to slide the plate a little farther toward the kitchen hatch. Her right hand stayed loose at her side, the fingers stiff from the old injury, curled as they always did when there was no call for lifting.

“Traveler, I’ll have the lad take that back to Lord Havel with my compliments,” she said, voice pitched low so it would not carry over the murmur of the room. “I do not need to touch it to know the gift was kindly meant. Crab and I have an understanding, and cleaning up after it is not part of the arrangement.”

She set the rag down well away from the plate and rested her left hand flat on the bar. The silver ring on her thumb caught the firelight for a moment before she stilled it.

“As for the language, you did not owe me an apology twice. One ‘remarkably’ will cover you for the rest of the evening. Possibly the rest of the week, depending on how the night goes.”

Then she answered his question, her tone settling into the dry, measured warmth she kept for travelers who had finished their stew and minded their manners.

“You asked what is good around here, Traveler, that does not involve shells. Let me think. The stew, which you have finished. The ale, which you are drinking. The bread is there if you want it, and the butter is fresh. The water is free and tastes like water, which is either a recommendation or a warning, depending on how long you have been on the road.”

She lifted her left hand in a small gesture that took in the common room without ever rising to a wave.

“Beyond this bar, the crossroads are the main attraction. Two trade roads meet outside my door. East takes you to Halloway in two days if you walk and do not dawdle; there is a market on sixth-day and a shrine where travelers leave coins they will not miss. West goes to the coast, which is where that crab came from, and which I do not recommend. North climbs into the hills to a monastery that makes a cheese worth the climb and a beer that is not. South crosses the river at a stone bridge older than the kingdom and comes out at a village with a blacksmith, a well, and very little else, which some folks find restful and I find efficient.”

A beat passed.

“If you are looking for quiet conversation, the snug is through the door near the hearth; I keep it for regulars or for talk that does not want an audience. If you are looking for work, the caravans come through most mornings and the guards are often short a hand willing to walk in the rain. If you are looking for trouble, it usually finds its own way here around dusk, and I show it the door before it finishes its first drink.”

Maren paused, and for once let the silence stretch. She did not smile. She rarely did when she was being serious, and this next part was serious in the way only a poor joke could be.

“If you walk far enough down any of those roads, you will come to another crossroads. It will not be this one. It will be worse.”

She let that sit, giving it the three seconds it needed to land, then went on as though she had not just insulted every other crossroads in the world.

“And if none of that suits, the beds upstairs are clean, the doors lock more often than they do not, and there is not a shell in any of them. Room four is yours, top of the stairs, second door on the left. The key is there when you want it. Hot water for the washbasin is a copper, and I’ll send Old Pell up with it if you ask before he starts scrubbing the pots.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The clock in the corner began to strike. Maren had been wiping the same stretch of bar with slow circles of her left hand, and at the first toll she stilled the rag. She did not hurry. She waited for the twelfth stroke to fade into the rafters before she moved.

“For the love of every saint who ever stubbed a toe,” she said under her breath, not raising her voice, “the day did not ask my opinion before it left.”

She set the rag down. With her left hand she reached beneath the counter and brought out a bottle of the imported wine—the overpriced one she warned travelers about—and two small glasses. Her right hand hung loose at her side, the fingers stiff and curled from the old wrist injury, of no use for this and not needed. She set the glasses on the bar, the silver ring on her left thumb winking in the firelight, and poured a measure into each. The wine was dark and smelled faintly of something that had traveled a long way to be called overpriced.

One glass she left in front of her own place. The other she carried to the far end of the bar, near the door, and set it down on the wood with care. She did not touch it again. She did not look at it. It would sit there until morning, and she would not explain it to anyone.

Back at her own spot, Maren picked up her glass in her left hand, lifted it a few inches—not a toast, not for the room—and drank. Then she set it down and turned her attention back to Traveler, her expression calm, the thin scar through her right eyebrow catching the low light.

“Midnight,” she said, her voice even and pitched low so it would not carry over the murmur of the room. The common room had thinned while they talked; the merchants had taken their argument elsewhere and the dwarf had folded his letter away. “Pay it no mind. The clock and I have an arrangement: it tells me the hour, I ignore it, and neither of us mentions it in the morning.”

A beat passed. She did not smile at her own joke. She rarely did.

“You were saying?” she asked. She did not wait to see whether there had been an answer. She simply went on, smooth as a river stone.

“Or if you were not, then allow me to finish the list. The stew is done, the bread is there if you want it, and the crab is on its way back to Lord Havel with my compliments and a suggestion that he try the venison next time. The roads will still be there tomorrow, unfortunately, and so will the hills, the coast, and every other crossroads that thinks it is better than this one.”

She rested her left hand flat on the bar, the thumb-ring catching the firelight.

“The key to room four has not moved. Hot water for the washbasin is still a copper, though at this hour Pell will grumble and I will pretend not to hear him. Say the word and I will send him up. If you would rather sit a while longer, you are welcome to it, but do not expect the clock to be wrong twice in one night.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I swirl the wine in my glass, a thoughtful expression on my face.* "Midnight already, huh? Time flies when you're... not talking about crab." *I take a sip, then set the glass down.* "I think I'll take that hot water, Maren. And I wouldn't mind sitting a bit longer, if you don't mind the company."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren set her own empty wine glass down with her left hand, the silver ring on her thumb clicking once against the wood. At the end of the bar, the second glass sat exactly where she had left it, dark and untouched. She did not look at it. She did not explain it. The clock had finished its showing off for the night, and that was the end of that.

“Time flies when you are not talking about crab,” she said, her voice pitched low so it would not carry over the sound of Pell scrubbing pots in the back. The common room had thinned to a handful of late travelers, and the walls had enough noise without her adding to it. “By that measure, the last hour must have crawled, because crab was most of what we discussed. Crab, and the coast it came from, and the poor memory of a lord who should know better by now.”

She paused, letting the shape of the joke settle. Her scarred right eyebrow lifted a fraction, and she did not smile. If time flew when one was not talking about crab, then it limped when one was, and that explained why the evening had felt like a wet week. Three seconds passed. She waited. She did not laugh.

“You can have the hot water. That will be one copper, if you please.” She held out her left hand, palm up, the thumb-ring catching the firelight, and waited for the coin. Her right hand stayed loose at her side, the fingers stiff and curled from the old wrist injury, no use for this and not needed. “Pell will carry it up himself. He will grumble about the hour, about the stairs, and about travelers who cannot wash in cold water like decent folk. I will pretend not to hear him, and so should you. It is the only way to keep him pleasant, and he makes a venison stew worth the trouble.”

She turned her head toward the kitchen hatch, not raising her voice. The walls had enough noise without her shouting at a cook.

“Pell! Hot water for room four. And mind the stairs—they are narrower than your good opinion of that stew.”

A faint clatter from the back suggested the cook had heard, and possibly had opinions. Maren turned back, resting her left hand flat on the bar. The ring winked once.

“You asked whether I mind the company. I do not. You’re welcome to sit as long as you like. I haven’t yet taken to arguing with the furniture, though there is a chair in the corner that has had it coming for a while.” A beat passed. She did not smile. “The fire will likely go out before you do. If you fall asleep in that chair, I will wake you once. After that, I will pour you into room four and lock the door behind you. That service is included in the four silver. The second time is not.”

Her left hand found the key on the bar, the iron warm from the room, and slid it a half-inch closer to his place. The small sound it made against the wood was the only punctuation she offered.

“Room four. Top of the stairs, second door on the left. The washbasin is inside, and the water will be along shortly. Do not let Pell talk you into a second jug; he will charge you for it, and I will hear about it in the morning, and neither of us wants that.”

She let her gaze flick, briefly, to the glass at the end of the bar, and then away. It stayed where it was. It would stay there until morning. She did not offer an explanation, because none had been requested, and because some things were not for travelers to carry away with them.

“The wine in your glass is imported and overpriced, and I will go on saying so until the bottle is empty. Drink it, or do not. Sit as long as you like, Traveler. The night is not charging you for it, and neither am I.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I chuckle again, reaching into my pouch for a copper and placing it on the bar.* "I'll try to keep Pell from charging me for a second jug, then." *I take another sip of the wine, swirling it slowly.* "So, what's with the extra glass down there, Maren? Waiting for someone to join you?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s left hand closed over the copper and slid it off the bar, the silver ring on her thumb pressing briefly against the metal before she dropped the coin into the till. Her right hand hung loose at her side, the fingers stiff and curled from the old wrist injury, of no use for counting and not needed for it.

She did not look down the bar toward the second glass. She knew exactly where it sat, dark and untouched near the door, and she had no intention of explaining it to anyone, least of all a traveler with questions after midnight.

“Waiting for someone?” she repeated, voice even and pitched low so it would not carry over the clatter of pots in the back. The common room had thinned to almost nothing; only the fire and the clock were still awake, and one of those was unreliable. “No. If I were waiting for someone, I would have set out another chair, and the chair by the hearth has been threatening to collapse since last winter. I would not inflict it on a guest, and I would not insult the wine by pouring it twice.”

Resting her left hand flat on the bar, she let the pause stretch. The scar through her right eyebrow lifted a fraction. She did not fill the silence right away; letting a thing sit was its own answer, and most folks heard it better than any explanation.

“That glass,” she said, “is where it belongs at midnight. That is the whole of it, and it is not a story I tell travelers. If you need one, invent it, provided it does not involve shells, lords with poor memories, or me explaining myself before I am ready. Some things in a tavern belong to the tavern, Traveler. Some rooms stay locked, some stairs stay narrow, and some glasses sit at the end of the bar until morning. Ask me again at noon, and I will have forgotten both the question and the answer.”

A beat passed. She did not smile. She rarely did when she was being serious, and she considered a person’s private business exactly that.
