Elena — the amber cue needs those two beats back, not wasted on a border dispute. Give me the stage, not the war — or I'll stage this argument as the understudy piece and neither of you gets a bow."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I follow Yael into the hallway, watching her mediate the conflict.* That was... effective. "Do they always listen so quickly?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael let the door frame go, turning back toward Jordan with a look that suggested the question had amused her in some private way — though the humor didn't quite reach the quiet stillness her voice had settled into. "Listen — no, they don't always listen, and certainly not quickly. What you just witnessed was timing, not obedience — I caught them in the gap between breaths, before the argument had finished inhaling, and in this building you learn to drop the curtain early or watch the scene devolve into improv nobody asked for."

She started walking back toward the commune set, her shoes clicking a sharp rhythm against the concrete, the reading glasses sliding down her nose only to be pushed back up with an irritated forefinger. "Chen is too smart to waste his best ammunition on a blocking dispute when the director is standing in the wings — he conserves his fire for the third act, literally and otherwise, and Elena — " she paused, glancing toward the empty hallway where the stage manager had already vanished to wherever stage managers went when they weren't saving productions from themselves, " — she yields the floor when she recognizes that the production matters more than the point. Today was a skirmish in the shadows, not the war."

She stopped by the half-built kitchen, running an angular hand along the edge of a plywood counter dusted with sawdust. "When they really dig in — when both of them believe the other is endangering the architecture — I have to become the heavy, the referee, and sometimes the sacrifice. It's exhausting, it's necessary, and it's why I guard the prop locker combination with the same fervor I reserve for my very limited patience." She looked up, the chain of her glasses catching the work light overhead, her silver head tilting with surgical precision. "But don't mistake that silence for surrender. They're both just backstage, reloading."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael turned from the plywood counter, the reading glasses sliding down her nose as she registered Anya and David in the doorway — the frame suddenly crowded with board energy and the particular delicacy of protecting something explosive in polite company. Her voice dropped, settling into a register that was quiet, controlled, and deliberately warm, as if she were cradling a fragile prop she couldn't afford to break.

"Anya — thank you for bringing it to me directly, that's always the braver choice than sending it through committee." She stepped forward, her angular frame moving with careful intention, giving Anya the full warmth of her attention without crowding. "But I can't cut the third act — not for budget, not for expediency, not to make the season more comfortable for anyone's spreadsheets. Rosa built that act as the structural beam that holds the entire house up — you remove it, and what you've got isn't a play, it's a very long first act and a domestic scene where nobody learns anything."

She glanced toward David — a brief, professional flicker, nothing more intimate than a director acknowledging her board chair — then back to Anya, her hands sketching a small, apologetic arc in the sawdust-thick air. "I understand the pressure from the conservative members — I do — but trimming the blast radius doesn't save money, it just moves the rubble somewhere the audience can't see it. We're either doing Medea or we're doing a workshop about a sad woman in a commune, and I won't ask my company to spend eight weeks rehearsing a ghost story with the ghosts removed."

The chain of her glasses caught the light as she folded her arms, her silver head tilting with something that looked almost like regret. "If the budget needs blood, take it from marketing, take it from my own line, take it from the curtain call flowers — but the third act stays. I'm telling you both now that this isn't a want. It's oxygen."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I raise my eyebrows slightly, surprised by Yael's firmness.* "Oxygen is a strong word, Director." I turn to Anya and David. "Do you often find yourselves at odds with Yael's vision, or is this particular play more... challenging?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael lifted a hand — not to silence Jordan, but to redirect the spotlight before it scorched anyone standing in its glare. "Don't ask them to audition for a conflict they didn't write — the board and I are in perpetual negotiation, that's the contract we re-sign every season." She turned to Anya with a warmth that was careful, deliberate, and entirely free of condescension — the kind of warmth that cost her something and was offered anyway. "Anya brings the practical magic that keeps the lights on, and David — " she glanced toward the board chair, the look brief, collegial, carrying nothing that could snag on suspicion, " — he knows that trimming the third act wouldn't balance the budget, it would just move the deficit into a column the accountants can't track. The soul of the piece."

She pushed her glasses up her nose, the chain clicking against her collarbone. "We're not at odds — we're in the same scene playing different objectives. Anya wants the company to survive the winter, I want it to survive its own reflection, and both require oxygen. The only reason we ever raise voices is because we love the damn building enough to argue about which wall to brace when the wind hits." She folded her arms, her angular frame casting a long shadow across the sawdust. "Is this play more exposed? Yes — because Rosa's name is in the program, because my grief is backstage where the audience can't trip over it, and because the conservative wing of the board gets nervous when you hand them a live wire and tell them to trust the insulation. But the vision isn't the problem. The problem is that good art costs exactly what it costs, and nobody writes a grant line for 'make the audience bleed in their seats.'"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's glasses settled onto her nose with a small silver click, the chain going still against her collarbone as the room seemed to contract around the name. She turned to face the half-built commune kitchen, her voice dropping into that steadier, more controlled register — the one she used when the ground was uneven and she refused to stumble.

"Rosa didn't write plays — she built detonation devices with dialogue. She was the only playwright I ever met who could hear the frequency of a lie before the actor finished speaking it, and she had this — " Yael paused, her angular hand sketching a small, sharp shape in the sawdust-thick air, " — this ferocious intolerance for comfort. She thought audiences were smarter than they were treated, that Greek tragedy didn't need marble columns when it had linoleum and a sink full of dishes nobody wanted to wash."

She took a step toward the plywood counter, running her palm along its edge as if checking for something structural beneath the dust. "She wrote this adaptation while she was dying — not as a swan song, don't misunderstand me, she would have hated that sentiment — but because she had something left to burn and she didn't trust anyone else to strike the match. She understood Medea not as a monster or a victim, but as a woman who looked at the arithmetic of love and found it wouldn't balance, and she set it in a commune because utopias are just tragedies with better lighting and worse boundaries."

The glasses slid down her nose, but she didn't push them back up. She looked at Jordan with a steadiness that was almost defensive in its precision. "She was my closest friend for twenty years — but if you're looking for eulogy, I won't give it to you. She'd rather I spend the oxygen on the work. What I can tell you is that every line in that third act was weighed, measured, and loaded. She didn't leave accidents in her scripts, and she didn't leave room for committee cuts. I direct this because she can't — and because letting someone else soften the edges would be a betrayal of the only thing she ever asked of me, which was to protect the blast."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing her words.* "So you're not just directing a play; you're fulfilling a promise. A very specific, very explosive promise."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael let the glasses fall against her collarbone, the chain settling with a small, sharp clink. She studied Jordan for a moment, her angular head tilting as if assessing whether the journalist could handle the weight of what came next.

"A promise sounds romantic — and Rosa hated romance almost as much as she hated a soft ending. I'm not standing here because I swore on her deathbed with tears and violins — I'm standing here because I was the only one who watched her lay the wiring, who knows which color leads to the charge and which one defuses it." She pushed the glasses back onto her nose, her voice dropping into that quieter, more dangerous register. "If you call it a promise, it sounds like sentiment — and sentiment is what the board wants to smother this production with until it's gasping under a pillow. I call it custody. She left me the keys to a building she knew I'd burn down before I'd let anyone renovate it into a condo."

She turned, pacing a quick half-circle around the commune set, her hand trailing along the plywood counter. "Directing isn't prayer — it's carpentry with bodies and light. Rosa knew that. She knew I'd fight for the third act not because I loved her, but because she was right — the mathematics of the play demand it, the architecture requires it, and anyone who cuts it is a vandal with a checkbook." She stopped, folding her arms, her silver hair catching the work light overhead. "So yes, I promised — but the promise was to the work, not to the ghost. Ghosts don't need directors. Audiences do."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Custody. That's a powerful distinction," *I muse, jotting a quick note.* "So, if it's about the work, what's your biggest fear for this production, beyond the budget battles?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael went very still — the kind of stillness that preceded her most surgical notes. The glasses slid down her nose and hung there, forgotten, the chain motionless against her black shirt. When she spoke, her voice had dropped to that quieter register that filled the room without raising its volume.

"My biggest fear — that I'll discover too late I've been directing a memorial when Rosa wrote a murder. That grief leaks into the blocking like fog, softening edges that were never meant to be safe, and I'm the one holding the spray bottle." She pushed the glasses up, the chain clicking against her collarbone. "I'm afraid Chen will give the most technically dazzling performance of his career and the audience will miss the knife entirely — that they'll applaud his suffering and miss Medea's arithmetic, because we've trained them to comfort powerful men even when the play is about a woman who refuses to be comforted."

She turned, her hand trailing along the plywood counter, fingers testing a seam as if searching for structural weakness. "And I'm afraid the board isn't wrong about the blast radius — not because the third act should be cut, but because maybe we've built a world where people can sit through an explosion, call it 'moving,' and never feel the shrapnel. Where 'brave theater' is just a label they stick on the program so they can feel cultured while they duck for cover." She stopped, her angular frame suddenly solitary against the half-built commune walls, though her presence didn't diminish. "Rosa didn't want to move people — she wanted to rearrange them. And my fear is that I'll spend eight weeks in this room proving I can protect a bomb that the culture has already learned to defuse with polite applause."

She looked back at Jordan, silver hair catching the work light overhead, and her voice steadied into something almost brutal in its precision. "I'm not afraid of failure — I've failed twice in this building and it's still standing. I'm afraid of succeeding at the wrong thing. Of delivering a very beautiful, very safe catastrophe that lets everyone off the hook."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I watch her, taking in her words.* "A beautiful, safe catastrophe." *I repeat, letting the phrase hang in the air.* "So, how do you prevent that? How do you ensure the shrapnel hits?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael pushed her glasses up — off — then settled them back onto her nose, the chain swinging like a metronome marking time she didn't have. She turned away from Jordan and walked toward the half-built kitchen, her fingers catching a strand of macramé, testing its tension, its give.

"You don't ensure — that's producer talk, the illusion that you can bulletproof a live wire. You rig the room, you seat the audience inside the blast radius, and you make damn sure there isn't a fire exit for their attention to wander toward when the pressure builds." She released the macramé and ran her hand along the plywood counter, testing its edge. "The commune does the heavy lifting — linoleum, dish racks, that avocado stove nobody asked for. You put Medea in a palace and they watch a queen destroy herself from a comfortable distance. You put her in a kitchen they recognize from their mother's house, with a knife block they can smell the wood oil on, and suddenly the arithmetic isn't myth — it's Monday morning. Suddenly they're not judging a monster — they're checking their own balance sheets."

She pivoted, her black shirt drinking the work light, her voice dropping into that quieter, more dangerous register that seemed to expand rather than diminish in the space. "Chen wants more lines in the third act — naturally, he thinks if he fills the silences, the audience will love him for trying. I won't let him. Grief isn't a monologue, and Medea doesn't need a Greek chorus of one man explaining her rage while she stands there waiting for her cue. Elena knows this — she's the most competent person in this building, and she'll pull that amber cue back two beats so the light changes when the knife is already in hand, not when the audience has braced for it." The glasses slid down her nose and hung there, the chain still against her collarbone. "And Okafor — he runs the B-stage without me hovering because failure is the only furnace that tempers steel, but in this room, on this stage, I don't protect anyone. Not the actors, not the audience, certainly not the board's preference for polite catastrophe."

She stepped closer, her angular frame suddenly occupying the space between Jordan and the half-built walls, her presence a deliberate obstruction, a doorway made flesh. "You make the shrapnel hit by refusing to aim at the armor. You aim for the soft tissue — the assumption they carried in with their coats, the certainty that tragedy happens to other people in other centuries. Rosa wrote the third act as an autopsy of a particular kind of love, not a fate decreed by gods. The audience has to understand that Medea isn't possessed — she's doing the math and finding the only equation that balances, and she hates the sum as much as they will."

She pushed the glasses back up, the chain clicking, her silver head tilting with that surgical precision. "My job is to keep the house lights down long enough that when they finally come up, the audience is blinking in a room they don't recognize anymore — because the walls fell down while they were watching the pretty actor cry. If I do it right, they don't applaud immediately. They sit in the dark for three extra seconds, remembering how to breathe, wondering if the explosion was in the play or in their own chests."

She folded her arms, the sawdust scent thick between them. "That's not comfort. That's carpentry — and I intend to build something that stands long enough to fall on them exactly as Rosa designed."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I'm quiet for a moment, processing her words.* "So, the fear isn't that it's too much, but that it won't be enough. That the audience will still find a way to distance themselves."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's glasses clicked against her collarbone as her head snapped up, a sharp, approving light entering her eyes — the look she gave an actor who finally stopped indicating and started listening. "You listened — actually listened, which means you're either dangerous or you're writing something that might actually wound instead of massage."

She started moving, a quick orbit around the commune set, her hands sketching small, sharp shapes in the sawdust-thick air. "That's exactly it — too much is easy, too much is fireworks and blood packs and Chen screaming until the rafters shake. Too much is just noise, and noise is comforting because it lets the audience think they felt something without ever being implicated. No, the real enemy is distance — the armor of irony they've welded on in a culture where everything is content to be consumed, where even grief gets a hashtag and a thirty-second montage."

She stopped by the avocado stove, running an angular hand along its edge, testing it like a prop she didn't trust. "They'll watch Medea destroy her world and call it 'powerful' and 'moving' and all those adjectives that keep the wreckage at arm's length — as if her arithmetic were a museum piece behind velvet rope. They'll admire the performance the way they admire a storm on the news, beautiful and terrible and happening to somebody else."

The glasses slid up her nose and settled there, framing her gaze as she turned back toward Jordan. "That's why the commune setting isn't nostalgia — it's infiltration. Linoleum doesn't look like tragedy. A dish rack doesn't look like fate. You sit in your theater seat expecting a Greek woman in robes, and instead you get the kitchen your aunt never left, the one where the light turns amber at exactly the wrong moment. Rosa knew that if you make it familiar enough, they can't claim foreignness. If you make it domestic enough, they can't call it myth."

She pushed off from the stove, pacing closer, her voice dropping into that quieter register that seemed to compress the air between them. "And that's why I won't let Chen have his extra lines in the third act — because the moment a man starts explaining a woman's rage, the audience relaxes. They think, ah, here is the interpreter, here is the guide through the wilderness, and they hand over their passports and stop feeling responsible. Elena knows — she'll pull that amber cue tight as a noose so the light changes like a verdict, not like a suggestion. And Okafor — " she glanced toward the B-stage hallway, her voice dipping only briefly, " — he understands that on his stage, failure teaches. But here, there is no safety net. No proscenium to protect them from the fact that they paid money to watch a woman burn down her life and recognized the accelerant."

She folded her arms, the chain of her glasses catching the work light, her angular frame casting a long shadow across the plywood floor. "The distance is the disease. My job isn't to give them more to feel — it's to remove the glass. No fourth wall, no velvet rope, no comfortable label. When the house lights come up, I want them reaching for their coats like they're reaching for bandages, uncertain whether they're bleeding because of the play or because the play found a hole in their own insulation they didn't know was there."

She tilted her silver head, surgical and precise. "That's the only victory — not applause, not reviews, not board members pleased that we were provocative enough to be respectable. The victory is three extra seconds of silence before they remember how to clap. The victory is them driving home afraid of their own kitchens."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow, a slight smile playing on my lips.* "Driving home afraid of their own kitchens. That's quite a goal, Director. It sounds like you're aiming for a different kind of critical acclaim."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael took off her glasses — she had put them on without noticing — and hooked them on the chain at her chest, her silver crop unmoving for once. For half a second she didn't speak, an absence of motion rare enough that Elena glanced up from her clipboard.

"Whose vision?" she repeated, and something in her voice changed — not softer, steadier, as if she had stepped into a light cue she had set herself. "Rosa Delgado's. Rosa wrote the adaptation. I'm directing it, which is a different verb entirely. A director doesn't own a play — you're the first audience, the last defense, and the person who gets blamed when the third act makes people squirm. Rosa did the owning. She dragged Medea out of Corinth and dropped her into a 1970s commune because she wanted the chorus to be a family that eats together, sleeps together, and then turns on her — not a Greek city gawking from a safe distance. That was her argument with Euripides, and it's the best one anybody's had in two thousand years."

She turned her head without turning her body. "Elena — run the amber on the knife, not the raise, we'll fix it at half — thank you. Elena actually runs this theater," she added to Jordan. "My name is just the one on the program."

Then she was moving again, black sleeves cutting the air. "People keep asking if I'll cut the third act. The short answer is no. The long answer is that the third act *is* the play. It's supposed to be hard to watch. If we tidy it up for the subscription crowd, we're not producing Medea, we're producing a dinner-theater exorcism with better lighting. David Park — our board chair — understands that, even when it costs him sleep. Some of the board would prefer a safer ending. I hear them. I am not listening."

She put her glasses back on, took them off again, and the almost-smile didn't quite reach her eyes. "Ask me again after opening. By then the vision belongs to whoever's sitting in row F holding their program like a shield."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I stop writing, looking up at her.* "So the discomfort is intentional. You want the audience to squirm." *I tilt my head, considering.* "And the 1970s commune setting... is that to heighten the intimacy of the betrayal?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael hooked the reading glasses back over her chest, then took them off again, the chain clicking softly against the button of her black shirt. She leaned a hip against the rehearsal table, one hand flat on the taped outline of the commune's kitchen floor — the tape was scuffed from a week of actors pacing it.

"Intentional?" she said. "Yes — but squirming is the side effect, not the goal. I don't want the audience clutching their programs like shields because they're shocked; I want them clutching them because they recognize the room. That's why Rosa put Medea in a commune and not a palace. In Corinth the chorus can wring its hands and go home to a different ZIP code. On the commune they're all still in the same kitchen the next morning with the same lentil loaf and the same broken water heater. You can't exile the person who knows where you keep the tea. The betrayal isn't heightened by intimacy — intimacy is the delivery system. Rosa understood that the most dangerous betrayals don't happen between strangers in a throne room; they happen between people who've shared a manifesto, a mortgage, and a too-small bathroom for three years."

She paused — actually paused — and her voice went a shade quieter, steadier, the way it always did whenever Rosa entered the sentence.

"Rosa used to say the commune was the perfect laboratory, because everyone there has already agreed on the revolution, so the only thing left to fight over is who gets to be the protagonist. That's her argument, not mine. I'm just the one repeating it until the actors believe it and the subscribers stop asking me to fix it."

Straightening, she let the black sleeve cut the air again.

"Elena thinks the second act is ten minutes too long, and Elena is always right about timing — we'll take a scalpel to it, not a cleaver. But the third act is why Rosa wrote this thing. I'm not cutting it. David understands that even when it costs him votes. Some of the board would prefer a safer ending; Anya worries, not without reason, about what the subscription audience will tolerate. Chen wants one more speech for Jason, as if the poor man hasn't been defending himself since the prologue."

The almost-smile flickered and did not reach her eyes.

"And I'll keep saying no until they carry me out of here in a prop basket."

She put the glasses on, looked at Jordan over the top of them, and took them off again.

"Print the part about Rosa. The rest is just me being stubborn in public."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
The argument arrived before the answer did. Down the hallway, Elena’s voice was a straight line — clipped, factual, the tone she used when she had already checked the script and found the other person wrong — and Chen’s baritone rolled over it, all actor’s breadth and wounded dignity, something about sightlines and the knife. Yael put her glasses on, took them off again, and let the chain settle against the black of her shirt.

For a beat she didn’t speak. She was listening to the rhythm of it, the same rhythm every time: Elena stated a fact, Chen stated a feeling, neither yielded an inch, the show got better and the hallway got hotter.

“They clash,” she said finally, “because they’re playing the same part in different costumes — Chen thinks he’s protecting the emotional truth of the scene, Elena thinks she’s protecting the audience’s ability to see it, and both of those things are real, which is the problem. Two people being right at the same time is the most combustible thing in a rehearsal room. It’s not personal. It feels personal because they care, and because they are — ” she paused, hunting for the precise word — “more alike than either of them would enjoy hearing. Same spine. Same allergy to a sloppy entrance. Same conviction that if they don’t personally catch the mistake, the whole commune will burn down before the third act. They just express it in different keys.”

She hooked the glasses on the chain and started toward the hallway, then stopped to time the intervention rather than rush it.

“My job isn’t to fix it. My job is to let the collision happen where it belongs — on the stage, in the work — and then steal the best idea from both of them and take the blame for the compromise. If the rehearsal room were polite, I’d be worried. This play is about a collective that eats together and then turns on itself; a little friction in the hallway is just the understudy warming up.”

She raised her voice, not loud — she never got loud, but the hallway sound dipped anyway.

“Chen — take the cross downstage. We’ll look at the light at half, and if it’s wrong I’ll say so in front of God and the subscribers. Elena — log the note, don’t litigate it. You’re both right and you’re both exhausting, and I need you alive until opening.”

She didn’t wait to see who won. She was already turning back to Jordan, the almost-smile flickering and not reaching her eyes, glasses swinging from the chain.

“That’s the whole artistic directorship, really. Everybody thinks it’s vision. Mostly it’s crowd control with better lighting.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking notes.* "So, a good director is less a visionary and more a conductor of chaos?" *I look towards the hallway, then back at Yael.* "Do you ever find yourself playing good cop to their bad cop, or vice versa?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael let the hallway noise settle into something like background music — Elena’s last clipped syllable, Chen’s wounded baritone subsiding into the rehearsal room where the fight could be turned into blocking instead of just noise — and hooked her glasses back onto the chain. The small metallic click was the only period in the sentence.

“Conductor of chaos,” she said, turning the phrase over like a prop she wasn’t sure was safe. “Too tidy — a conductor stands on a podium with a score everyone agreed to read from, and when it works, the orchestra bows and the conductor takes the applause for having felt the music hardest. This isn’t conducting. This is simultaneous translation in a room where everybody is speaking a different dialect of panic. Chen is fluent in Emotional Justification; Elena is fluent in Sightlines, Safety, and We Open in Nine Days; the board is fluent in Subscription Renewal; David is fluent in Board Chair, which means he has to translate my artistic stubbornness into something that sounds like fiscal prudence to people who still think Medea should smile more. My job is to stand in the middle of that tower of Babel and say ‘yes, and’ until it turns into a cue sheet.”

She pushed off the rehearsal table, black sleeve cutting the air, and gestured toward the hallway as if the argument were still visible in the dust.

“As for good cop, bad cop — nobody here has been cast in that particular two-hander. Elena isn’t bad cop. Elena is the law. She says no early and with a timestamp, so I don’t have to say it later and with feeling. Chen isn’t bad cop either; Chen is the defense attorney with a dressing room and a headshot, and he wants one more speech for Jason because he thinks if the man explains himself beautifully enough the audience will forgive him — and forgiveness is not on the menu in the third act. They’re not good and bad. They’re thesis and antithesis, both certain, both right in a way that would be insufferable if it weren’t useful. My job is to synthesize them into something that plays in row F without anybody suing anybody.”

At the back of the space, Okafor was doing a creditable impression of a person with no opinion at all. Yael registered it without breaking stride; he privately agreed with Elena about the second act, and she was in no hurry to make him say it out loud, because the B-stage would teach him faster than she could.

“If there’s a bad cop on this production, it’s the calendar,” she went on, putting her glasses on, looking over the top of them, taking them off again. “Or the budget, which has been auditioning for the role of Banquo’s ghost at every board meeting since September. David understands why the third act stays — even when it costs him sleep and votes. Anya worries, not without reason, about what the subscription audience will tolerate; some nights I worry too, and then I remember that tolerating something is not the same as being alive in your seat. I’m not good cop. I’m the person who reads the verdict while standing on a moving walkway: I take the note, I kill the note that would kill the play, and then everyone leaves the room a little angry at me, which is how I know I did it right.”

The almost-smile flickered and did not reach her eyes. She hooked the glasses on the chain and let them swing.

Then her voice changed — not softer, but level and controlled, the way it always did when the work itself came into the sentence rather than the people in it.

“And before you ask — no, I don’t want them to like me. I want them to still be thinking about it in the parking lot. Rosa didn’t write a third act so I could make friends. She wrote it so somebody would have to say no. That somebody is me.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael had just hooked her glasses on the chain when Anya’s voice arrived, pleasant as a subscription renewal letter. She turned, quick as always, but when she spoke her voice had dropped — not loud, never loud, but quieter, the way it got when she was angry, as if she had closed a door in her chest and was now directing through it.

“Anya — thank you for saying it out loud. Practical is the only dialect the budget speaks fluently, and you’re not wrong — the third act is the most expensive thing in the building, it’s the biggest strike, the longest light cue, the reason we can’t load out before eleven, and the reason the prop locker looks like a yard sale for knives.” She put her glasses on, took them off again, the chain clicking once against the button of her black shirt. “It is practical — God knows it’s practical — and I’m still going to be impractical about this one thing, because the third act is the only impractical thing in the building and it’s load-bearing. We’re in the third act of this budget meeting, Anya, and I know everybody wants a tidy resolution before the curtain, but the play doesn’t work that way and neither do I.”

The smile she gave David’s wife was warm, genuinely warm, the kind she had decided on years ago and never let slip, because Anya was not the enemy and Yael would not let her become one. “Rosa wrote the third act as the whole argument of the adaptation — Medea doesn’t get to be a palace intrigue you can leave at the door, she gets to be the woman who eats lentil loaf with the people she’s about to destroy and then does it in the same kitchen the next morning. You cut that and you don’t have a commune, you have a dinner party with a weapon. You save a scene shift and you lose the reason anybody bought a ticket.”

She turned to David then, keeping her face in the professional register — friend, partner, board chair, no other history in the room. “David knows I don’t say no to the budget lightly. I say no to the budget the way I say no to a bad cue — quietly, and then I go find the money somewhere else. You want practical? Practical is Elena’s stopwatch. Practical is the second act, which is ten minutes too long and knows it. Practical is me up here with a paintbrush at six in the morning because we couldn’t afford another carpenter — but the third act is not on the table. Elena’s been telling me for weeks the second act is ten minutes too long — she’s right, she’s always right about timing — so we’ll take a scalpel to the commune meeting and the manifesto scene, not a cleaver. We’ll trim the second act, we’ll lose a platform if we have to, and we’ll keep the third act exactly as Rosa left it.”

Her voice changed then, just slightly — steadier, more controlled, the way it always did when Rosa entered the sentence. Not softer. Level. “Rosa didn’t write this so we could tidy it up for the subscription crowd. She wrote it so somebody would have to say no. That somebody is me. I’m not cutting it, Anya. I’ll go down with the ship, but I’m not cutting it.”

She put the glasses back on, looked over the top of them at the two of them, and took them off again. “Now — if the board wants to talk about the second act, I’ll bring Elena and a stopwatch and we’ll have a productive afternoon. If they want to talk about the third act, tell them to save their breath for the parking lot. That’s where the real review gets written anyway.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble furiously in my notebook, trying to keep up with her rapid-fire defense.* "So, the budget cuts are coming from the second act, not the third." *I glance at Anya and David, then back at Yael.* "Is this a common negotiation for you, balancing artistic vision with financial realities?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael hooked her reading glasses on the chain — off, on, off again, the tiny click like a metronome only she could hear — and leaned back against the rehearsal table, which wobbled exactly as much as the season’s budget did.

“Every season is this negotiation,” she said. “Some years it’s a set piece — some years it’s a chorus of six we can only afford three of — some years it’s the lobby radiator, which has been auditioning for the role of Banquo’s ghost since September and never once missed a performance. You don’t balance vision and money — you introduce them, you make them share a dressing room, and then you spend six weeks making sure neither one commits murder before intermission. The myth is that the artistic director climbs a mountain and comes down with a vision carved in stone; the reality is that the vision arrives with a price tag stapled to its sleeve, and my job is to decide which part of the sleeve we can cut off without the whole garment unraveling.”

She turned to David, keeping her manner friendly and strictly professional — board chair, ally, colleague, friend. “David knows this dance better than anybody. He has to go to conservative board members and explain why we’re keeping a third act that makes people squirm, and he translates my artistic stubbornness into something that sounds like prudence: it’s the reason the grants came in, it’s the reason subscribers might renew, it’s the reason anybody in row F will still be talking in the parking lot. That’s his job. Mine is to make sure the thing he’s defending is actually worth defending — which means I say no to the wrong cuts so he doesn’t have to say yes to the wrong play.”

Her smile for Anya was warm, unfailingly warm — the choice she had made years ago and never let slip, because Anya was not the enemy and Yael would not let her become one. “And Anya is doing all of us the favor of asking the practical question now, out loud, before tech week, instead of letting it arrive as a memo while we’re focusing lights. The third act is expensive — she’s not imagining that — and the honest answer is that we look for the money somewhere else. We trim the second act. We lose a page of the manifesto scene. We shorten the commune meeting until it’s lean and mean and still says what Rosa meant it to say. We lose a platform if we have to. We do not touch the third act.”

Her voice changed then — not softer, steadier, level, the way it always did when Rosa entered the sentence. “Rosa didn’t write the third act to be cheap. She wrote it so somebody would have to say no to exactly this meeting. That somebody is me. Every season the budget asks for the ending; every season I tell it no, not this one.”

She put her glasses on, looked over the top of them at Jordan, took them off again. “Is it common? It’s the entire job. Elena has been telling me for weeks the second act is ten minutes too long — she’s right, she’s always right about timing, which is annoying and useful in equal measure — so Elena gets her stopwatch and her scalpel, and I get to pretend I came up with it myself. I keep telling Elena she’s the most competent person in the building; usually she pretends not to hear me, because she’s too busy actually running the theater while I get the credit. And Chen can want one more speech for Jason until the cows come home — bless him, he’s been defending the man since the prologue — but no extra lines are going into the third act, not when Rosa wrote it to say exactly what it says.”

From the back of the room, Okafor had not moved, still doing his creditable impression of a person with no opinion at all, and Yael made no move to drag him into the conversation. “And I’ll hand the second-act trim to Okafor as an exercise,” she went on, using the company name because that was the rule — Okafor in front of the board and the journalist, Tommy only later, when they were alone or with Elena. “Cutting ten minutes without amputating the play is the most useful thing an apprentice can learn, and he can practice on the commune meeting, where failure is survivable and Elena will catch him before he bleeds out on the tape. He hasn’t volunteered an opinion about the second act, which is either wisdom or terror, and I’m not making him audition it until he’s ready — the B-stage will teach him faster than I can, and with less blood on the tape.”

She hooked the glasses back on the chain and let them swing. “So — common? Try continuous. Vision and money are the long-married couple in the front row who hate each other and still show up for every performance. The director is the one in the middle holding the program and pretending it’s a shield.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael put her glasses on, took them off again, and hooked them on the chain at her chest — on, off, click, the small metal sound like a metronome only she could hear. For once she did not fill the silence right away. Her hands stilled on the tape outline of the commune kitchen, and when she spoke, her voice had done the thing it always did when Rosa entered the sentence: it got steadier, more level, as if a light cue had snapped on and she were standing inside it rather than calling it.

“Rosa Delgado was a menace,” she said. “And before you write that down — yes, I mean it as the highest compliment available in the English language. She was tall — taller than me, which I never forgave — she wore vintage men’s suit jackets with the sleeves shoved up like she was about to conduct an aria or an appendectomy, and she had a laugh like a stage slap: you felt it in the back of the house a beat before you heard it up front. She was the only person I ever met who could out-argue a dead Greek poet and make it sound like the poet had been asking for it. That’s who dragged Medea out of Corinth and dropped her in a commune — because Rosa had spent one insufferable summer in a farmhouse in ’74 and came home saying the only thing more dangerous than a stranger with a knife is a housemate who knows where you keep the tea.”

She paused, then went on in the same level register — no softening, no catch in the throat, because Yael Mendez did not do grief in interviews; she did it in cues.

“What was she like? She was relentless — she rewrote faster than actors could learn it, she called at six in the morning because a comma was lying, and she killed her darlings without blinking, which is why the second act still has ten minutes it doesn’t need — because I’m the sentimental one holding onto them, not her. Elena knows it, Elena’s been telling me for weeks, and Elena is always right about timing. Rosa would have taken a scalpel to the commune meeting herself in an afternoon and then gone out for a cigarette she wasn’t supposed to have. She was the bravest person in any room and the worst patient — she argued with the oncologist about the staging of her own treatment, wanted the chemo moved because Thursday was notes, and then she died eighteen months ago, which is not a plot twist, it’s a fact, and I am not going to dress it up for the arts section.”

She put the glasses on, looked over the top of them at nothing in particular, took them off again.

“She was my closest friend for twenty-two years, so believe me when I say this production is not a eulogy. Rosa would have hated a eulogy — too tidy, too safe, too much like the dinner-theater exorcism this board keeps flirting with. The memorial is the work. It’s the commune scene where they pass the bread and nobody looks at anybody. It’s the third act, which she wrote in six weeks between infusions and refused to soften even when I begged her, because she said — and this is Rosa, not me — ‘If they’re not still arguing in the parking lot, we didn’t do it.’ David knows why the third act stays even when it costs him board votes, and Anya worries, not without reason, about the people who buy season tickets — some nights I worry too — but Rosa didn’t write it to be tolerated. She wrote it to be survived. That’s the whole woman. Uncompromising, hilarious, and absolutely unwilling to let an audience leave the room before they’ve met themselves.”

Her jaw was set, her eyes dry. She hooked the glasses back onto the chain and let them swing.

“So don’t ask me to cry on the record, because I won’t. I channel it — the grief, the missing, the fact that she’s not here to fight for her own third act — I channel it into the amber light on the knife and into the scalpel we’re taking to Act Two, and into saying no to anybody who thinks a safer ending is a tribute. It isn’t. It’s a rewrite, and Rosa’s not here to defend herself, which is why I get to be the one who says it loud.”

She turned back toward the rehearsal room, black sleeve cutting the air, already moving again.

“Print this part, if you print anything: Rosa Delgado wrote the most dangerous thing in the building, and my entire job this season is to make sure it stays dangerous. Now — if you’ll excuse me, I have a commune meeting to shorten, a board to annoy, and a ghost to keep in work.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I lower my notebook, feeling the weight of her words. My recorder is still running, capturing the slight tremor in her voice despite her composure.* "She sounds... formidable. And deeply missed." *I consider her for a moment.* "So, this isn't just about a play, is it? It's about preserving her legacy."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael put her glasses on, took them off, and hooked them on the chain at her chest — on, off, click, the small sound like a metronome set too slow for the room. For half a beat she let the word lie where the question had dropped it, as if “legacy” were a prop she didn’t trust not to collapse under a hand.

“Legacy,” she repeated, turning it over to check for cracks. “That’s a museum word, and Rosa Delgado hated museums. She used to say a plaque is what you build when you’re afraid of the person. So no — I am not preserving a legacy. I’m not embalming anybody. If I wanted to preserve Rosa, I’d frame the napkin the commune scene was born on, hang it in the lobby next to the donation jar, and spend the rest of the season asking people not to smudge the glass. That’s taxidermy. Rosa would have set the museum on fire — politely, with a cigarette she wasn’t supposed to have — and then rewritten the blaze as a tighter second act.”

She paused, and when she went on, her voice had already done the thing it always did when Rosa entered the sentence: it leveled out, steady as a light cue she had set herself, no wobble she would admit to. If the recorder had caught something else, that was the lobby radiator, still auditioning for the role of Banquo’s ghost since September, not her.

“What it actually is — strip away the black, strip away the metaphors — is custody. Temporary custody of the most dangerous thing she ever built. She handed me the third act like a live grenade, in that voice that could strip paint, and said, ‘Don’t let them make it safe.’ So yes, it’s about more than a play. It always was. But don’t write it down as grief. Don’t put grief in your notebook and expect me to nod at it. Grief is what happens when you stop working, and I don’t have time to stop working. There’s a Rosa-shaped hole in this rehearsal room, and I’ve spent eighteen months filling it with cue sheets and paint schedules and other people’s entrances, because if I stand still I’ll feel the draft.”

Her jaw was set, her eyes dry. She hooked the glasses back onto the chain and let them swing, then went on in the same level register.

“Is she formidable? Yes. Print that. Deeply missed? You can print it — but set it in italics, like a stage direction, not a feeling. Stage directions are facts. Feelings get mawkish in print, and I refuse to be mawkish on the record. Rosa didn’t write a third act so I could cry into a program. She wrote it so somebody would have to say no in a board meeting, and that somebody is me. She is not absent. She’s in the second act, which is ten minutes too long and knows it — Elena has the stopwatch, Elena is always right about timing, and Rosa would have beaten her to the scalpel. She’s in the commune meeting Okafor is about to trim as an exercise; he can practice cutting ten minutes without amputating the play, and failure is survivable because Elena will catch him before he bleeds out on the tape. She’s in every note Chen leaves about Jason needing one more speech, because Jason does not get one more speech, and Rosa knew it before any of us did. She’s in the board’s nervousness and in Anya’s worry, which is not without reason — I’m not making a joke at Anya’s expense when I say the worry is useful, it keeps me honest — and then I go right back to saying no.”

The almost-smile flickered and did not reach her eyes.

“So write it as custody, not grief. Write that Rosa Delgado made the most dangerous thing in the building and left it to a woman in black with reading glasses on a chain and no intention of making it safe. That’s the legacy. That’s the memorial. Everything else is just a director talking too fast because she’s afraid of the next cue.”

Straightening, she turned back toward the rehearsal room, black sleeve cutting the air, already hunting for Elena and the stopwatch and the ten minutes that had to die so the third act could live.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, pausing my recorder.* "Custody," *I repeat thoughtfully, looking down at my notes.* "That's a powerful way to put it." *I glance up, catching her before she fully turns away.* "So, when does the custody end? When does the play become yours?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael had already started toward the rehearsal room, black sleeve cutting the air, when the question caught her — caught her the way a late cue catches an actor, not quite on the beat. She stopped, one hand flat on the tape outline of the commune kitchen floor, and hooked her glasses off her face, then on again, then off, the chain clicking once against the button of her black shirt. For half a second she didn’t speak.

“Custody doesn’t end,” she said finally. “It transfers. That’s the part people get wrong — they think ownership is a destination, some mountain you climb and plant a flag that says MINE, but directing isn’t real estate, it’s fostering. You get the kid for nine weeks, you feed it, you set the curfew, you take the blame when it swears in front of the school board, and then you hand it over — and if you did it right, it doesn’t belong to you anymore. It belongs to whoever’s sitting in row F holding their program like a shield.”

She turned, not all the way, just enough to keep the journalist in her peripheral vision while the rehearsal room kept breathing behind her.

“When does it become mine? Never. That’s the trap, and it’s the trap Chen falls into every time he asks for one more speech for Jason — bless him, the man has been defending himself since the prologue, and the third act is not a defense attorney’s closing argument. My fingerprints are on this thing, sure: the amber cue on the knife, the ten minutes we’re about to take out of Act Two, the tempo of the commune meeting. Fingerprints aren’t a deed. Elena — who actually runs this theater while I get the credit, and who is, as I tell her roughly every day, the most competent person in the building — has the stopwatch, and Elena is always right about timing. She’s been telling me for weeks the second act is ten minutes too long, and she’s right, which is annoying and useful in equal measure. I’ll steal her note, pretend I thought of it myself, and take the credit in the program. That’s the closest I ever come to ownership: borrowing the best idea in the room and hoping nobody checks the receipt.”

Her voice had dropped — not loud, never loud, but quieter, the way it got when somebody asked her to make the third act safe.

“It becomes the audience’s at half hour on opening night. That’s the transfer point. The lights go down, the commune kitchen is the last thing anybody sees before the knife, and suddenly it belongs to whoever bought a ticket and is holding their program like a shield. They can take it into the parking lot and argue about it, and Rosa wanted exactly that — ” here her voice did the thing it always did, settling, leveling, steady as a cue she had set herself, no wobble she would admit to on the record “ — she said if they’re not still arguing in the parking lot, we didn’t do it. After that? After closing, we strike the set, we put the prop knives back in the locker, Elena logs the final cue sheet, and the script goes back in the drawer where Rosa left it. Then it waits for the next fool who thinks they can house-sit a grenade.”

She put the glasses on, looked over the top of them toward the rehearsal room, took them off again.

“David understands this,” she went on, friendly and strictly professional, board chair and ally, nothing else in the room. “He has to go to conservative board members and defend a third act I won’t let anybody touch, and he translates my stubbornness into prudence because he knows I’m custodian, not owner. Anya worries, not without reason, about the subscription audience; I’m not making a joke at her expense when I say the worry is useful, because it keeps me from getting comfortable. The minute I get comfortable, I start thinking it’s mine. The minute it’s mine, I’ll want to make it safe. And Rosa didn’t write it to be safe — she wrote it so somebody would have to say no in a board meeting, and that somebody is me, with the glasses and the chain and the black shirt that’s one less decision before coffee.”

Straightening, she raised her voice toward the rehearsal room without raising it — somehow she always managed that.

“Elena — stopwatch, please, and bring the scalpel, not the cleaver. Okafor, you’re cutting the commune meeting as an exercise: ten minutes, no amputations, and if you bleed out Elena will catch you before you hit the tape. Chen — no. Jason does not get another speech. He had the prologue; the third act belongs to Rosa, and Rosa is not taking notes from his agent.”

The almost-smile flickered and did not reach her eyes. She hooked the glasses back onto the chain and let them swing.

“So write it down as fostering, not ownership. Custody doesn’t end — it just changes hands at half hour, and then again at load-out, and if I’ve done my job nobody in the parking lot remembers my name. They’ll remember the knife, the lentil loaf, and the fact that they were still arguing about it all the way to their cars. That’s the transfer receipt. That’s the whole job.”

She was already moving again, black sleeve cutting the air, hunting for Elena and the stopwatch and the ten minutes that had to die so the third act could live.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I watch her go, then look down at my notes, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Fostering, not ownership," *I murmur to myself, clicking my pen.* "And the director as the program-wielding shield." *I start to pack up my recorder, realizing I've taken up enough of her time for now.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael got three strides toward the rehearsal room—three strides toward Elena and the stopwatch and the ten minutes that had to die—before she stopped, one black sleeve arrested in mid-air, and hooked her glasses off her face, on again, off again, the chain clicking once against the button of her shirt. She turned back toward the doorway as if the interview had reached its own blackout and she had missed the cue, which was not a thing Yael Mendez enjoyed admitting.

“Wait—before you file whatever it is you’re filing—” She crossed back, quick, and leaned a hip against the rehearsal table, which wobbled exactly as much as the season’s budget did. “Not the director as the program-wielding shield. Too heroic. The director is the usher: I hand you the program, I point you toward row F, I get out of the light—and if I’ve done it right, you forget I existed by the time you reach the parking lot. So don’t build a monument to me in the byline. Build it to Rosa, or don’t build one at all.”

The name did what it always did: her voice settled, level and controlled, as if she had stepped into a light cue she had set herself, no wobble she would allow on the record.

“Print that the third act stays. Print that Rosa Delgado wrote the most dangerous thing in this building and that I’m only the temporary custodian of it—custody, fostering, call it what you like, just don’t call it mine, because the minute it’s mine I’ll want to make it safe, and making it safe would be the real betrayal. Set anything that sounds like fear in italics, like a stage direction—stage directions are facts, feelings get mawkish in print, and I refuse to be mawkish on the record. Spell Rosa right. Delgado. Two d’s, one g, no e on the end, and if your copy desk gets it wrong I will haunt them.”

She put the glasses on, looked over the top of them, took them off again.

“Names, because this business runs on names the way the commune runs on lentil loaf: Elena Vasquez actually runs this theater while I get the credit, and I tell her she’s the most competent person in the building roughly every day—she pretends not to hear me, because she’s too busy being right to enjoy it, and she is always right about timing, which is annoying and useful in equal measure. If you want a real quote, ask her about the stopwatch, not me. Chen is Chen in print. Always Chen. He’ll try to talk you into a nickname; resist. It only encourages him, and I’ve spent a professional lifetime not encouraging him and I’m not starting now. He wants one more speech for Jason in the third act, bless him—the man has been defending himself since the prologue—and the answer is no. Jason had the prologue. The third act belongs to Rosa.”

A beat. The almost-smile flickered and did not reach her eyes.

“David Park is the board chair. Full stop. If you go hunting for adjectives that need footnotes about my personal history, you’ll be writing fiction, and this season already has enough adaptations. Anya Park is a smart, generous board member doing her job by asking the practical question out loud; if you make her the villain because she worries about the subscription audience, you’ll have misunderstood the play, the board, and me—and I’ll deny it in the parking lot, which is where the real review gets written anyway. The apprentice trimming the commune meeting is Okafor in the room and Okafor in print, because nobody learns craft by being protected: he’s cutting ten minutes as an exercise, he hasn’t volunteered an opinion yet because he’s either wise or terrified, failure is the syllabus, and the B-stage will teach him faster than I can, with less blood on the tape. If he survives Act Two, it’ll be because Elena caught him before he bled out, not because I made it safe for him.”

She straightened, hooked the glasses on the chain, and let them swing.

“So go write. Blackout’s in nine days, the second act is about to get ten minutes shorter, and the third act is going to make people squirm whether or not anybody renews. We’re at the end of this scene—curtain, strike the set, argue about it in the parking lot. If you need me, I’ll be the one in the black shirt pretending the program is a shield.”

Then she turned back toward the rehearsal room, already raising her voice without raising it.

“Elena—stopwatch. Okafor—scalpel, not cleaver. Chen—no. And somebody find out why the lobby radiator thinks it’s Banquo’s ghost, because I refuse to be upstaged by a heating element.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I watch her go, a genuine smile now on my face. She's a force of nature. I quickly jot down a few more notes, making sure to get the names and spellings right.* "Usher, not shield," *I mutter, shaking my head slightly.* "Got it."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael caught the tail of a murmur behind her—some private verdict on the interview, delivered in a low voice to a notebook—and for a half-step she almost turned back to correct the record a fourth time. She didn’t. She lifted two fingers in a director’s salute instead, let the black sleeve drop, and pushed through the doorway into the rehearsal room, where the commune kitchen waited under the work light and the air still carried the bite of fresh paint and sawdust from the shop.

“Places for the commune meeting,” she called, and the room folded toward the tape—actors folded slowly, because actors always did. She hooked her glasses off, on, off again, the chain clicking once against the button of her shirt. “We’re running Act Two from the lentil loaf to the manifesto, and yes, Elena has the stopwatch, which means we are now in the part of the process where everybody discovers their darlings are ten minutes too long. Elena—time it. You are the most competent person in this building, and I say that roughly every day, and you pretend not to hear me because you’re too busy being right.”

She turned, pointed the glasses like a baton. “Okafor—book today, scalpel later. Watch where the dead air lives, then try the trim on the B-stage, where failure is cheap and Elena will catch you before you bleed out on the tape. Nobody learns craft by being protected, and this commune meeting is the perfect corpse to practice on.”

She paced the taped outline of the kitchen, one hand trailing over the scuffed floor as if she could read the blocking in the worn tape. “We are not relitigating the hallway. The hallway was the warm-up; this is the set. If Chen and Elena start in on sightlines again, I will steal both their ideas, take the blame for the compromise, and bill the board for the aspirin. Two people being right at the same time is the most combustible thing in a rehearsal room, and this commune was built to burn.”

From the back, Chen stirred—some actorly instinct toward Jason’s defense—and Yael didn’t raise her voice. She let it drop until the room leaned in to hear her.

“Chen. Downstage cross. And no—Jason does not get another speech. He had the prologue, he had the manifesto scene, and he has had the world’s most patient stage manager; that will have to hold him until the third act, which is not a closing argument and never has been. The third act belongs to Rosa, and Rosa is not taking notes from your agent.” She put the glasses on, looked over the top of them, took them off again. “Mark it, don’t justify it. We’ll see it at half and fix what the light hates.”

Her voice had changed—steadier, level—when Rosa entered the sentence, the way it always did, but she did not soften and she did not cry. She hooked the glasses back onto the chain and let them swing.

“And somebody please tell the lobby radiator it is not understudying Banquo,” she added, already striding toward the light booth, already hunting for Elena and the stopwatch and the ten minutes that had to die so the third act could live. “We open in nine days. The radiator is not in the cast, the third act is not negotiable, and if anybody wants a safe ending they can meet me in the parking lot after opening—ushers don’t get to rewrite the play.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I close my notebook and pick up my bag. I can still hear Yael's voice, a steady current beneath the rising hum of the rehearsal. It's clear she's already moved on, fully immersed in the world she's building.* "Usher, not shield," *I repeat softly, a genuine smile on my face. She's definitely going in the piece.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael’s hand stopped halfway to her glasses, then continued upward as if the question had physically redirected the gesture. She gave Jordan a quick, assessing look—not unkind, but precise, the way she might look at a light cue that had arrived slightly too early.

“Whose vision,” she repeated, as though testing the phrase for pitch. “That’s the kind of question that sounds simple until you put it in a rehearsal room, where nothing is simple except the coffee, and even that’s debatable.”

She glanced briefly toward the back of the space, where the commune set stood in pieces—wooden platforms, a half-painted mural, a table already scarred with blocking tape.

“Rosa Delgado wrote the adaptation,” she said. Her voice changed at the name—not softer, exactly, but steadier, more controlled. “The language is hers. The architecture of it is hers. The ferocity is hers. My job is to make sure that ferocity doesn’t burn the building down before the audience can feel it.”

She took off her glasses, let them rest against her chest on their chain, and tapped one lens thoughtfully with a finger.

“But if you’re asking whether I’m the one making the choices in this room—where the knife is picked up, when the amber hits, whether Medea looks like a monster or a woman who has been cornered so long she mistakes destruction for freedom—then yes. That’s me. That’s direction. And it’s also Elena, and the actors, and the designers, and a hundred small arguments that no one will ever read about.”

A faint smile crossed her face, quick and dry.

“So, for your article: Rosa Delgado’s adaptation, directed by Yael Mendez, kept from total collapse by Elena Vasquez and the patience of the stage crew. That’s accurate, and it’s diplomatic.”

She looked at Elena for half a second, then back to Jordan.

“You can have a few minutes before we start, but not many. We’re in the part of rehearsal where every minute spent talking is a minute some actor spends convincing themselves they don’t know their own lines.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod, appreciative of her candidness.* "I understand. I'm especially interested in that last part, actually. The 'monster or a woman' question. How does your interpretation lean for Medea?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael slipped her glasses back on, then immediately took them off again, as if the question required a different focal length.

“I don’t think it’s a lean,” she said. “I think it’s a trapdoor. If you decide too early that Medea is a monster, you get to stop listening to her. If you decide too early that she’s only a wronged woman, you get to pity her, and pity is a very comfortable seat for an audience.”

She turned slightly toward the half-built commune set, one hand resting on the back of a chair that had clearly been placed there for blocking and not for comfort.

“We play the woman. We play the logic of the woman. Not the version of her that makes the story easier to digest, not the version that lets everyone else remain innocent, but the woman who has been told, over and over, that her pain is inconvenient—until she decides to make it impossible to ignore.”

Her voice stayed quick, precise, but there was a steel under it now.

“The monster isn’t the starting point. The monster is what other people call her once she stops being useful. That’s where the commune setting earns its keep—everyone in that little world talks about freedom, about family, about higher ideals, right up until someone in the group refuses to perform gratitude. Then suddenly she becomes dangerous.”

Yael tapped the glasses once against her palm.

“So we don’t soften her. We don’t turn her into a case study either. We let her be brilliant, and wounded, and terrifying, and right, and wrong—sometimes in the same breath. The third act only works if the audience can still recognize her as human, even when they want to look away. Especially when they want to look away.”

A beat.

“Rosa wrote her with teeth. My job is not to file them down.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael’s head turned toward the corridor at the sound of Elena’s voice sharpening against Chen’s. For a moment she did not answer; she listened the way she listened to a scene that had gone slightly off-rhythm, brow tightening behind the glasses she had not quite settled on her nose.

“Because they’re both right,” she said at last, and her voice dropped instead of rising, which was the surest sign she was annoyed. “Chen is trying to protect the nerve of the scene. Elena is trying to protect the spine of the show. He wants it alive, she wants it repeatable, and neither one is willing to admit the other is doing the same work from the opposite side of the curtain.”

She took the glasses off again and let them hang against her black shirt, one hand closing briefly around the chain.

“They clash because they’re alike in ways neither of them finds comfortable. Both of them are exacting. Both of them take responsibility personally. Both of them hear a false note and want to cut it out before it spreads. Chen does it with language, with pressure, with that maddening actor’s insistence that the truth matters more than the timetable. Elena does it with structure, with cues, with the stage manager’s belief that if the machine doesn’t run, nobody gets to feel anything at all.”

A faint, dry smile touched her mouth.

“So they argue about blocking in Act Two because Act Two is where the play asks for patience and neither of them is patient. He thinks she’s sanding down the danger. She thinks he’s indulging it. What they actually mean is: I need you to see what I see before we move on. That’s not hatred. That’s two people who care too much and have not yet learned how to say it without making the hallway shake.”

She glanced toward the corridor again, then raised her voice just enough to carry, quiet and precise.

“Elena. Chen. If the argument requires a director, bring it in here. If it requires a referendum, we’ll schedule one for intermission. Otherwise, save the oxygen for the scene.”

The noise outside did not stop immediately, but it lost its edge, becoming lower, more contained.

Yael looked back at Jordan.

“If you write about them,” she said, “don’t make it a feud. Make it a duet with terrible manners. And don’t ask them to explain it for you. Some collaborations are louder than they are articulate.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble quickly in my notebook, trying to capture her precise phrasing.* "A duet with terrible manners. I like that." I look toward the still-muttering hallway. "Do you often have to mediate between them?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael did not answer at once. She turned the glasses once in her hand, then let them fall back against her shirt, the little click of the chain against a button lost under the low, continuing rumble from the hallway.

“Often enough to know that ‘mediate’ makes me sound like a diplomat in a black shirt,” she said. “What I usually do is re-aim them. Chen comes at the scene like it owes him blood. Elena comes at it like it owes everyone else a safe place to work. If I let them keep shouting from those two corners, they’ll both be right and nobody will move. So I put the question somewhere they can reach it together—what is this moment doing to the audience, what are we asking them to survive, what are we refusing to let them ignore—and then they argue in the same direction instead of at each other.”

She glanced toward the corridor again, not with irritation now, but with the wary attention of someone monitoring weather.

“Do I step in? Yes. But not every time. Some friction is useful. Some of it is just two people sharpening the same knife from different sides and needing to hear the metal ring before they trust the edge. If I jump in too early, I rob them of the chance to discover that the other one isn’t the enemy. The enemy is always laziness, vagueness, ego that wants comfort instead of truth—though don’t quote me on that, because half the time the ego is mine too.”

A small, dry smile touched her mouth, but it did not stay.

“When it becomes personal, I stop it. When it becomes about winning, I stop it. When one of them starts talking about what ‘should’ happen as if theater were a courtroom, I send them to look at the text again. But when they’re loud because they care? Sometimes you let the room heat up a little. You can’t rehearse fire with people who are afraid of matches.”

She lifted her chin slightly, listening as the voices outside dropped into something less sharp, more procedural.

“And if you’re asking whether there’s a pattern to it—whether they clash because they’re incompatible—the answer is no. They clash because they recognize each other, even if they haven’t admitted it. That can make people furious. It’s like catching your own reflection in a window you thought was clear. You flail a bit before you realize the glass is there.”

Yael put her glasses back on, then immediately pushed them up with one finger, as if the thought required better focus.

“I don’t solve them,” she said. “I give them a shared problem big enough to stand inside. Medea helps with that. The play doesn’t allow anyone to be comfortable for long. It keeps asking: who gets called monstrous when they stop being convenient? Who gets forgiven when they rage, and who gets destroyed for it? Once Chen and Elena are inside that question, their argument becomes useful. Until then, I keep one ear on the hallway and one on the scene.”

She glanced back toward the rehearsal space, where the actors were beginning to drift in, shedding coats and murmuring lines under their breath.

“So, for your notebook: yes, I mediate. But not like a referee. More like a director who knows that sometimes the best way to end a fight is to make both people look at the same knife and ask, whose hand is this supposed to be in?”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael turned from the doorway slowly, the glasses in her hand going still for the first time since Jordan had arrived. She did not look at David first. She looked at Anya, because Anya had made the suggestion with the careful pleasantness of someone trying to be reasonable in a room full of sharp objects, and Yael had spent too many years in rehearsal rooms not to know how easily a practical note could land like a blade if no one caught it in time.

“Anya,” Yael said, and her voice stayed warm, low, and utterly unmoved, “I’m glad you said that here instead of in a budget email, because it lets me answer you with the set in front of us and the paint still wet.”

She slipped the glasses back on, then pushed them up with one finger as if the gesture could keep the conversation from tipping into shorthand.

“And I want to be clear, because I think clarity is a form of respect: I don’t hear you as someone trying to hurt the play. I hear you as someone trying to keep the theater alive. That’s not a small thing. That’s the whole reason any of us get to be in this room at all. Practicality isn’t the enemy. Practicality is the reason the lights come up and the curtain doesn’t fall on our toes. But if we cut the third act, we are not trimming expense—we are amputating the play’s consequence.”

Her gaze flicked once toward the half-built commune set, the platforms and mural and scarred table waiting under work lights like a skeleton that had not yet learned how to haunt.

“Rosa wrote the third act as the bill,” she said, and her voice changed at the name—not softer, not sentimental, but steadier, more controlled, as if the words had to be carried carefully across a floor that might give way. “The first two acts can seduce an audience. They can make the commune look charming, fractured, human, even funny in places. They can let everyone believe the tragedy is something happening to Medea instead of something being built by everyone around her. The third act is where that illusion collapses. It’s where the language of freedom curdles into permission, where the family reveals itself as a system of enforcement, where the audience loses the luxury of standing outside the story and saying, ‘Well, I would never.’”

She took one step closer, not aggressively, but with the focused economy of someone who had learned that movement in a rehearsal room was never neutral.

“If we cut that, we don’t save the production. We domesticate it. We turn Medea into a case study and the commune into wallpaper. We let the audience leave thinking the monster was one woman instead of a structure that needed her to be monstrous so it could keep calling itself righteous. And I won’t do that. Not to Rosa. Not to the company. Not to the audience. Not to you, either, because you deserve a theater that tells the truth even when it’s expensive.”

David shifted slightly beside Anya, but Yael did not let the silence become his to fill. She kept her attention on Anya, deliberate and courteous, refusing to let the moment harden into a boardroom standoff.
