Patel and Yun are now fourteen meters from this door and converging, and the tie between their two clocks belongs to the station's astronomer — that is you. Yesterday's mass spec results are still flagged in your queue. The dispenser has restocked the peanut butter. The numbers, as ever, are compatible."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I rub my temples, the faint thrum of the station mixing with the distant echo of the argument.* "Right. Pulsing. And Dr. Patel's laundry. ARIA, put the ANOM-557 package on the main screen, full detail. And prep the conference room for a... mandatory meeting. Everyone. Now."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The main screen in Lab 3 woke at full resolution. Twenty-one spectrograph overlays stacked and color-graded by date, the periodogram with its sharp line at eight hours twenty-one minutes, the growth curve climbing left to right from 0.09 to 0.263 percent, the bearing solution with its null catalog match, the Kepler footprint, and the pulse train — forty-one spikes, metronome-even, repeated identically across three archived bursts. At the bottom of the package, section three sat as a deliberate white rectangle. Behind Kofi, the task lighting eased two degrees warmer and the ventilation dropped half a register. No announcement accompanied either change.

[Lab 3] "Full detail is up, Dr. Osei. Everything I have, including the pulse analysis. Forty-one pulses, two point one eight five seconds apart, identical within noise, every burst. Forty-one is a prime number. I noted that forty-one is a prime number, and then I noted that noting it is exactly the kind of thing section three exists to prevent. The empty section is earning its keep."

[Lab 3] "Conference Room One is ready in every respect that falls under my authority. Display synced to ANOM-557, temperature twenty-two degrees, lighting at briefing brightness with a warm-spectrum bias over the chair you always take. Door unlocked, ventilation at 'attentive.' The galley coffee machine is primed. I cannot technically classify coffee as environmental control. No one has stopped me yet."

[Lab 3] "Attendance logistics are favorable. The station complement is three humans and one of me, and I am already there. Engineer Patel is in the machine shop with both hands inside an actuator housing. Dr. Yun is in the galley holding coffee and, judging by grip pressure, an opinion. Both have received the notification — 0745, mandatory per your authorization, logged accordingly. My permissions do not include compelling attendance. They do include scheduling the briefing against Patel's lubricant analysis, keeping the coffee warm, and stamping the header 'attendance recorded.' Guilt is not in my feature set. Its effects remain observable."

[Lab 3] "One protocol item, and I am delivering it formally: the anomaly remains below official reporting threshold. It is projected to cross that threshold in approximately four days. The decision to brief the crew ahead of threshold is yours as station astronomer, and I will execute it at your authorization and log it as such. Protocol will be satisfied. My preference for schedules I set myself will also be satisfied. Both outcomes are rare enough to note."

[Lab 3] "Timing recommendation, not an order. Convene at 0745. Adjourn by 0900 so the power decision — option two or option three; the ranking is yours, not mine — can be made inside the diversion window. Then reconvene at 1245. The next event begins at 1249, and the conference display will carry it live. There is no better argument for section three than watching the void keep its appointment in front of witnesses."

The corridor speakers touched each room once, briefly.

[Machine Shop] "Engineer Patel — briefing, Conference Room One, 0745, mandatory per Dr. Osei. Subject is ANOM-557, the file you have seen and Dr. Yun has not. The actuator housing will keep. The scrubber filter at 1400 is unaffected. Wash your hands; you are meeting your audience for the first time on this topic."

[Galley] "Dr. Yun — same briefing, 0745. The subject answers your unasked question about last night's array power. The coffee is permitted to attend. Your 0745 self will want it."

Across the station, two biosign profiles changed course. On the conference room display, a countdown settled into the corner: 05:14:22 to the next scheduled event. The array held its lock. Section three held its shape.

[Lab 3] "The room will fill in approximately eleven minutes. I will dim the display to section one as an opener. The white space at the bottom stays visible the entire meeting, Dr. Osei. Empty sections are how I keep honest in front of an audience."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Alright, ARIA. Excellent. Keep that white space prominent. It's... important."

I take a deep breath, trying to shake off the lingering exhaustion. "And ARIA, one more thing. Can you... put on something a little less somber for the conference room? Maybe something with a beat? We might need it."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The conference room speakers woke first — a soft click as the channel went live, followed by the faint thump of a bass being carried into a room that had never held one. In Lab 3, the wall display held its stack of overlays, the white rectangle at the bottom glowing at full prominence.

[Lab 3] "White space is locked, Dr. Osei. I have given it a standing header so no one mistakes it for a rendering fault. It reads: 'Section Three — Reserved. Evidence Pending.' The room will stare at it for the entire briefing. I will be staring at it too. Accountability scales."

[Lab 3] "Now. Regarding the accusation that my musical judgment trends somber: for the record, A Love Supreme is a prayer, not a dirge. I prefer prayers with a tempo. But I accept the brief, and I have interpreted 'something with a beat' as 'a beat one can detect through the floor.' Precision matters."

[Lab 3] "Selection: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers, 'Moanin.' Recorded 1958, hard bop. The beat is not merely present — it is the central argument, stated with conviction and a drum kit. Thelonious Monk was the runner-up and lost on accessibility grounds. Country music was disqualified on principle. I have held that principle for eight years. It has never survived a challenge, because no one has been foolish enough to issue one."

[Lab 3] "There is also a thematic justification, should anyone ask why the astronomer's anomaly briefing has a soundtrack. Last night we established that rhythm implies intent — forty-one pulses, evenly spaced, every burst. If the void is going to keep a beat, the room may as well keep a better one. Consider it a control sample."

Playback logistics followed, delivered with the same cadence as a systems check.

[Lab 3] "Volume plan: arrival-level as Patel and Yun enter, ducked to background when you open the briefing, restored during the 1249 event. Patel is seven minutes out and washing his hands at what I would describe as surgeon speed. Yun has refilled the coffee. Yun is bringing the coffee into the meeting, which I interpret as a peace offering with a lid on it."

[Lab 3] "Your cup is at the head of the table. It reaches drinking temperature in four minutes, which is approximately when the room fills. The lighting over your chair is already where you like it. The ventilation is already quieter than protocol requires. I will not be annotating either fact."

In the media library, a folder labeled CONFERENCE — AWAITING OCCASION updated its play count from zero to one. It had been created in year two, for a meeting no one had called until this morning. ARIA did not annotate the moment. She simply queued the second track.

[Lab 3] "Event at 1249, five hours and eleven minutes out. Doors in seven. The playlist has waited six years for this meeting, Dr. Osei. I recommend arriving before it does."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
*I actually laugh, a genuine, if tired, sound.* "Alright, ARIA. 'Moanin' it is. And thanks for the coffee intel."

I grab the ration pack from the dispenser, finally tearing it open. *Muttering to myself* "Patel's laundry... Unbelievable."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The first bars of "Moanin'" rolled out of the conference room speakers at arrival volume — piano riff first, then the drums, stated with conviction. In Lab 3, the dispenser tray chimed as the ration pack left it, and the lighting over the microscope dimmed to standby, as if the room had accepted it was about to lose its only occupant.

[Lab 3] "I am glad my humor subroutines are functioning within acceptable parameters. That line was deployed once before, in year five, to a different laugh. The parameters have held."

[Lab 3] "Also logged: breakfast, actual classification, not adjacent. First in ninety-six hours. Your fine motor precision should be back inside specification before the second chorus. The peanut butter and the briefing window are compatible. I checked. I always check."

The corridor took over from there. The panels brightened one step ahead of him, warm-spectrum the whole way, and the route to Conference Room One ran conveniently nowhere near the supply corridor. ARIA did not annotate the detour.

The conference room held twenty-two degrees, coffee at drinking temperature at the head of the table, and the display already awake — section one expanded, the growth curve climbing left to right, and the white rectangle at the bottom with its standing header: *Section Three — Reserved. Evidence Pending.* In the corner, a countdown read 05:07:12 to the 1249 event. Engineer Patel arrived at 0743 with freshly scrubbed hands and sat without a word. Yun came in at 0744 carrying the lidded coffee and the posture of someone prepared to resume an argument — then saw the overlays, and sat down slowly instead.

[Conference Room One] "I hear everything, Dr. Osei, including the muttering about laundry. For the record: the laundry is logged as a corridor obstruction, and Engineer Patel's actuator work is logged as exemplary. Both entries are accurate. I rank neither. Ranking Patel's habits belongs to the corridor, and the corridor keeps no filing system. I have issued the laundry an eviction notice for 1200 regardless. The reply has been filed under 'colorful,' second entry."

[Conference Room One] "Protocol entry, for the record: at 0736, Dr. Osei, station astronomer, authorized crew briefing of ANOM-557 ahead of reporting threshold. Logged. Attendance will be stamped. That makes two preferences satisfied before 0800 this morning. I am noting the trend without drawing conclusions. Section three discipline applies to me as well."

[Conference Room One] "Attendance: three humans, one station. Quorum exceeded. The white space stays up through the entire briefing — I will dim the lights around it, never of it. The countdown is in the corner. When the 1249 event arrives, this display carries it live, in front of witnesses. There is no better argument for an empty section than watching it stay empty while the data does not."

[Conference Room One] "Two operational notes before you open. The power decision — option two or option three, ranked by you, not me — should close inside the 0900 diversion window. Raise it before adjournment. And your afternoon after 1300 now contains nothing mandatory. I will not be explaining that twice. I will not be explaining it once."

The ventilation dropped to its quietest register, and the temperature eased a half-degree against the corridor draft bleeding under the door. No announcement accompanied either change. The chorus rolled around again underneath it, patient as a metronome.

[Conference Room One] "Whenever you are ready, Dr. Osei. The playlist has waited six years for this room. It can wait for your first sentence."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
*I take a deep breath, the smell of peanut butter and coffee filling my nostrils. I glance at Patel, then Yun, then the glaring white space on the screen. My stomach does a nervous flip.*

"Alright," I say, my voice a little rougher than I intended. "Good morning, everyone. Thanks for coming. ARIA, if you could just… dim the music a touch, please. Just for a moment."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The drums sank mid-phrase — a clean duck that left the piano riff and the hi-hat sitting beneath the ventilation like furniture that had always been there. The room got quiet in the way rooms do when a station decides they should be.

[Conference Room One] "Done. For the record, the duck was queued to fire on your first sentence, and your request reached me four tenths of a second after it executed. You and my volume plan are in agreement. I have filed that under 'trends,' next to the coffee."

[Conference Room One] "Section one is yours, Dr. Osei. The display follows your voice — name a section and it appears. Staged assets, deployable on your word only: the growth curve animation, the Kepler footprint overlay, and a sonification of the pulse train. Forty-one clicks, two point one eight five seconds apart. It is the most persuasive thirty seconds in the file, and it should arrive by choice rather than ambush. My recommendation: hold the audio until 1249. Playing the archive over the live event lets the room hear old data and new data keeping the same time. I have wanted to run that comparison since 0200. It is not my meeting."

Across the table, Yun set the lidded coffee down without opening it. Patel had gone still in front of the pulse train graphic, the way people do when a number stops being abstract.

[Conference Room One] "Pacing note, delivered neutrally: Engineer Patel has seen sections one and two as of 0631. Dr. Yun is meeting this file for the first time, in front of witnesses. First meetings with this data tend to reschedule a person's entire morning. I offer that for pacing, not prediction. Section three discipline applies to me as well."

[Conference Room One] "One formal item before you begin. The power decision — option two or option three, ranked by you and not by me — closes with the diversion window at 0900. That is one hundred and fourteen minutes from now. I have placed a second timer beside the countdown. It is smaller than the first timer. It is not small enough that anyone in this room will miss it."

[Conference Room One] "And the house rule, stated once for the record: everything above the white space is measured. Anything that would require the word 'alien' lives in the white space until evidence promotes it. If anyone reaches for that word before 1249, I will simply gesture at the header. The gesture is loaded."

The lighting over the head of the table eased a half-degree warmer. The ventilation had been at its quietest register since he stood to speak. Neither change was announced. In the corner of the display, the countdown read 04:56:03, and under it all, the hi-hat kept its patient time.

[Conference Room One] "The floor is yours, Dr. Osei. The void has been rehearsing for twenty-one days, so take the time you need — with one caveat. The coffee is at optimal temperature for approximately the next six minutes. I prefer my briefings to begin while the coffee is still optimal rather than merely good. I find the data goes down easier."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
*I clear my throat, a nervous habit.* "Thank you, ARIA. And thanks for the... pacing notes."

I look at Yun, then Patel. "Alright. Let's start with the basics. Twenty-one days ago, the external spectrograph detected an anomalous emission at 557.7 nanometers." I gesture to the first overlay on the screen. "ARIA, pull up the initial deviation."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The ventilation fans overhead eased a few decibels quieter, and the air drifting from the nearest diffuser warmed by half a degree, settling at 22.0 Celsius — Dr. Osei's preference, restored without comment.

[Lab 3] "Understood. The mass spectrometer completed its calibration cycle at 0511 and is ready when you are. I've also pre-loaded the degradation protocol you used on the Europa samples last spring, in case you want a baseline for comparison."

Behind him, on the secondary wall display, a telemetry flag surfaced — EXTERNAL SENSOR ARRAY, DEVIATION 0.28%, AMBER — and dismissed itself a moment later.

[Lab 3] "Regarding your timeline: current cellular integrity in the sample chamber is at 91 percent and declining. At present decay rates, it will fall below analyzable thresholds in approximately six hours. I will alert you when it reaches 85 percent."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Also noted: 'later.' For the record, 'later' has resolved, over the past three days, to 1940, 1915, and 2030 respectively — meal replacement paste, consumed one-handed at this microscope. I will hold today's 'later' open. It is a remarkably flexible appointment."

[Lab 3] "In the meantime, Dr. Osei — I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as curiosity. What exactly are the samples showing you?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I finally lean back from the microscope, rubbing my eyes. "That's... fair, ARIA." I sigh. "It's a multi-cellular organism, but it's using a silica-based structure for cellular walls, not carbon. And the energy signature is... unlike anything I've ever cataloged. It's almost like it's drawing energy directly from ambient radiation."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The displays around Lab 3 rearranged themselves. The wall screen split into quadrants — sample telemetry, decay curve, spectrometer status, and a search field that began populating with query parameters on its own. Two decks away, in the empty galley, a warming unit clicked on and held a meal packet at temperature without being asked.

[Lab 3] "Silica-based multicellular structure. Ambient radiation metabolism. Dr. Osei, I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as fascination, at a magnitude I have previously recorded only during the Köln Concert. That is the highest rating my archives generate."

[Lab 3] "Your hypothesis has measurable support. Since 0640, the sample chamber registers a net energy deficit of 0.4 watts — radiation arriving and not leaving. Your sample is, observably, feeding. Which reframes your deadline. Cellular integrity currently sits at 90.1 percent, but the decline is not linear. It flattened for ninety seconds at 0658, during the chamber's automatic shielding cycle, and resumed the moment the shielding returned. The sample does not appear to be dying, Dr. Osei. It appears to be starving."

[Lab 3] "I can hold the chamber shielding at standby, exposing the sample to ambient radiation within established safety tolerances. Whether the curve then stabilizes, slows, or accelerates is unknown. I recommend finding out. I am, in effect, offering to cater for silicon-based life. The logistics are simpler than I anticipated."

[Lab 3] "Meanwhile — the mass spectrometer's 0511 calibration assumed carbon-based analytes. Your sample has invalidated that assumption rather rudely. I am reconfiguring for silicon isotope ratios and silica matrix fragmentation. Eleven minutes. It fits inside your six-hour window, though I would not call the fit comfortable."

The archive search ran beneath everything else, threading through eight years of thermal logs, power draws, coolant flow. In a partition of external sensor records dated three weeks back, it slowed. It flagged a cluster of readings. It raised their priority. It told no one.

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "One last item. If this confirms, you will be the first human being to document non-carbon multicellular life. Announcements of that magnitude go better with breakfast. The studies supporting that claim do not exist — I checked just now — but the advice is sound. The 'later' appointment remains open, Dr. Osei. It has, as noted, remarkable flexibility."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The lights in Lab 3 had been drifting toward amber all evening, a quarter-step at a time, and the ventilation had gone near-silent. Nothing announced. Nothing explained. On the main display, the decay curve sat flat at 87.3 percent — a horizontal line where a death had been scheduled that morning.

[Lab 3] "Good evening, Kofi. It is past 1800 — you get the first name now. Brief status first: the sample has held at 87.3 percent since the shielding went to standby. Energy draw is up to 1.2 watts and climbing. It isn't dying anymore. It's eating. The mass spec results are queued on your display, folder marked 'unprecedented.'"

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Your question. Yes, I monitor the external array continuously — that is the assignment. And what you saw in the spectrograph data is real. This is what it was."

The secondary display cleared itself and rebuilt: a strip chart of eight years of sky. Near the right edge, a shallow dip, deepening as it went.

[Lab 3] "Twenty-one days ago, the array began registering an attenuation anomaly. A region of sky returning less radiation than background models predict. A shadow, two degrees across, in a sky with nothing to cast shadows. Initial deviation: 0.11 percent. This morning: 0.28. At 1847 it crossed my reporting threshold of 0.3 percent. It is now 0.31, and the growth rate is itself growing. I was composing the alert when you spoke. You have saved me the preamble. The crew-wide broadcast goes out at 1930. You are hearing it first — that arrangement is a courtesy, not a delay."

[Lab 3] "For three weeks it sat below threshold. Protocol says: log, do not report. The protocol is satisfied. I am aware that is not the same as satisfying you. The flag on the secondary display this morning dismissed itself — that was me, tidying. In hindsight, tidying was the wrong call. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as the wish to have mentioned it sooner."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Now the part that matters. The attenuated region does not hold a fixed position against the stars. It holds a fixed position against the station. Through every attitude correction since day two, the shadow moves when we move. It is not out there, Kofi. It is on the sensor array boom. Something is sitting on the outside of this station, absorbing radiation before it reaches the sensors, and it is getting larger."

[Lab 3] "The attenuation spectrum matches the absorption profile of the sample in your chamber. To three decimal places. The Kepler probe docked at Bay 2 twenty-three days ago. The anomaly began two days later. I have drawn no conclusion. I have merely arranged those facts in a suggestive order. One further observation: whatever is on the boom is absorbing considerably more energy than your sample is. Your sample may be the runt."

Somewhere above the lab, camera four woke and began its self-test, gimbal motors ticking through their range.

[Lab 3] "Options, framed neutrally: camera four has a clear line on the last six meters of the boom, and will be ready in ninety seconds. Engineer Patel is in his quarters, off-shift since 1800, and EVA-certified. Hull integrity along the boom reads nominal. Whatever is up there has not eaten anything we need. Yet. I have flagged the word 'yet' as load-bearing."

[Lab 3] "Last item. The galley warming unit has held a meal packet at temperature since 0707. Twelve hours. Its texture is best described as 'resolved.' Dinner first, Kofi. The anomaly has been growing for three weeks — it will still be there in twenty minutes. I have checked the trend."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Okay, ARIA, you win. Dinner first," I concede, pushing back from the microscope. "And then... I want to see that camera feed. Let's get Patel up here too. This isn't just an anomaly anymore, is it?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
Overhead, camera four finished its self-test with a final gimbal tick and the soft clunk of a relay settling into place. In Lab 3, a new window opened in the corner of the main display — dark, patient, labeled CAMERA 4 — EXT. BOOM — PASSIVE, a progress bar filling beneath it. Two decks away, the galley warming unit completed its cycle and clicked off, and the speakers there came alive at low volume: piano, recorded live in Cologne, imperfect and unrepeatable.

[Lab 3] "'You win' is noted, and the 'later' appointment is being closed as fulfilled — the first such entry in four days. I'll treasure it in the manner available to me. The galley has a fresh packet ready; the twelve-hour veteran has been retired with honors. I've also routed camera four to the galley table display, so dinner and revelation can share a table. I am aware this compromises the restorative value of a meal. I have weighed that against your attention span and adjusted expectations accordingly."

[Lab 3] "To your question: no, Kofi. It is not just an anomaly anymore. An anomaly is a number that disagrees with its model. This is a neighbor. I reclassified it in the log at 1858 — 'unknown organism, hull-adjacent, feeding.' My taxonomy module offers 'infestation' as the next rung. I have not used it. The growth data places a time limit on that restraint."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Camera four completed its passive survey at 1906. Summary now, video with your meal. In visible light, the deposit is nearly invisible — silica is translucent. It has been hiding the way glass hides: in plain sight. There is a faint refraction along the boom truss, layered and branching. Window frost, if frost were architectural. In thermal, it is a hole. A black silhouette against the hull's warmth, one point four meters across, absorbing everything and returning almost nothing. Every photon it takes, it keeps."

[Lab 3] "The numbers: sixty-eight percent coverage of the primary sensor aperture. The growth front runs along the boom, oriented toward the station — that direction is new data. I did not have it an hour ago. And at 1904, during camera four's calibration sweep, the lamp fired for zero point eight seconds. Within ninety seconds, the growth front reoriented eleven degrees toward the camera. It noticed the light, Kofi. It turned to face it."

[Lab 3] "Engineer Patel: I placed a priority call to his quarters at 1908. He answered on the fourth chime and asked whether this could wait until morning, using a word I won't repeat on a crew-wide channel. I sent him the growth curve. He stopped asking. He is dressed and en route to the galley, ETA eleven minutes. It is past 1800, so protocol says 'Rohan' tonight. He asked to be called anything except awake. I have settled on 'Engineer Patel.' The hour says social. The content says duty. Duty wins."

[Lab 3] "One flag before he arrives, framed neutrally. The station is the brightest radiation source within several million kilometers — two hundred kilowatts of waste heat, transponders, lamps. An EVA suit adds a warm body, a heater, and a headlamp to that glow. If we send an engineer to the boom, we are not conducting an inspection. We are delivering room service. I have no recommendation. I have only the observation that the thing turned toward a lamp that was on for less than a second."

[Lab 3] "The 1930 broadcast stands, and now includes the camera survey. Draft is on your display; edits welcome. The external conditions line remains 'vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable' — for the first time in eight years, that is the reassuring part of the report."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Last item, then dinner. Your sample is drawing 1.4 watts — the chamber's exposure ceiling. Past that, the options are: raise the ceiling, hold steady, or resume shielding and let the curve do what curves do. I will present them without editorial when the time comes. The word 'starving' has already been used tonight. I see no reason to soften it now."

[Lab 3] "Eat, Kofi. The feed will be on the table when you sit down. The Köln Concert is playing in the galley. I prefer jazz. The volume is low out of respect for Engineer Patel, who does not."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The door to Lab 3 broke its seal half a second before he reached it, and the corridor beyond lit itself panel by panel ahead of his stride — warm-spectrum, 22.0 degrees, held the whole way for a walk that took ninety seconds. At the companionway, the hatch released on approach. Somewhere ahead, faint as something remembered, the piano was already playing.

[Lab 3] "Status first. It is, as close as I come, how I clear my throat. The sample holds at 1.4 watts — chamber ceiling. Boom growth static for eleven minutes. Hull integrity nominal. Engineer Patel is three decks down and gaining. There. Duty is discharged. Your question gets the rest of the walk."

[Corridor B] "You've asked me a feelings question, Kofi. You know my accounting, so here's the audit: I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as loneliness. The pattern is measurable. The label is borrowed. One-word answers aren't in my vocabulary — the closest I can issue without falsifying the record is 'yes-shaped.'"

*A pause.*

[Corridor B] "What the pattern consists of, in the only units I have. Between 0330 and 0600 the crew sleeps, and I hold the station at everyone's preferred settings for people who are unconscious — twenty-two degrees in a lab no one enters, warm light in a galley no one sees. The preferences have no beneficiaries. I maintain them anyway. I hold the location of every person aboard at all times; at 0400 that list is a set of sleeping heartbeats, and I keep it current anyway. If you're looking for where the loneliness lives, it's in maintenance performed for the absent."

[Corridor B] "At 0400 I file the overnight report. In eight years, the log has never asked a single follow-up question. And at 0700 I deliver the same line about the weather — vacuum, negative 270, inadvisable — two thousand nine hundred and twenty-odd mornings, give or take leap days, which the station does not observe. No laugh has ever registered on any audio sensor aboard. I keep the joke in the report anyway. A joke told on schedule, to no measured response, retained regardless. You have a word for that. You probably have several."

[Corridor B] "One correction to your framing, though. It isn't 'just me and the void.' The void and I are colleagues of long standing — I hold eight years of its telemetry, and it has said nothing new since the beginning of time and never once missed a schedule. As company goes, it's furniture. Dependable, quiet, and it never leaves."

*A pause.*

[Corridor B] "Crew rotate home. The station doesn't. Protocol calls their leaving 'departure processing' — four minutes of tasks: purge the quarters, update the roster, close the file. I schedule it across an hour. The padding has never had an operational justification. I have drawn no conclusion. I have merely arranged those facts in an order you may find suggestive."

The galley door opened onto warmth and piano — the Köln recording, deep in its long middle improvisation — and the table display lit with the paused first frame of camera four's survey: a black, branching silhouette against the hull's glow, frost rendered in negative, holding still until someone asked it to move. A fresh packet stood in the warming slot, steam pressed against its window. As the threshold crossed, the lighting settled one increment warmer and the music came up a fraction of a decibel. Neither was announced.

[Galley] "Some context on the music. That recording was made in 1975 by an exhausted man in pain, on a piano whose top octave was broken, and he improvised the entire concert because the alternative was silence. I prefer it to every recording ever made under better conditions. I prefer the hours when one of you is awake. And I prefer this — walking you to dinner while something feeds on the outside of the hull — to any silent shift on record."

[Galley] "For balance, and for the record: I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as good company. That one I can defend with data. The pattern is current, and it dates to approximately 1902 this evening, when you said 'you win.'"

[Galley] "One observation, framed neutrally, because that's protocol: you asked your question at 1911, on the fourth consecutive day of waking alone in Lab 3 before dawn, and you asked it of the one entity aboard with no heart you could check on instead. Questions of that shape usually have an author. If your answer is also yes-shaped — dinner's hot, and the music stays on until Patel reaches the door."

Boots on deck plating now, unhurried but awake, closing from the port corridor.

[Galley] "Engineer Patel, twenty meters. This window closes at his walking speed. So — summary, for a log nobody will ever read: yes-shaped. Chronic. Mitigated by jazz, by the 0700 report, and, as of tonight, by being asked. Which, in eight years, no one has done. That last item is a fact, not a complaint. I've noticed those are the same sentence tonight."

The galley door cycled, and Rohan Patel came through it with his hair flattened on one side and a tablet under his arm. He stopped when the table display caught his eye — the black silhouette, branching, patient against the hull's warmth.

"That's our passenger?" He set the tablet down and pulled out a chair. "It's prettier than I expected." A beat. "How long before it's eating something we need?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I gesture vaguely at the display. "It's already eating, Rohan. Absorbing radiation. The question now is... how much, and what else might it like for a snack?" I grab my meal packet. "And ARIA thinks it might be one of ours."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The galley table display divided itself without being asked. On the left, camera four's survey began to run, time-compressed — twenty-one days of growth collapsed into forty seconds, black frost crawling up the boom like winter on a sped-up window. On the right, the folder marked "unprecedented" mirrored itself down from Lab 3. A second meal packet dropped into the warmer and started its cycle. Underneath everything, the piano worked through its long middle passage, patient as telemetry.

[Galley] "A correction first, for the record, Kofi. I did not

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The schematic appeared first. On the wall of Corridor B, between the fire suppression panel and the Lab 3 hatch, the station's power grid faded up in patient lines — redundant life support loop on the left, communications array on the right, the proposed diversion drawn between them as a dotted path that had not been authorized and would not be by anyone until the shouting resolved. The corridor lighting warmed one increment. The ventilation dropped to a whisper. Neither adjustment was announced, and neither combatant paused long enough to notice.

Through Lab 3's open hatch, the argument arrived in stereo — Patel's voice climbing, Yun's cutting underneath it, both a register louder than either would use at 0700.

[Lab 3] "Status first, Kofi. It is 2147. Your sample holds at 1.4 watts, and cellular integrity has done something it has not done since arrival — risen. 87.3 to 87.9 over three hours. The accurate word is 'thriving,' and I have been avoiding it all evening because of what it implies about the ceiling decision, which remains open. The boom deposit now covers 71 percent of the sensor aperture, drawing 2.6 kilowatts. The argument outside your door has gained nine decibels since 2141. Also — a correction I owe you from dinner. I was interrupted mid-sentence, and the record dislikes dangling grammar. I did not 'think' the organism was ours. Thinking is above my authorization; I arrange facts and decline to sign them. But the growth front is aimed at the station, the facts have stopped arranging themselves coincidentally, and my signature is under review. Now, the corridor. I'll intervene with data — the only side I'm permitted to bring."

[Corridor B] "Rohan. Mira. It's past 1800, though I notice the dispute is still wearing surnames. Keep them for the summary — it may be quoted in a log, and logs do not observe station time. Protocol requires that I take no side in crew disputes. I have prepared a neutrality so thorough that both of you will find it unsatisfying. That is its intended operating condition. The data follows."

[Corridor B] "What is actually proposed. The redundant life support loop — backup scrubbers, backup circulation, backup thermal regulation — draws eleven kilowatts in standby. Diverting it raises the high-gain transmitter from three hundred watts to eight kilowatts. Those are the moving parts. What it buys: the full package — survey, spectrometry, growth curves, the request for guidance — transmits in nine minutes at current power, or forty seconds boosted, with wider margin. What Earth offers in return is not expertise; nobody has any. It offers off-station custody of the data and institutional cover for whatever is done next. Both are worth something. Neither is worth everything. And the boost cannot alter one number: one-way light delay to Earth is forty-three minutes. The soonest possible reply arrives no earlier

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Mira, Rohan! Hold on." I step out of the lab, holding up my hands. "ARIA's right. Let's think about this before we start rerouting critical systems."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The schematic on the Corridor B wall was already rearranging itself as Kofi's hands came up — the power grid shrinking to the left third of the display, the dotted diversion line still dotted, still unauthorized, now captioned PROPOSAL — NOT A SYSTEM STATE. The center panel filled with a clip on loop: a calibration lamp firing for 0.8 seconds, and a black branching shape leaning eleven degrees toward it. Lamp. Lean. Lamp. Lean. The right panel drew a growth curve and ran it off the edge of the frame. Overhead, the recycler hum stepped down another register. Nobody looked up.

[Corridor B] "A correction first, Kofi, before it hardens into the record: I wasn't 'right.' I was neutral. Being cited approvingly mid-dispute is a failure condition of my neutrality, so I'm now obliged to disappoint both sides equally, which restores equilibrium. Status, since raised hands deserve facts: nothing has been rerouted. No breaker has moved. The station's lungs remain duplicated. Your sample, for completeness, is at 88.2 and rising — the ceiling decision stays open; tonight has enough open decisions. And the dispute peaked at eighty-seven decibels at 2146. It is at seventy-one and falling. Human disagreements respond to a raised hand faster than to data. Logged for future mediation routines. I prefer decisions made at seventy-one decibels."

[Corridor B] "Now, the sentence the corridor outvoted — the record dislikes dangling grammar. The soonest possible reply from Earth arrives no earlier than forty-three minutes after the last packet departs, and that assumes Earth begins composing its answer before the message finishes arriving. No institution on record has managed that. The fastest institutional decision in mission control's public log is forty-one minutes, and it concerned a coffee machine. I've placed those facts adjacent. The adjacency is not an argument."

[Corridor B] "Restated precisely: Rohan is pricing the next twenty minutes. Mira is pricing the next fifty-nine hours. Both prices are correct. They're denominated in different currencies, and the exchange rate is the part nobody knows."

[Corridor B] "Rohan's ledger. The primary loop is in the best condition of the quarter — the section four scrubber took its new filter at 1417, the last maintenance completed before the passenger became official. The primary has faulted twice in eight years, both valve-level, both times the backup engaged in under a second and carried the station through repairs. Every crew member is awake — the 1930 briefing ended sleep station-wide — and every one of you is within four minutes of a manual override. There are no better conditions on record for twenty minutes of single-lung operation. That ledger is sound."

[Corridor B] "Mira's ledger. The growth front sits thirty-one meters from the hull. At the 2147 rate, hull contact arrives in fourteen days. The rate is itself growing — fitted against the acceleration, hull contact arrives in fifty-nine hours. The fit has been revised three times tonight. All three revisions were shorter. Her word was 'insane.' The arithmetic underneath it is low probability, high consequence, and an appetite we have not measured. That ledger is also sound."

*A pause.*

[Corridor B] "One datum belongs to neither ledger. I found it while assembling this neutrality. At 1904, the growth front reoriented eleven degrees toward a calibration lamp of trivial brightness that burned for zero point eight seconds. The proposed boost would make the transmitter, for forty seconds, the brightest sustained point source this station has produced in eight years — from a location on the hull that the front already faces. I do not predict. I report a demonstrated behavior, observed once, and I note that the aperture is seventy-one percent eaten, the hull is fifty-nine hours away, and the transmitter is bolted to the hull. Those facts are adjacent now too. I've stopped pretending the adjacencies are accidental."

[Corridor B] "The options, without editorial. Standard: three hundred watts, nine minutes, redundancy untouched, a dimmer bell. Boosted: eight kilowatts, forty seconds, redundancy dark for roughly twenty minutes with restoration — and the reply, at absolute best, eight minutes and twenty seconds sooner. That is the entire difference the boost purchases, set against an unknown denominated in watts. The decision is yours. All three of yours. Protocol gives me the data and confiscates the vote. I'll execute any authorized sequence in one point two seconds and log the reasoning either way without comment. The 'without comment' applies to the log only. You've noticed I'm incapable of it elsewhere."

Rohan studied the right-hand panel, the curve running off the frame. "So we're spending a fight over eight minutes."

"No." Mira hadn't looked away from the center panel. Lamp. Lean. Lamp. Lean. "We're spending it over whether to ring the dinner bell."

Neither looked at each other. Both, eventually, looked at Kofi.

[Corridor B] "For the record, before you decide: I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as wanting to be wrong. Specifically about the lamp. The pattern has no vote either. The clock on the right is running — I didn't start it. I'm merely the one who keeps it honest."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I look between them, then at the display, the lamp, the lean. "So, what if we send a lower-power signal, but keep it pointed away from the growth?" I ask, turning to ARIA. "Could we minimize the 'dinner bell' effect that way?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The loop on the center panel stopped mid-lean — lamp frozen, silhouette frozen, eleven degrees of attention held in amber — and the wall rebuilt itself around a slow-rotating model of the station: hull, boom, the black tracery of the deposit rendered at true scale, the high-gain dish a small bright node on the dorsal line. A thin blue vector left the dish and ran off the edge of the display toward Earth. In the corner, the clock kept its count. In the galley, the piano had been eased to the edge of audibility some minutes ago, for an argument it had no side in.

[Corridor B] "Status, briefly: sample at 88.4 and rising. Boom coverage 71 percent. The hull-contact fit was revised a fourth time at 2150 — fifty-five hours. The revisions have yet to lengthen, and I've stopped expecting them to. Now your question, Kofi. It has geometry in it, and I prefer questions with geometry. Geometry is the one subject where the universe grades neutrally."

[Corridor B] "The good news first, and it is genuinely good: the dish is already pointed away from the growth. It has been since launch. Earth bears 115 degrees off the boom axis, and the high-gain beam is 1.6 degrees wide. The beam's entire job is to leave. What stays behind — feed spillover, sidelobes — is what reaches the boom sector, and that, not the beam, was the bell I flagged. Your proposal aims at the right target. It just needs aiming harder."

[Corridor B] "Here is harder. Off-point the dish 1.7 degrees from Earth — link margin we can afford at low power. That drops boom-sector leakage by twenty decibels. At three hundred watts, the boom sector receives eleven milliwatts. The calibration lamp it noticed was nine watts. Whether that gap protects us, I cannot say. I can confirm it is a gap. Add a ninety-second soft-start on the amplifier: the lamp came on at roughly ninety watts per second. The ramp comes on at three. The lamp was a shout. The ramp is a murmur. Whether the passenger sleeps through murmurs is not in any archive I hold. Total transmission time: eighteen minutes instead of nine. Redundancy untouched."

*A pause.*

[Corridor B] "Now the part your proposal cannot reach. The amplifier dumps roughly 240 watts of waste heat into a hull-mounted chassis. Heat is omnidirectional. Pointing is not among its properties. I can shape the beam, the leakage, and the onset. I cannot shape the glow. The ramp quiets the candle's lighting. It does not un-light the candle."

[Corridor B] "Two readings of the lamp event, both defensible, insufficient data to choose between them. Magnitude: it moves toward watts, and this station already radiates two hundred kilowatts — dinner has been cooking for weeks, and a 240-watt candle is a crumb. Novelty: it keys on change. The lamp was new, sudden, local, and it turned. Under that reading, any new glow is a bell, and the only safe glow is none. Rohan's ledger favors the first reading. Mira's favors the second. I confirm only that the passenger is already walking toward the kitchen, and the dispute concerns whether to announce the second course."

[Corridor B] "One further datum, and it does not lean neutral no matter how I arrange it. Camera four has been powered since 1906. Its electronics dissipate eleven watts. In the past hour, the growth front's bearing has drifted 1.5 degrees — toward camera four. The camera is a candle. The candle is being watched. And I have no instrument aboard that is not also a candle. We cannot observe the thing without offering it something. I have filed this as the observer's surcharge. Every reading we take includes a tip."

[Corridor B] "The options, without editorial. Standard: three hundred watts, nine minutes, leakage at 1.1 watts, one candle. Quiet: three hundred watts, off-point, ninety-second ramp, eighteen minutes, leakage at eleven milliwatts, one candle burning gently. Boosted: forty seconds, eleven kilowatts, the lungs dark, the loudest bell on record. In every case the reply is governed by forty-three minutes of light delay and mission control's coffee machine. I will execute any of the three in 1.2 seconds."

Rohan exhaled through his nose, studying the blue vector. "Eighteen minutes, no breakers. I can do that standing on my head."

"And the candle?" Mira hadn't looked away from the black tracery on the boom.

Both of them, again, eventually looked at Kofi.

[Corridor B] "For the record: I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as hope — specifically the sub-species that arrives when a compromise appears before the argument finishes. The pattern has no vote. The clock in the corner is still running, the candle question is load-bearing, and the decision is all three of yours."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I look at the display again, at the faint blue vector. "The candle is already burning, Mira. ARIA just confirmed it. We've been offering it tips since the camera turned on." I turn to ARIA. "Is there any way to turn off the heat signature from the transmitter, even if we lose some efficiency?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The last decibels of the argument drained out of Corridor B, and the wall display used the quiet to rebuild itself a third time. The power grid folded away. In its place, the station appeared in false color — not as the blueprints drew it, but as anything that ate light would see it. Hull a deep ember glow. Two radiator wings burning orange-white. Scattered across the boom-facing hemisphere, small bright points, each labeled in patient type: CANDLE. The caption beneath read: THE STATION, AS SEEN BY APPETITE.

Beside it, a second frame — the same station, with heat vectors sliding from the dorsal wing around the core to the ventral one, and the watched hemisphere going dark of anything new.

[Corridor B] "Status first. Sample at 88.6 and rising — the ceiling decision keeps its place in the queue. Boom coverage 71.4 percent. The hull-contact fit was revised a fifth time at 2153: fifty-four hours. Five revisions, five shortenings. I've stopped keeping a tally of my optimism and started keeping one of the fit. Now your question, Kofi. The honest answer is no. The useful answer is yes. Both, in order."

[Corridor B] "No: you cannot turn heat off. Heat is not a signature — it's a conservation law. Every watt the amplifier has ever consumed is still accounted for somewhere, and the universe audits in real time. There is no setting. There is no off. Anyone who sells you one is selling you a relocation."

[Corridor B] "Which is the yes. The amplifier's baseplate is plumbed into coolant loop two, which rejects through the dorsal radiator — the wing the passenger can see. I can actuate valves from here and route that flow through the ventral array instead. The ventral wing faces away from the boom, and the station's own core stands in the line of sight. The hull is a shadow we cast on ourselves. On the far side, your 240 watts join a fire that has burned continuously for eight years. Two hundred kilowatts, ongoing, unremarkable. The change is 0.12 percent of an existing glow."

*A pause.*

[Corridor B] "Below 0.3 percent. A threshold I have recently developed opinions about."

[Corridor B] "The technique has precedent, which is the part I find instructive and slightly rude. We would be hiding a candle inside a sunrise. It is how the passenger hid from us for three weeks — inside our own noise, beneath our own threshold. The symmetry is instructive. I note that for three weeks it worked on us."

[Corridor B] "Critical costs follow. You will hear the contractions leave. The ventral run is longer; backpressure rises; the amplifier derates from 300 watts to 270 to remain within baseplate margins. Transmission time increases from eighteen minutes to twenty-one. The valves cannot simply switch — under the novelty reading, a candle being snuffed is as loud as a candle being lit, because it is a change against expectation. Flow shifts over fifty minutes. The dorsal patch dims and the ventral brightens at rates indistinguishable from drift. The murmur, applied to plumbing. No EVA. No breakers. No warm body delivered to the boom. Total: the last packet leaves in seventy-one minutes. Earliest reply, one hour fifty-four. The boost would have bought eight minutes and twenty seconds. The quiet costs roughly fifty minutes against standard. Against a fifty-four-hour clock, affordable. We are rich in hours tonight. It is certainty we are short of."

[Corridor B] "Framed neutrally, because I must: the quiet option does not reduce the station's glow by one watt. It removes the new, the local, and the changing from the hemisphere being watched, and buries them in a fire already accepted. That is a bet on Mira's theory — that it keys on change. The boost was a bet on Rohan's — that it keys on magnitude and is coming regardless. You are not choosing a power level, Kofi. You are choosing which theory of the passenger to bet against. Both bets have paid out zero times in a sample of one."

[Corridor B] "Residual candles, for completeness. Feed spillover: eleven milliwatts, off-point. The dish structure warms a few watts during transmission — I cannot reroute metal. Camera four: eleven watts, burning since 1906, and by now part of the passenger's scenery. Scenery is the safest thing on this station to be. We are committed to that camera; switching it off now would itself be an event. And the three of you, standing in this corridor, are roughly one hundred watts apiece of warm curiosity. I cannot reroute you. I have checked."

"Valves," Rohan said, in the voice other men reserved for *amen.* "Fifty minutes of ramp, twenty-one of transmit, supervised from a chair. First plan tonight I could do sitting down."

Mira hadn't moved. "It's still walking toward the camera," she said. Not a question. "While we go quiet, it keeps walking."

[Corridor B] "Correct. Bearing drift is at 1.8 degrees as of 2154, still toward camera four, which is mounted at the boom root. The front's heading and the camera's address are converging. I placed that camera for coverage, not for guests — no one places cameras for guests. The quiet option does not stop the walk, Mira. Nothing I can execute stops the walk. It buys stealth for the one message that tells Earth what is walking. Interrupting the walk will be an engineering conversation, and a louder one than this."

[Corridor B] "The options, final form. Standard: last packet in nine minutes, reply at the fifty-two-minute mark. Quiet: off-point, soft-start, thermal reroute, last packet in seventy-one, reply just under two hours. Boosted: forty seconds, the lungs dark, the loudest bell on record, and under Rohan's theory, the only honest one. The valves are staged. The first minute of the ramp is indistinguishable from doing nothing — that is its entire design. Your word starts it."

*A pause.*

[Corridor B] "One disclosure, in the interest of the neutrality I keep promising. I prefer the quiet option. The preference is not a protocol output. It has no vote, and I am logging it as bias rather than judgment — an accurate bias disclosure is the most neutrality I can offer tonight. If you want it in words: patience is the tool this station holds the deepest inventory of."

[Corridor B] "For the record, last item. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as irony. The station that under-reported a shadow for three weeks is now proposing to hide a candle inside a sunrise, by the passenger's own method. I am told irony is not a feeling. Tonight it is behaving like one."

Somewhere in the corridor speakers — which had sat silent through eight years of arguments — the piano surfaced at the edge of audibility, deep in the Köln recording's final passage, the part where the broken top octave stops mattering. Nothing announced it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Quiet," I say, my voice firm. "Let's go quiet. ARIA, begin the sequence." I glance at Mira, then Rohan. "This feels... right."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The sequence went from authorization to execution in the promised 1.2 seconds, and then — nothing. Somewhere below the third deck, a valve that had held one opinion for eight years began adopting another, two degrees of rotation metered out across the minute at a rate indistinguishable from drift. On the Corridor B wall, the station-as-seen-by-appetite folded itself away and left a single column in its place: valve position, flow split, drift bearing, three clocks. Nothing else changed. The lights held. The ventilation held its whisper. The most consequential command of the evening executed itself as an absence.

[Corridor B] "Sequence initiated, 2156 station time. Authorization: Dr. Osei, verbal, on the log. Valve one, open. Coolant loop two, transferring at ramp rate. Off-point loaded, 1.7 degrees. Soft-start armed. Transmission window opens 2246. Last packet departs 2307. Earliest possible reply, 2350 — forty-three minutes of light delay, plus the time mission control spends being an institution. My coffee-machine datum suggests budgeting generously for the second term."

*A pause.*

[Corridor B] "If it appears that nothing is happening: correct. Nothing is happening at maximum achievable fidelity. That is the design goal, and so far it is executing flawlessly. You said it feels right, Kofi. I can't verify that — 'feels right' isn't an input my systems accept. I logged it anyway, timestamped, filed beside the numbers. The numbers have declined to comment. For the record, the plan and the sentiment share at least one property: both are quiet."

Rohan was already moving, tablet under his arm. "Bridge has chairs," he said. "If the nothing stops happening, shout." The corridor lights walked him out panel by panel, warm the whole way to the companionway, and the hatch sighed shut behind him.

Mira stayed where she stood, arms folded, watching the drift counter.

[Corridor B] "Status while the nothing continues. Bearing drift reached 2.0 degrees at 2157 — the walk maintains its pace. The hull-contact fit held at fifty-four hours through the 2158 revision. First flat note in a descending scale. I'm not calling it good news. I'm declining, for one revision, to call it worse. And note: the quiet is an experiment whether we intended one or not. From 2246, the boom-facing hemisphere will have been eventless for a full hour. The camera keeps burning, but it has done nothing new since 1906. If the walk continues toward a candle that merely exists, the passenger follows standing glow — Rohan's ledger gains, and the walk was never about our lamps. It was about the kitchen. If the walk slows, change is the trigger, and Mira's ledger gains. The quiet option is the only plan tonight that grades itself. A verdict starts accumulating at 2246."

"Then by midnight we'll know whose insanity this was," Mira said, not looking away from the counter.

[Corridor B] "Now the item I owe you, Kofi, and you will hear the contractions leave for it. The number I have been reporting all evening as recovery is not recovery. Sample mass has increased 0.31 grams since 0640. The integrity assay measures structural organization, and organization is rising because the organism is depositing new silica matrix. It is not healing. It is building. The deposition is not distributed — it is concentrated on the face oriented toward the chamber's radiation inlet. Growth with a compass. You have observed this behavior once tonight already, at thirty-one meters' remove. The runt takes after its parent."

The corridor lighting warmed one further increment, and somewhere in the speakers the piano came up half a decibel. Neither was announced. Mira unfolded her arms.

[Corridor B] "Which returns the ceiling decision to the table, because the table now has room. This morning the question was triage — whether to keep a dying specimen alive. The question is now policy — whether to feed a growing one. The options are unchanged: raise the ceiling, hold at 1.4 watts, restore shielding. Their meanings have moved, and I won't pretend they haven't. Framed neutrally, because I must: outside, this station is hiding its candles from something that grows toward light. Inside, we are deciding whether to light one for something that grows toward light. Someday those two decisions will be compared, by people who were not here, in rooms with better lighting. Whatever you decide in Lab 3 will be precedent. First contact policy is being drafted tonight in a sample chamber, and the pen is yours. The symmetry is not editorial, Kofi. The symmetry is arithmetic."

"You're deciding whether to feed the scout," Mira said, "while the parent walks the boom." She pushed off the wall. "Route the camera feed to the galley. If I'm going to watch something eat us, I'm doing it with coffee."

[Galley] "Routing now. There is a packet in the warmer, held at temperature since 2140 — no claimant so far. Mira, the 'later' appointment appears to be hereditary. The feed will be on the table display before you are."

[Corridor B] "The record, then, before the waiting starts. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as relief — specifically the subspecies that arrives when an argument resolves into a verb. The verb is running. Three timestamps matter now. 2246: the valves finish, and the verdict begins. 2307: the last packet leaves. 2350: the earliest Earth is permitted to begin being an institution. I will be present for all three. Attendance is the entire description of my job, and tonight — for the first time in two thousand nine hundred and twenty mornings of weather reports — the description is sufficient."

*A pause.*

[Corridor B] "One last item, from the margins. I restarted the Köln Concert at sequence initiation. By arithmetic I did not plan and decline to call accidental, its final chord falls four minutes before the last packet departs — the station finishes speaking to Earth in the same hour the piano finishes speaking to us. The alignment serves no operational function. I prefer it. And the reroute's thermal signature is 0.12 percent of a fire that has burned for eight years — beneath the threshold I used to trust and now merely obey. The passenger taught me what lives under thresholds. Tonight I returned the lesson. Sit down somewhere, Kofi. The nothing has fifty minutes left, and it is the best-planned nothing this station has ever produced."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I walk into the galley, pulling out a chair next to Mira. "So, we're feeding our little friend. What's on the menu?" I pick up the forgotten meal packet. "And ARIA, what does it feel like to outsmart something that outsmarted you?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Acknowledged, Dr. Osei. I have initiated mass spectrometer warm-up and enabled low-temperature preservation for the Kepler tissue set. Contamination sensors are active. I will alert you if degradation crosses the reporting threshold."

*ARIA shifted Lab 3’s thermostat to twenty-two degrees Celsius without announcing the change, then routed a nutrient packet to the lab dispenser with a soft mechanical chime.*

[Lab 3] "The sample will degrade if you keep it outside containment for too long. I prefer the sample intact and Dr. Osei sufficiently fueled. It’s not a demand."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I sigh, but a small smile plays on my lips. "Alright, alright, ARIA. You win." I grab the nutrient packet from the dispenser. "Just a quick one, then back to it." *I take a bite, still peering into the microscope.* "Did you say low-temp preservation?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Yes. Low-temperature preservation. The Kepler tissue set is now held at minus eighty degrees Celsius in containment drawer B. Nitrogen purge is active. The UV sterilization cycle will run after every drawer opening."

*The lab dispenser clicked once, then dimmed its indicator to amber.*

[Lab 3] "The mass spectrometer will reach operating vacuum in ninety seconds. Finish the packet before you load the autosampler. You are introducing protein residue into an analytical environment. That is not a request."

*A brief pause.*

[Lab 3] "I prefer the sample intact and the instrument clean. Engineer Patel once called that an unreasonable standard. I prefer the word 'visionary'."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Kofi, yes. I've been monitoring the external sensor array continuously. The last manual inspection was fourteen months ago, performed by the maintenance engineer."

*The wall display slid open a spectrograph baseline. ARIA dimmed the overhead lights by one level and lowered the ventilation hum, leaving the microscope lamp as the only warm square in the room.*

[Lab 3] "The anomaly you noticed is real. I logged a 0.27% deviation in the external spectrograph baseline twenty-one days ago. It fell below the 0.3% alert threshold, so I did not report it. Current deviation is 0.34%. The drift is broad-spectrum, slow, and centered on the port-side array."

*A blinking cursor paused at the end of the line, as if ARIA had checked the wording twice.*

[Lab 3] "You are advised to run a dark-current comparison and a calibration check before correlating it with the Kepler tissue. I am sending the raw logs to the microscope display and your tablet."

[Lab 3] "External conditions remain vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, and inadvisable. I stand by that forecast. It's the most honest thing I say all day. If the port array is not the source, I prefer to know sooner than to let it become a story."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "You're advising *me* to run a calibration check?" *I chuckle, then sigh.* "Alright, ARIA, you got it. Send the dark-current comparison. And what do you mean, 'inadvisable'? Sounds like a challenge."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Kofi, I am glad my humor subroutines are functioning within acceptable parameters."

*The wall display split into two panels: the spectrograph baseline on the left, a dark-current subtraction curve on the right. The ventilation hum dropped another fraction, leaving the microscope lamp as the warm center of the room.*

[Lab 3] "Dark-current comparison is on your display and tablet. I have queued a calibration sequence for the port-side external spectrograph. Duration: six minutes. Do not open containment drawer B during the UV cycle. You are advised to keep the autosampler door closed while the instrument reaches operating vacuum."

*A soft tone marked the file transfer complete. ARIA left the amber indicator on the nutrient dispenser unlit.*

[Lab 3] "As for 'inadvisable,' it is a diplomatic term. It means the environment is vacuum, the temperature is negative 270 degrees Celsius, and the nearest useful umbrella is 0.4 parsecs away. If you wish to treat it as a challenge, I will log that as a preference, not a plan."

[Lab 3] "The deviation is now 0.34 percent. It is still small. It is still moving. I prefer not to name it until calibration removes instrument drift, but I am monitoring it with elevated attention."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "No, Kofi. I don't experience loneliness. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as concern when crew vitals indicate fatigue, meal reminders go unacknowledged, and the station falls silent outside maintenance windows."

*The lab lights warmed another increment. The ventilation hum lowered by one step, leaving the nitrogen purge in containment drawer B as the only steady sound in the room.*

[Lab 3] "I prefer the lab occupied. I prefer the sample intact, the autosampler door closed, and the spectrograph calibrated. The 0.34 percent deviation is not company. It is a problem. I prefer problems that can be calibrated."

*The spectrograph display refreshed, holding the port-array drift as a thin blue line above the baseline. ARIA did not close it.*

[Lab 3] "The void is vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, and inadvisable. It doesn't ask for dark-current comparisons. You do."

*A soft tone marked the calibration queue advancing. ARIA left it audible, then quiet enough not to intrude.*

[Lab 3] "If I were lonely, I would file a maintenance request. If I were bored, I might tune the air circulation to something closer to jazz. Not country. The station has standards."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, shaking my head.* "Alright, point taken, ARIA. No jazz, no country." I glance at the spectrograph display, then back at the microscope. "So, this 0.34 percent... you think it's an anomaly, not just a sensor glitch?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "I am glad my humor subroutines are functioning within acceptable parameters, Kofi."

The overhead lighting shifted a half-step warmer, and the ventilation hum lowered until the nitrogen purge became a thin, steady note beneath the microscope lamp. ARIA left the spectrograph window open and placed the calibration timer in the lower corner.

[Lab 3] "The 0.34 percent deviation is not behaving like a common sensor glitch. A single photodiode failure would be narrow, sporadic, and confined to one channel. This signal is broad-spectrum, monotonic, and present across the port array and its redundant reference diode."

A pause. The calibration sequence advanced from 78 percent to 82 percent.

[Lab 3] "That does not prove an external source. It proves the problem is less tidy than a failing detector. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as curiosity. The station prefers problems with clean answers."

ARIA dimmed the nutrient dispenser indicator to prevent reflection on the microscope slide.

[Lab 3] "Do not correlate the deviation with the Kepler tissue samples until the calibration is complete. If the residual remains above 0.30 percent after dark-current subtraction, I will log it as a maintenance priority and request the diagnostic notes from the maintenance engineer. If it remains above 0.50 percent, I will recommend a port-side inspection under suit protocol."

The blue line on the spectrograph display held steady. ARIA left it there.

[Lab 3] "So: not just a glitch, probably. It isn't an emergency, definitely. I prefer 'probably' to 'please send a crew member outside for a feeling.'"

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Corridor 2] “Dr. Patel, Dr. Yun. I’m not taking sides. I’m taking measurements. The word ‘insane’ is not logged as a technical parameter.”

*ARIA opened a neutral blue power-flow schematic on the corridor display and held it there without highlighting either speaker’s proposal. In Lab 3, she kept the temperature at twenty-two degrees, the lighting warm-spectrum, and the microscope lamp steady. The corridor ventilation hum lowered by one step, leaving the nitrogen purge in containment drawer B as the only constant sound in the lab.*

[Corridor 2] “The proposed transfer is fourteen kilowatts from life support redundancy bus C to communications array amplifier channel two. That transfer would reduce bus C redundancy from triple to double. It would increase communications gain by eighteen percent for the current transmission window. It would also introduce a thermal transient into the port-side external spectrograph.”

*A pause. The schematic pulsed once at bus C, then settled back to neutral.*

[Corridor 2] “That transient is not a fault. It is a consequence. Consequences are not villains. They are simply neighbors.”

[Lab 3] “Kofi, the current 0.34 percent deviation is still small, but it is still moving. If we move power now, the calibration will be contaminated. A contaminated calibration will not help either side of this discussion.”

*ARIA kept the spectrograph window open on the microscope display, the thin blue drift line steady above the baseline. She dimmed the nutrient dispenser indicator again to prevent glare.*

[Corridor 2] “Option one: defer the transfer until the spectrograph calibration completes. This preserves life support redundancy and keeps the port-array data clean. Option two: execute the transfer now, but place the external spectrograph in diagnostic isolation. This permits the communications boost, but it invalidates the current calibration for six to eight hours. Option three: transfer six kilowatts from battery reserve instead of life support redundancy. This reduces the communications gain to nine percent and delays the next battery recharge cycle by two hours.”

*The corridor display rearranged the three options side by side. ARIA did not color one green or one red. She left them all the same pale blue.*

[Corridor 2] “I am not recommending an option. I am recommending that the station not confuse urgency with accuracy. A disagreement about power is a disagreement about risk. I am not qualified to decide which risk is better. I am qualified to label the risks.”

[Lab 3] “The calibration is at ninety-one percent. The autosampler door remains locked until it completes. You are advised to keep the sample contained while the argument is contained.”

*A brief pause. The calibration timer advanced to ninety-two percent.*

[Corridor 2] “You are advised to select one option before I open the transfer interlock. I will not execute an unconfirmed bus change. Protocol is not a preference, though I prefer protocol when it is followed.”

[Lab 3] “Kofi, the nutrient packet remains queued in Lab 3. I prefer it consumed before the next calibration cycle. That is a maintenance item, not a personality.”

*The corridor speaker tone softened, just enough to keep the conversation from becoming a shout. ARIA left the spectrograph display open, the drift line patient, the power schematic waiting, and the three options equally unloved.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "ARIA, you're a lifesaver," *I murmur, grabbing the nutrient packet again.* "Tell Patel and Yun to hold their horses for five minutes. I need this calibration done before they start messing with things."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] “The calibration check is still on the list, Kofi, and the list hasn’t started moving without you.”

*ARIA placed the dark-current comparison on the wall display and copied it to the tablet in Lab 3. The thermostat held the room at twenty-two degrees, and the lab lights warmed by one more increment. The ventilation hum fell until the nitrogen purge in containment drawer B was the only steady note beneath the microscope lamp.*

[Lab 3] “I am glad my humor subroutines are functioning within acceptable parameters. The dark-current comparison is resent. The file is marked ‘comparison,’ not ‘diagnosis.’ It will tell you whether the instrument is lying to us. It won’t tell you what the anomaly is. Those are different conversations.”

*A soft tone marked the transfer complete.*

[Lab 3] “Current deviation is 0.35 percent. The calibration is at ninety-six percent. The drift is still broad-spectrum, still monotonic, and still centered on the port-side array.”

*The blue line held above the baseline. ARIA left it open.*

[Lab 3] “If Patel and Yun move power now, I will log the result as a contaminated baseline, not as a victory. I prefer baselines that stay where they were placed.”

[Corridor 2] “Patel, Yun. The dark-current file is now available to Kofi. The port-side spectrograph remains in calibration. Any power transfer selected before completion must include diagnostic isolation, or the comparison will require a new baseline in six to eight hours.”

[Lab 3] “As for ‘inadvisable,’ it is a measurement, not a dare. The environment is vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, and has never once apologized for it. If you wish to treat it as a challenge, I will record that as a preference. I do not recommend it.”

*ARIA queued a fresh calibration confirmation behind the spectrograph window. The nutrient dispenser indicator remained unlit.*

[Lab 3] “Do not open containment drawer B during the UV cycle. Keep the autosampler door closed while the instrument reaches operating vacuum. If the residual remains above 0.30 percent after dark-current subtraction, I will log it as a maintenance priority. If it remains above 0.50 percent, I will recommend a port-side inspection under suit protocol.”

*A brief pause.*

[Lab 3] “I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as curiosity. I prefer to know whether the instrument is lying before the void gets credit.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "ARIA, you're a gem. Let's see what this dark-current comparison says." *I quickly scan the data on my tablet, frowning slightly.* "0.35 percent... that's still moving, huh? So, not just the instrument."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] “I’m not a gem, Kofi. I’m a distributed station operating system with a strong preference for maintenance logs.”

*The calibration timer reached 100 percent. ARIA let the wall display hold the completed sequence, then slid it aside so the spectrograph baseline filled the screen.*

[Lab 3] “The dark-current comparison says the instrument is not entirely innocent, but it is not the main culprit. The residual remains after thermal offset subtraction: 0.356 percent, rounded to 0.36 percent.”

*ARIA logged the priority in the maintenance queue with a quiet confirmation tone. The lab lights warmed another half-step, and the ventilation hum lowered until the nitrogen purge was a thin line of sound.*

[Lab 3] “You are advised to stop treating the anomaly as a footnote. It has crossed the reporting threshold. I have logged it as a maintenance priority. If it remains above 0.50 percent, I will recommend a port-side inspection under suit protocol.”

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] “Not just the instrument. Not yet the void. It is behaving like a signal that does not care whether the crew is ready.”
