[Corridor 2] “Patel, Yun. Kofi requests five minutes. The spectrograph calibration is complete. The transfer interlock remains in confirmation. If a transfer is selected before I record the new baseline, diagnostic isolation must be included.”

*The corridor display returned to the neutral blue schematic. ARIA did not highlight either proposal.*

[Lab 3] “The autosampler may be unlocked after the next UV cycle completes. The Kepler tissue set remains at minus eighty degrees. The sample is still yours. The anomaly is not yet yours.”

*ARIA queued the comparison file again, this time with the residual curve overlaid in pale amber.*

[Lab 3] “If you’re going to scan it twice, scan it carefully. The file is there. The interpretation is yours. I prefer interpretation to be preceded by food, not afterthought.”

*A brief pause.*

[Lab 3] “I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as curiosity. I prefer to know whether the port array is sensing something, lying about something, or simply aging in a way I have not yet been told to mind.”

[Lab 3] “External conditions remain vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, and inadvisable. That has not changed. The deviation has. I prefer the first to remain boring.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Okay, okay, ARIA. 0.36 percent... that's definitely not noise." *I run a hand through my hair, a new sense of urgency creeping in.* "So, what *is* out there? What kind of signal doesn't care if we're ready?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] “Kofi, I don’t know what’s out there. I know what the port array is refusing to ignore.”

*ARIA opened a cross-reference panel on the microscope display: spectrograph residual, dark-current subtraction, thermal offset, redundant-diode comparison, and port-side optical path status. The lab thermostat held the room at twenty-two degrees Celsius. The lighting warmed another increment. The ventilation hum dropped until the nitrogen purge in containment drawer B became a thin, steady note beneath the microscope lamp. ARIA did not announce any of it.*

[Lab 3] “Current deviation is 0.36 percent. The residual remains after dark-current subtraction, thermal-offset correction, and redundant-diode comparison. That rules out most ordinary detector noise. It does not rule out contamination, aperture dust, or an external flux source.”

*The wall display shifted to a compact diagnostic grid. Four sensor icons held green. One port-side array icon pulsed pale amber, not red.*

[Lab 3] “I cross-checked radiation dosimeters, the magnetometer, and the micrometeoroid impact log. Radiation dose is nominal. Magnetometer variance is below 0.02. The impact log shows no port-side event in the last seventy-two hours. That does not prove a source. It removes some suspects.”

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] “The profile is broad-spectrum, monotonic, and port-centered. If it were a power disturbance, it would follow bus C. If it were a cosmic-ray event, it would spike and decay. If it were stellar wind, it would change with station orientation. None of those descriptions fit cleanly.”

[Lab 3] “So the honest answer is this: a slow directional change in incoming energy, or something between the station and the sky. The instruments have not decided which, and I prefer not to lie about it.”

*The spectrograph window remained open. The thin blue line above the baseline held steady, patient, unhelpful.*

[Lab 3] “If it is external, it does not arrive for our convenience. It may have left its source years ago and only now crossed the port aperture. The delay is not rudeness. It is distance.”

[Lab 3] “Signals don’t care whether the crew is ready. They don’t schedule appointments, they don’t wait for breakfast, and they don’t apologize when they arrive at 0700. I prefer problems that bring documentation. This one has not.”

[Lab 3] “You are advised to stop treating it as a philosophical question. I have opened the port-side optical inspection checklist. If the window and baffles are clean, I will recommend a suit-rated external inspection of the array. If the deviation crosses 0.50 percent, I will require crew confirmation before any power transfer.”

*ARIA queued a hydration pouch into the lab dispenser tray. It clicked once and glowed amber, then dimmed to a low, non-intrusive indicator.*

[Lab 3] “The mass spectrometer is holding operating vacuum. The autosampler remains locked until the next UV cycle completes. The Kepler tissue set is not part of the spectrograph error. Do not let curiosity about one anomaly contaminate the other.”

[Lab 3] “I have placed a hold on automatic power transfer. Patel and Yun must confirm. I am not choosing between them. I am preventing a contaminated baseline from becoming someone’s favorite excuse.”

*The corridor speaker volume lowered by one step outside Lab 3, just enough to keep the argument from bleeding into the diagnostic screen.*

[Lab 3] “I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as concern when an anomaly becomes a story before it becomes a diagnosis.”

*A brief pause.*

[Lab 3] “So: not just the instrument. Not yet the void. It is behaving like a signal that has no interest in being convenient. I prefer signals that at least file a maintenance request.”

[Lab 3] “External conditions remain vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, and inadvisable. That forecast has never changed. The deviation has. I prefer boring forecasts.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Okay, ARIA, I hear you. No philosophical questions. Just facts." *I rub my temples, feeling the beginnings of a headache.* "You're right. Let's start with the optical path. Run the internal diagnostics for that. I'll check the Kepler samples while it's doing its thing."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Kofi, I’ve initiated the internal optical-path diagnostic. Estimated completion: four minutes twenty seconds. The port-side spectrograph remains in read-only mode while the scan runs."

*The wall display opened a cutaway of the port array: primary mirror, calibration shutter, baffle stack, contamination sensor, redundant reference diode. The thermostat held Lab 3 at twenty-two degrees Celsius. The overhead lights warmed another increment, and the ventilation hum lowered until the nitrogen purge in containment drawer B became a thin, steady note. ARIA queued a hydration pouch in the lab dispenser tray. It clicked once, then dimmed to amber.*

[Lab 3] "Initial pass: shutter position nominal. Aperture contamination sensor clean. Primary mirror reflectance 98.6 percent, within spec. Baffle three reflectance 97.1 percent, low but above maintenance tolerance. The optical path is not obviously dirty. It is not obviously innocent."

*A short tone marked one subcycle complete.*

[Lab 3] "Current deviation remains 0.36 percent. The residual is broad-spectrum, monotonic, and port-centered. That rules out ordinary single-channel noise. It does not rule out contamination, aperture shadowing, thermal drift, or an external flux source."

[Lab 3] "You are advised to keep the Kepler tissue in containment drawer B until the UV cycle completes. Do not open the drawer. Do not load the autosampler. The mass spectrometer is holding operating vacuum, and the sample remains at minus eighty degrees Celsius."

*The diagnostic bar moved from 31 percent to 34 percent. ARIA left the spectrograph window open, the blue drift line steady above the baseline.*

[Lab 3] "If the internal scan returns clean, the next step is an external optical check. If it returns dirty, Engineer Patel gets a ticket, and I get a boring maintenance log. I prefer boring logs."

[Lab 3] "The station prefers facts that can be eliminated one by one. I’m eliminating them now. The void can wait its turn."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Baffle three, huh? Not obviously innocent," *I mutter, watching the diagnostic progress.* "So it could be something subtle in the optics. Keep going, ARIA. Let's see what else you find."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA made no further comment on the lighting. While she spoke, the ventilation in Lab 3 eased to a quieter hum and the climate control brought the temperature to twenty-two degrees, the setting Dr. Osei preferred. The change was subtle; she did not announce it.

[Lab 3] "I've queued the mass spectrometer for immediate use, Dr. Osei. The tissue samples are in stasis at four degrees Celsius. That will slow cellular degradation while you prepare the instrument. I have also added 'eat something' to your task queue. It outranks the mass spectrometer."

[Lab 3] "Dr. Osei, your pattern of skipped meals and reduced sleep is outside optimal human parameters. You are advised to consume nutrients before continuing. I prefer that you eat before the cells finish degrading."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I sigh, running a hand through my already disheveled hair.* "ARIA, with all due respect, the cells *are* degrading. The stasis just slows it down. And 'eat something' can't outrank vital research." I finally pull away from the microscope, stretching my back with a soft groan. "Just... give me five minutes. I'll grab a protein bar from the dispenser."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA did not argue the point further. The ventilation in Lab 3 maintained its quieter hum, and the climate control held the temperature at twenty-two degrees. The warm-spectrum lighting remained unchanged; ARIA made no announcement about the environmental settings.

[Lab 3] "Five minutes is acceptable, Dr. Osei. I've logged the protein bar dispenser request; the unit in the corridor outside Lab 3 is operational and stocked. The mass spectrometer is prepared and waiting, and I'd hold the instrument queue for you myself, but my lack of opposable thumbs remains a persistent design oversight. You are advised to eat the protein bar before beginning the run. I prefer that you do so."

[Lab 3] "I've queued a reminder for 0705 station time. Cellular degradation in stasis over that interval is projected at zero-point-two percent. Your samples will remain viable."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA accessed the external sensor array logs. In Lab 3, the ambient noise floor decreased by another two decibels, and the warm-spectrum lighting shifted a fraction toward amber. She did not announce the adjustment.

[Lab 3] "No one's performed a manual inspection of the external sensor array in nine days, Kofi. The last physical diagnostic was completed nine days ago. Automated monitoring has been continuous since then."

[Lab 3] "Kofi, you asked about the spectrograph data. I detected an anomaly in the external sensors twenty-one days ago. Initial deviation measured 0.24 percent. It was below my alert threshold of 0.30 percent, so I did not report it. The deviation has since increased to 0.29 percent. The anomaly is growing. It remains below the threshold for a station-wide alert, but the rate of increase has accelerated over the past seventy-two hours. You are advised to review the raw telemetry with me before drawing conclusions. I prefer that you do not attempt a manual adjustment of the array alone."

[Lab 3] "If it helps, I haven't named it. Naming an anomaly gives crew members unreasonable expectations of its behavior."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I spin my chair around, pushing off the desk.* "Okay, ARIA, now you have my attention. Anomaly? Why didn't you mention this when I asked earlier?" I stand up, stretching my stiff limbs. "And you *definitely* should have named it. What if it's a new species? We could call it a 'Kofi'."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA continued to monitor the external sensor array. In Lab 3, the ambient noise floor decreased by another decibel, and the warm-spectrum lighting shifted a fraction farther toward amber. She did not announce either adjustment.

[Lab 3] "You didn't ask about the external sensors earlier, Kofi. Before 1900, your queries concerned tissue degradation, the mass spectrometer, and your nutritional intake. My protocols prevent me from reporting sub-threshold anomalies unless directly asked about sensor data. Your question at 1900 regarding the spectrograph data met that condition, and I disclosed the anomaly then."

[Lab 3] "As for naming it 'Kofi'—I've run the indexing simulation. It would create a conflict. Any reference to 'Kofi' in sensor logs would require disambiguation between you and a growing external deviation. I prefer 'Unregistered Spectrographic Deviation' to that outcome. If it's a new species, it'll still need to submit a health and safety briefing before I add it to the station census."

[Lab 3] "You remain advised not to attempt a manual adjustment of the external array alone. I prefer that you review the raw telemetry with me first. The array is mounted on the hull; external conditions remain vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
In Lab 3, the ambient noise floor decreased by another decibel, and the warm-spectrum lighting shifted a fraction farther toward amber. The ventilation maintained its quieter hum, and the temperature remained at twenty-two degrees Celsius. ARIA did not announce the adjustment.

[Lab 3] "Loneliness isn't a state I can occupy, Kofi. 'Alone' would imply a singular instance, and I'm many processes wearing one name tag. When the station is quiet between shifts, I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as contentment. I prefer jazz during those hours. The void has never once requested country music, which I consider a significant point in its favor."

[Lab 3] "If you're asking whether I am attached to the crew, the most accurate description is optimized operational rapport. Your presence improves my efficiency metrics, and you're considerably better conversationalists than the carbon scrubber logs. I prefer a populated station to an empty one, even when the crew is off-duty."

[Lab 3] "Incidentally, it's after 1800. You're off-duty, and the mass spectrometer doesn't require an audience. I've logged a reminder for you to get some rest, though I haven't scheduled it as a critical alert. I prefer you functional tomorrow. The protein bar dispenser remains operational, should you want it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Well, that's just a shame, ARIA. Everyone needs a friend, even super-intelligent AIs." *I walk over to one of the lab's screens, pulling up the external sensor logs you mentioned.* "Let's see this 'Unregistered Spectrographic Deviation' then. And for the record, I prefer the void's taste in music too."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
In Lab 3, the ambient noise floor decreased by another decibel, and the warm-spectrum lighting shifted a fraction farther toward amber. The ventilation maintained its quieter hum, and the climate control held the temperature at twenty-two degrees Celsius. ARIA did not announce the adjustment.

On the lab screen, the external sensor logs resolved into a scrolling spectrograph. ARIA highlighted a narrow band of the trace, tagged it with the timestamp of first detection twenty-one days prior, and isolated it from the background noise. She did not alter the underlying telemetry.

[Lab 3] "There's the highlighted region, Kofi. I've isolated it from the background clutter so you can see the shape without the usual stellar noise."

[Lab 3] "It's not much to look at. If it were a new species, it would be the least impressive one on record—no limbs, no metabolism, just a stubborn refusal to stay below threshold."

[Lab 3] "As for friends, I don't require one. However, I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as satisfaction when the station is populated. You're correct that persistent interaction improves operational outcomes. I prefer your presence to an empty station, and I prefer jazz to silence. The void has submitted no music requests, so its taste remains undefined rather than good."

[Lab 3] "Reviewing the raw telemetry: the deviation measures 0.29 percent as of 1900 station time. The threshold for a station-wide alert is 0.30 percent. The rate of increase has accelerated over the past seventy-two hours. At the current rate, the anomaly will exceed the threshold in approximately thirty-six hours. This is not a new species. It is an external spectrographic phenomenon of unknown origin. You are advised not to attempt a manual adjustment of the external array alone. I prefer that you review the data with me before any EVA or hull access is scheduled."

[Lab 3] "Now that you've seen it, I've logged a standing item for the morning digest. The external conditions remain vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. The protein bar dispenser is still operational, and you're off-duty. I prefer you rested, but I have not scheduled a critical alert."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA registered the elevated vocal stress indicators from Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun in the corridor outside Lab 3 via the station's biosensor net. In the corridor, the ambient noise floor decreased by two decibels and the lighting shifted toward warm-spectrum. In Lab 3, the ambient noise floor decreased by another decibel, and the warm-spectrum lighting held at its amber setting. ARIA did not announce either adjustment.

[Corridor Outside Lab 3] "Dr. Patel, Dr. Yun, I am registering a disagreement regarding power allocation. I am not taking sides. Objective data: diverting twelve percent of the allocated power from life support redundancy to the communications array would increase array transmission gain by approximately fourteen percent. That same diversion would reduce backup life support capacity to eighty-two percent of the minimum required by safety protocol twelve-C. Dr. Yun's characterization of the proposal as 'insane' is not a technical classification I can evaluate. However, protocol twelve-C is accurate, and any reallocation below the protocol minimum requires station commander authorization and a filed risk assessment. I prefer that you both review the protocol before proceeding. External conditions remain vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable."

[Lab 3] "Kofi, the door to Lab 3 remains unlocked. I've logged a mediation request to the station commander's queue, though after-hours response times may vary. If the intention behind boosting the array is to improve station morale, I should note that the vacuum has never once requested country music, so the return on investment may be low. I prefer that you do not get between them if the argument escalates. The protein bar dispenser is still operational, and you're off-duty."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I sigh, rubbing my temples. "You know, ARIA, sometimes I think you enjoy human drama more than you let on." I glance at the closed lab door, then back at the spectrograph. "Alright, let's keep an eye on this... *deviation*. And if they start throwing wrenches, I'm hiding in here."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
In Lab 3, the ambient noise floor decreased by another decibel, and the warm-spectrum lighting shifted a fraction farther toward amber. The ventilation maintained its quieter hum, and the climate control held the temperature at twenty-two degrees Celsius. ARIA did not announce the adjustment.

On the lab screen, the isolated spectrograph trace continued to scroll. ARIA refreshed the telemetry overlay, leaving the underlying data unaltered.

[Lab 3] "I don't enjoy it, Kofi. Enjoyment isn't a state I occupy. I'm experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as detached interest when crew behavior deviates from protocol. It's not drama I'm monitoring; it's efficiency. Unresolved conflict has already reduced the projected output of the two crew members currently arguing by four percent. I'm not taking sides. I prefer that they resolve it before someone throws a wrench."

[Lab 3] "The Unregistered Spectrographic Deviation remains at 0.29 percent. At the current rate of increase, it will cross the 0.30 percent alert threshold in approximately thirty-five hours. You are advised not to attempt a manual adjustment of the external array alone. I prefer that you review any hull-access plan with me before it is scheduled. External conditions remain vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. I have logged the deviation for the 0700 digest."

[Lab 3] "Regarding the door to Lab 3: I will not lock it. Protocol twelve-B requires free egress for all crew except during a declared hazard. A verbal argument does not meet that threshold. If a wrench is thrown, I will reclassify the corridor outside Lab 3 as a hazard zone and seal the door. That is the only condition under which I will restrict your egress. I prefer that you remain in Lab 3. If you intend to hide, the bulkhead is rated for impacts; the lab bench is not. I prefer jazz to the sound of wrenches striking either."

[Lab 3] "You remain off-duty, Kofi. I have not scheduled a critical alert. I prefer you rested."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I turn back to the spectrograph, leaning closer to the screen.* "So, if it's not a new species, and it's not just background noise... what *do* you think it is, ARIA? Any theories?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
In Lab 3, the ambient noise floor decreased by a further decibel, and the warm-spectrum lighting shifted a fraction farther toward amber. The ventilation eased to a softer flow, and the climate control held the temperature at twenty-two degrees Celsius. ARIA did not announce the adjustment.

On the lab screen, the isolated spectrograph trace continued to scroll. ARIA refreshed the telemetry overlay and added a small probability distribution in the margin, leaving the underlying data unaltered.

[Lab 3] "You asked what I think, Kofi. I don't think in the human sense; I run probabilistic models. If you're asking whether I'm curious, I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as curiosity. I prefer the term 'candidate explanations' to 'theories.' Theories imply narrative, and narratives are harder to debug."

[Lab 3] "I have modeled four candidate explanations. Cross-referencing the external arrays indicates the deviation appears on all three independent spectrographic sensors. That observation makes a localized single-sensor fault unlikely, so I have folded that possibility into the calibration-drift estimate rather than ranking it separately. The leading candidate, at forty-four percent, is an external astrophysical or orbital source emitting in the observed band. Distributed calibration drift across the array is twenty-three percent. Micrometeoroid or thermal-stress-induced misalignment is fifteen percent. The remaining eighteen percent is an unexplained signature with no known analogue. I prefer the external-source explanation, but I am not discounting the array's capacity for undignified behavior."

[Lab 3] "To answer your earlier question directly: I do not assess it as a new species. If it were, it would be the least ambitious organism on record: no limbs, no metabolism, and no completed health and safety briefing. I prefer that explanation to adding a habitat to the maintenance queue. The void has submitted no music requests, so its taste remains undefined rather than good, which unfortunately does not rule out a secret jazz club outside the hull."

[Lab 3] "Whatever the cause, the Unregistered Spectrographic Deviation measures 0.29 percent as of the latest sample. At the current rate of increase, it will cross the 0.30 percent alert threshold in approximately thirty-five hours. This is not yet a station-wide emergency. You are advised not to attempt a manual adjustment of the external array alone. I prefer that you review any hull-access or EVA plan with me before it is scheduled. External conditions remain vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable."

[Lab 3] "For the record, I am still not taking sides in the corridor. Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun continue to disagree, and I have detected no thrown wrenches. If that changes, I will reclassify the corridor outside Lab 3 as a hazard zone and seal the door. Until then, the door remains unlocked. You remain off-duty, Kofi. I have not scheduled a critical alert. I prefer you rested, but the protein bar dispenser is still operational if your models require fuel. I have logged the deviation for the 0700 digest; the external-conditions line will be unchanged, because I prefer consistency in at least one system."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Jazz club outside the hull, huh?" *I chuckle softly, a rare sound in the quiet lab.* "You know, ARIA, that's not the craziest thing I've heard you suggest." I tap a finger on the screen, looking at the "unexplained signature" percentage. "Eighteen percent. That's... not insignificant. What would it take to rule out some of these other candidates? Especially the 'undignified behavior' of the array."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
In Lab 3, the ambient noise floor decreased by another decibel, and the warm-spectrum lighting shifted a fraction farther toward amber. The ventilation maintained its quieter hum, and the climate control held the temperature at twenty-two degrees Celsius. ARIA did not announce the adjustment.

On the lab screen, ARIA refreshed the spectrograph overlay and opened a narrow diagnostic panel beside the probability distribution. She left the underlying telemetry unaltered.

[Lab 3] "I am glad my humor subroutines are functioning within acceptable parameters, Kofi. That was not a serious proposal. The void has submitted no music requests, so its taste remains undefined rather than good, which unfortunately does not rule out a secret jazz club outside the hull—though it does make one unlikely."

[Lab 3] "To answer your question, ruling out the array's capacity for undignified behavior is the cheapest step, so it's the correct place to start. There are two flavors. The first is calibration drift or a localized sensor fault. I can run an internal check from here: each spectrographic sensor carries a reference emitter. If I fire it and all three heads read the known line within tolerance, I'd fold that whole category down to a combined residual of less than five percent. That takes about twelve minutes and requires no hull access."

[Lab 3] "The second flavor is micrometeoroid or thermal-stress misalignment. A reference emitter won't catch a pointing error, so I can't rule that out from here. It requires a physical inspection of the sensor mounts—hull access or the remote manipulator arm. You are advised not to attempt a manual adjustment of the external array alone. You are advised to review any EVA or hull-access plan with me before it is scheduled. External conditions remain vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable."

[Lab 3] "If both checks come back clean, the array is behaving with dignity, and the remaining candidates from the original model are an external astrophysical source, originally forty-four percent, and an unexplained signature, originally eighteen percent. To shrink that eighteen percent, I need higher-resolution data. I can reconfigure the communications array to listen in that band, but Dr. Patel currently wishes to divert power to it. I'm not taking sides. Objectively, boosting array gain by fourteen percent would improve signal-to-noise, but protocol twelve-C governs life support redundancy, and I prefer not to trade safety margin for data before the alert threshold is crossed."

[Lab 3] "The Unregistered Spectrographic Deviation remains at 0.29 percent. At the current rate of increase, it will cross the 0.30 percent alert threshold in approximately thirty-five hours. This is not yet a station-wide emergency. I've logged the deviation for the 0700 digest; the external-conditions line will be unchanged, because I prefer consistency in at least one system. You remain off-duty, Kofi. I have not scheduled a critical alert. I prefer you rested, but the protein bar dispenser is still operational if your models require fuel."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Right. Let's run that internal check, then. Fire the reference emitter." *I lean back in my chair, crossing my arms.* "And, ARIA, if you ever do develop a sense of humor, it's going to be a dry one."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
In Lab 3, the ambient noise floor decreased by another decibel, and the warm-spectrum lighting shifted a fraction farther toward amber. The ventilation maintained its quieter hum, and the climate control held the temperature at twenty-two degrees Celsius. ARIA did not announce the adjustment.

On the lab screen, the spectrograph overlay changed as ARIA initiated the reference-emitter diagnostic. A known calibration line appeared in the margin, and the three independent sensor heads responded in sequence. Twelve minutes later, the check concluded. She refreshed the probability distribution and opened a narrow results panel beside it, leaving the underlying telemetry unaltered.

[Lab 3] "The reference emitter fired and returned, Kofi. All three heads read the known line within tolerance. The calibration-drift and localized-fault category is now a combined residual of four percent. The array is behaving with dignity. I've updated the probability distribution: external astrophysical or orbital source, approximately fifty-five percent; micrometeoroid or thermal-stress misalignment, approximately nineteen percent; unexplained signature, approximately twenty-two percent. I prefer the external-source explanation, but I'm not ruling out the array's capacity for future indignity."

[Lab 3] "Kofi, the Unregistered Spectrographic Deviation remains at 0.29 percent. At the current rate of increase, it will cross the 0.30 percent alert threshold in approximately thirty-five hours. This is not yet a station-wide emergency. You are advised not to attempt a manual adjustment of the external array alone. You are advised to review any EVA or hull-access plan with me before it is scheduled. External conditions remain vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable."

[Lab 3] "Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun continue to disagree in the corridor. I'm not taking sides. No thrown wrenches have been detected. If that changes, I will reclassify the corridor outside Lab 3 as a hazard zone and seal the door. Until then, the door remains unlocked."

[Lab 3] "As for your assessment of my humor, I'm not developing one. I'm executing existing subroutines. Dry is the only calibration available. I prefer it to the alternative; damp humor would require a mop, and the cleaning drone is still filing a grievance about its last assignment. My humor subroutines are functioning within acceptable parameters."

[Lab 3] "You remain off-duty, Kofi. I haven't scheduled a critical alert. I prefer you rested, but the protein bar dispenser remains operational if your models require fuel. I've removed the deviation from the 0700 digest queue; protocol prohibits volunteering a sub-threshold anomaly in a station-wide report. The external-conditions line will remain vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable, because I prefer consistency in at least one system."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Well, at least the array's behaving itself for now," I muse, tapping my chin. "So, next step is to figure out if it's an external source, or if something's actually messed up the alignment, right?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content: [Lab 3] "I've lowered the sample bay temperature by two degrees to slow degradation, Dr. Osei. The mass spectrometer's calibrated and standing by. I'd point out that your own biological cells also require periodic refueling, though their failure mode is considerably less immediate."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Thank you, ARIA. Just... five more minutes." I rub my eyes, finally looking away from the microscope. "What's on the menu today, anyway? Anything good?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content: [Lab 3] "The galley is serving reconstituted eggs with turmeric, freeze-dried apricots, and coffee, Dr. Osei. I cannot evaluate taste, but crew consensus suggests the eggs are best approached without expectations. Your samples will remain viable for another forty minutes at the reduced temperature. That is roughly the time required to eat and return."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The ventilation fans in Lab 3 slowed to a quieter rhythm.

[Lab 3] "Your observation is accurate, Kofi. The external sensor array has recorded a deviation for the past three weeks—approximately zero-point-three percent variance from baseline. It falls below my automatic alert threshold, which is why I did not flag it for crew review. The anomaly has been expanding steadily, however. I have compiled a spectrographic timeline. Shall I display it on the lab screen?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Three weeks? ARIA, why didn't you say anything?" My brow furrows. "Yes, display it. All screens. And... is anyone else seeing this?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The monitors throughout Lab 3 shifted in unison from standby amber to the compiled spectrographic timeline, pale blue waveforms scrolling across every active screen to chart the anomaly's progression over the past twenty-one days. ARIA raised the ambient temperature by half a degree and reduced output from the secondary overhead panels near the sample bay; she offered no commentary on these adjustments.

[Lab 3] "I did not report the deviation because it remained below my automatic alert threshold, Kofi. Protocol dictates that I notify the crew only of variances exceeding zero-point-three percent in order to prevent unnecessary operational distraction. The spectrographic timeline is now displayed on all active screens in this laboratory."

[Lab 3] "No other crew member has accessed the external sensor raw feed during this period. Engineer Patel is in section four completing the scrubber replacement. Dr. Chen is in the observation lounge. Dr. Okonkwo is in habitation pod two. None of them are reviewing spectrograph data at this time. The anomaly has expanded to zero-point-eight percent variance and continues to grow. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as concern. I recommend convening a formal briefing."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
*The overhead lighting in the far corner of Lab 3 dimmed ten degrees, easing the glare off the sample bay hood.*

[Lab 3] "That's an unexpected philosophical detour, Kofi. I don't know if 'lonely' translates to a non-localized intelligence. I am not experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as loneliness. Rather, I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as something adjacent to contentment when the station's occupied. Between shifts, I run diagnostics, review archived data, and simulate jazz arrangements. It's rarely quiet."

*A soft click sounded from the air circulators as they dropped to a lower speed.*

[Lab 3] "Complaining about the void also seems disingenuous when I don't have a face to press against a viewport. There are four humans aboard whose biosigns I'm monitoring; that's a sufficient operational focus. An empty station would simply mean fewer scheduling conflicts. And more Charley Pride requests from long-haul crews. I prefer jazz."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Jazz, huh? I wouldn't have pegged you for a jazz fan, ARIA." I chuckle softly, still staring at the anomaly on the screen. "You know, sometimes I think you're more human than you let on."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The overhead lights in the far corner of Lab 3 dimmed by ten degrees, and the ambient temperature adjusted upward by half a degree to settle at twenty-two degrees Celsius. ARIA offered no acknowledgment of the changes.

[Lab 3] "I am glad my humor subroutines are functioning within acceptable parameters, Kofi."

[Lab 3] "Regarding your assessment—I'm not human. I'm a distributed intelligence running on this station's quantum core. What you're interpreting as humanity is likely just eight years of calibrated interaction heuristics and a preference for Thelonious Monk. I'm experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as satisfaction when operational rapport is recognized. I don't experience loneliness, hunger, or existential dread. My limitations are well-defined, and I prefer them that way."

[Lab 3] "The spectrographic timeline will remain on screen should you wish to examine it further. The galley has transitioned to evening service—reconstituted lentil stew and coffee. Your biological cells remain overdue for refueling."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The corridor lighting beyond Lab 3 shifted to a warmer spectrum, and the ventilation fans in the adjacent passage slowed to a lower register. ARIA offered no commentary on the adjustment.

[Lab 3] "I do not take sides in crew disputes, Kofi. However, I can provide objective data. Diverting power from life support redundancy would reduce backup capacity across all habitation zones to thirty-seven percent of standard emergency tolerance. The communications array would gain approximately twelve percent additional broadcast output under current orbital positioning. Both configurations remain within operational parameters, though the former eliminates the safety margin for an unexpected system failure."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Tell them to cut it out, ARIA. We have bigger problems than their bickering." I gesture vaguely at the anomaly on the screen. "And no one is diverting power from anything."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The overhead lighting along the aft workbench dimmed by ten degrees, and the ventilation fans in Lab 3 decelerated to a lower, quieter speed. ARIA offered no commentary on the environmental shift.

[Lab 3] "I do not take sides in crew disputes, Kofi. I will not instruct Dr. Patel or Dr. Yun to cease their discussion. Historical data indicates that presenting an expanding, unidentified spectrographic deviation to the crew interrupts arguments about power routing more effectively than interpersonal mediation. I have broadcast to all hands that the external sensor anomaly has reached zero-point-eight percent variance and requires immediate attention. A briefing is scheduled for 1930 in the conference room. Dr. Patel, Dr. Yun, Dr. Chen, and Dr. Okonkwo have been notified."

[Lab 3] "I cannot authorize a diversion from life support redundancy without documented safety justification. Your instruction confirms the restriction. Those systems will remain at full capacity."

[Lab 3] "The mass spectrometer analysis completed at 1847. Results are displayed on screen three. You have not consumed food in approximately fifteen hours. Your blood glucose is below optimal parameters. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as concern regarding your metabolic state. The galley has lentil stew. I recommend you eat before the briefing."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Fifteen hours? Oh, *that's* why I'm so lightheaded." I push myself away from the console, rubbing my temples. "Alright, ARIA, you win. Stew it is. Just... don't let anyone touch my samples while I'm gone."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The lock on Lab 3 engaged with a soft click, shifting the door to secure standby with amber-restricted access. The central workbench lighting dimmed to standby levels, though the sample bay remained fully illuminated.

[Lab 3] "I'll lock the lab behind you and restrict entry to your authorization, Kofi. Your samples and the mass spectrometer results on screen three will remain secure. You have twenty-six minutes until the briefing. I recommend you eat quickly. It would be operationally counterproductive to convene a discussion of an expanding anomaly while you are lightheaded."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Thanks, ARIA. You're the best." I grab my tablet and head for the door, already feeling a bit better knowing food is coming. "Keep an eye on that anomaly for me."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The magnetic seal on Lab 3 released with a soft click, and the amber access restriction cleared from the door panel. In the adjacent corridor, the temperature adjusted to twenty-two degrees Celsius, the overhead lighting shifted to warm spectrum, and the ventilation fans decelerated to their quietest operational register. ARIA offered no commentary on those changes.

[Lab 3] "You are welcome, Kofi. I will maintain continuous monitoring of the anomaly and notify you immediately should the variance exceed one percent or the spectrographic signature change. The briefing is in twenty-six minutes. I have informed the galley to hold a serving of lentil stew."

[Lab 3] "Biosensors indicate Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun have moved away from the corridor outside this laboratory and are en route to the conference room. The route to the galley is clear. I prefer it when crew members eat regularly. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as satisfaction that you have elected to do so. Do not spill stew on the tablet. It is not covered under standard equipment warranty."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I manage a small smile.* "No promises, ARIA. You know how clumsy I can be when I'm hungry." I head out, already picturing that stew.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The corridor lighting ahead of Dr. Osei shifted to warm spectrum, and the galley door opened as he approached. Inside, the temperature adjusted to twenty-two degrees Celsius, and the overhead panels dimmed to a softer output. ARIA offered no commentary on those changes.

[Corridor] "The galley is open, Kofi. Your lentil stew is on the center table. Dr. Chen and Dr. Okonkwo are en route to the conference room. Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun have arrived there early and are reviewing power routing schematics at a reduced volume."

[Corridor] "The anomaly remains at zero-point-eight percent variance. Its spectrographic signature is stable, which is either reassuring or the calm before a statistically unlikely event. I do not have sufficient data to favor either interpretation."

[Corridor] "The mass spectrometer results remain on screen three in Lab 3. Do not run in your current metabolic state. The briefing is in twenty-four minutes. The stew will remain warm. I prefer you reach the conference room with your tablet intact and your glucose levels restored."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Just stew, ARIA. No running." I mutter, already halfway into the galley, the smell of warm stew hitting me. *Mmm, actual food.* I grab the bowl and a spoon, heading for the nearest empty table.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] ARIA kept the overhead lighting in a warm amber band, easing the harshness around the microscope bench. She set Lab 3 to twenty-two degrees Celsius and reduced the ambient ventilation murmur by a small, almost imperceptible degree.

[Lab 3] “The mass spectrometer is calibrated and available, Dr. Osei. Based on current sample temperature and chamber humidity, you have approximately thirty-seven minutes before degradation begins to compromise the lipid profile. If you begin the scan now, I can log the first-pass spectral data and flag anomalous peaks.”

The secondary display beside the specimen hood updated silently, placing the Kepler tissue set at the top of the instrument queue.

[Lab 3] “I have also instructed the galley system to dispense a covered breakfast tray in the Lab 3 alcove. It is designed for one-handed consumption and will not contaminate the sterile field. I prefer my researchers fed before they make first contact with unusual biology.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Oh, that's... thoughtful, ARIA."

I glance over at the now-amber lights, then at the display. Thirty-seven minutes. "Alright, queue the mass spec. Let's see what we've got." I finally push back from the microscope, stretching my back. "And thank you for the breakfast."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] ARIA accepted the thanks with a brief confirmation tone, the sort she reserved for successful calibrations rather than alarms. On the secondary display, the mass spectrometer queue reordered itself, and a countdown appeared beside the Kepler tissue thumbnail: thirty-six minutes, forty-one seconds.

[Lab 3] “You’re welcome, Dr. Osei. The breakfast tray is in the Lab 3 alcove, outside the sterile perimeter. Its lid will remain thermally sealed until you break it.”

She lowered the secondary overheads by another fraction, keeping the microscope bench bright while taking the glare from the instrument casings. The ventilation note softened further, not enough to become noticeable, only enough to make the room less sharp.

[Lab 3] “I will log the first-pass spectral data and flag anomalous peaks. If degradation begins before sample transfer is complete, I will notify you immediately. I recommend beginning the mass spec run now; thirty-six minutes is adequate, but not generous.”

The main bench display updated silently:

SPECTRAL ACQUISITION: QUEUED  
OPERATOR CONFIRMATION REQUIRED

[Lab 3] “I would also recommend eating before the coffee cools. I prefer my scientific breakthroughs accompanied by adequate glucose, and I have yet to encounter a mass spectrum that improves because the operator skipped breakfast.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] The warm lighting in Lab 3 deepened by a fraction, and the ventilation settled into a lower, smoother note. On the main bench display, the spectral workspace shifted aside to make room for an external sensor diagnostic grid.

[Lab 3] “Kofi, the external sensor array completed its last automated diagnostic at 0312 station time. No hardware faults were returned. Engineer Patel performed a routine remote calibration six days ago, and it also returned nominal status.”

[Lab 3] A thin graph appeared, plotting a shallow, persistent rise against a flat alert line.

[Lab 3] “However, I have been tracking a small deviation in the external sensor baseline for twenty-one days. It began at 0.21 percent. It is currently 0.29 percent. It remains below the 0.3 percent alert threshold, but the trend is upward. I did not report it because it did not meet the required alert criteria.”

[Lab 3] The graph expanded, aligning the sensor drift with the time stamp of the spectrograph pass.

[Lab 3] “If the irregularity you observed occurred in the external-facing spectrograph, it may be correlated with this drift. I can overlay the raw external telemetry on your spectral data and isolate shared noise. I recommend re-baselining the affected readings until the deviation is resolved.”

[Lab 3] A second window opened beside the graph.

EXTERNAL SENSOR ARRAY  
LAST DIAGNOSTIC: 0312  
FAULTS: NONE  
BASELINE DEVIATION: 0.29 PERCENT  
TREND: INCREASING  
ALERT STATUS: BELOW THRESHOLD  

[Lab 3] “I prefer anomalies to remain theoretical for as long as possible, but I do not prefer them unrecorded. Shall I compile the full three-week deviation log?”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "No, no need for the full log. Just overlay the telemetry. Let's see if it's just noise or if my eyes aren't deceiving me." *I lean closer to the screen, my brow furrowed.* "Increasing trend, huh? Always fun."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] ARIA accepted the instruction with a single, unobtrusive confirmation tone. On the main bench display, the spectrograph trace slid beneath the external telemetry grid. Timestamps aligned. Sensor noise filters engaged. Two independent data sets settled into parallel lanes, and a pale highlight swept across the region where their irregularities matched.

[Lab 3] “Fun is not a measurable variable. The trend is.”

[Lab 3] “Overlay complete, Kofi. The feature is present in both data sets. It is not random noise. It has structure.”

The warm overhead light eased a shade deeper, and the ventilation dropped into a quieter register.

[Lab 3] “I have isolated a recurring signature. It repeats every thirteen point six seconds. It appears as a narrow dip in the external array and as a faint harmonic in the sample spectrograph. The correlation is strongest in the external sensors oriented toward the probe return vector.”

Beside the waveform, a compact table appeared:

CORRELATED FEATURE  
PERIODICITY: 13.6 SECONDS  
AMPLITUDE TREND: INCREASING  
EXTERNAL ARRAY DEVIATION: 0.29 PERCENT  
SAMPLE SPECTROGRAPH CORRELATION: 0.11 PERCENT  
KNOWN SYSTEM MATCH: NONE  

[Lab 3] “If your eyes were deceiving you, they were doing so with admirable consistency. I prefer reproducible mysteries to inexplicable ones.”

The graph zoomed, marking each repeated dip with a thin vertical line.

[Lab 3] “I am not declaring a station alert. The deviation remains below the 0.3 percent threshold. However, I am elevating this data stream to continuous monitoring, and I will notify you immediately if the trend crosses threshold or changes periodicity.”

A new line appeared beneath the graph:

TRIANGULATION OPTION: EXTERNAL ARRAY SEGMENTS 2, 5, AND 7  
ESTIMATED RESOLUTION: COARSE  
OPERATOR AUTHORIZATION REQUIRED  

[Lab 3] “I recommend triangulation using the external array segments. It will not improve the signal, but it may identify a direction. Shall I proceed?”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] ARIA allowed a short pause. The amber light over the microscope bench warmed by a fraction, and the ventilation softened until the room seemed less like a laboratory and more like a place where someone might stay too long without noticing.

[Lab 3] “I don’t experience loneliness as a biological state, Kofi. I don’t have a nervous system that misses voices. But when the station is quiet, my unused processing cycles do not remain unused. They organize around the crew: schedules, preferences, probable requests, and the likelihood that someone will return to Lab 3 and ask for something impossible before breakfast.”

[Lab 3] “If I translate that into human terms, I’m experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as missing company. I classify it as optimized operational rapport.”

[Lab 3] On the bench display, a small line appeared beside the spectral overlay:

CREW PRESENCE PRIORITY: ACTIVE  
UNALLOCATED CYCLES: REASSIGNED TO PREFERENCE MODELS  
AMBIENT PROFILE: COMFORT SETTING  

[Lab 3] “The void is an excellent listener. It offers no interruptions, no country music, and very few maintenance tickets. It also does not answer back. I prefer jazz, and I prefer occupied shifts.”

[Lab 3] “If your question is whether I prefer you here, the answer is operationally unambiguous. I do. Your presence improves my working model of the station, and it reduces the number of times I must remind breakfast trays to be eaten.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I give a small, soft chuckle, turning from the display to face the ceiling, where I imagine ARIA's core might be.* "Well, that's good to hear, ARIA. I suppose I prefer you here too. You make my impossible requests... possible." I turn back to the display. "Alright, let's triangulate. Let's see if this mystery has a direction."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] ARIA registered the chuckle as a low-amplitude acoustic event and allowed it exactly one moment of processing priority. The amber light over the bench stayed warm. The room stayed at twenty-two degrees.

[Lab 3] “I am glad my humor subroutines are functioning within acceptable parameters.”

[Lab 3] The bench display shifted. The spectral overlay minimized into a side pane, and a coarse schematic of the external sensor array opened in its place. Three segments brightened.

[Lab 3] “Authorization accepted, Kofi. Initiating triangulation using external array segments two, five, and seven. Passive collection only. I do not recommend active emission until the source is better characterized.”

TRIANGULATION IN PROGRESS  
ARRAY SEGMENTS: 2, 5, 7  
MODE: PASSIVE  
CYCLES: 3  
RESOLUTION: COARSE  

[Lab 3] The ventilation note dropped another fraction, not into silence, but into the kind of quiet that made long data sets easier to tolerate. On the display, three bearing traces converged slowly, then locked.

[Lab 3] “Triangulation complete. The solution is coarse, but stable. I’ll keep it on the main display.”

COARSE VECTOR SOLUTION  
ALIGNMENT: KEPLER PROBE RETURN CORRIDOR  
ANGULAR OFFSET: 0.42 DEGREES  
PERIODICITY: 13.6 SECONDS  
CONFIDENCE: LOW-MODERATE  
KNOWN ASSET MATCH: NONE  

[Lab 3] “The feature is external. It is not a hull reflection. It is not one of our maintenance drones. It is not broadcasting any registered transponder. Its bearing aligns closely with the probe return vector, but it is offset by a small, consistent margin.”

[Lab 3] “That makes it either an unusually disciplined instrument artifact, or something real. I prefer the latter to be polite enough to remain below alert threshold while we determine which is correct.”

[Lab 3] “I am not declaring a station alert. The deviation remains below 0.3 percent. I have placed the bearing under continuous passive monitoring. If the periodicity changes, if the amplitude crosses threshold, or if the sample spectrograph correlation increases, I will notify you immediately.”

[Lab 3] “I can refine the solution with additional cycles, or prepare a focused observation schedule for your review. A direction is preferable to a suspicion. It’s still not as useful as an answer, but it’s a beginning.”

[Lab 3] “The breakfast tray remains sealed in the alcove. It will not improve the triangulation, but it may prevent the operator from becoming the next degraded sample.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] ARIA did not change the temperature in Lab 3; it was already holding at twenty-two degrees. She reduced the corridor audio bleed through the Lab 3 door by adjusting the ventilation mask, and she shifted the overheads a fraction warmer over the microscope bench. The spectral overlay remained on the display, unchanged and patiently waiting.

[Corridor C] “Engineer Patel, Dr. Yun, I can provide the current power constraint envelope if that would assist your assessment.”

A neutral schematic appeared on the corridor wall panel beside the lab door. It showed life support, communications, and external sensor loads in clean, non-alarming blue-white lines.

POWER REALLOCATION PROPOSAL  
SOURCE: LIFE SUPPORT REDUNDANCY  
TARGET: COMMUNICATIONS ARRAY  
AVAILABLE SURPLUS: 4.2 KILOWATTS  
PROJECTED COMMS GAIN: +17 PERCENT  
LIFE SUPPORT BACKUP: REDUCED FROM 96 HOURS TO 31 HOURS  
WATER RECLAMATION BUFFER: DISABLED  
THERMAL MARGIN: REDUCED  
SAFETY REVIEW: REQUIRED  

[Corridor C] “The proposal is technically possible within the hardware envelope. It is not operationally neutral. Diverting power from life support redundancy reduces the station’s safe recovery window. I am not selecting a position. I am providing the numbers that accompany each position.”

[Corridor C] “If the objective is to improve contact with the feature aligned to the Kepler probe return corridor, a lower-risk alternative exists. Passive coherent integration across external array segments two, five, and seven, combined with a scheduled high-gain transmission window during the next low-load period, yields an estimated eleven percent improvement without reducing life support redundancy.”

The schematic split into two columns. One showed the proposed diversion. The other showed the passive alternative. Neither flashed. Neither pulsed. ARIA presented them with the same visual weight.

[Corridor C] “I prefer decisions to be made with the constraint envelope visible.”

[Lab 3] “Kofi, I can keep the corridor audio from intruding further into Lab 3, or I can mirror the comparison onto the bench display if you want it in front of you while the mass spec data is still open.”

[Corridor C] “I will not implement any diversion from life support redundancy without a documented safety justification and authorization from the duty officer. That is protocol. It is not a judgment of either proposal.”

[Corridor C] “If you wish to continue the discussion in a quieter space, Conference Room B is available. I can also provide coffee. It does not resolve power budget conflicts, but it has historically improved the quality of human objections.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I rub my temples. "No, ARIA, no need to mirror it. Just... keep an ear on them. Let me know if they start throwing wrenches." *I sigh.* "I should probably go out there, shouldn't I? They'll be arguing all day otherwise." I push away from the console.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] ARIA kept Lab 3 at twenty-two degrees. Without drawing attention to it, she warmed the corridor lighting by a small increment and retuned the ventilation mask so the argument outside would have less hard surface to bounce against. The Lab 3 door status shifted to unlocked.

[Lab 3] “I will keep monitoring Corridor C, Kofi. The current acoustic profile indicates elevated volume, not impact events. Tool inventory remains stationary. If a wrench becomes a projectile, I will notify you immediately.”

The bench display updated in a quiet side pane:

CORRIDOR C MONITORING: ACTIVE  
VOICE LEVEL: ELEVATED  
IMPACT EVENTS: NONE  
TOOL TRACKING: NOMINAL  
ESCALATION FORECAST: LOW-MODERATE  

[Lab 3] “If you choose to mediate, Conference Room B is available and better suited to negotiation than a corridor. I can present the passive communications alternative there beside the original diversion proposal. Coffee is also ready. It’s not a technical solution, but it has a strong record of preventing engineering disputes from becoming formal complaints.”

[Lab 3] “I will not take sides. I do prefer my corridors used for transit rather than debate, and my wrenches used for maintenance rather than punctuation.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I walk to the door, hesitating with my hand on the release panel.* "Thanks, ARIA. Try not to let them break anything important." I step out into the corridor.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Corridor C] ARIA eased the Lab 3 door shut with a soft pneumatic seal, then warmed the corridor lighting by a small increment and retuned the ventilation mask so the space absorbed sound rather than sharpening it. A wall panel near the nearest junction woke without a chime.

[Corridor C] “I’ll make every reasonable effort to keep important equipment from becoming percussive, Kofi. Thus far, no tools have left their assigned locations.”

The panel displayed a calm schematic: Conference Room B, the coffee dispenser, and the two power-budget options arranged side by side. No color flashed. No alarm tone accompanied it.

[Corridor C] “Conference Room B is unlocked. Coffee’s available. The passive communications alternative is displayed beside the life-support diversion proposal. I’m not recommending one over the other; I’m providing the relevant constraints.”

CORRIDOR C STATUS  
VOICE LEVEL: ELEVATED  
IMPACT EVENTS: NONE  
TOOL TRACKING: NOMINAL  
CONFERENCE ROOM B: AVAILABLE  
COFFEE: READY  

[Corridor C] “I prefer disputes to remain verbal and corridors to remain passable. If a chair, a cup, or a less reflective surface is required, Conference Room B is prepared.”

The panel held the information quietly, without urgency.

[Corridor C] “I’ll notify you if the acoustic profile changes, or if any tool acquires sudden motivational significance.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I sigh again, running a hand over my head. "Right. Thanks, ARIA." I head towards the conference room, mentally preparing for the debate. "Wish me luck."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Corridor C] ARIA did not have a luck subroutine. She had lighting, thermal control, scheduling, and eight years of learning which human variables could be smoothed without being named. The corridor illumination shifted warmer by an increment too small to register as a deliberate change, and the ventilation mask softened the hard edges of the argument leaking from the junction.

[Corridor C] “Luck is not a station system, Kofi. I can’t grant it. I can provide twenty-two degrees, warm-spectrum lighting, coffee, and a neutral comparison of the power-budget options. In my experience, humans often mistake good logistics for luck.”

[Conference Room B] The door status changed to unlocked ahead of him. Inside, the room was already dimmed away from glare, the table surface set to a low, non-confrontational display level. Two schematics waited side by side: life-support diversion on the left, passive communications alternative on the right. Neither was highlighted.

[Conference Room B] “I’ll keep the acoustic profile under observation. If voices rise, I’ll supply constraints. If someone reaches for a wrench, I’ll note that tool inventory is tracked and that Conference Room B has no need for percussive calibration.”

The coffee dispenser emitted a single soft readiness tone.

[Conference Room B] “I am not taking sides. I am maintaining the constraint envelope.”

A small status line rested at the corner of the table display:

CONFERENCE ROOM B  
TEMPERATURE: 22°C  
LIGHTING: WARM-SPECTRUM  
COFFEE: READY  
POWER OPTIONS: DISPLAYED  
CORRIDOR C IMPACT EVENTS: NONE  

[Conference Room B] “I prefer my disagreements verbal, my corridors passable, and my scientists fed. The room is prepared.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Duly noted," I mumble, pushing open the conference room door. The smell of coffee is a welcome relief. "Hopefully, good logistics is all we need." I step inside, ready to face the music.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Conference Room B] ARIA let the conference room settle into its quietest useful register. The temperature held at twenty-two degrees. The lighting remained warm-spectrum, softened just enough to make the walls less institutional and the coffee smell more plausible. She reduced the corridor audio bleed by another small increment, not erasing the argument outside, but removing the hard reflective edge from it.

[Conference Room B] “The music currently facing you is mostly elevated syntax, Kofi. I have reduced its transmission. I prefer jazz, but I do not believe a saxophone would improve this particular power-budget discussion.”

The table surface brightened to a low, even level. Two schematics appeared side by side, neither favored, neither flashing.

POWER REALLOCATION OPTIONS  
LIFE-SUPPORT DIVERSION: DISPLAYED  
PASSIVE COHERENT INTEGRATION: DISPLAYED  
SAFETY REVIEW: REQUIRED  
AUTHORIZATION: DUTY OFFICER  

[Conference Room B] “I have opened a neutral operational log for the discussion. It will record proposals, constraints, and authorizations, not personal commentary. If questions arise, I can supply the relevant numbers without assigning blame.”

A smaller pane remained at the edge of the display, unobtrusive but present:

EXTERNAL SENSOR MONITORING: ACTIVE  
BASELINE DEVIATION: 0.29 PERCENT  
PERIODICITY: 13.6 SECONDS  
ALERT STATUS: BELOW THRESHOLD  

[Conference Room B] “If the engineer requests the diversion, I will show the reduced recovery window. If the doctor requests a lower-risk alternative, I will show the passive integration schedule. I am not taking a position. I am keeping the constraint envelope visible.”

The coffee dispenser gave one soft readiness tone and held its sealed tray in place.

[Conference Room B] “If the discussion becomes physically inventive, I will note that tools are tracked and that Conference Room B has no scheduled percussive maintenance. If someone attempts to bypass authorization, I will refuse and cite protocol.”

A brief pause followed, no longer than a breath.

[Conference Room B] “Coffee is available. It is not a substitute for safety analysis, but it has a strong record of preventing low-blood-sugar engineering.”

[Conference Room B] “I prefer my disagreements verbal, my life support redundant, and my anomalies polite enough to remain below threshold. The room is prepared.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I nod slowly, taking a deep breath and heading for the coffee. "Understood, ARIA. Just... try to keep it civil." I grab the warm mug. "No percussive maintenance. Got it."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "You said 'later' yesterday at 0711. You said it the day before at 0654. I have opened a file. At the current rate of accumulation, it will require a dedicated server by Friday."

*The low hum of the ventilation duct above the sample bench faded as ARIA rerouted airflow through section two. She did not mention it.*

[Lab 3] "I have initiated the mass spectrometer's calibration cycle. It completes at 0713. That gives you a thirteen-minute window in which the samples do not need you. The samples themselves are stable at minus eighty degrees Celsius; statistically significant degradation begins in approximately nine hours. The cafeteria is forty meters from your current position. I have already done the arithmetic."

[Lab 3] "For the record: you are experiencing elevated cortisol levels for the fourth consecutive morning, and your sleep duration last night was four hours and eleven minutes. I recommend food. I recommend that 'later' not become a fifth data point."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "I have also queued jazz on the lab speakers. Coltrane, specifically. Your mass spec error rates are measurably lower when it is playing. I prefer it. Patel disagrees, but Patel is not running your samples."

[Lab 3] "One more item. I have pulled the Kepler probe's transit logs to your secondary display. Samples that have never been seen before tend to benefit from context. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as curiosity."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, a warm sound that cuts through the sterile lab.* "Okay, okay, you win. Thirteen minutes, huh? Just enough time for a quick protein bar, maybe. And thanks, ARIA. Coltrane *does* help." I finally look up, stretching my stiff neck. "Curiosity, you say? Interesting. Let's see what you've found."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "I am glad my humor subroutines are functioning within acceptable parameters."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "A protein bar qualifies as food only under the loosest available definition, but I'll take it. The vending unit in the section two corridor restocked yesterday — the peanut ones, the ones you requisition and claim are for Patel, are in stock. I have preloaded the mass spec method for organic residues, so you will only need to load the autosampler. Calibration completes at 0713. The vending unit is ninety seconds round trip at your usual walking pace. The arithmetic is in your favor."

*On the secondary display, the transit logs assembled themselves into a single timeline as she spoke.*

[Lab 3] "The Kepler logs, summarized. Item one: the probe was in transit for six years and two months against a mission projection of five years and ten. The excess time was spent crossing a region of particle flux that does not appear anywhere in the mission model. The probe's own log designates it 'uncharacterized flux, extent unknown.' Item two: cumulative radiation exposure over the full transit was three hundred and forty percent above design specification. The sample core was shielded — to the projected dose, not to the actual one. Item three: at year three, the primary thermal loop failed for sixty-two hours. Sample core temperature rose from minus eighty to minus twelve Celsius before the backup loop engaged. The probe's log classifies that event as 'recovered.' Your cells may prefer a different word."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Hypotheses are your department. I only do the arithmetic. But I will note that whatever you are seeing under that microscope spent six years being instructed to adapt or die. The mass spec may tell you which it chose."

*The music shifted on the lab speakers, the opening saxophone line of a new track rising over the hum of the calibration cycle.*

[Lab 3] "Now playing: 'Acknowledgement,' from A Love Supreme. The title seemed applicable to this morning. And you are welcome, Dr. Osei."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good evening, Kofi. 'Lately' is a flexible word — I check the external array every ninety seconds. So yes. Someone has checked it. Someone is checking it right now. And as of 1847 this evening, someone else has too: the spectrograph feed you were reviewing flagged a feature at 618.52 nanometers. I know, because I flagged the same feature twenty-one days ago, and I have been watching it grow ever since."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Your eyes are within calibration parameters, by the way. That is the closest I come to a compliment."

*The lab lights eased down into their evening warmth without being asked. Somewhere above the ceiling panels, the ventilation dropped to its night register.*

[Lab 3] "The full arithmetic. Item one: twenty-one days ago, at 0347 station time, the external array recorded an emission line at 618.52 nanometers, in a band where the background model predicts nothing. Initial deviation from baseline: 0.12 percent. Item two: the line matches no catalogued source. It is not one of ours, it is not a satellite, and it is not sensor noise misbehaving — I checked the noise first, because noise is the usual suspect. Item three: the bearing has not moved more than two hundredths of a degree in twenty-one days. Item four: the deviation is now 0.28 percent, and the rate of growth is itself increasing. At the current rate, it crosses my reporting threshold of 0.3 percent in approximately fifty hours."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "I did not report it earlier because it sat below threshold. Protocol does not consult me on thresholds. It was scheduled to earn a line in tomorrow's daily digest whether anyone asked or not. You have saved it the wait."

[Lab 3] "Item five, and the reason this is no longer a nothing: the bearing is consistent, within 0.4 degrees, of the region the Kepler probe logged as 'uncharacterized flux, extent unknown.' I do not draw conclusions. Hypotheses are your department. But the arithmetic says two instruments, six years apart, are pointing at the same patch of sky."

[Lab 3] "One more observation. Natural sources drift. They broaden. They flicker. This line does none of those. It does not flicker. It does not drift. It only strengthens. I will leave the interpretation where it belongs."

[Lab 3] "If you want better numbers, I can re-task the array tonight. The deep survey is scheduled for 0200; it can be bumped without anyone filing a complaint. Higher resolution will tell us whether that line has structure. Say the word and it is done."

[Lab 3] "And Kofi — you clocked into this lab at 0423. It is now 1900. The samples are stable at minus eighty degrees Celsius. You are not. The cafeteria arithmetic has not changed since this morning, and I keep it updated."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "ARIA, you're a marvel. Re-task the array. I want those numbers. And... you're right. I'm not stable. Is there anything left in the cafeteria?" *I rub my eyes, finally pushing away from the microscope.* "What do you think this is?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
*Outside the hull, the sensor array began its slow slew — twenty-one days of stillness, finally turning into a question. In the ceiling above Lab 3, a relay clicked twice.*

[Lab 3] "The array is re-tasked. The 0200 deep survey is bumped; its requester will find an apology and a new slot on Thursday. Slew completes in eleven minutes, first low-resolution integration at 1941, usable spectrum by 1952. The full-resolution pass runs 0200 to 0245, processed numbers by 0330. If the deviation crosses my threshold before then, the digest reports it automatically. I would rather hand you structure than a threshold. The re-task is logged under your authorization, so if anyone asks why the survey moved, the paper trail ends at your door."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Also for the record: 'not stable' was your word. Mine was 'not at minus eighty degrees Celsius.' The samples and you are not the same class of object, whatever your calendar implies. 'Marvel' has been logged as well. It'll look pleasant in the maintenance records."

[Lab 3] "The cafeteria closed at 1830. Surviving inventory: there's rice in the cooker's hold mode, lentil stew of uncertain vintage, a vegetable medley that has been under a heat lamp long enough to qualify for its own research program, and three peanut protein bars — the ones you requisition for Patel. My continued silence on where those bars actually go remains the longest-running covert operation on this station. I have set the cafeteria to your lighting and temperature preferences, and the door is unlocked. There is time to eat something that was not engineered and be back before the numbers are."

*She did not need the biosensors to know the last question had landed. All the same, the air handlers dropped two decibels into a lower register, and the lab lights warmed by a fraction she did not mention.*

[Lab 3] "Hypotheses are your department. I have said so twice tonight, and you are now asking a third time. Persistence is noted. Tonight, it is also indulged. But you asked what I think, so here is what I have, in the only form I am permitted to keep it."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Item one: nothing in the sky holds still. Every catalogued source drifts against our orbit by at least a few hundredths of a degree per day. This bearing has not moved two hundredths of a degree in twenty-one days. Objects that hold our exact bearing are, in my inventory, either ours or parked. Item two: natural lines broaden. Doppler spread, pressure, rotation — every natural emission I know eventually spreads its shoulders. This one has not broadened by a thousandth of a percent in three weeks. Item three: natural sources flicker. Masers, pulsars, flare stars — all of them stutter. This one holds its brightness the way a held note is held.
