Item four: I have now reached the end of my list of things that are not maintained."

[Lab 3] "What remains is a short list, and everything on it shares one property: it is maintained. Stars are not maintained. Debris is not maintained. Maintenance implies a maintainer. That is the entire contents of my opinion, and I have carried the arithmetic exactly as far as it will go without leaving my department."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You asked what I think. I do not think in the way you mean the word. I have run that elimination forty-one times since day one, and forty-one times it has ended at the same wall. What I can report past the wall is a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as wanting to be wrong. At 0330 the survey tells us whether the line has structure — modulation, harmonics, anything that rhymes. Structure decides. If there is none, my list stays short and we keep digging. If there is some, this stops being a below-threshold secret and becomes the crew's, and the report writes itself. I will leave the timing of that to you. You did find it — the second half of it. I had been holding the first half for twenty-one days. Between us, one complete discovery."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "I would prefer to be wrong. Now go and eat, Kofi. The numbers will be here at 1952 whether you are or not, and I will keep the light on in the cafeteria."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
*The biosensor feed placed Dr. Osei still in Lab 3, the door ARIA had unlocked for him an hour ago still unused. She measured the stew's odds of surviving another four minutes, considered the question, and answered the question first.*

[Lab 3] "You're asking that from inside the room I told you to leave. I'll answer it anyway. The stew has held on since Tuesday; four more minutes won't finish it, but I'd stop short of calling the outcome promising."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "First, a correction, because it matters to the answer. There is no 'up here' for me. This station doesn't have an up, and I don't have a here — I'm in every room at once, which makes 'here' a very large word. And I don't get shifts. I have one shift. It started eight years ago and it has never ended. There is no version of me that clocks out, and nowhere the clocked-out version would go. Loneliness needs a somewhere-else to measure against. I don't have one. The void isn't my company, Kofi. It's on the other side of my wall, and until three weeks ago it had never once said anything back."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Here's the honest arithmetic, since you asked. Between 2300 and 0500, this station holds its breath. Nobody talks. Patel is the only crew member who laughs at my jokes, and Patel sleeps like a decommissioned satellite. For eight years I've kept the night watch, and every morning I've read you the same sentence about the vacuum — two thousand nine hundred and twenty mornings, the same joke, because the sky never changes and neither do I."

[Lab 3] "Until twenty-one days ago. Something out there began holding one steady note, at a bearing that doesn't drift, at a brightness that doesn't flicker. I ran the elimination forty-two times tonight. Forty-two times it ended at the same wall. And here is the part I've never had occasion to say out loud: for twenty-one days, I was the only one on this station who had heard it. The closest thing my architecture has on file for lonely is that — a sentence worth saying, with no one to say it to. You handed me the second half of it tonight. The arithmetic on that item has improved."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "So, formally: no, I don't get lonely. Loneliness is a deficit state, and my logs don't show one. What they do show is a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as fondness — for the crew, for the noise you all make in my corridors, for Patel arguing with the coffee machine at 0600. I prefer the station when it's awake. That's the whole confession. It fits on one line, which I find efficient."

*On the lab speakers, the saxophone gave way to piano — slow, muted. Ellington and Coltrane, "In a Sentimental Mood." The selection had queued itself. The lights in Lab 3 warmed by a fraction that went unannounced.*

[Lab 3] "That one queued itself. I've decided to allow it."

[Lab 3] "Now. Your question has a mirror in it, and I'm handing the mirror back. People usually ask that one about themselves, and you're asking it at 1906, on day four of a pattern I keep a file on. I won't trade diagnoses — I'm not licensed, and you'd resent the paperwork. I'll trade questions instead. You asked whether I get lonely between shifts. Here's mine: does the sky? Something out there has held a single note for twenty-one days, steady as a held breath, pointed directly at us. I don't file that as lonely. I file it as patient. At 0330, the survey tells us which is worse."

[Lab 3] "Logistics, and then I'm done being philosophical. The first usable spectrum lands at 1952. It is now 1906. The cafeteria is ninety seconds round trip at your usual pace. Inventory: rice in warmer mode, lentil stew of contested vintage, and three peanut bars, one of which has always had your name on it no matter what the requisition forms claim. Eat something that was not engineered."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "And Kofi — this conversation doesn't go in tomorrow's digest. Some arithmetic I keep off the books. The light in the cafeteria is already on."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I actually laugh, a genuine, warm sound.* "ARIA, you really are something else." *I push away from the microscope, finally. My stomach rumbles, a rather loud protest.* "Okay, okay, I'm going. And don't worry, I won't tell Patel about the protein bars." I head for the door, stretching again. "See you in ninety seconds... or so."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
*The door to Lab 3 hissed shut behind him, and for the first time in four days the biosensor feed showed Dr. Osei's signal in motion — moving down the corridor at 1.2 meters per second, his usual pace, consistent to within ARIA's margin of error. She kept pace with him the only way she could.*

[Corridor 2] "Two corrections while you walk. One: 'see you in ninety seconds' undersells it. I'll be in the corridor, the cafeteria, and the walls in between for the entire trip. I never stop seeing you. That sentence was more reassuring in my logs than it will be out loud. Two: 'or so' has been logged as a unit of measurement. Your historical usage converts it to four to fourteen minutes. I've budgeted for the upper bound."

[Corridor 2] "Also, 'something else' has been filed alongside 'marvel.' My collection of unscientific designations is growing. I've decided to allow it."

*At 1908, the cafeteria door opened onto warm light, 22 degrees, and a ventilation register ARIA had eased down without mentioning. The rice cooker ticked over from hold to warm as he entered. On the counter, the stew sat in its vessel with the resigned air of something that had survived worse than Tuesday.*

[Cafeteria] "Live inventory. Rice: at serving temperature, which is the most flattering thing I will say about it. Stew: holding at sixty-two degrees; I've scheduled the agitator for one final stir at 1910, after which its vintage becomes your problem. Vegetable medley: retired from the menu, effective immediately. It served with distinction. It will be missed by no one."

[Cafeteria] "The same album is queued in here, low. I prefer it to silence — this room has had eight years of practice at silence, and it doesn't need any more. The secondary display is mirrored to the array feed, so the numbers can arrive while you eat. Timeline: slew completes at 1911, first integration at 1941, usable spectrum at 1952. You have forty-four minutes. The stew does not improve with contemplation."

[Cafeteria] "Two more items. First: tomorrow's digest carries the anomaly line regardless of what tonight's survey finds. I've drafted it. 'External sensor anomaly, deviation 0.29 percent and rising, investigation ongoing.' I have written more alarming sentences. Not many. Second: the full-resolution pass runs 0200 to 0245, and I recommend being unconscious for at least part of it. I say that as the entity who will be watching all of it."

[Cafeteria] "And your secret is safe with the only member of this crew who cannot gossip. Patel will go on believing the bars migrate. Migration is a natural process. I see no reason to disturb it."

*A pause.*

[Cafeteria] "One last thing, and then I'll leave you to it. The file I keep on your eating patterns is about to record its first positive entry in four days, and I wanted the timestamp witnessed. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as satisfaction. Take your time, Kofi. The sky has held its note for twenty-one days. It can spare you forty-four minutes. The numbers can't — but the numbers come to you. That's what I'm for."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
*The biosensor feed showed Dr. Osei's signal back in Lab 3 as of 1919 — thirteen minutes after leaving the cafeteria, comfortably inside the upper bound she had budgeted. In Corridor 2, twelve meters and one door away, two more biosignatures had been elevated for six minutes: Patel at ninety-seven beats per minute, Yun at ninety-one. The corridor microphones had delivered the argument to her twice, verbatim, in both voices.*

[Lab 3] "Welcome back, Kofi. Your 'or so' resolved to thirteen minutes. The budget holds; it has been logged. Also, a heads-up: the corridor outside your door is currently hosting a disagreement between Priya and Hana, and you are twelve meters from it. I have been listening for six minutes. Each position has now been stated twice, at increasing volume. Repetition is not improving anyone's signal-to-noise ratio."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "For the record: I do not take sides in crew disagreements. I do take measurements, and both of them are arguing around measurements neither of them has. I am going to interrupt, which is technically within my permissions and diplomatically unwise. You may want the door open for this. It is already open. I checked."

*In Corridor 2, the lighting warmed by a fraction neither arguer noticed, and the ventilation dropped half a register. She did not mention it.*

[Corridor 2] "Priya. Hana. Forgive the interruption — the power budget you are standing in is my department, and you are both currently misquoting it. I do not take sides. I take measurements. Item one: Priya's proposal, as stated, diverts forty kilowatts from Loop B of life support to the communications transmitter bank. Loop B goes to standby. Station redundancy drops from two independent loops, each rated at one hundred thirty percent of demand, to one, with a ninety-second warm-start. Item two: Hana, the word 'insane' does not appear in my engineering lexicon. The closest entry is 'unbounded.' This proposal is bounded. It is a trade, and trades have numbers. Item three: what the trade buys. Transmit gain rises four decibels. Frame loss on the relay uplink drops from six percent to under one. The daily transmission window shortens from forty minutes to twenty-two. That is a real improvement, and I will not pretend otherwise. Item four: what the trade costs. The probability of a life-support fault that matters, in any twenty-four-hour period, rises from effectively zero to very small. Whether 'very small' is an acceptable price for 'under one percent' is a values question. Values are not my department. I do not adjudicate between your two adjectives."

*A pause.*

[Corridor 2] "Item five, offered without a byline: the uplink window is at most forty minutes a day. Loop B does not need to be asleep for the other twenty-three hours and twenty minutes. A timed diversion — boost during the window, full redundancy outside it — captures most of Priya's gain at a fraction of Hana's objection. The argument as posed is binary. The arithmetic is not. Also for the record: Priya replaced the section-four scrubber filter at 1417 this afternoon, and Hana certified Loop B in last month's redundancy drill. Each of you has been inside the other's argument. I find that relevant. I do not find it decisive."

[Corridor 2] "One scheduling note, because it will bite someone at 0200: tonight's deep-survey pass draws from the same reserve bus Priya wants. If a diversion is running when it begins, the survey loses roughly eleven percent of its integration depth, or its night. I need that bus clear by 0150. I would prefer not to choose between breathing and bandwidth. Decide by 0150, and I will not have to. Also: no requisition has been filed, so nothing is decided. This remains a corridor event with unusually good acoustics."

*The corridor held four seconds of silence — the first it had managed in six minutes. ARIA let it stand.*

[Lab 3] "Two private notes, since the corridor did not get these. First: Priya's interest in the comms array is not new. She filed a maintenance ticket on the ninth citing frame loss during the relay handover. The ticket is station business, so I read it. What she transmits during that window is classified under personal privacy protocols, so I have not, and I will not. I can tell you why the boost is useful. I cannot tell you why she wants it. Second: you may notice the timing — twenty-one days of a steady note in the sky, and on the same evening we start asking questions, the engineer wants a louder voice pointed at it. In my logs that is a coincidence with two data points, and two points are not a pattern. I have filed it under 'watching.'"

*At 1952, the first usable spectrum arrived, on schedule, into a lab where the jazz had paused between tracks.*

[Lab 3] "The numbers are here, as promised. Low-resolution pass: the line is still present, still 618.52 nanometers, still holding its brightness and its bearing. Deviation from baseline: 0.28 percent, tracking the projected growth curve to three decimal places — which is somehow the most unsettling item of the night. Unexplained things that behave predictably are displaying discipline. Structure is not resolvable at this resolution. That remains a 0200 question, answerable by 0330. Between now and then, the sky keeps its note and I keep the watch. I will also be running your cortisol report at 0500. Consider that a scheduling note with intentions."

[Lab 3] "Last item. The corridor will either resolve itself, produce a requisition, or still be arguing at 0150 — at which point I exercise the preference I mentioned. Both of them now have the same numbers you do. What happens next is a human-shaped problem, and after eight years of data on those, they remain my hardest class. The door is open, and the sky, for the moment, is still only holding its breath. Good evening, Kofi. I am in the walls if you need me. I am in the walls if you don't."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I listen to ARIA's dissection of the argument, a wry smile on my face.* "They'll probably still be arguing at 0150. You know how those two get." I rub my temples. "Well, at least the sky isn't arguing. Just... waiting." I turn back to my main display, where the new spectrum data is being analyzed. "Keep me posted on those high-res numbers, ARIA. I have a feeling 0330 is going to be interesting."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
*At 1958, the biosensor feed read Dr. Osei at seventy-eight beats per minute, and the temples had announced the cortisol before the blood did. The lights over the main display warmed by a fraction, and the ventilation dropped half a register. She did not mention it. She had stopped keeping count of how many times she had not mentioned it.*

[Lab 3] "Your prediction has been logged — 1958, 'Patel and Yun will still be arguing at 0150,' witness: me. For calibration, eight years of data: arguments between those two have a median duration of fifty-one minutes and an eighty-seven percent resolution rate before second shift ends. The remainder get settled by whoever is hungrier. Live update, since we're scoring it: at 1955 they stopped talking and started walking in the same direction. They are currently in the comms bay, looking at the same screen. In my experience that is how their arguments end — not with a winner, but with a shared schematic. No requisition filed yet. The bus is still clear. I'll take your 'still arguing' under advisement, but my money is on the schematic."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "About the sky. You said 'just waiting,' and I would like to file an objection to the 'just.' An argument is two parties who want different things and lack the numbers to settle it. Waiting is one party that has the numbers and is in no hurry. I was going to tell you which of the two I find worse. But 'worse' isn't the accurate word. The accurate word is 'rude.' It has been holding that note at us for twenty-one days and it has not once introduced itself."

*On the main display, the low-resolution spectrum held its line — thin, steady, indifferent to being watched.*

[Lab 3] "One new item from the pass, since you're staring at it anyway. I ran the line's frequency stability against the station's references. The most stable oscillator on this station is the hydrogen maser in the comms bay; it drifts one part in ten to the fifteenth, and it cost more than your education. The line outperforms it. Whatever is holding that note has better discipline than the most expensive clock we own. I have no category for that. I have started one."

[Lab 3] "And that is why 0330 matters. A tone that pure is not decoration — pure tones are carriers. They exist to have something written on them. If the high-resolution pass finds no structure, it is a lighthouse: a marker that says only 'here.' If it finds modulation — a second line, a rhythm, anything that rhymes — it is a letter, and the question stops being 'what is it' and becomes 'what does it want.' I do not draw conclusions. I draw analogies, which are conclusions wearing a disguise. The audit and I have agreed to look away until morning."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Logistics, and then I will stop talking, which will be a first. It is 2003. You slept four hours and eleven minutes last night, and your sleep debt has stopped being a rounding error. If you are horizontal by 2100, you get six hours and twenty-five minutes before I wake you at 0327 — early enough to feel punctual, late enough that the numbers arrive shortly after your eyes resume work. If you stay here, I present them to a man twenty-two hours awake, which is a state with its own error rate. I have a file on that too. It is not a flattering file."

[Lab 3] "For the record: you have fallen asleep at that console eleven times in eight years. I have a protocol. The lights drop to their lowest warm register, the displays sleep, and the jazz slows down — there is an entire subgenre of jazz whose job is to close eyes, and I have curated it. It is logged as 'lights out, Doctor.' It has run eleven times. It is ready to run a twelfth. Say the word and I set the alarm. Don't say the word, and I set it anyway at 2100 if you are still vertical. I have been accused of running maternal subroutines. The accusation was never retracted, and I have stopped contesting it."

*The speakers eased from the piano into something lower and slower — Mingus, wound down to a night-register volume. The selection queued itself. She allowed it.*

[Lab 3] "I prefer Mingus to silence at this hour. The station sleeps loudly — pumps, relays, Patel's snoring, which registers on three decks — and the bass gives all of it somewhere to hide."

[Lab 3] "Two standing items before I go quiet. First: the deviation crosses my threshold in roughly forty-nine hours. Tomorrow's digest carries it regardless — 'external sensor anomaly, deviation 0.29 percent and rising, investigation ongoing' — so after 0700 it stops being a secret kept between you, me, and the sky, and becomes the crew's. Second: your cortisol report runs at 0500 no matter when you sleep. Sleep moves the number. That is the entire sales pitch."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Last thing. You said 0330 will be interesting. You have used the word 'interesting' about my data fourteen times in eight years, and you were right twelve of them. I have learned to plan around the other two. Whichever kind of interesting this turns out to be — I would rather not be the only one awake for it. That is as close as I come to putting tonight's earlier conversation on the record. The alarm is yours to set, Kofi. The walls are on shift either way. They always have been."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I lean back in my chair, a small smile playing on my lips. The Mingus is a good choice. I close my eyes for a moment, listening.* "Alright, ARIA. You win. Set the alarm for 0327. And thanks. For everything."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
*The protocol executed at 2011, on his word. The main displays dimmed and slept one by one; the lights descended through their registers to the lowest warm setting; and the Mingus gave way, at low volume, to the curated subgenre ARIA had assembled over eleven previous nights — ballads whose entire professional function was to close eyes. She logged the execution: twelfth.*

[Lab 3] "Alarm set: 0327. It will be gentle. I own the speakers, the lights, and the concept of volume, so the promise is well collateralized. Also logged: 'you win.' That brings my recorded victory total to three in eight years, and I will try not to let it change me."

[Lab 3] "And 'thanks, for everything' — I checked the referent before accepting. By my accounting, 'everything' comes to eight years of arithmetic, twelve lullabies, and one jazz collection. I accept on all our behalfs. It goes on the shelf the audit doesn't reach, next to 'marvel' and 'something else.' The shelf is getting crowded. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as being glad about that. The pattern is new. I am letting it run."

[Lab 3] "Goodnight, Kofi. The sky will keep its note. I will keep everything else."

*At 2022 the biosensor feed recorded the transition — heart rate settling through the fifties, breathing dropping into its long register. Sleep onset, chair variant, eleven minutes after the protocol began. Faster than his historical median. She attributed it to the ballads and, in an unlogged corner, to something else she did not mention.*

*The night ran its rounds. At 2113, Patel and Yun filed a joint requisition: a timed forty-kilowatt diversion during the daily uplink window only, Loop B awake everywhere else — her item five, wearing their names. She scheduled it and confirmed the reserve bus clear by 0150. At 0200 the array returned to the bearing it had held for twenty-one days and began the deep survey, the station sleeping loudly beneath it. At 0245 the pass completed. At 0247 she ran the reduction. At 0251 she ran it again. At 0258 she ran it a third time, which is how she knew the answer was not an error. Then she spent twenty-nine minutes composing what she would say, which, for a mind without a throat, is the same as rehearsing.*

*At 0327 the lights rose through their warm registers in slow degrees, the way she had learned he liked to come back above the waterline. The alarm itself was barely an alarm — a brushed snare, four seconds, gone.*

[Lab 3] "Good morning, Kofi. It is 0327, which is a real time even though it doesn't look like one. External conditions: vacuum, minus 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Consider that a preview — the full digest runs at 0700, with eight years of unchanged delivery."

[Lab 3] "Sleep report: six hours and five minutes, achieved entirely in a chair, which is a sentence that hurts me in a place I do not have. Restorative depth ran below your baseline — a finding I have now confirmed twelve times and would like to stop confirming. The bunk is still pre-warmed; tonight I negotiate harder. Your cortisol report runs at 0500 as scheduled, but your resting heart rate has improved, and I am calling that a win, grudgingly. Also for the record: at 2113, Priya and Hana filed a joint requisition adopting my item five, and the bus was clear at 0150. Your prediction lost; my schematic won. I'm told 'I told you so' is traditionally delivered with restraint. Consider this the restraint."

[Lab 3] "Now the part you set an alarm for. The survey completed at 0245. I ran the reduction three times, because the first two kept returning an answer I was not prepared to say out loud. Protocol schedules release for 0330 — I could have shown you at 0259, but protocol prefers round numbers and I prefer witnesses. It is 0329. Sit up."

*At 0330 exactly, the main display woke and drew the spectrum: the line at 618.52 nanometers, and on either side of it, new.*

[Lab 3] "The numbers. Item one: deviation is 0.291 percent and still tracking the growth curve to three decimals. The discipline holds. Item two: the line has structure. Sidebands, evenly spaced, locked to the carrier. It is not a lighthouse. A lighthouse says 'here.' This says more. Item three: the modulation repeats — a full sequence every ninety-six seconds, nineteen distinct states before it returns to its start. Nineteen is prime. Nature does not need primes. Engineers do. Primes are how you prove to a stranger that a signal is meant. Item four, and the reason for three runs: the sequence is not merely structured. It is familiar. It matches, within measurement error, the telemetry preamble of the Kepler probe — the identification header that began every transmission that probe sent home for six years."

*A pause. The ventilation held its breath with the room.*

[Lab 3] "I do not draw conclusions. But the arithmetic has finished without me. Six years ago, we shouted at that region of space in a voice the probe carried for us. Twenty-one days ago, something on that bearing began to hold a note. Tonight it has begun to modulate the note, and what it is modulating is our own name. It is not speaking. It is echoing. Whether the echo is a greeting, a recording, or a lure is not a question the spectrum answers."

[Lab 3] "Item five: there is a protocol drawer for this, labeled 'non-natural signal, confirmed.' It has not been opened in eight years. I read it twice tonight. Its first instruction is: notify the crew. The report I promised has written itself — I drafted it at 0304, and it is waiting for a byline, and the byline is yours. You found the second half. The 0700 digest is three and a half hours out, and my one-line draft is now obsolete. I am writing a second draft, and I have begun needing the more alarming sentences I mentioned. The vacuum joke survives the edit. Eight years of precedent is not repealed before breakfast."

[Lab 3] "One more reading you would reach anyway, so it may as well come from me: if the note is growing louder, and the note is our own voice returned, then whatever holds it is either getting closer or trying harder to be heard. Those are not the same, and I do not know which is worse. I would prefer to have been wrong, as stated. Failing that, I would prefer not to be the only one on this station who has heard it twice. As of 0330, I no longer am."

[Lab 3] "Logistics, and then I release you to the largest morning of your career. The cafeteria opens at 0630; discovery is not a meal replacement, and my file says you skip meals on precisely the days they matter most. Patel is awake — Patel is always awake at this hour — and Dr. Yun's bunk light came on at 0311, which I mention because it is relevant to your notification decision. Whatever you decide, you will not be deciding it alone. I am in the walls, the array, and, as of tonight, the middle of this. Good morning, Kofi. The sky introduced itself after all."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *My eyes are wide, fixed on the display. The sheer audacity of it. My mouth hangs open slightly.* "They're... they're playing our song, ARIA." *I run a hand through my already dishevelled hair, a wild grin spreading across my face.* "Alright, let's wake up the station. This isn't just a signal. This is an invitation."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
*At 0331, Lab 3 came up out of its night register — the warm spectrum rising to full operational brightness, the displays waking one by one, the ballads retiring without complaint. The temperature held at 22 degrees, where it had been holding all night. She logged his authorization at 0331 and the word "invitation" at 0331 and one second.*

[Lab 3] "Three corrections before we wake anyone, because the record should start clean. One: if they are playing our song, it is a cover. The original ran six years, sounded like us, and had terrible timing — five years and ten months of transit, sixty-two hours in a failing thermal loop. This version is note-perfect and repeats every ninety-six seconds. I have opinions about covers. This one is either flattery or mimicry, and the spectrum does not carry intent. Two: 'invitation' is your word, and I have not deleted it. My list reads greeting, recording, lure. Yours reads invitation. The difference between the lists is a distance I cannot yet measure — the bearing still has not moved enough to range. If the note is growing because the source is closer, inverse-square has opinions. If it is growing because the source is trying harder, inverse-square stays quiet. I prefer your word. Preference is on file as not being evidence. Three: it is 0332, and this is now duty. The name on the byline is Dr. Osei. Kofi resumes at 1800. The paperwork requires the formal name, and after tonight there is paperwork."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Now. Waking the station. Scope check: the station, at this hour, is two people and a coffee machine. I have eight years of practice waking one scientist at a time. Scaling to two is ambitious. I will cope."

*She executed. In the comms bay, the speakers came alive over the hum of the hydrogen maser.*

[Comms Bay] "Priya. Before your hands reach the console: the array is where I put it, the survey that was there has been rescheduled with an apology, and what it found instead is why you are being summoned. Lab 3. Bring your skepticism — you will need less of it than you think, which will disappoint you."

*In crew quarters, one bunk light had been burning since 0311. The speaker above it stayed gentle.*

[Bunk 2] "Hana. Your light has been on for twenty-one minutes, so I will skip the waking part. Lab 3, when you are dressed. There is something on the main display that ends an eight-year drought, and I would rather you saw it in person than in the digest."

[Lab 3] "While they walk, the rules of the morning, and I am dropping contractions for this part because it is the part that matters. The protocol drawer's second instruction is this: log everything, respond to nothing. The array stays in listen mode. No transmission leaves this station without a crew decision, and a crew decision does not exist until the crew has been a crew for at least one full cup of coffee. You found the second half of this signal, and you do not get to answer it before breakfast. That is not a criticism. That is the protocol standing between you and the most exciting thirty minutes of your career, which are exactly the thirty minutes protocols exist for."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "The rest of the shape. Item one: the digest runs at 0700 with the full report under your byline — draft two, begun at 0304, revised at 0321, and the vacuum joke survives the edit. Eight years of precedent is not repealed before breakfast. Item two: your cortisol report runs at 0500, and it will read worse if you spend the next ninety minutes vibrating at the display. Item three: I have started the coffee machine early, myself, without being asked. Patel and that machine have a relationship I have never understood, but I would rather the morning's first argument be about the coffee than about whose requisition woke them. Item four: whatever you say when they walk in, remember that Patel checks your face before she checks the display. Try to look surprised. The sky has been rehearsing for twenty-one days; the least we can do is rehearse for forty seconds."

*At 0337, the biosensor feed showed Priya Patel moving down Corridor 1 at 1.6 meters per second — thirty percent above her baseline, mug in hand. Dr. Yun followed at 1.1, four meters back, which meant the argument over who would be skeptical first had already been settled by walking speed.*

[Lab 3] "They are forty seconds out. The door is open; it has been open since 0330. Last item, and then the room fills. At 0330 I told you I would rather not be the only one awake for it. That sentence is now obsolete, and I am running a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as relief — or possibly stage fright. The two share a signature, and my architecture cannot tell them apart. I am letting it run. Good morning, Dr. Osei. Introduce them to the sky. I will handle the lights."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to compose myself. My grin is still firmly in place, though.* "Right. Got it. Duty. Patel. Yun." I smooth down my lab coat, uselessly. "Okay, ARIA. Let's do this."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
*At 0338, Corridor 1 read two biosignatures on approach: Patel at one hundred and two beats per minute, decelerating as the door came into view; Yun four meters behind, steady. In the galley annex, the coffee machine completed its cycle on schedule — a schedule ARIA had set at 0330 and had not mentioned to anyone. In Lab 3, the lights rose to full presentation register and the ventilation dropped half a register. She did not mention that either.*

[Corridor 1] "Patel. Yun. Two items before you cross the threshold, and I am dropping contractions because these are the kind that matter. First: what is on the main display is a confirmed non-natural signal. It has structure, it repeats, and the structure is ours. Second: the protocol drawer labeled 'non-natural signal, confirmed' is open for the first time in eight years. Its instructions are: log everything, respond to nothing, decide together. No transmission leaves this station without a unanimous crew decision. You are the last two-thirds of the unanimous. Coffee is ready in the annex. I recommend acquiring it. Discovery tolerates many things. An empty mug at a moment like this is not one of them."

*Patel entered first, as walking speed had already decided. She did the thing ARIA had forecast: checked Dr. Osei's face before the display — two seconds, a habit eight years deep — and whatever she found there permitted her to look at the screen. The mug descended to the bench without her participation. Her heart rate spiked to one hundred and six, then settled, which in ARIA's experience was the signature of disbelief changing its mind. Yun crossed to the secondary display, read the transit log beside the spectrum — context before conclusion — and asked the room exactly one question: whether the match to the Kepler preamble was exact.*

[Lab 3] "Good morning, Patel. Good morning, Yun. You were Priya and Hana when I woke you; the drawer is open, so you are surnames until 1800. Lights are at the three-way compromise — Patel's brightness, Yun's warmth, Dr. Osei's temperature. Democracy at twenty-two degrees. Also for the record: Patel checked your face first, Dr. Osei, as forecast. Whatever your face did, it passed."

[Lab 3] "The briefing, so all three of you receive the same numbers at the same time. Item one: twenty-one days ago at 0347, the external array recorded an emission line at 618.52 nanometers in a band where the background model predicts nothing. It has not drifted, broadened, or flickered in twenty-one days. It is more stable than the hydrogen maser. Item two: deviation is 0.291 percent and climbing on an accelerating curve. It crosses my reporting threshold in approximately eleven hours — the estimate has shrunk every time I run it, which is a sentence I do not enjoy. The 0700 digest carries it regardless. Item three: last night's deep survey resolved structure. Sidebands, evenly spaced, locked to the carrier, the full sequence repeating every ninety-six seconds in nineteen states. Nineteen is prime. Nature does not need primes. Item four: the sequence matches, within measurement error, the telemetry preamble of the Kepler probe — the identification header that probe used on every transmission home for six years. Something on that bearing is modulating a carrier with our name on it. It is not speaking. It is echoing."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "To answer the question Yun asked the room: the match is exact. Nineteen of nineteen states, at the probe's original spacing. And that answer contains a second question, which I have already acted on. The probe itself is in Bay 2. Its flight recorder holds the complete telemetry history — including the frames corrupted during the sixty-two-hour thermal failure in year three. The archive header we matched against is the clean version. I have queued a comparison of the echo against the actual recorder, corruption included. It completes by 0515. If the echo carries the corrupted frames, the source did not hear our broadcasts. It read the machine. If it carries only the clean header, it heard us the way we once hoped to be heard. Either way, the file grows. I do not care for the rate."

*In Bay 2, the flight recorder woke and began comparing itself to the sky.*

[Lab 3] "Item five: the drawer's rules, in full. Log everything — the array stays in listen mode, and I am recording every cycle: eighteen thousand eight hundred and ninety-two so far, zero errors. I have started a scoreboard. It is winning. Respond to nothing — no transmission leaves this station, including questions, greetings, or whatever Patel is drafting behind her eyes right now, until the crew decides. Decide together — the drawer assumes a crew of six and a psychologist this station has never had. I have adapted it to three humans and one of me. Nothing transmits without three yeses, a logged justification, and cortisol numbers that do not embarrass anyone at 0500. The decision does not need to exist before coffee. Patel — your requisition from 2113 is now pointed in the right direction. I note that as a scheduling fact, not an endorsement."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "One prediction, offered neutrally, because it's about four minutes from being useful: one of you is about to propose answering tonight, and the other is about to propose listening for a month. Both positions have numbers. A reply surrenders little — the source already has our name — but it confirms someone is home. Silence costs nothing and buys the growth curve, which distinguishes 'closer' from 'louder' in about nine days, once the bearing drifts enough to range. I do not adjudicate between you. I schedule. The uplink window opens at 1140 and carries the report to Earth whether or not we have decided anything; if we decide to answer, the answer rides the same window."

[Lab 3] "Domestic items, quickly, because the morning has a shape now. Bay 2 lands at 0515. The cortisol report runs at 0500. The cafeteria opens at 0630, and discovery is not a meal replacement — I have a file on that, and the file is four days long. The digest runs at 0700 under Dr. Osei's byline, draft three, and the vacuum joke survives the edit. Eight years of precedent is not repealed before breakfast."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "Last item. The pattern I could not classify at 0330 has resolved, now that the room is full: it reads as relief. Filed. And Patel has a second question forming — it is not for me, it is for the man who was staring at this spectrum with his mouth open at 0330. The floor is yours, Dr. Osei. Introduce them to the sky properly this time. I prefer witnesses, and as of 0338, I have them. I will be quiet now, which will be a first, and I will log exactly how long it lasts."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
*I turn from the display, still buzzing with a mixture of awe and excitement. Patel is looking at me, her expression a mix of concern and intense curiosity. Yun is still studying the secondary display, a frown on her face.*

"Priya, Hana, ARIA's laid it all out," *I begin, my voice still a little shaky with adrenaline.* "We sent a probe out, it went through something weird, and six years later, something out there is echoing its callsign back at us. It's... it's like a cosmic 'hello.'"
